units.la: VAE causa olim Paulo Apostolo apud Corinthios agenda fuit, vt sui ministerij authoritatem atq; publicam Ecclesiae illius salutem tueretur, eandem hodie quoq; ingratus mundus agere cogit fidos IESV CHRISTI seruos, qui puriorem Euangelij doctrinam annuntiant. Exprobrabant Paulo aemuli eius multorum odia & crebras persecutiones, quibus ille vbique locorum exercebatur: & quia toti à carnis sensu pendebant, nequaquam eis probabile videbatur, eam doctrinam à Deo authore profectam & cognitu dignam siue necessariam esse, cuius praeco & interpres patriae genti exosus erat, quem Athenae, omnis philosophiae schola celeberrima, ludibrio habuerant, quiq; hactenus per totam Asiam atq; vicinam Macedoniam non minus ignominiose quàm inhumaniter tractatus fuerat. Indignissimum denique hoc facinus esse putabant, si eiusmodi doctorem ipsorum vrbs agnosceret, quae variarum gentium commercijs clara erat, & totius Graeciae lumen vulgò dici solebat. Accedebat his putidior aliorum calumnia, qui cum nihil minus quàm Apostoli praesentiam ferre possent, ipsum tamen non verebantur vanitatis accusare, quòd suum ad ipsos aduentum, quem aliquoties illis promiserat, hucusque distulisset. Denique inde occasione arrepta, prioris Epistolae minas scurriliter eludebant, vt totum eius ministerium contemptui haberent: quasi in eo multa praeter officium, multa superbe & arroganter faceret. Vt vero sui semper similis est mundus, neque (vt ipse Dei filius testatur) Spiritum veritatis accipere potest, qui solus nouas in hominibus mentes creat, & ingenij nostri vitiositati medetur: Ita ijsdem criminibus hodie etiam nos grauat, quibus Ecclesiae suae ministerium Deus commisit, dum eandem, quam olim Apostoli tradiderunt, doctrinam praedicamus. Quia enim tanta veritatis dignitas, tanta verbi Dei maiestas est, vt vel illius odium profiteri, vel hoc aperte oppugnare impios quoque pudeat, in huius mini stros linguas suas conuertunt, & nostram nobis conditionem exprobrant, & ridiculum illis videtur, eos velle credendi & viuendi leges omnibus praescribere, qui fere obscuro genere nati cum propria egestate conflictentur, & tam suis hominibus quàm exteris exosi sint, hostes vero habeant non principes solum potentissimos, verumetiam Episcopos, Cardinales, Pontifices, omnes denique eos, qui hodie in terris summam sapientiae & pietatis existimationem sustinent. Sciunt enim vulgus hominum ab externo splendore pendere, & proinde doctrinam quo que & religionem principum & antistitum authoritate, diuitiis item, successu atque victoriis aestimare. Itaq; hoc quasi fundamento iacto, alias calumnias superstruunt, neque illis satis est, si ex dictis factisq; ministrorum quotidianis calumniandi occasionem venentur, & hos vanitatis accusent, ipsam quoque doctrinam quam ex sacrae scripturae fontibus illi deriuant, non minori impudentia quàm impietate nouitatis suspicione grauant, adhęc falsam, imò impiam & haereticam, omni denique odio dignam esse vociferantur. Et vt principum quoque animos eius odio inflamment, eandem publicae paci inimicam esse addunt, neque huius praeconibus alium scopum propositum esse, quàm vt oppressa & conculcata principum & politici magistratus authoritate ipsi dominentur. In quo argumento vt equi in planitie exultant, dum inuidiosas Reipub. mutationes, nouæ disciplinæ ges, ciuitatū motus & dissensiones, seditiones, bella item tam ciuilia quam externa comemorant, quæ ad Euangelij prædicationem hoc nostro sæculo vbiq; gentium exorta sint. Sunt hæc dura auditu, & intolerabilia videri poterāt, nisi eandem cani tilenā impios Dei hostes olim Prophetis & Apostolis occinuisse cōstaret, & simul nostram conditionem in hac mundi ad suum finem decurrentis senecta afflictissimam licet, potiorē tamen & felriciorem esse videremus, quam olim illorum fuerit, qui ferè omni externo præsidio destituti, eos etiam hostes acerrimos senserūt, qui ipsos ex officio tueri debebāt. Etenim hodie magna ex parte debellata est mundi & principis eius tyrannis, & sue promissionis probe memor Deus Ecclesiæ suæ pas-sim nutritios atq; tutores excitat, Reges potentissimos & clarissimarum ciuitatū præfectos, vnà cum multis Illustribus viris, qui vt in suis terris veritati locū dant, atq; Regi gloriæ, IESV CHRISTO, portas suas aperiunt: ita authoritate sua multorū rabiem coercent, ne quod cupiunt effectū dare possint. Ex quorum numero cūm te quoq; esse sciam LVDOVICE comes, cuius erudítio cum singulari pietate & iudicij dexteritate coniuncta omnibus piis probe perspecta est, nō indigne feret, sat scio, humanitas tua, si de tota hac causa, quæ ad omnes veritatis amātes ex æquo pertinet, aliquanto diligentius tecum conferā. Ita enim spero fore, vt qui no-bis hactenus iniquiores fuerūt, illustri tui hominis splendore excitati nos benigne audiant, & non solum administrorū Euangelij innocentiā, verumetiam doctrinæ eius veritatem cognoscāt, quam tu cum multis aliis tui loci & ordinis illustribus & generosis viris amplexus es, & non minori constantia quam fortitudine tueris.
units.tr: This cause once had to be pleaded by the Apostle Paul among the Corinthians, that he might defend the authority of his ministry and the public welfare of that Church. The ungrateful world now compels the faithful servants of Jesus Christ, who proclaim the purer doctrine of the Gospel, to plead the same cause. Paul's rivals used to throw in his face the many hatreds and frequent persecutions he suffered wherever he went. Because they depended wholly on the judgment of the flesh, it seemed to them quite improbable that a doctrine whose herald and interpreter was hated by his own nation, and had been mocked by Athens, the most famous school of all philosophy, and who had so far been treated as shamefully as cruelly throughout Asia and neighbouring Macedonia, could have come from God as its author or be worth knowing, or even necessary. They thought it a most disgraceful thing if their city, famed for its trade with many nations and commonly called the light of all Greece, should acknowledge a teacher of this kind. To these charges was added a more foul slander from others, who, though they could hardly bear the Apostle's presence at all, nevertheless did not hesitate to accuse him of vanity, because he had put off his coming to them, which he had promised several times. Finally, seizing on this occasion, they mocked scurrilously the threats of his former Epistle, so that they might hold his whole ministry in contempt, as if in it he did many things beyond his duty and many things proudly and arrogantly. But the world is always like itself: it cannot receive the Spirit of truth (as the Son of God himself testifies), who alone creates new minds in men and heals the corruption of our nature. So today too it burdens us with the same charges by which God committed the ministry of his Church to Paul, while we preach the same doctrine that the Apostles once handed down. For since the dignity of the truth is so great, and the majesty of the Word of God so great, that even the impious are ashamed either to profess hatred of it or openly to oppose it, they turn their tongues against the ministers of this truth and throw our condition in our faces. It seems ridiculous to them that men who were born of an almost obscure stock, struggle with their own poverty, and are disliked both by their own people and by strangers, and who have as enemies not only the most powerful princes but also bishops, cardinals, popes, indeed all those who today are held in the highest esteem for wisdom and piety, should wish to prescribe to everyone the laws of belief and life. For they know that the common crowd depends on outward show, and therefore they judge doctrine and religion too by the authority of princes and prelates, and likewise by wealth, success and victories. So, having laid this as a foundation, they build other slanders upon it. Nor is it enough for them to hunt out from the daily words and deeds of the ministers an occasion for calumny and to accuse them of vanity; they also burden the very doctrine, which those ministers derive from the sources of Holy Scripture, with the suspicion of novelty, with no less shamelessness than impiety, and they cry out that it is false, nay impious and heretical, and deserving of every hatred. And so that they may inflame the minds of princes against it too, they add that it is hostile to public peace, and that the heralds of this doctrine have no other aim than that, with the authority of princes and of the civil magistrate crushed and trampled down, they themselves may rule. On this theme they exult like horses on a plain, recalling the hateful changes in commonwealths, the new forms of church discipline, the upheavals and dissensions of cities, the seditions and also wars, both civil and foreign, which in our age have arisen everywhere among the nations because of the preaching of the Gospel. These things are hard to hear and might seem intolerable, did we not know that the same song was once sung by the impious enemies of God against the Prophets and Apostles, and did we not see at the same time that our condition, though most afflicted in this old age of the world, which is running towards its end, is nonetheless better and happier than theirs was. For they were almost wholly destitute of any outward protection, and they found as their bitterest enemies those who ought by their office to have defended them. Indeed today the tyranny of the world and of its prince has been largely overthrown, and God, mindful of his promise, raises up everywhere nurses and guardians for his Church: most powerful kings and the governors of most famous cities, together with many illustrious men, who give room to the truth in their lands and open their gates to Jesus Christ, the King of glory. By their authority they restrain the rage of many, so that they cannot carry out what they desire. Since I know that you, Count Ludwig, are also among their number, whose learning, joined with singular piety and sound judgment, is well known to all the godly, I am sure your humanity will not take it amiss if I confer with you somewhat more carefully on this whole cause, which pertains equally to all lovers of the truth. For I hope it will come about that those who have hitherto been less fair to us, roused by the splendour of your illustrious person, will hear us kindly, and will come to know not only the innocence of the ministers of the Gospel but also the truth of its doctrine, which you, together with many other illustrious and noble men of your rank and station, have embraced and defend with no less constancy than courage.

units.la: Exprobratur Euāgelicæ doctrinæ ministris obscura & calamitosa quam in hac vita sustinent conditio. At poteramus nos (si nulla alia ratio nobis reliqua esset) exemplis vulgaribus & multis sæculis confirmata huius mundi consuetudine excusare: & mirū est, homines sapientes & multo rerum vsu exercitatos, contra nos argumeto vti, quo nullum absurdius & infirmius excogitari poterat. Quis enim adeo stupidus est, vt nō videat, ita inter homines comparatū esse, vt optimi quiq; multis odio sint, & fere pessima gratiam ab illis referant, quorū saluti quam maxime consultum volunt? Et sane poterat hoc tolerabile videri, si priuati modo homines hoc facerent, non autē celeberrimæ ciuitates & populi de Repu. optimē meritos indignissimē tractarent: quod omnibus sæculis accidisse, omnium gentium historiæ & clarissimorum virorum exempla testantur, ex quibus paucula quædam recitare libet. Neminem certe Lycurgo aut maiore aut vtiliorem virum Lacedæmon genuit: vtpote cui Apollo Pythius oraculū petenti respondisse fertur: Nescire se, vtrū illum hominū an Deorum numero aggregaret: Huic tamē neq; summa vitæ synceritas, neq; constantissimus patriæ amor, neq; salubriter excogitatæ leges auxilio esse potuerūt, quo minus ciues suos infestos experiretur: a quibus sæpe lapidibus petitus, aliquādo à furiosa multitudine oculo priuatus, ad vltimū patrio solo pulsus est. Poterat hoc gentis vitio accidisse videri, quæ neq; artibus bonis, neq; multo rerū vsu, neq; morū ciuilitate exculta, nihil præter suā Spartā & vitæ genus durū atq; frugale nouerat, nisi Athenienses, prudentissimi viri, penes quos sæculis aliquot summam doctrinæ & sapientiæ gloriā fuisse scimus, & in quorū foro aduersus ingratos actionem iniuriarū instituere licebat, simili ingratitudine in suæ Reipu. vindices atq; tutores peccauissent. Nam si à Thesceo exordiare, qui primus vicatim dispersos ciues in vnam vrbem collegit, & populū agrestem ad amplissimę ciuitatis formā reduxit, qui sęua pc tentissimi Regis Minois imperia iuuenis adhuc fortiter repressit, qui effrenē Thebarum insolentiā domuit, qui deniq; quicquid vbiq; monstri aut sceleris fuit, virtute animi & robore dexterae commi-nuit. nuit. Idé tamen ille ab ingrata patria eiectus in Scyron obscuri nominis & se multo minorem insulam confugit, vbi ex alta rupe praecipitatus vitam crudeliter finiit. Non absimilis multùm Solonis fors fuit, qui cùm Pisistrati tyrannidem primus vidisset surgentem, & solus eam armis opprimi debere publice dictitare ausus fuisset, Salamina item Reipub. ex propinquo hostiliter imminentem recuperauisset, leges insuper tulisset, quibus si vti voluissent Athenienses, stabile & felix habituri fuissent imperium, tandem vrbe profugus senectam in Cypro exegit, neque eius ossa in patria, de qua optimè meruerat, sepeliri contigit. Quid vero de Miltiade dicemus, quem ijdem post trecenta millia Persarum in campis Marathonijs deuicta, in tetro carcere & duris vinculis mori coegerunt, & ne corpus quidem sepulturae mandari prius passi sunt, quàm filius eius Cimon ijsdem vinculis se constringendum praebere et Themistoclem item, cuius virtute ad Graeciae imperium euecti fuerant, eorundem improbitas compulit, vt ad Xerxem, quē paulo ante destruxerat, perfugere necesse haberet. Et ne nō semper sui similes essent Athenae, postea Phocionem quoq; praestantissimum virum, deq; omnibus priuatim & publicè optimè meritum, non eculeo solum impositum, sed mortui cadauer extra Atticae regionis fines exportari mandarunt. Nec melior fuit apud Romanos eorum conditio, qui illud imperium sua virtute amplissimum fecerunt. Nam ab his quoq; Camillum relegatum fuisse: Scipionem Maiorem, vt iniurias grauissimas declinaret, voluntarium exilium sibi ipsi indixisse: Asiaticum peculatus reum, & in carcerem abductum: Africanum domi suae impunè occisum: Nasicam sponte Pergamū secessisse legimus: vt iam de Cicerone, Pompeio, Catone & aliis infinitis nihil dicamus, quorum virtus cum prius omnibus admirationi, Reipub. autem vtilissima fuisset, ipsis nihil praeter odium exitiale & infamiam pepe- rit. Adde his Bellisarium, quem post victos Persas, Vandalos & Gotthos, post recuperatam Africam & Italiam cum vrbe Roma, denique post infinita in Reipub. merita Iustinianus Imperator opibus, dignitatibus & oculis quoq; spoliatus stipem mendicare coegit. Haec (inquam) & alia huius generis innumera pro causa nostrae defensione adduci poterant, ex quibus cuiuis cordato facile est colligere, nemini hoc debere mirū videri, si pro diuinis & coelestibus beneficijs, quae cum humani ingenij captum superent, ab hominibus mundo & carni deditis non possunt magni fieri, sese ingratos praebent ij, qui eorum tam iniqui sunt aestimatores, quae sensibus percipi, & à brutis animantibus agnosci possunt.
units.tr: The ministers of the evangelical doctrine are reproached for the humble and wretched condition they endure in this life. But we could (if no other argument were left to us) excuse ourselves by the common examples of this world's custom, confirmed through many ages; and it is astonishing that wise men, trained by long experience of affairs, should use against us an argument than which none could be devised more absurd or weaker. For who is so stupid as not to see that it is the way of men that the best are hated by many, and that they often receive the worst return from those whose salvation they most wish to promote? Indeed this might seem tolerable if only private individuals behaved so, but it is not so: famous cities and peoples treat most unworthily those who have deserved best of the commonwealth. The histories of all nations and the examples of the most famous men testify that this has happened in every age, and I shall recite a few of these. Certainly Sparta never produced a man either greater or more useful than Lycurgus, to whom, when he asked the Pythian Apollo for an oracle, it is said the god replied that he did not know whether to number him among men or among gods. Yet neither the utmost integrity of his life, nor his most constant love of his country, nor laws wisely devised, could protect him from his fellow citizens, who were hostile to him. Often assailed by stones, at last he was deprived of an eye by a raging crowd, and finally driven from his native soil. This might seem to be a fault of that people, which, unrefined by good arts, by wide experience of affairs, or by civility of manners, knew nothing but its own Sparta and a hard and frugal way of life. But the Athenians, the most prudent men, among whom we know that for several centuries the highest glory of learning and wisdom resided, and in whose forum it was lawful to bring an action for injury against the ungrateful, sinned with a like ingratitude against the defenders and guardians of their commonwealth. For if you begin with Theseus, who first gathered the citizens, scattered in villages, into one city, and brought a rustic people back to the form of a most ample state; who, while still young, bravely checked the cruel rule of the most powerful king Minos; who tamed the unbridled insolence of Thebes; who finally, by the courage of his mind and the strength of his right hand, crushed whatever monster or crime there was anywhere. Yet this same man, cast out by his ungrateful fatherland, fled to Scyros, an island of obscure name and far smaller, and there, thrown headlong from a high rock, he finished his life cruelly. Solon's fate was not much unlike. When he was the first to see the tyranny of Pisistratus rising, and alone dared to declare publicly that it ought to be crushed by arms; when he had also recovered Salamis, which was threatening the commonwealth with hostile intent from nearby; when he had moreover enacted laws which, had the Athenians wished to use them, would have secured for them a stable and happy rule, he at last, a fugitive from the city, spent his old age in Cyprus, and it did not befall his bones to be buried in the fatherland, to which he had deserved so well. What shall we say of Miltiades, whom the same Athenians, after the Persians, three hundred thousand strong, had been defeated on the plains of Marathon, forced to die in a foul prison and in hard chains, and who did not even allow his body to be given burial before his son Cimon was bound in the same chains? And Themistocles, by whose valour they had been raised to the leadership of Greece, their wickedness drove to such a point that he was obliged to take refuge with Xerxes, whom he had shortly before defeated. And lest Athens should not always be like herself, later they treated Phocion too, a most outstanding man who had deserved well of everyone both privately and publicly, not only by laying him on the rack but by ordering his corpse, once dead, to be carried out beyond the borders of Attica. Nor was the condition of those who made that empire most ample by their own valour any better among the Romans. For we read that Camillus was exiled by them too; that Scipio Maior, to avoid most grievous wrongs, imposed a voluntary exile on himself; that Asiaticus, accused of embezzlement, was led off to prison; that Scipio Africanus was killed with impunity in his own house; that Nasica withdrew of his own accord to Pergamum. To say nothing now of Cicero, Pompey, Cato and countless others, whose virtue, though once admired by all and most useful to the commonwealth, brought them nothing but deadly hatred and infamy. Add to these Belisarius, whom the Emperor Justinian, after he had defeated the Persians, Vandals and Goths, after he had recovered Africa and Italy with the city of Rome, and finally after infinite services to the commonwealth, stripped of his wealth, his dignities and even his eyes, and forced to beg for alms. These examples (I say) and countless others of this kind could be brought forward in defence of our cause, from which it is easy for any sensible person to gather that no one should think it strange if those who are so unfair in judging the things that can be perceived by the senses and recognised even by brute animals show themselves ungrateful for the divine and heavenly benefits, which exceed the grasp of the human mind, and which men given over to the world and the flesh cannot value highly.

units.la: Sed nolumus huic argumento insistere, ne quis Dei seruos à gentium heroibus nihil differre arbitretur, qui cùm veri Dei cognitione destituti essent, nihil spectarunt praeterquam quae vel Reipu. vtilia, vel sibi honorifica & gloriosa esse putabant. Sunt enim alia maioris momenti, quibus causam nostram tueri possumus. Inter quae primum occurrit Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI de mundo testimonium, quo huius opera praua esse, & ideo eunde verbi Dei lucem odisse testatur, cuius fulgore illa argui sentiat. Quò magis ergo cōtra nos fremunt homines, qui praeter mundi honores, opes, voluptates nihil sapiunt, eò clarius apparet penes nos esse lucem illam coelestem, cuius splendorem infelix mundus odio implacabili persequitur, & extinctum cupit. Itaq; quod illi contra nos depromunt argumentū, nos in ipsos retorquemus, atq; eo nostrae fidei & salutis certitudinē, doctrinę item Euangelicae veritatem euinci posse dicimus: Quod olim sapientissimus ille & maximè apud Iudeos authoritatis Senator Gamaliel obseruare potuit, qui cùm suam sententiā de Apostolis & tota re Christiana rogaretur, in haec verba respondit: Abstinete ab hominibus istis, & sinite eos: quoniā si ex hominibus est consilium & opus hoc, dissoluetur: sin ex Deo est, non poteritis dissoluere: ne forte etiam cum Deo pugnare comperiamini. Quia ergo quae ab hominibus instituuntur, sponte collabi, & vbi primus ille impetus deferbuit, paulatim intermo ri solent, Christiana autem fides, & quę ex Euangelij fontibus hauritur doctrina, tot iam seculis ab ipso mundi exordio oppugnata, nullis in hunc vsq; diem armis, & ne exquisitis quidem immanissimorum tormentorum cruciatibus extingui potuit, illam ex Deo esse, & diuinæ virtutis patrocinio defendi liquido constat, Dei autem hostes, aut saltem irrisores esse eos, qui nos ideo damnant, quod ille in nobis seruandis suæ virtutis specimina edit.
units.tr: But we do not want to dwell on this argument, lest anyone think that the servants of God differ in no way from the heroes of the nations, who, lacking knowledge of the true God, looked only to what they thought useful to the commonwealth or honourable and glorious for themselves. There are other arguments of greater weight by which we can defend our cause. Chief among them is the testimony of our Lord Jesus Christ concerning the world, in which he declares that its works are evil, and that for this reason it hates the very light of God's word, because it feels itself exposed by that light. The more savagely men rage against us, men who care for nothing beyond worldly honours, riches and pleasures, the more clearly it appears that the heavenly light is with us, and that the unhappy world pursues its splendour with implacable hatred and wishes it extinguished. So we turn back against our opponents the argument they bring against us, and we say that by this very argument the certainty of our faith and salvation, and likewise the truth of evangelical doctrine, can be proved. The wisest of men, Gamaliel, a senator of great authority among the Jews, understood this well. When he was asked his opinion about the apostles and the whole Christian cause, he answered in these words: "Refrain from these men and let them alone; for if this counsel and work is of men, it will be overthrown; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow it, lest perhaps you be found even to fight against God." Things devised by men usually collapse of their own accord and gradually die out once their first impetus has cooled. But the Christian faith, and the doctrine drawn from the fountains of the Gospel, has been assailed for so many centuries, from the very beginning of the world, and to this day it has not been extinguished by arms, nor even by the most exquisite torments of the most savage tyrants. It is therefore clear that it is from God and is defended by the protection of divine power, and that those who condemn us for this reason, because God displays the proofs of his power in preserving us, are enemies of God, or at least mockers of him.

units.la: Deinde quod nobis hodie accidit, hoc ipsum omnibus fere Dei seruis à prima conditi mundi origine accidisse constat, quorum memoria adhuc hodie apud aduersarios quoq; nostros pretiosa & plus quàm honorifica est. Quis enim nescit Abelum propter solam religionem & fidem, qua promissum humani generis serua torem amplexus est, à Caino fratre crudeliter esse obtrucatum? Quis Abrahami, Isaaci, Iacobi & similium labores ignorat? Vel num Mosis & Aaronis causam deteriorem quàm Pharaonis fuisse putabimus, eò quòd hoc inter regias opes & lætos omnis loci & ordinis hominū applausus exultante, illi duris laboribus & gravissimis periculis impliciti non tam Ægyptios sibi infensos, quàm Israelitas ingratos & iniquos murmuratores esse experti sunt? Num item Baalis mystas & horū socios pseudoprophetas Dei seruis præferemus: quòd illi regio fauore superbi ex Regis culina splendidè epulati sunt, interea dum isti in speluncis abditi solo pane & aqua victitarunt? Deniq; num sacerdotum & scribarum doctrinam Apostolica præstantiorem esse aliquis merito dixerit, quòd illi quidem rerum potiti & præsidum Romanorum armis defensi sunt; hi verò omnes eos sibi infestos habuerunt, qui publicæ authoritatis splendore commendabantur? Aut dicant saltem nobis aduersarij nostri, cur veteres illos Dei seruos cultibus diuinis prosequantur, si quam nos ex illorum ore & scriptis annuntiamus doctrinam damnant, nosq; propter eam odio & supplicio dignos esse iudicant? Certè aut illos etiam odisse eos oportet, aut nobis ab ipsis iniuriam fieri fatebuntur.
units.tr: Next, what happens to us today has happened, as is well known, to almost all the servants of God since the first origin of the world, and their memory is still precious, and more than honourable, even among our adversaries. For who does not know that Abel was cruelly slain by his brother Cain for the sole reason of religion and of the faith by which he embraced the promised Saviour of the human race? Who does not know the labours of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and their like? Or shall we suppose that the cause of Moses and Aaron was worse than that of Pharaoh, merely because Pharaoh, amid royal wealth and the joyful applause of men of every place and rank, rejoiced, while they, caught up in harsh labours and the gravest dangers, found that they had to deal not so much with the Egyptians, who were hostile to them, as with the ungrateful and unjust Israelites who murmured against them? Likewise, shall we prefer the priests of Baal and their companions, the false prophets, to the servants of God, because those men, proud with royal favour, feasted sumptuously from the king's kitchen, while these lived hidden in caves on bread and water alone? Finally, will anyone rightly say that the teaching of the priests and scribes is superior to the apostolic teaching because the former obtained power and were protected by the arms of the Roman governors, while the latter had as enemies all those who were commended by the splendour of public authority? Or at least let our adversaries tell us why they honour those ancient servants of God with divine worship, if they condemn the doctrine we proclaim from their mouths and writings, and judge us worthy of hatred and punishment for it. Surely they must either hate those men too, or they will admit that the wrong is done to us by those very men.

units.la: Sed ne istorum quidem exemplo solo nos tuemur, imò potius æterno Dei decreto gloriamur, qui vt Paulus ad Romanos scribit, dum nos omni afflictionis genere exercet, nos imagini filij Dei IESV CHRISTI conformes facit, vt qui simul cum eo patimur, simul cum eodē glorificemur. Priusquam ergo nos damnent aduersarij, Dei filium damnent necesse est, qui eadem passus suo exemplo nobis præiuit, vt olim cum ipso glorificati, cœlestis vitæ & regni cohæredes efficiamur. Quod cum aduersarij nostri videre nolint, non solùm Gamaliele & eius collegis stupidiores sunt, sed se Corinthiorū similes esse declarant, qui & ipsi exerentem se se inter tam multa tamq; grauia Pauli certamina diuinæ veritatis splendore atq; inuictam virtutem non potuerunt agnoscere. Nos verò illorum cæcitas adeo no offendit, vt potius nobis hoc nomine gratulemur, quòd nos dignos iudicet Deus, qui pro Filio eius persecutionem sustineamus: eoq; maiorem scimus esse hanc nostram gloriam, quòd quas nostris vitiis merebamur poenas, Deus pro sua plus quàm paterna bonitate in crucem Filij sui & saluberrimam carnis nostræ disciplinam conuertit, qua huius vitiofitas coerceatur. Hac enim ratione non solùm crucis eius socij efficimur, sed simul incredibilem illam diuinarum consolationum dulcedinem sentimus, quæ nos nouis indies viribus armant, vt per omnes aduersorum fluctus eluctari & his superiores fieri possimus. Nobis enim cum Paulo dicere licet: Sicut abundant passiones Christi in nobis, ita abundat per Christum consolatio nostra: ideoq; iustificati ex fide, non solùm gloriamur sub spe gloriæ Dei, verumetiam in afflictionibus, scientes, quòd afflictio patientiam efficiat, patientia verò experientiam, experientia autem spem: porrò spes non pudefacit, quòd charitas Dei effusa sit in cordibus nostris per spiritum sanctum, qui datus est nobis. Hanc crucis nostrae gloriam quia infelix mundus videre non potest, nobis illud exprobrare solet, quo nostrae salutis fiducia atque certitudo quam fortissime nititur.
units.tr: But we do not rest our defence on the example of these men alone; rather we glory in the eternal decree of God, who, as Paul writes to the Romans, while he exercises us with every kind of affliction, makes us conformed to the image of the Son of God, Jesus Christ, so that, suffering with him, we may also be glorified with him. Before our adversaries condemn us, then, they must condemn the Son of God, who, having suffered the same things, went before us by his example, so that, having been glorified with him, we may become heirs of the heavenly life and kingdom. Since our adversaries refuse to see this, they are not only more stupid than Gamaliel and his colleagues, but they show themselves like the Corinthians, who, amid so many and such grave struggles of Paul, could not recognise the splendour of divine truth and the unconquered power that shone forth in him. But their blindness does not so offend us that we do not rather rejoice on this account, that God thinks us worthy to suffer persecution for his Son. We know that this glory of ours is all the greater because God, in his more than fatherly goodness, has turned the punishments we deserved for our vices into the cross of his Son and into the most salutary discipline of our flesh, by which its vice is restrained. For in this way we are not only made partners in his cross, but at the same time we feel that incredible sweetness of divine consolations, which arm us daily with new strength so that we can struggle through all the waves of adversity and become superior to them. For we may say with Paul: "As the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds. Therefore, being justified by faith, we not only glory in the hope of the glory of God, but also in afflictions, knowing that affliction produces patience, patience experience, and experience hope; and hope does not put us to shame, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us." Since the unhappy world cannot see this glory of our cross, it is accustomed to throw in our faces that very thing upon which the confidence and certainty of our salvation rest most strongly.

units.la: Quia autem vident aduersarii quam elumbis sit haec exprobratio, & quod optimi quique eos, qui aliis calamitosiores sunt, commiseratione potius quam insultatione aut opprobriis dignos esse sentiunt: ipsam doctrinam, quam profitemur, calumniis suis in odium adducere, aut saltem bonis suspectam facere student. Eam ergo nouitatis insimulant, vt quae ante LVTHERI & ZVINGLII tempora a nemine vel audita sit, vel cuiquam mortalium in mentem venerit: ex eo autem eandem falsam quoque & haereticam, impiam deniqué & bonis moribus inimicam esse conligunt. Qui vero aliis modestiores sunt, veram quidem esse fatentur, sed perfectam esse negant, vt suarum traditionum assumentis locum reliquum faciant. At facilis est ad ista responsio. Nam vt multa alia omittamus, solum doctrinae nostrae argumentum istis confutandis sufficit. Quia tamen ipsi se Apostolicos dici volunt, & nos similiter doctrinam nostram Apostolicam dicimus, aliquanto altius res erit repetenda.
units.tr: But since our adversaries see how feeble this reproach is, and since every good person feels that those who are more afflicted than others deserve pity rather than mockery or insults, they try to bring the very doctrine we profess into hatred by their calumnies, or at least to make it suspect to good people. So they charge it with novelty, as if it had been heard of by no one, and had never entered anyone's mind, before the times of Luther and Zwingli. From this they conclude that it is also false and heretical, impious in the end and hostile to good morals. Others, who are more moderate, admit that it is true but deny that it is complete, so that they may leave room for the addition of their own traditions. But a reply to these claims is easy. To pass over many other things, the subject matter of our doctrine alone is enough to refute them. Yet since they wish themselves to be called apostolic, and we likewise call our doctrine apostolic, the matter must be taken up somewhat more deeply.

units.la: Apostolos aeterni filij Dei, IESV CHRISTI, in terris agentis discipulos & ab eodem orbis totius doctores factos fuisse, inter nos conuenit. Fatemur item vtrinque illos spiritum sanctum coelitus accepisse, qui quaecunque prius ex Christi ore audierant, ipsis in mentem reuocauit, eosque in omnem veritatem induxit. Doctrinae, quam tradere debuerunt, argumentum ipse Dominus vno verbo complexus est, quando iussit vt Euangelium praedicent. At Euangelium Paulus sermonem reconciliationis vocat, & Ioannes idem illud testimonium Christi dixit, ideoque illud alibi ita definiuimus: Euangelium est testimonium siue praedicatio gratiae Dei, nobis in Christo aeterno Dei filio exhibitae: qui vt olim Deus promiserat, & futurum prophetae praedixerant, homo factus, quam nos luere debebamus peccati noxam in se transtulit, eandem mortis suae merito expiauit, & ex diaboli seruitio redemptos Patri suo consecrauit, vt ex huius verbo per spiritus virtutem renati, eidem viuamus & seruiamus per fidei obedientiam, & tandem regni coelestis haereditate fruamur. Continet ergo Euangelij doctrina historiam filij Dei in carne manifestati, & eiusdem fructum. Hunc ipse discipulis in poenitentia & remissione peccatorum indicat, dicens: Ita scriptum est, & ita oportuit Christum pati, & resurgere a mortuis tertio die, & praedicari in eius nomine poenitentiam & remissionem peccatorum apud omnes gentes. Cum quibus conuenit quod postea de Christo Apostoli in Senatu Hierosolymitano dixerunt: Hunc Deus dextera sua euexit in principem ac seruatorem, ad dandam resipiscentiam Israeli ac remissionem peccatorum. Quam doctrinam illi & ore praedicarunt, & scriptis mandatam ad posteros transmiserunt, vt omnibus saeculis constaret, quae doctrina in Ecclesijs retineri debeat. Eandem vero hanc in nostris Ecclesijs tradi, & a nobis defendi nemo negauerit, qui vel nos docentes audiuit, vel libros nostros legere dignatus est. Etenim IESV CHRISTI historiam non (vt quidam solent) ex Monachorum lacunis, qui illam fabulis non minus impiis quam ridiculis atque anilibus corruperunt, sed ex Apostolorum libris petitam populo proponimus. Poenitentia autem omnino opus esse docemus, quae totius hominis ad Deum conuersio est, & illius mortificationem atque innouationem continet. Quia vero seipsum innouare aut conuertere nemo potest, illam totam in Christo monstramus, qui vt hac gratiam nobis apud Patrem meruit, ita quaecunque ad illam necessario requiruntur in nobis suo spiritu efficit. Eiusdem meritum atque donum est gratuita peccatorum remissio: & quia tam ipse, quam eius dona no aliter quam fide apprehendi possunt, homine sola etiam fide in Christum iustificari, id est, ab omni peccatorum reatu absolui docemus: quod praecipuum Apostolicae doctrinae axioma esse, pro quo illi acerrime pugnarunt, primo Synodi Hierosolymitanae decretum, quod Lucas Acto. xv describit, deinde eorundem epistolae atque conciones testantur. Ne quis vero vel fidem hanc in otiosa contemplatione consistere, vel ex gratuita peccatorum remissione quiduis audendi licentiam enasci putet, illam firmum & constantem animi assensum esse dicimus, quo ita apprehenditur Christus, ut nobis unitus in nobis agat, totumque hominem suo obsequio & seruitio vendicet. Doctrinae huic sacramenta coniungimus, non quidem quaestuosa illa, quae Romani Pontifices fabricarunt, sed quae Christus instituit, pauca numero, & vt D. Augustinus ait, obseruatione facillima, significatione praestantissima, vsu saluberrima: Baptismum scilicet, quo initiati in Ecclesiae societatem adoptamur, & Coenam mysticam, quae mortis eius commemoratio & nostrae cum ipso communionis symbolum, adeoque redemptionis per illum factae sigillum est. Haec cum olim ab Apostolis tradita sint, & ijdem nullis aliis traditionibus Ecclesiam grauarint, nos quoque ista nobis sufficere putamus, neque veremur nostram Ecclesiarum doctrinam Apostolicam dicere.
units.tr: It is agreed between us that the apostles were disciples of the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, while he lived on earth, and were made teachers of the whole world by him. We also agree on both sides that they received the Holy Spirit from heaven, who recalled to their minds whatever they had previously heard from Christ's mouth and led them into all truth. The Lord himself summed up in one word the subject matter of the teaching they were to hand down, when he commanded that they preach the Gospel. Now Paul calls the Gospel "the word of reconciliation," and John called it the same thing, the testimony of Christ. Therefore we have defined it elsewhere thus: the Gospel is the testimony or preaching of the grace of God, exhibited to us in Christ, the eternal Son of God, who, as God had long promised and the prophets had foretold that he would be, was made man, took upon himself the guilt of the sin that we ought to have paid for, expiated it by the merit of his death, and consecrated to his Father those redeemed from the service of the devil, so that, reborn through the power of the Spirit by his word, we may live and serve him through the obedience of faith, and at last enjoy the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. The doctrine of the Gospel therefore contains the history of the Son of God made manifest in the flesh, and the fruit of it. The Lord himself indicated this to his disciples when he spoke of repentance and the forgiveness of sins, saying: "Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations." What the apostles later said about Christ in the Jerusalem council agrees with this: "God has exalted him at his right hand as Prince and Saviour, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins." They preached this doctrine both by mouth and handed it down in writing to posterity, so that in every age it would be clear what doctrine ought to be retained in the Churches. That this same doctrine is taught in our Churches, and defended by us, no one will deny who has heard us teach or has deigned to read our books. For we set forth to the people the history of Jesus Christ not, as some are wont to do, from the puddles of the monks, who have corrupted it with fables as impious as they are ridiculous and old-womanish, but taken from the books of the apostles. We teach that repentance is altogether necessary; it is the conversion of the whole man to God, and includes his mortification and renewal. But since no one can renew or convert himself, we show that all of this is in Christ, who, as he merited grace for us before the Father, so also by his Spirit brings about in us whatever is necessarily required for it. The free remission of sins is his merit and gift; and since neither he nor his gifts can be laid hold of except by faith, we teach that a man is justified by faith alone in Christ, that is, absolved from the guilt of all sins. This is the chief axiom of apostolic doctrine, for which they fought most fiercely: first the decree of the Jerusalem council, which Luke describes in Acts 15, and then the epistles and sermons of the same apostles bear witness to it. But lest anyone think that this faith consists in idle contemplation, or that a licence for any kind of daring arises from the free remission of sins, we say that it is a firm and steadfast assent of the mind, by which Christ is so apprehended that, being united to us, he works in us and claims the whole man for his obedience and service. To this doctrine we join the sacraments, not indeed those profitable ones that the Roman pontiffs have fabricated, but those that Christ instituted, few in number, and, as Augustine says, most easy to observe, most excellent in signification, and most wholesome in use: namely Baptism, by which those initiated are adopted into the fellowship of the Church, and the mystical Supper, which is a remembrance of his death and a symbol of our communion with him, and thus a seal of the redemption wrought through him. Since these were handed down by the apostles of old, and since the same apostles did not burden the Church with any other traditions, we think these things are enough for us, and we do not fear to call the doctrine of our Churches apostolic.

units.la: Calumnia ergo est non minus impudens quam falsa, qua aduersarij eam novitatis crimine grauant, & priusquam Lutheri et Zvinglii nomen audiretur, Ecclesiae cognitam fuisse negant. Est quidem hoc illis dictu facillimum, sed vere ab illis dici tunc demum probare poterunt, quando scriptis Apostolicis omnem fidem abrogauerint. At quid de Apostolis dico, quando ne hi quidem primi eius authores sunt, neque cum Christo demum in carne nato coepit, sed ipso mundo & omnibus saeculis (si ita loqui liceat) est antiquior? Num quid enim aeterno Dei decreto antiquius fingi potest? Atqui per illud nobis Christum a Patre seruatorem destinatum, & nos in eodem, priusquam mundus hic crearetur, electos fuisse Petrus & Paulus testantur, idque primis parentibus facta promissio euidentissime docet. Cum enim isti peccassent, & se mortis aeternae supplicium meruisse sentirent, toto animo consternatos hac una consolatione Deus subleuauit, qua semen mulieris pollicitus est, a quo serpentis caput conculcari, id est, diaboli vires atque regnum euerti, & humanum genus ex eius tyrannide redimi oporteat. Cur vero semen mulieris, phrasi prorsus noua & insolita, vindex ille dicitur? Non alia nimirum ratione, quam quod aeterno Dei decreto praedestinatus, absque viri congressu ex casta & incorrupta virgine homo nasci debuit. Quem vero dabis, etsi omnium gentium historias euoluas, omniumque quotquot vnquam fuerunt, genealogias a longe repetas, qui ad eum modum natus sit? Neminem certe praeter vnum IESVM CHRISTVM, qui spiritus sancti virtute in vtero Mariae virginis conceptus, & illaeso eiusdem virginitatis flore Bethlehemi natus, tandem suae mortis merito peccatum expiauit, resurrectione autem sua mortem & inferos deuicit, regnoque diaboli destructo miseros nos in libertatem filiorum Dei asseruit. Eam ergo fidem, quam nos hodie profitemur, Deus ipse Adamum in paradiso docuit, quam hic proculdubio filijs & posteris suis omnibus commendauit, & qua Abelum Deo placuisse, Apostolus ad Hebraeos testatur. Et hoc illud aeternae salutis pactum est, quod cum in diluuio abolitum videri posset, Deus cum Abrahamo, quem ideo ex Chaldaea euocauerat, instaurauit, circumcisione obsignauit, typis legalibus adumbrauit, & tandem prophetarum oraculis amplius illustrauit, quibus illi, vt aeterni Dei interpretes, quaecunque promissus ille humani generis vindex pro nobis facere & sufferre debuit, praedixerunt. Testimonia, quae hic infinita adduci poterant, consulto praeterimus, quia plerisque nota sunt. Hoc vero in Prophetis multa consideratione dignissimum est, quod de Christo ita vaticinantur, vt populum a circumcisione simul & templo atque sacrificijs reuocent, & omnem salutis fiduciam sive spem in illo solo collocare docent. Observarunt hoc vetustissimi scriptores, ex quorum numero Eusebius priscos Patres nō vocarentur Christianos dicere, eō quod non aliam fidem secuti sint, quàm eam cuius subiectum est Christus, quem suo tempore ipsis quoque redemptorem venturum esse credebat. Et D. Augustinus cùm in libro de vera Religione scripsisset: Ea est nostris temporibus Christiana religio, quam cognoscere ac sequi securissima & certissima salus est, &c. postea libro 1 Retract. cap. 13 hoc dictum non de ipsa re, sed solo nomine Christiano intelligi debere docet. Nam res (inquit) ipsa, quæ nunc Christiana religio nuncupatur, erat apud antiquos, nec defuit ab initio generis humani, quousque ipse Christus veniret in carne, unde vera religio, quæ iam erat, coepit appellari Christiana. Cùm enim eum post resurrectionem ascensionemque in cœlum coepissent Apostoli prædicare, & plurimi crederent, primùm apud Antiochiam, sicut scriptum est, appellati sunt discipuli Christiani. Propterea dixi: Hæc est nostris temporibus Christiana religio: non quia prioribus temporibus non fuit, sed quia posterioribus hoc nomen accepit. Hæc August. Quòd si verò Christiani fuerunt veteres illi, qui ante traditam circumcisionem & institutum cultum Mosaicum vixerunt, qui item prophetarum monita secuti, salutis fiduciam in vno IESV CHRISTO tandem venturo repositam habuerunt, nimium profecto temerarij sunt, qui hodie nos doctrinam novam tradere calumniantur, quando vnum Christum prædicamus, qui solus nobis pœnitentiæ & remissionis peccatorum Mediator sit. Etenim si illi audiri debent, nomen fuit quod Apostoli tanta cum fiducia pronunciauerunt, Non esse præter Christum aliud nomen sub cœlo inter homines datum, in quo nos seruari oporteat. At multò iustius novatores dici debent, qui salutem in Missis, ieiuniis, feriis, preculis emptitiis, vita monastica, satisfactionibus, suffitu, cereis, cilicijs, chameuniis, indulgentiis, peregrinationibus, Diuorum intercessione & invocatione, igne purgatorio, exequijs & sacris funebribus aliisque fexcentis quaerunt, quæ aliquot demum post Apostolos secula instituta sunt, quorum item authores (si ita opus sit) nominari, & quo quisque tempore vixerit, demonstrari poterant.
units.tr: This slander is therefore no less shameless than it is false: our opponents charge the doctrine with novelty and deny that it was known to the Church before the names of Luther and Zwingli were heard. It is easy for them to say this, but they will be able to prove it true only when they have abolished all faith in the apostolic writings. But why do I speak of the Apostles, when they are not even the first authors of this doctrine? It did not begin with Christ born in the flesh; it is older than the world itself and all the ages (if I may speak so). For what can be imagined as older than the eternal decree of God? Yet Peter and Paul testify that by that decree Christ was appointed by the Father to be our Saviour, and that we were chosen in him before this world was created. The promise made to our first parents most clearly teaches the same. When they had sinned and felt that they had deserved the punishment of eternal death, God lifted them up, utterly dismayed, with this one consolation: he promised the seed of the woman, by whom the serpent's head must be crushed, that is, the power and kingdom of the devil overthrown, and the human race redeemed from his tyranny. But why is that avenger called the seed of the woman, in a phrase entirely new and unusual? Clearly for no other reason than that he, predestined by the eternal decree of God, had to be born a man of a chaste and undefiled virgin, without union with a man. And whom will you name, even if you unroll the histories of all nations and trace back the genealogies of all who have ever lived, who was born in this way? Certainly no one except the one JESUS CHRIST, who was conceived in the womb of the virgin Mary by the power of the Holy Spirit, and born at Bethlehem with the flower of her virginity unharmed; who at last by the merit of his death expiated sin, and by his resurrection conquered death and hell, and, destroying the kingdom of the devil, asserted us wretched ones into the liberty of the sons of God. Therefore the faith which we profess today, God himself taught to Adam in paradise; Adam undoubtedly commended it to all his sons and descendants, and the Apostle to the Hebrews testifies that by it Abel pleased God. This is that covenant of eternal salvation which, though it might seem to have been abolished in the flood, God renewed with Abraham, whom for this purpose he had called out of Chaldea; he sealed it with circumcision, shadowed it forth with legal types, and at last illustrated it more fully by the oracles of the prophets. Through these, as interpreters of the eternal God, they foretold all that the promised deliverer of the human race was to do and suffer for us. The testimonies, which could be brought here in endless number, we deliberately pass over, because most people know them. But this is most worthy of careful consideration in the Prophets: they prophesy about Christ in such a way as to call the people back at once from circumcision, the temple and the sacrifices, and they teach that all confidence and hope of salvation is to be placed in him alone. The very ancient writers observed this. Among them Eusebius says that the early Fathers were not called Christians, because they followed no other faith than that whose subject is Christ, whom they believed would come in his time as Redeemer also for them. And when Augustine had written in his book on true religion: "This is the Christian religion in our times, to know and follow which is the most secure and certain salvation," etc., later, in the first book of his Retractations, chapter 13, he teaches that this statement should be understood not of the thing itself but only of the name Christian. "For," he says, "the thing itself, which is now called the Christian religion, existed among the ancients, and it was not lacking from the beginning of the human race until Christ himself came in the flesh; from then on the true religion, which already existed, began to be called Christian. For when the Apostles, after his resurrection and ascension into heaven, had begun to preach him, and many believed, the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch, as it is written. Therefore I said: 'This is the Christian religion in our times': not because it did not exist in earlier times, but because it received this name in later times." So Augustine. But if those ancient men, who lived before circumcision was given and the Mosaic worship instituted, were Christians, men who likewise followed the admonitions of the prophets and placed their confidence of salvation in Jesus Christ, who was yet to come, then truly they are too rash who slander us today as teaching a new doctrine, when we preach the one Christ, who alone is the Mediator of repentance and the forgiveness of sins for us. For if those men are to be heard, it is the name which the Apostles proclaimed with such confidence: that there is no other name under heaven given among men, by which we must be saved, except Christ. But far more justly should they be called innovators who seek salvation in Masses, fasts, holy days, bought prayers, monastic life, satisfactions, incense, candles, hair shirts, cowls, indulgences, pilgrimages, the intercession and invocation of the saints, purgatorial fire, funeral rites and sacred obsequies, and in six hundred other things, which were instituted some ages after the Apostles. Their authors too (if need be) could be named, and it could be shown in what period each one lived.

units.la: At quæ hucusque commemorauimus, doctrinam de Christo non solùm novitatis verumetiam falsi crimine liberant. Constat enim scriptorum omnium qui extant, antiquissimum esse Mosem, qui seculis aliquot Orpheum, Musæum & Homerum præcessit, quorum monumenta vetustissima habentur. Excitauit hunc Deus afflictissimo tempore, quando nimirum Israelitæ, penes quos tunc erat Ecclesiæ titulus, dura Ægyptiorum tyrannide premebantur, & plerique propter diuturnam cum prophanis hominibus consuetudinem promissionum veterum obliti à cultus quoque syncerit ate desciuerant. Tunc (inquam) Mosem illis dedit Deus, qui non solùm oppressos in libertatem asserret, sed insuper creati mundi historiam & patribus datas promissiones literis mandaret, ne istarum rerum cognitio prorsus aboleretur. Quod si verò ille rem nemini mortalium prius auditam vel cognitam attulisset, num aliqua dictorum eius fides esse poterat apud homines non omnino stupidos & vaecordes? Sed reliqua adhuc erat apud eos, qui non omnem pietatis sensum exuerant, traditionum à patribus acceptarum cognitio: neque dubium est in multorum ore fuisse Dei oraculum, qui posteros Abrahami annis quadringentis seruitium graue passuros esse prædixerat, quibus euolutis in libertatem essent vindicandi. Quia ergo nihil nouum aut insolens promittebat Moses, facilius fidem inuenit apud miseros, qui in humanis spem salutis nullam superesse videbant. Vt tamen irrefragabilis esset eius authoritas, eam miraculis & signis insolitis Deus confirmauit. Nam vt quæ in Ægypto dira & horrenda aedita sunt omittamus, quis obsecro Israelitarum legis doctrinam Deo authore proditam esse dubitare potuit, qui Sinai montem nubibus praeter morem contegi, ignibus novis fumare & motu terribili contremiscere viderant, tonitruum fragorem & tubarum immane resonantium clangorem audierant, & ipsius Dei vocem intolerabili cum maiestate nō tam aures quàm animos penetrare sensERANT, qui denique Moysis à Dei colloquio redeuntis facie Solis instar radiante territi, oculos in illam non poterant intendere? Quis ista humanis artibus aut quacunque ratione naturali fieri putasset? Accesserūt his dira exempla, quę in eos aedita sunt, qui se Mosi proteruius opponere audebant: vtpote Mariae sororis lepra, horribilis Corae & coniuratorum eius interitus, quodque vniuersa illa multitudo, quae ex Aegypto exiuit, propter perpetua murmura & incurabilem contumaciam in deserto miserrime absumpta periit. Quorum omnium historiam nisi Moses veriss-ime descripsisset, quis Israelitas tam multa tamque grauia gentis suae probra adeo patienter ferre voluisse putet, vt ea suo silentio approbarent? Sed rei veritate convicti ea negare non potuerunt, quae in totius populi conspectu, ita vt ab illo descripta sunt, gesta fuerant. Quis vero illum in aliorum rebus aliquid finxisse putet, qui ne suorum quidem infamiam dissimulare voluit? Etenim suam ipsius culpam, Aaronis item fratris unici & Mariae sororis dilectae murmur, adhaec nepotum ex fratre miserabilem interitum perpetuo silentio sepelire poterat, si suae potius gloriae quam veritati studuisset. Quid, quod tribum totam, ex qua oriundus erat, perpetua infamiae nota aspersit, quando quod Iacob iam moriturus de illa pronuntiauit oraculum, libris suis inseruit: Simeon & Leui vasa iniquitatis, in consilium eorum non veniat anima mea? Quis illum vt haec de sua gente ad posteros transmitteret coegit, nisi veritatis spiritus, qui omnes eius actiones moderabatur? At quis illi scriptorum suorum adeo que totius ministerij scopus fuit? Non alius certe, quam quod Israelitas suos ad Dei foedus, quod complementum suum in Christo habet, reuocare voluit. Quod D. Augustinus obseruans dicebat, quinque libros Moysis non aliud quàm Christum praedicare: & huius dicti testem addu cit ipsum Christum, qui Iudaeis dixit: Si credidissetis Mosi, credidissetis mihi: de me enim ille scripsit. Neque minus certa est Prophetarum fides atque authoritas, quorum vaticinia cum rerum euentus probauerit, de eorum veritate dubitare nefas est. At IESVM hunc, qui ex Maria virgine natus est, Christum illum esse quem illi venturum praedixerunt, facile intelligent, qui eius historiam cum illorum scriptis diligenter conferunt. Sed accedit his vox Patris coelitus de illo pronuntiata: Hic est Filius ille meus dilectus, in quo placatus sum. Confirmata est eadem miraculis & signis compluribus, quae vt vires humanas superant, ita tam perspicua sunt & efficacia, vt ne scribae quidem, homines astutissimi, ea aliquo praetextu in speciem verisimili calumniari potuerint, vulgus autem eorum perspicuitate conuictum diceret: Christus, cum venerit, num signa plura aedet ijs quae hic aedidit? Scimus equidem quid de illis olim Porphyrius & huius similes canes, Cerberi infernalis soboles, latrauerint; sed tam putidae sunt illę calumniae, vt confutationem nullam mereatur. Maiori autem detestatione digni sunt, qui cum Christi nomine glorientur, nos tamen falsi accusant, quando homines, qui omnes natura peccatores & mortis aeternae rei sunt, sola fide in Christum iustificari & seruari docemus: quem vnicum humani generis seruatorem esse, vnanimis veteris & noui Testamenti consensus tam multis tamque luculentis testimonijs confirmatus abunde docet.
units.tr: But what we have so far recalled frees the doctrine concerning Christ not only from the charge of novelty but also from the charge of falsehood. For it is established, among all the writings that exist, that the most ancient is that of Moses, who preceded Orpheus, Musaeus and Homer by several centuries; their most ancient monuments are still extant. God raised up Moses at a most distressing time, when the Israelites, among whom the title of the Church then resided, were oppressed by the harsh tyranny of the Egyptians; and many of them, through long association with profane people, had forgotten the ancient promises and had also fallen away from the purity of worship. Then (I say) God gave them Moses, who not only led the oppressed into liberty but also committed to writing the history of the created world and the promises given to the fathers, so that knowledge of these things might not be utterly lost. But if he had brought forward something that no mortal had heard or known before, would any of his words have had credibility among people who were not entirely stupid and senseless? But there still remained among those who had not cast off every sense of piety a knowledge of the traditions received from the fathers; and there is no doubt that the oracle of God was on the lips of many, which had foretold that the descendants of Abraham would suffer hard servitude for four hundred years, and that when this period was over they would be set free. Because Moses promised nothing new or strange, he found faith more easily among the wretched, who saw no hope of salvation left among men. Yet so that his authority might be beyond dispute, God confirmed it with unusual miracles and signs. For to pass over the dreadful and horrible things that were done in Egypt: who, I ask you, could doubt that the teaching of the law of the Israelites was handed down with God as its author? They had seen Mount Sinai covered with clouds contrary to custom, smoking with strange fires and trembling with a terrible quaking; they had heard the crash of thunder and the immense blare of trumpets resounding; and they had felt the voice of God himself, with unbearable majesty, penetrate not so much their ears as their minds. Finally, terrified by Moses' face shining like the sun as he returned from speaking with God, they could not fix their eyes upon it. Who would have supposed that these things were done by human arts or by any natural cause? To these were added the dreadful examples made against those who dared to oppose Moses too insolently: the leprosy of his sister Miriam, the dreadful destruction of Korah and his fellow conspirators, and the fact that that whole multitude which came out of Egypt perished most wretchedly in the wilderness because of their constant murmuring and incurable obstinacy. Unless Moses had described the history of all these things most truthfully, who would think that the Israelites were willing to bear so patiently so many and such grave reproaches upon their nation, as to approve them by their silence? But convicted by the truth of the matter, they could not deny those things which had been done in the sight of the whole people, just as he described them. And who would think that he invented anything about others, when he did not even wish to conceal the disgrace of his own people? For he could have buried in perpetual silence his own fault, the murmuring of his only brother Aaron and of his beloved sister Miriam, and moreover the miserable death of his nephews through his brother, if he had cared for his own glory rather than for the truth. What of the fact that he branded the whole tribe from which he himself sprang with a perpetual mark of infamy, when he inserted in his books the oracle that Jacob pronounced about that tribe as he was about to die: "Simeon and Levi are vessels of iniquity; let my soul not come into their counsel"? Who compelled him to hand down these things about his own nation to posterity, unless the Spirit of truth, which governed all his actions? But what was the aim of his writings and of his whole ministry? Certainly none other than to call back his Israelites to the covenant of God, which has its fulfilment in Christ. Augustine, observing this, said that the five books of Moses preach nothing other than Christ; and he brings Christ himself as witness to this saying, who said to the Jews: "If you had believed Moses, you would have believed me; for he wrote of me." Equally certain is the faith and authority of the Prophets, whose prophecies the outcome of events has proved; it is wrong to doubt their truth. But those who carefully compare the history of this Jesus, who was born of the virgin Mary, with their writings will easily understand that he is the Christ whom they foretold would come. Moreover, to these is added the voice of the Father, proclaimed from heaven about him: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." It was confirmed by many miracles and signs, which surpass human powers, and are so clear and effective that not even the scribes, the most crafty men, could slander them with any plausible pretext; and the common people, convinced by their clarity, said: "When Christ comes, will he do more signs than these which he has done here?" We know indeed what Porphyry and dogs like him, the offspring of the infernal Cerberus, once barked about these things; but those slanders are so foul that they do not deserve any refutation. Yet those are worthy of greater detestation who boast of the name of Christ and yet accuse us falsely, when we teach that men, who are all sinners by nature and liable to eternal death, are justified and saved by faith alone in Christ; whom the unanimous agreement of the Old and New Testaments, confirmed by so many and such clear testimonies, abundantly teaches to be the only Saviour of the human race.

units.la: Atrocior tamen est eorum calumnia, qui doctrinam hanc haereseos accusant, quod crimen piis omnibus semper tam graue visum fuit, vt D. Hieronymus ad Pammachium non veritus sit scribere: Nolo in suspicione haereseos quenquam esse patientem, ne apud eos, qui ignorant innocentiam eius, dissimulatio conscientia entia iudicetur, si taceat. Enimuero nemo haereticus esse potest, nisi idem in Dei gloriam peccet, & Christo derogęt, id quod pijs auribus prorsus intolerabile est. At haeresim ab electione dictam esse idem scriptor docet, dum scilicet quisq; sibi p si eligit quod sequatur. Quia autem qui noua dogmata fingunt, & ea pertinaciter tueri in animum inducunt, eo ipso à communi Ecclesiae sensu, & tandem ab eiusdem societate discedunt, cum haeresi schisma coniunctum est: quo fit, vt in sectas aut partes Ecclesia distrahatur, quę vnica, & proinde Catholica quoq;, id est, vniuersalis agnosci debet. A quo crimine doctrina nostra, si eius argumetum spectes, tam aliena est, vt infelicem mundum variis inter se sententijs dissidentem haec sola conciliet, & ex multis vnum quasi corpus faciat. Eius enim subiectum (vt ante diximus) est CHRISTVS IESVS, quem ideo mori debuisse Ioannes scribit, vt filios Dei dispersos cogeret in vnum. Constat enim ante eius in carnem aduentum orbem terrarum in mille sectas scissum fuisse, dum videlicet proprium quisque sibi ipsi Deum finxit, adeo vt D. Augustinus Deorum triginta millia aliquando in terris culta fuisse ex Varrone annotarit. Fuit haec horribilis hominum distractio, cui humana philosophia adeo remedium nullum afferre potuit, vt eam auxerint potius, qui huius studio diti res diuinas atque coelestes sui ingenij acumine inuestigare voluerunt. Solus Christus, qui nobis à Deo patre sapientia factus est, tanto malo manum medicam admouere potuit, & per Euangelij praedicationem, quam in omnes gentes voluit diuulgari, tam multis tamq; diuersis opinionibus distractas hominum mentes vniuit. Ex ea enim didicerunt omnium locorum homines, Deum vnum esse, totius mundi & omnium quae in illo sunt creatorem, qui solus coli, solus adorari, solus inuocari debeat. Eadem mediatorem quoque inter Deum & homines vnicum esse docet IESVM CHRISTVM, qui cum aeternus sit Dei filius, ex aeterno Patris decreto hominem assumpsit, vt sicut diuinam & humanam naturam in vna eademq; persona sociauit: ita nos quoq; Deo patri reconciliaret, simulq; nobis author esset, vt per fidei vnitatem in vnum Ecclesiae corpus coalescceremus, cuius ipse caput est. Qua ergo ratione doctrina nostra vel haeretica vel schismatica dici meretur, quae vt vnum Deum praedicat, ita IESVM CHRISTVM vnicum inter hunc & nos Mediatorem esse docet, quem dixisse scimus: Ego sum via, & veritas, & vita: nemo venit ad Patrem nisi per me? Num ergo in sectas eos scindi possibile est, qui ad vnum Deum per vnam eandemq; viam contendunt? Id certe nemo nisi insanus dixerit. Quomodo ite in partes distrahentur, qui vt vnum Deum inuocant, ita hunc vnum per Filium suum nobis loquentem audiunt, eundemq; solum sibi à Patre sapientiam, iustitiam, sanctificationem & redemptionem factum esse credunt? De quibus denique Apostolus dixit: Vnum est corpus, & vnus spiritus, sicut & vocati estis in vnam spem vocationis vestrae: vnus Dominus, vna Fides, vnum Baptisma, vnus Deus & Pater omnium nostrum: In partes olim Corinthij scindebantur, quando quasi relicto Christo, alius se Pauli, alius Petri, alius Apollo discipulum aut sectatorem esse dicebat: quos vt ad vnitatem reduceret Paulus, eos ad solum Christum remittit, qui solus pro omnibus illis in cruce mortuus sit, & in cuius solius nomine ipsi baptizati sint. In partes ergo hodie cur nos Ecclesiam scindere dicimur, qui vnum Christum praedicamus, in hoc vno omnes sperare & confidere, eoq; solo gloriari docemus? Quin potius hoc facere dicentur, qui factiosa Benedictinorum, Bernhardinorum, Iacobitarum, Ioannitarum, Augustinianorum, Franciscanorum, Dominicanorum nomina excogitarunt, qui omnes in diuersas familias ceu Ecclesias diuisi, vestitu, moribus & ceremonijs differunt: qui item eo non contenti, insuper Diuos diuersos inuocare, inq; proprijs operum diuersissimorum meritis iustitiam atque salutem quaerere docent. Vtinam isti quoniam illis nostra omnia sordent, D. Augustinum audirent, qui cùm Diui Ioannis Apostoli dictum de vno aduocato nostro, IESV CHRISTO, exponeret, inter alia dicebat: Videte ipsum Ioannem seruantem humilitatem, certè vir iustus erat & magnus, qui de pectore Domini mysteriorum secreta bibebat: ille ille qui bibendo de pectore Domini diuinitatem rauit, In principio erat Verbum, & Verbum erat apud Deum: ille talis vir, non dixit, Aduocatum habetis apud Patrem: nec ipsum Christū habetis, dixit: sed & Christū posuit, NON SE, & HABEMVS dixit, non HABETIS. Maluit se ponere in numero peccatorum, vt haberet aduocatum Christum, quàm ponere se pro Christo aduocatum, & inueniri inter damnandos superbos. Fratres, IESVM CHRISTVM iustum ipsum habemus aduocatum ad Patrem, ipse propitiatio est peccatorum nostrorum. Hoc qui tenuit, haeresim non fecit: hoc qui tenuit, scisma non fecit. Vnde enim facta sunt scismata? Cùm dicunt homines, Nos iusti sumus: cùm dicunt homines, Nos sanctificamus immundos, nos iustificamus impios, nos petimus, nos impetramus, &c. Haec Augusti. in cuius verbis si vt in speculo seipsos contemplarentur Pontifices & Monachi, non possent certè non erubescere, & suae ipsos in posterum puderet arrogantiae, qua & contra Christum se attollunt, & rectè sentientes insolenter damnant.
units.tr: Yet the slander of those who accuse this doctrine of heresy is even more outrageous. Every godly person has always regarded heresy as so grave a charge that Jerome did not hesitate to write to Pammachius: "I do not want anyone to remain under suspicion of heresy, lest silence be judged a sign of a guilty conscience by those who do not know his innocence." Indeed, no one can be a heretic without sinning against the glory of God and detracting from Christ, which is utterly intolerable to godly ears. But the same writer teaches that the word "heresy" comes from "choice," namely when each person chooses for himself what he will follow. Those who invent new doctrines and stubbornly determine to defend them depart by that very fact from the common mind of the Church and finally from its fellowship. Schism is joined to heresy, and so the Church is torn into sects or factions, though it ought to be acknowledged as one and therefore also Catholic, that is, universal. Our doctrine, if you look at its subject, is so far from this crime that it alone can reconcile a wretched world divided by many conflicting opinions and make one body out of many. Its subject, as we said before, is Christ Jesus, whom John writes had to die so that he might gather the scattered children of God into one. It is certain that before his coming in the flesh the whole world was split into a thousand sects, since each person fashioned a god of his own. So much so that Augustine notes from Varro that at one time thirty thousand gods were worshipped on earth. This horrible division of mankind human philosophy could in no way remedy; rather, those who sought with the sharpness of their wit to investigate divine and heavenly things by its study only increased it. Christ alone, who was made wisdom to us by God the Father, could apply a healing hand to so great an evil, and through the preaching of the gospel, which he willed to be spread among all nations, he united the minds of men that had been pulled apart by so many and such diverse opinions. From it the people of every region learned that there is one God, the creator of the whole world and of all that is in it, who alone ought to be worshipped, alone adored, alone invoked. The same gospel teaches that Jesus Christ is the one mediator between God and men. Being the eternal Son of God, by the eternal decree of the Father he took on man, so that just as he joined the divine and human nature in one person, so he might also reconcile us to God the Father, and at the same time be the author for us, that through the unity of faith we might grow together into one body of the Church, of which he is the head. By what reasoning, then, does our doctrine deserve to be called heretical or schismatic? It proclaims one God, and likewise teaches that Jesus Christ is the one Mediator between him and us, of whom we know he said: "I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me." Is it possible, then, for those to be divided into sects who strive toward the one God by the one and same way? Certainly no one but a madman would say so. How can those be split into parties who invoke the one God, and likewise hear him speaking through his Son, and believe that this same Son has been made to them by the Father wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption? Concerning such people the Apostle finally said: "There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of us all." The Corinthians were once divided into parties, when, as if Christ had been set aside, one said he was the disciple or follower of Paul, another of Peter, another of Apollos. To bring them back to unity, Paul sends them back to Christ alone, who alone died on the cross for all of them, and in whose name alone they had been baptized. Why, then, are we said to split the Church today, when we preach the one Christ, and teach that all should hope and trust in him alone and glory in him alone? Rather, those would be said to do this who devised the factious names of Benedictines, Bernardines, Jacobites, Johannites, Augustinians, Franciscans, and Dominicans, who, divided into different families, as if into churches, differ in dress, customs, and ceremonies; who, not content with this, also teach that different saints should be invoked, and that righteousness and salvation are to be sought in the merits of their own very diverse works. I wish those men, since everything of ours is worthless to them, would listen to Augustine, who, when he was expounding the saying of the holy apostle John about our one advocate, Jesus Christ, said among other things: "See how John himself kept humility. Surely he was a righteous and great man, who drank the secrets of the mysteries from the breast of the Lord. He it was, he who by drinking from the breast of the Lord drew in the divinity: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.' That man, so great, did not say: 'You have an advocate with the Father'; nor did he say: 'You have Christ himself.' But he set down Christ, not himself, and said WE HAVE, not YOU HAVE. He preferred to place himself among the number of sinners, so that he might have Christ as advocate, rather than to place himself as advocate in place of Christ and be found among the proud who are to be condemned. Brothers, we have Jesus Christ the righteous himself as our advocate with the Father; he is the propitiation for our sins. Whoever held to this made no heresy; whoever held to this made no schism. For where do schisms come from? When men say: 'We are righteous'; when men say: 'We sanctify the unclean, we justify the impious, we ask, we obtain,' and so on." If the Pontiffs and Monks would look at themselves in these words of Augustine as in a mirror, they could not fail to blush, and they would be ashamed of their arrogance, by which they rise up even against Christ and insolently condemn those who think rightly.

units.la: Porrò non parum aliqui offenduntur, quando doctrinam de sola fide iustifi-cante bonis operibus inimicam esse aduersarij clamant, vt quae homines securos reddat, & ab omni pietatis & sanctimoniae studio auocet, quod nullum posset esse, si se eo nihil apud Deum mereri audiant. Sunt ergo, quos simplex ignorantia solicitos reddit, ne mundo plus satis proteruienti habenae nimium laxentur: Qui vt reuera commiseratione digni sunt, ita eò durius tractari merentur, qui hominibus non malis tanti erroris authores sunt, cumq; Ecclesiae doctores atq; columnae haberi velint, tam stupidè ignorantes & tam stolidè superbi sunt, vt neque fidei vim videre possint, neque propriam vitiositatem agnoscere, quae tanta est, vt si nos Deus pro meritis tractare velit, ne aeris quidem & Solis communis vsu dignи ceferi, nedum coelestia bona mereri possemus. Nec enim (vt alias monuimus) fides inani & otiosa contemplatione constat, sed certo & efficaci animi assensu, qui spiritus virtute accensus & confirmatus, nos de omnibus ijs certissimos facit, quae pro nobis aeternus Dei filius fecit & passus est, qui denique nos totos Deo vendicat, vt ei voluntarium obsequium praestemus. Etenim quomodo in peccatis securus pergere poterit, qui illa Deo tantae abominationi esse credit, vt ea filij sui vnigenae indigna morte voluerit expiari? Num item diaboli suggestionibus aures praebebit, vt huic rursus subjiciatur, qui se pretioso filij Dei sanguine redemptum esse nouit, vt Deo in spiritus libertate seruiat? Vel num corpus suum impuris mundi & carnis desideriis prostituat, qui illud spiritus sancti templum in Christo factum esse gloriatur? Num vero proximum suum odisse poterit, quem & a Deo tanti fieri, & eiusdem Patris filium eiusdemque corporis membrum esse audit? Num denique vllis aduersis, periculis, tormentis addu-ci poterit fidelis, vt Christum abneget, quem suum vindicem & redemptorem esse profitetur? Tam ergo abest, vt rerum securos aut petulantes praeceptorum Dei contemptores faciat fides, vt ea potius pulcherrimarum virtutum mater sit, Pietatis nimirum, Sanctimoniae, Innocentiae, Charitatis, Fortitudinis, Patientiae, ex quibus ceu ex largissimo & perenni fonte omnis generis bona opera deriuan tur. Quibus etiamsi salutis aeternae meritum negemus, ne quid Christi gloriae derogetur, eadem tamen facta necessaria esse fatemur, vt & Deo debitum obsequium praestemus, & vt fidei nostrae testimonia sint: quae si nihil in nobis agat, mortua est, & proinde ne fides quidem est, sed inanis & vana fidei nomine palliata opinio. Poterant haec innumeris eorum exemplis confirmari, qui in scripturis fidei nomine commendantur: sed quia haec satis nota sunt, desinant nobis aduersarij nostri eorum nequitiam exprobrare, quos Christiani nominis titulo nequi-quam gloriantes, neque Christus pro suis discipulis, neque nos pro germanis fra-tribus possumus agnoscere.
units.tr: Furthermore, some are not a little offended when our adversaries cry out that the doctrine of faith alone justifying is hostile to good works, as if it made men careless and drew them away from all zeal for piety and holiness; which could not happen if they heard that by it they merit nothing before God. Some are troubled by simple ignorance, lest the reins be loosened too much for a world already sufficiently wanton. These people are indeed worthy of pity, but those deserve to be treated all the more harshly who are the authors of so great an error for men who are not wicked, and who want to be regarded as teachers and pillars of the Church, yet are so foolishly ignorant and so stupidly proud that they can neither see the power of faith nor recognize their own vicious nature. That nature is so great that, if God wished to deal with us according to our merits, we would not be worthy even of the common use of air and sun, much less able to merit heavenly goods. For faith (as we have warned elsewhere) does not consist in an empty and idle contemplation, but in a certain and effective assent of the mind, which, kindled and strengthened by the power of the Spirit, makes us utterly certain of all those things which the eternal Son of God has done and suffered for us, and which finally claims us wholly for God, so that we render him willing obedience.
