For how will one who believes that sins are so abominable to God that he willed them to be expiated by the unworthy death of his only-begotten Son continue securely in sin? Or will he again lend his ears to the suggestions of the devil so as to submit himself to him, who knows he has been redeemed by the precious blood of the Son of God, so that he may serve God in the freedom of the Spirit? Or will he prostitute his body to the impure desires of the world and the flesh, who glories that in Christ it has been made a temple of the Holy Spirit? Indeed, can he hate his neighbor, whom he hears is held in such esteem by God, and who is a son of the same Father and a member of the same body? Finally, can the faithful man be led by any adversities, dangers, or torments to deny Christ, whom he professes to be his defender and redeemer? So far is faith from making men careless of their affairs or wanton despisers of God's commands, that it is rather the mother of the most beautiful virtues: of piety, holiness, innocence, charity, fortitude, and patience, from which, as from a most abundant and perpetual spring, all kinds of good works flow. Even if we deny that these merit eternal salvation, lest anything be taken from the glory of Christ, we nonetheless confess that these same works are necessary, both so that we may render to God the obedience owed to him and so that they may be testimonies of our faith. If faith does nothing in us, it is dead, and therefore it is not even faith, but an empty and vain opinion cloaked in the name of faith. These things could be confirmed by countless examples of those who are commended in the Scriptures for their faith. But since these are well known, let our adversaries cease to reproach us with the wickedness of those who boast in vain of the title of the Christian name, whom neither Christ can acknowledge as his disciples, nor can we acknowledge as true brothers.

units.la: Sed illis etiam hic respondendum est, qui etsi Euangelio doctrinam veram & salutarem contineri fateantur, eandem tamen imperfectam esse aiunt, & proinde quaedam ei addi oportere, quae ab Apostolis vel omissa, vel saltem literis nō man-data sint. Et tuentur isti sententiam suam verbis Christi, qui discipulis dixerit. Ad huc multa habeo quae vobis dicam, sed non potestis portare modo. Deinde Apo-stolos non omnia, quae cognitu & obseruatu necessaria sunt, libris abs se scriptis comprehendisse, sed multa insuper viua voce modo tradidisse dicunt, quae quasi per manus accepta & ad posteros transmissa sint, & propterea parem cum Apo-stolicis scriptis authoritatem mereantur. Sunt denique, qui nec hoc quidem faten-tur, sed multa ipsos quoque Apostolos totamque Ecclesiam primitiuam latuisse cla-mant, quae suo demum tempore Patribus certis reuelata, & irrefragabili Conci-liorum authoritate stabilita sint. At facilis est ad ista omnia responsio.
units.tr: But here too we must answer those who, although they admit that the true and saving doctrine is contained in the Gospel, nevertheless say that it is imperfect, and that therefore certain things ought to be added to it, which the Apostles either omitted or at least did not commit to writing. These men support their view with the words of Christ, who said to the disciples: "I have many more things to tell you, but you cannot bear them now." Next, they say the Apostles did not include in their books all that is necessary to know and observe, but additionally handed down many things by living voice alone, which, as if received by hand and transmitted to posterity, deserve equal authority with the apostolic writings. Finally, there are some who do not even admit this, but cry out that many things were hidden even from the Apostles and the whole primitive Church, and were revealed only at a later time to certain Fathers and established by the unshakeable authority of Councils. But the answer to all these is easy.

units.la: Quoad primum, agnoscimus Domini verba, sed quàm parum ista aduersario-rum instituto seruiant, ex aliis locis colligi potest. Nam idem paulo ante discipu-los consolaturus inter alia dixit: Non amplius vos dicam seruos, quia seruus ne-scit quid faciat dominus eius: Vos autem dixi amicos, quia omnia quae audiui a Patre meo, nota feci vobis. En eo argumento inter seruos & amicos suos distin-guit Christus, quod hos nihil eorum celarit, quae ex Patre suo audierat. Aut ergo nihil eius quod ad salutem cognitu & obseruatu necessarium est, ignorarunt A-postoli, aut Christum quoque aliquid horum latuisse oportet: quod dictu non ab surdum modo, verumetiam impiissimum est. Quod ergo se adhuc multa habere dicit, quae non possint portare, id pro temporis illius ratione dictum esse putabi-mus, quando dolore & tristitia praeoccupati non attendebant ijs, quae dicebant-tur. Vt enim absenti loqui dicitur, qui cum ebrio litigat: ita frustra ei de rebus ar-duis verba feceris, cuius animus curis & cogitationibus aliis distractus peregrina-tur. Sed mirum est aliquos tam auidè arripere quod ad affirmandam Apostolo-rum ignorantiam ipsis videtur facere, eosdem autem non obseruare quae ibidem subiicit Dominus, vt omni ignorantiae suspicione eos liberet, dicens: Cùm autem venerit spiritus ille veritatis, introducet vos in omnem veritatem. Repetit his spi-ritus sancti promissionem, quem omnis veritatis magistrum siue doctorem habi-turi sint. Ergo ne Christus (inquis) hucusque eos aliquid celauerat, vt ideo doctore nouo opus fuerit? Ne hoc quidem. Prius enim ijsdem dixerat: Paracletus ille, spiritus sanctus, quem mittet Pater in nomine meo, ille vos docebit omnia, & sug-geret vobis omnia quae dixi vobis. Hos locos si inter se conferas, videbis Christū fideliter docuisse suos Apostolos, vtpote qui magnus ille Propheta est, quem om-nes audire debent: discipulos autem propter intellectus sui nondum illuminati ruditatem spiritu opus habuisse: qui non nouum quid & prius inauditum tra-dere, sed quae ipsis excidérant rursus suggerere, & ita eos in omnem veritatem in-troducere debuit. At Christum promisisse stetisse, & spiritum sanctum misisse, non solum Lucas, verumetiam miraculosa quae in Apostolis sese exeruit, illius vir-tus testatur, & Ecclesia tota solenni atque annua tanti beneficij commemoratio-ne fatetur. Ergo nihil eorum illos latuit, sine quorum cognitione salus nobis con-stare non potest. Quis vero eosdem tam infidos vel negligentes dixerit, vt Eccle-siam Christi, cuius oeconomi & dispensatores constituti erant, aliquid celare vo-luerint, quod scire nostra interest? In dispensatore illud potissimum requiri Pau-lus ait, vt quis fidus esse comperiatur: quapropter idem ille Corinthijs scribebat:
units.tr: As to the first, we acknowledge the Lord's words, but how little they serve the opponents' purpose can be gathered from other passages. For shortly before, comforting the disciples, he said among other things: "I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master does; but I have called you friends, because I have made known to you all that I heard from my Father." By this argument Christ distinguishes between servants and his friends: that he concealed nothing from these friends of what he had heard from his Father. Therefore either the Apostles were ignorant of nothing that is necessary to know and observe for salvation, or Christ must also have hidden some of these things; which is not only absurd to say but most impious. So when he says he still has many things to tell that they cannot bear, we shall take this to have been said in view of the circumstances of that time, when they, preoccupied with grief and sadness, were not attending to what was being said. For just as one is said to speak to an absent person when he argues with a drunkard, so you would speak in vain about difficult matters to someone whose mind is distracted by other cares and thoughts and wanders abroad. But it is strange that some so eagerly seize upon what seems to them to support the claim of the Apostles' ignorance, yet do not notice what the Lord adds in the same place, to free them from every suspicion of ignorance, saying: "When that Spirit of truth comes, he will lead you into all truth." Here he repeats the promise of the Holy Spirit, whom they were to have as the teacher or master of all truth. "Then did Christ (you say) hide things from them until now, so that a new teacher was needed?" Not even this. For he had said earlier to them: "That Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you." If you compare these passages with each other, you will see that Christ faithfully taught his Apostles, since he is that great Prophet whom all must hear; but the disciples, because of the roughness of their understanding, not yet enlightened, needed the Spirit, who was to deliver not something new and previously unheard of, but to bring back to them what had slipped from their minds, and so lead them into all truth. That Christ promised this, and that the Holy Spirit was sent, is attested not only by Luke but also by the miraculous power which showed itself in the Apostles, and the whole Church confesses it in its solemn and annual commemoration of so great a benefit. Therefore nothing was hidden from them of that without whose knowledge salvation cannot stand for us. Who, moreover, would call these men so faithless or negligent that they wished to conceal from the Church of Christ, whose stewards and dispensers they had been appointed, anything which it is in our interest to know? Paul says that what is chiefly required in a steward is that he be found faithful; for this reason he wrote to the Corinthians:

units.la: Ego à Domino accepi, quod & tradidi vobis. Et quamuis hoc de sola Cœna mystica dictum videri possit, hoc ipsum tamen postea ad totum ministerium suum & abs se prædicatam Euangelij doctrinam extendit, dicens: Tradidi vobis imprimis quod & acceperam: quòd Christus mortuus sit pro peccatis nostris, secundum scripturas: & quòd sepultus sit, & quòd suscitatus sit tertio die, secundùm scripturas, &c. Quòd si vero ne hoc quidem de tota eius doctrina intelligendum esse aduersarij dicant, age respondeant illi nobis, qua ratione Paulus falsi crimine liberari possit, quando Corinthios hoc nomine commendat, quòd in omni sermone omnique cognitione ditati sint? Quòd item in omnibus abundent fide, sermone & cognitione? Quis item si ab Apostolis traditæ doctrinæ aliquid necessario addi oportet, illum non dixerit impie arrogantem fuisse, quando anathema pronuntiare ausus est omnes eos (siue illi homines siue Angeli fuerint) qui præter id quod ipse prædicauit, Euangelizant?
units.tr: "I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you." And although this might seem to be said only of the mystical Supper, Paul afterwards extended it to his whole ministry and to the doctrine of the Gospel which he preached, saying: "I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures," and so on. But if our opponents say that not even this is to be understood of his whole doctrine, then let them answer us this: by what reasoning can Paul be freed from the charge of falsehood, when he commends the Corinthians for this, that they have been enriched in every word and every knowledge, and that they abound in all things in faith, word and knowledge? Likewise, if something must necessarily be added to the doctrine delivered by the Apostles, who would not say that he was impiously arrogant, when he dared to pronounce anathema on all those, whether men or angels, who preach the gospel other than what he himself preached?

units.la: Fatemur ista (inquiunt) sed illos literis omnia mandauisse negamus, quæ ad plenam religionis Christianæ & Ecclesiæ constitutionem faciunt. Vt verò sibi psi semper constat seductionis spiritus? Et quis alius hoc vobis perfugium monstrauit o boni, quàm ille, qui olim Christianæ fidei turbatores, vt similia loquerentur, impulit? Irenæus certè, vetustissimus scriptor, hoc argumentum Valentinianis & aliis sui sæculi hæreticis tribuit, de quibus libro tertio cap. secundo sic scribit: Cùm ex scripturis arguuntur hæretici, in accusationem conuertuntur ipsarum scriptu rarum, quasi non recte habeant, nec sint ex authoritate, & quòd variè sint dictæ & quòd ab his qui traditionem nesciunt, veritas ex scripturis inueniri non possit: Non enim per literas traditam illam, sed per viuam vocem, &c. Hæc Irenæus.
units.tr: "We admit these things," they say, "but we deny that they committed to writing everything which pertains to the full religion of Christianity and the constitution of the Church." But how is it that the spirit of deception always remains consistent with itself? And who else, good sirs, showed you this refuge, than he who once impelled the disturbers of the Christian faith to speak similarly? Irenaeus, certainly the oldest writer, ascribes this argument to the Valentinians and other heretics of his age, and in the second chapter of the third book he writes of them thus: "When heretics are refuted from the Scriptures, they turn the accusation against the Scriptures themselves, as if they were not right, nor of authority, and as if they were variously stated, and as if the truth could not be found in them by those who do not know the tradition: for that tradition was not handed down in writing, but by living voice," and so on. Thus Irenaeus.

units.la: Ego verò illos Apostolis atrocem iniuriam facere dico, si quod dicunt ita intelligi velint, quasi vniuersam humanæ salutis summam eiusque consequendæ ratione vna cum vera & perfecta Ecclesiæ œconomia libris suis non comprehenderint. Etenim illos in toto salutis negotio nihil præter CHRISTVM IESVM nouisse, Paulus, qui cum in tertium cœlum raptus fuerit plus quiddam quàm alij omnes scire videri poterat, de seipso testatur. Quoad verò Christi in carne nati historiam, scimus equidem non singula, quæ ille à pueris fecit & dixit, vt neque miracula eiusdem omnia, ab Euangelistis descripta esse: sed quæ scripta sunt, ea sufficere dicimus, vt nos in ea cognitione ac fide instruant, quæ nos tam illius quàm salutis æternæ in illo participes facit. Ita enim Ioannes ait: Multa etiam alia signa æditit IESVS coram discipulis suis, quæ non sunt scripta in hoc libro: hæc autem scripta sunt, vt credatis quòd IESVS est Christus ille Filius Dei, & vt credentes vitam habeatis per nomen eius. Quoad verò eius fructum, qui ad nos redit, & quem in pœnitentia & peccatorum remissione consistere diximus, quam vita æterna comi tatur, quid obsecro doctrinæ illorum deest? Annon omnes homines peccati conuincunt, qui primus ad pœnitentiam gradus est? Annon modum conuersionis ad Deum diligenter tradunt, qui in vno Christo habetur: qui vt nobis vnica ad Patrem via est, ita solus etiam nos cum illo in gratiam reducit? Annon de fidei effectis differunt, sub quibus non solùm pax conscientiæ, verumetiam constantia in aduersis, sanctimoniæ item & charitatis officia continentur? Dies totus non sufficeret recensendis testimonijs, quibus hoc poterat demonstrari. Sufficiat ergo quod Paulus ad Ephes. de prima eius epistolæ parte tertio cap. scribit: Deus per reuelationem notum fecit mihi mysterium (sicut ante scripsi paucis) quo perlecto poteritis intelligere, quæ sit mea intelligentia in mysterio Christi. Quòd si vero Apostolus quæcunque ipse de Christo nouerat primis eius epistolæ capitibus complexus est, qua fronte negant nostri illi Apostolorum scriptis comprehendi, quæ vt sciamus & credamus sunt necessaria? Adde his, quòd idem ad Timoth. dixit. Hæc xit: Haec tibi scribo, sperans fore, vt veniam ad te valde cito: Quod si tardius venero, vt noris quomodo oporteat in domo Dei versari, quae est Ecclesia Dei viui. Vt ergo salutis aeternae doctrinam nobis perfecte tradiderunt: ita Ecclesiae quoque vera oeconomia ex illorum scriptis constitui potest, & recte in domo Dei versamur, si quae ab illis praescripta nobis sunt, probe obseruemus. Sed audiamus D. Pauli de veteris Testamenti libris testimonium: Tota scriptura (inquit) θεόπνευστος, id est diuinitus inspirata, & vtilis est ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem quae est in iustitia: vt perfectus sit homo, ad omne opus bonum perfecte instructus. Dignitatem ergo omni humana maiorem habet scriptura, cum a Deo inspirata, & hoc authore tradita sit. Visus vero eiusdem est, vt doctrinae seruiat, non vt in scriniis asseruetur, aut ex collo pendeat, vt superstitiosi quidam de Euangelio Ioannis facere solent. Indicantur etiam doctrinae species: Redargutio, quae peccata detegit, & homines intra animos suos conuincit: Correctio, qua delicta emendantur: Institutio, qua quid fieri quidue omitti debeat, docemur. Quibus alibi consolationem adiicit, quae in aduersis patientes & inuictos facit. Finis autem omnium statuitur, hominis perfectio, quae ad omne opus bonum instructos reddit. At quae ratio est, quae nos doctrinam imperfectam dicere iubeat, quae suos sectatores perfectos facit? Et si ista de veteris testamenti libris dixit Apostolus, quae dementia est, doctrinam, quae ex his deriuatur, imperfectam nunc dicere, postquam illis scripta Apostolica accesserunt? Num ergo horum accessio imperfectam fecit scripturam, quae prius perfecta erat? Quanto igitur felicior fuit veterum conditio, quibus Legis & Prophetarum libri sufficere potuerunt, si iidem Apostolorum scriptis aucti & illustrati, adhuc aliis atque aliis addita mentis opus habent? Hoc si vere dicitur, Christus certe iugum legis non abstulit, sed grauius fecit. Sunt haec tam absurda, vt qui eis confutandis velit diutius insistere, merito ridiculus videri possit.
units.tr: But I say that these men do a grave injury to the Apostles, if they wish what they say to be understood as meaning that the Apostles did not include in their books the whole sum of human salvation and the way of attaining it, together with the true and complete economy of the Church. For that the Apostles knew nothing in the whole business of salvation except Christ Jesus, Paul bears witness about himself, since he was caught up into the third heaven and could seem to know more than all the others. As for the history of Christ born in the flesh, we know indeed that not every single thing he did and said from boyhood, nor all his miracles, were described by the evangelists; but we say that what has been written is sufficient to instruct us in that knowledge and faith which make us partakers both of him and of eternal salvation in him. Thus John says: "Jesus did many other signs before his disciples which are not written in this book; but these are written that you may believe that Jesus is Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life through his name." As for the fruit which comes to us, which we said consists in repentance and the remission of sins, and with which eternal life is joined, what, I ask you, is lacking in their teaching? Do they not convict all men of sin, which is the first step of repentance? Do they not diligently teach the way of conversion to God, which is found in Christ alone, who, as he is the only way to the Father for us, so alone also reconciles us to him in grace? Do they not discourse on the effects of faith, under which are contained not only peace of conscience but also constancy in adversity, and likewise the duties of holiness and charity? A whole day would not suffice to recount the testimonies by which this could be shown. Let it suffice, then, that Paul writes to the Ephesians in the third chapter of the first part of his letter: "God made known to me the mystery by revelation (as I wrote briefly before), by reading which you can understand my understanding in the mystery of Christ." But if the Apostle embraced in the first chapters of his letter whatever he knew about Christ, with what face do those men deny that what we need to know and believe for salvation is comprised in the apostolic writings? Add to this what he said to Timothy: "I write these things to you, hoping to come to you very soon; but if I am delayed, that you may know how one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God." Therefore, just as the Apostles delivered to us the doctrine of eternal salvation perfectly, so also the true economy of the Church can be established from their writings, and we rightly conduct ourselves in the house of God if we carefully observe what they have prescribed to us. But let us hear St Paul's testimony about the books of the Old Testament: "All Scripture," he says, "is θεόπνευστος [theopneustos], that is, divinely inspired, and is profitable for teaching, for refutation, for correction, for instruction which is in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work." Scripture therefore has a dignity greater than anything human, since it is inspired by God and handed down by this author. Its purpose is indeed to serve doctrine, not to be kept in boxes or hung from the neck, as some superstitious people are wont to do with the Gospel of John. The kinds of teaching are also indicated: refutation, which detects sins and convicts men within their own minds; correction, by which faults are amended; instruction, by which we are taught what ought to be done or omitted. To these he elsewhere adds consolation, which makes people patient and unconquered in adversity. The end of all is stated to be the perfection of man, which renders him equipped for every good work. But what reason is there that bids us call imperfect a doctrine which makes its followers perfect? And if the Apostle said these things about the books of the Old Testament, what madness is it to call now imperfect the doctrine derived from them, after the apostolic writings have been added to them? Does the addition of these make imperfect a Scripture which was previously perfect? How much happier, then, was the condition of the ancients, to whom the books of the Law and the Prophets could suffice, whereas we, enlarged and illuminated by the writings of the Apostles, still have need of one thing and another added to our minds? If this is truly said, Christ certainly did not take away the yoke of the law, but made it heavier. These things are so absurd that whoever wishes to insist on refuting them at length may rightly seem ridiculous.

units.la: Fatemur equidem Orthodoxos patres interdum traditionis Apostolicae meminisse, & inter hos Irenaeum imprimis, qui ad Apostolorum tempora proximus accessit. Sed eo nomine idem ille non aliud quam fidei articulos, qui symbolo, quod nos Apostolicum dicimus, comprehenduntur intellexit: qui breue sunt omnium, quae praedicarunt & scripserunt, compendium. Vt tamen concedamus, Apostolos multa Ecclesiis tradidisse, de quibus nihil scriptum extet, ea tamen non de dogmatibus, neque de sacramentorum legitimo vsu, sed de indifferentibus ceremoniis aut statutis intelligi debent, in quibus propter loci & gentis (adde & temporum) diuersitatem non eadem vbique forma seruari potest. De his Paulus Corinthiis dicebat: Caetera cum venero disponam. Id vero ad fidei & salutis dogmata nequaquam extendi debet. Constat enim spiritum sanctum, quo rectore Apostoli vsi sunt, sibi ipsi semper & in omnibus constare: Nihil ergo potuerunt tradere Ecclesiis, quod ab illorum scriptis dissentiret: neque ab impostura crimine liberari possent, si aliud scriptis, aliud viua voce tradidissent. Itaque quod improbis quibusdam apud Corinthios calumniatoribus Paulus dixit: Quales sumus verbo per epistolas cum absumus, tales etiam reipsa cum adsumus: hoc ipsum de tota eorum doctrina debet intelligi, siue eam coram docendo propositerint, siue literis complexi sint.
units.tr: We admit that the orthodox Fathers sometimes mention apostolic tradition, and among them Irenaeus above all, who lived closest to the time of the apostles. But by that term he meant nothing other than the articles of faith contained in the creed we call Apostolic, which is a brief summary of everything the apostles preached and wrote. Yet even if we grant that the apostles handed down to the churches many things that were never written down, those things should not be understood as doctrines or as the lawful use of the sacraments, but as indifferent ceremonies or regulations, which cannot be observed in the same form everywhere because of differences of place, people and (add) times. Paul said of such matters to the Corinthians: "The rest I will set in order when I come" (1 Cor. 11). That cannot possibly be extended to the doctrines of faith and salvation. For it is certain that the Holy Spirit, under whose guidance the apostles spoke, has always been consistent with himself and in all things. So they could hand down nothing to the churches that disagreed with their writings; nor could they be cleared of the charge of deceit if they taught one thing in writing and another by word of mouth. Therefore what Paul said against certain wicked slanderers among the Corinthians, "Such as we are in word by letters when we are absent, such we are also in deed when we are present" (2 Cor. 10), must be understood of their whole teaching, whether they set it forth in person by teaching or embraced it in writing.

units.la: Porro vt Pauli aduersariis non satis fuit illius doctrinam oppugnauisse, sed eius quoque personam exosam facere conati sunt, quando illum priori epistola nimis pro imperio & minaciter scripta totam Ecclesiam turbauisse, & adhuc multa insolentius facere dixerunt: Ita hodie multi Euangelicae doctrinae ministros hoc nomine accusant, quod pacem publicam turbent, & inter homines priuatos dissensiones serant, quod item imperium in omnes affectent. Quibus ego paucis respondeo. sponderé poteram: Agnosco Achabi spiritum, qui olim Eliæ prophetæ dicebat: Annon tu es ille, qui turbat Israelem? Sed vt illud Achab immani & impio veritatis odio accensus dixit: ita hodie idem affectus plerosq; mouet, vt eadem de nobis garriant: multos vero ignorantia & quòd eorum quæ fiunt causas non penitius inspiciunt, decipit, vt eiusmodi calumniis fidè habeant. Nimius Corinthijs visus fuit Paulus in priori epistola. At si horribilem, quæ tunc apud eos fuit, totius Ecclesiæ faciem consideres, sectas nimirum cum Christi professione pugnantes, effrenem scortandi licentiam, turpem in ferendo incesto indulgentiam, illicita cum prophanis gentibus commercia, idololatriæ societatem, contentiones, scurriles de mortuorum resurrectione sermones, immanem deniq; purioris doctrinæ & disciplinæ Christianæ contemptum: fatearis oportet, nihil à Paulo tam durum tamq; graue dici potuisse, quod illorum improbitas non abunde meruerit. Si vero hæc illius rigorem excusat, cur nos æquo rigidiores dicimur hodie, quando ijsdem moribus viuitur, & pleriq; licentia maiori leges omnes tam politicas quàm ecclesiasticas conculcant? Dissensiones quidem fatemur exoriri inter eos, quibus Euangelium prædicatur, quæ interdum motus publicos pariunt: sed istorum causas ex Euangelio manare, constanter negamus. Est enim hoc pacis nuntium, quo post fidem in Christum nihil perinde vt charitas mutua à nobis exigitur. At quia maior hominum pars mundo dedita illius lucem odit, neq; eos ferre potest, quos abs se dissentire videt, fit quod Christus futurum prædixit, vt pater aduersus filios, hi aduersus patrem, fratres item aduersus fratres, cuniuges item & qui prius amicissimi erant, inter se dissideant: Culpa vero omnis in aduersarijs hæret, qui non contenti propria inobedientia, insuper alios quoque relicta & abnegata veritate ad superstitiones redire cogunt, aut saltem cogere volunt: Quibus cùm pij obsequi neque possint neque debeant, non vtique hi, sed alteri illi dissensionum atq; turbarum authores sunt.
units.tr: Furthermore, as if it were not enough for Paul's opponents to attack his teaching, they have also tried to make his person hateful, saying that in his former letter he wrote too imperiously and threateningly, disturbed the whole Church, and did many things even more insolently. So today many accuse the ministers of the evangelical doctrine on this same ground: that they disturb the public peace, sow dissensions among private persons, and likewise aim at dominion over everyone. To these I answer briefly. I could answer with a promise, but I recognise the spirit of Ahab, who once said to the prophet Elijah: "Is it you who troubles Israel?" (1 Kings 18). But just as Ahab, inflamed with a monstrous and impious hatred of the truth, said this, so today the same feeling moves many to chatter the same things about us; and ignorance, together with their failure to look more closely into the causes of what happens, deceives many into giving credence to such slanders. Paul seemed too severe to the Corinthians in his former letter. But if you consider the dreadful face of the whole Church at that time, namely sects fighting against the profession of Christ, unbridled licence for fornication, shameful tolerance of incest, unlawful dealings with the profane nations, fellowship in idolatry, quarrels, scurrilous talk about the resurrection of the dead, and finally a monstrous contempt for the purer doctrine and Christian discipline, you must admit that nothing so harsh and severe could have been said by Paul which their wickedness did not richly deserve. But if these things excuse his severity, why are we said to be far too severe today, when the same morals prevail, and most people trample underfoot with greater licence all laws, both civil and ecclesiastical? We admit that dissensions arise among those to whom the gospel is preached, and these sometimes produce public disturbances; but we constantly deny that their causes flow from the gospel. For this is the message of peace, by which, after faith in Christ, nothing is demanded of us more than mutual love. But because the greater part of mankind, given over to the world, hates its light and cannot bear those whom it sees dissenting from it, what Christ foretold comes to pass: the father will be against the son, the son against the father, brothers likewise against brothers, spouses and those who were most friendly before will be at odds with one another. The whole blame, however, rests with the adversaries, who, not content with their own disobedience, also compel others, and wish to compel them, to return to superstitions, having abandoned and renounced the truth. Since the godly can neither and ought not to obey them, it is not they but those others who are the authors of the dissensions and disturbances.

units.la: Quod vero aut quale est illud imperium siue dominium, quod Euangelij precones affectant? Num aliis imperare velle dicetur, qui vt omnes per fidei obedientiam Dei verbo se subjiciant, hortatur? Aut num tyrannidem affectare putabuntur, qui toti in eo sunt, vt ex diaboli & Antichristi tyrannide assertos in libertatem filiorum Dei vendicent? Enimuero istos homines, qui nobis regni cupiditatē exprobrant, ego in re seria ludere potius quàm serio loqui existimo. Quæ enim ratio illis esse potest, vt hoc nomine eos accusent, qui neq; existimationē suam contra improbos tueri, neq; se & familiam suam commodè alere possunt? Alit suos pro sestores liberaliter Medicina, Iuris prudentia vero suos diuitijs & dignitatibus auctos principum assessores facit. Similiter qui inter Papisticæ superstitionis defensores ingenio valent & studio feruent, ij fere sacerdotijs pinguissimis donantur, Coenobijs opulentissimis præficiuntur, Episcopi fiunt potentes, deniq; in purpuratorum Senatum adoptantur, vt cum regibus luxu & fastu certent, ijsdemq; pro nutu imperent. At qui Euangelium prædicant, ne sua quidem patrimonia tueri possunt, quæ fere iuuenes adhuc insumunt, dum vel domi bonas literas addiscunt, vel scholas exteras sequuntur. Ad Ecclesiæ vero ministerium tandem vocati, dum cœlestis regni thesauros fideliter dispensant, dum aliorum saluti cum propriæ vitæ periculo consulunt, dum eiectis per ipsos verbi flagello sacrificis & Monachis, multi quotidie ex horum bonis ditescunt, ipsi tunc demum officio suo fungi putantur deprauatis hominibus, quorum magnus vbiq; est numerus, si omnibus contemptui sint, si egeant, si mendicent. Qui enim in hos præ aliis liberales videri volunt, aureos dant centum aut ducentos annuos: At liberis plena est domus: conuolat vndiq; hospites, qui vel honorificè excipiendi sunt propter suam dignitatem, vel viatico iuuandi propter egestatem: sumptus faciendi sunt in libros, alenda familia: artem interea nullam exercet, ut ne à sua scilicet auocentur: interea dum æs alienum miseros cruciat, dum vxorē & liberos difficulter alunt, dum filias ob dotis inopiam domi asseruare, filios inopes ad scholas mendicatum extrudere coguntur: dum in creditorum conspectum venire erubescunt, dum per plateas circumeunt & ambages quærunt, ut in eam nō veniant, in qua creditor habitat; denique vulgi ludibrijs, improborum odijs, maledicorum conuitijs, vi denique aperta petuntur, plerique illos regnare dicunt, & durum in omnes exercere dominium. Vah regnum egregium, solis nimirum suis regibus formidabile. Quis hic non exclamet: o mores, o tempora, o sceleratam mundi ingratitudinem. Fateor equidē, non omnium esse hanc culpam, & inueniri hodie pios principes & vrbium magistratus veré Christianos, qui magnis impensis scholas aperiunt, stipendia iuuenibus studiosis constituunt, fidos Ecclesiarū pastores liberaliter alunt: at hi paucissimi dici possunt, si cum aliorum turba conferantur, quibus cum Iuda Iscariote nimia videtur omnis impensa, quando per Euangelij prædicationem odor bonæ fragrantiæ Christo excitatur, qui totam eius domum siue Ecclesiam replens ad alios diffunditur. Neque ista scribo, quod de mea sorte priuata conquerar, quæ talis hucusque fuit, ut me Deo imprimis, deinde amplissimo Senatui populoque Tigurino gratias magnas debere libenter & merito fatear: vel quod otio nostro consultum, aut cupiditati nimiæ, qua aliqui ex nostris ardent, satisfactum velim: sed ut illorum iniquitas omnibus manifesta fiat, qui cum ipsi per ministros regnent & voluptuentur, illis cum egestate conflictantibus regni affectationem exprobrat. Vtinam vero illi reuera regnarent, & excusso Satanæ iugo, Spiritu illo regio se duci paterentur, qui solus efficit, ut Deo in libertate veré Christiana seruiamus.
units.tr: But what sort of rule or dominion is it that the heralds of the gospel are said to aim at? Will he be said to wish to rule others who exhorts everyone to submit himself to God's word in the obedience of faith? Or will those be thought to aim at tyranny who are wholly intent on rescuing men from the tyranny of the devil and Antichrist and asserting them into the liberty of the sons of God? Indeed, I think these men who charge us with a lust for kingship are playing in a serious matter rather than speaking seriously. For what reason can they have for accusing of this those who can neither defend their own reputation against the wicked, nor support themselves and their families decently? Medicine generously supports its practitioners for their own sake, and the study of law makes its own men, enriched with wealth and honours, assessors to princes. Likewise, those among the defenders of papistical superstition who excel in talent and burn with zeal are for the most part rewarded with the fattest priesthoods, set over the wealthiest monasteries, become powerful bishops, and are finally admitted into the senate of purple-clad men, so that they vie with kings in luxury and pomp and give orders to them at a nod. But those who preach the gospel cannot even protect their own patrimonies, which they often spend while still young, while they learn good letters at home or attend foreign schools. And when at last they are called to the ministry of the Church, while they faithfully dispense the treasures of the heavenly kingdom, while they look after the salvation of others at risk to their own lives, while through them, by the scourge of the word, priests and monks are cast out and many daily grow rich from their goods, they are then at last thought to discharge their office only by depraved men, of whom there is everywhere a great number, if they are held in contempt by all, if they are in want, if they beg. For those who wish to appear generous towards these men beyond others give a hundred or two hundred gold coins a year. But the house is full of children; guests flock in from every side, who must be received with honour because of their rank, or helped with travelling money because of their poverty; money must be spent on books and the family must be fed; meanwhile they practise no trade, so that they will not be drawn away from their calling. Meanwhile, while debt torments them in their misery, while they can scarcely feed their wife and children, while they are forced to keep their daughters at home for lack of a dowry and to send their penniless sons out to school as beggars; while they blush to come into the sight of their creditors, while they go round the streets and seek roundabout ways so as not to come to the street where the creditor lives; finally, while they are assailed by the mockery of the common people, the hatred of the wicked, the abuse of slanderers, and, lastly, by open violence, many say that they rule and exercise a harsh dominion over everyone. What an splendid kingdom, surely terrifying only to its own kings! Who would not cry out here: O manners, O times, O the wicked ingratitude of the world! I admit that this fault does not belong to all, and that today there are found pious princes and truly Christian magistrates of cities, who at great expense open schools, establish stipends for studious young men, and generously support the faithful ministers of the Churches. But these can be called very few compared with the crowd of others, to whom, like Judas Iscariot, all expense seems excessive, although through the preaching of the gospel the odour of a sweet fragrance is raised up to Christ, which fills his whole house, that is, the Church, and spreads to others (2 Cor. 2). I do not write these things because I complain of my own private lot, which so far has been such that I gladly and rightly confess that I owe great thanks first to God, and then to the most distinguished Senate and people of Zurich; nor because I wish to provide for our leisure or satisfy the excessive greed with which some of ours burn; but so that the iniquity of those men may be made plain to all, who, while they themselves rule and live in luxury through their ministers, reproach others with a lust for dominion while those others struggle with want. Would that they really ruled, and, having shaken off the yoke of Satan, allowed themselves to be led by that royal Spirit who alone makes it possible for us to serve God in true Christian liberty.

units.la: Sed video me longius excurrisse, quam initio statuerā. Apud te autem LVDO VICE Comes illustris, liberius de his dixi, partim tua bonitate & clementia fretus, quam non obscuris indiciis iampridē perspexi: partim quod in huius causę cognitione, tibi neque animū deesse scia, cum totus Christi & veritatis amore ardeas: neque iudicij facultate, cum & diligenti lectione religionis nostræ mysteria scruteris, & longo rerū vsu ea probe cognita habeas, de quibus multi in vmbra disputant. Et quia querela hæc nō minus iusta, quam causæ totius defensio necessaria est, meo instituto illam imprimis conuenire putaui, cum in posteriore D. Pauli ad Corinth. epistolā, meis Homilijs illustrata, præfari statuissem. Cuius argumentū quam pro bé nostris temporibus seruiat, mox intelligent, qui eā diligentius inspexerint. Mihi certē dignissima visa est, quæ hodie exponeretur, quādo eadē & Ecclesiæ & ministrorū eius fors est, quæ olim fuit, cum Paulus illā scriberet. Præstiti ego in opere laborioso quod potui, & mihi probe cōscius sum, me hoc potissimū spectauisse, vt & Apostoli sensum explicarē, & vt per ea, quæ illē Corinthijs scripsit, nostri seculi vitijs mederer. Quod si in epistolam plerisq; in locis obscura & difficile meus hic labor aliquā lucem intulit, illud omne mihi à Patre luminū obtigisse fateor, & non tā mihi ipsi quàm illis gratulor, quibus prodesse volui. Sub tuę vero clementię auspicio Homilias istas in lucē dare libuit LVDOVICE comes: quia illa iampridē merebatur, vt mei erga te studij atq; obseruantiæ aliquod testimoniū publicè exaret. Vt autē huic meo operi ex illustri nominis tui splendore authoritate aliquā accessurā esse non diffido apud eos, quibus tua virtus & cū summa dignitatis atq; fortunarū amplitudine coniuncta humanitas probe cognita est: Ita hoc meū officiū tibi non ingratū fore spero, cū & me abs te diligi & te sacrarū literarū studiosissimum esse scia. Deus Opt. Max. faxit, ut quod in prouehēda cōmuni veritatis causa hactenus fecisti, diu possis facere; idemq; te cū generosissima coniuge in finem vsque seruet ad sui nominis gloriam & publicam Ecclesiæ vtilitatem. Datæ Tiguro primaria Heluetiorum ciuitate. VIII. Calend. Septemb. Anno in carne nati filij Dei, M. D. LXXII.
units.tr: But I see that I have run on longer than I had intended at the start. Yet I have spoken more freely about these matters to you, Ludovicus, illustrious Count: partly relying on your kindness and clemency, which I have long perceived from not obscure indications; partly because I know that you lack neither the will nor the judgment for the examination of this cause, since you burn with the whole love of Christ and of truth, and since you both study the mysteries of our religion diligently by reading and, through long experience of affairs, have them well understood, which many dispute about in the shade. And since this complaint is no less just than the defence of the whole cause is necessary, I judged it fitting to my plan especially to put it in front of the preface to the second epistle of St Paul to the Corinthians, which I had resolved to preface with my Homilies. Those who examine it more carefully will soon understand how well its argument serves our own times. To me it has seemed most worthy to be expounded today, since the Church and its ministers now face, perhaps, the same situation that existed when Paul wrote to them. In this laborious work I have done what I could, and I am well aware that my aim was above all to explain the sense of the Apostle and, through what he wrote to the Corinthians, to remedy the vices of our age. If my labour has thrown some light on an epistle that in many places is obscure and difficult, I acknowledge that all of this has come to me from the Father of lights, and I congratulate not so much myself as those whom I wished to benefit. Under the auspices of your clemency, Count Ludovicus, I have been pleased to bring these Homilies into the light, because they have long deserved that some public testimony of my zeal and respect toward you should be set forth. And since I do not doubt that, from the splendour of your illustrious name, this work of mine will gain some authority among those who know well your virtue and the humanity joined with the great dignity and wealth of your fortunes, so I hope this duty of mine will not be unwelcome to you, since I know both that I am loved by you and that you are most devoted to the sacred letters. May God, the best and greatest, grant that what you have hitherto done in advancing the common cause of truth, you may be able to do for a long time; and may He preserve you, together with your most noble wife, to the end, to the glory of His name and the public benefit of the Church. Given at Zurich, the chief city of the Helvetians, on the 8th day before the Kalends of September, in the year M.D.LXXII after the birth of the Son of God in the flesh.

units.la: IN POSTERIOREM D. PAVLI APOSTOLI EPISTOLAM AD CORINTHIOS, HOMILIAE RODOLPHI GVALTHERI TIGVRINI. CAPVT I.
units.tr: THE SECOND EPISTLE OF ST PAUL THE APOSTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS: HOMILIES OF RUDOLPH GWALTHER OF ZURICH. CHAPTER 1.

units.la: HOMILIA I.
units.tr: HOMILY 1.

units.la: PAulus Apostolus IESV CHRISTI per Dei voluntatem, & Timotheus frater, Ecclesiae Dei quae est Corinthi, vnà cum sanctis omnibus, qui sunt in tota Achaia. Gratia sit vobis & pax à Deo Patre nostro, & Domino IESV CHRISTO. Benedictus Deus ac Pater Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, Pater illc misericordiarum, & Deus omnis consolationis qui nos consolatur in omni afflictione nostra, vt possimus in quauis afflictione positos consolari, ea ipsa consolatione, qua nosipsos Deus consolatur.
units.tr: Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the Church of God which is at Corinth, together with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia. Grace be to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Blessed be God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction with that same comfort with which God himself comforts us.

units.la: RIOREM ad Corinthios epistolam ideo scripserat Paulus Apostolus, quòd Ecclesia illa multis modis depravata & corrupta esset per impostores quosdam, qui omnis generis errores cum morum licentia & impunitate inuexerant. Et quantum conijcere possumus, non omni fructu illa caruit. Nam admoniti & correpti multa vitia emendarunt. Interim tamen non defuerunt, qui disciplinae & correptionis impatientia & fidissimi huius monitoris odio accensi, sua pertinacius defendebant, & vt hoc aliquo praetextu plausibili facere possent, illum in suspicionem & odium trahere conabantur. Itaq; ex perpetuis persecutionibus, quibus vbiq; gentium exagitabatur, occasione arrepta, illum hominem esse aiebant turbulentum & praecipitis ingenij, qui sua importunitate ac insolentia seipsum simul atq; Euangelium omnibus inuisum faceret: ideoq; ipsos nequaquam reprehendi debere, si eius monitis siue mandatis subijci nollent, quem nulla alia gens siue ciuitas ferre posset. Deinde quia aduentum suum quem in priori epistola promiserat, diutius differebat, illum vanitatis quoq; vel potius stoliditae iactantiae insimulabant, qui procul ab ipsis absens minis grauissimis fulminaret, non auderet autem in ipsorum conspectum prodire, & coram cum praesentibus congredi. Accedebant his alij, qui totum eius Apostolatum in dubium vocabant, quasi minus bona fide in eo ageret, multa item faceret insolenter atq; nimis pro imperio. Itaq; tam gravibus tamq; necessarijs causis adductus Paulus, priori epistolae hanc alteram submisit, quae tota fere in genere Iudiciali versatur. Nam ad calumnias istas ex ordine respondet, & simul eos, qui inter ipsos infirmi & simpliciores erant, argumentis instruit, quibus seipsos & fidem suam aduersus pastores & improbos eorum conatus possint tueri. Quae causa est, vt suam authoritatem sic asserat, vt simul multa subinde interserat de Euangelio, de ministerio item Noui testamenti, de constantia in fide, de beneficentia in pauperes, deq; alijs religionis Christianae exercitijs, quae singula suo loco videbimus.
units.tr: Paul the apostle had written the earlier epistle to the Corinthians because that church had been corrupted and depraved in many ways by certain impostors, who had introduced errors of every kind together with licence and impunity in morals. As far as we can conjecture, it was not without fruit. For, admonished and rebuked, they amended many faults. Meanwhile, however, there were not lacking those who, impatient of discipline and correction and inflamed with hatred of this most faithful monitor, defended their own ways more stubbornly, and who, in order to do so under some plausible pretext, tried to bring him into suspicion and odium. So, seizing the occasion of the constant persecutions with which he was harassed everywhere among the nations, they said that he was a turbulent man of hasty temper, who by his importunity and insolence made himself and the gospel hateful to all; and therefore they ought not to be blamed if they were unwilling to submit to his admonitions or commands, which no other people or city could bear. Then, because he kept postponing the visit he had promised in the first letter, they accused him of vanity, or rather of foolish boasting: he, absent and far from them, thundered with the most severe threats, but did not dare to appear before their eyes and meet them face to face. To these were added others who called his whole apostleship into doubt, as if he acted with less than good faith and did many things insolently and too much in the manner of a ruler. Therefore Paul, moved by causes so grave and so necessary, sent this second letter after the first, which is almost wholly of a judicial kind. For he answers those calumnies in order, and at the same time equips with arguments those among them who were weak and simpler, so that they might defend themselves and their faith against the ministers and the wicked attempts of those men. This is why he so asserts his authority, while at the same time frequently interposing much about the gospel, about the ministry of the New Testament, about constancy in faith, about beneficence toward the poor, and about the other exercises of the Christian religion, each of which we shall see in its place.

units.la: Nunc obseruatu dignissimum est, tantum Apostolum posse tot tamq; egregia suae fidei & integritatis specimina aduersarios habuisse tam pertinaces, quorum calumnias ne inter eos quidem effugere potuit, quos ipse primus Christo lucrifecerat, & qui quod Christiani atq; salutis aeterna hæredes essent, ipsi soli debebant. Est hoc memorabile ingratitudinis exemplum, & naturæ fiue ingenij humani per omnia depravatissimi argumentum quàm maximè euidens. Nam extant huius generis multa alia. Tales enim Moses sensit Israelitas suos, quorum causa ipse delitias aulæ & honores amplissimos sponte reliquerat. Eadem omnium Prophetarum fors fuit in hoc seculo, vt iam de æterno Dei Filio, IESV CHRISTO, nihil dicamus, qui ex innumeris & incomparabilibus beneficijs in Iudæos collatis nihil aliud quàm contemptum & gentis totius odium, adhæc indignam & infamem mortem retulit. Nemo igitur miretur, si quid huius etiam hodie fiat, & Euangelicæ veritatis præcipui instauratores pessime audiant inter eos, quibus ipsi libertatis in Christo & salutis administri fuerunt. Etenim vt improbi & petulantes quidam olim Paulum ambitionis & tyrannidis accusarunt, qui cum inter Iudæos maximus esset, omnia propter Christum reliquerat: ita hodie multi ijsdem criminibus grauantur iniquissimè, qui in Papatu potentia & diuitijs excellere atque omnium capitibus pro sua libidine insultare poterant, nisi publicam multorum salutem suis commodis priuatis antiquiorem habuissent. Quod cum res ipsa loquatur, multorum tamen tanta est stoliditas, vt putidissimis hominum vanissimorum calumnijs aures præbeant.
units.tr: Now it is most worthy of observation that so great an apostle could have had such stubborn adversaries, despite so many and such excellent proofs of his faith and integrity. He could not escape their calumnies even among those whom he himself had first won to Christ, and who, being Christians and heirs of eternal salvation, owed this to him alone. This is a memorable example of ingratitude, and a most clear proof of the utterly depraved nature or disposition of man. For there are many other instances of this kind. Thus Moses found his Israelites such, for whose sake he had willingly left the delights of the court and very high honours. The same lot fell to all the prophets in their age, not to mention the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, who, from innumerable and incomparable benefits conferred on the Jews, obtained nothing but contempt and the hatred of the whole nation, and besides an unworthy and infamous death. Let no one therefore wonder if something of this kind happens even today, and if the chief restorers of evangelical truth are treated most badly by those to whom they were ministers of liberty in Christ and of salvation. For just as some wicked and petulant men once accused Paul of ambition and tyranny, though he, being the greatest among the Jews, had left everything for Christ's sake, so today many are most unjustly burdened with the same charges. In the Papacy they could have excelled in power and riches and trampled the heads of all at their pleasure, had they not held the public welfare of many more important than their private advantages. Although the thing itself speaks for them, so great is the stupidity of many that they lend their ears to the most foul calumnies of the most vain men.

units.la: Quid verò interea facient (inquis) fideles veritatis ministri? Hoc ipsum, quod Paulum fecisse videmus. Ferant patienter fortem suam, quæ ipsis cum Prophetis & Apostolis, imò cum Dei Filio, IESV CHRISTO, communis est. Interea autem non negligant ministerij sui authoritatem, sed calumnias eiusmodi quoad eius fieri potest diluant, non quidem priuatæ gloriæ studio, sed ne veritatis doctrina propter ipsos in periculum veniat. Fecit hoc olim Moses magna cum grauitate, quando Core cum coniuratis suis sacerdotij simul & reipub. ordinem, ab ipso Deo constitutum, seditiosis artibus turbare conabatur. Idem Prophetæ etiam non semel fatigitarunt. Ipse denique Christus, quo nemo manfuetior aut patientior vnquam in terris comparuit. Ignauia ergo, non patientia, dici meretur, si qui Dei gloriam & æternæ veritatis doctrinam in sua persona prophanari & euerti patiuntur. His præmissis ad primam epistolæ partem accedamus, quæ tria continet.
units.tr: What, you ask, will the faithful ministers of the truth do meanwhile? Exactly what we see Paul did. Let them patiently bear their cross, which they share with the prophets and apostles, indeed with the Son of God, Jesus Christ. Meanwhile let them not neglect the authority of their ministry, but refute such calumnies as far as can be done, not from a desire for private glory, but lest the teaching of the truth be endangered on their account. Moses did this once with great gravity, when Korah with his conspirators tried by seditious arts to disturb the order of priesthood and commonwealth established by God himself. The prophets too did the same more than once. Lastly Christ himself, than whom no one more gentle or patient ever appeared on earth. Therefore it deserves to be called cowardice, not patience, when people suffer the glory of God and the doctrine of eternal truth to be profaned and overthrown in their own person. With these things premised, let us come to the first part of the epistle, which contains three things.

units.la: Primò author eius nominatur his verbis: Paulus Apostolus IESV CHRISTI per voluntatem Dei, & Timotheus frater. Vbi ante omnia obseruabis, quòd non contentus nomen suum præfixisse, Apostolum quoque Christi se dicit, & talem quidem, qui non temere aut priuato consilio hoc munus subierit, sed ex Dei voluntate ad illud fit vocatus. Quod ipsum non ambitiose, sed propter æmulos suos facere alibi diximus, qui ipsum germanum Christi Apostolum esse negabant. Itaque doctrinæ suæ & salutis ipsorum potius rationem habet, quàm suæ existimationis. Simul autem admonemur, nullos alios in Ecclesia audiri debere, quàm qui ad munus docendi legitimè vocati sunt. Nam vt infra cap. 3. testatur Paulus, nemo ex seipso ad aliquid idoneus est: quos verò Deus vocat & mittit, eos donis quoque necessarijs instruit. Id autem sibijpsis polliceri non possunt, qui non expectata illius vocatione, sua sponte currunt, vt ipse apud Prophetam loquitur. Non dubitent autem se ex Dei voluntate vocari, quotquot ab Ecclesijs legitimè & religiosè vocantur. Quod propter eos monemus, qui omnes immediatè ab ipso Deo, vt olim Prophetas & Apostolos vocari oportere arbitrantur.
units.tr: First, the author is named in these words: Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timothy our brother. Here you will observe, above all, that not content with having prefixed his name, he calls himself an apostle of Christ too, and indeed one who did not undertake this office rashly or on his own counsel, but was called to it by the will of God. We have said elsewhere that he did this not out of ambition, but on account of his rivals, who denied that he was a true apostle of Christ. Thus he has regard to their teaching and their salvation rather than to his own reputation. At the same time we are admonished that no others should be heard in the Church except those who are lawfully called to the office of teaching. For, as Paul testifies below in chapter 3, no one is sufficient of himself for anything; but those whom God calls and sends he also equips with the necessary gifts. Those who do not wait for that calling but run of their own accord cannot promise this to themselves, as he says through the prophet. Let all who are lawfully and devoutly called by the churches not doubt that they are called by the will of God. We say this on account of those who think that everyone ought to be called immediately by God himself, as the prophets and apostles once were.

units.la: Deinde Timotheum sibi collegam adiungit, eò quòd hunc prius ad illos miserat. 1. Cor. 16. Fuit is Pauli discipulus, ætate iuuenis quidem, sed fide constans & donis præclaris ornatus. Poterat autem Paulus eum discipulum, vel saltem filium dicere, vt quam in ipsum habebat authoritatem exprimeret. Sed fratris nomine eum dignatur, partim propter communionem, quam credentes omnes inter se habent in Christo, partim propter ministerij societatem. Alibi certè sibi parem facit, vt in vltimo cap. prioris epist. vidimus. Est hoc magnæ modestiæ argumentum, quæ omnes Christi ministros decet, ne ambitiosius sibi imperium vendicent in conseruos, quod improbos suæ domus dissipatores facere Christus testatur. Quod ipsum in Repub. quoq; obseruatu plus quàm necessarium est. Intolerabilis enim & plerunq; noxia est illorum insolentia, qui soli sapere, soli omnia gubernare, collegis denique præscribere volunt.
units.tr: Then he associates Timothy with himself as colleague, because he had sent him to them earlier. 1 Cor. 16. Timothy was Paul's disciple, young in age indeed, but constant in faith and adorned with excellent gifts. Paul could have called him disciple, or at least son, so as to express the authority he had over him. But he deigns to call him brother, partly on account of the fellowship which all believers have with one another in Christ, and partly on account of their partnership in the ministry. Elsewhere indeed he makes him his equal, as we saw in the last chapter of the former epistle. This is an argument of great modesty, which becomes all ministers of Christ, lest they claim for themselves a more ambitious rule over their fellow servants, which Christ testifies makes wicked destroyers of his household. This is also more than necessary to observe in the commonwealth. For the insolence of those is intolerable and very often harmful, who want to be wise alone, to govern everything alone, and finally to prescribe to their colleagues.

units.la: Secundò, quibus epistola hæc inscripta sit, indicatur: Ecclesiæ Dei quæ est Corinthi, vnà cum sanctis omnibus, qui sunt in tota Achaia. Prioris epistolæ Inscriptio generalior fuit, & omnium locorum credentes comprehendit. Hanc restringit aliquantulum, ita tamen, ut ijs qui Corinthum incolebant vniuersos totius Achaiæ fideles coniungat. Erant enim hi per totam regionem illam dispersi, & credibile esse in quibusdam locis pauciores fuisse, quam ut ipsi cœtus publicos instituere & verbi administrum alere possent. Solebant hi interdum in vrbem venire, ut cum Ecclesia, quæ illic frequentior erat, communicarent, quod hodie etiā fieri consueuit in ijs locis, vbi fideles propter Antichristi tyrannide moccultius & cautius res suas instituere coguntur. Admonet ergo hac Inscriptionis parte Paulus Corinthios, ut illos quoq; pro fratribus suis agnoscant, nec temere à suis cœtibus eos excludant. Debent hoc omnes obseruare, qui in locis celebrioribus agunt, & Ecclesias habent legitimè constitutas: Ne videlicet exteros nihil ad se pertinere putent. Vt enim in CHRISTO IESV nullum vel gentis vel sexus vel conditionis discrimen est: ita fidei vinculum omnes omnium locorum credentes sub vno capite Christo constringit, ut vnum corpus efficiantur. Charitas item Christiana, quæ cum fide semper coniuncta est, neminem fastidit, quem Christi sanguine & merito redemptum atq; sanctificatum esse audit. Barbari nimis & profecto parum Christiani sunt hodie, qui gentiles suos eundem cum ipsis Christum profitentes ob causas leuissimas temere abijciunt.
units.tr: Secondly, the letter indicates to whom it is addressed: to the church of God which is at Corinth, together with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia. The inscription of the earlier letter was more general and took in believers in every place. This one narrows it somewhat, yet in such a way that it joins to the people living at Corinth all the faithful of the whole of Achaia. For these were scattered throughout that entire region, and it is credible that in some places there were too few of them to set up public assemblies and maintain a minister of the Word. They would sometimes come into the city to share in the Church there, which was larger. Even today this is customary in those places where the faithful, because of the tyranny of Antichrist, are forced to order their affairs more secretly and cautiously. Paul therefore admonishes the Corinthians, in this part of the inscription, to acknowledge those others too as their brothers and not rashly exclude them from their assemblies. All should observe this who live in more famous places and have legitimately constituted churches, namely, that they should not think strangers are no concern of theirs. For just as in Christ Jesus there is no distinction of nation, sex or condition, so the bond of faith binds all believers in every place under the one head, Christ, so that they become one body. Likewise Christian charity, which is always joined with faith, despises no one whom it hears to have been redeemed and sanctified by the blood and merit of Christ. Those are too barbarous, and surely scarcely Christian, who today rashly cast off their own compatriots, who profess the same Christ as they do, for the very slightest causes.

units.la: At priusquam ab hoc loco discedamus, obseruabis, Ecclesiam Dei à Paulo dici eos, qui tot modis depravati & corrupti erant. Dictum de hoc in prioris epistolæ Inscriptione, idem tamen sæpius repeti debet propter eos, qui vel nimio & præcipiti zelo abrepti temere quosuis damnant, vel propria pusillanimitate superati de salute sua dubitant; vel etiam desperant, quando se professioni suæ non per omnia respondere vident. In primo genere hodie sunt Anabaptistæ, & quicunque alij, qui Ecclesias omnes pro impuris habent, in quibus non omnia ex ipsorum placito aut voluntate instituuntur. Tentant hi multa magno cum conatu, ut breui nobis aureum seculum reducturi videantur. Sed plerunq; fit, quod Satyricus canit: Parturiunt montes, nascetur ridiculus mus. Et vtinam non interdum sub plausibili disciplinæ titulo, quo suam Excommunicationem palliant, disciplinam omnem euerterent, & Ecclesiarum ante coniunctissimarum concordiam turbarent. Posteriores autem illi meminerint, nos non per nostra opera sanctificari, sed per fidem, sicuti Apostolici Concilij decreto docemur. Ea autem quantulacunq; sit, ad Christum apprehendum sufficit. Is vero non rigidus perfectionis summæ (quæ nullus adhuc carnis moleg gravatis obtingit) exactor est, sed mitis & benignus seruator, qui omnes qui laborant, ad se vocat, & quæ nobis desunt, suæ obedientiæ & iustitiæ merito farcit siue supplet. Quoad ergo aliqua ex parte in Ecclesia hæremus, quæ eius corpus est, de salute nostra nequaquam debemus desperare.
units.tr: Before we leave this passage, you should observe that Paul calls the Church of God those who were depraved and corrupted in so many ways. This was said in the inscription of the earlier letter, but it must be repeated often, on account of those who, carried away by excessive and hasty zeal, rashly condemn whoever they please, or who, overcome by their own timidity, doubt their salvation, or even despair when they see that they do not in every respect match their profession. Of the first kind today are the Anabaptists and others who hold that all churches are impure in which not everything is ordered according to their own pleasure or will. They attempt many things with great effort, as if they were about to bring back the golden age to us in a moment. But it usually happens as the satirist sings: "The mountains will labour, and a ridiculous mouse will be born." And would that they did not sometimes overturn all church discipline under the plausible title of discipline, with which they cover their excommunication, and disturb the harmony of churches that were once most closely united! But let those latter men remember that we are sanctified not by our own works but by faith, as we are taught by the decree of the apostolic council. And this faith, however small it may be, is enough to lay hold of Christ. He is not a harsh exactor of the highest perfection (which no one burdened with the weight of the flesh has yet attained), but a gentle and kind saviour, who calls to himself all who labour, and supplies by the merit of his obedience and righteousness what is lacking in us. So long as we cling in some measure to the Church, which is his body, we must by no means despair of our salvation.

units.la: Subjicitur Inscriptioni salutatio sive benedictio apostolica: Gratia sit vobis & pax à Deo Patre nostro, & Domino IESV CHRISTO. Diximus de his quædam in priori epistola, quibus in præsenti addimus, nos salutationibus istis de nostra felicitate & salute certiores fieri. Nam eas neque inanes neque irritas esse apud eos, qui Christum fide vera apprehenderunt, ipsius verbis docemur, dicentis: In quamcunq domum intraueritis, primum dicite: Pax huic domui: Et si ibi fuerit filius pacis, requiescet super illum pax vestra. At concurrunt hic alia quoq; quæ consideratione merentur.
units.tr: To the inscription is added the apostolic salutation or blessing: "Grace be to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." We have said some things about these in the earlier letter; now we add that these greetings assure us of our happiness and salvation. We are taught by the words of Christ himself that they are neither empty nor vain among those who have truly laid hold of Christ by faith, when he says: "Whatever house you enter, first say, 'Peace be to this house.' And if a son of peace is there, your peace shall rest upon him." But other points also arise here which deserve consideration.

units.la: Primum, quod hæc nobis Apostoli precantur à Deo Patre nostro. Ex eo enim apparet, nos non esse gentem, quæ Deum nullum habeat, aut quam Deus ignoret, siue negligat. Clamant quidem impij, quando nos aut socios nostros affligi & in extremis periclitari vident: Vbi nunc est Deus illorum? At nos ijsdem respondere possumus: Atqui Deus noster in cœlis est, qui facit quicquid voluerit. Et cur non ita respondeamus, quos ipse germanius & æternus Dei Filius precari docuit: Pater noster, qui es in cœlis? Ἀθεοι potius & gens sine Deo dici merentur, qui Deos sibi finguntincertos, dubios, & quos hinc inde in terris monstrant, quasi locis certis astrictis hæreant.
units.tr: First, that the apostles pray for us these things from God our Father. For from this it is clear that we are not a people who have no God, or whom God does not know or neglects. The impious indeed cry out, when they see us or our companions afflicted and in extreme danger: "Where now is their God?" But we can answer them: "Yet our God is in the heavens, and he does whatever he pleases." And why should we not answer thus, we whom the eternal Son of God himself taught to pray: "Our Father, who art in heaven"? Rather, those who fashion gods for themselves, uncertain and doubtful gods, whom they point to here and there on earth, as if they clung to fixed and confined places, deserve to be called atheists [ἄθεοι] and a people without God.

units.la: Alterum, quod Deus ille verus & æternus nobis Pater est. Est quidem omnium gentium Deus atq; Dominus, vt qui non illas modo, verumetiam malos dæmones suo nutu atq; imperio coerceat. At idem non nisi ijs, qui in Christum credunt, Pater est. His enim solis datur Spiritus ille adoptionis, in quo clamant, Abba Pater. Esᶜ hæc dignitatum omnium, quæ homini obtingeri possunt, maxima, eademq; omnes felicitatis verę partes complectitur. Quid enim ijs deesse poterit, qui Deum Patrem habent, cuius est terra & plenitudo eius? Regis filius vbicunq; fit in patris regno, certa vitæ subsidia inuenit. Ita nobis quoq; vbiq; gentium prospicitur, qui vbi vbi fumus, in Patris nostri ditione sumus, vbi is merum imperium obtinet. Vt vero nobis certa & firma sit consolatio ista, IESVM CHRISTVM semper ob oculos habere oportet, qui vt suos nobis hanc dignitatem meruit, ita suos ab ea excidere nunquam patietur. Per eundem quoq; nobis gratia & pax obtingit, id est, fauor Dei perpetuus & certa conscientiæ tranquillitas, qui regni Dei Patris nostri thesauri sunt.
units.tr: Second, that this true and eternal God is our Father. He is indeed the God and Lord of all nations, since by his nod and command he restrains not only them but also the evil demons. Yet he is Father only to those who believe in Christ. For to these alone is given that Spirit of adoption, by whom they cry, "Abba, Father." This is the greatest of all the dignities that can fall to a human being, and it embraces all the parts of true happiness. For what can be lacking to those who have God as Father, whose is the earth and its fullness? Wherever a king's son is, in his father's kingdom, he finds sure support for his life. Thus we too are cared for in every part of the world: wherever we are, we are in the dominion of our Father, wherever he holds sovereign power. But so that this consolation may be sure and firm for us, we must always keep Jesus Christ before our eyes, who has earned this dignity for his own, and who will never allow his own to fall from it. Through him also grace and peace come to us, that is, the perpetual favour of God and the sure tranquillity of conscience, which are the treasures of the kingdom of God our Father.

units.la: Porrò vsus istorum omnium hic nobis esse debet, vt ijs bene & recte vtamur ad Dei gloriam & nostram salutem. Etenim si Deum verum profitemur, non vt gentes Epicuri delirij impijs deceptas hinc inde vagari nos conuenit, sed illi vni adhærere. Si Deus ille nobis Pater est, hunc supra omnia amare, hunc vnum obseruare & colere conuenit. Si æternus Dei Filius noster redemptor atq; Dominus est, cauendum vtiq; nobis fuerit, ne fidem ipsi datam fallamus, aut turpem ab eo faciamus secessionem. Et cum in illo gratiam Dei & pacem obtinuerimus, cura hæc nobis præcipua sit, ne in vasa iræ degeneremus, neue contra illum murmuremus, aut temere cum ijs lites suscipiamus, quos ille eorundem nobiscum bonorum confortes esse vult. Habes ergo in benedictione illa Apostolica philosophiæ Christianæ summam, quæ tunc demum nobis salutaris fiet, si cum θεωρίᾳ siue contemplatione πρᾶξιν ipsam coniunxerimus.
units.tr: Moreover, the use of all these things ought to be ours here, that we use them well and rightly, to the glory of God and our own salvation. For if we profess the true God, it is fitting that we not wander hither and thither, deceived by the impious raving of Epicurus, but cling to him alone. If that God is our Father, it is fitting that we love him above all things, and that we alone obey and worship him. If the eternal Son of God is our Redeemer and Lord, we must certainly take care not to betray the faith given to him, or make a shameful withdrawal from him. And since we have obtained the grace and peace of God in him, let this be our chief concern: that we not degenerate into vessels of wrath, nor murmur against him, nor rashly enter into quarrels with those whom he wills to be sharers with us in these same goods. You have, then, in that apostolic blessing the sum of Christian philosophy, which will become salutary for us only if we join practice [πρᾶξις] itself to contemplation [θεωρία].

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad epistolæ Exordium, quod totum οἰκονομία siue gratiarum actione constat, qua Dei erga se bonitatem ita prædicat, vt simul mirifico artificio sese apud Corinthiorum animos insinuet, atq; aduersariorum calumnias diluat. Hi enim (vt initio diximus) persecutiones & afflictiones perpetuas ipsi exprobrabant, vt eum propter iuge omnia turbandi studium odio dignum esse demonstrarent. Ad ea igitur respondens afflictiones suas excusat, & his adeo neminem offendi debere docet, vt potius in eis diuinæ bonitatis argumenta agnoscere ipsum, amare debeant, qui hæc omnia propter ipsos fuisset, ad quos fructus præcipuus redundet. Benedictus Deus (inquit) & Pater Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, Pater ille misericordiarum, &c. Quibus verbis hoc omnino vult dicere: Scio quid de me loquantur, qui vt me vobis suspectum & inuisum reddant, persecutiones mihi vitio vertunt, quibus vbiq; gentium exerceor, & quæ meum ad vos aduentum hucusq; impediuerunt. Possem ego istis prolixe respondere, & eorum calumnias grauiter, sicuti merentur, confutare: Sed malo ipsis omissis circa diuinæ misericordiæ & bonitatis prædicationem occupari, quæ mihi in omnibus periculis affulget. Etenim o benedictum Deum illum & Patrem Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, qui reuera Pater misericordiarum & Deus omnis consolationis dici meretur: eo quòd nos consoletur in omni afflictione nostra, &c. Sunt verba hæc plana satis & perspicua, digna tamen, quæ singula aliquanto diligentius excutiantur. Etenim memorabile exemplum continent, quo admonemur, in afflictionibus non ea modò spectari debere, quæ carni molesta sunt, verumetiam quæ in medijs illis occurrunt diuinæ bonitatis argumenta. Ita mox patebit, nos ampliorem habere gratias agendi quàm quiritandi occasionem.
units.tr: Let us now pass to the exordium of the letter, which consists entirely of a thanksgiving [οἰκονομία], in which he proclaims God's goodness toward himself, so that at the same time, with remarkable skill, he insinuates himself into the minds of the Corinthians and refutes the calumnies of his opponents. For these men (as we said at the beginning) constantly reproached him with persecutions and afflictions, in order to show that he was worthy of hatred because of his unending zeal for stirring up trouble. Answering these charges, therefore, he excuses his afflictions, and teaches that no one should be offended by them. Rather, they should acknowledge in them the proofs of divine goodness, and love him who suffered all this on their account, since the principal fruit redounds to them. "Blessed be God," he says, "and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, etc." By these words he wants to say this: "I know what they say about me. In order to make me suspect and hateful to you, they charge me with the persecutions by which I am harassed everywhere among the nations, and which have hitherto hindered my coming to you. I could answer them at length and refute their calumnies severely, as they deserve. But I prefer to set them aside and to occupy myself with proclaiming the divine mercy and goodness, which shines upon me in all dangers. For O blessed God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who truly deserves to be called the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, because he comforts us in all our affliction, etc." These words are plain and clear enough, yet they are worth examining each one somewhat more carefully. For they contain a memorable example, by which we are admonished that in afflictions we should look not only at what is troublesome to the flesh, but also at the proofs of divine goodness that present themselves in the midst of them. Thus it will soon become evident that we have more occasion for giving thanks than for complaining.

units.la: Itaq; videamus initio, qualem nobis Deum Apostolus describat. Benedictus (ait) Deus & & Pater Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI. Non debent autem hæc ita intelligi, quasi alius sit Deus, alius verò Pater Christi. Sed ita loquitur, partim vt Deum verum à falsis gentium Dijs distinguat, & non alium esse offendat Deum, quàm qui in Scripturis traditur, qui verbum æternum, siue Filium, ab æterno ex se genuit, Deum verum (vt patres Niceni loquuntur) ex Deo vero, sibi consubstantialem, per quem omnia creauit, & cuius merito nos quoq; redempti sumus: partim propter huius loci argumentum. Quia enim de afflictionibus dicturus erat, quas ipsi exprobrabant æmuli eius, docere vult, ea quæ propter Christum patiuntur pij, non debere Dei irati argumentum putari, cum hic Pater sit Christi, & hunc Filium suum dilectum esse cœlitus testetur. Et facit ad huius doctrinæ confirmationem, quòd quem paulò ante dixit nostrum Patrem esse, nunc Christi Patre vocat. Ex eo enim colligimus, vnum & eundem IESV CHRI-STI & nos STI & nostrûm omnium Patrem esse, & ideo nos Christi fratres esse, quod ipsemet non obscure testatur, quando nos orare iussit his verbis: Pater noster, qui es in cœlis: quando item à mortuis resuscitatus Magdalenæ dicebat: Vade ad fratres meos, & dic eis: Ascendo ad Patrem meum, & Patrem vestrum: ad Deum meum, & Deum vestrum. Illic enim in Mediatoris persona loquitur & suæ mortis atq; resurrectionis fructu exponit: qui est, quòd Deu ita nobis placauit, vt qui ipsi Pater est natura, nobis quoq; Pater factus sit ex gratia, quos propter ipsum in filios adoptarit.
units.tr: Let us first see, then, what kind of God the Apostle describes to us. "Blessed (he says) be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ." These words ought not to be understood as though God were one and the Father of Christ another. Rather he speaks thus partly to distinguish the true God from the false gods of the nations, and to show that the God meant is none other than the one delivered in the Scriptures, who from eternity begot from himself his eternal Word or Son, true God (as the Nicene fathers put it) from the true God, consubstantial with himself, through whom he created all things, and by whose merit we too have been redeemed; and partly on account of the argument of this passage. For since he was about to speak of afflictions, which his rivals were throwing in his face, he wishes to teach that the sufferings which the godly undergo for Christ ought not to be taken as a sign of God's anger, since this God is the Father of Christ and from heaven bears witness that this is his beloved Son. And it serves to confirm this teaching that the one whom he a little before called our Father he now calls the Father of Christ. For from this we gather that one and the same God is the Father of Jesus Christ and of us all, and that therefore we are brethren of Christ; which he himself does not obscurely attest when he bade us pray with these words: "Our Father, who art in heaven"; and likewise when, raised from the dead, he said to Mary Magdalene: "Go to my brethren and say to them: I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God." For there he speaks in the person of the Mediator and sets forth the fruit of his death and resurrection, which is that God has so reconciled himself to us that he who is by nature Father of himself has also become our Father by grace, adopting us as sons for his sake.

units.la: Deinde Patrem misericordiarum dicit Hebraica phrasi pro misericorde, vel potius omnis misericordiæ fonte & authore. Plurali autem numero vtitur, vt omnia, quæ in natura rerum extant, diuinæ bonitatis & misericordiæ argumenta comprehendat.
