Quicquid enim boni habemus, id omne ex Deo est: de quo cum ipsi nihil possimus mereri, gratuitum sit oportet, quicquid nobis largitur. Est autem obseruatu dignum, Deum passim in Scripturis à bonitate & misericordia commendari. Causæ huius rei sunt. Prima, quòd hæc in omnibus eius operibus eminet, sicuti Psalmus testatur: Misericordia eius superat omnia opera eius. Altera, quòd ex misericordia nobis applicantur & salutaria siunt, quæcunq; in illo eximia & magnifica sunt. Nam si iustitiam eius solam respicias, terreberis peccatorum tuorum conscientia. Si veritatem, mox occurret, omnes homines natura mendaces, & proinde à Deo alienos esse. Si omnipotentiam & maiestatem, tua infirmitas coram ea consistere non poterit. Si sapientiam, tuæ te stultitiæ pudebit & ignorantiæ, qui in media luce cæcutias. At si misericordiam eius infinitam & plus quàm paternam simul nobis ob oculos ponamus, mox spes bona animis nostris affulgebit, ipsum omnia quæ habet nobis communicare velle, vt nostræ saluti inseruiant: eoq; magis spes ista confirmabitur, quò diligentius miserias nostras expenderimus, quæ si nullæ essent, misericordia illius locum habere non poterat. Huc refer, quæ de illa traduntur. Psal. 103. Isa. 49, & c.
units.tr: Then he calls him "the Father of mercies," in the Hebrew manner of speaking, for "merciful," or rather the fountain and author of all mercy. He uses the plural number so that it may embrace all the tokens of divine goodness and mercy that exist in the nature of things. For whatever good we have, all of it comes from God; and since we can merit nothing from him, whatever he bestows upon us must be of free gift. It is worth noting that Scripture everywhere commends God for goodness and mercy. The reasons for this are these. First, because this shines forth in all his works, as the Psalm testifies: "His mercy is above all his works." Second, because all those things in him which are outstanding and magnificent become applicable to us and salutary through mercy. For if you look at his justice alone, you will be terrified by the consciousness of your sins. If his truth, at once it will occur to you that all men are liars by nature and therefore alienated from God. If his omnipotence and majesty, your weakness will be unable to stand before it. If his wisdom, you will be ashamed of your folly and ignorance, which grope blindly in the midst of light. But if we set before our eyes at the same time his infinite mercy, which is more than paternal, at once a good hope will shine upon our minds, that he is willing to share with us all that he has, so that they may serve our salvation; and this hope will be the more confirmed the more carefully we weigh our miseries, for if there were none, his mercy could have no place. Refer here what is said of that mercy in Psalm 103 and Isaiah 49, and so on.

units.la: Tertiò, Deum omnis consolationis Patrem dicit. Id vero subijcit ceu argumentum misericordiæ, vt eos confirmet, qui de Dei misericordia dubitant, quando pios perpetuis afflictionibus exerceri vident. Tunc enim multorum fides grauissimè tentatur, & audiuntur fere voces istæ: Egregia sanè misericordia, homines insontes & meliora meritos in assiduis tormentis & cruciatibus spectare, gemitus & eiulatus eorum audire, nec tamen opem ferre miseris. Num verò credendum est, Deum eorum calamitatibus affici, quos ita negligit? Sic Iobum olim Satan tentauit, & huius generis multa illi obganniebat vxor. Docet ergo Paulus, Deum, etsi non semper ex calamitatibus & periculis liberet, nihilominus tamen non deesse eum misericordiæ suæ: nam eundem tunc afflictos consolari, vt omnibus ferendis possint sufficere. Ideoq; expresse Patrem omnis consolationis dicit, & per expositionem addit: Qui consolatur nos in omni afflictione nostra. Non ait, Qui nos potest consolari: sed, Qui consolatur. Ita enim docet, illum nunquam deesse suo officio, adeoq; hoc ei proprium & perpetuum esse, quòd semper suis adsit, semper consoletur, semper viribus nouis labascentes suspulciat. Habemus igitur in illo duplicem consolationem. Vnam in præsenti seculo, quam adhibet, dum nos (vt Paulus alibi docet) non patitur supra vires tentari. Alteram, quæ in futuro seculo habetur, quando omnibus miserijs liberatos ad se transferet in sedes beatæ immortalitatis, vbi lachrymæ omnes abstergentur, & omnis gemitus atq; dolor cessabunt. De hac consolatione diuiti illi epuloni Abrahamus loquitur, quando Lazarum nunc solatio frui ait, ipsum autem merito cruciari qui omnia sua in vita male anteacta receperit. Debent autem priorem illam diligentes meditari quicunq; in hoc seculo affliguntur, vt ea perspecta in futuræ felicitatis spe confirmentur, quæ nos omnibus malis superiores facit.
units.tr: Third, he calls God "the Father of all consolation." He adds this as a proof of mercy, to strengthen those who doubt God's mercy when they see the godly constantly exercised by afflictions. For then the faith of many is most severely tested, and words of this sort are heard almost everywhere: "A fine mercy indeed, to watch innocent men, who deserve better, in continual torments and agonies, to hear their groans and wailing, and yet not to bring help to the wretched. Ought we really to believe that God is affected by the calamities of those whom he so neglects?" So once Satan tested Job, and his wife barked many things of this kind at him. Paul therefore teaches that God, although he does not always free from calamities and dangers, nevertheless does not lack his mercy; for he consoles those who are afflicted, so that they may be sufficient to bear all things. And so he expressly calls him the Father of all consolation, and by way of explanation adds: "who comforts us in all our affliction." He does not say, "who can comfort us," but "who comforts." For thus he teaches that God never fails in his office, and that it is his peculiar and perpetual property always to be present with his own, always to comfort them, always to lift up those who totter with fresh strength. We have, then, a twofold consolation in him. One in the present age, which he supplies, while he (as Paul teaches elsewhere) does not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength. The other is had in the age to come, when he will transfer all those freed from miseries to himself, into the seats of blessed immortality, where every tear will be wiped away and every groan and pain will cease. Abraham speaks of this consolation to the rich glutton, when he says that Lazarus now enjoys comfort, while he himself, who received all his evil deeds in life, is rightly tormented. Those who are afflicted in this age ought to diligently meditate upon the former consolation, so that, having grasped it, they may be strengthened in the hope of future happiness, which makes us superior to all evils.

units.la: Simul autem obseruabis hoc loco, Paulum, qui dum hæc scriberet, adhuc sub cruce exercebatur, & quidem propter vnum Christum & Euangelium eius, solius tamen misericordiæ meminisse, qua ipsum Deus consoletur. Atqui iustitiam Dei implorare, & vindictam minitari poterat, qua Deus suorum iniurias vlciscitur. Sed consolatio eiusmodi vt non solida est (eò quòd in nobis quoq; multa sunt, quæ puniri merentur) ita qui ad illam confugiunt, ijs fere nimis arroganter de semetipsis sentiunt, quasi ipsi digni sint, propter quos alij puniantur. Atqui omnes precari cogimur: Memor sis miserationum tuarum ô Domine, & bonitatis tuæ: quoniam à seculo sunt. Peccatorum autem adolescentiæ meæ & scelerum ne sis memor: memor autem mei sis secundùm benignitatem tuam. Item: Ne ingrediaris in iudicium cum seruo tuo: Remitte nobis debita nostra, ut nos remiserimus debitoribus nostris. Admonent ista, quid de illis iudicemus, qui dum affliguntur, ex impatientia murmurant, quasi ipsis iniuriam faciat Deus. Quin potius eius misericordiam agnoscis, qui cædit nos, ut sanet, occidit item ut viuificet? Deinde in mentem renoca, quàm multus quamq; efficacibus consolationibus, te hucusq; refocillatu seruarit: quibus nullus apud te locus fuisset, nisi ista pateretis. Deniq; ad alios homines respice, & multos inuenies, qui grauiora quàm tu patiuntur, ideoq; te nullam habere videbis de Deo quiritandi occasionem.
units.tr: At the same time, you will observe in this place that Paul, who while writing these things was still exercised under the cross, and indeed on account of Christ alone and his Gospel, nevertheless remembers only the mercy by which God consoles him. Yet he could have implored God's justice and threatened vengeance, by which God avenges the injuries of his own. But consolation of this kind is not solid (because there are also many things in us which deserve punishment), and so those who flee to it generally think of themselves too arrogantly, as though they were worthy that others should be punished on their account. Yet all of us are compelled to pray: "Remember your tender mercies, O Lord, and your goodness, for they have been from of old. Do not remember the sins of my youth and my transgressions, but remember me according to your kindness." Likewise: "Do not enter into judgment with your servant. Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." These words warn us how we should judge those who, while they are afflicted, murmur from impatience, as though God were doing them an injury. Rather, do you not recognize the mercy of him who strikes us in order to heal, and likewise kills in order to make alive? Then call to mind how many and how efficacious the consolations are with which he has hitherto refreshed you, consolations which would have had no place with you unless you were suffering these things. Finally, look at other men, and you will find many who suffer heavier things than you, and so you will see that you have no occasion of complaining against God.

units.la: Quarto vsum & finem misericordiæ sibi factæ Paulus indicat: Ut possimus in quauis afflictione positos consolari, ea ipsa consolatione, qua nos ipsos Deus consolatur. Vt enim qui rerum aliquarum vsum sibi longa experientia compararunt, easdem alijs facilius & felicius possunt tradere: Ita qui multis aduersis agitati vim diuinæ consolationis sæpius senserunt, ij alios melius consolari possunt, & ad opem ferendam propensiores sunt. Vidit hoc prophanus Poeta, qui barbaram mulierem loquentem inducit. Non ignari mali miseris succurrere disco. Sciunt etiam isti quæ consolationis argumenta sint efficacissima. Fatetur ergo Apostolus, se hoc Dei consilium agnoscere, & ita fructum omnem suarum afflictionum Corinthijs communem facit: Quod vt apud bonos ipsi beneuolentiam parabat, ita vehementer arguebat æmulorum ingratitudinem, qui afflictiones ei exprobrabant.
units.tr: Fourth, Paul points out the use and end of the mercy shown to him: that, being placed in any affliction, we may be able to console others with that very consolation by which God consoles us. For just as those who have acquired for themselves a long experience of certain matters can more easily and happily pass them on to others, so those who, tossed about by many adversities, have often felt the power of divine consolation can console others better and are more inclined to bring help. The pagan poet saw this, when he introduces a barbarian woman speaking: "Not ignorant of evil, I learn to help the wretched." Those men also know which arguments of consolation are most effective. The Apostle therefore acknowledges that he recognizes this to be God's purpose, and thus makes the whole fruit of his afflictions common to the Corinthians. This both won him goodwill among good men and sharply reproved the ingratitude of his rivals, who threw his afflictions in his face.

units.la: Est autem diligentiori consideratione dignus hic locus, quo admonemur, Deum qui singularia edit iustitiæ suæ exempla in sceleratos, vt ea multis alijs ad pietatem documento sint, similiter misericordiam quoq; & bonitatem suam exemplis peculiaribus declarare, non propter eos modo, qui illis tunc fruuntur, sed vt plures alij ijsdem confirmentur. Docet hoc Dauid suo exemplo in Psalmis non semel. Et Paulus in priori ad Timoth. sibi factam misericordiam omnibus peccatoribus applicat. Et notum est illud Christi Petro dicentis: Tu conuersus aliquando, confirma fratres tuos. Est hoc memorabile prouidentiæ Dei argumentum, quæ nos hominum afflictissimorum exemplis erigit atq; confirmat, & sæpe etiam eorum, qui dignas sceleribus suis pœnas exoluunt. Debent ergo diligenter obseruari, quæcunq; sunt huius generis.
units.tr: It is worth considering this passage more carefully, for it reminds us that God, who displays singular examples of his justice against the wicked so that they may serve as a lesson in piety to many others, likewise declares his mercy and goodness by particular examples, not only for those who then enjoy them but so that many others may be strengthened by the same. David teaches this by his own example in the Psalms more than once. And Paul, in his first letter to Timothy, applies the mercy shown to himself to all sinners. And that saying of Christ to Peter is well known: "When you have been converted, strengthen your brothers." This is a notable argument of God's providence, which raises up and strengthens us by the examples of the most afflicted men, and often also of those who pay the penalties their crimes deserve. Therefore such examples of this kind ought to be carefully observed.

units.la: Imprimis autem officij sui meminerint, qui singulari gratia Dei se in aduersis subleuari sentiunt: vt nimirum quicquid inde accipiunt, id ad aliorum vtilitatem conferant. Itaq; si quando ex periculis liberati pace tuta fruimur, alijs periclitantibus opem feramus, aut si id non possumus, saltem pijs consolationibus & nostri doloris significatione illorum molestias leuemus. Idem faciant erga egenos opulenti, erga perplexos & consilij inopes, qui sapientia instructi sunt. Sumus enim membra eiusdem corporis, vt in priori epist. audiuimus: cum Deus mundi huius machinam cum omnibus eius partibus nostro vsui destinauit, iniqui erimus donorum eius dispensatores, si quæ nobis data sunt cuiquam negemus, qui illis opus habet. Arguit hoc eorum duritiem, qui otio & pace abundantes fratrum pro fide periclitantium cura nulla tanguntur, dummodo ipsis lasciuire & delitiari per illos liceat. Peiores sunt, qui insuper eis insultant, & in cruce pendentibus acetum felle mixtum propinant, dum omnia eorum improbè calumniantur. Quibus adnumerari debent, qui dum Euangelij prædicatione tutò fruuntur, alijs sub duro tyrannorum imperio laborantibus illius micas negant, neq; libellos aliquos in illorum consolationem aut institutionem ædi volunt, ne ipsi in alicuius odium incurrant. Accidit hís fere, vt dum omnia tuta metuunt, seipsos periculis grauissimis intricent, & tunc alios quoq; erga se duriores experiantur. Deum Opt. Max. precor, vt omnium animos emolliat, & difficillimis hisce temporibus regat, vt mutuis consolationibus confirmati per aduersa omnia eluctemur ad beatæ immortalitatis portum, quem nobis CHRISTVS IESVS sui sanguinis pretio acquisiuit. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Above all, those who feel that they are sustained in adversity by the singular grace of God should remember their duty, namely, that whatever they receive from this they should put to the use of others. So if at any time, freed from dangers, we enjoy a safe peace, let us bring help to others who are in peril; or if we cannot do that, at least let us lighten their troubles by pious consolations and by showing our own sorrow for them. Let the wealthy do the same toward the needy, and toward those who are perplexed and lack counsel, they who are furnished with wisdom. For we are members of the same body, as we heard in the first letter; since God has destined the frame of this world with all its parts for our use, we shall be unfaithful stewards of his gifts if we deny to anyone who needs them what has been given to us. This exposes the hardness of those who, abundant in leisure and peace, are moved by no care for brothers imperiled for the faith, provided they may themselves indulge and revel in their own comforts. Worse are those who moreover insult them and give vinegar mixed with gall to those hanging on the cross, while wickedly slandering everything they do. To these must be added those who, while they enjoy the preaching of the Gospel in safety, deny even its crumbs to others labouring under the harsh rule of tyrants, and refuse to have any little books published for their consolation or instruction, lest they themselves incur someone's hatred. It usually happens to such people that, while they fear every safe course, they entangle themselves in the gravest dangers, and then they find others harsher toward them in turn. I pray to God, most good and most great, that he soften the hearts of all, and govern us in these most difficult times, so that, strengthened by mutual consolations, we may struggle through all adversities to the harbour of blessed immortality, which Christ Jesus acquired for us at the price of his own blood. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA II.
units.tr: HOMILY II.

units.la: Quoniam sicut abundant passiones Christi in nobis: ita per Christum abundat etiam consolatio nostra.
units.tr: Since as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds.

units.la: INter alia, quibus Pauli æmuli ipsum apud Corinthios suspectum & contemptum reddere conabantur, præcipuum fere fuit, quòd apud imperitos rerum persecutiones, quibus ille exercebatur, odiosè exagitabant, vt nimirum omnibus persuaderent, ipsum talem esse, quem nemo bonus & moderati ingenij homo ferre posset, & proinde merito eum ab ipsis quoq; contemni. Prudenter ergo ab eo epistolam hanc orditur, & vt scandalum hoc è medio tollat, initiò statim magnificè prædicat Dei misericordiam, qui ipsum hucusque inter medias afflictiones ita consolatus sit, vt non modò ipse eas vincere potuerit, verumetiam alios suo exemplo atq; doctrina consolari. Facit ad horum confirmationem locus iste, quem modò recitauimus.
units.tr: Among the other charges by which Paul's rivals tried to make him suspected and despised among the Corinthians, the chief was that they maliciously magnified, before the ignorant, the persecutions with which he was afflicted, so as to persuade everyone that he was such a man as no good and reasonable person could tolerate, and that he therefore deserved to be despised even by them. Wisely, then, he begins this letter with this, and to remove the scandal he at once praises God's mercy in lavish terms, because God has so consoled him in the midst of his afflictions until now that he has been able not only to overcome them himself but also to console others by his example and teaching. This passage which we have just recited serves to confirm them.

units.la: Nam οξολογίας istius, qua Dei misericordiam celebrauit, rationem reddit his verbis: Quoniam sicut abundant passiones Christi in nobis: ita per Christum abundat etiam consolatio nostra. Quasi diceret: Non equidem inficior multa mihi quotidie aduersa accidere, imò verè dicere possum, ms omnibus ijs, quæ Christus passus est exerceri, adeò vt afflictionum fluctus in me omnem suum impetum effundere videantur. Non autem propterea me miserum aut infelicem esse existimo, neque de Dei rigore quiritor. Vt enim Deus ista immittit, vt propter Filium suum dilectum, ea patiar: ita per eundem me liberalissimè consolatur atque confirmat, vt omnibus istis superandis posssim sufficere. Eius ergo consolatione suffultus, neque ipsis aduersorum vndique mihi insultantium procellis, neque iniquis æmulorum meorum iudicijs moueor, quò minus cum læta & publica gratiarum actione suscipiam quicquid ille dederit. Hic verborum istorum sensus est, quibus Paulus non solum scandalum remouet, quod ex ipsius persecutionibus nascebatur, verumetiam consolationem pijs omnibus propinat, qua in suis tentationibus confirmentur. Ea autem eo solidior & efficacior est, quòd argumento ex communi sensu aut legibus naturæ deducto nititur. Æquum enim est, vt qui propter aliquem affligitur, ab eodem retributionem accipiat, aut saltem gaudij & felicitatis, qua ille fruitur, particeps fiat. Quia ergo nos cum Christo, & propter eius Euangelium patimur, fieri non potest, quin ù consolationis spiritu nobis adsit, ne sub onere isto succumbamus.
units.tr: For he gives the reason for that thanksgiving [ἐξομολογίας] in which he celebrated God's mercy, in these words: "Since as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds." It is as if he said: "I do not deny that many adversities befall me every day; indeed I can truly say that I am subjected to all the things which Christ suffered, so that the waves of afflictions seem to pour their whole force upon me. Yet I do not therefore think myself wretched or unhappy, nor do I complain of God's severity. For just as God sends these things so that I may suffer them for his beloved Son, so through the same Son he consoles and strengthens me so generously that I am sufficient to overcome all of them. Supported by his consolation, I am moved neither by the storms of adversities raging against me on every side, nor by the unjust judgments of my rivals, so as not to receive gladly and openly with thanksgiving whatever he has given." This is the sense of those words, by which Paul not only removes the scandal that arose from his persecutions, but also offers to all the godly a consolation by which they may be strengthened in their own temptations. And this consolation is the firmer and more effective because it rests on an argument drawn from common sense or the laws of nature. For it is fair that one who suffers on account of someone should receive a reward from that same person, or at least share in the joy and happiness which he enjoys. Since therefore we suffer with Christ and for his gospel, it cannot be that the Spirit of consolation is not present with us, so that we do not sink under that burden.

units.la: Est autem hoc Pauli dictum, ô viri Christiani, dignissimum, quod diligentius à nobis consideretur. Breuiter enim comprehendit omnia, quæ nobis, quoad crucem & huius seculi afflictiones, cognitu necessaria sunt. Inter quæ primum est, Christianis hominibus nunquam defore crucem & aduersa, quibus in hac vita exercentur. Docemur deinde, quid de cruce nostra & afflictionibus sentire, vnde item consolationem, consilium aut opem petere debeamus. Præterea Mediatorem nobis ostendit, cuius intercessione seruamur. De istis ergo, quod Dominus dederit, ex ordine dicemus.
units.tr: This saying of Paul, O Christian men, is most worthy of being considered by us more carefully. For it briefly comprehends all that we need to know concerning the cross and the afflictions of this age. Among these, the first is that Christian people will never lack the cross and the adversities with which they are exercised in this life. Next we are taught what we ought to think about our cross and afflictions, and from where we ought to seek consolation, counsel or help. Moreover, he shows us the Mediator by whose intercession we are saved. Let us therefore speak of these things in order, as the Lord shall give.

units.la: Et primum quidem cognitu perquàm necessarium est, crucem videlicet pijs ac verè Christianis nunquam defore: ne ea, vt re insolita & noua offendamur. Id enim multis accidit, qui tamnon Iudaico errore decepti, in Christo nihil aliud præter opes, dignitates, pacem & otium sperant, posthabitis bonis cœlestibus, quæ ille nobis meruit: quæ sunt, peccatorum remissio, reconciliatio cum Deo, & pax conscientiæ, quæ omnem mundi huius intellectum superat. Quæ causa est, ob quam Christus discipulos frequenter de cruce ferenda præmonuit, & quoties ipsi de regno eius terreno disputarunt, toties illos ad patientiam & fidei constantiam hortatus est. Idem regulam omnibus Christianis communem præscribit: Si quis vult post me venire, abneget semetipsum, tollat crucem suam quotidie, & sequatur me. Et hanc proprio exemplo commendat, dicens: Non est seruus maior hero suo: Si me persecuti sunt, vos quoque persequentur. Et rursus: Veniet tempus, quando qui vos occiderit, putabit se cultum Deo præstare. Denique, in mundo afflictionem habebitis, sed bono animo estote, ego vici mundum. Ex quibus Paulus hoc suum dictum collegit: Omnes qui volunt pie viuere in CHRISTO IESV, persecutionem patientur. 2. Timoth. 3.
units.tr: And first it is most necessary to know that the cross will never be lacking to the godly and truly Christian, lest we be offended by it as something unusual and new. For this happens to many who, though not deceived by the Jewish error, hope from Christ for nothing else but wealth, dignities, peace and leisure, while setting aside the heavenly goods which he has merited for us, namely the forgiveness of sins, reconciliation with God, and the peace of conscience which surpasses all understanding of this world. This is the reason why Christ often warned his disciples about bearing the cross, and whenever they disputed about his earthly kingdom, he exhorted them to patience and constancy of faith. He prescribes the same rule common to all Christians: "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me." And he commends this by his own example, saying: "A servant is not greater than his master. If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you." And again: "The time will come when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God." Finally: "In the world you will have affliction, but be of good cheer, I have overcome the world." From these things Paul gathered his own saying: "All who wish to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution." 2 Timothy 3.

units.la: Neque aliter fieri posse patebit, si rem penitius inspexerimus. Nam & communibus humani generis calamitatibus, quæ ex peccato plurimæ & graues exortæ sunt, Christiani homines sunt obnoxij, & multa alia incidunt, quibus crux eorum aggrauatur. Etenim nunquam mutabit ingenium suum mundus hic, qui vt Veritatis lucem odit, eo quòd opera eius mala sunt: ita neque eos
units.tr: It will be clear that it cannot be otherwise, if we look into the matter more deeply. For Christian people are subject both to the common calamities of the human race, which have arisen in great number and severity from sin, and many other things befall them by which their cross is made heavier. For this world, which hates the light of truth because its works are evil, will never change its nature; so neither can it bear

units.la: Luc. 9. Matth. 16. Ioan. 16. ferre potest, penes quos lux ista fulget, aut quorum ministerio in illa accendenda Deus vtitur. Deinde in pijs quoq;, etsi de fide & religione recte sentiunt, nœui tamen & vitia inueniuntur, quæ castigationem merentur, ne latius serpant, neue in suis Deus ferre putetur, quæ in alijs seuerius punit. Itaque à sua fere domo (vt Petrus ait) iudicij sui initium facit, & in suis castigandis atque corrigendis opera impiorum vtitur, ne quando illi quoq; cum mundo incurabili & pœnitere nescio pereant. Adde his, quòd cum natura huius vitæ & seculi amantes simus, opus omnino est, vt crebris afflictionum incursionibus vexatos tandem satietas vitæ & mundi tædium capiat, vt animis ad Deum eleuatis ad cœlestem patriam aspiremus. Possent & aliæ huius generis causæ adduci, quas breuitatis causa omittimus. Nam qui istas non ofcitanter perpenderit, mox intelliget, Deum nemini iniuriam facere, neque habere nos, quod de eius rigore aut seueritate nimia conqueramur.
units.tr: Luke 9. Matthew 16. John 16. those in whom this light shines, or through whose ministry God uses to kindle it. Then too, even among the godly, who think rightly about faith and religion, blemishes and faults are found which deserve correction, lest they spread more widely, and lest God be thought to tolerate in his own people what he punishes more severely in others. Thus, as Peter says, he begins his judgment almost at his own house, and uses the works of the wicked in chastising and correcting his own, lest at some time they too perish with the incurable world, which knows not how to repent. Add to these that, since we are lovers of this life and this age, it is altogether necessary that, being harassed by frequent assaults of afflictions, we should at last be seized by a satiety of life and a weariness of the world, so that with our minds lifted up to God we may aspire to the heavenly homeland. Other causes of this kind could also be adduced, which we omit for the sake of brevity. For whoever weighs these things carefully will soon understand that God does no wrong to anyone, and that we have no cause to complain of his severity or excessive harshness.

units.la: Nam quòd aliqui hoc nouum & insolens esse clamant, quòd hodie persecutiones passim feruent, eo suam ignorantiam produnt. Qua ratione enim nouum aut insolens dici potest, quod vt in ipso mundi exordio cœpit, ita quasi continua successione ad nos vsque est propagatum? Etenim primus ex Adamo natus germanus Dei cultor fraterna manu miserabiliter cecidit. Quàm dura verò Sethi & posterorum eius conditio fuerit inter impios Cainitas, facilè æstimabit, qui horum mores & studia animo perpenderit, propter quæ Deus terris diluuiû immisit, & genus humanum, vno Noa cum suis excepto, perdidit. Quis verò huius labores, pericula, curas & molestias verbis explicet, qui Cainitarum petulantiam tam diu pertulit, mundi totius miserabilem interitum spectauit, filij ludibria sustinuit, omnia deniq; passus est, quæ homini molesta & intolerabilia videri possunt? De Abrahamo quid dicemus quem ab eo tempore, quoDeo vocante solum natale reliquit, perpetuæ curæ partim domesticæ, partim exteræ, pericula item, labores, tentationesq; grauissimæ exercuerunt? Atqui is ille est, quem credentium patrem vocat Apostolus. Eadem Isaaci sors fuit, & grauior adhuc multoq; durior Iacobi, qui iam senex à Pharaone de ætate sua interrogatus, non aliud respondere potuit, quàm vitam suam peregrinationem breuem quidem, sed laboris & ærumnarum plenam fuisse. Poterant his connumerari Ioseph, Moses, Iosua, Dauid, Prophetæ, Apostoli & quotquot vnquam Deo fideles fuerunt, qui eò magis afflicti sunt, quò alacrius & studiosius communi omnium saluti studuerunt consulere. Et quod de priuatis hominibus dicimus, hoc ipsum de tota fidelium Ecclesia debet intelligi: quam similiter ab ipsa rerum origine perpetuis persecutionibus obnoxiam fuisse nemo negare potest, qui Scripturas sacras & historiam ecclesiasticam vel à primo limine (quod dicitur) salutauit.
units.tr: For when some cry out that this is new and unusual, that persecutions now rage everywhere, they betray their own ignorance. For in what sense can it be called new or unusual, when it began at the very beginning of the world and has been handed down to us in a kind of continuous succession? For the first man born of Adam, a true worshipper of God, fell wretchedly by the hand of his brother. And how hard the condition of Seth and his posterity was among the impious Cainites, he will easily judge who weighs in his mind their manners and pursuits, on account of which God sent the flood upon the earth and destroyed the human race, except for Noah with his family. Who could explain in words the labours, dangers, cares and troubles of Noah, who endured for so long the wantonness of the Cainites, saw the miserable destruction of the whole world, endured the mockery of his own son, and at last suffered all things which can seem grievous and intolerable to a man? What shall we say of Abraham, whom from that time, when at God's call he left his native land, perpetual cares, some domestic and some foreign, as well as dangers, labours and most grievous temptations exercised? Yet he is the one whom the Apostle calls the father of believers. The same was the lot of Isaac, and that of Jacob was heavier still and much harder, who, already an old man when Pharaoh asked him about his age, could answer nothing else than that his life had been a brief pilgrimage, indeed, but full of toil and hardship. To these could be added Joseph, Moses, Joshua, David, the prophets, the apostles, and as many as have ever been faithful to God, who were all the more afflicted the more eagerly and zealously they strove to care for the common salvation of all. And what we say of private persons ought to be understood in the same way of the whole Church of the faithful; that no one can deny that it has been subject to perpetual persecutions from the very origin of things, if he has greeted the sacred Scriptures and ecclesiastical history, as they say, from the very threshold.

units.la: Fuerunt hæc aliquanto diligentius repetenda propter eos, quos nostri seculi turbæ, seditiones & bella, quæ contra fideles Christi cultores suscipiuntur, ita offendunt, ac si nihil huius vnquam in terris accidisset. Quæ causa est, vt alij quidem de fidei doctrina & tota salutis nostræ ratione dubitent: alij verò Corinthiorum exemplo turbas hasce Euangelij præconibus acceptas ferant, quorum morositate & importunis siue seditiosis concionibus principes viri irritentur. Fatemur equidem aliquos istorum zelo inconsulto abreptos multa sæpe importunè, quædam etiam petulantius facere. Veruntamen turpissimè falluntur, qui eam Euangelij prædicandi rationem institui posse sibi persuadent, quæ mundo quoque probetur. Quid enim hic nos tentemus, quando hoc neque Prophetis neque Apostolis, imò ne Christo quidem datum fuit, qui vt mansuetissimus fuit omnium hominum, ita doctrinæ suæ miracula saluberrima in multorum vtilitatem coniungebat? Pollicetur quidem ille suis discipulis pacem, sed suam pacem, quam à pace huius mundi distinguit, cui illos exosos fore aperte testatur. Et alibi ait: Putatis quòd aduenerim pacem daturus in terra? Non, dico vobis, imò dissidium. Erunt enim ab hoc tempore quinque dissidentes in domo vna, tres aduersus duos, & duo aduersus tres. Dissidebit pater aduersus filium, & filius aduersus patrem: mater aduersus filiam, & filia aduersus matrem: socrus aduersus nurum suam, & nurus aduersus socrum suam. Item: Inimici hominis erunt domestici eius. Hæc cùm nobis Dei Filius, qui ipsa est veritas, iam olim prædixerit, simulq; constet, infelicem hunc mundum nunquam ab ingenio suo discessurum esse, cuius proprium est (vt supra diximus) lucem Veritatis odisse: minime nobis mirum videri debet, si nouissimis hisce temporibus, quæ corruptissima fore idem Dominus
units.tr: These things needed to be repeated somewhat more carefully, on account of those who are so offended by the disturbances, seditions and wars of our age, which are waged against the faithful worshippers of Christ, as if nothing of this kind had ever happened on earth. This is the reason why some doubt the doctrine of faith and the whole plan of our salvation, while others, after the example of the Corinthians, lay these tumults at the door of the heralds of the Gospel, whose stubbornness and importunate or seditious sermons irritate men of rank. We admit indeed that some of them, carried away by unwise zeal, often do many things imprudently and some things even too boldly. Yet they are utterly mistaken who persuade themselves that a way of preaching the Gospel can be devised that will also please the world. For why should we attempt this here, when it was granted neither to the Prophets nor to the Apostles, nor even to Christ himself, who, though the gentlest of all men, nonetheless joined to his teaching most wholesome miracles for the benefit of many? He indeed promised his disciples peace, but his own peace, which he distinguishes from the peace of this world, and he plainly testifies that they would be hated for it. And elsewhere he says: "Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division. For from now on there will be five divided in one house, three against two and two against three. The father will be divided against the son, and the son against the father; the mother against the daughter, and the daughter against the mother; the mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law, and the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law." Likewise: "A man's enemies will be those of his own household." Since the Son of God, who is truth itself, has foretold these things long ago, and since it is certain that this unhappy world will never depart from its nature, whose property it is (as we said above) to hate the light of truth, it ought not to seem strange to us if in these most corrupt latter times, which the same Lord warned would be the most corrupt,

units.la: 1.Pet.4. Dominus monuit, principes tam ecclesiastici quàm politici, vnà cum stolido & infelici vulgo, aduersus Euangelij doctrinam eiusq; sectatores tumultuantur, & persecutiones sanguinarias instituunt. Sufficiat nobis, si ipsi, quantum in nobis est, cum omnibus pacem colamus. Quòd si vero aliquibus hoc non sufficit, qui insuper vt fidem in IESVM CHRISTVM abnegemus, à nobis exigere audent: tunc quiduis potius facere aut sufferre parati simus, quàm mundo obsequi in eo, quod cum Dei ignominia & salutis nostrae iactura coniunctum est.
units.tr: (1 Pet. 4.) Princes, both ecclesiastical and civil, together with the foolish and wretched common people, rage against the doctrine of the Gospel and its followers, and institute bloody persecutions. Let it suffice for us, if we ourselves, so far as lies in us, cultivate peace with all. But if to some this is not enough, and they dare to demand of us that we also deny our faith in Jesus Christ, then let us be prepared to do or suffer anything rather than yield to the world in that which is joined with the dishonour of God and the loss of our salvation.

units.la: Caeterum vt in hoc certamine, quo nullum carni gravius accidere potest, instructiores simus, alterum huius loci caput diligentius considerari oportet, vt discamus, quid de afflictionibus piorum iudicari debeat, & quo loco apud Deum habeantur. Nam si mundi iudicia admittamus, illas digna & iusta impietatis supplicia & Dei irati argumenta esse dicet, quibus hic palam testatur, illorum fidem atque religionem sibi quàm maxime improbari. Quae causa est, quòd multi pijs sub cruce gementibus fidem suam atque factam ab ipsis externi cultus mutationem exprobrant: idq; tanta cum scurrilitate & petulantia, vt ne sacrosancto quidem Dei nomini parcant. Exemplum huius impietatis memorabile, in Sennacheribo, Assyriorum tyranno, sacra historia proponit. Et Babylonijs à Iudaeis inter ipsos exulantibus per ludibrium postulauisse legimus, vt sui Dei laudes & hymnos in festis decantari solitos, tunc ipsis canerent. Cui impietati maius quid & gravius addidit Balthazar Rex, quando vasa sacra, ex templo Hierosolymitano direpta, in conuiuio luxuriosò sui similibus proceribus apposuit, qui inde occasione arrepta Deos suos & horum auspicijs partas victorias celebrauerunt, non sine veri aeternique Dei ludibrio. Fiunt huius generis multa hodie, si quando fideles Christi cultores cladem aliquam accipiunt, & hostium libidini subijciuntur. Tunc enim voces illas audire licet: Iamne apparet, quae nam fides vera quae religio orthodoxa sit? Vbi iam Euangelium illud est, quod isti nouatores nunquam non in ore habuerunt? Vbi Christus ille, quo solo illi confisi sunt? &c. Haec & his similia (inquam) passim pijs Christi martyribus occinuntur. Qui vero non tam crudeles & inhumani sunt, vt tamen Christianos hominum miserrimos & infelicissimos esse putant, qui pro re incerta & dubia, vel saltem indifferenti, sese omnium odijs atque ludibrijs, imò tormentis quoque diris & infandis cruciatibus exponant. At neminem ista debent offendere, quando aeternum Dei Filium, IESVM CHRISTVM, similibus conuitijs in cruce confixum fuisse scimus, vt iam de prisci s martyribus nihil dicatur.
units.tr: Moreover, that we may be better equipped in this struggle, in which nothing more grievous can befall the flesh, we must consider more carefully the second head of this passage, so that we may learn what ought to be judged concerning the afflictions of the godly, and in what esteem they are held before God. For if we admit the judgements of the world, it will say that these afflictions are worthy and just punishments of impiety and proofs of God's wrath, by which, as it openly declares, their faith and religion are most strongly disapproved by him. This is why many taunt the pious, groaning under the cross, with their faith and with the change of external worship made by them, and they do so with such buffoonery and insolence that they do not spare even the most holy name of God. Sacred history sets before us a memorable example of this impiety in Sennacherib, the tyrant of the Assyrians. And we read that the Babylonians, mocking the Jews who were exiles among them, demanded that they sing to them the praises and hymns of their God, which they were accustomed to chant at festivals. King Belshazzar added something greater and more grievous to this impiety, when he set the sacred vessels, plundered from the temple at Jerusalem, before his nobles at a luxurious banquet; and they, seizing the occasion, celebrated their gods and the victories won under their auspices, not without mockery of the true and eternal God. Many things of this kind happen today, whenever the faithful worshippers of Christ suffer some defeat and are given over to the lust of their enemies. Then one may hear those voices: "Now it is plain which faith is true and which religion is orthodox! Where now is that Gospel which those innovators always had in their mouths? Where is that Christ in whom alone they trusted?" etc. These and similar things (I say) are everywhere sung against the godly martyrs of Christ. But there are others, not so cruel and inhuman, who nonetheless think that Christians are the most wretched and unhappy of men, who expose themselves, for an uncertain and doubtful matter, or at least an indifferent one, to the hatred and mockery of all, and even to dire tortures and unspeakable torments. Yet no one ought to be offended by these things, since we know that the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, was fixed to the cross with similar reproaches, not to mention the ancient martyrs.

units.la: Itaque Paulum audiamus, qui quae ipse patiebatur, passiones Christi vocat: Sicut (inquit) abundant passiones Christi in nobis, ita, &c. Id vero non temere aut arroganter dicit, sed vere: eò quod afflictiones, quas Christiani homines sustinent, in Dei conspectu Christi crux siue passiones reuera sunt atq; censentur: partim quidem quòd illas propter solius Christi nomen sustinent: partim verò, quòd ipse Christus in illis affligitur. Quia enim hic caput nostrum est, & nos membra corporis eius sumus, non potest non sibi factum putare, quicquid suis factum fuerit. Fatetur hoc ipse, quando in nouissimi iudicij eiusque processus descriptione fideles & pios sic alloquitur: Venite benedicti Patris mei, possidete regnum paratum vobis à iactis fundamentis mundi. Esuriui enim, & dedistis mihi quod ederem: sitiui, & dedistis mihi potum, &c. Et rursum impijs: Maledicti, abite à me in ignem aeternum, qui paratus est diabolo & Angelis eius. Esuriui enim, & non dedistis mihi quod ederem: sitiui, & non dedistis mihi potum, &c. Quibus consentit, quod apud Prophetam de suo erga Ecclesiam suam zelo differens, inter alia dicit: Qui vos tangit, tangit pupillam oculi mei. Sed & ipse Paulus quod in praesenti dicit, id ex Christi ore didicerat, quando ad Damasci portas propter impium & crudelem in fideles conatum fulmine prostratus, illum sibi intonantem audiuit: Saul Saul, cur me persequeris? Quia ergo ab eo tempore fidus Christi minister fuerat, merito afflictiones, quibus exercebatur, Christi passiones vocat: nec se propter illas miserum aut infelicem esse putat, quin potius praecipuam felicitatis suae partem in eo collocat, quòd Dei Filius ipsum, suae crucis socium habere dignetur. Et sanè vere beati sunt quibus hoc datur, vere autem miseri & mortalium omnium infelicissimi sunt, qui dum pios hostiliter persequuntur, illum sibi hostem faciunt, cui omnis potestas data est in coelo & in terra, & qui olim poenas aeternis eorum impietatem multabit.
units.tr: Let us therefore hear Paul, who calls the sufferings which he himself endured "the sufferings of Christ": "As (he says) the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so, etc." He does not say this rashly or arrogantly, but truly: because the afflictions which Christian men endure are in the sight of God really and indeed reckoned to be the cross or sufferings of Christ, partly indeed because they endure them for the sake of the name of Christ alone, and partly because Christ himself is afflicted in them. For since he is our head and we are the members of his body, he cannot but regard as done to himself whatever is done to his own. He himself confesses this, when in describing the last judgement and its proceedings he addresses the faithful and pious thus: "Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me something to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink," etc. And again to the wicked: "Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me something to eat; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink," etc. Agreeing with this is what he says through the Prophet, speaking of his zeal for his Church: "He who touches you touches the apple of my eye." But Paul himself also learned from the mouth of Christ what he says at present, when, struck down by lightning at the gates of Damascus on account of his impious and cruel assault upon the faithful, he heard Christ thundering to him: "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" Therefore, since from that time he had been a faithful minister of Christ, he rightly calls the afflictions with which he was exercised the sufferings of Christ; nor does he think himself wretched or unhappy on account of them, but rather places the chief part of his happiness in this, that the Son of God deigns to have him as the companion of his cross. And indeed they are truly blessed to whom this is granted, but truly wretched and the most unhappy of all mortals are those who, while they hostilely persecute the godly, make for themselves an enemy in him to whom all power has been given in heaven and on earth, and who will one day punish their impiety with eternal penalties.

units.la: Elucet ergo hîc ô fideles Christi serui ingens & eximia crucis nostræ gloria, quæ sola, si dili-gentius consideretur, nos abunde consolari potes{ne vllis afflictionibus succumbamus. Merentur omnes homines, vt propter innatam naturæ vitiofitatem & pessimos, qui ex ea protuberant, fructus æternis inferorum cruciatibus puniantur: ideoq; quæcunq; patiuntur impij & à Christo alieni, hæc Dei ipsis irati argumenta, & nisi conuertantur, æternarum pœnarum præludia sunt. At pios Christi sui cultores ea gloria & honore Deus dignatur, vt quæ ipsi patiuntur in Christi passiones commutet, vt nimirum huius similes facti in cruce, imo crucis eius socij, olim eiusdem quoq; coheredes sint in cœlesti gloria. Fit hoc plerunque, quando non alia quàm Christi causa eos mundus persequitur: eoq; illustrior est hæc gloria, quando ne hostes quidem dissimulant, de fide & Euangelij doctrina agi, quam diutius ferre nec velint, nec possint. Tunc enim reuera Simeones illi sancti siunt Christiani homines, qui Filij Dei cruce post ipsum ferunt, & ad quos promissio pertinet: Vbi ego sum, ibi volo sit etiam minister meus. Item: Si cum Christo morimur, cum eodem viuemus: si cum illo sufferimus, cum eode regnabimus. At quod nam euidentius suæ bonitatis spe-cimen Deus nobis dare, aut quam gloria maiorem nobis conferre poterat? Finge Regem aliquem potentissimum, qui homini facinoroso & suspendiû sitte rotam merenti, non modò culpam omnem condonet, verumetiam equestri ordine donatum cum filio suo vnico regni hæredem in prima acie collocet, vt illic contra publicos regni hostes suæ virtutis tyrocinium siue specimen præbeat. Quis tantam Regis istius clementiâ non prædicet? Quis istum se totum Regi suo debere negaret? Quis item non gloriosa & summis votis expetenda diceret vulnera, quæ idem iste ex prælio referret? Aut num illorum ipsum iure posset pudere? Atqui eadem est omnium nostrum conditio. Omnes enim peccaueramus, & à Deo perfidâ feceramus secessionem. Omnes ergo rebelles facti extremum & æternum supplicium merebamur. At nostri misertus Deus nô solum culpam omnem condona-uit, sed eandem Filij sui vnigeniti sanguine emit, nos deniq; indignos in filiorum locum adopta-uit, & per baptismum in militiam Filij sui adscripsit, vt cum eo sub glorioso & victorioso crucis vexillo aduersus communem hostem diabolum & satellites eius dimicemus, stipendij autem loco regni sui cœlestis hæreditatem pollicetur. Quis ergo hanc plus quàm paternam illius bonitatem nô exosculetur & celebret? Aut num aliquis tam ignauus aut stolidus fuerit, vt ipsum periculi, vulnerum aut plagarum istarum pudeat, quæ ipsi cum Christo communes sunt? Hæc consideratio certè olim beatos Martyres ita cõfirmauit, vt alacri animo ad mortis supplicia accesserint, car-nifices amicè salutârint, palos & vncos exosculati sint, & Deo gratias egerint, qui isto honore ipsos dignabatur. Fuit ex horum numero Ignatius, Antiochena Ecclesiæ episcopus, qui cum Ro-mam ad bestias duceretur, fideles, qui Romæ erant, epistola ad eos ex itinere præmonuit, ne qua ratione hoc eius tam dirum supplicium impedire conarentur. Et inter alia sic scribit: Dei esse tri-ticum cupio, teriq; ac moli dentibus bestiarum, vt Deo mundus aut purus panis inueniar. Itaque ad hoc blandè allicite bestias, vt meum sepulchrum fiant, neque de meo corpore quicquam inhu-matum relinquat, quod me dormiente cuiquam graue aut molestum sit. Et rursus: O optatissimas bestias, quæ parata meum corpus expectant: quas vtinam breui tempore videam, &c. Idem ani-mus eademque sententia Magni illius Constantini fuit, qui in Nicena Synodo patrum cicatri-ces exosculabatur, quas illi ex plagis sub Diocletiano acceptis gestabant. Agnoscebat enim in his singularem Dei gratiam, qui tanto honore dignos duxerat, vt (quod Paulus noster alibi dicit) stigmata IESV CHRISTI haberent in suis corporibus.
units.tr: Here, then, O faithful servants of Christ, shines the great and remarkable glory of our cross, which alone, if it is considered more carefully, is enough to console us fully, so that we do not give way under any afflictions. All men deserve to be punished with eternal torments in hell, because of the corruption innate in our nature and the wicked fruits that spring from it. Therefore whatever the impious and those estranged from Christ suffer is a sign of God's anger against them, and, unless they are converted, a foretaste of eternal punishments. But God honours his pious worshippers of Christ with such glory and dignity that he changes what they suffer into the sufferings of Christ, so that, made like him in the cross, indeed fellow-sharers of his cross, they will also be fellow heirs of the same heavenly glory. This happens for the most part when the world persecutes them for nothing other than Christ's cause, and this glory is all the more illustrious when even their enemies do not conceal that the matter at issue is faith and the doctrine of the Gospel, which they neither wish nor are able to bear for long. For then truly those holy Simons become Christians, who carry the cross of the Son of God after him, and to whom the promise pertains: "Where I am, there my minister shall be also" (John 12). Likewise: "If we die with Christ, we shall also live with him; if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him" (2 Tim. 2). But what clearer proof of his goodness could God give us, or what greater glory could he bestow upon us? Imagine some most powerful king who, to a wicked man deserving the gallows and the wheel, not only pardons all his guilt, but also, having made him a knight and having placed his only son, the heir of the kingdom, beside him, puts him in the front line, so that there he may show a proof or training of his valour against the public enemies of the kingdom. Who would not proclaim the clemency of such a king? Who would deny that he owes himself wholly to his king? Who would not also call the wounds that the same man brings back from battle glorious and to be sought with the highest desire? Or could he rightly be ashamed of them? Yet the condition of all of us is the same. For we had all sinned and had made a treacherous departure from God. Therefore, having become rebels, we all deserved the extreme and eternal punishment. But God, having mercy on us, not only pardoned all our guilt, but also redeemed it with the blood of his only-begotten Son; finally, having found us unworthy, he adopted us into the place of sons, and through baptism enrolled us in the army of his Son, so that under the glorious and victorious banner of the cross we might fight with him against the common enemy, the devil, and his henchmen, and he promises as our pay the inheritance of his heavenly kingdom. Who, then, would not embrace and celebrate this goodness of his, which is more than paternal? Or would anyone be so cowardly or foolish as to be ashamed of the danger, the wounds, and the blows that are common to him and Christ? This consideration certainly so strengthened the blessed Martyrs of old that they approached the punishments of death with a cheerful spirit, greeted the executioners in a friendly way, kissed the stakes and hooks, and gave thanks to God, who deemed them worthy of such honour. Among their number was Ignatius, bishop of the Church of Antioch, who, when he was being led to Rome to the beasts, warned the faithful who were at Rome, in a letter written to them on the journey, not to try in any way to prevent his dreadful punishment. And among other things he writes thus: "I desire to be the wheat of God, and to be ground by the teeth of the beasts, so that I may be found pure bread for God. So gently entice the beasts to become my tomb, and let them leave nothing of my body undisturbed, lest I be a burden or trouble to anyone when I am asleep." And again: "O most desired beasts, which stand ready to receive my body; would that I might see them soon, etc." The same spirit and the same opinion belonged to that great Constantine, who at the Nicene Synod kissed the scars of the fathers, which they bore from the wounds received under Diocletian. For he recognised in them the singular grace of God, who had thought them worthy of such honour that (as our Paul says elsewhere) they might bear the marks of the Lord Jesus Christ in their bodies.

units.la: Etsi verò ista proprie ad eos pertineant, qui propter fidem in Christum eiusq; professionem liberiorem affliguntur, debet tamen doctrina atq; consolatio ista ad omnes alias quoq; afflictiones extendi. Nam siue morbis infestemur, siue cum egestate conflictemur, siue propter admissa scelent pœnas debitas luamus, ex his quoq; crucem Christi nobis fabricare possumus, si ea propter ipsum patienter feramus, & exemplum, quo is nobis præiuit, imitemur. Eius enim hæc regula est, vt su-pra diximus: Si quis vult post me venire, abneget semetipsum, & tollat crucem suam quotidie, & sequatur me. Crux autem vniuscuiusq; dicuntur aduersa, quæ Deus cuiq; ferenda imponit. Itaq; si in his patientes sumus ex fide, eò quòd æternus Dei Filius his grauiora & duriora propter nos passus est, insons nimirum pro sontibus, iustus pro iniustis, tunc Christi crucem ferre dicemur. Cur enim hoc aliquis neget, cum & in eius solius merito omnem salutis fiduciam repositam habeamus, & exempli eius vestigijs insistamus? Hinc ergo consolationem communem petant omnes Christi cultores, quocunque tandem tentationis aut aduersorum genere exerceantur.
units.tr: Although these things properly pertain to those who are afflicted more severely for their faith in Christ and their profession of it, yet this teaching and consolation ought to be extended to all other afflictions as well. For whether we are troubled by illnesses, or struggle with poverty, or pay the penalties due for sins we have committed, we can also make the cross of Christ for ourselves out of these, if we bear them patiently for his sake and imitate the example that he has gone before us in. For this is his rule, as we said above: "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me" (Luke 9). Now the adversities that God lays upon each person to bear are called that person's cross. So if we are patient in these things out of faith, because the eternal Son of God suffered heavier and harder things for us, innocent for the guilty, righteous for the unrighteous, then we shall be said to carry the cross of Christ. For why would anyone deny this, since we have placed all our confidence of salvation in his merit alone, and we tread in the footsteps of his example? Let all the worshippers of Christ, therefore, seek from this common consolation, whatever kind of temptation or adversity they may be exercised by.

units.la: At quia caro nostra infirmior est, quàm vt hæc ei semper possint sufficere, prodest ipsissimum omnis consolationis fontem atque authorem nouisse (quod tertium huius loci caput est) vt intelligamus, quò nos recurrere oporteat, vt aduersus omnes tentationum insultus confirmemur. Est is solus verus & æternus Deus, cuius bonitatem Paulus hoc loco multiuariàm commendat. Initio enim eum Patrem misericordiarum, & Deum omnis consolationis dicit. Deinde se inter afflictiones omnis generis ab illo consolationes solidas percipere testatur, idque in eum finem, vt alios in quauis tentatione consolari possit. His in præsenti addit: Sicut abundant passiones Christi in nobis, ita per Christum abundat etiam consolatio nostra. Sensus est, Deum consolationes suas nobis augere & vberiores facere pro ratione nobis imminentium afflictionum. Id verò non ex suo cerebro confinxit Apostolus, sed ex veteri Scriptura desumpsit, vbi sic canit diuinus ille Psaltes: Pro æstu multarum cogitationum intra me, recrearunt animam meam consolationes tuæ. Finis autem & vsus istorum nobis hic esse debet, ne alibi quàm apud vnum Deum consolationem, opem aut consilium quæramus, si quid grauius nobis incumbit. Nam quæcunque in rerum natura sunt, vtut præclara & magnifica appareant, fluxa tamen & caduca sunt. Omnis caro fœnum (ex Dei mandato clamat Propheta) & omnis gloria carnis, flos agri. Ieremias verò maledictum pronuntiat eum, qui homini fidit, & carnem facit brachium suum. Dauidis item Regis potentissimi admonitio est: Ne fidatis principibus, filijs hominum, in quibus non est salus: Nam vbi animam efflauerit, reuertetur corpus eius in terram suam, & tunc intercidunt omnes cogitationes eius. Et his mox addit: Beatus autem, qui Deum Iacobi habet in auxilijs, & spem in Domino Deo suo: Qui cælum & terram fecit, mare & omnia quæ in eis sunt, quique custodit æternum veritatem. Etenim solus ille Dominus exercituum est, qui creaturis omnibus pro suo nutu imperat, & proinde solus etiam in omni necessitate nobis subuenire potest. Idem bonus ille & clementissimus Pater est, qui etiamsi non semper ex aduersis & periculis liberet, semper tamen nos consolatur atque confirmat, ne in illis succumbamus, neque nos (vt alibi dictum est) supra vires tentari finit. 1. Corinth. 10.
units.tr: But because our flesh is too weak for these things always to be enough for it, it is useful to know the very source and author of all consolation (which is the third head of this place), so that we may understand where we ought to run in order to be strengthened against all the assaults of temptations. He is the only true and eternal God, whose goodness Paul commends here in many ways. For at the beginning he calls him the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation. Then he testifies that amid afflictions of every kind he receives solid consolations from him, and that to this end: that he may be able to console others in any temptation. To these he adds for the present: "As the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds." The meaning is that God increases his consolations for us and makes them more abundant in proportion to the afflictions threatening us. Now the Apostle did not invent this from his own brain, but took it from the old Scripture, where that divine Psalmist sings thus: "In the heat of many thoughts within me, your consolations have refreshed my soul." But the purpose and use of these things here ought to be that, if anything weighs more heavily upon us, we seek comfort, help, or counsel nowhere else than from the one God. For whatever things are in nature, however splendid and magnificent they appear, are nevertheless fleeting and perishable. "All flesh is grass" (the Prophet cries out by God's command), "and all the glory of flesh is the flower of the field." Jeremiah, moreover, pronounces a curse upon him who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm. There is also a warning from David, the most powerful king: "Do not trust in princes, in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation; for when he breathes out his spirit, his body returns to its earth, and then all his thoughts perish." And soon after he adds: "Blessed is he who has the God of Jacob for his help, and his hope in the Lord his God, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them, who keeps truth for ever." For that Lord alone is the Lord of hosts, who commands all creatures at his will, and therefore alone can help us in every need. He is that good and most merciful Father who, even if he does not always deliver us from adversities and dangers, always consoles and strengthens us, so that we do not give way under them, nor does he allow us (as was said elsewhere) to be tempted beyond our strength. 1 Cor. 10.

units.la: Exempla, quæ hoc probant, in Scripturis plurima occurrunt. Prodeat inter ea primus Abrahamus, pater credentium, cuius tota vita afflictissima fuit. Educitur ex natali solo, vt exul & peregrinus fit, qui domi inter suos splendide viuere poterat. Mox moritur pater Thare, quem peregrinationis suæ comitem fidissimum sibi delegerat. Vbi verò terram à Deo monstratam attigit, fame exceptus in Ægyptum descendere compellitur. Illic vxor dilectissima rapitur à Rege non sine manifesto pudicitiæ periculo. In Chanaan reuersum iurgia seruorum à Lotho nepote suo cogunt discedere: quod ei procul dubio acerbissimum fuit, cum ille solus esset, qui exilij molestias atq; curas in gente barbara lenire posset. Deinde hostilibus armis terra vicina petitur, & Lothus captus recuperatur. Accedunt his turbæ domesticæ propter Saræ sterilitatem, & in extremam senectam differtur feminis promissi natiuitas. Tandem cum in Isaaco spem omnē haberet fundatam, illum propria manu immolare iubetur: quæ tentatio plus quàm mille gladijs animum paternum vulnerare poterat. Sequitur mox coniugis charissimæ obitus. Sed inter omnia hæc abundauit consolatio, quam Deus adhibuit, & qua confirmatus his omnibus superior factus est. Idem de Isaaco & Iacobo dicere possumus, quibus rectè Iobum coniunxeris & Dauidem, qui cum foris & intus grauissimè tentaretur, Dei tamen consolationibus sese confirmari ac sustentari sensit. Neque alia est Noui Testamenti ratio, in quo gratiæ & bonitatis Dei iubar nobis propius atque vberius affulget. Et extant illic dulcissimæ Christi promissiones: Venite ad me qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego refocillabo vos. Si quis sitit, veniat ad me. Non relinquam vos orphanos, veniam ad vos. Et rogabo Patrem, qui alium consolatorem dabit vobis, Spiritum Veritatis. Ecce ego vobiscum sum vsque in consummationem seculi, &c.
units.tr: Examples that prove this occur in great numbers in the Scriptures. First among them comes Abraham, the father of believers, whose whole life was full of affliction. He is led out of his native land and becomes an exile and a stranger, though at home among his own people he could have lived in splendour. Soon his father Terah dies, the most faithful companion he had chosen for his journey. When at last he reaches the land shown him by God, he is received by famine and forced to go down into Egypt. There his most beloved wife is seized by the king, not without a clear danger to her chastity. When he returns to Canaan, quarrels among the herdsmen force him to part from his nephew Lot, which was undoubtedly most bitter to him, since Lot was the only one who could ease the troubles and cares of exile among a barbarous people. Then the neighbouring land is attacked by enemy arms, and Lot is taken captive and recovered. To these are added troubles in his household over Sarah's barrenness, and the birth of the promised seed is deferred into extreme old age. At last, when he had placed all his hope in Isaac, he is commanded to sacrifice him with his own hand; this trial could wound a father's heart more than a thousand swords. Soon follows the death of his dearest wife. Yet amid all these things the consolation that God supplied abounded, and by it he was strengthened and made superior to them all. The same we may say of Isaac and Jacob, to whom we may rightly join Job and David, who, though he was most grievously tested both outwardly and inwardly, nevertheless felt himself strengthened and sustained by God's consolations. The order of the New Testament is no different, in which the radiance of God's grace and goodness shines upon us more closely and more richly. And there stand Christ's sweetest promises: "Come to me, all you who labour and are heavy laden, and I will refresh you." "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me." "I will not leave you orphans; I will come to you." "And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Comforter, the Spirit of truth." "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age," etc.

units.la: Ista verò simul nos officij nostri admonent, vt bonitatem istam Dei agnoscamus, & hac eiusdem gratia contenti simus, neue ei temere præscribamus, licet non semper votis nostris annuat,
units.tr: These things, however, at the same time remind us of our duty: that we should acknowledge this goodness of God and be content with this grace of his, and not rashly prescribe terms to him, even though he does not always grant our prayers.

units.la: {a} In afflictionibus quo confugere debeamus & interdum nos durius tractare videatur. Docebit hoc infra Cap. duodecimo Paulus proprio exemplo, vbi plura de hac re dicendi locus dabitur. Hoc solum nunc monuisse sufficiat, eos qui Deo praescribere audent, eundem simul tentare, quod scelus grauissimum esse, non vno loco Scripturae docent. Hic igitur imprimis opus est obedientia fidei, qua illum (vt Dauid docuit) expetemus cum silentio & spe. Et cur id graue nobis videatur, quando cum afflictionibus tam multa tamen illustria diuinae bonitatis argumenta concurrunt? Etenim per se magnum est, quod Deus nos propter nomen suum affligi vult. Maius, quod afflictos respicit, quos plerique fastidiunt. Maximum, quod per eosdem de mundo & eius principe diabolo triumphat.
units.tr: {a} In afflictions, to what we ought to flee, and sometimes he seems to deal with us too harshly. Paul will teach this in the twelfth chapter below by his own example, where there will be occasion to say more about this matter. For now it is enough to have given this warning: that those who dare to prescribe to God and at the same time to test him commit a most grievous sin, as Scripture teaches in more than one place. Here, therefore, what is chiefly needed is the obedience of faith, by which we shall wait for him (as David taught) in silence and hope. And why should this seem hard to us, when so many illustrious tokens of divine goodness run alongside the afflictions? For it is in itself a great thing that God wishes us to be afflicted for his name's sake. Greater still is that he looks upon the afflicted, whom most people despise. Greatest of all is that through them he triumphs over the world and its prince, the devil.

units.la: At quia nos fere impatientiores facit, quod ea sola spectamus, quae carni dura & acerba sunt, neglectis bonis, quorum nobis afflictiones causa sunt, vtile fuerit earum fructus inspicere, & mox patebit, in illis praeclarissimarum virtutum materiam proponi, ex quibus tota vitae Christianae summa dependet. Comprehendit has Paulus ad Romanos sic scribens: Gloriamur sub spe gloriae Dei, neque id solum, verumetiam gloriamur in afflictionibus, scientes quod afflictio patientiam efficiat, patientia vero experientiam, experientia autem spem: porro spes non pudefacit, quod charitas Dei effusa sit in cordibus nostris per Spiritum sanctum, qui datus est nobis. Primus afflictionum fructus patientia esse dicitur, quia huius materiam nobis praebent, neque sine illis hac locum habere posset. Est autem patientiae virtus praestantissima, vt quae nos omnibus aduersis superiores facit, & in qua Christo teste, animas nostras possidemus. Patientiae fructus siue proles est (vt sic loquar) experientia, quae nouis quotidie exemplis Dei bonitatem nobis commendat, nosq; in certa eius fiducia confirmat. Experientia haec spem parit, qua constanti & intrepido animo promissam nobis a Deo opem expectamus: quando eius fidem toties experti de illa porro dubitare non possumus. Solet enim ex anteactis argumentari fides (vt alibi Dauidis exemplo docuimus) eo quod Deum semper sui similem esse nouit. At hac ratione concepta spes non pudefacit, quia non lubrico fundamento, sed aeterna Dei Veritate nititur, quae infallibilis est: dilectione item eiusdem plus quam paterna, quam inexhaustam esse non Scriptura modo, sed ipsa quoq; rerum experientia testatur. His adde, quod afflictiones vitae & morum emendationi seruiunt, quod humiles & modestos reddunt, & superbia cristas deprimunt, & dilectionis mutua fomenta praebent, quae tunc maxime locum habent, quando vel nos alieno auxilio opus habemus, aut nostram operam ab aliis requiri audimus. Itaque quando aduersis vndique premimur, tunc meminerimus nos in Dei schola siue palaestra versari, qui nos ad omnia vitae Christianae officia erudire statuerit. Quis vero id indignius ferat? Aut quis non agnoscat in eo Dei bonitatem, quando se nouis quotidie viribus fulciri sentit?
units.tr: But because we are for the most part made more impatient by looking only at those things which are harsh and bitter to the flesh, while neglecting the good things for which our afflictions are the cause, it will be useful to examine their fruits, and soon it will become plain that in them is set forth the matter of the most excellent virtues, on which the whole sum of the Christian life depends. Paul sums these up in writing to the Romans: "We glory in hope of the glory of God, and not only so, but we also glory in afflictions, knowing that affliction produces patience, patience experience, and experience hope; and hope does not put us to shame, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us." The first fruit of afflictions is said to be patience, because they supply us with its matter, and without them patience could have no place. Patience is a most outstanding virtue, since it makes us superior to all adversities, and by it, Christ being witness, we possess our souls. The offspring, so to speak, of patience is experience, which day by day commends God's goodness to us with fresh examples and confirms us in a sure trust in him. This experience brings forth hope, by which with a steadfast and fearless mind we await the help promised us by God; since we have so often found his faithfulness, we cannot afterwards doubt it. For faith is wont to reason from past events (as we have shown elsewhere by the example of David), because it knows that God is always like himself. But hope conceived on this ground does not put us to shame, because it rests not on a slippery foundation but on the eternal truth of God, which is infallible; and likewise on his love, more than fatherly, which Scripture and also the very experience of things attests to be inexhaustible. Add to these that afflictions serve the amendment of life and morals, that they make us humble and modest, cast down the crests of pride, and provide the mutual warmth of love, which is especially in play when we need the help of others, or hear that our own labour is required by others. Therefore, when we are pressed on every side by adversities, let us remember that we are in God's school or wrestling-ground, which he has determined to train us for all the duties of the Christian life. Who indeed would bear this with indignation? Or who would not recognise in it the goodness of God, when he feels himself strengthened with fresh powers every day?

units.la: Etsi vero ista passim in Scripturis tradantur, tanta est tamen carnis nostrae infirmitas, vt facile labascamus aut vacillemus, si quando afflictiones graviores & frequentiores incidunt. Etenim si nostram conditionem cum Dei maiestate, omnipotentia, iustitia & seueritate conferamus, tantus animis nostris terror oboritur, vt neque Dei promissionibus fidere, neq; ex veteribus exemplis consolationem petere possimus, eo quod neque haec neque illas ad nos putemus pertinere. Quapropter Mediatore nobis opus est, cuius fiducia niti possimus. Hunc Paulus nobis ceu digito monstrat, dum consolationem nostram per CHRISTVM abundare scribit. Et hunc quidem solum nominat, eo quod extra eum nihil est, quod in isto carnis fluctuantis certamine nos confirmare possit. Hic enim solus is est, de quo Pater caelitus pronuntiauit: Hic est Filius ille meus dilectus, in quo placatus sum. Ideo alibi dicebat Paulus, Vnus Deus, vnus Mediator Dei & hominum homo IESVS CHRISTVS. In hunc ergo nos respicere conuenit, quoties inter afflictionum assultus conscientias quoque nostras grauius tentari sentimus. Nam vt mox sequitur, hic ille est, in quo omnes promissiones sunt Etiam & Amen. Itaque si in mentem tibi veniat, te hominem miserum, infirmum & mortalem coram Dei Maiestate comparere aut consistere non posse: mox id etiam animo reputa, Dei Filium carnem nostram in personae vnitatem assumpsisse, & eandem peractio nostrae redemptionis negotio, in caelos subuectam ad Patris dexteram collocauisse, vt nobis aditum pararet ad thronum gratiae, adeoq; certos faceret, nostrae etiam carni aliquando in caelis atque ipso Dei conspectu locum fore. Quod si conscientia te accusat, indignum esse clamet, quem Deus respiciat: rursus ad Christum recurrito, qui peccatis grauatos ad se inuitat, seq; vt illos seruaret in mundum venisse docet. Similiter, si Crucis scandalum obijciatur, vt te propter illam Deo minus gratum & acceptum esse cogites, hic quoque in Christum respice, qui non solùm praedixit quid in hoc mundo passuri simus, verumetiam exemplo suo nobis praeiuit, & quascunque ferimus afflictiones proprio sanguine consecrauit, ne porrò Dei irati argumenta censeantur. Haec si probè considerentur, mox animis nostris pax Dei affulgebit, quae omnem huius mundi intellectum superat, eoq; efficacior est, quò magis omni aduersorum genere premimur. Quò Ioannes Apostolus respexit, quando fidem dixit nostram esse victoriam: de ea nimirum fide loquens, qua IESVM CHRISTVM apprehendimus, & qua patres olim ea superarunt, quae humanis viribus perfici non potuissent, vt ad Hebraeos capite 11. multis exemplis docetur. Arguit hoc eorum superstitionem, qui in necessitatibus, relicto Christo ad Divos coelites, ceu patronos & Mediatores confugiunt. Atqui hos suo seculo iam defunctos esse constat, vt de Dauide Paulus loquitur: nunc autem exuti curis omnibus in coelo beati & felices agunt. Quod verò ex illis ad nos redit, id omne doctrina & exemplo eorum comprehenditur. Illam ergo audiamus, & eorundem exemplum imitati, patienter feramus huius vitae incommoda, fiduciam verò omnem collocemus in Deo per IESVM CHRISTVM, qui vt fidus noster apud Patrem Mediator est, sic petra quoque inuicta est, aduersus quam neportae quidem inferorum praevalere possunt. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Although these things are indeed handed down throughout the Scriptures, our flesh is nevertheless so weak that we easily totter or waver whenever heavier and more frequent afflictions befall us. For if we compare our condition with the majesty, omnipotence, justice and severity of God, such terror arises in our minds that we can neither trust God's promises nor seek consolation from the examples of old, because we think neither these nor those pertain to us. Therefore we need a Mediator on whom we can rest our trust. Paul points to him for us, as it were with his finger, when he writes that our consolation abounds through Christ. And he names this one alone, because outside him there is nothing that can strengthen us in this struggle of the wavering flesh. For he alone is the one of whom the Father proclaimed from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Therefore elsewhere Paul said, "One God, one Mediator between God and men, the man Jesus Christ." To him, then, we ought to look whenever amid the assaults of affliction we feel our consciences too severely tested. For as the passage goes on to say, he is the one in whom all the promises are "Yes, and Amen." So if it comes into your mind that you, a wretched, weak and mortal man, cannot appear or stand before the majesty of God, immediately consider this too: that the Son of God assumed our flesh into the unity of his person, and, having completed the work of our redemption, carried it up into heaven and placed it at the right hand of the Father, in order to prepare for us access to the throne of grace, and so to make us certain that our flesh too will one day have a place in heaven and in the very sight of God. But if conscience accuses you and cries out that you are unworthy that God should look upon you, run back again to Christ, who invites to himself those burdened with sins, and teaches that he came into the world to save them. Likewise, if the scandal of the Cross is thrown in your face, so that you think you are less pleasing and acceptable to God because of it, look here too to Christ, who not only foretold what we were to suffer in this world, but also went before us in his own example, and consecrated with his own blood whatever afflictions we bear, lest they be reckoned signs of an angry God. If these things are duly considered, the peace of God will soon shine upon our minds, which surpasses all understanding of this world, and it is the more effective the more we are pressed by every kind of adversity. To this the Apostle John looked when he said that our faith is our victory: speaking, of course, of that faith by which we JESUS CHRIST lay hold of, and by which the fathers of old overcame those things which could not be accomplished by human strength, as is taught by many examples in Hebrews chapter 11. This refutes the superstition of those who, in their needs, leaving Christ, flee to the heavenly saints as patrons and mediators. Yet it is certain that these have already departed this life in their age, as Paul speaks of David; now, freed from all cares, they live blessed and happy in heaven. What comes back to us from them is all comprehended in their teaching and example. Let us therefore hear that, and imitating their example, patiently bear the discomforts of this life; but let us place all our trust in God through JESUS CHRIST, who, as our faithful Mediator with the Father, is also an unconquered rock, against which the gates of hell cannot prevail. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA III.
units.tr: HOMILY III.
