units.la: Siue autem premimur, id fit pro vestra consolatione ac salute, quae efficitur in tolerantia earundem passionum, quibus & nos afficimur: Siue consolationem accipimus, id fit pro vestra consolatione ac salute: Et spes nostra firma est de vobis, quod sciamus, vos, sicuti socij estis passionum, ita etiam socios fore consolationis.
units.tr: Whether we are afflicted or comforted, it is for your consolation and salvation. Our affliction works your consolation and salvation through the patient endurance of the same sufferings that we also undergo, and our comfort is likewise for your consolation and salvation. Our hope for you is firm, because we know that just as you share in our sufferings, so you will also share in our consolation.

units.la: Quemadmodum homo natura à Cruce & afflictionibus abhorret: ita ferè de illis maligne iudicat, quos grauius illis tentari, & cum assiduis aerumnis plus quam alios confligere videt. Accidit hoc apud Corinthios Paulo Apostolo. Vt enim hic in propagando regno Christi plus alijs Apostolis laborauit: ita hostes quoq; plures ei excitauit Satan, quorum insidijs, calumnijs & aperta vi undiq; petitus & grauissime exagitatus est. Cum autem eò maioris fieri deberet, ex eo aemuli eius calumniandi occasionem arripiebant, vt apud rudes & rerum imperitos, suspectum facerent, quasi ipse sua importunitate turbarum & seditionum materiam siue occasionem praeberet. Haec igitur causa eum mouit, vt epistolam hanc ab afflictionibus & periculis suis exordiatur: quarum rationem ita reddit, vt primò Dei gratiam in illis elucere demonstret: deinde se propter illas amore potius quàm odio aut contemptu dignum esse doceat, quando propter ipsos haec omnia patiatur, ad quos praecipua afflictionum suarum vtilitas redeat. Id nuper in genere docuit, quando à gratiarum actione exorsus est, vt vel ita demonstraret, quam parum aduersis huius seculi moueatur. Hoc ipsum verò nunc diligentius illustrat, & propius applicat ad eorum institutionem.
units.tr: Human nature shrinks from the Cross and from afflictions, and so people commonly judge harshly those whom they see tried more severely and struggling with constant hardships more than others. This happened to the Apostle Paul among the Corinthians. For just as he laboured more than the other Apostles in spreading the kingdom of Christ, so Satan stirred up more enemies against him, and by their plots, slanders and open violence he was assailed on every side and harassed most grievously. Yet the more his work grew, the more his rivals seized the chance to slander him, so that among the simple and inexperienced they might make him look suspect, as if he himself, by his troublesome conduct, were the source and occasion of tumults and sedition. This, then, is what moved him to begin this letter with his afflictions and dangers. He gives an account of them in such a way that, first, he shows the grace of God shining forth in them; second, he teaches that on account of them he is worthy of love rather than hatred or contempt, since he suffers all these things for their sake, and the chief benefit of his afflictions returns to them. He taught this in general terms recently, when he began with thanksgiving, so as to show how little he is moved by the adversities of this age. Now he illustrates it more carefully and applies it more closely to their instruction.

units.la: Siue autem premimur (inquit) id fit pro vestra consolatione ac salute, &c. Prius consolationes cum afflictionibus coniunxerat, vt illas nunquam defuturas esse doceret. Nunc de singulis seorsim agit: quia etiamsi nunquam deßt omnis consolatio, eadem tamen non semper sensu carnis percipitur, neque ita manifeste ab omnibus agnoscitur. Imò frequenter electis quoque accidit, vt Deum sui oblitum esse arbitrentur. Hinc enim voces illae emanant: Quousq; obliuiscēris mei Domine? num perpetuo? Quousq; faciem tuam à me abscondis? Item: Deus meus, Deus meus, cur me deseruisti? Vt longè abes à salute mea, à verbis rugitus mei? Deus meus, inuoco per diem, & non respondes, &c. Nec mirum his tentationibus sanctos infestari, quando Christum pro assum‐ptae humanae infirmitatis ratione similes querelas in cruce iudisse scimus. Ut ergo huic tentationi remedium adhibeat Paulus, docet, afflictiones per se salutares esse, etiamsi absque consolatione considerentur. Id autem proprio exemplo demonstrat, de iis loquens, quae ipse perpetiebatur.
units.tr: "Whether we are oppressed," he says, "it is for your consolation and salvation," and so on. Previously he had joined consolations with afflictions, to teach that the consolations would never be lacking. Now he deals with each separately, because although all consolation never fails, it is not always perceived by the feeling of the flesh, nor is it so clearly recognised by everyone. Indeed it often happens even to the elect that they think God has forgotten them. From this come those words: "How long wilt thou forget me, O Lord? for ever?" and "How long wilt thou hide thy face from me?" Likewise: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" and "Why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring? O my God, I cry in the day, and thou answerest not," and so on. Nor is it surprising that the saints are troubled by these temptations, since we know that Christ, according to the nature of the human weakness he had assumed, uttered similar complaints on the cross. So, to supply a remedy for this temptation, Paul teaches that afflictions are salutary in themselves, even when they are considered without consolation. He demonstrates this by his own example, speaking of those things which he himself was suffering.

units.la: Si premimur aut affligimur (inquit) id fit pro vestra consolatione ac salute, quae efficitur in tolerantia earundem passionum, quibus et nos afficimur, vel quas et nos patimur. Potest hoc membrum bifariam exponi. Primo, Paulum et reliquos Apostolos, quaecunque perpessi sunt, ideo perpessos esse, ut salutem, quam nobis Dei Filius suae mortis merito peperit, toti mundo annuntiarent, et ea praedicatione afflictis conscientiis consolationem veram atque solidam afferrent. Etenim constat, mundum illis non aliam ob causam infensum fuisse: cum neque reipub. formas mutarint, neque scelera ulla designaverint, hoc autem unum egerint, ut quam plurimos Christo adducerent. Et quoad Paulum, Iudaei hunc ubique gentium persecuti sunt, quod patribus ipsorum promissam salutem gentibus quoque praedicaret, quas illi pro prophanis et a Deo alienis habebant. Ob hanc causam Lystris seditionem excitarunt, ut postea apud Corinthios quoque, sicuti Lucas in Actis scribit. Haec item ratio illos movit, ut eundem in templo caperent, occisuri quoque, nisi Centurionis Romani armis servatus fuisset. Et de eo ipse in priori ad Thessalonicenses conqueritur. Hanc istius loci expositionem Chrysostomus sequitur, cui si insistere libeat, sensus hic erit: Iniqui nimis in nos sunt, qui propter persecutiones, quibus assidue exercemur, nos suspectos habent, aut ministerium nostrum calumniantur, quasi id Deo minus gratum aut acceptum sit. Etenim omnia ista nos immerentes et nullius scelieris conscii propter vos sufferimus: et nisi forti atque invicto animo sustineremus quaecunque mundus et huius princeps Satan nobis obiciunt, nunquam vobis salus annuntiata esset, et iampridem in tenebris superstitionum atque peccatorum laqueis perijissetis, &c.
units.tr: "If we are oppressed or afflicted," he says, "it is for your consolation and salvation, which is brought about in the endurance of the same sufferings which we also undergo." This clause can be explained in two ways. First, that Paul and the other Apostles endured whatever they suffered so that they might proclaim to the whole world the salvation which the Son of God won for us by the merit of his death, and that by this preaching they might bring true and solid consolation to troubled consciences. For it is certain that the world was hostile to them for no other reason: they did not change the forms of government, nor did they plot any crimes, but did only this, that they might lead as many people as possible to Christ. And as for Paul, the Jews persecuted him everywhere among the Gentiles, because he preached to the Gentiles also the salvation promised to their fathers, whom the Jews regarded as profane and alien to God. For this reason they stirred up a riot at Lystra, and afterwards also among the Corinthians, as Luke writes in the Acts. This same motive moved them to seize him in the temple, intending to kill him too, had he not been rescued by the arms of a Roman centurion. Paul complains about this himself in his first letter to the Thessalonians. Chrysostom follows this explanation of the passage, and if we care to adhere to it, the sense here will be: "Those people are too unjust towards us who regard us with suspicion because of the persecutions with which we are constantly exercised, or who slander our ministry as if it were less pleasing or acceptable to God. For we suffer all these things undeservedly, and conscious of no crime, for your sake. And unless we endured with a strong and unconquered spirit whatever the world and its prince Satan throw at us, the salvation would never have been announced to you, and long ago you would have perished in the darkness of superstitions and in the snares of sin," and so on.

units.la: Arguit ille sensus mundi huius ingratitudinem, qui plerunque iis infensus est, qui pro eius salute dies noctesque excubant, laborant, periclitantur: imo quod turpius est, quae illi propter ipsius salutem perpetiuntur, eis exprobrat, quasi sceleribus suis ea meruerint. Venit hic mihi in mentem historia siue fabula, quae ad arguendam improbitatem hanc probe convenit. Erat quidam uxor morosa et infida, quam tamen ille ardentius, quam ipsa mereretur amabat. Accidit ut contra leges noctu per plateas discurrens ab excubitoribus publicis comprehenderetur, et tristino die iudicum sententia damnaretur, ut lapidem non parui ponderis catena alligatum cum publica infamia et totius populi ludibrijs per urbem traheret. Fuit hoc marito grave admodum, et proinde misericordia propositum motus a magistratu precibus impetravit, ut uxoris supplicium in se transferret, sed ipsum pro illa infamem faceret. Quam vero illa pro tam inofficioso officio gratiam ei retulit? Teffimam sane. Nam quoties inter ipsos iurgium incidit, eam quoque liberius admoneret maritus, mox illa ei lapidem illum infamem exprobrabat, quem cum omnium ludibrio per urbem traxisset. At quid aliud faciunt, qui hodie persecutiones, exilia, egestatem et alia adversa verbi Dei administris exprobrant? Cur enim hi illa sustinent? Non aliam certe ob causam, quam quod omnium saluti consulere volunt, et ideo superstitiones, idololatriam et scelera liberius arguunt. Quod autem iste sit, hoc ipsum omnibus seculis factum esse constat bonis atque fidis principibus, qui in Repub. feruanda fideles fuerunt. Quo loco Mosem, Samuelem, Davidem, Ezechiam, et ex prophanis historijs Themistoclem, Miltiadem, Camillum, Scipiones, Ciceronem cum innumeris aliis producere poteramus. Ex quibus omnibus apparet, Deum olim verissime per Hoseam dixisse: Perditio tua ex te est, o Israel, ex me autem salus tua. Neminem ergo infelicis mundi ingratitudo, qua etiam hodie antiquum ingenium refert, offendat: quin discant potius singuli officium facere, ad quod destinati sunt, retributionem vero a Deo expectent, qui remunerator est iustus et liberalis. Et haec quidem de primo huius loci sensu dicta sunt.
units.tr: That sense exposes the ingratitude of this world, which is generally hostile to those who keep watch, labour and endanger themselves day and night for its salvation. Worse still, it reproaches them for the sufferings they undergo for its salvation, as if they had deserved them by their own crimes. Here there comes to my mind a story, or fable, which is well suited to exposing this wickedness. There was a certain man with a fretful and unfaithful wife, whom nevertheless he loved more ardently than she deserved. It happened that she, running about the streets at night contrary to the laws, was seized by the public watchmen, and on a gloomy day was condemned by the judges' sentence to drag a stone of no small weight, fastened by a chain, through the city, with public disgrace and the mockery of the whole people. This was very grievous to the husband, and so, moved by pity, he obtained from the magistrate, by his entreaties, that he might take the punishment of his wife upon himself and bear the infamy in her place. But how did she repay him for such a dutiful service? Certainly with the greatest ingratitude. For whenever a quarrel arose between them, and the husband rebuked her a little more freely, she at once threw in his face that infamous stone which she had dragged through the city to the mockery of all. But what else do those people do today who reproach the ministers of God's Word with persecutions, exiles, poverty and other adversities? For why do these men endure them? Surely for no other reason than that they want to consult the salvation of all, and therefore they more freely denounce superstitions, idolatry and crimes. That this is so has been true in every age of good and faithful rulers, who were faithful in preserving the commonwealth. Here we could bring forward Moses, Samuel, David, Hezekiah, and from profane histories Themistocles, Miltiades, Camillus, the Scipios, Cicero, along with countless others. From all these it is plain that God long ago said most truly through Hosea: "O Israel, thy destruction is of thyself; but in me is thy help." Let no one, therefore, be offended by the ingratitude of the unhappy world, which even today shows its ancient character; rather let each learn to do the duty for which he has been appointed, and let him expect his recompense from God, who is a just and generous rewarder. And these things have been said about the first sense of this passage.

units.la: Quoad alterum, de exemplo possunt haec verba intelligi, ut se cum reliquis Apostolis ideo affligi ac premi dicat, ut ipsorum exemplo Christiani homines confirmentur, et consolationem habeant, si quid simile ipsis quoque accidat. Ut enim Imperatoris labores et diligentes vigiliae militibus animum addunt, ut ipsi quoque ad quaevis subeunda alacriores sint: Ita vulgus Christianorum stianorum nouas fidei & patientiæ vires concipit, si doctores atque duces suos ad quiduis pro Christo ferendum paratos & intrepidos esse videat. Et huic sensui fauet, quod adijcit: Quæ salus efficitur in tolerantia earundem passionum, quas etiam nos perpetimur. Nam ita dicere videtur: Dum meos labores atque ærumnas cernitis, meo exemplo haud dubiè confirmamini, vt si quid si- mile vobis accidat, id patienter sufferatis, & sic (quod olim Christus monuit) in patientia vestra possideatis animas vestras.
units.tr: As for the second sense, these words may be understood as referring to example: Paul says that he is afflicted and oppressed together with the other Apostles so that Christians may be strengthened by their example and have comfort, should anything similar happen to them too. For just as the labours and diligent watches of a commander put courage into the soldiers, so that they too are more eager to undergo whatever must be endured, so the crowd of Christians conceives new strength of faith and patience when it sees its teachers and leaders ready and fearless to bear anything for Christ. This sense is also favoured by what he adds: "which is brought about in the endurance of the same sufferings which we also undergo." For he seems to say: "As you watch my labours and hardships, you will undoubtedly be strengthened by my example, so that if anything similar happens to you, you will bear it patiently, and thus, as Christ once warned, you will possess your souls in your patience."

units.la: Porrò quod istum sensum obseruabis, quis nobis vsus esse debeat persecutionum & afflictio- num omnium, quas olim sancti cultores Dei perpessi sunt. Est ea doctrina hæc non vtilis modò, verum etiam necessaria. Alij enim dum illas vident vel narrari audiunt, territi offenduntur, vt de fidei etiam Christianæ veritate dubitare incipiant. Alij nimia constantia & fortitudi- nis ipsorum admiratione abrepti, Deos ex illis nouos faciunt, vel saltem gloriam, quæ soli Chri- sto debetur, in illos transferunt, quasi salus nostra eorum merito perfici debuerit. Et hi ad tuen- dum errorem suum non huius solum loci authoritate abutuntur, verumetiam verbis, quæ in epi- stola ad Colossenses scribit: Gaudeo de ijs, quæ patior pro vobis, & quæ deerant afflictionibus Christi vicissim expleo in carne mea pro corpore ipsius, quod est Ecclesia. At certum est, nihil huius, quod isti colligunt, voluisse Paulum dicere, qui nos per Christi meritum plene redemptos esse sciebat, quod alibi diserte docet, & quidem in illo ipso loco, quem ex epistola ad Colossenses adduximus. Paulo ante enim de Christo multa magnificè differens, inter alia dicit: Quoniam in eo placuit Patri, vt omnis plenitudo inhabitaret, & pace per sanguinem crucis eius facta, per eum reconciliare omnia sibi (per eum, inquam) tum quæ in terra, tum quæ in cœlis sunt. Itaq; vos quondam abalienatos & hostes, mente operibus malis intenta, nunc sanè reconciliauit in corpo- re illo carnis suæ per mortem: vt sisteret vos sanctos & irreprehensibiles & inculpatos coram se. Quid igitur Paulo restabat, vt Colossensibus porrò mereretur, quos Deus pro sanctis & inculpa- tis agnoscebat, quiq; huc iam plenè reconciliati erant? Quid, quod idem nefas esse putat in quo- quam alio gloriari, præterquam in cruce IESV CHRISTI? Vel num illum hoc apostoli- cum dictum ignorauisse putabimus: Non est in alio quoquam salus: Nec enim est aliud nomen sub cœlo datum inter homines, in quo nos oporteat saluos fieri? Quis ergo (inquis) sensus est eo- rum, quæ Colossensibus scribit? Idem illis dicit, quod hic clarius & simplicius explicat: Nimi- rum, quòd ideo affligatur, quòd ipsis & reliquis gentibus Euangelium prædicet, & vt ipsi conso- lationem habeant, dum suo exemplo confirmantur, & ita in tolerantia afflictionum salutem suam possideant. Ideo quod dicit, Gaudeo de ijs, quæ patior pro vobis: idem est ac si dixisset: Quæ pa- tior in vestrum commodum aut bonum: Vel ideo, quòd Euangelium æternæ salutis vobis annun- tio. Deinde reliquias afflictionum Christi dicit quæ perpetiebatur: non quòd Christi passioni quic- quam desit, quoad nostræ redemptionis meritum (sciebat enim hunc iam moriturum dixisse: Con- summatum est) sed quòd vt Christum in proprio corpore pati oportuit, vt nos redimeret: illa quotidie in corpore eius mystico, quod est Ecclesia, completur, dum sibi factum putat quicquid membris suis fit: dumq; simul in his mortis suæ vim exerit, vt omnibus aduersis superiores facti in illo triumphent, viuant & regnent, qui afflictionum eius participes ac socij fuerunt. Itaq; af- flictiones sanctorum, quoad nos huc vsum habent, quòd suo exemplo plures alios attraxerunt ad diligentiorem doctrinæ eorum considerationem, multorum item fidem suo exemplo confirma- runt, qui prius nimiùm pusillanimes vacillabant. Exempla huius generis in historia Ecclesias- tica passim occurrunt, & nostro seculo multa similia fiunt ijs in locis, vbi persecutiones feruent, & diris supplicijs fideles Christi martyres excruciantur. Ideo Tertullianus sanguinem fide- lium semen Ecclesiæ esse dicebat: nimirum quòd eo plures alij excitentur, vt ad fidem conuersi Ecclesiæ se coniungant. Et idem ad Scapulam scribit: Non deficiet hæc secta, quam tunc ædifi- cari scias, quando cædi videtur. Potuit hoc pro sua astutia obseruare impius fidei abnegator Iu- lianus, qui artibus potius & dolis contra Christianos agendum esse putabat, ne crudeliter in eos sæuiendo patientiæ & constantiæ materiam ipsis præberet, & plures alios in tantæ virtutis ad- mirationem excitaret. Ad hoc igitur nobis quoque exempla ista seruiant, vt nostram patien- tiam atque fortitudinem confirment: vt item doctrinam eorum secuti vni Deo confidamus, &
units.tr: Moreover, in regard to this sense, you should observe what use we ought to make of all the persecutions and afflictions which the holy worshippers of God suffered of old. This teaching is not only useful but also necessary. For others, when they see these things or hear them told, are frightened and take offence, so that they begin to doubt even the truth of the Christian faith. Others, carried away by admiration for the extraordinary constancy and courage of these saints, make gods of them, or at least transfer to them the glory that is due to Christ alone, as if our salvation ought to be accomplished by their merit. To defend their error, these men abuse not only the authority of this passage but also the words he writes in the epistle to the Colossians: "I rejoice in the sufferings I endure for you, and fill up what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ in my flesh, on behalf of his body, which is the Church." But it is certain that Paul did not mean anything of what they infer, since he knew that we have been fully redeemed through the merit of Christ, as he teaches expressly elsewhere, and indeed in that very passage from the epistle to the Colossians which we have quoted. For a little before, speaking magnificently of Christ, he says among other things: "Because in him it pleased the Father that all fullness should dwell, and through the blood of his cross, peace having been made, to reconcile all things to himself through him (through him, I say), both those which are on earth and those in heaven. And so he has now reconciled you, who were once alienated and enemies, your minds intent on evil works, in that body of his flesh through death, so as to present you holy and blameless and irreproachable before him." What then remained for Paul to merit for the Colossians, whom God already recognised as holy and blameless, and who had already been fully reconciled? And what of the fact that he thinks it wrong to glory in anything except the cross of Jesus Christ? Or shall we think that he was ignorant of the apostolic saying: "There is no salvation in any other; for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved"? What then (you ask) is the sense of what he writes to the Colossians? It says the same thing to them that he explains more clearly and simply here: namely, that he is afflicted because he preaches the gospel to them and to the other nations, and so that they may have consolation, being strengthened by his example, and thus in the endurance of afflictions possess their salvation. When he says "I rejoice in the things I suffer for you," it is as if he had said: "What I suffer is for your advantage or good, or because I announce to you the gospel of eternal salvation." Then he calls the remnants of Christ's afflictions what he himself endured: not that anything is lacking to Christ's passion as regards the merit of our redemption (for he knew that Christ, about to die, had said: "It is finished"), but because, just as it was necessary for Christ to suffer in his own body in order to redeem us, so those things are daily fulfilled in his mystical body, which is the Church, while he counts as done to himself whatever is done to his members; and at the same time he exerts the power of his death in them, so that those who have been sharers and companions in his afflictions, having become superior to all adversities, triumph in him, live and reign. Thus the afflictions of the saints, as far as we are concerned, have this use: that by their example they have drawn many others to a more diligent consideration of their teaching, and have also strengthened the faith of many who before were too fainthearted and wavered. Examples of this kind occur everywhere in ecclesiastical history, and in our own age many similar things happen in places where persecutions rage and faithful martyrs of Christ are tortured with dreadful punishments. Therefore Tertullian used to say that the blood of the faithful is the seed of the Church: doubtless because by it many others are roused to join the Church, having been converted to the faith. And in his letter to Scapula he writes: "This sect will not fail, which you know is built up when it seems to be cut down." The impious apostate from the faith, Julian, could have observed this with his cunning; he thought that one should act against the Christians by arts and tricks rather than by cruelly raging against them, lest he provide them with matter for patience and constancy and stir many others to admire such great virtue. Therefore let these examples serve us too, to strengthen our patience and fortitude; and likewise, following their teaching, let us trust in the one God alone, and

units.la: Sozomenus lib. 5. cap. 4. hunc vnum innocemus per IESVM CHRISTVM: quoad vitam vero & mores, innocentia studeamus ac sanctitati:in periculis vero & aduersis constantes simus in finem vs- que. Hic verus cultus sanctorum est, qui vt ipsorum honorem & famam illustrat, ita gloriae Dei nihil detrahit.
units.tr: Sozomenus lib. 5. cap. 4. invoke this one alone through Jesus Christ; as regards life and morals, let us cultivate innocence and holiness; in dangers and adversities let us be steadfast to the end. This is the true worship of the saints, which brings honour and fame to them, and takes nothing away from the glory of God.

units.la: At simul hoc loco istud quoq; considerationem diligentiorem meretur,quomodo vniuscuiusq; salus per tolerantiam afflictionum perfici dicatur. Nam ad hoc etiam dictum aliqui offendunt, qui afflictionibus expiationis meritum & satisfactionem pro peccatis tribuunt, non absq; lucu- lenta Christi ignominia, cui soli haec gloria debetur. Sed dicti huius ratio est, quod per afflictio- nes nobis fidei exercendae atq; confirmandae materia praebetur, sicuti nuper ex epistola ad Roma- nos annotauimus, vbi dicitur: Afflictio patientiam efficit, patientia vero experientiam, experi- entia spem, porro spes non pudefacit, &c. Nec est quod aliquis hic nobis piorum gemitus, lachry- mas aut querelas obiiciat, quas interdum inter ista certamina fundunt: Nam etiamsi aliquid hu- manum patiantur, vincunt tamen dum in Dei prouidentiam & Christi promissiones respiciunt, quae ipsos de Dei bonitate & regni caelestis spe dubitare non sinunt.
units.tr: But at the same time this passage also deserves more careful consideration, namely how each one's salvation is said to be accomplished through the endurance of afflictions. For some take offence at this saying too, those who attribute to afflictions the merit of expiation and satisfaction for sins, not without a considerable dishonour to Christ, to whom alone this glory is due. But the reason for the saying is that through afflictions we are given material for exercising and strengthening faith, as we noted recently from the epistle to the Romans, where it is said: "Affliction produces patience, patience experience, experience hope, and hope does not disappoint," and so on. Nor need anyone here object to us the groans, tears or complaints of the pious, which they sometimes pour out amid these struggles: for even if they suffer something human, they nevertheless conquer, while they look to God's providence and Christ's promises, which do not allow them to doubt God's goodness and the hope of the heavenly kingdom.

units.la: Porro facit ad huius doctrinae confirmationem alterum huius loci membrum, quo de consola- tionibus quoq; disserit,dicens: Siue consolationem accipimus, id fit pro vestra consolatione ac salu- te, &c. Id est, quod me interea Deus consolatur & recreat, id quoque non mei solius causa facit, sed propter vos, vt ipsi quoq; consolatione percipiatis, sic q; in salutis fiducia & certitudine confir- memini. Id vero confirmat, dum addit: Et spes nostra firma est de vobis, &c. Quasi diceret: Non dubito quicquam de vestra constantia, quin fortiter eluctaturi sitis per omnia pericula, nec de- serturi stationem, in quam vos Deus collocauit. Ita vero non solum remouet scandalum, quod ex suis persecutionibus nasceabatur, verumetiam illos erigit, vt ad quiduis ferendum alacriores fiant. Nam perinde ista dicit, ac si Imperator militibus certam victoriae spem faciat, dum se de ipsorum virtute nihil dubitare dicit: aut si medicus aegroto dicat: Spes mihi certa & firma est, te breui conualituum, itaque animo laeto sis, vt tibi appropinquantem salutem acceleres atque iu- ues. Est q; in verbis istis admodum memorabile, quod cum consolatione salutem subinde coniun- git. Eo enim docet, Deum nos non inanibus verbis latare, sed salutem simul certam eos conci- pere, qui consolationes eius intra animum suum admittunt. Vbi rursus admonemur, non ea mo- do spectari debere, quae in nos confert Deus, verumetiam quae in aliis proponit gratiae sua & li- berationis exempla, vt eorum consideratione in salutis spe atque fiducia confirmemur. Arguit hoc inuidos, qui aliorum felicitate ringuntur, quales hodie multos passim est videre. Isti ve- ro non solum animos tormento crudelissimo excruciant, quo (vt Satyricus poeta canit) Si- culi tyranni nullum maius inuenerunt, verumetiam fructu dulcissimo saluberrimoque sei- psos spoliant, quo frui poterant, si aliorum exemplis recte vterentur, & in his relucentem Dei bo- nitatem obseruarent.
units.tr: Moreover, another part of this passage, in which he also discourses about consolations, contributes to the confirmation of this teaching, saying: "Whether we receive consolation, it is for your consolation and salvation," and so on. That is: whatever God meanwhile consoles and refreshes me, he does not do for my sake alone, but on account of you, so that you too may receive consolation, and thus be confirmed in the confidence and certainty of salvation. He confirms this when he adds: "And our hope for you is firm," and so on. As if he said: I do not doubt anything about your constancy, that you will bravely struggle through all dangers, nor will you desert the post in which God has placed you. Thus he not only removes the scandal that arose from his persecutions, but also raises them up, so that they become more eager to endure anything. For he speaks just as if an emperor were to give his soldiers a sure hope of victory, saying he has no doubt of their courage; or as if a doctor said to a sick man: "I have a sure and firm hope that you will soon be well, so be of good cheer, that you may hasten and help the salvation approaching you." And in these words there is something very memorable: he repeatedly joins salvation with consolation. For thereby he teaches that God does not comfort us with empty words, but that those who admit his consolations within their soul at the same time conceive a certain salvation. Here again we are reminded that we ought to look not only at what God bestows on us, but also at the examples of his grace and deliverance which he sets forth in others, so that by considering them we may be confirmed in the hope and confidence of salvation. This rebukes the envious, who pine away at the happiness of others, such as one may see in many people everywhere today. These men not only torment their minds with the most cruel torture, which (as the satirist sings) the tyrants of Sicily found no greater, but also deprive themselves of the sweetest and most wholesome fruit, which they could enjoy if they used the examples of others rightly and observed the goodness of God shining in them.

units.la: Caeterum inter ista meminisse oportet, doctrinam atque consolationem istam ad eos solos pertinere, qui a Deo sibi impositam crucem atque molestias patienter ferunt: non ad eos,qui ten- tationibus sponte cedunt, carni delitias faciunt, cum mundo impio & reprobo colludunt, denique nihil ferre volunt pro Christo & nominis eius gloria. Falluntur isti non minus permitiose quam turpiter, quod pacem mundi huius cum Christi seruitio coniungi, Euangelium denique ita praedicari posse sibi persuadent, vt nemo quantumuis prophanus aut improbus eo offenda- tur. Sed longe aliter nos Christus docet, qui vt omnes, qui ipsi nomen dant, ad crucem inuitat: ita mundi hoc ingenium esse testatur, vt propter operum atque studiorum suorum turpitudinem veritatis lucem ferre nequaquam possit. Ideo Apostolis dicebat: In mundo afflictionem habebi- tis. Ad hanc ergo ferendam toto animo praeparemur: & qui affliguntur, simul meminerint, non de sua solum, verumetiam aliorum hominum salute agi, & proinde ita se gerant, vt quibusuis Christianae fortitudinis & constantiae exempla praebeant, quibus confirmati salutem suam perfi- ciant in IESV CHRISTO, redemptore nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Yet among these things we ought to remember that this teaching and this consolation pertain only to those who patiently bear the cross and the troubles laid upon them by God, and not to those who willingly give way to temptations, indulge the flesh, collude with the impious and reprobate world, and, in short, are unwilling to suffer anything for Christ and for the glory of his name. These men are deceived no less dangerously than shamefully, for they persuade themselves that the peace of this world can be joined with the service of Christ, and that the Gospel can be preached in such a way that no one, however profane or wicked, is offended by it. But Christ teaches us quite otherwise. He invites all who give their name to him to the cross, and he testifies that the nature of the world is such that, on account of the baseness of its works and pursuits, it can by no means bear the light of truth. Therefore he said to the apostles: "In the world you will have affliction." Let us therefore prepare ourselves with our whole heart to bear this. And let those who are afflicted remember at the same time that it is not only their own salvation but also the salvation of other men that is at stake; and so let them conduct themselves that they may offer examples of Christian courage and constancy to anyone, by which, being strengthened, they may bring their own salvation to completion in Jesus Christ our redeemer, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA IIII.
units.tr: Homily 4.

units.la: Non enim volumus vos ignorare fratres, de afflictione nostra, quae nobis euenit in Asia; nos summè grauatos fuisse supra vires, adeò vt prorsus animi penderemus, etiam quod ad vitam: Sed ipsi apud nos decretum mortis habuimus, ne consideremus in nobis ipsis, sed in Deo qui excitat mortuos: Qui ex tanta morte liberauit, & liberat: in quo speramus nos adhuc etiam liberatum iri: Vobis etiam vnà pro nobis operam conferentibus ad deprecandum, vt donum ex multis personis in nos collatum, per multos celebretur gratiarum actione pro nobis.
units.tr: For we would not have you ignorant, brothers, of the affliction that befell us in Asia: we were weighed down excessively, beyond our strength, so that we despaired even of life. Indeed, we had the sentence of death within ourselves, so that we should not trust in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead. He delivered us from so great a death, and he does deliver us, and in him we hope he will deliver us again, while you also help us by prayer, so that the gift bestowed on us through many persons may be celebrated through many thanksgivings on our behalf.

units.la: QVoniam Dominus & Seruator noster, IESVS CHRISTVS, electos suos ad crucem vocat, ea autem caro nostra maximè offenditur, non tam vtile quàm necessarium est veram atq; solidam de cruce & afflictionibus doctrinam in Ecclesia extare. Quae causa est, quod Apostoli hanc frequenter inculcant. Et facit ad eius illustrationem imprimis huius epistolae exordium, quo Paulus de ijs, quae ipse perpetiebatur multis ac diligenter disserit. Vbi didicimus hucusq; primò Christi passiones apud Deum censeri, quaecunq; pij in hac vita sufferunt. Deinde, Deum suis nunquam deesse, sed eos sub cruce laborantes per Christum consolari. Postremò, piorum exempla, siue illi affligantur siue consolationem accipiant, aliorum saluti seruire, qui ex illis non consolationes modò, sed insuper certam firmamq; salutis suae fiduciam concipiant. Istis loco demonstrationis proprium exemplum & non diu ante editum subijcit, eoq; simul testatur, se adeò non pudere afflictionum, quas ferat, vt potius ipsi volupe sit eas commemorare, vt multorum institutioni & consolationi seruiant.
units.tr: Since our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ calls his chosen ones to the cross, and since our flesh is greatly offended by this, it is not merely useful but necessary that a true and solid doctrine of the cross and of afflictions should exist in the Church. This is why the Apostles press it so often. And the opening of this epistle, in which Paul discusses at length and with care what he himself was suffering, serves especially to illustrate it. From it we have learned, first, that all the sufferings the godly undergo in this life are counted by God as the sufferings of Christ. Second, that God never abandons his own, but comforts through Christ those who labour under the cross. Last, that the examples of the godly, whether they are afflicted or receive comfort, serve the salvation of others, who from them gain not only consolation but also a firm and certain confidence in their own salvation. To confirm these points, he sets before us his own example, very recent, and in doing so he bears witness that he is so far from being ashamed of the afflictions he endures that he is actually glad to recall them, so that they may serve the instruction and comfort of many.

units.la: Non enim volumus (inquit) vos ignorare fratres, de afflictione nostra, quae nobis euenit in Asia, &c. Subest exordiolo isti noua beneuolentiae captatio, quando eos tanti abs se fieri testatur, vt nihil eos celare possit, & ne ea quidem, quae sciebat ab aemulis suis in partem deteriorem rapi, vt nouam haberent calumniandi occasionem. Videtur autem locus hic totus intelligi debere de historia, quam Lucas in Actis cap. decimo nono describit. Venit enim Paulus Ephesum, & illic totum biennium docuit, & interea multa fecit per totam Asiam, adeò vt ex principibus quoq; amicos sibi pararet. Tandem cum Dianae Ephesiae cultus frigere inciperet, multis quotidie ad Christi fidem accedentibus, seditionem contra illum excitauit Demetrius quidam aurifaber, qui ex cultu illo hucusq; quaestum fecerat cum alijs ex eodem artificio viuentibus. Ita enim fieri solet, vt Euangelicae veritatis hostes acerrimi sint, qui religionem sibi quaestum faciunt: hanc verò suis impijs conatibus praetexunt, vt causam suam plausibiliorem reddant, & plures in partes trahant: quod multis exemplis cum veteribus tum recentioribus probari poterat. Habet enim nostrum quoque seculum Demetrios suos, qui vbique gentium Euangelij doctrinae simili astutia atque temeritate obstrepunt. Sed vt ad Paulum redeamus, credibile est, eum in summo discrimine constitutum fuisse: quando amici quantumuis potentes illi permittere noluerunt, vt in publicum progressus furenti turbae sese committeret, neque etiam diutius illic subsistere posset. Ipse certe in praesenti rem omnem diligentissimè descriptam suo instituto applicat: cuius partes ex ordine inspiciemus.
units.tr: "For we would not have you ignorant, brothers," he says, "of our affliction which befell us in Asia," and so on. This introduction contains a fresh attempt to win goodwill, since he declares that the Corinthians are so precious to him that he can conceal nothing from them, not even what he knew his rivals would twist to their worse sense, so that they might have a new occasion for slander. This whole passage ought to be understood as referring to the history that Luke describes in Acts chapter nineteen. Paul came to Ephesus and taught there for two whole years, and in the meantime did much throughout the whole of Asia, so that he won friends even among the leading men. Finally, when the worship of Diana of Ephesus began to grow cold, since many were coming to faith in Christ every day, a certain Demetrius, a silversmith who had made a profit from that worship, together with others who lived by the same trade, stirred up sedition against him. For it usually happens that the bitterest enemies of evangelical truth are those who make a profit from religion, and they put forward their impious schemes as a pretext, so as to make their cause look more plausible and draw more people to their side. This could be proved by many examples, both ancient and more recent. Our own age too has its Demetriuses, who everywhere in the world bring the same cunning and recklessness to bear in clamouring against the doctrine of the Gospel. But to return to Paul: it is credible that he was placed in the greatest danger, since his powerful friends did not allow him to go out into public and entrust himself to the raging crowd, and neither could he remain there any longer. In the present passage, at any rate, he applies the whole matter, described with the greatest care, to his purpose. Let us examine its parts in order.

units.la: Primò periculi magnitudinem describit, & illud amplificat quoque, vt & Dei gloria illustretur, & seipsum ad gratiarum actionem ardentiorem excitet. Ita enim solent sancti homines, sicuti in Psalmis, in Ezechiae Regis Cantico & multis similibus locis est videre. Ingrati animi indicium est, periculum extenuare vbi te liberatum videris. Audiamus ergo Apostolum de suo periculo differentem. Nolo (inquit) vos ignorare, nos summè grauatos fuisse supra vires, adeò vt prorsus animi penderemus, etiam quod ad vitam, &c. Primò summè se grauatum fuisse dicit, Metaphora sumpta vel à baiulis, quibus onera intolerabilia imponuntur: vel à nauibus onerarijs, quae saburra grauantur, aut mercibus ita onerantur, vt eas commodè ferre non possint.
units.tr: First, he describes the magnitude of the danger, and he also magnifies it, both so that God's glory may be illustrated and so that he himself may be roused to a more ardent thanksgiving. Holy men usually do this, as can be seen in the Psalms, in the Canticle of King Hezekiah and in many similar places. It is a sign of an ungrateful mind to minimise a danger once you see yourself delivered from it. Let us then hear the Apostle speaking of his danger: "I would not have you ignorant," he says, "that we were weighed down excessively, beyond our strength, so that we despaired even of life," and so on. First, he says that he was weighed down excessively. The metaphor is taken either from porters, on whom intolerable burdens are laid, or from merchant ships, which are weighed down with ballast or loaded with cargo so heavily that they cannot carry it comfortably.

units.la: Proprio exemplo confirmat quae dixit.
units.tr: He confirms what he has said by his own example.

units.la: Periculum amplificat. Deinde addit, Supra vires. Atqui alibi gloriatur, se omnia posse in CHRISTO IESV, & Deum fidelem esse dixit in priori epistola, qui nos supra quam ferre possimus, tentari non sinat. Sed in praesenti de viribus humanis, id est, naturalibus & quae homini propriae sunt, loquitur. In his mera est imbecillitas, adeo ut ne vires quidem dici mereantur, quado ne cogitare possumus ea, quae nos decent. Illic vero simul virtutem fidei comprehendit, quam in Christo habemus, & quam Deus pro tentationum ratione aut pondere indies confirmat, ne illis succumbamus. Itaque cum hic se supra vires grauatum dicat, omnem liberationis gloriam uni soli Deo tribuit. Tertio tantum fuisse pondus ait istius discriminis, ut prorsus animi penderet, quod ad vitam, id est, ut de vita quoque dubitaret. Est enim idem quod consilij inopem esse, & perplexum dubiumq; haerere, ut nescias quid statui debeat. Itaque sensus est, eo rem deductam fuisse, ut nulla euadendi spes reliqua esset in humanis, nec etiam videre posset, quo se verteret. Et facit ad huius amplificationem quod sequitur: Sed ipsi apud nos, vel in nobismetipsis, aut in animo nostro, decretum mortis habuimus, id est, apud me iam decretum erat mori, sine omni praesentis huius vitae iam prorsus sublata.
units.tr: He magnifies the danger. Then he adds, "beyond our strength." Yet elsewhere he boasts that he can do all things in Christ Jesus, and in the earlier epistle he said that God is faithful and will not allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear. But here he is speaking of human strength, that is, natural strength, the kind that belongs to man by nature. In these matters there is pure weakness, so that they do not even deserve to be called strength, since we cannot even think the things that befit us. There, however, he also comprehends the power of faith that we have in Christ, which God strengthens day by day according to the measure or weight of the temptations, so that we do not give way under them. Therefore, when he says here that he was weighed down beyond his strength, he ascribes the whole glory of his deliverance to God alone. Third, he says the weight of that peril was so great that he was utterly in suspense, even as to life, that is, that he doubted even about his life. For to be at a loss for counsel and to remain perplexed and uncertain, so that you do not know what ought to be decided, is the same thing. The sense, then, is that the matter had been brought to such a point that no hope of escape remained among human means, and he could not even see where to turn. And what follows also serves to magnify this: "But we ourselves had the sentence of death within ourselves," that is, in ourselves, or in our own mind, I had already decided to die, with every hope of this present life already entirely taken away.

units.la: Docet autem locus iste, quanta sit omnium hominum, in hac carne viuentium, imbecillitas. Videntur aliqui interdum sibi fortes & in omnem euentum instructissimi. Sed in periculis improuisis, se omnis consilij expertes esse sentiunt, & qui prius sapientissimi habebantur, sibijpsis minus quam alij possunt consulere. Quid vero de morte dicemus, cuius terrores si obijciantur, mox omnes vires nostrae succumbunt? Exempla infirmitatis huius etiam in sanctissimis extant, quos Deus interdum eo usque delabi patitur, ne donorum eius excellentia confidentiores facti aduersus gratiam eius superbiant: quod Paulus infra cap. duodecimo diserte de semetipso testatur. Nemo igitur offendatur, si vel propriae infirmitatis sensu se percelli, vel alios meticulosiores videat, quos ad omnem fortunam probe instructos esse putabat. Quid enim faciant homines, quando aeternus Dei Filius naturae nostrae, quam ex Virgine Matre assumpsit, infirmitatem non dissimulauit? Vide Ioan. 12. Luc. 22.
units.tr: This passage, however, shows how great is the weakness of all men who live in this flesh. Some men sometimes seem strong and fully prepared for any outcome. But when unforeseen dangers arise, they feel that they lack all counsel, and those who were thought most wise can give themselves less counsel than others can. And what shall we say of death, at whose terrors, if they are set before us, all our strength soon gives way? Examples of this weakness are found even among the holiest men, whom God sometimes allows to fall so far, lest, made more confident by the excellence of his gifts, they grow proud against his grace. Paul bears explicit witness to this about himself in chapter twelve below. Therefore let no one be offended if he is struck by a sense of his own weakness, or sees others more fearful than he had thought, whom he supposed well equipped for every fortune. For what can men do, when the eternal Son of God did not hide the weakness of our nature, which he took from the Virgin Mother? See John 12, Luke 22.

units.la: Admonemur praeterea, sanctos de vita sua ut plurimum solicitos esse, & eius seruandae rationes quaerere. Hinc est, quod interdum fuga sibi consulunt, aut alijs medijs, quae Deus monstrat, utuntur. Fecit hoc frequenter Dauid. Et Apostolis Christus dicebat: Si persecuti vos fuerint in una ciuitate, fugite in aliam. Etenim quamuis intelligant, se vitam suam Deo debere, quia tamen ipsi eius finem siue horam nesciunt, non possunt eam temere profundere, imo ne negligere quidem debent, nisi hoc ita Deum velle videant, ut ex huius corporis carcere ad coelestem patriam emigrent. Damnatur ergo sanctorum exemplis & totius Scripturae consensu ἀπάθεια siue indolentia illa Stoica, quae si posset locum aliquem inuenire inter homines, non alios quam ἀσόργους, id est, homines communi sensu & naturalibus affectionibus carentes faceret, qui ab Apostolo inter nouissimorum temporum pestes numerantur. 2. Tim. 3.
units.tr: We are also reminded that the saints are for the most part anxious about their lives and seek ways of preserving them. Hence it is that sometimes they consult their safety by flight, or make use of other means that God shows them. David often did this. And Christ said to the Apostles: "If they persecute you in one city, flee into another." For although they understand that they owe their life to God, yet because they do not know its end or hour, they cannot squander it rashly, nor indeed ought they to neglect it, unless they see that God wills it so, that they should migrate from the prison of this body to the heavenly fatherland. Therefore the Stoic ἀπάθεια [apatheia], or that indifference, is condemned by the examples of the saints and by the consensus of all Scripture. If it could find a place among men, it would make none but ἀσόργους [asorgous], that is, men lacking common feeling and natural affections, who are numbered by the Apostle among the plagues of the last times. 2 Tim. 3.

units.la: At quaerat aliquis, Cur Deus tantum Apostolum & electum suae gratiae organum in tantum discrimen & angustias tam graues deuenire passus sit? Causam ergo ipse indicat: Ne confidemus in nobis ipsis, sed in Deo qui excitat mortuos. Innata est enim homini suijpsius & propriae virtutis siue dignitatis fiducia: quod in multorum exemplis quotidie experimur: imo hoc in semetipsis singuli sentiunt, quam diu aliqua sese efferendi occasio offert. Contraximus vitium hoc ex primis parentibus, quos ea fiducia decepit, quod suis viribus se ad praestantiorem conditionem euadere posse putarent. Itaque huius vestigia non in vulgo solum hominum, verumetiam in sanctis apparent, qui tanto magis hic periclitantur, quanto alijs donorum excellentia praestant. Quae causa est, ut saepius in extremas angustias redigantur, & (ut paulo ante monuimus) nihil praesidij in humanis videre possint. Accidit hoc frequenter Dauidi, quem in Psalmis quiritari audimus: Serua me Deus: quoniam penetrarunt aquae ad animam usque. Demersus sum in limum profundissimum, in quo non est fundus: decidi in aquas profundissimas, & aquae obruunt me. Defessus sum vociferando, aret guttur meum, defecerunt oculi mei suspicientes ad Deum meum, &c. Quo etiam referri potest, quod cum ob populi censum ipsi optionem detulisset Dominus deligendi poenam, quam vellet, idem exclamauit: Supra modum angor, inci-damus
units.tr: But someone may ask: why did God allow the Apostle, the chosen instrument of his grace, to fall into such great danger and such severe distress? The Apostle himself gives the reason: that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead. A confidence in one's own strength and worth is innate in man, as we daily see in many people; indeed, each person feels it in himself whenever an opportunity to raise himself up presents itself. We have drawn this fault from our first parents, whom that confidence deceived, since they thought they could by their own powers rise to a higher condition. So its traces appear not only among the common people but also in the saints, who are in greater danger here the more they excel others in the greatness of their gifts. This is why they are often driven into extreme distress and, as we noted a little earlier, can see no help in human affairs. This happened often to David, whom we hear complaining in the Psalms: "Save me, O God, for the waters have come up to my soul. I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing; I have come into deep waters, and the floods overwhelm me. I am weary with crying; my throat is dry; my eyes fail while I wait for my God," and so on. To this may also be referred what happened when the Lord, because of the census of the people, gave him the choice of which punishment he would take, and he cried out: "I am in great distress; let us fall

units.la: Psal. 69.
units.tr: Psal. 69.

units.la: 2. Sam. 24. damus quæso in manum Domini, &c. Simile exemplum in Ezechia Rege habemus, quem disciplina eiusmodi opus habuisse ex ijs apparet, quæ cum Babyloniorum legatis egit. Rectè igitur hoc Dei consilium observauit Paulus, quem Christus ipse organum electum dixerat, qui donis præstantissimis supra omnes eminebat, & in regni Dei propagatione plus aliis omnibus laborauerat, qui denique reuelationibus verè diuinis de ijs edoctus erat; quæ neque sensu humano percipi, neque verbis exprimi possunt. Et est locus iste dignissimus consideratu, in quo hæc potissimum obseruabis.
units.tr: 2. Sam. 24. into the hand of the Lord, I beg you, and so on. We have a similar example in King Hezekiah, who clearly needed this kind of discipline, as is evident from what he did with the envoys of the Babylonians. Paul therefore rightly observed this counsel of God. Christ himself had called him a chosen instrument; he surpassed all others in the most outstanding gifts, had laboured more than all the rest in spreading the kingdom of God, and was finally taught by revelations truly divine, which can be grasped by no human sense nor expressed in words. This passage is well worth considering, and in it you will chiefly observe the following.

units.la: Primum, nocentissimam esse nostrijpsius fiduciam, & eandem Deo quàm maximè displicere. Nisi enim talis esset, nequaquam illam in electis suis tanto afflictionum pondere, ceu virgis gravioribus, coerceret & castigaret. Id verò non præter rationem fieri, quius facile intelliget, qui eius effecta propius inspexerit. Nam rationis vsum aufert, ut homo confidentia nimia quasi ebrius, seipsum prorsus ignoret. Quò fit, ut plerique res viribus suis maiores tentent, sub quorum pondere turpiter succumbunt: vel etiam pharisaico spiritu decepti, propriæ iustitiæ fiducia efferantur, non sine manifesto gratiæ Dei misericordiæ & meriti IESV CHRISTI contemptu. Accedit huic malo, quòd Dei gloriam sibi ipsis confidentes illi vendicant, seque ipsos Deo æquant, dum se sibi ipsis ad omnia sufficere arbitrantur, quod solius Dei proprium esse constat. Tertiò Dei dona corrumpit fiducia illa, dum relicto vero eorum vsu, ea nobis ipsis simul atque aliis noxia facimus, quæ salutis nostræ adminicula esse debebant. Denique securos facit, & admonitionum omnium contemptores: ex quo non aliud quam exitium præsens enasci potest. Exempla, quæ istis fidem faciant, passim in ijs habentur, quos opum, honorum, amicitiarum atque fœderum fiducia perdidit. Quis autem Deo placere putet eos, in quibus vitia tam multa tamque grauia concurrunt, quæ singula eius iram provocant?
units.tr: First, our own confidence is most harmful, and it displeases God most of all. For if it were not so, he would never restrain and chastise it in his chosen ones with such a weight of afflictions, as with heavier rods. That this does not happen without reason will be easily understood by anyone who looks more closely at its effects. For excessive confidence takes away the use of reason, so that a man, like a drunkard, altogether forgets himself. Hence it happens that many attempt things greater than their strength and shamefully collapse under their weight; or else, deceived by a Pharisaical spirit, they are puffed up with confidence in their own righteousness, not without a plain contempt for God's mercy and for the merit of Jesus Christ. To this evil is added that those who trust in themselves claim for themselves the glory that belongs to God, and make themselves equal to God, while they think they are sufficient for everything in themselves, which is plainly proper to God alone. Second, that confidence corrupts God's gifts: when we leave their true use, we turn into harm for ourselves and for others the very things that ought to have been aids to our salvation. Finally, it makes men careless and scorners of all warnings, and from this nothing but present ruin can arise. Examples that confirm this are found everywhere among those whom confidence in wealth, honours, friendships and alliances has destroyed. Who, however, would think that those pleases God in whom so many and such grave faults come together, each of which provokes his anger?

units.la: In quo igitur nos confidere oportet inter tot rerum discrimina atque pericula, quæ nos vndique circumstant? Est hoc cognitu necessarium, quia facile succumbimus, nisi spei & fiduciæ nostræ certum aliquod & solidum fundamentum habeamus. Id verò Paulus nobis suo exemplo monstrat, quando subijcit: Sed in Deo, qui excitat mortuos. Ergo soli Deo fidere debemus. Ad hoc obstringit nos fœderis cum Abrahamo facti primus articulus: Ego sum Deus Sthadai, ambula coram me. Cui consentit primum Decalogi præceptum: Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, qui eduxi te ex terra Ægypti, è domo seruitutis: Ne sint tibi Dij alieni coram me. Quibus addi debet primus Symboli apostolici articulus: Credo in vnum Deum, &c. Quæ omnia totius Scripturæ consensu confirmantur. Et enim vt hoc passim Deus exigit, ita nullum scelus magis detestatur & seuerius punit, quàm idololatriam & superstitionem, qua vel fiduciam nostram, vel cultum ipsi soli debitum, aliò transferimus. Et merito quidem in eo tam seuerus est, quando gloria eius tunc quàm maximè illustratur, quando ab ipso vno pendemus, & ipsi vni fidimus. Vt enim Regem is potissimum honorat, qui illi confidit, eumque suum vindicem & protectorem agnoscit: Ita qui spem & fiduciam salutis omnem in Deo collocatam habent, ij verum & solidum honorem illi deferunt, non qui circa ceremonias qualescunque occupantur, quibus ille nequaquam opus habet. Ideo hunc sibi gratissimum cultum esse docet, si in afflictionibus constituti ipsum vnum invocemus. Et hoc ipsum æterna nostrarum animarum salus exigit, cuius fiducia certa & firma nobis esse non potest, quoad non in vnum Deum respicimus, præter quem Deus iustus & saluans nullus est. Isaiæ 45.
units.tr: In whom then must we trust amid so many dangers and perils that surround us on every side? This is necessary to know, because we easily give way unless we have some certain and solid foundation for our hope and trust. Paul shows us this by his own example when he adds: "but in God, who raises the dead." Therefore we ought to trust in God alone. The first article of the covenant made with Abraham binds us to this: "I am God Shaddai; walk before me." The first commandment of the Decalogue agrees with it: "I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. You shall have no other gods before me." To these should be added the first article of the Apostles' Creed: "I believe in one God," and so on. All these things are confirmed by the agreement of the whole of Scripture. For just as God everywhere requires this, so he detests and punishes no crime more severely than idolatry and superstition, by which we transfer either our trust or the worship due to him alone to something else. And he is rightly so severe in this, since his glory then shines most brightly when we depend on him alone and trust in him alone. For just as a king is especially honoured by the one who trusts in him and acknowledges him as his defender and protector, so those who place all their hope and confidence of salvation in God pay him true and solid honour, not those who busy themselves with whatever ceremonies, of which he has no need at all. Therefore he teaches that this is the most pleasing worship to him, if we, when placed in afflictions, call upon him alone. And the eternal salvation of our souls itself requires this, since we cannot have a sure and firm confidence in it so long as we do not look to the one God, besides whom there is no righteous and saving God. Isaiah 45.

units.la: At quoniam infinita sunt, quæ fidem hanc nostram impediunt, rationibus nos in ea confirmari necesse est. Inter quas prima adduci poterat fluxa & fallax omnium quæ in hoc seculo habentur, conditio. Omnis caro fœnum (dicit Propheta) & omnis gloria carnis flos agri. Itaque non possunt non falli, qui in illis fidunt, quæ carni magnifica videntur. At Paulus in præsenti solius omnipotentiæ Dei meminit, & huius argumentum adduxit, quòd excitet mortuos. Conueniebat hoc ipsi loco, cùm de periculi magnitudine disseruisset, quæ illum vitæ dubium fecerat. Itaque communem resurrectionem, quæ olim futura est, præsenti negotio applicans, illius specimen quoddam æditû fuisse dicit, quando ipsum Deus ex tanta morte, id est, ex manifesto & præsentissimo vitæ periculo eripuerit. Ex eo autem spem certam se concipere ait, quòd in posterum quoque Deus ipsum sit liberaturus. Quo loco obiter admonemur, nos quoties vel ex morbo aliquo letali, vel graviori periculo eripimur, toties in spe resurrectionis futurae confirmari debere. E contra, quoties pericula & calamitates inextricabiles nos undique premere videntur, tunc mortuorum resurrectio nobis in mentem veniat, ut ex ea colligamus, non impossibile esse Deo nos ex illis liberare, qui olim corpora nostra, iam in cineres & pulverem redacta, nobis gloriosa & incorruptibilia restituet. Hoc argumento certe olim Dominus per Ezechielem eos consolatus est, qui in Babylone sic undique premebantur, ut nulla liberationis spes in humanis superesset. Ezech.37.
units.tr: But since there are countless things that hinder this faith of ours, it is necessary for us to be confirmed in it by reasons. Among these, the first that could be brought forward is the fleeting and deceptive condition of all that is held in this age. "All flesh is grass," says the prophet, "and all the glory of flesh is like the flower of the field." Therefore those who trust in things that seem splendid to the flesh cannot but be deceived. But Paul, in the present passage, calls to mind the omnipotence of God alone, and he brings forward as proof that God raises the dead. This fitted the place well, since he had just spoken of the greatness of the danger that had made his life doubtful. So, applying the common resurrection, which is to come one day, to his present situation, he says that it was a kind of sample of it when God rescued him from such a death, that is, from a plain and very present danger to his life. From this, he says, he conceives a sure hope that God will also deliver him in future. Here we are reminded in passing that whenever we are rescued from some deadly sickness or a more serious danger, we ought to be confirmed by it in the hope of the future resurrection. On the other hand, whenever dangers and calamities seem to press us from every side without any way out, then the resurrection of the dead should come to mind, so that we may conclude from it that it is not impossible for God to deliver us from those troubles, since he who will one day restore our bodies, now reduced to ashes and dust, will give them back to us glorious and incorruptible. Certainly the Lord once used this very argument through Ezekiel to comfort those who in Babylon were so pressed on every side that no hope of deliverance remained in human affairs. Ezek. 37.

units.la: Quia vero multa alia quoque fidem nostram tentare & labefactare solent, proderit alia etiam Dei attributa ob oculos ponere. Cogitamus forte, nos miseriores & abiectiores esse, quam ut Deus ille omnipotens nostri aliquam rationem habere debeat, aut etiam habere velit. Hic ergo cum omnipotentia & divina illius maiestate misericordiam quoque consideremus plus quam paternam, quae eo erga nos propensior est, quo nos miseriores & imbecilliores esse videt. Et huc illud Davidis pertinet: Sicut pater miseretur liberorum, ita Dominus miseretur timentium eum. Ipse enim novit conditionem nostram, recordans quod sumus pulvis. Ita si nos peccatorum nostrorum multitudine terreri sentiamus, ex illius iustitia consolatio petatur, quam ille nobis in Filio suo, IESV CHRISTO, communicavit. Quod si iniusta vi tyrannorum opprimimur, tunc ad Dei tribunal provocemus, qui gemitus & suspiria suorum audit, nedum querelas & clamores, quos illis dolor acerbior exprimit. At in dubium rapit Satan promissiones Dei. Hic nobis eiusdem Veritas succurrat, de qua illud Isaiae debet intelligi: Verbum Domini manet in aeternum. Et illud Christi: Caelum & terra transibunt, verba autem mea non transibunt. Discamus deniq; ex anteactis argumentari quemadmodum in praesenti Paulus facit. Constat enim sibi ipsi semper Deus, & cum viscera miserationum inexhausta habeat, non potest non manum suam exercere, quando materiam misericordiae exercendae sibi propositam esse videt in iis, quos ab aeterno in filios adoptavit.
units.tr: Because many other things also commonly try and shake our faith, it will be useful to set before our eyes the other attributes of God as well. Perhaps we think that we are too wretched and too abject for that almighty God to have, or even to want to have, any regard for us. Here, then, let us consider his mercy, which is more than fatherly, together with his omnipotence and divine majesty; it is the more inclined toward us the more wretched and weak it sees us to be. To this belongs that saying of David: "As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear him." For he knows our condition, remembering that we are dust. So if we feel ourselves terrified by the multitude of our sins, let us seek comfort from his righteousness, which he has bestowed on us in his Son, Jesus Christ. But if we are oppressed by the unjust violence of tyrants, then let us appeal to the judgment seat of God, who hears the groans and sighs of his people, and much more the complaints and cries that a more bitter pain wrings from them. But Satan tries to cast doubt on God's promises. Here let the truth of God come to our aid, of which that saying of Isaiah must be understood: "The word of the Lord abides for ever." And that saying of Christ: "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away." Finally, let us learn to reason from past events, as Paul does in the present case. For God is always consistent with himself, and since he has inexhaustible bowels of mercy, he cannot but exercise his hand when he sees that there is matter for exercising mercy set before him in those whom he adopted as sons from eternity.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui ne arrogantius hoc Dei beneficium iactare, & suae dignitati siue meritis tribuere putetur, aliquam eius causam in Corinthiis esse fatetur, quorum precibus adiutus sit, simulq; eos quid porro pro ipso facere debeant, admonet. Vobis etiam (inquit) una pro nobis operam conferentibus ad deprecandum, ut donum ex multis personis collatum in nos, per multos celebretur gratiarum actione pro nobis. Per donum intelligit liberationem illam, de qua modo dixerat, & sic eam in gratuitam Dei misericordiam refert. Itaque hic verborum istorum sensus est: Nemo me ista dicere putet, quasi Deum mihi debitorem faciam, aut me supra vos ambitiosius extollam. Quicquid enim in me contulit Deus, id totum χάρισμα, id est, gratuitum donum est, quod non tam mei quam vestrum omnium respectu ille mihi contulit. Itaque tam abest, ut contra vos superbiam, ut potius me vestrum debitorem esse libenter fatear. Nam vos quoque vestram operam mihi contulistis, quando salutem meam publicis precibus commendavistis Deo, quas ipse exaudiuit, & in posterum quoque exaudiet: ut quemadmodum nunc me multorum precibus donavit, ita multorum quoque gratiarum actione ipsius bonitas celebretur. Ita vero non obscure innuit, aemulos suos praeter officium facere, dum ei hanc gratiam Dei inuidean t, & ex eo ariripiant calumniandi occasionem, pro quo gratias Deo debebant agere.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who, so that he should not be thought to boast of this benefit of God more arrogantly, or to attribute it to his own dignity or merits, admits that there is a cause for it in the Corinthians, by whose prayers he was helped, and at the same time reminds them what they ought further to do on his behalf. "You also," he says, "helping us together by prayer, so that the gift bestowed upon us through many persons may be celebrated through many by thanksgiving on our behalf." By the gift he means that deliverance of which he had just spoken, and so he refers it to the free mercy of God. The sense of these words, then, is this: let no one think that I say these things as if I were making God my debtor, or as if I were lifting myself above you with ambition. For whatever God has bestowed on me, it is all a χάρισμα, that is, a free gift, which he bestowed on me not so much with regard to me as with regard to you all. So far am I from being proud against you, that I rather willingly confess myself to be your debtor. For you too have contributed your labour to me, when you commended my salvation to God by public prayers, which he has heard and will hear again in the future; so that, just as he has now granted me to many persons' prayers, so his goodness may be celebrated by the thanksgiving of many. In this way he also hints not obscurely that his rivals act beyond their duty, while they begrudge him this grace of God and seize from it an occasion for slander, for which they ought rather to give thanks to God.

units.la: Fuit ergo veteris aut primitivae Ecclesiae mos, ut pro Euangelii administris preces publicae haberentur. Exempla eius moris Lucas in Actorum libro Cap. quarto & duodecimo commemorat. Et petijt saepe Paulus, ut Ecclesiarum precibus adiuuaretur. Estque hoc plus quam necessarium. Quia enim publicae salutis ministri sunt, variis insidiis eos Satan aggreditur, ut opus Domini impediat, omnis autem illorum error cum publico Ecclesiae totius periculo coniunctus est. Arguit hoc corruptissimos nostri seculi mores, quando ij quoque, qui Christianum nomen profitentur, Euangelij doctores diris devouent & execrantur, ac si illi turbarum & malorum omnium authores sint: quod olim Ieremiae etiam in faciem exprobratum fuisse scimus. Sunt hi mortalium ingratissimi & digni qui impostoribus praeda fiant. Quid vero de illis iudices, qui proditorio animo cum apertis Ecclesiae & Euangelij hostibus colludunt, & horum impios conatus in pastoribus suis opprimendis adiuuant? Obseruabis praeterea hic generalem doctrinam: Deus, quamuis nobis ex gratuita misericordia benefaciat, adiuuari tamen salutem nostram aliorum precibus. Imo vt alij pro alijs oremus perquam necessarium est propter infirmitatem nostram, quae multis adminiculis opus habet, & vt hoc officio amorem mutuum inter nos accendamus. Etenim si tantus Apostolus preces Ecclesiae requisiuit, seque illis adiutum esse publicè confessus est, quid nos faciamus, qui cum illo nequaquam sumus conferendi? Ad charitatem autem hic magnus atque efficacissimus stimulus est, si cogitemus, eos qui nihil posse videntur, preces tamen habere, quibus nos apud Deum iuuent. Sunt ergo nimium securi & barbari, qui & ipsi rarius precantur, & preces publicas ceu inutiles & superuacaneas negligunt. Quales autem censeri debent Chananaei illi nundinatores, qui preculas suas incondito murmure & plerunque non intellectas praecipitant, ab alijs conducti, & ita ex illis quaestum faciunt? Sunt hi Simonis Magi sectatores, & ideo eadem cum illo sententia damnantur: Pecunia vestra sit vobiscum in perditionem.
units.tr: There was therefore a custom of the old or primitive Church that public prayers should be offered for the ministers of the Gospel. Luke records examples of this custom in the Acts of the Apostles, chapters four and twelve. And Paul often asked to be helped by the prayers of the churches. And this is more than necessary. For since they are ministers of public salvation, Satan attacks them with various snares, to hinder the work of the Lord, and every error of theirs is joined with the public danger of the whole Church. This shows the most corrupt morals of our age, when even those who profess the Christian name curse and execrate the teachers of the Gospel with dreadful imprecations, as if they were the authors of all the troubles and evils; which we know was once also thrown in the face of Jeremiah. These people are the most ungrateful of mortals and deserve to become the prey of impostors. What then shall we judge of those who, with treacherous minds, collude with the open enemies of the Church and the Gospel, and help their impious attempts to oppress their ministers? You will observe here also a general doctrine: although God bestows benefits on us from free mercy, nevertheless our salvation is aided by the prayers of others. Indeed, it is most necessary that we pray for one another, because of our weakness, which needs many supports, and so that by this duty we may kindle mutual love among ourselves. For if so great an Apostle sought the prayers of the Church, and publicly confessed that he had been helped by them, what should we do, who are in no way to be compared with him? Now a great and most effective spur to charity here is, if we consider that those who seem able to do nothing nevertheless have prayers by which they may help us before God. Therefore they are too careless and barbarous, who both themselves pray rarely and neglect public prayers as useless and superfluous. But what must we think of those Canaanite money-changers, who rush through their little prayers with an unintelligible murmur, and mostly not understood, hired by others, and so make a profit from them? These are followers of Simon Magus, and therefore are condemned with the same sentence as he: "May your money perish with you."

units.la: Postremò officij quoque locus iste admonet eos, qui se à Deo exauditos esse sentiunt: quod est, vt Deo benefactori & vindici suo gratias agant, & id quidem publicè, ne quid dissimulare videantur, & vt plures alios suo exemplo excitent. Praecipit hoc Deus, in Psalmo dicens: In die tribulationis tuae inuoca me, & liberabo te, & glorificabis me. Id verò vt iustum aequumque est: ita licentiam carnis efficacissimè cohibet, ne à Deo acceptis beneficijs abutamur. Ideo Dauid dicebat, gratiarum actionem quouis sacrificio acceptiorem esse apud Deum. Horum itaque memi- nerimus in omnibus actionibus & studijs nostris, spem verò nostram confirmet, quod preces nostras exaudiri scimus à Deo Patre propter Filium eius aeternum, IESVM CHRISTVM, cuius haec promissio est: Si quid petieritis per nomen meum, ego faciam. Item: Si manseritis in me, & verba mea in vobis manserint, quicquid volueritis petetis, & fiet vobis. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Lastly, this passage also admonishes those who feel that they have been heard by God: that is, that they should give thanks to God, their benefactor and deliverer, and indeed publicly, lest they seem to dissemble anything, and that they may stir up many others by their example. God commands this in the Psalm, saying: "Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me." And indeed, as is just and fair, this most effectively restrains the licence of the flesh, so that we do not abuse the benefits received from God. Therefore David used to say that thanksgiving is more acceptable to God than any sacrifice. Let us therefore keep these things in mind in all our actions and endeavours, and let our hope be confirmed by the knowledge that our prayers are heard by God the Father for the sake of his eternal Son, JESUS CHRIST, whose promise this is: "If you ask anything in my name, I will do it." Likewise: "If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, you shall ask whatever you will, and it shall be done for you." To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA V.
units.tr: HOMILY V.

units.la: Nam gloriatio nostra haec est, testimonium conscientiae nostrae, quod cum simplicitate & sinceritate Dei, non cum sapientia carnali, sed cum gratia Dei versati sumus in mundo, potissimum autem apud vos. Non enim alia scribimus vobis quam quae legitis, aut etiam agnoscitis: spero autem vos etiam ad extremum agnituros. Sicut & aliquatenus agnouistis nos gloriationem vestram esse, quemadmodum & vos nostra estis in die Domini IESV.
units.tr: For our boast is this: the testimony of our conscience, that we have lived in the world, and especially among you, in the simplicity and sincerity of God, not in carnal wisdom but in the grace of God. We write to you nothing other than what you read or even acknowledge, and I hope you will acknowledge it to the end. Just as you have in some measure acknowledged that we are your boast, as you also are ours in the day of the Lord Jesus.

units.la: Respondit hucusque Paulus aduersariorum suorum calumniae, qua ei persecutiones exprobrabant, quasi sua importunitate quosuis contra se prouocaret, & odio dignus esset. Transit ergo nunc ad aliud crimen, quod ei obijciebatur: Leuitatem nimirum in promissis. Quia enim se Corinthum venire velle saepius promiserat, multa item quae apud eos corrigenda erant, in suum aduentum reiecerat, quibusdam etiam minatus erat, quorum proteriam tunc dignis modis coercere vellet, hactenus autem rebus Asiaticis impeditus (eo quod illic Deus ipsi nouam quotidie negotiorum grauissimorum materiam obijceret) aduentum suum distulerat: aduersarij ex eo nouam arripiebant calumniandi occasionem, vt vanum iactatorem esse dicerent, qui literis quidem magnificis multa polliceretur, & imbecilliores minis quoque terreret, non auderet autem prodire in conspectum, & coram cum illis agere, qui se ipsi opponebant. Ita verò eadem opera pijs, qui inter ipsos erant, insultabant, qui eius aduentu freti hucusque in veritate tuenda constantes fuerant, & adhuc illum magno cum desiderio expectabant. Vt ergo istis consulat, causam hanc agit quam diligentissimè.
units.tr: Up to this point Paul has answered the calumny of his opponents, by which they reproached him with persecutions, as if by his importunity he provoked everyone against himself and deserved to be hated. He now turns to another charge brought against him, namely fickleness in his promises. He had often promised that he would come to Corinth, and he had put off until his arrival many matters that needed correcting among them. He had even threatened some people whose wantonness he wished to restrain in fitting ways when he came. Hitherto, however, he had been hindered by affairs in Asia, since God kept presenting him each day with new and very weighty business there, and so he had postponed his coming. His opponents seized on this as a fresh occasion for slander, saying that he was a vain boaster who promised much in grand letters and frightened the weaker with threats, but did not dare to show himself in person and deal face to face with those who opposed him. In doing so they also insulted the godly among them, who, trusting in his coming, had so far stood firm in defending the truth and still awaited him with great longing. So, to look after these people, he handles this matter with the greatest care.

units.la: Orditur autem à praefatiuncula, qua hunc locum cum ijs, quae proximè praecesserunt connectit, simulque in genere asserit fidem suam, qua in munere Apostolico hucusque versatus sit. Nam gloriatio nostra (inquit) hæc est testimonium conscientiæ nostræ, &c. Summa omnium istorum est, se posse iure gloriari, quòd officio suo fideliter functus sit, cum alibi, tum maximè apud ipsos.
