Ita verò loquitur, non quòd alibi minus fideliter egerit, sed quòd plus studij & laboris apud Corinthios impendi oportebat, partim propter electorum multitudinem, quam in ea vrbe esse, ex Dei reuelatione intellexerat, partim propter pericula, quæ vndique ipsi incumbebant, adeò vt alibi testetur, se cum timore & tremore multo inter eos fuisse. Accedebat his mora diuturnior, cum illic sefquiannum substitisset. Id verò probat conscientiæ suæ testimonio, quòd perinde est, ac si Deum testem produceret. Hic enim solus corda renesque hominum scrutatur, & quo animo omnia fiant, nouit. Vbi tamen meminisse oportet, Paulum conscientiæ testimonio non gloriari, quasi per illud in Dei conspectu iustificetur quoad æternæ salutis negotium. Non enim de hoc, sed de munere apostolico hic aît, in quo nullius fraudis sibi conscius erat. Quoad illud, nihil sibiipsi vnquam tribuit, & perpetuò ratum manet, quòd dixit alibi: Nullius mihi conscius sum, sed non ideo iustificatus sum. 1. Corinth. 4.
units.tr: He begins with a short preface, by which he links this passage with what immediately preceded, and at the same time asserts in general terms his own faithfulness in the apostolic office up to now. For "our boast," he says, "is this: the testimony of our conscience," and so on. The sum of all this is that he can rightly boast that he has discharged his office faithfully, both elsewhere and especially among them. He does not say this because he had acted less faithfully elsewhere, but because more zeal and labour had to be spent among the Corinthians, partly because of the multitude of the elect whom he had learned by God's revelation to be in that city, and partly because of the dangers which pressed on him from every side. So much so that he elsewhere testifies that he was among them "in fear and much trembling." To these things was added a longer delay, since he had stayed there a year and a half. He proves this by the testimony of his conscience, which is just as if he were calling God to witness. For He alone searches hearts and reins, and knows with what intention everything is done. Yet we must remember here that Paul does not boast of the testimony of his conscience as though by it he were justified before God as regards the matter of eternal salvation. For he is speaking here not of that, but of his apostolic office, in which he was aware of no fraud. As for the former, he never ascribed anything to himself, and what he said elsewhere remains firmly true: "I am conscious of nothing against myself, yet I am not thereby justified" (1 Cor. 4).

units.la: Debet autem testimonium hoc omnibus, qui in publico aliquo munere versantur, sufficere aduersus calumnias & iniqua hominum de ipsorum studio & laboribus iudicia. Nam nullum testimonium certius, nullus testis grauior ac fide dignior est conscientia, quæ sibiipsi mentiri non potest. Ideo Paulus frequenter ad illam prouocat. In Concilio certè Sacerdotum coram Anania Pontifice orationem suam sic exorditur: Viri fratres, ego omni conscientia bona seruiui Deo ad hunc vsque diem. Et in posteriori ad Timoth. Gratiam habeo Deo, cui seruio à maioribus cum pura conscientia, &c. Ad Hebræos item: Confidimus quòd bonam habemus conscientiam, in omnibus cupientes honestè conuersari. Ita Dauid olim sæpius apud Dei tribunal de mente bene sibi conscia gloriabatur, cùm inter homines suæ defensioni locum nullum esse videret. Et idem ante hunc fecerat Samuel, cùm ipso absque culpa sua reiecto Israelitæ Regem sibi dari petijssent. Quorum omnium exemplis discant singvli ita se gerere, vt ipsi quoque propriæ conscientiæ testimonio freti, improborum hominum iudicia iniqua possint contemnere. Curent tamen, ne quid hic temere aut cum dolo faciant. Qui enim conscientiæ suæ testimonio in fallendis aliis abutuntur, ij à proprio corde condemnantur, quòd multis infelicissimè cessisse scimus. Nam si cor nostrum condemnet nos (inquit Apostolus) maior est Deus corde nostro. Quomodo autem huius iudicium sustinebunt, qui se à proprio corde iam damnari sentiunt? Porro quoad huius loci argumentum, hæc obseruatu digna occurrunt.
units.tr: This testimony ought to suffice for all who hold some public office against slanders and the unjust judgements of men about their diligence and labours. For no testimony is more certain, no witness more weighty and more worthy of trust, than conscience, which cannot lie to itself. Therefore Paul often appeals to it. Certainly in the council of priests, before Ananias the high priest, he begins his speech thus: "Brethren, I have served God in all good conscience until this day" (Acts 23). And in the second letter to Timothy: "I thank God, whom I serve from my forefathers with a pure conscience," and so on. Likewise to the Hebrews: "We trust that we have a good conscience, desiring to live honestly in all things" (Heb. 13). So too David of old often boasted before the tribunal of God of a mind well aware of its own innocence, when he saw that among men there was no place for his defence. And Samuel had done the same before him, when the Israelites, after he had been rejected without fault of his own, asked for a king to be given them. Let each person learn from all these examples to conduct himself so that, relying also on the testimony of his own conscience, he may despise the unjust judgements of wicked men. Yet let them take care not to act rashly or deceitfully here. For those who abuse the testimony of their conscience in deceiving others are condemned by their own heart, and we know that this has turned out very unhappily for many. For "if our heart condemns us," says the Apostle, "God is greater than our heart" (1 John 3). But how will they bear His judgement who already feel themselves condemned by their own heart? Moreover, as to the argument of this passage, the following points deserve notice.

units.la: Primùm, quòd existimationem suam tanta animi constantia tuetur, vt se innocentia sua gloriari dicat. Facit hoc non ambitiosè, sed ex officio: quia in nominis sui existimatione Euangelij doctrina, atque omnium, qui ipsi crediderant, salus periclitabatur. Imitentur ergo Apostoli exemplum omnes Ecclesiarum ministri, vnà cum omnibus ijs qui ad Reipub. gubernacula assident. Sunt enim nimium ignaui & seruiles, qui surdis auribus omnia negligunt, quæ de ipsis alij sentiunt & loquuntur. Decet quidem modestia & iniuriarum patientia omnes Christianos: at simul videre oportet, ne existimationi nostræ suum derogetur pondus, quo Deus nos alijs formidabiles esse vult. Vidit hoc olim Moses etiam, qui cùm hominum mansuetissimus esset, acerrimè tamen sese maleuolis opposuit, qui ipsum conabantur in contemptum adducere, vt simul à Deo institutum Ecclesiæ & Reipub. ordinem euerterent. Quàm verò infelices & nulla prorsus venia digni sunt, qui ipsi suam existimationem prostituunt morum licentia, & tunc demum se modestiæ laudem mereri sibi persuadent, si nihil à vulgo ignobili aut priuatis hominibus differant?
units.tr: First, he defends his reputation with such firmness of mind that he says he boasts of his innocence. He does this not out of ambition but out of duty, because the teaching of the gospel and the salvation of all who had believed in him were endangered by the loss of his good name. Let all ministers of the Churches, therefore, imitate the apostles' example, together with all who sit at the helm of civil government. For they are far too lazy and servile who, with deaf ears, neglect everything that others think and say about them. Modesty and patience under injuries certainly befit all Christians; but at the same time we must see to it that the weight of our reputation, by which God wills us to be formidable to others, is not diminished. Moses also saw this, who, although he was the meekest of men, nevertheless resisted most sharply those ill-disposed persons who tried to bring him into contempt, so that they might at the same time overthrow the order of the Church and of the commonwealth instituted by God. How wretched, and utterly unworthy of any pardon, are those who prostitute their own reputation by a licence of morals, and persuade themselves that they deserve praise for modesty only if they differ in nothing from the ignorant common crowd or from private persons!

units.la: Deinde, quare gloriatur Paulus? Quòd in mundo versatus sit, vt Christi ministrum decet. Ergo suæ in hoc mundo conuersationis rationem ministri habere debent, ne videlicet aliquid suæ vocatione indignum faciant. Nam etsi ministerij dignitas, Verbi item Dei & Sacramentorum effectus, nequaquam ex ministri persona dependeant, attamen propter auditores grauitati & honestati morum eos studere decet, ne propter ipsos ministerium vnà cùm Dei verbo vilescat. Arguunt hæc immanem Pontificum insolentiam, qui adeò non curant ista, vt ne tunc quidem ab aliquo reprehendi velint, si & suum officium negligant, & miserorum hominum animas secum ad inferos rapiant. Neque eo contenti, eandem immunitatem suis creaturis, Episcopis nimirum; mirum, sacrificis & monachis totique clero suo fecerunt, ut nemini aliquod in ipsos ius sit, & nefarium scelus putetur, aliquem ex illis in scelere quoque deprehensum durius aut contumeliosius tractare. Imitantur hos aliqui ex Euangelij ministris, qui cum improbissime viuant, tamen se audiri volunt, & nunquam non illud Christi in ore habent: In cathedra Mosis sedent Scribae & Pharisaei: omnia ergo quaecunque iusserint vos seruare, seruate & facite: secundum opera autem eorum ne feceritis. At simul huius quoque meminisse debebant, quod per Prophetam Dominus pronuntiauit: Honorantes me honorabo: qui vero me contemnunt, ignominia afficiuntur. Cuius sententiae exemplum horribile in filijs Heli mox edidit. Quibus adde, quae ignauis & mali exempli Sacerdotibus apud Malachiam dicuntur: Si non audieritis, neque posueritis super cor, ut detis gloriam nomini meo, dicit Dominus exercituum: mittam in vos execrationem, maledicamque benedictionibus vestris: quin maledixi iam, quia non ponitis super cor. Ecce ego increpabo vobis semen, & spargam stercus in facies vestras, &c. Non ergo absque peculiari Spiritus suggestione conscripti sunt Canones Apostolici (non fictitij illi, qui hoc nomine circumferuntur, sed qui in Apostolorum scriptis extant) de episcoporum & diaconorum officijs: qui si homine diligentius obseruarentur, regnum Dei felicius propagari posset, & maior esset ministrorum & totius Ecclesiastici ministerij authoritas.
units.tr: Next, why does Paul boast? Because he has lived in the world as becomes a minister of Christ. Therefore ministers must take account of their conduct in this world, lest they do anything unworthy of their calling. For although the dignity of the ministry, the efficacy of the Word of God and of the sacraments, by no means depends on the person of the minister, nevertheless, for the sake of the hearers, it becomes them to strive for gravity and honesty of morals, lest the ministry along with the Word of God be made contemptible on their account. These things condemn the monstrous arrogance of the Papists, who care so little for them that they do not even wish to be rebuked by anyone when they neglect their duty and drag the souls of wretched men down to hell with them. Not content with this, they have granted the same immunity to their creatures, namely the bishops, (what a marvel!) priests, monks and their whole clergy, so that no one has any right against them, and it is thought an unspeakable crime to treat any of them more harshly or contemptuously even when caught in a crime. Some ministers of the gospel imitate these men: though they live most wickedly, they still want to be heard, and always have on their lips that saying of Christ: "The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' seat; so whatever they bid you observe, observe and do; but do not do according to their works" (Matt. 23). But at the same time they ought to remember what the Lord declared through the prophet: "Those who honour me I will honour; but those who despise me shall be held in dishonour" (1 Sam. 2). He soon gave a terrible example of this sentence in the sons of Eli. Add to these what is said by Malachi to the slothful priests who gave a bad example: "If you will not hear, nor lay it to heart to give glory to my name, says the Lord of hosts, I will send a curse upon you, and I will curse your blessings; indeed I have already cursed them, because you do not lay it to heart. Behold, I will rebuke your seed and spread dung on your faces," and so on (Mal. 2). Therefore the Apostolic canons (not those fictitious ones that go about under this name, but those which are found in the writings of the apostles) concerning the duties of bishops and deacons were not written without a peculiar prompting of the Spirit. If these were observed more diligently by men, the kingdom of God could be propagated more happily, and the authority of the ministers and of the whole ecclesiastical ministry would be greater.

units.la: At simul videre oportet, in quibus nam consistat conuersatio illa, qua Paulus gloriatur? Quod cum simplicitate (inquit) & synceritate Dei, non cum sapientia carnali, sed cum gratia Dei versati sumus in mundo, potissimum autem apud vos. Primo simplicitatem & sinceritatem Dei sibi tribuit. Duplicitas cordis dicitur, quando aliud simulatur verbis & gestibus, aliud autem corde tectum latet. Est hoc vitium terrerrimum & inter homines exosissimum, utpote quo nullum efficacius est ad turbandum amicitias, sine quibus vita haec non potest consistere. Hominum vero nocentissimi sunt, qui in Ecclesia aut in Repub. corde duplici versantur. Hi enim sub publicae salutis praetextu suas res agunt, & omnia cauponantur. Exempla in omnibus historijs occurrunt, quibus commemorandis non est opus, cum quotidie hoc ipsum passim omnes boni non sine dolore & gemitu sentiant. Recte ergo Paulus simplicitatem & sinceritatem Dei, id est, diuinam, aut ad exemplum Dei institutam, sibi vendicat, & ita procul abs se remouet omnem dolum malum, adulationem, inuidiam, odium, seque quaecunque fecerit, bona fide & animo simplici atque ingenuo fecisse testatur, non ut suis commodis priuatim, sed publicae omnium saluti seruiret, Deiq; gloriam illustraret.
units.tr: But we must also see in what that conduct consists in which Paul glories: "that in simplicity and sincerity of God, not in carnal wisdom but in the grace of God, we have conducted ourselves in the world, and especially among you." First, he claims for himself the simplicity and sincerity of God. A double heart is one where something is pretended in words and gestures while something else lies hidden in the heart. This is a most terrible vice, and among men most hateful, since nothing is more effective for disturbing friendships, without which this life cannot stand. The most harmful men are those who act with a double heart in the Church or in the commonwealth. For under the pretext of public welfare they pursue their own affairs, and everything becomes a matter of bargaining. Examples occur in every history, and there is no need to recall them, since all good people feel this very thing everywhere every day, not without pain and groaning. Rightly, then, Paul claims for himself the simplicity and sincerity of God, that is, a divine sincerity, or one established on the model of God's own. In this way he removes far from himself every evil deceit, flattery, envy and hatred, and testifies that whatever he has done, he has done in good faith and with a simple and open mind, not to serve his own private advantage but the public welfare of all, and to make the glory of God shine forth.

units.la: Deinde addit: Non in sapientia carnali. Sub ista comprehendit quicquid non habetur ex Dei spiritu, sed nostro studio & industria paratur, & in mundo existimationem sapientiae sustinet: qualia sunt astutia in rebus agendis, sophistica, verborum splendor, eloquentia, & si quae alia sunt his similia. Haec omnia sibi deesse fatetur, ut etiam in prioris epistolae Cap. secundo. At istorum loco vendicat sibi gratiam Dei, sub qua Spiritus dona omnia continentur, quibus Deus Apostolos suos atq; primitiuam Ecclesiam olim exornauit: quae erant Scripturarum veterum vera cognitio, linguae, animi fortitudo, dicendi libertas, miraculorum virtus, denique ut quouis loco & tempore possent ea dicere, quae necessitas postulabat. Gratiae autem vocabulo hic vtitur consulto, ut mitiget gloriationis vocabulum, quo prius arrogantius vsus esse videri poterat. Ita enim innuit, ista se non ex semetipso habere, sed authorem omnium agnoscere Deum, qui ea sibi ex gratia dederit.
units.tr: Then he adds: "not in carnal wisdom." Under this term he includes whatever is not had from the Spirit of God but is prepared by our own zeal and industry, and that holds the reputation of wisdom in the world. Such things are cunning in managing affairs, sophistry, a show of words, eloquence, and whatever else is similar to these. He confesses that he lacks all these, as he also does in the second chapter of the earlier epistle. But in their place he claims for himself the grace of God, under which are contained all the gifts of the Spirit, with which God once adorned his Apostles and the primitive Church: namely, a true knowledge of the Old Scriptures, languages, fortitude of mind, freedom of speech, the power of miracles, and finally the ability to say, in any place and at any time, whatever necessity required. He uses the word grace here deliberately, so as to soften the word "glorying," which might have seemed too arrogant before. For he thus hints that he does not have these things from himself, but acknowledges God as the author of all, who has given them to him by grace.

units.la: Et haec illa sunt, quae in Ecclesiarum ministris, imo in magistratibus quoque, imprimis requiruntur, & sine quibus nihil recte agitur. Ante omnia animi integritate & synceritate opus est, ut ingenue agant & dicant omnia, nec alicui fucum faciant. Quid enim magis alienum a Veritatis ministro esse potest, quam si mendacijs & fallacijs quenquam decipiat? Reges quoque Spiritus Sanctus eos praecipue commendat, quorum cor rectum fuit cum Domino. Nec enim fieri potest, ut hominibus fideles sint, quibus leue videtur cum Deo ludere, & religione ad suas cupiditates abuti. Deinde non fidant carnis sapientiae aut vllis humanis praesidijs, sed in vnius Dei gratiam toto animo recumbant. Possunt hoc intrepida fiducia facere ministri, eo quod Dei promissiones habeant, quibus Spiritum suum illis aduocatum, patronum & protectorem pollicitus est. Quod ipsum de ijs quoque potest dici, qui Rempub. administrant. Nec aliqua causa est
units.tr: And these are the things which are chiefly required in the ministers of the Churches, indeed in magistrates as well, and without which nothing is rightly done. Above all there is need of integrity and sincerity of mind, so that they act and speak everything openly, and make a pretence to no one. For what can be more foreign to a minister of the Truth than to deceive anyone with lies and deceits? The Holy Spirit also especially commends those kings whose heart was upright before the Lord. For it cannot happen that men are faithful to other men when they think it a light matter to trifle with God and to abuse religion for their own desires. Next, let them not trust in the wisdom of the flesh or in any human protections, but let them rest with their whole mind in the grace of the one God alone. Ministers can do this with fearless confidence, because they have God's promises, in which he has pledged his own Spirit to them as advocate, patron and protector. The same can be said of those too who administer the commonwealth. Nor is there any cause

units.la: Matt.23. 1.Sam.2. Mala.2. 1.Tim.3. 2.Tim.1.2.3. Tit.1.3. 1.Pet.5. &c. quæ fiduciam hanc debeat aut possit in dubium vocare: quando impossibile est, vt eos deserat Deus, qui ipsius negotium agunt, & ei fideles sunt. Maledicti vero pronunciantur, qui vel in hominum gratiam, vel quacunque alia de causa opus Domini faciunt maligne. Vide Ierem. 49.
units.tr: Matt. 23. 1 Sam. 2. Mal. 2. 1 Tim. 3. 2 Tim. 1, 2, 3. Tit. 1, 3. 1 Pet. 5. etc., which ought or could call this confidence into doubt, since it is impossible for God to desert those who carry out his business and are faithful to him. But those are pronounced accursed who do the work of the Lord maliciously, whether to win men's favour or for any other reason. See Jer. 49.

units.la: Postquam vero Paulus de sua in munere Apostolico fide in genere disseruit, nunc propius ad rem ipsam accedit, & quia multi eum vanitatis insimulabant, quasi multa graviter & minaciter scriberet, multa item de semetipso in epistolis suis polliceretur, minus autem præstaret, ad horum calumniam ita respondet. Non enim alia scribimus vobis, quam quæ legitis, aut etiam agnoscitis, &c. Videtur hæc ridicula locutio. Quis enim aliud scribat, quam quod postea legatur? aut quis legere possit, quod nusquam scriptum extat? Sed proverbialis locutio est. Aliud enim scribunt quam quod legitur, qui ambigue scribunt, & consulto verborum cothurnos fingunt, dum locutionibus utuntur dubijs, quæ in diuersos sensus trahi ac non uno modo exponi possunt. Hi ipsi postea, si res in controversiam veniat, se aliud scripsisse clamant, quam lectum sit, id est, non eam esse suorum verborum sententiam, quam hi colligunt, quibus ipsi voluerunt fucum facere. Exempla huius impostura hodie multa videmus circa infelicem illam de Cœna Domini mysticA controversiam, in qua multi bono quidem zelo, sed nimis inconsulta temeritate novas loquendi formulas excogitarunt, quas utraque pars admittere posse videbatur: & ulterius progressi in aliorum confessiones, cum publicas tum privatas, manum iniecerunt, vt his quoque sensum alienum affingerent, quem deinde pro vero & genuino incautis obtruderent. Accidit deinde eis quod omnibus solet accidere, qui non bona fide in dirimendis controversijs agunt. Dum enim utrique parti placere volunt, utrique nebulas offundunt, quibus tandem per Veritatis aurām dissipatis & abstersis, ipsi omnibus suspecti & exosi sunt. Recte igitur Paulus, se exiftorum numero esse negat, dicens: Non scribimus alia, quam quæ legitis, id est, non aliter accipiatis ea quæ scribimus, quam verba sonent: neque alium sensum illis affingi cupimus, quam quem ipsi agnoscitis cum ea mente & voluntate convenire, quam iampridem ex iis didicistis, quæ vobiscum coram egi, cum in vrbe vestra versarer. Et spero, vos me talem agnituros esse in finem vsque, qualem olim vidistis & audiuistis. Et hæc quidem potissimum ad ea referri debent, quæ in priori epistola de suo aduentu scripserat, ob cuius dilationem diuturniorem amuli, vel potius aduersarij eius, ipsum vanitatis accusabant.
units.tr: But after Paul has spoken in general about his faithfulness in the Apostolic office, he now comes closer to the matter itself. Since many accused him of vanity, as if he wrote many weighty and threatening things, and in his epistles promised many things about himself, but performed less, he answers this calumny thus: "For we write to you nothing other than what you read, or even acknowledge, etc." This seems a ridiculous way of speaking. For who would write anything other than what is afterwards read? Or who could read what is nowhere written? But it is a proverbial way of speaking. For those write something other than what is read who write ambiguously and deliberately contrive the buskins of words, using doubtful expressions which can be drawn into different senses and cannot be explained in only one way. These same men afterwards, if the matter comes into dispute, cry out that they wrote something other than what was read, that is, that this is not the meaning of their words which those gather, whom they wished to deceive with their pretence. We see many examples of this imposture today in that unhappy controversy about the mystical Supper of the Lord, in which many, with a good zeal but with too thoughtless rashness, have devised new formulas of speech, which both parties seemed able to admit. Going further, they laid hands on the confessions of others, both public and private, so that they might attach to these also a foreign sense, which they then forced upon the unwary as true and genuine. Then there happened to them what usually happens to all who do not act in good faith in settling controversies. For while they wish to please each party, they throw clouds over both, and when these are at last dispersed and wiped away by the breath of Truth, they themselves become suspect and hateful to all. Rightly, then, Paul denies that he belongs to the number of such men, saying: "We write nothing other than what you read," that is, you should not understand what we write otherwise than the words sound, nor do we wish any other sense to be attached to them than that which you yourselves acknowledge agrees with the mind and will which you have long since learned from those things I discussed with you in person, when I was living in your city. And I hope that you will recognise me to the end as the man you once saw and heard. These words should chiefly be referred to what he wrote in the earlier epistle about his coming, on account of whose long delay his rivals, or rather his adversaries, accused him of vanity.

units.la: Admonentur autem hoc Pauli exemplo ministri omnes, constantiam ipsos decere cum in cmnibus suis actionibus, tum maxime in doctrina. Vt enim Christus sibi ipsi semper constat, & idem est hodie, heri & in secula: ita Verbum quoque eius non mutatur, sed manet in æternum. Nemo igitur in eius doctrina quicquam mutare, aut eius prædicationem pro suo arbitrio aliter instituere debet, quam Deus ipse mandauit. Quia enim is non alia ratione quam in Spiritu & Veritate colitur, nullus cultus et probari poterit, quem illi exercent, quibus de eius voluntate ex Verbo suo non satis constat. Obseruarunt hoc magno studio Apostoli, qui vt Euangelium vnanimi consensu prædicarunt, ita nihil vnquam mutarunt in doctrina semel ex Spiritus suggestione tradita. Poterat hoc prolixè demonstrari, si religionis & doctrinæ Christianæ capita quis ex ordine percurrere, eaque simul diligentius examinare vellet. Sed quia in re manifesta demonstrationibus minime opus est, hoc potius curent, qui hodie Apostolici videri ac dici volunt, vt Apostolorum vestigijs insistant, & ab his traditam doctrinam constanter seruent in Ecclesijs, quas ipsorum fidei Dominus credidit.
units.tr: All ministers, moreover, are admonished by this example of Paul that constancy befits them, both in all their actions and especially in doctrine. For as Christ always remains himself, and is the same today, yesterday and for ever, so his Word too is not changed but abides for ever. Therefore no one ought to change anything in his doctrine, or to order his preaching otherwise at his own discretion than God himself has commanded. For since he is worshipped in no other way than in Spirit and Truth, no worship which those men practise can be approved, who are not sufficiently certain of his will from his Word. The Apostles observed this with great care: they preached the Gospel with one accord, and so they never changed anything in the doctrine once delivered by the suggestion of the Spirit. This could be demonstrated at length, if someone wished to run through the heads of the Christian religion and doctrine in order and examine them more carefully together. But since demonstrations are by no means needed in a matter so plain, let those who today wish to be called and seen as Apostolic take care rather to tread in the footsteps of the Apostles, and to keep constantly in the Churches the doctrine handed down by them, which the Lord has entrusted to their faith.

units.la: At quod de illis dicitur, non minus ad vulgus Christianorum pertinet. Nam his quoque nihil magis necessarium est, quam vt in agnita veritate in finem vsque perseuerent, neque se abea illis rationibus dimoueri patiantur. Vt enim non multum profuerit iter rectum initio ingressum esse, nisi in eodem insistas, neque ad auia qualiacunque declines: Ita in salutis via non magnos progressus facient, qui non in eadem constantes fuerint, vt (quod in Lege passim inculcatur) neque ad dextram neque ad sinistram deflectant. Id vero cum nostris viribus præstare non possimus, modeste de nobis ipsis sentire, de Deo autem spem bonam concipere debemus, quod is ipsum in nobis consummaturus sit. Et de eo nos suo exemplo Paulus admonet, quando se fidere dicit, quod in finem vsque talem experturi sint, qualem initio fuisse viderant. Nam qui sibi ipsis fidunt, deque suis viribus magnifice sibi pollicentur, ijs fere idem quod Petro accidit, ut turpius alijs labantur, quos prae se antea contemserunt. Confirmat autem nos promissio boni illius pastoris, IESV CHRISTI, qui se oues suas nouisse dicit, neque passurum ut quis illas e manibus suis rapiat. Et qui filios irae dilexit, quomodo sibi per Filij sanguinem reconciliatos abijciat, siue negligat?
units.tr: But what is said of those men applies no less to the common run of Christians. For nothing is more necessary for them too than to persevere to the end in the truth they have acknowledged, and not to let themselves be turned away from it by those arguments. Just as it does little good to have set out on the right road at the start unless you keep to it and do not wander off along whatever side paths present themselves, so those who are not steadfast in the same course will not make great progress on the way of salvation: they must not turn aside to the right or to the left, as the Law repeatedly urges. Since we cannot accomplish this by our own strength, we ought to think modestly of ourselves and to place our good hope in God, who will bring it to completion in us. Paul admonishes us of this by his own example, when he says that he is confident that they will in the end experience the same kind of people they had been from the beginning. For those who trust in themselves and promise great things from their own powers usually suffer the same fate as Peter, falling more shamefully than others whom they had earlier despised. Moreover, the promise of that good Shepherd, Jesus Christ, strengthens us: he says that he knows his sheep and will not allow anyone to snatch them from his hands. And he who loved the children of wrath, how will he cast off or neglect those whom he has reconciled to himself through the blood of his Son?

units.la: Quid vero illud est, quod Corinthios in se perpetuo in extremum vsque agnituros esse, dicit Apostolus? Quòd(inquit)gloriatio vestra sumus, quemadmodum & vos nostra estis in die Domini IESV. Gloriatio vestra sumus, ait. Id est, ita tam erga vos quàm erga alios in toto meo apostolatu me gessi, ut me Apostolo & doctore iure possitis gloriari. Id vero non ea intentione dicit, quòd eos abs se denominari & Paulinos dici velit (nam de eo magna cum gravitate totam illam Ecclesiam in priori epistola monuerat) sed quia solide & syncerciter eis tradiderat, quacunque ad Veritatis & aeternae salutis doctrinam pertinebant, adeò ut quoad cognitionem & scientiam nullis Ecclesijs essent inferiores. Et vt dictum hoc molliat, quod ambitiosius aliquibus poterat videri, gloriam hanc ipsis quoque communicat, quando vicissim eos suam gloriationem esse, id est, tales per suum ministerium factos esse dicit, ut ipse quoq; vberrimam habeat de illis gloriandi materiam. Etenim si nullum aliud argumentu fuisset, sola tamen Ecclesiae illius in corruptissima vrbe constitutio docere poterat, Paulum fidelem & germanum esse Christi Apostolu. Quo referri debet, quòd alibi eos sui Apostolatus sigillu esse dixit. Ne quis tamen ipsum de gloria huius seculi loqui, aut de ea solicitum esse suspicetur, addit: In die Domini IESV: & simul particulam istam opponit iniquis aemulorum iudicijs, ut ostendat, se illa non magni facere, quando in gloriosó illo Christi aduentu totus mundus cogniturus sit, qua fide cum ipsis & cum alijs egerit.
units.tr: But what is this that the Apostle says, that he will have the Corinthians as his own until the very end? "For," he says, "we are your boast, just as you are ours in the day of the Lord Jesus." "We are your boast," he says; that is, I have so conducted myself, both toward you and toward others, throughout my whole apostolate, that you may rightly glory in me as your Apostle and teacher. He does not say this with the intention of wanting them to be named after him and called Paulines (for he had earlier admonished that whole Church with great seriousness on this very matter in his first letter), but because he had taught them soundly and sincerely everything that pertained to the doctrine of truth and eternal salvation, so that in knowledge and learning they were inferior to no churches. And to soften this statement, which might have seemed rather boastful to some, he shares this glory with them as well, when in turn he says that they are his boast, that is, that through his ministry they have been made such that he too may have the richest material for glorying in them. For even if there were no other argument, the mere founding of that Church in the most corrupt city could have shown that Paul was a faithful and true Apostle of Christ. To this should be referred what he says elsewhere, that they are the seal of his apostleship. Lest anyone suspect, however, that he is speaking of the glory of this age or is anxious about it, he adds: "in the day of the Lord Jesus," and at the same time he sets this phrase against the unjust judgments of his rivals, to show that he does not value those judgments, since at that glorious coming of Christ the whole world will come to know with what fidelity he dealt with them and with the others.

units.la: Est autem locus hic dignissimus obseruatu: quia docet, quae vera & solida sit gloria tam ministrorum quam Ecclesiarum. Gloriantur hodie Episcopi latissimis suarum dioecesium finibus, & pro ijs interdum bella quoque mouent non necessaria. Multi earum quoque gentium & vrbium Episcopi dicuntur, quas neque viderunt vnquam, neque videre cupiunt. Ambiunt praeterea purpuram Cardinalitiam, augent redditus annuos, inuadunt Abbatias & Ecclesias opulentiores, ut ex harum stipendijs maiorem partem sibijpsis decidant. Superbiunt item seruorum aulicorum inutili turba, equis multisque phaleratis, rhedis auro & ostro fulgentibus, mitris bicornibus, pedus argenteis & alia eius generis supellectile. Et ista quidem stolidum vulgus admiratur, seque Semideos quosdam videre putat, quoties personatos illos pastores intuetur. Sed vanissima est haec gloria, neque olim consistere poterit in die Domini IESV. Imò iam nunc his argumentis sese produnt, quòd praeceptorum Christi immemores regnum terrenum affectent, & huius mundi gloriam tam ipsi quàm Ecclesiae ministerio praeferant. Simulq; stulti illi laruarum eiusmodi admiratores se non germanas Christi oues esse offendunt, quando vocem alienam audiunt, neque ab illo vno pendent. Meminerint ergo pastores, hanc ipsorum gloriam veram & solidam esse, si Ecclesias secundum Dei Verbum bene instituas habeant, ut has Christo sistere possint, ceu sponsam castam & integram. De eo infra Paulus gloriabitur, & Baptista suum ministerium hoc potissimum nomine commendat. Vicissim populi gloria est, si ministros habeat fideles, qui doctrina simul & vitae exemplo praeluceant. Potest hoc ipsum ad Rempublicam quoque transferri. Gloriantur plerunque principes latis regnorum finibus, & his propagandis studeunt: & e contra populus illorum vitiorijs atque triumphis superbit. Sed vtrique leuitate & stultitia peccant. Etenim vera principum gloria est, non aliena inuadere, sed sua prudenter & bene gubernare, ius dicere, leges bonas condere, populum habere honestatis amantem, frugalem, pacificum, & obsequentem. Hoc olim in Solomonis aula nobilis illa Sabae Regina obseruabat, & admirabatur. Populi autem gloria est, principes habere pios, religiosos, iustitiae & pacis amantes, & horum edictis obtemperare. Idem de parentibus & liberis, heris & seruis, de coniugibus item debet intelligi: & si doctrinam hanc omnes diligentius obseruarent, felicior esset & tranquillior omnis loci & ordinis hominum conditio.
units.tr: This passage is well worth noting, for it teaches what true and solid glory is, both for ministers and for churches. Today bishops glory in the vast extent of their dioceses, and sometimes even wage unnecessary wars on their account. Many are called bishops of peoples and cities which they have never seen and have no desire to see. Besides this, they covet the cardinal's purple, increase their yearly revenues, seize abbeys and richer churches, so that they may pour the greater part of their revenues into their own pockets. They also take pride in a useless crowd of courtly servants, in horses and many decorated carriages, in carriages gleaming with gold and purple, in two-horned mitres, silver crosiers and other furnishings of that kind. The foolish crowd admires these things and thinks it sees some demigods whenever it looks upon those masked shepherds. But this glory is most empty, and it will not endure on the day of the Lord Jesus. Indeed, even now they betray themselves by these very signs, since, forgetful of Christ's precepts, they aspire to an earthly kingdom and prefer the glory of this world both to the ministry of the Church and to themselves. At the same time, those foolish admirers of such masks show that they are not the true sheep of Christ, since they hear a strange voice and do not depend on him alone. Let ministers therefore remember that their glory is true and solid only if they have churches well ordered according to the Word of God, so that they can present them to Christ as a chaste and whole bride. Paul will glory in this later on, and the Baptist commends his own ministry chiefly on this ground. In turn, the glory of the people lies in having faithful ministers who shine forth both in doctrine and by the example of their lives. This can also be applied to the commonwealth. Princes often glory in the wide boundaries of their realms and strive to enlarge them, and on the other hand the people take pride in their victories and triumphs. But both sin through levity and folly. For the true glory of princes is not to invade what belongs to others, but to govern their own affairs wisely and well, to dispense justice, to enact good laws, and to have a people who love honesty, are thrifty, peaceable and obedient. The noble Queen of Sheba observed and admired this in the court of Solomon. The glory of the people, on the other hand, is to have princes who are godly, religious, and lovers of justice and peace, and to obey their edicts. The same should be understood of parents and children, masters and servants, and likewise of spouses; and if everyone observed this teaching more diligently, the condition of every place and order of men would be happier and more tranquil.

units.la: Corinthij quomodo gloria Pauli dicenter in die Domini
units.tr: How the Corinthians are Paul's glory in the day of the Lord

units.la: Priusquam vero dicendi finem faciamus, hoc nobis quoque expendendum est, qua ratione Paulus dicat Corinthios suam gloriam fore in die Domini. Atqui constat, Ecclesiam illam tunc modis omnibus corruptissimam fuisse, & hodie in illis locis Mahumeticas superstitiones atq; barbariem dominari. Sed non spectauit Apostolus, quales plerique essent, sed Dei oraculum respexit, qui se in illa vrbe populum multum habere dixerat. Itaque ad electos restringi debet, quod hic dicitur, quos hypocritas & reprobos permixtos esse sciebat. Neque ipsi fraudi esse debuit posterorum perfidia atque defectio. Quis enim de nondum natis rationem reddere cogatur? Sunt haec diligentius hodie observanda propter inquietos illos rerum turbatores, qui Ecclesias omnes impuras & omni vitiorum genere infectas esse clamant, in quibus aliqui mali conspiciuntur, & se quoque polluti dicunt, nisi ab illis separentur. Nec eo contenti, infantes quoque per baptismum in Ecclesiae societatem adoptari nolunt, quia fidem nondum possint profiteri, neque constet quales aliquando futuri sint. Longe alia certe Pauli sententia fuit, qui de Corinthijs sibi gloriandum esse putauit. Et Isaias olim sub Achas rege in gente perditissima discipulos sibi a Deo datos esse agnoscebat. Ecce (inquit) ego & pueri, quos dedit mihi Dominus: miraculum & portentum sumus in Israele. Quod ipsum de plerisque prophetis poteste dici. Quem vero isti omnes vnquam reiecerunt, quo minus circumciderentur? Aut num illi propter aliquos improbos ac petulantes templi atq; Ecclesiae communionem deseruerunt? Nemo igitur temere de Ecclesijs iudicet, aut aliquorum salute desperet. Nemo praecipiti affectu abreptus Ecclesias facile deserat. Frequenter enim fit, vt qui scismata & dissidia faciunt, multo grauius peccent ijs, quos ipsi flagitiosissimos mortalium esse putant. Singuli potius simplicitati & constantiae in vera fide studeant, vt conscientia bona & integra confiteri possint in magno illo die, quando ad iudicium veniet magnus ille pastorum princeps, IESVS CHRISTVS: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Before we bring this discourse to an end, we must also consider in what sense Paul says that the Corinthians will be his glory in the day of the Lord. It is certain that that Church was then thoroughly corrupt in every way, and today Mahumetan superstitions and barbarism hold sway in those places. But the Apostle did not look at what most of them were like; he looked to the oracle of God, who had said that he had a great people in that city. Therefore what is said here must be restricted to the elect, since he knew that hypocrites and reprobates were mixed in with them. Nor should the faithlessness and defection of their descendants have been a reproach to him, for who can be called to give an account of those not yet born? These things must be observed more carefully today because of those restless disturbers of affairs who cry out that all churches are impure and infected with every kind of vice, in which some wicked persons can be seen, and who say that they themselves will be polluted unless they are separated from them. Not content with this, they also refuse to admit infants into the fellowship of the Church through baptism, because they cannot yet profess faith and it is not clear what they will be in time to come. Paul's judgment was certainly quite different, for he thought he had cause to glory in the Corinthians. And Isaiah, long ago under King Ahaz, acknowledged that the disciples given him by God were among a most wicked nation: "Behold," he says, "I and the children whom the Lord has given me are a sign and a wonder in Israel." The same could be said of most of the prophets. But did all of them ever reject those whom they had been commanded to circumcise? Or did they desert the communion of the temple and the Church because of some wicked and wanton persons? Let no one therefore judge the churches rashly, or despair of the salvation of some. Let no one, carried away by hasty feeling, easily abandon the churches. For it often happens that those who create schisms and dissensions sin far more gravely than those whom they consider the most shameful of mortals. Rather, let each person strive for simplicity and steadfastness in the true faith, so that with a good and clear conscience they may be able to confess on that great day, when that great Prince of shepherds, Jesus Christ, comes to judgment, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA VI.
units.tr: HOMILY VI.

units.la: Itaque hac fiducia prius volui ad vos venire, vt secundam gratiam habueritis: & per vos transfire in Macedoniam, & rursum ex Macedonia venire ad vos, & a vobis deduci in Iudaeam. Hoc ergo cum deliberarem, numquid leuitate sum vsus? aut num quae delibero, secundum carnem delibero, vt sit apud me Etiam & Non? Imo fidelis Deus, quod sermo noster apud vos non fuit Etiam & Non. Nam Dei Filius, IESVS CHRISTVS, qui inter vos per nos praedicatus est, per me scilicet, & Syluanum ac Timotheum, non fuit Etiam & Non, sed fuit Etiam in ipso (quotquot enim sunt promissiones Dei, in ipso sunt Etiam, & in ipso sunt Amen) ad Dei gloriam per nos. Porro qui nos confirmat vobiscum in Christum, & qui vnxit nos, Deus est: Qui etiam obsignauit nos, deditq; arrhabonem Spiritus in cordibus nostris.
units.tr: Therefore, in this confidence I wished to come to you first, so that you might have a second grace; and to pass through you into Macedonia, and to come back again from Macedonia to you, and to be sent on by you into Judea. When I was deliberating this, did I use levity? Or do I deliberate according to the flesh, so that with me there is Yes and No? Indeed, God is faithful, that our word to you was not Yes and No. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you through us, namely through me, and Silvanus and Timothy, was not Yes and No, but in him it is Yes (for however many the promises of God are, in him they are Yes, and in him they are Amen) to the glory of God through us. Moreover, God is the one who establishes us with you in Christ, and who has anointed us; he also sealed us and gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts.

units.la: Quoniam mundus Veritatis lucem odit, eo quod per eam opera ipsius prava arguuntur, nihil in huius ministris tam minutum est, quod non notet maligno oculo atque calumnietur: non quidem quod vitia, quibus hi laborant, emendata cupiat, sed vt doctrinam in contemptum adducat, aut inuisam atq; exosam reddat. Accidit hoc ipsi Christo Domino nostro, quem modo propter commercia cum publicanis, modo propter discipulorum leuiuscula delicta, modo alias obcausas accusauerunt. Non debent ergo similibus offendi Ecclesiarum ministri, vt propterea ab officio discedant: quia tamen improbi illi per ipsorum latus Veritatis doctrinam iugulare conantur, exigit hoc partim Dei gloria, partim multorum salus, vt suam authoritatem qua possunt diligentia afferant. Idem ergo Paulus facit quoad Corinthios, apud quos multi hoc vnum agebant, vt labefactata ipsius authoritate, synceriorem Euangelij doctrinam exploderent. Ideo ei persecutiones exprobrabant: quibus initio statim fortiter respondit. Deinde vanitatis & mendacij insimulabant, eo quod suum ad ipsos aduentum diutius differret. Cum his nuper coepit agere, & in genere docuit, se ab omni fuco & simulatione alienissimum fuisse, inter ipsos vero ita vixisse, ut merito de sua fide possit gloriari, & quidem in ipsius Christi conspectu. In praesenti autem propius ad calumniam diluendam accedit, & mora admissa totius q; consilij sui rationem reddit.
units.tr: Since the world hates the light of truth, because by its light its wicked works are exposed, nothing is so small in the ministers of the truth that it does not mark it with an evil eye and slander it. Not indeed because they wish the faults from which these men suffer to be corrected, but so that they may bring the doctrine into contempt, or make it hated and detested. This happened to Christ our Lord himself, whom they accused sometimes on account of his dealings with the tax collectors, sometimes on account of the trivial faults of his disciples, and sometimes on other grounds. Therefore the ministers of the Churches ought not to be offended by similar things so as to abandon their office; yet since those wicked men try to cut the throat of the doctrine of truth through the ministers' side, the glory of God and the salvation of many demand in part that they defend their authority with all the diligence they can. So Paul does the same with regard to the Corinthians, among whom many were doing this one thing: that, by undermining his authority, they might reject the purer doctrine of the Gospel. Therefore they reproached him with persecutions, to which he replied at once and bravely at the outset. Then they accused him of vanity and falsehood, because he had delayed his coming to them for so long. He has recently begun to deal with these charges and has taught in general that he was most remote from all pretence and dissimulation, and that among them he had lived in such a way that he could rightly glory in his faith, and indeed in the sight of Christ himself. But now he draws closer to refuting the calumny, and, having admitted the delay, he gives an account of the whole reasoning of his plan.

units.la: Principio ostendit, se nullius levitatis debere accusari, eo quod si quae culpa sit in eius mora aut dilatione adventus sui, ea in ipsis tota haereat, qui illius fuerint ei authores. Hac fiducia (inquit) prius volui ad vos venire: quod nimirum sperarem, vos agnoscere, qua fide & integritate inter vos versatus sim, neque mihi alia mei consilij ratio fuit, quam ut qui prius per sesquiannum apud vos fidem docui & plantaui, nunc secundam quoque gratiam, id est, alterum beneficium vobis conferrem, & ad vos reversus uberiori doctrina animos omnium rigarem, collapsa restituerem, vitiosa corrigerem, labefactata instaurarem, denique vos in fide magis confirmarem. Hac (inquam) mei consilij summa fuit, quae me monuit, ut per vos in Macedoniam transire, deinde ex Macedonia ad vos redire, & tandem vobis me deducentibus in Iudaeam profectus statuerem.
units.tr: First he shows that he ought not to be accused of any levity, since if there is any fault in his delay or postponement of his coming, it clings wholly to them, who were the authors of it for him. "In this confidence," he says, "I wished to come to you first": namely because I hoped that you would recognise with what faith and integrity I had lived among you. Nor was there any other reason for my plan than this: that I, who had previously taught and planted the faith among you for a year and a half, might now also confer on you a second grace, that is, another benefit; and, returning to you, might water the minds of all with richer teaching, restore what had collapsed, correct what was faulty, restore what had been weakened, and finally confirm you more firmly in the faith. This (I say) was the sum of my plan, which advised me to pass through you into Macedonia, then return from Macedonia to you, and at last, with you sending me on, set out and go into Judea.

units.la: Quid vero hic reprehensione dignum est? Num levitatis accusari mereor, quod ex Apostoli officio vos inuisere, & donum aliquod spirituale vobis conferre volui? Atqui levitatis crimine notantur, qui labores nihil ad se pertinentes & quibus ipsi non possunt sufficere, subeunt. Vel num me secundum carnem, id est, inconsulto & praecipiti affectu abreptum hoc consultauisse dicetis, & ideo mihi accidisse, ut apud me sit Etiam & Non, id est, ut in meis promissis lubricus atque levis inueniar, dum ea non praesto? Equidem scio homines quidem proponere, Deum autem dirigere gressus suos consilia nostra, prout ipsi libuerit: neq; mihi ipsi unquam tantum tribui, ut in mea potestate esse putarim ad vos venire, vel minus. Ideo diserte dixi me venturum esse, si ita velit Dominus. Quia ergo nihil a functione apostolica alienum promisi, & insuper consilium meum Dei decreto atq; voluntati subieci, quae ratio est, cur levitatis accuser?
units.tr: But what here is worthy of reproach? Do I deserve to be accused of levity because I wished to visit you from the duty of an Apostle and to confer some spiritual gift upon you? Yet those are marked with the charge of levity who undertake labours that do not concern them and for which they themselves are not sufficient. Or will you say that I took this counsel according to the flesh, that is, carried away by an unconsidered and hasty impulse, and that therefore it has come about that with me there is Yes and No, that is, that I am found fickle and light in my promises, since I do not perform them? Indeed I know that men propose, but God directs their steps, and our plans are as he pleases. Nor have I ever claimed so much for myself as to think it was in my power to come to you, or not to come. Therefore I expressly said that I would come, if the Lord so wills. Since, then, I promised nothing foreign to the apostolic office, and in addition subjected my plan to the decree and will of God, what reason is there why I should be accused of levity?

units.la: Est autem in Pauli exemplo observatu dignissimum, quod vanitatis crimen tanta cum diligentia amolitur. Ut enim mendacio in quouis homine nihil inhonestius aut illiberalius fingi posse est: ita non aliud est a functione Ecclesiastica magis alienum. Qui enim hanc obeunt, ij Veritatis ministri sunt, cuius Verbum praedicare debent, & ita quidem ne huic aliquid vel abs se vel ab alijs confictum admisceant. Quid enim paleae cum tritico? inquit Dominus. Obseruent ergo quoad doctrinam, ne vanis promissionibus aliquos laltent, ut de ipsis Propheticum illud dici possit: Populi mi, qui te beatum dicunt, te decipiunt, & viam gressuum tuorum dissipant: Item, Ne quem minus fallacibus terreant, & (ut alius Propheta ait) bellum contra eos sanctificent, qui non dederint in os ipsorum. Curent praeterea, ut nomini & titulis suis respondeant, ut denique in sermone quotidiano veritati studeant, ne dum hic vaniores sunt, seipsos quoad doctrinam quoque suspectos reddant. Quis enim de caelestibus loquentes audiat, quos in terrenis & temporarijs mendaces esse videt? Proderit hic plurimum, si non immiscean se rebus a sua functione alienis, & quae ipsis minus compertae esse possunt: si ite temperantia & frugalitati studeant, ne quando aere alieno grauati tandem creditores suos fallere, & saepius mentiri cogantur. Pertinent huc Apostolici canones, quibus praecipitur, ne Episcopi vino dediti sint, ne quaestum turpem faciant, ut denique domui suae bene praesint, &c. qui si ab omnibus observarentur, non ita vilesceret ministerij authoritas.
units.tr: Moreover, in Paul's example the charge of vanity is most worthy of observation, since he removes it with such care. For just as nothing more dishonourable or ungentlemanly can be imagined in any man than a lie, so nothing is more alien to the ecclesiastical office. For those who discharge it are ministers of the Truth, whose Word they ought to preach, and indeed in such a way as not to mix anything with it, whether invented by themselves or by others. "For what has chaff to do with wheat?" says the Lord. Let them therefore be careful in doctrine, lest they deceive anyone with empty promises, so that the prophetic saying may be applied to them: "My people, those who call you blessed deceive you, and scatter the way of your steps." Likewise: let them not terrify anyone with less than deceitful things, and (as another prophet says) sanctify war against those who have not put anything into their mouths. Let them also take care that they answer to their name and titles, and finally that they strive for truth in daily speech, lest, while they are more vain here, they also make themselves suspect in doctrine. For who would listen to those speaking of heavenly things, when he sees them lying about earthly and temporal matters? It will be of great benefit if they do not meddle in affairs foreign to their office, and in matters which may be less well known to them; if they devote themselves to moderation and thrift, lest at some time, burdened with debt, they are at last forced to cheat their creditors and to lie more often. To this belong the Apostolic canons, which command that bishops not be given to wine, that they not make shameful gain, and finally that they rule their own households well, and so on. If these were observed by all, the authority of the ministry would not be so cheapened.

units.la: At quod de ministris dicitur, omnes homines, cuiuscunq; loci sint, ad se transferre debent. Quam enim turpe sit mentiri, gentium quoq; sapientes intellexerunt. Id sane in virum bonum cadere, Cicero negat: & idem eum, qui semel a veritate deflexit, non maiore religione ad periurium, quam ad mendacium perduci posse ait. A Christiano cerce homine alienissimum esse debet mendacium, quando huius patrem diabolum esse, Christus testatur. Meminerint ergo horum singuli, & non in verbis modo verum etiam in factis veritati studeant, ne quis ipsos aliud simulare aliud vero reipsa agere dicat. Imprimis autem in religionis causa caueant, ne Spiritui sancto mentiantur, quod scelus atrocissimum esse, Ananiae exemplo docemur. Act. 5.
units.tr: But what is said of ministers, all men, of whatever place, ought to apply to themselves. The wise men of the Gentiles also understood how shameful it is to lie. Cicero denies that this befalls a good man; and he says that the man who has once turned aside from the truth can be led no less to perjury than to lying, without any greater scruple. A lie ought to be most alien to a Christian man, since Christ testifies that its father is the devil. Let each of them therefore remember this, and strive for truth not only in words but also in deeds, lest anyone say that they pretend one thing and in reality do another. Above all, let them take care in matters of religion not to lie to the Holy Spirit, which we are taught by the example of Ananias to be a most atrocious crime. Acts 5.

units.la: Admonet praeterea Pauli exemplum, quae ratio in capiendis consilijs teneri debeat. Abstit ab his ante omnia levitas, ne illa praecipitemus. Est enim magna affectuum vis, ira nimirum, odij, amoris atque similium, qui fere animos excaecant, ut solis praesentibus intenti, non ulterius proficiant. Ideo de ira dicebat Apostolus, eam non operari iustitiam. Quod ipsum de reliquis etiam affectibus intelligi debere, res ipsa docet. Mora igitur & examine diligenti, adeoque (quod proverbio dicitur) consilio in nocte opus est. Recte enim Sophocles monuit, non eundem finem cursus & consilij esse. In cursu enim vincit, qui celerrimus est: in consultando autem mora de multis nos admonet, celeritas vero periculosa est: & qui ea vruntur, fere tandem non sine ignominia sua dicunt. Non putaram quod dictum a sapiente viro alienissimum esse debere, Scipio non minus verè quam graviter monuit. Deinde ne consultemus secundum carnem, id est, confidenter, quasi quae ipsi statuimus, decreta sint irrevocabilia. Possumus enim falli tunc quoque, quando animi intentio bona & zelus omnino sanctus est: cuius rei memorabile exemplum in Nathano historia sacra pro ponit, qui consilium, quod Davidi de templo aedificando confidentius dederat, mox proprio ore revocare coactus fuit. Adde hīs, quod omnia nostra à Dei providentia pendent (vt iam ante monuimus) qui non semper per nos id fieri vult, quod per se bonum est. Semper ergo meminerimus conditionis illius, qua Iacobus nos consilia nostra moderari iubet, & de qua in explicatione ultimi Cap. epistolae priores diximus: vt nimirum addamus: Si Dominus voluerit. Ita enim nihil sine Deo suscipiemus, multo minus autem statuemus quod cum ipsius voluntate pugnet. Peccant in utroque, quicunque confidentius agunt, & ideo vt plurimum suis consiliis falluntur, & ex sua confidentia ignominiam reportant. Vt vero doctrina haec nos in officio continet, ita consolationem quoque dulcissimam suggerit, qua aduersus eorum machinationes confirmemur, qui contra Christum & Ecclesiam eius conspirant. Consultant hi secundum carnem, & quod ipsi statuunt, id cum aeterna Dei decreto pugnat, qui Filium suum vnxit Regem super Zionem montem suum sanctum, vt suos feruet & regat, rebelles autem & contumaces sceptro suo ferreo coerceat. Illis ergo rectissimè feruit comminatio illa, quae apud Isaiam habetur: Societatem inite o populi, at inferiores eritis: auscultate qui in longinquis estis regionibus: accingamini, at inferiores eritis: accingamini inquam, at inferiores eritis: inite consilium, & fiet irritum: loquimini sermonem, sed non stabit: quia nobiscum est Deus. Isa. 8.
units.tr: Moreover, the example of Paul advises what principle ought to be kept in taking counsel. Above all, levity must be kept away, lest we act rashly. For there is great power in the affections, namely anger, hatred, love and such like, which generally blind the minds so that, intent only on what is present, they make no further progress. Therefore the Apostle said of anger that it does not work the righteousness of God. The thing itself shows that the same must be understood of the other affections as well. Therefore delay and careful examination are needed, and indeed (as the proverb says) counsel is needed at night. Rightly Sophocles warned that the end of a race and the end of a plan are not the same. For in a race he wins who is swiftest; but in deliberating, delay warns us about many things, while haste is dangerous, and those who use it generally end, not without their own disgrace. Scipio, no less truly than gravely, warned of something which I did not think should be said by a wise man to be most alien to him. Next, let us not deliberate according to the flesh, that is, confidently, as if what we have decided were irrevocable decrees. For we may be deceived even when the intention of the mind is good and the zeal entirely holy. Sacred history sets before us a memorable example of this in Nathan, who was forced to recall with his own mouth the counsel he had given David too confidently about building the temple. Add to these that all our affairs depend on the providence of God (as we have already warned), who does not always wish to be done through us what is good in itself. Let us therefore always remember that condition by which James bids us moderate our plans, and about which we spoke in the explanation of the last chapter of the earlier epistle: namely that we add, "If the Lord wills." For thus we will undertake nothing without God, and much less decide upon anything that conflicts with his will. Those who act with confidence sin in both ways, and therefore for the most part are deceived in their plans, and from their confidence bring back disgrace. Just as this teaching keeps us in our duty, so it also offers a most sweet consolation, by which we are strengthened against the schemes of those who conspire against Christ and his Church. These men take counsel according to the flesh, and what they decide conflicts with the eternal decree of God, who anointed his Son King over his holy mountain Zion, to feed and rule his own, and to restrain the rebellious and stubborn with his iron sceptre. Therefore that threat which is found in Isaiah fits them most rightly: "Join together, O peoples, and you will be broken; listen, you who are in distant regions: gird yourselves, and you will be broken; gird yourselves, I say, and you will be broken: take counsel, and it will come to nothing; speak the word, but it will not stand; for God is with us." Isa. 8.

units.la: Porrò vt ad Paulum redeamus, quia aemuli levitatem ei ideo exprobrabant, vt hoc praetextu (sicut initio monuimus) doctrinam eius suspectam facerent, commodè ad hanc delabitur, & argumento ex illa petito probat, se ab omni vanitate sine mendacio semper alienissimum fuisse. Quo loco observari debet, quod omissis iis, quae in ipsius personam dicebantur, doctrinae suae veritatem asserit. De hac igitur potius quàm de sua exi-stimatione omnes ministri ecclesiarum solliciti esse debent. Sic autem hanc partem orditur: Fidelis Deus, quod sermo nostcr apud vos non fuit Etiam & Non. Praemittit iurisiurandi formulam, quae pro Hebraeorum more Apostopesim habet. Nam sensus est: Quàm verax & fidelis est Deus, tam certum est, sermonem, id est, praedicationem apud vos non fuisse Etiam & Non, id est, non fuisse variam, inconstantem sibi, ipsi contrariam. Id verò probat. Nam Dei Filius, qui praedicatus est inter vos per nos, per me scilicet, & Syluanu ac Timotheu, non fuit Etiam & Non: sed fuit Etiam in ipso. Argumentum hoc à subiecto Euangelij sumitur, & vt magis perspicuum fit, ita formari poterit: Euangelio, cuius nos administri sumus, nihil aliud praedicatur, quàm Dei Filius, IESVS CHRISTVS: At hic non est varius, qui instar Protheï in omnes formas vertatur, sed ipsissima est Veritas, sibi semper constat. Ergo praedicatio quoq; nostra vera, certa & firma fuit, neq; aliqua in parte à seipsa dissentit. Ad confirmationem & amplificationem Minoris facit quod sequitur: Quotquot enim sunt promissiones Dei, in ipso sunt Etiam & Amen ad Dei gloriam per nos. Quasi diceret: Tam abest, vt Christus possit varius & inconstans dici, vt potius hic ille sit, in quo omnes promissiones suum habent complementum. Convenit enim hoc dictum cum illo Ioannis: Lex per Mosem data est, gratia & veritas per IESVM CHRISTVM facta est. Peculiari autem loquendi formula Paulus vtitur, in qua vocem Graecam vàí cum Hebraea Amen coniungit: partim vt Christum & meritum eius tam ad gentes quàm ad Iudaeos pertinere doceat, de quo saepe dictum est: partim vt nos nostri officij admoneat. Vt enim Graecum vàí, quod Latini per Etiam exprimunt, assensionis siue confirmationis nota est: ita voce Amen Hebraei vtebantur olim, quoties suo consensu confirmabant quae Deus loquebatur, aut quod huius nomine ministri proponebant. Vide Deut. 27. 1. Cor. 14. Est autem totus hic locus admodum memorabilis, quia Euangelij dignitatem mirifice commendat. Argumentum siue subiectum huius est vnus IESVS CHRISTVS, qui ideo alibi Prophetarum & Apostolorum fundamentum dicitur, & quem vnum Apostoli nouerunt atque praedicarunt. Quis vero ille est? Aeternus verusque Dei Filius, qui praefinito tempore verum hominum in personae vnitatem assumpsit, vt pro peccatis totius mundi victima factus, promissiones Dei omnes completeret, atque ratas faceret. In illo sane vno praestita est promissio primis parentibus facta: Semen mulieris conculcabit caput serpentis. Idem ille benedictum illud Abrahami semen est, de quo dictum fuerat: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes terrae. Hic Schilo ille vel Sospitator, quem venturum esse Iacob praedixerat, quando sceptrum a Iuda esset transferendum. Hic est, quem typi legales adumbrarunt, & quem Moses Prophetam illum Magnum dixit, quem omnes audire debeant. Denique (vt Petrus testatur) hic solus ille est, de quo omnes Prophetae iaminde a Samuele vaticinati sunt. Est ergo Euangelium ipsissimum Dei Verbum, de quo olim Isaias dixit, Verbum Domini manet in aeternum. Quapropter hodie etiam hoc solum praedicari debet, & ita quidem, vt per illud vnus Christus annuntietur, non ambiguus, non varius, non qui villis adminiculis opus habeat, sed qui idem est heri, hodie & in aeternum, solusque nobis seruandis sufficit. Et debent ex eo in omni tentationum genere consolationem petere Christiani homines, quod promissiones Dei omnes in eo complementum suum habere, & proinde illum nobis vere placatum esse sciunt. Idem Euangelij doctrina suo Amen succinere aut subscribere debent ad gloriam Dei, id est, sic vt suo testimonio Dei veritatem commendent, adeoque obsignent (vt Ioannes loquitur) quod Deus verax sit. Neque dubitare quenquam conuenit de eorum, quae nobis in illo promittuntur, veritate. Quia ad omnes pertinet vsitatum illud IESV CHRISTI dictum: Fiat tibi secundum fidem tuam. Item: Fides tua te seruauit: abi in pace.
units.tr: Now let us return to Paul. Since his rivals used to charge him with fickleness, so that by this pretext (as we noted at the start) they might make his teaching suspect, he comes conveniently to this point and, from an argument drawn from that very charge, proves that he was always far removed from vanity and falsehood. Here it should be observed that, setting aside what was said against his person, he asserts the truth of his teaching. All ministers of the churches ought to be concerned about this rather than about their own reputation. He begins this part as follows: "God is faithful, that our word to you was not 'Yes and No'." He puts first a form of oath, which in the Hebrew manner takes the shape of an aposiopesis. The sense is: as truly and faithfully as God is true and faithful, so surely our word, that is, our preaching among you, was not "Yes and No," that is, was not varying, inconstant, and self-contradictory. He then proves this. For the Son of God, who was preached among you through us, that is, through me, Silvanus and Timothy, was not "Yes and No," but was "Yes" in him. This argument is taken from the subject matter of the Gospel, and to make it clearer it may be framed thus: Nothing else is preached in the Gospel, whose ministers we are, than the Son of God, Jesus Christ. But he is not variable, who turns himself into every shape like Proteus, but is Truth itself, always consistent with himself. Therefore our preaching too was true, certain and firm, and in no part does it disagree with itself. What follows serves to confirm and amplify the minor premise: "For however many are the promises of God, in him is the 'Yes,' and in him the 'Amen,' to the glory of God through us." As if he said: Christ is so far from being capable of being called variable and inconstant that rather he is the one in whom all the promises have their fulfilment. For this agrees with John's saying: "The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ." Paul uses a particular form of speech, in which he joins the Greek word for "yes" [ναί] with the Hebrew "Amen." He does this partly to teach that Christ and his merit pertain to the Gentiles as much as to the Jews, which has often been said, and partly to remind us of our office. For just as the Greek [ναί], which the Latins render by "etiam," is a mark of assent or confirmation, so the Hebrews of old used the word "Amen" whenever they confirmed by their consent what God spoke, or what ministers proposed in his name. See Deut. 27 and 1 Cor. 14. This whole passage is indeed most noteworthy, because it wonderfully commends the dignity of the Gospel. The argument or subject of it is the one Jesus Christ, who for this reason is elsewhere called the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles, and whom the Apostles alone knew and preached. Who then is he? The eternal and true Son of God, who in the appointed time took true humanity into the unity of his person, so that, made a victim for the sins of the whole world, he might fulfil all the promises of God and make them sure. In him alone indeed was performed the promise made to our first parents: "The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent." He is that blessed seed of Abraham, of whom it was said: "In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed." He is that Shiloh or Saviour whom Jacob foretold would come when the sceptre was to be taken from Judah. He is the one whom the legal types foreshadowed, and whom Moses called that great Prophet whom all should hear. Lastly, as Peter bears witness, he alone is the one of whom all the Prophets have prophesied from Samuel onward. The Gospel, therefore, is the very Word of God, of which Isaiah once said: "The word of the Lord remains for ever." Wherefore today this alone too ought to be preached, and in such a way that through it Christ alone is proclaimed: not ambiguous, not variable, not one who needs some props, but who is the same yesterday, today and for ever, and alone is sufficient for our salvation. Christians ought to draw comfort from this in every kind of temptation, knowing that all God's promises find their fulfilment in him, and that therefore he has truly been reconciled to us. The doctrine of the Gospel ought likewise to answer with its own "Amen," or to subscribe, to the glory of God, that is, so that by their testimony they commend the truth of God, and so seal (as John puts it) that God is true. Nor ought anyone to doubt the truth of those things promised to us in him. For that common saying of Jesus Christ applies to all: "Let it be done to you according to your faith." And again: "Your faith has saved you; go in peace."

units.la: Caeterum ne quid Paulus sibi ipsi arrogantius tribuere putaretur, apertius docet, vnde fit haec Euangelicae doctrinae certitudo, & simul Corinthios propriae conscientiae testimonio conuincit, sic dicens: Porro qui nos confirmat vobiscum in Christum, & qui vnxit nos, Deus est: qui etiam obsignauit nos, deditque arrhabonem Spiritus in cordibus nostris. Quasi diceret: Quid verbis opus est? Ista non ex nostro cerebro fingimus, sed ab ipso Deo confirmati dicimus: neque ex Christianorum numero aliquis tam impudens reperietur, qui Deum veracem esse non fateatur, aut qui promissiones eius in Christo plene praestitas esse neget. Et idem ille nos vnà vobiscum confirmat in Christum, vt videlicet huic inseramur ceu germani palmites, inque eius fide constanter perseueremus, dum nos vngit & obsignat, arrhamq; Spiritus sui cordibus nostris inserit. Quod si ergo Christiani estis, vtique hanc Spiritus virtutem sentitis, & eius testimonio atq; inspiratione confirmati nihil dubitatis, quin in Christo vobis abunde exhibita sint, quaecunque ad generis humani salutem faciunt. At cum nos nihil praeter hunc vnum praedicemus, adeoq; aperte fateamur, nos nihil aliud nouisse praeter IESVM CHRISTVM, neque nomen aliud sub caelo hominibus datum esse, in quo nos seruari oporteat: cur praedicatio nostra vanitatis ant falsi insimulatur, quam Spiritus sanctus in omnium credentium animis tam certo tamq; luculento testimonio confirmat? Hic verborum istorum sensus est, quae tacitam reprehensionem continent, quae vtinam hodie in omnium animis resonaret, qui Christiani quidem dici volunt, Corinthijs autem leuiores & deteriores nos haereticos dicunt, quod in vno Christo promissiones Dei omnes confirmatas & impletas esse, & proinde omnem salutis fiduciam in illo vno collocari debere docemus. Insunt tamen verbis istis quaedam alia etiam, quae obseruare conuenit.
units.tr: But lest Paul be thought to claim anything for himself too arrogantly, he teaches more openly whence this certainty of the Gospel teaching comes, and at the same time he convicts the Corinthians by the testimony of their own conscience, saying: "Now he who establishes us with you in Christ, and who has anointed us, is God; who also has sealed us and given us the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts." As if he said: Why do we need words? We do not make these things up in our own brains, but we speak as men confirmed by God himself. Nor will anyone among the number of Christians be found so shameless as not to confess that God is true, or to deny that his promises have been fully performed in Christ. And the same God establishes us together with you in Christ, so that we are grafted into him like true branches and persevere constantly in his faith, while he anoints and seals us and inserts the pledge of his Spirit into our hearts. If therefore you are Christians, you certainly feel the power of this Spirit, and, confirmed by his testimony and inspiration, you do not doubt that everything which serves the salvation of mankind has been abundantly offered to you in Christ. But since we preach nothing but this one thing, and openly confess that we know nothing except Jesus Christ, and that there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved, why is our preaching accused of vanity or falsehood, when the Holy Spirit confirms it in the minds of all believers with such a certain and clear testimony? This is the sense of these words, which contain a tacit rebuke. Would that it resounded today in the minds of all who wish to be called Christians, yet who, being lighter and worse than the Corinthians, call us heretics because we teach that all God's promises have been confirmed and fulfilled in the one Christ, and that therefore all confidence of salvation ought to be placed in him alone. Nevertheless there are also certain other things in these words which it is fitting to observe.

units.la: Primum, quod ijs, quae de doctrina & praedicationis Euangelicae certitudine dixit, mox nostra fidei certitudinem subiungit. Eo docemur non sufficere Euangelij doctrinam, imo nihil nobis prodesse, nisi eam nostro assensu vel fide apprehendamus. Sunt enim ex Relationum numero, Praedicatio Verbi Dei & Fides. Quare Paulus dicebat: Quomodo credent ei, de quo nihil audierunt? quomodo autem audient absque praedicante? Et quae nam vtilitas ad eos redeat, qui multa quidem vere dici audiunt, ijsdem vero fidem non habent? Imo nisi Dei Verbo credamus, iam in illum contumeliosi sumus, & (vt Ioannes scribit) Ieum mendacij arguimus, ideoque Euangelium audimus in nostræ damnationis testimonium. Est ergo incredulitatis peccatum multò grauius quàm plerique putent: quod vtinam serio expenderent, qui hodie nuda & inani fidei professione gloriantur. Possunt illi oculos hominum fallere, Deum vero fallere non poterunt, cuius oculi(vt Propheta ait)per totam terram discurrunt, & intimos cordium recessus penetrant.
units.tr: First, that immediately after what he said about the certainty of the doctrine and preaching of the Gospel, he adds the certainty of our faith. By this we are taught that the doctrine of the Gospel does not suffice, indeed that it profits us nothing, unless we lay hold of it by our assent or faith. For the preaching of God's Word and faith belong to the class of correlatives. So Paul said: "How will they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without a preacher?" And what use is it to those who hear many things truly spoken but do not believe them? Indeed, unless we believe God's Word, we already insult him and (as John writes) we make him a liar, and so we hear the Gospel to our own condemnation. The sin of unbelief is therefore much graver than most people think. Would that those who today boast of a bare and empty profession of faith would weigh this seriously. They may deceive the eyes of men, but they will not deceive God, whose eyes (as the Prophet says) run through the whole earth and penetrate the inmost recesses of hearts.

units.la: Vnde autem (inquis) fides ista & eius certitudo nobis obtingit? Est quæstio hæc vtilis & necessaria cognitu: quia hic multi impingunt, dum vel suæ rationis figmenta admittunt, vel ad alio- rum authoritatem confugiunt: quos omnes falli necesse est, quando mysteria hæc omnem humani intellectus captum superant, & maior semper fuit incredulorum numerus, qui sese Dei Verbo & voluntati opposuerunt. Itaq; Paulus omnem hanc gloriam vni Deo tribuit. Is est qui Filium suum nobis dedit Seruatorem, & in eodem nobis per Euangelium salutem plenam atque omnibus numeris absolutam offert. Idem animos nostros fide donat, qua eum ampleƈtimur, qui nobis per Verbum prædicatur. Confirmat denique nos in Christum, vt in fide stabiles & salutis nostræ certi, non fluctuemus.
units.tr: But from where, you ask, does this faith and its certainty come to us? This question is useful and necessary to know, because here many stumble, either admitting the inventions of their own reason or fleeing to the authority of others. All of them must be deceived, since these mysteries surpass every grasp of human understanding, and the number of unbelievers who have set themselves against the Word and will of God has always been greater. Therefore Paul ascribes all this glory to God alone. He is the one who gave his Son to us as Saviour, and in the same Son offers us through the Gospel a full salvation, complete in every respect. He also gives our minds faith, by which we embrace him who is preached to us through the Word. Finally, he confirms us in Christ, so that we may be steadfast in faith and certain of our salvation, and not wavering.

units.la: Sed præstat ordinem quoque videre, quo nobiscum Deus agit. Primùm vngit nos. Dicitur hoc de Spiritu sanctificationis, quo nos sibi fecit Reges & Sacerdotes. Hi enim antiquitus vnge- bantur. Et tales quidem sunt omnes Christiani. Nam Reges agunt, quando diabolo, mundo, peccato & carni imperant: quod regnum est omnium præstantissimum, cui nullum aliud in terris conferri meretur. Idem Sacerdotes sunt, dum seipsos Deo sistunt viuentem hostiam, dum alij alios docent, monent, hortantur & mutuis precibus iuuant.
