Est præterea Vnctionis huius effectus, quòd in omnem Veritatem inducit, ne porrò ambigamus de iis, quæ ad nostræ salutis causam pertinent. Deinde obsignat nos Deus. Potest hoc non inepte ad baptismum referri, qui vt olim Circumcisio fœderis & iustitiæ fidei sigillum erat: ita ille nobis gratiæ, sanctificationis & iustitiæ sigillum est, quæ omnia in Christo habemus. Et vult Deus suos tam intus quàm foris obsignatos esse, vt & ipsi de salute sua certi sint, & ab aliis sestis diuisi ita se gerant, vt eos ex mundo hoc selectos esse omnibus constet. Additur his tertium, arrha Spiritus, quam Deus dat in cordibus nostris. Id verò non de donis spiritualibus intelligi debet, quæ interdum incredulis quoque & Christo parum fidis dari solent: sed de Spiritu adoptionis, in quo clamamus, Abba Pater. Hunc non temere arrham dicit Apostolus. Est enim arrha id, quod in sponsionibus & contractibus datur confirmationis ergo, & quo vtrinque obstringuntur, tam qui illam dant, quàm qui accipiunt. Eadem omnino est Spiritus sancti ratio. Hunc enim nobis dat Deus, vt pignoris & testimonij loco fit, illùd nobis velle Deum & Patrem esse propter Filium suum æternum, IESVM CHRISTVM, qui noster frater factus est, vt nos quoque in filiorum Dei numerum cooptaret. Vicissim nos illi per Spiritum obstringimur, ne posthac mundo & carni viuamus, sed ex Verbi semine renati, toti Deo consecremur.
units.tr: But it is worth seeing also the order in which God deals with us. First, he anoints us. This is said of the Spirit of sanctification, by whom he has made us kings and priests. For these were anointed of old. And indeed all Christians are such. For we act as kings when we rule over the devil, the world, sin and the flesh, which is the most excellent of all kingdoms, and no other on earth deserves to be compared with it. Likewise we are priests, when we present ourselves to God as a living sacrifice, when we teach, admonish and exhort one another, and help each other by mutual prayers. Moreover, the effect of this anointing is that it leads us into all truth, so that we no longer doubt those things which pertain to the cause of our salvation. Then God seals us. This can not inappropriately be referred to baptism, which, as circumcision once was, is the seal of the covenant and of the righteousness of faith; thus baptism is to us the seal of grace, sanctification and righteousness, all of which we have in Christ. And God wills his people to be sealed both inwardly and outwardly, so that they may be certain of their own salvation, and, set apart from others, may so conduct themselves that it is evident to all that they have been chosen out of this world. To these is added a third thing, the earnest of the Spirit, which God gives in our hearts. This ought not to be understood of spiritual gifts, which are sometimes given even to unbelievers and to those little faithful to Christ, but of the Spirit of adoption, in whom we cry, Abba, Father. The Apostle does not call him an earnest rashly. For an earnest is that which is given in agreements and contracts as a confirmation, and by which both parties are bound, both those who give it and those who receive it. The reasoning concerning the Spirit of God is altogether the same. For God gives him to us so that he may serve as a pledge and testimony to us that God is willing to be our Father on account of his eternal Son, Jesus Christ, who became our brother so that he might also enroll us in the number of the sons of God. In turn, we are bound to him through the Spirit, so that henceforth we should not live to the world and the flesh, but, born again from the seed of the Word, be wholly consecrated to God.

units.la: Ista verò primùm omnem nostræ salutis gloriam vni Deo vendicant, ne quid nostræ digni- tati, aut viribus nostris tribuamus. Sic enim de istis Paulus disserit, vt seipsum quoque ijs admi- meret, quos à Deo vngi & obsignari, arrha denique Spiritus sancti confirmari oporteat. Deinde consolationem continent dulcissimam, quæ in tentationibus de salute nostra nos dubitare non sinit.
units.tr: These things, first of all, claim all the glory of our salvation for God alone, so that we attribute nothing to our own worth or our own strength. For Paul discourses on these matters in such a way that he also reminds those who ought to be anointed by God and sealed, and finally confirmed by the earnest of the Holy Spirit, of themselves. Next, they contain a most sweet consolation, which does not allow us to doubt our salvation in temptations.

units.la: Qui enim nos foris & intus obsignauit, nos ignorare vel negligere non potest. Nouit Dominus qui sint sui, & idem pastor ille bonus atque omnipotens est, ex cuius manu oues nemo potest rapere. Sunt ergo impij gratiæ Dei hostes & animarum homicidæ, qui hominem de salute sua certum fieri posse negant, & ita infelices in desperationis præcipitium adducunt. Postremò officij nostri nos ista admonent, ne huic tam fideli & salutiferæ obsignationi & confirmationi reclamemus. Qui enim id faciunt postquam intra animum suum conuicti sunt, ij in Spiritum sanctum peccare incipiunt, & nisi pedem mox retrahant, tandem desperationis laqueo abripiuntur. Agnoscamus ergo magnitudinem beneficij diuini, nobis in IESV CHRISTO exhibiti, & credamus Euangelio, neque posthac nobis aut mundo viuamus, sed ipsi vni, qui redemit nos, & suo Spiritu vnctos atque obsignatos sibi consecrauit. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: For he who has sealed us outwardly and inwardly cannot be ignorant of us or neglect us. The Lord knows who are his own, and he is that same good and almighty Shepherd, out of whose hand no one can snatch the sheep. Therefore those who deny that a man can be made certain of his salvation are enemies of the grace of God and murderers of souls, and so they lead the unhappy into the precipice of despair. Lastly, these things admonish us of our duty, that we should not resist this so faithful and salutary sealing and confirmation. For those who do so, after they have been convicted in their own consciences, begin to sin against the Holy Spirit, and unless they quickly draw back their foot, they are at last snatched away by the snare of despair. Let us therefore acknowledge the greatness of the divine benefit exhibited to us in Jesus Christ, and believe the Gospel, and henceforth live not to ourselves or to the world, but to him alone who redeemed us, and who, anointed and sealed by his Spirit, has consecrated us to himself. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA VII.
units.tr: HOMILY VII.

units.la: Ego vero testem Deum inuoco in animam meam, quod ut parcerem vobis nondum venerim Corinthum. Non quod dominemur vestrae fidei, sed quod administri simus gaudij vestri. Na fide statis.
units.tr: But I call God as witness against my soul, that it was to spare you that I have not yet come to Corinth. Not that we lord it over your faith, but that we are workers for your joy. For you stand by faith.

units.la: Magno studio & diligentia Paulus hucusque leuitatis crimen siue suspicionem a se depulit: non quidem priuati honoris & gloriae causa, sed ne Euangelij doctrina propter ipsum in dubium veniret, & ita multorum salus periclitaretur. Didicimus itaque eius exemplo, quid in asserenda nominis sui existimatione omnes spectare debeant, qui vel in Repub. vel in Ecclesia gradum aliquem eminentiorem tenent. Quia autem quaedam de doctrina suae certitudine consulto interposuerat, quam aduersarij imprimis petebant, redit in praesenti propius ad rem ipsam, & cur consilium de sua ad ipsos profectione mutarit, apertius docet, & sic quidem, ut culpam omnem in ipsos transferat, suam vero erga eos beneuolentiam diserte testetur. Ex quibus cordatiores quique facile colligere poterant, nimium proteruos & iniquos esse eos, qui Apostolum ea culpa grauare conabantur, cuius ipsi erant praecipui authores.
units.tr: With great zeal and care, Paul has so far repelled the charge of fickleness, or even the suspicion of it. He did this not for the sake of private honour or glory, but so that the teaching of the gospel would not be called into doubt because of him, and so that the salvation of many would not be put at risk. From his example we learn what all those should consider when defending their good name, whether they hold some higher rank in the commonwealth or in the Church. Since he had deliberately left some points open about the certainty of his teaching, which his opponents above all demanded, he now comes closer to the matter itself. He explains more clearly why he changed his plan about going to them, and he does so in such a way that he places all the blame on them while plainly declaring his own goodwill towards them. From this, any who were more sensible could easily infer that those who tried to burden the Apostle with that fault, when they themselves were its chief authors, were far too bold and unjust.

units.la: Initio causam hanc magna cum grauitate, & non sine iurisiurandi formula proponit: Ego vero testem Deum inuoco in animam meam, quod ut parcerem vobis nondum venerim Corinthu. Summa omnium est, se aduentum suum hucusque distulisse, non quod ex leuitate aut inconstantia consilium suum mutarit, sed ne cogeretur seuerius & durius cum ipsis agere: Eam enim fuisse apud eos rerum faciem, ut praesens non potuisset ipsis parcere, quo minus seueritate & rigore Apostolico vteretur. Ergone (dicat aliquis) indulgentia peccauit Paulus? Nequaquam. Nam licet noluerit coram eos durius tractare, literas tamen ad illos dedit, quibus acriter eos corripuit, nec aliquid dissimulauit, quod reprehensionem mereretur. Verum tamen si coram vidisset Ecclesiae huius conditionem corruptissimam & multorum mores dissolutos, eosdem seuerius castigare coactus fuisset, ne authoritatem suam publice omnium contemptui & ludibrio exponeret, cum nocentissimo multorum scandalo. Nam si indulgentius quid egisset, alij quidem omnem de poenitentia cogitationem abiecissent, alij vero contumaciores facti, absque omni pudore perrexissent in sua proteruia. Vt enim patris existimatio tota corruit, si ipso spectante liberi agant petulantius, idem tamen aliqua ex parte excusari potest, si ignorare putetur quae illi faciunt, & hi ipsi in aliquo adhuc metu continentur: Ita in Ecclesia & Repub. fieri solet. Si in conspectu pastorum siue magistratuum aliqui immodestius & turpius sese gerant, ipsis ad omnia conniuentibus, non potest non omnis eorum authoritas collabi, quae aliqua manet, quoad improbi illi ista se non impune facturos putant, si ad illos deferantur. Vidit hoc olim Cato, seueriissimus morum Censor, qui in festis Floralibus cum religionis praetextu confirmatam petulantiam abolere aut corrigere non posset, e theatro discessit, ne quid sua grauitate indignum spectaret, & populi leuitati subscribere videretur. Erant haec diligenter obseruanda Ecclesiarum ministris, viris item Senatoriis, quando primi ludunt, primi potant & inebriantur, primi scurrilia tractant, & ita non solum mali exempli authores fiunt iis, quos debebant in officio continere, verumetiam authoritatem suam turpiter prostituunt.
units.tr: At the outset he sets out the matter with great seriousness and not without the form of an oath: "But I call God as witness against my soul, that it was to spare you that I have not yet come to Corinth." The sum of it is this: he has put off his coming until now, not because he changed his plan out of levity or inconstancy, but so that he would not be forced to deal with them more severely and harshly. For the situation among them was such that, if he came in person, he could not spare them, and he would have to use Apostolic severity and rigour. "Then," someone may say, "did Paul sin through indulgence?" Certainly not. Although he was unwilling to treat them more harshly face to face, he nevertheless wrote to them, sharply rebuking them, and he passed over nothing that deserved reproof. Yet if he had seen with his own eyes the very corrupt condition of this Church and the loose morals of many, he would have been compelled to punish them more severely, lest he expose his authority to the open contempt and mockery of all, with the most harmful scandal to many. For if he had acted more leniently, some would have cast off all thought of repentance, while others, becoming more stubborn, would have gone on in their wantonness without any shame. Just as a father's reputation collapses entirely if his children behave more insolently in his presence, yet the same father can be partly excused if he is thought not to know what they are doing, and they themselves are still held in some fear, so it usually happens in the Church and the commonwealth. If, in the sight of ministers or magistrates, some behave in an unseemly and shameful way while those officials overlook everything, the whole authority that remains to them is bound to collapse, since the wicked believe they will not get away with these things if they are reported to those officials. Cato, the most severe censor of morals, saw this long ago. At the Floral Games, when under the pretext of religion a confirmed wantonness could not be abolished or corrected, he left the theatre so that he would not watch anything unworthy of his dignity and so that he would not seem to give his approval to the fickleness of the people. Ministers of the Churches, and likewise men of the senatorial order, must carefully observe this: when they are the first to play, the first to drink and get drunk, the first to indulge in obscene jokes, they not only become authors of a bad example to those whom they ought to keep in their duty, but they also shamefully prostitute their own authority.

units.la: Vt vero ad Paulum redeamus, obseruatu dignum est, quod de Corinthijs ista scribit, quos in epistola priori tanta cum grauitate corripuit. Ex eo enim apparet, non statim secutam fuisse poenitentiam perfectam & plenam vitiorum omnium emendationem. Imo credibile est, multos nouas calumniandi occasiones ex eius acrimonia captauisse, & ferocius aduersus illum eiusque sectatores proteruisse: quemadmodum hodie multos istorum similes facere videmus. Attamen vicit tandem pars melior, & multa deinceps in melius restituta, multa item emendata sunt. Ergo non statim animum despondere debent qui ad Ecclesiae aut Reipub. gubernacula sedent, si primo conatu non tantum proficiant, quantum volunt. Nam (vt prouerbio olim dixerunt) non vno ictu deijcitur quercus: & altius in hominum animis radices agit semel admissa opinionum atque morum licentia, quam ut subito euelli possit. Itaque operi bene incepto fortiter insistere, & cunctantes vrgere, stimulare & impellere oportet, & omnes rationes quaerere, quibus permoueri queant. Admonet nos de hoc ipsius Dei exemplum, qui vt poenas mirifica longanimitate differre solet, ita nouis subinde admonitionibus, correptionibus & adhortationibus apud eos instat, qui adhuc pertinacius ei reluctantur. Interim meminerint hi ipsi, non impune laturos se contumaciam suam: quia ut lento pede procedit vindicta divina, sic tarditatem suam gravitate supplicij compensat. Et notum est illud Pauli, quo poenitere nescijs interminatur dicens: Num divitias benignitatis eius, & tolerantiae ac lenitatis contemnis, ignorans quòd benignitas Dei ad resipiscentiam te allicit? Sed pro duritia tua & corde resipiscere nescio, thesaurizas tibi ipsi iram in diem irae & declarationis iusti iudicij Dei, &c. Vide Roma. 2. Cap. Exempla, quibus haec probantur, sunt passim obvia.
units.tr: But to return to Paul: it is worth noting what he writes about the Corinthians, whom he had rebuked so sternly in his earlier letter. For this shows that repentance did not follow at once, nor a complete and full amendment of all their vices. Indeed, it is credible that many seized on the sharpness of his letter as a fresh occasion for slander, and grew more fierce in their wantonness against him and his followers, just as we see many like them doing today. Nevertheless, the better part finally prevailed, and afterwards many things were restored for the better and many were corrected. Therefore those who sit at the helm of the Church or the commonwealth should not lose heart at once if, after the first attempt, they do not achieve as much as they wish. For (as the ancients said in a proverb) an oak is not felled with one blow; and once licence in opinions and morals has been admitted, it takes root more deeply in men's minds than it can be suddenly torn out. So one must press firmly on with a work well begun, urge, goad and drive on those who hesitate, and seek out every means by which they may be moved. God's own example also admonishes us on this point: he is accustomed to delay punishments with wonderful patience, yet he continually presses those who still resist him more stubbornly with new admonitions, rebukes and exhortations. Meanwhile, let those very people remember that they will not escape unpunished for their obstinacy. For the divine vengeance advances with a slow foot, yet it makes up for its delay by the severity of its punishment. And that saying of Paul is well known, in which he threatens those who refuse to repent: "Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance? But because of your hardness and your impenitent heart, you are storing up for yourself wrath on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God," and so on. See Rom. 2. Examples that prove these things are found everywhere.

units.la: Caeterum priusquam hinc defecedamus, diligentius expendi debet Pauli exemplum, qui iusiurandi gravissimum interponit. Simile quid nuper etiam fecit, sed obscurius, cum diceret: Fidelis Deus, &c. Hic vero apertius & maiori cum pondere verborum ait: Ergo vero testem Deum invoco in animam meam. Facit hoc, quia res erat magni momenti, & (ut iam saepe monuimus) non tam de ipsius persona agebatur, quam de doctrina, quam pseudoapostoli hac ratione oppugnabant. Licet ergo iurare in causis gravibus, & hoc olim quoque multi fecerunt, quorum fides & pietas in Scripturis commendatur. Abrahamus certè famulum suum iureiurando obstringit, ut Isaaco filio uxorem quaerat de sua gente: & ipsemet Abimelecho iurat, cum quo foedus fecerat. Et Iacobum Labano socero iuramentum dedisse legimus. Quid quòd Deum ipsum Abrahamo iurasse, Moses tradit, quod Apostolus ad Hebraeos scribens diligenter observavit: & idem ille, ut per suum nomen iuremus, non uno loco mandat. Arguunt haec Anabaptistarum errorem, qui dum iuramenta omnia simpliciter damnant, eadem opera Remp. turbant, & huius vinculum praecipuum dissoluunt. Nituntur Christi verbis, qui ne omnino iuremus praeceperit. Sed de temerariis iuramentis illic Dominus loquitur, qualia tunc inter Iudaeos in quotidiano usu erant, & hodie etiam nimis vulgaria sunt. Neque aliter Apostolos Christi praeceptum intellexisse, propria ipsorum exempla docent. Netamen in illud aliquo modo peccetur, primo probe videndum est, ne iuramentis temere, sed in solis gravibus causis utamur, quas hac ratione vel determinari vel confirmari necesse est. Deinde ne quibusvis illud committatur. Peccant in eo multi hodie, qui iusiurandum illis quoque cum publica authoritate adhibent, quorum fides tam dubia est, ut nemo eis teruntium, aut si quid vilius est, velit credere.
units.tr: Yet before we leave this point, Paul's example of swearing, in which he uses the most solemn oath, ought to be weighed more carefully. He had done something similar a little earlier, but less openly, when he said: "God is faithful," and so on. Here, however, he speaks more plainly and with greater weight of words: "But I call God as witness against my soul." He does this because the matter was of great importance and (as we have often pointed out) it concerned not so much his own person as the teaching which the false apostles were attacking in this way. It is therefore lawful to swear in serious causes, and many have done so in the past, whose faith and piety are commended in the Scriptures. Abraham certainly bound his servant by an oath to seek a wife for his son Isaac from his own people; and he himself swore to Abimelech, with whom he had made a covenant. We read that Jacob also gave an oath to his father-in-law Laban. Moses records, moreover, that God himself swore to Abraham, which the Apostle carefully noted when writing to the Hebrews. And that same God, in more than one place, commands us to swear by his name. These things refute the error of the Anabaptists, who, while condemning all oaths outright, at the same time throw the commonwealth into confusion and dissolve its chief bond. They rely on the words of Christ, who seems to forbid us to swear at all. But the Lord there speaks of rash oaths, such as were then in everyday use among the Jews and are even today far too common. The examples of the Apostles themselves show that they understood Christ's precept in no other way. Yet so that one does not sin in this respect in some way, we must first take great care not to use oaths rashly, but only in serious causes, which of necessity must be settled or confirmed in this way. Secondly, care must be taken that oaths are not given for just any matter. Many today sin in this, who require an oath even from those in public office, whose faith is so doubtful that no one would be willing to believe them about a trifle, or about anything of even lesser weight.

units.la: Debet autem observari diligenter formula iurandi, qua Paulus utitur: Testem invoco Deum in animam meam. Habent singula verba Emphasim. Deum testem citat, quia ipsius verbis multi palam contradicebant. Nec citat modo, verumetiam invocat: Et quidem in animam suam, id est, cum periculo animae aut vitae suae: ut innuat, hunc vindicem & ultorem fore, si quem sub nominis sui praetextu fallat. Quo loco docemur, per solius Dei nomen iuramenta concipi & dari debere. Quia solus hic arcana omnium novit, & corda quoque hominum scrutatur. Solus item vindicandi ius habet, si qui peierent: & solus eos tueri potest, qui bona fide agunt. Adde, quòd plerunque cum invocationis formula iuratur (sicuti in hoc etiam Pauli exemplo videmus) & ideo non postremum divini cultus pars est iusiurandum. Quae causa est, quòd ne per alienos Deos iuremus, tam saepe tamque graviter in Lege & Prophetis prohibetur. Dominum Deum tuum timebis (inquit Moses) & illum coles, iurabisque per nomen eius. Ieremias item dicebat: Et iurabis, Viuit Dominus. Et Isaias de conuersione Aegyptiorum ad fidem Christianam vaticinans, inter alia fidei exercitia hoc quoque numerat: In die illa erunt quinque civitates in terra Aegypti, quae loquentur lingua Chananaica, & iurabunt per Dominum exercituum. Apud Sophoniam vero Deus illis excidium minatur, qui per ipsum simul & Milchom, id est, patronum sive Deum tutelarem iurent, quae ipsi sibi finxerint: quod hodie faciunt, qui in iurisiurandi formula Deo vero Diuos coniungunt. Coniuncuntur hi sanctissimorum Martyrum exemplis, qui quaevis potius supplicia subire voluerunt, quam per alterius Dei nomen iurare. Iuliani certè milites cùm aliquid huius per incogitantiam fecissent, tandem de scelere atrocitate admoniti, sponte se ad supplicium obtulerunt, ut hanc divino nomini factam iniuriam eluerent.
units.tr: The form of oath which Paul uses must be carefully observed: "I call God as witness against my soul." Each word has its emphasis. He calls God as witness, because many were openly contradicting his words. He not only calls him as witness, but also invokes him, and indeed against his own soul, that is, at the risk of his soul or his life, so as to indicate that God will be the avenger and punisher if anyone deceives under the pretext of his name. From this place we are taught that oaths ought to be framed and given only through the name of the one God alone, because he alone knows the secrets of all and also searches the hearts of men. He alone also has the right to avenge perjury, and he alone can protect those who act in good faith. Add to this that an oath is very often sworn with a formula of invocation (as we see in this very example of Paul), and therefore an oath is not the least part of divine worship. This is why the Law and the Prophets so often and so strictly forbid us to swear by other gods. "You shall fear the Lord your God," says Moses, "and serve him, and you shall swear by his name." Jeremiah likewise said: "And you shall swear, As the Lord lives." And Isaiah, prophesying of the conversion of the Egyptians to the Christian faith, counts among other exercises of faith this also: "In that day there shall be five cities in the land of Egypt that speak the language of Canaan and swear to the Lord of hosts." But in Zephaniah God threatens destruction on those who swear both by him and by Milchom, that is, by a patron or guardian god, whom they have invented for themselves; and this is what those do today who, in the formula of an oath, join the saints to the true God. They are joined to the examples of the most holy martyrs, who preferred to undergo any torture rather than swear by the name of another god. When the soldiers of Julian, through carelessness, had done something of this kind, and were at last reminded of the atrocity of their crime, they voluntarily offered themselves for punishment, so as to wipe away the injury done to the divine name.

units.la: Ut vero caveri debet, ne iurando in cultum Deo uni debitum peccemus: ita proxima nobis cuique esse debet, ut sanctè & bona fide praestetur quod iuratum est. Si qui enim fallunt, ij Deum extrema contumelia afficiunt. Quis enim vir bonus ferat, aliquem sub nominis aut sigilli sui praetextu saltu falli? Et tu Deum qui ipsissima est Veritas, hoc dissimulaturum putas, si mendacium, dolos & fraudes tuas ipsius nomine palliare audeas? Exempla in periuros edita in historijs passim habentur, & quaedam tam atrocia, ut gentibus quoque periurium horrori fuerit. Sed o nostri saeculi infelicitatem, quando iurandi levitas, quae apud omnes in quotidiano usu est, eo plerosque adducit, ut ne a periurijs quidem abhorreant: imo sibi laudi ducant, si quem fallere possint. Meminerint ergo singuli, se quoties iurant, toties Deum testem invocare in animam suam, etiamsi conditio illa non semper diserte exprimatur.
units.tr: But just as we must take care not to sin by swearing, so that we give to God alone the worship owed to Him, so each of us ought to be equally careful that what has been sworn is performed sincerely and in good faith. For those who deceive do the greatest insult to God. What good man could endure someone being deceived under cover of his name or seal? And do you think God, who is Truth itself, will overlook it if you dare to disguise your lies, deceit and frauds with His very name? Examples of perjurers punished are found everywhere in histories, and some are so atrocious that even the heathen nations regarded perjury with horror. But alas for the unhappiness of our age, when the lightness of swearing, which is in everyday use among everyone, leads most people to such a point that they do not shrink even from perjury; indeed, they count it a credit if they can deceive someone. Let each one therefore remember that whenever he swears, he calls God to witness against his own soul, even if the condition is not always stated in so many words.

units.la: Caeterum potuerat quibusdam arrogantius a Paulo dictum videri: Ut parcerem vobis, nondum veni Corinthum. Parcere enim is dicitur, qui cum puniendi ius habeat, aut nocere possit, vel etiam invitos cogere, id tamen non facit. Ideo objiceret aliquis: Ergo ne tantum iuris tibi in nos sumis, ut nos pro tuo arbitrio tractare possis? aut cuius praesentia omnibus terrori esse debeat, adeo, ut quod tu vis aut iubes, omnes velle & facere cogamur? Haec certe non lenis pastoris aut benigni patris, sed tyranni ingenium referunt. Itaque Paulus praeoccupatione dictum illud mitigat, dicens: Non quod dominemur vestrae fidei, sed quod administri simus gaudij vestri, &c. Sensus verborum est: Nemo hoc ita accipiat volo, quasi mihi in conscientias vestras ius & imperium vendicem, & fidei vestrae dominari velim. Scio enim nos Apostolos & quotquot alij Euangelium praedicant, non dominos esse Ecclesiarum (quae unum IESVM CHRISTVM profitentur, domino & capite suo agnoscunt) sed tantum administros esse vestri gaudij, id est, tranquillitatis & pacis conscientiarum, quae ex gratia & reconciliationis cum Deo per Christum factae cognitione nascitur. Quoad fidem vestram, vos illa fletistis hactenus, & ea sola, licet multis alijs vitijs laboraretis, vos tamen sulciuit, ne toti corruerituis. Idcirco ego non aliud quaero, quam ut haec fides vestra confirmetur, & gaudium illud vestrum vobis solidum & integrum maneat. Insunt autem huic loco multa observatu dignissima, de quibus ex ordine dicemus, quantum nunc videbitur sufficere.
units.tr: Moreover, Paul's words, "But I spare you, for I did not yet come to Corinth," could have seemed rather arrogant to some. For a man is said to spare when he has the right to punish or could harm someone, or even force unwilling people, and yet does not do so. Someone might therefore object: "Do you claim such a right over us, that you can treat us according to your own will? Or should your presence be such a terror to all that we are compelled to want and do whatever you wish or command? These things certainly savour not of the gentle shepherd or kindly father, but of the temper of a tyrant." Paul therefore softens this statement by forestalling the objection, saying: "Not that we lord it over your faith, but that we are helpers of your joy," and so on. The sense of the words is this: let no one take it to mean that I wish to claim for myself a right and dominion over your consciences, and to lord it over your faith. For I know that we apostles, and all others who preach the gospel, are not lords of the churches (which profess the one Jesus Christ and acknowledge Him as their Lord and Head), but only helpers of your joy, that is, of the tranquillity and peace of conscience, which arises from the knowledge of grace and of reconciliation with God made through Christ. As for your faith, you have stood firm in it until now, and although you have laboured under many other faults, it alone has upheld you so that you have not utterly fallen. Therefore I seek nothing else than that this faith of yours be confirmed and that your joy remain solid and entire for you. There are, however, many points in this passage most worthy of notice, which we shall discuss in order, as far as seems sufficient for now.

units.la: Primum inter illa est praeclarum fidei encomium. Ut enim fide Corinthij steterunt, ita hac so la omnes seruantur. Etsi enim salus, quam nobis Christus meruit, ad totum hominem pertineat, & proinde ad corpus quoque: tamen eius percipiendae ratio in anima consistit. Ideo Paulus alibi dicebat exercitationem corporalem parum habere utilitatis. Et quid de ceremoniarum observatoribus Deus per Prophetas olim pronunciauerit, satis notum est. Recte ergo rursus a nostro Apostolo dictum est: Regnum Dei non est cibus aut potus, sed iustitia, & pax & gaudium in Spiritu sancto. Item: Bonum est gratia confirmabiliri cor, non cibis, quibus non sunt adiuti, qui in ipsis veri sati sunt. Atqui gratia ista per solam fidem apprehenditur in CHRISTO IESV, qui illam nobis meruit: & ideo iustus fide sola viuere dicitur. Itaque huius nobis prima cura esse debet, ne cum Martha illa Bethaniensi circa multa occupati, quod maxime necessarium est negligamus Luc. 10.
units.tr: The first of these is the notable praise of faith. For as the Corinthians stood by faith, so all are preserved by faith alone. For although the salvation which Christ merited for us pertains to the whole man, and therefore to the body as well, nevertheless the manner of receiving it consists in the soul. Hence Paul elsewhere said that bodily exercise is of little profit. And what God pronounced of old through the prophets concerning the observers of ceremonies is well enough known. So again our Apostle rightly says: "The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit." Likewise: "It is good that the heart be strengthened by grace, not by foods, by which those who have been occupied with them have not been helped." But this grace is apprehended by faith alone in Christ Jesus, who merited it for us; and therefore the righteous is said to live by faith alone. Thus our first care ought to be that, being occupied with many things like that Martha of Bethany, we do not neglect what is most necessary (Luke 10).

units.la: Admonemur praeterea, non temere damnari debere eos, qui fidei principia salua habent. Scimus enim quot modis Corinthij corrupti fuerint, quamque multis vitijs laboratint: Attamen Paulus illos hucusque fide fletisse ait, ne toti perierint. Sunt ergo nimis temerarij, qui hodie viros de Ecclesia optime meritos damnant propter unum aliquod dogma, absque quo fides potest consiste-re: quale est, quod de crassa & corporali siue substantiali corporis Christi praesentia & eiusdem Capernaitica vel orali manducatione ex Papae penu siue culina deprompserunt: cuius cum nulla mentio fiat in fidei aut symboli Apostolici articulis, & idem omnis vetustas ignorarit, illi tamen nos fanaticos, Sacramentorum prophanatores, haereticos & indignos esse clamant, quos terra haet ferat, eo quod non cum ipsis ineptire volumus. Abutuntur hi contra nos Iacobi loco: Quisquis totam Legem seruauerit, offenderit autem in uno, factus est omnium reus. Atqui nihil illic Apostolus de dogmatibus loquitur, sed hypocritas arguit, qui ut operum iustitiam stabilirent, praecepta quaedam Legis leuiora & ipsis conuenientia seligebant, quorum observatione deinde gloriabantur; securi de alijs, quae grauioris momenti sunt: cuius iactantiae exemplum in iuuene illo proponitur, quem Christus de vita aeterna quaerentem, & Legis observatione gloriantem, ad diligentiorem illius inspectionem remittit. Horum iactantiam Iacobus inutilem esse docet, quia unius praecepti transgressio sufficit, ut nos reos agat ad Dei tribunal, qui iam olim maledictum pronunciauit eum qui non omnia seruarit, quae in Lege nobis mandantur. Perperam ergo Rhadamanti illi hoc ad fidem detorquent, vt hac nos prorsus carere probent, quia in illis nolumus eis consentire, quae nullo fidei articulo comprehenduntur. At nos Deo immortales gratias agimus, quod ea fide hucusque stetimus, quam Apostoli ex Spiritus sancti suggestione toti orbi praedicarunt, quam Martyres sancti suo sanguine confirmarunt, & in qua patres omnes seruati sunt: & oramus Deum misericordiarum Patremque omnis consolationis, vt in ea nos in finem vsque confirmet: quod illum facturum esse firmiter speramus.
units.tr: We are also warned not to condemn rashly those who hold the principles of faith intact. For we know in how many ways the Corinthians were corrupted and how many faults they laboured under. Yet Paul says that they had thus far been preserved by faith, so that they did not utterly perish. Therefore those are far too rash who today condemn men who have deserved very well of the Church, on account of some single doctrine without which faith can stand. Such is the doctrine which they have drawn from the Pope's pantry or kitchen, concerning the gross and corporal, or substantial, presence of Christ's body and its Capernaitic or oral eating. Since no mention of this is made in the articles of faith or of the Apostles' Creed, and all antiquity has been ignorant of it, they nevertheless cry out that we are fanatics, profaners of the sacraments, heretics, and unworthy of the earth, merely because we do not wish to trifle with them. They abuse against us the passage of James: "Whoever has kept the whole law but has offended in one point has become guilty of all." Yet the Apostle there says nothing about doctrines; he rebukes hypocrites who, in order to establish the righteousness of works, selected certain lighter precepts of the law that suited themselves, and then boasted of keeping them, being careless about the other matters of weightier importance. An example of this boasting is set before us in that young man whom Christ, when he asked about eternal life and boasted of keeping the law, sent back to a more diligent examination of it. James teaches that the boasting of such men is useless, because the transgression of a single precept suffices to bring us as guilty before God's judgment seat; God long ago pronounced a curse on him who has not kept all the things commanded in the law. Those Rhadamanthine judges therefore wrongly twist this passage to apply to faith, in order to prove that we lack faith altogether, because we refuse to agree with them in those matters which are comprised in no article of faith. But we give immortal thanks to God that we have stood thus far in that faith which the Apostles, moved by the Holy Spirit, preached to the whole world, which the holy martyrs confirmed with their blood, and in which all the fathers were preserved; and we pray God, the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, to confirm us in it to the end, which we firmly hope He will do.

units.la: Nostros autem aduersarios ex fraterna charitate monemus, vt quod alterum huius loci capur est[?], diligentius inspiciant, & sibi ipsis applicent, Pauli exemplum nimirum, qui se fidei Corinthiorum dominari velle negat. At si quisquam hominum in Ecclesiam aliquam ius habuit, Paulus id in Corinthios habuit. Per ipsum enim regeniti erant, & ideo alibi se patrem ipsorum esse demonstrat. Noluit tamen in conscientias sibi ius vsurpare, vt fidei illorum dominetur, eosque credere cogat, quae ipsi pro suo arbitrio placerent. Vidit enim electum illud organum, fidem non alio fundamento, quam Verbo Dei, innixi, ex quo etiam nascitur. Quae deinde causa est, quod totum hominem Deo vendicat, vt nihil possit aut velit admittere, quod ab huius voluntate, nobis in Scripturis sacris manifestata, dissentire sentit. Sufficit hoc arguendum omnibus, qui lodie in fidem & conscientias aliorum sibi ius sumunt. Faciunt hoc prae aliis Romani Pontifices, qui dogmata nova & nouos fidei articulos ex suo cerebro fingunt, & eosdem omnibus obtrudunt, qualia sunt quae de Missae sacrificio pro peccatis viuentium & mortuorum, de Confessione prinata, de Purgatorio igne, indulgentijs, satisfactionibus, imaginum cultu, ieiunijs, feriis, peregrinationibus & sexcentis aliis ab illis traduntur: nec traduntur modo, sed vimis pro imperio obtruduntur, dum simul clamant, Esse de necessitate salutis, vt omnis anima Romano Pontifici subiiciatur atque obtemperet. Nec eo contenti, haereticos dicunt omnes eos, qui vel in minimo ab ipsis dissentiunt, contra eosdem excommunicationibus fulminant, & bella cum extera tum ciuilia aduersus eos concitant. Hi sunt fidei dominatores intolerabiles, & vel vno hoc indicio sese produnt, quam parum habeant Spiritus Apostolici. Vetuit Dominus, ne in corpora & fortunas dominentur. Et notum est illud Petri: Pascite gregem, qui penes vos est, curam illius agentes non coacte, sed libenter, non turpiter affectantes lucrum, sed prompto animo: neque vt dominantes clerus, sed vt qui sitis exemplaria gregis. Quis ergo illos ferat, qui a regula Apostolica tam procul discedunt? Sequuntur hos proximo gradu, qui sub plausibili disciplinae titulo Excommunicationem Papisticam reducunt, & sacramenta fidei negant ijs, quos a fide alienos esse nondum probaucrunt, neque etiam certo scire possunt, num a fide alieni sint. Hi cum multos disciplinae Christianae acerrimos vindices, & de Christi Ecclesia optime meritos, eam vnam ob causam quod ab illis ex Papatu reductam disciplinae formulam, vel Excommunicationem probare nolunt, summae impietatis & atheismi simul accusent, annon imperium sibi vendicant in Ecclesia, & fidei aliorum se dominari velle ostendunt?
units.tr: We admonish our adversaries, however, out of brotherly love, that they look more carefully at the second point of this passage and apply it to themselves: namely, Paul's example, who denies that he wishes to lord it over the faith of the Corinthians. Yet if any man ever had a right over a church, Paul had it over the Corinthians. For through him they had been begotten, and therefore elsewhere he shows that he is their father. Nevertheless he would not usurp for himself a right over their consciences, to lord it over their faith and compel them to believe whatever they pleased by their own judgment. For that chosen instrument saw that faith rests on no other foundation than the Word of God, from which it is also born. From this it follows that he claims the whole man for God, so that he can neither admit nor wish anything that he perceives to dissent from His will, which has been made known to us in the holy Scriptures. This suffices as a rebuke to all who today assume for themselves a right over the faith and consciences of others. The Roman Pontiffs do this above all others, who fabricate new doctrines and new articles of faith out of their own brains, and force them upon everyone, such as those they hand down concerning the sacrifice of the Mass for the sins of the living and the dead, private confession, the fire of purgatory, indulgences, satisfactions, the veneration of images, fasts, holy days, pilgrimages, and six hundred other things. Nor do they merely hand these down, but thrust them upon people with great violence, as if by command, while at the same time they cry out that it is necessary for salvation that every soul be subject to and obey the Roman Pontiff. Not content with this, they call heretics all who differ from them even in the smallest point, and hurl excommunications against them, and stir up wars against them, both foreign and civil. These are intolerable lords of faith, and by this single sign alone they betray how little they have of the Spirit of the Apostles. The Lord forbade that men should lord it over bodies and property. And that saying of Peter is well known: "Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint but willingly, not for filthy lucre but with a ready mind; neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock." Who then could endure those who depart so far from the Apostolic rule? In the next rank follow those who, under the plausible title of discipline, bring back the Papal excommunication, and deny the sacraments of faith to those whom they have not yet proved to be alien from the faith, nor can they know for certain whether they are alien from it. When they accuse of the highest impiety and atheism at once many most zealous defenders of Christian discipline, who have deserved very well of the Church of Christ, for the sole reason that they are unwilling to approve of the form of discipline or of excommunication brought back from the Papacy, do they not claim for themselves dominion in the Church, and show that they wish to lord it over the faith of others?

units.la: Ergo ne (inquis) permittendum est, vt quisque sibi fidem fingat, & pro suo arbitrio in Ecclesia & Dei cultu omnia instituat? Hoc certe multi ex hoc loco & similibus colligunt. Fides (aiunt) donum Dei est, & vt quis hanc animo concipiat a nemine potest cogi, quare permitti debet, vt vnusquisque suo sensu abundet, vt alibi Apostolus loquitur. Atqui nihil minus, quam quod isti colligunt, sensit Apostolus. Enimuero fides Dei donum est, nec quisquam venit ad Christum, nisi Pater eum traxerit: at solet hic illam per certa media largiri, nimirum per Verbi praedicationem & Spiritus Sancti in cordibus nostris agentis virtute. Ergo illud solum audire, & Spiritui locum dare, non autem hominum placita eos sequi oportet, qui fidem consequi cupiunt. Deinde fatemur, nullius animum aut voluntatem cogi posse vt credat: at in officio contineri possunt homines superstitiosi simul & impij, ne quod male sentiunt, cum aliorum scandalo effutiant. Eadem enim opinionum sive dogmatum ratio est, quae scelerum. Quis hominis sanguinarij & homicidia perpetua spirantis animum mutare, aut alium fingere potest eum, qui natura furax & alieni appetens est? Nemo vtique praeter vnum Deum. Idem tamen hic tales legum disciplina & suppliciis coercere iubet, et quantum his proficiatur, quotidie cernimus. Quapropter hoc ipsum in fide quoq; & religione debet obseruari, quando de his quoque leges dedit Deus, ne cui ab ipso traditam doctrinam
units.tr: So (you say) must we not permit each person to make up his own faith and to arrange everything in the Church and the worship of God as he pleases? Many people certainly draw this from this passage and similar ones. Faith, they say, is a gift of God, and no one can be compelled to conceive it in his mind; therefore everyone should be allowed to abound in his own sense, as the Apostle says elsewhere. Yet the Apostle thought nothing less than what they infer. Faith is indeed a gift of God, and no one comes to Christ unless the Father draws him; but God usually bestows it through certain means, namely through the preaching of the Word and through the power of the Holy Spirit working in our hearts. Therefore those who desire to attain faith ought to hear that alone and give room to the Spirit, and not follow the opinions of men. Next, we grant that no one's mind or will can be compelled to believe. But superstitious and impious men can be restrained from blurting out what they think amiss, to the scandal of others. For the principle governing opinions or doctrines is the same as that governing crimes. Who can change the mind of a bloodthirsty man who breathes murder continually, or make into another man one who is by nature a thief and covets what belongs to others? No one, surely, except the one God. Yet the same God orders such men to be restrained by the discipline of laws and punishments, and we see every day how much these accomplish. Wherefore the same ought to be observed also in faith and religion, since God has given laws about these matters too, so that no one may be permitted to alter the doctrine handed down by him

units.la: Deut.13. nam aut cultus formam mutare permittatur. Quoad nostrum sensum, non hoc vult Apostolus, vt quisque pro suo arbitrio statuat quod velit, sed vnumquenque certum esse iubet intra conscientiam suam quid sequatur. Id enim Graeco vocabulo πληροφορια significatur. Vnde vero πληροφορια ista aut fidei nostrae certitudo? Non aliunde certè quàm ex Dei Verbo, à quo vno nos ille ita pendere iubet, vt non faciamus quod nobis bonum videtur in oculis nostris. Quia enim cor hominis prauum, varium & inscrutabile est, nihil vnquam certum firmumque habebit, quisquis huius placita, quae in horas mutantur, sequi voluerit. At fidei simul atque salutis suae certus erit, qui solius Dei verbo nititur, quod sibi ipsi semper constat, & in aeternum manet.
units.tr: Deut.13. or the form of worship. As to our sense, the Apostle does not mean that each person should decide for himself whatever he wishes, but he bids each one to be certain within his own conscience what he is to follow. For this is signified by the Greek word plērophoria [πληροφορια], full assurance. But where does this full assurance, or the certainty of our faith, come from? Certainly not from anywhere other than the Word of God, on which alone he bids us depend, so that we do not do what seems good in our own eyes. For since the heart of man is wicked, changeable and unsearchable, whoever follows its opinions, which change from hour to hour, will never have anything certain or firm. But he who rests on the Word of God alone will be certain of his faith and of his salvation, since that Word is always consistent with itself and remains for ever.

units.la: Ex his iam colligi potest, quod nam ministrorum Ecclesiae officium, & quis totius prædicationis Euangelicae finis sit? Paulus se & Apostolos reliquos administros esse docet gaudij ipsorum: per quod pacem conscientiae quam Christus nobis peperit, intelligi supra diximus. Hanc ergo ministri fideliter tradere, & toti in eo esse debent, vt homines intelligant, Deum ipsis propitium esse factum in Christo, vtque huic in sanctitate seruiant, atque huius gratiae sensu confirmati in afflictionibus quoq; constanter perseuerent. Nemo igitur temere minis non necessarijs deijci debet, quin potius contritis medicinam adhibere, nutantes verò & labascentes fulcire conuenit, ne desperent. Quod ante hinc aliqui colligunt, non debere corripi eos, qui cum publico scandalo delinquunt, in proximo Sermone confutabitur. Nunc teneamus, nos sola fide consistere posse in conspectu Dei, hanc autem solo Verbo Dei gubernari, in quo non aliud illius fundamentum monstratur, quàm dilectus & vnicus Dei Filius, IESVS CHRISTVS, in quo Pater sibi reconciliauit omnia, quaecunq; in caelo & in terra sunt. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: From these things it can now be gathered what the office of the ministers of the Church is, and what the aim of all evangelical preaching is. Paul teaches that he and the other Apostles are servants of their joy, by which, as we said above, we understand the peace of conscience that Christ has won for us. Ministers, therefore, ought to hand this on faithfully, and devote themselves wholly to ensuring that people understand that God has been made propitious to them in Christ, and that they serve him in holiness, and that, strengthened by the sense of this grace, they persevere constantly even in afflictions. Therefore no one should be cast down rashly by unnecessary threats; rather, medicine should be applied to the broken, and the wavering and tottering should be propped up, lest they despair. What some have previously inferred from this, that those who sin with public scandal ought not to be rebuked, will be refuted in the next sermon. For now let us hold that we can stand in the sight of God by faith alone, and that this faith is governed by the Word of God alone, in which no other foundation of it is shown than the beloved and only Son of God, Jesus Christ, in whom the Father has reconciled to himself all things that are in heaven and on earth. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: HOMILIA VIII.
units.tr: SERMON VIII.

units.la: HOc autem apud me statui, ne rursus ad vos cum tristitia veniam. Nam si ego vos tristitia afficiā, quis est qui me exhilaret, nisi is ipse qui tristitia ex me afficitur? Et hoc ipsum vobis scripsi, ne cum venero tristitiam capiā ex iis, de quibus oportebat me gaudere: confisus de vobis omnibus, meum gaudium omnium vestrum gaudium esse. Nam ex multa oppressione & anxietate cordis scripsi vobis, per multas lachrymas: non vt tristitia afficiamini, sed vt cognoscatis charitatem, quam habeo abundantissimam erga vos.
units.tr: I have also resolved this in my own mind, that I will not come to you again in sorrow. For if I grieve you, who is there to cheer me but the very one whom I have grieved? And I wrote this very thing to you, so that when I came I would not be grieved by those over whom I ought to have rejoiced, since I trusted all of you, that my joy is the joy of all of you. For I wrote to you out of much affliction and anguish of heart, with many tears: not so that you would be grieved, but so that you would know the very great love I have for you.

units.la: Icuti homo ex innata vitiositate ad omne malū proclivius est et vitijs delectatur: ita eos aequo animo ferre non potest, qui prauis ipsius studijs obstant, & saluti publicae consultiū volunt. Quare si semel odio aduersus eos indulgere caeperit, nihil non sibi licere putat, neque vllis beneficijs vinci aut emolliri potest, vt rectius de illis iudicet. Exempla huius ingratitudinis & contumaciae in Scripturis multa proponuntur, inter quae admodum memorabile est, quod in Mose habemus. Reliquerat is aulae delicias & spem regni, vt Israelitas ex dura Pharaonis tyrannide liberatos Deo consecraret: beneficia in eosdem infinita contulerat, & ipso Deo teste, mortalium erat mitissimus. Quid vero hisce officijs apud eos meruit? Vnum hoc, quòd impostorem dicunt, & tyrannidis in ipsos affectatae accusant. Eadem post hunc Prophetarum sors fuit, vt iam de Christo Domino nihil dicam, qui per illos locutus est. Neque meliorem fuisse Apostolorum conditionem, vel vnius Pauli exemplo admonemur. Docuerat is Corinthi diu, & vt eos Christo lucrifaceret, nullos labores, nulla pericula subire detrectauerat. Et ab illis digressus non tamen curam eorum deposuerat, quò minus de illis sciscitaretur, & abusus atq; vitia, quae apud eos obrepebant, scriptis ad illos literis amice corrigeret. Qua vero ab eis gratia retulit? Nō aliam, quàm quòd ab æmulis eius decepti, quaecunq; ab eo fiebant calūniati sunt, & minimā quaq; odiosius exagitarunt. Cuius generis fuit, quòd mendacij & vanitatis accusarunt, eò quòd sum ad ipsos aduentum bucusq; extraxisset. Debent exempla eiusmodi diligenter obseruari, ne hodie similibus offendamur. Interim horum memores ministri eò diligentius curent, ne Veritatis doctri na propter ipsos in contemptum veniat. Hoc certe Paulus monuit, ut vanitatis suspicione tanta cum diligentia abs se remouerit. Argumentum praecipuum fuit, quo se excusat, se ideo nondum aduenisse, ut ipsis commodius parcere posset, neq; cogeretur ut seueritate Apostolica, quam ipsorum vitia merebatur, & à qua non potuisset sibi absque publico scandalo temperare, si coram omnia vidisset. Id nunc apertius explicat, & paulatim ad causam hominis incesti descendit, propter quem in priori epistola quaedam in illos duriuscule dixerat, ex quibus maleuoli calumniandi ansam arripiebant.
units.tr: Just as a man, by his innate wickedness, is more inclined to every evil and takes pleasure in vices, so he cannot bear with equanimity those who stand in the way of his depraved pursuits and wish for the public good. Hence, if once he has begun to indulge hatred against such people, he thinks nothing is forbidden to him, and he cannot be won over or softened by any benefits so as to judge them more fairly. Many examples of this ingratitude and obstinacy are set before us in the Scriptures, among which the one we have in Moses is very memorable. He had abandoned the delights of the court and the hope of a kingdom, so that he might lead the Israelites, freed from the harsh tyranny of Pharaoh, to God. He had conferred countless benefits upon the same people, and, with God himself as witness, he was the gentlest of mortals. Yet what did he earn from them for these services? This only: that they called him an impostor and accused him of aiming at tyranny over them. The lot of the Prophets after him was the same, not to mention Christ the Lord himself, who spoke through them. Nor are we shown that the condition of the Apostles was any better, even by the example of Paul alone. He had taught at Corinth for a long time, and in order to win them for Christ he had shrunk from no labours and no dangers. And when he had departed from them, he had not laid aside his care for them, so that he did not inquire about them, and he kindly corrected, by letters written to them, the abuses and faults that were creeping in among them. But what thanks did he receive from them? None other than that, deceived by his rivals, they slandered whatever he did and criticised even the smallest things more spitefully. Of this kind was their charge that he was deceitful and vain, because he had put off his coming to them until now. Examples of this sort ought to be carefully observed, so that we are not offended by similar things today. Meanwhile, let ministers who remember these things take all the more care that the teaching of the truth does not fall into contempt on account of themselves. Paul certainly warned against this, that he should so diligently remove from himself any suspicion of vanity. The chief argument by which he excuses himself is that he had not yet come, so that he could spare them more conveniently, and would not be compelled to use the apostolic severity that their faults deserved, and from which he could not have refrained without public scandal, had he seen everything in person. He now explains this more openly, and gradually comes down to the case of the incestuous man, on account of whom he had said somewhat harsh things to them in the earlier letter, from which malicious people seized an occasion for slander.

units.la: Principio docet, quomodo illis pepercerit? Hoc autem apud me statuì sine decreui ne rursus ad vos cum tristitia veniam. Sensus est: Quia semel vos contristaui, ego mihi hanc legem posui, me nolle iterum eodem modo venire. Loquitur autem de epistola priori, per quam quasi praesens adesset cum illis egerat. Et causam reddit, cur nolit suo aduentu nouam tristitiam sine molestiam ipsis exhibere. Nam si ego (inquit) vos tristitia afficiam, quis est qui me exhilaret, nisi is ipse qui tristitia ex me afficitur? Sunt haec summae & ardentis dilectionis verba, quae συμπαθειαν & mutuam affectionem gignebat, ut illorum maerore atque molestia ipse etiam afficeretur, neque gaudere posset, quando ipsos contristatos esse videbat. Perinde ergo haec verba sonant, ac si amicus amico comun dissimo, aut pater filio unico & charissimo dicat, Mene putas aliquid ferre aut facere posse, quod tibi doleat? Ita certè te amo & complector animo meo, ut omnia mihi tecum communia sint, neque aliud aequè atque tuum commodum quaero. Non potero igitur tibi alicuius molestiae author esse, quae non in me quoque redundet. Et quis me tunc nouo gaudio reficere poterit, nisi te excusso maerore alacriore factu & pro more rursus gaudere videa? Haec & similia Apostolus in praesenti Corinthijs dicit, ut exacerbatos impostorum calumnijs animos ipsorum emolliat, sibiq; obsequentiores reddat.
units.tr: First he shows how he spared them. "But I have determined this in my own mind, not to come to you again in sorrow." The sense is: since I once grieved you, I have set this rule for myself, that I will not come again in the same way. He speaks of the earlier letter, through which he had dealt with them as if he were present. And he gives the reason why he does not wish, by his coming, to bring them fresh sorrow and trouble. "For if I grieve you," he says, "who is there to cheer me but the very one whom I have grieved?" These are words of the highest and most fervent love, which produced [συμπάθεια] and mutual affection, so that he himself was affected by their sorrow and distress and could not rejoice when he saw them grieved. Accordingly these words sound just as if a friend said to a friend, or a father to his only and dearest son: "Do you think I can bear or do anything that would pain you? I love and embrace you so truly in my heart that all things are shared between us, and I seek nothing so much as your good. Therefore I cannot be the author of any trouble to you that does not also fall back upon me. And who could then refresh me with new joy, unless I see you shaking off your sorrow, becoming more cheerful, and rejoicing again as is your custom?" These and similar things the Apostle says to the Corinthians at present, so that he may soften their minds, which had been exasperated by the slanders of impostors, and make them more compliant to him.

units.la: Est autem exemplum hoc obseruatu dignissimum, ut discamus, quo animo Ecclesiarum ministri erga suae fidei creditos esse debeant. Non potuit Paulus gaudere, nisi gaudetibus Corinthijs. At ipsi baetenus gaudijs suis nimiu indulserant, quando omniu securi liceter peccabant, in gentiu sacris comesfabantur, & quaeu alia pro suo arbitrio faciebant, adeo, ut quidam excusso futuri iudicij metu Sardanapalicum illud in ore haberent: Ede, bibe, lude, post mortem nulla voluptas. At nō de eiusmo di gaudio loquitur Paulus, sed de spirituali illo & sancto, quod ij intra animos suos concipiunt, qui à peccatis conuersi cum Deo in gratia redierunt. Cotristabatur ergo eorum peccatis, quod tiuc durius cum illis agere cogeretur, & saluti ipsorum metueret. Rursus gaudio nouo reficiebatur, quando ipsos ex animo resipuisse, & proinde Deo reconciliatos esse videbat. Debet hoc vtriusq; fieri, neq; salvae erunt Ecclesiae, nisi mutuus iste affectus inter pastores & oues locum habeat. Itaque ministri propter populi peccata doleant, & non nisi moesto animo ad illorum correptionem accedant, neq; ex eo voluptatem capiant, si qui durius tractandi sint, sed emendationem illorum omni studio quaerant. Talis olim Moses fuit, qui dies noctesq; pro populo precabatur, & ut huic parceretur, ex libro vitae deleri cupiebat. Tales Prophetae fuerunt. Samuel certè seipsum maerore coficiebat, quod Saule à Deo reiectum esse audiret. Et notae sunt acerbissimae querelae atq; lamentationes, quibus Ieremias populi contumaciam saepius, deinde excidium quoq; deplorauit. Horum igitur exempla hodie imitentur, quicunq; in Ecclesia cum aliquo fructu versari volunt. Et arguuntur hi ministri socordes & gregi sui ofores, quorum illi quidem nullis vitijs, quantumuis enormibus contristantur, sed sufq; deque ferunt omnia: hi vero vitijs suorum gaudent, quod bilem suam releuandi occasionem sibi oblatam esse videant. Taceo nunc perfidos familiae Dei turbatores, qui ipsi cum ebriosis bibunt, ludunt, proteruiunt, & suo exemplo confirmant eos, quorum peccata pijs lachrymis deflere debebant. Quid vero de personatis illis pastoribus dicemus, qui Ecclesias, quarum titulis superbiunt, prorsus negligunt, neque ad eas vnquam veniunt alio proposito, quam ut pecunias colligant: quo fit ut tenuiorus fortunae hominibus molestiae & tristitiae authores sint, quos subleuare potius debebant.
units.tr: This example is also most worthy of notice, so that we may learn with what spirit the ministers of the Churches ought to regard those entrusted to their faith. Paul could not rejoice unless the Corinthians rejoiced. Yet hitherto they had indulged their own pleasures too much, since, secure from all judgement, they sinned freely, ate at the sacrifices of the Gentiles, and did whatever they pleased, to such an extent that some, having shaken off the fear of the coming judgement, kept on their lips that Sardanapalian saying: "Eat, drink, play; after death there is no pleasure." But Paul is not speaking of that kind of joy, but of that spiritual and holy joy which those conceive within their souls who, converted from sins, have returned to God in grace. He therefore grieved over their sins, because he was then compelled to deal more severely with them, and he feared for their salvation. Again he was refreshed with new joy when he saw that they had repented from the heart, and so had been reconciled to God. This ought to happen on both sides, and the Churches will not be safe unless this mutual affection holds between ministers and sheep. Therefore ministers should grieve over the sins of the people, and approach their correction only with a sorrowful mind, and should not take pleasure in it if some have to be treated more harshly, but should seek their amendment with all zeal. Such was Moses of old, who prayed for the people day and night, and wished, so that they might be spared, to be blotted out of the book of life. Such were the Prophets. Samuel certainly wasted away with grief when he heard that Saul had been rejected by God. And the most bitter complaints and lamentations are well known, with which Jeremiah often bewailed the people's obstinacy, and then their destruction as well. Let whoever wishes to live with some fruit in the Church therefore imitate these examples today. And those ministers are rebuked who are careless and neglectful of their flock: some of them are not grieved by any sins, however grave, but take everything lightly; others rejoice in the vices of their people, because they see in them an occasion offered to relieve their own bile. I say nothing now of the treacherous disturbers of God's household, who themselves drink, play and behave wantonly with drunkards, and by their example confirm those whose sins they ought to have mourned with devout tears. And what shall we say of those masked pastors, who utterly neglect the churches in whose titles they take pride, and never come to them with any purpose other than to collect money, with the result that they are causes of trouble and sorrow to people of humbler means, whom they ought rather to relieve?

units.la: At vicissim populum quoque hic locus officij admonet, ut qui digne corripiuntur, pastorum suorum fidem atque amorem paternum agnoscant, deque illis rursus exhilarandis cogitent. Vt enim bonae indolis filij gaudere non possunt, quàm diu patrem ipsis succenfere, & propter ipsos in luctu & mærore constitutum esse vident: ita qui germani Dei filij sunt, non possunt non dolere, quàm diu ex præconum verbi Dei sermonibus audiunt, hunc peccatis ipsorum irasci. Arguuntur ergo hic, qui scelerum correptionem clamant superuacaneam esse, & aliqua liberius accusari indignissimè ferunt, in hoc unum intenti, ut Euangelicæ libertatis prætextu ad peccandi licentiam abutantur. Horum ferè voces sunt. Iampridem nos iugum Antichristi & sacrificorum monachorumq; eius excussimus, ergo nouum istud subire nolumus, quod Concionatores isti, omnium mortalium importunissimi, nobis imponere conantur: Item: Debebant illi nobis gaudij & tranquillitatis administri esse, & ecce quid aliud faciunt, quàm quod rixantur, minantur, fulminant, & iurgijs perpetuis omnia turbant? &c. Errant autem isti homines multis modis. Primò enim, bene quidem faciunt quicunq; Antichristi iugum iniquum & intolerabile excutiunt, sed id in eum finem fieri debet, ut eius loco iugum Christi suauissimum saluberrimumq; in se recipiant. Nec enim nos exleges esse vult Deus, qui omni reiecta disciplina, affectuum carnis impetu feramur. Impiorum & hostium Christi voces sunt: Rumpamus vincula eorum, & iora eorum abijciamus. Et Belialis filij in Scriptura dicuntur impij & ad exitium deuoti homines, eò quod absq; omni legum & disciplinæ iugo viuere soleant. Deinde gaudium carnale quærunt isti homines, & pacem huius mundi, quam Christus discipulis suis diserte negauit, ut nuper diximus. Præterea, non intelligunt, neq; ministros neq; vulgus Christianorum posse gaudij illius sancti & salutiferæ tranquillitatis conscientiarum participes fieri, nisi sanctus ille & optatissimus dolor præcedat, qui ex peccatorum agnitione & sensu iræ Dei nascitur. Ad eum verò opus est redargutione & correptione, quæ pœnitentiam gignit veram, qua Angelos quoq; cœlites exhilarari Christus ait, & quæ totum hominem nouo gaudio recreat, dum se cum Deo in gratiam redijsse sentit: sicuti in filij prodigi parabola, in Zachæi item & similium exemplis est videre. Neminem ergo improborum istorum voces moueant, qui suarum cupiditatum licentiam non solum gloriæ Dei, verumetiam propriæ simul & publicæ omnium saluti præferunt.
units.tr: In turn, this passage also reminds the people of their duty: that those who are rightly corrected should acknowledge the faithfulness and paternal love of their pastors, and think about cheering them again. For just as the sons of a good disposition cannot rejoice as long as they see their father angry with them and sorrowing and distressed on their account, so those who are true sons of God cannot but grieve, as long as they hear from the sermons of the heralds of God's Word that he is angry at their sins. Therefore those are rebuked here who cry out that the correction of wickedness is superfluous, and who take very ill being accused at all with any freedom, intent on this one thing: that under the pretext of evangelical liberty they may abuse it as licence to sin. Their words are roughly these: "For a long time now we have shaken off the yoke of Antichrist and of his priests and monks, so we do not wish to take on this new one, which those preachers, the most troublesome of all mortals, try to impose upon us." Again: "They ought to have been ministers of our joy and tranquillity, and look what they do instead, except quarrel, threaten, thunder, and throw everything into confusion with constant wrangling?" etc. But these men are wrong in many ways. For first, those who throw off the unjust and intolerable yoke of Antichrist do well indeed, but this ought to be done with the aim that in its place they may take upon themselves the most gentle and most wholesome yoke of Christ. For God does not wish us to be lawless, to be carried headlong, with all discipline cast aside, by the impulse of the desires of the flesh. These are the voices of the impious and enemies of Christ: "Let us break their bonds and cast away their cords." And in Scripture the impious men doomed to destruction are called sons of Belial, because they are accustomed to live without the yoke of any law or discipline. Next, these men seek carnal joy and the peace of this world, which Christ plainly denied to his disciples, as we said a little while ago. Moreover, they do not understand that neither ministers nor the common run of Christians can share in that holy joy and saving tranquillity of conscience unless that holy and most desirable sorrow goes before it, which arises from the recognition of sins and the sense of God's wrath. For this, rebuke and correction are needed, which produce true repentance, over which Christ says the angels of heaven also rejoice, and which refreshes the whole man with new joy when he feels that he has returned into favour with God, as may be seen in the parable of the prodigal son and likewise in the examples of Zacchaeus and similar cases. Therefore let the voices of these wicked men move no one, who put the licence of their own lusts before not only the glory of God, but also the salvation of themselves and of the public as a whole.

units.la: Quod autem in Ecclesia fieri necesse est, hoc in Repub. quoq; non minus debet obseruari. Doleant populi sui incommodis magistratus, & non sine gemitu multas siue pœnas à transgressoribus exigant. E contra populus principibus suis gaudium parere studeat, dum se illis fidelem & obsequentem præbet. Debet idem priuatim quoq; fieri inter parentes & liberos: ut illi quidem ex liberorum delictis & contumacia pium & acerbum dolorem concipiant: hi verò cogitent, quantum scelus sit molestiam & tristitiam illis exhibere, ex quibus geniti & non sine maximo labore educati sunt: & proinde illis exhilarandis intenti sint. Filius sapiens (inquit Solomon) exhilarat patrem, at filius stultus mæror est matri suæ. Et rursus: Eius oculos, qui patrem subsannat, & matris doctrinam spernit, corui torrentis eruant, & aquilarum pulli deuorent. Prouerbiorum 20. & 30.
units.tr: What must happen in the Church must be observed no less in the commonwealth. Magistrates should grieve over the troubles of their people and not exact many penalties from wrongdoers without groaning. For their part, the people should strive to bring joy to their rulers by showing themselves faithful and obedient to them. The same should happen privately between parents and children. Parents should feel a godly and bitter grief over their children's offences and disobedience. Children, for their part, should consider what a wicked thing it is to cause pain and sorrow to those from whom they were born and by whom, with great toil, they were raised, and so they should be eager to gladden them. "A wise son," says Solomon, "gladdens his father, but a foolish son is a grief to his mother." And again: "The eyes of the one who mocks his father and despises his mother's instruction, let the ravens of the valley pluck out, and the young eagles devour." Proverbs 20 and 30.

units.la: Sed ut ad Paulum redeamus, obijceret aliquis: Sine tristitiam nobis afferres, hucusq; Corinthum noluisti venire, cur ergo epistolam scripsisti tam acrem & vehementem, quæ totam Ecclesiam contristauit? Hanc ergo obiectionem præoccupat Paulus, & prioris epistolæ rigorem excusat. Primò à causa finali argumentum petit: Et hoc ipsum vobis scripsi, ne cùm venero tristitiam capiam ex ijs, de quibus me oportebat gaudere. Fateor me aliquanto acrius scripsisse, id quod vobis mærorem & tristitiam peperit: id verò feci, non quòd vestro dolore ego gauderem, sed ne quando vobis molestiam maiorem exhibere cogerer, & præsens maiori cū acerbitate exequi, quod me absente mitius perfici potuit per epistolam. Itaq; patres fidos & cordatos imitatus sum: qui si ipsis peregrè agentibus domi suæ multa à suis præter officium fieri audiant, mox aut literis scriptis, aut aliquibus domum missis curant, ut quacunque ratione id fieri possit, omne id corrigatur, priusquam ipsi ad suos redeant, ne domum reuersi cum dolore cogantur molestiam grauiorem subire, quando ex suorum conspectu gaudium & foris exhaustorum laborum recreationem concipere cupiunt. Decet hoc omnes, qui vel Ecclesiæ pastores sunt, vel in Repub. versantur: Ut vitiis maturam medicinam adhibeant, neq; differant id quod citius fieri potest. Ita enim minori cum animorum offensione fit, quod fit, quod si diuturniori vsu confirmetur, vix absq; summa difficultate, & sæpe non sine periculo perficitur.
units.tr: But to return to Paul: someone might object, "If you were going to bring us sorrow, why did you refuse until now to come to Corinth? Why then did you write a letter so sharp and vehement that it saddened the whole Church?" Paul anticipates this objection and excuses the severity of his earlier letter. First he draws the argument from his purpose: "And this very thing I wrote to you, lest when I come I should have sorrow from those over whom I ought to rejoice." I admit that I wrote somewhat more sharply, and this brought you grief and sorrow. I did it, however, not because I took pleasure in your pain, but so that I would not be forced to cause you greater trouble when present, and to carry out with greater harshness what could have been done more gently by letter in my absence. In this I have imitated faithful and sensible fathers. When they are abroad and hear that many things contrary to duty are being done at home by their families, they soon arrange, either by written letters or by sending someone home, that everything be corrected by whatever means are possible before they themselves return. They do this so that, coming home, they will not be forced to suffer the greater pain of trouble, when they long to find joy in the sight of their own people and recreation from the labours they have endured abroad. This applies to all who are ministers of the Church or who take part in the commonwealth: they should apply a timely remedy to faults and not put off what can be done sooner. For in this way what has to be done is done with less offence to minds; but if the evil is allowed to become entrenched by long practice, it is scarcely accomplished without the greatest difficulty, and often not without danger.

units.la: Secundum argumentum ab ipsorum persona sumitur. Nam ipsem, quam de ipsis optimam conceperit, exponit, & qua fretus epistolam illam scripserit, Confisus (inquit) vobis omnibus, meum gaudium omnium vestrum gaudium esse. Id est, plane mihi persuasi, me a vobis non minus amari, quam ego vos amo, & ideo ea, quae mihi gaudium pepiunt, vobis quoq; iucundissima & gratissima esse. Quia ergo non alia re perinde ut vestro in pietate profectu gaudeo, non potui non vos liberius admonere de iis, quae vestrum illum profectum impediebant. Quo loco observabis, Paulum universaliter loqui de omnibus Corinthiis. Atqui sciebat, non eundem esse omnium animum, imo aliquos pessime erga se affectos esse, adeo ut omnia eius improbe & scurriliter calumniarentur. Nec tamen his animo seruili blandiri sive adulari voluit: sed singulari prudentia hoc agit, ne meliores cum iniquis illis misceendo, illos etiam offendat, simulq; alteros quoq; sua lenitate sibi conciliet, & in posterum obsequentiores habeat. Deniq; Christiana charitatis haec verba sunt, quae de omnibus bene sperat, nec facile locum dat suspicionibus. Debent igitur in eo quoq; Paulum imitari omnes doctores, ne seipsos exosos faciant, dum aequo morosiores nemini fidunt, & temere conceptis suspicionibus indulgent: neue animum mox despondeant, quando apud aliquos fructra laborare videntur. At ita (inquis) saepe falluntur. Quid tum postea? Falluntur enim absq; sua salutis iactura: interim hypocritae illi, aut etiam aperte proteruientes (si rem propius inspicias) ipsos fallunt, non illos, quorum facilitate abutuntur. Et tutius est sic falli dum officium facis, quam temerario aut praecipiti nimis iudicio tuo decipi, dum de illis desperas, qui etsi nunc professioni suae non respondeant, sunt tamen ex electorum numero, quos Deus suo tempore traheret. Hoc vtinam observarent omnes, qui in omnium conscientias suo iudicio penetrant, & nimia severitate multos abstrerent, qui si commode tractarentur, poterant in viam reduci ut verbo Dei colla submitterent.
units.tr: The second argument is taken from the persons themselves. For Paul sets out the very good opinion he had formed of them, and on what confidence he wrote that letter: "Trusting in you all, that my joy is the joy of you all." That is, he was fully persuaded that he was loved by them no less than he loved them, and therefore that the things which gave him joy would also be most pleasing and welcome to them. Since he rejoices in nothing so much as in your progress in godliness, he could not help admonishing you more freely about those things which hindered that progress. Here you will observe that Paul speaks in general terms of all the Corinthians. Yet he knew that their minds were not all the same; indeed some were very badly disposed towards him, so that they slandered everything he did wickedly and scurrilously. Still, he did not wish to flatter or fawn upon them with a servile spirit. Rather, with singular prudence he acted so that by mingling the better with the unjust he would not offend the better, and at the same time would win over the others by his gentleness and make them more obedient in future. Finally, these words are the words of Christian charity, which hopes well of all and does not readily give room to suspicions. Therefore all teachers ought to imitate Paul in this as well, so that they do not make themselves hated by being too severe, trusting no one and indulging rash suspicions, nor lose heart at once when they seem to labour in vain among some. "But," you say, "they are often deceived." What then? They are deceived without loss to their salvation. Meanwhile those hypocrites, or those who are openly shameless (if you look at the matter more closely), deceive themselves, not those whose good nature they abuse. And it is safer to be deceived in this way while doing your duty than to be misled by a rash or overhasty judgement, despairing of those who, though they do not now live up to their profession, are nonetheless among the number of the elect whom God will draw in his time. Would that all who pry into the consciences of everyone by their own judgement would observe this, and would not drive away by excessive severity many who, if they were handled suitably, could have been brought back to the way and submitted their necks to the Word of God.

units.la: Addit his Paulus tertium argumentum a propria persona, quo modum quoq; exponit, quem tenuerit, cum priorem ad illos epistolam daret. Nam ex multa oppressione & anxietate cordis scripsi vobis, per multas lachrymas: non ut tristitia afficiamini, sed ut cognoscatis charitatem, quam habeo abundantissimam erga vos. Quasi diceret: Non mihi gaudio vel voluptati fuit, quod acrius & severius me scribere oportuit: quin potius id mihi dolore acerbissimum attulit, adeo, ut ego non minus quam vos contristatus fuerim, & fortasse etiam acerbius atq; acutius. Et hoc facit descriptio maeroris, quem inter scribendum senserit. Scripsi (inquit) ex multa oppressione, sic nimirum, ut me vndiq; premi sentirem.
