Deinde corde anxius & quasi in angustias coactatus fui, ut nescirem quo me verterem. Et tantus fuit ille dolor, ut lachrymas quoque plurimas mihi expresserit. Deniq; omnis mei instituti non hic finis mihi fuit, ut vos conturbarem, sed ut meum erga vos studium & charitatem, qua vos in animo meo complector, & quam omni officiorum genere declarare cupio, cognosceretis.
units.tr: Paul adds to these a third argument, taken from his own person, by which he also sets out the manner he had kept when he gave his earlier letter to them. "For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you, with many tears; not that you should be grieved, but that you might know the love I have in abundance for you." As if he were saying: it was no joy or pleasure to me that I had to write more sharply and severely; rather, it brought me the most bitter grief, so that I was saddened no less than you, and perhaps even more keenly and sharply. This is what the description of the sorrow he felt while writing conveys. "I wrote," he says, "out of much affliction," so that, of course, I felt myself pressed down on every side. Then my heart was anxious, and I was as if driven into straits, so that I did not know where to turn. And that grief was so great that it drew many tears from me. Finally, the whole aim of my undertaking was not to disturb you, but that you might know my zeal for you and the love with which I embrace you in my mind, and which I wish to declare by every kind of service.

units.la: Nec temere ista Paulum dicere putabimus, quae Stoicus aliquis de semetipso noluisset fateri. Sed Christiana religio non extinguit naturales animi affectiones, quas in Christo quoq; locum habuisse scimus, qui interdum lachrymas fudit, interdum animi dolorem voce & gemitu testatus est. Et quoad Paulum, quia bene sperabat de Corinthiis, deq; ipsis ut sigillo sui apostolatus gloriari solebat, non potuit non acutius dolere, quando eos spei suae minus respondere videbat. Ita enim natura comparatum est, ut intolerabilior sit dolor, cuius nobis authores sunt, de quibus propter amorem vehementissimum, quo eos diligimus, nihil tale cogitabamus. Sic Christus toto animo turbabatur, quando se a discipulo proditum iri cogitabat. Et marito nihil molestius accidere potest, quam si eum vxor fallat, de cuius fide & pudicitia semper optime sperauit. Quod ipsum parentibus quoq; accidit, si inter liberos suos eos proteruiores factos videant, quos ipsi aliquando seneRectutis suae baculum fore sibi persuaserant.
units.tr: We should not think that Paul said these things rashly, things which some Stoic would not have been willing to admit about himself. Christian religion does not extinguish the natural affections of the mind, which we know also had a place in Christ, who at times shed tears and at other times testified by voice and groaning to the grief of his soul. As for Paul, since he hoped well of the Corinthians, and was accustomed to glory in them as the seal of his apostleship, he could not help feeling more keenly when he saw them falling short of his hope. For it is the nature of things that the grief is harder to bear when its authors are those for whom, because of the most intense love with which we cherish them, we had thought nothing of the kind. So Christ was troubled in his whole soul when he thought that he would be betrayed by a disciple. And nothing can happen more painful to a husband than for his wife to deceive him, one in whose faithfulness and chastity he has always hoped the best. The same happens to parents, if they see among their children those become more insolent whom they had once persuaded themselves would be the staff of their old age.

units.la: Est autem obseruatu dignissimum, quod Paulus charitatem suam, qua Corinthios prosequebatur, agnosci voluit, non ex indulgentia & ignaua omnium, quae inter illos fiebant, dissimulatione, sed ex correptione paterna, quam delinquentibus adhibuerat. Nam ut Solomon ait, paterfilium, quem diligit, castigat. Et ideo Deus, qui ipsissima charitas est, fere iudicium suum a suis inchoat, ne cum mundo poenitere nescio condemnentur. Idem ergo faciant, quicunq; in Ecclesia, sive Repub. parentum loco sunt. Vicissim agnoscant hoc dilectionis paternæ argumentum siue officium esse ij, qui corripiuntur, & proinde id patienter ferant. Atqui scio (inquis) aut saltem non absq; grauibus coniecturis suspicor, multa hostili animo & ex odio fieri. Esto, attamen eadem ad te redit vtilitas, si eam quoq; correctionem patienter admittas, quæ ex tui amantissimo rediret, si ab eo corripereris. Cur igitur illum odio prosequaris, qui vel iniuitus tibi beneficium dat, dum ipse prauo suo affectui indulget?
units.tr: It is well worth noting that Paul wished his love for the Corinthians, with which he pursued them, to be recognised not from an indulgent and idle overlooking of everything that was going on among them, but from the fatherly correction he had applied to those who did wrong. For, as Solomon says, a father chastises the son whom he loves. And so God, who is love itself, almost always begins his judgment with his own people, lest they be condemned together with the world, which does not know how to repent. Therefore let all who stand in the place of parents, or in the commonwealth, do the same. In turn, let those who are corrected acknowledge that this is a sign and duty of paternal love, and so bear it patiently. But, you say, I know, or at least I suspect on no slight grounds, that many things are done with a hostile mind and out of hatred. Granted; yet the same benefit returns to you if you also patiently accept the correction that would come from one who loved you most, if you were rebuked by him. Why then do you pursue with hatred the one who, even against his will, does you a kindness, while he himself indulges his own wicked passion?

units.la: Deinde multum facit locus hic ad afferendam doctrinæ apostolicæ authoritatem. Quia enim erga hominum salutem ita affecti fuerunt, vt eorum perditionem atq; interitum gemitu & lachrymis prosecuti sint, adhæc totius mundi odia in se prouocarint, imò mortem quoq; subierint, vt quàm plurimos seruarent, nemo illos suspectos habere poteßt, quòd ex prauo affectu aliquid vel dixerint vel fecerint, quod nobis fraudi esse queat. Prædicauerunt autem illi nobis vnum IESVM CHRISTVM, qui miseris mortalibus vnicus pœnitentiæ simul & remissionis peccatorum author atque Mediator sit. Hunc ergo totis animis amplectamur, & in meriti eius fiducia constanter in finem vsque perseueremus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, this passage is of great value in establishing the authority of the apostolic teaching. For since they were so affected toward the salvation of men that they pursued their perdition and destruction with groaning and tears, and moreover stirred up the hatred of the whole world against themselves, and even underwent death itself, so that they might save as many as possible, no one can regard them as suspect, as if they had said or done anything out of a wicked disposition that could be to our harm. Now they preached to us the one Jesus Christ, who is the only author and Mediator of repentance and of the forgiveness of sins for wretched mortals. Let us therefore embrace him with all our hearts, and persevere constantly in trust in his merit to the end. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA IX.
units.tr: HOMILY IX.

units.la: Quòd si quis tristitiam attulit, non mihi tristitiam attulit, sed ex parte, ne aggrauem vos omnes. Sufficit huiusmodi homini ista obiurgatio à pluribus facta: Vt è contrario potius vos ei condonetis, eumq; consolemini, ne quo modo redundante tristitia absorbeatur eiusmodi homo. Quapropter precor vos, vt tratam faciatis in illum charitatem. Nam in hunc finem etiam scripsi, vt cognoscere probationem vestri, num ad omnia obedientes sitis. Cui verò condonatis, etiam ego condono: nam & ego si quid condonaui, cui condonaui, propter vos id feci in conspectu Christi, vt ne præoccupemur à Satana. Non enim illius machinationes ignoramus.
units.tr: But if anyone has caused sorrow, he has not caused it to me, but in part, so that I may not burden you all. This rebuke, given by many, is enough for such a man. So on the contrary you should rather forgive him and comfort him, lest such a man be swallowed up by excessive sorrow. Therefore I beg you to confirm your love towards him. For I also wrote with this aim, that I might know your proof, whether you are obedient in all things. Whomever you forgive, I also forgive. For if I have forgiven anything, to the one I forgave, I did it for your sake in the sight of Christ, so that we would not be overreached by Satan. For we are not ignorant of his schemes.

units.la: IN priori epistola Paulus Corinthios durius aliquanto tractauerat, cùm propter alia vitia, quæ apud eos obrepserant, tum propter hominem incestum, quem æquo diutius tolerauerant non sine magno scandalo & religionis Christianæ ignominia. Et quia apud eos non erat magistratus Christianus, neq; apud gentes incestus capitalibus pœnis plectebantur, quas Deus illis decreuerat non potuit Legem vrgere Paulus, quæ apud Mosem extat. Ideo quod vnum reliquum erat, iuf-fit impurum illum vnanimi totius Ecclesiæ consensu Satanæ tradere. Erat hæc non vulgaris aut simplex exclusio à cœtibus sacris, sed pœnam habebat coniunctam, qua miseri illi in corpore simul & animo suo torquebantur. Nam eo dono primitiuam Ecclesiam à Domino armatam fuisse, in capite duodecimo prioris epistolæ audiuimus, vt haberent Christiani homines, qui tunc magistratus nouos ex suis creare non poterant, quo improborum petulantia aut improbitas coerceretur. Paruerant Corinthij mandato Pauli, & id non sine fructu. Nam vt ex præsenti loco colligi poteßt, miser ille ita discruciatus esset, vt periculum esset, ne totus dolore aut desperatione absorberetur. Quæ causa fuit, vt multi nouam arriperent calumniandi occasionem, & Paulum crudelitatis accusarent. Ideo nuper se excusare cœpit docens, quæ ipsi huius seueritatis ratio fuerit, & quòd ipse ex ea non minus doloris senserit, quàm quisquam alius. Nunc autem docet, quid porrò cum illo homine agere debeant, vt & eius saluti, & publico Ecclesiæ dolori consulatur.
units.tr: In the earlier letter Paul had dealt with the Corinthians rather harshly, both on account of other vices that had crept in among them and on account of the incestuous man, whom they had tolerated for too long, not without great scandal and disgrace to the Christian religion. Since there was no Christian magistrate among them, and since among the Gentiles incest was not punished by the capital penalties that God had prescribed for it, Paul could not press the law that stands in Moses. So he ordered that the one remaining measure be taken: that this impure man be handed over to Satan by the unanimous consent of the whole Church. This was not an ordinary or simple exclusion from the sacred assemblies; it carried a penalty, by which those wretched men were tormented in both body and soul. For we heard in the twelfth chapter of the earlier letter that the primitive Church was armed by the Lord with this gift, so that Christians, who could not then create new magistrates from among themselves, would have a means by which the insolence or wickedness of the bad could be restrained. The Corinthians obeyed Paul's command, and not without result. For, as can be gathered from the present passage, that wretched man had been so tormented that there was a danger he would be swallowed up entirely by grief or despair. This was the reason that many seized the new occasion to slander, and accused Paul of cruelty. So he has now begun to excuse himself, teaching what the reason for this severity was, and that he himself felt no less grief from it than anyone else. Now, however, he teaches what they ought further to do with that man, so that both his salvation and the public grief of the Church may be provided for.

units.la: Vt verò totam hanc epistolam mira prudentia atque artificio temperauit, ne plus satis exacerbatos magis irritaret: ita hic quoq; sensim ad causam hanc delabitur. Si quis (inquit) tristitiam attulit, non mihi tristitiam attulit, sed ex parte, &c. Non nominat hominem, neque scelus ab eo commissum odiose exagitat. Erant enim omnia satis nota, & quia nunc de eius restitutio-ne agebatur, non opus erat aliquid dicere, quod vel illum vel Corinthios amplius contristaret. Itaque hic verborum istorum sensus est: Si quis tristitiam siue molestiam aliquam in vestra Ec-clesia excitauit, is non mihi tristitiam attulit, id est, illud non ita interpretatus sum, quasi iniu-ria illa ad me priuatim potissimum redundaret, neq; vt priuatim dolorem vlturus in illu vos se-uerius animaduertere iussi: Sed ex parte modo, vel quadamtenus, id mihi molestum fuit, quod ta-le quid accidisset inter vos, quos ego vt filios & fratres dileƈtissimos compleƈtor, & de quorum fi-de & virtute passim apud Ecclesias gloriari soleo. Neque alium mei consilij aut mandati finem propositum habui, quam ne vos omnes grauarem nimia indulgentia. Pertinet exemplum hoc ad omnes Ecclesiarum ministros, quorum est sic res suas instituere, vt eadem ratione suam seueritatem aut rigorem excusare possint omnibus, quibus in vitijs corripendis nimij esse videntur. Sed ea est mundi infelicis cæcitas, vt licet aliqui eadem cum Paulo vere dicant, pauci tamen eorum fidem agnoscant.
units.tr: Just as he tempered this whole letter with remarkable prudence and skill, so as not to irritate further those who were already too exasperated, so here too he gradually comes to this matter. "If anyone," he says, "has caused sorrow, he has not caused it to me, but in part," and so on. He does not name the man, nor does he harshly denounce the crime committed by him, since everything was sufficiently well known; and since what was now being dealt with was his restoration, there was no need to say anything that might grieve either him or the Corinthians further. So the sense of these words is this: if anyone has caused some sorrow or distress in your Church, he has not caused it to me, that is, I have not so taken it as if that injury fell upon me particularly and privately, nor have I ordered you to punish him more severely in order to avenge a private grief. Rather, it was troubling to me only in part, or to some extent, that such a thing had happened among you, whom I embrace as my most beloved sons and brothers, and of whose faith and virtue I am accustomed to boast everywhere among the Churches. Nor have I had any other aim in my counsel or command than that I might not burden you all by excessive indulgence. This example pertains to all ministers of the Churches, whose duty is so to order their affairs that by the same reasoning they can excuse their own severity or strictness to all those whom they seem too harsh toward when correcting faults. But such is the blindness of this unhappy world that, although some say the same things as Paul truly, few acknowledge their faith.

units.la: Continet autem locus hic memorabilem doƈtrinam: Nimirum publicis sceleribus, si impuni-ta dimittantur, totas Ecclesias atque Respub. grauari. Facit enim impunitas illa, vt paucorum exemplo multi alij corrumpantur, & latius subinde serpat contagio apud eos, qui natura ad ma-lum procliues sunt. Deinde indulgentia ista confusionis speciem habet, quæ omnes simul eodem reatu inuoluit, & quæ causa est, vt publicis pœnis simul omnes à Deo multentur. Exemplum habes in primi mundi hominibus, quando filij Dei cum filiabus hominum primum per coniugia il-licita misceri cœperunt. Debebant tunc principijs obstare parentes, & quicunque authoritate a-lijs præstabant: sed quia id non fecerunt, & fortassis hoc ad fouendam pacem & concordiam pu-blicam vtile atque commodum putarunt (quibus rationibus etiam hodie commercia eiusmodi ab huius seculi sapientibus excusantur) breui temporis progressu malu factum est immedicabile, & secuta est tandem vniuersalis licentia, quam vniuersali omnium terrarum diluuio coerceri at-que elui oportuit. Simile quid postea Sichemitis accidit, quando filij regij libido impunita abijt.
units.tr: This passage contains a noteworthy teaching: namely, that if public crimes are left unpunished, whole Churches and the commonwealth are burdened. For such impunity causes many others to be corrupted by the example of a few, and the contagion creeps more widely among those who are naturally inclined to evil. Moreover, that indulgence has the appearance of confusion, which involves everyone alike in the same guilt, and which is the cause that all are together punished by God with public penalties. You have an example in the men of the first world, when the sons of God first began to mix with the daughters of men through unlawful marriages. The parents and whoever held authority over others ought then to have resisted the beginnings; but because they did not do so, and perhaps thought this useful and advantageous for fostering public peace and harmony (on which grounds even today such unions are excused by the wise men of this age), the evil in a short time became incurable, and at last universal licence followed, which had to be restrained and washed away by the universal deluge of all the lands. Something similar happened later to the Shechemites, when the lust of the king's son went unpunished.

units.la: Quibus adde quod in deserto factum, quando filij Israel cum Moabiticis & Madianiticis puel-lis scortati sunt. Grauauit ea licentia totum populum, nec accensus in eam Dei furor prius extin-ctus est, quam dum Phinees diuino zelo motus memorabile vindiƈtæ iustæ exemplum ædidit in viro principe, qui contumacius & impudentius in publico quoque scortari pergebat. Et quantam cladem cum publica totius gentis & cultus diuini ignominia coniunƈtam filiorum Heli licentia Israelitis attulerit, sacra historia prolixè docet. Quid vero de apertis flagitijs dicere attinet, quando occulta & ignota scelera interdum eos grauant, qui adeo non conscij sunt eorum, vt ne admis-sa quidem esse sciant? Pertinent huc Achan & Ionas, ex quibus hic quidem à conspeƈtu domini fugiens nautas rerum plane ignaros in summum discrimen adduxit, ille verò sacrilegio suo in Ierichuntina præda commisso Israelitis publicæ cladis author extitit. Quibus exemplis Deus osten-dere voluit, quàm grauiter omnibus ijs irascatur, qui eius mandata ex destinata animi malitia transgrediantur: & quàm diligenter in scelera inquirere debeant, qui ad Reipub. gubernacula destinati sunt, ne dum paucis parcunt indulgentius, simul omnes in periculum adducant. Debet huc referri Lex, quæ Deuteronom. capite duodecimo habetur de expiatione cædis, cuius author ignoratur. Ea enim docet quanta cura opus sit in puniendis publicorum scandalorum authoribus. Similiter qui puniuntur, ij patienter ferre discant castigationem, quam suis deliƈtis meruerunt. Nimium enim iniquus & inhumanus sit oportet, qui sua flagitia communi patriæ fraudi vel exitio esse velit.
units.tr: To these add what happened in the wilderness, when the sons of Israel committed fornication with Moabite and Midianite girls. That licence burdened the whole people, and the wrath of God, kindled against it, was not quenched until Phinehas, moved by divine zeal, gave a memorable example of just vengeance upon a leading man who continued to fornicate more stubbornly and shamelessly even in public. And sacred history tells at length how great a disaster, joined with public disgrace to the whole nation and to the worship of God, the licence of the sons of Eli brought upon the Israelites. What need is there to speak of open crimes, when hidden and unknown sins sometimes burden those who are so unaware of them that they do not even know they have been committed? Achan and Jonah belong here: the latter, fleeing from the presence of the Lord, brought sailors who were wholly ignorant of the matter into the greatest peril; the former, by his sacrilege in the spoil of Jericho, became the author of public ruin for the Israelites. By these examples God wished to show how gravely he is angered at all who transgress his commands from settled malice of mind, and how diligently those who are appointed to the helm of the commonwealth ought to inquire into crimes, lest by sparing a few too indulgently they bring all into danger. The law in Deuteronomy chapter twelve, concerning the expiation of a murder whose author is unknown, should be cited here. For it teaches how great care is needed in punishing the authors of public scandals. Likewise, those who are punished should learn to bear patiently the chastisement that they have deserved by their misdeeds. For a man must be very unjust and inhuman if he wishes his own disgraceful acts to be a disgrace or ruin to his common country.

units.la: Porrò docet Paulus, quid porrò faciant cum homine illo incesto: nimirum vt culpam ei con-donent, & restitutum Ecclesiæ pijs consolationibus confirment. Et addit: Precor vos, vt ratam faciatis in illum charitatem. In Græco ἐκχωρήσαι ponitur, quod aliquid legitimè & cum publica authoritate siue consensu statuere significat. Vult ergo, vt quemadmodum cum publico consensu eum multarint: ita publico etiam consensu eum in Ecclesiæ consortium recipiant, & pro fratre atq; Ecclesiæ membro agnoscant, cui charitas debeatur. Petitioni autem rationes interserit. Pri-mam: Sufficit huiusmodi homini ista obiurgatio à pluribus, id est, à tota Ecclesiæ multitudine facta. facta. Græca vox ἐπιτιμία obiurgationem, increpationem, vel etiam multam significat. Vnde colligimus, illum in publico Ecclesiæ cœtu durissimè obiurgatum & correptum fuisse cum denunciatione sententiæ, quam Paulus ad eos perscripserat, vt eam ipsi exequerentur. Secuta est mox pœna aut castigatio quædam, qua Satan, cui traditus fuerat, eius corpus & animum afflixit. Quia autem hæc suum habuerant effectum, adeò vt ille culpam suam agnosceret, seq; ipsum serio dolore conficeret, Paulus hæc sufficere ait, & eos longius progredi vetat. Inq; eum finem alteram adhuc rationem subijcit: Ne quo modo redundante tristitia absorbeatur eiusmodi homo. Solet hoc bifariam fieri. Tales enim aut desperatione vitii succumbunt, vt Cain & Iudas: aut mundo & secu-li huius studijs se totos addicentes in omnem licentiam effunduntur, si nullam reconciliationis spem sibi reliquam esse arbitrentur. Hoc ergo Corinthios cauere vult Paulus, ne misero illi exitium ferat ea disciplina, quæ saluti debebat seruire.
units.tr: Next, Paul teaches what they should further do with that incestuous man: namely, that they should forgive him his fault, and confirm him, restored to the Church, with pious consolations. And he adds: "I beg you to confirm your love towards him." The Greek word ekchōrēsai [ἐκχωρήσαι] is used here, which signifies to decide something lawfully and with public authority or consent. He wills, therefore, that just as they punished him by public consent, so by public consent they should receive him back into the fellowship of the Church, and acknowledge him as a brother and member of the Church, to whom love is owed. He adds reasons to his request. The first: "Sufficient for such a man is this rebuke by the many," that is, by the whole multitude of the Church. The Greek word epitimia [ἐπιτιμία] signifies rebuke, reproof, or even a fine. From this we gather that he had been most sharply rebuked and reproved in the public assembly of the Church, with the pronouncement of the sentence that Paul had written to them, so that they themselves might carry it out. Soon afterwards some penalty or chastisement followed, by which Satan, to whom he had been handed over, afflicted his body and soul. Since these measures had their effect, so that he acknowledged his fault and was consumed by serious grief, Paul says that this is enough and forbids them to go any further. For this same end he adds another reason: "lest by any means such a man be swallowed up by excessive sorrow." This usually happens in two ways. For such people either succumb to despair over their vice, as Cain and Judas did, or, giving themselves wholly to the pursuits of the world and of this age, they pour themselves into every licence, if they think no hope of reconciliation is left to them. Paul therefore wants the Corinthians to guard against that discipline, which ought to serve his salvation, bringing ruin upon the unhappy man.

units.la: Habemus hoc loco exemplum obseruatu dignissimum, quo admonemur, vt disciplina publicè in Ecclesia exerceri, vtq; eadem ab ijs, qui illam peccando meruerunt, ferri debeat. Disciplina quidem Ecclesiæ non vtilis modò verumetiam necessaria est propter innatam nobis naturæ vitiositatem, qua fit vt ad omne malum natura proclives simus, & cordis humani figmenta ab ineunte ætate prava sint. Quibus accedunt multiplices scelerum occasiones, quas seueriùs reprimi & coerceri oportet, ne in licentiam erumpant. Forma autem disciplinæ non vna & eadem apud omnes Ecclesias constitui potest, sed pro ratione locorum & hominum agere oportet, qua de re non vno loco D. Augustinus diligenter disputat. Finis autem idem vbique spectari debet: vt qui peccarunt, pœniteant, & ad Deum serio conuersi feruentur: non autem vt diutius excrucientur cum animarum periculo. Medicinæ enim instar est hæc castigatio, & proinde non debet in carnificinam commutari: quin potius quicunque à peccatis ad Deum conuertuntur, absque mora in gratiam recipiendi sunt. Debet enim Ecclesia Dei exemplum imitari, qui apud Prophetam ait: Si auersus fuerit impius ab omnibus peccatis suis quæ fecit, & custodierit omnia statuta mea, feceritque iudicium & iustitiam, viuendo viuet, & non morietur: Omnes præuaricationes, quas fecit, non venient in memoriam, sed in iustitia sua, quam fecit, viuet. Et rursus: Momento, vt loquutus fuero de aliqua gente aut regno, vt euellam, extirpem aut perdam, reddieritque ea gens, contra quam locutus eram, à malitia sua, iam me quoque pœnitebit mali, quod ei facere constitueram. Quibus consentit & illud: Reuertimini ad me, & ego reuertar ad vos. Confirmantur promissiones istæ infinitis exemplis, inter quæ admodum memorabilia sunt, Dauidis, Zachæi, Petri, peccatricis item illius, quæ peccatorum pœnitentia acerbè dolens Christi pedes lachrymis suis abluit, & capillis extersit. Quibus iure addideris Hierosolymitanos cives, quos adhuc cæde ac sanguine Filij sui, IESV CHRISTI, madentes in gratiam Deus recepit, quando animis totis compunctì, ab Apostolis salutis consilium petebant. Et huc pertinet, quod Paulus bis illud quasi Ἀνεκτικῶς dictum repetit: Huiusmodi homo. Eo enim admonet, in disciplinæ executione non tam delictum ponderari, quàm delinquentis ingenium, adeoq; communis nostræ naturæ infirmitatem respici debere, quid nimirum vnusquisq; ferre possit, vel minus. Estq; hic imprimis multa & diligenti cura opus, ne modum excedamus. Vt enim nobismetipsis facile condonamus, quæ præter omne officium designauimus: ita in aliorum delictis castigandis natura seueriores sumus: eò quòd nos tanto sanctiores & iustiores esse arbitramur, quantò implacabiliores durioresque nos præbemus. Vt autem non probatur medicus, qui eodem morbo laborantibus idem pharmacum propinat, nulla constitutionis illorum & accidentium, quæ morbos comitari solent, ratione habita: ita nemini cordato probari poterunt rigidi illi censores, qui eadem seueritate in quibusuis castigandis vtuntur. Et imprimis eorum rigor hic damnatur, qui veterum quorundam exemplum imitati, pœnitentiæ annos, aut saltem menses plures præscribunt, & satisfactiones reducunt theatricas, quibus qui iam pœnitentiam serio agunt, non sine publica ignominia Ecclesiæ satisfaciant. At quid huius Scriptura docet? Aut num quid simile vnquam fecisse Apostoli? Vel; num ad Ecclesiam totam pertinere negabimus, quod Christus singulis priuatim præcipit, vt fratri in die septuagies septies peccanti, & toties culpam deprecanti ignoscant atque condonent? Certè non volet Deus Ecclesiam suam ipso rigidiorem & difficiliorem habere. Objiciunt hic nobis satisfactionem magistri, periculum esse, ne qui poenitentiam simulent, & Ecclesiam fallant. Quibus ego respondeo: Non tam Ecclesiam fallunt, quam seipsos, qui hic dolo malo agunt. Nam ita Spiritui Sancto mentiuntur, qui quam acriter vlcisceatur fucum sibi factum, Ananiæ & Sapphiræ exemplo docemur. Simulabat equidem Achab quoque poenitentiam, aut saltem non omnino serius neque durabilis erat dolor, quem ex Eliæ comminatione conceperat. Attamen aliqua ex parte Deo probabatur, quod faciebat. Nimium ergo morosi & fastidiosi sunt, qui tam anxie hodie metuunt, ne a quoquam fallantur simulata resipiscentia. Atqui periculum maius hic timeri debebat, ne tu tuo iudicio falsus cum adhuc excrucies & diutius suspendas, qui iampridem Deo satisfecit. Quam enim veniam mereberis, si tu propter humanæ rationis figmenta, & superstitiosas potius quam necessarias constitutiones, eum ab Ecclesiæ coetu & Cænæ mysticæ visu excludas, quem Deus iam filiorum loco habet, imo quem Filij sui corpore & sanguine pascit & alit?
units.tr: We have in this passage an example most worthy of notice, by which we are admonished that discipline is to be exercised publicly in the Church, and that those who have deserved it by sinning must bear it. Church discipline is not only useful but necessary, because of the inborn wickedness of our nature, by which we are prone to every evil, and the imaginations of the human heart are wicked from early youth. To these are added many occasions of sin, which must be checked and restrained more severely, lest they break out into licence. The form of discipline cannot be one and the same in all Churches, but must be adapted to the circumstances of places and people, a matter on which Augustine discusses carefully in more than one place. The aim, however, should everywhere be the same: that those who have sinned may repent, and, turning seriously to God, may be brought back. This correction is like medicine, and therefore it must not be turned into torture. Rather, whoever turns from sins to God must be received into grace without delay. The Church of God ought to imitate the example of him who says through the Prophet: "If the wicked turn away from all his sins that he has committed, and keep all my statutes, and do judgment and justice, he shall live and not die. None of the transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him; in his righteousness that he has done he shall live" (Ezek. 18). And again: "At what instant I shall speak concerning a nation or a kingdom, to pluck up, to break down, and to destroy it, if that nation turn from its evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do to it" (Jer. 18). To these agrees that saying: "Turn ye unto me, and I will turn unto you" (Zech. 1). These promises are confirmed by countless examples, among which those of David, Zacchaeus and Peter are very memorable, and also that of the sinful woman who, grieving bitterly for her sins, washed Christ's feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. To these you may rightly add the citizens of Jerusalem, still dripping with the blood of his Son, Jesus Christ, whom God received into grace when, pricked to the heart, they asked the Apostles for counsel of salvation. To this also belongs Paul's repeated use, twice, of the phrase "such a man" (huiusmodi homo), which is, as it were, said ἀνεκτικῶς [with forbearance]. By it he admonishes that in carrying out discipline one must weigh not so much the offence as the character of the offender, and must therefore take account of the weakness of our common nature, of what each person can in fact bear, or less. Here above all, much careful and diligent attention is needed, lest we exceed the proper measure. For just as we readily pardon ourselves for things that we have marked out as beyond all duty, so we are more severe in punishing the faults of others, because we think ourselves the more holy and just the more implacable and harsh we show ourselves. As a physician is not approved who gives the same medicine to all who suffer from the same disease, without regard to the constitution of those patients and the symptoms that usually accompany the disease, so those rigid censors who use the same severity in punishing whatever offences will not be approved by any sensible person. Above all, the rigour of those is condemned who, imitating the example of certain ancients, prescribe years, or at least many months, of penance, and bring back theatrical satisfactions, by which those who are already repenting in earnest must make satisfaction to the Church without public disgrace. But what does Scripture teach about this? Or did the Apostles ever do anything similar? Or shall we deny that what Christ commands individuals privately, that they forgive a brother who sins against them seventy times seven times in a day, and who each time asks pardon, pertains to the whole Church? Certainly God does not wish his Church to be harsher and more unyielding than he himself is. Here the Papists object to us the satisfaction of the teacher, and the danger that men may feign repentance and deceive the Church. To them I answer: they do not so much deceive the Church as themselves, who act here with malicious deceit. For such men lie to the Holy Spirit, and we are taught by the example of Ananias and Sapphira how sharply he avenges a fraud practised upon him. Ahab, to be sure, also feigned repentance, or at least his grief, which he conceived from Elijah's threat, was not altogether sincere or lasting. Yet in some measure what he did was approved by God. Those men are therefore too peevish and fastidious who nowadays fear so anxiously that they may be deceived by anyone's feigned repentance. Yet a greater danger here ought to be feared: that you, deceived by your own judgment, should go on tormenting and keeping in suspense a man who long ago made satisfaction to God. For what pardon will you deserve if, on account of the fancies of human reason and superstitious rather than necessary regulations, you exclude from the assembly of the Church and from sight of the holy Supper the one whom God already regards as a son, indeed whom he feeds and nourishes with the body and blood of his own Son?

units.la: Sed inspiciamus eum quoque, de quo hic agitur, ut quomodo disciplina ferri debeat, discamus. Hic certe agnovit peccatum suum, ex animo poenituit, & toto corde contritus patienter tulit poenam, quæ ipsi ab Ecclesia impositæ fuerat. Ex eo igitur fructum retulit amplissimum, ut nimirum cum Deo reconciliatus sit, & nunc Paulum habeat deprecatorem & patronum, qui prius illum accusauerat. Imo memorabile gratiæ Dei exemplum factus est, ex quo etiam hodie consolationem petere possunt peccatores, qui vasa iræ & ignominiæ esse videntur. Ita olim fecerunt sancti Dei cultores, quos non puduit, quasi dignitatis suæ oblitos, sese verbi Dei correptioni subijcere: sicuti in Dauide est videre, qui non contentus Nathano culpam fateri, tandem in Psalmis quoque confessus est, quos toti Ecclesiæ decantandos proposuit, ut sicuti scandali publici author fuerat, ita suo exemplo omnibus poenitentiam veram commendaret. Id vero nunquam fiet absque vera & seria peccatorum agnitione, quam nos ex Lege petere oportet, & simul cogitare, quam graue scelus sit Ecclesiam Dei offendere. Si enim, quovis supplicio dignus est, qui puerulo scandalum dat, quid de illo fiet, qui toti Ecclesiæ mali exempli author fuerit? Qui iStud probè expendunt, ijs nulla seueritas posse nimia videri, & ideo patienter ferent, quod de illis Deus statuerit. Vt vero hic caueri debet simulatio aut hypocrisis, ita non minus a desperationis præcipitio nobis cauendum est, ne idem nobis quod Caino, Sauli & Iudæ accidat. At hic præ aliis periclitantur, qui ad proprias satisfactiones confugiunt, quasi his peccata ipsorum expiari oporteat. Quid enim hic inuenient, quam quo magis terreantur, quando sanctissimi quique orant: Ne ingrediaris Domine in iudicium cum seruo tuo? Item: Remitte nobis debita nostra. Itaque ad thronum gratiæ nos confugere decet, & huius promissiones animo repetere, inque Christi meritum respicere, qui omnes ad se vocat, neque vllum ad se venientem reijcit. Vt vero ad præsentis loci tractationem redeamus, poterant quædam obijcere Corinthij, ad quæ Paulus respondet.
units.tr: But let us also look at the man of whom this is spoken, so that we may learn how discipline ought to be borne. He certainly recognised his sin, repented from his heart, and, wholly crushed in spirit, patiently bore the punishment that the Church had imposed on him. From this he reaped a very great fruit: namely, that he was reconciled with God, and now has Paul as his intercessor and patron, the one who had earlier accused him. Indeed he has become a memorable example of the grace of God, from which even today sinners who seem to be vessels of wrath and shame may draw comfort. So the holy worshippers of God have done in times past, men who were not ashamed, as if forgetful of their dignity, to submit themselves to the correction of God's Word. This may be seen in David, who, not content with confessing his guilt to Nathan, at last also confessed it in the Psalms, which he proposed to be sung by the whole Church, so that, just as he had been the author of public scandal, so by his own example he might commend true repentance to all. This, however, will never happen without a true and serious acknowledgement of sins, which we ought to seek from the Law, and at the same time consider how grave a crime it is to offend the Church of God. For if he who gives scandal to a little child deserves any punishment, what will become of him who has been the author of a bad example to the whole Church? Those who weigh this carefully will think that no severity can be too great for them, and so they will patiently bear whatever God has decreed concerning them. But just as pretence and hypocrisy must be guarded against here, so we must also guard against the headlong plunge of despair, lest what happened to Cain, Saul and Judas should happen to us. Yet those are in greater danger than others who take refuge in their own satisfactions, as if their sins had to be expiated by these. For what will they find here except that they become the more terrified, when the holiest men pray: "Enter not into judgment with thy servant, O Lord" (Ps. 143), and again: "Forgive us our debts" (Matt. 6)? Therefore it is fitting for us to flee to the throne of grace, to call its promises to mind, and to look to the merit of Christ, who calls all to himself and rejects none who come to him. But to return to the treatment of the present passage: the Corinthians could raise certain objections, to which Paul replies.

units.la: Primo enim dicerent: Atqui tu prius iußisti, ut iStum Satanæ tradamus, & noStram accusauisti negligentiam siue indulgentiam, qua in illo tolerando vsi fuimus. Quæ ergo hæc inconstantia? Vnde tam subita consilij mutatio? Præoccupat ergo, & ita rationem reddit prioris consilij, vt simul quod nunc petit alijs rationibus amplius confirmet. Nam in hoc scripsi (inquit) vt cognoscerem probationem vestri, num ad omnia obedientes sitis. Quasi diceret: Non is mihi animus fuit, fratres, vt vos aduersus miserum iStum hoStiliter accenderem, eumque perderem: sed potius, vt & eius saluti consulerem, & simul experimentum sumerem de vobis, an mihi in omnibus obedire parati sitis. Atqui vtrumque iam obtinui, quando & illum pœnituit serio sui sceleris, & vos vestro officio præclare functi estis. Quid ergo reStat, quam vt eo recipiendo non minus clementer agatis, quam seueriter egistis in illo eijciendo.
units.tr: For first they might say: "But you formerly ordered us to hand this man over to Satan, and you accused our negligence or indulgence, which we showed in tolerating him. What, then, is this inconstancy? Whence this sudden change of mind?" Paul therefore anticipates this and gives an account of his earlier counsel in such a way that, at the same time, he confirms more fully by other reasons what he now asks. For, he says, "I wrote for this purpose, that I might know the proof of you, whether you are obedient in all things." As if he said: "It was not my intention, brothers, to inflame you hostilely against that wretched man and to destroy him, but rather both to consult his salvation and at the same time to test you, whether you were ready to obey me in all things. Yet I have now obtained both: he has seriously repented of his crime, and you have discharged your duty admirably. What remains, then, except that in receiving him you act no less mercifully than you acted severely in casting him out?"

units.la: Quo loco obseruabis, Paulum Corinthiorum obedientiam probare aut explorare voluisse: Nimirum, vt ex ea omnibus constaret, eos Euangelium vere & serio amplexos esse. Huius enim finis est obedientia fidei, vt infra docebit. Debet ergo etiam hodie Christianorum hominum fides probata esse: quando non sufficit ore ad Dominum accessisse, cor autem procul ab eo remotum siue alienatum habere. Consistit autem experimentum fidei in eo, vt Apostolorum doctrinæ atque monitis obtemperent. Nec enim isti ex suo cerebro nobis tradiderunt, quae ipsis placerent, sed ab aeterno Dei Filio missi, & quid docerent instructi fuerunt. Arguuntur ergo hic fucati Christiani, qui IESV CHRISTI quidem nomen plenis buccis iactant, & quid per illud fecerint, prolixe commemorant, nullum autem in tota sua vita & moribus obedientiae verae experimentum praebent. Sunt hi ex eorum numero, quibus olim ab illo dicetur: Non noui vos: discedite ame procul qui iniquè agitis. Nec tamen illorum tyrannidi locus iste patrocinatur, qui simpliciter ab omnibus obedientiam exigunt, quae ipsis vt legitimis Apostolorum successoribus debeatur: ea autem tradunt, quae cum Apostolorum doctrina διὰς ἀπιστῶν pugnant. Illis ergo obedire nemo potest, nisi qui Apostolis se immorigerum praebere velit.
units.tr: Here you will observe that Paul wanted to test or explore the obedience of the Corinthians, so that it would be plain to everyone that they had truly and earnestly embraced the Gospel. For the end of this obedience is the obedience of faith, as he will teach below. So even today the faith of Christians ought to be proved, since it is not enough to have approached the Lord with the mouth while keeping the heart far away from him or estranged from him. Faith is tested by whether people obey the teaching and admonitions of the Apostles. For these men did not hand down to us what pleased themselves, drawn from their own brains; they were sent by the eternal Son of God and were instructed in what they were to teach. So here fake Christians are rebuked: those who boast loudly of the name of Jesus Christ and relate at length what they have done through it, yet show no proof of true obedience in their whole life and conduct. They belong to the number of those to whom he will one day say: "I never knew you; depart from me, you who work iniquity." Nor does this passage support the tyranny of those who simply demand obedience from everyone, as if it were owed to them as the lawful successors of the Apostles, while they hand down things that are at odds with the teaching of the Apostles. No one can obey such men unless he is willing to set himself against the Apostles.

units.la: Sed rursus obijcerent Corinthij: Quid vero, si hoc etiam consilio mutato mox aliud iubeas? Num pro tuo arbitrio in horas nos quoque nostra decreta mutabimus? Respondet ergo Paulus: Cui vero condonatis, etiam ego condono, &c. Quasi diceret: Nihil periculi est, fratres. Nam quicquid hic egeritis, id apud me ratum erit. Et si cui culpam admissam condonatis, eam ipse quoque condono. Imo, quod huic incesto iampridem ego ignoni, id propter vos feci, idque in conspectu Christi, id est, ingenuè & syncerè, vt qui sciam mihi non cum hominibus solum, sed cum Christo rem esse, in cuius ministerio versor. Quia autem scio hunc nolle, vt peccatores pereant, sed vt oues, quae errant, ad gregem suum reducantur, nolim vobis nimij rigoris author esse, qui cum eius voluntate pugnet.
units.tr: But the Corinthians might object again: "What if, after you have changed your mind on this matter, you soon order something else? Will we too change our decisions from hour to hour at your pleasure?" Paul therefore answers: "To whom you forgive anything, I forgive too, etc." As if he said: "There is no danger, brothers. Whatever you do here will be ratified by me. And if you forgive anyone the offence he has committed, I too forgive it. Indeed, what I have long since pardoned this incestuous man, I did for your sake, and that in the sight of Christ, that is, sincerely and honestly, since I know that I have to do not only with men but with Christ, in whose ministry I serve. But since I know that he does not want sinners to perish, but wants the sheep that have gone astray to be brought back to his flock, I would not wish to be the author for you of excessive severity, which would conflict with his will."

units.la: Admonet locus hic omnes Verbi Dei administros, vt meminerint semper, se in IESV CHRISTI conspectu agere. Est enim is praesens Ecclesiae suae sicuti dixit: Ecce ego vobiscum sum vsque in consummationem seculi. At cum idem nihil illa pretiosius & charius habeat, ferre non possit, vt quicquam in eius ministerio fiat, quod cum fidelium periculo coniunctum sit, aut vt dolo multo agant, qui illius pastores se esse profitentur. Ananias, cum in re pecuniaria Spiritui sancto mentitus esset, morte subitanea periit. Quid ergo de illis fiet, qui in rebus maioris momenti fraudulentius agunt, id sine sub nomine Christi praetexcu? Hoc vtinam diligentius meditarentur Romani Pontifices, & omnes alij, quibus voluptas est cum Christo & Ecclesia eius ludere, vt quaestum faciant, & male in illa vsurpatam tyrannidem tueantur. At quod de Ecclesiae ministris dicitur, id qui in magistratu sunt, non minus ad se pertinere putent. Nam horum quoque consessui Deus interest, qui non solum sententias eorum audit, sed quo animo & in quem finem illas dicant, intelligit. Denique priuatim quoque singuli meminerint, omnes nos in Dei conspectu versari, cui olim rationem reddere oporteat.
units.tr: This passage admonishes all the ministers of God's Word to remember always that they act in the sight of Jesus Christ. For he is present with his Church, as he said: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age." Since he holds nothing more precious and dear than his Church, he cannot bear that anything should be done in his ministry which endangers the faithful, or that those who profess themselves his ministers should act with much deceit. Ananias, having lied to the Holy Spirit in a matter of money, died a sudden death. What then will become of those who act more fraudulently in matters of greater importance, and cover this under the name of Christ? I wish the Roman Pontiffs and all others who take pleasure in mocking Christ and his Church would meditate more carefully on this, those who make profit and defend the tyranny that has been wrongly usurped in the Church. But what is said of the ministers of the Church, those who hold civil office should think applies no less to themselves. For God is present also at the assemblies of these men, and he hears not only their opinions but understands with what intention and to what end they state them. Finally, let each individual also remember privately that we all live in the sight of God, to whom we must one day give an account.

units.la: Porro concludit locum hunc Paulus graui admonitione: Vt ne praeoccupemur a Satana. Et rationem addit: Non enim illius machinationes ignoramus. Ostendit his verbis, non iam de vno tantum homine, sed de tota Ecclesia agi, cui Satan per hanc occasionem insidias struat. Et sane non leue periculum Corinthijs imminebat, ne nimio rigore in charitatis Legem peccarent, miserum item illum ad desperationem adductum ab Ecclesia prorsus alienarent, & simul dissidij alicuius grauioris essent authores. Monet ergo, vt de eo diligenter cogitent, & meminerint, cum quo hoste ipsis res sit: cum Satana nimirum, qui in omnem occasionem intentus, non modo a ministris nos oppugnat, ea suggerendo, quae palàm impia & noxia sunt: verumetiam a dextris, id est, sub pietatis & boni zeli praetexta. Sic olim Saulem cultus diuini & clementiae praeposte- rae fuco decepit. Et hodie multi crudeles fiunt cum fratrum infirmorum exitio, dum vt disciplinae (cuius summam fere in Excommunicatione sua constituunt) acerrimi vindices habeantur, omnia absque moderatione faciunt.
units.tr: Paul concludes this passage with a grave warning: "that we be not forestalled by Satan." And he adds a reason: "For we are not ignorant of his schemes." By these words he shows that the matter concerns not just one man but the whole Church, against which Satan lays snares through this occasion. And indeed no small danger threatened the Corinthians: that by excessive rigour they might sin against the law of charity, and that they might utterly alienate that wretched man, driven to despair, from the Church, and at the same time become the authors of some more serious division. He therefore warns them to think carefully about this and to remember with what enemy they have to deal: namely Satan, who, alert to every opportunity, attacks us not only from the left, through ministers, by suggesting things that are openly impious and harmful, but also from the right, that is, under the pretext of piety and good zeal. So once he deceived Saul with the mask of divine worship and a perverted clemency. And today many become cruel, to the destruction of weak brothers, while they are regarded as the fiercest champions of discipline (whose chief part they almost wholly place in their excommunication) and do everything without moderation.

units.la: Erant haec diligentius cogitanda ijs, qui in aliorum conscientias temere inquirunt, contra illud Pauli: Probet vnusquisque seipsum: qui item nimijs satisfactionibus infirmos fatigant, & plus satis afflictos aequo diutius suspendunt. Niruntur isti hoc exemplo: sed quam parum hoc illis seruiat, facilè videbunt, qui omnes eius circumstantias propius inspexerint. Paulus enim toti Ecclesiae Corinthiorum rem hanc mandauit, & incestum hominem in publico coetu damnari, eundemque publico totius Ecclesiae consensu denuo recipi voluit. At nostri illi paucis quibusdam Senioribus hoc omne negotium demandant, & nouum magistratum ijs etiam in locis constituunt, vbi magistratus verè Christianus regnat. Apostolus itẽ nullius satisfaćtionis theatricæ meminit, qua miser ille porrò vexari debeat: at isti in eo suæ illius potestatis gloriam & autho- ritatem potissimùm consistere putant, si omnium ludibrio prius eos exponant, qui in Ecclesiam recipi debebant. Et hanc rationem multis quidem illi, ceu imprimis necessariam commendant: at quàm infeliciter illa multis olim cesserit, quàm multa quamque grauia scandala ex satisfa- ćtionibus istis enata sint, & quàm intolerabilem tyrannidem nobis pepererit sub Papatu ex ve- teri Ecclesia seruatus presbyterorum vel Seniorum pœnitentiariorum ordo, norunt omnes, qui Ecclesiasticam historiam non ofcitanter legerunt. Quis verò spondebit, ne quando in similem tyrannidem degeneret, quod hodie quidam zelo non malo quidem, sed tamen inconsulto, insti- tuunt? Annon idem hodiè Satanæ ingenium est, quod olim fuit? Vel, annon specimina iam non vno in loco vidimus, quæ quid porrò sperari debeat, satis admonent? Ne ergo plus sibi arrogent Ecclesiarum ministri, quàm à Domino ipsis datum est: & subinde occinant sibi ipsis Paulinum hoc: Caue, ne à Satana præoccuperis. Si enim hoc timeri debuit viuentibus adhuc Christi Aposto- lis, tamen, sedulò officium suum facientibus, quid hodie sperare possumus, quando præclara illa Spiritus sancti dona, quibus vetus Ecclesia ornata fuit, maxima ex parte cessarunt, Episcopi autem apertam tyrannidem exercent: & qui Euangelij administri sunt, plerunque dormiunt? In summa, disciplina omnino opus est: ea autem sic institui debet, ne facilè in tyrannidem degene- rare possit, neue temere damnentur, aut abalienentur, quos lucrifacere & ad Ecclesiæ gremium colligere debebamus. Finis totius negotij sit, vt qui peccarunt, in viam redeant: qui Ecclesiam offenderunt, coerceantur, & bono exemplo eandem ædificent: vt denique omnes vno corde, vno spiritu & vno ore honorent IESVM CHRISTVM, Dominum nostrum: cui debetur bene- dićtio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Those who rashly pry into the consciences of others should have considered these things more carefully, against that saying of Paul: "Let each one examine himself." Likewise those who wear down the weak with excessive satisfactions and keep those already more than sufficiently afflicted in suspense for longer than is fair. They lean on this example, but how little it serves them will be easily seen by those who look more closely at all its circumstances. For Paul committed this matter to the whole Church of the Corinthians, wishing that the incestuous man be condemned in the public assembly and then received again by the public consent of the whole Church. But those men of ours hand over this whole business to a few elders and set up a new magistracy for them even in those places where a truly Christian magistrate rules. The Apostle therefore makes no mention of any theatrical satisfaction by which that wretched man must further be harassed; but these men think the glory and authority of their power consists chiefly in this, if they first expose to the mockery of all those who ought to be received into the Church. They commend this practice to many as especially necessary, but how unhappily it turned out for many in the past, how many and how grievous scandals arose from such satisfactions, and what intolerable tyranny an order of penitentiary presbyters or elders, preserved from the ancient Church, brought upon us under the Papacy, all know who have not read ecclesiastical history carelessly. But who will guarantee that what some today institute, out of zeal that is not wicked but nevertheless ill-advised, will not in time degenerate into a similar tyranny? Is not the nature of Satan today the same as it was of old? Or have we not already seen examples in more than one place which sufficiently warn us what we ought to expect? Therefore let the ministers of the Churches not claim more for themselves than the Lord has given them, and let them repeat to themselves this saying of Paul: "Take care lest you be forestalled by Satan." For if this had to be feared while the Apostles of Christ were still alive and faithfully doing their duty, what can we hope for today, when those excellent gifts of the Holy Spirit with which the ancient Church was adorned have for the most part ceased, the bishops exercise open tyranny, and those who are servants of the Gospel for the most part sleep? In sum, discipline is altogether necessary; but it must be so arranged that it cannot easily degenerate into tyranny, and that those are not rashly condemned or alienated whom we ought to win back and gather into the bosom of the Church. Let the aim of the whole business be that those who have sinned return to the way, that those who have offended the Church be restrained, and that by a good example they build it up; and finally that all with one heart, one spirit and one mouth honour Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA X.
units.tr: Homily X.

units.la: Porro cùm venissem Troadem ad prædicandum Euangelium Christi, & ostium mihi apertum esset in Domino, non habui relaxationem in Spiritu meo, eò quòd non inuenissem Titum fratrem meum. Sed cùm illis valedixissem, abij in Macedoniam. Deo autem gratia, qui facit vt semper triumphemus in Christo, & odorem notitiæ suæ manifestum facit per nos in omni loco. Nam Christi bona fragrantia sumus Deo, in iis qui seruantur, & in iis qui pereunt: His quidem odor mortis ad mortem, illis verò odor vitæ ad vitam: & ad hæc quis idoneus? Non enim, vt plerique, cauponamur sermonem Dei: sed vt ex Deo in conspectu Dei in Christo loquimur.
units.tr: When I came to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ, and a door was opened to me in the Lord, I had no rest in my spirit, because I did not find Titus, my brother. So, after saying farewell to them, I went on into Macedonia. But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and through us spreads the fragrance of his knowledge in every place. For we are the aroma of Christ to God, among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to the one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life. And who is sufficient for these things? For we are not, like many, peddlers of the word of God; rather, we speak as from God, in the sight of God, in Christ.

units.la: Quemadmodum in liberorum educatione parentes hoc imprimis spectare debent, vt liberi se ab ipsis amari sentiant: Ita verbi Dei administris, quoad Ecclesias & singulos Chri- stianos, hæc præcipua cura esse debet: Quia nisi omnibus persuasum fit, illos animo syncero & in- tegro nihil præter Dei gloriam, & totius Ecclesiæ salutem quærere, suspećta & exosa plerisque erit doćtrina eorum, neque locum inuenire poterit obedientia fidei, qua omnibus opus est, qui sa- lutem in Christo assequi cupiunt. Hinc est, quòd veteres Prophetæ multis argumentis suum er- ga populum studium declarauerunt: & hoc ipsum diligenter obseruauit Paulus cum Corinthijs agens. Quia enim sciebat multos hoc vnum agere, vt toti Ecclesiæ suspećtum facerent, quasi ho- stili in ipsos animo præditus, non aliud quàm suum honorem atque priuatum commodum venaretur, magno studio calumniam istam diluit. Et huc imprimis pertinet, quod nuper de hominis incęsti restitutione dixit: Eo enim nimium rigorem excusauit, cuius ipsum multi insimulabant. Quia vero ijdem apud vulgus Christianorum subinde vrgebant diuturniorem moram, qua suum ad Corinthios aduentum differebat, non contentus ijs, quae nuper dixit, nunc eodem reuer-sus morae illius rationem reddit diligentem. Exponit enim quid interea fecerit, vbi fuerit, & quam praeclaris argumentis siue effectis Deus Euangelij sui praedicationem non vno in loco con-firmarit. Docemur autem Apostoli exemplo, qua fide & diligentia Ecclesiae & Reipub. praefecti agere debeant: ea nimirum, vt de singulis possint rationem reddere. Nam etsi non semper fucum deprehendant homines, rationem tamen certo ab illis exiget Deus, cuius oculos nemo potest fallere.
units.tr: Just as in bringing up children parents must above all make sure that the children feel they are loved by them, so for the ministers of God's word the chief concern must be for the churches and for each individual Christian. For unless everyone is convinced that they seek nothing but the glory of God and the salvation of the whole Church with a sincere and upright heart, their teaching will be suspect and hateful to most people, and the obedience of faith, which everyone who wishes to attain salvation in Christ needs, will find no place. Hence it is that the ancient prophets showed their zeal for the people by many proofs, and Paul, dealing with the Corinthians, took great pains over this very thing. For since he knew that many were doing this one thing, namely making him suspect to the whole Church, as if he were animated by hostility towards them and sought only his own honour and private advantage, he wiped away that slander with great earnestness. And this above all relates to what he said recently about the restoration of the incestuous man: for there he excused the excessive severity of which many accused him. But because these same people were constantly pressing among the Christian crowd the long delay with which he was postponing his coming to the Corinthians, he is not content with what he said recently, but now returns to the same matter and gives a careful account of that delay. For he explains what he did in the meantime, where he was, and by what remarkable arguments, or effects, God confirmed the preaching of his gospel not in one place only. Moreover, we are taught by the example of the apostle with what faith and diligence those set over the Church and the commonwealth ought to act: namely, so that they can give an account of each individual. For although people may not always detect deceit, God, whose eyes no one can deceive, will certainly demand an account from them.

units.la: Principio docet Paulus, quae causa ipsum detinuerit, cum iam in procinctu esset vt ad eos ve-niret. Veni (inquit) ex Epheso Troadem, vt inde in Macedoniam traijcerem, & per hanc ad vos vsque venirem, sicuti in priori epistola promiseram, &c. Quia vero ex Epheso compendio-siori nauigatione per mare Ionium Corinthum venire potuisset, causam reddit, cur Troadem po-tius abierit: Nimirum Euangelij praedicandi causa, & quod in illis locis ostium ipsi aperuisset Deus. Verumtamen (inquit) etsi praeclaram illic haberem agendi occasionem, tamen non habui relaxationem in Spiritu meo, id est, animus meus quiescere non potuit, quod Titum, fratrem dilectum, & quem ad vos praemiseram, illic non inuenirem. Itaque rebus apud Troadem dispositis, mox in Macedoniam profectus sum. Ista vero in eum finem narrat, vt offendat se non de-fuisse suae promissioni, per ipsos autem stetisse, quo minus ad eos venerit: quia Titum diutius apud se detinuerint, quem voluerit prius ad se redire, vt per ipsum de rebus eorum certior fieret. Ex eo autem colligit, nimium iniquos in se esse Corinthios, qui ei vitio vertant moram hanc, cu-ius ipsi authores fuerint non sine magna ipsius molestia.
units.tr: First, Paul teaches what kept him back when he was already about to come to them. "I came," he says, "from Ephesus to Troas, so that from there I might cross over into Macedonia, and through it come to you again, as I had promised in my earlier letter," and so on. But since he could have come from Ephesus to Corinth by a shorter voyage across the Ionian Sea, he gives the reason why he rather went to Troas: namely, for the sake of preaching the gospel, and because God had opened a door to him in those parts. Nevertheless, he says, although I had a splendid opportunity for work there, I had no rest in my spirit, that is, my mind could not be at peace because I did not find there Titus, my beloved brother, whom I had sent on ahead to you. So, when matters at Troas had been settled, I set out at once for Macedonia. He tells this in order to show that he had not failed to keep his promise, but that it was through them that he had not come to them: for they had kept Titus with them longer, whom he had wished to return to him first, so that through him he might learn about their affairs. From this he concludes that the Corinthians are too unfair to him, since they find fault with this delay, of which they themselves were the authors, and not without great inconvenience to him.

units.la: His vero magnum eius Ecclesiae studium atque amorem declarat, ex quo apparet, quot curis & quam anxijs cogitationibus diuinum illud pectus distractum & excruciatum fuerit. Vnius Corinthiacae Ecclesiae cura eum ita exercuit, vt quiescere non posset. Atqui Ecclesiarum, quot-quot tunc inter gentes erant, cura ei incumbebat, vt infra testabitur. Quid ergo non passus est, cum tot vndique aretibus oppugnaretur? Facit hoc (vt nuper monuimus) plurimum ad asse-rendam Apostolicae doctrinae authoritatem. Quis enim falsi insimulet eos, quibus hominum salus tam vehementer cordi fuit? Et debent horum exemplis omnes ministri excitari, vt eos imiten-tur. Cogitent se gregi Dominico praefectos esse, de quo olim rationem reddituri sint: & proinde zelum ardentem animo concipiant, qui nullum locum apud ipsos ignaviae & socordiae concedat. Nec enim digni sunt, qui gradum hunc in Ecclesia teneant, si susq; deq; omnia ferant. Transfe-rant hoc ipsum ad se Reipub. praefecti, quos nisi eadem cura excoquat, nunquam fructum dignum ex sua gubernatione referent. Et sane, qui nostrorum temporum mores & statum diligentius ex-penderint, quiescere non poterunt: quando plerique, pessimis studijs dediti priuatam simul atque publicam salutem negligunt. Epaminondas olim, cum Thebani diem festum agerent, armatus muros circuibat, & cur id faceret rogatus, dicebat: Vt ciuibus meis tutus epulari liceat. Quam ergo turpe fuerit, Christianos principes ab homine ethnico vinci, dum ipsi primi poculis vacant, & securi in omnem licentiam effunduntur?
units.tr: Here again he shows his great zeal and love for that church, from which it is clear how many cares and how anxious thoughts that divine heart was pulled apart and tormented by. The care of the Corinthian church alone so troubled him that he could not rest. Yet the care of all the churches that then existed among the Gentiles also rested upon him, as he will testify below. What, then, did he not suffer, when he was assailed on every side by so many troubles? This (as we noted recently) contributes greatly to establishing the authority of apostolic teaching. For who could accuse of falsehood men for whose salvation people's hearts were so intensely concerned? All ministers ought to be stirred up by their examples, so that they may imitate them. Let them consider that they are set over the Lord's flock, of which they will one day have to give an account; and accordingly let them conceive a burning zeal in their minds, which allows no place to idleness and sloth among them. For they are not worthy to hold this office in the Church if they bear everything with indifference. Let those who govern the commonwealth take this to heart too: unless the same care refines them, they will never bring forth worthy fruit from their administration. And indeed, those who weigh the morals and condition of our times more carefully will be unable to rest, since most people, given over to the worst pursuits, neglect both private and public welfare. Epaminondas once, when the Thebans were keeping a festival, went round the walls armed, and when asked why he did this, he said: so that my fellow citizens may feast safely. How shameful, then, it is that Christian princes should be outdone by a heathen man, while they themselves, first of all, are given over to their cups and, secure, pour themselves out into every licence!

units.la: Porro quaerat aliquis, Cur Paulus reliçta Troade, vbi ostium ei aperuerat Dominus, in Ma-cedoniam festinarit, vt inde Corinthum veniret? Videtur enim reprehensione dignus, qui consi-lium suum leuiter mutarit, & a Deo oblatam occasionem neglexerit. Sed facilis est eius excusa-tio. Primo enim maior erat necessitas Corinthi, & quia ad ipsum, vt pote ordinarium gentium Apostolum, cura omnium Ecclesiarum pertinebat, non debuit vni sic adhaerere, vt maiori necessitate laborante negligeret. Deinde plus quiddam Corinth. Ecclesiae debebat, quam primus fundauerat, & quam ipsi Deus peculiari mandato commendarat, vt Luc. in Actis docet. Adde, quod interea Troadem non neglexit, sed non nisi rebus illic dispositis & recte constitutis (sicuti ex Graeco vo-cabulo, ἀποταξάμενος, colligi potest) discesserit. Rursus ergo docemur, Episcoporum esse, vt omnibus passim pro virili consulant, interim tamen suarum Ecclesiarum cura peculiari tangantur, quibus ordinarie praefecti sunt. At qui nostro tempore dominantur, ne has quidem curant, sed eis Regum aulas, & saepe castra quoq; praeferunt: & iam seculis aliquot nulla vel Regum vel Conciliorum au-thoritate in ordinem redigi potuerunt, vt apud Ecclesias residere velint. Ita in omnibus membris sese prodit Antichristi spiritus mendax. 1. Ioan. 4.
units.tr: But someone may ask: why did Paul, leaving Troas, where the Lord had opened a door to him, hurry into Macedonia so as to come from there to Corinth? For he seems deserving of blame, since he lightly changed his plan and neglected an opportunity offered by God. But his excuse is easy. First, there was greater need at Corinth, and since the care of all the churches belonged to him as the ordinary apostle of the Gentiles, he ought not to have clung so closely to one place that he neglected a place labouring under greater need. Secondly, he owed something more to the Corinthian church, which he had founded first, and which God had himself committed to him by a special command, as Luke teaches in Acts. Add to this that he did not neglect Troas in the meantime, but left only after things there had been arranged and properly set in order (as can be gathered from the Greek word ἀποταξάμενος [apotaxamenos]). Again, then, we are taught that it is the duty of bishops to take thought for all people everywhere, as far as they can, while nonetheless being especially concerned for their own churches, over which they are set in the ordinary way. But those who in our time lord it over others do not even care for these, and they prefer royal courts, and often military camps too, to them; and for some centuries now, neither by the authority of kings nor of councils have they been brought back into order so as to be willing to remain among their churches. Thus the lying spirit of Antichrist shows itself in all its members. 1 John 4.

units.la: Caeterum ne curiosis potius quàm necessarijs peregrinationibus vacauisse putaretur Paulus, ostendit ministerium suum interea nequaquam infructuosum fuisse: quia in omnibus illis locis prædicarit, & quidem non sine luculento multorum profectu. Id verò per ἀοξολογίαν siue gratiarum actionem enuntiat, ne quid arrogantius dicendo odium sibi conciliet, vt̀s, simul æmulorum malignitatem perstringat, quos inuidia non sinebat tam luculenta gratia Dei sese in ipso exerentis argumenta cernere. Sic autem ait: Deo gratia, qui facit vt semper triumphemus in Christo, & odorem notitiæ suæ manifestum facit per nos in omni loco. Quasi diceret: Nonnulli quidem vestrum me vanum iactatorem esse putant, alij crucem & afflictiones perpetuas mihi exprobrant. Sed nisi inuidia affectus totos excæcauisset, videre possent me non inutilem Christi seruum esse, neq; mihi afflictiones exprobrarent, in quibus Christi per me vbiq; locorum triumphantis virtus tam clarè elucet. Itaque iudicent alij vt liber, ego tamen habeo quòd Deo gratias agam: quia nu-squam locorum venio, vbi non eximia victoriæ per Euangelium partæ trophæa relinquam. Nam Deus vbique odorem notitiæ suæ per nos manifestum facit, &c. Ita verò dicit Euangelij prædicationem, quia per illam innotuit mysterium illud salutis, quod à seculis absconditum fuit. Deinde quia fragrantia est Deo acceptissima, dum per illam ei homines instar sacrificij adducuntur, vt ipse Paulus alibi de gentibus per se conuersis loquitur. Sed & alia Euangelij effecta hoc simile exprimit. Vt enim odor penetrandi vim habet mirificam: ita Euangelium quoq;, quod alibi per venti & ignis parabolas docemur. Deinde vt odor bonus cerebrum & cor recreat atq; confortat: sic Euangelio refocillantur afflictæ hominum conscientiæ. Denique vt odor manet, quamuis vnguentum aut omne id, vnde exortus est, è medio auferas: ita licet Apostoli alio digrederentur, manebat tamen Euangelij per ipsos prædicati effectus: quod ipsum hodie etiam fieri videmus. Horum omnium Corinthios Paulus admonet, vt his auditis non patiantur se vinci ab alijs Ecclesijs, neue eam doctrinam contemnant, quæ alibi fructus tam eximios atque salutares ferat.
units.tr: Moreover, lest Paul be thought to have been busy with curious rather than necessary journeys, he shows that his ministry in the meantime was by no means unfruitful, since he preached in all those places, and indeed not without a remarkable advance of many people. He expresses this by thanksgiving [ἀνθομολογίαν], so that by saying something too arrogant he might not win hatred for himself, and at the same time he rebukes the malice of his rivals, whom envy did not allow to see such splendid proofs of God's grace shining forth in him. He speaks thus: Thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and through us spreads the fragrance of his knowledge in every place. As if he were saying: some of you think that I am a vain boaster, others reproach me with the cross and continual afflictions. But if envy had not blinded their whole minds, they could see that I am not a useless servant of Christ, and they would not reproach me with afflictions, in which the power of Christ triumphing everywhere through me shines out so clearly. So let others judge as they will; I nevertheless have reason to give thanks to God, because I never come to any place without leaving behind outstanding trophies of victory won through the gospel. For God everywhere makes manifest the fragrance of his knowledge through us, and so on. He calls the preaching of the gospel this because through it that mystery of salvation, which had been hidden from ages past, became known. Then, because it is most acceptable to God as a fragrance, since through it people are brought to him like a sacrifice, as Paul himself says elsewhere about Gentiles converted through him. But he also expresses by this image other effects of the gospel. For just as a smell has a remarkable power of penetration, so too the gospel, which elsewhere we are taught through the parables of wind and fire. Again, just as a good smell refreshes and strengthens the brain and heart, so afflicted human consciences are revived by the gospel. Finally, just as a smell remains even when you remove the ointment or whatever it was that gave it off, so although the apostles went away elsewhere, the effects of the gospel preached by them remained; and we see this happening even today. Paul warns the Corinthians of all these things, so that, having heard them, they should not allow themselves to be outdone by other churches, nor despise that doctrine which bears such remarkable and salutary fruit elsewhere.

units.la: Porrò diligentius considerari debet, quod Deo gratias agit, qui ipsum triumphare faciat in Christo. Triumphare dicebantur apud Romanos, qui bostibus deuictis demum redibant, & victoriam cum publica pompa testabantur. Solebant præferri spolia bostibus erepta, signa item & imagines verbum captarum, aut etiam deuictarum classium: ducebantur bostium duces captiui. Imperator in curru magnifico sublimis ferebatur, quem legatus eius eques sequebatur, milites verò gloriæ & gaudij huius participes ordine incedebant. Ista omnia Dei Filio, IESV CHRISTO, rectissimè tribuuntur. Venit us in mundum, & cum boste communi Satana congressus eum vicit, & tandem cum triumpho carnem à nobis assumptam in cœlos intulit, captiuam ducens captiuitatem, vt ad Ephesios scribit Apostolus. Idem quoq; Euangelij præcones triumphi sui socios & gloriæ participes facit, quoties etiam ipsi mundo et diabolo superiores fiunt, atq; homines ex huius seruitio ereptos Christo adducunt & mancipant. Ad hunc modum Paulus vincebat & triumphabat, licet vbique locorum iniurijs exciperetur & fere cum ignominia eijceretur.
units.tr: Moreover, we must consider more carefully that he gives thanks to God, who always leads him in triumph in Christ. Among the Romans, those were said to triumph who, after defeating their enemies, returned home and displayed their victory with public pomp. The spoils taken from the enemy were carried before them, likewise the standards and images of captured cities, or of defeated fleets, and the enemy's captive leaders were led along. The commander rode high in a splendid chariot, followed by his mounted officer, while the soldiers, sharing in this glory and joy, marched in order. All of this is most rightly attributed to the Son of God, Jesus Christ. He came into the world and, engaging in combat with Satan, their common enemy, he conquered him, and at last he carried our assumed flesh into the heavens in triumph, leading captivity captive, as the Apostle writes to the Ephesians. In the same way he also makes the heralds of the Gospel partners in his triumph and sharers in his glory, whenever they themselves prevail over the world and the devil, and snatch people from their slavery to these and bring them to Christ and bind them to him. In this manner Paul was conquering and triumphing, although in every place he was met with injuries and was almost always driven out with disgrace.

units.la: Estq; hic victoria nostræ modus probè obseruandus contra scandalum crucis. Si enim carnem audias, clamat illa: Egregij sanè victores & triumphatores, qui passim caeduntur, spoliantur, pellun-tur, trucidantur. At si rem ipsam inspicias, illi reuera victores sunt. Vincunt enim, qui in causa, de qua contenditur, superiores fiunt, succumbentibus in eadem ipsorum aduersarijs. Id verò in præsenti causa siue certamine fieri solet. Quando enim Euangelium in gente aliqua prædicatur, mox sese opponit Satan & per suos ministros turbas dat, ex quibus seditiones & bella cum ciuilia tum externa suscitantur, funditur multorum sanguis, & sæpe Ecclesiæ dissipantur. Num verò causam suam obtinent impij? Nequaquam. Imò hac ratione latius propagatur Ecclesia, & Euangelij scintillæ, ceu ex incendio aliquo hinc inde dispersæ multos alios accendunt. Cuius rei exemplum Lucas in Actis Cap. octauo memorabile describit. Quis ergo neget victoriam penes eos esse, qui quoad corpus loco cedere coguntur? Idem cum singulis Christianis priuatim fit. Vincunt hi primùm seipsos, quando seipsos abnegant, & vnum Christum sequuntur. Deinde tyrannis quoque superiores fiunt sua patientia. Conferamus enim tyrannum aliquem, fidei persecutorem, cum martyre Christiano. Pugnant illi de fidei confessione, quam ille quidem prohibere conatur, hic verò liberam & integram retinere contendit. Ille minacibus edictis agit, carceres extruit, flagella, ecleos, glaleos, gladios, faces, cruces & mille alias tormentorum species profert: Hic solam fidem Spiritus virtute armatam omnibus istis opponit. Tandem moritur iste in fidei confessione, quae eo illustrior est, quòd eandem sanguine suo obsignat. Ille verò, qui verbis solis sonantem ferre noluit, sanguine confirmatam & in media morte victricem audire atque videre cogitur. Itaque anima istius victrix in coelos subuolat, angelis Dei laetum Paeana ipsi succinentibus, & fidei tam praeclarae tamque constantis memoria in terris triumphat. Ille verò odio & ira inflammatus ringitur, & toti mundo ludibrium factus, laetum pijs omnibus spectaculum praebet. Huc pertinent exempla, quae Apostolus ad Hebraeos scribens multa congerit, & quae historiam Ecclesiasticam legentibus passim occurrunt. Potuit illa obseruare (vt supra diximus) impius ille apostata Iulianus, qui artibus potius & dolis Christianos circumuenire studebat, quàm tormentis & supplicijs aggredi, ne illis patientia illius victricis materiam siue occasionem praeberet. Libet autem hic commemorare, quod de muliere Edessana Theodoretus scribit. Cùm Valens Imperator Edessae episcopum Arianum violenter obtruderet, ciues Christiani vnà omnes vrbe relicta, extra hanc congregabantur. Quod indignè ferens tyrannus praefecto gentis, cui nomen erat Modestus, in manus dedit, vt coetum illum armata manu dissiparet. Resciuit crudelem conatum mulierculà quaedam & cum infante, quem vnus gestabat, ad locum illum magna cum festinatione contendit. A praefecto autem, quem obuium sibi habuit, interrogata, quò nam festinaret? respondit: Ad meas fidei socios, vt cum illis occidar. Cur verò infantem tecum abripis? dixit praefectus. Cui illa: Vt & ipse mecum mortem hanc optatissimam obeat. Obstupuit Modestus, & imperatori nuntiauit, conatum hunc prorsus inutilem fore, & si ita pergamus (inquit) nobis quidem ipsis infamiam accersemus, istorum verò hominum alacritatem atque constantiam vincere nunquam poterimus. Poterant huius generis exempla multa proferri, & similia nostro seculo passim vidit ingratus & infelix mundus. Recte ergo dilectus ille discipulus dicebat, fidem esse victoriam nostram, quamundus vincatur.
