Itaque neminem offendant impiorum tyrannorum conatus, & dira piorum supplicia: quin meminerimus, Christum per crucem triumphare, & proinde ad omnes Christianos pertinere quod Constantino crucis signum in coelo spectanti dictum fuit olim: In hoc signo vinces.
units.tr: Here we must carefully observe the manner of our victory, which stands against the scandal of the cross. For if you listen to the flesh, it cries out: "Surely these are remarkable victors and triumphers, who are cut down everywhere, stripped, driven out, and slaughtered!" But if you look at the matter itself, they are truly the victors. For those win who become superior in the cause that is contested, while their adversaries in that same cause give way. And in the present cause or struggle this is usually what happens. For when the Gospel is preached among some people, Satan immediately sets himself against it and stirs up tumults through his ministers, from which both civil and foreign seditions and wars arise, the blood of many is poured out, and often the churches are scattered. But do the wicked gain their cause? By no means. Rather, in this way the Church is spread more widely, and the sparks of the Gospel, scattered here and there like those from some great fire, kindle many others. Luke describes a memorable example of this in the eighth chapter of the Acts. Who then could deny that victory belongs to those who are forced to give up their place in body? The same thing happens with individual Christians in private. First they conquer themselves, when they deny themselves and follow Christ alone. Then by their patience they also become superior to tyrants. For let us set a tyrant, a persecutor of the faith, beside a Christian martyr. They contend over the confession of faith, which the one tries to forbid, while the other strives to keep it free and whole. The one acts with threatening edicts, builds prisons, and brings out whips, racks, chains, swords, torches, crosses, and a thousand other kinds of torments. The other opposes to all these only the faith, armed with the power of the Spirit. At last the martyr dies in the confession of faith, which is the more glorious because he seals it with his blood. But the tyrant, who was unwilling to bear the sound of the word alone, is compelled to hear and see that faith confirmed by blood and victorious even in death. So the victorious soul of the martyr flies up to heaven, with the angels of God singing a joyful paean to him, and the memory of such a noble and steadfast faith triumphs on earth. But the tyrant, inflamed with hatred and rage, gnashes his teeth, and, made a laughingstock to the whole world, offers a joyful spectacle to all the godly. To this belong the examples which the Apostle gathers in great number in writing to the Hebrews, and those which meet readers everywhere in ecclesiastical history. That impious apostate Julian, as we said above, could observe these things. He strove to overcome Christians by arts and tricks rather than to attack them with torments and punishments, so that his patience would not give them the material or occasion for victory. It is worth recalling here what Theodoret writes about a woman of Edessa. When the emperor Valens was forcing an Arian bishop upon Edessa, the Christian citizens all left the city and gathered outside it. The tyrant, taking this badly, handed over to the prefect of the province, whose name was Modestus, an armed force to break up that assembly. A certain little woman learned of the cruel attempt and hurried with great haste to that place, carrying an infant that she held in her arms. When the prefect, whom she met, asked her where she was hurrying, she replied: "To my fellow believers, so that I may die with them." "Why then do you carry the infant with you?" said the prefect. She answered: "So that he too may meet this most desired death with me." Modestus was astonished and reported to the emperor that the attempt would be entirely useless, and he said, "If we go on like this, we will only bring infamy upon ourselves, and we will never be able to overcome the eagerness and constancy of these people." Many examples of this kind could be brought forward, and the ungrateful and unhappy world has seen similar things everywhere in our own age. Rightly, then, that beloved disciple said that our faith is the victory by which the world is overcome. Therefore let not the attempts of impious tyrants, nor the dreadful punishments of the godly, disturb anyone. Rather, let us remember that Christ triumphs through the cross, and therefore what was once said to Constantine, when he saw the sign of the cross in the heavens, pertains to all Christians: "In this sign you will conquer."

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, cui aliquis poterat obijcere: Si vbiq; gentium triumphas, & Deus suae notitiae odorem per te in omni loco manifestum facit, cur non omnes credunt Euangelio? cur doctrinam tuam non omnes recipiunt? Imò cur plerique illam reijciunt, & contra te hostiliter insurgunt? Respondet ergo per Anthypophoram: Nam Christi bona fragrantia sumus Deo, in ijs qui seruantur, & in ijs qui pereunt, &c. Christi bonam fragrantiam dicit Apostolos, eo quod odorem sacrificij & meriti eius in orbe circumferant. Christum igitur pretiosissimo vnguento aut thymiamati, seipsum verò & omnes alios Euangelij ministros vnguentarijs confert. Emphasin autem habet particula, DEO. Nam sensus est: Vt tut de nobis mundus hic iudicet, & multi nos non admittant, attamen Deo, cuius serui sumus, optima sumus fragrantia Christi, non in ijs modo qui seruantur, verumetiam in reprobis qui pereunt. Nec enim ea Euangelij conditio est, vt necessariò credant & seruentur omnes, qui illud audiunt: sed in multis ea est corruptio & ingenij prauitas, vt eis mortem afferat, quod alijs est odor vivificus, quo seruantur, &c.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, to whom someone might object: "If you triumph everywhere among the nations, and God makes the fragrance of his knowledge manifest through you in every place, why do not all believe the Gospel? Why do not all receive your teaching? Indeed, why do most reject it and rise up in hostility against you?" He answers by way of anthypophora: "For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God, among those who are saved and among those who perish," and so on. He calls the apostles the good fragrance of Christ because they carry about the odour of his sacrifice and merit through the world. Thus he compares Christ to a most precious ointment or incense, and the apostles and all other ministers of the Gospel to perfumers. The particle "to God" carries emphasis. For the sense is this: however the world may judge us, and however many may not admit us, nevertheless, to God, whose servants we are, we are the excellent fragrance of Christ, not only among those who are saved but also among the reprobate who perish. For it is not the condition of the Gospel that all who hear it must necessarily believe and be saved. Rather, in many people there is such corruption and perversity of nature that what is a life-giving fragrance to others, by which they are saved, brings death to them.

units.la: Docet ergo locus iste, quae sit Euangelij fors, & vt de eo debeamus iudicare. Per se est odor vitae, siue vivificus: quia Christum praedicat & nobis offert, qui vita est. Ideo Petrus ei dicebat: Tu verba vitae aeternae habes. Et Angelus Cornelio Centurioni de Petro loquens: Is tibi loquetur verba, per quae seruêris tu & domus tua. Idem ipse Christus innuit, dicens: Amen dico vobis, qui audit verba mea, & credit ei qui misit me, habet vitâ aeternam. Item: Profecti in orbem vniuersum, praedicate Euangelium omni creaturae: Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, saluus erit. Quòd ergo multis exitio est Euangelium, ipsorum culpa fit, qui illud vel omnino non audiunt, vel eo audito exasperantur & praefractiores fiunt, ideoq; sibi ipsis audiunt in testimonium. Exempla quibus hoc probetur, multa sunt. Audit Dei Verbum Pharao, sed eo offensus clamat: Quis ille Deus Hebraeorum, cui ego obedire debeo? Et ante hunc in ipsa rerum origine Cainum ex Dei admonitione contumaciorem factum fuisse scimus. Et prophetarum sermonibus multi irritati
units.tr: This passage therefore teaches what the lot of the Gospel is, and how we ought to judge it. In itself it is a fragrance of life, or life-giving, because it preaches Christ and offers him to us, who is life. Therefore Peter said to him: "You have the words of eternal life." And the angel, speaking to the centurion Cornelius about Peter, said: "He will speak words to you by which you and your household will be saved." Christ himself indicated the same thing when he said: "Truly I say to you, whoever hears my words and believes him who sent me has eternal life." Likewise: "Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved." That the Gospel is therefore a ruin to many is their own fault, for they either do not hear it at all, or, having heard it, they become exasperated and more stubborn, and so they bear witness against themselves. There are many examples by which this is proved. Pharaoh heard the word of God, but, offended by it, he cries out: "Who is that God of the Hebrews, whom I am bound to obey?" And we know that even before him, at the very beginning of things, Cain became more obstinate after God's admonition. And many were provoked by the words of the prophets.

units.la: Ioan.6. Act.11. Ioan.5. Marc.16. ex illis calumniandi occasionem arripuerunt. De Christi autem praedicatione hoc diserte beatus ille senex Simeon praedixit, quando positum esse ait alijs in ruinam, alijs in resurrectionem. Quibus conuenit quod ipsemet dicit: In iudicium ego in hunc mundum veni, ut qui non vident, videant: & qui vident, caeci fiant. Quid, quod idem, quando Euangelium praedicabitur, subitam & irreconciliabilem separationem fore docet inter eos, qui prius coniunctissimi erant? Neque debet hoc alicui mirum aut impossibile videri, quando similia exempla in rerum natura videmus, ut nimirum causae eiusdem effecta diuersa sint pro subiecti ratione. Sol etenim oculos sanos illuminat, lippientes prorsus excaecat. Idem ceram molliorem facit, latum indurat. Unguentum pretiosum cerebri sani homines recreat, porcos occidit. Ex eodem flore apes mella, aranea venena colligunt. Mel quibusdam cibis suauis simul & salutaris est, at cholica laborantes offendit. Ignis aurum & metalla reliqua excoquit, ligna & spinas prorsus consumit. Denique ut ignis vis non solum in suauis thymiamatis incensione sentitur, dum huius odorem longe lateq; diffundit, verumetiam in stercoribus, quae adusta intolerabilius foetent: Ita Christi virtus, quae per Euangelium agit, non modo in electorum conuersione & instauratione ad veram vitam cernitur: sed tunc imprimis sese conspicuam praebet, quando impiorum cogitationes arguit, Antichristum iugulat, & omnem altitudinem deijcit, quae aduersus Deum sese effert.
units.tr: Ioan.6. Act.11. Ioan.5. Marc.16. They seized on these as an occasion for slander. Concerning the preaching of Christ, the blessed old man Simeon foretold this plainly, when he said that he was set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel. To this agrees what he himself says: "For judgement I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind." Moreover, when he teaches that when the gospel is preached there will be a sudden and irreconcilable separation between those who were previously most closely joined, why should this seem strange or impossible to anyone? We see similar examples in nature, namely that the effects of one and the same cause are different according to the nature of the subject. The sun, for instance, illuminates healthy eyes but utterly blinds those with sore eyes. The same sun softens wax and hardens mud. Precious ointment refreshes healthy men's brains but kills pigs. From the same flower bees gather honey and spiders gather poison. Honey is at once sweet and wholesome food for some, yet it offends those who suffer from colic. Fire refines gold and other metals, but it utterly consumes wood and thorns. In short, the power of fire is felt not only in the burning of sweet incense, as its fragrance spreads far and wide, but also in dung, which when burnt stinks more intolerably. So too the power of Christ, which works through the gospel, is seen not only in the conversion and restoration of the elect to true life; it shows itself most clearly when it convicts the thoughts of the impious, slays Antichrist, and casts down every height that lifts itself up against God.

units.la: Sunt haec diligentius obseruanda propter Anabaptistas, qui ex auditorum moribus, aut etiam ex nostri seculi turbis, temere de Euangelio pronuntiant. Falluntur hi suo iudicio turpissime, dum quod inter electos & reprobos est ingeniorum discrimen non obseruant. Discant potius singuli animis honestis & discendi cupidis ad audiendum Euangelium accedere, & mox fructum ex eo saluberrimum percipient, ut cum Davide dicant: Magis expetibilia sunt Domine verba tua, quam aurum praestantissimum: dulciora item fauis multo melle stillantibus. Simul vero hinc consolationem petant ministri, qua sese aduersus iniqua mundi iudicia confirment. Nam si illi officio suo probe fungantur, Deo optima suauissimaq; Christi fragrantia erunt, ut res cadat inter homines: quorum contumacia illis fraudi esse non poterit. Quod ipsum sibi quoque applicare debent pij magistratus aut principes, quando se nequicquam cum aliquorum improbitate luctari vident. Nam horum ceruices frangct tandem Deus, illorum vero studium atque industriam dignis praemijs remunerabitur.
units.tr: These things must be observed more carefully on account of the Anabaptists, who rashly pronounce judgement on the gospel from the conduct of the hearers, or even from the disturbances of our age. They are shamefully mistaken in their judgement, since they do not notice the difference of disposition between the elect and the reprobate. Rather, let each person come to hear the gospel with an honest mind and a desire to learn, and he will soon receive the most wholesome fruit from it, so that he can say with David: "Your words, O Lord, are more to be desired than the finest gold, sweeter also than honey dripping from the honeycomb." At the same time, let ministers seek from this comfort by which they may strengthen themselves against the unjust judgements of the world. For if they discharge their office faithfully, they will be a most pleasing and sweet fragrance of Christ to God, whatever the outcome may be among men; and men's obstinacy cannot harm them. Godly magistrates and princes too ought to apply this to themselves, when they see that they struggle in vain against the wickedness of some. For God will at length break the necks of these men, while the zeal and industry of the others will be rewarded with due prizes.

units.la: Porro ijs, quae dixerat, tacitam antithesim Paulus subijcit: Et ad haec quis idoneus? Non enim, ut plerique cauponamur Verbum Dei, sed ut ex Deo in conspectu Dei in Christo loquimur. Sensus verborum hic est: Multi quidem hoc nomine gloriantur, quod germani Christi ministri sint, & ijdem nihil non sibi arrogant, quasi ad omnia sint idonei. Sed tanta est huius functionis dignitas atque grauitas, ut omne humani ingenij captum superet, nec quisquam ei sufficere queat, nisi quem Dominus idoneum fecerit. Id ego in mepso etiam agnosco, qui quicquid sum, gratia Dei sum, qui me ab vtero matris segregauit in Euangelium Filij sui IESV CHRISTI. Interim quoad meam in hoc munere fidem, sanctè testari possum, me non esse ex eorum numero, qui Verbum Dei cauponantur: sed quia me in Dei conspectu agere scio, nihil temere, sed omnia ex Dei mandato loquor, ut me verum Christi seruum esse probem. Cauponandi autem vocabulum Metaphoram habet, ab cenopolis aut unguentarijs sumptam, qui vina & unguenta adulterant, ut plus lucri faciant. Et illa pseudoapostolos perstringit, qui partim legales traditiones Euangelio miscebant, partim doctrinae illius ysum corrumpebant, cum gloriae & quaestui priuato studerent, & turpi dissimulatione conniuerent ad multa, quae acrem reprehensionem merebantur. At hic duo nobis obseruanda veniunt.
units.tr: Further, after what he had said, Paul adds an implied contrast: "And who is sufficient for these things? For we are not, as many are, hucksters of the word of God, but we speak in Christ, as from God and in the sight of God." The sense of the words is this: many indeed boast of this, that they are true ministers of Christ, and these same men arrogate everything to themselves, as if they were fit for all things. But the dignity and weight of this office is so great that it exceeds the capacity of human intellect, and no one can be sufficient for it unless the Lord has made him fit. I recognise this in myself too: whatever I am, I am by the grace of God, who set me apart from my mother's womb for the gospel of his Son Jesus Christ. Meanwhile, as far as my faith in this office is concerned, I can solemnly testify that I am not one of those who peddle the word of God; but because I know that I act in the sight of God, I speak nothing rashly, but everything at God's command, so that I may prove myself a true servant of Christ. The word "peddling" is a metaphor, taken from wine-sellers or perfumers, who adulterate wines and ointments in order to make more profit. And it censures those false apostles who partly mixed legal traditions with the gospel, partly corrupted the use of that teaching, while they pursued glory and private gain, and with shameful dissimulation connived at many things that deserved sharp rebuke. But two things here must be observed by us.

units.la: Primum, quid potissimum vitari debeat in doctrina? Fucatio nimirum, qua adulteratur, ut suam simplicitatem aut synceritatem non retineat. Fit hoc bifariam. Primo, quando ei coniunguntur humanae traditiones, quod est palear cum tritico miscere, ut Deus ipse per Ieremiam loquitur. Est & haec doctrinae corruptio nocentissima, eo quod cultum Dei prorsus inutilem reddit, adeoq; totum euertit. Huius enim verba sunt: Frustra me colunt docentes doctrinas hominum. Item: Omnis plantatio, quam non plantauit Pater meus caelestis, eradicabitur. Deinde fucus quoque fit docendo, quando doctrina quidem proponitur vera, sed non recte secatur, ut omnium institutioni & tutioni & ædificationi possit seruire. Fit hoc, quando hominū fauore captant doctores, & quasi sublato sale illo Euangelico, quo prurientis carnis petulantiam coërceri oportebat, blandius agunt, ne quem offendant. Hos Propheta canes mutos, Christus autem salem infatuatum vocat, qui ad nihil vtilis foras eijcitur, vt à prætereuntibus conculcetur. In vtroque peccatur hodie, quando multi hominum decreta Dei Verbo æquare audent: multi item principibus viris & alijs, ex quibus lucrum sperant, turpissimè blandiuntur, imò ad vulgi quoque scelera conniuent, vt commodius & quietius viuant.
units.tr: First, what above all must be avoided in teaching? Namely, falsification, by which doctrine is adulterated so that it does not keep its simplicity or sincerity. This happens in two ways. First, when human traditions are mingled with it, which is like mixing chaff with wheat, as God himself says through Jeremiah. This corruption of doctrine is most harmful, because it renders the worship of God utterly useless and so overthrows it entirely. For these are his words: "In vain do they worship me, teaching the doctrines of men." Again: "Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted." Second, falsification also happens in teaching when the doctrine proposed is indeed true, but is not rightly divided, so that it cannot serve for the instruction, admonition and building up of all. This happens when teachers seek to win the favour of men, and, as if the gospel salt had been removed, by which the wantonness of the lusting flesh ought to be restrained, they act more flatteringly, so as not to offend anyone. The prophet calls these dumb dogs, and Christ calls them salt that has lost its savour, which is cast out as useless to be trampled underfoot by passers-by. Today sin is committed in both ways: many men dare to set the decrees of men on a level with the word of God; many also shamefully flatter princes and other men from whom they hope for gain, and indeed connive even at the wickedness of the common people, so that they may live more comfortably and quietly.

units.la: Alterum ergo est, vt quid fieri debeat, videamus: Hoc nimirum, vt Pauli exemplum ministri imitentur, in quo tria habemus. Primum, vt ex synceritate agatur, non ex carnis sapientia, aut prauorum affectuum arbitrio. Hoc adulterationi, de qua modo diximus, opponitur, & cum puritate doctrinæ modum quoque tradendi verum atque ædificationi seruientem comprehendit. Alterum, vt ex Deo loquantur doctores, ne loco panis Euangelici toxica & letalia pharmaca Ecclesiæ apponant. Sunt enim mysteriorum Dei Dispensatores, non suorum placitorum satores. Imo legati sunt Domini exercituum, vt Malachias ait: & proinde capitale scelus admittunt, si à mandatis, quæ ille eis dedit, vel latum unguem discedant. Ideo Ieremiæ dicebatur: Ecce ego pono verba MEA in os tuum. Et Ezechieli: Sumes verbum ex ore meo, & monebis eos ex me. Quibus consentit, quod Paulus se ex Deo in Christo loqui scribit. Postremum est, vt cogitent se in Dei conspectu agere, qui ipsos videat & audiat, imò corda quoque & cogitationes eorum norit, & cui olim rationem reddere cogentur. Qui ista sibi perpetuò ob oculos & in mentem reuocant, ij non facile ignauia aut perfidia peccabunt.
units.tr: Let us see, then, what ought to be done in the other respect: namely, that ministers should imitate the example of Paul, in which we have three things. First, that they act from sincerity, not from carnal wisdom or the choice of depraved passions. This is opposed to the adulteration of which we have just spoken, and together with the purity of doctrine it also embraces the manner of delivering the truth, which serves for building up. Second, that teachers speak from God, lest they set before the Church poisons and deadly drugs in place of the bread of the gospel. For they are dispensers of the mysteries of God, not sowers of their own opinions. Indeed, they are ambassadors of the Lord of hosts, as Malachi says; and therefore they commit a capital crime if they depart a hair's breadth from the commands which he has given them. That is why it was said to Jeremiah: "Behold, I put my words in your mouth." And to Ezekiel: "You shall take the word from my mouth, and warn them from me." To these things agrees what Paul writes, that he speaks from God in Christ. Last, they should consider that they act in the sight of God, who sees and hears them, and indeed knows their hearts and thoughts, and before whom they will one day be compelled to give an account. Those who keep these things constantly before their eyes and in their minds will not easily sin through sloth or faithlessness.

units.la: Quod autem de Verbi administris dicitur, hoc ipsum ad se transferre debent principes viri, quibus Reipub. gubernatio commissa est. Nam hi quoque Dei negotium agunt, cuius est iudicium, vt Scripturæ docent. Agant igitur omnia corde syncero & integro, neque suæ rationis siue affectuum placita, sed Dei iudicia enuntient. Meminerint item, se in Dei conspectu agere, qui in illorum consessu præsens adsit, & ab ipsis olim rationem exiget, deque eorundem manibus requiret sanguinem populi sui, quem iniquè opprimunt. O si de istis serio cogitarent Pontifices & Reges. Sed quia isti tacent, & res suas agunt, singuli priuatim salutem propriam curent, & Dei bonitatem agnoscant, qui salutarem Euangelij sui fragrantiam nobis subinde offundit, & eidem se totis animis accommodent, vt vita illa vera & æterna fruantur, quam nobis suæ mortis merito acquisiuit IESVS CHRISTVS: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: What is said of the ministers of the Word, the same rulers to whom the government of the commonwealth has been entrusted ought to apply to themselves. For they too carry out the business of God, whose is the judgement, as the Scriptures teach. Let them therefore do everything with a sincere and upright heart, and announce not the opinions of their own reason or passions, but the judgements of God. Let them also remember that they act in the sight of God, who is present in their assembly and will one day demand an account from them, and will require at their hands the blood of his people, whom they unjustly oppress. O that the Pontiffs and Kings would seriously think about these things! But since they are silent and pursue their own affairs, let each one individually take care of his own salvation, and acknowledge the goodness of God, who continually pours out upon us the saving fragrance of his gospel, and let him devote himself wholeheartedly to it, so that he may enjoy that true and eternal life which Jesus Christ has won for us by the merit of his death: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: HOMILIA XI.
units.tr: HOMILY XI.

units.la: INcipimus rursus nosipsos commendare? nū egemus, vt nonnulli, commendatitijs epistolis apud vos, aut commendatitijs à vobis? Epistola nostra vos estis, inscripta in cordibus nostris, quæ intelligitur & legitur ab omnibus hominibus: dum palàm fit vos esse epistolam Christi, subministratam à nobis, inscriptam non atramento, sed Spiritu Dei viui: non in tabulis lapideis, sed in carneis tabulis cordis. Fiduciam autem eiusmodi habemus per Christum apud Deum: Non quòd idonei simus ex nobisipsis ad cogitandum quicquam velut ex nobisipsis: sed quod idonei sumus, id ex Deo est.
units.tr: Do we begin again to commend ourselves? Or do we need, as some do, letters of commendation to you, or from you? You are our letter, written in our hearts, known and read by all men. It is plain that you are the letter of Christ, delivered through us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on the fleshy tablets of the heart. We have this confidence through Christ toward God: not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as if from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God.

units.la: Vlta nuper Paulus Apostolus de suo ministerio præclarè dixit, quòd nimirum circa illud occupatus Corinthum hucusque non potuerit venire, ne in Asia sibi apertum Euangelij ostium negligeret, quòd item Deus per ipsum vbique gentium triumphet, quòd denique bona fit IESV CHRISTI fragrantia tam in ijs qui pereunt, quàm in ijs qui seruantur: adhæc quòd non fit ex eorum numero, qui Euangelium cauponantur, vt ex eo quæstum faciant, aut priuato honori consulant: sed ingenuè & syncerè, vt eos decet qui in Dei conspectu agůt, se omnia dixisse & fecisse testatus est. Nõ potuit autè ignorare, quid ad ista dicturi essent eius æmuli: En Thrasonem gloriosum & iactatorem, en hercèm inuictum, qui solus de toto orbe terrarum triumphat, solus Euangelium fideliter & ingenuè prædicat, &c. Ad ista ergo per Præoccupationem respondet, & hîc nihil abs se fingi, sed omnia verissimè dici demonstrat. Vtque tota hæc causa minus haberet inuidiæ, ista occasione de toto Noui testamenti ministerio disserit, & hoc cum Mosaico aut Leuitico confert, vt ea collatione doceat, non debere sibi & reliquis Apostolis vitio verti, si liberius & maiori cum fiducia agant, quando hoc olim Mosi licuerit, qui ministerium habuerit minus gloriosum. Continet autem Pauli exemplum generalem doctrinam, vt qui functionem aliquam à Deo sibi creditam sustinent, non patiantur eam improborum calumniis in contemptum rapi, sed fortes sint in authoritate sua tuenda.
units.tr: Paul the Apostle recently spoke splendidly about his ministry: that, being occupied with it, he had not been able to come to Corinth until now, so as not to neglect the open door of the Gospel in Asia; that likewise God triumphs everywhere through him among the nations; and finally that he is the good fragrance of Jesus Christ both among those who perish and among those who are saved. Besides this, he testifies that he is not one of those who peddle the Gospel to make profit from it or to seek private honour, but that he has said and done everything sincerely and openly, as befits those who act in the sight of God. He could not have been unaware of what his rivals would say in reply: "Behold the boastful, swaggering Thrasö! Behold the unconquered Hercules, who alone triumphs over the whole world, who alone preaches the Gospel faithfully and sincerely," and so on. He therefore answers these charges in advance, and shows that nothing is invented by him but everything is said most truly. And so that this whole matter might attract less ill will, he discusses on this occasion the ministry of the whole New Testament and compares it with the Mosaic or Levitical ministry, in order to teach by this comparison that he and the other Apostles should not be blamed if they act more freely and with greater confidence, since this was once permitted to Moses, whose ministry was less glorious. Paul's example, moreover, contains a general teaching: that those who discharge some office entrusted to them by God should not allow it to be dragged into contempt by the slanders of the wicked, but should be brave in defending their authority.

units.la: Incipimus (inquit Apostolus) rursus nosipsos commendare? num egemus, vt nonnulli, commendatitijs epistolis apud vos, aut commendatitijs à vobis? Exordium Mimesi constat, qua aduersariorum calumniam perstringit. Quasi diceret: Scio quid ad ista æmuli mei dicturi sint, me propriæ laudis præconem & ebuccinatorem esse, & vnum hoc agere, vt me apud vos ea ratione insinuem, atque vobis vicißim commendationes eliciam, quibus mihi apud alios quoque authoritas paretur. Sed non hæc mea sors est, vt mihi (sicuti nonnullis) apud vos literis commendatitijs opus sit, aut vt à vobis tales ad alios emendicare oporteat. Ipsi enim scitis quis sim, & ipsum opus quod ago, me abunde ijs commendat, qui rem ipsam rectius intueri & expendere volunt, neque prauos carnis affectus in consilium admittunt. Ita verò hæc proponit, vt non obscurè aduersarios pungat, quos non propria virtus commendabat, sed alienis commendationibus nitebantur, per quas in Corinthiorum Ecclesiam irrepserant. Et quia mox de Legis ministerio differet, credibile est, tales Hierosolyma venisse ab ijs commendatos, qui illic Legalibus ceremoniis adhuc pertinaciùs addicti erant, & easdem Ecclesijs gentium per suos illos emissarios obtrudere conabantur, vt Lucas in Actorum libro prolixè narrat.
units.tr: "We begin again to commend ourselves," the Apostle says. "Do we need, as some do, letters of commendation to you, or from you?" The opening consists of mimesis, by which he sharpens the slander of his opponents. As if he were saying: "I know what my rivals will say in reply: that I am a herald and trumpeter of my own praise, and that I do this one thing, that I may insinuate myself among you by this method and in turn draw commendations from you, by which authority may be secured for me among others as well. But this is not my lot, that I should need letters of commendation from you (as some do), or that I should have to beg such letters from you to take to others. For you yourselves know who I am, and the work I do commends me sufficiently to those who wish to see and weigh the matter itself more rightly, and who do not admit perverse fleshly passions into their judgement." He puts this forward in a way that does not hide his sting at his opponents, who were not commended by their own virtue but relied on the commendations of others, through which they had crept into the Church of the Corinthians. And since he will soon speak of the ministry of the Law, it is credible that such men had come to Jerusalem commended by those who were still more obstinately attached there to the legal ceremonies, and were trying to thrust these same ceremonies on the churches of the Gentiles through their emissaries, as Luke relates at length in the Book of Acts.

units.la: Interim non debent Pauli verba sic accipi, quasi per se nefas sit, commendatitias literas vel ab aliquo accipere, vel alicui dare. Nam vt id fiat, non raro necessitas iubet. Et vult Apostolus alibi ministrum Ecclesiæ, qui eligendus est, ab exteris quoque bonum testimonium habere, quò minus in probrum incidat, & in laqueum calumniatoris. Nec desunt exempla, quæ morem istum inter optimos quosque diligenter obseruatum semper fuisse docent. Apollo certè Corinthijs ab Aquila & Priscilla commendatus fuit, cùm illuc profectionem instituisset. Et Paulus Timotheum suum & Titum aliosque similes non semel Ecclesijs commendauit. Quid, quòd idem de vnius muliercula, Phœbes, side & industria apud totam Romanorum Ecclesiam testimonium perhibere dignatur? At hîc duo vitia caueri debent: Vnum, ne leues simus, aut nimium faciles in quibusuis commendandis. Peccant hîc multi hodie, qui non alio proposito aliquos alijs commendant, quàm vt ipsi illis liberentur. Ita verò sæpe fraudis alienæ ministri atque socij fiunt, suamque authoritatem suspectam faciunt. Alterum, ne qui commendantur, de se conceptam spem fallant, sed aliorum testimonijs respondere studeant, ne ipsis fraudi sit hoc charitatis officium.
units.tr: Meanwhile, Paul's words should not be taken as if it were in itself wrong either to receive letters of commendation from someone or to give them to someone. For necessity often requires that this be done. And the Apostle elsewhere wants a minister of the Church, who is to be chosen, to have a good testimony also from outsiders, so that he may not fall into reproach and into the snare of the slanderer. Nor are examples lacking which teach that this custom was always carefully observed among the best men. Apollos was certainly commended to the Corinthians by Aquila and Priscilla when he had resolved to set out for there. And Paul commended his Timothy, Titus and others like them to the churches more than once. What of the fact that he also thinks it worth bearing witness to the faith and diligence of a single humble woman, Phoebe, before the whole Church of the Romans? But two faults ought to be guarded against here. The first is that we should not be light or too ready in commending anyone. Many today sin here, who commend some people to others with no other purpose than to be freed of them themselves. In this way they often become the agents and partners of another's fraud, and make their own authority suspect. The second is that those who are commended should not disappoint the hope conceived of them, but should strive to answer to the testimony of others, so that this office of charity does not turn to their own harm.

units.la: Cæterum rationem reddit Paulus, cur ipse commendatitijs literis apud Corinthios non opus habeat: Nam epistola nostra vos estis, inscripta in cordibus nostris, quæ intelligitur & legitur ab omnibus hominibus, &c. Epistolam suam illos esse dicit, quia in Ecclesia eorum apparebat, ipsum Apostoli fidelis & strenui officio functum fuisse, qui vrbem luxu, libidine & omni vitiorum genere infamem ad Christi fidem converterat. Quo sensu eosdem alibi Apostolatus sui sigillum vocat. Itaq; istius loci sensus est: Cur ego aliorum literis commendatitijs ornatus ad vos veniam, vel à vobis emendicatis cömendationibus ad alios proficiscar? Atqui vos ipsos viuæ epistolæ loco habeo, quæ de mea fide & industria testatur. Quòd enim vos Christiani estis, quòd Ecclesia apud vos qualiscunque constituta est, hoc omne mihi debetis, qui primus vobis Euangelium prædiprædicaui. Quàm diu ergo tales fueritis, tam diu de meo erga vos studio testimonium feretis luculentum & locuples, quod solum sufficere poterit omnibus iis confutandis, qui me Apostolum esse negant, aut fidem meam dubiam siue suspectam facere conantur. Non temere autem epistolam hanc in corde suo inscriptam esse ait. Id enim perinde est, ac si diceret: Etenim quemadmodum ego legem Christi cordibus vestris inscripsi, vt ex Euangelij semine renati & prorsus alij facti sitis: ita vicissim vos in meo corde inscriptos habeo & circumfero, vt quocunque locorum venio, ex vobis habeam mei ministerij siue apostolatus testimonium. Et hæc epistola (inquit) vbique locorum legitur & intelligitur ab omnibus hominibus: dum videlicet res ipsa docet, vos esse epistolam Christi, quæ per meum ministerium parata est, non atramento, neque in tabulis lapideis (vt olim Lex data fuit) sed Spiritu Dei viui in carneis tabulis cordis.
units.tr: Moreover, Paul gives the reason why he himself has no need of letters of commendation to the Corinthians: "For you are our letter, written in our hearts, known and read by all men," and so on. He says they are his letter because in their church it was evident that he had discharged the faithful and vigorous office of an Apostle, having converted to faith in Christ a city infamous for luxury, lust and every kind of vice. In this sense he elsewhere calls them the seal of his apostleship. So the sense of this passage is: "Why should I come to you adorned with the letters of commendation of others, or set out to others with commendations begged from you? Indeed, I regard you yourselves as a living letter, which bears witness to my faith and diligence. For that you are Christians, and that a church has been established among you in whatever condition, you owe all this to me, who first preached the Gospel to you. So long as you remain such, you will bear a clear and abundant testimony to my zeal toward you, which alone will be enough to refute all those who deny that I am an Apostle, or who try to make my faith doubtful or suspect." He does not say that this letter is written in his heart without reason. For this is just as if he said: "Just as I have written the law of Christ on your hearts, so that you, born again from the seed of the Gospel, have become altogether other people, so in turn I have you written in my heart and carry you about, so that wherever I go I have from you the testimony of my ministry or apostleship. And this letter," he says, "is read and understood by all men in every place, since the thing itself shows that you are the letter of Christ, prepared through my ministry, not with ink, nor on tablets of stone (as the Law was once given), but by the Spirit of the living God on the fleshy tablets of the heart."

units.la: Rursus autem suo exemplo Paulus docet, quæ vera & solida sit hominis cuiuscunque commendatio: Ea nimirum, quæ non verbis nudis aut titulis inanibus constat, sed quam res ipsa aut opus confirmat. Nam quod vulgo aiunt, ipsum opus de opificis arte & industria verissimè testatur. Frustra enim hanc commendauerit, si opera non respondeant. Ideo Paulus, quotiescunque manum Christi Apostolum esse docere vult, semper Ecclesias adducit in medium, quas per Euangelium collestas & plantatas Christo acquisiuerat. Erat hoc obseruandum nostri sæculi Episcopis, qui nihil præter inanes titulos spirant, & ornatu siue apparatu theatrico sese venditant: cùm interim Ecclesiarum curam quasi nihil ad se pertinentem reiciant. Sunt hi philosophorum similes, quos Lucianus ridet, quòd philosophiam pallio & barba profiterentur, à virtute autem & sapientia essent alienissimi. Ita enim isti præter mitram illam suâ bicornem, pedum & pallium nihil habent, quo se Episcopos esse probent: vt iam de illis nihil dicam, qui ab Ecclesijs suis procul absunt, nec contenti eo quòd ipsi non docent aliquos, simul etiam alios, quos Deus excitat, docendi munere fungi non patiuntur. Quid obsecro isti cum Paulo commune habent, qui Corinthios cordi suo inscriptos habuit, & omnium Ecclesiarum cura angebatur, quoties se gentium Apostolum à Deo constitutum esse cogitabat?
units.tr: Again, by his own example Paul teaches what the true and solid commendation of any man is. It is that which does not consist of bare words or empty titles, but which the thing itself or the work confirms. For what people commonly say, that the work itself bears the truest witness to the skill and industry of the craftsman, is true. For a man would commend himself in vain if his works did not match. So Paul, whenever he wants to show that he is an Apostle sent by the hand of Christ, always brings forward the Churches which he had gathered and planted for Christ through the Gospel. This ought to have been observed by the bishops of our own age, who breathe nothing but empty titles and advertise themselves by theatrical display and pomp, while meanwhile they cast off the care of the churches as if it did not concern them. They are like the philosophers whom Lucian ridicules, who professed philosophy by their cloak and beard, but were most remote from virtue and wisdom. For in the same way those men have nothing, apart from their two-horned mitre, their crook and their cloak, by which they might prove themselves bishops. I say nothing now of those who are far from their own churches, and who, not content with failing to teach others themselves, also do not allow others, whom God raises up, to discharge the office of teaching. What, I beg you, do such men have in common with Paul, who had the Corinthians written on his heart, and who was burdened with the care of all the churches whenever he considered that God had appointed him Apostle to the Gentiles?

units.la: Cæterùm diligentius exponit Paulus, quales epistola sint Corinthij, & ita de illis loquitur, vt paucis omnia comprehendat, quæ de Ecclesia bene constituta deque legitimo & ordinario Verbi ministerio dici possunt. Primò enim epistolam Christi eos dicit, quos prius suam dixerat. Ita verò dicuntur illi, non ideo solùm quòd fidem in Christum profiterentur, & cum Ecclesia Sacramentis communicarent: sed (vt Chrysostomus annotauit) quòd Legem Domini cordibus suis inscriptam haberent, adeoque sponsa & peculium Christi essent, cuius doctrina & virtus in illis non obscurè elucebat. Tales esse conuenit omnes, qui Ecclesia Christi dici & haberi volunt. Omnibus enim ille loquitur: Si diligitis me, præcepta mea seruate. Cui illud Iacobi astipulatur: Ostende mihi fidem tuam in factis tuis. Meminerint denique homines Christiani, epistolam ipsos esse, quæ ab omnibus legitur & intelligitur. Sunt enim è mundo selecti, adeoque instar lucerna & ciuitatis sunt, quæ in altissimo monte sita ab omnibus circumquaque venientibus spectatur. Arguit ergo locus iste eos qui sic viuunt, vt nihil Christiano nomine dignum in ipsis inuenias. Quomodo enim epistola Christi dici merentur, in quibus nihil præter diaboli characteres cernere licet, ebrietatem scilicet, intemperantiam, luxum, libidines vagas, auaritiam, fraudes, vsuras, odium, vindictæ priuatæ studium, mendacia, & blasphemias, execrationes, conuitia, periuria & alia huius generis, quibus suorum corda ille inscribere consueuit?
units.tr: Paul also describes in more detail what kind of church the Corinthians are, and he speaks of them in a way that sums up in a few words everything that can be said about a well-ordered church and about the lawful and ordinary ministry of the Word. First, he calls them the letter of Christ, though he had earlier called them his own. They are called that not only because they professed faith in Christ and shared in the sacraments with the church, but also (as Chrysostom observed) because they had the law of the Lord written on their hearts, and so were the bride and the special people of Christ, whose teaching and power shone out clearly in them. All who wish to be and be called the church of Christ ought to be like this. For he speaks to everyone: "If you love me, keep my commandments." James agrees with this: "Show me your faith by your works." Finally, let Christians remember that they are a letter, which everyone reads and understands. For they have been chosen out of the world, and so they are like a lamp and a city set on a high mountain, which can be seen from all around by everyone who comes near. This passage therefore condemns those who live in such a way that you cannot find in them anything worthy of the Christian name. For how can they deserve to be called the letter of Christ, in whom nothing can be discerned but the marks of the devil: namely drunkenness, intemperance, luxury, wandering lusts, greed, fraud, usury, hatred, the pursuit of private revenge, lies, blasphemies, curses, reproaches, perjuries, and other things of this kind, with which he is accustomed to inscribe the hearts of his own people?

units.la: Deinde Corinthios epistolam Christi dicit Paulus abs se subministratam: qua locutione medium & ordinem denotat, quo Ecclesiæ constituuntur. Solus quidem Deus est, qui suos iam inde ab æterno elegit & prædestinauit: idem eosdem suo tempore vocat, trahit, & Spiritu suo animatos indissolubili fidei & charitatis vinculo connectit. Ideo Christus dicebat: Nemo venit ad me, nisi Pater meus traxerit eum. Et Isaias Christianos homines Dei discipulos fore prædixit. Idem tamen ad hæc conficienda hominibus ministris vtitur, non quidem quòd horum ministerio opus habeat, sed vt suam bonitatem in eo etiam declaret, dum nos sui operis socios & quasi opitulatores habere dignatur. Obseruandum hoc est diligenter, ne Verbi ministerium, ceu inutile & superuacaneum, negligamus, vel etiam explodamus: vt hodie phanatici quidam, qui Spiritu solo & nescio quo Verbo non scripto gloriantur. Semper enim ratum erit Apostoli nostri dictum: Quomodo credent absque praedicante? Item: Fides ex auditu est, auditus vero per Verbum Dei. Interim non minus caueri debet, ne ministris nimium additi, illis tribuamus quod vni soliqué Christo debetur. Qua de re in prioris epistolae Cap. tertio satis dictum est. In praesenti tamen rursus de eo admonet Paulus, dum addit: Non atramento, sed Spiritu Dei viui. Ea enim locutione inter externum ministerium & effectum Verbi Dei ita distinguit, ut hunc solius Spiritus sancti opus esse doceat. Etenim ut atramento fides scribi non potest, ita neque ministri vox aliquid proficiet, nisi Spiritus virtute animi illuminentur & emolliantur.
units.tr: Next, Paul calls the Corinthians a letter of Christ that has been delivered by him. By this expression he indicates the means and the order by which churches are established. God alone chooses and predestines his people from eternity; he also calls them in their time, draws them, and, animated by his Spirit, binds them with the indissoluble bond of faith and love. Hence Christ said: "No one comes to me unless my Father draws him." And Isaiah foretold that Christians would be the disciples of God. Yet God nonetheless uses human ministers to accomplish these things, not because he needs their ministry, but so that he may also show his goodness in this, while he deigns to have us as partners and, as it were, helpers in his work. This must be carefully observed, lest we neglect or even reject the ministry of the Word as useless and superfluous, as some fanatics today who boast of the Spirit alone and of I know not what unwritten Word. For the saying of our Apostle will always stand: "How will they believe without someone preaching?" Likewise: "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the Word of God." Meanwhile, we must take equal care not to attribute to the ministers too much, giving them what is owed to the one and only Christ. We have said enough about this matter in the third chapter of the former epistle. Yet here Paul again warns us about it, when he adds: "Not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God." By this expression he distinguishes between the external ministry and the effect of the Word of God, so as to teach that the effect is the work of the Holy Spirit alone. For just as faith cannot be written with ink, so the voice of the minister will accomplish nothing unless minds are enlightened and softened by the power of the Spirit.

units.la: Addit hîs tertiû: Non in tabulis lapideis, sed in tabulis cordis carneis. Alludit ad Legis promulgationem, simulq; ad veteres promissiones de regno Messiae & Ecclesia, quibus pollicetur Deus quòd Legem suam cordibus credentium inscribere velit. Et videtur hoc membrum ideo subiecisse, ut sensim delabatur ad institutam Leuitici siue legalis ministerij & Euangelici siue Apostolici collationem. Legem enim Dei digito in duas tabulas lapideas inscriptam fuisse, Moses testatur. Adumbrabat hoc ingenij humani duritiem & intractabilem contumaciam, quae non nisi Dei digito emolliri potest, ut Legem eius admittat. Istis opponit tabulas cordis carneas, id est, cor tractabile & Dei Spiritu mollitum, quale olim Prophetae promiserunt. Itaque caro hic in bonam partem sumitur, pro corde (ut diximus) tractabili & per regenerationem sic mutato, ut iam spontaneus sit homo ad Dei obsequium, qui prius huic contumaciter reluctabatur. Ut vero haec quoque omnem salutis nostrae gloriam vni soliqué Deo vendicant: ita Christianos hominès officij sui admonent, ne videlicet corda sua indurent, sed IESV CHRISTI praeceptis ex fide non fucata obediant, quem totius Euangelij scopum esse, alibi diximus.
units.tr: He adds a third point: "Not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of fleshly hearts." He alludes to the promulgation of the Law, and at the same time to the old promises about the kingdom of the Messiah and the Church, in which God promises that he will write his law on the hearts of believers. And I think he added this clause so that he might gradually pass over to a comparison between the Levitical or legal ministry, as it was instituted, and the Evangelical or Apostolic ministry. For Moses bears witness that the law of God was written with the finger of God on two tablets of stone. This signified the hardness of the human mind and its stubborn obstinacy, which cannot be softened, so as to admit God's law, except by the finger of God. Against these he sets fleshly tablets of the heart, that is, a heart that is pliable and softened by the Spirit of God, such as the prophets formerly promised. So "flesh" is taken here in a good sense, for a heart that is (as we have said) pliable and so changed through regeneration that a man is now willing to obey God, when before he resisted stubbornly. But these words too claim all the glory of our salvation for the one God alone, and they remind Christians of their duty: that they should not harden their hearts, but obey the precepts of Jesus Christ from a sincere faith, which we have elsewhere said is the aim of the whole gospel.

units.la: Porrò ut ad Paulum redeamus, ne aduersarij ex ijs, quae dixerat, nouam arriperent calumniandi occasionem, & ipsam arrogantius haec scribere clamarent, noua Praeoccupatione occurrit, & cur tanta cum fiducia haec dixerit, docet: simul autem occasione ista redit ad expositionem planiorem disti illius, quod sub finem Cap. secundi audiuimus: Et ad haec quis idoneus? Sic vero scribit: Fiduciam autem eiusmodi habemus per Christum apud Deum: Non quòd idonei simus ex nobis ipsis, &c. Sensus est: Ista tam confidenter loquimur, non quòd nostris viribus aut inductria fretinos ad tam grauem Euangelici ministerij prouinciam obeundam idoneos putemus. Agnosco enim communem sortem hominum, qui ex semetipsis ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei sunt. Quare fiduciam istam habemus per Christum, qui nos Deo reconciliauit, mihiq; hanc gratiam meruit, ut meo ministerio vti dignetur. Itaque si aliquam ad rem idonei sumus, hoc omne ex Deo est, qui in nobis operatur & velle & facere. Est autem huius loci vsus duplex.
units.tr: Moreover, to return to Paul: lest his opponents should seize on what he had said as a new occasion for slander, and should cry out that he was writing these things too arrogantly, he meets the objection in advance, and he explains why he has said these things with such confidence. At the same time, this leads him back to a fuller explanation of that question which we heard at the end of the second chapter: "And who is sufficient for these things?" He writes thus: "Such confidence we have through Christ toward God. Not that we are sufficient of ourselves," and so on. The sense is this: "We speak so confidently not because we think that we are fit to undertake so weighty a charge of the Evangelical ministry by our own strength or industry. For I acknowledge the common lot of men, who are not even fit of themselves to think anything." Therefore we have this confidence through Christ, who has reconciled us to God and has merited for me this grace, that he deigns to use my ministry. So if we are fit for anything at all, all this is from God, who works in us both to will and to do. The use of this passage is twofold.

units.la: Primum de Euangelij dignitate nos admonet, & quòd tam hoc quàm totum eius ministerium ex Deo sit. Nam quod Paulus de seipso dicit, id de omnibus debet intelligi, qui in Ecclesia & Verbi ministerio versantur. Erat ille à pueris institutus in Lege, & sub Gamaliele, praeceptore tunc temporis celeberrimo, profecerat supra omnes aequales suos. Adhaec secundum exquisitissimam sectam Pharisaeorum inculpatus & irreprehensibilis vixerat. Nihil tamen ista profuissent ad Euangelij ministerium, nisi illum Deus noua Spiritus gratia illuminatum ad illud obeundum fecisset idoneum. Idem de Mose dici potest, qui in omni Aegyptiorum disciplina enutritus, de infantia sua conqueritur, quando se à Deo ad hoc munus vocari audit. Quod ipsum Isaiae accidisse, eius verba testantur: Vae mihi, quoniam obmutui, eò quòd homo sim pollutus habens labia. Et Ieremias clamabat: Ah Domine Deus, en non noui loqui, quoniam puer sum. Magnum ergo & arduum sit oportet munus hoc, cui nemo quantumuis eximius sufficit, nisi eum Deus peculiari gratia dignetur.
units.tr: First, it reminds us of the dignity of the Gospel, and that this ministry, like the whole of it, is from God. For what Paul says of himself must be understood of all who are engaged in the Church and in the ministry of the Word. He had been trained in the Law from boyhood, and had made progress under Gamaliel, the most famous teacher of his time, beyond all his equals. Besides, he had lived blameless and irreproachable according to the most exact sect of the Pharisees. Yet all these things would have been of no use for the ministry of the Gospel, unless God had enlightened him with a new grace of the Spirit and made him fit to undertake it. The same can be said of Moses, who, though brought up in all the learning of the Egyptians, complained of his inability from his infancy when he heard that he was being called by God to this office. The words of Isaiah bear witness that the same thing happened to him: "Woe is me, for I have been silenced, because I am a man of unclean lips." And Jeremiah cried out: "Ah, Lord God, behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am a boy." This office must therefore be great and arduous, since no one, however outstanding, is sufficient for it unless God deigns to favour him with a special grace.

units.la: Docent haec, neminem nisi à Deo vocatum hanc functionem subire aut suscipere debere. Quia non possunt Dei gratiam sperare, qui huius vocationem non expectant. Etenim apud Ieremiam quibusdam ille succensét quòd non missi ab ipso cucurrissent ad praedicandum. Quod Apostolus nostrer ad Romanos scribens obseruauit, cum diceret: Quomodo praedicabunt, nisi missi fuerint? Arguit hoc Anabaptistarum temeritatem, qui sola ignorantia & plus quàm barbara inscitia freti, sese ad docendum ingerunt, & tunc demum se vere Apostolicos esse arbitrantur, si prorsus illiterati & idiotae sint. Sed ijdem Apostolorum exemplo conuincuntur, quos Christus ad hoc munus proprorumpere noluit, donec Spiritum sanctum accepissent, qui ea linguarum & Scripturarum cognitione illos miraculose instruxit, quam nemo hodie multorum annorum studiis posset consequi. Discant ergo, qui ad ministerium Ecclesiæ animum appulerint, legitimam vocationem expectare, & si ea obtingat, in illo diligentes sint, precibus ad Deum assidue vacent, & vitam suam sic instituant, ne tanto munere indigni, aut ad illud minus idonei censeri possint. Quod ipsum si pariter observent, qui magistratum gerunt, in Ecclesia simul & Repub. res felicius gerentur.
units.tr: These things teach that no one ought to undertake or take up this function unless he has been called by God. For those who do not wait for this calling cannot hope for God's grace. Indeed, in Jeremiah God rebukes certain people because they ran to preach without being sent by him. Our Apostle observed the same when he wrote to the Romans: "How will they preach unless they have been sent?" This condemns the rashness of the Anabaptists, who, relying only on ignorance and a more than barbarous lack of learning, thrust themselves forward to teach, and think themselves truly apostolic only if they are utterly illiterate and untrained. But the example of the Apostles refutes them. Christ did not want them to come forward for this office until they had received the Holy Spirit, who miraculously instructed them in languages and Scriptures in a way that no one today could attain by many years of study. Let those, therefore, who have set their minds on the ministry of the Church learn to wait for a lawful calling; and if it comes to them, let them be diligent in it, devote themselves constantly to prayer to God, and order their lives so that they cannot be judged unworthy of so great an office, or too unfit for it. If those who bear the magistracy would likewise observe this, affairs in the Church and in the commonwealth alike would be managed more happily.

units.la: Porrò quod de Apostolico siue Ecclesiastico munere Paulus dicit, hoc ipsum ad omnes homines pertinet, quoad æternæ salutis causam. Si enim nemo ex semetipso idoneus est, ut hanc verbis dignis cum aliorum profectu & ædificatione proponat, quanto minus aliquis salutem proprijs viribus vel fibijpsi vel alijs mereri poterit? Sufficit ergo locus hic ad euertendam eorum arrogantem atque confidentem sententiam, qui τῷ αὐτεξουσίῳ & sui arbitrij libertate gloriantur. Fefellit aliquos in hac causa vetus Interpres, qui Græcam vocem, quà hic Paulus vtitur, ἱκανότητα, per Sufficientiam exposuit. Ex eo enim collegerunt, hominem habere quidem ex semetipso aliquas vires aut facultates, sed quæ non sufficiant, & proinde eum nouo gratiæ Dei auxilio indigere. Ita vnius vocabuli impropria expositione Satan hominibus imposuit, ut eo loco ad nocentissimi erroris defensionem abuterentur, quo vix alius euidentior & efficacior est ad destruendam virium & meritorum nostrorum fiduciam. Etenim inter omnes hominis actiones, tam internas quàm externas, omnium leuissima & liberrima est cogitatio: adeo ut Germanico proverbio cogitationes à vetligalibus immunes esse dicantur. Attamen ne hæ quidem in nostra potestate sunt, ut eas possimus pro nostro arbitrio ad res bonas atque salutares inclinare, aut ne instabiles vagentur continere. Experiuntur hoc pij frequenter inter precandum, quando illis inuitis cogitationes absurdissimæ, & interdum turpes atque infandæ obrepunt, quibus mens à seria Dei inuocatione auocatur. Quid ergo nobis reliquum manet, quo gloriemur? Vidit hanc Pauli mentem esse D. Chrysostomus, qui cum Græcorum more alibi τὸ αὐτεξούσιον & liberum hominis arbitrium magnificè prædicet, huius tamen loci perspicuitate coactus, ita eum interpretatur: ἐχ' ἕτως ἐπὶ πεποίθησιν ἔχομεν, ὡς τὸ μὲν ἡμέτερον ἂναι, τὸ δὲ τῆς θεοῦ, ἀλλὰ τὸ πᾶν αὐτῶν ἀναθῆναι. Id est, non eo sensu nos fiduciam habere dixi, ut pars quidem nostra, pars autem Dei sit, sed hoc totum ad hunc refero. Cuius Generis testimonia infinita ex alijs quoque Patribus orthodoxis, imprimis autem ex D. Augustino proferri poterant, qui totius Ecclesiæ doctrinam suo sæculo contra Pelagianos acerrimè propugnauit.
units.tr: Moreover, what Paul says about the apostolic or ecclesiastical ministry applies to all people as far as the cause of eternal salvation is concerned. If no one is by himself fit to set forth this word worthily, to the profit and building up of others, how much less can anyone earn salvation by his own powers, either for himself or for others? This passage is therefore enough to overthrow the arrogant and confident opinion of those who boast of free will [τῷ αὐτεξουσίῳ] and the liberty of their own choice. The old translator misled some on this point, for he rendered the Greek word that Paul uses here, ikanotēta [ἱκανότητα], as "sufficiency." From this they concluded that man has some powers or faculties of his own, but that these are not enough, and so he needs the new help of God's grace. By this improper rendering of a single word, Satan deceived men, so that they used the passage to defend a most harmful error, though scarcely any other passage is clearer or more effective for destroying our confidence in our own powers and merits. Indeed, of all human actions, inward and outward, thought is the lightest and freest; so much so that by a German proverb thoughts are said to be exempt from taxes. Yet even thoughts are not in our power, so that we can at will turn them to good and saving things, or restrain them from wandering unsteadily. The godly often experience this while praying, when, against their will, the most absurd and sometimes foul and unspeakable thoughts creep in, and the mind is drawn away from the serious invocation of God. What then remains for us to boast of? Chrysostom saw that this was Paul's meaning. Although elsewhere, in the Greek manner, he greatly praises autexousion [αὐτεξούσιον] and man's free choice, yet, compelled by the clarity of this passage, he interprets it thus: "We do not have confidence in such a way that one part is ours and another part God's, but we refer the whole of it to him" [οὐχ οὕτως ἐπὶ πεποίθησιν ἔχομεν, ὡς τὸ μὲν ἡμέτερον εἶναι, τὸ δὲ τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀλλὰ τὸ πᾶν εἰς αὐτὸν ἀναφέρειν]. That is: I did not mean that we have confidence in such a sense that one part is ours and one part God's; rather I refer this whole matter to him. Countless testimonies of this kind could also be brought from other orthodox Fathers, and especially from St. Augustine, who in his own age most vigorously defended the doctrine of the whole Church against the Pelagians.

units.la: Obseruemus igitur hoc loco, hominem natura sua non modo peccatorem, verumetiam omnibus viribus destitutum nasci. Genuit enim Adam (ut Moses scribit) filios suos in sua imagine, id est, corrupta illa & vitiosa natura, quam per peccatum obliterata imagine Dei, contraxerat. Quò fit, ut (quod Dauides de seipso fatetur) omnes in peccato concipiamur atque nascamur. Sunt ergo vitiosæ & corruptæ omnes hominis facultates. Intellectus non percipit ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei. Voluntas ad malum natura inclinat, & ideo figmenta cordis nostri prava sunt. Vires autem, quibus resistamus, aut nosmetipsos in officio contineamus, omnino nullæ sunt. Vnde sequitur, regeneratione nobis opus esse, quæ nisi fiat, Regnum Dei (ipso Christo teste) ne videre quidem possumus, nedum ingredi. At hæc multò minus in nostro arbitrio siue potestate posita est. Quid enim hic faciat homo, qui neque ad primam generationem, qua peccator & mortalis natus est quicquam contulit, neque corporis sui staturæ quicquam addere, imo ne capillum quidem in capite suo nigrum aut album facere potest? E supernis ergo renascamur oportet, nimirum ex semine Verbi æterni & immortalis per Spiritus sancti virtutem, quæ sola mysterium hoc perficitur. Hinc noua lux menti affulget, quæ intellectum nostrum diuinorum & cœlestium capacem reddit. Sequitur mox voluntatis ad meliora propensio, Deo nimirum hanc trahente & inclinante. Idem vires nouas sufficit, ut omnia iam in Christo possimus, qui paulo ante ne ad cogitandum quidem eramus idonei. Hic enim Mediator & canalis instar est, per quem dona Dei cœlestia in nos deriuantur. Quapropter ipse dicebat: Sine me nihil potestis facere. Verissimè ergo alibi Paulus exclamat: Quid habes, quod non accepisti? Quod si accepisti, quid gloriaris, quasi non acceperis? Est itaque hæc apostolica & orthodoxa doctrina, quam in Ecclesijs retinere plus quàm necessarium est: eò quòd sine hac nobis constare non potest certa salutis fiducia, quæ necessario fluctuat, nisi tota in Dei gratiam & misericordiam recumbat per IESVM CHRISTVM, Mediatorem & Seruatorem nostrum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Let us therefore observe here that man is born not only a sinner by nature, but also destitute of all powers. For Adam (as Moses writes) begot his sons in his own image, that is, in that corrupt and vicious nature which he had contracted when, through sin, the image of God was effaced. Hence it comes about that (as David confesses of himself) we are all conceived and born in sin. All the faculties of man are therefore vicious and corrupt. The understanding does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God. The will is inclined by nature to evil, and so the imaginations of our heart are evil. Indeed, we have no powers at all by which we might resist or keep ourselves in obedience. It follows that we need regeneration; unless this happens, we cannot even see the Kingdom of God (as Christ himself testifies), much less enter it. But this is far less within our own choice or power. For what can a man do here, who contributed nothing to his first birth, by which he was born a sinner and mortal, and who cannot add anything to the stature of his body, or even make a single hair on his head black or white? We must therefore be born again from above, namely from the seed of the eternal and immortal Word, through the power of the Holy Spirit, by which alone this mystery is accomplished. Hence a new light shines upon the mind, which makes our understanding capable of divine and heavenly things. Then follows the inclination of the will toward better things, God drawing and inclining it. The same God supplies new powers, so that we can now do all things in Christ, we who a little before were not even fit to think. For this Mediator is like a channel through which God's heavenly gifts flow down to us. Therefore he himself said: "Without me you can do nothing." Most truly, then, Paul elsewhere cries out: "What have you that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?" This, then, is the apostolic and orthodox doctrine, which it is more than necessary to retain in the Churches, because without it a certain confidence of salvation cannot stand, and that confidence necessarily wavers unless it rests wholly on the grace and mercy of God through Jesus Christ, our Mediator and Saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XII.
units.tr: HOMILY XII.

units.la: Qui etiam fecit, vt idonei essemus ministri Noui testamenti, non literæ, sed Spiritus: Nam litera occidit, Spiritus autem vivificat. Quòd si mortis ministerium literis informatum in saxis, fuit gloriosum, adeò vt non possent intueri filij Israel in faciem Mosis, propter gloriam vultus eius, quæ abolenda erat: quì non potius ministerium Spiritus erit gloriosum? Nam si ministerium condemnationis fuit gloriosum, multò magis ministerium iustitiæ abundat gloria. Etenim quod glorificatum fuit, ne glorificatum quidem fuit in hac parte, quoad excellentissimam gloriam. Nam si quod aboletur fuit gloriosum, multò magis est gloriosum id quod manet.
units.tr: "Who also made us able ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life. But if the ministry of death, engraved in letters on stones, was glorious, so that the children of Israel could not look steadily at the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance, which was to be done away, how much more glorious will the ministry of the Spirit be? For if the ministry of condemnation was glorious, the ministry of righteousness abounds much more in glory. For what was glorified was not glorified at all in this respect, compared with the surpassing glory. For if what is being abolished was glorious, what remains is much more glorious."

units.la: Paulus Apostolus in tota hac epistola frequenter de suo ministerio disserit, & qua fide atque diligentia in illo versatus sit, docet. Id vero non facit ambitiose, sed quòd æmulorum & impostorum quorundam calumnijs cogeretur, qui vt doctrinæ eius fidem derogarent, ipsum verum & germanum Christi Apostolum esse negabant, & præter hoc alia quoque multa congerebant, quibus eum in contemptum adducere conabantur. Confutauit autem nuper istorum calumnias ipsius Ecclesiæ Corinthiacæ testimonio, offendens, nimium imprudentes esse qui eius ministerium atque fidem in dubium vocent, cùm ipsimet viuæ epistolæ loco sint, quæ de ipsius fide & industria abunde testetur. Simul tamen ne quid arrogantius dicere videatur, omnem sui ministerij gloriam vni foliquè Deo transcribit, qui homines sua natura vitiosos, & ad omnia ineptos, suis donis ornare, & rebus arduis destinare soleat. Id vero nunc ad suam personam propius applicat, & simul ea occasione transit in generalem ministerij Euangelici commendationem, cuius dignitatem & gloriam multò excellentiorem esse docet, quàm olim Mosaici aut Legalis ministerij fuerit. Causa huius disputationis fuit, quòd illo tempore passim Ecclesijs obreperent homines partim ambitiosi partim superstitiosi, qui Legis doctrinam cum Euangelio commiscebant, & vt illius ritus possent facilius quibusuis persuadere, magnificis verbis prædicabant, quanta cum maiestate illa olim à Deo fuisset promulgata: Eoque fundamento iacto, in Apostolos innuebant, vt qui nimium sibijpsis tribuerent, & in Mosem iniurij essent, cuius ministerium Deus singulari gloria ornauisset. Adista respondens Paulus, Legis quidem gloriam non vulgarem fuisse fatetur, eandem tamen nullam esse demonstrat, si cum Euangelio & eius doctrina conferatur. Vnde colligit, quòd cum Mosi licuerit libere & cum fiducia agere, quæ ad Legis authoritatem defendendam faciebant, hoc ipsum multò magis licere Euangelij doctoribus, qui ministerium sublimius & præstantius sustineant. Denique æquum esse docet, vt Lex Euangelio locum cedat, & omnes in vno IESV CHRISTO acquiescant, qui per hoc prædicatur. Est ergo locus hic admodum memorabilis, quia Euangelium supra omnia alia doctrinarum genera extollit, & omnes ad illius amorem atque studium excitat.
units.tr: The apostle Paul often speaks in this whole letter about his ministry, and shows with what faith and diligence he has laboured in it. He does not do this out of ambition, but because he was forced to by the slanders of certain rivals and impostors. To undermine faith in his teaching, they denied that he was a true and genuine apostle of Christ, and besides this they heaped up many other charges by which they tried to bring him into contempt. Recently he refuted their slanders by the testimony of the Corinthian Church itself, pointing out that those are very ill-advised who call his ministry and his faith into doubt, since the Corinthians themselves are, as it were, a living letter that bears full witness to his faith and industry. At the same time, lest he seem to say anything too arrogant, he ascribes all the glory of his ministry to God alone, who is accustomed to adorn with his gifts men who are by nature sinful and unfit for everything, and to appoint them to difficult tasks. Now he applies this more closely to his own person, and on this occasion passes over to a general commendation of the evangelical ministry, teaching that its dignity and glory are far more excellent than those of the Mosaic or legal ministry of old. The reason for this discussion was that at that time, everywhere in the churches, there crept in men some ambitious and some superstitious, who mixed the doctrine of the Law with the Gospel. So that they could more easily persuade anyone of its rites, they preached with grand words how great the majesty was with which it had once been published by God. Having laid this foundation, they hinted against the apostles, as if they claimed too much for themselves and were unfair to Moses, whom God had adorned with singular glory. Answering this, Paul admits that the glory of the Law was no small thing, yet shows that it is no glory at all when compared with the Gospel and its teaching. From this he infers that if Moses was allowed to act freely and confidently in whatever served to defend the authority of the Law, the teachers of the Gospel are much more entitled to do so, since they carry on a higher and more excellent ministry. Finally, he teaches that it is right for the Law to give place to the Gospel, and for all to rest in the one Jesus Christ, who is proclaimed through it. This passage is therefore most memorable, because it exalts the Gospel above all other kinds of teaching and stirs all people to love and zeal for it.

units.la: Porrò pulchrè ista cum ijs, quæ proximè præcesserunt connectit, vt vniuersam sui ministerij conditionem commodius & plenius explicet. Cùm enim dixisset, Deum esse, qui homines ad res magnas idoneos faciat, id ad se transferens mox subdit: Qui etiam fecit, vt idonei essemus ministri Noui testamenti, non literæ, sed Spiritus, &c. Fatetur ergo ingenuè, se non ministerium modò à Deo habere, verumetiam eiusdem donum esse, quòd ad illud obeundum idoneus fit. Præcipuum puum tamen huius loci caput est, quòd se cum reliquis Apostolis noui Testamenti ministrum fa-ctum esse ait. Eo enim dicto impostores perstringit, qui cum Legis doctrinam importunius vrge-rent, se non Noui, sed potius Veteris testamenti ministros esse declarabant, idq; non sine ignominia Christi, qui vmbras illas abolere debuit, nec sine graui causa dixerat: Lex & Prophetæ vsq; ad Io-annem, ab eo tempore Regnum Dei annuntiatur: qui deniq; iam moriturus magna voce testatus est, consummata iam & impleta esse, quæcunq; in veteri Testamento promissa atq; typis tam le-galibus quàm propheticis adumbrata fuerunt. Ioan.19.
units.tr: Moreover, he connects these points skilfully with what came just before, in order to explain the whole condition of his ministry more fittingly and fully. For when he had said that it is God who makes men fit for great things, he applies this to himself and at once adds: "who also made us fit to be ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the Spirit," and so on. He therefore frankly confesses that he has his ministry not only from God, but that it is also God's gift that he is fit to discharge it. The chief point of this passage, however, is that he says he has been made a minister of the New Testament along with the other apostles. For by this statement he strikes at impostors who, when they pressed the doctrine of the Law more insistently, declared themselves ministers not of the New but of the Old Testament. This was not without dishonour to Christ, who ought to have abolished those shadows, and who had said, not without serious reason, "The Law and the Prophets were until John; from that time the kingdom of God is preached." Finally, about to die, he testified with a loud voice that everything promised in the Old Testament and foreshadowed by types, both legal and prophetic, was now finished and fulfilled. John 19.

units.la: Addit autem Expositionis loco: Non literæ, sed Spiritus. Et huius quoq; dicti rationem red-dit: Quia litera occidat, Spiritus autem viuificet. Quæ verba consideratione diligentiorem me-rentur, quia illis semper abusi sunt homines phanatici & purioris doctrinæ hostes. Olim certè Ori-genes, vir alioqui eruditus & in Ecclesiæ ministerio laboriosissimus, huius loci falsa interpretatio-ne deceptus, Philonem plus quàm Iudaicè in sacris philosophantem sequutus est: & quia per lite-ram expositionem literalem, id est, grammaticam atq; historicam, per Spiritum verò spiritualem siue mysticam intelligebat, allegorijs partim ineptis, partim absurdis ac violentis omnia inuoluit potius quàm explicuit. Fuit hæc multorum errorum causa, & posteris temporibus graues turbas toti Ecclesiæ dedit, cùm Episcopi quidam Origenis libros publicè ab omnibus damnandos esse con-tenderent, alij verò tanti viri famæ & existimationi parcendum esse putarent. Sed & hæreticis occasio data fuit quiduis fingendi per ineptas & impias Scripturarum detorsiones. Quorum exem-plum hodie ferè Monachi sequuntur, quibus ea demum optima ostentandæ eruditionis & acumi-nis sui materia esse videtur, si Allegorijs pro suo arbitrio in Scripturis ludant. Hodie autem sunt, qui per literam vetus Testamentum intelligunt, & proinde eius libros simpliciter reijciunt, quasi indignos, qui in Ecclesia exponantur. Horum facilè principes sunt Anabaptistæ, qui si se veteris Testamenti authoritate stringi & vrgeri sentiunt, mox clamant, se non literam, sed Spiritum quæ-rere: quia litera occidat, Spiritus viuificet. Alij literam dici putant Verbum Dei scriptum, & hoc nomine ea quoq; comprehendunt, quæ in Scripturis sensu planissimo dicuntur, adeò vt allegorias aut expositiones argutiores quærere non sit opus: per Spiritum verò occultam quandam inspira-tionem intelligi debere contendunt, quæ nos de Dei voluntate edoceat, & cui non minus quàm Ver-bo in Scripturis reuelato debeat tribui. At hi dum toti spirituales fieri volunt, sese diabolo illu-dendos propinant. Quia enim à Verbo Dei scripto discedunt, impostturis omnibus patent, & eò vsq; tandem deueniunt, vt Dei Spiritum siue inspirationem esse putent, quicquid vel malus damon eis suggerit, aut ipsi ex suo cerebro pro suorum affectuum arbitrio commininscuntur.
units.tr: But he adds, by way of explanation, "not of the letter but of the Spirit," and he also gives the reason for this: "because the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life." These words deserve careful consideration, because fanatics and enemies of purer doctrine have always abused them. Origen, certainly, a man otherwise learned and most diligent in the ministry of the Church, was long ago deceived by a false interpretation of this passage. He followed Philo, who philosophized in sacred matters more than a Jew should. Because he understood "letter" to mean the literal exposition, that is the grammatical and historical, and "Spirit" to mean the spiritual or mystical, he wrapped up everything in allegories, some silly, some absurd and forced, rather than explaining it. This was the cause of many errors, and in later times it caused great troubles for the whole Church, when some bishops insisted that Origen's books should be publicly condemned by everyone, while others thought that the reputation and esteem of so great a man should be spared. But heretics too were given the opportunity of inventing whatever they liked through silly and impious twisting of the Scriptures. Monks today mostly follow this example, for whom it seems the best material for showing off their learning and cleverness, if they play with allegories in the Scriptures as they please. Today, however, there are some who understand the Old Testament according to the letter, and therefore simply reject its books as unworthy to be expounded in the Church. The leaders of these are easily the Anabaptists. If they feel themselves pressed and hemmed in by the authority of the Old Testament, they at once cry out that they seek not the letter but the Spirit, "because the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life." Others think that the letter is the written Word of God, and under this name they also include those things which in the Scriptures are stated in the plainest sense, so that there is no need to seek allegories or more subtle expositions. By the Spirit, however, they insist, must be understood some hidden inspiration, which teaches us the will of God, and which is to be credited no less than the Word revealed in the Scriptures. But while these people wish to become wholly spiritual, they expose themselves to be mocked by the devil.
