For since they depart from the written Word of God, they lie open to every sort of deception, and at last come to think that whatever an evil demon suggests to them, or whatever they themselves invent out of their own brain according to the feelings of their passions, is the Spirit of God or inspiration.

units.la: At si loci huius circumstantias omnes vnà cum statu, quem Paulus sibi propositum habuit, spectemus, literam dicit ipsissimam Legem Mosis, non alio quàm literali sensu intellectam, qualis tunc inter Iudæos habebatur: neq; de ea solum parte loquitur, quæ ceremonias tradit, verumetiam de ipso Decalogo, qui totius Legis compendium continet. Literam verò dicit Legem, quia literis descripta fuit in tabulis lapideis (vt ipse mox exponet) quod argumentum erat, per illam Spiritum illum viuificum non posse conferri. Etenim non potuit Moses aliud, quàm à Deo acceptam Legem Israelitis suis voce & scriptis proponere, eandem verò animis eorum imprimere non potuit, multò minus autem vires largiri, quibus illi satisfacerent. Deniq; litera dicitur Lex, quia per se simpli-citer & secundùm solam literam considerata non aliud nobis confert, quàm doctrinam, qua quid fieri quidue vitari debeat admonemur: non autem nos viribus nouis instruit, vt id possimus præ-stare, quod à nobis exigit Deus. E contra Euangelium Spiritus dicitur: primùm, quia hoc non in tabulis vel saxeis vel ex quacunq; alia materia factis descriptum acceperunt Apostoli, sed Spiri-tu magistro & doctore vsi sunt, qui illud cordibus eorum inscripsit, sicuti olim Deus per Ieremiam promiserat. Deinde quia cum Euangelij prædicatione Christus coniunctus est, qui (vt infra dice-tur) Spiritus & vita Legis est, eamq; in nostris cordibus viuificam ac salutarem reddit: qui de-niq; nos ex Verbi semine regenerat, vt vitam viuamus nouam & Deo acceptam. Quòd denique per Euangelium Spiritus sanctus datur, qui & adoptionis Spiritus & salutis nostræ arrhabo est. Qua nota olim Ioel quoq; vetus Testamentum à nouo distinxit, quòd tunc Deus Spiritum suum liberalissimè super omnem carnem effusurus sit. Itaq; Apostoli & quicunq; postea hos legitimè electi & missi Euangelium prædicant, Spiritus administri dicuntur, non quòd ipsi Spiritum in sua potestate habeant, eumq; pro suo arbitrio, quibus volunt, conferre possint: sed quòd Euangelij prædicatio medium & organum illud ordinarium est, per quod Deus Spiritum suum electis confert, dum ipse seruorum suorum ministerio benedicit, adeoq; per illos factæ plantationi & rigationi incrementum addit, sicuti in priori epistola Paulus docuit. Et huc faciunt exempla eorum, quibus vt primum Euangelio audito crediderunt, Spiritus sanctus non sine miraculo datus est, vt repente mutati linguis quoq; variis loquerentur: quod in primitiua Ecclesia tam fuit vulgare, vt Paulus Galatarum stoliditatem, qui ab Euangelio ad Legis doctrinam defecerant, hoc argumento arguat, dicens: Hoc solum cupio discere à vobis, Ex operibus Legis Spiritum accepistis, an ex prædicatione fidei? Adeò amentes estis, cum Spiritu inceperitis nunc carne perficimini?
units.tr: But if we consider all the circumstances of this passage, together with the purpose Paul had in view, he means by "letter" the very Law of Moses, understood only in the literal sense in which it was then held among the Jews. He speaks not only of that part which sets out the ceremonies, but also of the Decalogue itself, which contains the summary of the whole Law. He calls the Law "letter" because it was written on tablets of stone (as he will explain shortly), which showed that through it that life-giving Spirit could not be conferred. For Moses could do nothing but set before the Israelites, by voice and in writing, the Law received from God; he could not imprint it on their minds, much less give them the strength to satisfy it. Finally, the Law is called "letter" because, considered simply and according to the letter alone, it gives us nothing but teaching, by which we are warned what must be done and what avoided. It does not equip us with new strength to do what God requires of us. The Gospel, on the contrary, is called Spirit: first, because the apostles did not receive it written on tablets of stone or any other material, but had the Spirit as their teacher and instructor, who wrote it on their hearts, as God had long ago promised through Jeremiah. Next, because Christ is joined with the preaching of the Gospel, who (as will be said below) is the Spirit and life of the Law, and who makes it life-giving and saving in our hearts, and who finally regenerates us from the seed of the Word, so that we may live a new life acceptable to God. Lastly, because through the Gospel the Holy Spirit is given, who is the Spirit of adoption and the pledge of our salvation. On this ground Joel also distinguished the Old Testament from the New, because God was then going to pour out his Spirit most generously upon all flesh. Therefore the apostles, and all who afterwards were lawfully chosen and sent to preach the Gospel, are called ministers of the Spirit. Not that they have the Spirit in their power, to bestow on whomever they wish at their pleasure, but because the preaching of the Gospel is the ordinary means and instrument by which God gives his Spirit to the elect, while he himself blesses the ministry of his servants and so adds increase to the planting and watering done by them, as Paul taught in the earlier letter. The examples of those who, as soon as they believed on hearing the Gospel, received the Holy Spirit not without a miracle, so that they at once spoke in various tongues, point the same way. This was so common in the primitive Church that Paul, rebuking the foolishness of the Galatians who had fallen away from the Gospel to the teaching of the Law, argues from this very fact, saying: "This only I want to learn from you: did you receive the Spirit from the works of the Law, or from the preaching of faith? Are you so foolish that, having begun in the Spirit, you are now being made perfect by the flesh?"

units.la: Hæc probè considerata simul docent, quo sensu Paulus dicat, literam occidere, Spiritum verò viuificare. Et de hoc quidem non est opus multis dicere. Quid enim aliud faciat Spiritus Christi, qui totus vita est? Quoad Legem autem, quam literæ vocabulo significari diximus, occidere dicitur, non quidem quòd ipsa per se noxia aut letalis sit, sed nostro vitio. Per se enim (vt alibi Paulus scribit) spiritualis est, bona est, sancta est. Et ipse Moses de ea differens ait: Obtestor hodie aduersus vos cœlum & terram, vitam & mortem propositi vobis, benedictionem & maledictionem: elige igitur vitam, vt viuas tu & semen tuum, &c. Et nota sunt, quæ in Psalmis habentur, Legis præconia: Lex Domini integra est, conuertens animam: testimonium Dei verum, imperitis sapientiam suppeditans: Decreta Domini recta, cor exhilarantia: præceptum Domini rectum illuminans oculos. Quæ cum verissimè dicantur, sequitur legem occidere, non suo, sed nostro vitio, adeoq; (vt vulgo loquuntur) per accidens. Dum enim nos de Dei voluntate edocet, eadem opera peccatum, quod prius ignorabamus, arguit, & ita reos agit transgressionis. Vnde Paulus de seipso dicebat: Peccatum non cognoui, nisi per Legem. Deinde naturæ & ingenij nostri vitiositate fit, vt in vetitum nitamur, quoq; magis prohibentur peccata, eò maiori eorum desiderio accendamur. Quibus accidit, quòd maledictionem omnibus denuntians Lex qui non omnia eius præcepta obseruant, eadem sententia omnes homines iugulat: quando constat neminem, ne inter sanctissimos quidem inueniri, qui de vera & perfecta omnium præceptorum Dei obseruatione gloriari possit. Et quàm vana atq; inutilis sit eiusmodi gloriatio, in dimitis illius iuuenis exemplo apparet, qui cum initio se præcepta omnia seruasse dixisset, mox tristis & toto animo consternatus discedit, quando Christus id quod in Lege præcipuum est ei mandans, in animum eius altius penetrauit. Pertinent autem ad totius loci huius explicationem, quæ Paulus copiosius scribit ad Rom. 7. Cap. Quibus si coniunxeris, quæ Diuus Augustinus in libro de Spiritu & litera tradidit Cap. quarto & aliis sequentibus, videbis nos de his non tam nostram sententiam, quàm veteris & orthodoxæ Ecclesiæ doctrinam protulisse.
units.tr: These things, considered carefully together, show in what sense Paul says that the letter kills but the Spirit gives life. There is no need to say much more about this. For what else does the Spirit of Christ, who is wholly life, do? As for the Law, which we have said is signified by the word "letter", it is said to kill, not because it is in itself harmful or deadly, but because of our fault. For in itself (as Paul writes elsewhere) it is spiritual, good, and holy. Moses himself, speaking of it, says: "I call heaven and earth to witness against you today, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: choose therefore life, that you and your seed may live," etc. The praises of the Law found in the Psalms are also well known: "The law of the Lord is perfect, converting the soul; the testimony of God is true, giving wisdom to the simple; the judgments of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart; the commandment of the Lord is pure, enlightening the eyes." Since these things are said most truly, it follows that the Law kills not by its own fault but by ours, and so (as people commonly say) accidentally. For while it teaches us the will of God, at the same time it exposes the sin we did not previously know, and so makes us guilty of transgression. Whence Paul said of himself: "I did not know sin except through the Law." Then, through the corruption of our nature and mind, it happens that we strive after what is forbidden, and the more sins are prohibited, the more we are inflamed with desire for them. Moreover, since the Law pronounces a curse on all who do not observe all its precepts, it slays all men by the same sentence, for it is clear that no one, not even among the holiest, can be found who could boast of a true and perfect observance of all God's commandments. How vain and useless such boasting is appears from the example of that young man, who at first said that he had kept all the precepts, but soon departs sad and utterly dismayed, when Christ, commanding him the thing which is chief in the Law, penetrated more deeply into his heart. The explanation of this whole passage belongs to what Paul writes more fully at Rom. 7. If you join these with what the blessed Augustine taught in his book On the Spirit and the Letter, chapter four and the following ones, you will see that on these matters we have set forth not so much our own opinion as the teaching of the old and orthodox Church.

units.la: Confutantur autem hîs omnes, qui dum hodie etiam Legis opera vrgent, iustificationem ex nostrorum operum meritis pendere docent. Sunt hi literæ occidentis ministri, nec pro Christi ministris haberi possunt, qui Apostolos suos Spiritus ministros fecit, & veteris Testamenti ministerium abrogauit. Quòd si vero Legis diuinæ operibus, quoad hanc causam, nihil tribui debet, quid de hominum traditionibus dicemus, quibus fere omnia ea opera nituntur, quibus hodie se vendiant, qui optimi & iustissimi videri volunt? Atqui constat illas iam olim Dei sententia damnatas esse cum toto cultu, qui secundum eas instituitur. Arguit etiam locus iste eorum errorem, qui toti circa res externas occupantur, deq; illis non solum disputationes, verumetiam contentiones grauissimas non sine publico scandalo instituunt. Quales sunt, qui de reali corporis Christi præsentia in Cœna, deq; eiusdem corporali manducatione, quæ ore fiat, contendunt. Quid verò omnes illi Christo respondebunt, qui corpus suum ideo ex terris hisce in cœlos subuexit, vt Spiritui suo locus fit, neq; nos ex corporis eius præsentia pendeamus? Quin ergo omissis rixis, quæ superstitioni potius quàm pietati seruiunt, in hoc fumus, vt Spiritu donemur, qui Christum in nobis viuificet, nosq; in eius vijs dirigat?
units.tr: Hereby are refuted all those who, while today also urging the works of the Law, teach that justification depends on the merits of our works. These are ministers of the letter that kills, and cannot be regarded as ministers of Christ, who made his apostles ministers of the Spirit and abrogated the ministry of the Old Testament. But if nothing should be attributed to the works of divine Law in this cause, what shall we say of human traditions, on which almost all those works rest by which men today seek to commend themselves, who wish to seem the best and most just? Yet it is certain that these were condemned long ago by the judgment of God, together with the whole worship instituted according to them. This passage also refutes the error of those who are wholly occupied with external things, and about them institute not only disputes but very grave contentions, not without public scandal. Such are those who contend about the real presence of Christ's body in the Supper, and about its bodily eating, which is done with the mouth. But what will all those answer to Christ, who for this very reason lifted his body from this earth into heaven, so that room might be made for his Spirit, and so that we might not depend on the presence of his body? Why then, leaving aside the quarrels, which serve superstition rather than piety, do we not strive to be given that Spirit who may quicken Christ in us and direct us in his ways?

units.la: Porrò accedit Paulus ad amplificandam & extollendam ministerij Euangelici dignitatem contra pseudoapostolos, qui apud rerum imperitos multa magnificè de Lege garriebant: & quantum ex tum ex hoc loco colligere licet, vrgere imprimis solebant illius promulgationem terroris, gloriae & maiestatis plenam, & quae de facie Mosis noua luce coruscante dicuntur, quam is ex familiari colloquio cum Deo retulit. Quod autem ex eo colligebant, Legem videlicet adhuc doceri, neq; Euangelio inferiorem æstimari debere, id per Concessionis speciem validissimè confutat. Nam omnium quae sequuntur, hæc summa est: Fateor quacunq; de Legis gloria & dignitate dicuntur, neque is ego sum, qui eam, ceu inutilem aut noxiam, cum ignominia abijci velim: sed si cum Euangelio conferatur, hoc multò gloriosius & præstantius esse dico, & proinde huius ministerium maiorem habere dignitatem, neque Mosaico aut Legali ministerio postponi debere: quin potius hoc nobis agendum esse, vt Lege, quæ iam ceu emerita suum finem attigit, cum honore sepulta, Euangelium emineat & triumphet, &c. Ista vero eleganti & multiplici comparatione illustrat atque confirmat.
units.tr: Furthermore, Paul proceeds to magnify and exalt the dignity of the Gospel ministry against the false apostles, who among the ignorant talked grandly about the Law. As far as can be gathered from this passage, they especially used to urge its proclamation, full of terror, glory and majesty, and what is said about the face of Moses shining with a new light, which he brought back from his familiar converse with God. What they inferred from this, namely that the Law is still to be taught and ought not to be esteemed inferior to the Gospel, he refutes most strongly by a figure of concession. For the sum of all that follows is this: "I grant whatever is said of the glory and dignity of the Law, nor am I one who would wish to cast it off with dishonour as useless or harmful; but if it is compared with the Gospel, I say that this is much more glorious and excellent, and therefore that its ministry has greater dignity and ought not to be placed behind the Mosaic or legal ministry. Rather, we must bring it about that the Law, which has now reached its end as one that has served its time, is buried with honour, and the Gospel stands out and triumphs," etc. He illustrates and confirms this with an elegant and manifold comparison.

units.la: Primum comparationis huius membrum est: Quòd si mortis ministerium literis informatum in saxis, fuit gloriosum, adeò vt non possent intueri filij Israel in faciem Mosis, propter gloriam vultus eius, quæ abolenda erat, quî non potius ministerium Spiritus erit gloriosum? Legem ministerium mortis dicit, quia prævaricationis causa (vt Augustini verbis vtar) posita peccati conuictos sibijpsis relinquit, neq; viribus nouis armat, quibus nos liberemus. Hinc enim non aliud quàm mors sequitur, quam eadem omnibus, qui eius præcepta transgrediuntur, denuntiat. Euangelium vero ministerium Spiritus dicitur, quia Spiritum nobis confert. Cum autem ex visitata Comparationis regula vitam morti opponere debuisset, Spiritum dicere maluit, vt doceret, nos per Euangelium non obiter modo ex morte liberari, verum etiam Spiritu vitæ donari, vt peccatis defuncti vitam in Christo nouam viuamus, quæ ad cœlestis & æternæ possessionem hæreditatis nos deducat. Quantò ergo gloriosior est vita quàm mors, & quantò laudabilius est vitæ restituere quàm occidere, tantò etiam maior est Euangelij dignitas quàm Legis & Legalis ministerij. Facit autem ad huius argumenti amplificationem atq; confirmationem, quòd repetit Legem literis in tabulas saxeas inscriptam fuisse, cum Euangelium cordibus hominum à Dei Spiritu inscribatur. Quibus adde, quòd lapideæ tabulæ durum quid & crassum denotabant, sicuti insculptio (quod Chrysostomus obseruauit) illam ad solam Iudæorum gentem pertinere docebat: cum Euangelij Spiritus longè lateq; per omnes terras diffundatur. Accedit hus, quòd gloria illa & maiestas Legis, quam impostores pseudoapostoli subinde iactabant, in sola Mosis facie reluxit: Euangelij verò effectus per totam hominis Christiani vitam sese diffundit, & per illud ad cœlestem illam gloriam deducimur, cuius specimen & gustum aliquem Christus tribus discipulis in corporis sui claritatione exhibuit. Matth. 17. Adhæc splendorem istum faciei solus Moses sibi habuit: at Christus, qui in Euangelio prædicatur, omnes in se credentes gloriæ suæ participes facit. Istis vero arguuntur inepte fastidiosi, qui legales ritus & omnem externum splendorem sic admirantur, vt spiritualem illam dignitatem fere prorsus negligant, quam nobis Euangelium in Christo offert. Erant tales multi apud Corinthios: & hodie multi audiuntur, quibus Euangelij simplex doctrina sordet, præ pompa illa theatrica & vitreo splendore, quibus Papatus sese ostentat.
units.tr: The first member of this comparison is: "If the ministry of death, engraved in letters on stones, was glorious, so that the children of Israel could not look upon the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance, which was to be abolished, why will the ministry of the Spirit not be rather glorious?" He calls the Law a ministry of death because, being put in place for the sake of transgression (to use Augustine's words), it leaves those convicted of sin to themselves and does not arm them with new strength by which they might be freed. For from this nothing but death follows, which it announces to all who transgress its precepts. But the Gospel is called the ministry of the Spirit because it confers the Spirit upon us. Yet, when by the usual rule of comparison he ought to have opposed life to death, he preferred to say Spirit, to teach that through the Gospel we are freed from death not merely in passing, but are also given the Spirit of life, so that, dead to sins, we may live a new life in Christ, which leads us to the possession of the heavenly and eternal inheritance. Therefore, as life is more glorious than death, and as it is more praiseworthy to restore life than to kill, so the dignity of the Gospel is greater than that of the Law and the legal ministry. Moreover, it serves to amplify and confirm this argument that he repeats that the Law was inscribed in letters on tables of stone, whereas the Gospel is inscribed on the hearts of men by the Spirit of God. Add to this that the stone tables signified something hard and gross, just as the inscription (as Chrysostom observed) taught that the Law pertained to the Jewish nation alone, whereas the Spirit of the Gospel is spread far and wide through all lands. Furthermore, that glory and majesty of the Law, which the impostors, the false apostles, kept boasting of, shone only in the face of Moses; but the effect of the Gospel spreads through the whole life of the Christian, and through it we are led to that heavenly glory, of which Christ gave a specimen and some taste to his three disciples in the brightness of his body, Matt. 17. Moreover, that splendour of the face Moses kept to himself alone; but Christ, who is preached in the Gospel, makes all who believe in him partakers of his glory. These things rebuke those foolishly fastidious people who so admire the legal rites and all external splendour that they almost entirely neglect that spiritual dignity which the Gospel offers us in Christ. There were many such among the Corinthians, and today many are to be heard for whom the plain doctrine of the Gospel is contemptible in comparison with that theatrical pomp and glassy glitter by which the Papacy displays itself.

units.la: Sequitur alterum comparationis huius membrum: Nam si ministerium condemnationis fuit gloriosum, multò magis ministerium iustitiæ abundat gloria. Faciunt ista ad prioris membri explicationem: Nam ministerium condemnationis vocat Legem, quam prius mortis ministerium dixerat, vt ostendat, illam non peculanter, vt tyranni solent, aliquem occidere, sed de peccato legitimè conuictis sententiam mortis denuntiare. At si huius ministerium fuit gloriosum, quanto gloriosius censeri debet ministerium iustitiæ? Vbi rursus exigebat comparationis lex, vt pro iustitia iustificationem aut absolutionem à peccatis diceret: sed docere vult, nobis per Euangelium non modò simplicem absolutionem, sed ipsissimam IESV CHRISTI iustitiam conferri, quam ita nobis propter fidem in illum Deus imputat, vt tota nostra sit, nosq; propter illam æterna gloria coronemur. Ideo in priori epistola, Christum nobis à Deo iustitiam factum esse dixit. Et infra illus pro nobis peccatum factum dicet, vt nos per illum iustitia Dei efficeremur. Quibus consentit, quòd Ieremias Messiæ nomen fore ait: IEHOVA iustitia nostra. Quia verò visibilem illam gloriam Legis, quæ in eius promulgatione & facie Mosis relucente apparuerat, nonnulli aduersus omnia argumenta pertinacius vrgebant, ad huius membri confirmationem adijcit: Etenim quod glorificatum fuit, ne glorificatum quidem fuit in hac parte, quoad excellentissimam gloriam. Seusus est: Fuit quidem gloria magna Legis, sed per se considerata: At si illam cum Euangelio conferas, iam nulla erit, sed mox euanescet, perinde vt stellae & lucernae ad Solis exortum suum splendorem occultant. Ita Chrysostomus olim hunc locum exposuit.
units.tr: Next comes the second part of this comparison: For if the ministry of condemnation was glorious, much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory. These words explain the first part. He calls the Law "the ministry of condemnation," having earlier called it "the ministry of death," to show that it does not kill someone arbitrarily, as tyrants do, but pronounces the sentence of death on those lawfully convicted of sin. But if the ministry of the Law was glorious, how much more glorious must the ministry of righteousness be considered? Here the rule of comparison required him to say "justification" or "absolution from sins" in place of "righteousness." But he wishes to teach that through the Gospel we are given not merely simple absolution but the very righteousness of Jesus Christ. God imputes this to us on account of faith in him, so that it becomes wholly ours, and by it we are crowned with eternal glory. Therefore in the former epistle he said that Christ was made righteousness for us by God. And below he will say that he was made sin for us, so that through him we might be made the righteousness of God. Jeremiah agrees with this when he says that the name of the Messiah will be: "The LORD our righteousness." Since some stubbornly urged the visible glory of the Law, which had appeared at its promulgation and in the shining face of Moses, against all arguments, he adds in confirmation of this part: "For what was made glorious was not glorious at all in this respect, compared with the surpassing glory." The sense is this: the Law indeed had great glory, considered in itself; but if you compare it with the Gospel, it will be as nothing and will soon fade, just as stars and lamps lose their brightness at the rising of the sun. Chrysostom long ago expounded this passage in this way.

units.la: Restat tertium comparationis membrum: Si quod aboletur fuit gloriosum, multo magis est gloriosum id quod manet. Habuit quidem Lex vsum suum praeclarum, sed qui ad tempus correctionis vsque (vt alibi loquitur Apostolus) durare debuit. Et notum est illud Christi: Lex & prophetae vsque ad Ioannem, &c. Euangelij verò ministerium firmum immutatumque manebit vsque ad finem mundi. Quod propter eos obseruari debet, qui nouam indies in Ecclesia rerum mutationem expectant: ex quorum numero olim Chiliastae fuerunt, qui aureum quoddam seculum & pacem vniuersalem sibi pollicebantur. Sequuntur hoc multi hodie, quorum aliqui Veritatis cognitionem ne Apostolorum quidem temporibus plene manifestatam fuisse dicere audent, quo facilius figmenta sua quibusuis possint obtrudere. Atqui Paulus de ministerio loquitur, quod ipse cum alijs Apostolis obibat, & illud manserum dicit, imo hac nota illud à Lege distinguit, quod hac suo tempore debuerit aboleri. Non est ergo, vt aliquam mutationem vel doctrinae vel fidei & religionis expectemus. Nam quaecunque fit contra Euangelium, quod olim Apostoli praedicarunt, ea erronea, falsa & noxia est.
units.tr: The third part of the comparison remains: If what is being abolished was glorious, much more glorious is what remains. The Law did indeed have its excellent use, but it was to last only until the time of correction (as the Apostle says elsewhere). And that saying of Christ is well known: "The Law and the prophets were until John," and so on. But the ministry of the Gospel will remain firm and unchanged until the end of the world. This must be noted on account of those who daily expect some new change in the Church. Among their number were once the Chiliasts, who promised themselves a golden age and universal peace. Many follow them today, some of whom dare to say that the knowledge of the truth was not fully revealed even in the times of the Apostles, so that they may more easily force their fictions upon anyone. Yet Paul speaks of the ministry which he himself performed along with the other Apostles, and he says that it remains. Indeed, by this mark he distinguishes it from the Law, which had to be abolished in its own time. There is therefore no reason for us to expect any change either in doctrine or in faith and religion. For whatever is contrary to the Gospel that the Apostles once preached is erroneous, false and harmful.

units.la: Porro in tota hac comparatione non oscitanter obseruari debet, Paulum tam duriter loqui de Lege & ministerio eius, cum non ignoraret, quam graue hoc esset Iudaeis suis & multis alijs, qui per illam iustificari & seruari se posse sperabant. At mouit eum, quod illam videret tunc temporis praecipuam remoram esse, qua purior Euangelij praedicatio impediebatur. Nam vbicunq; hanc tradebant Apostoli, mox ipsis digressis obrepebant falsi fratres, qui Legem illi commiscendo Ecclesias turbabant. Oportuit ergo aperte agere, & ficum ficum, scapham scapham dicere. Hinc illa tam grauia Legis epitheta, Ministerium mortis, ministerium condemnationis, formata in saxis, quodq; eam aboleri oportuerit. Debet hoc obseruari in omnibus controuersis articulis, nec eos audiamus, qui nos de Missa, de imaginibus, purgatorio, Papa, indulgentijs & similibus, aut nihil omnino, aut blandè atque molliter dicere vellent. Atqui haec illa sunt, quibus multi in superstitionum tenebris detinentur, &c. Liberè ergo dicendum, quod à Deo auocent, Christi merito derogent, & exitium afferant. Si enim hoc licuit Apostolis de Lege dicere, quam olim Deus tanta cum maiestate & gloria promulgauerat, quis nos iure accusabit, si idem de hominum traditionibus pronuntiemus?
units.tr: Moreover, in this whole comparison it must not be carelessly overlooked that Paul speaks so harshly of the Law and its ministry, although he was not unaware how grievous this would be to his own Jews and to many others who hoped to be justified and saved through it. But he was moved because he saw that at that time the Law was the chief hindrance by which a purer preaching of the Gospel was impeded. For wherever the Apostles preached this, as soon as they had departed, false brethren crept in and troubled the churches by mixing the Law with the Gospel. It was therefore necessary to act openly and to call a fig a fig and a boat a boat. Hence those severe epithets for the Law: the ministry of death, the ministry of condemnation, "engraved in stones," and the fact that it had to be abolished. This should be observed in all controverted articles. We should not listen to those who would have us speak of the Mass, images, purgatory, the Pope, indulgences and similar matters either not at all or gently and softly. Yet these are the very things by which many are held in the darkness of superstition. Therefore we must speak freely about what draws people away from God, detracts from the merit of Christ, and brings ruin. For if the Apostles were permitted to speak in this way of the Law, which God had once promulgated with such majesty and glory, who could justly accuse us if we pronounce the same judgment on the traditions of men?

units.la: Admonet praeterea nos locus iste de Euangelij dignitate & eius vsu. Est ministerium Spiritus & iustitiae, cordibus inscribitur, vitam confert, durat denique & manet in aeternum, & ipsi Lex Mosis quantumuis gloriosa cedere debuit. Quanto magis igitur philosophia, Canones, traditiones, Concilia & omnis generis decreta, quae ab hominibus conduntur? Nec tibi persuadeas aliquid in eo vtiliter nouari aut mutari posse. Non mixturam, non assumentum vllum patitur. Et qui seruari volunt, per CHRISTVM IESVM seruentur oportet. At is sibijpsi semper constat, & idem est hodie, heri & in seculum. Interim officij sui diligenter meminerint Christiani homines. Si enim Spiritum vitae accepimus, non decet nos vt ad priorem vxzorutα (vt Chrysostomus loquitur) id est, mortalitatem relabamur, sed vt vitam nouam in Christo viuamus studendum est. Quid multis? Agnoscamus Dei beneficium, qui nouissimis hisce temporibus Euangelium Filij sui IESV CHRISTI manifestare dignatus est. Huic credamus, & eidem adhaereamus, qui etsi cum Iudaismo gentilismum quoque sustulerit, ipse tamen idem semper manet, neque vlli mutationi est obnoxius. De hoc enim Pater pronuntiauit: Ego constitui Regem meum super Zion montem meum sanctum: & huic vaticinio Angelus succinens, dicit: Et Regni eius non erit finis. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, this passage reminds us of the dignity of the Gospel and of its use. It is the ministry of the Spirit and of righteousness; it is written on hearts, it confers life, and in the end it endures and remains forever. Even the Law of Moses, however glorious, had to give way to it. How much more, then, must philosophy, canons, traditions, councils and every kind of decree devised by men give way? Do not persuade yourself that anything in the Gospel can be usefully renewed or changed. It admits no mixture and no addition of any kind. Those who wish to be saved must be saved through Christ Jesus. He is always consistent with himself, and is the same today, yesterday and forever. Meanwhile, Christians should diligently remember their duty. For if we have received the Spirit of life, it is not fitting that we relapse into our former state (as Chrysostom puts it), that is, into mortality. Rather we ought to strive to live a new life in Christ. What more is there to say? Let us acknowledge the goodness of God, who in these last times has deigned to reveal the Gospel of his Son Jesus Christ. Let us believe in him and cling to him. Though he has abolished Gentilism along with Judaism, he himself remains the same and is subject to no change. For the Father declared concerning him: "I have set my King upon Zion, my holy mountain." And an Angel, echoing this prophecy, says: "And of his kingdom there shall be no end." To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XIII.
units.tr: Homily XIII.

units.la: Itaque cùm eiusmodi spem habeamus, multa in loquendo libertate vtimur: Nec sumus sicut Moses, qui imponebat velamen faciei suae, ne intuerentur filij Israel in finem eius quod aboletur. Itaque obcaluerunt mentes eorum. Nam vsque in diem hodiernum, in lectione Veteris testamenti, manet non retectum velame illud: quod per Christum tollitur. Quin ad hunc vsque diem, cùm legitur Moses, velamen cordi eorum impositum est. Postquam autem conuersus fuerit ad Dominum, tolletur velamen.
units.tr: Since we have this kind of hope, we speak with great boldness. We are not like Moses, who put a veil over his face so that the children of Israel might not look at the end of what was being abolished. Their minds were hardened, for to this day, when the Old Testament is read, that same veil remains unlifted, since it is taken away through Christ. Indeed, to this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart. But when they turn to the Lord, the veil will be removed.

units.la: Praecipua causa errorum atque vitiorum, quae in Ecclesiam Corinthiorum irrepserant, haec fuit, quòd non rectè sentirent de Euangelij praedicatione, quam Paulus illis bona fide & simplici perspicuoq; dicendi genere tradiderat. Mali verò huius primi authores erant, qui totum Noui testamenti ministerium extenuabant, & partim humanae rationis figmenta, partim Legis Mosaicae doctrinam, qualis tunc inter Iudaeos tradebatur, cum Euangelio miscebant. Loquebantur bi magnificè de Lege, quanta in eius promulgatione maiestas eluxisset, & imprimis hoc apud rudiores vrgebant, quòd Mosis facies ex colloquio cum Deo fulgorem radiantem cotraxisse scribitur, quem filij Israel propius intueri non potuerint. Itaque non absque causa Paulus de Euangelij doctrina & toto Noui testamenti ministerio prolixè ac diligenter disserit, & nuper elegcanti Comparatione docuit, huius dignitatem multò excellentiorem esse, quàm olim Mosaici fuerit. Id nunc ad causam, de qua ipsi cum aemulis controuersia erat, propius applicans, demonstrat, quanto praestantior sors sit tam ministrorum quàm omnium credentium Noui testamenti, quàm olim Mosis & populi Israelitici fuerit. Ea verò occasione in Legis abusum digreditur, & simul scandalum removet, ad quod multi offendebant, quando Iudaeos videbant indomita plane & incurabili contumacia Christum persequi & eius Euangelio contradicere.
units.tr: The chief cause of the errors and vices that had crept into the Church of the Corinthians was that they did not think rightly about the preaching of the Gospel, which Paul had handed down to them in good faith, in a plain and clear manner of speaking. The authors of this evil were those who belittled the whole ministry of the New Testament and mixed the Gospel with fabrications of human reason and with the teaching of the Mosaic Law as it was then taught among the Jews. They spoke of the Law in grand terms, saying how great a majesty had shone forth in its promulgation, and above all they pressed this upon the more ignorant, that Moses' face is written to have acquired a radiant brightness from his conversation with God, a brightness the children of Israel could not look upon closely. So it was not without reason that Paul discussed at length and carefully the doctrine of the Gospel and the whole ministry of the New Testament, and in a recent elegant comparison he taught that its dignity is far more excellent than that of the Mosaic ministry once was. Now, applying this more closely to the matter about which he was in dispute with his rivals, he shows how much more outstanding is the lot of both the ministers and all believers of the New Testament than that of Moses and the Israelite people of old. On this occasion he digresses into the abuse of the Law, and at the same time removes the stumbling block that offended many, when they saw the Jews persecuting Christ and opposing his Gospel with a stubbornness that was utterly unbending and incurable.

units.la: Connectit autem locum hunc cum ijs quae proximè praecesserunt, dum ex ijs sic infert: Itaque cum eiusmodi spem habeamus, multa in dicendo libertate vtimur. Quae verò illa spes? Nimirum quòd Euangelij doctrina semper ad finem mundi vsque duratura sit, neque vnquam cessaturum eius ministerium. Ea spe (inquit) freti, tam multa aut magna in dicendo libertate vtimur. In Graeco habetur παρρησία, quae vox proprie libertatem dicendi significat. At quia huic coniuncta esse solet fiducia & perspicuitas, vt aperte quod res est dicatur, voluit haec omnia Paulus vna voce complecti, & simul ijs respondere, qui ipsius in dicendo libertatem atque ingenuitatem accusabant. Quasi diceret: Nemini mirum videri debet, nos tanta cum fiducia animi & dicendi libertate Euangelium IESV CHRISTI praedicare, & ea seuerius apertiusq; corripere, quae cum illius simplicitate pugnant. Licuit olim Mosi in suo ministerio liberè edicere, quaecunq; à Deo acciperet. Licuit eidem peccantes durius tractare, & contumaciter aduersus se & ordinem à Deo institutum tumultuantes, non verbis modò acrioribus corripere, verumetiam exemplis horrendis punire: sicuti in aurei vituli confectione, in seditione Coritica & saepe aliàs factum fuisse legimus. Cur ergo nobis non idem liceat, qui ministerium à Deo accepimus multò excellentius & praestantius? Aut cur mundi huius & hominum vanissimorum comminationibus nos perterrefieri patiamur, qui Euangelium perpetuò mansurum scimus, vt hic mundus fremat et tumultuetur?
units.tr: He links this passage with what came just before, when he infers from it: "Since we have this kind of hope, we speak with great boldness." What, then, is that hope? Surely that the doctrine of the Gospel will endure until the end of the world, and that its ministry will never cease. Relying on this hope (he says), we speak with such great and open boldness. In the Greek it is παρρησία [parrhēsia], a word which properly means freedom of speech. But since confidence and plainness are usually joined with this, so that what is the case is stated openly, Paul wanted to embrace all of this in one word, and at the same time to answer those who accused him of boldness and frankness in speaking. As if he were saying: No one ought to be surprised that we preach the Gospel of Jesus Christ with such confidence of mind and freedom of speech, and rebuke with greater severity and openness those things that conflict with its simplicity. Moses once was free in his ministry to declare plainly whatever he received from God. He was also allowed to deal more harshly with sinners, and to punish those who stubbornly raged against him and the order instituted by God, not only with sharper words but with dreadful examples; as we read was done in the making of the golden calf, in the sedition of Korah, and often on other occasions. Why, then, should we not have the same liberty, we who have received a ministry far more excellent and outstanding from God? Or why should we allow ourselves to be terrified by the threats of this world and of the most vain of men, since we know that the Gospel will remain forever, however much this world may rage and riot?

units.la: Vbi obseruabimus ad omnes Euangelij ministros pertinere quod Paulus de semetipso dicit: Quia enim Deus vult omnis loci & ordinis homines salvos fieri, & in Veritatis cognitionem venire, nihil dissimulare, nihil tectius aut obscurius proponere, nihil ambiguis locutionibus fucare debent ij, quibus Veritatis doctrina credita est. Admonet de eo Christus, qui Apostolos quae in occulto audierint, per plateas vulgare: & quae ipsis in aurem dicta sunt, ex tectis publicè omnibus annuntiare iubet. Et Isaiae dicitur: Clama ex gutture, exalta tubae instar vocem tuam, & annuntia populo meo peccata sua. Neque terreat aliquem mundi potentia & ferocia, qui cum Veritatis lucem oderit, eius praedicationem vel legibus certis circumscribere, vel omnino impedire et abolere
units.tr: Here we note that what Paul says of himself pertains to all ministers of the Gospel: since God wishes men of every place and rank to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, those to whom the doctrine of the truth has been entrusted must conceal nothing, set forth nothing more covertly or obscurely, and disguise nothing with ambiguous expressions. Christ warns about this, who bids the apostles to proclaim in the streets what they have heard in secret, and to announce publicly from the housetops what has been said to them in the ear. And it is said by Isaiah: "Cry aloud, lift up your voice like a trumpet, and declare to my people their sins." Nor should anyone be terrified by the power and fierceness of the world, which, since it hates the light of the truth, tries either to limit its preaching by fixed laws or altogether to hinder and abolish it.

units.la: Matth. 10; Isa. 58. conatur. Perrumpet enim per omnia obstacula Dei Spiritus, qui in Euangelio sese exerit, & ardeat oportet ignis ille, quem Dominus accensum vult. Stultus omnium iudicio putaretur, qui Austri vel Boreæ spirantis flatus impedire vellet, aut incendij iam grassantis & ipsa tectorum fastigia superantis vim vna aut altera aquæ guttula restinguere. Et tu eos aliquid effecturos putas, qui Spiritus sancti per Euangelium spirantis flatum obturare, & ignis illius diuini atq; cœlestis ardorem extinguere conantur? Etenim Euangelium reuera Verbum illud Domini est, quod omnibus in nihilū redactis manebit in æternum. Omnis caro fœnum (clamat ex Dei mandato Isaias) & omnis gloria carnis flos agri. Exaruit fœnum, flos defluxit, Verbum autem Domini Dei nostri manet in æternum. Quibus consentit istud Christi: Cœlum & terra transibunt, verba autem mea non præteribunt aut intercident. Est ergo inconsulta plane & impia eorum temeritas, qui Euangelij prædicationem certis finibus circumscribere, aut illius cursum suis machinationibus remorari in animum inducunt. Quid enim illi aliud quàm in cœlum expuunt, & contra stimulum calcitrant, vt sibi ipsis ignominiam & exitium accersant? Rursus nimium ignaui sunt, qui cum in tam sublimis ministerij dignitatem à Deo euecti sint, sibi tamen à mundo hoc infelici & mox peituro metuunt.
units.tr: Matth. 10; Isa. 58. For the Spirit of God, who shows himself in the Gospel, will break through all obstacles, and that fire which the Lord wishes to be kindled must blaze. Anyone who tried to stop the blast of the blowing south or north wind, or to quench with a single drop of water a fire already raging and rising above the very roofs of houses, would be judged foolish by everyone. And do you think that those will accomplish anything who try to block the breath of the Holy Spirit blowing through the Gospel, and to extinguish the heat of that divine and heavenly fire? For the Gospel is truly that Word of the Lord which will remain forever, when all things have been reduced to nothing. "All flesh is grass," cries Isaiah on God's command, "and all the glory of flesh is the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower falls, but the Word of the Lord our God stands forever." Christ's words agree with this: "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away or perish." Therefore the rashness of those who determine to limit the preaching of the Gospel within fixed bounds, or to delay its course by their own schemes, is plainly ill-advised and impious. For what else do they do but spit at heaven and kick against the goad, bringing shame and ruin upon themselves? Moreover, they are too cowardly who, though they have been raised by God to the dignity of so high a ministry, nevertheless fear this unhappy world, which is soon to perish.

units.la: Quia verò semel in Mosis & Legis mentionem Apostolus incidərat, repetit quod nuper de facie eius fulgente aut corruscante dixerat, cuius splendorem Israelitæ ferre non potuerunt: vt quoad hunc quoq; maiorem Apostolorum dignitatem esse euincat. Non sumus (inquit) sicut Moses, qui imponebat velamen faciei suæ, ne intuerentur filij Israel in finem eius, quod aboletur, &c. Quasi diceret: Ne mihi Mosem obieceritis & ex facie eius emicantes fulgoris cœlestis radios. Quid enim hoc Israelitis contulit? aut quæ nam fuit splendoris illius vtilitas? Nulla sane. Quin potius oculos illorum perstrinxit, vt illum non possent coram intueri. Itaque ei velo opus fuit, quo ad populum verba facturus faciem suam tegeret. At nos non ita agimus, qui facie retecta & voce libera IESVM CHRISTVM prædicamus, longè maioris atque salubrioris claritatis seu gloriæ Mediatorem, &c.
units.tr: But since the Apostle had once come upon the mention of Moses and the Law, he repeats what he had recently said about his face shining and gleaming, whose brightness the Israelites could not bear, in order to prove that the dignity of the apostles is greater in this respect too. "We are not," he says, "like Moses, who put a veil over his face so that the children of Israel might not look at the end of what was being abolished," and so on. As if he were saying: Do not throw Moses in our faces, with the rays of heavenly brightness shining from his face. For what did this benefit the Israelites? Or what was the usefulness of that brilliance? None at all. Rather, it dazzled their eyes, so that they could not look upon him openly. Therefore he needed a veil, so that he might cover his face when he addressed the people. But we do not act in this way. With face unveiled and voice free, we proclaim Jesus Christ, the Mediator of a far greater and more wholesome brightness or glory, and so on.

units.la: Ilis verò simul docet, quanto melior feliciorq; fit conditio Christianorum in Nouo testamento, quàm olim Israelitarum sub Mose fuerit. Illis velo opus fuit, quia non potuerunt intueri in finem eius quod aboletur. Id verò de Lege dicitur, quam abolendam fuisse nuper dixerat, & cuius finem, id est, verum legitimumq; vsum Israelitæ videre siue intelligere non potuerint. Est autem finis Legis Christus, & proinde vsus illius est, vt pædagogi instar nos ad hunc deducat: sicut in epistola ad Galatas prolixè docetur. At nos (inquit) Christum coram cernimus, & eundem absq; omni inuolucro omnibus spectandum proponimus, vt finem & summam felicitatis suæ & salutis æternæ videant atq; intelligant. Ita verò demonstrat, libertatem illā dicendi, qua Euangelij præcones vtuntur, si rectè æstimetur, nemini molestam, sed ipsis quoq; auditoribus vtilem esse, qui per eam ad Christum adducuntur, vt in eo felicitatis veræ & æternæ participes fiant. Est præterea hoc non vulgare diuini fauoris argumentum, quòd aperte & libere per ministros suos ille nobiscum loquitur. Beati ergo qui patienter ferunt, & quæ dicuntur ad suam institutionem accommodant, vt in melius indies proficiant.
units.tr: By these words he also teaches how much better and happier the condition of Christians is under the New Testament than that of the Israelites under Moses. They needed a veil because they could not look upon the end of what was being abolished. This is said of the Law, which he had just said was to be abolished, and whose end, that is, its true and lawful use, the Israelites could not see or understand. Now the end of the Law is Christ, and therefore its use is to lead us to him, as a schoolmaster would, as is taught at length in the Epistle to the Galatians. But we (he says) behold Christ face to face, and set him forth without any covering for all to see, so that they may see and understand the goal and sum of their happiness and eternal salvation. In this way he shows that the freedom of speech which the heralds of the Gospel use, if it is rightly judged, is troublesome to no one, but is useful even to the hearers themselves, who through it are brought to Christ, so that they may become partakers in him of true and eternal happiness. Moreover, this is no common evidence of divine favour, that he speaks openly and freely with us through his ministers. Blessed, then, are those who bear patiently and apply to their own instruction what is said, so that they may make progress for the better day by day.

units.la: Cæterum non ideo solum tam diligenter de Mose & Legis ministerio disserit Paulus, vt ministerij Euangelici & Noui testamenti dignitatem supra illud extollat: sed simul aliud quoq; agit, quod non minoris erat momenti: Nam scandalum è medio tollit, quo nullum tunc erat nocentius, & quo fidei in Christum prædicatio magis impediretur. Erat hoc, quòd Iudæi, qui soli hucusque electus ille populus, Dei peculium & regnum illud sacerdotale fuerant, quosq; Moses solos gentem sapientem esse dixerat, quibus deniq; promissiones omnes datæ erant, Christum ex ipsis natum adeò non agnoscebant, vt potius eius prædicationi sese hostiliter opponerent: quod Corinthi quoque tanta cum improbitate factum fuisse Lucas scribit, vt Paulus pedum puluere in illos excussó, ad gentes se conuerteret. Eo certè cordatiores quique ita offendebantur, vt exististimarent, nimium imprudenter facere eos, qui abiecta patria & auita religione, eum vellent Redemptorem & Seruatorem suum profiteri, qui à propriis gentilibus fastidiretur. Vt ergo scandalum hoc remoueat Paulus, ostendit hanc Iudæorum contumaciam nonnouam aut prius inauditam, sed iam olim præsignificatam guratam esse: idq; per velamen illud Mosaicum docet, cuius mysterium omne diligentius explicat, sic dicens: Itaq; occalluerunt mentes eorum: Nam vsq; in hodiernum diem in lectione Veteris testamenti manet non retectum velamen illud, quod per Christum tollitur. Et mox amplius hoc exponens, per repetitionem addit: Quin ad hunc vsq; diem, cum legitur Moses, velamen cordi eorum impositum est: postquam autem conuersus fuerit ad Dominum, tolletur velamen. Quorum omnium hic sensus est: Non est, quod istorum hominum incredulitas & contumacia aliquem offendat. Si enim quod in Legis promulgatione (de cuius maiestate illi tantopere gloriantur) factum est, diligentius excutiamus, iam tunc caecitatis illius praeludium hoc fuisse patebit, quo Deus toti mundo declarare voluit, quale populi istius ingenium semper futurum esset, & quam infelix conditio. Dum enim Mosis faciem non potuerunt intueri, & proinde eam velo contegi oportuit, haud obscure significauit Deus, illos verum Legis sensum & vsum nunquam percepturos esse, sed potius sibi ipsis velum oppositurös, quo minus sub Legis inuolucris delitescentem Christum possint agnoscere. Et quod tunc obscurius adumbratum fuit, nunc reipsa fieri videtur. Manet enim velamen istud vsq; in hodiernum diem non retectum, quoties Vetus testamentum siue Lex istis hominibus recitatur. Unde vero hoc? Quia per solum Christum illud tollitur, qui sua luce Veteris testamenti vmbras discussit. Quem cum illi reiiciant, velum cordi ipsorum impositum manebit, quoad ad Christum conuersi, in eo verum & germanum Legis sensum atq; vsum videre poterunt. Quare ipsorum in Christo perseqvendo contumacia adeo neminem offendere debet, vt potius eorum exemplo territi illum amplecti & constanter retinere omnes debeant, ne quid simile cum Iudaeis patiantur.
units.tr: Paul does not discuss Moses and the ministry of the Law so carefully only to raise the dignity of the Gospel ministry and the New Testament above it. He also deals with something else, no less important: he removes a stumbling block, and none was then more harmful or more likely to hinder the preaching of faith in Christ. The stumbling block was this. The Jews, who alone had been God's chosen people until then, God's own possession and "kingdom of priests," the nation Moses called alone wise, and to whom all the promises had finally been given, did not acknowledge Christ born from among them. Instead they set themselves hostilely against his preaching. Luke writes that this happened at Corinth too, with such wickedness that Paul shook the dust from his feet against them and turned to the Gentiles. Indeed, the more thoughtful were offended and judged that those people acted very unwisely, abandoning their country and ancestral religion, when they wished to profess as their Redeemer and Saviour one whom his own countrymen despised. So that Paul may remove this stumbling block, he shows that this obstinacy of the Jews is neither new nor previously unheard of, but was foreshadowed long ago in a figure. He teaches this through the Mosaic veil, whose whole mystery he explains more carefully, saying: "Their minds were hardened; for to this day, when the Old Testament is read, the same veil remains unlifted, since it is taken away through Christ." Then, explaining this further, he adds by way of repetition: "Indeed, to this day, when Moses is read, a veil lies upon their heart; but when one turns to the Lord, the veil will be taken away." The sense of all this is: the unbelief and obstinacy of these men should not offend anyone. For if we examine carefully what happened when the Law was published (the majesty of which they boast about so greatly), it will be clear that this was a prelude to that blindness, by which God wished to show the whole world what the character of this people would always be, and how unhappy their condition. For since they could not look upon Moses' face, and therefore it had to be covered with a veil, God plainly signified that they would never perceive the true sense and use of the Law, but would rather place a veil before themselves, so that they could not recognise Christ hidden under the wrappings of the Law. What was then shadowed more obscurely is now seen to happen in fact. For the veil remains unlifted to this day whenever the Old Testament, or the Law, is read to these men. Why is this? Because it is taken away only by Christ, who by his light dispelled the shadows of the Old Testament. Since they reject him, the veil will remain on their heart; but once they have turned to Christ, they will be able to see in him the true and genuine sense and use of the Law. Therefore their obstinacy in persecuting Christ ought to offend no one. Rather, warned by their example, everyone should embrace him, hold fast to him constantly, and so avoid suffering anything like what the Jews suffered.

units.la: Porrò vt ista nostrae institutioni magis seruiant, diligentius paulo Iudaici populi conditio inspicienda erit. Fuit is (vt antea quoq; diximus) dilectus ille populus Dei, quem primogenitum suum vocat, & in quo cultus sui sedem constituerat. Imo vt olim illis solis Legem suam dedit, ita nostro adhuc seculo eos quasi depositarios & custodes oraculorum Dei esse videmus, sicuti Paulus quoq; ad Romanos fatetur. Nam Legis & prophetarum libros penes se habent, ijsdem suo exilio testimonium ferunt luculentum, simulq; eorum temeritatem coercent, quos non puderet Scripturas sacras corrumpere, nisi fraudem illam per Iudaeos argui & deprehendi posse scirent. Verumtamen neq; olim vetus illa dignitas illis profuit, neq; hodie eis prodest, quod in Mosis atq; Prophetarum scriptis dies noctesq; versantur. Olim enim cum Legem ipsis Deus daret, huius ex monte Sinai concionantis voce ferre non potuerunt. Idem Mosis faciem rutilantem timuerunt, vt eam velo contegi oporteret. At velum seruitutis quoq; symbolum antiquitus fuisse, in prioris epistolae capite vndecimo diximus. Itaq; ex Lege non aliud quam terrores & metum, adeoq; seruitutis spiritum retulerunt. Accessit his gratius malum, Excaecatio nimirum cum incurabili cordis indurratione coniuncta: qua factum est, vt in solam Legis literam intenti, nihil praeterea admiserunt, ex quo verum huius sensum atq; vsum addiscerent. Id vero illis exitium attulit, sicuti olim Isaias praedixerat. Nam causa fuit, quod partim suorum operum iustitiam ex Lege non intellecta statuerunt, partim ex ceremoniis legalibus impunitatem scelerum omnium sibi ipsis polliciti securè peccarunt, neq; vllis admonitionibus, imo ne correptionibus quidem, ad resipiscentiae studium adduci potuerunt. Imò dum veteres promissiones secundum literam modo intellexerunt, Christum sibi ipsis longè alium, quàm is reuera sit, finxere, & proinde eius humili specie offensi sunt, quo minus illum amplecterentur.
units.tr: Moreover, so that these matters may serve our instruction more fully, the condition of the Jewish people must be examined a little more carefully. That people (as we said before also) was the beloved people of God, whom he calls his firstborn, and in whom he had established the seat of his worship. Indeed, just as he once gave his Law to them alone, so even in our own age we see them as the depositaries and guardians of God's oracles, as Paul also confesses to the Romans. For they hold the books of the Law and the Prophets, they bear a clear testimony to the truth by their exile, and at the same time they restrain the rashness of those who would not be ashamed to corrupt the sacred Scriptures, did they not know that such fraud can be exposed and detected through the Jews. Yet that old dignity neither profited them then, nor does their day and night occupation with the writings of Moses and the Prophets profit them now. For when God gave them the Law, they could not bear the voice of him speaking from Mount Sinai. They feared the radiant face of Moses, so that it had to be covered with a veil. Moreover, we said in the eleventh chapter of the earlier epistle that the veil was also anciently a symbol of servitude. Thus from the Law they brought back nothing but terrors and fear, and so the spirit of bondage. A more serious evil was added to these: blindness, namely, joined with an incurable hardening of the heart. As a result, intent only on the letter of the Law, they admitted nothing else from which they might learn its true sense and use. This indeed brought ruin upon them, as Isaiah had foretold long before. For the cause was that, partly, they established a righteousness of their own works from the Law, which they did not understand, and partly, relying on the legal ceremonies, they promised themselves impunity for all their sins and sinned securely, and could not be brought to the zeal of repentance by any admonitions, or even by rebukes. Indeed, while they understood the ancient promises only according to the letter, they fashioned for themselves a Christ quite different from what he really is, and so they were offended by his humble appearance, so that they did not embrace him.

units.la: Quo exemplo admonemur, quàm periculosum atq; noxium sit, non rectè aestimare Dei beneficia, & neglecto germano verbi diuini sensu externis titulis confidere aut superbire. Quod enim Iudaeis olim accidit, hoc ipsum hodie multos pati videmus. Nam reuelat quidē toti mundo verbum suum Deus: multi vero de eius obscuritate, difficultate, & quod seipsos extricare nō possint queruntur. Unde autem hoc illis accidit? Quia ipsi oculis suis velum obtendunt, dum affectibus se duci patiuntur, & carnis suae rationes audiunt. Alij enim in Christo regnum terrenum, opes, honores, pacem huius mundi & otium quaerunt, vt olim discipuli quoq; fecerunt, neq; alium Christum animo concipiunt, quàm qualis Messias ille Iudaeorum est, quem infelices adhuc hodie expectant. Alij peccandi licentiam & impunitatem desiderant, & ad hanc Christi merito & fidei in illum professione
units.tr: From this example we are warned how dangerous and harmful it is not to judge God's benefits rightly, and, neglecting the genuine sense of the divine Word, to trust in or take pride in outward titles. For what happened once to the Jews, we see many suffering today. God indeed reveals his Word to the whole world, yet many complain of its obscurity and difficulty, and that they cannot disentangle themselves. But why does this happen to them? Because they themselves cover their eyes with a veil, while they allow themselves to be led by their passions and listen to the reasons of their flesh. For some seek in Christ an earthly kingdom, riches, honours, the peace and leisure of this world, as the disciples also once did, and they conceive of no other Christ than the kind of Messiah the Jews have, whom these unhappy people still await today. Others desire licence to sin and impunity, and by the merit of Christ and their profession of faith in him they

units.la: Iudaeorum infelix conditio.
units.tr: The unhappy condition of the Jews.

units.la: Proprij sensus fiducia noxia. non minus, quàm olim circumcisione & sacrificijs Iudæi, abuntur. Multi cum Euangelio veteres superstitiones coniungunt, & ita nouum illud vinum in vtres veteres recondunt, quibus non potest{} contineri. Alij doctrinæ veritatis traditiones humanas assuunt, quibus totam deformant, ipsi verò ambidextri fiunt, & in vtrumq; latus claudicant. Hinc ergo noua pro peccatis sacrificia prodeunt, hinc Diuorum intercessio & inuocatio nascitur, hinc purgatorium, indulgentiæ, sacra pro defunctis & sexcenta alia instituuntur, quæ singula IESV CHRISTI merito derogant, & religionem hominibus auaris atq; indoctis quæstum faciunt. Et isti quidem omnes, si quando admonentur, vt rectius sentiant, atq; aliter res suas instituant, non aliud quàm rationis humanæ argumenta nobis obijciunt, quibus addunt consuetudines, longi temporis præscriptionem, Regum potentissimorum exempla, Pontificum authoritatem, Conciliorum & Patrum decreta, victorias deniq;, quibus superstitiones quasi cœlitus confirmatas esse clamant. Atqui eadem ratione Neronis, Domitiani, Valeriani, Diocletiani & similium exempla adducere poterant, qui omnes Imperij maiestate & triumphis illustres fuerunt, Christi verò fidem hostiliter persecuti sunt. Et miror eos carnificum obluisci in hoc argumento, qui suam crudelitatem olim in sanctis Martyribus cum totius populi applausu exercuerunt. Ista ergo dum infelices illi vndique colligunt, non aliud quàm vela contexunt, quibus indies magis excæcati tandem in sua contumacia male pereant.
units.tr: The harmful trust in one's own judgement. They are no less deceived than the Jews once were by circumcision and sacrifices. Many join old superstitions to the Gospel, and so pour that new wine into old wineskins, which cannot hold it{} (as Christ says). Others stitch human traditions onto the teaching of truth, by which they disfigure the whole of it, and they themselves become ambidextrous and limp on both sides. From this come new sacrifices for sins; from this the intercession and invocation of the saints arise; from this purgatory, indulgences, masses for the dead and six hundred other things are instituted. Each of these detracts from the merit of Jesus Christ, and they make religion a source of profit for greedy and unlearned men. And all these people, whenever they are admonished to think more rightly and to order their affairs otherwise, bring against us nothing but arguments of human reason, to which they add custom, the prescription of long time, the examples of the most powerful kings, the authority of the Pontiffs, the decrees of Councils and Fathers, and finally victories, by which they cry out that their superstitions have been confirmed as if from heaven. Yet by the same reasoning they could cite the examples of Nero, Domitian, Valerian, Diocletian and the like, who were all illustrious for the majesty of their empire and their triumphs, but who hostilely persecuted the faith of Christ. And I marvel that they forget the executioners in this argument, who once carried out their cruelty against the holy martyrs to the applause of the whole people. Therefore, while those unhappy men gather these things from every side, they are doing nothing but weaving veils, by which, growing daily more blinded, they finally perish in their obstinacy.

units.la: Quid verò faciendum, ne quid huius nos quoq; patiamur? Docet hoc breui sententia Paulus, quando de Israelitico siue Iudaico populo dicit: Postquam conuersus fuerit ad Dominum, tolletur velamen. Conuenit hoc quoq; cū typo veteri. Moses enim quando à populo ad Dominum reuertebatur, velum deponere solebat: ita nimirum innuente Spiritu sancto, ipsos quoq; absque velo Legis sensum perspecturos esse, si se totos ad promissum patribus seruatorem, & æternum Dei Filium, IESVM CHRISTVM, conuertant. Et huc facit, quod in Lege illis Moses dixit: Diuijciet vos Dominus in populos, & reliqui eritis pauci numero in gentibus, ad quas vos Dominus ducet: seruietis ibi Diis, qui sunt opus manuum hominis, nempe ligno & lapidi, qui non vident, neq; audiunt, neq; comedunt, neq; odorantur. Inde tum quæres DOMINVM Deum tuum, atq; inuenies, siquidem eum inuestigaueris toto corde & toto animo tuo, &c. Et Paulus in epistola ad Romanos Iudæis in sola conuersione ad Christum spem salutis reliquam esse docet.
units.tr: What then must we do, lest we also suffer something of this kind? Paul teaches this in a brief saying, when he speaks of the Israelite or Jewish people: "When they shall turn to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away." This agrees also with the old type. For Moses, whenever he returned from the people to the Lord, used to lay aside the veil: the Holy Spirit thus signified, no doubt, that they too would perceive the meaning of the Law without a veil, if they turned themselves wholly to the Saviour promised to the fathers, the eternal Son of God, JESUS CHRIST. And to this purpose is what Moses said to them in the Law: "The Lord will scatter you among the peoples, and you will be left few in number among the nations to which the Lord shall lead you; there you will serve gods that are the work of human hands, namely wood and stone, which neither see nor hear, nor eat, nor smell. From there you will then seek the Lord your God, and you will find him, provided you search for him with all your heart and all your soul," etc. And Paul, in the epistle to the Romans, teaches that for the Jews the only hope of salvation remaining is in conversion to Christ alone.

units.la: Salus in sola conuersione ad Christum habetur.
units.tr: Salvation is had in conversion to Christ alone.
