units.la: Dominus verò Spiritus ille est: vbi autem Spiritus ille Domini, illic libertas. Nos autem omnes retecta facie gloriam Domini vt in speculo intuentes, in eandem imaginem transformamur ex gloria in gloriam, sicut à Domini spiritu.
units.tr: Now the Lord is that Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. But we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.

units.la: QVoniam homo natura sua ad malum proclivis est, iis etiam ad exitium suum abuti solet, quae saluti ipsius servire debebant. Exemplum huius rei memorabile in Iudaeis habemus. Elegerat hos ex omnibus aliis gentibus Deus, ut suum esset peculium, & ijsdem Legem dederat, quae & vitae morum, praecepta tradit, & omnia salutis aeternae mysteria continet. Et ne in externis caeremonijs servilius haerèrent, non modò promissiones olim patribus dederat de benedictione illo semine, in quo omnes gentes terrae benedici & servari oportebat: verumetiam postquam Legem promulgatam & externum cultum iam probè institutum, Moses illos ad Prophetam illum Magnum remiserat, quem audire debebant omnes, qui servari volunt: & quem non alium esse, quam IESVM CHRISTVM, Petrus & Stephanus Protomartyr docent. Quid vero illi? Promissionum veterum simul & admonitionis Mosaicae immemores, & in solam Legis literam intenti, neglecto eius sensu spirituali, qui ad Christum deducebat, totum Legis usum perverterunt. Quo factum est, ut extincta apud eos unici veri, Seruatoris cognitione, salutem in frigidissimis caeremonijs & suorum operum iustitia quaesiuerint, seque ipsos iustitia simul & omni salutis spe spoliarint, quam Deus in Filio suo, IESV CHRISTO, ipsis offerebat. Factum hoc est non modò Prophetarum tempore, quando omnia adhuc obscuriora & umbris involuta erant: verumetiam manifestato iam in carne Filio Dei, eum hoc nomine persecuti sunt, quod per eius doctrinam operum Legis iustitiam euerti, & salutis rationem tradi viderent longè alia ab ea, quam ipsi hactenus secuti fuerant. Et tanta erroris semel concepti vis fuit, ut inter eos quoque, vix omni studio & labore euelli potuerit, qui audito Euangelio, iam nomen Christo dederant. Nam ex his prodierunt, viuentibus adhuc Apostolis, qui Euangelio Legem miscebant, & operum iustitiam exigendo Ecclesias passim turbabant. Tales in Corinthiorum quoque Ecclesiam irrepserant, qui ut causam suam facilius obtinerent, Legem magnificè praedicabant, & indignissimum facinus esse clamabant, si ea aboleretur iam, quae olim tanta cum maiestate à Deo lata fuisset: simulque patrum exemplo nitebantur, qui omnes iam multis seculis sub illa vixissent & servati essent. Diligenter ergo hanc causam agit Paulus, & nuper quidem longè maiorem Euangelij gloriam & dignitatem esse ostendit, neque aliquem hic patrum exemplo defendi posse, quando ne hi quidem per Legis opera servati, in illis autem praefigurata sit exaecatio illa & contumax incredulitas, quae hodie adhuc in posteris eorum conspiciatur. Id nunc amplius illustrat, simulque docet, quanto felicior sit fidelium Christi conditio, qui per Euangelij praedicationem illuminati sunt, quam veterum qui sub Mose & Legis disciplina vixerunt.
units.tr: Because man by nature is inclined to evil, he is accustomed to abuse even those things that ought to serve his own salvation. We have a memorable example of this in the Jews. God had chosen them from all the other nations to be his own peculiar people, and had given them the Law, which both prescribes the precepts of a moral life and contains all the mysteries of eternal salvation. And so that they would not cling too slavishly to the outward ceremonies, God had not only long ago given the fathers promises about that blessing seed through whom all the nations of the earth were to be blessed and saved. Moreover, after the Law had been promulgated and the outward worship duly instituted, Moses had also sent them on to that great Prophet, whom all who wish to be saved ought to hear, and who, as Peter and Stephen the first martyr teach, is none other than Jesus Christ. But what did they do? Forgetful both of the ancient promises and of the admonition of Moses, and intent only on the letter of the Law, they neglected its spiritual sense, which leads to Christ, and so perverted the whole use of the Law. As a result, the knowledge of the one true Saviour was extinguished among them, and they sought salvation in the coldest ceremonies and in the righteousness of their own works. In doing so they deprived themselves both of righteousness and of every hope of salvation, which God offered them in his Son, Jesus Christ. This happened not only in the time of the Prophets, when everything was still more obscure and wrapped in shadows, but also after the Son of God had been manifested in the flesh. They persecuted him under this charge: that through his teaching they saw the righteousness of the works of the Law overthrown, and a way of salvation taught that was quite different from the one they had followed until then. And so strong was the force of an error once conceived that it could scarcely be uprooted, even by every effort and labour, among those too who, having heard the Gospel, had already given their name to Christ. For from these there arose, while the Apostles were still living, men who mixed the Law with the Gospel and, by demanding the righteousness of works, everywhere disturbed the Churches. Such men had crept also into the Church of the Corinthians. To win their cause more easily, they praised the Law extravagantly and cried out that it would be a most shameful deed if that which God had once given with such majesty were now abolished. At the same time they relied on the example of the fathers, who had all lived under it for many centuries and had been saved. Paul therefore treats this cause carefully. First he shows that the glory and dignity of the Gospel is far greater, and that no one can here be defended by the example of the fathers, since not even they were saved by the works of the Law, and since in them was foreshadowed that blindness and obstinate unbelief which can still be seen today in their descendants. Now he illustrates this more fully, and at the same time teaches how much happier is the condition of the faithful in Christ, who have been enlightened through the preaching of the Gospel, than that of the ancients who lived under Moses and the discipline of the Law.

units.la: Sunt autem nonnulla ex ijs, quae nuper dixit, repetenda. Illic inter alia uno verbo respondet ineptis & superstitiosis Legis admiratoribus, qui in eius litera pertinacius haerebant: Littera occidit, Spiritus viuificat. Vt ergo constet, quis nam sit Spiritus ille viuificans, in praesenti ait: Dominus vero Spiritus ille est. Quasi diceret: Dixi, nos Apostolos non literae, sed Spiritus ministros esse, & ita omnino fieri oportere, quia littera occidat, Spiritus autem viuificet. Vt ergo rem dilucidius expediam, & ne quid haereatis, Spiritum illum, cuius ministri sumus, ipsum Dominum IESVM CHRISTVM esse dico. Is literam Legis, adeoque Legem totam viuificat, si quis ad illum omnia referat, aut hunc in illam inferat. Dicitur autem Christus Spiritus Legis, quia ipse nos à damnatione Legis liberatos in vitam nouam restituit. Deinde, quia Legi, quae per carnem nostram infirmatur, ut nos seruare nequeat, ipse succurrit dum sua obedientia id sarcit, quod in nobis desiderabatur, imò quod nobis praestitu erat impossibile. Ita hoc mysterium Paulus ipse exponit, ad Romanos sic scribens: Siquidem cum impotens esset Lex, eò quod nihil posset in carne, Deus suo ipsius Filio misso in similitudine carnis peccato obnoxiae, etiam de peccato condemnauit peccatum in carne, ut ius illud Legis compleatur in nobis. Quo etiam referri potest, quòd chirographum Legis, quo nos damnabamur, cruci affixum proprio sanguine deleuisse scribitur, adeò ut iam nulla condemnatio illis timenda sit, qui ipsi per fidem veram sunt insiti. Et huc facit etiam, quod in praesenti addit: Vbi autem Spiritus ille Domini, illic libertas, scilicet à metu siue terrore Legis, peccati, damnationis & mortis. Cur enim peccati seruus posthac dicatur, cuius iustitia Christus est? Cur damnetur is, quem Dei Filius, cui omne iudicium à Patre datum est, absoluit? Cur mortem timeat, aut huic obnoxius dicatur is, cuius vita in Christo est non minus, quàm olim circumcisione & sacrificijs Iudæi, abutuntur. Multi cum Euangelio veteres res superstitiones coniungunt, & ita nouum illud vinum in vtres veteres recondunt, quibus non potes{ } contineri. Alij doctrinæ veritatis traditiones humanas affuunt, quibus totam deformant, ipsi verò ambidextri fiunt, & in vtrumq; latus claudicant. Hinc ergo noua pro peccatis sacrificia prodeunt, hinc Diuorum intercessio & inuocatio nascitur, hinc purgatoriũ, indulgentiæ, sacra pro defunctis & sexcenta alia instituuntur, quæ singula IESV CHRISTI merito derogant, & religionem hominibus auaris atq; indoctis quæstum faciunt. Et isti quidem omnes, si quando admonentur, vt rectius sentiant, atq; aliter res suas instituant, non aliud quàm rationis humanæ argumenta nobis obijciunt, quibus addunt consuetudines, longi temporis præscriptionem, Regum potentissimorum exempla, Pontificum authoritatem, Conciliorum & Patrum decreta, victorias deniq;, quibus superstitiones quasi cœlitus confirmatas esse clamant. Atqui eadem ratione Neronis, Domitiani, Valeriani, Diocletiani & similium exempla adducere poterant, qui omnes Imperij maiestate & triumphis illustres fuerunt, Christi verò fidem hostiliter persecuti sunt. Et miror eos carnificum obluisci in hoc argumento, qui suam crudelitatem olim in sanctis Martyribus cum totius populi applausu exercuerunt. Ista ergo dum infelices illi vndique colligunt, non aliud quàm vela contexunt, quibus indies magis excæcati tandem in sua contumacia male pereant.
units.tr: Some of the things he said recently must be repeated. There, among other things, he answers in a single phrase those foolish and superstitious admirers of the Law who clung more stubbornly to its letter: "The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life." So that it may be clear who that life-giving Spirit is, he says in the present passage: "Now the Lord is that Spirit." As if he were saying: I have said that we Apostles are ministers not of the letter but of the Spirit, and that it must be so, because the letter kills but the Spirit gives life. So that I may explain the matter more clearly, and so that you may not be puzzled, I say that the Spirit whose ministers we are is the Lord Jesus Christ himself. He gives life to the letter of the Law, and so to the whole Law, if anyone refers everything to him, or reads him into it. Christ is called the Spirit of the Law because he himself, having freed us from the condemnation of the Law, restores us to a new life. Again, the Law, which is weakened through our flesh so that it cannot save us, is helped by Christ himself, who by his obedience makes good what was lacking in us, indeed what was impossible for us to supply. Paul himself explains this mystery, writing thus to the Romans: "For what the Law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh, that the righteousness of the Law might be fulfilled in us." To this can also be referred what is written, that he nailed to the cross, by his own blood, the handwriting of the Law by which we were condemned, so that no condemnation is now to be feared by those who have been grafted into him through true faith. To this also belongs what he adds here: "Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty," namely liberty from the fear or terror of the Law, of sin, of condemnation and of death. For why should he any longer be called a slave of sin whose righteousness is Christ? Why should he be condemned whom the Son of God, to whom all judgement has been given by the Father, absolves? Why should he fear death, or be called liable to it, whose life is in Christ? The Jews once abused circumcision and sacrifices no less than many now abuse the Gospel. Many join old superstitions to the Gospel and so pour the new wine into old wineskins, which cannot hold it. Others add human traditions to the teaching of truth, by which they deform the whole of it, and themselves become ambidextrous, limping on both sides. From here arise new sacrifices for sins; from here are born the intercession and invocation of the saints; from here are instituted purgatory, indulgences, masses for the dead and six hundred other things, each of which detracts from the merit of Jesus Christ and makes a trade of religion for greedy and ignorant men. And all these men, whenever they are admonished to think more rightly and to order their affairs otherwise, object to us nothing but arguments of human reason. To these they add custom, the prescription of long time, the examples of most powerful kings, the authority of Popes, the decrees of Councils and of the Fathers, and finally victories, by which they cry out that their superstitions have been confirmed as if from heaven. Yet by the same reasoning they could cite the examples of Nero, Domitian, Valerian, Diocletian and others like them, all of whom were famous for the majesty of their empire and their triumphs, yet who hostilely persecuted the faith of Christ. I am amazed that they forget the executioners in this argument, who once carried out their cruelty against the holy martyrs to the applause of the whole people. Therefore, while those wretched men gather these things from every side, they are doing nothing but weaving veils, by which, growing ever more blinded day by day, they will at last perish miserably in their obstinacy.

units.la: Quid verò faciendũ, ne quid huius nos quoq; patiamur? Docet hoc breui sententia Paulus, quando de Israelitico siue Iudaico populo dicit: Postquam conuersus fuerit ad Dominũ, tolletur velamen. Conuenit hoc quoq; cũ typo veteri. Moses enim quando à populo ad Dominũ reuertebatur, velum deponere solebat: ita nimirum innuente Spiritu sancto, ipsos quoq; absque velo Legis sensum perspecturos esse, si se totos ad promissum patribus seruatorem, & æternum Dei Filium, IESVM CHRISTVM, conuertant. Et huc facit, quod in Lege illis Moses dixit: Disijciet vos Dominus in populos, & reliqui eritis pauci numero in gentibus, ad quas vos Dominus ducet: seruietisq; ibi Diis, qui sunt opus manuum hominis, nempe ligno & lapidi, qui non vident, neq; audiunt, neq; comedunt, neq; odorantur. Inde tum quæres DOMINVM Deum tuum, atq; inuenies, siquidem eum inuestigaueris toto corde & toto animo tuo, &c. Et Paulus in epistola ad Romanos Iudæis in sola conuersione ad Christum spem salutis reliquam esse docet. Etenim vt probè obseruauit Chrysostomus ea est Legis conditio, vt si ab ea recedas ad Christum, tunc illius sensum verum videre, eamq; tibi salutarem facere possis: sin verò relicto Christo illius literæ intentus in ea sola hæreas, ne ipsam quidem intelliges, & proinde per eam impedieris potius quàm iuuabe-ris. Debet hoc ipsum nostris quoq; hominibus aptari. Nec enim errorum & superstitionum nocen-tissimarum finis erit, donec relictis omnibus aliis figmentis, ad Christum conuersi hunc vnum respiciant, vnum hunc audiant, & in illo solo per fidem veram acquiescant. Ita videbunt, illum non opes & huius seculi regna, sed cœlestia bona & æternæ salutis thesauros nobis largiri: eidem quoq; omnem deberi nostræ salutis gloriam: neq; per illius meritum peccandi licentiam & impunitatem inuehi, sed potius argui scelerum atrocitatem. Iidem non mouebuntur etiam porrò hominum authoritate, consuetudine, victorijs, quando omnibus his Christum præstare vident, qui in ipso mundi exordio promissus, in hunc usq; diem Ecclesiam suam defendit, & omnibus seculis per crucem de hostibus suis triumphauit. Istis ergo intenti Deum assiduè precemur, vt is procul amoto carnis & cogitationum carnalium velo, faciem Filij sui IESV CHRISTI nobis retegat, in qua vna salus & bonorum omnium satietas inueniri potes{ }. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: But what must be done, so that we ourselves do not suffer any of this? Paul teaches this in a brief sentence, when he speaks of the Israelite or Jewish people: "When they shall have turned to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away." This agrees also with the old type. For Moses, whenever he returned from the people to the Lord, used to put off the veil. The Holy Spirit thus signified that they too would perceive the sense of the Law without a veil, if they turned wholly to the Saviour promised to the fathers, the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ. To this also belongs what Moses said to them in the Law: "The Lord shall scatter you among the peoples, and you shall be left few in number among the nations to which the Lord shall lead you. There you shall serve gods, the work of men's hands, namely wood and stone, which neither see nor hear, neither eat nor smell. But from there you shall seek the Lord your God, and you shall find him, if you seek him with all your heart and all your soul," and so on. And Paul, in his Epistle to the Romans, teaches that for the Jews the only remaining hope of salvation lies in conversion to Christ. For, as Chrysostom rightly observed, the condition of the Law is this: if you turn away from it to Christ, then you can see its true sense and make it salutary for yourself; but if, having left Christ, you cling only to its letter, you will not even understand it, and so you will be hindered by it rather than helped. The same must be applied to our own people. There will be no end to errors and most harmful superstitions until, having turned to Christ and set aside all other fictions, they look to him alone, hear him alone, and rest in him alone through true faith. Then they will see that he bestows upon us not the riches and kingdoms of this age, but heavenly goods and the treasures of eternal salvation; that the glory of our salvation is due to him alone; and that through his merit no licence to sin and no impunity is introduced, but rather the atrocity of wickedness is condemned. Such men will not be moved any further by the authority of men, by custom, or by victories, since they see that Christ surpasses all these things, he who was promised at the very beginning of the world, who to this day defends his Church, and who in every age has triumphed over his enemies through the cross. Intent on these things, then, let us pray constantly to God that, having removed far away the veil of the flesh and of carnal thoughts, he may unveil for us the face of his Son Jesus Christ, in whom alone salvation and the fulness of all good things is to be found. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XIV.

units.la: Dominus verò Spiritus ille est: vbi autem Spiritus ille Domini, illic libertas. Nos autem omnes retecta facie gloriam Domini vt in speculo intuentes, in eandem imaginem transformamur ex gloria in gloriam, sicut à Domini spiritu.
units.tr: Now the Lord is that Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. But we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.

units.la: QVoniam homo natura sua ad malum proclivis est, ijs etiam ad exitium suum abuti solet, quæ saluti ipsius seruire debebant. Exemplum huius rei memorabile in Iudæis habemus. Elegerat hos ex omnibus alijs gentibus Deus, vt suum esset peculium, & ijsdem Legem dederat, quæ & vitæ morum, præcepta tradit, & omnia salutis æternæ mysteria continet. Et ne in externis ceremonijs seruilius hærerent, non modò promissiones olim patribus dederat de benedictio illo semine, in quo omnes gentes terræ benedici & seruari oporteat: verumetiam postea Legem promulgatam & externum cultum iam probè institutum, Moses illos ad Prophetam illum Magnum remiserat, quem audire debeant omnes, qui seruari vDelint: & quem non alium esse, quàm IESVM CHRISTVM, Petrus & Stephanus Protomartyr docent. Quid verò illi? Promissionum veterum simul & admonitionis Mosaicæ immemores, & in solam Legis literam intenti, neglecto eius sensu spirituali, qui ad Christum deducebat, totum Legis vsum peruerterunt. Quo factum est, vt extincta apud eos vnici veri, Seruatoris cognitione, salutem in frigidissimis ceremonijs & suorum operum iustitia quæsiuerint, seq; ipsos iustitia simul & omni salutis spe spoliarint, quam Deus in Filio suo, IESV CHRISTO, ipsis offerebat. Factum hoc est non modò Prophetarum tempore, quando omnia adhuc obscuriora & vmbris inuoluta erant: verumetiam manifestato iam in carne Filio Dei, eum hoc nomine persecuti sunt, quòd per eius doctrinam operum Legis iustitiam euerti, & salutis rationem tradi viderent longè alia ab ea, quam ipsi hactenus secuti fuerant. Et tanta erroris semel concepti vis fuit, vt inter eos quoq; vix omni studio & labore euelli potuerit, qui audito Euangelio, iam nomen Christo dederant. Nam ex his prodierunt, viuentibus adhuc Apostolis, qui Euangelio Legem miscebant, & operum iustitiam exigendo Ecclesias passim turbabant. Tales in Corinthiorum quoque Ecclesiam irrepserant, qui vt causam suam facilius obtinerent, Legem magnificè prædicabant, & indignissimum faciunt esse clamabant, si ea aboleretur iam, quæ olim tanta cum maiestate à Deo lata fuisset: simulq; patrum exemplo nitebantur, qui omnes iam multis seculis sub illa vixissent & seruati essent. Diligenter ergo hanc causam agit Paulus, & nuper quidem longè maiorem Euangelij gloriam & dignitatem esse ostendit, neq; aliquem hic patrum exemplo defendi posse, quando nec hi quidem per Legis opera seruati, in illis autem præfigurata sit excæcatio illa & contumax incredulitas, quæ hodie adhuc in posteris eorum conspiciatur. Id nunc amplius illustrat, simulq; docet, quanto felicior sit fidelium Christi conditio, qui per Euangelij prædicationem illuminati sunt, quàm veterum qui sub Mose & Legis disciplina vixerunt.
units.tr: Because man is by nature inclined to evil, he is accustomed to abuse even those things which ought to serve his salvation. We have a memorable example of this in the Jews. God had chosen them out of all other nations to be his own peculiar people, and had given them a Law which both sets out the precepts of moral life and contains all the mysteries of eternal salvation. And lest they cling too slavishly to the external ceremonies, he not only had long before given the fathers promises about that blessed seed in whom all the nations of the earth ought to be blessed and saved; but also, after the Law had been promulgated and the external worship had been properly instituted, Moses had sent them on to that great Prophet, whom all who wish to be saved ought to hear, and whom Peter and Stephen the first martyr teach to be none other than Jesus Christ. But what did they do? Forgetful of the ancient promises and of the admonition of Moses, and intent only on the letter of the Law, they neglected its spiritual sense, which led to Christ, and perverted the whole use of the Law. As a result, with the knowledge of the one true Saviour extinguished among them, they sought salvation in the coldest ceremonies and in the righteousness of their own works, and so deprived themselves both of righteousness and of every hope of salvation, which God was offering them in his Son, Jesus Christ. This happened not only in the time of the Prophets, when all things were still more obscure and wrapped in shadows; but also, after the Son of God had been manifested in the flesh, they persecuted him on this account: that they saw his teaching overthrowing the righteousness of the works of the Law and setting forth a way of salvation quite different from the one they had followed hitherto. And so strong was the force of this error once conceived that it could scarcely be uprooted, even with every zeal and effort, among those who, having heard the Gospel, had already given their names to Christ. For from these there arose, while the Apostles were still living, men who mixed the Law with the Gospel and, by demanding the righteousness of works, everywhere disturbed the churches. Such men had also crept into the church of the Corinthians, who, to win their cause more easily, extolled the Law magnificently and cried out that it was most unworthy to abolish now what had once been given by God with such majesty; at the same time they relied on the example of the fathers, who had all lived under it for many centuries and had been saved. Paul therefore handles this matter carefully, and has just shown that the glory and dignity of the Gospel are far greater, and that no one can here be defended by the example of the fathers, since these too were not saved by the works of the Law, and since in them was prefigured that blindness and stubborn unbelief which is still seen today among their descendants. He now illustrates this more fully, and at the same time teaches how much happier is the condition of the faithful in Christ, who have been enlightened through the preaching of the Gospel, than that of the ancients who lived under Moses and the discipline of the Law.

units.la: Sunt autem nonnulla ex ijs, quæ nuper dixit, repetenda. Illic inter alia vno verbo respondet ineptis & superstitiosis Legis admiratoribus, qui in eius litera pertinacius hærebant: Littera occidit, Spiritus viuificat. Vt ergo constet, quis nam sit Spiritus ille viuificans, in præsenti ait: Dominus verò Spiritus ille est. Quasi diceret: Dixi, nos Apostolos non litera, sed Spiritus ministros esse, & ita omnino fieri oportere, quia litera occidat, Spiritus autem viuificet. Vt ergo rem dilucidius expediam, & ne quid hæreatis, Spiritum illum, cuius ministri sumus, ipsum Dominum IESVM CHRISTVM esse dico. Is literam Legis, adeoq; Legem totam viuificat, si quis ad illum omnia referat, aut hunc in illam inferat. Dicitur autem Christus Spiritus Legis, quia ipse nos à damnatione Legis liberatos in vitam nouam restituit. Deinde, quia Legi, quæ per carnem nostram infirmatur, vt nos seruare nequeat, ipse succurrit dum sua obedientia id farcit, quod in nobis desiderabatur, imò quod nobis præstitu erat impossibile. Ita hoc mysterium Paulus ipse exponit, ad Romanos sic scribens: Siquidem cum impotens esset Lex, eò quòd nihil posset in carne, Deus suo ipsius Filio misso in similitudine carnis peccato obnoxiæ, etiam de peccato condemnauit peccatum in carne, vt ius illud Legis compleatur in nobis. Quo etiam referri potest, quòd chirographum Legis, quo nos damnabamur, cruci affixum proprio sanguine deleuisse scribitur, adeò vt iam nulla condemnatio illis timenda sit, qui ipsi per fidem veram sunt insiti. Et huc facit etiam, quod in præsenti addit: Vbi autem Spiritus ille Domini, illic libertas, scilicet à metu siue terrore Legis, peccati, damnationis & mortis. Cur enim peccati seruus posthac dicatur, cuius iustitia Christus est? Cur damnetur is, quem Dei Filius, cui omne iudicium à Patre datum est, absoluit? Cur mortem timeat, aut huic obnoxius dicatur is, cuius vita in Christo est
units.tr: Some of the points he has just made must, however, be repeated. There, among other things, he answers in a single word those foolish and superstitious admirers of the Law who clung more obstinately to its letter: "The letter kills, the Spirit gives life." So that it may be clear who that life-giving Spirit is, he says now: "Now the Lord is that Spirit." As if he said: I have said that we Apostles are ministers not of the letter but of the Spirit, and that it must necessarily be so, because the letter kills but the Spirit gives life. So that I may explain the matter more clearly, and that you may not be in doubt, I say that the Spirit whose ministers we are is the Lord Jesus Christ himself. He gives life to the letter of the Law, and so to the whole Law, if anyone refers all things to him, or reads him into it. Christ is called the Spirit of the Law because he himself, having freed us from the condemnation of the Law, restores us to a new life. Next, because he comes to the aid of the Law, which is weakened through our flesh and cannot save us, and by his obedience supplies what was lacking in us, indeed what was impossible for us to supply. Paul himself explains this mystery in this way, writing to the Romans: "For since the Law was powerless, in that it could do nothing through the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh even concerning sin, so that the righteousness of the Law might be fulfilled in us." To this also may be referred what is written, that he blotted out with his own blood the handwriting of the Law, by which we were condemned, fastening it to the cross, so that now no condemnation is to be feared by those who have been grafted into him through true faith. And to this bears also what he adds now: "And where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty", namely liberty from the fear or terror of the Law, of sin, of condemnation and of death. For how can someone be called a slave of sin from now on, when his righteousness is Christ? How can he be condemned whom the Son of God, to whom all judgment has been given by the Father, absolves? How can he fear death, or be called subject to it, whose life is hidden in Christ?

units.la: Spiritus Legis est Christus.
units.tr: The Spirit of the Law is Christ.

units.la: Rom. 8.
units.tr: Rom. 8.

units.la: Colos. 2. abscondita? Videtur autem in præsenti hanc particulam ijs opponere, quæ ruper de velo Mosis & Iudæorum, quod seruitutis symbolum fuit, dixerat. Itaq; docere vult, quòd vbi Christus nobis illucescit, tunc hominum mentes illuminentur, vt se in libertatem Filiorum Dei translatos esse sentiant, & proinde Spiritu adoptionis donati non amplius ex seruili metu, sed voluntarij & alacri animo Deo seruiant: qualem fore Christi populum, olim Dauid prædixit.
units.tr: Col. 2. Yet in the present passage he seems to set this clause against what he said just before about the veil of Moses, which was a symbol of servitude. So he wishes to teach that where Christ shines upon us, the minds of men are enlightened, so that they feel themselves translated into the liberty of the sons of God; and therefore, endowed with the Spirit of adoption, they no longer serve God out of servile fear, but with a willing and cheerful mind, as Christ's people was once foretold by David.

units.la: Itaq; facit locus iste ad explicationem locorum, in quibus Lex magnificè prædicatur, sicuti nuper quædam ex Psalmo 19. adduximus: vbi animam conuertere, imperitis sapientiam submistrare, cor exhilarare, oculos item illuminare dicitur. Ista enim tunc præstat, quando per Christum animatur, qui eius finis, impletio & vita est. Quòd si hunc ab ea remoueas, tunc non aliud agit, quàm quòd peccatum arguit, accusat, concupiscentias in carne latentes irritat, mortis reos agit, condemnat, terret deniq; & in angustias extremas adducit, vt cum Paulo cogamur clamare: Miserum me, quis me liberabit ex corpore mortis huius? Rom.7.
units.tr: Hence this passage serves to explain the places in which the Law is magnificently praised, as we lately quoted from Psalm 19, where it is said to convert the soul, to give wisdom to the simple, to gladden the heart, and likewise to enlighten the eyes. For it does these things when it is quickened by Christ, who is its end, fulfilment and life. But if you remove him from it, then it does nothing other than convict of sin, accuse, stir up the lusts lying hidden in the flesh, hold men guilty of death, condemn, finally terrify and bring them into the utmost straits, so that with Paul we are compelled to cry out: "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?" Rom. 7.

units.la: Docemur itaq; horum consideratione, quæ nam vera libertas sit, ad quam omnes homines aspirare debent: Ea nimirum, quæ in vno vindice & seruatore nostro IESV CHRISTO, habetur. Hic solus peccati nexus dissoluit: Solus ex diaboli tyrannide & seruitio tristi asseruit: mortem deuicit vnà cum eo qui mortis habebat imperium. Solus item Spiritu adoptionis donat, & ex seruis peccati filios Dei facit. Deniq; vs est, de quo verissimè Paulus alibi pronuntiauit: Per hunc vobis remissio peccatorum annuntiatur, & ab omnibus, à quibus non potuistis per Legem Mosis absolui, per hunc omnis qui credit absoluitur. Ideo ipse in Euangelio dicebat: Si Filius vos liberauerit, verè liberi eritis. Ioan.8.
units.tr: We are taught by considering these things what true liberty is, to which all men ought to aspire: namely that which is had in our one deliverer and saviour, Jesus Christ. He alone loosens the bonds of sin; he alone has rescued us from the tyranny of the devil and from sad servitude; together with him who held the power of death he has conquered death. He alone also bestows the Spirit of adoption, and from slaves of sin makes us sons of God. Finally, he is the one of whom Paul most truly declared elsewhere: "Through him forgiveness of sins is announced to you, and from all those things from which you could not be absolved by the Law of Moses, through him everyone who believes is absolved." In the Gospel, too, he himself said: "If the Son shall set you free, you will be truly free." John 8.

units.la: Euertuntur ergo huius loci authoritate omnes superstitiones, & omnes cultus arbitrarij (quas ἐθελοθρησκείας Græci vocant) ab hominibus confictî & instituti, vt per eos peccatorum remissionem & vitam æternam consequantur. Quia enim libertas in solo Christo habetur, vtiq; adhuc peccati & diaboli mancipia sunt, quicunq; illum nondum apprehenderunt, qualiacunq; alia illa sint hominum iudicio, quibus occupantur. Quid, quòd ijdem fere hominum superstitiosissimorum, imò auarissimorum, aut ventris gulæq; mancipiorum serui sunt vilissimi? Nec enim eorum modò decretis omnibus, vel somnijs potius, obedire, verumetiam eosdem alere, imò saginare, imò diuites facere coguntur. Sic olim Baalis sacerdotü seruus fuit Achab, qui Eliam regni turbatorem iniustè vocabat. Et quàm turpem atq; infelicem tā animæ quàm corporis seruitutem seruiant viri principes, qui Romanis Pontificibus obedire & ab eor u nutu toti pendere solent, vel cæcus videat. Nam ad pedū osculā cernui procumbunt, equū ascensuris ipsi stapedes tenent, prandentibus & cœnantibus ministrant, ex illorum arbitrio bella suscipiunt & gerunt: imò in suæ fidei commissum populum sæuiunt, si ita iubeant Pontifices. Idem deniq; impuris sacrificis & indo Eis monachis peccata sua in aurem confitentur, ijsdem arcana quoq; consilia credunt, & quàmuis Reges atq; Imperatores ab hoc hominum genere non semel proditos esse norint, eorū tamen dolos cauere neq; possunt, neq; volunt. Nec est, quòd obedientiam ista Deo probari putent, idq; tunc in primis, si ieiunijs, cilicijs aliisq; exercitijs superstitiosis sese macerent. Sunt enim hæc illorū opera omnia mortua, cum absq; fide fiant: & proinde neq; Deoplacere, neq; ijs à quibus fiunt, vitā conferre possunt. Si enim ab ipso Deo lata Lex mortua est & occidit, nisi per Christi Spiritum viuifice tur, quanto magis illud de hominū figmentis sentire debemus, quæ Deus iā olim toties damnauit?
units.tr: By the authority of this passage, therefore, all superstitions are overthrown, and all arbitrary worships (which the Greeks call ethelothreskeias [ἐθελοθρησκείας], self-chosen worship) devised and instituted by men, so that through them they may obtain forgiveness of sins and eternal life. For since liberty is had in Christ alone, certainly all those who have not yet laid hold of him are still slaves of sin and of the devil, whatever other things they are occupied with, however they may seem in the judgment of men. What of the fact that they are very often the most abject slaves of the most superstitious, indeed the most avaricious men, or of the slaves of their belly and throat? For they are compelled not only to obey all their decrees, or rather their dreams, but also to feed them, indeed to fatten them, indeed to make them rich. So once Ahab was a slave of the priests of Baal, who unjustly called Elijah the troubler of the kingdom. And how shameful and unhappy a servitude of both soul and body the princes serve, who are accustomed to obey the Roman pontiffs and to depend wholly on their nod, even a blind man can see. For they bow down with their faces to the ground to kiss their feet; when they are about to mount a horse they hold the stirrups for them; they wait on them at dinner and supper; by their judgment they undertake and wage wars; indeed they rage against the people committed to their trust, if the pontiffs so command. Finally, the same princes confess their sins in the ear of impure priests and of the Indian monks, trust them with their secret counsels, and although kings and emperors have known more than once that they have been betrayed by this class of men, they can neither guard against their deceits nor wish to. Nor is there any reason why they should think that such obedience is pleasing to God, especially if they weary themselves with fasts, hair shirts and other superstitious exercises. For all these works of theirs are dead, since they are done without faith; and therefore they can neither please God nor bring life to those by whom they are done. For if the Law itself, given by God, is dead and kills, unless it is quickened by the Spirit of Christ, how much more ought we to think this of the inventions of men, which God has already so often condemned?

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui hoc libertatis per Christum nobis partæ beneficium exemplo communi Christianorum illustrat, eaq; occasione docet, quanto præstantior & beatior sit hominum conditio, quàm illorum, qui olim sub Mose fuerunt. Nos autem omnes (inquit) retectâ facie gloriam Domini vt in speculo intuentes, in eandem imaginem transformamur ex gloria in gloriam, sicut à Domini Spiritu. Scio aliquos ista de solis Euangelij administris exponere, sed vt supra de Israelitis omnibus narrauit, quæ horum sub Mose conditio fuerit: ita hic in omnium fidelium Christi persona loquitur, vt quantum ista Iudæis præstent, doceat. Itaque hic verborum istorum sensus est: Si durum aut mirum alicui videtur, libertatem illam certam & salutis fiduciam ad vnum Christum astringere, cogitate quæso diligentius, quæ veteris populi conditio fuerit. Olim solus Moses ingrediebatur nubem, vt cum Domino colloqueretur, & gloriæ eius con-spectu frucspectu frueretur. At nunc Patre nobis per Christum placato, omnes credentes in illius conspectum admittuntur, & liberum tutumq; habent ad thronum gratiæ accessum, deinde vulgus Israelitarum ne Mosis quidem splendorem ferre potuit: At nobis licet facie retecta & ab omni velamine liberata ad Deum ipsum appropinquare, & clamare, Abba pater. Præterea solius Mosis facies splendorem illum & cœlestis lucis radios ex colloquio familiari cum Deo concepit: At nos simul omnes gloriam Domini ceu in speculo intuentes, in eandem gloriam transformamur ex gloria in gloriam, sicut à Spiritu Domini, id est, Dei Spiritu hoc in nobis agente, qui suam virtutem aperte & euidenter in nobis transformandis exerit. Continet locus hic omnia, aut saltem præcipua Christianæ doctrinæ & salutis humanæ mysteria, & non sine dulcissima consolatione eam dignitatem & gloriam exponit, quæ nobis per meritum IESV CHRISTI parta est, ideoq; singulæ partes propius excuti debent.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who illustrates this benefit of liberty won for us through Christ by the common example of Christians, and on that occasion teaches how much more excellent and blessed the condition of men is than that of those who lived under Moses. "But we all," he says, "with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord." I know that some expound these words only of the ministers of the Gospel. But just as above he described what the condition of all Israelites under Moses was, so here he speaks in the person of all faithful believers in Christ, to show how much these things surpass the Jews. So the sense of his words is this: if it seems hard or strange to anyone that this sure liberty and confidence of salvation is bound to Christ alone, consider more carefully, I beg you, what the condition of the old people was. Formerly Moses alone entered the cloud to speak with the Lord and enjoyed the sight of his glory. But now, with the Father reconciled to us through Christ, all believers are admitted into his presence, and have free and safe access to the throne of grace. Moreover, the common crowd of Israelites could not even bear the brightness of Moses; but we, with face uncovered and freed from every veil, may draw near to God himself and cry, "Abba, Father." Furthermore, the face of Moses alone took on that brightness and the rays of heavenly light from familiar converse with God; but we all together, beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same glory, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord, that is, by the Spirit of God working this in us, who displays his power openly and plainly in transforming us. This passage contains all, or at least the principal, mysteries of Christian doctrine and of human salvation, and it sets forth, not without the sweetest consolation, the dignity and glory that has been won for us through the merit of Jesus Christ; therefore each part ought to be examined more closely.

units.la: Primò enim docemur, veram & salutarem Dei cognitionem non aliunde quàm ex Euangelio percipi posse. Deum enim (vt Ioannes ait) nemo vidit vnquam (nimirum carnis sensu & intelleƈtu duƈtus) sed Filius ille Vnigenitus, qui est in sinu Patris, ea nobis manifestauit, quæ ad eum cognoscendum nobis sufficiunt. Idem est splendor & charaƈter personæ eius, adeo, vt qui Filium vidit, is simul Patrem viderit. At Filius Dei, IESVS CHRISTVS, in Euangelio se nobis videndum & cognoscendum proponit: illic nobis concionatur, illic miraculosis operibus suam virtutem humana maiorem declarat, nosque de Patris sui voluntate edocet, quoad omnia, quæ nostræ saluti seruiunt, ex quibus certò sequitur non posse non falli & errare omnes eos in Dei cognitione, quotquot Christum ignorant, & extra hunc per humanæ philosophiæ ambages vagantur. Vnde rursus hoc quoq; colligimus, inanes & inutiles esse cultus omnes, quorum institutio & regula non ex solo Euangelio petitur. Nam vt Deum absq; eius cognitione colamus, impossibile est: eundem verò cognoscere nemo poterit, nisi Vnigenitum eius Filium in Euangelio loquentem audiat.
units.tr: First, we are taught that the true and saving knowledge of God can be gained from nowhere but the Gospel. For (as John says) no one has ever seen God (namely, when led by the sense and understanding of the flesh); but that Only-begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father has revealed to us those things that are sufficient for us to know him. The same is the brightness and express image of his person, so that whoever has seen the Son has at the same time seen the Father. But the Son of God, Jesus Christ, presents himself to us in the Gospel to be seen and known: there he preaches to us, there by miraculous works he declares his power, greater than human, and teaches us about his Father's will in all things that serve our salvation. From this it certainly follows that all who are ignorant of Christ, and wander outside him through the windings of human philosophy, cannot but be deceived and go astray in the knowledge of God. Hence we again conclude that all forms of worship are empty and useless whose institution and rule are not sought from the Gospel alone. For to worship God without knowing him is impossible; and no one can know him unless he hears his Only-begotten Son speaking in the Gospel.

units.la: Secundò de fine prædicationis Euangelicæ & cognitionis Dei, quæ per illam nobis obtingit, hic locus nos admonet. Est ille, vt ad eandem imaginem gloriæ Dei transformemur. Non ergo mortua & inanis contemplatio hic commendatur, sed viua & efficax, quæ Dei imaginem in nobis instauret. Scimus enim initio secundùm hanc Adamum conditum fuisse: sed amisit eam, quando contra Dei mandatum ex arbore vetita comedit. Itaque peccator & peccati mancipium factus in sua imagine, id est, in vitiosa & corrupta natura, quam ex peccato contraxit, omnes suos filios genuit, & ea ratione peccatum in omnem eius posteritatem deriuatum est. Ergo vt huic naturæ nostræ vitiositati mederetur, & Dei imaginem in nobis instauraret, Vnigenitus Dei Filius in mundum venit: qui vt peccata nostra expiauit, ita in se credentes Spiritu suo donat, & ex Euangelij sui semine renatis in eodem gloriam Dei ita nobis spectandam proponit, vt qui in illam serio intuentur, & collatum ipsis redemptionis beneficium diligentius cum fide vera expendunt, ipsi quoque nouis gratiæ Dei radijs illustrati ad primam illam imaginem transformentur, & hunc suum redemptorem æternum Dei Filium, IESVM CHRISTVM, vita sua tota referant. Quò Apostolus noster respiciens, ad Galatas dicebat, Viuo, non amplius ego, sed viuit in me Christus: & vitam, quam nunc viuo in carne, per fidem viuo, quæ est in Filium Dei. Vt verò Christiani homines in hac mortali carne Filij Dei imaginem gerunt: ita olim in resurrectione toti glorificabuntur, vt quoad corpus quoque illi conformes & similes efficiantur. De quo idem Paulus ad Philippenses sic scribit: Ciuitas aut municipium nostrum in cœlis est, vnde etiam Seruatorem expeƈtamus, Dominum IESVM CHRISTVM: qui transformabit corpus nostrum humile, vt cõforme fiat corpori suo glorioso, &c. Id verò de solis veris & germanis Christianis debet intelligi, non de fucatis aut hypocritis: multò minus autè de sceleratis, qui quam ore profitentur fidem, factis abnegant, & ideo diaboli potius quàm Christi imaginem referunt, dum mentiuntur, furantur, rapiunt, cædes spirant, libidinibus vagis & illicitis diffluunt, blasphemijs, execrationibus, deierationibus, periurijs & disterijs turpissimis atquè scandali plenis toti crepant. Quis enim penes istos libertatem illam esse dixerit, cuius Spiritus Christi author est? Quapropter Apostolus cùm ad Romanos scribens dixisset: Nulla est condemnatio his, qui sunt
units.tr: Second, this passage reminds us of the aim of the Gospel preaching and of the knowledge of God that comes to us through it. Its aim is that we be transformed into the same image of God's glory. Therefore it is not a dead and empty contemplation that is commended here, but a living and effective one, which restores the image of God in us. For we know that at the beginning Adam was created according to this image; but he lost it when, against God's command, he ate from the forbidden tree. And so, having become a sinner and a slave of sin, he begot all his sons in his own image, that is, in the vicious and corrupt nature that he had contracted through sin, and in this way sin has been derived to his whole posterity. Therefore, to heal this vicious nature of ours and restore the image of God in us, the Only-begotten Son of God came into the world; who, as he atoned for our sins, so gives his Spirit to those who believe in him, and, to those reborn from the seed of his Gospel, sets forth the glory of God to be beheld in such a way that those who look on it earnestly and weigh with true faith the benefit of redemption offered to them more diligently are themselves also illumined by the new rays of God's grace and transformed into that first image, and refer their whole life to Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God, their Redeemer. Looking to this, our Apostle said to the Galatians: "I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me; and the life that I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God." And as Christians bear the image of the Son of God in this mortal flesh, so one day at the resurrection they will be wholly glorified, so that they are made conformed and similar to him also in body. Of this same thing Paul writes to the Philippians thus: "Our citizenship is in heaven, from which also we eagerly await a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform our lowly body, so that it may be conformed to his glorious body," etc. But this must be understood of true and genuine Christians only, not of the pretenders or hypocrites, and much less of the wicked, who deny the faith by their deeds while they profess it with their mouths, and therefore bear the image of the devil rather than of Christ, while they lie, steal, rob, breathe out murder, indulge in wandering and illicit lusts, and wholly resound with blasphemies, curses, oaths, perjuries and most shameful quarrels full of scandal. For who could say that that liberty belongs to such people, when the Spirit of Christ is its author? Therefore the Apostle, when writing to the Romans, had said: "There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ," and soon adds, by way of an added exclamation [ἐπιφώνησιν]: "Namely, for those who do not walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit." Likewise: "If you live according to the flesh, you will certainly die; but if by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you will live." To these you may fittingly add also this exhortation of the same Apostle: "I beg you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living, holy sacrifice, acceptable to God, your rational worship; and do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is, good, acceptable and perfect."

units.la: Vera Dei cognitio ex solo Euangelio discitur.
units.tr: The true knowledge of God is learned from the Gospel alone.

units.la: Finis Euangelij & cognitionis Dei.
units.tr: The aim of the Gospel and of the knowledge of God.

units.la: Rom.8. in Christo:mox addit per ἐπsignυσιν: Nempe ijs,qui non secundùm carnem incedunt, sed secun‐dùm spiritum. Item: Si secundum carnem vixeritis,futurum est ut moriamini:sed si spiritu actiones carnis mortificaueritis, viuetis. Quibus merito hanc quoq; eiusdem Apostoli exhortationem addideris: Precor vos fratres,per miserationes Dei,ut sistatis corpora vestra hostiam viuam, sanctam,acceptam Deo,rationalem illum cultum vestrum: Et ne configuremini seculo isti,sed transformemini per renouationem mentis vestrae ad hoc, ut probetis quae sit voluntas Dei, bona illa, accepta & perfecta.
units.tr: Rom. 8., in Christ. He soon adds by way of explanation [ἐπεξήγησις]: namely, to those who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. Likewise: "If you live according to the flesh, you are bound to die; but if by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you will live." To these you may fitly add that exhortation of the same Apostle: "I beseech you, brethren, by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your reasonable service. And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the will of God, that which is good, acceptable and perfect."

units.la: Tertiò, modum quoq; huius transformationis Paulus exprimit, dicens: Ex gloria in gloriam, id est,successiue, & quasi per gradus. Ergo non uno momento hoc opus tam arduum perficitur, sed incrementis quotidianis constat glorificatio nostra. Ut enim in morbos subitò quidem incidimus,ex ijsdem verò subitò restitui aut convalescere non possumus: ita in hoc spirituali naturae nostrae vitiosissimae restitutione fieri consueuit. Imò quoad in carne vixerimus, quae natura ad malum proclivis est, ad summam illam perfectionem peruenire non possumus. Cernimus enim nunc quasi per speculum, sed ex parte tantum, & quantum nunc satis est: sed profectu quotidiano opus est, ut aliquando in virum perfectum adolescamus: neq; hic iocordiae locus est, quando in sanctissimis quoq; naevos & lapses esse videmus. Arguit hoc eos, qui quasi metam iam attigerint, ignaui cessant, vel etiam à tergo respiciunt. Quia enim ea animae conditio est, ut otiari aut quiescere non possit, sed in actione sit perpetua, non potest non ad prava opera declinare, nisi eam circa veram pietatis exercitia perpetuo occupatam teneamus. Agnouerunt hoc sancti omnes, & ideo precantur in Psalmis, ut Deus ipsos confirmare, in semitis suis deducere, & quod in ipsis inchoauerit opus, perficere dignetur. Psal.51.25.119.90,&c.
units.tr: Thirdly, Paul also expresses the manner of this transformation when he says: "from glory to glory," that is, successively and as if by degrees. Therefore this so arduous work is not completed in a single moment, but our glorification consists in daily increments. For just as we fall suddenly into diseases but cannot be restored or recover from them suddenly, so this spiritual restoration of our most corrupt nature usually takes place. Indeed, as long as we live in the flesh, which is inclined to evil, we cannot attain that supreme perfection. For now we see "as through a mirror," but only in part, and as much as is enough for now; yet we need daily progress, so that at some point we may grow into a perfect man. Nor is there any place here for sloth, since we see that even the most holy have blemishes and lapses. This refutes those who, as if they had already reached the goal, cease idly or even look back over their shoulders. For the condition of the soul is such that it cannot be at rest or idle, but is in constant activity; it cannot help turning to wicked works unless we keep it perpetually occupied in the true exercises of piety. All the saints have recognised this, and therefore they pray in the Psalms that God would deign to confirm them, lead them in his paths, and complete the work he has begun in them. Psal. 51. 25. 119. 90, etc.

units.la: Postremò causam efficientem huius transformationis Paulus indicat,dum ait: Sicut à Domini Spiritu. Nec enim haec simplex similitudinis nota est, sed potius rem ipsam exprimit, & transformationem iRam ita fieri docet, ut constet eam Spiritus Dei opus esse, non humanarum virium. Ideo Christus,hominem coelitus renasci oportere,dicebat. Quis enim Deum spectet, quando ne in Solem quidem intueri possumus? Certè ad Angelorum apparitiones sanctissimos quosq; consternatos concidisse legimus. Et cum corporis vitia, quae nobis agnata sunt, emendare non sit in nostra potestate,quanto minus naturam totam, quam ex primo parente contraximus mutare licebit? Itaq; Deus hic manum admoueat opus est. At si Spiritus Domini ad huius imaginem nos transformat,quis obsecro spiritus ille est, qui Francisco, Dominico & aliis ineptissimarum impiissimarumq; superstitionum authoribus similes fieri docet? Euertitur certè hic omnis superstitionum officina. Nostrum fuerit Dei bonitatem agnoscere, & mediis quibus hic in nobis transformandis utitur,nos accommodare, omniq; studio ad hunc finem contendere, ut Dei imaginem in nobis instaurata,ipsum glorificemus per IESVM CHRISTVM: cui debetur benedictio,honor,gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Last of all, Paul indicates the efficient cause of this transformation when he says: "as by the Spirit of the Lord." This is not a mere sign of likeness, but expresses the thing itself, and he teaches that the transformation is so brought about that it is evidently the work of God's Spirit, not of human powers. For this reason Christ said that a man must be born again from heaven. For who can look upon God, when we cannot even look upon the sun? Certainly we read that the holiest men, when the angels appeared to them, were struck down in terror. And since we have no power to correct the defects of the body that have been born with us, how much less will it be lawful for us to change our whole nature, which we have drawn from our first parent? Therefore God must put his hand to this work. But if it is the Spirit of the Lord who transforms us into this image, what spirit, I ask you, is it that teaches us to become like Francis, Dominic and the other authors of the most foolish and most impious superstitions? Surely here the whole workshop of superstitions is overthrown. It is our part to acknowledge the goodness of God, to adapt ourselves to the means by which he uses to transform us, and to strive with all zeal toward this end, that, the image of God being restored in us, we may glorify him through Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: PRO terea cum ministerium hoc habeamus, prout misericor‐diam consecuti sumus, non segnescimus. Sed abdicauimus re‐gumenta turpitudinis,non incedentes cum calliditate, neq; falsantes sermonem Dei, sed declaratione veritatis commendantes nos‐pfos apud omnem conscientiam hominum in conspectu Dei.
units.tr: Therefore, since we have this ministry, as we have obtained mercy, we do not lose heart. But we have renounced the hidden things of shame, not walking in craftiness, nor adulterating the word of God, but by the manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God.

units.la: MVLTA hucusque Paulus praeclarè dixit in Euangelij commendationem, & hoc Legge Mosaica praestantius esse docuit, eò quòd vitae & iustitiae ministerium sit, & plenam tradat IESV CHRISTI cognitionem,per quam nos quoque transformemur ad Dei imaginem,quae in Adamo collapsa & obliterata fuit. Finis omnium hic est, ut eos in viam reuocet, qui à pseudoapostolis decepti Legem cum Euangelio miscebant, quasi huius doctrina ad salutem non sufficiat. Nobis vero eorundem hic usus esse debet, ut procul relictis omnibus aliis doctrinis, unum Euangelium audiamus. Si enim Moysis Legem huic cedere oportuit, quis non videat, quam inepte & iniquè faciant, qui hominum traditiones ei praeferunt, aut saltem aequant? Quia vero de Pauli persona potissimum agebatur, cuius authoritatem aduersarij labefactare studebant, ut facilius omne in Ecclesiam ius & imperium sibi vendicarent, redit nunc ad ea, quae sub finem Cap. secundi & initium tertij tractare coeperat, & amplius docet, se in munere Euangelico bona fide versatum esse, sic ut nullius doli aut sceleris sibi ipsi conscius sit.
units.tr: Up to this point Paul has said many excellent things in commendation of the Gospel, and has taught that it is more excellent than the Law of Moses, because it is the ministry of life and righteousness and delivers the full knowledge of Jesus Christ, through which we too are transformed into the image of God, which was corrupted and effaced in Adam. The whole aim here is to call back those who, deceived by false apostles, mixed the Law with the Gospel, as if its doctrine were not sufficient for salvation. For us, however, the lesson should be this: setting aside all other doctrines, we should hear the Gospel alone. For if the Law of Moses had to yield to it, who does not see how foolishly and wickedly those act who prefer human traditions to it, or at least place them on a level with it? But because the discussion concerned chiefly the person of Paul, whose authority his adversaries were trying to weaken, so that they might more easily seize for themselves all right and power in the Church, he now returns to what he had begun to treat at the end of the second chapter and the beginning of the third. He teaches further that he has conducted himself faithfully in the office of the Gospel, so that he is conscious of no deceit or wrongdoing.

units.la: Esti, observatu dignissimum Pauli exemplum, cui non satis fuit suae functionis dignitatem atque praestantiam demonstrauisse, nisi suam quoque in ea obeunda fidem atque industriam omnibus perspectam & testatam faceret. Etenim est quidem magna ministerij Euangelici dignitas, & non temere, qui in eo versantur, legati Domini exercituum dicuntur, & eosdem Dei Filius salem terrae & lucem mundi vocat, domus item suae dispensatores, adeoque seruatores hominum. Sed ad salutem non sufficit, in sublimiori aliquo gradu constitutum esse, sed ut te eo dignum esse reipsa probes necesse est. Ad omnes enim pertinet Christi dictum: Cui multum datum est, ab eo multum exigetur: & apud quem multum depositum fuerunt, ab eo multum repetent. Itaque quoties ministri de muneris sui excellentia cogitant, tunc simul meminerint, quid ab ipsis requirat Dominus, & quod olim omnium quae fecerunt rationem illi reddere cogentur. Transferant hoc etiam ad se, qui magistratum aliquem gerunt. Nam horum quoque dignitas maxima sit oportet, quos Scriptura Deos dicere dignatur. At nisi Deo atque populo eius fideles, adhaec iustitiae cultores, & strenui iudiciorum Dei vindices sint, graues poenas dabunt, quas Prophetae illis non uno loco minantur, & quas multorum exemplis confirmatas esse constat.
units.tr: Indeed, this is a most notable example of Paul, who thought it not enough to have shown the dignity and excellence of his office, unless he also made his faith and diligence in discharging it evident and attested to all. For the dignity of the evangelical ministry is indeed great, and not without reason those who serve in it are called ambassadors of the Lord of hosts; the Son of God also calls them the salt of the earth and the light of the world, and the stewards of his house, and thus the saviours of men. But it is not enough for salvation to be placed in some higher rank; you must truly prove by your conduct that you are worthy of it. For Christ's saying applies to all: To whom much has been given, of him much will be required; and from whom much has been entrusted, of him much will be demanded. Therefore, whenever ministers think of the excellence of their office, let them at the same time remember what the Lord requires of them, and that they will one day be compelled to render an account of all they have done. Let those who hold any magistracy apply this to themselves as well. For the dignity of these also must be very great, since Scripture deigns to call them gods. But unless they are faithful to God and to his people, and likewise lovers of justice and vigorous avengers of God's judgments, they will pay heavy penalties, which the prophets threaten to them in more than one place, and which are known to have been confirmed by the examples of many.

units.la: Sed Paulum audiamus, qui diligenter ac grauiter exponit, quis & qualis hucusque fuerit in suo ministerio, & qualis porrò futurus sit. Id vero ea ratione facit, ut arrogantiae suspicionem omnem diligenter declinet. Nam cum ijs, quae proximè praecesserunt, locum hunc connectens, sic scribit: Propterea cum ministerium hoc habeamus, prout misericordiam consecuti sumus, non segnescimus, &c. Quasi diceret: Non ista in eum finem dico, ut me supra omnes insolenti propriae dignitatis fiducia extollam. Scio enim mihi non imperium, sed ministerium commissum esse, idque ex gratuita misericordia, cum indignissimus essem, qui vel extremum in Ecclesia locum tenerem, cuius persecutor fueram. Quapropter adeo non efferor aut superbio, ut potius haec me cura subinde solicitum teneat, ne aliquando segnescam, neue aliquid mea functione indignum committam, quod me cogat latebras quaerere, aut ad excusationes confugere, quae homines probos & ingenuos minus decent. Itaque ab omni astutia & fraude alienus, Verbum Dei sic tracto, ut mihi liceat tam hominum conscientias quam Deum meae fidei & integritatis testes appellare. Est autem locus hic admodum insignis, & dignus, quem nunquam non sibi ipsi occinant omnes Ecclesiarum ministri: quare singula ex ordine inspiciamus.
units.tr: But let us hear Paul, who carefully and gravely sets forth who and what he has been hitherto in his ministry, and what he will be henceforth. He does this so as diligently to avoid any suspicion of arrogance. For, linking this place with what immediately precedes, he writes thus: Therefore, since we have this ministry, as we have obtained mercy, we do not lose heart, etc. It is as if he said: I do not say these things to lift myself above all others with an insolent confidence in my own dignity. For I know that I have been entrusted not with rule but with ministry, and that from free mercy, when I was most unworthy even to hold the lowest place in the Church, I who had been its persecutor. Therefore I am so far from being puffed up or proud that rather this care keeps me anxious from time to time, lest I ever grow slack or commit anything unworthy of my office, which would compel me to seek hiding-places or to take refuge in excuses, which become honest and well-born men less. Thus, free from all craft and fraud, I handle the word of God in such a way that I may call upon men's consciences, as well as God, to witness my faith and integrity. This place, moreover, is very remarkable and worthy that all ministers of the churches should always rehearse it to themselves. Let us therefore look at its parts one by one.

units.la: Primum occurrit, quod Apostolatum sive munus Ecclesiasticum, quod obibat, subinde ministerium dicit. Conuenit hoc cum ijs, quae Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS discipulis suis dixit, quando serui eos confert expectantibus dominum suum à nuptijs breui rediturum.
units.tr: First, he calls the apostleship, or ecclesiastical office, which he discharged, a ministry. This agrees with what our Lord Jesus Christ said to his disciples, when he compares them to servants waiting for their lord, who will return shortly from the wedding.

units.la: Sed & ipsa Apostoli vox dignitatem eiusmodi denotat, quae cum ministerio coniuncta est. Dicuntur autem tales ministri duplici ratione. Primùm, quia Christi serui sunt, qui eos vocat, & ad hanc functionem destinat. Ideo frequenter Paulus in epistolarum inscriptionibus se IESV CHRISTI seruum dicere consueuit: quod ipsum Petrus quoque & Iacobus faciunt. Deinde, quia Ecclesiae seruiunt, in qua illos Deus ut oeconomos & dispensatores constituit. Vnde satis apparet, Ecclesiam non propter ipsos, sed hos propter Ecclesiam institutos esse. Quod unum abunde sufficit ad arguendam eorum arrogantiam, qui sibi in Ecclesiam ius & imperium vendicant, contra Petri Apostoli admonitionem, qua ne quid huius fiat, grauissimè monuit. Meminerint potius se ministros esse, & quidem Dei gratia esse quicquid sunt, deque officio suo potius faciendo, quam de dominio in haereditatem Domini exercendo cogitent.
units.tr: But the very word apostle also denotes a dignity of this kind, which is joined with ministry. Such ministers are called so for a twofold reason. First, because they are servants of Christ, who calls them and appoints them to this function. Therefore Paul was accustomed frequently to call himself the servant of Jesus Christ in the inscriptions of his epistles, which Peter and James also do. Second, because they serve the Church, in which God has appointed them as stewards and dispensers. From this it is quite clear that the Church was not instituted for their sake, but they for the sake of the Church. This one point is enough to refute the arrogance of those who claim for themselves right and rule over the Church, contrary to the admonition of the Apostle Peter, by which he most seriously warned that nothing of this kind should happen. Rather let them remember that they are ministers, and that whatever they are, they are by the grace of God; and let them think about doing their duty rather than about exercising lordship over the inheritance of the Lord.

units.la: Debet hoc ipsum in omnibus aliis muneribus atq; dignitatibus obseruari, quae aliquam habent excellentiae aut eminentiae speciem. Nam si rem propius contemplemur, ita Deus res hominum instituit, vt quicunq; in gradu sublimiori sedent, serui potius aut ministri sint, quàm domini: serui (inquam) Dei, qui omnium functionum author atq; distributor est: aeque hominum quoq; quibus ideo praefecti sunt, vt pro illis vigilent, atq; saluti eorum consulant. Est hoc satis evidens in ijs, qui ad Reipub. gubernacula sedent. Quòd hi excellunt alios, id Dei donum est, qui vt Psal. docet, pauperem ex pulueribus & tenuem abiectum{?} hominem ex stercore erigit, vt eum inter populi sui principes collocet. At eorundem haec summa gloria, & omnis quam habent authoritatis vnica causa est, quòd Dei serui sunt, quales Paulus alibi dicit. Agnouit hoc Constantinus ille Magnus, laudatissimus Imperator, qui in Nicena Synodo hoc potissimum nomine gloriabatur, quòd se episcoporum ὡς ἂν ἂν ἡμῶν, id est, conseruum posset dicere. Quod autem illud munus est, in quo principes viri Deo seruiunt? Illud nimirum, quòd populum suae fidei creditum regere, ius dicere, bonos tueri, commodis publicis consulere, pacem publicam summo studio conseruare, deniq; toti in eo esse debent, vt omnes Deum sancte colant, & inter se vitam viuant honestam, tranquillam & pacificam. Quid vero hoc aliud est, quàm publicum totius populi, & simul priuatum vniuscuiusq; seruum esse, qui consilio, auxilio, defensione opus habet? Haec qui diligentius expendunt, si certe quiescere non possunt, tamq; abest vt sua dignitate superbiant, aut securi delitientur, vt potius aliis secure dormientibus, aut genio indulgentibus, ipsi vigilent. Vidit ista Rex ille barbarus, qui oblatum sibi diadema diu contemplatus, tandem cum gemitu dicebat: O nobilem & pretiosum magis quàm felicem pannum, quem si quis nosset tot curis & sollicitudinibus refertum esse, ne lumi quidem iacentem tolleret. Eadem parentum quoque conditio est: qui etsi liberis praesient, eorundem tamen serui sunt, quoad educationis molestias, institutionem, labores & curas, quas vt illis honestè prospiciant, sustinent. De patrefamilias certè rectè olim Graecus Senarius pronunciauit, vnum hunc in domo sua seruum esse: nimirum quòd in eius humeros tota domus cura recumbit. Sic maritus vxoris quidem caput est, sed ita, vt huic seruiat, sicuti caput videndo, audiendo, olfaciendo, cibos per os admittendo, reminiscendo, cogitando, loquendo, toti corpori & singulis in eo membris suum obsequium praestat. Idem de scholarum praefectis, omnibus denique alijs dici potest, qui aliquod ius & imperium in alios obtinent. Estq; hoc singulare bonitatis & sapientiae diuinae argumentum, quae cum nostris ministerijs minimè opus habeat, ijs tamen vti dignatur, simul verò sic res hominum temperat atque moderatur, vt qui in altiori fastigio constituti sunt, pluribus alijs seruiant. Hoc ipsum autem inferioris quoq; conditionis homines officij sui admonet, vt ijs sese obedientes & gratos praebeant, quos ipsis Deus praefecit.
units.tr: This same principle ought to be observed in all other offices and dignities which have some appearance of excellence or eminence. For if we consider the matter more closely, God so ordains the affairs of men that those who sit in higher rank are servants or ministers rather than lords: servants, I say, of God, who is the author and distributor of all functions, and likewise of the men over whom they are set, so that they may watch over them and look to their salvation. This is quite evident in those who sit at the helm of the commonwealth. That they surpass others is a gift of God, who, as the Psalm teaches, raises the poor man from the dust and lifts the needy and abject man from the dunghill, so as to set him among the princes of his people. But the whole glory of these men, and the sole cause of all the authority they have, is that they are servants of God, such as Paul elsewhere calls them. Constantine the Great, that most praised emperor, recognised this, who at the Council of Nicaea gloried chiefly in this name, that he could call himself a fellow-servant of the bishops [ὡς ἂν ἡμῶν]. What, then, is the office in which princely men serve God? Surely it is this: to rule the people entrusted to their faith, to administer justice, to protect the good, to look after the public welfare, to preserve public peace with the greatest zeal, and finally to devote themselves wholly to ensuring that all worship God devoutly and live among themselves an honest, tranquil and peaceful life. And what else is this than to be the servant of the whole public and at the same time of each private person, who needs counsel, help and defence? Those who weigh these things more carefully, if indeed they cannot rest, are so far from taking pride in their dignity, or from lying safe and secure, that rather, while others sleep securely or indulge their pleasures, they themselves keep watch. That barbarian king saw this, who, having long gazed at the diadem offered to him, said at last with a groan: O cloth more noble and precious than happy, which if anyone knew to be filled with so many cares and anxieties, he would not pick it up even if it lay on the ground. The same is the condition of parents also: although they preside over their children, they are nonetheless their servants, in respect of the troubles of their upbringing, the instruction, the labours and the cares which they endure in order to provide honourably for them. Indeed, a Greek senarius rightly once pronounced of the head of a household that he alone is the servant in his house, namely because the whole care of the household rests upon his shoulders. So the husband is indeed the head of the wife, but in such a way that he serves her, just as the head serves the whole body and each of its members by seeing, hearing, smelling, admitting food through the mouth, remembering, thinking and speaking. The same may be said of the heads of schools and, in short, of all others who hold some right and power over others. And this is a singular proof of divine goodness and wisdom, which, although it has no need of our ministries, nevertheless deigns to use them; and at the same time it so tempers and governs the affairs of men that those who are set on a higher height serve the more. Moreover, this very thing reminds men of inferior condition of their duty, that they should show themselves obedient and grateful to those whom God has set over them.

units.la: Porro ad Paulum reuertamur, qui vt in suo ministerio versatus sit diligenter narrat. Et primò quidem, se non segnescere aut deficere ait. Graeca vox significat malis aut aduersis fatigari & quasi vinci, vt à statione nobis credita discedamus. Itaque se in commisso sibi munere constanter perseuerare ac pergere testatur: quod illum reuera fecisse, totus Actorum liber docet, vt iam de ijs nihil dicamus, quae infra capite vndecimo scribuntur, & quorum in prioris epistolae Capite quarto meminit. Etenim ab ipso die vocationis suae agitatus est omni periculorum genere, laboribus assiduis, peregrinationibus per terras & maria, aemulorum calumnijs, certaminibus item contra falsos fratres, & infinitis alijs casibus, quos ex ordine recensere longum foret. In omnibus tamen vicit, & vt Euangelicae doctrinae atque fidei puritatem tueretur, omnibus ea animi constantia sese opposuit, adeo, vt Petro quoque in faciem resisteret, cum illum in Iudaeorum gratiam dissimulatione minus ingenua non sine scandalo eorum vti viderct, qui ex gentibus crediderant. Vide Galatas secundo Capite.
units.tr: Let us return to Paul, who describes carefully how he conducted himself in his ministry. First, he says that he does not grow slack or lose heart. The Greek word means to be worn out or overcome by evils or adversities, so that we abandon the post entrusted to us. He therefore testifies that he persevered constantly and kept going in the office committed to him. The whole book of Acts shows that he really did this, not to mention what is written below in chapter eleven and what he mentioned in chapter four of the first epistle. From the day of his calling he was harried by every kind of danger, by constant labours, by journeys over land and sea, by the slanders of his rivals, by contests with false brothers, and by countless other misfortunes, which would take too long to list in order. Yet he prevailed over all of them, and to defend the purity of the evangelical doctrine and faith he set himself against everyone with such firmness of mind that he even resisted Peter to his face, when he saw him, out of regard for the Jews, dissembling in a way that was not honest and not without scandal to those who had believed from the Gentiles. See Galatians, chapter two.

units.la: Decet eadem constantia & fortitudo omnes Ecclesiae ministros. Sunt enim innumera, quibus tentantur, inter quae molestissima illis est ingratitudo eorum, quorum saluti ipsi quàm maximè consultum volunt, & quòd laborem suum fere irritum & infructuosum esse vident. Hoc certe Eliam olim mouit, vt de fuga cogitaret, imò mori cuperet. Et Ieremias de sua forte grauissimè conqueritur, vt inter alia dicat: Vae mihi o mater mea, quòd me peperisti virum litigatorem, & virum controuersiae vniuersae terrae. Sed hic meminisse oportet, nos in Dei ministerio laborare, qui agonothetes simul & remunerator est liberalissimus, & omnibus dici, quod olim discipulo suo quidam dixit Dominus: Nemo, qui ubi manum aratro admouit, à tergo respicit, idoneus est ad regnum Dei. Breue item est tempus illud, quo nobis in hac palaestra cum mundi ingratitudine & contumacia luctandu est: eos autem, qui in finem usque perseuerant, immarcesibilis corona iusti-tiae manet, quam Deus omnibus praeparauit, qui ei fideliter seruiunt. Pertinet hoc ipsum ad Reip. praefectos, quorum eadem fere sors est, quae Ecclesiae ministrorum, ut ingratos & rebelles esse iudicant eos, pro quorum salute ipsi laborant & vigilant. Sed nunquam deerit illis Deus, si in eius gloria tuenda fideles sint. Eius enim promissio est: Honorantes me honorabo. Et exempla sunt in Dauide, Ezechia, Constantino, Theodosio & multis aliis, qui per infinita pericula eluctati immortalem gloriam sibi pararuerunt, & nunc cum Christo beati & felices regnant. Obseruent hoc ipsum singuli priuatim in fidei & religionis causa, ne inter persecutionum pericula deficiant. Cur autem se vinci patiantur, quando maior est qui in nobis agit, quam qui in mundo infelici tumultuatur & furit? Et quantae illius vires sint, quamq; efficax consolatio sit, qua suis luctan-tibus adest, Martyrum multorum exempla docent, qui carnificum quidem manus patientia sua fatigarunt, ipsi vero omnibus tormentis superiores facti sunt.
units.tr: The same constancy and courage befit all the ministers of the Church. There are countless trials by which they are tested, and among them the most troublesome is the ingratitude of those whose salvation they most earnestly seek, and the sense that their labour is almost fruitless and unproductive. This certainly moved Elijah once to think of flight, and indeed to wish to die. And Jeremiah complains very bitterly of his lot, saying among other things: "Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me a man of strife and a man of contention for the whole earth." But here we must remember that we labour in the service of God, who is both the judge of the contest and the most generous rewarder, and that what the Lord once said to a disciple applies to everyone: "No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God." That time in which we must wrestle in this arena with the ingratitude and obstinacy of the world is also brief, but for those who persevere to the end there remains the unfading crown of righteousness, which God has prepared for all who serve him faithfully. This applies also to the rulers of the commonwealth, whose lot is nearly the same as that of the ministers of the Church: they are judged ungrateful and rebellious by those for whose salvation they labour and keep watch. But God will never fail them, if they are faithful in defending his glory. For his promise is: "Those who honour me, I will honour." And there are examples in David, Hezekiah, Constantine, Theodosius and many others, who, struggling through endless dangers, won for themselves immortal glory, and now reign blessed and happy with Christ. Let each individual likewise take this to heart in the cause of faith and religion, lest he fail amid the perils of persecution.
