Itaque eadem est omnium nostrum conditio, quae eorum, qui liquorem aliquem pretiosissimum in testaceo vel ceolo aut ampulla vitrea per glaciem ferunt. Quod ut plus quam paternam Dei bonitatem nobis commendat, qui nobis, cum tales simus, tantum thesaurum credere dignatur: ita nos admonet, ut caute agamus, ne unquam pedes nostri labantur aut offendant: adeo q; (quod alibi monet Apostolus) salutem nostram in timore & tremore operemur. Sunt etenim nimium stulti, qui ipsi lubricitates quaerunt, dum sese conditionibus periculosis ingerunt, & carnem per se plus satis lasciuientem fouent. Quo enim in sublimiori gradu consistimus, eo maiori cura & studio nobis opus est.
units.tr: Some general doctrine should also be drawn from this, which all may apply to themselves. For God offers this most precious treasure to everyone through the Gospel, and it is received by us through faith alone. But who are we? Earthen vessels indeed, as the creation of our first parent, whom Moses writes was made of clay, can remind us. We are frail, then, however great we may be. The soul is exposed to various passions and is tossed about and troubled. The body is weak and perishable, a workshop of a thousand diseases, and it is mortal. The course of our whole life is slippery and full of danger, since we are naturally inclined to evil and are always being tempted besides by the allurements of the world and the suggestions of the devil. So the condition of all of us is the same as that of people who carry some very precious liquid in an earthen pitcher or a glass flask across ice. This should commend to us God's goodness, which is more than fatherly, in deigning to entrust so great a treasure to us, though we are such as we are. It also warns us to act cautiously, lest our feet ever slip or stumble, and so, as the Apostle elsewhere says, to work out our salvation "with fear and trembling" [φόβου καὶ τρόμου]. For those are very foolish who seek out slippery places for themselves, throwing themselves into dangerous situations and nourishing a flesh that is already wanton enough. The higher the step on which we stand, the greater care and diligence we need.

units.la: Porro ad statum huius loci propius accedit Paulus, ut doceat, propter ipsorum vilem atque afflictam conditionem nihil decedere Euangelio, sed hac ratione illustrari potius Dei potentiam, qua inter tot casus mirifice seruentur. Habet autem totus hic locus tacitam comparationem, qua pseudoapostolos perstringit, qui in otio viuebant, deque multorum fauore atque amicitiis gloriabantur. His enim ista opponit. Quasi diceret: Glorientur illi ut libet, nos nihil horum possumus producere, sed iis contenti sumus, quae nobis euentura Christus praedixit: persecutionibus nimirum, exilijs, carceribus, plagis & omni afflictionum genere, quibus indies exercemur. Sed videamus singula:
units.tr: Moreover, Paul comes closer to the point of this place, to teach that, because of their lowly and afflicted condition, nothing is lost to the Gospel, but rather that God's power is thereby made more illustrious, since it preserves them wonderfully amid so many dangers. This whole passage contains a tacit comparison, by which he attacks the false apostles, who lived at ease and boasted of the favour and friendships of many. He sets these things against them, as if to say: let them boast as they please; we can produce none of these things, but we are content with those which Christ foretold would befall us, namely persecutions, exiles, prisons, blows and every kind of affliction, with which we are exercised daily. But let us look at the individual points.

units.la: Primum, In omnibus premimur, inquit: sed non coarctamur, vel in angustias redigimur. Exa primitur hoc membro, quae Euangelij & ministrorum eius sors sit. Veritas in terris hisce peregrina, & vix aliud magis quam illa inuisum & exosum est, eo quod mundus fere opinione ducitur, & plerique fuco inani sese vendicant. Itaque qui Veritatis luce fucum & errores arguunt, ij ubique locorum hostes inueniunt, domi, foris, imo inter intimos & sibi familiarissimos. Et qui lucem iam prorsus extinguere nequeunt, ij saltem hoc agunt, ut in angustum redigant, & arctioribus finibus concludant. Sed est hoc impossibile, quia ignem iltum Deus ardere, & Spiritum suum libero flatu omnes terras penetrare vult. Et quod in praesenti Paulus dicit, hoc res ipsa probat. Premebantur Apostoli initio statim Hierosolymis, ne in nomine IESV praedicarent: nec edictis modo minacibus agebant Sacerdotes, sed carceribus & plagis ignominiosis. Instituta est mox persecutio tam saeva, ut ne domi quidem intra privatos parietes Christianis tutis esse liceret. Sed adeo non coarctatum est hoc furore incendium iltud saluberrimum, ut eius scintilla vicinam Iudaeam, Samariam, Phaeniciam illuminarint, & inde per totum orbem dispersae sint. Idem postea factum est, cum ne inter gentes Euangelium praedicaretur, Iudaei obstiterunt. Nam adeo nihil profecerunt, ut solius Pauli illius praedicationem ab Hierosolyma in Illyricum usque extenderit, & eadem viuentibus adhuc plerisque Apostolorum in toto orbe fuerit diuulgata. Poterant hic commemorari, quae sub Romanis Imperatoribus acciderunt, sed cum nostro seculo hoc ipsum fiat, veteribus exemplis non est opus. Agnoscant modo singuli, hoc diuinae virtutis argumentum esse, qua totum hoc negotium gubernatur.
units.tr: First, "We are pressed on every side," he says, "but not crushed, or driven into a corner" [οὐ στενοχωρούμενοι]. In this clause is set out what the lot of the Gospel and of its ministers is. Truth is a stranger in this world, and scarcely anything is more hated and detested than it, because the world is mostly led by opinion, and most people pass themselves off with empty pretence. So those who expose pretence and errors by the light of truth find enemies everywhere, at home, abroad, and even among their closest and most intimate friends. And those who cannot at all put out the light, at least aim to hem it in and confine it within narrower bounds. But this is impossible, because God wills that fire to burn and his Spirit to penetrate all lands with its free breath. What Paul says here, the very event proves. At the start the Apostles were hard pressed at Jerusalem, so that they might not preach in the name of Jesus. The priests acted not only with threatening edicts but with prisons and shameful beatings. Soon a persecution was set up so fierce that it was not even safe for Christians to be at home within their private walls. Yet that most salutary fire was so far from being confined by this rage that its spark lit up the neighbouring Judaea, Samaria and Phoenicia, and from there they were scattered through the whole world. The same thing happened afterwards, when the Jews opposed the preaching of the Gospel even among the Gentiles. For they achieved so little that the preaching of that one Paul alone spread from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, and while many of the Apostles were still living, it was made known throughout the whole world. Instances from the time of the Roman emperors could be mentioned here, but since this same thing is happening in our own age, there is no need of ancient examples. Let each one only acknowledge that this is a proof of divine power, by which this whole enterprise is governed.

units.la: Secundo ait Paulus: Haesitamus, sed non prorsus haeremus. ἀπορούμενοι non simpliciter dubitare, sed simul consilij inopem esse significat. Ideo ἐξαπορούμενοι supra Cap. primo pro desperare potuit, quod fere sequitur ex priori, nisi Deus nobis dexter affulgeat. Itaque sensus huius membri est: Saepe quidem difficultates obijciuntur, ut carnis rationi nulla euadendi via pateat: sed tunc non ut impij solent, sed abiecta haeremus: quia Deus mox nos extricat, neque supra vires tentari finit. Tale quid initio statim Damasci expertus fuerat, cum Aretas regis praefectus ipsi insidias frueret, ut infra Cap. 12. pluribus dicetur. Docet autem locus hic, non desperandum esse inter pericula, si quando in humanis nulla effugij via apparet. Nam si Deus liberare nos velit, facile is viam inuenit, cui naturae quoque leges cedunt. Exemplum eius rei memorabile in transitu Israelis per mare rubrum habemus. Quid, quod interdum per hostes nobis opem fert? quod Dauid expertus est, quando Philistaei Saulem ab illius persecutione reuocarunt. Et Persas Iulianum ab Ecclesiae cerunicibus retraxisse, historiae testantur: & Valentem fidei catholicae hostem acerrimum, Gothi perdiderunt, a quibus ille in acie vitus, & in tugurio, quo confugerat, exustus est. Non dubitemus ergo, tunc diuinum auxilium incipere, quando humanum defecit, ut olim Philo dicebat. Quod si vero velit Deus nos diutius periclitari, vel etiam periculis succumbere, feramus patienter quod ille dederit.
units.tr: Second, Paul says: "We are perplexed, but not utterly at a loss" [ἀπορούμενοι, ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἐξαπορούμενοι]. The word aporoumenoi means not simply to doubt, but at the same time to be without resources of counsel. That is why in the first chapter exaporoumenoi could be rendered as "to despair", which almost follows from the former, unless God shine upon us with favour. So the sense of this clause is: difficulties are often thrown in our way, so that no path of escape opens to human reason. But then we do not, as the impious usually do, give up; we stand firm, because God soon extricates us and does not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength. He had experienced something like this at the very beginning, at Damascus, when the governor of King Aretas was laying snares for him, as will be told at more length below, in chapter 12. This place teaches, however, that one must not despair amid dangers if, in human affairs, no way of escape appears. For if God wishes to free us, he easily finds a way, to which even the laws of nature yield. We have a memorable example of this in Israel's passage through the Red Sea. What of the fact that sometimes he brings us help through our enemies? David experienced this when the Philistines called Saul back from pursuing him. And histories bear witness that the Persians drew Julian back from the necks of the Church, and that the Goths destroyed Valens, the most bitter enemy of the catholic faith, who was wounded in battle and burned in the hut into which he had fled. Let us not doubt, then, that divine help begins when human help fails, as Philo once said. But if God wishes us to be in danger for a longer time, or even to yield to dangers, let us bear patiently what he has sent.

units.la: Tertio dicit Paulus: Persecutionem patimur, sed in ea non deferimur. Facit ad huius membri explicationem atq; confirmationem totus Actorum liber, qui persecutiones Apostolorum perpetuas, & noua subinde diuini auxilij exempla continet: quibus adde, quae infra Cap. 11. audiemus. Ad pertinet hoc quoq; ad omnes credentes. Nam omnibus dictum est: In mundo afflictionem habebitis, sed confidite, ego vici mundum. Et ut suos omnes ad crucem ferendam vocat Dominus, ita omnibus se tutorem & vindicem fore pollicetur. Id vero praestat, siue liberet ex periculis, seu minus. Nam etiamsi nos perpetuis persecutionibus exerceri velit, semper tamen nobis adest, nosq; in fide confirmat, ut per nos de mundo eius q; principe triumphet.
units.tr: Third, Paul says: "We are persecuted, but not forsaken" [διωκόμενοι, ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἐγκαταλειπόμενοι]. The whole Book of Acts, which contains the perpetual persecutions of the Apostles and fresh examples of divine help from time to time, serves to explain and confirm this clause. To these you may add what we shall hear in chapter 11 below. This also applies to all believers. For it has been said to all: "In the world you will have tribulation, but be of good cheer, I have overcome the world" [Ioh. 16.]. And just as the Lord calls all his people to bear the cross, so he promises to be the protector and avenger of all. And he does this whether he delivers them from dangers or not. For even if he wishes us to be exercised by continual persecutions, he is always present with us and confirms us in faith, so that through us he may triumph over the world and its prince.

units.la: Quartum sequitur: Deijcimur, at non perimus. Simile ab ijs sumptum, qui inter luctandum prostrati aut lapsi, mox iterum in pedes exiliunt, & luctam cum aduersario instaurant. Accidit autem saepe pijs, ut prostrati & nunquam emersuri videantur: quo pertinet, quod Paulo Lystris accidit: & idem Corinthi se in maximo timore & tremore versatum esse fatetur. Quid, quod infirmitate aliquando vincuntur sancti, ut fidem quoq; vel dissimulent, vel etiam aperte negent? cuius rei exemplum in Petro habemus. Sed tunc illis manum porrigit Deus, & nouis viribus instauratos erigit, ut ad officium redeant. Admonet ergo nos huius membri consideratio, ne tunc quidem nos ipsum omnem abijce: e debere, quando nos vitios & lapsos esse sentimus, adeo ut indigni videamur, quorum curam Deus porrò habeat. Christus enim non extinguit linum fumigans, neque arundinem quassatam conterit. Imò nostro bono nos aliquid humanitus pati finit, vt in posterum minus confidentes, ab ipso solo pendeamus, & pugnam fortius instauremus. Et hic imprimis locum habet quod proverbio dicitur: Vir fugiens denuo pugnabit: ideoque alios quoque non temere debemus damnare, quibus simile quid accidit.
units.tr: Fourth follows: "We are cast down, but not destroyed" [καταβαλλόμενοι, ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἀπολλύμενοι]. This is taken from those who, when knocked down or slipping while wrestling, soon rise again to their feet and renew the struggle with their opponent. It happens often to the godly that they seem to be laid low and never likely to rise again. To this belongs what happened to Paul at Lystra, and he confesses that he himself was at Corinth in the greatest fear and trembling. And what of the fact that the saints are sometimes overcome by weakness, so that they either hide their faith or even openly deny it? We have an example of this in Peter. But then God stretches out his hand to them and raises them up, restored with new strength, so that they return to their duty. The consideration of this clause therefore admonishes us not to cast away all hope of ourselves even then, when we feel that we are faulty and fallen, so much so that we seem unworthy of God's continuing care. For Christ does not quench the smoking flax, nor break the bruised reed [Matth. 12.; Isa. 42.]. Indeed, for our good he allows us to suffer some things as men do, so that in future, being less confident, we may depend upon him alone, and renew the fight more vigorously. And here above all applies the proverb: "A man who has fled will fight again." Therefore we ought not rashly to condemn others too, to whom something similar has happened.

units.la: Interim meminerimus, toto hoc loco commendari Euangelicae doctrinae & fidei Christianae certitudinem, quae inter tot & tanta pericula propagata, & in hunc vsque diem defensa atque seruata est. Gentium superstitiones nemo vnquam aperta vi persecutus est, quin potius vnanimi totius orbis consensu receptae & probatae fuerunt. Eadem tamen manifestato in carne Dei Filio collapsae sunt, neque eas vel vnanimis populorum consensus, vel Romani Imperij amplitudo & potentia aduersus Euangelij praedicationem defendere potuit. E contra doctrina de CHRISTO IESV, & quae huic nititur fides, iam inde ab initio mundi persecutionibus obnoxia fuit: durat tamen adhuc, & durabit vsque in finem saeculi. Ista nos consolentur inter turbas & machinationes, quibus mundus hic illam euertere studet.
units.tr: Meanwhile let us remember that this whole passage commends the certainty of the Evangelical doctrine and of the Christian faith, which, amid so many and so great dangers, has been propagated, and to this day has been defended and preserved. No one ever attacked the superstitions of the Gentiles with open force; rather, they were received and approved by the unanimous consent of the whole world. Yet these same superstitions collapsed once the Son of God was manifested in the flesh, and neither the unanimous consent of the peoples nor the greatness and power of the Roman Empire could defend them against the preaching of the Gospel. On the contrary, the doctrine concerning CHRIST JESUS, and the faith that rests upon it, has been exposed to persecutions from the very beginning of the world; yet it endures still, and will endure until the end of the age. Let these things console us amid the tumults and schemes by which this world seeks to overthrow it.

units.la: Porrò quod per partes exposuerat Paulus, id nunc summatim comprehendit, dicens: Quoliebet mortificationem Domini IESV in corpore circumferentes; &c. Ita verò vocat afflictiones quotidianas, quae ipsis in horas mortem minabantur, & has eodem sensu mortificationem Christi dicit, quo supra Cap. primo passiones Christi dixerat: Nimirum, quòd ista propter hunc sustinerent, & quòd in sibi factū putat, quicquid suus fit. Et ita ipse mox exponit: Semper enim nos qui viuimus (scilicet in Christo & ex eius virtute) in mortem tradimur propter IESVM. Et cur hoc? Vt etiam vita IESV manifesta fiat in mortali carne nostra. Dicit autem vitam IESV, viuificam illam virtutem, qua in mortem deuicit, vt per hanc ad vitam coelestem transferit, in qua nunc regnat atque suos tuetur. Itaque hic verborum istorum sensus est: Nemo nos propter vitae genus afflictissimum & persecutiones continuas contemnat, aut Euangelium ideo minoris faciat. Quicquid enim patimur, id omne propter Christum patimur: qui vt in nobis affligitur, ita nos sibi conformes facit, simulque sua vitam in nobis manifestat, dum nos adhuc in mortali carne agentes mirificè seruat, & quotidie ex mille mortibus eripit. At hoc dicendo, simul acriter pungit ministerij sui contemptores, quòd nimirum iniuria haec, qua ipsum & reliquos Apostolos afficiant, in aeternū Dei Filium IESVM CHRISTVM, redundet.
units.tr: Moreover, what Paul had set out part by part, he now sums up briefly, saying: "always carrying about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus," etc. He calls by this name the daily afflictions which threatened them with death every hour, and he speaks of these as the mortification of Christ in the same sense in which, above in the first chapter, he had spoken of the sufferings of Christ. Namely, because they endured these things on account of him, and because he counts as done to himself whatever is done to his own. And so he himself explains at once: "For we who live (that is, in Christ and by his power) are always delivered over to death for Jesus' sake." And why this? "So that the life of Jesus may also be made manifest in our mortal flesh." He calls it the life of Jesus, that life-giving power by which he conquered death, so that through it he might carry us into the heavenly life, in which he now reigns and keeps his own safe. Thus the sense of these words is this: let no one despise us on account of the most wretched manner of life and our continual persecutions, or hold the Gospel the less in esteem because of them. For whatever we suffer, we suffer it all for Christ; who, as he is afflicted in us, so he makes us conformed to himself, and at the same time manifests his life in us, while we, still living in mortal flesh, he wondrously preserves and daily snatches from a thousand deaths. But in saying this, he also sharply stings those who despise his ministry: because this injury, by which they wound him and the other Apostles, redounds upon the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ himself.

units.la: Rursus autem hoc etiam loco admonemur, quid de afflictionibus piorū iudicari debeat? Primò, quòd ipsius Christi passiones siue mortificationes sint. Vt enim corpus affligi dicitur, quando vnum modo membrum vulneratur aut laeditur, imprimis autem caput curam membri affecti ad se pertinere putat: ita inter Christum & eius corpus, Ecclesiam, eadem planè est compassionis ratio. Quoties ergo pius aliquis vincitur, caeditur, relegatur, occiditur, toties haec ipsa Christum pati putemus. Quanta ergo impietas est pios & credentes affligere? quàm infelices icem & miseri, qui pios affligendo, Christi iram aduersus se prouocant? Deinde Christo nos conformes faciunt afflictiones eiusmodi. Est haec praecipua, quae homini potest obtingere, gloria. Quis enim nolit similis censeri filio Regis, qui in acie periclitatus per honesta vulnera victoriā de hostibus retulit? Tertiò ad gloriam Christi & nostram salutem afflictiones faciunt. Ita enim manifestatur vita Christi in nobis, id est, certò demonstratur, eum reuera viuere & regnare, imò vitae & mortis esse domi num. Nisi enim is esset, neq; suos in tantis periculis tueri, neq; in medio hostium dominari posset, sicut de illo Dauid vaticinatur. Nos verò afflictionibus mortificati quoad carnem, per illas ad vitam nouam ingredimur. Pertinet ergo ad huius loci expositionem, quod Paulus ad Colossenses scribit: Mortui estis, id est, dum in hac carne viuitis, mortem quasi circumfertis: Vita autem vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo, cuius virtutem nunc quidem experimini: Olim verò quando Christus, vita illa nostra, patefactus fuerit, tum & vos cum eo patefietis gloriosi, & ceu arca reclusa toti mundo patebit vita & gloria vestra, cuius nobis Mediator est Christus. Consentit his Ioannes Apostolus, sic scribens: Charissimi, nunc filij Dei sumus, sed nondum patefactum est quod erimus: scimus autem fore, vt cum ipse patefactus fuerit, similes ei simus: quoniam videbimus eum sicuti est. Ista ergo nos in tentationibus consolentur, ne iniquis saeculi mundi iudicijs moueamur.
units.tr: Again, in this place we are also taught what ought to be judged concerning the afflictions of the godly. First, that they are the very sufferings or mortifications of Christ himself. For just as the body is said to be afflicted when only one member is wounded or injured, and the head especially considers the care of the affected member to belong to itself, so between Christ and his body, the Church, there is plainly the same relation of compassion. Whenever, therefore, some godly person is overcome, beaten, banished, or killed, let us think that Christ himself suffers this. How great, then, is the impiety of afflicting the godly and believing! How unhappy and wretched are those who, by afflicting the pious, provoke the wrath of Christ against themselves? Next, afflictions of this kind make us conformed to Christ. This is the chief glory that can befall a man. For who would not wish to be counted like the son of a King, who, having been endangered in the battle line, has won the victory over the enemy through honourable wounds? Third, afflictions serve the glory of Christ and our salvation. For thus the life of Christ is manifested in us, that is, it is clearly shown that he truly lives and reigns, and indeed is the Lord of life and death. For unless he were such, he could neither keep his own safe in such great dangers, nor rule in the midst of enemies, as David prophesied of him. But we, mortified as to the flesh by afflictions, through them enter into a new life. Therefore, to the exposition of this passage belongs what Paul writes to the Colossians: "You are dead," that is, while you live in this flesh you carry death about as it were; "but your life is hidden with Christ in God," whose power you now indeed experience; but one day, when Christ, that our life, shall be revealed, then you too shall be revealed with him in glory, and your life and glory, of which Christ is our Mediator, shall lie open to the whole world like an unlocked chest. John the Apostle agrees with these things, writing thus: "Beloved, now we are the sons of God, but it is not yet made manifest what we shall be; we know, however, that when he shall be manifested, we shall be like him, since we shall see him as he is." Let these things, therefore, console us in temptations, so that we are not moved by the unjust judgments of the wicked world.

units.la: Caeterum concludit hanc Comparationem Paulus: Itaque mors quidem in nobis agit, vita vero in vobis. Quasi diceret: Quid multis opus est? In nobis nihil quàm mortem cernitis, quae ut hostis aliquis, omnes vires contra nos exerit, & ad nos opprimendos comites sive satellites suos omnes educit, egestatem nimirum, exilia, vincula, tormenta, famem, & quaecunque excogitari alia possunt. At in his vos spectare decebat, ad quos nam omnis iustorum fructus redeat. Ad vos nimirum, in quibus vita agit. Propter vos enim periculis istis exercemur, ut nimirum Verbum vitae omnibus praedicemus, & eosdem nostro exemplo confirmemus, qui iam ad fidem adducti sunt. Itaque nostri sunt labores, nostra pericula, nostrae mortes, quas subimus: vos autem iustorum omnium fructum percipitis. Sic ipse Paulo posset exponet: Omnia propter vos, ut gratia illa copiosissima, pluribus gratias agentibus, redundet in gloriam Dei. Subiectē autem huic clausulae acrem exprobratio ingratitudinis, qua aemuli Paulo afflictiones suas exprobrabant, ex quibus fructus tam luculentus ad ipsos redibat. Causa huius vitii illis praecipua fuit, quòd Christianismum sibi fingerent absque cruce: quae opinio hodie etiam multos decipit, ut iniquissimè de Evangelii praedicatione iudicent.
units.tr: Moreover, Paul concludes this comparison: "So death works in us, but life in you." As if he were saying: Why need there be many words? In us you see nothing but death, which, like some enemy, exerts all its forces against us and brings out all its companions or attendants to overwhelm us: namely want, exile, chains, torments, hunger, and whatever else can be devised. But in these things you ought to look to where the whole fruit of the righteous returns: namely, to you, in whom life works. For it is on your account that we are exercised by these perils, so that we may indeed proclaim the Word of life to all, and confirm by our example those who have already been brought to the faith. Thus our labours, our dangers, and the deaths that we undergo are ours; but you receive the fruit of all the righteous. Paul could thus put it in his own words: "All things are for your sake, so that grace, abounding more and more, may through the thanksgiving of many redound to the glory of God." Then to this conclusion he attaches a sharp rebuke of ingratitude, by which his rivals reproached Paul for his afflictions, though from them so splendid a fruit came back to themselves. The chief cause of this vice in them was that they imagined a Christianity without the cross; an opinion which today also deceives many, so that they judge most unjustly concerning the preaching of the Gospel.

units.la: Quod autem Paulus de Corinthiis queritur, hoc omnibus fere accidit, qui aliorum salutem promovere cupiunt. Olim certè non alia Mosis fors fuit. Cùm enim propter Israelitas, gentiles fusos, à Regis gratia excidisset, & cum diuitiis amplissimis honores atque dignitates tantumnon regias reliquisset, ut illos ex dura servitute afferret, eosdem tamen ingratissimos expertus est, ad quos omnis laborum & periculorum fructus redierat. Idem Prophetae postea passi sunt, quos publicae salutis studium mouit, ut periculis atque odiis multorum sese exponerent. Et reliqui Apostoli, perinde ut Paulo pessimam gratiam infelix mundus retulit. Quid ergo miramur, si hodie idem fiat? Fit idem plerunque iis, qui in repub. administranda fideles sunt. At non propterea segnescere debent, sed potius officium sedulò facere, & spem in Deo collocatam habere, qui in sua vocatione laborantes non deseret, sed propitius illis aderit, ut tandem in ipsis manifestetur vita illa gloriosa IESV CHRISTI Domini nostri: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: What Paul complains of in the Corinthians happens to almost all who wish to promote the salvation of others. Certainly Moses' lot was no different in times past. For when, on account of the Israelites, the Gentiles' victims, he had fallen from the favour of the King, and had left behind wealth and honours, indeed almost royal dignities, in order to rescue them from harsh slavery, he nevertheless found them most ungrateful, to whom the whole fruit of his labours and dangers had returned. The Prophets afterwards suffered the same, whom zeal for the public welfare moved to expose themselves to the dangers and hatred of many. And the other Apostles, just as the unhappy world repaid Paul with the worst return. Why, then, do we wonder if the same happens today? It happens most often to those who are faithful in administering the commonwealth. Yet on that account they ought not to grow slack, but rather to perform their duty diligently, and to have their hope placed in God, who does not forsake those labouring in their calling, but will be propitious and present to them, so that at last that glorious life of Jesus Christ our Lord may be manifested in them: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XVIII.
units.tr: HOMILIA XVIII.

units.la: Et quia habemus eundem Spiritũ fidei, secundùm illud quod scriptum est: Credidi, & ideo locutus sum: nos quoque credimus, quamobrem etiam loquimur: Scientes fore, ut qui excitauit Dominum IESVM, nos quoque per IESVM excitet, & sistat vobiscum. Nam haec omnia propter vos, ut gratia illa copiosissima, pluribus gratias agentibus, redundet in gloriam Dei. Propterea non segnescimus: sed etiamsi homo noster externus corrumpitur, internus tamen renouatur quotidie. Momentanea enim levitas oppressionis nostrae excellenter excellenter aeternũ pondus gloriae conficit nobis: dum non spectamus ea quae cernuntur, sed ea quae non cernuntur. Nam quae cernuntur temporaria sunt: at quae non cernuntur, aeterna.
units.tr: And because we have the same spirit of faith, according to what is written: "I believed, and therefore have I spoken," we also believe, and therefore we also speak. Knowing that he who raised up the Lord Jesus will raise us also by Jesus and will present us with you. For all these things are for your sake, so that grace, which is most abundant, may overflow through the thanksgiving of many to the glory of God. Therefore we do not lose heart; even though our outward man is wasting away, our inward man is renewed day by day. For our momentary light affliction produces for us an eternal weight of glory far beyond all comparison, since we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are unseen are eternal.

units.la: Quoniam aliqui Corinthiorum Evangelij doctrinam contemptui habebant, eò quòd Apostolos ubique gentium contemni, & multorum odijs atque persecutionibus obnoxios esse viderent, Paulus nuper multis docuit, hoc adeò nihil derogare Evangelio, ut potius in eo elucet admirabilis Christi virtus, qui dum ipsos inter medias mortes servat, aperte testatur, se mortis & vitae dominum esse, & negotium hoc omne ipsius auspiciis gubernari. Ea autem occasione de seipso & reliquis Apostolis magnificè locutus erat, simulque obiter perstrinxerat Corinthiorum ingratitudinem, qui non agnoscant, laborum & periculorum omnium, quae ipsi sustineant, fructum ad se pertinere: cùm Apostoli in hoc unum intenti sint, ut Ecclesias passim Christo colligant, collectas servent, & ita multos vitae aeternae participes faciant. At poterant ista à maleuolis accipi, quasi arrogantius loqueretur, & vulgus Christianorum præse contemneret, ut qui hodie in Papatu
units.tr: Since some of the Corinthians held the teaching of the gospel in contempt, because they saw the apostles everywhere despised and exposed to the hatred and persecutions of many, Paul has just taught that this in no way detracts from the gospel, but rather that in it the wonderful power of Christ shines forth. Christ, while he preserves them in the midst of deaths, clearly declares that he is the lord of death and of life, and that this whole business is governed under his authority. On that occasion he had spoken magnificently of himself and the other apostles, and at the same time had touched in passing on the ingratitude of the Corinthians, who did not acknowledge that the fruit of all the labours and dangers they endured belonged to them. Yet the apostles are intent on this one thing alone: that they gather churches to Christ everywhere, keep them gathered, and so make many partakers of eternal life. But these words could be taken by ill-wishers as if he spoke too arrogantly and despised the common mass of Christians in comparison with himself, as the Papists do today, who boast that they alone are spiritual and are the clergy of the Lord.

units.la: papatu patuse solos spirituales & clerum Domini esse iactant. Ideo in præsenti huius tantæ fiducia rationem reddit, sic vt Deo quidem omnem ministerij sui gloriam transcribat, Corinthios vero eiusdem victoriæ & salutis socios faciat.
units.tr: Therefore, in the present passage he gives an account of this so great confidence, in such a way that he indeed ascribes all the glory of his ministry to God, and makes the Corinthians sharers in the same victory and salvation.

units.la: Sic vero orditur: Et quia habemus eundem Spiritum fidei, secundum illud quod scriptum est: Credidi, & ideo locutus sum: nos quoque credimus, quamobrem etiam loquimur. Dauidis exem-plum adducit, ne quis fiduciam hanc dicendi nouam & Dei seruis inusitatam esse putet. Extat locus in Psalmo CXVI. Continet is gratiarum actionem, quà Dei laudes celebrat, qui ipsum ex Ab-solomi & coniuratorum eius manibus liberatum in regnum restituerat. Vtque illustrius fit beneficium istud, magnitudinem periculi describit: Circumdederant me laquei mortis, angustiæ inferni inuenerant me: angustiam & dolorem inueneram. Et in nomine Domini inuocabam: Obsecro Deus, eripe animam meam, &c. Et tandem subijcit: Credidi, & ideo locutus sum: cum affligerer va-ds, & cum dicerem in præcipitatione mea: Omnis homo mendax, &c. Id est, cum regno & vrbe e-iectus, omnes eos perfidos experirer, qui mihi imprimis fidem & obedientiam debebant, nihilomi-nus eam fidem retinui, quòd Deus iustus scelerum vindex, & fidelis suorum redemptor sit, eaque fide suffultus ipsum inuocaui. Hæc nunc sibi accommodans Paulus, ita dicere videtur: Si Dauidi olim in extremis angustijs constituto licuit Deum inuocare, sibique certam polliceri de iniquis hostibus victoriam, cur mihi & collegis meis, Apostolis, non idem liceat? Atqui eundem habemus Spiritum fidei, & proinde idem, quod ille olim dixit, dicere possumus. Voluit autem Spiritum fidei potius quàm fidem dicere, vt huius efficaciam simul atque authorem exprimat: eundem videlicet Spiritum, qui olim in Dauide egerit, ne eius fides in periculis succumberet.
units.tr: He begins thus: "And because we have the same spirit of faith, according to what is written: 'I believed, and therefore have I spoken,' we also believe, and therefore we also speak." He brings forward the example of David, lest anyone think that this boldness in speaking is new and unusual for the servants of God. There is a passage in Psalm 116. It contains a thanksgiving by which he celebrates the praises of God, who had restored him to the kingdom after he had been freed from the hands of Absalom and his conspirators. And so that this benefit may be the more illustrious, he describes the magnitude of the danger: "The snares of death encompassed me; the pains of hell laid hold upon me; I found trouble and sorrow." And "I called upon the name of the Lord: O Lord, deliver my soul," and so on. And at last he adds: "I believed, and therefore have I spoken; I was greatly afflicted, and I said in my haste: All men are liars," and so on. That is to say: when I had been cast out of kingdom and city, and found all those faithless men, who especially owed me faith and obedience, nevertheless I held to that faith, because God is a just avenger of crimes and a faithful redeemer of his own, and supported by that faith I called upon him. Now applying this to himself, Paul seems to say: If it was once lawful for David, placed in the greatest straits, to call upon God and to promise himself certain victory over wicked enemies, why should it not likewise be lawful for me and my fellow apostles? But we have the same spirit of faith, and therefore we can say the same thing that he once said. He chose to say "the spirit of faith" rather than "faith," so that he might express at once the efficacy of faith and its author: namely, the same Spirit who once worked in David, lest his faith should give way in dangers.

units.la: Est ergo idem Spiritus Veteris & Noui testamenti: Obseruari hoc debet propter Manichæ-os, quorum furores hodie in Anabaptistis sese exerunt, qui Veteris Scripturæ libros & exempla, vt nihil ad nos pertinentia, reijciunt. Atqui easdem nobiscum promissiones acceperunt veteres, quæ omnes in Christo sunt Etiam & Amen. Pater item omnium credentium dicitur Abrahamus. In vnum quoque Christum illi olim respexerunt, & eandem in venturo collocarunt fiduciam, quam nos in exhibito collocatam habemus. Eadem denique est nostra & illorum hæreditas: quando nos cum Abrahamo, Isaaco & Iacobo in regno Dei accubituros esse Christus testatur. Quibus adde, quòd in præsenti Paulus eundem Spiritum fidei, quem nos habemus, veteribus tribuit. Ergo quæ cum illis Deus olim egit atque locutus est, ad nos quoque pertinent, vt ex ijs cum fidei tum vitæ præcepta atque exempla petamus. Simul autem ista docent, quo Spiritu ducantur, qui in periculis alios quàm vnum Deum per nomen IESV CHRISTI inuocant.
units.tr: Therefore there is one and the same Spirit of the Old and New Testament. This must be observed on account of the Manichees, whose madness shows itself today in the Anabaptists, who reject the books and examples of the Old Scripture as having nothing to do with us. Yet the ancients received the same promises as we do, which are all "Yes and Amen" in Christ. Abraham is also called the father of all believers. Those men of old also looked to one Christ alone, and placed the same trust in the Christ who was to come that we place in the Christ who has been revealed. Finally, our inheritance and theirs is the same, since Christ testifies that we shall recline at table in the kingdom of God with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. To these things add that here Paul ascribes to the ancients the same spirit of faith that we have. Therefore what God once did and spoke with them pertains to us too, so that from these we may seek both the precepts and the examples of faith and of life. At the same time these examples teach by what Spirit those are led who in dangers call upon other gods than the one God through the name of Jesus Christ.

units.la: Exprimitur simul hoc loco fidei ingenium. Hæc totum hominem Deo vendicat, ideoque tam in di-ctis quàm factis sese exerit, vt Iacobus dicit: Ostende mihi fidem tuam ex factis tuis, & ego ostendam tibi fidem meam ex factis meis. Et quia viuum verèque efficax Dei donum, adeoq; ve-rissima hominis χτιλεχία est, perpetuo actu sese declarat, & quò magis premitur, eò magis cum aduersaria vi luctatur, & linguas simul atque manus soluit ad ea, quæ nostri sunt officij. Hinc fit, quòd credentes in aduersis ad Deum clamant, & contra crudelissima tyrannorum edicta fidem suam liberè & palam fatentur. Exempla eius rei in Daniele & socijs habemus, & innumerabi-lia in Martyribus extant, qui omnes vitam potius inter dira tormenta profundere, quàm à Dei vnius inuocatione abstinere voluerunt. Arguunt hæc nostri sæculi Pseudonicodemos, qui confes-sionem, quæ ore fit superuacaneam esse aiunt, eò quòd fides in corde latens atque seruata ad salu-tem sufficiat. Fingunt illi fidem, quæ nihil quàm inanis & mortua persuasio est, aut ex proprio cerebro concepta opinio. Atqui aliter Christus docet, qui se pro suis agnituram esse negat, quos sui nominis apud mundum hunc degenerem puduerit. Et notum est illud Pauli: Corde creditur ad iu-stitiam, ore autem fit confessio ad salutem. Arguuntur etiam hi, qui in sua functione socordes & ignaui sunt, nec aliquid audent pro gloria Dei & salute publica. Etenim, si fidem haberent, procul dubio intrepide loquerentur & facerent, quæcunque officij ipsorum ratio requirit.
units.tr: At the same time the nature of faith is expressed in this place. Faith claims the whole man for God, and therefore it shows itself both in words and in deeds, as James says: "Show me your faith by your works, and I will show you my faith by my works." And because it is a living gift of God, truly effective, and therefore the truest [κτίσις] of man, it always declares itself by action; and the more it is pressed down, the more it struggles against the adverse force, and it loosens both tongue and hands for the things that belong to our duty. Hence it comes about that believers cry out to God in adversity, and openly and freely confess their faith against the most cruel edicts of tyrants. We have examples of this in Daniel and his companions, and countless ones exist among the martyrs, who all chose rather to pour out their lives amid dreadful torments than to refrain from calling upon the one God. These things refute the Pseudo-Nicodemites of our age, who say that confession made with the mouth is superfluous, because faith lying hidden in the heart and kept is sufficient for salvation. They feign a faith which is nothing but an empty and dead persuasion, or an opinion conceived in one's own brain. Yet Christ teaches otherwise, who says that he will not acknowledge before his Father those whom shame has kept from confessing his name in this degenerate world. And that saying of Paul is well known: "With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." Those also are rebuked who are slothful and idle in their office, and dare to do nothing for the glory of God and the public good. For if they had faith, they would undoubtedly speak and act fearlessly, whatever the nature of their office requires.

units.la: Quid vero credidit Paulus, quod tam fortem atque intrepidum fecit? Scientes (inquit) fore, vt qui excitauit Dominum IESVM, nos quoq; per IESVM exciter, & sistat vobiscum, &c. Re-surrectionis suæ nomine hoc loco liberationem ex periculis maximis intelligit, quæ Cap.primo mortem dixerat. Fiduciam vero liberationis istius concepisse se scribit ex resurrectione Christi, & proinde sensus verborum est: Quoniam scimus Deum Filium suum ex mortuis excitauisse, ex eo firma fide colligimus, eundem nos facilius multo ex quouis vitae discrimine liberare posse: imo non dubitamus, quin nos iam in medijs mortis tenebris versantes erepturus sit, ut me vobis restituat, & praesentem sistat. Nam propter vos omnia ista fiunt, quibus nunc exerceor, & ideo propter vos quoque liberabor: ut copiosissima illa gratia, id est, praeclarum hoc & illustre liberationis meae beneficium, publica totius Ecclesiae gratiarum actione celebratum, ad nominis sui gloriam exuberet. Conueniunt his, quae primo Cap. in eandem sententiam dixit.
units.tr: But what did Paul believe that made him so bold and fearless? "Knowing," he says, "that he who raised up the Lord Jesus will raise us also by Jesus and will present us with you," and so on. Here by his resurrection he understands deliverance from the greatest dangers, which in the first chapter he had called death. He writes that he conceived confidence of this deliverance from the resurrection of Christ, and so the sense of the words is: Since we know that God raised his Son from the dead, from this we gather by firm faith that he can much more easily deliver us from any peril of life. Indeed we do not doubt that he will snatch us, even now dwelling in the midst of the shadows of death, so as to restore me to you and present me alive. For all these things, by which I am now exercised, happen for your sake, and therefore I too shall be delivered for your sake, so that that most abundant grace, that is, this remarkable and illustrious benefit of my deliverance, celebrated by the public thanksgiving of the whole Church, may overflow to the glory of his name. These things agree with what he said to the same effect in the first chapter.

units.la: In his autem primo obseruabis, quod fiduciam suam argumento ex Christi resurrectione desumpto confirmat. Facit hoc secundum ipsius Domini exemplum, qui quoties cū discipulis suis de sua morte disseruit, semper eosdem resurrectionis suae promissione consolatus est. In eandem ergo nos quoque respicere conuenit. Vt enim ea nostrae salutis complementum continet: ita sola scandalo crucis medetur, dum illum voluntarium pro nobis passum esse, adhaec vitae mortisq; dominum esse demonstrat. Eadem quia mortis terrores discutit, simul animat nos ne vllis periculis succumbamus. Ideo cum Paulus ad Roman. dixisset: Christus est, qui mortuus est, imo vero, qui etiam excitatus est, qui etiam est ad dexteram Dei, qui etiam postulat pro nobis: mox laetum illud & plenum consolationis epinicium subijcit: Quis nos separabit a charitate Christi? num afflictio? &c. Roman. 8.
units.tr: In these words, first, you will note that he strengthens his confidence with an argument drawn from Christ's resurrection. He does this after the example of the Lord himself, who, whenever he spoke with his disciples about his death, always comforted them with the promise of his resurrection. So we too ought to look to the same thing. For just as it contains the completion of our salvation, so it alone heals the scandal of the cross, since it shows that he suffered voluntarily for us and that he is Lord of life and death. And because it dispels the terrors of death, it at the same time encourages us not to yield to any dangers. Therefore, when Paul had said in Romans: "It is Christ who died, yes rather, who was also raised, who is also at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us," he immediately adds that joyful and comforting song of triumph: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall affliction?" and so on. Romans 8.

units.la: Obseruabis praeterea, quod omnia, quae tam ipse quam collegae ipsius Apostoli reliqui patiebantur, propter Corinthios fieri dicit, Atqui erant illi iam salui ex Christi merito, quem fide apprehenderant. Sed in eo laborarunt Apostoli, vt salutis notitiam indies ad plures alios propagarent, & quos iam Christo lucrifecerant, in officio continerent. Est hoc luculentum φιλανθρωπίας aut bonitatis Dei argumentum, qui homines sibi amicissimos tot laboribus & periculis exerceri voluit propter mundum hunc, qui totus in malo iacet, vt Ioannes ait. Prouidentiae item singularis opus est, quod eos, quos in fide nouit firmiores esse, periculis obijcit, vt in eis primus hostium furor hebetetur, simulque infirmiores fidei & patientiae exempla habeant, quibus confirmentur. Factum hoc nuper in Gallia, quando Tridentini Concilij furorem in fratres nostros, qui illic sunt, effundi voluit, quod non ignoraret, quid facturi fuissent alij, quos otij abundantia in fide frigidiores iam fecerat si tempestas illa in ipsos primos fuisset deriuata. Si quid ergo huius alibi quoq; fit, agnoscamus Dei consilium, & fauore atq; precibus nostris prosequamur eos, qui pro communi causa periclitantur.
units.tr: Further, you will note that everything which both he himself and the other apostles suffered, he says is done on account of the Corinthians. Yet those men were already saved through the merit of Christ, whom they had grasped by faith. But the apostles labored in order to spread the knowledge of salvation daily to many others, and to keep in duty those whom they had already gained for Christ. This is a clear proof of God's love of mankind, or his goodness, who willed that men most dear to him should be exercised with so many labors and dangers for the sake of this world, which, as John says, lies wholly in evil. It is also the work of a singular providence that he exposes to dangers those whom he knows to be firmer in faith, so that the first fury of the enemies may be blunted on them, and at the same time the weaker in faith may have examples of faith and patience by which they may be strengthened. This happened recently in France, when the fury of the Council of Trent wished to pour itself out upon our brethren who are there, though it was not unaware of what the others would have done, whom an abundance of leisure had already made colder in faith, if that storm had been diverted upon them first. If, therefore, something of this kind happens elsewhere too, let us recognize the counsel of God, and by our favor and prayers let us support those who are in peril for the common cause.

units.la: Adhaec docemur hoc loco gratiarum actionem deberi Deo pro acceptis beneficijs. Vult enim hic, vt gloriam nominis sui pro virili prouehamus. At quid obsecro illi conferre possumus praeter gratiarum actionem, cum neque ille nostri indigeat, neque nos aliquid ex nobismetipsis habeamus? Illa vero, vt de animi nostri pietate testatur, & confessionis species est: ita plures alios exemplo excitat, vt idem faciant. Ideo in Lege Deus sacra eucharistica instituit, & gratiarum actionem publicam sanctè in Psalmis vouent, qua nullū sacrificiū Deo magis acceptū & pretiosius esse, Dauid testatur. Christus quoque abolitis omnibus sacrificijs, Coenam suam mysticam instituit, qua mortem ipsius praedicemus, quo nomine illam veteres Eucharistiam siue Gratiarum actionem, & propter hanc sacrificium quoque dixerunt. At in hac etiam parte plurimum peccatur. In aduersis quidē plurimi ad Deum clamant: at qui liberati beneficium eius agnoscant, pauci sunt. Quid, quod plerique eius beneficijs abutuntur? Quòd si vero Corinthij simul omnes publicè Deo debuerunt gratias agere, si Paulus ipsis restituisset, quid nos non debemus Domino, qui hoc nouissimo tempore cum Apostolis ipsum quoque Christum per Euangelij doctrinam nobis restituit, quae sub Antichristianis tenebris diu sepulta latuerat? Quàm ingens hoc beneficium sit, sentiunt qui adhuc tyrannide pseudocleri papistici premuntur. Ex nobis vero multos satietas iam coepit, quam fames noua breui discutiet.
units.tr: Besides, we are taught in this place that thanksgiving is owed to God for benefits received. For he wishes us to advance the glory of his name as far as we can. But what, I beg you, can we offer him besides thanksgiving, since he has no need of us, and we have nothing of our own? Indeed, thanksgiving, as it bears witness to the piety of our mind, is also a kind of confession; and by example it stirs many others to do the same. Therefore God instituted sacred thank-offerings in the Law, and in the Psalms they vow public thanksgiving devoutly; David testifies that no sacrifice is more acceptable and precious to God than this. Christ too, having abolished all sacrifices, instituted his mystical Supper, in which we proclaim his death; for this reason the ancients called it the Eucharist, that is, Thanksgiving, and on account of this they also called it a sacrifice. Yet in this part too there is very much sin. In adversity indeed very many cry out to God, but those who acknowledge his benefit when they are delivered are few. And what of the fact that many abuse his benefits? But if the Corinthians all together ought to have given thanks to God publicly, when Paul had restored them to themselves, what ought we not to owe to the Lord, who in these last times, with the apostles, has restored to us Christ himself through the teaching of the gospel, which had long lain buried under Antichristian darkness? How great this benefit is, those feel who are still oppressed by the tyranny of the Papists' false clergy. But among us many have already begun to grow weary of it, a hunger that is new will soon shake them out of that.

units.la: Porrò redit Paulus ad id, quod initio huius Cap. dixit, & ostendit quibus fulcris fidem suam fultentet, vt non succumbat tot tantisque laboribus: & de his quidem sic disserit, vt suo exemplo Corinthios quoque instruat & confirmet. Quae ergo hic dicuntur, singuli sibi ipsis accommodare debent, vt iisdem argumentis suam quoque fidem ad constantiam arment. Propositio est: Propterea non segnescimus, id est quicquid aduersi aut periculi inciderit; ego tamen non deficio in fide, quò minus perseuerem, & per omnia obstacula eluctor. Quod vere ab illo dici, totus Actorum liber abunde probat. Atqui hoc imprimis omnes Verbi administros decet, imò vt constantia se armet, plus quam necesse est: quia infinita sunt, quae eos tentant, inter quae praecipuum fere est Ingratitudo hominum, & quòd se nequicquam laborare putant. Hoc certè Mosem, Eliam, Ieremiam & plures alios fatigauit olim, qui in Dei seruitio praestantissimi fuerunt. Et hodie multos decipit, quòd quid hucusque fecerint & passi sint solummodo respiciunt, non autem obseruant, quid porrò agendum restet. Hinc voces illae importunae proficiscuntur: Nos abunde satis laborauimus, satis periclitati sumus, satis diu hoc saxum voluimus. Laborent nunc alij quoque & periclitentur: nos rude donari meremur. At quanto iustius sic loqui poterat Paulus? Sed longè alia eius sententia atque mens fuit, cum se non segnescere dicat propter ea, quae hucusque fecerat. Et alibi post innumeros labores, obsecrantibus illum pijs, vt sibi parceret, se non vinciri modò verum etiam mori pro Christo paratum esse testatur. Et quis frugi seruum dixerit eum, qui ipse sibi absque berisui consensu feras facit? Sed audiamus rationes Pauli.
units.tr: Furthermore, Paul returns to what he said at the beginning of this chapter, and shows by what supports he sustains his faith, so that it does not give way under so many and such great labors; and about these things he speaks in such a way as to instruct and strengthen the Corinthians too by his own example. Therefore, what is said here each person ought to apply to himself, so that by the same arguments he may also arm his own faith for constancy. The proposition is this: "For this reason we do not lose heart," that is, whatever adversity or danger befalls, "yet I do not fail in faith, so that I do not persevere and struggle through all obstacles." That the whole book of Acts abundantly proves that these words were truly spoken by him. Yet this above all befits all ministers of the Word, indeed that they arm themselves with constancy more than is necessary, because there are endless things that tempt them, among which the chief is nearly the ingratitude of men, and the thought that they labor to no purpose. This certainly wearied Moses, Elijah, Jeremiah and many others long ago, who were most outstanding in the service of God. And today it deceives many, because they look only at what they have done and suffered up to now, and do not consider what still remains to be done. Hence those troublesome cries arise: "We have labored enough, we have been in danger enough, we have rolled this stone long enough. Let others now labor and be in danger too; we deserve to be released as a discharged soldier." But how much more justly could Paul have spoken thus! Yet his judgment and mind were quite different, when he says that he does not lose heart on account of what he had done up to that point. And elsewhere, after countless labors, when devout men begged him to spare himself, he testifies that he is prepared not only to be bound but even to die for Christ. And who would call a servate worthy who takes holidays for himself without his master's consent? But let us hear Paul's reasons.

units.la: Primam nuper ex Christi resurrectione desumpsit, & ea docuit, facillimum esse Deo in media etiam morte suos seruare. Eam nunc expolit, & ita carnis obiectioni respondet: At interim tu laboribus consumeris, & tandem omnino peris. Offendit ergo nihil periculi subesse, dicens: Nam etiamsi externus homo noster corrumpitur, internus tamen renouatur quotidie. Per prosopopoeiam in vna hominis Christiani persona duos homines fingit, Externum & Internum. Externum dicit, non corpus solum, sed quaecunque ad hoc spectant, & praesentis vitae conseruationi seruiunt, qualia sunt, opes, honores, voluptates licitae, gaudia, integrior hominis valetudo. Internus homo similiter, non anima sola aut spiritus dicitur: sed potius noua illa creatura, quam ex regeneratione habemus, adeoque ipse fidelis, qui non carnalibus desiderijs seruit, sed totus spiritu Christi regitur, & huic obtemperat. Quare per Concessionem ista loquitur Apostolus: Fateor sane, multum mihi interea decedere, quoad corpus & vitae huius praesentis commoda. Qui enim inter Iudaeos diuitijs abundabam, dignitatibus florebam, omnibus charus eram, commodissimè item & hilariter viuebam: nunc bonis exutus incertis sedibus hinc inde oberro, contumelijs multorum proscindor, periculis quotidie nouis obijcior, laboribus frangor, decurrente simul ad suum finem hac vita, de qua mihi porrò non multum polliceri possum. Interea autem internus homo, quoad mentem & nouam, quae mihi ex regeneratione Spiritu obtigit, creaturam, indies renouatur, dum nouas subinde fidei & spei vires concipio, & ad officium faciendum alacrior fio. Non possum ergo segnescere aut defatigari, cum me indies robustiorem fieri sentiam. Simile quid infra Cap. duodecimo sibi à Domino dictum fuisse scribit: Sufficit tibi gratia mea: quia virtus mea in infirmitate perficitur.
units.tr: He first took the argument from Christ's resurrection, and taught that it is most easy for God to preserve his people even in the midst of death. Now he refines this, and so answers the objection of the flesh: "But meanwhile you are worn out with labors, and at last you will utterly perish." He shows therefore that there is no danger lurking, saying: "For even if our outward man is wasting away, yet our inward man is renewed day by day." By prosopopoeia he imagines two men in the one person of a Christian, the outward and the inward. By the outward he means not only the body, but everything that pertains to it and serves the preservation of the present life, such as wealth, honors, lawful pleasures, joys, the better health of the man. Likewise the inward man is not called the soul alone or the spirit, but rather that new creature which we have through regeneration; and thus the faithful man himself, who does not serve carnal desires, but is wholly ruled by the Spirit of Christ and obeys him. Therefore the Apostle says these things by way of concession: "I admit indeed that much is taken from me in the meantime, as far as the body and the advantages of this present life are concerned. For I who among the Jews abounded in riches, flourished in dignities, was dear to all, and lived most comfortably and cheerfully, am now stripped of goods, wander here and there without any settled home, am torn by the insults of many, am exposed daily to new dangers, am broken by labors, while this life at the same time runs to its end, of which I can promise myself little more. Meanwhile, however, the inward man, as regards the mind and the new creature which has come to me by regeneration through the Spirit, is renewed day by day, while I continually conceive fresh strength of faith and hope, and become more eager to do my duty. I cannot therefore lose heart or be worn out, since I feel myself becoming stronger every day." He writes that something similar was said to him by the Lord in the twelfth chapter below: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness."

units.la: Rursus autem commedatur nobis hoc loco vsus praecipuus afflictionum: qui est quòd nos ad vitam caelestem praeparant, inq; ijs instructiores reddunt, quae ad hanc consequendam faciunt. Quod enim Paulus de seipso dicit, hoc de omnibus Christianis debet intelligi, & facit ad huius loci explicationem quod habetur ad Romanos quinto Cap. Afflictio patientiam parit, patientia autem experientiam, &c: de quo cum alibi dixerimus, eadem hic repetere non est opus. Hoc tamen in praesenti addimus, quòd vt aurum ex igne splendidius prodit: sic fides afflictionum flammis excocta nos illustriores facit. Singuli ergo haec sibijpsis applicent, & obseruent Dei consilium, qui corpori aut carni vitae praesentis commoda subducit, vt nos cogat relictis terrenis ad caelestia aspirare. Sic opes aufert, vt discamus non in his, sed in Deo viuente confidere. Valetudinem corporis affligit, ne ea ad libidine & voluptates illicitas abutamur: sed membra nostra faciamus arma iustitiae Dei, nosque totos huic sistamus viuente hostia. Aduersis nos undiq; premit, vt huius saeculi pertaesi, animos in patriae caelestis desiderium attollamus. Vinculis & carceribus coercet, vt mens liberius Deum colat. Deniq; vita ipsa auferitur, vt eam cum aeterna & immortali commutemus. Ita enim fieri oportet, quando corruptibilis haec natura ad ἀφθαρσίας id est, conditionis illius incorruptibilis non est capax, quanobis Christus in caelis parauit. Haec vt consolationem dulcissimam pijs afferunt, ita docent quoq; quàm vani sint impiorum conatus, qui fidei lucem & regnum Dei in credentibus opprimi posse putant tormentis & diris exemplis suppliciorum. Quod enim hic dicitur, hoc omnium saeculorum exemplis iampridem confirmatum est, & hodie multa fiunt passim, quae his fidem faciunt. Sequitur altera Pauli ratio, à fine & fructu crucis aut afflictionū desumpta. Momentanea enim leuitas oppressionis nostræ excellenter excellenter æternum pondus gloriæ conficit nobis, &c. Finem afflictionum nobis lætissimum à Deo propositū esse docet, quem certò tandem assequamur. Amplificat verò argumentū hoc eleganti antithesi. Momentaneo enim opponit id, quod excellentissimè æternum, adeoq; ipsa æternitate (vt sic dicam) æternum est. Leuitati item pondus, afflictioni gloriam opponit. Vere autem momentaneas dicit afflictiones, quia citò præteruolant, neque diu durare possunt, quando vita ipsa momentanea & (vt Iacobus scribit) vapor est subitò exurgens & euanescens. Simul autem modum exponit, quo comparationem istam ad consolationem aut fidei suæ confirmationem applicet: Dum scilicet non spectamus ea quæ cernuntur, sed ea quæ non cernuntur. Et huius quoq; dicti rationem reddit: Nam quæ cernuntur, temporaria sunt: at quæ non cernuntur, æterna. Ita vero docet suo exemplo Paulus, quæ Christianorum hominum meditationes esse debeant. Conferant inter se diligenter conditionem vitæ præsentis & futuræ. Quæcunq; ad illa faciunt, & subiensum cadunt, temporaria sunt. Transit enim figura mundi huius, & eauum nostrum (vt Dauidis verbis vtar) est quasi non sit, & in imagine vadit homo. Et debet hoc tam de lætis quàm tristibus, secundis & aduersis intelligi. Nihil in hoc sæculo perpetuū & stabile. Futura autem illa, vt nō videntur, ita nullis casibus obnoxia sunt, sed æternum durant. De his Propheta olim pronuntiauit: Quæ oculus non vidit, & auris non audiuit, neque in cor hominis ascenderunt, ea parauit Dominus iis, qui ipsum diligunt. Et Christus thesauri nobis in cœlo repositi meminit, quem neque erugo & tinea exedant, neque fures furari possint. Vsus istorum nobis hic esto, ne propter aduersa stationem nostram deseramus, neue propter huius vitæ commoda aliquid faciamus præter officiū. Hæc enim euanida sunt, neq; certò constat, quàm diu eis frui possimus: at quæ ignauis defectoribus parata sunt pœnæ, æternæ sunt. De illis enim dictū est: Vermis eorū non morietur, et ignis eorū non extinguetur. Vide concionē Simeonis Seleuciæ episcopi, qua centū Martyres, qui simul omnes à Sapore Persarum rege occidebātur, consolatus est. Sozomenus.lib.2. Cap.10.
units.tr: Again, the principal use of afflictions is commended to us in this passage: they prepare us for the heavenly life and make us better equipped for the things that lead to it. What Paul says of himself should be understood of all Christians, and what is written in Romans 5 helps to explain this place: "affliction produces patience, patience experience," and so on. I have discussed this elsewhere, so there is no need to repeat it here. Yet this we add at present: as gold comes out more brilliant from the fire, so faith, refined in the flames of affliction, makes us more illustrious. Let each one therefore apply these things to himself and observe the counsel of God, who withdraws from the body or the flesh the comforts of present life, so that, leaving earthly things, we are forced to aspire to heavenly ones. So He takes away wealth, that we may learn to trust not in such things but in the living God. He afflicts bodily health, lest we abuse it for lust and illicit pleasures, but that we make our members weapons of God's righteousness and present ourselves wholly as a living sacrifice. He presses us on every side with adversities, so that, weary of this age, we may lift our minds to desire the heavenly fatherland. He restrains us with chains and prisons, so that the mind may worship God more freely. Finally, life itself is taken away, so that we may exchange it for the eternal and immortal. For so it must be, since this corruptible nature is not capable of [ἀφθαρσία], that is, of that incorruptible condition which Christ has prepared for us in heaven. As these things bring the sweetest consolation to the godly, so they also teach how vain are the efforts of the impious, who think that the light of faith and the kingdom of God can be crushed in believers by torments and dreadful examples of punishment. For what is said here has been confirmed long ago by the examples of all ages, and today many things happen everywhere that bear witness to it. Next follows another reason of Paul's, taken from the end and fruit of the cross or of afflictions: "For our momentary light affliction works out for us an eternal weight of glory," and so on. He teaches that God has set before us a most joyful end of afflictions, which we shall certainly attain at last. He strengthens this argument by an elegant antithesis. For he sets against the momentary what is supremely eternal, and so eternal, as I may say, by eternity itself. Likewise he sets glory against affliction and weight against lightness. Indeed he calls the afflictions truly momentary, because they quickly fly past and cannot last long, since life itself is momentary and (as James writes) a vapour that rises suddenly and vanishes. At the same time he sets out the way in which he applies this comparison to his own consolation and the confirmation of his faith: namely, while we do not look at the things that are seen, but at the things that are not seen. He also gives the reason for this saying: "For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal." By his own example Paul teaches what the meditations of Christians ought to be. Let them carefully compare the condition of the present life with that of the future. Whatever belongs to the former and is subject to its changes is temporal. For "the fashion of this world passes away," and "our age" (to use David's words) "is as nothing," and "man walks in an image." This must be understood of joyful things as much as of sad, of prosperity as much as of adversity. Nothing in this age is lasting and stable. But those future things, as they are not seen, so they are subject to no chances, but endure forever. Of these the prophet once declared: "What eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and what has not entered into the heart of man, the Lord has prepared for those who love Him." And Christ speaks of the treasure laid up for us in heaven, which neither rust nor moth consumes and thieves cannot steal. Let us make use of these things here, so that on account of adversity we do not desert our post, nor for the comforts of this life do anything beyond our duty. For these are fleeting, nor is it certain how long we may enjoy them; but the punishments prepared for idle deserters are eternal. Of them it was said: "Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched." See the sermon of Simeon, bishop of Seleucia, with which he consoled the hundred martyrs who were being put to death together by Sapor, king of the Persians. Sozomen, book 2, chapter 10.

units.la: Sed priusquam dicendi finem faciamus, propius aliquanto inspici debet locutio qua momentaneam afflictionem æternum pondus gloriæ nobis conficere dicit. Hanc enim quidam intelligunt, quasi afflictionibus gloriam cœlestem & vitam æternam merearmur. Sed obseruare oportet, hic de solis credentibus agi, qui dum affliguntur, Christo conformes fiunt. Nihil ergo hæc ad impios, quibus afflictiones scelerum pœnæ sunt, & nisi resipiscant, infernalium suppliciorum præludia. Quoad pios, hi quidem per afflictiones multas (vt alibi dicitur) ingrediuntur in regnum Dei, nō autē hoc illis merentur. Primò enim non sunt hæ comparandæ cum gloria illa æterna: quæ olim revelabitur. Deinde regnum cœlorum hereditas est, cuius ius ex regeneratione dependet, & non nisi Dei filijs debetur. Quod ergo huius sæculi aduersa nobis adiumento sunt ad æternam salutem, id ex eo est, quòd Christus ea suo merito sanctificauit, & propter hunc Deo probatur nostra in his ferendis patientia. Deinde, quòd carnem in ordinem redigunt, ne eius affectus praui nos transfuersos abripiant. At si fides desit, ne hoc quidem præstant, sed potius murmuratores faciunt. Itaque vniuersa nostræ salutis gloria vni Deo transcribi debet, qui nos ex gratuita misericordia elegit, & Filium suum, IESVM CHRISTVM, nobis redemptorem dedit, in quo vno habentur, quæ ad salutē faciunt. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But before we make an end of speaking, the expression by which he says that a momentary affliction works out for us an eternal weight of glory ought to be examined somewhat more closely. For some understand it as if by afflictions we merited heavenly glory and eternal life. But it must be observed that Paul here speaks only of believers, who, while they are afflicted, are made conformable to Christ. Therefore these words do not concern the impious, for whom afflictions are punishments for their crimes and, unless they repent, previews of infernal torments. As for the godly, indeed, through many afflictions (as is said elsewhere) they enter into the kingdom of God, yet they do not merit it by them. For, first, these afflictions are not to be compared with that eternal glory which will one day be revealed. Next, the kingdom of heaven is an inheritance, whose right depends on regeneration and is owed only to the sons of God. Therefore, that the adversities of this age help us toward eternal salvation comes from this: Christ has sanctified them by His merit, and because of Him our patience in bearing them is approved by God. Next, they bring the flesh into order, so that its depraved affections do not carry us off course. But if faith is lacking, they do not even accomplish this, but rather make us murmurers. Therefore the whole glory of our salvation ought to be ascribed to God alone, who chose us out of free mercy and gave us His Son, JESUS CHRIST, as our redeemer, in whom alone are contained the things that pertain to salvation. To Him be blessing, honour, glory and power forever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: HOMILIA XIX.
units.tr: HOMILY XIX.

units.la: SCimus enim, nos, si terrestris huius domus nostræ tabernaculum dissolutum fuerit, ædificium ex Deo habituros, domicilium videlicet non manufactum, æternum in cœlis. In hoc enim suspiramus, expetentes domicilio nostro, quod è cœlo est, superindui: siquidem etiam induti, non nudi reperiemur.
units.tr: For we know that if the tent of this earthly house of ours is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this we groan, longing to be clothed upon with our habitation which is from heaven; since indeed, having been clothed, we shall not be found naked.

units.la: TSI Deus per Euangelij prædicationem miseris mortalibus æternæ salutis thesaurum in Filio suo, IESU CHRISTO, offerat: pauci tamen Euangelium, vt par erat, recipiunt. Causa inter alias non postrema est, quòd illi crucem & persecutiones coniunctas esse vident. Quia enim carnis ratio Dei fauorem huius seculi commodis metitur, non potest sibi persuadere, eam doctrinam ex Deo esse, Deoq; probari, cuius ministri & sectatores tot casibus atque periculis exagitantur. Opus itaque est, vt hic diligenter instituamur, ne publicum hoc scandalum fidei & saluti nostræ officiat, Ideo Paulus, cum sciret multos ministerium suum propter persecutiones, quibus assiduè vexabatur, suspectum habere, multis docuit hucusque illas Euangelio nihil derogare, neque se propterea animo frangi. Rationes adduxit: primam, quia ex his pateat, doctrinam hanc diuinitus conseruari: alteram, quia salus nostra aduersis iuuetur atque prouehatur. Nam quantum externo homini decedit, tantum accedit interno. Quibus tertiam adiecit, quòd momentaneæ huius seculi afflictiones sempiternis beatæ immortalitatis præmijs compensabuntur. His modò subtexit diligentiorem huius doctrinæ explicationem, cuius hic status est, vt nos aduersus omnia vitæ huius incommoda atque pericula, fide constanti atq; patientia inuicta armet, simulq; carnis imbecillitati medeatur, quæ à cruce abhorret, & proinde huius terroribus facile succumbit.
units.tr: Although God, through the preaching of the Gospel, offers to wretched mortals the treasure of eternal salvation in his Son, Jesus Christ, few nevertheless receive the Gospel as they should. Among other causes, one that is not least is that they see the cross and persecutions joined together with it. For since the reasoning of the flesh measures God's favour by the advantages of this world, it cannot persuade itself that that teaching is from God and approved by God, when its ministers and followers are harassed with so many misfortunes and dangers. It is therefore necessary that we be carefully instructed on this point, lest this public stumbling block harm our faith and our salvation. For this reason Paul, knowing that many viewed his ministry with suspicion because of the persecutions with which he was constantly troubled, has so far taught that these do not detract from the Gospel, nor is he broken in spirit on that account. He gave reasons: first, because it is evident from them that this doctrine is preserved by divine power; second, because our salvation is aided and advanced by adversities, for as much as is taken from the outward man is added to the inward. To these he added a third: that the momentary afflictions of this age will be compensated with everlasting rewards of blessed immortality. Now he goes on to explain this doctrine more fully, the purpose of which is to arm us against all the discomforts and dangers of this life with a steadfast faith and an unconquered patience, and at the same time to remedy the weakness of the flesh, which shrinks from the cross and therefore easily gives way to its terrors.

units.la: Sic autem orditur: Scimus enim, nos, si terrestris huius domus nostræ tabernaculum dissolutum fuerit, ædificium ex Deo habituros, domicilium videlicet non manufactum, æternum in cælis. Perstat in instituta comparatione vitæ præsentis & futuræ, quæ credentibus in cælo parata est. Et vt nuper duos homines finxit, Externum & Internum: ita nunc duo fingit domicilia; Tabernaculum videlicet, vel domum luteam, & Ædificium solidum, firmum & stabile, quod perpetuò duret. Et per illud quidem, non corpus solum, sed totam hominis in hoc seculo conditionem intelligit: per hoc verò beatum illum tam corporis quàm animæ statum, in quem olim credentes in cælesti patria euehentur. Itaq; sensus verborum est, Non posse se multùm moueri cruce & periculis, quæ ipsi mortem perpetuò minentur: eò quòd hæc non aliud sit, quam ruinosi & sordidi tabernaculi destructio, in quo nunc vitam miseram & calamitosam agimus, ex quo item in æterna Regni Dei palatia simus transferendi. Sed vtile fuerit, si verba singula excutiamus.
units.tr: He begins thus: For we know that if the tent of this earthly house of ours is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. He persists in the comparison, already drawn, between the present life and the future life, which is prepared in heaven for believers. And just as a little earlier he portrayed two men, the outward and the inward, so now he portrays two dwellings: a tent, that is, a house of clay, and a building solid, firm and stable, which will last forever. By the former he means not the body alone, but the whole condition of man in this age; by the latter, that blessed state of both body and soul into which believers will one day be carried up in the heavenly fatherland. The sense of the words, then, is that they cannot be much moved by the cross and dangers, which constantly threaten them with death, since these are nothing other than the destruction of a ruinous and squalid tent, in which we now lead a wretched and calamitous life, and from which we are likewise to be transferred to the eternal palaces of the Kingdom of God. But it will be useful if we examine the individual words.

units.la: Primo, Scimus, inquit. Vnde verò hæc sciuit Apostolus? Quis enim vnquam (vt prophani homines loquuntur) e cælis redijt, vt ista nobis annuntiaret? Annon ipse scribit, hominem animalem non percipere ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei? At Paulus non vt homo animalis, sed vt renatus in Christo, & vt ex fide loquens considerari debet. Hæc enim, quia non carnis sensu, sed Dei Spiritu & verbo ducitur, certa & indubitata notitia apprehendit ea, quæ neq; videntur, neq; ratione humana intelligi possunt. Ideo in epistola ad Hebræos substantia dicitur eorum quæ sperantur, & eorum quæ non videntur demonstratio. Et Petrus cognitionem eiusmodi cum fide coniungit, quando CHRISTVM IESVM publicè confitens, dicit: Et nos credimus & cognouimus, quòd tu es Christus, Filius ille Dei viuentis.
units.tr: First, he says, "We know." But whence did the Apostle know this? For who has ever returned from heaven (as profane men put it) to announce these things to us? Does not he himself write that the natural man does not receive the things that are of the Spirit of God? But Paul must be considered not as a natural man, but as one reborn in Christ and speaking from faith. For he, being guided not by the sense of the flesh but by the Spirit and Word of God, grasps with certain and undoubted knowledge those things which are neither seen nor can be understood by human reason. Therefore in the Epistle to the Hebrews faith is called the substance of things hoped for and the evidence of things not seen. And Peter joins knowledge of this kind with faith, when, publicly confessing Jesus Christ, he says: "And we believe and know that you are Christ, the Son of the living God."

units.la: In his ergo apparet discrimen, quod est inter filios Dei, & homines mundo aut carni addictos. Hi sola opinione ducuntur, & nihil certi habent in ijs, quæ ad diuinorum & cælestium bonorum cognitionem faciunt. Argumentum eius rei est, quòd felicitatem sibi pollicentur ex rebus vanissimis, quæ cum fluxæ & caducæ sint, nihil conferre possunt ad vitam verè beatam: quales nimirum sunt opes, honores, corporis forma & decor, voluptates, vulgi fauor, potentum amicitiæ, quæ omnia in horas mutantur, & suos admiratores turpiter fallunt. Itaque non possunt de certa scientia gloriari, cum exemplis quotidianis confutentur. At germani filij Dei in huius promissiones respiciunt, quæ vt eos ad æterna & cælestia bona remittunt: ita neminem fallunt, cum omnes iam olim in Christo impletæ sint. Deinde ijdem Dei Spiritu confirmantur, qui salutis arrhabo certissimus est, neq; eos fluctuari finit. Vide Rom. 8.
units.tr: In these things, then, appears the difference between the sons of God and men given over to the world or to the flesh. The latter are led by opinion alone and have nothing certain in those matters which pertain to the knowledge of divine and heavenly goods.
