The proof of this is that they promise themselves happiness from the most vain things, which, since they are fleeting and perishable, can contribute nothing to a truly blessed life: such as wealth, honours, bodily beauty and grace, pleasures, the favour of the crowd, the friendship of the powerful, all of which change within the hour and shamefully deceive their admirers. Therefore they cannot glory in certain knowledge, since they are refuted by daily examples. But the genuine sons of God look to the promises of Christ, which lead them to eternal and heavenly goods, and so deceive no one, since all of them were fulfilled in Christ long ago. Furthermore, the same sons are strengthened by the Spirit of God, who is the most certain pledge of salvation and does not allow them to waver. See Romans 8.

units.la: Interim hoc teneamus, non satis esse, vt cum alijs dicamus, nos ista scire, sed necesse est, vt vnusquisq; apud se probè persuasus sit, sibi post huius vitæ curriculum, locum in cælis paratum esse, in quo tam corpus quàm anima beatitate vera & æterna fruantur. Alioqui nulla consolatio efficax, nulla spei certitudo esse poterit, quæ animum pacatum & tranquillum reddat. Et no-
units.tr: Meanwhile let us hold to this: it is not enough for us to say with others that we know these things; but it is necessary that each one be thoroughly persuaded in himself that a place in heaven has been prepared for him after the course of this life, where both body and soul may enjoy true and eternal blessedness. Otherwise no effective consolation, no certainty of hope, can exist to make the mind calm and tranquil.

units.la: Hh tum est illud Prophetae: Iustus ex sua fide viuet. Opus ergo est diligenti promissionum Dei consideratione, & huic exempla cum vetera tum recentia comungere oportet, vt illas nobis ipsis applicare discamus. Sic Paulum in praesenti facere videmus, vt postea quoque, quando Romae captiuus mortis supplicium in omnes horas expectabat. Tunc enim verba ista, plenissima consolatio nis protulit: Ego iam libor, & tempus meae resolutionis instat: Certamen istud praeclarum decertaui, cursum consummaui, fidem seruaui: quod superest, reposita est mihi iustitiae corona, quam reddet mihi Dominus in illo die, iustus ille iudex: non solum autem mihi, sed simul omnibus, qui expetierint illustrem illum ipsius aduentum. En sibi peculiariter applicat, quod omnibus pijs promissum & praeparatum esse sciebat. Idem Iobus olim fecit, quando communem illam beatae resurrectionis spem ita ad se reflringit, quasi sibi soli dicta sint, quae de illa suo seculo tradebantur. Quod ipsum Dauid quoque in Psalmo 16. & plures alij sancti fecerunt. Horum itaq; exempla imitemur, neq; fallet nos spes nostra, quae vt aeterno Dei verbo nititur, ita infinitis electorum exemplis confirmata est.
units.tr: Hence the saying of the prophet: "The righteous shall live by his faith." There is need, therefore, of careful consideration of the promises of God, and we ought to join to them examples both old and recent, so that we may learn to apply those promises to ourselves. Thus we see Paul doing in the present passage, and also later, when, a captive at Rome, he was awaiting the punishment of death every hour. For then he brought forth these words, a most full consolation: "I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day; and not only to me, but also to all who have loved his appearing." See, he applies to himself peculiarly what he knew to be promised and prepared for all the godly. Job did the same once, when he so restricted to himself that common hope of blessed resurrection, as if what was delivered about it in his age had been said to him alone. David himself also did this in Psalm 16, and several other saints. Let us therefore imitate their examples, and our hope will not fail us, which, as it rests on the eternal Word of God, so it is confirmed by the countless examples of the elect.

units.la: Quid vero illud est, quod Paulus sciuit, & quod credentes aut Christiani omnes scire debent? Quae nimirum sit vita praesentis & futurae conditio. Debet enim vtraq; semper coniungi in ista consideratione. Nam huius vitae conditionem infelicem, aerumnosam & instabilem esse, genium quoque philosophi intellexerunt. Heraclitus certe ideo res mortalium continuis lachrymis, Democritus autem risu perpetuo prosequebatur. Alij vero optimum dicebant esse, vel non nasci, vel statim a partu mori. Et Thraces suorum natales deflebant, funera vero ducebant cum gaudio & tripudijs. Sed quia isti omnes futurae vitae cognitionem aut nullam omnino, aut saltem non certam neq; solidam habuerunt, praesentis quidem illos taedere potuit, nulla autem futurae spe fefellerunt confirmati. At longe aliter Christiani, qui non in praesentibus haerent, sed animos supra terras in coelum euehunt, & vtriusq; vitae statum diligentius expendunt. Audiamus ergo nos quoq; Paulum de vtroq; loquentem.
units.tr: But what is it that Paul knew, and what all believers or Christians ought to know? Namely, what is the condition of the present life and of the future. For both ought always to be joined in this consideration. For even the philosophers of genius understood that the condition of this life is unhappy, full of hardship and unstable. Heraclitus, indeed, therefore followed human affairs with continual tears, but Democritus with perpetual laughter. Others said it was best either not to be born, or to die immediately after birth. And the Thracians wept at the births of their people, but led their funerals with joy and dancing. But since all those men had either no knowledge of the future life at all, or at least no certain and solid knowledge, they could be wearied of the present, yet, lacking confirmation in any hope of the future, they were deceived. Christians, however, are far otherwise: they do not cling to present things, but lift their minds above the earth into heaven, and weigh the condition of each life more carefully. Let us therefore listen to Paul speaking of both.

units.la: Praesentis ergo conditionem terrestris nostrae domus tabernaculum dicit. Theodoretus domus nomine vniuersam vitae nostrae in terris conuersationem intelligit, per tabernaculum vero corpus hoc significari dicit. Illam vero terrenam dicit, quia vt homo ex terra originem habet, ita terrenis subsidijs ei ad vitam tuendam opus est. Tabernaculi autem simile rem hanc omnem elegantissimè adumbrat, & huic causae optimè seruit. Nam tabernaculorum vsus est, vbi sedes certas non habent homines, sed hinc inde migrantes, nunc hic nunc illic tentoria aut tabernacula erigunt. Talis Abrahami, Isaaci & Iacobi vita fuit in terra Chanaan. Talis Scytharum quoque esse fertur, & Arabum, quos olim Nomades dixerunt, quod cum pascuis tentoria quoque sua mutarent. Atqui eadem est omnium nostrum conditio. In terris enim hisce peregrini sumus, neque habemus hic ciuitatem permanentem aut stabilem, cum patria nostra in coelis sit. Quo Petrus respiciens, scribebat: Iustum arbitror, quam diu sum in hoc tabernaculo, excitare vos per commonitionem: cum sciam breui futurum, vt deponam hoc tabernaculum meum, &c. Deinde tabernacula, quando primum eriguntur, amoenissima sunt, eadem vero mox marcescunt: Sic vitae nostrae initium iucundum est, propter aetatis florem, vires corporis integras, ingenij & memoriae acumen, & omnis generis voluptates: quibus interdum opes quoque & honores siue dignitates publicae accedunt. Sed haec omnia incerta & euanida sunt. Cum aetate enim formae decor deperit, vires deficiunt, hebetatur ingenium, diffluit memoria, augentur curae, labores, morbi, tandemq; dierum saturi (vt Scriptura loquitur) tam nobisipsis quam aliis oneri sumus. Postremo, vt tabernacula tandem soluuntur & destruuntur, vel sponte corruunt: Sic vita haec ad suum finem quotidie decurrit, & vbi eum attigerit, iam aut morbis ex improuiso incidentibus soluitur, aut violenter abrumpitur, vel si nihil huius fiat, paulatim euanescit. Nam fiat oportet, quod primo parenti dixit Deus: Terra es, & in terram reuerteris. Quae ergo stultitia est praesentibus addictum viuere, aut in illis aliquam spem collocare? Nam vt omnia nobis ex voto succedant, non possunt tamen, qui cordatiores sunt, non perpetuis solicitudinibus discruciari, quando de instabili rerum humanarum conditione & mortis hora incerta cogitant. Taceo nunc, quod ne gaudia quidem huius mundi syncera sunt, cum semper triste quid & acerbum coniunctum habeant. Conferamus autem cum his futuræ vitæ statum, quem Paulus ædificium ex Deo, domicilium non manufactum, æternum item in cœlis nominat. Primò ædificium ex Deo dicit. Atqui in hac quoque vita corpus nostrum, & quæcunque ad hoc spectant, ex Deo habemus. Sed quoad futuram, longius prospicit Apostolus: quòd nimirum ea absque omnibus medijs naturalibus sola Dei virtute sustentetur, & proinde corruptioni non sit obnoxia. Ideo expositionis loco subijcit: Domicilium videlicet non manufactum. Quod hominum manibus fit, ab ijsdem etiam potest destrui. At alia longè est domus illius cœlestis conditio, quæ nobis à iactis mundi fundamentis parata, & æterni Filij Dei sanguine acquisita, mansiones habet stabiles, sicuti ipse Christus illas vocat. Et in præsenti Paulus domicilium illud diserte æternum dicit, quo nomine ab omni corruptione prorsus eximitur. Ut minus dubitemus, locum eius in cœlis monstrat. Quis verò in cœlos ius habeat, aut manum suam eò vsque extendat? Sunt hæc singula dulcissimæ consolationis plena: quare hic nobis eorum vsus esse debet, ut quemadmodum Paulus ista contemplatione confirmatus, pericula omnia contempsit, & invicta animi constantia per omnes casus atque adversa elucatus est, neque horruit huius mortalis tabernaculi dissolutionem: ita nos quoque intrepida animi fiducia feramus quicquid Dominus dederit. Cur enim timeamus ea quæ momentanea sunt, & quando quàm maximè nocere videntur, vehiculi instar nos ad cœlestium bonorum possessionem deducunt?
units.tr: So he calls the present condition of our earthly home a tent. Theodoret understands by "house" our whole way of life on earth, and says that "tent" signifies this body. He calls it earthly because, just as man takes his origin from the earth, so he needs earthly supports to sustain his life. The likeness of a tent portrays this whole matter most elegantly and serves the point very well. Tents are used where people have no fixed dwellings but move from place to place, pitching their tents or booths now here, now there. Such was the life of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the land of Canaan. It is also said to have been the life of the Scythians and the Arabs, whom men once called Nomads, because they moved their tents as they moved their pastures. Yet the condition of all of us is the same. For we are strangers in these lands, and we have here no abiding or permanent city, since our fatherland is in heaven. Looking to this, Peter wrote: "I think it right, as long as I am in this tent, to stir you up by reminding you, since I know that soon I must put off this tent of mine," and so on. Next, tents are most pleasant when first pitched, but soon they wither. So the beginning of our life is pleasant, on account of the flower of our age, the vigour of our bodies, the sharpness of wit and memory, and every kind of pleasure; to these there sometimes come riches, honours and public dignities. But all these things are uncertain and fleeting. For with age the beauty of form fades, strength fails, the wit is dulled, memory slips away, cares, labours and sicknesses increase, and at last, "full of days" (as Scripture says), we become a burden both to ourselves and to others. Finally, as tents are at last taken down and destroyed, or fall of their own accord, so this life runs daily towards its end, and when it reaches that end, it is either dissolved by sicknesses that come on unexpectedly, or violently cut off, or, if none of this happens, it gradually fades away. For what God said to our first parent must come to pass: "You are earth, and to earth you shall return." What folly, then, is it to be given over to the present life, or to place any hope in it? For though all things may turn out for us as we wish, those who are wiser cannot help being tormented by perpetual anxieties, when they think of the unstable condition of human affairs and the uncertain hour of death. I say nothing now of the fact that even the joys of this world are not pure, since they always have something bitter and sour joined to them. Let us compare with these the state of future life, which Paul calls a building from God, a dwelling not made with hands, and eternal in the heavens. First, he calls it a building from God. Yet in this life too we have our body, and whatever pertains to it, from God. But the Apostle looks further ahead to the future life: that it is sustained, without any natural means, by the power of God alone, and therefore is not subject to corruption. So, by way of explanation, he adds: "a dwelling not made with hands." What is made by human hands can also be destroyed by them. But the condition of that heavenly house is entirely different: it has been prepared for us from the foundation of the world, and was won by the blood of the eternal Son of God, and it has abiding mansions, as Christ himself calls them. And here Paul expressly calls that dwelling eternal, by which name it is entirely exempt from all corruption. So that we may have no doubt, he points out its place in the heavens. But who has a right to the heavens, or can stretch his hand so far? Each of these things is full of the sweetest consolation. Therefore we ought to use them here, so that, as Paul was strengthened by this contemplation and despised all dangers, and shone with unconquered firmness of spirit through all chances and adversities, and did not shrink from the dissolution of this mortal tent, so we too may bear with fearless confidence whatever the Lord has given. For why should we fear things that are momentary, and which, when they seem most harmful, carry us, like a vehicle, to the possession of heavenly goods?

units.la: At quia non satis est ista scire, aut etiam de ijs differere posse, nisi ea nobisipsis applicemus, id nunc Paulus suo exemplo docet, sic dicens: Etenim in hoc scilicet corpore aut terreno tabernaculo nostro suspiramus, expetentes domicilio nostro, quod è cœlo est, superindui: siquidem etiam induti, non nudi reperiemur. Docet his verbis, tam certam esse hanc spem, ut diligentius considerata præsentis vitæ tædium, cœlestis verò & æternæ desiderium ardentissimum pariat. In hoc corpore (ait) nihil quàm gemitus & suspiria sentimus. Unde verò hæc enascuntur? Quòd ex tabernaculo hoc ruinoso liberari, & domicilio nostro æterno, quod è cœlo est, superindui expetimus. Ita verò dicit corpus illud clarificatum, quod nobis in resurrectione dabitur (ut in prioris epistolæ capite decimo quinto didicimus) vel potius ipsam gloriam, qua tunc corpora nostra donabuntur. Innuit hoc Superinduendi verbum, & quòd domicilium è cœlo dicit. Nec enim tunc corpus novum è cœlo dabitur, sed hoc ipsum, quod moriendo cecidit, & sepultum in pulverem aut primam materiam redijt, illud (inquam) resurget, superinduetur autem nova gloria: cœlesti nimirum, & eiusmodi conditione, quæ regni illius æterni capax sit. Cœleste ergo dicitur, non quoad materiam, sed quòd gratia & virtute Dei cœlitus sese exerente gloriosum, incorruptibile & immortale fiet.
units.tr: But since it is not enough to know these things, or even to be able to speak of them, unless we apply them to ourselves, Paul now teaches this by his own example, saying: "For in this body, or tent of ours on earth, we groan, desiring to be clothed upon with our dwelling which is from heaven; if indeed, being clothed, we shall not be found naked." By these words he teaches that this hope is so certain that, when it is carefully considered, it produces weariness of the present life and a most ardent longing for the heavenly and eternal. In this body (he says) we feel nothing but groans and sighs. But whence do these arise? Because we desire to be freed from this ruinous tent and to be clothed upon with our eternal dwelling, which is from heaven. And he means by this the glorified body which will be given to us in the resurrection (as we learned in the fifteenth chapter of the first epistle), or rather the glory itself with which our bodies will then be endowed. The word "to be clothed upon" and the phrase "from heaven" hint at this. For a new body will not then be given from heaven; rather that very body which fell in death, and was buried and returned to dust or to primal matter, will rise again (I say), and will be clothed upon with new glory: heavenly, of course, and of such a condition as is capable of that eternal kingdom. It is therefore called heavenly not with respect to its matter, but because, made glorious, incorruptible and immortal by the grace and power of God exerting itself from heaven, it will become so.

units.la: Cæterùm, ne tantum bonum omnibus hominibus promisçue, & proinde impijs quoq; commune facere putetur, illud ad solos Christi fideles restringit, addens: Siquidem etiam induti, non nudi reperiemur. Alludit ad parentis nostri Adami historiam. Is cum peccauisset, se nudum esse vi dit, nec pudore solùm suffusus, verumetiam peccati conscientia ita consternatus est, ut ne vocem quidem Dei aduentantis ferre potuerit. Eadem est omnium nostrùm conditio, quoad natales nostros. Nam in peccato concepti & geniti, non tam corpore quam anima nudi nascimur. Et ut Adam ex ficorum foliis subcinctoria aut tegumenta contexit, quibus turpitudinem suam velaret: Ita pleriq; hominum ad suæ rationis figmenta conuersi, multa contexunt, speciosa quidem carnis iudicio, quibus iniustitia suam palliare, & Dei oculos fallere studeent. Sed sunt hæc verè ficulnea, & noxia magis quàm vtilia præsidia. Quia quàm primùm Deus sua voce intonans quærit, qui nā & quo loco fuerimus, & vbi nunc simus, mox propriæ conscientiæ testimonio conuicti trepidamus, & cùm nullus fugæ locus sit, terram potius nobis debiscere, quàm in illius conspectu prodire vellemus. Quis enim vocem illam terribilem sustineat? Maledictus, quisquis nō fecerit quæ-cunq; scripta sunt in libro Legis: & dicet omnis populus, Amen. Intellexerunt sanctissimi quiq; ea sententia vniuersum genus humanum damnari, & ideo precati sunt, Domine, ne ingrediaris in iudicium cum seruo tuo. Et nos similiter precari iubemur: Remitte nobis debita nostra, &c.
units.tr: Moreover, lest it be thought that so great a good is made common to all men indiscriminately, and therefore also to the wicked, he restricts it to Christ's faithful alone, adding: "if indeed, being clothed, we shall not be found naked." He alludes to the history of our parent Adam. When he had sinned, he saw that he was naked, and he was overcome not only with shame but also with such consternation from the consciousness of sin that he could not even bear the voice of God approaching. Our condition is the same as to our birth. For conceived and born in sin, we are naked not so much in body as in soul. And just as Adam sewed together coverings or aprons from fig leaves to hide his shame, so many men, turning to the inventions of their own reason, weave many things together, fine indeed by the judgment of the flesh, with which they strive to cloak their unrighteousness and deceive the eyes of God. But these are truly fig-leaf defences, and more harmful than useful. For as soon as God, thundering with his voice, asks who we are, and where we were, and where we now are, straightaway, convicted by the testimony of our own conscience, we tremble, and since there is no place to flee, we would rather the earth open beneath us than come forth into his sight. For who can bear that terrible voice? "Cursed is everyone who does not do all the things written in the book of the Law; and all the people shall say, Amen." The holiest men understood that by this sentence the whole human race is condemned, and therefore they prayed: "Lord, do not enter into judgment with your servant." And we too are commanded to pray in the same way: "Forgive us our debts," and so on.

units.la: Deut. 27.
units.tr: Deut. 27.

units.la: Itaq; longè alia vestè, quàm quæ hominum manibus contexatur, opus est. Monstrauit hanc Adamo Deus, quando de femine mulieris ei concionatus est, cuius merito & virtute serpentis, idest, diaboli caput conculcari, & ex eius imperio siue tyrannide humanum genus redimi oportet. Atqui semen hoc est æternus Dei Filius, qui absque viri congressu ex intemerata Virgine verus homo natus est, & proinde vere & propriè semen mulieris dicitur. Hic nobis à Patre factus est Sapientia, Satisfactio, Iustitia, Sanctificatio & Redemptio, & ideo solus vestis illa nuptialis est, quæ peccatorum nostrorum sœditatem tegit, & nouum decorem nobis confert, quo ornati in Dei iudicio comparere, & in nuptiis illis cœlestibus locum honestum obtinere possumus. Induitur autem is per solam fidem: quia extra hanc nulla ratio aut medium inuenitur, per quod illum apprehendamus, & tam ipsius quàm bonorum, quæ nobis meruit, participes efficiamur. Ideo ad Galatas Apostolus noster scribebat, Omnes filij Dei estis, per fidem in CHRISTO IESV. Nam quicunque in Christum baptizati estis, Christum induistis: Ad hæc ergo mysteria in præsenti respiciens Paulus, eos cœlesti & æterno domicilio superinduendos dicit, qui in illo die non nudi reperiantur, sed Christi iustitiam per fidem induerint, cùm in terris hisce vitam mortalem viuerent. Et his solis seruiunt promissiones: Vbi ego sum, illic volo sit minister meus. Pater, volo, ut vbi ego sum, illic etiam sint, quos dedisti mihi: Nihil ergo ista ad aperte scelera-tos, aut mendaces hypocritas, qui sese in Ecclesiam absque veste nuptiali, imò prorsus nudi, vel suorum operum centonibus male tecti, insinuant: quibus non profuerit, si aliquandiu locum aliquem inter pios teneant: quia nulla temporis longi præscriptione excusatur hypocrisis. Quamobrem singulis dicetur: Amice, quomodo huc intrauisti, non habens vestem nuptialem? Obmutescent tunc illi, quia non habebunt, quod iudici respondeant: & proinde eijcientur in tenebras exteriores.
units.tr: Therefore we need a garment of a quite different kind from one woven by human hands. God showed this to Adam when he spoke to him of the seed of the woman, by whose merit and power the head of the serpent, that is, of the devil, must be trampled, and by whose command or tyranny the human race must be redeemed. Now this seed is the eternal Son of God, who, without union with a man, was born true man of the undefiled Virgin, and therefore is truly and properly called the seed of the woman. He has been made to us by the Father wisdom, satisfaction, righteousness, sanctification and redemption; and therefore he alone is that wedding garment which covers the foulness of our sins and confers on us a new beauty, by which we, adorned, can appear before the judgment of God and obtain an honourable place at those heavenly nuptials. He is put on through faith alone, because outside of faith no means or method is found by which we may lay hold of him and be made partakers both of him and of the goods which he merited for us. Therefore our Apostle wrote to the Galatians: "You are all sons of God, through faith in Christ Jesus. For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ." Looking to these mysteries in the present passage, Paul says that they will be clothed upon with the heavenly and eternal dwelling who on that day are not found naked, but have put on the righteousness of Christ through faith while they lived their mortal life on these lands. And the promises serve these alone: "Where I am, there my servant also will be." "Father, I desire that where I am, there also may be those whom you have given me." Therefore these things have nothing to do with those who are openly wicked, or lying hypocrites, who creep into the Church without the wedding garment, indeed utterly naked, or badly covered with the patchwork of their own works; for them it will not help if they hold a place among the godly for some time, since no lapse of time excuses hypocrisy. Wherefore it will be said to each one: "Friend, how did you come in here, not having a wedding garment?" Then they will be silent, because they will have nothing to answer the judge, and therefore they will be cast out into the outer darkness.

units.la: Venit autem toto hoc loco diligenter considerandus fidei verae effectus multiplex atque saluberrimus. Primùm enim, nos in mortali adhuc corpore agentes Christi iustitia induit, quae causa est, ut peccata nobis non imputentur. Ita vero nos in eorum censu ponit, quos Scriptura vere beatos pronuntiat. Deinde excitat nos, ne euanidis huius seculi studijs atque voluptatibus nos decipi & circumduci patiamur: sed totis animis ad cœlestia aspiremus. Adhæc mortem nobis leuem & optabilem facit, quam omnes natura horrent: Qui enim bonorum cœlestium dulcedinem iam fide degustarunt, ij dissolui cupiunt, ut propius cum Christo coniungantur. Neque eis graue est mori, quacunque ratione id fiat, quando genus mortis saluti ipsorum nihil derogat. Idem ergo ad migrandum semper parati sunt, ut is qui carceri tetro conclusus liberationem auidè expectat. Alia longè est impiorum sors, qui cùm iustitia Dei careant, perpetuis conscientiæ terroribus discruciantur. Idem terrenis interea addicti, cœlestia negligunt: ad mortis mentionem toti horrent ac trepidant: & tandem quia nudi inueniuntur, anima simul & corpore æternum pereunt. Agnoscamus ergo inæstimabile illud Dei beneficium, quod nobis in Filio suo IESV CHRISTO contulit, eumq; fide amplexi, eidem seruiamus in Spiritu & veritate. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Now we must carefully consider the many and most salutary effects of true faith that arise from this passage. First, while we are still living in our mortal body, faith clothes us with the righteousness of Christ, which is the reason our sins are not imputed to us. In this way it places us among those whom Scripture rightly pronounces blessed. Next, it stirs us not to be deceived and led astray by the fleeting pursuits and pleasures of this age, but to aspire with all our hearts to heavenly things. Besides this, it makes death light and desirable to us, which all people by nature dread. For those who have already tasted by faith the sweetness of the heavenly goods long to be dissolved, so that they may be joined more closely with Christ. Nor is it hard for them to die, by whatever means it comes, since the manner of death takes nothing away from their salvation. So they are always ready to depart, like one shut up in a foul prison who eagerly awaits his release. The lot of the ungodly is far different: since they lack the righteousness of God, they are tormented by constant terrors of conscience. Meanwhile they, given over to earthly things, neglect the heavenly; at the mention of death they shudder and tremble entirely, and at last, because they are found naked, they perish eternally in both soul and body. Let us therefore acknowledge that inestimable benefit of God, which he has bestowed on us in his Son Jesus Christ, embrace him by faith, and serve him in spirit and in truth. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XX.
units.tr: HOMILY XX.

units.la: Etenim qui sumus in hoc tabernaculo, suspiramus onerati: in quo non cupimus exui, sed superindui, vt absorbeatur mortalitas à vita. Porrò Deus is est, qui nos ad hoc ipsum condidit: qui etiam dedit nobis arrhabonem Spiritus. Confidentes igitur semper, & scientes nos aduenas esse in corpore, peregre absumus à Domino. Per fidem enim incedimus, non per aspectum.
units.tr: For we who are in this tabernacle groan, being burdened, not because we wish to be unclothed, but to be clothed upon, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. Now God is the one who has made us for this very purpose, and who has also given us the pledge of the Spirit. Therefore, being always confident, and knowing that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord (for we walk by faith, not by sight).

units.la: Dicit Paulus de afflictionibus & periculis, quibus exercebatur, ita disserit, vt non suæ modò fidei constantiam atque inuictam animi patientiam testetur, verumetiam suo exemplo Christianos omnes doceat, quales ipsi esse debeant, si quid durius & grauius patiantur. Postremum in hac tractatione fuit vitæ præsentis cum futura comparatio: in qua illi quidem luteum & caducum tabernaculum tribuit, huic verò domum cœlestem ac æternam. Simul autem ostendit, pijs adeò non grauem esse mortem, qua tabernaculum hoc destruitur, ut potius hoc fieri cupiant, ut cœlesti gloria superinduantur, & cum Christo in cœlis viuant: quod omnibus à Deo promissum & præparatum esse docet, qui dum hic viuunt, Christum ex fide vera induerint. At si dum ista proponuntur, in nosipsos altius descendamus, illa captum nostrum superare sentiemus, & multa occurrent, quæ nobis scrupulos injiciunt, ut nonnihil hæreamus atque dubitemus. Quapropter nunc diligentius rem hanc tractat Apostolus, & objectionibus, quæ hic mouentur, præcipuis respondet.
units.tr: Paul speaks of the afflictions and dangers with which he was being tried, and he argues in such a way that he not only bears witness to the steadiness of his own faith and his unconquered patience of mind, but by his own example also teaches all Christians what they ought to be if they suffer anything harder and more grievous. The last point in this discussion was the comparison of the present life with the future one. In it he calls the present a frail and perishable tabernacle of clay, but the future a heavenly and eternal house. At the same time he shows that death, by which this tabernacle is destroyed, is not so grievous to the godly that they do not rather desire it, so that they may be clothed upon with heavenly glory and live with Christ in heaven. He teaches that this has been promised and prepared by God for all who, while they live here, have put on Christ by true faith. But if, while these things are set before us, we go deeper into ourselves, we shall feel that they exceed our capacity, and many things will occur which put scruples in our way, so that we hesitate and doubt somewhat. Therefore the Apostle now treats this matter more carefully and answers the chief objections raised here.

units.la: Et initio quidem duas simul complectitur. Prima est, quòd mortis horror aliqua ex parte in pijs quoque & electis adhuc locum habet: quod ut multorum exemplis demonstrari potest, ita vnius Christi abunde sufficit, qui ad diræ suæ mortis recordationem toto animo perturbatus fuit, & præ animi angustia sudorem sanguineum profudit. Nec facile aliter fieri potest, cùm mors ex peccato originem ducat, & huius pœna à Deo constituta sit. Nam quamuis per Christi meritum eius conditio mutata, & pijs transitus, ex hac lachrymarum valle in vitam æternam facta sit, adhuc tamen de peccati atrocitate nos admonet, & quid porrò mereamur docet, si Deus stricto iure nobiscum agere instituat. Est præterea utilis hic mortis horror: quia obstat, quò minus in grauioribus angustijs desperatione superati, nobismetipsis manum inferamus. Cùm enim hoc multi nunc faciant, quid non facturi essent plerique alij, nisi hoc quasi fræno retinerentur? Altera obiectio est, frustra mortis desiderio homines Christianos gloriari, quando inter ethnicos olim inuenti sint, qui in illam sese alacri animo coniecerint. Et vetera quidem exempla habemus in Decijs, Curtijs, Gymnosophistis: quibus Manichæos & Donatistas connumerare licet, quorum vestigijs hodie fere Anabaptistæ insistunt. Et inter Turcas sunt, quibus iucundum est pro Lege Mahumetis sui morte oppetere. At istos omnes vel desperatio olim mouit, quam poetæ per furias intellexerunt: vel præsentis vitæ tædium cum impatientia coniunctum: vel ambitio immodica: vel pertinax defendendæ semel conceptæ opinionis studium: non autem, quòd melioris vitæ aliquam cognitionem aut spem habuerint. Ideo Paulus ad istas obiectiones respondens, longè aliam esse docet Christianorum hominum conditionem, atque proprias pij istius desiderij, quo illi ardent, causas exponit, dicens: Etenim qui sumus in hoc tabernaculo, suspiramus onerati, in quo non cupimus exui, sed superindui, ut absorbeatur mortalitas à vita. Sensus est: Gemimus quidem in hoc misero corporis tabernaculo, & semel dissolui vel liberari cupimus: non autem conscientiæ desperabundæ stimulis exagitati, aut quòd fortem nobis à Deo destinatam impatientius feramus: sed quòd nos carnis sarcina peccatrici, eiusque prauis desiderijs grauari sentimus, quò minus ad cœlestia queamus eluctari. Itaque, si proprie loquendum sit, non cupimus exui hoc corporis tabernaculo, tanquam per se mali & detestabilis: sed potius superindui, ut quod mortale & caducum in nobis est, absorbeatur à vera illa & gloriosa vita, quæ nobis in cœlo præparata est.
units.tr: At the outset he takes up two together. The first is that the horror of death still has some place, in some measure, even in the godly and the elect. This can be shown by the examples of many, but the example of Christ alone is enough, who, when he recalled his dreadful death, was troubled in his whole soul and, in the anguish of his mind, sweated drops of blood. Nor can it easily be otherwise, since death arises from sin and its penalty has been appointed by God. For although by Christ's merit his condition has been changed, and for the godly the passage from this valley of tears into eternal life has been made, yet death still reminds us of the atrociousness of sin, and teaches what we would deserve if God were to begin to deal with us by strict right. Moreover, this horror of death is useful, because it stands in the way so that, overcome by despair in heavier distresses, we do not lay hands upon ourselves. For since many now do this, what would most others not do, unless they were held back as if by a bridle? The second objection is that Christians boast in vain of the desire for death, since among the heathen of old there were found those who threw themselves into it with a cheerful mind. We have ancient examples in the Decii, Curtius, and the Gymnosophists, and to these one may add the Manichaeans and Donatists, whose footsteps the Anabaptists today almost follow. And among the Turks there are those who find it pleasant to meet death for the law of their Mahomet. But all these were moved either by despair, which the poets understood through the Furies; or by weariness of the present life joined with impatience; or by immoderate ambition; or by a stubborn zeal for defending an opinion once conceived; but not because they had any knowledge or hope of a better life. Therefore Paul, answering these objections, teaches that the condition of Christian men is far different, and sets out the proper causes of the godly desire by which they burn, saying: "For we who are in this tabernacle groan, being burdened, in which we do not wish to be unclothed, but to be clothed upon, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life." The sense is this: we indeed groan in this wretched tabernacle of the body and desire to be released or freed once for all; yet not driven by the goads of a despairing conscience, nor because we bear with too much impatience the lot appointed us by God; but because we feel that we are weighed down by the sinful burden of the flesh and its wicked desires, which keep us from struggling upward toward heavenly things. Thus, if we speak properly, we do not wish to be stripped of this bodily tabernacle as if it were evil and detestable in itself; rather we wish to be clothed upon, so that what in us is mortal and perishable may be swallowed up by that true and glorious life which has been prepared for us in heaven.

units.la: Rursus autem hic exprimitur ingenium piorum siue electorum Dei, & in quo à reprobis huius seculi filijs differant. Hi si non omnia pro voto eis succedant, mori volunt, cùm aliâs de vita futura nunquam cogitent. Pij autem, etsi non alieni sint ab affectionibus humanis, & proinde ingemiscant quoque & suspirent, quoties carnis infelici massa se grauari sentiunt, fortem tamen suam patienter ferunt, cùm sciant, se inter labores & molestias huius seculi Deo gratissimum obsequium præstare posse, si in fidei obedientia constanter perseuerent. Grauantur ergo non tam communibus ærumnis, quàm innata carnis vitiositate, quæ illos non semper finit animos altius ad cœlestia attollere. Itaque quòd mori cupiunt, ex eo est, quòd ϑνητὸν siue mortalitatem omnem semel à vita absorberi vellent. Eodem enim sensu mortalitas hic ponitur, quo corpus mortis ad Romanos septimo capite, ut nimirum non tam fortem mortalem denotet, quàm innatam vitiositatem, qua fit, ut in dies peccando nunquam non mortem mereamur. Nam etsi nos ab ea Christus liberauerit (sicuti Paulus loco nunc citato fatetur) attamen nondum plenè effectum suum habet redemptio nostra, sed olim perficietur, quando ille in nubibus cœli ad iudicandum veniet. Ideo cùm in Euangelio de horrendis & periculosis nouissimorum temporum motibus dissereret, discipulis dicebat: His autem incipientibus fieri, attollite capita vestra, quoniam appropinquat redemptio vestra. Ut ergo semel hunc locum expediamus, gemunt pij in hoc corporis sui tabernaculo, quia se à patria exulare, & corpus hoc ergastuli instar esse sentiunt, ex quo mens liberari cupit, vt in cœlos transferatur.
units.tr: Here again the disposition of the godly, or the elect of God, is set forth, and the point in which they differ from the reprobate sons of this age. The latter, if not everything succeeds for them as they wish, want to die, although otherwise they never think about the future life. The godly, however, although they are not strangers to human feelings, and therefore also groan and sigh whenever they feel themselves weighed down by the unhappy mass of the flesh, nevertheless bear their lot patiently, since they know that among the labours and troubles of this age they can render to God the most acceptable service, if they persevere constantly in obedience of faith. They are burdened, then, not so much by the common hardships as by the innate sinfulness of the flesh, which does not always allow them to raise their minds higher toward heavenly things. Therefore their desire to die arises from this: they would wish that all mortality [θνητόν] be once for all swallowed up by life. For mortality is here taken in the same sense as "the body of death" in Romans chapter seven, so that it signifies not so much the mortal lot as the innate sinfulness by which we are made to deserve death at every moment as we sin day by day. For although Christ has freed us from it (as Paul confesses in the passage just cited), nevertheless our redemption does not yet have its full effect, but will be perfected in time, when he comes in the clouds of heaven to judge. Therefore, when in the Gospel he was discoursing about the dreadful and perilous movements of the last times, he said to his disciples: "But when these things begin to happen, lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near" (Luke 21). So, to explain this passage once for all: the godly groan in this tabernacle of their body, because they feel that they are exiles from their homeland, and that this body is like a prison, from which the mind desires to be freed, so that it may be carried up into heaven.

units.la: Admonet etiam locus hic, quantum futura vita præstet præsenti. Hæc, si rem ipsam propius considereS, nihil nisi mortalitas est: vt quæ obnoxia sit omnibus ærumnis, quæ cum morte in mundum introierunt, & quarum finis nullus est, donec illa huius vitæ filum abruperit. Imò quoad in carne hac viuimus, mortem nobiscum circumferimus, quæ corpus hoc cum omnibus huius vitæ subsidijs tandem quasi absorbet, vt nos seruare non possint. At futura illa verè vita est, & adeò nullis obnoxia est casibus, vt ipsam quoque mortem & mortalitatem omnem absorbeat. Nam vt Theodoretus annotauit, quemadmodum lux tenebras discutit, sic vita æterna mortem omnino abolet. Recte ergo huius spe fideles triumphant, & cum Paulo dicunt: Quis nos separabit à charitate Christi? Num afflictio? num angustia? num persecutio? num fames? num nuditas? num periculum? num gladius? Imò in his omnibus plus quàm victores sumus per eum, qui dilexit nos. Nam mihi persuasum est, quòd neque mors, neque vita, &c. nos separare poterit à charitate Dei, quæ est in CHRISTO IESV, Domino nostro. Stulti ergo reuera, imò amentes sunt, qui mortalem hanc & miseram vitam futuræ præferunt, & huius seculi studijs sic addicti sunt, vt cœlestia bona negligant. Etenim quis non absque omni mora è domo ruinam minante, aut mox arsura exilire cupiat? Quis non velit quàm ocyssimè in littus exponi ex naui, quam mox naufragium facturam intelligat? Atqui non alia est totius mundi conditio, qui breui totus ardebit & corruet. Sibi ergo dictum putent omnes, quod olim Angeli Lotho dixerunt: Serua vitam tuam, neq; respectes post te, neq; consistas in tota ista planitie, effuge montem versus, ne forte absumaris. Gen.19.
units.tr: This passage also reminds us how much the future life excels the present. If we consider the matter itself more closely, this present life is nothing but mortality: it is subject to all the calamities which entered the world with death, and of which there is no end until it breaks the thread of this life. Indeed, as long as we live in this flesh, we carry death about with us, which at last swallows up this body together with all the supports of this life, so that they cannot preserve us. But that future life is truly life, and is so free from all chances that it swallows up even death itself and all mortality. For, as Theodoret has noted, just as light dispels darkness, so eternal life altogether abolishes death. Rightly, then, the faithful triumph in the hope of it, and say with Paul: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall affliction, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us. For I am persuaded that neither death nor life, etc., will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Rom. 8). Truly foolish, indeed mad, then, are those who prefer this mortal and miserable life to the future one, and who are so given over to the pursuits of this age that they neglect heavenly goods. For who would not wish to leap out of a house that threatens ruin, without any delay, or out of one that is about to burn? Who would not want to be put ashore from a ship as quickly as possible, when he understands it is soon going to be wrecked? Yet the condition of the whole world is no different, which will shortly burn entirely and fall. Let all, then, take to themselves what the angels once said to Lot: "Save your life; do not look behind you, nor stop anywhere in all this plain; flee to the mountain, lest perhaps you be consumed" (Gen. 19).

units.la: Porrò si ista ad nostræ rationis calculum reuocemus, vires & captum hominis longè superant. Caro enim conditione hac calamitosa & misera delectatur, & vt qui casæ siue tugurio assueuit, ægre ab eo diuellitur, etiamsi palatium regium sibi paratum esse audiat: ita homo huius vitæ consuetudine captus, vix adduci potest, vt volens eam relinquat. Impedit nos etiam innatus nobis mortis horror, de quo diximus. Cum ratione item pugnare videtur, vt corpus idem, quod in terram abijt, resurgat, quodq; insuper ἀφθαρσία & immortalitate donetur. Adhæc, si qui ista fidem adhibent, periculum est, ne vel confidentius sibi ipsis aliquid tribuant, vel securiores facti, minus intenti sint in oblatas sibi salutis occasiones. Itaque omnibus istis vitijs Paulus occurrit, & simul doctrinam hanc omnem amplius confirmat, dicens: Porrò Deus is est, qui nos ad hoc ipsum condidit: qui etiam dedit nobis arrhabonem Spiritus. Sensus verborum est: Non debent hæc alicui mira vel absurda videri, aut etiam impossibilia. Deus enim is est, qui ista agit. Is initio hominem ex terra lutoue desumptum, ad suam imaginem condidit, cuius non postrema dos est Immortalitas. Ergo, vt immortales simus, nos creauit. Idem nos lapsos & perditos restituit per Filium suum, qui caput veteris serpentis contriuit, & vnâ mortis vires atque imperium destruxit. At quis omnium istorum fructus esset, si adhuc morte æternum detineremur? Siue ergo primam hominis creationem, siue eiusdem restitutionem in Christo spectemus, immortalitatis beatæ spes sese offert. Accedit his arrhabo Spiritus sancti, qui spem istam confirmat sicuti supra quoque capite primo diximus.
units.tr: Moreover, if we bring these things to the reckoning of our reason, they far exceed the strength and grasp of man. For the flesh delights in this wretched and miserable condition, and, like one who has grown used to a hut or hovel, is reluctant to be torn from it, even when he hears that a royal palace has been prepared for him. So man, captivated by the habit of this life, can scarcely be brought to leave it willingly. Also the horror of death, innate in us, hinders us, as we have said. Likewise it seems to conflict with reason that the same body which has gone into the earth should rise again, and be endowed moreover with incorruption [ἀφθαρσία] and immortality. Besides, if some give credit to these things, there is a danger that they may either attribute something to themselves too confidently, or, having become too secure, be less alert to the opportunities of salvation offered to them. Therefore Paul meets all these faults, and at the same time confirms this whole doctrine more fully, saying: "Now he who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who also has given us the earnest of the Spirit." The sense of the words is: these things ought not to seem to anyone wonderful or absurd, or even impossible. For it is God who does these things. He at the beginning formed man from the earth and clay, and made him in his own image, whose not least gift is immortality. Therefore he created us that we might be immortal. The same God, having restored us when we had fallen and were lost, did so through his Son, who crushed the head of the old serpent and at once destroyed the power and dominion of death. But what would be the fruit of all these things if we were still held eternally by death? Whether, then, we look to the first creation of man or to his restoration in Christ, the hope of blessed immortality presents itself. To these is added the earnest of the Holy Spirit, who confirms that hope, as we said above also in the first chapter.

units.la: Admonent nos ista de certitudine salutis nostræ. Hæc tota ex Deo est, & æterno eius decreto nititur, quod per primas promissiones patribus olim reuelauit, & tandem missô in carnem Filio suo executus est. Agnoscamus ergo hoc totum gratuitæ misericordiæ beneficium esse, & pro inde nihil hic nostris siue viribus siue meritis tribuamus. Deinde hinc petamus solida consolationis argumenta, quibus confirmati, nullis tentationibus succumbamus. Quis enim æterno Dei decreto obstabit, quò minus effectum suum habeat? Num peccatum? Atqui Deus est, qui iustificat. Num Satan? Atqui hunc iampridem deuicit Dei Filius, eiusq; caput contriuit, omnemq; potentiam euertit. Num mundus? Atqui fides est victoria nostra quæ vincit mundum. Num tyranni? At hi nihil iuris aut potestatis habent in animas nostras, multò minus autem in cœlos, vt nos ab eorum possessione excludant. Num ipsa mors? Atqui hæc luteum istud tabernaculum dissoluit, vt suo tempore idem nobis gloriosum & æternum restituatur. Vt ergo ædificaturi, dum veteres parietes demoliuntur, nouo ædificio locum parant: ita per mortem nostræ reparationis & glorificationis materia paratur. Ista verò non solùm in Scripturis traduntur, verumetiam intra animos nostros Spiritus Sancti testimonio confirmantur. Sunt ergo impudentissimi impostores, & noxiissima Satanæ organa, qui hominem de salute sua certum fieri posse negant, & ita simplicium fidem labefactant, quos potius consolationibus Euangelicis fulcire debebant.
units.tr: These things admonish us concerning the certainty of our salvation. All of this is from God and rests upon his eternal decree, which he long ago revealed to the fathers through the first promises, and at last, having sent his Son into the flesh, carried into effect. Let us acknowledge, therefore, that this whole thing is a benefit of free mercy, and accordingly let us ascribe nothing here to our own strength or merits. Then from this let us seek firm grounds of consolation, by which, being strengthened, we may not yield to any temptations. For who will stand in the way of God's eternal decree, so that it does not attain its effect? Sin? But it is God who justifies. Satan? But the Son of God has long since conquered him, crushed his head, and overthrown all his power. The world? But our faith is the victory which overcomes the world. Tyrants? But these have no right or power over our souls, much less over the heavens, so as to shut us out from possession of them. Death itself? But death dissolves this clay tabernacle, so that in its time the same body may be restored to us glorious and eternal. Just as builders, while the old walls are being pulled down, prepare a place for a new building, so through death the material of our renewal and glorification is prepared. These things are not only handed down in the Scriptures, but are also confirmed within our minds by the testimony of the Holy Spirit. They are therefore most shameless impostors and most harmful instruments of Satan, who deny that a man can be made certain of his salvation, and so weaken the faith of simple people, whom they ought rather to uphold with evangelical consolations.

units.la: Nos potius Paulum audiamus, qui huius fiduciæ effectum amplius exponit, sic vt totam Christiani hominis vitam nobis ceu in tabula spectandam proponat. Propositio aut summa omnium est, se nullis periculis siue afflictionibus, imò ne mortis quidem terroribus, superari & frangi posse, vt in ministerio sibi commisso remissius agat. Id verò ex ijs, quæ proximè præcesserunt, sic infert: Confidentes igitur semper, & scientes nos aduenas esse in corpore, peregre absumus à Domino: Per fidem enim incedimus, non per aspectum. Confidentem se esse profitatur, id est, animo præsenti & ad quæuis subeunda parato, quicquid tandem accidat. Videtur autem ad Christi præceptum respicere, qui apud Ioannem discipulis dicebat: In mundo afflictionem habebitis, sed confidite, ego vici mundum. In præsenti verò suæ fiduciæ rationem Paulus affert, quæ cum ijs, quæ nuper dixerat, conuenit: Scientes nos aduenas esse in corpore, peregre absumus à Domino. Quod nuper lutei tabernaculi cum domicilio cælesti & fixo compactione docuit, id nunc peregrinantium & in patria agentium exemplo illustrat. Quasi diceret: Qui peregre agunt, iis non nouum aut insolens est, si non omnia ipsis ex voto succedant. Sciunt enim se longius abesse à parentibus & amicis, in quibus præcipuam spem habent collocatam. Atqui eadem plane est condicio omnium conditio. Patriam enim nostram in cœlis habemus, & ibidem Pater quoque noster est, quem inuocamus. Quoad ergo in hoc corpore vitam agimus, aduenæ ac peregrini sumus in terris, absumus autem à Deo, qui nobis Pater est, & in cuius domo patrimonium & hæreditatem nostram reconditam habemus. Itaque non possumus ceu casu improuiso consternari, & animo deici, si in hoc quasi exilio constituti aliquid aduersum aut triste accidat.
units.tr: Let us rather listen to Paul, who sets out more fully the effect of this confidence, so that he presents to us the whole life of the Christian to be viewed as on a painted panel. The proposition, or the sum of all, is that he cannot be overcome or broken by any dangers or afflictions, nor even by the terrors of death, so that he may act more calmly in the ministry committed to him. He draws this conclusion from what immediately precedes: "Therefore, being always confident, and knowing that while we are at home in the body we are absent from the Lord (for we walk by faith, not by sight)." He professes that he is confident, that is, of a present mind and prepared to undergo whatever may happen. He seems, moreover, to have in view the precept of Christ, who said to his disciples in John: "In the world you will have affliction, but be of good confidence; I have overcome the world." In the present passage Paul gives the ground of his confidence, which agrees with what he said just before: "Knowing that while we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord." What he taught just before, concerning the frailty of the earthly tabernacle compared with the heavenly and fixed dwelling, he now illustrates by the example of those who travel abroad and live in a foreign land. As if he said: For those who travel abroad, it is nothing new or strange if not everything turns out for them as they wish. For they know that they are far from their parents and friends, in whom they have placed their chief hope. Yet the condition of all is plainly the same. For we have our country in heaven, and there our Father also is, whom we call upon. So long as we live in this body, we are strangers and pilgrims on earth, and we are absent from God, who is our Father, and in whose house our inheritance and patrimony is laid up. Therefore we cannot be dismayed as by an unforeseen accident, and cast down in spirit, if, being placed in this, as it were, exile, something adverse or sad happens to us.

units.la: Rursus autem hoc loco apparet discrimen inter pios & impios, electos & reprobos: quid item illos quidem in periculis animosos & mortis contemptores faciat, hos autem terroribus immodicis deiectos perdat: Pij se in terris peregrinos esse, per mortem verò ad Dominum migrare nolunt, vt huc vere vniantur. Non possunt ergo vllis periculis succumbere, neque eos formidant, qui necem ipsis minitantur. Nam hi illis viam in cœlos aperiunt, & carnis infelicis carcere eos liberant. Adhæc horum memores, minus occupantur circa res huius seculi, & quò propius ad finem vitæ se peruenisse vident, eò minus de temporarijs solliciti sunt, liberalitati autem & beneficentiæ impensius student. Impij verò cùm præter huius seculi vitam non aliam vllam norint aut sperent, non possunt non contremiscere ad ea, quæ illius interitum afferunt. Idem verò, cùm se mortales norint, tamen circa opum studium perinde tumultuantur, ac si immortalitatem ipsis Deus promisisset: & quò propius ad metam suam peruenerunt, eò plura cupiunt: perinde ac si quis longinqua profectione iam quasi perfecta, de viatico solicitus esse incipiat, quando patriæ mœnia iam in conspectu habet. Sunt hi stultissimi mortalium, præsens autem huic stultitiæ remedium afferri potest, si hæc Pauli verba memori mente perpetuò versemus.
units.tr: Again, in this place there appears the difference between the godly and the ungodly, the elect and the reprobate: and what makes the former bold in dangers and despisers of death, but casts the latter down and destroys them by excessive terrors. The godly know that they are strangers on earth, and they are unwilling to remove through death to the Lord, so that they may be truly united with him. Therefore they cannot yield to any dangers, nor do they fear those who threaten them with death. For these open for them the way into heaven, and free them from the prison of unhappy flesh. Moreover, mindful of these things, they are less occupied with the affairs of this age, and the nearer they see themselves to the end of life, the less anxious they are about temporal things, and they study more eagerly liberality and beneficence. The ungodly, however, since they know and hope for no other life beyond this life of the age, cannot but tremble at those things which bring its ruin. Yet the same people, though they know they are mortal, nevertheless are in such tumult over the pursuit of wealth as if God had promised them immortality; and the nearer they come to their goal, the more they desire: just as if someone, on a long journey already almost completed, were to begin to be anxious about his provision for the road, when he already has the walls of his country in view. They are the most foolish of mortals; and a remedy for this folly can be applied at once, if we constantly turn over these words of Paul in a mindful spirit.

units.la: Poterat autem aliquis obijcere: Atqui alias dixisti, corpora nostra esse templa Spiritus sancti, in quibus Deus ipse habitet: & Christi promissio est, quòd nos nolit orphanos relinquere, sed nobis adesse velit vsque in consummationem seculi. Quomodo igitur nunc dicis te peregre abesse à Domino? Respondet ergo ad hanc quæstionem: Per fidem enim incedimus, non per aspectum. Sensus huius dicti est: Vera quidem sunt, quæ alibi diximus, tamque arcta est inter Christum & nos coniunctio, vt nihil nos separare possit ab eius dilectione: & idem nobis nunquam non adest suo Spiritu & virtute, qua in nobis efficaciter agit. Sed quoad nos & totam hanc vitam, quam in corpore agimus, tota hæc conuersatio fide & spiritu constat, nec adhuc coram cum illo versari & regni illius cœlestis thesauris frui datur. Idem ergo hic dicit, quod pluribus in Cap.13. prioris epistolæ expositit: Cernimus nunc per speculum, & per ænigma: tunc autem coram cernemus, &c. Et ad Colossen: Vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo: quando Christus, vita illa nostra, patefactus fuerit, tum etiam vos cum eo declarabimini gloriosi. Coloss.3. Apparet autem ex hoc & similibus locis, quàm procul Apostoli abfuerint à crassa illa Caepernaitarum nostri seculi opinione de corporali & substantiali IESV CHRISTI in terris hisce præsentia. Nam si hanc credidisset Paulus, nulla cum ratione dicere poterat, nos dum in carne hac viuimus, peregre abesse à Domino. Nec etiam in Cœnæ Dominicæ reformatione scri-psisset: Quotiescunque hunc panem comederitis, & hoc poculum biberitis, annunciate mortem Domini DONEC VENIT. Sed procul dubio ad illius verba respexit: Vos in mundo estis, ego non amplius sum in mundo. Quæ locutio cum ijs, quæ Matthæi 18. & 28. habentur: Vbi duo aut tres congregati fuerint in nomine meo, ego ero in medio eorum: Ecce ego vobiscum sum vsque in consummationem seculi: non aliter conciliari potest, nisi illam de corporis eius absentia intelligamus. At hodie huius præsentiam corporalem quidam tam pertinaciter vrgent, vt ipsos cœlos quoque in terras detrahant. At dicant illi, quomodo peregrini in terris dicamur, si iam nunc cœli cum Christo nobis adsunt? Quia ergo hæc non minus inepta quàm falsa sunt, discamus procul relictis curiosis disputationibus, animos per fidem in cœlos attollere, vt illic IESVM CHRISTVM apprehendamus, in quo vno vita & salus est. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: But someone might object: "Yet elsewhere you said that our bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, in which God himself dwells; and it is Christ's promise that he will not leave us orphans, but wishes to be with us even to the end of the age. How, then, do you now say that you are absent from the Lord as a pilgrim?" He answers this question thus: "For we walk by faith, not by sight." The sense of this saying is: What we have said elsewhere is true, and so close is the union between Christ and us that nothing can separate us from his love; and he is never absent from us, by his Spirit and power, by which he works effectively in us. But as far as we and this whole life which we live in the body are concerned, the whole of this conduct consists in faith and spirit, nor is it yet granted to us to live openly with him and to enjoy the treasures of his heavenly kingdom. He therefore says here what he set out more fully in chapter 13 of the former epistle: "Now we see through a mirror, and in a riddle; but then we shall see face to face," etc. And to the Colossians: "Your life is hidden with Christ in God: when Christ, who is our life, shall be made manifest, then you also shall be made manifest with him in glory." Colossians 3. It appears from this and similar places how far the apostles were from that gross opinion of the Capernaites of our age concerning the bodily and substantial presence of Jesus Christ on this earth. For if Paul had believed it, he could not have said with any reason that we, while we live in this flesh, are absent from the Lord. Nor would he have written in the reform of the Lord's Supper: "As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes." But without doubt he had in view the words: "You are in the world, I am no longer in the world." Which saying cannot be reconciled with those things found in Matthew 18 and 28: "Where two or three are gathered together in my name, I am in the midst of them," and "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age," except by understanding it of his bodily absence. But today some press his bodily presence so stubbornly that they drag even the heavens down to earth. Let them say, however: how are we called pilgrims on earth if already now heaven and Christ are present to us? Since these notions are no less foolish than false, let us learn, leaving aside curious disputations, to lift our minds through faith into heaven, so that we may there lay hold of Jesus Christ, in whom alone is life and salvation. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXI.
units.tr: HOMILY XXI.

units.la: Confidimus autem & probamus potius migrare è corpore, & ad Dominum ire habitatum. Quapropter etiam ambimus & incolentes & migrantes ei esse accepti. Omnes enim nos comparere oportet coram tribunali Christi vt vnusquisque reportet quæ in corpore fecerit secundùm id quod fecit, vel bonum vel malum.
units.tr: Yet we are confident, and would rather depart from the body and go home to the Lord. Therefore we also make it our aim, whether living at home or away, to be pleasing to him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.

units.la: Quoniam vitæ huius cupiditas omnibus innata est, eadem vero nos à cœlestibus bonis & vera vita abstrahit: non tam vtile quàm necessarium est, vt de præsenti simul & futura vita recte iudicare discamus. Docet id Paulus diligenter: qui nuper quidem, nos quoad hanc vitam, tabernaculum luteum & ruinosum incolere dixit, domum vero in cœlis habituros stabilem & nullis casibus obnoxiam. Deinde huius seculi vitam peregrinationi confert, in qua nunc absimus peregre à Domino, neque aliter quàm per fidem apprehendi queat: Conueniunt ista cum totius Scripturæ tam Veteris quà Nouæ doctrina, & cum consensu sanctorum, qui omnes hoc ipsum semper confessi sunt, & huius peregrinationis suæ finem ardentibus suspirijs desiderauerunt. Hic ergo nobis etiam istorum vsus esse debet, vt terrenis quidem bonis vtamur pie & sobrie, quoad Deo placuerit nos hic agere, interim vero conditionis nostræ instabilis memores, toto animo ad cœlestia aspiremus: vbi vita nostra cum Christo in Deo recondita est. Id vero in præsenti nos Paulus suo exemplo amplius docet.
units.tr: Since the desire for this life is innate in all, and the same desire draws us away from heavenly goods and the true life, it is not so much useful as necessary that we learn to judge rightly both the present life and the future life. Paul teaches this diligently. He said that for now we dwell in this life as in a tent of clay and ruin, but that we shall have a house in heaven, stable and exposed to no calamity. Then he compares this life of the age to a pilgrimage, in which we are now absent from the Lord, abroad, and can be grasped only by faith. These things agree with the teaching of all Scripture, both Old and New, and with the agreement of the saints, who all have always professed this very thing and have longed with burning sighs for the end of their pilgrimage. Here, then, we too ought to make use of these things: to use earthly goods piously and soberly, as long as it pleases God that we live here, yet at the same time, mindful of our unstable condition, to aspire with our whole soul to heavenly things, where our life is hidden with Christ in God. Paul teaches this more fully in the present passage by his own example.

units.la: Confirmat quod dixit, nos per fidem incedere, non per speciem: Confidimus autem, & probamus potius migrare è corpore, & ad Dominum ire habitatum. Quasi diceret: Nemo putet, nos ita nunc peregre abesse à Domino, vt incerta sit nostræ salutis spes. Nam fiducia eius tam certa est, vt si optio detur, malimus emigrare ex hoc mundo, & corporis istius ergastulo, & ad Dominum abire, vt illic domicilium nobis paremus fixum & stabile. Conueniunt hæc cum ijs, quæ ad Philippenses postea scripsit: Cupio dissolui, aut migrare & esse cum Christo. Et cum Dauidico illo: Væ mihi, incolatus meus prolongatur. Psalm.120.
units.tr: He confirms what he said, that we walk by faith and not by sight: "Yet we are confident, and would rather depart from the body and go home to the Lord." As if he said: let no one think that we are so far away from the Lord now that our hope of salvation is uncertain. For our trust in him is so sure that, if the choice were given, we would prefer to emigrate from this world, out of the prison of this body, and go to the Lord, so as to prepare for ourselves there a fixed and stable dwelling. These things agree with what he wrote later to the Philippians: "I desire to depart and be with Christ." And with that Davidic word: "Woe is me, my sojourning is prolonged" (Ps. 120).

units.la: Obseruabis autem hoc loco, fide non modò mortis metum discuti, verumetiam sanctum eius desiderium accendi. Vt enim bonæ indolis filius, vt vt apud exteros peregre agens amicis & hospitij commoditatibus delectetur, cum læta tamen & gaudij plena spe cum diem expectat, quo auulsus ab exteris domum redeat, & parentum conspectu exhilaretur: Ita qualiscunque sit piorum in terris conditio, præponderat tamen patriæ cœlestis & bonorum, quæ illic nobis reposita sunt,
units.tr: Notice in this place that by faith not only is the fear of death dispelled, but also a holy desire for it is kindled. As a son of good disposition, living abroad among strangers, takes delight in friends and the comforts of hospitality, yet while he waits for the day with joyful and hopeful expectation, when he may be taken from strangers, return home, and be cheered by the sight of his parents, so, whatever the condition of the godly on earth may be, the hope of the heavenly fatherland and of the goods laid up for us there nonetheless outweighs it.

units.la: Salutis spes certissima.
units.tr: The most certain hope of salvation.

units.la: Fides accendit mortis desiderium. sunt, desiderium, ut ad ea contendere cupiant. Est ergo perquàm evidens τῆς ἀπιστίας seu incredulitatis indicium, si qui mortis metu superati turpiter & immoderatè eiulant, & ut præsenti vita consulant, multa præter officium faciunt. Verumtamen hic probè tenendum est, hunc piorum affectum longè alium esse ab eo, quo impij mori cupiunt, non cœlestis patriæ amore, sed præsentis vitæ & laborum tædio atque impatientia. Pios solùm cœlestium bonorum & ipsius Christi desiderium trahit. Quoad verò in hac vita Deo servire possunt, moram hanc patienter ferunt. Et ita Paulum affectum fuisse, non hic modò locus, sed ille alter etiam, quem paulò ante adduximus, docet: Nam mihi (inquit) vita Christus est, & mori lucrum. Verum verò viuere in carne mihi operæpretium sit, & quid eligam ignoro. Coarctor enim utrinque, desiderans migrare, & esse cum Christo: Nam id longè optimum est. Sed permanere in carne, magis necessarium est propter vos. Philippen. primo capite.
units.tr: Faith kindles the desire for death. Thus it is a plain sign of unbelief (τῆς ἀπιστίας, that is, of incredulity) when those overcome by fear of death wail shamefully and immoderately, and, in order to provide for present life, do many things beyond their duty. Yet here we must firmly hold that this affection of the godly is very different from that by which the wicked wish to die, which comes not from love of the heavenly fatherland but from weariness and impatience with present life and its labours. Only the desire for heavenly goods and for Christ himself draws the godly. As long as they can serve God in this life, they bear the delay patiently. That Paul was so disposed is shown not only by this place but also by that other one which we cited a little while ago: "For to me," he says, "life is Christ, and to die is gain. But if to live in the flesh is worth the effort for me, I do not know what to choose. For I am torn both ways, desiring to depart and be with Christ, for that is by far the best. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake" (Phil. 1).

units.la: Facit eodem quod in præsenti subijcit: Quapropter etiam ambimus & incolentes & migrantes, id est, sive diutius in hoc infelici tugurio viuendum, sive moriendum sit, ut Domino placeamus accepti. Exprimit his verbis vitæ Christianæ scopum, quem omnes sibi propositum habere debent, qui fidem in Christum profitentur. Est is, ut Domino placeamus. Ut enim uxor fidelis tota in eo est, ut marito placeat, & si hoc impetrer, non multum petulantium & improborum sermonibus mouetur: utque servus frugi in solius heri voluntatem respicit, cui si probetur, aliorum de se iudicia facilè contemnit: Ita erga Deum affecti esse solent, quotquot illius filij sunt germani: & in hoc ipso à filijs huius seculi procul differunt. Vellent enim hi quoque placere Deo, ut vitæ æternæ (si quæ est, ut ipsi loquuntur) participes fieri possint. At qui in hac carne agentes, quoad vitam & mores hunc scopum sibi propositum habeant, paucos est videre. Imò hæc plerisque sola videtur sapientia esse vera, si se mundo approbent, & hominibus placeant. Sed de illis proprissimè dicuntur apostolica illa: Si hominibus placerem, Christi servus non essem. Item: Amicitia huius mundi est inimicitia cum Deo. At longè aliud electorum & filiorum Dei ingenium est, qui sive viuere, sive mori oporteat, Deo placere student. Id verò assequuntur, quotquot æternum Dei Filium, IESVM CHRISTVM, fide non fucata apprehendunt. Hic enim solus est, qui Patrem nostris peccatis iratum, nobis placauit, ut propter hunc nos pro dilectis filijs agnoscat, qui prius iræ filij eramus. Ut autem studeamus Deo probari, multa nos mouere possunt. Primùm, quòd in hunc finem sumus conditi. Ut enim omnes creaturæ hominis vsibus seruiunt, adeoque hunc suum dominum atque principem agnoscunt: Ita nos ad suam imaginem Deus condidit olim, ut eius seruitio dediti, ipsum colamus & glorificemus. Deinde IESVS CHRISTVS propter nos mortuus est & resurrexit, ut vitiatam in nobis Dei imaginem instauraret, & ut nos sive viuamus, sive moriamur, ipsius simus peculium atque coheredes, sicuti Paulus ad Romanos scribens testatur. Quibus adde, quòd cùm mundi huius iudicio mors nulla nobis gloriosior obtingere possit, quàm si pro patria dulci in acie pugnantes occumbamus: multò felicius & gloriosius moriantur oportet, quibus datur vitam & sanguinem suum pro æterno Dei Filio profundere. In eo certè imprimis consistit Christianorum hominum dignitas & prærogatiua, qua præ aliis fruuntur, quòd Deum moriendo quoque colunt atque glorificant. Multum ergo fallitur infelix mundus suo de Christi seruis atque Martyribus iudicio, dum eos hominum miserrimos atque calamitosissimos esse arbitratur. Hi enim sanguine suo Deum honorant, & reuera beatissimi illi phœnices sunt, qui in medijs flammis vitam hanc corruptibilem cum incorruptibili commutant, & depositis carnis nostræ infelicibus exuuijs, in cœlos subuolant. At qui hos martyrat tyranni, & quicunque alij ex ipsorum supplicijs voluptatem capiunt, ij sibi ipsis quidem inter homines infamiam perpetuam conciliant, in futuro autem seculo sempiternis inferorum cruciatibus mancipantur. Quis ergo umbratilem, qua nunc superbiunt, eorum gloriam aut felicitatem admiretur? Aut quis non malit cum Christo mori, ut cum eodem viuere & regnare detur?
units.tr: He says the same thing in what follows: "Therefore we also make it our aim, whether living at home or away," that is, whether we must live longer in this wretched hovel or must die, so that we may be pleasing to the Lord. In these words he expresses the goal of the Christian life, which all who profess faith in Christ ought to have set before themselves. It is this: to be pleasing to the Lord. For just as a faithful wife is wholly intent on pleasing her husband, and if she obtains this she is little moved by the talk of wanton and wicked people, and just as a diligent servant looks only to the will of his one master, and if he is approved by him easily despises the judgments of others about himself, so all the true children of God are wont to be disposed toward God, and in this very thing they differ far from the children of this age. For these too would wish to please God, so that they might be made partakers of eternal life (if there is any, as they themselves say). But of those who, living in this flesh, have this goal set before them in life and conduct, there are few to be seen. Indeed, to most this alone seems to be true wisdom, if they commend themselves to the world and please men. But the words of the apostle apply most properly to such people: "If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a servant of Christ" (Gal. 1). Likewise: "Friendship with this world is enmity with God" (James 4). But the disposition of the elect and sons of God is far different, for whether they must live or die they strive to please God. Yet all who grasp the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, with unfeigned faith attain this. For he alone is the one who reconciled to us the Father, angry on account of our sins, so that on account of him he might acknowledge us as beloved sons, who were formerly sons of wrath. Now, many things can move us to strive to be approved by God. First, that we were created for this end. For just as all creatures serve the uses of man, and thus acknowledge him as their lord and prince, so God formerly created us in his image, so that, devoted to his service, we might worship and glorify him. Next, Jesus Christ died and rose again for us, so that he might restore the image of God corrupted in us, and so that, whether we live or die, we might be his own possession and co-heirs, as Paul testifies in writing to the Romans. To these add that, since by the judgment of this world no death can befall us more glorious than to fall fighting in the line of battle for a sweet fatherland, much more happily and gloriously ought those die to whom it is given to pour out their life and blood for the eternal Son of God. In this indeed chiefly consists the dignity and privilege of Christian men, which they enjoy above others: that they honour and glorify God even by dying. Therefore the unhappy world is greatly mistaken in its judgment of Christ's servants and martyrs, while it thinks them the most wretched and calamitous of men. For they honour God with their blood, and truly they are the most blessed phoenixes, who in the midst of the flames exchange this corruptible life for an incorruptible one, and, laying aside the wretched cast-off garments of our flesh, fly up into heaven. But those tyrants who torment the martyrs, and all others who take pleasure in their punishments, they indeed win for themselves perpetual infamy among men, but in the age to come they are consigned to the everlasting torments of hell. Who then would admire the shadowy glory or happiness in which they now exult? Or who would not rather die with Christ, so that he may be granted to live and reign with him?

units.la: Quia autem Paulo cum Corinthijs res erat, inter quos maximus erat hominum carnalium numerus, quos ista non multum mouent, eò quòd putent sufficere, si studia sua & mores hominibus probentur: aliud argumentum subiungit, quo istos quoque perterrefaciat. Nam ad Dei tribunal omnes eos citat, qui dolo malo se insinuabant Ecclesiæ, ipsum verò & alios fideles Christi Apostolos calumnijs suis in contemptum & suspicionem adducebant. Sic autem scribit: Omnes enim nos comparere oportet coram tribunali Christi, ut unusquisque reportet, quae in corpore fecerit, secundum id quod fecit, vel bonum, vel malum. Quasi diceret: Non temere hoc moneo, ut Deo placere studeamus. Nam etiamsi fucata pietatis specie nos toti mundo approbemus, nulla tamen ex eo ad nos redibit utilitas certa & solida. Olim enim dies ille praefinitus illucescet, quo omnes homines ad IESV CHRISTI tribunal sistentur, ubi non secundum speciem aut fucum externum, neque ex communi hominum sensu sive arbitrio iudicabitur: sed unusquisque in suo corpore feret eorum quae unquam fecit retributionem, sive illa bona sive mala fuerint. Conuenit cum hoc loco, quod in priori epistola Capite quarto dixit: Ne ante tempus quicquam iudicetis, vsque dum venerit Dominus, qui & illustrabit ea, quae occulta tenebrarum, & manifesta faciet consilia cordium: & tunc laus erit unicuique a Deo. Proderit autem praesentis huius loci verba singula expendere, cum circa hanc doctrinam totius salutis nostrae cardo versetur.
units.tr: Since Paul was dealing with the Corinthians, among whom there was a very large number of carnal people, who are not much moved by such things (because they think it is enough if their pursuits and morals are approved by men), he adds another argument by which he may terrify them as well. For he summons before God's tribunal all those who were insinuating themselves into the Church with evil deceit, while they brought Paul himself and the other faithful apostles of Christ into contempt and suspicion by their calumnies. He writes thus: "For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that each one may receive the things done in the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil." As if he said: "I do not give this warning rashly, that we should strive to please God. For even if we commend ourselves to the whole world by a false show of piety, no sure and solid advantage will come to us from it. For that appointed day will one day dawn, on which all men will be brought before the tribunal of Jesus Christ, where judgment will not be made according to outward appearance or false show, nor according to the common opinion or whim of men; but each one will bear in his own body the repayment of whatever he has ever done, whether those deeds were good or evil." This agrees with what he said in the first epistle, chapter four: "Judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the things hidden in darkness and make manifest the counsels of hearts; and then each one will have his praise from God." It will be useful to weigh the individual words of the present passage, since the hinge of our whole salvation turns on this doctrine.

units.la: Primò eos denotat, qui iudicio sistendi sint, & in genere OMNES dicit, ut omnis loci aut ordinis homines comprehendat. Neminem ergo tunc vel aetas excipiet, vel sexus, vel natio, vel dignitas, vel potestas, vel opes, vel egestas, nihil denique eorum, quae in mundo vel magnifica habentur, vel contemptu & odio digna putantur. Ut enim in quovis vitae genere aut statu, per se bono & honesto, possumus gratum Deo obsequium praestare: sic etiam in quovis peccari & aeternae salutis iactura fieri potest, si ab officio nostro discedamus.
