Falluntur ergo vehementer, qui ex gradu sublimiori, aut opum abundantia, impunitatis spem concipiunt, vel quos sua pauperras aut vitae genus contemptibilius securos facit, quoad salutis causam. Nec enim de fortunis iudicium feretur, sed de nobis & studijs nostris.
units.tr: First, he marks out those who are to be brought to judgment, and he says ALL in general, so that he embraces men of every place and rank. Therefore no one then will be exempted, whether by age, sex, nation, dignity, power, wealth, or poverty, nothing at all of those things which in the world are held to be splendid or are thought worthy of contempt and hatred. For just as in any kind of life or station, which is good and honourable in itself, we can render God acceptable service, so too in any station we may sin and suffer the loss of eternal salvation, if we depart from our duty. Therefore they are greatly mistaken who conceive hope of impunity from a higher rank or abundance of wealth, or whom their poverty or manner of life makes too secure as regards the cause of salvation. For judgment will be passed not on fortunes, but on us and on our pursuits.

units.la: Deinde nos comparere, vel (ut Graeci vocabuli vim melius exprimamus) manifestos fieri oportere dicit. Poterat dicere, Sisti, quia voce in epistola ad Romanos usus fuerat. Sed quia multi iudicio sistuntur, qui sua vel astutia vel dicendi facultate iudices fallunt, sic potius loqui voluit, ut ostendat, quod etsi nunc multi lateant, in illo tamen die toti mundo notum fore, qui nam & quales singuli fuerint. Nam ut Daniel scribit: Libri omnes aperientur, & omnium conscientiae patebunt, adeoq; retegentur tunc omnium oculis, quae nunc probe tecta & aeterno silentio sepulta esse putantur. Et quis de eo dubitet, quando in hac etiam vita raro ita celari possunt atrociora scelera, ut non tandem manifesta fiant, & id quidem plerunque eorum indicio, qui illa patrauerunt, & poenas sibi paratas esse non ignorant? Quantum vero momenti haec consideratio ad pietatis studium afferret, si in ea essemus diligentiores?
units.tr: Next, he says that we must appear, or (to express the force of the Greek word better) be made manifest. He could have said "be set before", since he had used that word in the epistle to the Romans. But because many are brought before judgment who by their cunning or by their gift of speech deceive the judges, he preferred to speak thus, to show that although many now lie hidden, yet on that day it will be known to the whole world who and what each one has been. For as Daniel writes: "All the books will be opened, and the consciences of all will be laid bare," so that those things which are now thought well covered and buried in eternal silence will then be exposed to the eyes of all. And who would doubt it, since even in this life the most atrocious crimes can rarely be so concealed that they do not at last become manifest, and that mostly through the confession of those who committed them, who are not ignorant that punishments are prepared for them? And how great a weight this consideration would bring to the pursuit of piety, if we were more diligent in it!

units.la: Habet quoque emphasim verbum, OPORTET. Poterat enim dicere, nos aliquando comparituros in iudicio: Sed omnes comparere aut manifestos fieri OPORTET, inquit: Nimirum, quia Deus sic decreuit, cuius consilium manet in aeternum. Nam Domino exercituum aliquid constituente, (ut Prophetae verbis utar) quis illud faciet irritum? Et facit ad huius loci confirmationem, quod cum tuba Dei & voce archangeli Christus veniet, & angelos suos mittet, qui omnes omnium seculorum & nationum homines ad suum tribunal colligant. Nemo igitur vel astutia sua sese subducere, vel violenter resistere poterit, quo minus se quoque huic iudici sistat. Exigit praeterea hoc iustitia Dei, ut cum quotidie multorum scelera puniat, multos autem impunitos dimittat, tandem hi quoque digna factis suis praemia accipiant. Siue ergo Dei iustitiam, sive iudicis potentiam, sive infirmas hominum vires spectes, OPORTET sane omnes nos comparere.
units.tr: The word MUST also carries emphasis. He could have said that we shall at some time appear in judgment; but he says that all must appear or be made manifest, namely because God has so decreed, whose counsel remains for ever. For when the Lord of hosts has determined something (to use the words of the Prophet), who will make it void? And it serves to confirm this place that Christ will come with the trumpet of God and the voice of the archangel, and will send his angels, who will gather all the men of all ages and nations to his tribunal. Therefore no one will be able either to withdraw himself by his cunning or to resist by force, so as not to present himself also before this judge. Moreover the justice of God requires that, since he punishes the crimes of many every day, while he lets many go unpunished, at last these also should receive rewards worthy of their deeds. Whether you look at the justice of God, or the power of the judge, or the weak strength of men, we must all indeed appear.

units.la: Vbi autem comparebimus? Coram tribunali Christi. Huic enim omne iudicium dedit Pater, & idem vir ille praedestinatus est, per quem electos quidem suos seruare, impios vero punire decreuit. Aeternus nimirum Dei Filius, IESVS CHRISTVS, qui pro nobis in cruce diram mortem subijt, & cui nunc omnis potestas data est in coelo & in terra. Hunc ergo iudicem suum in assumpta hominis natura agnoscere & ferre cogentur, qui nunc illum Seruatorem suum agnoscere nolunt, secundum illud Prophetae: Videbunt in quem pupugerunt. Et huc referri debet, quod de signo Filij hominis in nubibus tunc compariturò, ipse praedixit. Matth.24.
units.tr: Where shall we appear? Before the tribunal of Christ. For the Father has given all judgment to him, and that same man was predestined by whom he decreed to preserve his elect, but to punish the wicked: the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, who for us underwent a dreadful death on the cross, and to whom now all power is given in heaven and on earth. Therefore they will be compelled to acknowledge and endure this as their judge in the nature of man which he assumed, those who now refuse to acknowledge him as their Saviour, according to the word of the Prophet: "They shall look on him whom they have pierced." And to this must be referred what he himself foretold of the sign of the Son of man, who will then appear in the clouds. Matt. 24.

units.la: Porrò finem quoque istius actionis totius indicat Paulus: Vt vnusquisque reportet quæ per corpus, id est, in corpore ipsi debentur, siue gloriam, siue ignominiam, secundum id quod fecerit vel bonum vel malum. Erit ergo iudicium istud iustum prorsus & æquum, cùm neque iudicem alius fallere, neque sententia, quæ tunc feretur, executionem impedire possit. Facit autem locus hic quàm maximè ad afferendam corporum nostrorum resurrectionem. Nam nisi eam admittamus, Paulum ex spiritus sancti suggestione loquentem mendacij arguemus, qui vnumquemque in corpore reportaturum dicit, quæ ipsi debentur. Nec est, quòd eos audiamus, qui corpora quidem surrectura dicunt, sed alia quàm hæc nostra sint, in quibus nunc viuimus. Ita enim Dei iustitia periclitaretur, si vel glorificarentur in cœlis, vel apud inferos torquerentur corpora, quæ neque peccassent, neque virtutis ac pietatis organa, aut certaminum, quibus in hac vita pij exercentur, socia fuissent: qua de re alibi prolixè est dictum.
units.tr: Furthermore Paul also indicates the end of this whole action: "That each one may receive what is due through the body, that is, in the body, whether glory or shame, according to what he has done, whether good or evil." This judgment therefore will be altogether just and equitable, since no one can deceive the judge, nor can any sentence which is then passed be hindered in its execution. This place also bears most strongly on proving the resurrection of our bodies. For unless we admit it, we shall charge Paul, speaking by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, with falsehood, since he says that each one will receive in the body what is due to him. Nor should we listen to those who say that bodies will indeed rise, but other bodies than these our own in which we now live. For thus the justice of God would be endangered, if bodies which had not sinned, and which were not instruments of virtue and piety, nor partners in the struggles in which the godly are exercised in this life, were either glorified in the heavens or tormented in hell. On this matter it has been treated at length elsewhere.

units.la: Nunc vsum istius doctrinæ spectare oportet. Nam etsi sæpius de eo dixerimus, vtile tamen & necesse est eadem crebrius repetere. Consistit autem ille potissimum in duobus. Primum est, vt ex ea consolatione habeant pij, qua seipsos in omni genere tentationum confirment. Laborat tibi fama propter calumnias, quæ tibi fiunt? Cogita tunc, fore tempus, quando innocentia tua ipsius Christi testimonio publicè approbabitur. Videntur nunc mortalium omnium abiectissimi esse, qui Deo ex fide vera seruiunt? Sed olim apparebit, eos germanos esse Dei filios. Affliguntur nunc illi inedia, siti, morbis, carceribus & diris exquisitissimorum suppliciorum tormentis? Sed erit tunc remuneratio, quæ ad animam simul & corpus redundabit. Imò tunc vindicem suum pij cum incomparabili gloria videbunt, pro cuius nomine nunc affliguntur. Ita olim hoc articulo vsi sant sanctissimi cultores Dei: vt alibi Iobi & Pauli exemplo docuimus. Alterum est, vt ista ad nostram institutionem accommodemus aduersus peccati & mundi illecebras. Tentaris securitate & ignauia? mox igitur animo repete, quis & qualis ad iudicium venturus sit Christus Dominus. Blanditur tibi voluptas & gulæ studium? hic oppone, quod de epulonis diuitis miserabili apud inferos conditione in Euangelio dicitur. Superbiæ spiritu turgere incipis? Succurrat mox, te breui reum fore ad Christi tribunal. Quòd si veritatis odium te ad maiorem audaciam & impietatem extimulet, vt illius ministros atque sectatores diris incessere & aperta vi oppugnare libeat: tunc in mentem veniant, quæ Christus olim hostibus suis minatus est: fore nimirum, vt ferreo sceptro eos comminuat, qui virga Euangelij sui gubernari nolunt. Item: Qui vos tangit, tangit pupillā oculi mei. Et rursus: Quod vni ex minimis istis fecistis, mihi fecistis. Etenim si tanta est iudicij istius grauitas, vt nunc conscientiæ de illo diligentius cogitantis terrores sustinere non possimus: quanto intolerabilius erit, iudicis sententiam coràm audire, & mox sequentem eius executionem sentire? Ad primum sanè iudicis illius aspectum plangent omnes tribus terræ. Quid multis opus est? Discant omnes hunc sibi totius vitæ & actionum omnium scopum proponere, vt Deo placeant, seq; ipsos fide constanti & sanctimonia non fucata præparent in occursum Domini nostri & venturi iudicis, IESV CHRISTI, vt ad eius tribunal læta conscientia audiamus dulcissimam istam & verè saluificam vocem: Venite benedicti Patris mei, & possidete regnum, paratum vobis ab exordio mundi. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Now we must look to the use of this doctrine. For although we have often spoken of it, yet it is both useful and necessary to repeat the same things more often. Its use consists chiefly in two things. The first is that the godly may draw from it such consolation as will strengthen them in every kind of temptation. Is your reputation suffering because of the calumnies done to you? Think then that there will come a time when your innocence will be publicly approved by Christ's own testimony. Do those who serve God in true faith now seem to be the most abject of all mortals? But one day it will appear that they are the true sons of God. Are they now afflicted by hunger, thirst, diseases, prisons and the dreadful torments of the most exquisite punishments? But there will then be a reward, which will extend to the soul and the body together. Indeed then the godly will see their Avenger, whose name they now suffer for, with incomparable glory. Thus the most holy worshippers of God have used this article of faith in former times, as we have taught elsewhere by the examples of Job and Paul. The second is that we apply these things to our instruction against the allurements of sin and the world. Are you tempted by security and sloth? Then at once call to mind in your heart who and what kind of judge Christ the Lord will be when he comes. Does pleasure flatter you and the desire of gluttony? Then set against it what is said in the Gospel of the miserable condition of the rich glutton in hell. Do you begin to swell with the spirit of pride? Let it come to mind at once that you will shortly be accused before the tribunal of Christ. But if hatred of the truth stirs you on to greater boldness and impiety, so that you are pleased to assail its ministers and followers with dreadful reproaches and to attack them with open force: then let come to mind what Christ once threatened to his enemies: that he will surely crush with an iron sceptre those who refuse to be governed by the rod of his Gospel. Likewise: "He who touches you touches the apple of my eye." And again: "What you have done to one of these least, you have done to me." For if the weight of that judgment is so great that we cannot now bear the terrors of a conscience which thinks about it carefully, how much more intolerable will it be to hear the sentence of the judge before us, and soon after to feel its execution? At the first sight of that judge indeed all the tribes of the earth will mourn. What need is there of many words? Let all learn to set this before themselves as the aim of their whole life and of all their actions: to please God, and to prepare themselves by constant faith and unfeigned holiness for the meeting of our Lord and coming judge, Jesus Christ, so that before his tribunal with a joyful conscience we may hear that most sweet and truly saving voice: "Come, blessed of my Father, and possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXII.

units.la: Scientes igitur terrorem illum Domini, homines persuademus, Deo autem manifesti sumus: & spero nos etiam conscientijs vestris manifestos esse. Enimuero non iterum nosipsos commendamus vobis: sed vobis occasionem præbemus gloriandi de nobis: vt habeatis quid aduersus eos, qui ex facie gloriam captant, at non ex corde. Nam siue insanimus, Deo insanimus: siue sana mente sumus, vobis sana mente sumus. SPiritus Sanctus in Scripturis non solum doctrinam Prophetarum & Apostolorum proponit, verumetiam diuersa de illis hominum iudicia describit, odia item, insidias & persecutiones, quibus exagitati sunt. Visus istorum nobis hic esse debet, vt si quid huius etiam hodie fieri videmus, non offendamur, quin potius constantes simus in retinenda ea fide & doctrina, quam illi tanto cum consensu nobis tradiderunt: imo tunc recurramus ad argumenta illa, quibus illi suae doctrinae authoritatem aduersus impiorum calumnias defenderunt. Debet hoc obseruari in tota hac Pauli epistola: in qua multa ille de suo ministerio, deq; sua fide & integritate disserit, qua in illo obeundo hucusque fit visus. Argumentum eius nuper euidens adduxit, quod nullis periculis, & ne morte quidem se absterreri patiatur, quo minus inuicta animi fiducia pergat. Nam se hoc vnum spectare dicit, vt siue diutius ipsi viuendum, siue iam nunc moriendum sit, Deo placere queat: neque se hominum iudicijs multum moueri, quando nos omnes olim apud Christi tribunal manifestari oporteat, vbi singulis digna suis factis praemia retribuentur. Quod autem in genere dixit de nouissimo Christi ad iudicium aduentu, id nunc sibi ipsi propius applicat, & docet, vt illius consideratione in suo ministerio confirmetur. Quo exemplo omnis loci & ordinis homines docentur, non sufficere generalem IESV CHRISTI cognitionem, sed vt quaecunque de illo dicuntur singuli ad se transferant necesse esse, & se quoq; olim ad illius tribunal sistendos esse meminerint.
units.tr: Knowing, then, the terror of the Lord, we persuade men, but we are manifest to God; and I hope we are also manifest to your consciences. For we are not again commending ourselves to you, but giving you occasion to boast about us, so that you may have something to answer those who glory in appearance and not in heart. For if we are beside ourselves, we are beside ourselves for God; if we are in our right mind, we are in our right mind for you. The Holy Spirit in the Scriptures not only sets forth the teaching of the Prophets and Apostles, but also describes the various judgments of men about them, likewise the hatreds, plots and persecutions by which they were harassed. The example of these men ought to be before us here, so that if we see anything of this kind happening even today, we are not offended, but rather remain steadfast in holding to that faith and teaching which they handed down to us with such great agreement. Indeed, then we should have recourse to those arguments by which they defended the authority of their teaching against the slanders of the impious. This should be observed throughout this whole Epistle of Paul, in which he discourses at length about his ministry, and about his faith and integrity, which have so far been seen in his discharge of it. He has lately brought forward a clear argument, that he does not allow himself to be terrified by any dangers, not even by death, so that he does not go on with unconquered confidence of mind. For he says that he has this one aim: that, whether he must live longer or must die now, he may be able to please God; and that he is not much moved by the judgments of men, since we all must one day be made manifest before the tribunal of Christ, where each is repaid with rewards worthy of his deeds. What he said in general about the last coming of Christ to judgment, he now applies more closely to himself, and teaches that he is strengthened in his ministry by the consideration of it. By this example men of every place and rank are taught that a general knowledge of Jesus Christ is not enough, but that each must apply to himself whatever is said about him, and remember that he too must one day stand before his tribunal.

units.la: Sic autem rem istam proponit: Scientes igitur terrorem illum Domini, homines persuademus, Deo autem manifesti sumus, &c. Terrorem Domini dicit terribile illud Christi tribunal, cui omnes homines sisti oportere dixerat. Et de quo Daniel olim sic scripsit: Cuius solium flammae ignis, & rota eius ignis flagrans: Igneum flumen dimanabat egrediebatur, ab eo, & millies mille ministrabant ei, ac decies mille myriades ante ipsum stabant. Ad ista & alia huius generis respiciens Paulus, sic videtur dicere: Cum non ignoremus quid futurum sit, imo frequenter cogitemus de magno illo die, quo ratio reddenda erit de omnibus, quae nobis a Deo in mandatis data sunt: non possumus non diligenter & serio versari in nostro Apostolatu. Itaque hominibus passim persuadere conamur, vt ipsi quoque Deum illum timeant, & IESVM CHRISTVM fide vera ampleCtantur, ne dies ille ipsis tristis & intolerabilis illucescat. Et quo animo istud omne a nobis fiat, Deus nouit, qui corda & renes scrutatur. Caeterum spero, fidem & integritatem nostram, non illi solum, verumetiam vobis iam perspectam esse: qui si velitis fateri quod verum est, propria conscientiae testimonio conuicti cogemini dicere, me nullum fidi doctoris officium apud vos praetermisisse. Ita vero pseudoapostolorum & aemulorum calumnijs partim ipsius Dei, partim propriae ipsorum conscientiae testimonium opponit.
units.tr: He sets the matter out in this way: Knowing, then, the terror of the Lord, we persuade men, but we are manifest to God, etc. By the terror of the Lord he means that dreadful tribunal of Christ, before which he had said all men must appear. Of it Daniel once wrote thus: Whose throne was a flame of fire, and its wheels a burning fire; a river of fire flowed and issued from before him; thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. Looking to these things and others of this kind, Paul seems to say: Since we do not ignore what is to come, indeed often think of that great day on which an account must be rendered for all the things that have been committed to us by God, we cannot but labour diligently and earnestly in our Apostleship. Therefore we try everywhere to persuade men that they too should fear that God, and embrace Jesus Christ with true faith, so that that day does not dawn upon them as sad and unbearable. With what intention all this is done by us, God knows, who searches hearts and minds. Moreover, I hope that our faith and integrity are now known not only to him but also to you; if you are willing to confess what is true, you will be compelled, convicted by the testimony of your own conscience, to say that I have omitted no duty of a faithful teacher among you. Thus he sets against the slanders of the false apostles and rivals the testimony partly of God himself and partly of their own consciences.

units.la: Est autem in his verbis obseruatu dignissimum, quod de suo & collegarum suorum ministerio loquens, non Docendi aut Praedicandi, sed Suadendi vocabulo vtitur. Quia enim Regnum Dei non in sermone aut nuda inanie cognitione consistit, non satis est scire quid credas & facias: sed vt id reuera praestes necesse est. At multa hic nobis obstant: Innata nimirum vitiositas, qua fit, vt figmenta cordis nostri ab ineunte aetate praua sint: intellectus nostri tarditas, qui non percipit ea quae sunt Spiritus Dei: exemplum mundi, qui totus in malo iacet, & varijs voluptatum atque scelerum illecebris nos ab officio reuocat: quibus accedit tyrannis & aperta vis impiorum, qui synceros Christi cultores hostiliter persequuntur. Quapropter Verbi administros omnes ingenij vires cum ardenti zelo intendere oportet, vt persuadeantur qui vel moras nectunt, vel iam iter ingressi pedem referunt. Videmus enim quotidie & passim fieri, quod Lotho & vxori eius accidisse Moses scribit, cum e Sodomis exire iuberentur. Hinc illa Prophetarum vehementia in dicendo, qua ex mandato Dei vsi sunt, dicentis: Clama ex gutture, exalta instar tubae vocem tuam, &c. Hinc illa Ioannis Baptistae libertas, qui neque Sacerdotibus, neque Senioribus, neque Herodi Regi parcendum esse putauit, cum hos omnes multa praeter officium facere videret. Hinc etiam manarunt acres illae conciones Apostolorum, quibus Iudaeorum principibus immane illud parricidium, in Dei Filium recens patratum, publice exprobrauerunt. At quae nostri seculi mollities est, vel malitia potius, plerique putant sufficere, si obiter praedicetur Veritatis doctrina, & nimios clamant esse eos, qui huic obiurgationes, increpationes, & poenarum denunciationes admiscent. Atqui sufficeret simplex Verbi praedicatio, si mox facerent homines quod rectum
units.tr: In these words it is worth most careful notice that, speaking of his own ministry and that of his colleagues, he does not use the word teaching or preaching, but persuading. For since the Kingdom of God does not consist in speech or bare empty knowledge, it is not enough to know what you should believe and do, but it is necessary that you actually perform it. Yet many things stand in the way here: our innate viciousness, by which it comes about that the imaginations of our heart are evil from our earliest age; the dullness of our understanding, which does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God; the example of the world, which lies wholly in evil and calls us back from duty by its various allurements of pleasures and crimes; to which is added the tyranny and open violence of the impious, who hostilely persecute the sincere worshippers of Christ. Therefore all the ministers of the Word must bend the powers of their minds with ardent zeal, so that those are persuaded who either delay or, having already set out on the way, turn back. For we see every day and everywhere what Moses writes happened to Lot and his wife, when they were ordered to come out of Sodom. Hence came that vehemence of the Prophets in speaking, which they used by the command of God, who said: Cry aloud, lift up your voice like a trumpet, etc. Hence came the freedom of John the Baptist, who thought that neither the priests, nor the elders, nor King Herod was to be spared, since he saw all of them doing many things beyond their duty. From this too flowed those sharp sermons of the Apostles, by which they publicly reproached the leaders of the Jews for that monstrous parricide recently committed against the Son of God. But the softness, or rather the malice, of our age is such that most people think it enough if the doctrine of truth is preached in passing, and they cry out that those are excessive who mix rebukes, reproofs and denunciations of punishments with it. And yet simple preaching of the Word would suffice, if men straightaway did what they understand to be right.

units.la: Isa. 58. rectum esse intelligunt. Sed quid fiat, nemo tam caecus est qui non videat. Regnat vbiq; gentiũ superstitiones, & ab his ne ij quidé immunes sunt, qui Euangelij doctrinā profitentur, cum interim mundo placere studeat, et pro Veritate in nullius odiū incurrere velint. Regnat ite, imò grassantur apud omnis loci homines vitia, quibus Dei ira accenditur: qualia sunt, ebrietas, luxuria, libidines vagae, avaritia, vsurae, fraudes, rapina, caedes, & quaecunque alia solent ista comitari: neque vllis iudiciorum Dei exemplis, quae is multa & non vulgaria edit, infelix mundus mouetur. Quae ergo diligentia nimia, quae dicendi vehementia non necessaria videri potest, quando vix centesimus quisque se de ijs persuaderi patitur, sine quibus salus nostra non potest consistere.
units.tr: Isa. 58. Yet what is happening, no one is so blind as not to see. The superstitions of the nations reign everywhere, and even those who profess the doctrine of the Gospel are not free from them, while they are eager to please the world and do not want to incur the hatred of anyone for the sake of the truth. Vices reign and rage among men in every place, and by these the wrath of God is kindled: such as drunkenness, luxury, wanton lusts, avarice, usury, frauds, robbery, murders, and whatever else usually accompanies these; and the unhappy world is not moved by any of the examples of God's judgments, which he has shown in many and not ordinary ways. What excessive diligence, then, what vehemence of speech can seem unnecessary, when scarcely one in a hundred allows himself to be persuaded of those things without which our salvation cannot stand?

units.la: Quid vero illud est, quod Apostoli omnibus hominibus persuasum esse voluerunt? Terror sive timor Domini, qui ex certa cognitione atque indubitata IESV CHRISTI ad iudicium venturi fide nascitur. Est hic articulus plus quam necessarius, qui & inculcetur ab Ecclesiarum ministris, & in cuius meditatione homines Christiani assidue versentur. Nā haec fere nocentissima est salutis remora, quod pleriq; praesentis modò saeculi boni inenti perpetuam sibi impunitatem pollicentur, quando multos inter absurdissimas superstitiones & atrocissimorum scelerum licentiam feliciter agere, & seipsos non statim puniri vident postquam ijsdem studijs sese addixerunt. Tunc enim comminationes Verbi Dei ridere, & Prophetas quoq; insultare audent, & audiuntur voces illae nefariae: Vbi est pollicitatio aduentus Domini? Non est Deus, qui mortalia curet: Deus non videt, Dominus non audit: Foedus fecimus cum inferis, & pactum cum morte pepigimus, &c. Et eiusmodi quidem illusores omnibus saeculis fuerunt: quae causa fuit, quod Apostoli huius articuli frequenter meminerunt, & diligentissimè quidem apud eos, qui humanae sapientiae studio decepti, lusum iocumque esse putabant omnia, quae de illo in Scripturis traduntur, quales cū Corinthijs omnes fere Graecos, & quidem Athenienses imprimis fuisse constat. Et huc pertinent, quae apud Felicem praesidem coram Agrippa Rege dixit Paulus, & quae Petrus apud Cornelium testatus est, vt iam ea omittamus, quae in posteriori sua epistola idem ille scripsit de illusoribus, qui nouissimis temporibus futuri sint. Et ne vnquam articuli huius obliuio Christianus possit obrepere, disertis verbis eum in Symbolo, quod Apostolicum vocant, expresserunt.
units.tr: But what is it that the Apostles wanted to be persuaded into all men? The terror or fear of the Lord, which arises from a sure knowledge and an undoubting faith that Jesus Christ is coming to judgment. This article is more than necessary; it must be impressed by the ministers of the Churches, and Christian men must be constantly occupied in meditating on it. For this is almost the most harmful hindrance to salvation, that most people of the present age, good at inventing, promise themselves perpetual impunity, since they see that they live happily amid most absurd superstitions and the licence of most atrocious crimes, and that they are not punished at once after they have devoted themselves to the same pursuits. For then they dare to mock the threats of the Word of God and even to insult the Prophets, and those wicked voices are heard: Where is the promise of the Lord's coming? God does not care for mortal things: God does not see, the Lord does not hear: we have made a covenant with the dead, and struck a pact with death, etc. Indeed, such scoffers have existed in all ages; and for this reason the Apostles often remembered this article, and most diligently so among those who, deceived by the study of human wisdom, thought that everything that is handed down about it in the Scriptures was play and jest; of which sort it is clear that almost all Greeks, and especially the Athenians, were, together with the Corinthians. To this belong what Paul said before Governor Felix in the presence of King Agrippa, and what Peter testified before Cornelius, not to mention what the same man wrote in his second letter about the scoffers who will come in the last times. And lest the forgetting of this article should ever creep upon a Christian, they expressed it in plain words in the Creed which they call Apostolic.

units.la: At hic quaerunt multi, qui fiat, quod non omnes mouentur articulo isto? Quibus respondeí potest: Quia eum pauci ea ratione considerant, qua Paulum vsum fuisse audimus. Hic non contentus hominum de se iudicio, neque si aemulorum calumnias propriae conscientiae testimonio confutauisset, insuper se in Dei conspectu versari cogitauit, qui omnia eius nota atque perspecta habeat. Decet hoc omnes homines, vt suam fidem atque industriam Deo approbare studeant. Possunt enim homines suo iudicio falli, at Deus falli non potest, cum corda simul & cogitationes omnium norit, & eius oculi (vt Prophetá ait) discurrant per vniuersam terram. Et vt ipsi perpetuò lateamus aut scelera nostra semper occultemus, impossibile est. Habet enim vindices oculos Deus (vt Graeci loquuntur) & Veritatem alij Temporis filiam esse non inepte dixerunt, eò quod illud omnia reuelat. Exemplum eius rei memorabile in Dauide proponit scriptura, qui cum adulterium & indignam Viriae caedem mirifico astu simul & authoritate regia celaret (quis enim tale quid de illo vel mussitare ausus fuisset?) Dei tamen oculos latere non potuit, qui per Nathanum seruum suum non priuatam modò, sed publicam quoque tanti scelerisconfessionem ei extorsit: vt nimirum hanc Psalmis de seipso compositis populo decantandam proponeret. Quod infinitis alijs, tam bonis quàm malis accidisse scimus. Et esto inueniantur interdum, quorum flagitia, quoad hic viuunt, perpetuo silentio tecta manent, ijdem tamen magnum illum nouissimi iudicij diem subterfugere non poterunt, quando libri aperientur (vt nuper ex Daniele docuimus) & omnium conscientiae angelis simul atque hominibus patebunt. Meminerimus ergo omnem virtutis simulationem inanem esse; nisi quod videri volumus, reipsa praestemus. Itaque quod Solomon olim monuit, terror aut timor iste Domini, de quo in praesenti Paulus loquitur, praecipua hominis sapientia est. Nam solus ille indomitos carnis affectus quasi frano coercet, & fidei obedientiam gignit, quae nos posse illicita corruptae naturae nostrae desideria exorbitare non finit. Applicent ergo sibi ipsis singuli doctrinam istam, & imprimis quidem Verbi Dei administri. His enim commisit illeud, quo nihil vel in terris vel in caelo pretiosius ha-
units.tr: But many people ask here why not everyone is moved by this article. To this it can be answered that few consider it in the way we hear Paul did. Not content with other people's judgement of him, and not satisfied that the testimony of his own conscience refuted his rivals' slanders, he thought that he also lived in the sight of God, who knows and sees all that is his. This becomes all people, that they should strive to approve their faith and diligence before God. Men can be deceived in their own judgement, but God cannot be deceived, since he knows the hearts and thoughts of all, and his eyes (as the Prophet says) range through the whole earth. Nor is it possible for us to lie hidden forever or to keep our sins always concealed. God has eyes that avenge (as the Greeks put it), and not without reason some have said that Truth is the daughter of Time, because Time reveals all things. Scripture sets before us a memorable example of this in David, who concealed his adultery and the shameful murder of Uriah with wonderful cunning and royal authority (for who would have dared to murmur anything of that sort about him?). Yet God's eyes could not be hidden from him. Through Nathan his servant, God wrung from him a confession of so great a crime, not only a private one but a public one as well, so that he might set it forth to be sung by the people in the Psalms he composed about himself. We know that this has happened to countless others, both good and bad. And although there are sometimes those whose disgraceful deeds remain covered by perpetual silence while they live here, they will nonetheless be unable to escape that great day of the last judgement, when the books are opened (as we recently taught from Daniel) and the consciences of all are laid open to the angels as well as to men. Let us remember, then, that all pretence of virtue is empty, unless we actually do what we wish to appear to do. Therefore, that fear or dread of the Lord of which Paul speaks in this place is, as Solomon long ago warned, the chief wisdom of man. For it alone restrains the untamed affections of the flesh, as if with a bridle, and begets an obedience of faith, which does not allow us to stray into the unlawful desires of our corrupt nature. Let each one therefore apply this teaching to himself, and above all the ministers of God's Word. For to them has been entrusted that which has nothing more precious and dear, either on earth or in heaven: namely the Church, which he redeemed with the price of his own blood and washed, that he might make her his own and a partner in all good things. He also equips them with the gifts necessary to make them sufficient for this office, which by its nature far exceeds human strength. And the time will come when he will require an account from them, as Christ clearly teaches in the parable of the talents. If then they are slothful and of poor fruit, or if (as many are wont to do) they have sold their authority to a shameful license of conduct, they will never bear it unpunished. For the Lord will come when they least expect it, and he will cast them, condemned by the same judgement by which traitors are usually punished, into outer darkness. And the Holy Spirit abundantly teaches, through the dreadful example of the sons of Eli, what awaits many even in this age. But this concern pertains no less to those who hold the magistracy. Arrogance there deceives many, who persuade themselves that the people are wholly under their control and that they are the masters of affairs, and so may, at their own pleasure, make and unmake laws and twist or even entirely repeal public rights. Yet the people of God is a special possession, which acknowledges that the magistrate is its own, and which is present in their assemblies, and understands not only what they say or do but also with what intention they do everything. Let magistrates therefore announce their judgements, seek solely the glory of God, and strive to the utmost of their strength for public peace and welfare, and above all (as the Psalm admonishes) let them hold the blood of their subjects precious. Let them also be terrified by the examples which God has set forth in every age against tyrants, who either were the authors of license for the people or oppressed them insolently. Let parents and masters too apply these things to themselves, and remember that their children are a deposit from God, who wishes them to be consecrated to himself and will require them at their hands. Let them therefore take care that he may bear the same testimony concerning them that Moses writes he bore of Abraham. Finally, this confidence pertains to wives, servants, subjects, the rich and the poor: all of whom will live more honourably and comfortably here, and will in time be admitted to the possession of eternal life, if they strive to keep themselves in their duty by this sincere fear of God.

units.la: Cur pauci articulo isto moueantur? bet & charius: Ecclesia videlicet, quæ proprij sanguinis pretio redemit, & abluit vt eam sibi ipsam & bonorum omnium consortem faceret. Eosdem quoque donis necessarijs instruit, vt functioni huic, quæ per se humanas vires longè superat, possint sufficere. Et veniet tempus, quando de illis rationem exiget, sicuti Christus in talentorum parabola diserte docet. Quòd si ergo segnes et malæ frugis fuerint, vel etiam (quod multi solent) ipsi authoritatem suam turpi morum licentia proflituerint, id nunquam inultum ferent. Venient enim Dominus, cùm minimè putarint, & eodem, quo proditores puniri solent, iudicio damnatos in tenebras exteriores eijciet. Et quid plerosque in hoc etiam sæculo maneat, horribili illo filiorum Heli exemplo Spiritus Sanctus abunde docet. At non minus ad eos quoque hæc cura pertinet, qui magistratum gerunt. Imponit illic multis arrogantia, quòd populum sui omnino iuris, seque rerum dominos esse sibi persuadent, quibus liceat pro suo arbitrio leges figere & refigere, iura denique publica torquere, vel etiam omnino abrogare. Atqui populus Dei peculium est, qui & hunc pro suo agnoscit, & illorum consessibus medius adest, & non solum quid dicant aut faciant, verumetiam quo animo omnia agant, intelligit. Huius ergo iudicia enuntient, eiusdem gloriam vnicè quærant, paci & saluti publicæ pro virili studeant, imprimis autem (vt Psalmus admonet) pretiosum ducat sanguinem subditorum suorum. Terreant item eos exempla, quæ omnibus sæculis in tyrannos edidit Deus, qui vel populo licentiæ authores fuerunt, vel eundem insolenter oppresserunt. Transferant ista ad se quoque parentes, & liberos suos depositum Dei esse meminerint, qui hos sibi consecratos esse velit, & eosdem de manibus ipsorum requisiturus sit. Curent ergo, vt hic de ipsis idem testimonium ferat, quod olim de Abrahamo illum tulisse, Moses scribit. Pertinet deniq; confidentio ista ad coniuges, seruos, subditos, diuites, pauperes: qui omnes & hic honestius atque commodius viuent, & olim ad vitæ æternæ possessionem admittentur, si ingenuo hoc Dei timore sese in officio continere studeant.
units.tr: Why are so few people moved by this article? It is also dearer and more precious to him: the Church, which he redeemed by the price of his own blood and cleansed so that he might make it his own and a partaker of all good things. He also equips those ministers with the gifts they need, so that they may be equal to this office, which far exceeds human strength. A time will come when he will call them to account, just as Christ plainly teaches in the parable of the talents. If then they prove slothful and fruitless, or even (as many are wont to do) sell their authority for a shameful license of conduct, they will never bear it unavenged. For the Lord will come when they least expect it, and he will cast them, condemned by the same judgment with which traitors are usually punished, into outer darkness. And how the greater part of them will fare even in this age, the Holy Spirit amply teaches by the dreadful example of the sons of Eli. But this concern pertains no less to those who hold the magistracy. Arrogance besets many of them, for they persuade themselves that the people belong entirely to them and that they are the masters of affairs, so that they may set and repeal laws at their own pleasure, twist public rights, or even abolish them altogether. Yet the people of God is a peculiar possession, which acknowledges that the magistrate is its own, which is present in the councils of rulers, and which understands not only what they say or do but also with what intention they do everything. Let magistrates therefore pronounce their judgments in the sight of God, seek his glory alone, study with all their strength for the peace and welfare of the commonwealth, and above all (as the Psalm admonishes) hold the blood of their subjects precious. Let them also be frightened by the examples which God has set forth in every age against tyrants, who either were the authors of license for the people or oppressed them arrogantly. Let parents and masters likewise apply these things to themselves, and remember that their children are a deposit from God, who wishes them to be consecrated to himself and will require them at their hands. Let them therefore take care that God may bear the same testimony to them as Moses writes he once bore to Abraham. Finally, this admonition pertains to wives, servants, subjects, rich and poor alike. All of these will live more honorably and more comfortably here, and will in time be admitted to the possession of eternal life, if they earnestly strive to keep themselves in their duty by this sincere fear of God.

units.la: Sed vt ad Paulum redeamus, poterant ista aliquibus ambitiosius dicta videri; quare rursus se excusat, & quo animo & in quem finem ea dixerit, docet. Enimuero non iterum nosipsos commendamus vobis: sed vobis occasionem præbemus gloriandi de nobis, &c. Particula, I TERVM, Paulum hac per Mimesim dicere ostendit, qua aduersariorum de se sermones perstringit. Solebant enim illi quacunque occasione oblata exclamare: En Thrasonem rursus in suas laudes digredientem, &c. Ostendit ergo, se nihil minus facere, quàm quod isti calumniantur: sed hæc omnia propter ipsos & ipsorum vtilitatem dici, & ideo duas causas adducit, quibus moueatur. Vnam, vt vobis occasionem præbeamus gloriandi de nobis, id est, vt argumenta habeatis, quibus ministerium meum & quam ex nobis didicistis doctrinam possitis defendere. Erat hoc plus quàm necessarium: quia fide ministri labefactata, huic tuto credi non potest, & simul multorum falsis periclitatur. Cùm ergo Paulus multorum calumniis peteretur, opus erat Corinthios argumentis instruì, ne de eius ministerio & authoritate dubitarent. Altera, vt habeatis quid aduersus eos, qui ex facie gloriam captant, at non ex corde, id est, qui magnificè sese extollunt, quasi germani sint IESV CHRISTI Apostoli, cùm nihil huius in corde suo habeant, imò proprij cordis testimonio falsi convincantur. Adhæc ex facie gloriam captare dicuntur, qui non nisi laruis externis sese vendicant, verborum ornatu & eloquentiæ ostentatione superbiunt, nihil autem habent in re- cessu, quod germanos Christi ministros esse testetur. Tales erant isti, qui Corinthiorum Ecclesiam turbabant. Gloriabantur de suo zelo & fide, qua publicæ omnium salutí consultum vellent: cùm non nisi sua quærerent. Deinde Hierosolymitanæ Ecclesiæ authoritatem prætexebant, seque Apostolorum, qui illic agerent, discipulos esse iactabant: cùm pharisaici essent impostores. Præterea philosophiæ & eloquentiæ exîstimatione sese ostentabant, à fide autem & vera pietate, quæ in puro cordis affectu consistit, erant alienissimi. Aduersus istos (inquit Paulus) ego vos armis instruo, ne ab eis decipiamini. Ita vero obiter Corinthiorum ingratitudine arguit, qui nõ agnoscebant eum proipsis laborare, sed quasi hæc nihil ad se pertinerent, admittebant calumnias eorum, qui eius authoritatem labefactabant. Fit hoc ipsum hodie. Imperiū in Ecclesias omnes iampridem sibi vendicarunt Pontifices & Episcopi, qui ex sola facie gloriā captant: quòd nimirum Apostolorum successores et Christi vicarij sint, quòd ad ipsos totius orbis Ecclesiarū cura pertineat, quòd zelo domus Dei vrantur. Accedunt hîs opes immodicæ, multus auri & gemmarum splendor, vestis pur- purā purae dignitas, mitrae bicornes & tiarae triplices, galeri, pallia, peda, cruces aureae & argenteae, sexcenta item alia, quae rudis populi oculos possunt perstringere. Quales autem sint, ipsorum dicta & facta abunde docent, & illos cum Christo simul & eius Ecclesia ludere, vel Vnius Alexandri VI. dictum probat, qui cum aliquando de re Christiana sermo incidisset, exclamavit: Atqui haec bona est perfuasio, quia per hanc nos regnamus. At dum ista fideles Christi servi arguunt, ne rudiores larvis eiusmodi capiantur, multi suspecti fiunt, qui illos affectui indulgere & res suas quaerere calumniantur quo fit, ut illis fere exosi sint, pro quorum salute ipsi contra communes Ecclesiae & religionis Christianae hostes pugnant. Sed non debent ista aliquem offendere, quo minus officium faciat. Nam qualiacunque sint mundi infelicium de nobis iudicia, arguì tamen oportet eorum impostoras, qui vulgi simplicitate ad tyrannidem suam stabiliendam abutuntur. Tueantur ergo Veritatis doctrinam, & alios quoque argumentis instruant, quibus adversus impostores illos eandem tueri possint.
units.tr: But to return to Paul: these things might seem to some to have been said somewhat boastfully. Therefore he again makes his excuse and shows with what intention and to what end he has said them. "For again we do not commend ourselves to you, but give you occasion to glory on our behalf," etc. By the word "again" Paul shows that he is speaking in this way by imitation, thereby ridiculing the words of his opponents about himself. For they were accustomed, whenever any occasion offered, to cry out: "Behold Thrasso again launching into his own praises," etc. He shows, therefore, that he does nothing less than what they slander him for, but that all these things are said for their sake and for their benefit, and he brings forward two reasons that move him. The first is that he gives them occasion to glory on his behalf, that is, that they may have arguments by which they can defend my ministry and the doctrine they have learned from me. This was more than necessary, for once the faith in a minister is shaken, his teaching cannot be safely believed, and at the same time the faith of many is put in danger by falsehoods. Since Paul was therefore being attacked by the calumnies of many, it was necessary that the Corinthians be equipped with arguments, so that they would not doubt his ministry and authority. The second reason is that you may have something to answer those who seek glory from the face and not from the heart; that is, who puff themselves up magnificently, as if they were the true apostles of Jesus Christ, when they have none of this in their heart and are convicted by the testimony of their own heart as false. Moreover, those are said to seek glory from the face who claim for themselves nothing but external masks, who take pride in the ornament of words and the display of eloquence, but have nothing inside that bears witness that they are genuine ministers of Christ. Such were those who were troubling the Church of the Corinthians. They boasted of their zeal and faith, by which they wished to provide for the public welfare of all, when they sought only their own interests. Then they pretended the authority of the Church of Jerusalem and boasted that they were disciples of the apostles who labored there, when they were Pharisaic impostors. Besides, they displayed themselves by the esteem of philosophy and eloquence, while they were utterly estranged from faith and true piety, which consists in a sincere disposition of the heart. Against these men (says Paul) I arm you, so that you may not be deceived by them. In passing he also rebukes the ingratitude of the Corinthians, who did not acknowledge that he labored on their behalf, but, as if these things were no concern of theirs, admitted the calumnies of those who undermined his authority. The same thing happens today. Popes and bishops, who seek glory from the face alone, have long since claimed for themselves dominion over all the Churches: namely, that they are successors of the apostles and vicars of Christ, that the care of the Churches of the whole world belongs to them, that they burn with zeal for the house of God. To these are added immoderate riches, a great display of gold and gems, vestments of purple worthy of purple, double-horned mitres and triple tiaras, galeri, palliums, pedums, golden and silver crosses, and six hundred other things that can dazzle the eyes of the common people. What sort of men they are, however, their words and deeds amply show, and the saying of one Alexander VI proves that they mock both Christ and his Church. For once, when the talk turned to the Christian religion, he exclaimed: "Indeed this belief is good, for through it we reign." But while the faithful servants of Christ denounce these things, lest the simpler sort be caught by such masks, many come under suspicion, and they are slandered as indulging their own passions and seeking their own affairs. As a result, they are almost hated by those for whose salvation they fight against the common enemies of the Church and of the Christian religion. Yet these things ought not to deter anyone from doing his duty. For whatever the judgments of the unhappy world about us may be, the impostures of those who abuse the simplicity of the crowd to establish their tyranny must nonetheless be exposed. Let them therefore defend the doctrine of the truth, and let them also equip others with arguments by which they may defend it against those impostors.

units.la: Porrò clarius aliquanto seipsum explicat Paulus, dicens: Nam sive insanimus, Deo insanimus: sive sana mente sumus, vobis sana mente sumus. Insaniam sive insipientiam dicere solet, quando de seipso & ministerio suo magnificentius loquitur. Sic infra Cap. undecimo hoc argumentum tractaturus, inter alia dicit: Quod dico, non secundum Dominum dico, sed ut per insipientiam. Et rursus Cap. duodecimo post longam eorum, quae per ipsum Deus fecerat, expositionem subijcit: Fui insipiens gloriando, vos me coegistis. Ita vero loquitur, partim quod per se videatur parum cordati hominis indicium esse proprias laudes cantare: partim ex adversariorum iudicio, qui hinc occasione arrepta ipsum stoliditatis arrogantiae accusabant. Huic opponit σωφροσύνη, quod sana mente uti significat, & quoad huius loci sensum, idem est, quod de seipso modestius sentire & loqui. Itaque sic vult dicere Apostolus: Si quando adversariorum calumniis coacti, nostram authoritatem tuemur, deque ministerio nostro ea dicimus, quae dicere res ipsa iubet, vobis quidem insanire videor, sed id me non multum movet: quia Deo insanimus, id est, hoc unum agimus, ut Dei Verbo sua authoritas salva maneat, neque illi per impostores illos sua fides derogetur. Rursus, si quando humilius de meipso & ministerio nostro loquor (quae vobis demum unica sapientia esse videtur) id vobis damus, adeoque propter vos facimus, ne nimium graveminì, & ut nostro exemplo humilitatem & modestiam discatis. In summa, hic mihi scopus propositus est, ut Deo & Ecclesiae serviam, & multorum saluti consulam. Dum ergo hoc consequi studeo, non multum moror, quid de me iudicent, qui suis potius affectibus servire volunt, quam Dei gloriam tueri.
units.tr: Paul explains himself a little more clearly, saying: "For whether we be beside ourselves, it is to God: or whether we be sober, it is for your cause" (2 Cor. 5:13). He usually calls it madness or folly when he speaks of himself and his ministry too boastfully. So in chapter eleven, when he is about to treat this same subject, he says among other things: "That which I speak, I speak not after the Lord, but as it were foolishly" (2 Cor. 11:17). And again in chapter twelve, after a long account of what God had done through him, he adds: "I am become a fool in glorying; ye have compelled me" (2 Cor. 12:11). He speaks in this way partly because boasting of one's own praises seems in itself to be a sign of a man who lacks sense, and partly because of the judgement of his opponents, who, seizing on this occasion, accused him of foolish arrogance. He sets against this sōphrosynē [σωφροσύνη], which means being of sound mind, and, as far as the sense of this passage goes, it is the same as thinking and speaking of oneself with more modesty. So the Apostle means this: "If at any time, compelled by the slanders of our opponents, we defend our authority and say about our ministry what the matter itself requires, you may think me mad. But that does not move me much, because we are beside ourselves for God, that is, we do this one thing, that the authority of God's Word remain safe and that its credibility not be diminished by those impostors. Again, if at any time I speak more humbly of myself and my ministry (which to you alone seems to be wisdom), I do this for your sake, and so I do it on your account, so that you may not be too burdened, and that by our example you may learn humility and modesty." In sum, my aim here is set before me: to serve God and the Church, and to look after the salvation of many. So while I strive to attain this, I do not greatly care what those think of me who would rather serve their own passions than defend the glory of God.

units.la: Observemus nos hoc loco, quàm iniquè mundus de Verbi Dei administris iudicet. Odit enim huius lucem, & extinctam cupit, ut iam saepe diximus. Itaque qui in mundo meliores sunt, ij Verbi praecones stultescere, aut etiam prorsus insanire dicunt. Etenim carnis iudicio stultissimum videtur, omnia velle ex Verbi illius praescripto facere, contemptis omnium aliorum exemplis proprium vitae genus sectari, aliorum studijs sese opponere, odia & inimicitias sibi accersere propter Veritatis cognitionem, quae plerisque dubia esse, & (ut Philosophus dicebat) in puteo profundo delitescere videtur. Hinc illa prophanorum hominum de servis Dei iudicia, quorum Scriptura non uno loco meminerunt. Cùm Iehu à quodam illorum in regem vnctus esset, & is mox se alio proripuisset, interrogavit mox illum alius: Quam ob causam ingressus est ad te Vesanus ille? Isaias item se cum suis discipulis portenti instar esse querebatur in Israële. Similiter Paulo de Regno Dei differenti Festus acclamavit: Insanis Paule, multae litterae te ad insaniam redegerunt. Et cùm primum Spiritu donati essent Apostoli, & linguis variis Euangelij doctrinam praedicarent, multi eos musto plenos dixerunt. Hodie phanatici dicimur, capitosi, rerum civilium imperiti, imprudentes & temerarij rerum novatores. Sed quid mirum, quando Christus modò insanire, modò daemonio agitari dictus fuit? et quis ignorat, quàm scurriliter ipsum exceperit Pilatus quando se ideo in mundum venisse dicebat, ut Veritati testimonium ferat? Horum ergo memores Ecclesiarum ministri, in officio suo fidi & constantes sint, alij verò omnes Dei Verbum patienter audiant, vitaque sua omne secundum illius praescriptum instituant, ut olim in adventu Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, salute & vita aeterna fruantur. Huic debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Let us observe here how unjustly the world judges the ministers of God's Word. For it hates its light and wishes it extinguished, as we have often said already. Therefore those who are the better sort in the world call the heralds of the Word foolish, or even quite mad. For in the judgement of the flesh it seems most foolish to want to do everything according to the prescription of that Word, to despise the examples of all others and pursue a way of life of one's own, to set oneself against the pursuits of others, and to draw hatred and enmity upon oneself for the sake of knowing the truth, which seems doubtful to most people and (as the philosopher used to say) lies hidden in a deep well. Hence come those judgements of profane men about the servants of God, which Scripture mentions in more than one place. When Jehu had been anointed king by one of them, and he had soon hurried away elsewhere, another immediately asked him: "Why did that madman come to you?" (2 Kings 9:11). Isaiah likewise complained that he and his disciples were like a portent in Israel (Isa. 8:18). Similarly, when Paul was discoursing about the kingdom of God, Festus shouted: "Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad" (Acts 26:24). And when the Apostles were first filled with the Spirit and preached the doctrine of the Gospel in various tongues, many said that they were full of new wine (Acts 2:13). Today we are called fanatics, hot-heads, men ignorant of civil affairs, and rash and reckless innovators. But what is surprising about that, when Christ himself was said at one time to be mad and at another to be possessed by a demon? And who does not know how scornfully Pilate received him when he said that he had come into the world for this reason, to bear witness to the truth (John 18:37)? Mindful of these things, therefore, let the ministers of the Churches be faithful and steadfast in their office, and let all others listen patiently to God's Word and order their lives entirely according to its prescription, so that, as at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, they may enjoy salvation and eternal life. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXIII.

units.la: Charitas enim illa Christi constringit nos: ut qui hoc statueri mus, quòd si vnus pro omnibus mortuus fuit, ut pote omnes mor tui fuerunt: & ille pro omnibus mortuus est, ut qui viuūt, post hac non sibi viuant, sed ei, qui pro ipsis mortuus est & resurrexit. Itaque nos posthac neminem nouimus secundum carnem: quòd si etiam nouimus Christum secundum carnem, nunc tamen non amplius nouimus. Si quis igitur est in Christo, noua creatura est. Vetera praeterierunt, ecce noua facta sunt omnia.
units.tr: For the love of Christ constrains us, since we judge this: that if one died for all, then all died; and he died for all, so that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them and rose again. Therefore from now on we regard no one according to the flesh. Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, now we no longer know him so. So if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new.

units.la: Paulus Apostolus hucusque suam authoritatem contra aemulorum suorum calumnias diligenter asseruit, eaque occasione multa dixit de suo erga Ecclesiam studio. Id vero non fecit, ut suae modo existimationi consuleret, sed potius ne Euangelij doctrina apud Corinthios in contemptum veniret, utq; simpliciores argumentis instrueret, quibus fidem suam tueri, & doctrinae saniorus aduersarios arguere atque confutare possent. De istis vero omnibus sic disserit, ut simul suo exemplo doceat, quibus stimulis singuli seipsos excitare debeant in suis functionibus, quas illis Deus creadit. Quo cumprimis facit, quod de nouissimo IESV CHRISTI aduentu dixit, ad cuius tribunal omnes nos sisti & manifestari oporteat. At ne quis ipsum ignobili solum & seruili timore vrgeri putaret, nunc praecipuam sui studij causam indicat, quae ipsum segnescere aut laboribus periculi sue fatigari non sinat: sed excitet potius, ut contemptis hominum de se iudicijs, totus in eo sit, ut quamplurimos Christo adducat, & fidem in hunc longè lateq; propaget.
units.tr: The Apostle Paul has so far carefully defended his authority against the slanders of his rivals, and on that occasion he has said much about his zeal for the Church. He did not do this merely to look after his own reputation, but rather so that the teaching of the Gospel would not fall into contempt among the Corinthians, and so that he might equip the simpler folk with arguments by which they could defend the faith and refute and confute the opponents of sounder doctrine. He discusses all these matters in such a way that, by his own example, he also teaches what goads each person ought to use to stir himself up in the functions that God has entrusted to him. Especially to this purpose is what he said about the last coming of Jesus Christ, before whose judgement seat we must all be presented and made manifest. But lest anyone think that he is driven only by a base and servile fear, he now names the chief motive of his zeal, which does not allow him to grow sluggish or to be worn down by the labours and dangers, but rather rouses him so that, having despised people's judgements about himself, he may devote himself wholly to bringing as many as possible to Christ and to spreading the faith far and wide.

units.la: Charitas enim illa Christi (inquit) constringit nos, &c. Paulo ante se hoc necessario facere dixit, quia nouissimi iudicij terror ipsum vrgeat, at nunc se Christi charitate magis adhuc constringi testatur. Debet autem ea hoc loco Actiue simul & Passiue accipi: pro dilectione nimirum, qua Christus nos diligit, & pro ea, qua nos eum complectimur. Itaque hic verborum sensus est: Videor quibusdam affectui priuato indulgere, dum tanta cum constantia Christo gloriam suam vendico, ut omnes ab illo vno pendeant. Sed longè alia mihi mens est. Ita enim monet officium, quo illi obstrictus sum: & ut nihil porrò dicam de terrifico illius ad iudicium aduentu, & magno illo die, quo omnes ad eius tribunal sistemur, ipsa charitas, qua ille nos complexus est, & qua nos eum vicissim complecti debemus, nos quasi vinculis quibusdam constringit, ut non possimus non apud omnes instare, ut debitum illi obsequium praestent. Etenim cum inter homines (ipso Christo teste) hic summus dilectionis gradus sit, ut quis animam suam pro amicis suis deponat: ipse vt huc superaret, pro inimicis & rebellibus mori dignatus est. Quis ergo illum satis digne diligat? Ego certè me eius amori nunquam respondere posse sentio, qui me, crudelissimum Ecclesiae suae persecutorem, singulare gratiae & bonitatis suae exemplum facere dignatus est. Non possum ergo nō me ei totum impendere, &c. Ista autem vere dici à Paulo, Apostolorum facta testantur, qui vt initio omnia quae habebant, propter Christum reliquerunt, & multis ab eo interdum deficientibus, ipsi constanter ei adhaeserunt: ita postea cum gaudio pertulerunt carceres, plagas, conuicia, opprobria, imò voluptes eis fuit pro illo mori, quem communis omnium nostrum vita authorem esse sciebant. Testis locupletissimi instar est totus Actorum liber, qui illorum res gestas, & imprimis quidem Pauli, prolixè describit. Ipse certè in Miletana Synodo dicit: Nunc ecce, ego vinctus Spiritu profici scor Hierosolymam, quae illic obuentura sint mihi, ignorans: nisi quòd Spiritus sanctus per singulas ciuitates testificatur, dicens, quòd vincula & afflictiones me manent. Verum nullius rationem habeo, neque vita mea chara est mihijpsi, ut consummem cursum meum cum gaudio, & ministerium quod accepi à Domino IESV, ad testificandum Euangelium gratiae Dei. Quibus consentiunt ea, quae aliquanto post suis ab itinere suscepto ipsum dehortantibus, Cesarea respondit: Quid facitis facitis flentes & comminuentes cor meum? enimuero ego non solum vinciri, sed & mori paratus sum in Ierusalem pro nomine Domini IESV. Vide Actor 20. & 21.
units.tr: For the love of Christ (he says) constrains us, etc. A little before, he had said that he was doing this out of necessity, because the terror of the final judgement pressed upon him; but now he testifies that he is constrained even more by the love of Christ. The word here must be taken both actively and passively: namely, the love with which Christ loves us, and the love with which we embrace him. So the sense of the words is this: "I seem to some to indulge a private feeling, since I claim glory for Christ with such constancy, that all things depend upon him alone. But my mind is quite different. For duty, by which I am bound to him, so admonishes me; and, to say nothing further of his terrifying coming to judgement and of that great day on which we shall all be brought before his tribunal, the very love with which he has embraced us, and with which we ought in turn to embrace him, binds us as with certain chains, so that we cannot help urging everyone to render him the obedience that is due." For since among men (as Christ himself testifies) this is the highest degree of love, that someone lay down his life for his friends, he himself deigned, in order to surpass this, to die for enemies and rebels. Who then loves him sufficiently worthily? I, at least, feel that I can never respond to his love, he who deigned to make me, the most cruel persecutor of his Church, a singular example of his grace and goodness. I cannot therefore refrain from devoting myself wholly to him, etc. That these words were truly spoken by Paul is attested by the deeds of the Apostles, who at the beginning left all that they had for Christ's sake, and when many at times fell away from him, they themselves clung to him constantly; afterwards they bore prisons, blows, reproaches, and insults with joy, and indeed it was a pleasure to them to die for him whom they knew to be the author of the life of us all. The whole book of Acts, which describes their deeds at length, and especially those of Paul, is like a most abundant witness. He himself certainly says in the Synod of Miletus: "Behold, now I go bound in the Spirit to Jerusalem, not knowing what will befall me there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies in every city, saying that bonds and afflictions await me. But I count my life of no account, nor is it dear to myself, so that I may finish my course with joy, and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify the Gospel of the grace of God." In agreement with this is what he replied, some time after he had undertaken the journey, to those who were urging him to turn back: "What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? Indeed I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus." See Acts 20. & 21.

units.la: In praesenti autem docet suo exemplo Apostolus, quae nam efficacissima ratio sit, qua nos excitemus ad veram fidei obedientiam, inque ea nos confirmemus aduersus tentationes, quae nos inter pericula graviora abstterrere solent. Diligens nimirum atque seria amoris siue dilectionis Christi consideratio. Natura enim sic comparatum est, ut non possimus no redamare eos, a quibus nos ardetissime amari nobis persuasimus. At quis de Christi amore dubitet, qui hunc pro nobis sanguinem suum effudisse, & seipsum dirae atque infamis crucis supplicio tradidisse audit, ut nos ex morte in vitam assereret? Quid ergo de illis dicemus, qui Christi gloriam securi negligunt, neque aliquid audent pro ea asserenda, imo homines pluris quam illam faciunt? Sunt isti profecto adhuc alieni a vera Filij Dei cognitione, neque credi potest, eos unquam serio cogitasse de eius dilectione, qua & ille nos complexus est, & qua vicissim nos illum prosequi debebamus.
units.tr: In the present passage the Apostle teaches, by his own example, what is the most effective reason for stirring ourselves up to a true obedience of faith, and for strengthening ourselves in it against the temptations that are wont to frighten us amid greater dangers. This is namely a diligent and serious consideration of the love or affection of Christ. For nature has so ordered things that we cannot but love in return those whom we have convinced ourselves love us most ardently. But who could doubt the love of Christ, who hears that he shed his blood for us and gave himself up to the punishment of the dreadful and infamous cross, so that he might bring us from death to life? What then shall we say of those who carelessly neglect the glory of Christ, and do not dare to assert anything on its behalf, indeed who value men more than it? Such people are certainly still strangers to the true knowledge of the Son of God, nor can it be believed that they have ever seriously thought about that love of his, by which he embraced us, and by which we in turn ought to pursue him.

units.la: Caeterum explicat seipsum Paulus, & quomodo ex dilectione Christi argumentetur, docet: Vt qui hoc statuerimus, siue ad hunc modum colligamus: Quod si vnus pro omnibus mortuus fuit, utique omnes mortui fuerunt: & ille pro omnibus mortuus est, ut qui viuunt, posthac non sibi viuant, sed ei qui pro ipsis mortuus est & resurrexit. Ex causa mortis Christi argumentatur, quod nimirum nos per eam redimi oportuerit: & potest argumentum sic formari: Christus pro ijs mori debuit, qui iampridem mortui seipsos viuificare non poterant (Nec enim qui sani & valididi sunt, opus habent medico, sed inualidi) At illum pro omnibus mortuum esse, Scriptura non vno loco testantur: & ipsius verba sunt: Sic Deus dilexit mundum (Mundi vocabulo vniuersum genus humanum comprehenditur) vt Filium suum, Vnigenitum illum, pro eo traderet, &c. Item: Panis, quem dabo, caro mea est, quam dabo pro mundi vita. Et rursus: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis, &c. Ite in orbem vniuersum, & praedicate Euangelium omni Creaturae, &c. Ergo totum mundum, id est, omnes homines peccatis demersos & in ijs obrutos fuisse oportet, adeo vt nemo sibijpsi subuenire potuerit. Quis vero hunc tam ardentem Christi amorem, & quod ex eo ad nos redundauit aeternae salutis beneficium digne praedicauerit? Quid autem ex his colligit Paulus? Pro omnibus mortuus est, vt qui viuunt, posthac non sibi viuant, sed ei, qui pro ipsis mortuus est & resurrexit. Continetur hoc argumento vniuersa salutis ratio, in qua haec ex ordine consideranda veniunt.
units.tr: Moreover Paul explains himself, and shows how he argues from the love of Christ: "That we who have judged this, or so gather: If one died for all, then all died; and he died for all, so that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them and rose again." He argues from the cause of Christ's death, namely that we needed to be redeemed by it; and the argument can be framed thus: Christ ought to have died for those who long since were dead and could not make themselves alive (for those who are well and strong have no need of a physician, but the sick do). But Scripture testifies in more than one place that he died for all, and his own words are: "God so loved the world" (the word "world" comprehends the whole human race) "that he gave his only-begotten Son for it," etc. Likewise: "The bread which I shall give is my flesh, which I shall give for the life of the world." And again: "Come to me, all you who labour," etc. "Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature," etc. Therefore the whole world, that is, all men, must have been sunk in sins and buried in them, so that no one could help himself. Who has worthily proclaimed this so ardent love of Christ, and the benefit of eternal salvation that has flowed from it to us? But what does Paul gather from these things? "He died for all, so that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them and rose again." In this argument is contained the whole order of salvation, in which the following points come to be considered in turn.

units.la: Primum, qui & quales sint omnes homines, si ex innata sibi & propria conditione aestimetur. Omnes mortuos fuisse dicit, & quidem ex Dei decreto, qui Adamo dixerat: Quacunque hora comederis ex fructu arboris huius, morte morieris. Comedit autem ille, & peccator mortisque reus factus, in hac sua vitiosa & infelici conditione posteros suos omnes genuit. Ideo de gentibus omnibus Paulus ad Ephesios sic scribit: Et vos vnà viuificauit, cum essetis mortui in offensis & peccatis: in quibus olim versati estis, vt esset vita mundi huius, secundum principem, cui potestas est aeris, & Spiritus nunc agentis in hominibus contumacibus. Inter quos & nos omnes olim conuersati sumus in cupiditatibus carnis nostrae, facientes quae carni ac cogitationibus libebant, eramusque natura filij irae, vt etiam reliqui. Ad quorum confirmationem faciunt, quae ad Roman. septimo Cap. de semetipso scribit, vbi legem peccati in membris suis inueniri queritur, & corpus suum corpus mortis vocat: nimirum vt demonstret peccatum in electis quoque adhuc locum habere, imo certamina subinde noua aduersus Spiritum instaurare, in quibus Dei gratia & auxilio peculiari opus fit. Quod si quis negare audeat, neque hoc in semetipso agnoscere velit, is aut Christum pro ipso mortuum esse, simul negabit, aut eius morte falsi contincetur. Euertit ergo locus iste non solum merita operum nostrorum, verumetiam vires nostras omnes. Quid enim faciat, aut facere possit mortuus? Ideo supra Cap. tertio, nos ne cogitare quidem aliquid posse dixit, tanquam ex nobis ipsis.
units.tr: First, let us consider what all people are, and what they are like, if we judge them by their own innate and natural condition. Paul says that all were dead, and this by God's decree, since God had said to Adam: "On the day you eat of the fruit of this tree, you will surely die." Adam ate, and having become a sinner and liable to death, he begot all his descendants in this same wretched and corrupt condition. So Paul writes to the Ephesians about all the Gentiles: "And you, when you were dead in trespasses and sins, in which you once walked, following the prince of the power of the air, the spirit now working in the sons of disobedience. Among them we also all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the wishes of the flesh and of the thoughts, and we were by nature children of wrath, as the others were." Passages from Romans 7, where he speaks of himself, support this: there he complains that he finds a law of sin in his members, and calls his body "the body of death." He does so to show that sin still has a place even in the elect, and indeed that they must again and again renew their struggles against the Spirit, in which the grace of God and his special help are needed. If anyone dares to deny this, and is unwilling to recognise it in himself, then he will at the same time deny that Christ died for him, or else he will be found to be false about that death. This passage therefore overturns not only the merits of our works but all our powers. For what can a dead man do, or what can he be able to do? That is why above, in chapter 3, he said that we are not even able to think anything of ourselves, as if from ourselves (2 Cor. 3:5).

units.la: Secundo loco, vnde nobis per peccatum mortuis vita obtingat, Paulus docet. Ex eo nimirum, qui pro nobis mortuus est & resurrexit. Est is Vnigenitus ille Dei Filius, qui ex Virgine Maria homo factus est, vt ea, quae ad humani generis redemptionem requirebantur, posset perficere. Is mortuus est, vt peccata nostra expiaret quae in ipsum Pater nostri misertus deriuarat, sicuti ab Isaia fuit praedictum. Ita vero simul Legem, cuius sententia ad mortem deposcebamur, eneruauit, & quod ex ea aduersus nos conscriptum erat chirographum aboleuit. Idem non mortuus modo est, verumetiam resurrexit ex mortuis, ut mortem vna cum eo, qui huius habebat imperium, destrueret, & nobis vitam restitueret. Verissimè ergo de semetipso pronuntiauit: Ego sum Resurrectio & Vita. Et haec quidem omnia Paulus gratuitae dilectioni tribuit, qua nos ille complexus est: quod ut rursus omnem nostri meriti aut dignitatis fiduciam euerti, ita nos in illo solo acquiescere docet, quando praeter eum nomen nullum sub caelo hominibus datum est, in quo nos seruari oporteat, &c. Act. 4. Cap.
units.tr: Second, Paul teaches from where life comes to us who are dead through sin: namely, from him who died and rose again for us. He is that only-begotten Son of God, who was made man of the Virgin Mary, so that he might accomplish what was required for the redemption of the human race. He died so that he might expiate our sins, which the Father of mercy had laid upon him, as Isaiah foretold. In this way he also annulled the Law, by whose sentence we were condemned to death, and abolished the certificate of debt that had been written against us by it (Col. 2:14). He did not only die, but also rose from the dead, so that he might destroy death, together with him who held its power, and restore life to us. Most truly, then, he said of himself: "I am the Resurrection and the Life" (John 11:25). Paul ascribes all these things to free love, by which he embraced us; and so that all confidence in our own merit or worth may be overturned, he teaches us to rest in him alone, since "there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved," etc. (Acts 4:12).

units.la: Tertiò, quod sit hominis Christiani officium, hoc loco admonemur: Ut qui viuunt, id est, qui vitae illius verae per ipsum participes facti sunt, non sibi ipsis, sed ei viuant. Ergo ad solos Christianos, qui vere credunt, doctrinae huius fructus debet restringi. Nam etiamsi Christus pro omnibus mortuus sit, omnes item ad se invitet, eiusque meritum omnibus seruandis sufficiat, non tamen omnes in eo vitam consequuntur, quia non omnes credunt: imò plerique hominum dum praua carnis desideria illius Verbo praeferunt, ipsimet sibi perditionis authores sunt. At qui illum per fidem amplexi, vitâ illam veram gustauerunt, si iam non amplius sibi ipsis viuunt, sed ei, cuius morte & resurrectione se redemptos esse credunt. Sibi ipsis autem viuunt, qui suae rationis dictata sequuntur, affectibus & desiderijs suis indulgent, neque aliquam habent vel voluntatis diuinae, vel iustitiae, aut receptae inter homines consuetudinis rationem. E contra Christo viuere dicuntur, qui se totos huic impendunt & consecrant, & in illo homines quoque amore fraterno & syncero complectuntur. Et hoc est Christiani hominis officiu, de quo in praesenti Paulus disserit, quodque negligere non possunt, quotquot exhibitum sibi in Christo aeternae salutis beneficium recte agnoscunt. Nam exigit hoc Lex naturae, & de eodem mos inter homines probos & honestos receptus nos admonet. Qui enim alicuius liberalitate ex vinculis aut triremi, ad quam damnati erant, redimuntur: ii se totos debent redemptori suo, & si huic ingrati sint, quouis supplicio digni esse iudicatur. Quid ergo nos IESV CHRISTO negare possumus, qui cum propter peccata nostra ad aeternos inferorum carceres damnati essemus, nos sanguinis sui pretio redimere dignatus est? Quis non ingratos, iniustos, iniquos, imò indignos quos terra ferat, dixerit eos, qui seipsos non illi totos consecrant? Tales certè ne hominum quidem nomine digni sunt, cum neque naturae legibus obtemperent, neque Dei & creaturarum, quas ille propter nos creauit, exemplo moueantur, ut suum faciant officium. Etenim Deus, cùm sibi ipsi sufficiat, neq; alicuius creaturae seruitio opus habeat, non tamen sibi soli viuit & regnat: sed quicquid habet bonorum, id omne in creaturas suas transfundit: & hominem ideo condidit, ut eum suae gratiae & bonitatis consortem faceret. Et si omnes huius mundi partes consideremus, vna cum brutis animalibus, nihil in his omnibus inuenies, quod non alicuius usui seruiat. Quis ergo hominem dixerit esse eum, qui omnibus aliis neglectis, & nulla beneficij per Christum sibi exhibiti ratione habita, sibi soli viuit, suisque modò desideriis indulget?
