In horum consideratione si omnes diligentius versarentur, nullius certè laboris & studij eos taederet in promouenda Dei gloria & aliorum salute.
units.tr: Third, here we are reminded what the duty of a Christian man is: that those who live, that is, those who have been made partakers of that true life through him, should live not to themselves but to him. Therefore the fruit of this teaching ought to be restricted to Christians alone, who truly believe. For even though Christ died for all, and invites all to himself, and his merit is sufficient to save all, yet not all obtain life in him, because not all believe; indeed, most men, while they prefer their evil desires of the flesh to his Word, become the authors of their own destruction. But those who have embraced him by faith and have tasted that true life, no longer live to themselves, but to him, by whose death and resurrection they believe they have been redeemed. Those live to themselves who follow the dictates of their own reason, indulge their passions and desires, and have no regard for the divine will, for justice, or for the custom accepted among men. On the other hand, those are said to live to Christ who devote and consecrate themselves wholly to him, and in him embrace men also with sincere brotherly love. This is the duty of the Christian man, of which Paul is speaking here, and which all who rightly recognise the benefit of eternal salvation offered to them in Christ cannot neglect. For the law of nature requires this, and the custom received among upright and honourable men reminds us of the same. For if someone is redeemed by another's generosity from chains or from the galley to which he had been condemned, he owes himself wholly to his redeemer, and if he proves ungrateful to him, he is judged worthy of any punishment. What then can we deny to Jesus Christ, who, when we were condemned to the eternal prisons of hell for our sins, deigned to redeem us by the price of his own blood? Who would not call ungrateful, unjust, unrighteous, indeed unworthy of the earth that bears them, those who do not consecrate themselves wholly to him? Such people are certainly not worthy even of the name of men, since they obey neither the laws of nature nor the example of God and of the creatures, which he made for our sake, so as to perform their duty. For God, although he is sufficient for himself and has no need of the service of any creature, nevertheless does not live and reign for himself alone, but pours out into his creatures all the good things he possesses; and he made man so that he might make him a partaker of his grace and goodness. And if we consider all the parts of this world, together with the brute animals, you will find nothing among all these things that does not serve some use. Who, then, would call a man one who, neglecting all others and taking no account of the benefit shown to him through Christ, lives to himself alone and merely indulges his own desires? If all people were to consider these things more carefully, they would certainly never grow weary of any labour or effort in promoting the glory of God and the salvation of others.

units.la: Quia vero homines Christiani, non sibi ipsis, sed soli Christo viuere debent, sequitur eos etiam errare, qui homines quoscunque ex carne, id est, ex ijs quae carnis iudicio magnifica sunt, metiuntur & aestimant, sic ut ab his potius quàm ab vno Christo pendeant. Erat hoc admodum vulgare apud Corinthios, adeò ut ex doctoribus suis quidâ denominari vellet, & nimia istorum admiratione decepti in diuersas sectas & factiones scinderentur. Et qui inter ipsos erant pseudoapostoli nō nisi titulis inanibus sese venditabant. Ergo quod modò dixit, nunc huic etiam vitio applicat, et ut ei medeatur, sic infert: Itaque nos posthac neminem nouimus secundum carnem, &c. Quasi diceret: Glorientur alij carne, quòd ex Iudaeis progeniti, quòd circumcisi, quòd Hierosolymae à germanis & praecipuis Apostolis instituti sint: nos tamen qui ab vno Christo pendemus, & huic soli viuere instituimus, non possumus ista magni facere, aut aliquem propter ea maioris aestimare. Faciunt ad huius loci explicationem, quae Paulus ad Philippen. scribit: Si quisquam alius videtur fiduciam habere in carne, ego magis habeo: Circumcisus octauo die, ex gete Israëlis, tribus Beniamin, Hebraeus ex Hebraeis, religione Pharisaeus: quòd ad zelû, perseguens Ecclesiâ: quòd ad iustitiâ quae est in Lege, irreprehensus. Sed quae mihi erat lucra, ea duxi propter Christi damnum esse, etc. Vide locum Phil.3.
units.tr: But because Christian men ought to live not to themselves but to Christ alone, it follows that those also are mistaken who measure and value men of every kind according to the flesh, that is, according to those things that are magnificent by the judgement of the flesh, so that they depend upon these rather than upon Christ alone. This was very common among the Corinthians, so that some wished to be named after their teachers, and, deceived by an excessive admiration for them, were split into various sects and factions. And the false apostles who were among them boasted of nothing but empty titles. So what he has just said, he now applies to this fault too, and to cure it he goes on: "Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh," etc. As if he were saying: let others glory in the flesh, because they are descended from Jews, because they were circumcised, because they were appointed at Jerusalem by the brethren and the chief apostles; but we, who depend on Christ alone and have resolved to live to him alone, cannot esteem these things highly, or value anyone more highly for them. To explain this passage, one may compare what Paul writes to the Philippians: "If anyone else thinks he has confidence in the flesh, I have more: circumcised on the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee in religion; as to zeal, persecuting the Church; as to the righteousness which is in the Law, blameless. But whatever gains I had, these I counted as loss for the sake of Christ," etc. See the passage, Phil. 3.

units.la: At hic apparet, quàm errent, qui hodie omnes ad Romanam sedem astringunt, vt & huic omnes animæ obtemperent, ex salutis necessitate esse aiunt: idq; propter successionem Apostolicam, qua Pontifices Romani superbiunt. Nam vt hanc illis demus, eadem tamen ex carne est: & non ex personis fides probatur, sed personas ex fide probari necesse est; ideoq; non personarum, sed doctrinæ & fidei successio in hac controversia spectari debet: quod olim Tertullianus quoq; monuit. Quis enim nescit, omnibus fere seculis nequissimos impostores fidei Dei seruis successisse? Christi certe tempore in Mosis cathedra sedebant Annas, Caiaphas, Alexander, & horum similes nō minus impij quàm inepti architecti, qui lapidem illum pretiosissimum reiecerunt, quem Deus vt caput anguli esset, destinauerat. Et quid obsecro successioni nudæ tribui debet, quando Paulus seipsum pro anathemate habere iubet, si aliud quid prædicet præter id, quod iam prædicatum erat? Galat. 1.
units.tr: But here it becomes clear how wrong those are who today bind everyone to the Roman see, and say that it is necessary for salvation that all souls obey it, and this on account of the Apostolic succession in which the Roman Pontiffs take such pride. For even if we grant them this succession, it is still of the flesh; and faith is not proved by persons, but persons must be proved by faith. Therefore in this controversy the succession to be considered should be not of persons but of doctrine and faith, as Tertullian long ago also warned. For who does not know that in almost every age the most wicked impostors have succeeded to the servants of God's faith? At the time of Christ, certainly, Annas, Caiaphas, Alexander and their like sat in the chair of Moses, no less impious than they were inept builders, who rejected that most precious stone which God had destined to be the head of the corner. And I ask, what should be granted to bare succession, when Paul bids himself be accursed if he preaches anything else than what had already been preached? Gal. 1.

units.la: Quoad verò huius loci argumentum, aduersarij Paulo ista dicenti, Christum obijciebant, qui ipse ex Iudæis natus, circumcisus, legi obnoxius & Iudaicæ gentis Apostolus fuisset. Illis ergo respondet, dicens: Quod si etiam nouimus Christum secundum carnem, nunc tamen non amplius nouimus. Sensus est: Nemo hic mihi Dominum & Seruatorem nostrum IESVM CHRISTVM obijciat, in quo eadem illa inueniantur, quibus æmuli mei seipsos vobis commendant. Nam olim quidem ista in illo agnouimus, & eadem tunc suum vsum habuerunt, quando ex æterno Patris decreto illum ex Dauidis stirpe verum hominem nasci, circumcidi & Legi subijci oportuit, vt noster vindex factus nos à Lege & maledictione, quæ nos premebat, liberaret. At nunc cùm omnia peregerit, quæcunq; in carne fieri oportuit, & iam moriturus eà omnia iam consummata esse testatus sit, carnem denique suam ex terris hisce in cœlos euexerit, illum non amplius ex carne æstimamus, sed ex eo, quòd æternus est Dei Filius, in quo omnis plenitudo Deitatis habitat corporaliter, qui vt nobis à Patre vindex & redemptor datus est, ita nunc pro nobis apud Patrem intercedit, fidelis Pontifex in omnibus quæ illic sunt agenda. Quare non in carnis eius præsentia, aut aliqua carnis prærogatiua hæremus, vt Iudæi (qui quia ex ipsis natus est, illum ad ipsos solos pertinere putant) sed animis per fidem supra cœlos euectis, eum ad dexteram Patris quærimus, vbi sedet Rex & Pontifex noster in æternum, &c. Hic loci huius sensus germanus & simplicissimus est, & ipsius Christi authoritate confirmatur, qui quoties aliqui in solam carnem eius intenti fuerunt, eos ad Ascensionem suam & Spiritum remisit. Capernaitæ certè trassum quid de carnis suæ manducatione cogitantibus, dixit: Quid igitur, si videritis Filium hominis ascendentem eò, vbi erat prius? Et in vltima Cœna discipulos, qui propter ipsius discessum mœrebant, consolaturus ait: Ne turbetur cor vestrum: creditis in Deum, etiam in me credite. In domo Patris mei mansiones multæ sunt, &c. Et ibidem: Rogabo Patrem, & alium consolatorem dabit vobis, vt maneat vobiscum in æternum: Nempe Spiritum illum Veritatis, &c. Rursus nunc vado ad eum, qui misit me, & nemo ex vobis interrogat me: Quò vadis? Sed quia hæc locutus sum vobis, tristitia impleuit cor vestrum. Sed ego veritatem dico vobis, expedit vobis, vt ego abeam: nam nisi abiero, Consolator ille non veniet ad vos, &c. Quibus addi potest, quòd quoties in ijs occupatus fuit Christus, quæ ex Patris cœlestis mandato pro hominum salute agenda erant, neq; matrem neq; fratres aut secundùm carnem sibi cognatos agnouit. Etenim cùm puer adhuc in templo doceret, & postlongam & solicitam inquisitionem illic inuento Virgo mater diceret: Fili, cur ita fecisti nobis? ecce pater tuus & ego cruciati quærebamus te: Respondit ille: Quid est quòd quærebatis me? an nesciebatis, quòd in ijs quæ Patris mei sunt, oportet me esse? Et in nuptijs de vini penuria à matre requisitus dicebat: Quid mihi tecum mulier? nondum venit hora mea. Quò etiam pertinet, quòd cùm docenti quidam dixisset: Ecce mater tua & fratres tui foris stant, quærentes tibi loqui: mox ei respondit: Quæ est mater mea, & qui sunt fratres mei? Et extensa manu in discipulos, dixit: Ecce mater mea, & fratres mei: Quisquis enim fecerit voluntatem Patris mei, qui est in cœlis, ipse meus frater, & soror, & mater est. Ex his omnibus Paulus à maiori ad minus argumentatur: Si ne Christus quidem ipse secundùm carnem spectari debet, quantò minus homines, qui toti nihil nisi caro sunt, priusquam Dei Spiritu innouantur?
units.tr: As for the argument of this passage, Paul's opponents, when he said these things, objected Christ to him, who himself was born of the Jews, circumcised, bound to the Law, and an apostle of the Jewish nation. To them, therefore, he replies, saying: "Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer." The sense is this: let no one object to me our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, in whom those same things are found by which my rivals commend themselves to you. For indeed we once recognised these things in him, and they then had their use, when by the eternal decree of the Father it was necessary that he be born a true man from the stock of David, be circumcised and be subject to the Law, so that, made our redeemer, he might free us from the Law and from the curse which pressed upon us. But now that he has accomplished all things that had to be done in the flesh, and has testified that all these things are now finished as he is about to die, and at last has lifted his flesh from this earth into heaven, we no longer judge him by the flesh, but by the fact that he is the eternal Son of God, in whom all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily, who, as he was given to us by the Father as deliverer and redeemer, so now intercedes for us with the Father, a faithful High Priest in all things that are to be done there. Therefore we do not cling to the presence of his flesh or to any prerogative of the flesh, as the Jews do (who, because he was born from among them, think he belongs to them alone), but with minds lifted above the heavens by faith we seek him at the right hand of the Father, where our King and High Priest sits for ever, etc. The true and simplest sense of this place is confirmed by the authority of Christ himself, who, whenever some were intent only on his flesh, sent them back to his Ascension and to the Spirit. Thus he said to the Capernaites, who were thinking crudely of eating his flesh: "What then, if you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before?" And in the last supper, wishing to console the disciples who grieved at his departure, he says: "Let not your heart be troubled; you believe in God, believe also in me. In my Father's house are many mansions," etc. And in the same place: "I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever," namely that Spirit of Truth, etc. "Again, now I go to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, Where are you going? But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart. But I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go away; for unless I go away, that Comforter will not come to you," etc. To these may be added that whenever Christ was occupied with the things that had to be done for the salvation of men by the command of the heavenly Father, he acknowledged neither mother nor brothers, nor those related to him according to the flesh. For when, as a boy, he was teaching in the temple, and after a long and anxious search the Virgin mother found him there and said, "Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in anguish," he answered: "Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in the things of my Father?" And at the wedding, when his mother asked him about the lack of wine, he said: "Woman, what is that to me and to you? My hour has not yet come." To this also belongs the fact that when someone said to him as he was teaching, "Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking to speak to you," he immediately answered: "Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?" And stretching out his hand towards his disciples, he said: "Behold my mother and my brothers. For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother." From all these things Paul argues from the greater to the lesser: if not even Christ himself is to be regarded according to the flesh, how much less men, who are wholly nothing but flesh until they are renewed by the Spirit of God?

units.la: Diligentius ista annotamus, quia olim quidam hoc loco abusi sunt, vt carnem Christi à diuinitate absorptam, & iam Deificatam esse euincerent. Quorum errorem, olim publica Ecclesia Catholicæ & Orthodoxæ authoritate damnatum, hodie instaurant, qui nobiscum de corporali carnis Christi præsentia & manducatione contendunt. At Paulus hic Christum carnem veram habere, nequaquam negat: sed à carnis præsentia & superstitiosa eius fiducia homines Christianos suo exemplo avocare vult, ut talem agnoscant, qualis nunc est, quoad regnum & officium suum. Fecit enim caro eius, quicquid in terris facere debuit. Nunc in cœlis habet quod agat, quibus illam capi oportet usq; ad diem restitutionis omnium. Ibi eius visus est, ut arrhæ loco nobis certam spem faciat, quod nos quoq; corporibus nostris illuc transferendi simus: quod tunc fiet, quando ipse in carne sua veniet ad iudicandum vivos & mortuos. Simul ergo confutatur hic crassus illorum error, qui carnem Christi corporaliter, realiter, substantialiter in Cœna præsens adesse, & in vel sub vel cum pane contrectari, & à dignis simul & indignis realiter & oraliter manducari docent. Accusant illi nos, quod Capernaitarum more crassum quid somniemus. At hoc ipsi faciunt, & simul aliis crassissimarum cogitationum authores sunt, dum illis non sufficit, si IESVM CHRISTVM, verum Deum & Hominem fide manducari dicamus, nisi eiusdem corpus vere & realiter manibus nostris contrectari, in os nostrum inseri, dentibus conteri, & vere atq; corporaliter deglutiri fateamur. At quis obsecro Cyclops aut Anthropophagus de suis epulis crassius & crudelius loqui poterat? Et qua fronte isti cum Paulo dicent: Quod si etiam novimus Christum secundum carnem, nunc tamen non amplius novimus? cum & meritum & Spiritus Christi, vnà cum fide & omnibus eius attributis illis nullius momenti esse videantur, nisi carnalem corporis eius præsentiam atq; manducationem cum illis confitearis?
units.tr: We note these things more carefully because some men once abused this passage to prove that the flesh of Christ had been absorbed into the divinity and was now deified. Their error, long ago condemned by the public authority of the Catholic and Orthodox Church, is today revived by those who contend with us about the bodily presence and eating of the flesh of Christ. But Paul here does not at all deny that Christ has true flesh; rather, by his own example he wishes to call Christian people away from the presence of the flesh and from superstitious trust in it, so that they may acknowledge him as he now is, as to his kingdom and office. For his flesh has done whatever it was to do on earth. Now it has in heaven what it has to do, where it must be held until the day of the restoration of all things. There his flesh is seen, so that, as a pledge, it gives us a certain hope that we too are to be transferred thither in our bodies; which will happen when he himself comes in his flesh to judge the living and the dead. At the same time, therefore, that crude error of those is refuted who teach that the flesh of Christ is present in the Supper corporeally, really and substantially, and is handled in, under or with the bread, and is really and orally eaten by both worthy and unworthy. They accuse us of dreaming something crude in the manner of the Capernaites. Yet they themselves do this, and at the same time are the authors of very gross thoughts to others, since it is not enough for them that we say Jesus Christ, true God and Man, is eaten by faith, unless we also confess that his body is truly and really handled by our hands, put into our mouth, ground by our teeth, and truly and bodily swallowed. But who, I ask, could speak more crudely and cruelly of his feasts than a Cyclops or a man-eater? And with what face will they say with Paul, "Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer," when the merit and Spirit of Christ, together with faith and all its attributes, seem to them of no account unless you confess with them his carnal presence in the body and his eating?

units.la: Sed audiamus huius loci conclusionem: Si quis igitur est in Christo, nova creatura est. In Christo esse dicuntur, qui ei per fidem insiti, & proinde veri & germani Christiani sunt. Et sensus est: Christianum hominem ex nulla carnis prærogatiua, sed ex regenerationis & innovationis effectu æstimari debere. Idem ergo hic dicit, quod ad Galatas: In CHRISTO IESV neq; Circumcisio quicquam valet, neq; præputium, sed nova Creatura. Unde autem hæc obtingit, aut ex quibus signis agnoscitur? Hoc idem ille in eadem epistola docet his verbis: In Christo neq; Circumcisio quicquam valet, neq; præputium, sed fides per charitatem agens. Ita vero vocat fidem veram & viuam, ut hanc à mortua distinguat, de qua Iacobus loquitur, quando nos non sola fide iustificari scribit. Quia vero quod in præsenti dicit, ijs qui adhuc à Lege toti pendebant, durum videri poterat, rationis loco subijcit: Vetera præterierunt, ecce nova facta sunt omnia. Quasi diceret: Nemo mihi veteres ritus & multorum sæculorum præscriptione confirmatum cultum obijciat. Scitis enim, Nouum testamentum olim per Ieremiam promissum fuisse. Hoc Christus in sanguine suo nobis monstrauit, cum in Cœna mystica solennem suæ mortis memoriam instituisset: & ideo iam moriturus dicebat: Consummatum est. Et mox spiritum suum Deo Patri reddens, velum templi totum disrupit. Sunt ergo abrogata iam vetera illa, quæ hucusq; tam magnifica visa sunt, & Dominus per suæ mortis meritum nouam atq; veteri præstantiorem cultus diuini faciem induxit, simulq; impleuit omnia, quæ olim sub typis & figuris illis adumbrabantur. Opus ergo est, ut reliquis veteribus istis, ei posthac in Spiritus nouitate seruiamus.
units.tr: But let us hear the conclusion of this passage: "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation." Those are said to be in Christ who have been grafted into him by faith and are therefore true and genuine Christians. And the sense is this: a Christian man must be judged not by any prerogative of the flesh, but by the effect of regeneration and renewal. Here he therefore says the same thing as to the Galatians: "In Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creature." But whence does this come, or from what signs is it recognised? The same man teaches this in the same letter in these words: "In Christ neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love." He calls faith true and living in such a way as to distinguish it from dead faith, of which James speaks when he writes that we are justified not by faith alone. But because what he says at present might seem hard to those who still wholly depended on the Law, he adds a reason: "The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new." As if he said: let no one object to me the old rites and a worship confirmed by the prescription of many centuries. For you know that the New Testament was promised long ago through Jeremiah. Christ showed this to us in his own blood, when in the mystical Supper he instituted the solemn memorial of his death; and therefore, as he was about to die, he said: "It is finished." And soon, giving up his spirit to God the Father, he tore the whole veil of the temple. Those old things, which until now have seemed so magnificent, are therefore now abrogated, and the Lord, through the merit of his death, has introduced a new face of divine worship, more excellent than the old, and at the same time has fulfilled all those things which were once foreshadowed under those types and figures. It is therefore necessary that, leaving those other old things, we serve him henceforth in the newness of the Spirit.

units.la: Debet hinc generalis doctrina peti: nihil esse inter omnia externa, quæ carni magnifica & præclara videntur, cuius aliqua sit in æternæ salutis utilitas, nisi Spiritu Christi innouemur. Nam (ut paulo ante diximus) veri Christiani sunt, qui illi sunt insiti. Quotquot ergo extra Christum vagantur, & circa quascunq; alias res occupantur, ij Christiani non sunt. At qui in Christo sunt, ijdem nova Creatura sunt. Nec enim convenire possunt inter se Caro & Spiritus, ut alibi Paulus ait. Manent quidem in electis reliquiæ carnis & peccati, ex quibus pugna illa exoritur, de qua ad Rom. 7. Cap. legimus. Sed non in ea succumbunt credentes, sed ius suum in illis Spiritus obtinet. Quod si vero vetera illa aboleri oportuit, quæ stultitia, vel potius dementia esset, in eorum locum substituere superstitiosorum hominum figmenta? In huius ergo loci meditatione diligenti nos assiduè exerceamus, & in uno IESV CHRISTO collocata omni salutis nostræ fiducia, eidem uni viuamus, ut ipse in nobis regnet & triumphet: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: From this a general doctrine should be drawn: among all the external things that seem splendid and admirable to the flesh, there is none that is of any use for eternal salvation, unless we are renewed by the Spirit of Christ. For (as we said a little earlier) those are true Christians who are engrafted into him. Therefore, all who wander outside Christ and busy themselves with other things are not Christians. But those who are in Christ are a new creature. For, as Paul says elsewhere, flesh and Spirit cannot agree with one another. Indeed, remnants of the flesh and of sin remain in the elect, and from these arises that struggle which we read about in Romans chapter 7. But believers do not yield to it; the Spirit maintains its right over them. But if those old things had to be abolished, what folly, or rather madness, would it be to substitute in their place the inventions of superstitious men? Let us therefore exercise ourselves diligently in meditating on this passage, and, with all confidence of our salvation placed in Jesus Christ alone, let us live to him alone, so that he may reign and triumph in us, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXIV.

units.la: Hæc autem omnia sunt ex Deo: qui reconciliauit nos sibi per IESVM CHRISTVM, deditq; nobis ministerium reconciliationis. Etenim Deus erat in Christo, mundum reconcilians sibi, non imputando eis peccata ipsorum: posuitq; in nobis sermonem reconciliationis huius. Itaq; nomine Christi legatione fungimur, velut Deo precante per nos, oramus Christi nomine: Reconciliamini Deo. Fecit enim eum qui non norat peccatum, pro nobis peccatum, vt nos efficeremur iustitia Dei in eo.
units.tr: Now all these things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation. For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not counting their sins against them, and he has placed in us the word of this reconciliation. So we serve as ambassadors in the name of Christ, as though God were pleading through us; we beg you in Christ's name, be reconciled to God. For he made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

units.la: Vt quemadmodum Deus miseris mortalibus per Euangelij prædicationem omnes gratiæ suæ thesauros atq; plenam salutem offert: ita ab eius gratia & salute excidunt, qui Euangelium audire dedignantur. Ideo Paulus in ijs, quæ proximè præcesserunt, ministerij sui rationem sic reddidit, vt simul summam doctrinæ Euangelicæ & totius religionis Christianæ complexus sit, quæ est: Homines, qui natura peccatores & filij iræ sunt, per IESV CHRISTI meritum redemptos, & eiusdem Spiritu innouatos esse: & propterea illos huic vni viuere, omnibus autem alijs, quæ mundo magnifica videntur, renuntiare debere, vt omnis salutis nostræ gloria vni Christo transcribatur. Quia autem illic quædam obscurius dicta videri poterant, eadem in præsenti illustrat, & duo tradit, quæ in toto hoc negotio obseruatu & cognitu quàm maximè necessaria sunt. Primum, qua ratione Deus homines sibi reconciliarit. Alterum, vt nos reconciliationis istius participes efficiamur. Est ergo locus hic vnus ex præcipuis, qui in Scripturis habentur: vt qui summam eius doctrinæ continet, quæ in Ecclesia perpetuò debet retineri. Quapropter non pigeat singulas illius partes diligentius inspicere.
units.tr: Just as God offers miserable mortals, through the preaching of the Gospel, all the treasures of his grace and full salvation, so those who disdain to hear the Gospel fall away from his grace and salvation. That is why Paul, in the passages immediately preceding, gave an account of his ministry in such a way that he also embraced in brief the sum of the Gospel teaching and of the whole Christian religion. That sum is this: men, who by nature are sinners and children of wrath, have been redeemed through the merit of Jesus Christ and renewed by his Spirit; and therefore they ought to live to him alone, and renounce all those things which seem splendid to the world, so that the whole glory of our salvation may be ascribed to Christ alone. But since some things there might seem more obscurely stated, he now clarifies them, and sets out two points which are most necessary to observe and know in this whole matter. First, by what method God reconciled men to himself. Second, how we are made partakers of this reconciliation. This passage, then, is one of the principal ones contained in the Scriptures, since it holds the sum of that teaching which must always be retained in the Church. Therefore let us not hesitate to examine each of its parts more carefully.

units.la: Principio præsentem locum cum ijs, quæ præcesserunt, connectens, summam omnium, quæ diGurus est, præmittit. Ea est, Deum homines sibi reconciliauisse per Filium suum IESVM CHRISTVM, beneficium verò hoc nobis offerre per Apostolorum ministerium, qui Euangelium in toto orbe terrarum prædicare debeant. Id verò sic enuntiat: Hæc autem omnia sunt ex Deo, qui reconciliauit nos sibi, &c. Omnia ex Deo esse ait, quod in genere verum est, & de omnibus intelligi potest, quæ in cælo & in terris siue sunt, siue fiunt. Nam & omnia condidit Deus, & idem omnia gubernat, & demittit (vt Psaltes canit) vt videat quæcunque in cælo & in terra sunt. Sed in præsenti de ijs agitur, quæ ad humanæ redemptionis atque salutis negotium pertinent, de quibus hucusq; dixerat: Christum videlicet pro nobis mortuum, nosq; in illo nouam Creaturam factos esse, & ideo nos huic vni viuere, atque procul relictis omnibus, quæ caro admiratur, in hoc vnum intentos esse debere, vt nos verè per illum innouatos esse vniuersa vita nostra testemur. Hæc (inquit) omnia ex Deo sunt, qui nos infelices sibi per Christum reconciliare dignatus est, nobis autem Apostolis ministerium reconciliationis istius commisit.
units.tr: At the outset, connecting this passage with what has gone before, he sets down a summary of everything he is about to say. It is this: God has reconciled men to himself through his Son Jesus Christ, and offers this benefit to us through the ministry of the Apostles, who ought to preach the Gospel throughout the whole world. He expresses it thus: Now all these things are from God, who reconciled us to himself, etc. He says that all things are from God, which is true in general and can be understood of all things that are or come to pass in heaven and on earth. For God created all things, and he also governs all things, and, as the Psalmist sings, he looks down to see whatever is in heaven and on earth. But here he is speaking of those things which pertain to the business of human redemption and salvation, of which he had spoken up to this point: namely, that Christ died for us, and that in him we have been made a new creature, and therefore that we ought to live to him alone, and, having left aside all those things which the flesh admires, to be intent on this one thing, so that we bear witness by our whole life that we have truly been renewed through him. All these things (he says) are from God, who has deigned to reconcile us wretched men to himself through Christ, and has committed to us Apostles the ministry of this reconciliation.

units.la: Obseruabis autem hoc loco diligenter, authorem omnium, quæ ad nostram salutem faciunt, vnum Deum nobis monstrari, idq; abjq; omni conditione, quæ vel tantillum nobis tribuat. Si enim nos spectes, nihil quàm vitiositatem totius nostræ naturæ extremam & prorsus deploratam inuenies. In peccato concipimur & nascimur. Ad bonum vires in nobis nullæ sunt, ne ad cogitandum quidem. Accedunt quotidiani lapsus, & omnis generis delicta, quibus recensendis nemo sufficiat; nos autem illa perpetuò clamare cogunt cum filio prodigo: Pater, peccaui in cælum & in te, neque sum dignus, qui posthac filius tuus dicar. Item: Ne ingrediaris Domine in iudicium cum seruo tuo: Si enim transgressiones nostras obseruES, quis consistet? Quòd ergo vnigenitus ille Dei Filius, IESVS CHRISTVS, in mundum venit, quòd idem ille hominem verum induit, quòd pro nobis in cruce mortuus mundi peccata expiauit, quòd in eo noua creatura, id est, ex peccatoribus iusti, ex filijs iræ filij dilecti, ex abdicatis regni cælestis hæredes, ex carnalibus spirituales facti sumus: quòd item ministri aut præcones Verbi dantur, qui hæc tanta bona nobis annuntient: id omne ex Deo est, qui ita dilexit mundum, vt Filium suum Vnigenitum traderet, vt omnis qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Sufficit hoc confutandis omnibus, qui suis viribus aut meritis aliquid tribuunt. Potest enim singulis dici: Ex Deo est illud omne quo gloriamini. Quid habes, quod non accepisti? quod si accepisti, quid gloriaris, quasi non acceperis? Et hanc quidem doctrinam sacrae literae passim inculcant, ut, sic fiat necesse est, ut certa nobis esse possit salutis per Christum partae fiducia. Nisi enim gratuita dilectionis & misericordiae Dei fundamento nitamur, non possumus non fluctuare, cum in nobis nihil omnino sit, in quo confidere possimus. Simul etiam nos officii nostri hac doctrina admonet: Ut nimirum omnia nostra ad unum Deum referamus, & (ut initio monuimus) illi uni viuamus, ut ipse in nobis glorificetur. Itaque turpissime falluntur, qui ex gratia Dei praedicatione licentiam praetextum venantur. Quia autem duo his verbis propositus Apostolus, utrumque diligentius explicat.
units.tr: Here you will carefully observe that the one God is shown to us as the author of all those things which contribute to our salvation, and that without any condition which would grant us even the smallest thing. For if you look at ourselves, you will find nothing but the utmost wickedness of our whole nature, and altogether desperate. We are conceived and born in sin. There are no powers in us toward good, not even to think. Daily lapses are added, and every kind of offence, which no one could sufficiently enumerate; and these things compel us to cry out continually with the prodigal son: Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you, and I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Likewise: Enter not into judgement, Lord, with your servant; for if you should mark our transgressions, who could stand? Therefore, that the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, came into the world; that he likewise put on true man; that he died on the cross for us and expiated the sins of the world; that in him we have become a new creature, that is, from sinners, righteous; from children of wrath, beloved children; from those cast out of the heavenly kingdom, heirs; from carnal, spiritual: that likewise ministers or heralds of the Word are given to announce these great blessings to us: all this is from God, who so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. This is enough to refute all who ascribe something to their own strength or merits. For it can be said to each one: All that you boast of is from God. What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it? Holy Scripture everywhere inculcates this doctrine, and it must be so, in order that we may have a sure confidence of salvation obtained through Christ. For unless we rest upon the foundation of the free love and mercy of God, we cannot help but waver, since there is absolutely nothing in us in which we could trust. This doctrine also reminds us of our duty: namely, that we refer all our things to the one God, and (as we noted at the beginning) live to him alone, so that he may be glorified in us. Therefore those are most shamefully deceived who seek a pretext for licence from the preaching of God's grace. But since the Apostle, in these words, set out two things, he explains each of them more carefully.

units.la: Primum est, quomodo nos Deus sibi reconciliarit in Christo. In eo enim fere offendit caro, dum non potest videre, quomodo unus Christus tantae rei sufficiat, ut nimirum per ipsum solum omnes omnium gentium & aetatum homines Deo reconcilientur. Dicit ergo: Etenim Deus erat in Christo, mundum reconcilians sibi, non imputando eis peccata ipsorum, &c. Deus (inquit) erat in Christo, non quidem communi modo ratione, qua in omnibus creatis est & agit, sed ea, quam ipse Apostolus in epistola ad Colossenses exprimit, quando omnem plenitudinem Deitatis in ipso habitare dicit σωματικῶς vel corporaliter, id est, vere & essentialiter, ut qui non homo solum sit, verumetiam Deus, eiusdem cum Patre substantiae, potestatis & dignitatis: quod ipsemet testatur, dicens: Ego & Pater unum sumus. Philippe, qui me videt, Patrem videt. Item: Non credis, quod ego in Patre sum, & Pater in me est? Ad ista ergo respiciens Paulus, in praesenti scribit: Etenim Deus erat in Christo: hoc nimirum volens dicere: Nemo miretur, nos in hac causa tam graui solius Christi meminisse, per quem Deo reconciliati sumus, neque huius vilis & ignobilis speciei, quam in carne sustinuit, aliquem offendat, ut eum tanto negotio solum sufficere non posse arbitretur. Nam hic ipse qui ex pauperrima Virgine Maria Bethlehemi in stabulo verus homo natus est, qui item in extrema egestate educatus esuriuit, sitiuit, alsit, & post infinitos labores, opprobria & convitia, diram atque infamem mortem in ara crucis subiit: is (inquam) verus & germanus Dei Filius est, Patri consubstantialis & coaeternus, ideoque verus ille Immanuel est, de quo olim Isaias vaticinatus fuit, & proinde tantae rei potuit sufficere. Nec temere hoc argumento Paulus utitur, qui Christum eodem usum fuisse sciebat, quando se bonum illum & fortem pastorem esse probare voluit, qui oues suas aduersus omnes insidias atque pericula possit seruare. Ego (inquit) do vitam ouibus meis, nec peribunt in aeternum, neque rapiet eas quisquam e manu mea: Pater meus, qui eas dedit mihi, maior omnibus est, nec quisquam potest eas rapere e manu Patris mei: Ego & Pater unum sumus. Ioan.10.
units.tr: The first is how God reconciled us to himself in Christ. For the flesh is largely offended here, since it cannot see how the one Christ is sufficient for so great a matter, namely that through him alone all men of all nations and ages should be reconciled to God. He therefore says: For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not counting their sins against them, etc. God (he says) was in Christ, not indeed in the common manner by which he is present in and acts upon all created things, but in that manner which the Apostle himself expresses in the epistle to the Colossians, when he says that all the fullness of the Godhead dwells in him bodily [σωματικῶς], that is, truly and essentially, so that he is not only man but also God, of the same substance, power and dignity as the Father; which he himself testifies, saying: I and the Father are one. Philip, he who sees me sees the Father. Likewise: Do you not believe that I am in the Father, and the Father in me? Looking to these things, Paul writes in the present passage: For God was in Christ. He clearly wishes to say this: let no one wonder that in so grave a matter we remember Christ alone, through whom we have been reconciled to God; nor let anyone be offended by the lowly and ignoble appearance which he bore in the flesh, so as to think that he cannot alone suffice for such a great business. For this very one, who was born as true man from the most poor Virgin Mary in a stable at Bethlehem, who was also reared in extreme want and hungered, thirsted and shivered, and after endless labours, reproaches and insults, underwent a dreadful and infamous death on the altar of the cross: he (I say) is the true and genuine Son of God, consubstantial and coeternal with the Father, and therefore is that true Immanuel of whom Isaiah long ago prophesied, and so could suffice for so great a matter. Nor does Paul use this argument rashly, since he knew that Christ had used the same, when he wished to prove that he was that good and strong shepherd who can preserve his sheep against all snares and dangers. I (he says) give life to my sheep, and they shall never perish, nor shall anyone snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who gave them to me, is greater than all, and no one can snatch them out of my Father's hand. I and the Father are one. John 10.

units.la: Discimus itaque ex hoc Pauli loco, Mediatorem reconciliationis eius, qua nos in gratiam Deus recepit, esse unum IESVM CHRISTVM, de quo ipse Pater olim per Isaiam pronuntiauit: Ecce seruus meus, quo nitar: electus meus, quo placatur anima mea. Et haec ipsa verba caelitus postea bis intonuit, ἀεκτικῶς de illo dicens: Hic est Filius ille meus dilectus, in quo placatus sum. Vere igitur ipse discipulis dixit: Ego sum Via, & Veritas, & Vita: nemo venit ad Patrem, nisi per me. Et Paulus ad Timotheum: Unus Deus, unus Mediator Dei & hominum, homo CHRISTVS IESVS. Quibus consentit Apostolicum illud axioma, quod coram Senatu Hierosolymitano publice simul omnes protestati sunt, non esse aliud nomen sub caelo inter homines datum, in quo nos seruari oporteat. Sunt loci isti diligenter obseruandi propter eos, qui gloriam, quae uni Christo debetur, in Diuos partiuntur, & eadem opera multos ab illo abducunt. At si Christus reconciliationis istius Mediator esse non poterat, nisi Deus esset verus & Patri coessentialis, nunquam ei aliqui per nos aequari poterunt, nisi eos quoq; Deos faciamus. Ita vero in principium fidei & religionis peccabimus, quod est: Audi Israel, Dominus Deus tuus, Deus unus est. Item: Etsi multi sint qui dicantur Dij, & in caelo & in terra: nobis tamen unus est Deus, Pater ille, ex quo omnia, & nos in ipso: & unus Dominus IESVS CHRISTVS, per quem omnia, & nos per ipsum. 1.Corinth.8.
units.tr: We learn therefore from this passage of Paul that the Mediator of that reconciliation, by which God has received us into favour, is the one Jesus Christ, of whom the Father himself long ago declared through Isaiah: "Behold my servant, in whom I lean; my chosen, in whom my soul is well pleased." And these same words he afterwards twice thundered from heaven, speaking of him [ἀεκτικῶς]: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Truly, then, he himself said to the disciples: "I am the Way, and the Truth, and the Life: no one comes to the Father except through me." And Paul to Timothy: "There is one God, and one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." To these agrees that apostolic axiom, which all the apostles together publicly declared before the Senate at Jerusalem: that there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved. These passages must be carefully observed because of those who divide the glory due to Christ alone among the saints, and by the same act draw many away from him. But if Christ could not be the Mediator of this reconciliation unless he were true God and co-essential with the Father, then others can never be made equal to him by us, unless we make them gods as well. Yet in doing so we would sin against the very foundation of faith and religion, which is: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one God." Likewise: "Although there are many who are called gods, both in heaven and on earth, yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we in him, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him." 1 Cor. 8.

units.la: Porro modum quoque reconciliationis cum Deo Paulus exprimit, dicens: Non imputans eis peccata: nimirum propter Christum, qui illa suae mortis merito expiauit. Rursus ergo totum mundum peccati arguit, simul autem eos consolatur, qui quòd se peccatores esse sentiunt, de reconciliatione cum Deo dubitant. Docet ergo hanc non in aliqua satisfactione nostra consistere, sed in eo, quòd nobis Deus peccata porrò non imputet, quae Filius suus dilectus in se transtulit, & pro ijsdem in ara crucis satisfecit. Est vero hoc nobis plus quàm necessarium, ne peccata nobis imputet Deus. Quia vbi peccatum, ibi ira Dei & mors. Cùm autem nemo mortalium illa expiare, aut pro suis delictis ipse satisfacere possit, vt ea ex gratia remittantur, & nobis non imputentur necesse est. Neque noua videri debet cuiquam doctrina ista, quando in ea omnes Scripturae tam Veteris quàm Noui testamenti consentiunt. Prima etenim promissiones salutem nō in aliquo hominum opere, sed in solo semine illo benedicto monstrant, quod suo tempore nasciturum sit. In Lege vero etsi sacrificia pro peccatis plurima fuerunt instituta, ipse tamen sacrificandi ritus illos de eo admonebat, quod hic Paulus docet. Sistebatur victima ad altare. Imponebat illi manus is, qui eam adduxerat, vel sacrificulus illius nomine. Inde mactabatur, & spargebatur sanguis ad cornua altaris, vel etiam versus velum Sancti sanctorum. Innuebat autem manuum impositio, peccata in eum transferri, cuius typus erat victima illa, & proinde non imputari amplius ijs, qui ea designauissent. Et Nathan cum Dauidem audiuisset ex animo dicentem, Peccaui Domino: mox respondebat: Dominus transtulit peccatum tuum. Sed & ipse Dauid docere volens, in quo vera hominis beatitas consistat, sic canit: Beatus is est, qui exoneratus est transgressione, & cuius peccatum tectum est: Beatus homo, cui Dominus iniquitatem non imputat. Quibus consentit, quod Deus ipse per Isaiam prò-nuntiauit: Ego ego ille ipse sum, qui deleo transgressiones tuas, idq; propter me, & peccatorum tuorum non recordabor. Et rursus: Ego delebo transgressiones tuas vt densas nebulas, & vt nubè peccata tua. Quibus addi debet parabola creditoris & debitoris, quam Christus in Euangelio in hac causa proposuit: & quod nos omnes ex eius mandato precamur: Remitte nobis debita nostra, &c. Et haec quidem sufficiunt contra ambitiosum illud commentum de satisfactionibus hominum, quas primitiua Ecclesia aliquot seculis ignorauit, & vtinam hodie adhuc ignorarentur.
units.tr: Further, Paul also sets out the manner of reconciliation with God, saying: "not counting their sins against them": that is, on account of Christ, who expiated those sins by the merit of his death. Thus again he convicts the whole world of sin, and at the same time he comforts those who, because they feel themselves to be sinners, doubt their reconciliation with God. He teaches, therefore, that this reconciliation does not consist in any satisfaction of ours, but in this, that God no longer imputes to us the sins which his beloved Son took upon himself and for which he made satisfaction on the altar of the cross. Indeed, it is more than necessary for us that God not impute our sins to us. For where sin is, there are the wrath and death of God. Since, however, no mortal can atone for those sins, or make satisfaction for his own offences, it is necessary that they be remitted by grace and not imputed to us. Nor should this doctrine seem new to anyone, since all the Scriptures of both the Old and the New Testament agree in it. For the first promises show that salvation lies not in any work of men but in that blessed seed alone, which was to be born in its appointed time. In the Law, indeed, although many sacrifices for sins were instituted, the very rites of sacrificing nevertheless reminded of that which Paul here teaches. The victim was set before the altar. The one who had brought it, or its priest in his name, laid his hands upon it. Then it was slain, and the blood was sprinkled on the horns of the altar, or even towards the veil of the Holy of Holies. The laying on of hands signified that sins were transferred to him whose type that victim was, and therefore were no longer imputed to those who had offered it. And when Nathan heard David saying from the heart, "I have sinned against the Lord," he at once replied: "The Lord has transferred your sin." And David himself, wishing to teach in what the true blessedness of man consists, sings thus: "Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute iniquity." With these agrees what God himself declared through Isaiah: "I, I am he who blots out your transgressions, and that for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins." And again: "I will blot out your transgressions like a thick cloud, and your sins like a mist." To these should be added the parable of the creditor and the debtor, which Christ proposed in the Gospel on this matter, and that prayer which we all offer at his command: "Forgive us our debts," and so on. These things are enough against that ambitious fiction of human satisfactions, which the primitive Church was ignorant of for several centuries, and would that they were still unknown today.

units.la: Accedamus nunc ad alterum huius loci caput, quo vt nos reconciliationis istius cum Deo participes efficiamur, Apostolus docet. Pertinet ad hoc, quod in propositione dixit: Dedit nobis ministerium reconciliationis. Id vero nunc exponens, ait: Posuit in nobis sermonem siue verbum reconciliationis huius. Ita vero dicit Euangelium, quia per hoc praedicatur, Deum nobis tum in gratiam redijsse. Itaq; sensus est: Deus, qui mundum sibi reconciliauit in CHRISTO IESV, is nobis Apostolis hoc in mandatis dedit, vt faustum illud laetumq; gratuitae reconciliationis nuntiū omnibus gentibus praedicemus, & sic hoc tā salutari beneficio fruantur omnes, qui Euangelium audiunt, & audito credunt. Facit ergo ad huius loci explicationem, quod Dominus discipulis dixit: Ita oportuit Christum pati & resurgere a mortuis tertio die, & praedicari in eius nomine resipiscentiam ac remissionem peccatorum in omnes gentes. Item: Profecti in vniuersum orbem praedicate Euangelium omni creaturae: Qui crediderit, & baptizatus fuerit, saluabitur: qui vero non crediderit, condemnabitur. Luc.24. Marc.16.
units.tr: Let us now come to the second part of this passage, by which Paul teaches that we are made partakers of this reconciliation with God. To this belongs what he said in his proposition: "He has given us the ministry of reconciliation." Now explaining this, he says: "He has placed in us the word or message of this reconciliation." The Gospel is called this because through it is proclaimed that God has returned us into favour. The sense, therefore, is this: God, who reconciled the world to himself in Christ Jesus, has given us apostles this charge, that we should proclaim to all nations that joyful and glad message of free reconciliation, and so all who hear the Gospel, and believing it, may enjoy this so salutary benefit. What the Lord said to the disciples therefore serves to explain this passage: "Thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name to all nations." Likewise: "Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned." Luke 24; Mark 16.

units.la: Itaq; Euangelij praedicatio legitimum illud & ordinarium medium est, per quod gratia Dei & tota salus, quae Christi merito quaesita & parta est, nobis applicatur. Hinc est, quòd Apostoli peccata remittere & seruare dicuntur: non quòd id in ipsorum sit arbitrio & potestate, sed quòd Euangelium praedicant, quo gratuita peccatorum remissio omnibus credentibus offertur, quodque Dei potentia est ad salutem omni credenti. Hae etiam claues sunt, quibus Ecclesiarum ministri credentibus caelos referant, incredulis autem & poenitere nescijs eosdem claudunt. Euangelio subseruiunt Sacramenta, quasi appendices & sigilla promissionum salutis, quae in illo proponuntur. In istis ergo sese exercere debent Ecclesiarum ministri, vt nimirum in Euangelij praedicatione fideles sint, & salutare illud reconciliationis nostrae cum Deo mysterium omnibus diligenter commendent, inq; eius fide quosuis, quantum in ipsis est, confirment, curent denique ne qui nouam rebellionem faciant, dum abnegata fide & calcato per Christum ipsis exhibito salutis aeternae beneficio, ad diaboli castra redeunt.
units.tr: Accordingly, the preaching of the Gospel is the lawful and ordinary means by which the grace of God and the whole salvation, which was obtained and procured by the merit of Christ, is applied to us. Hence it is that the apostles are said to remit and to retain sins: not because this lies in their own power and authority, but because they preach the Gospel, in which the free remission of sins is offered to all who believe, and which is the power of God unto salvation for everyone who believes. These are also the keys by which the ministers of the churches open heaven to believers, but shut it to unbelievers and to those who know not how to repent. The sacraments serve the Gospel, as appendages and seals of the promises of salvation which are set forth in it. Therefore the ministers of the churches ought to devote themselves to these things: that they be faithful in preaching the Gospel, diligently commend to all that saving mystery of our reconciliation with God, confirm as far as they can everyone in faith in it, and finally take care that no one commits a new rebellion, by renouncing the faith and trampling underfoot the benefit of eternal salvation offered through Christ, and returns to the camp of the devil.

units.la: Sunt haec diligenter obseruanda propter Romanos Pontifices, quorum immoderata potentia
units.tr: These things must be carefully observed because of the Roman Pontiffs, whose immoderate power

units.la: nidem. atque tyrannis huius loci authoritate validissime confutatur, imo funditus euersa ruit. Primo enim, cum Paulus ministerium reconciliationis Apostolis commissum esse dicat, illi imperium & dominium in Ecclesia sibi vendicant, & se Christi vicarios esse dicunt, quibus perinde ut huic data sit omnis potestas in coelo & in terra. Quod Paulum III I. nostro tempore aperte dixisse, cum aliquando ad eius mensam Monachi duo de Pontificia potestate ineptius disputarent, ex viro illustri audiui, qui tunc praesens adfuerat. Ea autem confidentia ijdem elati, diuina & humana turbant, & (quod Daniel fore praedixit) leges & tempora mutant, & mille modis, quibus per Christum parta salus nobis applicetur, a Magorum & incantatorum praestigijs non multum differentes, excogitarunt. Nam quod de Claudibus Christus dixit, illi ad Confessionem auricularem & absolutionem priuatam transtulerunt, quam susurro quasi Magico obmurmurant ijs, qui ad ipsorum genua procidunt. Deinde ex Coena Domini mystica Missam fabricarunt, quae tota susurris & cantu a nemine intelligo, atque gesticulationibus theatricis constat: & per hanc meritum Christi & salutem omnem, non viuentibus modo, qui illam spectant, verumetiam mortuis applicari fabulantur. Pugnat hoc cum vsu Coenae ordinario, qui est, ut commemoratio fit mortis Domini, & per hanc nobis acquisitae salutis sigillum. Fatemur quidem Sacramenta Euangelij appendices esse, sed eadem si absque illo considerentur, nihil sunt, & sine fide sumpta non quicquam prosunt. Accessit his Indulgentiarum mercatura, quas graui plumbo munitas, ceu amuleta quaedam, hominibus superstitiosis vendiderunt. Enata ex his est peregrinationum superstitio & reliquiarum cultus: quibus omnibus, si ieiunia, vota monastica, cucullas, cilicia, conductitias preculas, campanarum pulsum, suffitus, oleum, sputum, salem, rosaria, & quaecunque alia sunt huius generis adnumeres: mox videbis quam parum fidi sint in domo Domini dispensatores, qui eius familiam tot fructuum laboribus atque impensis inutilibus grauarunt. Quis vero hominum tales seruos domi suae ferret, qui omni ordine turbato pro sua libidine omnia agerent? Et nos Christum putemus tam ambitiosis & auaris hominibus Ecclesiam suam subiecisse, quam proprij sanguinis pretio sibi acquisiuit? Discant potius omnes se accommodare ei ordini, quem Paulus in praesenti ab ipso Deo institutum esse scribit.
units.tr: and tyranny is most powerfully refuted by the authority of this passage, nay, it is utterly overthrown and collapses from its foundations. For first, since Paul says that the ministry of reconciliation was committed to the apostles, they claim for themselves rule and lordship over the Church, and say that they are the vicars of Christ, to whom, as if to him, all power in heaven and on earth has been given. That Paul III, in our own time, openly said this, when two monks once disputed rather foolishly about papal power at his table, I heard from an illustrious man who was present at the time. Puffed up with this confidence, they throw into confusion things divine and human, and (as Daniel foretold would happen) they change laws and times, and by a thousand methods they have devised by which the salvation won through Christ is applied to us, differing not much from the tricks of magicians and enchanters. For what Christ said about the keys, they transferred to private auricular confession and absolution, which they mutter in a whisper, almost as a magic spell, to those who fall at their knees. Then from the mystical Supper of the Lord they fashioned the Mass, which consists entirely of whispers and chanting that no one understands, and of theatrical gestures; and through it they falsely claim that the merit of Christ and all salvation are applied not only to the living who watch it, but even to the dead. This conflicts with the ordinary use of the Supper, which is that the death of the Lord be remembered, and that it be a seal of the salvation acquired for us through it. We indeed confess that the sacraments are appendages of the Gospel, but if they are considered apart from it, they are nothing, and taken without faith they profit nothing. To these abuses was added the merchandising of indulgences, which they sold to superstitious people, stamped with heavy lead, like certain amulets. From these arose the superstition of pilgrimages and the cult of relics. If you add to all these fasting, monastic vows, cowls, hair shirts, hired little prayers, the ringing of bells, incense, oil, spittle, salt, rosaries, and whatever other things are of this kind, you will soon see how unfaithful were the stewards in the house of the Lord, who burdened his household with so many fruitless labours and expenses. And what man would tolerate such servants in his own house, who, with all order thrown into confusion, did everything according to their own lust? Shall we think that Christ has subjected his Church, which he won for himself at the price of his own blood, to such ambitious and greedy men? Rather, let all learn to accommodate themselves to that order which Paul writes was instituted by God himself in the present passage.

units.la: Et hinc occasione sumpta, ut ipse atque alij Apostoli hoc suum ministerium obeant, docet. Itaque nomine Christi (inquit) legatione fungimur, velut Deo precante per nos, oramus Christi nomine: Reconciliamini Deo, &c. Sunt singula emphatica, & sic causam iam proponi necesse erat, ut Euangelij praedicationem quae tunc a multis contemnebatur, ab omni contemptu vindicaret. Sic ergo vult dicere: Haec cum ita se habeant, nemo nobis vitio vertat, quod liberius & maiori cum fiducia agimus. Ut enim sic agamus, nostri ministerij author, & communis salutis necessitas exigunt: quae monent, ut tanquam legati Regis regum apud omnes insteimus qua possumus diligentia, ut se cum Deo reconciliari patiantur. At quia in Apostolis ordinarium Euangelij ministerium institutum est, debent ista de omnibus ministris exponi, ut quid de ipsis iudicari debeat, discamus.
units.tr: Taking occasion from this, he teaches how he and the other Apostles discharge their ministry. "Therefore," he says, "we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were pleading through us: we beg you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God, &c." Each word is emphatic, and the matter had to be put in this way so that the preaching of the Gospel, which was then despised by many, might be defended against all contempt. So his meaning is this: since these things stand as they do, let no one hold it against us that we act more freely and with greater confidence. The author of our ministry and the necessity of our common salvation require us to act this way. They urge us, as ambassadors of the King of kings, to press upon everyone, with all the diligence we can, that they allow themselves to be reconciled to God. But because the ordinary ministry of the Gospel was instituted in the Apostles, these things ought to be explained concerning all ministers, so that we may learn how judgment should be made of them.

units.la: Primo quia ministerij prius meminerat, & ministeriorum genera varia atque diuersa sunt, quale illud sit docet, quod ipsis Deus mandarit. Nam ipsos legatione fungi dicit, ipsius Christi nomine. Admonet de eo Apostoli vocabulum, quod Graecis legatum significat. Emphasim vero habet, quod ipsos legationem hanc ipsius Christi nomine obire ait. Eo enim innuit, ipsos non solum ab illo missos, verumetiam virtute ac Spiritu instructos esse. Id vero Verbi administros omnes officij admonet, ut nihil praedicent, quam quod in mandatis acceperunt: in eo autem fidi sint atque intrepidi, ne vel mundi illecebris, vel tyrannorum minis se ab officio dimoueri sinant. Etenim execrabilis ignauia est, Dei negotium timidius agere, qui ut ubique praesens adest, ita pro suo nomine laborantes deserere non possunt. At simul meminerint in legatis morum grauitatem requiri, ne leuitate sua & petulantia, causa, quam agunt, officiant, vel etiam heris suis inuidiam siue contemptum pariant. Curent ergo diligenter, ne vitae exemplo destruant, quod docendo aedificarunt. Huc pertinent, quae Paulus alibi de Episcopi vita & moribus praescripsit. Rursus vero singulorum est, Euangelij praecones pro legatis aeterni Filij Dei agnoscere, ne horum contemptus in ipsum Christum redundet.
units.tr: First, because he had just mentioned the ministry, and there are various and different kinds of ministries, he teaches what sort of ministry it is, the one God has commanded them. For he says they discharge an embassy in the name of Christ himself. He draws attention by the word "Apostle," which in Greek means one sent as an envoy. There is emphasis in his saying that they carry out this embassy in the name of Christ himself. By this he implies that they were not only sent by him but were also equipped with power and the Spirit. This reminds all the servants of the Word of their office: they should preach nothing but what they have received in their commission, and they should be faithful and fearless in this, so that neither the allurements of the world nor the threats of tyrants allow them to be turned aside from their duty. For it is a detestable cowardice to carry out God's business too timidly, since he who is present everywhere cannot abandon those who labour in his name. Yet at the same time they should remember that gravity of conduct is required of envoys, so that by their levity and wantonness they do not harm the cause they serve, or bring odium or contempt upon their masters. Let them therefore take care not to destroy by the example of their life what they have built by teaching. To this belongs what Paul elsewhere prescribed about the life and morals of a bishop. Again, it is the duty of each individual to acknowledge the heralds of the Gospel as envoys of the eternal Son of God, lest contempt for them redound upon Christ himself.

units.la: Deinde, quomodo legationem hanc obeant, docet: Velut Deo precante per nos, oramus Christi nomine: Reconciliemini Deo. Ostendit ipsos neq; obiter aut perfunctorie, neq; etiam imperiosius ac insolenter agere: sed tanto studio & animorum contentione communem salutis causam vrgere, vt cum doctrina & adhortatione preces quoq; coniungant, neque pudeat supplices fieri ijs, quos videant esse præfectiores. Id autem vere ab eo dici, non ipsorum modo concniones & scripta testantur, verumetiam quæ in Asia Paulus fecit, & quæ tam nota fuerunt omnibus, vt in frequenti illa episcoporum Asiæ Synodo, coram omnibus auderet dicere: Vos scitis, à primo die quo ingressus sum Asiam, quomodo vobiscum per omne tempus fuerim, seruiens Domino cum omni modestia & multis lachrymis ac tentationibus, quæ mihi euenerant ex insidijs Iudæorum: Vt nihil suffugerim eorum, quæ vobis conducerent, quin annuntiarem vobis, & docerem vos publice ac per singulas domos, &c. Debent autem exemplum hoc imitari omnes ministri, vt quacunq; possunt ratione instent, vt quam plurimos Christo lucrifaciant. Non pudeat ergo precari quoq; eos, qui vix alloquio digni videbantur: imprimis autem Deum orando fatigent, vt is suo Spiritu contumaciores emollire & flectere dignetur. At longè aliam viam Pontifices ingrediuntur, qui cum Apostolici haberi velint, pro imperio quiduis mandant, & seculari brachio atq; Regum armis muniti, vel inuitos cogunt obedire omnibus, quæ ipsi ex suo cerebro fingunt.
units.tr: Next, he teaches how they should discharge this embassy: "as though God were pleading through us, we beg you in Christ's name, be reconciled to God." He shows that they do not act carelessly or perfunctorily, nor again arrogantly and insolently, but press the common cause of salvation with such zeal and intensity of mind that they join prayers to teaching and exhortation, and are not ashamed to become suppliants to those whom they see to be above them. That this was truly said by him is attested not only by their sermons and writings, but also by what Paul did in Asia, and what was so well known to everyone that in the well-attended synod of the bishops of Asia he dared to say before all: "You know, from the first day that I set foot in Asia, how I was with you all the time, serving the Lord with all humility and with many tears and trials which befell me from the plots of the Jews; how I kept back nothing that would be useful to you, but declared it to you and taught you publicly and from house to house," &c. All ministers ought to imitate this example, so that by whatever means they can they press on, to win as many as possible to Christ. Let them not be ashamed, therefore, to beg even those who seemed scarcely worthy of being spoken to; above all, let them weary God with prayer, that he may deign to soften and bend the more obstinate by his Spirit. But the Pontiffs take a very different path. Although they wish to be thought Apostolic, they command whatever they please by authority, and, fortified by the secular arm and the arms of kings, they compel even the unwilling to obey all that they themselves invent from their own brains.

units.la: Est autem hic obseruatu dignissima plus quam paterna Dei bonitas, qua erga nos vtitur. Etenim ea est nostræ naturæ & sortis humanæ calamitas siue miseria, vt nobis opus sit perpetuis ad Deum supplicationibus ea postulare, quæ ad salutem sunt necessaria. At cum hic vel negligentes nimium, vel etiam præfecti & gratiæ eius improbi contemptores simus, ipse per seruos suos eòsq; se demittit, vt nobis quasi supplex fiat, & precibus apud nos obtinere studeat, vt quam ipse nobis offert gratiam amplectamur. Fecit hoc olim per Prophetas, vt in eorum sermonibus est videre. Apud Isaiam certè clamat: O vos omnes qui sitis, venite ad aquas, & vos quibus non est pecunia, venite: comparate & comedite, emite sine argento & sine pretio vinum & lac. Cur expenditis pecuniam pro non pane? &c. Et per eundem Prophetam queritur, se tota die manus suas expandisse ad populum desertorem. Imprimis autem pathetica & amoris paterni plena est illa actio, quam apud Mich. cum ipsum de instituit, dicens: Populi mi, quid feci tibi? aut qua nam re molestus ti bi fui? Respondè mihi. Num quod eduxi te de terra Ægypti, et de domo seruitutis te redemi? quod ite misi ante te Aaronē, Mosem & Mariam? Populi mi, recordare quæso, quid consultarit Balak, &c. Quis non admiretur tantam Dei indulgentiam? At superat hæc, quod cum tot seculis apud contumaces istos nihil profecisset, tandem Filium suum Vnigenitum misit, qui preces eàsdem apud eos repeteret. Et cum huic quoq; pessimam gratiam reculisset, idem Apostolos posteà se reliquit, qui legatione ista apud Iudæos simul & gentes ipsius nomine fungerentur, adeoq; supplices vbiq; clamarent: Reconciliamini Deo. Experimur hanc Dei bonitatem etiam nostro seculo, & passim ad rauim vsq; clamant Christi præcones, vt ebriosi, auari, vsurarij, scortatores, idololatræ, quotquot deniq; alij iram Dei hucusq; flagitijs suis irritauerunt, his relictis ad illum redeant, & gratiam eam amplectantur, cuius nobis Mediator est factus IESVS CHRISTVS. Accedunt ferijs ministrorum obtestationibus prodigia omnis generis, fames item, pestis, bella, seditiones, quibus omnibus Deus quasi cogere studet, vt ad mentem meliorem redeant ij, qui verbis flecti non possunt. Sed plerosq; plus quam belluinus stupor occupauit, vt nihil audiant vel sentiant: digni nimirum, contra quos sui iudicij rigorem Deus breui proferat.
units.tr: Here, moreover, is to be observed God's goodness, more than paternal, which he shows towards us. For such is the calamity or misery of our nature and human lot that we need to ask, by perpetual supplications to God, for those things which are necessary for salvation. And since here we are either too negligent or, indeed, proud and wicked despisers of his grace, he himself, through his servants, humbles himself so far that he becomes, as it were, a suppliant to us, and strives by entreaty to prevail upon us to embrace the grace which he offers. He did this once through the Prophets, as can be seen in their words. Certainly in Isaiah he cries: "O all you who thirst, come to the waters, and you who have no money, come: buy and eat, buy wine and milk without silver and without price. Why do you spend money for what is not bread?" &c. And through the same Prophet he complains that he has stretched out his hands all day to a rebellious people. Above all, that action is full of pathos and paternal love which he performs in Micah, when he addresses them, saying: "My people, what have I done to you? Or in what have I troubled you? Answer me. Did I not bring you up out of the land of Egypt, and redeem you from the house of bondage? Did I not send before you Aaron, Moses and Miriam? My people, remember, I pray, what Balak king of Moab consulted," &c. Who would not marvel at so great an indulgence of God? Yet this surpasses everything: that, when for so many ages he had accomplished nothing among these stubborn people, at last he sent his only-begotten Son, who repeated the same entreaties among them. And when they had rejected this Son too with the worst ingratitude, he afterwards left behind the same Apostles, who should discharge this embassy in his name among both the Jews and the Gentiles, and so cry out everywhere, as suppliants, "Be reconciled to God!" We experience this goodness of God even in our own age, and everywhere the heralds of Christ cry out until they are hoarse: drunkards, misers, usurers, fornicators, idolaters, and whoever else has hitherto provoked the wrath of God by their wickedness, let them leave these things and return to him, and embrace that grace of which Jesus Christ has been made our Mediator. Along with the daily entreaties of the ministers come portents of every kind, famine too, plague, wars, seditions, by all of which God strives, as it were, to compel to a better mind those who cannot be moved by words. But most people are seized by a stupor more than bestial, so that they hear nothing and feel nothing: doubtless they are worthy that God should soon display against them the rigour of his judgment.

units.la: Cæterum in præsenti ratione præcipuam Paulus adducit, qua Apostoli hominibus resipiscentiam persuadere studuerunt. Fecit enim (inquit) eum, qui non norat peccatum, pro nobis peccatum vt nos efficeremur iustitia Dei in eo. De Christo loquitur, quem omnis peccati immunem fuisse dicit, adeò, vt ne norit quidem peccare. Quia enim eius conceptio & natiuitas purissima fuit, & ab omni Originalis vitiositatis labe prorsus immunis, peccatum in illo locum habere non potuit. Etita facto opus erat, quia alioqui non potuisset pro nostris peccatis satisfacere. Illum (inquit) fecit peccatum pro nobis, id est, hostiam aut victimam pro peccatis nostris, dum eorum reatum illi imposuit, vt (si cuti Propheta ait) cum sceleratus fuerit reputatus. Cur vero id fecit Deus? Vt nos efficeremur iustitia Dei in eo, id est, vt nos, qui natura peccatores sumus, ad Dei tribunal pro iustis possemus comparere: Nimirum propter ipsum, qui nobis à Patre iustitia factus est. Ut enim Christus peccatum factus dicitur, quia nostrorum peccatorum reatus ei imputatus sive impositus fuit: ita nos iustitia Dei, sive coram Deo iusti dicimur, quia Filii sui iustitiam nobis Pater imputat, si illum vera fide amplectamur. Itaque natura quidem peccatores sumus, iustitia autem nostra omnis ex imputatione est, ut alibi diligentius est explicatum. Ita vero partes Euangelij summam Paulus comprehendit, ut nihil vehementius, nihil efficacius dici possit. Etenim ferreus sit oportet, qui Dei Patris nos tam amicè ad gratiam invitantis voce non movetur. Quis item non horreat peccatum, quod non aliter quàm indigna Filij Dei morte expiari potuit? Quis verò non ardeat eius iustitiae desiderio, quae sola nos apud Dei tribunal tuetur? Agnoscant ergo singuli hanc Dei Patris bonitatem indulgentissimam, & procul relictis vitae prioris studijs, IESVM CHRISTVM toto animo complectantur, seq; totos ei consecrent ut cum eodem ad regni cœlestis hæreditatem accedant. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, in the present passage Paul brings forward the chief argument by which the Apostles have sought to persuade men to repentance. "For he made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him." He speaks of Christ, whom he says was free from all sin, so much so that he did not even know how to sin. For since his conception and nativity were most pure, and altogether free from the stain of original corruption, sin could have no place in him. And this had to be so, because otherwise he could not have made satisfaction for our sins. He made him (he says) sin for us, that is, a sacrifice or victim for our sins, while he laid upon him the guilt of them, so that (as the Prophet says) he was reckoned among the wicked. But why did God do this? That we might be made the righteousness of God in him, that is, that we, who are sinners by nature, might be able to stand before the tribunal of God as righteous, namely on account of him who has been made righteousness for us by the Father. For just as Christ is said to be made sin, because the guilt of our sins was imputed or laid upon him, so we are called the righteousness of God, or are said to be righteous before God, because the Father imputes to us the righteousness of his Son, if we embrace him with true faith. Thus we are indeed sinners by nature, but all our righteousness is by imputation, as has been explained more fully elsewhere. Paul has so comprehended the sum of the parts of the Gospel that nothing more forceful and effective can be said. For he must be made of iron who is not moved by the voice of God the Father inviting us so lovingly to grace. Who likewise would not shudder at sin, which could not be expiated otherwise than by the unworthy death of the Son of God? And who would not burn with desire for that righteousness which alone protects us before the tribunal of God? Let each one therefore acknowledge this most indulgent goodness of God the Father, and, leaving far behind the pursuits of his former life, embrace Jesus Christ with his whole soul, and consecrate himself wholly to him, that with him he may come to the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: CAPVT VI. HOMILIA XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI. HOMILY XXV.

units.la: OPeram verò nostram conferentes etiam hortamur, ne frustra gratiam Dei vos receperitis. Dicit enim Deus: Tempore accepto exaudiui te, & in die salutis succurri tibi. Ecce nunc tempus acceptum, ecce nunc dies salutis. Nullam vlla in re præbentes offensionem, ne vituperetur ministerium: sed & in omnibus nos approbantes, ut Dei ministri.
units.tr: Lending our effort, we also urge you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For God says: "In an acceptable time I have heard you, and in the day of salvation I have helped you. Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation." We give no offence in anything, so that the ministry is not blamed, but in all things we commend ourselves as ministers of God.

units.la: SVB finem quinti capitis summam humanæ salutis Paulus breuiter complexus est, & huius legatos à Deo constitutos esse dixit Apostolos, qui omnis loci & ordinis homines summo studio vrgere debeant, ut quam Deus nobis in Filio suo, IESV CHRISTO, gratiam sponte offert, gratis animis amplectantur. Ex eo autem occasione sumpta, quod in genere dixit, nunc Corinthijs applicat, quos grauiter hortatur & vrget, ut in semel recepta fide constantes perseuerent, ne gratiam sibi factam à Deo, sua negligentia aut inobedientia inanem reddant. Argumenta adducet plurima, quæ singula suis locis videbimus. Admonentur autem Pauli exemplo omnes Ecclesiarum ministri, ut non solum de suo ministerio magnificè concionentur, eiusq; authoritate contra improbos illius contemptores afferant, sed ut eadem vtantur quoq; fortiter apud omnes, quos admonitione, hortatione, vel etiam correptione acriori opus habere vident.
units.tr: Near the end of the fifth chapter Paul briefly summed up the whole of human salvation, and said that the apostles were appointed by God as its ambassadors. They must press men of every place and rank with the utmost zeal, so that they willingly embrace the grace that God freely offers us in his Son, Jesus Christ. Taking occasion from what he had said in general terms, he now applies it to the Corinthians, whom he earnestly exhorts and urges to persevere steadfastly in the faith once received, and not to make void by their own carelessness or disobedience the grace God has bestowed on them. He will bring many arguments, which we shall see in their proper places. By Paul's example, all ministers of the churches are admonished not only to preach magnificently about their ministry and to bring its authority against the wicked who despise it, but also to use the same boldness before all whom they see in need of admonition, exhortation, or even sharper correction.

units.la: Propositio totius Cap. est: Operam verò nostram conferentes etiam hortamur, ne frustra gratiam Dei vos receperitis. In Græco habetur συνεργοῦντες, quod si literam respicias, Cooperantes significat, & hoc loco variè exponi potest: Vt nimirum vel ad Deum referas, cuius cooperarios sive adiutores verbi administros esse in priori epistola dixerat: Vel ad Corinthios, quos in pietatis studio adiuuare soleat (quæ sententia Chrysostomo & Theodoreto placuit:) Vel ad ipsum Euangelium, quod adhortationibus crebris adiuuatur, adeoq; viuificatur, ut suum effectum habeat apud auditores: Vel ad ipsos ministros sive Apostolos, qui opus Domini quasi in vnum collatis viribus vbiq; locorum vrgeant. Et non male omnes isti sensus argumento præsenti conueniunt.
