Itaque hoc dicere videtur: Quia ergo Deus sublime istud & salutiferum reconciliationis per Christum factæ ministerium nobis Apostolis commisit, quibus ceu socijs & adiutoribus vti dignatur: æquum est, ut nos quoq; coniunctis viribus negotium istud agamus, & hortationibus assiduis vobis quoq; ad pietatem adiumento simus, neq; patiamur vos in cursu bene cœpto deficere, ut salus iam parta vobis quasi ex manibus elabatur. Quod dum facimus, nemo nos vel morosos vel arrogantes esse putet: quia hoc omne ex officio, & quia vobis ita opus est, facimus.
units.tr: The theme of the whole chapter is: "But as we work together with you, we also exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain." The Greek has συνεργοῦντες [synergountes], which, if you look at the word itself, means "working together", and in this place it can be explained in several ways: either as referring to God, whose fellow-workers or helpers in the ministry of the Word he had called them in the earlier letter; or as referring to the Corinthians, whom Paul was accustomed to help in their pursuit of godliness (this is the view that pleased Chrysostom and Theodoret); or as referring to the Gospel itself, which is helped by frequent exhortations and so is made living, so that it has its effect on its hearers; or as referring to the ministers or apostles themselves, who press forward the work of the Lord in every place, as if their strength were joined into one. All these senses fit the present argument well. So he seems to say this: Since God has entrusted to us apostles this lofty and saving ministry of the reconciliation made through Christ, and deigns to use us as his partners and helpers, it is fitting that we too should carry on this business with united strength, and by constant exhortation be a help to you also in godliness, and not allow you to fail in the course you have begun well, so that the salvation already won is slipping, as it were, out of your hands. In doing this, let no one think us either fussy or arrogant, for we do all this out of duty, and because you have need of it.

units.la: Est autem hic non ociosè obseruandum, hæc Corinthijs dici, quos initio in fide plene & perfecte instifete institutos fuisse, & omni scientia atq; cognitione abundauisse, Paulus ipse testatus est. Eosdē verò admonitione & adhortatione ista opus habuisse partim abusus, qui apud eos publicè irrepse-rant, partim vitia quibus pleriq; illorum priuatim laborabant, satis ostendunt. Inter quae prorsus inexcusabile fuit, quòd eò licentiæ usq; progressi erant, vt idololatrarum quoq; epulis communica-rent: quæ etiam causa fuit, vt Apostolus sub finem capitis huius adhortationem istam imprimis ad publicam illam Christianæ professionis prophanationem restringat. At non minus omnes ho-mines admoneri necesse est, cùm propter innatam ingenij nostri vitiositatem, tum propter varias mundi illecebras, quibus nos Satan transuersos abripere studet. Omnibus ergo hanc Pauli ad-hortationem applicent ministri, ne qui gratiam Dei in vanum recipiant.
units.tr: It should not be passed over here that these things are said to the Corinthians, whom Paul himself bears witness were at the beginning fully and perfectly instructed in the faith, and abounded in all knowledge and understanding. That they nevertheless needed this admonition and exhortation is sufficiently shown partly by the abuses that had crept into their public life, and partly by the faults from which most of them suffered in private. Among these, it was utterly inexcusable that they had gone so far in licence as to take part in the feasts of idolaters. This was also the reason why the Apostol, near the end of this chapter, directs this exhortation chiefly against that public profanation of the Christian profession. But all people need to be admonished no less, both because of the innate sinfulness of our nature and because of the various allurements of the world, by which Satan seeks to drag us off course. Let ministers therefore apply this exhortation of Paul to all, so that none receive the grace of God in vain.

units.la: Fit hoc non vno modo. Primum, quando non contenti vno Christo, noua quaedam salutis subsidia ei coniungimus, quae homines superstitiosi ex suo cerebro finxerunt. Faciebant hoc Apostolorum tempore multi, qui Pharisaicæ doctrinæ fermento adhuc infecti, legem cum Euangelio miscebant, & circumcisione recepta seipsos Legi subijciebant. Quos in epistola ad Galatas Paulus acerrimè corripiens, inter alia dicit: Ecce, ego Paulus dico vobis, quòd si circūcidamini, Christus nihil vos iuuabit. Testor enim rursus omni homini, qui circumciditur, quòd debitor est totius Legis seruandæ. Vobis inanis factus est Christus per vosipsos, quicunq; per Legem iustificamini: à gratia excidistis. Quid grauius dici poterat, quàm Christum inanem fieri aliquibus, & eosdem à gratia excidere? At quanto verius hoc de illis dicetur, qui nō Legem Mosis, olim ab ipso Deo certas ob causas datam, sed vanissimorū hominum traditiones sequuntur? Obseruent hi, solum Christum esse viam, veritatem & vitam, nec alia via, quàm, per ipsum, ad Patrem veniri posse: eundem quoq; vnicum esse gregis Dei pastorem, ostium item in ouile Dei vnicum, fures autem & latrones esse eos, qui alia via in hoc perrumpere volunt. Deinde ij etiam gratiam in vanum recipiunt, qui Euangelium non applicant ad vitæ suæ & morum institutionem, vt fructum ferant sua professione dignum. De his in sementis parabola Dominus loquitur, & tales sunt, qui in viam vel in spinas verbi semen excipiunt: vbi vel à praui diaboli suggestionibus aufertur, vel à mundi exem-plo conculcatur, vel huius seculi curis atq; solicitudinibus suffocatur. Ita fit, vt iisdem vitiis, quibus antea laborarunt, se iterum polluant, & factis negent fidem, quam ore profitentur: quae mani-festa est nominis Christiani prophanatio. Discant hi seipsos Deo hostiam viuente sistere, vt Paulus ad Romanos monet. Postremo in vanum receperunt gratiam Dei, qui aliquoufq; progressi, tandem deficiunt, si quando crucem & pericula sibi imminere vident. Sunt hi, quos in loca lapidosa semen illud excipere Christus dicit, in quibus radices non potest agere. Itaq; cùm iam manu admota, ad mundi huius fauorem respiciant, & pacem atq; otium quærant, nō sunt idonei ad Regnum Dei. Hodie tria hæc hominum genera passim inueniuntur inter eos, qui Euangelium audiunt, & Christo nomen dedisse videri volunt: quare paucissimos est videre, qui verbum gratiæ non in vanum recipiant.
units.tr: This happens in more than one way. First, when, not content with Christ alone, we join to him certain new supports for salvation, which superstitious people have made up out of their own brains. Many did this in the time of the apostles, who, still infected with the leaven of Pharisaic doctrine, mixed the Law with the Gospel and, having received circumcision, subjected themselves to the Law. Paul, sharply rebuking these in his letter to the Galatians, says among other things: "Behold, I Paul say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing. For I testify again to every man who is circumcised that he is a debtor to keep the whole Law. Christ has become of no effect to you, whoever of you are justified by the Law; you have fallen from grace." What could be said more gravely than that Christ is made of no effect to some, and that they have fallen from grace? But how much more truly will this be said of those who follow not the Law of Moses, once given by God himself for certain reasons, but the empty traditions of very vain men? Let them observe that Christ alone is the way, the truth and the life, and that no one can come to the Father except through him; that he is also the one Shepherd of God's flock, and likewise the one door into the sheepfold of God, and that those who want to break in by any other way are thieves and robbers. Next, those also receive the grace of God in vain who do not apply the Gospel to the ordering of their life and conduct, so as to bear fruit worthy of their profession. The Lord speaks of such in the parable of the sower; they are those who receive the seed of the word on the path or among thorns, where it is either snatched away by the wicked suggestions of the devil, or trampled by the example of the world, or choked by the cares and anxieties of this age. So it happens that they defile themselves again with the same vices by which they were troubled before, and by their deeds deny the faith they profess with their mouths; this is a manifest profanation of the Christian name. Let such learn to present themselves to God as a living sacrifice, as Paul advises the Romans. Lastly, those receive the grace of God in vain who make some progress and then at last fall away, when they see the cross and dangers hanging over them. These are the ones whom Christ says receive that seed on rocky ground, where it cannot take root. So when they have already put their hand to the plough, yet look back to the favour of this world and seek peace and ease, they are not fit for the kingdom of God. Today these three kinds of people are found everywhere among those who hear the Gospel and wish to seem to have given their name to Christ; so that there are very few to be seen who do not receive the word of grace in vain.

units.la: Quapropter Ecclesiarum ministros meminisse oportet, legationis suæ summam non in eo con-sistere, vt homines semel in gratiæ Dei & salutis cognitionem adducantur, sed vt qui adducti sunt, in ea perseuerent, & (quod Petrus monuit) vocationem & electionem suam firmam efficere stu-deant. Vt enim fidi legati est, Regis sui mandata non obiter modo exponere ijs, ad quos missus est, verumetiam rationibus & argumentis instare, vt eadem illi rata habeant: Ita ministri non docere modò, verumetiam monere, hortari, arguere, increpare, instare deniq; debent opportunè & importunè, donec se aliquid profecisse videant. Docet idem agriculturæ parabola, qua Spiritus sanctus sæpe in hoc argumento vtitur, & quæ ei optimè conuenit, cùm Ecclesia Dei aruum atq; vinea sit. Non autem sufficit hic, vt singmuli officium faciant, sed vt concordi & vnanimi studio operas suas conferant necesse est. Vt enim animorum distractio in re quauis noxia, ita inter Ecclesiæ ministros pernitiosissima, adeoq; exitialis est. Nam Ecclesiam in sectas distrahit, noua dogmata parit, altercationes & rixas excitat, & ita animos addit apertis fidei hostibus, vt multa tentent, de quibus ne cogitarent quidem, si illos idem sentire & velle cernerent. Exempla, quibus hoc confirmetur, in historia Ecclesiastica passim habentur. Debebant sta nostro seculo diligentius considerari, quando pleriq; in vulgo Christianorum de gratia Dei nunquam, aut raro, cogitant, sed
units.tr: Therefore ministers of the churches ought to remember that the chief aim of their embassy does not lie in this: that people be brought once to the knowledge of the grace and salvation of God, but that those who have been brought in should persevere, and (as Peter admonished) strive to make their calling and election sure. For just as it is the duty of a faithful envoy not merely to set out in passing the commands of his king to those to whom he is sent, but also to press them with reasons and arguments so that they hold these as settled, so ministers ought not only to teach but also to admonish, exhort, reprove, rebuke, and finally to insist, in season and out of season, until they see that they have made some progress. The parable of the farmer teaches the same thing; the Holy Spirit often uses this image, and it suits very well, since the Church of God is a field and a vineyard. Here, however, it is not enough for each to do his own duty; they must bring their labours together with a harmonious and united zeal. For just as the division of minds is harmful in any matter, so among the ministers of the Church it is most destructive and deadly. For it splits the Church into sects, gives birth to new doctrines, stirs up quarrels and brawls, and so gives courage to the open enemies of the faith, so that they attempt many things which they would never even have thought of, if they saw that the ministers agreed and wished the same things. Examples confirming this are found everywhere in ecclesiastical history. These things ought to be considered more carefully in our own age, when most of the common crowd of Christians think about the grace of God never, or rarely, but

units.la: Lucae 8. Vt Dei gratia in vanum recipiatur. Galat. 5. Lucae 9. Ministri retine re studeant in Dei gratia eos, quos huic adduxerunt. Rom. 12. 1. Pet. 1. 2. Tim. 4. plus æquo securiores vitam viuunt plenam scandalorum: Ministri quoq; plurimi, quasi nihil porro ipsis agendum restet, vel cum improbis huius seculi filijs colludunt, vel inter se rixis & iurgijs minimè necessarijs digladiantur: interim verò ea collabi sinunt, quæ antecessorum cura & pio labore ædificata fuerunt. Sed quia hæc deplorari facilius quàm corrigi possunt, nos ad Paulum redeamus; qui quod propositum, argumentis validissimis confirmat.
units.tr: Luke 8. That the grace of God should not be received in vain. Gal. 5. Luke 9. Ministers should take care to keep in the grace of God those whom they have brought to it. Rom. 12. 1 Pet. 1. 2 Tim. 4. Many people live their lives too securely, and so live a life full of scandals. Most ministers too, as if nothing more remained for them to do, either make common cause with the wicked sons of this age or fight among themselves in quarrels and wrangles that are not in the least necessary. Meanwhile they allow to collapse what was built by the care and pious labour of their predecessors. But since these things are easier to lament than to correct, let us return to Paul, who confirms what he proposes with very strong arguments.

units.la: Primum à temporis circumstantia sumitur, & Isaiæ prophetæ authoritate confirmatur, apud quem Deus ista pronuntiat, quæ hic Paulus adducit. Locus extat capite 49. Vaticinatur illic Propheta de Christo, qui Ecclesiam suam ex omnibus gentibus collecturus sit, etiamsi Iudæi sei-psos ei minus obsequentes præbeant. Vtq; magis ad se pelliciat hominum animos, omnis generis bona pollicetur, quorum ille author siue mediator est omnibus, qui ipsum cum fide recipiunt. Primum his verbis explicat: Tempore accepto exaudiam te, in die salutis adiuuabo te. Quæ verba Paulus per præterita citat, dicens: Tempore accepto exaudiui te, & in die salutis succurri tibi. Id verò facit exemplo communi Prophetarum, qui de rebus futuris vaticinantes, præteritis vtuntur, vt promissionum Dei certitudinem & veritatem indubitatam exprimant. Infert autem ex his Prophetæ verbis Paulus: Ecce nunc tempus acceptum, ecce nunc dies salutis. Quod autem tempus acceptum nos dicimus, id Hebræi tempus Ratzon, id est, beneuolentiæ & gratiæ, aut beneplaciti vocant: & ita tempus illud dicitur, quod Deus præfiniuit ad hoc, vt humani generis mi-sertus cum eo in gratiam redeat: quod Paulus alibi tempus plenitudinis dicit, eò quòd perfecta & impleta fuerunt, quæcunq; prius fieri oportebat, vt nihil reflaret præter aduentum Filij Dei in carnem. Recte autem & proprie illud tempus acceptum, siue tempus gratiæ dicitur, quia eos quoq; recipit Deus (vt Chrysostomus annotauit) qui millies peccarunt: nec modò in gratiam recipit, verumetiam in pristinam gloriam, ad quam Adamus conditus fuerat, & libertatem filiorum suorum restituit. Est autem argumentum, quo Paulus vtitur, eiusmodi: Deus certum constituit tempus, quo miseros mortales in gratiam recipere vult, & bonorum cælestium hæredes facere: Ideo se huic tempori accommodare debent, quicunque gratiæ & salutis æternæ cupidi sunt. Atqui tempus illud est, quo Filium suum vnigenitum in mundum misit, qui nos illi reconciliauit, & suæ mortis merito partam salutem per Euangelium omnibus liberaliter offert: Ergo accommodate vos huic, ne gratia hæc vobis ex manibus elabatur, & à salute excidatis, quam iam apprehendi-se videbamini. Argumenti huius ratio ex communi ordine dependet, quem in tota rerum natura Deus instituit. Nam vt sapiens ille ait, certum tempus habent omnia, quæ sub sole fiunt: & aliud quidem tempus arationi, aliud sementi, aliud messi, aliud vindemiæ, aliud navigationi destinatum est: quæ momenta temporum si quis præterlabi sinat, frustra tentabit posteà, quæ suo tantum tempore vtiliter possunt fieri. Ita verò gratiæ quoq; suæ tempus certum definiuit Deus: quod si quis neglexerit, frustra illam posteà requiret.
units.tr: First he takes the argument from the circumstances of the time, and confirms it by the authority of the prophet Isaiah, in whom God announces the things that Paul here cites. The passage is in chapter 49. There the prophet prophesies concerning Christ, who would gather his Church from all nations, even though the Jews show themselves less obedient to him. And to draw men's minds more strongly to himself, he promises every kind of good thing, of which he is the author or mediator to all who receive him with faith. He first explains this in these words: "In an acceptable time I will hear you; in the day of salvation I will help you." Paul cites these words in the past tense, saying: "In an acceptable time I have heard you, and in the day of salvation I have helped you." He does this following the common practice of the prophets, who, prophesying of future things, use the past tense in order to express the certainty and unshakable truth of God's promises. From these words of the prophet Paul draws the inference: "Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation." Now what we call the acceptable time, the Hebrews call the time of ratzon [רצון], that is, of goodwill and grace, or of good pleasure; and so that time is called the time which God has appointed for this purpose, that, having compassion on the human race, he might be reconciled to it in favour. Paul elsewhere calls this the fullness of time, because everything that had to come before was completed and fulfilled, so that nothing remained but the coming of the Son of God in the flesh. Now that time is rightly and properly called the acceptable time, or the time of grace, because God receives even those (as Chrysostom observed) who have sinned a thousand times; he not only receives them into favour, but restores them to the former glory for which Adam had been created, and to the liberty of his sons. The argument Paul uses is of this kind: God has fixed a certain time in which he wishes to receive miserable mortals into favour and make them heirs of heavenly goods. Therefore all who desire grace and eternal salvation ought to conform themselves to this time. But that time is the one in which he sent his only-begotten Son into the world, who reconciled us to him, and who offers the salvation won by the merit of his death to all through the Gospel freely. Therefore accommodate yourselves to this, lest this grace slip from your hands and you fall away from the salvation which you seemed already to have grasped. The reasoning of this argument depends on the common order which God has established throughout the whole of nature. For, as that wise man says, all things that are done under the sun have their appointed time; there is a time set for ploughing, another for sowing, another for harvest, another for the vintage, another for sailing. If anyone lets these moments of time slip past, he will try in vain afterwards to do what could be done usefully only in its own time. So God has likewise fixed a certain time for his grace; if anyone neglects it, he will seek it in vain afterwards.

units.la: Vbi tamen nemo superstitiosas dierum aut horarum obseruationes animo concipere debet, circa quas multi occupantur. Sed in genere tempus gratiæ censeri debet totus ille omnium seculorum decursus, qui à nato ex virgine Christo ad finem mundi vsq; extenditur. Nam totum illud tempus Christo tribuitur, qui nobis gratiæ Dei Mediator atq; vnicus salutis author est. Deinde singuli tempus gratiæ sibi adesse sciant, quoties Deus ipsis per Euangelium aures vellicat, & vt Filium suum vnigenitum audiant, eiq; obtemperent, hortatur. Habent enim singulæ gentes & singuli homines suum tempus, quo lucem veritatis Deus illis reuelat: quod non obscurè Paulus innuit, quando in concione ad Lystrenses fatetur, permisisse Deum præteritis ætatibus gentes ambulare in suis viis. Et si Apostolorum acta legas, videbis illos non temere discurrisse per orbem terrarum, sed spiritum ducem secutos esse, qui eos modò hic modò illic prædicare iussit. Petrus cer-tè non sponte, sed à Deo euocatus Euangelium Cornelio Centurioni prædicat. Paulus & Barnabas à Spiritu sancto segregantur, vt Euangelium inter gentes prædicent. Imò Paulus aliquando in Asia docere à Spiritu Sancto prohibitus fuit: & cùm ex Mysia in Bithyniam proficisci statuisset, non permisit hoc idem Spiritus: nimirum, quòd iam tempus illud instaret, quo Macedonibus verbum gratiæ annuntiari oportebat. Et quoad singulos homines, permittit interdum Deus, vt qui ex electorum numero sunt, aliquandiu in superstitionibus & erroribus vagentur, imò per scelerum quoq; lacunas volutentur, suo autem tempore veritatis luce conuicti resipiscant, & ad Christum accedant, cuius gratiae exempla in publicanis, meretricibus & Paulo Euangelica historia proponit. Ita vero salutis aeternae donum Deus dispensat, ut vel ex eo constet, illum nos ex gratuita misericordia seruare, neq; vllis legibus esse astrictum. Ideo in praesenti tempus gratiae aut beneplaciti primo loco ponitur, & huic subijcitur dies salutis: nimirum, quia hanc sperare non liceret, nisi nos sua gratia & misericordia Deus dignaretur.
units.tr: Yet here no one should form in his mind superstitious observations of days or hours, with which many people are preoccupied. Rather, in general, the time of grace should be reckoned as the whole course of all the ages which stretches from Christ born of the virgin to the end of the world. For that whole time is attributed to Christ, who is the Mediator of God's grace for us and the sole author of salvation. Next, let each individual know that the time of grace is at hand for him whenever God pricks his ears through the Gospel and exhorts him to hear his only-begotten Son and obey him. For each nation and each man has its own time in which God reveals to them the light of truth. Paul hints at this not obscurely when, in his sermon to the Lystrians, he confesses that God had permitted the nations in past ages to walk in their own ways. And if you read the Acts of the Apostles, you will see that they did not wander haphazardly through the world, but followed the Spirit as their guide, who ordered them to preach now here, now there. Peter, certainly, did not preach the Gospel to the centurion Cornelius of his own accord, but being called by God. Paul and Barnabas are set apart by the Holy Spirit to preach the Gospel among the Gentiles. Indeed, Paul was once forbidden by the Holy Spirit to teach in Asia; and when he had resolved to set out from Mysia into Bithynia, the same Spirit did not permit it: plainly because the time was now at hand when the word of grace had to be announced to the Macedonians. And as for individual men, God sometimes allows those who are among the number of the elect to wander for a while in superstitions and errors, even to roll in the mire of crimes; but at their proper time, convicted by the light of truth, they repent and come to Christ. Gospel history sets before us examples of this grace in tax-collectors, harlots and Paul. Thus God dispenses the gift of eternal salvation in such a way that it is clear from this that he saves us out of free mercy and is bound by no laws. Therefore in the present passage the time of grace or of good pleasure is placed first, and the day of salvation is subjoined to it; plainly because we could not hope for this unless God deigned to show us his grace and mercy.

units.la: At hic tenere oportet, notam siue signum eius diei esse Euangelij praedicationem, per quam Deus & gratiam suam, & salutem nobis offert. Etenim serio is nobiscum agit, neque ludit nos inanibus promissis. Tunc ergo nos aduigilare conuenit, ne oblatam nobis salutis occasionem negligamus. Nam instar pluuiae aut imbris transeuntis est Euangelij praedicatio, & fere non redit ad eos, qui semel sibi oblatam excluserunt. Quoad singulos autem, poenitentiae & gratiae tempus est, quàm diu hac vita frui datur: quia quandocunq; nos peccatorum poenitet, & ad Deum conuerti mur, fores gratiae eius nobis patent. At huius vitae curriculum emensis nulla spes reliqua est: quia (ut Abraham diuiti epuloni dicebat) nemo ex inferis in coelos ascendere, aut ex his ad illos transire potest. Et notū est, quid fatuis virginibus acciderit, quae lampades suas in sponsi occursum nō praeparauerant. Quoties ergo Deus nos ad poenitentiā inuitat, & gratiam suam nobis in Christo offert, tunc tempus illud acceptū adesse, & illum ad ostium stare atq; pulsare cogitemus, & illum toto animo admittamus. Stulti nimium & infelices sunt, qui rem qua nulla magis necessaria est, in extremam senectam usq; differre instituunt, cùm ignorent, an vel in crastinum usq; superstites futuri, nedum num ad senectam peruenturi sint.
units.tr: But here we must hold that the mark or sign of that day is the preaching of the Gospel, through which God offers us both his grace and salvation. For he deals with us in earnest, and does not mock us with empty promises. Then, therefore, we ought to be watchful, lest we neglect the opportunity of salvation offered to us. For the preaching of the Gospel is like a passing shower or rain, and it scarcely returns to those who have once shut out the opportunity offered them. As for individuals, the time of repentance and grace lasts as long as it is granted to enjoy this life; for whenever we repent of our sins and turn to God, the doors of his grace stand open to us. But once the course of this life has been run, no hope remains; because (as Abraham said to the rich man in the feast) no one can ascend from the dead to heaven, or pass from there to those places. And it is well known what happened to the foolish virgins, who had not prepared their lamps for the coming of the bridegroom. Whenever, therefore, God invites us to repentance and offers us his grace in Christ, let us reflect that the acceptable time is then present, and that he is standing at the door and knocking; and let us admit him with our whole heart. Those are very foolish and unhappy who determine to put off until extreme old age a matter than which none is more necessary, when they do not know whether they will be alive even until tomorrow, let alone whether they will reach old age.

units.la: Porrò ut ad Paulum redeamus, quia administrorum verbi adhortationes parum efficaces sunt, nisi ipsi eas proprio exemplo confirment, & ita se gerant, ut appareat eos serio agere, neq; dubitare de ijs, quae aliis persuasa volunt, nunc seipsum Apostolus in exemplum proponit. Nos (inquit) vos hortamur, qui nullam vlla in re praebemus offensionem, ne vituperetur ministerium nostrum: sed & in omnibus nos approbamus ut Dei ministros. Quasi diceret: Si iniqua aut dura praescribere videor, meipsum respicite, & ut me geram videte: & spero vos mox intellecturos, me atq; collegas meos hoc ipsum summo studio agere, quod à vobis impetrare cupimus. Etenim in hoc sumus, ne quam alicui demus offensionem, ne (quod alibi dixi) dum alios hortamur, ipsi reprobi esse, & in vanum cucurrisse deprehendamur. Et poterat hoc dicere Paulus, cùm (ut alias audiuimus) à licitis quoq; abstineret. In sequenti autem sermone exponet, quibus studijs fidem suam Deo & hominibus approbet. Hoc autem dicendo, simul Corinthiorum stultitiam arguit, qui contemptis fidis & germanis Christi ministris, homines nequam & impostores, neq; vllis virtutibus apostolicis ornatos, in pretio habebant.
units.tr: Now, to return to Paul: because the exhortations of ministers of the Word have little effect unless they confirm them by their own example, and conduct themselves so that it appears they are in earnest and do not doubt the things they wish to persuade others of, the Apostle now sets himself forth as an example. "We," he says, "exhort you, giving no offence in anything, so that our ministry may not be blamed; but in all things we commend ourselves as ministers of God." As if he said: "If I seem to prescribe unjust or harsh things, look at yourselves, and see how I conduct myself; and I hope you will soon understand that I and my colleagues are doing with the greatest zeal the very thing we wish to obtain from you. For we take care not to give offence to anyone, lest (as I said elsewhere) while we exhort others, we ourselves be found to be reprobate and to have run in vain." Paul could say this, since (as we heard elsewhere) he even abstained from things that were lawful. In the following discourse he will set out by what efforts he commends his faith to God and to men. In saying this, he at the same time rebukes the folly of the Corinthians, who, despising the faithful and genuine ministers of Christ, held in esteem worthless men, impostors, adorned with none of the apostolic virtues.

units.la: Interim suo exemplo docet, quid eos facere conueniat, qui alios docere aut monere ac hortari instituerunt: Nimirum, ne quam ipsi dent offensionem. Non ait: Ne quem offendamus: Aut, ne quis offensionis ansam siue scandalum ex nobis arripiat. Id enim ministri cauere non possunt. Nā vt coguntur multa ex officio dicere, quae multos offendunt: ita multi scandalum arripiunt; vbi reuera nullum datum est. Exempli gratia: Si Ecclesiae minister vxorem ducat, multi offenduntur: si scorteatur, non item. Quis vero sanae mentis propter istos scortandum potius quàm nubendū esse dixerit? Et inter eos, qui Euangelicae doctrinae sectatores haberi volunt, multos dicendi & corripiendi libertas offendit, à qua tamen ministri sibi temperare non possunt, siquidem Deo & Ecclesiae fideles esse velint. Sufficit ergo, si curent, ne quam dent offensionem, ea faciendo, quae vel per se mala & inhonesta sunt, vel salte non necessaria sunt factu, & quae vtilius omitti poterant. Etenim qui calumniandi occasionem praebent non necessariam, qua Euangelicae doctrinae cursus impeditur, ij non vno scelere seipsos grauant. Nam & Dei consilii remorantur, quantum in ipsis est, qui ignem hunc vbiq; locorum ardere & indies latius propagari vult: & multorum saluti obstant, quibus seruandis potius studere debebant. Sunt igitur ex eorum numero, qui caco scandalu ponunt, quos Deus in Lege totius Ecclesiae consensu pro maledictis & execrationi obnoxijs censeri vult. Vtinam vero illud hodie omnes diligentius expenderent, quando apud omnis loci homines peccatur. Inter eos enim, qui Ecclesiarum praesules haberi volunt, plurimi sunt, qui nec ipsi docent, nec alios docere sinunt. Scribarum nimirum similes, qui nec ipsi in Regnum coelorum ingrediebantur, neque alios ingredi sinebant. Alij falsa docent, & non nisi sua quaerunt, ideoque infelicem populum in ignorantia & superstitionibus studiose retinent. Sunt rursus qui bene quidem docent, sed quod docendo aedificant, vitae suae exemplo destruunt: quales nimirum sunt vsurarij, fornicatores & adulteri, percussores, ebriosi, voluptuarij & Epicuri de grege porci. Quibus omnibus serviie filiorum Heli exemplum, & gravis illa Dei sententia, quam Malachias contra sui saeculi Sacerdotes pronuntiavit. Quod si ad viros politicos transfeamus, ibi quoque sunt, qui veritatis doctrinam perse quuntur. Quod qui non faciunt, ij saltem suo exemplo illa apud vulgus in contemptu adducunt, dum vel bona Ecclesiae impudenter diripiunt, vel scholas evertunt, et bonas leges improbe dissipant. Nec minus hoc loco parentes peccant, qui liberos suos negligunt, vel etiam ipsi mali exempli authores sunt: quibus adnumerari debent omnes, qui Christiani nominis professioni minus respondent. Hos omnes suo ore Christus damnat, quando ei, qui pusillum aliquem offenderit, utilius fore dicit, si mola asinaria ex collo ipsius suspensa demergeretur in mare. Meminerint ergo singuli, Regnum Dei non esse in sermone, sed in virtute, & ita viuant, ne gratiam Dei in vanum receperint, sed potius proficiant indies in IESV CHRISTO, Domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Meanwhile, by his own example he teaches what those ought to do who have undertaken to teach others, or to admonish and exhort them: namely, that they should give no offence themselves. He does not say, "that we should not offend anyone," or "that no one should take an occasion of offence or a stumbling-block from us." Ministers cannot guard against that. For since they are compelled by their office to say many things which offend many people, so many people take offence where in truth none has been given. For example: if a minister of the Church marries a wife, many are offended; if he fornicates, they are not. Yet who of sound mind would say that, for the sake of such people, one ought to fornicate rather than marry? And among those who wish to be regarded as followers of the Gospel doctrine, many are offended by the freedom of speech in admonishing and rebuking, a freedom from which ministers cannot refrain if they wish to be faithful to God and the Church. It is enough, then, that they take care to give no offence by doing things that are either evil and dishonourable in themselves, or at least not necessary to do, and which could have been more usefully left undone. For those who provide an unnecessary occasion for slander, by which the course of the Gospel doctrine is hindered, load themselves with more than one crime. For they delay the counsels of God, as far as in them lies, since God wills this fire to burn everywhere and to spread more widely day by day; and they stand in the way of the salvation of many, whose salvation they ought rather to have pursued. Therefore they belong to the number of those who lay a blind stumbling-block, whom God, by the consent of the whole Church in the Law, wills to be counted accursed and liable to execration. Would that all people would now weigh this more carefully, since everywhere, in every place, men sin. For among those who wish to be regarded as the leaders of the Churches, there are very many who neither teach themselves nor allow others to teach. They are indeed like the scribes, who neither entered into the kingdom of heaven themselves nor allowed others to enter. Others teach false things and seek only their own, and therefore eagerly keep the unhappy people in ignorance and superstitions. There are again those who teach well, but what they build up by teaching they tear down by the example of their life: such, surely, are usurers, fornicators and adulterers, murderers, drunkards, voluptuaries, and the Epicureans of the herd of swine. To all of these applies the example of the sons of Eli, and that grave sentence of God which Malachi pronounced against the priests of his age. And if we turn to the men of politics, there too are those who persecute the doctrine of the truth. Those who do not do this, at least by their example bring those things into contempt among the common people, while they either shamelessly plunder the goods of the Church, or overthrow the schools, or wickedly squander good laws. Nor do parents sin less in this respect, who neglect their children, or are themselves authors of a bad example; and all who respond less to the profession of the Christian name must be numbered among them. Christ condemns all these with his own mouth, when he says that it would be more useful for one who has offended some little one to have a millstone hung from his neck and be sunk in the sea. Let each one therefore remember that the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power, and so let them live that they do not receive the grace of God in vain, but rather make progress daily in Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY XXVI.

units.la: In tolerantia multa, in afflictionibus, in necessitatibus, in angustijs, in plagis, in carceribus, in tumultuationibus, in laboribus, in vigilijs, in ieiunijs: in puritate, in scientia, in longanimitate, in bonitate, in Spiritu Sancto, in charitate non simulata: in sermone veritatis, in virtute Dei, in armis iustitiae dextris ac sinistris: per gloriam & ignominiam, per convicia & laudes, ut seductores, & tamen veraces: ut ignoti, & tamen noti: ut morientes, & ecce viuimus, ut qui castigamur, nec tamen occidimur: ut dolentes, semper tamen gaudentes: ut pauperes, sed multos ditantes: ut nihil habentes, sed omnia obtinentes.
units.tr: In much patience, in afflictions, in necessities, in distresses, in stripes, in imprisonments, in tumults, in labours, in watchings, in fastings; by pureness, by knowledge, by long-suffering, by kindness, by the Holy Ghost, by love unfeigned; by the word of truth, by the power of God, by the armour of righteousness on the right hand and on the left; by honour and dishonour, by evil report and good report; as deceivers, and yet true; as unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and behold we live; as chastened, and not killed; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.

units.la: HOrtatus est nuper Paulus Corinthios, ut curent, ne gratiam Dei in vanum receperint, sed fide constanti & moribus vere Christianis salutem suam tueantur. Vt efficacior apud illos esset adhortatio ista, rationibus eam confirmauit, quarum prima a tempore sumitur, cuius occasionem non debeant negligere: alteram a proprio exemplo producit, docens, se nihil ab ipsis requirere, quod non ipsemet faciat, qui totus in eo fit, ne cui scandalum praebeat, sed se fideli Dei ministru esse factis & studijs suis omnibus publice testetur. Quod vero in genere proposuit, id nunc diligentius explicat per partes, & amplius suo exemplo docet, quibus virtutibus vacare & studere debeant, quicunque Deo probari volunt. Quia ergo ista omnium institutioni seruiunt, singula ex ordine videbimus.
units.tr: Paul has recently exhorted the Corinthians to take care that they do not receive the grace of God in vain, but that they keep their salvation by a steadfast faith and by lives truly Christian. To make this exhortation more effective with them, he confirmed it with reasons. The first is taken from time, whose opportunity they must not neglect. The second he draws from his own example, teaching that he asks nothing of them that he does not do himself. He is entirely given over to this, so that he gives no one offence, and by his deeds and all his efforts he shows publicly that he is a faithful minister of God. What he proposed in general terms, he now explains more carefully, part by part, and by his own example he teaches more fully which virtues all who wish to please God must cultivate and pursue. Since these serve the instruction of all, we shall look at each one in order.

units.la: Primo loco tolerantiam siue patientiam ponit, qua hic ceu fundamento aliarum virtutum opus est, quia omnes qui volunt pie viuere in Christo, persecutionem patientur, neque ex verbi semine fructus aliquis nasceatur, nisi patientia armati per omnia obstacula & propriae carnis illecebras eluctemur. Ideo patientiam multam sibi tribuit, ut offendat, non modica aut vulgari opus esse, quando multa undiq; occurrunt, quae Dei seruis molestiam & labores exhibent. Ne tamen patientiam iactare videatur, qua nulla opus sit (vt hodie personati Apostolici inter amplissimas opes atq; omnis generis delitias se multa pro Ecclesia Christi & publica salute pati atq; sufferre gloriantur,) multas & diuersas afflictionum species, quibus exercentur, enumerat.
units.tr: In the first place he sets down tolerance, or patience, which here is needed as the foundation of the other virtues. All who want to live godly lives in Christ will suffer persecution, and no fruit can spring from the seed of the Word unless we, armed with patience, struggle through every obstacle and the allurements of our own flesh. So he ascribes to himself much patience, to show that it is no small or ordinary thing, since many things meet us on every side that bring trouble and toil to the servants of God. Yet, lest he seem to boast of a patience that has no need of it (as today the masked Apostolic men, amid the greatest riches and every kind of luxury, glory that they suffer much for the Church of Christ and the public good), he lists the many and various kinds of afflictions with which he was exercised.

units.la: In his primae sunt necessitates, per quas penuriam rerum necessariarum intelligit, qua illum saepius laborauisse, ex eo apparet, quod interdum manuum suarum labore victum sibi parauit. Id vero credentium eius saeculi ingratitudinem arguit, qui tanto Apostolo tam illiberaliter prospe-xerunt. xerunt, cum interea gentium sacrifici & malorum daemonum mystae splendidè viuerent atque voluptuarentur. Sed est hæc sors seruorum Dei in hoc mundo, qui mendacia Veritati præferti, & ideo impostoribus magis quàm Verbi diuini administris fauet. Sic olim in speluncis pane & aqua non sine periculo alebantur Prophetæ, cum Baalis Sacerdotes ex regia mensa delitiaren-tur. Nemo igitur hodie offendatur, si quid simile accidit. Meminerint autem ingratissimi homi-nes, plerunque diabolo tandem ea cedere, quæ Christo & eius seruis negantur.
units.tr: Among these the first are necessities, by which he means the lack of things needed for life. That he often laboured under this is clear from the fact that at times he provided for himself by the labour of his own hands. Yet this condemns the ingratitude of the believers of that age, who provided so meanly for so great an Apostle, while the sacrificers of the Gentiles and the initiates of the wicked demons lived splendidly and indulged themselves. But this is the lot of the servants of God in this world, who prefer lies to Truth and therefore favour impostors more than the ministers of the divine Word. So in former times the prophets were fed in caves on bread and water, not without danger, while the priests of Baal lived in luxury from the royal table. Let no one, therefore, be offended today if something similar happens. But let the most ungrateful men remember that, in the end, what is denied to Christ and his servants usually goes over to the devil.

units.la: Secundo angustiæ siue anxietates nominantur: quibus pericula ineuitabilia intelligit, quæ nos omnis consilij & auxilij incertos reddunt. Tale fuit, quod in Asia ei accidit, quando de vita sua iam quasi desperauerat, vt Cap.primo audiuimus. Tertiò plagarum meminit, quas ipsum non semel perpessum esse constat. Nam Philippis virgis caesus, & apud Lystrenses lapidatus quo-que fuit. Infra quoque scribet, se à Iudæis quinquies plagas quadragenas, vna modò minus, accepisse. Quarto carceres addit, quibus eum frequenter conclusum fuisse, non est dubium, cùm to-ties verbera & plagas sustinuerit. Memorabilis tamen præ aliis est historia, quæ Actô.16. Cap. describitur de carceris custode ad fidem Christi conuersò per miraculum, quod in Paulo & Syla, qui in vinculis detinebantur, æditum esse videbat.
units.tr: Second, he names straits, or anxieties, by which he means unavoidable dangers that leave us uncertain of all counsel and help. Such was what happened to him in Asia, when he had nearly despaired of his life, as we heard in the first chapter. Third, he mentions stripes, which he is known to have suffered more than once. For at Philippi he was beaten with rods, and at Lystra he was also stoned. Later he will also write that he received from the Jews five times forty stripes less one. Fourth, he adds prisons, into which he was often shut; there is no doubt of this, since he endured so many beatings and blows. Yet the story described in Acts 16 is more memorable than the others: the jailer was converted to the faith of Christ through the miracle that he saw happen to Paul and Silas, who were held in chains.

units.la: Coniungit hîs quinto loco tumultuationes. Græca vox agitationes & confusos atque subitos motus significat, qui nos certas sedes habere non sinunt, sed solum subinde cogunt vertere. Quod fere in seditionibus fieri solet, in quibus plerunq; meliores præ aliis periclitantur. Istis vero Paulus iam inde ab initio suæ vocationis exagitatus fuit. Etenim Damasci tota vrbs commota, & præsidia militum portis impositæ fuerunt, vt non alia effugij via ei pateret, quàm per mœnia, ex quibus sportæ impositum discipuli demiserunt. Mox Antiochiæ in Pisidia per seditionem ex finibus eius regionis eiectus fuit. Grauiora autem Lystris passus Derbam se contulit. Eadem eius sors fuit in Macedonia, vbi publicæ seditiones contra illum excitatæ sunt sub legum Romanarum prætextu. Apud Corinthios verò, etsi diutius moram traxerit, parum tamen tuta ei fuit ciuitas illa, adeò vt se illic cum timore & tremore multo versatum esse, in priori epistola testetur. Superauit omnia hæc Ephesina seditio, quam Demetrius aurifaber concitauit, quæ illinc quoque Paulum abire coegit. Et hæc quidem omnia acciderunt, priusquam hanc epistolam scriberet. Ac-cesserunt deinde grauiora Hierosolymis, vbi per seditionem captus, & tandem Romam vsque deductus est.
units.tr: Fifth, he joins tumults. The Greek word means agitations, sudden and confused movements, which do not let us keep a settled home but force us again and again to move on. This usually happens in uprisings, in which the better people are commonly in greater danger than others. Paul was harassed by these from the very beginning of his calling. For at Damascus the whole city was stirred up, and guards were placed at the gates, so that no way of escape lay open to him except through the walls, from which the disciples let him down in a basket. Soon after, at Antioch in Pisidia, he was driven out of that region's borders by a sedition. At Lystra he suffered even worse, and then went on to Derbe. His lot was the same in Macedonia, where public uprisings were stirred up against him under the pretext of Roman laws. At Corinth, though he stayed there longer, that city was not very safe for him, so much so that he testifies in his former letter that he lived there with much fear and trembling. The uprising at Ephesus, which Demetrius the silversmith stirred up, surpassed all these, and it too forced Paul to leave that place. All these things happened before he wrote this letter. Later, at Jerusalem, there were even graver troubles, where he was seized in a riot and at last led all the way to Rome.

units.la: Debet autem hoc loco obseruari singulare diaboli stratagema, quiferè sicubi Euangelium primò prædicatur, illic publicos motus & seditiones excitat, vt ea ratione doctrinam hanc exosam & inuisam reddat. Scit enim optimos quosq; nihil perinde atque seditiones odisse, quibus nihil Reipub. periculosius accidere potest. Exempla huius generis multa vidimus nostro seculo, quæ Euangelij ministros excitare debent, vt prudenter & circumspectè agant, ne importunita-te nimia, aut non necessarijs mutationibus alicui occasionem tumultuandi præbeant. Quin potius commendent diligenter populo obedientiam, quæ magistratibus debetur, & eundem ad patien-tiam potius quàm ad vindictam instruant. Quod si nihilominus absq; ipsorum culpa motus publici exoriantur, tunc quoad eius fieri potest, intrepidi suam stationem teneant, neque illos moueant impiorum calumniæ, qui malum hoc omne ipsis & Euangelio acceptum ferunt. Sic Eliam olim fecisse legimus, quando turbati Israelis crimen ei immerenti Achab obijciebat. Et memorabilis imprimis est D.Ambrosij constantia, qua cum Mediolani propter basilicas, quas Cæsar Arianis tradi volebat, populus tumultuaretur, vsus est. Vide eius epistolam ad Marcellinam sororem, quæ in libro quinto trigesima tertia habetur.
units.tr: Here we must notice a singular stratagem of the devil: wherever the Gospel is first preached, he stirs up public disturbances and seditions, so that by this means he may make this doctrine hateful and odious. For he knows that the best people hate nothing so much as sedition, which can bring no greater danger to the commonwealth. We have seen many examples of this kind in our own age, and they ought to move the ministers of the Gospel to act prudently and circumspectly, lest by excessive importunity, or by unnecessary changes, they give anyone an occasion for tumult. Rather, let them diligently commend to the people the obedience owed to the magistrates, and train them to patience rather than revenge. But if, nevertheless, public disturbances arise without their fault, then, as far as possible, let them keep their position fearlessly, and let them not be moved by the slanders of the impious, who blame all this evil on them and on the Gospel. So we read that Elijah once did, when Achab charged him with the trouble of Israel, though he was innocent. Especially memorable is the constancy of St Ambrose, which he showed when the people at Milan were in an uproar over the basilicas that the emperor wanted to hand over to the Arians. See his letter to his sister Marcellina, which is found in the fifth book, number thirty-three.

units.la: Sed redeamus ad Pauli catalogum, qui sexto loco labores nominat, quos sanè multos & graues sustinuit. Nam in apostolatu suo plus aliis laborauit hinc inde terras obeundo, vt quàm plurimos Christo adduceret. Idem suis humeris Ecclesiarum omnium curam impositam esse sentiebat, cum gentium Apostolus & doctor esset designatus. Quibus accedebat, quòd sæpe manuum labore victu quoq; quærere cogebatur, vt initio diximus. Et poterant de eo Corinthij testari, qui tentoria texentem viderant. Et huc vigiliæ pertinent, quarum simul meminit, & quas partim labor ille textorius requirebat, partim ipsa quoq; docendi functio. Scimus enim non tutum fuisse tunc temporis hominibus Christianis cœtus diurnos habere, & ideo ferè noctu ad audiendum Verbum Dei, ad Sacramentorum distributionem & preces publicas convenire solebant. Exempla habes Act. 12. & 20. cap. Et Plinius secundus in suis ad Traianum Imp. epistolis eiusdem moris meminit. Ex eo per κακοῦ ηλίου initium sumpserunt vigiliæ Papisticæ, vna cum lampadibus & cereis, quæ hodie interdiu quoq; in illorum templis ardent, quibus homines superstitiosi salutis quoq; meritum tribuunt. At longè alia fuit veterum Christianorum conditio, quibus ignaui illi Penelopes sponsi tantum non illudunt & insultant, dum cum populi Christiani ludibrio ijs ad hypocrisim & quæstum abutuntur, quæ illi sic facere olim coacti sunt. Addit hîs Paulus ieiunia quoq; non quidem voluntaria (cur enim ista hic referret?) sed ea quorum ei causa erant vel penuria, vel negotiorum multitudo, vel peregrinationes non minus periculosæ: quàm laboriosæ: in quibus ne cibum quidem suo tempore semper capere licebat: quod Christo quoq; aliquando accidisse scimus, vt propter populi concursum ad mensam non posset accumbere.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul's list. Sixth, he names labours, which he certainly bore in great number and weight. For in his apostleship he laboured more than the others, travelling about many lands so that he might bring very many to Christ. He also felt that the care of all the Churches was laid on his shoulders, since he had been appointed Apostle and teacher of the Gentiles. To this was added that he was often compelled to seek his living by the labour of his hands, as we said at the beginning. And the Corinthians could bear witness to this, for they had seen him weaving tents. To this belong the watchings, which he also mentions, and which were partly required by that weaving work and partly by the duty of teaching itself. For we know that it was not safe in those times for Christians to hold daytime assemblies, and so they usually gathered almost at night to hear the Word of God, to receive the sacraments, and for public prayers. You have examples in Acts 12 and 20. Pliny the Younger, too, in his letters to the emperor Trajan, mentions this custom. From this, through [κακοῦ ηλίου], the Papistic vigils took their start, together with the lamps and candles, which today burn even by day in their temples, and to which superstitious people also attribute the merit of salvation. But the condition of the ancient Christians was quite different. Those idle suitors of Penelope almost mock and insult them, as they abuse for hypocrisy and profit, to the ridicule of the Christian people, the very things that those early Christians were once forced to do. To these Paul adds fastings as well, not voluntary ones (for why would he mention those here?), but fastings whose cause was either want, or the multitude of business, or journeys no less dangerous than laborious, in which he could not always take food even at its proper time. We know that this also once happened to Christ himself, who could not recline at table because of the crowd of people.

units.la: Et ista quidem sunt, in quibus Apostoli patientiam suam exercuerunt: quo loco admonemur, quàm duris quamq; variis casibus Deus seruos suos exagitari sinat. Quod enim Paulo accidit, hoc ipsum multis aliis accidisse scimus, qui Dei seruitio se totos consecrauerunt. Nec temere dictum est: Multæ sunt tribulationes iustorum. Item: Per multas afflictiones oportet nos ingredi in regnum Dei. Neminem ergo hodie similia exempla offendant. Est enim in hoc seculo vallis lachrymarum, neq; à malis immunes sunt, qui mundo & prauis suis desiderijs seruire in animum induxerunt: imò illos interdum horrenda exempla fieri videmus, dum improuisis calamitatibus oppressi, nulla autem spe auxilij diuini suffulti desperant, & belluino vlulatu nequicquam de suis aduersis quiritantur. Itaque soletur nos magnum illud, quod inter nos & illos est discrimen. Nos enim Deum habemus propitium: hunc illi sibi iratum sentiunt. Nobis item per aduersa iter ad cœlos patet, & in illis Christo conformes efficimur: illis verò hæc maiorum & æternorum cruciatuum sunt initia.
units.tr: These are the trials in which the apostles exercised their patience, and they show us how harsh and varied the afflictions are that God allows to batter his servants. What happened to Paul we know has happened to many others who have wholly devoted themselves to the service of God. It was not said without reason: "Many are the afflictions of the righteous." Likewise: "We must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations." So no one today should be scandalised by similar examples. In this world there is a vale of tears, and those who have resolved to serve the world and their own wicked desires are not exempt from evils. Indeed, we sometimes see dreadful examples among them, when they are crushed by unforeseen calamities, have no hope of divine help, and vainly complain of their misfortunes with a beastly howling. Let us therefore be comforted by the great difference between us and them. We have God propitious to us; they feel him angry with them. For us the way to heaven lies open even through adversity, and in them we are made conformed to Christ; for them these are the beginnings of greater and eternal torments.

units.la: Quia verò huius seculi afflictiones per se non seruant, nisi officiû faciamus, subijcit hîs Paulus virtutes verè Apostolicas, quibus homines Christianos instructos esse oportet. Nam se ista, quæ enumerauit, sufferre dicit: In puritate, in scientia, in longanimitate, in bonitate, &c. Primò puritatem nominat. Græce est ἁγνότης, quam castitatem verterunt: vnde occasione arripuerunt superstitiosi, vt locum hunc de Virginitate interpretarentur, quæ tandem impurum illum cœlibatum in Papatu peperit. Sed puritas ista totum hominẽ requirit, & initium eius ex corde est (sicuti Dominus apud Matthæum admonet) & inde ad omnes vitæ actiones extenditur. Decet ea omnes Christianos, & in coniugio quoq; locum habet, cuius thorum Apostolus ἀμίαντον, id est, impollutum dicit. Quò Paphnutius respiciens congressum cum propria coniuge castitatem esse dicebat. Sunt ergo parum Apostolici, qui sub cœlibatus prætextu per omne genus libidinis volutantur. Discant Christi serui alijs exemplar esse in puritate. 1. Tim.4.
units.tr: But since the afflictions of this age do not save us in themselves, unless we perform our duty, Paul adds the virtues that are truly apostolic and with which Christian men ought to be equipped. For he says that he endures these things which he has listed: "in purity, in knowledge, in longsuffering, in kindness," and so on. First he names purity. In Greek it is ἁγνότης [hagnotes], which they rendered as chastity, and from this the superstitious seized an occasion to interpret this passage as referring to virginity, which at last produced that impure celibacy under the Papacy. But this purity demands the whole man, and its beginning is in the heart (as the Lord admonishes in Matthew), and from there it extends to all the actions of life. It befits all Christians, and it also has its place in marriage, whose bed the Apostle calls ἀμίαντον [amianton], that is, undefiled. With this in mind Paphnutius used to say that intercourse with one's own wife was chastity. Those therefore are little apostolic who, under the pretext of celibacy, wallow in every kind of lust. Let the servants of Christ learn to be an example to others in purity. 1 Tim. 4.

units.la: Deinde Scientiam ponit, nimirum rerum spiritualium, quæ ad salutem sunt necessariæ. Comprehendit hæc docendi facultatem, qua nisi minister instructus sit, scientia eius non multùm proderit Ecclesiæ. Obtingit illa à solo Deo, patre luminum, vt Iacobus ait. Opus tamen fludio diligenti & assidua lectione, ad quæ Paulus Timoth. suum hortatur: precibus item ferijs & ardentibus. In his ergo sese exerceant, qui in Verbi ministerio cum laude & fructu aliquo versari volunt. Arguit hoc ignauos & mali exempli ministros, qui procul relictis libris pocula sectantur, aut venationi & aucupijs vacant, obliti nimirum, se ad homines capiendos à Domino destinatos esse.
units.tr: Then he sets down knowledge, of course of spiritual things, which are necessary for salvation. This includes the ability to teach, and unless a minister is equipped with it, his learning will not greatly benefit the Church. It is obtained from God alone, the Father of lights, as James says. Yet it requires diligent study and constant reading, to which Paul urges his Timothy, and likewise prayers, both earnest and fervent. Let those therefore who wish to engage in the ministry of the Word with praise and some fruit exercise themselves in these things. This rebukes the idle and ministers of bad example, who, having abandoned their books, chase after cups, or devote themselves to hunting and fowling, forgetting, of course, that they have been appointed by the Lord to catch men.

units.la: Tertio longanimitatis meminit, de qua dictum in prioris epist.cap.13. Opponitur ea iræ præcipiti. Opus illa doctori, cùm quia Dei minister (sc. qui tardus ad iram esse dicitur: tum quia hoc requirit hominum prauitas & contumacia, quæ nisi arte tractetur, fere incurabilis solet fieri. Neq; hic ministrum alicuius laboris & studij pigere debet, quando videmus quàm patientes et induστrij sint, qui elephantes, vrsos aut equos feroces instituere & cicurare statuerunt. Parum ergo proficiunt, qui mox ad excommunicationis fulmen recurrunt, aut gladio cædendos iudicant, qui vel in minimo ipsis contradixerint. Vtinam illi de colligendis potius ad Ecclesiam hominibus cogitarent, deq; ijs retinendis, qui sponte secessionem parant. Audiant illi Paulum Timotheo suo sic dicentem: Seruum Domini non oportet pugnare, sed placidum esse erga omnes, aptum ad docen-dum, tolerantem malos, cum lenitate erudientem eos, qui contrariè sunt animo affecti, si quando det eis Deus, vt conuersi agnoscant veritatem, &c. 2. Tim.2.
units.tr: Third, he mentions longsuffering, of which we spoke in the chapter 13 of the earlier epistle. It is opposed to hasty anger. A teacher needs it both because he is a minister of God (who, we are told, is slow to anger) and because the perversity and obstinacy of men demand it, which, unless they are handled with skill, are usually made almost incurable. Nor ought a minister to shrink from any labour or pains of this kind, when we see how patient and industrious those are who have undertaken to train and tame elephants, bears, or fierce horses. Those therefore accomplish little who at once have recourse to the thunderbolt of excommunication, or judge that men should be cut down with the sword if they have opposed them in even the smallest matter. Would that they thought rather of gathering men into the Church and of keeping hold of those who are preparing to secede of their own accord. Let them hear Paul saying thus to his Timothy: "The servant of the Lord must not fight, but must be gentle towards all, apt to teach, patient towards the wicked, correcting with gentleness those who are opposed to him, if perhaps God may grant them that they, having been converted, may recognise the truth," and so on. 2 Tim. 2.

units.la: Quarto bonitas ponitur, quæ cum longanimitate coniuncta est, & placidos facit, qui se om-nibus faciles & commodos præbent. Ex his ergo æstimari debent homines Christiani. Nam licet Paulus de seipso loquatur, & proinde eius exemplum imprimis ad Verbi administros pertineat, idem tamen hoc toti Corinthiorum Ecclesiæ proponit, vt ijsdem virtutibus omnes studeant, ne Dei gratiam in vanum receperint. Ad ista ergo sese examinent, quicunque nomen Christianum profitentur, ne corrupti mores falsi eos arguant.
units.tr: Fourth, kindness is set down, which is joined with longsuffering and makes men gentle, who show themselves easy and agreeable to all. By these qualities Christian men ought to be judged. For although Paul speaks of himself, and his example therefore pertains chiefly to the ministers of the Word, he nevertheless sets the same before the whole Church of the Corinthians, so that all may strive after the same virtues, lest they have received the grace of God in vain. Let all who profess the Christian name therefore examine themselves by these, lest corrupt morals convict them of falsehood.

units.la: At non sunt ista nostrarum virium, & ne ea præstemus ingenij nostri prauitas nobis impedi-mento est. Ne quid ergo Paulus sibi ipsi tribuere putetur arrogantius, docet etiam, quibus armis aut subsidijs adiutus ista perficiat. Et hic quidem ante omnia Spiritum sanctum nominat, quo Apostolos instructos fuisse scimus. Ita vero vno verbo omnem sui ministerij gloriam solidè vni Deo transcribit. Simul autem redit ad virtutum catalogum, quas Spiritus ille in nobis efficit, vt ijs tanquam organis vtatur ad ea perficienda, quæ facto opus sunt.
units.tr: But these are not within our own powers, and our own perversity of nature is an obstacle to our achieving them. So that Paul should not be thought to claim anything for himself too arrogantly, he also teaches by what weapons or aids he accomplishes these things. And here above all he names the Holy Spirit, by whom we know the apostles were equipped. In a single word he thus ascribes all the glory of his ministry solidly to God alone. At the same time he returns to the list of virtues which that Spirit produces in us, so that he may use them as instruments to accomplish those things which the deed requires.

units.la: In charitate (inquit) non simulata, in sermone Veritatis, in virtute Dei, in armis iustitiæ dextris ac sinistris. Charitatem primò nominat, quia regulæ instar est, quæ Dei dona omnia si-mul & actiones nostras ad suum finem dirigit, vt nimirum ædificationi aliorum seruiant. Etenim sine illa nihil recte fit, & qui ea destituuntur, ij fere Dei donis abuti solent cum aliorum contemptu & scandalo, vt alibi diximus. Ideo etsi communis sit omnium Christianorum tessera, ea tamen Verbi administri imprimis opus habent: quia nisi eius igne ardeant, aut laboribus & periculis succumbent, aut insolentiores facti omnia agent pro sua libidine. Quàm vehemens autem & quàm syncera fuerit Pauli charitas, eius labores atque pericula testantur: imprimis autem ardens illud studium, quo eorum saluti consultum voluit, quos erga se ingratissimos mortalium esse experiebatur: quales ex parte Corinthij fuerunt, Iudæi item, de quibus alibi diximus. Eius ergo exemplum imitentur, quicunque vel in Ecclesia vel Repub. laborant.
units.tr: "In love unfeigned," he says, "in the word of truth, in the power of God, with the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left." He names love first, because it is like a rule, which directs all the gifts of God and our actions together to their end, namely that they serve the edification of others. For without it nothing is done rightly, and those who lack it usually abuse God's gifts to the contempt and scandal of others, as we have said elsewhere. Therefore, although it is the common watchword of all Christians, ministers of the Word above all need it, because unless they burn with its fire, they will either succumb to labours and dangers, or, becoming more arrogant, will do everything according to their own lust. How vehement and how sincere Paul's love was, his labours and dangers bear witness, and above all that ardent zeal with which he wished to care for the salvation of those whom he found to be the most ungrateful of mortals towards him: such as the Corinthians in part were, and the Jews too, of whom we have spoken elsewhere. Let therefore whoever labours either in the Church or in the commonwealth imitate his example.

units.la: Charitati sermonem veritatis subijcit. Sic dicitur Euangelium, quia Christum prædicat, qui reuera Veritas est, cùm in eo promissiones omnes suum habeant complementum. Estq; hoc ordi-narium Spiritus Sancti organum, per quod fides datur, vt alibi ex epist. ad Roman. docuimus. Idem gladius quoque est, quo Apostoli olim orbem totum debellarunt, & quo etiam hodie Ministri pugnare debent. Nam eo Antichristum in hominum animis iugulari, Paulus in posteriori ad Thessalonicen. docet, & ipsi quotidie experimur. At hic diligenter cauere oportet, ne vllis hominum figmentis hebetetur. Quàm primùm enim ista admiscentur, iam Veritatis sermo dici non poterit.
units.tr: He adds the word of truth after love. The gospel is so called because it proclaims Christ, who is truly the Truth, since in him all the promises have their fulfilment. And this is the ordinary instrument of the Holy Spirit, through which faith is given, as we have taught elsewhere from the epistle to the Romans. It is also the sword with which the apostles once subdued the whole world, and with which ministers ought to fight even today. For Paul teaches in the second epistle to the Thessalonians that Antichrist is slain in the minds of men by it, and we ourselves experience this daily. But here we must take careful heed lest it be blunted by any inventions of men. For as soon as these are mixed in, it can no longer be called the word of truth.

units.la: Addit huic Paulus Dei virtutem, per quam Spiritus Sancti efficacitatem intelligit, quæ in Apostolis sese multis atque variis indicijs exeruit: vtpote magnanimitate, qua aduersus omnia pericula intrepidi constiterunt: mirabili item Euangelij propagatione, qua per omnis generis obstacula eluctati sunt: miraculis quæ multa & maxima ediderunt: impiorum pœnis, quos Satanæ tradiderunt multandos: quæ omnia tam perspicua fuerunt, vt hostibus quoque formidabiles fecerint, sicuti Actio.2.4.5.cap.est videre.
units.tr: Paul adds to this the power of God, by which he understands the efficacy of the Holy Spirit, which showed itself in the apostles by many and various signs: namely by the greatness of spirit with which they stood fearless against all dangers; likewise by the wonderful spread of the gospel, through which they struggled against every kind of obstacle; by the miracles which they performed in great number and magnitude; and by the punishments of the impious, whom they handed over to Satan to be punished. All these things were so manifest that they made even their enemies afraid, as may be seen in Acts 2, 4 and 5.

units.la: Coniunguntur his arma iustitiæ dextra & sinistra. Arma iustitiæ ea dicit, quibus iustitiæ seruitur. His se instructum dicit à dextris & sinistris, adeo vt ad omnem euentum paratus statione m suam fortiter tueri possit. Militi ergo se confert, vt infra quoq; Cap.10. Vt enim Christianorum omnium vita militiæ instar est: sic imprimis eorum, qui Ecclesiæ seruiunt. His enim nunquam non pugnandum est aduersus Satanam, mundum, peccatum, falsos fratres, propriam deniq; carnem, quæ nouas subinde remoras eis obijcit. Itaq; à Dextris quidem gladio Verbi opus est, quo hostem feriant: à sinistris autem scuto fidei, quo tela & ictus hostiles excipiant, vel eludant. His armis diabolo resistitur, & hæc ipsa victoria nostra est, qua mundum vincimus.
units.tr: The arms of righteousness are joined to these, on the right hand and on the left. By "arms of righteousness" he means those by which righteousness is served. He says that he is equipped with these on the right and on the left, so that, ready for any outcome, he can bravely hold his post. He therefore presents himself as a soldier, as he also does below in chapter 10. For the whole Christian life is like military service, and especially that of those who serve the Church. These men must always fight against Satan, the world, sin, false brothers and finally their own flesh, which keeps throwing up new obstacles before them. So on the right hand they need the sword of the Word, with which to strike the enemy; on the left, the shield of faith, with which to catch or deflect the enemy's missiles and blows. By these arms the devil is resisted, and this very victory is ours, by which we conquer the world.

units.la: Debet autem in ista commemoratione Pauli scopus subinde obseruari, qui seipsum quidem omnibus exemplum proponere voluit, simul autem Corinthiorum stoliditate arguere, qui præpostera pseudoapostolorum admiratione decepti, eos in pretio habebant, in quibus nihil cernebatur, quod Christi apostolos deceret. Nam Spiritu Sancto prorsus destituti, suis desiderijs indulgebant: charitate vacui, non Ecclesiæ ædificationem, sed sua commoda quærebant: Veritatis sermonem non pure sed suorum figmentorum paleis adulteratum prædicabant: nulla in ipsis erat Spiritus Dei virtus, sed inani modo ostentatione turgebant: deniq; ignaui milites, vel potius proditores, diabolo locum dabant. Vult ergo, ut tales agnoscant, fidos autem Christi seruos obseruent, qui dignis virtutibus commendentur. Nobis vero o fratres, idem iflorum vsus esse debet, ut fidos doctores à fucis ignauis discernere, & male fidos cauere discamus. Gloriantur quidem plerique Dei Spiritu, at non propterea illis credere, sed (ut Ioannes monet) spiritus probare debemus, an ex Deo sint. Et quis obsecro hodie eos Spiritu Dei duci dixerit, qui nulla necessitate coacti Ecclesias sibi creditas deserunt, vel etiam lucri causa permutant? qui Euangelium susq; deq; faciunt, & doctrinam hominum affectibus accommodant? qui denique ex acie discedunt, quando diaboli machinationibus resistere eos decebat? Nihil nunc de illis dico, qui cum mundo colludunt, & fidus Christi ministris odium conflant, ut ipsi in pretio habeantur.
units.tr: In this recollection of Paul, the aim must be kept in view. He wanted to set himself forth as an example to all, and at the same time to rebuke the foolishness of the Corinthians, who, perverted by their admiration for false apostles, held in high esteem those in whom nothing could be seen that befits the apostles of Christ. For, utterly destitute of the Holy Spirit, they indulged their own desires; empty of love, they sought not the building up of the Church but their own advantage; they preached the word of truth not purely but adulterated with the chaff of their own inventions; there was no power of the Spirit of God in them, but they puffed themselves up with empty display; in short, they were idle soldiers, or rather traitors, who gave place to the devil. He therefore wants them to recognise such men, and to observe the faithful servants of Christ, who are commended by worthy virtues. But for us, brothers, the same use of these matters ought to be made: that we learn to distinguish faithful teachers from idle drones, and to beware of those who are untrustworthy. Many boast of the Spirit of God, yet we must not believe them for that reason, but (as John warns) we ought to test the spirits, whether they are from God. And who, I ask, would say today that those are led by the Spirit of God who, though compelled by no necessity, desert the churches entrusted to them, or even change them for gain? Who make the Gospel of no account, and adapt the teaching of men to their passions? Who, finally, withdraw from the battle line when they ought to be resisting the machinations of the devil? I say nothing now of those who collude with the world and stir up hatred against the faithful ministers of Christ, so that they themselves may be held in esteem.

units.la: Cæterum ne vanus ardelio putaretur Paulus, ad rem ipsam accedit, & quæ tam ipsius quam Apostolorum omnium conditio sit, & per quam varia obstacula his donis armati eluctentur, diligentius exponit, sic dicens: Per gloriam & ignominiam, per convitia & laudes: ut seductores, & tamen veraces: ut ignoti, & tamen noti, &c. Primo, approbamus (inquit) nos ut Dei ministros per gloriam & ignominiam, id est, sive in pretio habeamur, sive contemnamur, constanter tamen perginus in functione, quam nobis Deus commisit. Ita ipse exponit, dum subdit: per convitia & laudes. Ab eo autem non temere orditur Apostolus. Paucos enim est videre, qui vel gloriam & laudes publicas, vel ignominiam & opprobria recte ferant. Ut enim natura gloriæ cupidi sumus: ita si ea nobis obtingat, ferè insolentiores facti, nihil nō nobis licere putamus, & potestate nostra abutimur. Hinc est quod fortunam non satis æque omnes ferunt, imprimis autem qui animo seruili præditi sunt, vulgi applausu & fauore excæcati spiritus maiores concipiunt, seq; insolentius efferunt. E contra generosiores, cum aduersa quæuis constanter ferant, contumeliarum tamen & iniuriarum ferè sunt immpatientissimi. Ionam certè ignominiæ nota terruit, ne Dei mandato obediret, qui eum Niniuen abire, & illi ciuitati imminens excidium denuntiare iusserat. Et Ieremias hoc nomine potissimum de sua sorte queritur, quod se omnium opprobrijs atq; conuitijs expositum esse videret. Similes item Dauidis querelas in Psalmis habemus. Imo hæc remora omnibus seculis multos impediuit, quo minus ad cognitionem Christi peruenirent, quod publicam infamiam metuerent. Exempla eius rei in Iudæorū Scribis & Pharisæis Euangelica historia proponit. Et quid hodie multi patiantur, notius est, quam ut opus sit narrare. Itaq; ut in vtramq; partem instructi simus necesse est. Quare quoad gloriam huius seculi, meminerimus, nos nihil ex nobisipsis habere, quod laudem mereatur, & ideo si quid habemus, id ad vnum Deum authore referri debere. Adde, conditionem nostram lubricam esse, nosq; thesaurum salutis gestare in vasis testaceis: & proinde tunc maximè casum timeri debere, quando egregiè stare videmur. Quoad verò contumelias & iniurias, famam quidem & nominis nostri existimationem tueri debemus, quatenus id Dei gloria & Ecclesiæ ædificatio requirit: quod si verò id non datur, & nobis clausa videmus omnia tribunalia, tunc cogitemus nihil nouum aut insolens nobis accidere, beatos autem esse eos, qui propter iustitiam male audiunt apud mundum hunc malum atq; adulterum. Etenim qualescunque nos hic æstimet, nomina tamen nostra in cœlis ascripta sunt, & olim corona iustitiæ donabimur. Luc.10. 2. Timoth.4.
units.tr: But lest Paul be thought an idle busybody, he comes to the matter itself, and explains more carefully what the condition of himself and of all the apostles is, and how, armed with these gifts, they struggle through various obstacles, saying: "By glory and dishonour, by evil report and good report; as deceivers, and yet true; as unknown, and yet well known," and so on. First, he says, "we commend ourselves as ministers of God by glory and dishonour", that is, whether we are held in esteem or despised, we nonetheless persevere steadfastly in the office which God has committed to us. He himself explains this when he adds: "by evil report and good report." The apostle does not begin this lightly. For few are found who bear public glory and praise, or public shame and reproach, rightly. As we are naturally eager for glory, so if it falls to us we often become more insolent, think ourselves permitted in everything, and abuse our power. Hence it is that not all bear good fortune with equal balance, and especially those of servile disposition, who, blinded by the applause and favour of the crowd, conceive greater notions of themselves and carry themselves more arrogantly. On the other hand, the more noble-minded, though they bear adversity steadfastly, are for the most part very impatient of insults and injuries. Jonah was certainly terrified by the stigma of shame, so that he did not obey God's command, who had ordered him to go to Nineveh and proclaim the destruction hanging over that city. And Jeremiah complains of his lot chiefly on this account, that he saw himself exposed to the reproaches and abuse of all. We have similar complaints of David in the Psalms. Indeed this obstacle has hindered many in every age from coming to the knowledge of Christ, because they feared public infamy. The Gospel history sets forth examples of this in the scribes and Pharisees of the Jews. And what many suffer today is too well known to need recounting. Therefore we must be prepared for both sides. As to the glory of this age, let us remember that we have nothing of ourselves which deserves praise, and that therefore, if we have anything, it must be referred to the one God as its author. Add that our condition is slippery, and that we carry the treasure of salvation in earthen vessels; and so we ought to fear a fall especially when we seem to stand most splendidly. As to reproaches and injuries, we ought indeed to guard our name and reputation, so far as the glory of God and the building up of the Church require; but if this is not granted, and we see all tribunals closed to us, then let us consider that nothing new or strange has happened to us, and that those are blessed who are ill spoken of for righteousness' sake in this evil and adulterous world. For however this world judges us, our names are nevertheless written in heaven, and one day we shall be given the crown of righteousness. Luke 10. 2 Timothy 4.

units.la: Sed pergit Paulus: Vt seductores (scilicet iudicamur) & tamen veraces sumus. Sensus est, se non moueri hominum iudicijs, qui impostorem ipsum esse dicant, sed hoc potius agere, ut veritatis minister sit fidelis. Ita affectos esse conuenit omnes Verbi Dei administros. Nam ex improborum calumnijs Veritati nihil decedit, quæ ut sibijpsi semper constat, ita emergit tandem suo tempore, & ofores suos merita ignominia confundit. Sunt ergo stultissimi mortalium, qui hodie à Concilijs pendent, & propter ea de Euangelio dubitant. Quid enim isto traditur aliud, quam quod Scripturæ passim docent, & quod cum principijs religionis Christianæ per omnia conuenit?
units.tr: But Paul goes on: "as deceivers (namely, we are judged) and yet we are true." The sense is that he is not moved by the judgements of men who say that he is an impostor, but rather takes care to be a faithful minister of the truth. All the ministers of God's Word ought to be disposed in this way. For the slanders of the wicked detract nothing from the truth, which, as it always remains consistent with itself, so in time it emerges, and it confounds its slanderers with the shame they deserve. Those, then, are the most foolish of mortals who today depend on councils and on that account doubt the Gospel.
