For what is taught in it other than what the Scriptures teach throughout, and what agrees in every point with the principles of the Christian religion?

units.la: Luc. 10. 2. Timoth. 4. nic? qualia sunt, de Deo uno colendo & adorando, deq; uno Seruatore & Mediatore IESV CHRISTO. Atqui omnia ista diserte in Scripturis per Dei Verbum traduntur, quod in aeter-num manet, quicquid infelix hic mundus blateret.
units.tr: Luke 10. 2 Timothy 4. Such as: that the one God is to be worshipped and adored, and the one Saviour and Mediator, Jesus Christ. Yet all these things are plainly delivered in the Scriptures through the Word of God, which remains for ever, whatever this unhappy world may babble.

units.la: Sequitur: Ut ignoti (scilicet reijcimur) & tamen noti sumus. Ignori dicebantur Apostoli, quòd homines peregrini essent: quod fere solent impij ijs exprobrare, qui ipsorum studijs prauis resistunt. Sic Lothum aduenam dicebant Sodomaei. At Paulus hoc membro perperam aduersariorum iudicium perstringit, qui peregrinitatem & obscuritatem Apostolis exprobrabant, qui tamen ex Spiritus Sancti effectis toti mundo iam abunde noti erant: quòd nimirum Dei serui essent, & huius negotium agerent. Quid, quòd ne mali daemones quidem id ignorabant? Notum est enim, quod spiritus Pythonis de Paulo & Syla Philippis pronuntiauit: Isti homines serui sunt Dei illius summi, qui annuntiant nobis viam salutis. Et apud Ephesios maleficis praestigiatoribus daemon dicebat: IESVM noui, & Paulum scio: vos autem qui estis? Quae ideo diligenter obseruari debent, ut videamus vel ipsius diaboli testimonio conuinci impios, qui ignorantiae praetextum suae contumaciae praetendunt. Admonemur autem hoc loco, in Verbi administris non tam spectandum esse, num natales habeant illustres, quàm num Dei ministri sint. Quia enim hic omnium gentium Dominus est, nemo propter gentem repudiatur. Ut ergo Regum legatis fides habetur, quia regij legati sunt, neque in eorum natales curiosius inquiritur: ita multo magis hoc in ijs observari debet, qui Dei legatos agunt, ut nuper Cap. quinto diximus.
units.tr: Next: "as unknown (namely, we are rejected), and yet we are well known." The apostles were called unknown because they were foreigners, which the wicked are wont to throw in the faces of those who resist their wicked pursuits. So the Sodomites called Lot a stranger. But Paul, in this clause, strikes at the mistaken judgement of his adversaries, who reproached the apostles with being foreign and obscure, when in fact, through the effects of the Holy Spirit, they were already abundantly well known throughout the whole world, since they were servants of God and were carrying on his business. Indeed, even the evil demons did not fail to know this. For it is well known that the spirit of the Python, speaking of Paul and Silas at Philippi, declared: "These men are servants of the most high God, who announce to us the way of salvation." And at Ephesus the demon said to the magicians: "I know Jesus, and I know Paul; but who are you?" These things ought to be carefully noted, so that we may see the wicked convicted even by the testimony of the devil himself, who put forward ignorance as a pretext for their obstinacy. We are admonished at this point that in the ministers of the Word we should look less to whether they have illustrious birth than to whether they are ministers of God. For since he is the Lord of all nations, no one is rejected on account of his people. Just as the envoys of kings are believed because they are royal envoys, and no inquisitive enquiry is made into their birth, so much more should this be observed in those who act as envoys of God, as we said recently in chapter 5.

units.la: Addit his Paulus: Ut morientes, & ecce viuimus. Id est, ea est nostra conditio, ut inter mille mortes versari, & iam nunc periisse videamur, & ideo nobis multi insultant: sed ecce viuimus, nimirum Dei virtute, qui inter pericula & in media morte nos seruat. Et emphasin habet particula ECCE. Ea enim stupidos illos pungit, qui Apostolos propter pericula contemptu dignos putabant, non obseruabant autem manum Dei ipsos tam fideliter protegentis. Ita hodie fit: imò fidelium ministrorum mortem multi auidè expectant, & ex ea sibijpsis certam victoriam polli-centur. Sed ecce viuunt illi, & viuit spiritus eorum, qui in successoribus aliquando efficacius agit, ut in Elisaeo olim factum fuisse videmus. Et huc refer, quae de duobus Prophetis siue testibus habentur in Apocalyp. Capite 11.
units.tr: Paul adds to these words: "As dying, and behold we live." That is, such is our condition: we dwell amid a thousand deaths, and already we seem to have perished, and therefore many mock us. "But behold, we live" — surely by the power of God, who preserves us amid dangers and in the very midst of death. The particle ECCE has emphasis. For it pricks those dullards who thought the Apostles worthy of contempt on account of their dangers, but did not observe the hand of God protecting them so faithfully. So it happens today: indeed, many eagerly await the death of faithful ministers and promise themselves certain victory from it. But behold, they live, and their spirit lives, which at times works more effectively in their successors, as we see was once done in Elisha. And refer to this what is found about the two prophets or witnesses in Apocalypse chapter 11.

units.la: Sed quae sequuntur, audiamus: Ut qui castigamur, nec tamen occidimur. Loquitur de perpetuis afflictionibus, quibus videbantur ab ipso Deo castigari, ut qui id suis sceleribus meruissent. Sed non occidimur, inquit. Quasi diceret: non vincunt nos afflictiones istae, quò minus salui & incolumes emergamus. Quo loco Chrysostomus nō ineptè obseruauit, afflictionum fructum denotari. Sunt hae castigationum instar, quibus Deus carnem nostram vel coercet, vel excitat, ne cum mundo incurabili & poenitere nescio condemnemur. Quia ergo earum nobis administri sunt hostes nostri, ijdem tunc quàm maximè benefaciunt nobis, quando nos volunt perdere.
units.tr: But let us hear what follows: "As chastened, and yet not killed." He speaks of continual afflictions, by which they seemed to be chastened by God himself, as men who had deserved this by their sins. "But we are not killed," he says, as if he said: these afflictions do not overcome us, so that we do not emerge safe and sound. In this place Chrysostom has observed, not unsuitably, that the fruit of afflictions is indicated. They are like chastisements, by which God either restrains or rouses our flesh, lest we be condemned together with a world that is incurable and does not know how to repent. Therefore, since our enemies are the ministers of these afflictions, they then do us the greatest good when they wish to destroy us.

units.la: Ideo subijcit Paulus: Ut dolentes, semper tamen gaudentes. Id est, nunquam non quidem nobis doloris materia obijcitur, quoad carnis iudicium: sed interim perpetuò gaudemus, quòd nimirum eo honore nos dignatur Deus, ut pro nomine eius aliquid feramus, quodq; illum in nobis vi-demus triumphare. Exemplum huius dicti in Apostolis habes Actio. 5. Cap. Et imprimis huc pertinet locus in epistola ad Romanos Cap. 5. vbi gaudij huius causae diligentius ex ordine exponuntur. Quibus adde, quòd pro afflictionum ratione, consolationes quoq; abundant, ut in primo Cap. huius epist. audiuimus. Etenim fidelis est Deus, qui nos supra vires tentari non finit. Haec qui attentius obseruant, ij in medijs doloribus gaudij veri & solidi materiam inueniunt.
units.tr: Therefore Paul adds: "As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing." That is, the matter of sorrow is never wanting to us, so far as the judgment of the flesh goes; but meanwhile we rejoice continually, because God deigns to honour us so that we bear something for his name, and because we see him triumphing in us. You have an example of this saying in the Apostles, Acts chapter 5. And especially to this belongs the passage in the epistle to the Romans chapter 5, where the causes of this joy are set out more carefully in order. To these add that, in proportion to the afflictions, consolations also abound, as we heard in the first chapter of this epistle. For God is faithful, who does not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength. Those who observe these things more attentively find in the midst of sorrows the matter of true and solid joy.

units.la: Additur his maius quid: Ut pauperes, sed multos ditantes. Ingratitudinem Corinthijs & omnibus horum similibus exprobrat: qui Apostolos propter paupertatem & inopiam despicatui habebant, à quibus ipsi aeternis Regni caelorum bonis ditabantur: neq; interea animaduertebant, se prae-cipuos esse egestatis Apostolorum authores, cùm eos negligerent, quibus ut patribus suis in Christo debebant prospicere. Quid verò de nostri seculi hominibus iudicari debet, quorum multi per Euangelium diuites fiunt, etiâ quoad hoc seculum: ijdem verò eius ministros cane & angue peius oderunt, eosdem cum inopia & fame conflictari sinunt, deinde autem contemptu dignos putant, eò quòd pauperes sint? Meretur horum scurrilitas graues poenas, quas suo tempore Deus ab eis exiget.
units.tr: Something greater is added: "As poor, yet making many rich." He reproaches the Corinthians and all like them with ingratitude: they held the Apostles in contempt on account of their poverty and want, though they themselves were enriched by them with the eternal goods of the kingdom of heaven; nor did they meanwhile notice that they themselves were the chief causes of the Apostles' destitution, since they neglected those whom they ought to have provided for, as their fathers in Christ. But what ought to be judged of the men of our own age, many of whom become rich through the Gospel, even as to this present age, yet hate its ministers worse than dog and snake, allow the same men to struggle with want and hunger, and then think them worthy of contempt because they are poor? The buffoonery of these men deserves heavy punishments, which God in his time will exact from them.

units.la: Cap. VI.
units.tr: Chapter VI.

units.la: Nunc postremum huius loci membrum videamus: Nihil habentes, sed omnia obtinentes, sive possidentes. Etenim omnia reliquerant Apostoli, & incertis sedibus oberrabant: ijdem tamen omnia obtinebant, quae ad vitae huius vsum erant necessaria. Quia vbique gentium erant homines Christiani, à quibus excipiebantur, & pro suae functionis dignitate tractabantur. Galatas certè hoc nomine Paulus commendat, quòd si fieri potuisset, oculos quoque suos effodissent ipsi dedissent. Et hoc illud est, quod discipulis suis Christus promisit: fore nimirum, vt qui propter ipsum & Euangelium eius relinquunt domos, agros, parentes, fratres, centuplum recipiant in hoc seculo, & in futuro vitam aeternam. Alia longè est hodie Apostolicorum Romanensium conditio, qui cum omnia possideant, pauperes tamen haberi volunt, & cum Regibus quoque dominentur, seruos tamen seruorum se dicunt. Quod quid aliud est, quam cum hominibus ludere sub Christi & religionis praetextu? Continet verò totus ille locus vniuersam doctrinam & consolationem, quam inter afflictiones meditemur. Est enim eadem omnium Christianorum fors. Nemo igitur secundum speciem externam iudicet, sed quales ijdem sint in Dei conspectu, diligentius expendat: & mox in illorum ignominia gloriam, in exilijs patriam verè stabilem, in doloribus vberrimam gaudij materiam, in morte denique vitam ipsis constare videbit. Vt enim athletae vulnerantur quidem, sed per vulnera coronas accipiunt: ita pij per vulnera & mille mortes ad immarcesibilem iustitiae coronam contendunt, quam illis praeparauit fidelis ille agonothetes, IESVS CHRISTVS, Dominus noster: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Now let us look at the last member of this place: "Having nothing, yet possessing all things." For the Apostles had left everything and wandered about without fixed dwellings; yet they nevertheless possessed all things that were necessary for the use of this life. For there were Christian men everywhere among the nations, by whom they were received and treated according to the dignity of their office. Paul certainly commends the Galatians on this account, because, if it had been possible, they would have plucked out their own eyes and given them to him. And this is what Christ promised to his disciples: that, namely, those who for his sake and the Gospel's leave houses, fields, parents, brothers, will receive a hundredfold in this age, and in the future age eternal life. The condition of the Roman Apostolics today is quite different: though they possess all things, they nevertheless wish to be considered poor, and though they rule even with kings, they call themselves servants of servants. What else is this than to trifle with men under the pretext of Christ and religion? That whole passage contains the entire doctrine and consolation which we should ponder amid afflictions. For all Christians share the same lot. Let no one therefore judge by outward appearance, but let him weigh more carefully what they are in the sight of God; and soon he will see that in their shame lies glory, in exiles a truly stable homeland, in sorrows the most abundant matter of joy, and in death finally life. For as athletes are indeed wounded, yet receive crowns through their wounds, so the godly, through wounds and a thousand deaths, strive for the unfading crown of righteousness, which that faithful president of the games, JESUS CHRIST, our Lord, has prepared for them: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXVII.

units.la: Os nostrum apertum est erga vos, Corinthij, cor nostrum dilatatum est, Non habitatis angustè in nobis, sed angusti estis in visceribus vestris. Loquor autem vt filijs de pari compensatione: Dilatamini & vos. Ne alieno iugo copulemini cum infidelibus.
units.tr: Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians, our heart is enlarged. You are not cramped in us, but you are cramped in your own affections. I speak to you as to children, asking for a fair return: enlarge yourselves too. Do not be yoked together with unbelievers.

units.la: Apostoli non solùm fidem in IESVM CHRISTVM docent, qua hunc & in ipso exhibitam nobis salutem amplectimur: verumetiam sedulò hortantur, vt in fide illa constanter in finem vsque perseueremus. Et huc facit tota huius Capitis tractatio. Huius enim summa est, vt Corinthij curent, ne Dei gratiam in vanum receperint: sed ita se gerant, vt ipsorum vita atque mores professioni fidei respondeant. Vtq; maioris momenti atque efficacior esset exhortatio ista, inter alias rationes commune Apostolorum exemplum adduxit, multis exponens, per quam multas quamq; graues difficultates atq; angustias ipsis eluctandum sit, vt sefidos Dei ministros esse probent. Caeterum ea erat Corinthiorum conditio, vt non admonitione vel exhortatione solummodo opus haberent, verumetiam increpationem seueriorem mererentur. Hanc ergo nunc subijcit, sed ita eandem temperat, ne eos, quos ferociores & intractabiliores esse sciebat, magis irritet: vtq; id e medio tollat, quod ipsius admonitionibus authoritatem derogabat: Nimirum, quòd nō recte erga ipsum essent affecti. Itaq; exemplu memorabile hic locus proponit, quo omnes Ecclesiarum ministri discant, vt ipsi quoq; eos tractare debeant, quorum vitia correptione seueriorem requirunt.
units.tr: The apostles not only teach faith in Jesus Christ, by which we embrace him and the salvation offered to us in him, but also earnestly exhort us to persevere constantly in that faith to the end. The whole treatment of this chapter bears on this. Its chief aim is that the Corinthians take care not to have received God's grace in vain, but conduct themselves so that their life and morals match their profession of faith. To make this exhortation weightier and more effective, among other reasons Paul sets forth the common example of the apostles, explaining through how many great difficulties and distresses they had to struggle in order to prove themselves faithful ministers of God. Yet the Corinthians' condition was such that they needed not only admonition and exhortation but also deserved a sterner rebuke. He now therefore adds this rebuke, but tempers it so as not to provoke further those whom he knew to be fiercer and more unmanageable. He also removes what undermined the authority of his admonitions, namely that they were not well disposed toward him. So this passage sets before us a memorable example, from which all the ministers of the churches may learn how they too ought to deal with those whose faults require a sharper correction.

units.la: Principio, suum erga illos amorem atq; studium declarat, vt increpationis acerbitatem mitiget. Os nostrum apertum est erga vos Corinthij, cor nostrum dilatatum est, &c. Aperto ore loqui dicuntur, qui libere & ingenuè dicunt, quod res est. Itaque sensus huius loci est: Libere vobiscum ago, nec quicquam dissimulo, quo minus quod intra animum sentio, id verbis quoque diserte eloquar. Et eius libertatis mihi causa est, quòd cor meum erga vos dilatatum est, id est, toto animo vos complector, & si possem, cor ipsum vobis impartiri velim, quo cùm non opus habeatis, hoc saltem ita dilatauì, vt omnibus vobis capiendis sufficiat. Est verò hoc magni amoris & studij ardentissimi argumentum. Nam si quos ex animo diligimus, cum ijs magno cum desiderio & libere colloquimur de ijs rebus, quas ipsis vtiles & necessarias esse scimus, & in eosdem nos totos effundere cupimus. Ista verò omnia in eum finem à Paulo dicuntur, vt Corinthios sibi conciliet, ne quae dicturus erat, ex odio vel inuidia manare putarent. Admonentur autem hoc exemplo omnes Ecclesiarum ministri, ut ipsi quoq; liberè & aperto ore loquantur, nec aliquid in cuiusquam gratiam dissimulent. Sunt enim Veritatis ministri, quâ vete- res nudam finxerunt, eò quòd latebras nullas quærit, neq; eam suijpsius pudet. Deinde, ut ita fiat, mundi huius improbitas & contumacia requirit, in quo plerique tergiuersantur, & vel ignorantiam prætexunt, vel quæ dicuntur, nihil ad se pertinere putant: eorum nimirùm similes, de quibus Dominus apud Ezechielem disserit, quòd Verbum suum perinde ut cantilenam aliquam audiat. Multi etiam quàmuis intra animos suos abunde conuicti sint, tamen respondere audeant, & Deo obloqui. Ideo speculatoribus conferuntur Prophetæ, & ijsdem tuba tribuitur, libera nimirùm & intrepida Verbi prædicatio, qua delinquentium vitia publicè arguant, & quosuis ad resipiscentiā excitent. Et Christus Dominus, quando ad populū verba facturus erat, os aperuisse, & interdum clamasse quoq; dicitur. Idem Apostolos quoq; monet, ut liberè & super tecta diuulgent, quæ ipsis in aurem dicantur. Qua in re illos fidelissimos fuisse, acres illæ concionès testantur, quas Hierosolymis ad populū & ad Senatum fiue Concilium eius loci habuerunt. In Paulo certè tam intrepida fuit dicendi libertas, & tâ ardens fidei sincerioris zelus, ut Petro quoq; publicè resistendum esse putarit, cum illum videret non satis recto pede secundum Euangelij veritatem incedere. Istorum ergo exempla imitetur ministri, neq; huius seculi sapientes audiant, qui ipsis sub modestiæ & charitatis prætextu silentium mandare & liberiorem Verbi prædicationem impedire satagunt. Sunt hi nimium alieni à primitiuæ Ecclesiæ ingenio atq; moribus, quæ feruente persecutione & undiq; imminentibus periculis, publicas preces pro Apostolis concipere solebat, ut cum omni libertate sermonem prædicarent, &c. Vide Actò. 4.
units.tr: First, he declares his love and zeal toward them, to soften the harshness of the rebuke. "Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged," and so on. Those are said to speak with an open mouth who speak freely and frankly what is the case. So the sense of this passage is: "I deal with you frankly, and I conceal nothing, so that I will also express in plain words what I feel within my mind." The reason for this freedom is that my heart is enlarged toward you, that is, I embrace you with my whole soul, and if I could, I would wish to impart my very heart to you. Since you have no need of it, I have at least enlarged it so that it suffices to receive all of you. This is indeed a sign of great love and most ardent zeal. For if we love certain people from the heart, we speak with them freely and with great eagerness about those things which we know to be useful and necessary for them, and we long to pour ourselves out wholly upon them. Paul says all these things with this end in view: that he might win the Corinthians to himself, so that they would not think that what he was about to say came from hatred or envy. All the ministers of the churches are admonited by this example to speak freely and with an open mouth too, and not to dissemble anything for anyone's favour. For they are ministers of Truth, whom the ancients pictured naked, because she seeks no hiding places and is not ashamed of herself. Next, the wickedness and obstinacy of this world require that this be done, in which most people shirk their duty, either pretending ignorance or thinking that what is said does not concern them. They are clearly like those of whom the Lord speaks in Ezekiel, who hear his word as if it were some song. Many, even though they are thoroughly convicted in their own minds, nevertheless dare to answer back and speak against God. Therefore the prophets are compared to watchmen, and the trumpet is given to them, that is, the free and fearless preaching of the Word, by which they publicly reprove the sins of wrongdoers and rouse anyone to repentance. Christ the Lord too, when he was about to speak to the people, is said to have opened his mouth and sometimes even to have cried out. He likewise bids the apostles to proclaim freely and from the housetops what is whispered to them. That they were most faithful in this matter is attested by those keen sermons which they delivered at Jerusalem to the people and to the senate or council of that place. In Paul there was certainly such a fearless freedom of speech, and such a burning zeal for purer faith, that he thought he must resist Peter openly when he saw him not walking uprightly enough according to the truth of the gospel. Ministers should therefore imitate these examples, and not listen to the wise men of this age, who strive to impose silence on them under the pretext of modesty and charity and to hinder the freer preaching of the Word. They are too far removed from the spirit and manners of the primitive Church, which, amid fierce persecution and dangers threatening on every side, used to offer public prayers for the apostles, that they might preach the word with all freedom, and so on. See Acts 4.

units.la: Cæterùm, quia hucusq; non multum apud Corinthios profecerat Paulus, & multi hoc ipsius ut tio siue culpa accidisse calumniabantur, qui nimium imperiose cum ipsis egisset, ita sese excusat, ut rè moram, quæ suæ doctrinæ seu prædicationis fructu huncusq; impedierit, in ipsis fuisse ostendat. Non habitatis angustè in nobis, sed angustiæ estis in visceribus vestris. In Græco habetur στενοχωρεῖσθε, quod in loco angustiori habitare significat, vbi ita coarctaueris, ut neminem prætereà ad te possis recipere. Id verò per Metaphoram ad animum transferens, sic vult dicere: Ego cor meum ita aperui vobis atq; dilatauì syncero amoris affectu, ut vobis omnibus apud me locus sit amplissimus, nec mihi graue est vos simul omnes, quotquot estis, animo meo copletti (Sic ipse in Cap. proximo exponet; dicens: Capite nos, nam ante dixi, vos esse in cordibus nostris ad simul moriendum, & ad simul vi- uendum.) Quòd autem meo hoc studio minus proficio, id ex eo est, quòd vos in vestris visceribus coarctamini: dum videlicet sinistro affectu, & nescio qua suspicione præoccupati, corda vestra quasi contrahitis: ut mihi non perinde apud vos locus sit: aliter haud dubiè de me iudicaturi, si meum erga vos studium, meas item curas & labores rectius inspiceretis. Itaq; eiusdem amoris recompensationem ut filijs præcipio: Dilatamini & vos: ut nimirum simili studio & amore me complettamini, quo ego vos completti soleo. Hic verborum istorum sensus est. Latet ergo sub illis non obscura ingratitudinis exprobratio. Quasi diceret: Quàm verò indignum est, me apud vos, qui multi estis, non tantum studij inuenire, quantum ego vnus in vos singulos confero? Ego enim vnus vobis omnibus in meo corde locum do, & hoc mihi voluptè est, vos in animo meo inscriptos gestare, deq; vobis vbiq; gentium gloriari: vos autem multi me vnum non capitis, &c. Poterat hoc, prout ipsi merebantur, multis & grauioribus verbis amplificare: sed quia aliquos irritabiliores esse sciebat, acerbitatem huius exprobrationis patris similli mitigat, quando se patris instar non aliud exigere dicit, quàm ut pari amore ipsum vicissim diligant. Et sanè erat hæc æquissima petitio, cùm alibi testatus esset, se ipsorum patrem esse in Christo, neq; hoc illi possent negare, cùm per eius ministerium regeniti essent in Dei filios. Vide 1.Cor. 4.
units.tr: Moreover, since Paul had not made much progress among the Corinthians up to this point, and many were slandering that this had happened through his fault or defect, because he had dealt too imperiously with them, he excuses himself in such a way as to show that the hindrance which had so far stood in the way of the fruit of his teaching or preaching lay in them. "You are not cramped in us, but you are cramped in your own affections." In the Greek it is στενοχωρεῖσθε [stenochōreisthe], which means to dwell in a narrow place, where you have so confined yourself that you can receive no one else into yourself. Transferring this figuratively to the mind, he means to say: "I have opened and enlarged my heart to you with a sincere affection of love, so that there is the very widest room for all of you in me, nor is it burdensome to me to hold all of you, however many you are, together in my mind." (He himself explains this in the following chapter, saying: "Make room for us; for I said before that you are in our hearts to die together and to live together.") But that I make less progress in this zeal of mine comes from this: that you are confined in your own affections, while you, preoccupied with a hostile disposition and some suspicion I know not what, as it were draw in your hearts, so that I do not have a corresponding place among you. Assuredly you would judge of me otherwise if you looked more rightly upon my zeal toward you, and likewise my cares and labours. Therefore, as to children, I command a return of the same love: "Enlarge yourselves too," that is, that you may embrace me with the same zeal and love with which I am accustomed to embrace you. This is the meaning of these words. Beneath them, therefore, lies no faint reproach of ingratitude, as if he said: "How unworthy it is that I find among you, who are many, not as much zeal as I alone bestow upon each one of you! For I alone give a place in my heart to all of you, and it is my delight to carry you inscribed in my mind and to boast of you among all nations; but you many do not contain me, who am one..." He could have amplified this in many and weightier words, as they deserved; but because he knew some to be more irritable, he softens the harshness of this reproach by calling himself a father, saying that as a father he asks for nothing other than that they love him in return with equal love. And indeed this was a most just request, since he had elsewhere testified that he was their father in Christ, and they could not deny this, since through his ministry they had been born again as sons of God. See 1 Cor. 4.

units.la: Describitur autem hoc Pauli exemplo ingenium verè & syncerę dilectionis. Solet illa hominū corda dilatare, ut suū studium & beneuolētiam ad omnes alios, adeoq; ad quosuis obuios extendat. Causa eius est, quòd in omnibus inueniunt, quæ ipsos ad commiseratio nem excitare possunt: quàdo alij in corpore affliguntur, alij cum paupertate conflictantur, alij animis suis sauciį sunt, & sub dura con scientiæ sarcina laborant. Ut ergo bonus ille Samaritanus visò seminece illo, quem latrones multis vulneribus mulctauerat, mox totis visceribus incaluit, atq; eius misertus opem illi tulit pro virili: ita Christiani homines affecti esse solet, quos diuinus ille charitatis ignis semel accendit. Præterea
units.tr: By this example of Paul is described the nature of true and sincere love. It is accustomed to enlarge men's hearts, so that it extends its zeal and goodwill to all others, and indeed to whomever they meet. The cause of this is that they find in all people things that can move them to compassion: when some are afflicted in body, others struggle with poverty, others are wounded in their minds and labour under the heavy burden of a troubled conscience. Just as that good Samaritan, when he saw that half-dead man whom robbers had mauled with many wounds, straightway his bowels were moved, and taking pity on him he brought him help to the extent of his power, so it is usual with Christians whom that divine fire of charity has once kindled. Moreover

units.la: L l linguas nobis soluit syncera dilectio, ut libere cum illis loquamur, quos videmus admonitione, correptione & consilio indigere. Quid vero de linguis loquor? Imò manus, pedes & membra omnia mo̅ uet charitas, ut quam egentibus debemus opem, libenter conferamus. Sunt ergo à charitate alienis̉simi, qui omnes occasiones quaerunt, quibus corda sua contrahere, & dilectionis officia quibusuis negare possint. Quibus etiam adnumerari debent, qui subdolè & maligne agunt, qui adulantur, simulant, & ita fallunt eos, quos prius falsa aliqua spe inescarunt.
units.tr: Tongues sincere love loosens for us, so that we speak freely to those whom we see in need of admonition, correction and counsel. But why speak only of tongues? Love moves our hands, feet and all our limbs, so that we gladly bring the help we owe to the needy. Those, then, are most estranged from charity who look for every opportunity to close their hearts and to refuse the duties of love whenever they can. Among them must also be counted those who act deceitfully and maliciously, who flatter and pretend, and so deceive those whom they had first enticed with some false hope.

units.la: Videmus item in hoc exemplo, quid vicissim petant ab alijs ij, qui charitate vera ardent. Nimirum non aliud, quàm parem amoris compensationem, id est, ut ipsi quoq; ab ijs redamentur, qui bus se totos impendunt. Sufficit ergo eis, si sua officia alijs accepta & grata esse, seq; vicissim ab illis diligi sentiant. Id vero non tam sua causa requirunt, quàm aliorum, quorum salutem nolunt propter ingratitudinem suam in periculum venire. Arguit hoc auaros Ecclesiarum ministros, quibus nihil sufficit, & quàmuis se Ecclesijs suis charissimos esse, & laboris sui fructum non paenitendum videant, subinde tamen quiritantur, & lucri aut opulentioris stipendij causa de illis deserendis cogitant. Imitantur hos multi alij priuatim, qui omnes non fratres, sed seipsos diligunt, & ex charitate quaestum faciunt.
units.tr: In this example we also see what those who burn with true charity in turn seek from others. Surely nothing more than an equal return of love, that is, that they too be loved by those to whom they devote themselves wholly. It is enough for them if they perceive that their services are welcome and acceptable to others, and that they in turn are loved by them. Yet they ask for this less for their own sake than for the sake of others, whose salvation they do not want to be endangered by others' ingratitude. This rebukes greedy ministers of the Churches, for whom nothing is enough. Although they see that they are most dear to their congregations and that the fruit of their labour is not to be regretted, they still complain from time to time and, for the sake of gain or a richer stipend, think about abandoning them. Many others imitate these in private life; they all love not their brothers but themselves, and make a profit out of charity.

units.la: At simul elucet hic quoq; indigna administrorum Verbi fors, quam plerique eandem cum fidis pa rentibus sibi obtingere senciunt. Vnus pater liberos complures gignit, educat, alit, vestit, singulos deniq; omni amore atq; studio prosequitur, adeò, ut propter illos saepe genium suum defraudet, curis conficiatur, noctes insomnes ducat, & labores atq; peritula quaeuis subeat? At ijdem illi simul omnes ipsum unum, si necessitas exigat, vix alere possunt, & ne ab illicitis quidem abstinet, ut patre aetate & laboribus confectum recreent. Quid, quod qui in una & angusta domo turbam liberorum aluerunt parentes, vix in multis & amplis eorundem iam adultorum aedibus angulum aliquem obtinere possunt, in quo ipsis securis & quietis, quod reliquum est vitae transfigere liceat? Idem solet fidis quoq; doctoribus accidere, qui homines ex Verbi semine regenerant & Christo adducunt, ut in eo seruentur. Exemplo nobis sunt Prophetae veteres, ex quorum numero si vel unum Ieremiam inspicias, hoc à nobis verissimè dictum esse patebit. Quid enim ille non fecit, & quid non pertulit pro populi Iudaici salute, quem ad interitum suum properare videbat? Quoties incautos monuit? quoties cunctatos hortatus est? quoties contumaces corripuit? quoties pro illis apud Deum intercessit? quàm acerbis lachrymis eorundem excidium deflevit? Et ne quid omitteret, cùm Nabuchodonozore in Babylonem sequi posset, vbi quiete & honoribus quoq; frui poterat, maluit tamen cum pauperculis & obscuris illis manere, quos in terra miserè vastata ille relinquebat, ne hos Verbi doctrina atq; consolatio ne fraudaret: imò eosdem non vno modo in se contumeliosos atq; iniquos, in Aegyptum secutus est. Quam vero pro omnibus illis officijs gratiam retulit? Non alia, quàm quòd tam senio, curis & laboribus fatigatum lapidibus obruerunt. Idem de alijs quoq; dici posset. Et quod Corinthij in Paulum designarunt, hoc ipsum alij quoq; Apostoli ab ijs passi sunt, qui eos pro patribus suis debebant agnoscere. Seruat hoc suum ingenium infelix mundus in hunc usq; diem. Nec est quòd iflud miremur, quando Christus olim non meliorem gratiam reportauit ab ijs, quos proprij sanguinis pretio redimere studuit. Et quid in ipsum Deum quotidie impijssimi homines designent, notius est, quàm ut multis demonstrari oporteat. Haec certè causa praecipua est, ob quam pauci ex Euangelio proficiunt.
units.tr: At the same time there shines forth here the unworthy lot of the ministers of the Word, which many feel falls to them in the same way as to faithful parents. One father begets, rears, feeds and clothes several children, and finally pursues each of them with all love and devotion, so much so that for their sake he often cheats himself of his own rest, is worn down by cares, spends sleepless nights, and undergoes labours and hardships of every kind. Yet those same children, all together, can scarcely support that one man, if necessity requires it, and they do not even refrain from unlawful means so as to refresh their father, worn out with age and toil. And what of this: parents who nourished a crowd of children in one small and narrow house can scarcely obtain some corner in the large and spacious houses of those same children, now grown up, where they may be allowed to spend in security and quiet what remains of their life? The same is wont to happen to faithful teachers, who regenerate men by the seed of the Word and bring them to Christ, so that they may be kept in him. The ancient prophets are examples for us; if you look at only one of them, Jeremiah, it will be plain that what we have said is most true. For what did he not do, and what did he not endure, for the salvation of the Jewish people, whom he saw hastening to their own destruction? How often did he warn the heedless? How often did he exhort the hesitant? How often did he rebuke the obstinate? How often did he intercede for them before God? With how bitter tears did he lament their ruin? And, so as to omit nothing, when he could follow Nebuchadnezzar to Babylon, where he could enjoy quiet and even honours, he preferred to remain with those poor and obscure people whom he was leaving in the wretchedly devastated land, so that he would not deprive them of the teaching and consolation of the Word. Indeed, he even followed these same people into Egypt, although they were insolent and unjust towards him in more than one way. What thanks, however, did he receive for all these services? None other than that they stoned him, worn out with age, cares and labours. The same could be said of others as well. And what the Corinthians did to Paul, the other apostles too suffered from those who ought to have acknowledged them as their fathers. Unhappy world keeps this disposition of its own even to this day. Nor is there cause for us to wonder at this, since Christ long ago received no better thanks from those whom he strove to redeem at the price of his own blood. And what the most impious men daily devise against God himself is too well known to need demonstrating to many. This is certainly the chief cause why few make progress from the Gospel.

units.la: Porrò his praemissis, redit nunc ad institutum Apostolus, & quod initio Capitis in genere monuit, ne gratiam Dei in vanum receperint, nunc ad id applicat, quo quàm maximè à fidei veritate auocabantur. Vt vero rem omnem rectius intelligamus, repetenda hic est illorum temporum conditio. Versabantur tunc homines Christiani inter ethnicos & idololatras, penes quos summa erat rerum potestas. Non poterant ergo ab horum commercijs prorsus abstinere quoad ea, quae ad communem vitae vsum spectant. Multi vero longius progressi, ut ciuibus suis, & imprimis magistratibus magis propitijs vterentur, in ijs quoq; cum illis communicabant, quae à professione fidei Christianae erant alieniss ima. Nam sacris illorum astabant, ad epulas in Deorum honorem institutas accedebant, festos dies agebant: nec dubium est, quin spectaculis quoq; interfuerint, quae & idololatriae pars erant (maximè si de ludis Isthmijs sermo fit, qui in vicinia in honorem Neptuni celebrantur, ut Plutarchus in Theseo scribit) & in quibus multa non crudeliter modò, verumetiam turpiter & inhonestè cum multorum publico scandalo fiebant. Accedebant his coniugia cum infidelibus, ad quae defendenda Pauli consilio abutebantur, quod in priori epistola de imparibus coniugijs dederat. Ita fiebat, ut multi quotidie in fide languidiores fierent, multi aliorum sceleribus polluerentur, multi indies in peius proficiendo gratiam Dei tantumnon vacuarent. Itaq; vehementiori correptione opus erat, quam ita adhibet, ut rursus appareat, ipsum non aliquo affectu sinistro abripi, sed honori & saluti ipsorum consultum velle.
units.tr: Having set out these things, the Apostle now returns to his purpose, and what he admonished at the beginning of the chapter in general, that they should not receive the grace of God in vain, he now applies to that by which they were most of all being drawn away from the truth of the faith. To understand the whole matter more correctly, we must here recall the condition of those times. Christians then lived among pagans and idolaters, in whose hands was the supreme power of affairs. They could not therefore abstain altogether from dealings with these men in matters that pertain to the common use of life. Many, however, went further, and in order to use their fellow citizens, and especially the magistrates, more favourably, they also took part with them in those things that were most alien to the profession of the Christian faith. For they stood by at their sacred rites, came to feasts instituted in honour of the gods, and kept festival days. Nor is there doubt that they were also present at the spectacles, which were part of idolatry (especially if the talk is of the Isthmian games, celebrated nearby in honour of Neptune, as Plutarch writes in his life of Theseus), and at which many things were done not only cruelly but also shamefully and dishonourably, to the public scandal of many. To these were added marriages with unbelievers, which they defended by an abuse of Paul's counsel that he had given in the earlier letter concerning unequal marriages. So it came about that every day many grew weaker in the faith, many were polluted by the crimes of others, and many, advancing daily for the worse, almost emptied themselves of the grace of God. Therefore a sharper rebuke was needed, and this he applies in such a way that it becomes clear again that he is not carried away by any sinister feeling, but wishes to consult their honour and salvation.

units.la: Propositio est: Ne iugo alieno copulemini cum infidelibus. Graeca vox ἑτεροζυγεῖν significat iugum alienum ducere, vel iugo alieno copulari: ut quando diversi generis iumenta ad unum iugum copulantur, quod ne fiat, Deus olim in Lege prohibuit. Non arabis (inquit) cum bove & asino simul. Nam quando hoc fit, uterq; iugum alienum ducit. Id verò ad fideles transfert Paulus, & Legis Allegoriam exponit: hoc nimirum Deum velle docens, ne qui ipsius populus dici volunt, cum infidelium operibus atq; studijs communicent. Est praeceptum hoc necessarium valde, cum natura ad malum proclives simus, exemplorum autem, & consuetudinis magna vis sit. At quia illo multi hodie abutuntur, dum temere quosvis abs se dissentientes damnant, & scismata faciunt non necessaria, duo nobis aliquanto diligentius sunt observanda.
units.tr: The proposition is: Do not be yoked together with unbelievers under a foreign yoke. The Greek word ἑτεροζυγεῖν [heterozygein] means to draw a foreign yoke, or to be coupled under a foreign yoke, as when animals of different kinds are yoked to one yoke; God forbade this of old in the Law. "You shall not plough," he says, "with an ox and an ass together" (Deut. 22). For when this happens, each of them draws a foreign yoke. Paul, however, transfers this to the faithful and expounds the allegory of the Law, teaching that God wills that those who wish to be called his people should have no fellowship with the works and pursuits of unbelievers. This precept is very necessary, since we are naturally prone to evil, and the force of examples and custom is great. But because many today abuse it, rashly condemning whoever dissents from them and making unnecessary schisms, two things must be observed by us somewhat more carefully.

units.la: Primum, quorum commercia prohibeat Apostolus? Infideles nominat, non quidem eos intelligens, qui cum fide vera & viva destituantur, eam tamen simulant, & Ecclesiae membra censeri volunt: sed eos, qui professionem à fide alienam sequuntur, & ne dici quidem volunt Christiani: quales illo tempore erant ethnici alienorum Deorum cultores & idololatrae, Iudaei item aperti Dei hostes, & crudelissimi Christi atque Ecclesiae eius persecutores: quales item hodie sunt Turcae, unà cum Papistis contumacioribus, qui Evangelij doctrinam & veram in unum IESVM CHRISTVM fidem haeresem damnant, imò ferro & igne hostiliter persequuntur. Ab horum iugo Paulus homines Christianos iubet abstinere.
units.tr: First, whose fellowship does the Apostle forbid? He names unbelievers, not indeed meaning those who lack true and living faith yet pretend to have it and wish to be counted members of the Church, but those who follow a profession alien to the faith and do not even wish to be called Christians: such as at that time were the pagans, worshippers of strange gods and idolaters, likewise the Jews, open enemies of God and most cruel persecutors of Christ and of his Church. Such also today are the Turks, together with the more obstinate Papists, who condemn the doctrine of the Gospel and the true faith in the one Jesus Christ as heresy, and indeed pursue it hostilely with sword and fire. From the yoke of these Paul bids Christians to abstain.

units.la: Abutuntur igitur hoc praecepto, qui illud de Christianis exponunt, qui vel in articulo aut dogmate aliquo minus necessario ab ipsis dissentiunt, vel aliquo scelere seipsos polluerunt: quos mox ab Ecclesiae consortio excludunt, vel si id non possint obtinere, ipsi ab Ecclesia secessionem faciunt, & ita fieri debere clamant, quia Paulus dixerit: Ne iugo alieno copulemini cum infidelibus. Hoc praetextu fere Anabaptistae Ecclesias scindunt. Sic quidam crassiores Lutherani nos omni commercio fidelium indignos esse dicunt, utpote haereticos & Papistis deteriores, quia crassam illam & plus quam Caperniaticam corporis Christi manducationem, in qua ipsi puppim proramq; salutis collocant, nolumus admittere. Sed utriq; vehementer errant. Iugum enim commune omnibus Christianis est, de quo Christus in Evangelio pronuntiat: Tollite iugum meum super vos, & discite à me, quod mitis sum & humilis corde: & invenietis requiem animabus vestris. Iugum enim meum facile est, & onus meum leve est. Quod verò illud iugum est? Audi illum rursus dicentem: Si quis vult post me venire, abneget semetipsum, & tollat crucem suam quotidie, & sequatur me. Non ergo alienum iugum cum infidelibus ducunt, qui in eiusdem Ecclesiae societate manent cum ijs, qui unum IESVM CHRISTVM Seruatorem profitentur, eius leges probant, ipsi obtemperare studient, in aduersis pro nomine eius perferendis patientes sunt, & fide pura in hunc unum intenti, exemplum eius sibi imitandum proponunt, & si cubi peccarunt, poenitentiam spondent, deq; vitijs suis emendandis serio cogitant. Temerarij autem nimis sunt, qui tales damnant propter dogma aliquod controversum, per quod neq; Christi merito, neq; fidei Christianae principijs aliquid derogatur. Et periculum est, ne qui istos temere damnant, & scismata in Ecclesia faciunt non necessarium, cum diabolo iugum ducant, qui dissensionibus & dissidijs gaudet, dum apertis fidei hostibus laetum spectaculum praebent cum publico Ecclesiae & totius orbis scandalo.
units.tr: Those therefore abuse this precept who apply it to Christians who differ from them on some article or dogma of lesser necessity, or who have defiled themselves with some crime. They straightaway exclude such people from the fellowship of the Church, or, if they cannot achieve this, they secede from the Church themselves, and shout that this must be done because Paul said: "Do not be yoked together with unbelievers." Under this pretext the Anabaptists nearly tear the churches apart. Likewise some cruder Lutherans say that we are unworthy of all fellowship with believers, as heretics and worse than the Papists, because we refuse to admit that crude eating of Christ's body, more than Capernaitic, in which they place the stern and the prow of salvation. But both are gravely wrong. For the yoke common to all Christians is the one of which Christ pronounces in the Gospel: "Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am meek and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light." What then is that yoke? Hear him again saying: "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me." Therefore they do not take on a foreign yoke with unbelievers who remain in the same fellowship of the Church with those who profess one Jesus Christ as Saviour, approve his laws, strive to obey him, are patient in adversities borne for his name, and, intent on him alone with pure faith, set his example before themselves to imitate; and if they have sinned at any time, they promise repentance and think seriously about amending their faults. But they are excessively rash who condemn such people on account of some disputed dogma, by which nothing is taken away from Christ's merit or from the principles of the Christian faith. And there is a danger that those who rashly condemn them, and make unnecessary schisms in the Church, yoke themselves with the devil, who delights in dissensions and quarrels, while they provide a joyful spectacle for the open enemies of the faith, to the public scandal of the Church and of the whole world.

units.la: Alterum hic observari debet, de quibus commercijs Paulus loquatur? Vtiq; non de ijs quae ad communem vitae usum pertinent, sed ijs quibus fidei confessio & religio Christiana vitiatur, aut quae nos palàm à Christo avocant. Quoad enim illa priora, multa nobis cum impijs communia sunt, quibus carere non possumus: utpote Sol, aer, aqua, ignis, telluris proventus, & quae alia sunt huius generis. Sunt etiam commercia cum gentibus externis necessaria, eò quod non omnis fert omnia telus. Itaq; quod alibi Paulus ait, è mundo exeat oportet, qui nulla prorsus in re cum impijs aut infidelibus comunicare velit. Sunt autem alia, quae ut non sunt necessaria, ita religioni & fidei Christianae inimica sunt, & eiusdem professionem polluunt. De his Pauli praeceptum debet intelligi.
units.tr: Here another point must be observed: what kinds of dealings does Paul speak of? Surely not those which pertain to the common use of life, but those by which the confession of faith and the Christian religion are corrupted, or which openly draw us away from Christ. For as to the former, many things are common to us and the impious, and we cannot do without them: such as sun, air, water, fire, the produce of the earth, and other things of this kind. There are also dealings with foreign nations that are necessary, because not every land bears everything. So when Paul elsewhere says, "He must go out of the world," he means one who does not wish to have any dealings whatever with the impious or unbelievers. But there are other things which, though not necessary, are hostile to religion and the Christian faith and pollute its profession. It is of these that Paul's precept must be understood.

units.la: In istis primus locus externo cultui debetur: qui ut ad unum Deum restringi, ita secundum huius praescriptum instituti debet & exerceri. Nam frustra me colunt (inquit ille) docentes doctrinas hominum. Peccant ergo & iugo alieno cum infidelibus copulantur, qui cultibus communicant alienis, qui vel in Deorum alienorum honorem instituti sunt, vel contra Dei institutum exercentur. Sic olim Israelitae peccarunt, quando vitulum aureum erigendo Aegyptiorum in cultu socij facti sunt. Peccarunt ijdem postea quoque, quando cum veri Dei professione Baalis cultum coniungebant, & ita (sicuti Elias ait) in utrumque latus claudicabant. Et hoc ipsum in Corinthijs Paulus in praesenti reprehendit, ut ex Cap. 10. prioris epist. apparet, ubi negat fieri posse, ut simul ex mensa Domini, & mensa daemoniorum comedant. Similis nostrorum culpa est hodie, qui cum Euangelij doctrinam profiteantur, interim tamen Missas audiunt, imagines adorant, peregrinationes suscipiunt, encaenijs & aliis festis superstitiosis intersunt, vel etiam cucullis tecti vitam monasticam sectantur. Gloriantur fere isti fide integra, quam in corde suo retineant. Sed calua est ea excusatio, quia scortationes (ut Prophetae verbis utar) a facie simul & uberibus removere oportet: nec minus professio fidei quam fides ipsa a nobis requiritur. Corde enim creditur ad iustitiam, ore autem fit confessio ad salutem. Et quis obsecro vir bonus uxorem posset ferre, quae corde quidem ipsum amaret, corpus vero suum alijs viris prostitueret?
units.tr: In these matters the first place is owed to external worship, which, as it is restricted to the one God, so must be instituted and practised according to his prescription. For (he says) "they worship me in vain, teaching the doctrines of men." Those therefore sin, and are yoked with unbelievers, who share in alien cults, which are either established in honour of alien gods or are practised against God's institution. So once the Israelites sinned, when by erecting the golden calf they became partners in the worship of the Egyptians. The same people sinned later too, when they joined the worship of Baal to the profession of the true God, and so (as Elijah says) they limped on both sides. Paul rebukes this very thing in the Corinthians here, as appears from chapter 10 of the former epistle, where he denies that they can eat both from the table of the Lord and from the table of demons. Our people are similarly at fault today: while they profess the doctrine of the gospel, they nevertheless attend Masses, adore images, undertake pilgrimages, take part in the encaenia and other superstitious festivals, or even, clothed in cowls, follow the monastic life. Such people boast almost of an entire faith, which they keep in their heart. But that excuse is worthless, because (to use the Prophet's words) harlotries must be removed both from the face and from the breasts; nor is profession of faith required from us any less than faith itself. For "with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." And what good man, I ask, could bear a wife who loved him indeed in her heart, but gave her body to other men?

units.la: Deinde ad hunc censum coniugium quoque pertinet. Est hoc ab ipso Deo institutum in eum finem, ut homo commodius in sanctitate & puritate vera Deo viuere ac seruire possit. Prima igitur in eo contrahendo religionis cura esse debet, ne cum alienis a fide copulemur. Ut enim nexus ille, Christo teste, artissimus est, adeo ut quae parentibus debetur pietas ei cedat: ita plurimum potest in animis permouendis & inclinandis, ut a Deo vero & cultus puritate recedant. Exempla in primi mundi hominibus, in Solomone item, in Ioramo Iosaphati filio & aliis similibus grauissima habemus: quae abunde docent, coniugia imparia non temere olim a Deo seuerissimis legibus prohibita fuisse. Et imprimis memorabilis est actio Esdrae, qui post reditum ex Babylone multorum coniugia rescidit, qui uxores alienigenas siue ethnicas duxerant. Quia ergo in eo Corinthij quoque peccabant, & quod Paulus in priori epist. monuerat, ne fidelis ab infideli coniuge tractabiliori temere discedat, ad hanc licentiam excusandam detorquebant, huic etiam praeceptum istud opponit, ne posthac cum infidelibus copulentur.
units.tr: Marriage also belongs to this category. It was instituted by God himself to this end, that a man might live and serve God more conveniently in holiness and true purity. The first care of religion in contracting it, therefore, must be that we not join ourselves with those alien to the faith. For just as that bond, Christ bearing witness, is most close, so that the piety owed to parents yields to it, so it has the greatest power to move and incline minds away from the true God and the purity of worship. We have the most weighty examples in the men of the first world, also in Solomon, in Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat, and others like them, which abundantly teach that mixed marriages were not lightly prohibited of old by God under the strictest laws. Especially memorable is the action of Ezra, who after the return from Babylon annulled the marriages of many men who had taken foreign or heathen wives. Since the Corinthians too were sinning in this, and to excuse this licence were twisting what Paul had admonished in the former epistle, that a believer should not lightly separate from a more amenable unbelieving spouse, he sets against this also the precept that they should not henceforth be yoked with unbelievers.

units.la: Debent huc etiam foedera & societates referri, quarum eadem plane est ratio. Etenim foedera inire per se licitum, & saepe necessarium est, ut vicini id faciant, cum pacis inter ipsos seruandae causa, tum ut hostibus facilius resistere possint. Abrahamum certe cum vicinis foedus ferijsse legimus, & hoc illi utile fuisse Lothi capti & rursus liberati historia testatur. Fecit illud ipsum filius quoque eius Isaac, nec id Scriptura sacra improbat. At hic ante omnia videre oportet, ut primas semper apud nos teneat foedus, quo nos sibi Deus ante obstrinxit, neue fidutiam, quae in illo uno collocata esse debet, in sociis collocetur. Deinde ne cum palam impijs & hostibus Dei societatem ineamus. Tertio, ne conditiones foederum iniquae sint & impiae, per quas fidei hostibus aliquid detur. Qui enim ista negligunt, multis magnisque difficultatibus se implicant. Nam sociorum fiducia decepti saepe bella non necessaria sibi ipsis accersunt, ex quibus interdum communis patria exitium sequitur: quod olim Zedechiae Regi accidisse constat. Vel a sociis derelicti in extremas angustias deueniunt: quod Ezechias passus est, quando cum Aethiopibus & Aegyptijs contra Dei mandatum, foedus percussit. Adhaec multa videre & ferre coguntur quae nollent, quicunque impiorum foederibus se obstringunt. Languidior in vera religione & pietate fit populus, audaciores autem & ferociores impij facti ex iure foederum multa exigunt & mandant, quorum, si illa nulla essent, non aliquā auderent mentionem facere. Accedit his malis longe gravius: quod opem ferre coguntur interdum ijs, quos Deus perditos vult, & ita cum illis in periculum veniunt. Et haec quidem omnia unus Iosaphat abunde expertus est, postquam cum impio Achabo foederis & affinitatis vinculo iunctus fuit. Quapropter ut coniugia infidelium Deus in Lege prohibuit, ita foederibus quoque illorum interdixit, & ad ea hoc etiam Pauli praeceptum potest extendi. At si in ijs caute agere nos conuenit, quae per se licita se licita sunt, quanto diligentiori cautione opus est in illicitis, à quibus Christianos homines perpetuò abstinere decet? qualia sunt alea infamis, compotationes luxuriosæ, choreæ & saltationes, mitiliæ mercenariæ societas, & si quæ alia sunt huius generis. Nam qui istis vel ex animi levitate, vel commodi alicuius spe communicant, ij impios in sua proteruia confirmant, religionem suspectam faciunt, seipsos quoq; inquinant, totamq; fidei professionem prophanant: & sequitur interdum manifesta eiusdem abnegatio, vt in Petri exemplo est videre. Meminerint ergo Christiani homines, se populum esse Deo consecratum, qui IESV CHRISTO in baptismo nomen dederit, & proinde procul relictis huius mundi inquinamentis, huic vni constanter adhæreant & bona fide seruiant, qui nouum illud fœdus siue testamentum proprij sanguinis pretio confirmauit, vt nos sibi cohæredes faceret. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Covenants and partnerships must also be referred here, for they have exactly the same reasoning. For to enter into covenants is lawful in itself, and often necessary, as neighbours do it, both for keeping peace among themselves and so that they may resist enemies more easily. We certainly read that Abraham made a covenant with his neighbours, and the story of Lot's capture and rescue attests that this was useful to him. His son Isaac did the same, nor does holy Scripture disapprove. But here above all one must see to it that the covenant by which God has bound us to himself always holds first place among us, and that the trust, which ought to be placed in that one alone, is not placed in allies. Next, that we not enter into fellowship openly with the impious and enemies of God. Third, that the conditions of covenants not be unjust and impious, by which something is given to enemies of the faith. For those who neglect these things entangle themselves in many great difficulties. Deceived by the trust of allies, they often bring upon themselves unnecessary wars, from which sometimes follows the destruction of the common fatherland; as is known to have happened to King Zedekiah of old. Or, deserted by their allies, they fall into the utmost straits, as Hezekiah suffered when, against God's command, he struck a covenant with the Ethiopians and Egyptians. Besides, all who bind themselves by covenants with the impious are compelled to see and bear many things they would not wish. The people grow more languid in true religion and piety, while the impious, made bolder and fiercer by the law of covenants, demand and command many things, of which, if those covenants did not exist, they would not dare make any mention. A far graver evil is added to these: they are sometimes compelled to bring help to those whom God wills to be destroyed, and so come into danger with them. All this Jehoshaphat alone experienced abundantly, after he was joined by the bonds of covenant and marriage to the impious Ahab. Therefore, just as God prohibited marriages with unbelievers in the Law, so he also forbade covenants with them, and this precept of Paul can be extended to them too. But if we ought to act with caution in those things which are lawful in themselves, how much more diligent caution is needed in unlawful things, from which Christians ought always to abstain? Such things are disreputable gambling, riotous drinking-parties, dances and leaping, mercenary soldiering, and whatever others are of this kind. For those who take part in these, whether from levity of mind or in hope of some advantage, strengthen the impious in their wantonness, make religion suspect, pollute themselves too, and profane the whole profession of faith; and sometimes a manifest denial of it follows, as may be seen in the example of Peter. Let Christians therefore remember that they are a people consecrated to God, who have given their name to Jesus Christ in baptism, and so, leaving far behind the pollutions of this world, they should cling constantly to him alone and serve him in good faith, who confirmed that new covenant or testament with the price of his own blood, to make us his co-heirs. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXVIII.

units.la: Quod enim consortium iustitiæ cum iniustitia? & quæ communio lucí cum tenebris? Quæ vero concordia Christo cum Belial? aut quæ pars fideli cum infideli? Et quæ consensio templo Dei cum simulachris?
units.tr: For what fellowship has righteousness with unrighteousness? And what communion has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what part has the believer with the unbeliever? And what agreement has the temple of God with idols?

units.la: INter alia, quibus Corinthiorum fides labefactabatur, præcipuè fere erat consuetudo nimia cum ethnicis & à fide prorsus alienis. Quia enim (vt nuper diximus) Christiani homines illo tempore ethnicis permixti habitabant, imò sub horum potestate erant, multi vt illos sibi æquiores haberent, non contenti necessarijs commercijs, illicitis quoq; communicabant. Id vero Paulus grauissimè reprehendit, & contra illos generale præceptum ex Lege protulit, Ne qui iugo alieno cum infidelibus copulentur. Debent hoc ipsum hodie etiam obseruare, quotquot Christo nomen dederunt, & fidem in eum profitentur. At ea est humanæ rationis cæcitas, vel contumacia potius, vt pauci hoc sibi persuaderi patiantur, multis verò hæc præcipua sapientia esse videtur; si qui se omnium moribus accommodare, & (quod prouerbio dicitur) foro vti possint. Ideo præceptum hoc suum Paulus rationibus grauissimis confirmat, quibus docet, quàm absurdum & ineptum, imò quàm hoc impium & iniquum sit, si fideles cum infidelium operibus atq; studijs communicent.
units.tr: Among the other things by which the faith of the Corinthians was being weakened, the chief one was excessive association with the heathen, who were wholly estranged from the faith. For since (as we said recently) Christians at that time lived mixed in with the heathen, and indeed were under their power, many, in order to be more acceptable to them, not content with necessary dealings, also took part in unlawful things. Paul severely rebuked this, and against them he brought forward the general precept from the Law: "Do not be yoked together with unbelievers." All who have given their name to Christ and profess faith in him ought to observe this same precept today as well. But human reason is so blind, or rather so stubborn, that few allow themselves to be persuaded of this, while to many it seems the chief wisdom, if a man can accommodate himself to everyone's manners and, as the proverb says, play the part of the marketplace. So Paul confirms this precept by very weighty reasons, by which he teaches how absurd and foolish, indeed how impious and unjust, it is for believers to share in the works and pursuits of unbelievers.

units.la: Prima, Quod enim consortium est iustitiæ cum iniustitia? Interrogationibus totam hanc argumentationem figurat, vt magis feriat eorum animos, qui in causa tanti momenti nimium securi erant ac negligentes. Hoc autem primo membro (sicuti Chrysostomus exponit) conferr nobilitatem Christianorum cum ignominiosa infidelium & idololatrarum conditione, vt illos excitet & moneat, ne dignitatem suam turpiter prostituant. Iustitiam enim dicit eos qui credunt: nimirum ad id respiciens, quod supra Cap. 5. dixit, Christum pro nobis peccatum factum fuisse, vt nos in ipso efficeremur iustitia Dei. Perinde ergo hic loquitur, ac si quis generosi alicuius & illustris viri filio, quem inter ganeones & nequissimos sodales turpiter per omne genus scelerum volutari videt, dicat: Quid facis ô dæmens? Cur non cogitas, qui tu sis, & cuius patris filius? qui item illi sint, quos sectari in animum induxisti? Quæ obsecro inter vos est æqualitas? quæ generis, fortunarum, dignitatis & honorum communio? Cur ergo non pudet te istorum, ex quibus nihil præter contumelias & ignominiam sperare potes, quæ aliquando ad totam tuam familiam, ex qua natus es, redundet? Ita in præsenti Paulus cum Christianæ fidei professoribus agit: Quæ hæc cæcitas est ô boni, quæ vos videre prohibet, in quam dignitatem vos euexerit Deus, & quàm infelix & ignominiosa sit istorum conditio, quorum studijs atq; operibus communicatis? Vos etenim in CHRISTO IESV iustitia Dei facti estis: illi quanti quanti sunt, peccatores, iniusti & à Dei iustitia alienissimi sunt. Quod verò inter iustitiam & iniustitiam consortiū esse poterit? Certè vbi hæc regnat, ibi illa exulat. Quin ergo vestram dignitatem sedulò tuemini, ne degeneres aliquando sitis, & à dignitate filiorum Dei prorsus excidatis. Docet autem locus iste, calumniatores impudentissimos esse eos, qui doctrinam de iustificatione fidei bonis operibus inimicam esse dicunt, perq; eam peccandi licentiam introduci. Qui enim iusti sunt, ij iustitiæ student, & fides bona illa arbor est, quæ optimis Deoque iucundissimis iustitiæ, charitatis & obedientia fructibus seipsam commendat, & suos cultores ab omni iniustorum consortio procul abstrahit. Atqui multos videmus (aiunt illi) qui fide quidem gloriantur, vitam vero viuunt sceleratam & impuram. Fateor. Num vero illorum nequitia fidei fraudi esse debet, quæ in omni Scriptura tam præclaris præconijs commendatur? Vel num doctri-nam à Spiritu sancto per Prophetas & Apostolos vnanimi consensu traditam mutabimus pro-pter mendaces fidei professores, quibus olim dicetur: Discedite à me omnes qui iniquè agitis: non enim omnis qui dicit, Domine Domine, intrabit in regnum meum: sed qui fecerit voluntatem Pa-tris mei, qui in cœlis est?
units.tr: The first: "For what fellowship has righteousness with unrighteousness?" By questions he frames the whole argument, so that it may strike more sharply the minds of those who were too secure and careless in a matter of such great moment. In this first member (as Chrysostom explains) he sets the nobility of Christians against the shameful condition of unbelievers and idolaters, so as to rouse and warn them not to prostitute their dignity disgracefully. For he calls those who believe "righteousness," clearly looking back to what he said above in chapter 5, that Christ was made sin for us, so that in him we might be made the righteousness of God. He speaks here just as if someone saw the son of a noble and illustrious man rolling shamefully in every kind of wickedness among gamblers and the most vile companions, and said: "What are you doing, madman? Why do you not consider who you are and whose son? And who are those whom you have resolved to follow? What equality, I beg you, is there between you? What common bond of birth, fortune, dignity and honours? Why then are you not ashamed of these men, from whom you can hope for nothing but insults and disgrace, which will at some time reflect on your whole family from which you were born?" In the same way Paul deals here with the professors of the Christian faith: "What blindness is this, good people, that prevents you from seeing to what dignity God has raised you, and how unhappy and disgraceful is the condition of those whose pursuits and works you share? For you have become the righteousness of God in Christ Jesus; they, however many they are, are sinners, unrighteous, and utterly alien from God's righteousness. What fellowship, then, can there be between righteousness and unrighteousness? Surely where the one reigns, the other is banished. Why then do you not carefully guard your dignity, lest you ever become degenerate and altogether fall from the dignity of the sons of God?" This passage also teaches that those are most shameless slanderers who say that the doctrine of justification by faith is hostile to good works and that it introduces a licence for sinning. For those who are righteous strive after righteousness, and faith is that good tree which commends itself by the best fruits of righteousness, charity and obedience, which are most pleasing to God, and which keeps its worshippers far away from all fellowship with the unrighteous. "Yet we see many," they say, "who indeed glory in faith, but live a wicked and impure life." I grant it. But ought the wickedness of these men to be a disgrace to faith, which is commended in all Scripture with such glorious praises? Or shall we change the doctrine delivered by the Holy Spirit through the Prophets and Apostles with one accord, on account of lying professors of faith, to whom it will one day be said: "Depart from me, all you who work iniquity; for not everyone who says, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter into my kingdom, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven"?

units.la: Secunda ratio est: Quæ communio luci cum tenebris? Christus lux mundi est, & idem suo in mundum aduentu omnes illuminat, quotquot ipsum cum fide recipiunt. Ideo Paulus Ephesijs scri-bebat: Eratis quondam tenebræ, nunc autem lux in Domino, vt filij lucis ambulate. Et quod Chri-stus discipulis dicebat: Vos estis lux mundi, hoc ipsum ad omnes pertinet, qui Euangelium per ipsos prædicatum profitentur. Ideo ex eo dicto generalem doctrinam ille infert: Sic luceat lux vestra co-ram hominibus, vt videant vestra bona opera, glorificentq; Patrem vestrum, qui est in cœlis. Quia ergo Christiani lux sunt, quis non videat, quàm absurdum sit, si ijdem cum tenebris communicare ve-lint, id est, cum mundo, qui tenebris gaudet, lucem vero odit, cuius radijs & fulgore opera eius pra-ua arguuntur? Habes hoc loco quod illis respondeas, qui necesse omnino esse dicunt, vt mundo nos accommodemus, cùm impossibile sit ab omni eius consuetudine abstinere. Etenim ipsi quoq; supra di-ximus, multa esse hominibus Christianis cum impijs atq; infidelibus communia, quoad huius vitæ vsum. Veruntamen cum eorundem prauis operibus, superstitione, idololatria communicare nequa-quam debemus. Alibi Paulus monet: Pacem habete cum omnibus, quantum in vobis est. At quàm primum de Dei cultu deq; obedientia, quam huic debemus, agitur, nequaquam in nostra potestate est ab ijs vel latum vnguem discedere, quæ ille nobis mandauit. Et quis non ineptum dixerit esse eum, qui lucernam, quæ gressus eius dirigere debebat, ipse tenebris & caligine obruat?
units.tr: The second reason: "What communion has light with darkness?" Christ is the light of the world, and by his coming into the world he enlightens all who receive him with faith. So Paul wrote to the Ephesians: "You were once darkness, but now are light in the Lord; walk as children of light." And what Christ said to the disciples, "You are the light of the world," applies to all who profess the Gospel preached by them. So from that saying he draws a general doctrine: "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven." Since, then, Christians are light, who does not see how absurd it would be for them to wish to have fellowship with darkness, that is, with the world, which delights in darkness and hates the light, by whose rays and brightness its evil works are exposed? Here you have an answer for those who say it is altogether necessary for us to accommodate ourselves to the world, since it is impossible to abstain from all its customs. For we ourselves have said above that there are many things common to Christians and to the impious and unbelieving, so far as the use of this life is concerned. But we must by no means share in their wicked works, superstition and idolatry. Paul elsewhere advises: "Live at peace with all, as far as lies in you." But as soon as the worship of God and the obedience we owe to him is at stake, it is by no means in our power to depart even a hair's breadth from what he has commanded us. And who would not call foolish the man who himself smothers with darkness and gloom the lamp that ought to guide his steps?

units.la: Sequitur tertia ratio: Quæ vero concordia Christo cum Belial? Iam ad vtriusq; partis siue fa-ctionis capita accedit. Fidelium enim caput Christus est, infidelium Belial siue diabolus, qui & princeps huius mundi dicitur. Ille iustitia est, sanctitas, lux, veritas, vita, fons deniq; & author vitæ vnicus. Diabolus è contra iniustus, impurus, immundus, tenebrarum princeps, mendax, ho-micida. Christus, vt nos redimeret, æterno Patris decreto sese humiliter submisit, obediens faetus vsq; ad mortem, & quidem mortem crucis: Diabolus autem, vt nos totos perdat, Deo hostiliter re-sistit, & omni eius iugo procul excusso (vnde Belialis nomen accepit) aduersus illum fremit atq; tu multuatur. Non poterunt ergo vnquam duo isti inter se conuenire. Imò in ipsa rerum origine hoc dissidium inter illos sancitum est, Deo ad serpentem dicente: Ponam inimicitiam inter te & mu-lierem, inter semen tuum & semen illius: Ipsum conculcabit tibi caput, & tu percuties aut mordebis ipsum in calcaneo. Neq; hoc ipse Satan, quantùmuis mendax & impudes diffitetur. Quoties enim in Euangelio illum ex infelicibus illis, quos totos obsederat, clamantem audimus: Quid mihi tecum rei est IESV, fili Dei? Venisti ante tempus ad nos cruciandum. Quàm ergo absurdè & iniquè agunt, qui cùm Christi cultores dici & haberi velint, cum diaboli seruis atq; mystis commercia ha-bent non necessaria, & quæ cum fidei Christianæ professione pugnant? Transfuga & proditor ha-betur, qui in hostiū castris cum illis colloquia occulta habere deprehenditur. Quis ergo fidelem Chri-sti militè dicat eū, qui cū diaboli seruis familiarius conuersatur, & cum eorundē studijs cōmunicat? Hoc vtinam diligentius expenderet, qui non contenti vulgaribus commercijs, insuper iuratos dia-boli seruos, magos nimirum, præstigiatores, incantatores, veneficos, diuinatores consulunt. Tales olim Deus ex populo suo excindere iussit; quare indigni sunt, qui inter Christianos nomen habe-ant. Itaq; vel hinc æstima, quid de toto clero Papistico iudices, quando nemo ignorat, artes illas in nullo hominum genere frequentius & maiori cum audacia exerceri, quàm inter sacrificulos & mo-nachos, quorum alij circa eas occupantur, vt tam propriè quàm aliorum curiositati satisfaciant: alij vero vt libidinē expleant, vel etiam de ijs sese vlciscantur, quibus malè volunt. Quid verò de Pontificibus Maximis dicemus, ex quorum numero multi per eiusmodi cum diabolo cōmercia ad sedem illam apostolicā (vt ipsi loquuntur) peruenerunt, vel artibus illis infames facti sunt? Nota certè sunt omnibus, quæ in historijs de Syluestro II. Gregorio VII. Alexandro VI. & similibus traduntur.
units.tr: There follows the third reason: "What agreement has Christ with Belial?" Now he comes to the heads of each party or faction. For Christ is the head of believers, and Belial, or the devil, is the head of unbelievers, who is also called the prince of this world. Christ is righteousness, holiness, light, truth, life, indeed the fountain and the sole author of life. The devil, on the contrary, is unrighteous, impure, unclean, the prince of darkness, a liar and a murderer. Christ, to redeem us, by the eternal decree of the Father humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death, and indeed the death of the cross. But the devil, in order to destroy us utterly, resists God with hostility, and having shaken off all his yoke (whence he received the name Belial), he rages and rushes in tumult against him. These two therefore can never come to terms with each other. Indeed, this enmity between them was established at the very origin of things, when God said to the serpent: "I will put enmity between you and the woman, between your seed and her seed; he shall crush your head, and you shall strike or bite him in the heel." Nor does Satan himself, however lying and shameless he is, deny this. For how often in the Gospel do we hear him crying out through those unhappy people whom he had wholly possessed: "What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us?" How absurdly and unjustly, then, do they act who, while wishing to be called and regarded as worshippers of Christ, have unnecessary dealings with the servants and initiates of the devil, dealings that fight against the profession of the Christian faith? A man who is caught holding secret conversations with the enemy in the enemy's camp is regarded as a deserter and a traitor. Who, then, would call faithful a soldier of Christ who associates more familiarly with the servants of the devil and shares in their pursuits? I wish those would weigh this more carefully who, not content with ordinary dealings, consult sworn servants of the devil, namely magicians, charlatans, enchanters, poisoners and diviners. God once commanded such people to be cut off from his people; therefore they are unworthy to have a name among Christians. So from this alone judge what you should think of the whole Papist clergy, since no one is unaware that those arts are practised more frequently and with greater boldness in no class of men than among the sacrificing priests and monks, some of whom are occupied with them in order to satisfy their own curiosity as well as that of others, and others in order to indulge their lust, or even to take revenge on those whom they wish ill. And what shall we say of the Supreme Pontiffs, of whom many through such dealings with the devil came to that apostolic see (as they themselves put it), or were made infamous by those arts? The things related about Sylvester II, Gregory VII, Alexander VI and others like them in the histories are certainly known to all.

units.la: Sed pergit Paulus, & quartum huius argumentationis membrum infert, in quo apertius ipsas personas utriusque partis inter se confert, Quae pars (inquit) fideli cum infideli? Id est, quid habent isti commune, quod inter eos diuidi oporteat? Num Christum? Atqui hic ad infideles non pertinet. Num Euangelium? Atqui huius lucem infideles oderunt & extinctam volunt. Num gratiam Dei? Atqui huius participes sunt soli credentes, super eos autem qui non credunt, manet ira Dei, ut Baptista testatur. Num Regnum coelorum? Atqui huius quoque haereditas fidelibus solis destinata, infidelibus autem tenebrae exteriores praeparatae sunt, vbi est fletus & stridor dentium. Num cultum externum & morum disciplinam? At in his quoque summa est inaequalitas. Illi enim in Spiritu & Veritate Deum colunt, hi vero circa ceremonias frigidas & inutiles occupantur. Hi morum honestati studeunt, & disciplinam patienter ferunt, illi vero cum licenter & turpiter omnia faciunt, tamen neque legibus bonis, neque correptione aliqua volunt coerceri. Quod si ergo nihil inter partes istas commune est, certe multo minus societas aliqua inter eas esse debet in iis, quae ad religionem spectant: & nimium absurde faciunt, qui cum illorum cultu externo vel caeteris studijs communicant. At hic meminisse oportet, haec imprimis ad festa pertinere.
