Hinc enim de istis dicendi occasionem Paulus arripuit, quod multi ex Christianorum numero ad sacras & solennes epulas ethnicorum accederent, ut in priori epistola audiuimus. Nobis ergo haec dici putamus, qui Euangelij quidem doctrina gloriamur, interim vero tam gentium quam Papistarum festa celebramus, & in eo quaerimus praecipuam vtilitatem, quod nos omnium affectibus possimus accommodare. Semper ergo nobis comparatione istam occinamus, nos ab omni impiorum non necessario consortio impollutos seruemus.
units.tr: But Paul goes on, and draws the fourth member of this argument, in which he more openly compares the persons of the two parties with each other: "What part," he says, "has the believer with the unbeliever?" That is, what do these people have in common that must be divided between them? Christ? But he does not belong to unbelievers. The Gospel? But unbelievers hate its light and want it extinguished. The grace of God? But only believers partake of it, while upon those who do not believe the wrath of God remains, as the Baptist testifies. The kingdom of heaven? But its inheritance is destined for believers alone, while for unbelievers the outer darkness is prepared, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth. External worship and the discipline of morals? But here too the inequality is great. For the one worships God in Spirit and in truth, while the others are occupied with cold and useless ceremonies. The one strives for honesty of life and bears discipline patiently, while the other does everything licentiously and shamefully, and yet will be restrained neither by good laws nor by any correction. If then nothing is held in common between these parties, certainly much less should there be any fellowship between them in matters that pertain to religion; and those act most absurdly who share in their external worship or in their other pursuits. But here we must remember that these things pertain chiefly to festivals. For Paul seized the occasion to speak of them because many from among the Christians attended the sacred and solemn feasts of the heathen, as we heard in the earlier epistle. We think therefore that these things are said to us, who indeed glory in the teaching of the Gospel, yet meanwhile celebrate the festivals both of the Gentiles and of the Papists, and seek in this their chief usefulness, that we may accommodate ourselves to everyone's affections. Let us therefore always sing this comparison to ourselves, and keep ourselves undefiled from every unnecessary association with the impious.

units.la: Porro adhuc propius ad rem ipsam Paulus accedit, hoc quoque addens: Et quae consensio templo Dei cum simulachris? Vbi multa & diligenti obseruatione dignum est, hoc membrum inter ea poni, quorum absurditas omnibus notissima est: Non conuenire scilicet iustitiae cum iniustitia, neque lucì cum tenebris, neque Christo cum Belial, aut fideli cum infideli. Quae cum contradictorie inter se opponantur, simul consistere non possunt. At non minus pro confesso hoc etiam sumit Apostolus, quod neque templo Dei cum simulachris possit conuenire: et proinde indignum esse, ut homines Christiani, qui viuum Dei templum sunt, cum ethnicorum sacris atque simulachris communicent, aut ad epulas accedant, quae inter simulachra in Deorum honorem instituuntur. Ratio huius dicti adducti potest, quod Deus simulachra a cultu suo procul reijcit, quando ne illa a nobis fiant prohibet, & ne ab alijs facta vlla vel interni vel externi cultus specie veneremur. Atqui Dei voluntas, tam diserte expressa nobis sufficere debet, ne quid praeterea quaeramus. Verumtamen, si quis pio & sancto zelo interroget, cur Deus simulachra tam grauiter damnet, & a cultu suo prorsus remota velit, rationes multae & graues adduci poterunt. Prima ex hisce Pauli verbis petitur; qui templo Dei cum simulachris conuenire posse negat. Nam hoc dicendo templum Dei distinguit a templis Deorum falsorum, qui ab infidelibus colountur. In his enim illorum imagines prostare necesse est, quia nihil aliud habent quo commendentur. Etenim Dij illi nulli sunt in rerum natura, ut in priori epist. ad Cap. audiuimus. Oportet ergo imaginibus aut simulachris eorum aeque fictitijs, ut illi sunt, rudi populo fucum fieri, ut eos & esse, & sacris suis propitios adesse credat. At nostep Deus vt reuera est, imo ipse omnium quae sunt ESSE est (qua de causa ab Hebraeis Iehoua dicitur) ita vbique praesens adest, & omnia penetrat atque implet, ideoque eum Graeci Θεὸν dixerunt. Eius enim verba sunt apud Prophetas: Annon Deus de propinquo ego sum, & non Deus de longinquo? Num abscondet se quisquam in latebras, ut eum videre nequeam? Annon caelum & terram ego impleo? Item: Caelum thronus meus est, terra vero scabellum pedum meorum. Quod Dauid probe obseruans dicebat: Quo discedam a Spiritu tuo? & quo a facie tua fugiam? Si ascendero in caelum, tu ibi es: & si sternam lectum meum apud inferos, tu ades. Si sumam pennas aurorae, & habitem in extrema parte maris: etiam ibi manus tua reget me, & dextera tua apprehendet me, &c. Quia ergo Deus omnipraesens est, nullo simulachro opus habet, quo eius tanquam absentis memoria conseruetur: & proinde stultum fuerit, illa in templis, quae ipsi consecrata sunt, colloc are. Deinde per simulachra maiestas Dei (vt Scriptura ait) commutatur cum imagine non homin us modo, verumetiam animalium atque volatilium. Quibus adde, quod Deum aliqua imagine effingere prorsus impossibile est. Est enim immensus, infinitus, omnipotens, & denique, quem neque sensus nostri, neque intellectus aut ratio nostra apprehendere possunt. Quare Propheta reverissimè olim dixit: Cui similem facietis Deum? aut quod namsimulachrum adornabitis ei? Quòd si verò Dei neque essentia neque maiestas imagine aliqua exprimi potest, sequitur, operam & impensas illis perire, qui illud conantur, adeoque simulachra omnia fallacia esse, & falsis imaginationibus veram Dei cognitionem ex hominum animis delere. Quapropter nihil cum illis commune potest habere Deus, qui ipsissima est Veritas. Non minus vere ergo quàm graviter olim Lactantius scripsit: Non est dubium, quin religio nulla sit, ubicunque simulachrum est. Et mox hoc dictum sic probat: Nam si religio ex divinis rebus est, divini autem nihil est, nisi in coelestibus rebus: carent ergo religione simulachra: quia nihil potest esse coeleste in ea re, quae fit ex terra: quod quidem de nomine ipso sapienti apparere potest. Quicquid enim simulatur id falsum fit, necesse est: nec potest unquam veri nomen accipere quod veritatem fuco & imitatione mentitur, &c. Vide lib. Instit. 2. Cap. 19.
units.tr: Moreover, Paul comes still closer to the matter itself, adding this also: "And what agreement has the temple of God with idols?" Here it is worth much careful attention that this member is placed among those things whose absurdity is best known to all: namely, that righteousness does not agree with unrighteousness, nor light with darkness, nor Christ with Belial, or the believer with the unbeliever. Since these are opposed to each other as contradictories, they cannot stand together. But the Apostle takes it no less as granted that the temple of God cannot agree with idols; and therefore it is unworthy that Christian men, who are the living temple of God, should share in the sacred rites and images of the heathen, or attend the feasts which are instituted in honour of the gods before the images. The reason for this saying can be adduced: God casts images far from his worship, since he forbids that they be made by us, and forbids us to venerate any images made by others under any appearance of inward or outward worship. But the will of God, so clearly expressed, ought to suffice us, so that we seek nothing further. Nevertheless, if anyone with pious and holy zeal asks why God condemns images so severely and wishes them utterly removed from his worship, many and weighty reasons can be given. The first is drawn from these words of Paul, who denies that the temple of God can agree with images. For in saying this he distinguishes the temple of God from the temples of false gods, which are worshipped by unbelievers. In these it is necessary that their images stand, because they have nothing else by which they may be commended. For those gods are nothing in the nature of things, as we heard in the earlier epistle at chapter 8. It is necessary, therefore, that by images or likenesses of them, which are as fictitious as they are, a deception be practised upon the rude people, so that they believe both that they exist and that they are present and favourable to their rites. But our God, as he truly is, indeed is himself the BEING of all that is (for which reason he is called Jehovah by the Hebrews), so he is present everywhere, and penetrates and fills all things; and therefore the Greeks called him Theos. For his words are in the Prophets: "Am I a God at hand, and not a God afar off? Can anyone hide himself in secret places so that I cannot see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?" Likewise: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool." David, observing this well, said: "Whither shall I go from your Spirit? or whither shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; and if I make my bed in hell, you are present. If I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost part of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me," etc. Since therefore God is omnipresent, he has no need of any image by which his memory, as of one absent, may be preserved; and therefore it would be foolish to place those things in temples which are consecrated to him. Next, through images the majesty of God (as Scripture says) is changed into the likeness not only of man but also of animals and birds. To these add that it is utterly impossible to portray God by any image. For he is immense, infinite, omnipotent, and, in short, one whom neither our senses nor our intellect or reason can grasp. Wherefore the Prophet very truly said of old: "To whom will you liken God? Or what likeness will you set up for him?" But if neither the essence nor the majesty of God can be expressed by any image, it follows that the labour and expense of those who attempt it are lost, and that all images are deceptive, and by false imaginations blot out the true knowledge of God from men's minds. Therefore God, who is very Truth itself, can have nothing in common with them. No less truly than gravely, Lactantius wrote of old: "There is no doubt that there is no religion wherever there is an image." And soon he proves this saying thus: "For if religion belongs to divine things, and nothing is divine except in heavenly things, then images lack religion, because nothing heavenly can be in that thing which is made from earth; which indeed can be seen from the very name. For whatever is simulated must necessarily be false, nor can that which lies by pretence and imitation ever receive the name of truth," etc. See the Institutes, book 2, chapter 19.

units.la: Colligimus ergo ex his, plus quam puerliter (ne quid gravius dicam) eos delirare, qui aliquem putant esse posse usum imagine in templis Christianorum, ut nimirum nos de Deo et eius operibus admoneant, & librorum instar sint, ex quibus homines illiterati & idiotae discant ea, quae alii ex Scripturis discere solent. Atqui magistros & doctores mendacij vocat Propheta imagines: nimirum, quòd Deum longè alium nobis fingant, quàm revera sit. Et sufficit adversus omnium istorum rationes unicum hoc Apostoli dictum: Quae consensio templo Dei cum simulachris? Neque hic mihi aliquis ogganniat, Paulum de spirituali templo loqui, quod nos sumus. Nam quoad materialia illa, non minus diserte praecepta Dei habemus, quae illa ne in his quidem ferunt. Et videtur hoc loco Apostolus à minori ad maius argumentari: In templis lapideis, quae Dei cultui consecrata sunt, simulachra nulla prostare debent, neque ijsdem bonos aliquos exhiberi debet: multò minus ergo, qui vivum Dei templum, & pretioso Christi sanguine consecratus est, seipsum illis aliquo modo polluere aut prophanare debet. Itaque horum memores, vitemus commercia cum infidelibus non necessaria, fide autem pura & integra adhaereamus uni Deo Patri, per IESVM CHRISTVM, redemptorem & Mediatorem unicum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: We gather therefore from these things that those are more than childish (to say nothing more severe) who think that images can have any use in the temples of Christians, namely, that they might remind us of God and his works, and serve as books from which unlettered and ignorant people may learn what others are accustomed to learn from the Scriptures. Yet the Prophet calls images "teachers of lies," namely because they fashion for us a God quite different from what he really is. And the single saying of the Apostle is sufficient against all their arguments: "What agreement has the temple of God with idols?" Nor let anyone here object to me that Paul speaks of the spiritual temple, which we are. For as to material things, we have no less plainly the precepts of God, which do not allow even these. And the Apostle seems here to argue from the less to the greater: in stone temples, which are consecrated to the worship of God, no images ought to stand, nor should any veneration be shown to them; much less, then, ought he who is the living temple of God, and consecrated by the precious blood of Christ, defile or profane himself with them in any way. Therefore, mindful of these things, let us avoid unnecessary dealings with unbelievers, and cling with pure and whole faith to the one God the Father, through JESUS CHRIST, the redeemer and sole Mediator: to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXIX.
units.tr: Homily XXIX.

units.la: Nam vos templū estis Dei viuentis, sicut dixit Deus: Habitabo in eis, & inambulabo, & ero illorū Deus, & ipsi erunt mihi populus. Quapropter exite è medio eorum, & separamini, dicit Dominus: & impurum ne attingite, & ego suscipiā vos: & ero vobis Pater, & vos eritis mihi filij ac filiae, dicit Dominus Omnipotens.
units.tr: "For you are the temple of the living God, as God said: I will dwell among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. Therefore come out from among them and be separate, says the Lord, and touch nothing unclean; and I will receive you, and I will be a Father to you, and you shall be my sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty."

units.la: Dominus & Seruator noster, IESVS CHRISTVS, discipulis suis admodum graviter dicit: Si de mundo essetis, mundus quod suum est diligeret: quia verò de mundo non estis, sed ego vos selegi de mundo, propterea odit vos mundus. Quibus verbis non modò illos armat adversus odia & persecutiones, quibus pij in mundo exercentur, verumetiam docet, quid nos interea facere conveniat. Nimirum, ut non quidem vicissim odijs certemus, vitemus autem, quoad eius fieri potest fludia mundi, quem Christo tam inimicum esse audimus. Ut enim neque boni filij, neque fidelis subditi est, cum patris sui oforibus aut principis sui hostibus familiarius conversari, vel etiam occultius colludere: Ita neque nos, qui Christo redemptore gloriamur, decet, ut mundo nos conformes faciamus, è quo nos ille sanguinis sui pretio redemit, ut nos totos sibi consecraret. Et hoc illud est, de quo Corinthios suos Paulus in praesenti diligenter admonet. Quia enim tantum sibi ipsis indulgebant, ut putarent licere sibi, ut pacis & concordia publica causa cum ethnicorum idololatria communicarent, docuit, nefas omnino esse, ut cum aliquo ingum ducamus à fidei nostrae professione alieno. Et quàm hoc indignum & iniquum sit, multiplici comparatione, vel potius antithesi aut oppositione demonstrauit. Quod enim consortium (inquit) iustitiæ cum iniustitia? & quæ communio luci cū tenebris? quæ verò concordia Christo cūBelial? aut quæ pars fideli cū infideli? & c. Vbi non oscitanter obseruari debet, quibus titulis siue nominibus eos insigniat, quibus illi placere re studebāt. Dicit eos iniustitiam, tenebras, Belial, infideles. Id verò facit, non conuiciandi libidine, sed vt suam dignitatem cum ethnicorum conditione infelici conferentes, ab eorum studijs prauis abhorrere discant. Estq; admonitio ista plus quam necessaria hodie, quando plerique mundi blan-ditijs sese decipi patiuntur, quòd de illo non rectè iudicent.
units.tr: The Lord and Saviour of us all, Jesus Christ, says to his disciples very seriously: "If you were of the world, the world would love what is its own; but because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you." By these words he not only arms them against the hatred and persecutions with which the godly are harassed in the world, but he also teaches what we ought to do in the meantime: namely, that we should not indeed contend with hatred in return, but should avoid, as far as possible, the pursuits of the world, which we hear is so hostile to Christ. For just as it is not fitting for a good son or a faithful subject to associate familiarly with his father's enemies or the enemies of his prince, or even to collude with them more secretly, so it does not become us, who glory in Christ the Redeemer, to conform ourselves to the world, from which he redeemed us at the price of his blood, that he might consecrate us wholly to himself. And this is what Paul carefully warns his Corinthians about in the present passage. For since they were indulging themselves so far that they thought it lawful to take part in the idolatry of the heathen for the sake of public peace and harmony, he taught that it is utterly wrong for us to yoke ourselves with anything foreign to our profession of faith. And to show how unworthy and unjust this is, he demonstrated it by a manifold comparison, or rather by antithesis or opposition. "For what partnership," he says, "has righteousness with lawlessness? And what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what part has the believer with the unbeliever?" etc. Here we must observe carefully the titles or names by which he marks them, the very things they were eager to please. He calls them lawlessness, darkness, Belial, unbelievers. He does this not out of a desire to revile, but so that, by comparing their own dignity with the unhappy condition of the heathen, they may learn to shrink from their wicked pursuits. And this admonition is more than necessary today, when most people allow themselves to be deceived by the flatteries of the world so that they do not judge rightly about it.

units.la: Quia verò postremum institutæ comparationis membrum fuit, nullam consensionem inter tem-plum Dei & simulachra intercedere posse, id nunc propius applicat Corinthijs, dum ipsos templum Dei esse docet. Nam vos (inquit) templum estis Dei. Id verò ipsius Dei verbis probat: Habitabo in eis, et inambulabo, & ero illorū Deus, & ipsi erunt mihi populus. Desumpta sunt hæc partim ex Leuitici XXV I. partim ex Ezechielis XXXVII. Cap. Apud Mosem enim sic loquitur Domi-nus: Ego ponam tabernaculū meū in medio vestri, & animus meus non fastidiet vos. Ego ambula-bo inter vos, & ero Deus vester, vosque eritis meus populus. Quibus consentiunt plane, quæ per Ezechielem postea dixit: Erit habitaculum meum in eis, & ego eorum Deus, ipsi verò meus erunt populus. Adista Paulus in præsenti alludens, ita dicere videtur: Si cui duriora videntur quæ dixi, vel etiam augusta & magnifica nimis, is non me iflorum authorem, sed hæc Dei verba esse co-gitet, &c. Nec est, vt quis ea de tabernaculo & arca fœderis olim dicta esse existimet. Nam suo populo loquitur Deus, in cuius locum vos successistis: & constat tabernaculum illud cum tota sua supellectile symbolum fuisse præsentiæ Dei, & quod tunc per arcam & propitiatorium adumbra-batur, id nos reuera præstitum habemus in IESV CHRISTO, vero illo Immanuele, de quo Euangelista scripsit: Verbum Caro factum est, & habitauit in nobis, &c.
units.tr: Since the last member of the comparison was that no agreement can exist between the temple of God and idols, he now applies this more closely to the Corinthians, teaching that they themselves are the temple of God. "For you," he says, "are the temple of God." He proves this by the very words of God: "I will dwell among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people." These words are taken partly from Leviticus 26 and partly from Ezekiel 37. For in Moses the Lord speaks thus: "I will set my tabernacle in the midst of you, and my soul shall not loathe you. I will walk among you, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people." Those words are plainly agreed with by what he said afterwards through Ezekiel: "My dwelling place shall be among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people." Paul, alluding to these things in the present passage, seems to say: "If what I have said seems too harsh to anyone, or even too lofty and magnificent, let him consider that it is not my word but God's words, etc." Nor should anyone think that these things were said long ago about the tabernacle and the ark of the covenant. For God speaks to his own people, into whose place you have succeeded; and it is certain that the tabernacle with all its furnishings was a symbol of the presence of God, and what was then foreshadowed through the ark and the mercy seat, we truly have fulfilled in Jesus Christ, that true Immanuel, of whom the Evangelist wrote: "The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us," etc.

units.la: Obseruabis autem hic ineffabilem Dei bonitatem, qua is nos prosequitur. Est hic immensus, infinitus, omnipotens, ipsis quoque cælis sublimior, vt Dauid in Psalmo canit. E contra nihil vi-lius, imbecillius, sordidius homine, siue corpus eius siue animam spectes. Hæc enim peccatis pollu-ta, illud morborum mille generibus obnoxium est, vtraque autem pars simul assiduis curis, dolo-re, laboribus conficitur: quod idem Dauid obseruans, canebat: Domine, quid est homo, quòd ratio-nem illius habeas? & filius hominis, quòd cogites de eo? Homo vanitati similis est, & dies eius vmbræ prætereunt. Verumtamen ita se demittit Deus, vt non modò nos respiciat & curet, ve-rumetiam inhabitet, dum videlicet Spiritum suum cordibus nostris inserit, qui nos illuminat, re-git atque mirificè seruat. Et id quidem non solum de tota credentium Ecclesia, verumetiam de sin-gulis debet intelligi, qui omnes ceu viui lapides (vt Petrus ait) per fidem super Christum, petram illam insuperabilem extruuntur, vt & in singulis Deus habitet, & ex omnibus simul communis illa & magna Dei domus, Ecclesia, coalescat. Et huc illud Christi debet referri: Si quis diligit me sermonem meum seruabit: & Pater meus diliget eum, & ad eum veniemus, & mansionem apud eum faciemus. Hoc vnum quicunq; paulò diligentius expendunt, ij facilè videbunt, quàm absur-dum & indignum sit, hominem, qui viuum & spirituale Dei templum est, imò qui per Christum ad Dei imaginem reparatus est, ad muta & inanima simulachra prosterni, in quibus neq; vita neq; sensus inest aliquis. De talibus certè verissimè illud dictum est: Homo, quando in honore est, non intelligit. Psal. 49.
units.tr: Here you will also notice the inexpressible goodness of God, by which he cares for us. He is immense, infinite, almighty, higher even than the heavens, as David sings in the Psalm. On the other hand, nothing is more worthless, weaker, or more squalid than man, whether you look at his body or his soul. For the one is polluted by sins, and the other is subject to a thousand kinds of diseases; and both parts together are worn down by constant cares, grief, and labours. David, observing this, sang: "Lord, what is man, that you have regard for him? Or the son of man, that you think of him? Man is like a breath; his days are like a passing shadow." Yet God so humbles himself that he not only looks upon us and cares for us, but also dwells in us, namely by inserting his Spirit into our hearts, who enlightens us, guides us, and wonderfully preserves us. And this must be understood not only of the whole Church of believers, but also of each individual, who, as living stones (as Peter says), are built up through faith upon Christ, that unshakeable rock, so that God may dwell in each one, and from all of them together that great common house of God, the Church, may be joined into one. To this also the saying of Christ should be referred: "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him." Whoever weighs this one thing a little more carefully will easily see how absurd and unworthy it is for a man, who is the living and spiritual temple of God, or rather who through Christ has been restored to the image of God, to prostrate himself before dumb and lifeless idols, in which there is no life or sensation at all. Of such people it is most truly said: "Man, when he is in honour, does not understand." Ps. 49.

units.la: Est præterea hic obseruandum, quod Deus dicit: Et inambulabo. Oportuit enim hoc addi, ne quis illum in Ecclesia otiosum stare putet, vt olim fictitiorum Deorum statuæ in gentium templis, et qualem hodie Christum Papistæ fingunt, quem illi ex crustula factum ædiculæ cancellis ferreis munitæ includunt, vbi otiosus stans ab imperitis adoratur. At non talis est Deus noster: qui ita in nobis habitat, vt simul inambulet, omnia nimirum videns, audiens, gubernans. Quomodo enim totam Ecclesiam suam, aut vnicum eius membrum ille negligeret, cuius prouidentia ad flores vsq; in agris nascentes & ad auiculas, imò ad coruorum voracium pullos vsque extenditur? Id verò vt nos in omni tentatione efficacissimè consolatur: ita officij quoque admonet, ne securi & ocitan-tes simus, neq; latebras nostræ ignauiæ aut etiam proteruiæ quæramus inutiles, sed Dei inter nos ambulantis & omnia inspicientis memores, sedulò officium faciamus, cui ille nos destinauit.
units.tr: Furthermore, it must be observed here that God says: "and I will walk among them." For it was necessary to add this, lest anyone think that he stands idle in the Church, as the statues of feigned gods once stood in the temples of the heathen, and as the Papists today fashion Christ, whom they enclose in a little shrine made of wafer-bread and fortified with iron bars, where, standing idle, he is worshipped by the unlearned. But our God is not like this: he so dwells in us that he also walks among us, seeing, hearing, and governing all things. For how could he neglect his whole Church, or any single member of it, whose providence extends even to the flowers growing in the fields, and to the little birds, indeed to the young of the voracious ravens? This truly comforts us in every temptation, and at the same time it admonishes us of our duty, that we should not be careless and idle, nor seek useless hiding places for our sloth or even our wantonness, but, mindful of God who walks among us and sees all things, we should diligently perform the duty for which he has appointed us.

units.la: Christiani sunt templum Dei.
units.tr: Christians are the temple of God.

units.la: Facit ad huius particulae confirmationem quod additur : Et ero illorum Deus, & ipsi erunt mihi populus. Nam Deum alicuius esse, idem est, quod vindicem & protectorem esse. Id vero omnia comprehendit, quae ad veram & perfectam hominis felicitatem faciunt. Etenim Deus ille Schadai dicitur, quia & sibi ipsi & omnibus aliis solus sufficit, inque seipso inclusum habet inexhaustum bonorum omnium, quibus nobis opus est, thesaurum. Ideo Dauid dicebat: Beatus ille populus, cuius Deus est IEHOVA, & felix ea gens, quam ille sibi in haereditatem delegit. Rursus Dei populum esse, est huic consecratum esse, ita ut ab eo uno pendeas, illi uni fidas & obedias, unum illum colas, adeoque in illo uno nobis omnia tibi reposita esse, quaecunque ad huius praesentis & futurae vitae felicitatem faciunt. Hic ergo nobis finis & usus sit omnium, quae Scripturae de Deo praedicant, ut nimirum illum Deum nostrum, id est, tutorem & vindicem nostrum esse firmiter credamus, & procul relictis mundi huius & carnis nostrae studijs, nos totos illi consecremus, ut suo Spiritu nos inhabitet atque regat. In eo enim verae pietatis atque religionis totius summa sive Colophon consistit, ut & Deum recte agnoscamus, & dignitatem nostram constanter tueamur, in quam ille nos ex gratuita misericordia euexit.
units.tr: What is added serves to confirm this part: "and I will be their God, and they shall be my people." For to be someone's God is the same as to be his defender and protector. And this comprehends everything that contributes to the true and complete happiness of man. Indeed, God is called Shaddai because he alone is sufficient both for himself and for all others, and he has within himself an inexhaustible treasure of all the good things we need. Therefore David said: "Blessed is that people whose God is Jehovah, and happy is the nation which he has chosen for his inheritance." Again, to be the people of God is to be consecrated to him, so that you depend on him alone, trust and obey him alone, worship him alone, and so that in him alone are laid up for us all things that contribute to the happiness of this present life and of the life to come. Therefore this is the end and use of all that the Scriptures proclaim about God: that we should firmly believe that he is our God, that is, our guardian and defender, and that, having put aside the pursuits of this world and of our flesh, we should consecrate ourselves wholly to him, so that he may dwell in us and rule us by his Spirit. For in this consists the sum, or the summit, of all true piety and religion: that we rightly acknowledge God and constantly maintain our dignity, into which he has raised us out of his free mercy.

units.la: Ideo Paulus ijs, quae modo dicta sunt, nouam exhortationem subijcit, ut illicita & non necessaria gentium atque idololatrarum consortia deuitent. Rursus autem Dei verbis utitur, quibus is olim populum suum allocutus est, ut doceat, eandem adhuc hodie illius voluntatem esse, quae olim fuerit. Quapropter, Exite (inquit) e medio eorum, & separamini, dicit Dominus, & impurum ne attingite, &c. Extat locus ille apud Isaiam in Cap. LII. Vaticinatur illic Propheta de liberatione aut reditu Iudaeorum ex Babylonico exilio, idque ita facit, ut simul vniuersalem humani generis redemptionem, cuius illa typus fuit, describat. Inter alia autem hisce verbis Sacerdotes alloquitur, quorum cura & custodia vasa templi credita erant, ut in profectionibus ea deferrent, sicuti in Lege mandatur. Debebant hi seipsos ab omni immunditia legali puros seruare. Id vero Paulus omnibus Christianis applicat, eo quod nos omnes Christus Deo Patri Sacerdotes fecit, quorum corpora (ut prius diximus) templum Dei viuum, adeoque vasa sunt, quibus Spiritus Sanctus vti dignatur. Monet ergo, ut veteris illius exhortationis memores idem ipsi quoque faciamus, quod olim fuit mandatum. Praestat ergo, ut singulas eius partes siue praecepta ex ordine videamus.
units.tr: Therefore, after what has just been said, Paul adds a new exhortation: that they should avoid unlawful and unnecessary associations with the Gentiles and idolaters. He again uses the words with which God once addressed his people, to teach that his will today is the same as it was then. So: "Go out from among them," he says, "and be separate," says the Lord, "and touch no unclean thing," and so on. That passage is found in Isaiah chapter LII. There the prophet foretells the deliverance, or return, of the Jews from the Babylonian exile, and he does so in such a way that he also describes the universal redemption of mankind, of which that return was a type. Among other things, he addresses the priests, to whom the care and custody of the temple vessels had been entrusted, so that they carried them on journeys, as the Law commands. They had to keep themselves free from all legal uncleanness. Paul applies this to all Christians, because Christ has made us all priests to God the Father, and our bodies (as we said before) are the living temple of God and so are the vessels which the Holy Spirit deigns to use. He therefore admonishes us to remember that old exhortation and to do ourselves what was once commanded. Let us therefore look at its individual parts, or precepts, in order.

units.la: Primum est: Exite e medio eorum. Debebant illi olim ex Babylone exire, vbi totis annis septuaginta captiui fuerant. A nobis autem requirit Dominus, ut Babylonem illam spiritualem relinquamus, quae totum Antichristi regnum comprehendit. Sic enim ipse Christus in Apocalypsi loquitur, quando illius ruinam atque excidium denuntiat: Exite de illa populo mei, ne participes sitis delictorum eius, & de plagis eius ne accipiatis. Non debet tamen hoc simpliciter de solo discessu aut migratione, quae corpore fit, accipi, quasi mox migrandum sit ex omnibus locis, in quibus vel superstitiones exercetur, vel flagitiose & inhonestè viuitur. Ita enim vix aliquis nobis in orbe terrarum angulus reliquus maneret, & ex mundo hoc nobis emigrandum esset, ut alibi Paulus dixit. Saepe autem fit, ut pijs tuto versari liceat inter homines superstitiosos & idololatras, neque cogatur eorum superstitionibus communicare, aut puriioris religionis exercitia omittere. Licet ergo tunc illis manere, quoad non diserto Dei mandato alio euocantur. Itaque hic locus de ipsis superstitionibus intelligi debet, ut his procul relictis, nullam cum eis habeamus communionem. Quod si vero id caueri non potest, nisi loci mutatio fiat, tunc e patrio quoque solo migrandum est, & coniunctissimi quique deferendi potius, quam verae fidei confessio violanda est. Sic Abraham natale solum reliquit, cum Deum sibi dicentem audiret: Exi e terra tua, ex patria tua, & de domo patris tui, ad terram quam ego ostendam tibi. Sic Petrus recte exiuit ex atrio summi Pontificis, cum illic Christi confessioni nullum locum esse videret. Idem faciant quotquot Christo fidem seruare volunt inuiolatam. Nec enim ille temere dixit: Qui amauerit patrem & matrem, filium & filiam supra me, non est me dignus. Matth. 10. Cap.
units.tr: The first is: "Go out from among them." Those men once had to go out of Babylon, where they had been captives for seventy years. From us, however, the Lord requires that we leave that spiritual Babylon, which embraces the whole kingdom of Antichrist. For Christ himself speaks in this way in the Apocalypse, when he announces its ruin and destruction: "Come out of her, my people, that you may not share in her sins, and that you may not receive of her plagues." Yet this should not be understood simply of departure or migration in body, as if we must at once move away from all places where either superstition is practised or people live in a shameful and dishonourable way. For in that case hardly any corner of the world would remain for us, and we would have to emigrate from this world altogether, as Paul said elsewhere. Often, however, it happens that the godly may live safely among superstitious people and idolaters, without being compelled to share in their superstitions or to give up the exercises of purer religion. It is therefore lawful for them to remain there, as long as they are not called away by a clear command of God. So this place should be understood of the superstitions themselves: that, leaving these far behind, we may have no fellowship with them. But if this cannot be guarded against unless a change of place is made, then one must also migrate from one's native soil, and the dearest ties should be left behind rather than the confession of true faith violated. Thus Abraham left his native land, when he heard God say to him: "Go out of your land, out of your country, and from your father's house, to the land that I will show you." Thus Peter rightly went out of the court of the high priest, when he saw there was no place there for the confession of Christ. Let all who wish to keep faith with Christ inviolate do the same. For he did not speak carelessly: "He who loves father or mother, son or daughter, more than me, is not worthy of me." Matt. chap. 10.

units.la: Alterum praeceptum nos separari iubet. Exponit eo, & docet Deus, ut exire debeamus ex Babylone: sic nimirum, ut publice testemur, nobis cum superstitionibus nihil commune esse. Et de eo Sacramenta quoque nos admonent, quorum hic non postremus usus est, quod nota sunt externa Ecclesiae, qua huius membra ab aliarum gentium superstitionibus distinguuntur & separantur. Sic olim CirCircumcisio Iudaicum populum à gentibus prophanis & incircumcisis separabat: quod ipsum & omnibus sacris & toto cultu Leuitico dici poterat. Sic baptismus inter nos & Iudaeos siue Turcas distinguit. Et Cœna Dominica inter alia, quæ illic habemus, nos admonet, vitandas esse omnes alias superstitiones, eò quòd fieri non possit, vt simul de mensa Domini & daemoniorum edamus. Vidit hoc Petrus, qui cùm post primam concionem Hierosolymitanis consilium salutis petentibus dixisset: Resipiscite, & baptizetur vnusquisque vestrum in nomine IESV CHRISTI, &c. tandem addit: Seruemini à natione ista prava. Quibus verbis separationem illam praecipit, de qua hic agitur.
units.tr: The second precept bids us be separated. God explains and teaches what we must do when we go out of Babylon: namely, that we publicly bear witness that we have nothing in common with superstitions. The sacraments also admonish us of this, and their use here is by no means the least, since they are the external marks of the Church, by which its members are distinguished and set apart from the superstitions of other nations. Thus circumcision once separated the Jewish people from the profane and uncircumcised nations; and the same could be said of all the sacred rites and the whole Levitical worship. So baptism distinguishes us from the Jews or the Turks. And the Lord's Supper, among the other things we have there, reminds us that all other superstitions must be avoided, because it is impossible to eat at once from the table of the Lord and from the table of demons. Peter saw this, who, after his first sermon, when the men of Jerusalem asked for counsel about salvation, said: "Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ," etc., and at last adds: "Save yourselves from this perverse generation." By these words he enjoins that separation of which this passage speaks.

units.la: Additur his tertium: Immundũ ne tetigeritis. Est haec locutio ex Lege petita, vbi tactus quoq; cadaueris aut rei alterius polluebat, vt esus quoque ciborum, quos Deus pro eius temporis ratione prohibuerat. Imprimis tamen Sacerdotibus interdictum erat, ne quid immundum tangerent. At Christianis hominibus nihil hic periculi est. Vt enim ipsi per Christi sanguinem purgati sunt, & à Legis ceremonijs liberati: ita purus omnia pura sunt, & Paulus alibi grauiter monet, ne eos audiamus, qui dicunt: Ne attigeris, neque gustaris, neque contrectaueris. Verè autem immundum est, quicquid cum fide in Christum pugnat & eius professione, adeò vt eius merito derogeT: qualia sunt idola, cultus illiciti & superstitiosi, scortatio item, ebrietas, & quaecunque sunt alia huius generis. Haec enim vt ex corde corrupto emanant, ita totum hominem & conscientiam eius polluunt, sicuti Christus docet. Ab istis ergo abstinere oportet omnes eos, qui templum Dei viuentis esse, & in Christo seruari cupiunt. Arguit hoc illorum leuitatem, qui externis superstitionibus communicant, & vitam viuunt scandali plenam, interim verò de animi puritate gloriantur. Quasi verò ex pura & limpidissima fontis scaturigine riuus sordidus ac luteus emanare possit. Sed de his sub initium proximi Cap. plura dicentur.
units.tr: A third is added: "Touch no unclean thing." This expression is taken from the Law, where even touching a corpse or another defiled thing made a person unclean, as did eating foods that God had forbidden for that age. Above all, however, the priests were forbidden to touch anything unclean. But for Christians there is no danger here. For just as they have been cleansed through the blood of Christ and freed from the ceremonies of the Law, so "to the pure all things are pure"; and Paul elsewhere earnestly warns us not to listen to those who say: "Do not handle, nor taste, nor touch." Truly unclean is whatever fights against faith in Christ and its profession, so that it detracts from his merit: such as idols, illicit and superstitious worship, and likewise fornication, drunkenness, and whatever else is of this kind. For just as these come forth from a corrupt heart, so they pollute the whole man and his conscience, as Christ teaches. All who wish to be the temple of the living God and to be kept in Christ must therefore abstain from these things. This points to the levity of those who take part in external superstitions and live lives full of scandal, while at the same time they boast of the purity of their minds. As if a foul and muddy stream could flow from a pure and most limpid spring! But these matters will be discussed at greater length at the beginning of the next chapter.

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad postremam huius loci partem, quia exhortationem istam Dominus promissione laetissima confirmat, simulque magis excitat suos, ne in re tam seria & tam magni momenti cunctentur siue moras nectant. Ego (inquit) suscipiam vos: & ero vobis Pater, & vos eritis mihi filij & filiae, dicit Dominus Omnipotens. Ista ex diuersis Veteris Scripturae locis Paulus contexuit, sensum magis quam literam secutus, vt saepe Apostoli solent, quando non de verbis, sed re ipsa agitur. Merentur autem hic quoque singula diligentiorem considerationem.
units.tr: Let us now pass to the last part of this passage, because the Lord confirms this exhortation with a most joyful promise, and at the same time stirs his people up more, so that they do not hesitate or delay in a matter so serious and of such great importance. "I will receive you," he says, "and I will be a Father to you, and you shall be my sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty." Paul has woven these words together from various places of the Old Testament, following the sense rather than the letter, as the Apostles often do when the matter itself, and not the wording, is at issue. Each of these points also deserves more careful consideration.

units.la: Primum, Ego (inquit) suscipiam vos. Opponit hoc odijs mundi, qui pios exibilare & excomunicare solet, vt indignos, qui communi cum alijs aere fruantur. Quasi diceret: Si mundi consortio relicto, vos totos mihi consecrareritis, omnes quidem vos fastidiet atque abominabuntur: sed ego vos ad me colliga, vbi vobis asylum erit tutissimum & portus salutis, in quo mundi infelicis conatus absque periculo spectare & ridere poteritis. Et quamuis illi vos execrentur, ego tamen vobis benedicam & fauore meo tuebor. Huc pertinet promissio Abrahamo facta: Benedicam tibi, & magnificabo nomen tuum, tuq; eris benedictio. Benedicam quoq; ijs qui tibi benedicunt, maledicentibus verò tibi maledicam. Quibus consentiunt quae in Psalmis habentur: Domini est salus, super populum tuum benedictio tua. Item: Tu benedices iusto o Domine, gratia tua veluti scuto tueberis ipsum. Et rursus: Ipsi quidem maledicent, tu autem benedices. Exemplum istarum promissionum euidens in Balaami historia extat, qui à Balak Moabitarum Rege conductus, vt Israelitarum castra diris deuoverer, quoties id facere tentauit, toties illis laeta & fausta omnia precatus est. Et in Euangelio caecum illum, quem Christus visu donarat, ob liberam fidei confessionem é Synagoga eijciunt Sacerdotes & Seniores Iudaeorum, sed eundem mox inuenit & ad se recipit aeternus Dei Filius. Nemine ergo terreant execrationes impiorum antistitum, nemo item tyrannorum minis moueatur, neque etiam aliquid tribuamus improborum iudicijs, qui nos probris & sannis prosequuntur, si ipsorum studijs relictis nouum vitae genus in Christo sectemur. Sunt enim haec inania fulgura ex vitro aut lebete emicantia, quorum ferè euentus est ridiculus.
units.tr: First, "I will receive you." He sets this against the hatred of the world, which is accustomed to hiss at and excommunicate the godly, as unworthy to enjoy the common air with others. As if he were saying: if, leaving the fellowship of the world, you consecrate yourselves wholly to me, indeed all will despise and abhor you; but I will gather you to myself, where you will have a most secure refuge and a harbour of salvation, from which you can watch and laugh at the unhappy efforts of the world without danger. And although they curse you, I will nevertheless bless you and protect you with my favour. To this belongs the promise made to Abraham: "I will bless you, and I will magnify your name, and you shall be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and curse those who curse you." The things in the Psalms agree with this: "Salvation belongs to the Lord; your blessing is upon your people." Also: "You, O Lord, will bless the righteous man; you will protect him with your favour as with a shield." And again: "They indeed will curse, but you will bless." A clear example of these promises stands in the history of Balaam, who, hired by Balak, king of the Moabites, to curse the camp of Israel, as often as he tried to do so, prayed for all things happy and prosperous for them instead. And in the Gospel the priests and elders of the Jews cast the blind man, whom Christ had given sight, out of the synagogue because he freely confessed the faith; but the eternal Son of God soon found him and received him to himself. Let no one, therefore, be frightened by the curses of impious leaders; let no one be moved by the threats of tyrants, nor give any weight to the judgments of wicked men, who assail us with insults and sneers, if we, leaving their pursuits, follow a new way of life in Christ. For these are empty flashes, gleaming from glass or from a bronze vessel, whose outcome is almost always ridiculous.

units.la: Deinde, se nobis patrem fore pollicetur Deus, qua promissione omnem beneuolentiam vnà cum cumulo beneficiorum omnis generis comprehendit. Parentes liberorum suorum obliuisci non possunt, & affectione, quam illis natura indidit, moti eorunde miserentur, vt quiduis potius ferre possint, quàm illis periclitantibus opem atque auxilium negare. Exemplum huius amoris memorabile in meretrice illa habetur, quæ ad Solomonis tribunal pro filiolo suo litigauit. Atqui Dei amor, quàm nos prosequitur parentū στοργὰς longè superat, quod ipsemet apud Isaiam testatur, dicens: Nū obliuiscitur mulier infantis sui, quò minus misereatur filij vteri sui? Sed esto, obliuiscantur illæ, ego tamē tui non obliuiscar. Quò etiā referri debet, quod in Psalmo canitur: Vt Pater miseretur liberorum, ita Dominus miseretur timentiū eum. Ipse enim nouit conditionē nostram, recordans quòd fimus puluis. Et ne quid de eo dubitemus, idem sub Patris nomine à nobis inuocari vult, & Spiritum adoptionis cordibus nostris ideo inserit, vt eo confirmati clamemus, Abba Pater. At in præsenti Emphasim habet, quod additur: Dicit Dominus Omnipotens. Sunt enim parentes, qui etsi liberos suos tenerrimè ament, eosdem tamen non possunt semper iuuare vt vellent. At Deus exercituum Dominus est, qui creatis omnibus imperat, & corda quoque hominum, tam bonorum quàm malorum in sua manu habet. Nunquam ergo ei desunt vires, quibus suos tueatur et liberet. Id orantes quoq; fatemur, quando dicimus: Pater noster, qui es in cœlis. Nam ijs verbis non tam locum denotamus, in quo ille habitet, quàm omnipotentiam eius exprimimus, qua omnibus imperat, quæ in cœlis & sub illis in tota huius mundi machina continentur. Quibus adde, quod Christo, quo Seruatore gloriamur, omnis potestas data est in cœlo & in terra, & quòd idem se pastorem illum bonum & fortem esse profitetur, è cuius manibus oues nemo possit rapere.
units.tr: Next, God promises that he will be a Father to us, and by this promise he embraces all goodwill together with a heap of benefits of every kind. Parents cannot forget their children, and moved by the affection which nature has planted in them, they take pity on them, so that they can bear anything rather than deny help and aid when their children are in danger. A memorable example of this love is found in that harlot who pleaded before Solomon's tribunal for her little son. Yet God's love, with which he cares for us, far surpasses the affection (στοργάς) of parents, as he himself testifies through Isaiah, saying: "Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? Yet let those forget, yet I will not forget you." To this also belongs what is sung in the Psalm: "As a father pities his children, so the Lord pities those who fear him." For he knows our frame, remembering that we are dust. And lest we doubt him, he also wishes to be invoked by us under the name of Father, and he places the Spirit of adoption in our hearts so that, strengthened by him, we may cry out, "Abba, Father." But in the present passage the emphasis lies in what is added: "Thus says the Lord Almighty." For there are parents who, however tenderly they love their children, cannot always help them as they would wish. But God is the Lord of hosts, who commands all created things and holds in his hand the hearts of men, both good and bad. Therefore he never lacks the strength by which he may protect and deliver his own. We also confess this when we pray and say: "Our Father, who art in heaven." For by these words we do not so much indicate the place in which he dwells as express his omnipotence, by which he rules all things that are contained in the heavens and beneath them, in the whole machine of this world. Add to this that to Christ, in whom we glory as our Saviour, all power is given in heaven and on earth, and that he professes himself to be that good and strong Shepherd, from whose hands no one can snatch the sheep.

units.la: Additur autē in præsenti tertiū quoq; Et vos eritis mihi filij et filiæ. Poterat hoc idē cum priori membro, aut saltē ad eius confirmationē dictū videri: sed simul nos officij admonet, & quid nos vicissim Deo debeamus docet: Nimirū, vt filij Dei simus germani & ingenui, qui hunc Patrē nostrū indulgentissimū amemus, colamus, timeamus, & eide obtemperemus: Ne videlicet nobis dici possit, quod in Prophetis olim de Iudæis ille pronuntiauit: Filios educaui & euexi, ipsi autē perfide desciuerunt à me. Agnoscit bos dominum suum, & asinus præsepe heri sui: At Israël non agnoscit, populus meus non intelligit. Ite: Filius honorat patrē, & seruus dominū suum: Si ergo ego pater sum, vbi honor est meus? Si verò dominus sum vester, vbi mei timor? Ista fibijpfis occinant, qui se fecuriores esse, & in ijs, quæ ad Dei cultum spectant, remissius aut frigidius agere sentiunt.
units.tr: In the present passage a third point is added as well: "And you shall be my sons and daughters." This could seem to be said along with the former member, or at least to confirm it; but at the same time it reminds us of our duty and teaches what in turn we owe to God. Namely, that we should be true and free-born children of God, who love, honour, fear and obey this most indulgent Father of ours; lest it be said to us what he once pronounced through the Prophets concerning the Jews: "I have reared and brought up sons, but they have rebelled against me. The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master's crib; but Israel does not know, my people does not understand." Come now: "A son honours his father, and a servant his lord. If then I am a father, where is my honour? And if I am your lord, where is my fear?" Let those sing these words to themselves who feel that they are rather secure, and who act more carelessly or coldly in those things which pertain to the worship of God.

units.la: At priusquam dicendi finem faciamus, hoc quoq; in tota ista tractatione diligenter obseruari debet, primo loco poni, quòd Deus noster Deus & Pater esse velit: & ex eo deinde inferri, quòd nos ipsius populus, filij & filiæ simus. Nisi enim ille seipsum ad nos demittat, nosq; nihil huius meritos ad istam dignitatē euehat, nūquam eius capaces erimus, multò minus autē nostris viribus eò peruenire poterimus. Quapropter tota hæc coniunctio cum Deo, ex qua omnis salus nostra dependet, gratuitæ misericordiæ opus atque donum est, neq; hic aliquid nostris viribus aut meritis debet tribui. Docet hoc ipsum ordo capitū fœderis olim cum Abrahamo factū, in quo præmittitur: Ego sum Deus Schadai: deinde autem infertur: Ambula coram me, & esto integer. Idem in Decalogi ordine est videre. Quòd ergo à nobis Deus obedientiam & præceptorum suorum obseruantiam requirit, non ideo fit, vt nos ad nostrorum operum merita remittat, sed vt officij admoneat, quod ipsi debemus pro ipsius in nos gratuita bonitate. Itaque turpiter paralogizant, qui ex eo meritum concludunt. Debitores enim sumus Deo, cui nunquā satis facere, nedum de illo quicquā mereri possumus. Nam si omnia fecerimus (inquit Dominus) quæ mandata sunt vobis, dicite: Serui inutiles sumus: quod debuimus facere, fecimus. Itaq; agnoscamus Dei bonitatē, qui nos filiorū loco adoptare dignatus est: officij autem nostri memores, IESVM CHRISTVM vera fide complettamur, qui vt nobis Seruator & doctor datus est; ita nos eum audire, ipsumq; vita & moribus nostris referre decet. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But before we make an end of speaking, this also must be carefully observed throughout this whole treatment: that God first wishes to be our God and Father, and that from this it then follows that we are his people, sons and daughters. For unless he were to lower himself to us, and raise us, who deserve nothing of this, to such dignity, we would never be capable of it, much less could we ever attain it by our own strength. Therefore this whole union with God, on which all our salvation depends, is the work and gift of free mercy, and nothing should here be attributed to our strength or merits. The order of the chapters of the covenant once made with Abraham teaches this same thing, in which it is first said: "I am God Almighty (El Shaddai)," and then it is added: "Walk before me, and be perfect." The same order can be seen in the Decalogue. Therefore, that God requires obedience from us and the observance of his precepts does not happen so that he may refer us to the merits of our works, but so that he may remind us of the duty which we owe to him for his free goodness towards us. Thus those reason shamefully who conclude merit from this. For we are debtors to God, to whom we can never make sufficient satisfaction, much less merit anything from him. For, the Lord says: "When you have done all the things that are commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done." Let us therefore acknowledge the goodness of God, who has deigned to adopt us in the place of children; and, mindful of our duty, let us lay hold of Jesus Christ with true faith, who has been given to us as Saviour and teacher; and as it is fitting that we hear him, so we should also reflect him in our life and conduct. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT VII. HOMILIA XXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. HOMILY XXX.

units.la: HAs igitur promissiones cum habeamus, dilecti, purgemus nos ipsos ab omni inquinamento carnis ac Spiritus, perficientes sanctificationem cum timore Dei.
units.tr: Since therefore we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.

units.la: ETSI homo ad Dei gloriam conditus, & proinde huius seruitio atq; cultui destinatus sit, vt plurimùm tamen hic peccat, dum vel negligenter agit, vel à cultus veritate declinat, & ex semetipso cultus instituit ridiculos partim, partim absurdos, quibus gloriæ Dei multum derogatur. Causa omnis erroris est, quòd pleriq; Deum sibi fingunt ex suo ingenio, qui vel humana non curet, vel nostri animi intentione contentus quiduis recipiat, quod nos ipsi offerimus. Nò temere ergo Deus cultus sui formâ ipse præscripsit, & vt eam constanter retineamus hortatur, ne proprij ingenij figmentis decepti exorbitemus. In illa autem hoc præ aliis vrget & inculcat, ne quod ipsi simulachrum faciamus, neue ab aliis facta colamus: Nimirum quod quia ipse summum atq; æternum bonum est, nulla potest imagine exprimi, nihil autem absurdius & contumeliosius fieri potest, quàm si eius maiestatem commutemus cum simulachro hominis mortalis, vel cuiuscunq; alterius creaturæ. Recte ergo Paulus tam multis hoc agit apud Corinthios, qui sub amicitiæ & concordiæ ciuilis prætextu, sibi licere putabant, vt ad idololatrarum sacra & epulas accederent. Ostendit enim nuper, quàm hoc absurdum sit, & veteres Dei admonitiones atq; promissiones ipsis in mentem reuocauit, vt intelligant, eandem semper Dei voluntatem fore, quæ olim fuerit Mosis atq; Prophetarum temporibus. Istius autem nunc generalem conclusionem subijcit, qua Christianos omnes tam in hac causa quàm in omnibus aliis officij sui admonet.
units.tr: Although man was created for the glory of God, and is therefore destined for his service and worship, yet for the most part he sins here, either by acting carelessly or by turning aside from the truth of worship, and devises for himself worship that is partly ridiculous and partly absurd, by which the glory of God is greatly diminished. The cause of every error is that most people fashion for themselves a God according to their own disposition, one who either does not care about human affairs, or who, content with the earnestness of our own mind, accepts whatever we ourselves offer. Not without reason, therefore, has God himself prescribed the form of his worship, and he urges us to keep it steadfastly, lest, deceived by the inventions of our own mind, we go astray. In that form he presses and inculcates this above others: that we make no image of him, nor worship images made by others. Clearly, since he is the supreme and eternal good, he cannot be expressed by any image; and nothing can be more absurd or more insulting than to exchange his majesty for the likeness of a mortal man or of any other creature. Paul therefore rightly deals with this at such length among the Corinthians, who, under the pretext of civil friendship and harmony, thought it allowed to them to attend the sacred rites and feasts of idolaters. For he has shown just now how absurd this is, and he has recalled to their minds the ancient admonitions and promises of God, so that they may understand that God's will will always be the same as it was in the times of Moses and the Prophets. He now adds a general conclusion of this, by which he admonishes all Christians, both in this matter and in all other duties of their office.

units.la: Has igitur promissiones (inquit) cum habeamus, dilecti, purgemus nosipsos ab omni inquinamento, &c. Dilectos vocat, vt & hoc et alia omnia, quæ hoc cap. dicturus est, ex animo amico et salutis ipsorum cupido proficisci intelligant, & proinde sese præbeant obsequentiores. Ex iis autem, quæ proximè dixerat, admonitionem siue exhortationem istam inferens, eius fundamentum præmittit: Cùm has & tantas habeamus promissiones. Quas nam? Quòd nimirum Deus nos pro templo suo agnoscit, in quibus sibi domicilium constituat: quòd item noster Deus & Pater esse vult, nosq; sui populi & filiorum loco habere: æquum fuerit, vt nos sanctos & ab omni scelere puros præbeamus: vt deniq; purgemus nos ab omni inquinamento tam carnis quàm spiritus. Habent huius admonitionis singulæ partes Emphasim quandam, & proinde diligentius ex ordine considerari merentur.
units.tr: "Since therefore we have these promises," he says, "beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement," etc. He calls them beloved so that they may understand that both this and all the other things he is about to say in this chapter come from a friendly heart and a desire for their salvation, and so that they may show themselves more compliant. Drawing this admonition or exhortation from what he had said just before, he first sets down its foundation: since we have such great promises. What promises? Namely, that God acknowledges us as his temple, in which he establishes his dwelling; that likewise he wishes to be our God and Father, and to hold us in the place of his people and children. It is fitting that we should show ourselves holy and pure from every wickedness; and finally that we should cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh as well as of spirit. Each part of this admonition has a certain emphasis, and therefore deserves to be considered more carefully, in order.

units.la: Primùm, præclara illa & ineffabilia bona, in quibus omnis nostra salus consistit, promissiones dicit. Eo autem innuit, Deum ista nobis, non propter aliquod meritum nostrum, sed ex gratia conferre. Patet hoc luce clarius, si tempus consideres, quando omnes illæ promissiones datæ sunt, quibus se nobis Deus obstrinxit: Tunc nimirum, quando nihil minus merebamur, sed potius digni eramus, quos ille nostro exitio relinqueret. Nam vt ab ipso Adamo exordiamur, quis obsecro & qualis ille fuit, quando semen mulieris ei pollicitus est Deus, cuius merito caput serpentis conculcari & humanum genus redimi oporteret? Nonne peccator fuit? nonne perfidus & seditiosus maiestatis diuinæ affectator? nonne nudus & omnis boni expers? nonne hypocrita, qui ficuum folijs peccati turpitudinem velare voluit? nonne profugus à Dei conspectu fuit, & in proprium exitium festinauit, quando illum Deus vocauit: Adam vbi es? Nullum ergo eius meritum fuit, sed promissionem illam ei Deus fecit ex gratuita misericordia. Idem fateamur oportet, si promissionis huius, quæ in diluuio abolita videbatur, instaurationem videamus. Ad hanc enim ex toto hominum genere delectus est Abrahamus. At quis nam ille tunc erat? Nonne inter Chaldæos, homines, superstitiosos & Deorum alienorum cultores, ijsdem cum eis moribus vixit? Id certè Iosua non obscurè testatur. Quòd ergo inde eum euocauit Deus, & in terram Chanaan deduxit, vt illic cum eo æternæ salutis fœdus instauraret, id ex amore gratuito factum est. His si addas Iacobi filios, proteruia, incestibus & parricidijs infames, Israelitas item in Ægypto idololatriæ ditos, in deserto autem ingratos atq; impios murmuratores, quo obsecro illorum merito factum dices, quòd Legem suam illis dedit Deus, quòd sibi eos peculium fecit, quòd sui cultus sedem inter eos constituit? quòd denique terram dedit lacte & melle fluentem? Ipse Moses certè hoc omne ad Dei gratiam refert, dicens: Non ideo vos ita dilexit & elegit Dominus, quòd plures fitis alijs populis (nam pauciores estis omnibus populis) sed quia dilexit vos, & seruare voluit iuramentum, quod iurauit patribus vestris, &c. Item: Non propter iustitiam tuam, & propter rectitudinem cordis tui, tu venis vt possideas terram hanc: sed propter impietatem gentium iste-rum, Dominus Deus expellit eas ante te: vt scilicet verbum, quod iurauerat patribus tuis, Abra-hamo, Isaaco & Iacobo, inconcussum seruaret. Scias igitur, quòd non propter iustitiam tuam das tibi Dominus Deus tuus terram istam bonam possidendam: cùm sis populus præfractæ ceruicis, &c. Atqui eadem est ratio promissionum, quæ apud Prophetas habentur. Fere enim præcedunt acerrimæ scelerum accusationes, obiurgationes acerbæ & diræ comminationes pœnarum, quas sua contumacia meruerint. Imò si eas consideres, quas nuper Paulus adduxit, Propheta his cos consolari voluit, quos propter inobedientiam & ingratitudinem suam in Babylonem abducendos fore prius dixerat. Potest idem de promissionibus dici, quæ ad gentes pertinent. Hæ enim omnes tunc sub tenebrarum potestate per omne genus superstitionum atque libidinis volutabantur, cùm Prophetæ de earum vocatione & conuersione ad Christum vaticinati sunt: & tales adhuc fuisse, quando Apostoli eis Euangelium prædicarunt, notius est, quàm vt demonstrari oporteat. Itaque, salus toti humano generi ex gratuita Dei misericordia obtigit, in qua vna nos acquiescere decet, ne eam nobis inutilem reddamus, dum nostram iustitiam conamur stabilire.
units.tr: First, he calls the splendid and inexpressible goods, in which all our salvation consists, promises. By this he implies that God confers these things on us not because of any merit of ours, but out of grace. This is clearer than light, if you consider the time when all those promises were given, by which God bound himself to us: namely, at a time when we deserved nothing less, but rather were worthy to be left by him to our destruction. For, to begin with Adam himself, who and what sort of man was he, I ask you, when God promised him the seed of the woman, by whose merit the serpent's head was to be crushed and the human race redeemed? Was he not a sinner? Was he not faithless and seditious, one who aspired to the divine majesty? Was he not naked and destitute of all good? Was he not a hypocrite, who wished to cover the shame of sin with fig leaves? Did he not flee from the sight of God and hasten to his own destruction, when God called him: "Adam, where are you?" He had no merit, then; God made that promise to him out of free mercy. We must confess the same if we look at the renewal of this promise, which seemed to have been abolished in the flood. For Abraham was chosen from the whole human race for this purpose. But what sort of man was he then? Did he not live among the Chaldeans, superstitious men and worshippers of strange gods, with the same customs as they? Joshua certainly bears witness to this plainly. That God therefore called him out from there and led him into the land of Canaan, to establish with him the covenant of eternal salvation there, was done out of free love. If to these you add the sons of Jacob, insolent, infamous for incest and parricide; the Israelites likewise, enriched with idolatry in Egypt, and in the desert ungrateful and impious murmurers: by whose merit, I ask you, do you say it was done that God gave them his law, that he made them his own special people, that he established the seat of his worship among them, and finally that he gave them a land flowing with milk and honey? Moses certainly refers all this to the grace of God, saying: "The Lord did not set his love upon you and choose you because you were more numerous than other peoples (for you are fewer than all peoples), but because he loved you and wished to keep the oath which he swore to your fathers," etc. Again: "Not because of your righteousness, nor because of the uprightness of your heart, do you come to possess this land; but because of the wickedness of those nations, the Lord your God drives them out before you, that he might keep the word which he swore to your fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, unshaken. Know therefore that the Lord your God gives you this good land to possess not because of your righteousness, since you are a stiff-necked people," etc. Yet the reason for the promises found among the Prophets is the same. For sharp accusations of sins, bitter rebukes and dreadful threats of punishments, which they had deserved by their stubbornness, almost always precede them. Indeed, if you consider those passages which Paul lately cited, the Prophet wished to comfort those whom he had said before would be led away to Babylon because of their disobedience and ingratitude. The same may be said of the promises which pertain to the nations. For all of them then wallowed under the power of darkness, in every kind of superstition and lust, when the Prophets prophesied of their calling and conversion to Christ; and that they were still such when the Apostles preached the Gospel to them is too well known to need demonstration. Therefore salvation has come to the whole human race from the free mercy of God, and in this alone we ought to rest, lest we make it useless to ourselves while we try to establish our own righteousness.

units.la: Deinde de vsu promissionum Dei hic locus nos admonet, quoad vitam & mores nostros: Quòd nimirum nos Deo obstringunt, vt nimirum ei obsequamur. Etsi enim nihil de eo possimus mereri, eidem tamen gratitudinem & voluntariam obedientiam debemus. Finge enim pauperis & mendici filium à viro honesto & opulento adoptari. Id certè ex misericordia & gratuito amore fieri omnes fatebuntur. Quis verò adoptiuum illum patri omne obsequium debere negauerit? Ita cùm Deus nobis Deus & Pater esse velit, communis sensus nos monet, vt nos ipsius populus simus, atque vt filij boni & ingenui ipsi obediamus. Et hoc plerunque, diserte verbis Scripturæ docent. In fœdere enim cum Abrahamo inito (vt nuper quoque diximus) dicit Dominus: Ego sum Deus Schadai, id est, ad omnia tibi sufficiens. Mox autem subiicit: Ambula coram me, & esto integer. In Lege item dicit: Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, qui eduxi te ex terra Ægypti, &c. Ex eo autem infert: Non habebis Deos alienos coram me. In Prophetis autem hoc tritissimum est, qui ingratos atque rebelles seueriter corripiunt, & ijsdem pœnas graues minantur. In Euangelio eandem rationem sequitur Deus. Nam cœlitus de Filio suo IESV CHRISTO pronuntians: Hic est Filius ille meus dilectus, in quo placatus sum: Mox addit: Ipsum audite. Et ex Christi mandato prædicationem de peccatorum remissione doctrina de pœnitentia præcedit: non vt hac illam mereamur, sed vt ea nos opus habere intelligamus, & ad illam amplectendam præparemur. Obseruarunt hoc semper Apostoli, qui quoties de gratuita Dei electione & in Christo facta humani generis redemptione loquuntur, semper hunc eius finem, quoad huius vitæ nostræ curriculum, indicant, vt inculpatè viuamus, & eius laudes prædicemus, qui nos ex tenebris in lucem eduxit. Et in præsenti Paulus promissiones Dei gratuitas ceu fundamentum ponit exhortationis istius, qua nos ad sanctimoniam & alia vitæ Christianæ officia excitat. Est hoc diligenter obseruandum propter eos, qui solam Dei gratiam prædicari volunt, officij autem sui nolunt admoneri, multò minus corripi: eorum similes nimirum, qui olim Prophetis dicebant: Ne prophetetis, ne stilletis, loquimini nobis blanda, &c. At quomodo ei gratia Dei prædicabitur, qui se illa opus habere non intelligit? Vel num gratiæ prædicatio scelerib-us & carnis licentiæ patrocinari debet? Id certè nemo cordatus aut honestus dixerit.
units.tr: Next, this passage admonishes us about the use of God's promises, as regards our life and conduct: namely, that they bind us to God, so that we should obey him. For although we can merit nothing from him, we nevertheless owe him gratitude and willing obedience. Imagine the son of a poor and beggarly man being adopted by an honorable and wealthy man. All will admit that this is done out of mercy and free love. Who, however, would deny that the adopted son owes the father every obedience? So, since God wishes to be our God and Father, common sense warns us that we should be his people, and that, as good and freeborn children, we should obey him. And Scripture teaches this very often, in plain words. For in the covenant made with Abraham (as we also said just now) the Lord says: "I am God Almighty, that is, sufficient for you in all things." Soon afterwards he adds: "Walk before me, and be upright." Likewise in the Law he says: "I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt," etc. From this he infers: "You shall have no other gods before me." Among the Prophets this is most commonplace: they sharply rebuke the ungrateful and rebellious, and threaten them with grievous punishments. In the Gospel God follows the same reasoning. For when he proclaimed from heaven concerning his Son Jesus Christ, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased," he immediately added: "Hear him." And by Christ's command, the preaching of the forgiveness of sins is preceded by the doctrine of repentance: not so that we may merit forgiveness by it, but so that we may understand that we have need of it, and be prepared to embrace it. The Apostles always observed this: whenever they speak of the free election of God and of the redemption of the human race accomplished in Christ, they always point to this end of it, as regards the course of our life: that we should live blamelessly and proclaim the praises of him who has brought us out of darkness into light. And in the present passage Paul lays down God's free promises as the foundation of this exhortation, by which he stirs us to holiness and the other duties of the Christian life. This must be carefully observed on account of those who wish that only the grace of God be preached, and do not want to be reminded of their duty, much less rebuked: men like those who once said to the Prophets: "Do not prophesy, do not preach; speak to us smooth things," etc. But how will the grace of God be preached to one who does not understand that he has need of it? Or ought the preaching of grace to defend sins and licence of the flesh? Surely no sensible or honest person would say that.

units.la: Sed videamus, quid Paulus ab hominibus Christianis requirat? Nimirum vt purgemus nos ipsos ab omni inquinamento carnis & spiritus. His verbis exponitur quod Propheta dixit: Immundum ne tetigeritis. Est autem duplex inquinatio seu immundities: Carnis nimirum & Spiritus, siue Externa & Interna. Quoad externam, in Lege quidem immundi censebantur, qui vel morticinum, vel leprosum, vel cruorem menstruum tetigissent, aut cibum aliquem vetitum gustauissent. Sed nihil huius præscribitur in præsenti, cum ceremoniæ illæ omnes in Christo abrogatæ sint. Itaque inquinamenta carnis dicuntur ea scelera, quæ ipsum quoque corpus polluunt, dum per eius ministerium patrantur: qualis est Scortatio & omnis illicita libido, de quibus in priori epistola dicitur: Qui fornicatur, in proprium corpus peccat. Ebrietas item, quæ totum hominem defædat, & ne in corpore quidem subsistit, sed ad animam vsq; suas vires extendit. Blasphemiæ & execratio-nes, quibus nes, quibus os & linguam polluimus: Illiciti cultus & sacra aliena, quorum communio plerunq; corpus quoq; inquinat, sicuti de Israelitis narratur, qui sacris Baal Pegor sese polluerunt, & insuper cum Moabitarum filiabus scortati sunt. Polluebantur etiam Corinthij, cum epulis in Deorum honorem institutis accumberent: & de eo imprimis loquitur hic Paulus, ut ex ijs apparet, quae praecesserunt. Hodie idem multis accidit, qui sacris Papisticis communicant, dum infantes suos ad baptismum Papisticum deferunt, & ea ratione in illorum ecclesiam adscribi curant: dum item cum illis ferias agunt, peregrinationes obeunt, Missas audiunt, ad simulachra prosternuntur. Haec (inquam) omnia, & quaecunq; huius generis sunt, ad carnis inquinamenta, seu ad immunditiem externam pertinent. E contra inquinamentum spiritus omnia comprehendit, quae in animo haerent: utpote opiniones falsas & impias de Deo, impuras cogitationes, pravas cupiditates & omnes affectus vitiosos, invidiam, aemulationem, odium, iram, avaritiam, vindictae desiderium, & horum similia. Ab istis omnibus vult nos abstinere Paulus, ut corpore simul & animo mundi simus: nec ab ijs modo abstineamus, quae solius Dei oculis patent, verum etiam ab omnibus externis, quae cum verae fidei & pietatis professione pugnant. Et Emphasim habet particula Vniuersalis: quia non satis est unum inquinamenti genus vitauisse, si interim alio, quoad corpus vel animam, polluaris.
units.tr: But let us see what Paul requires of us Christians. Namely, that we cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit. By these words is explained what the Prophet said: "Touch no unclean thing." Now there is a twofold defilement or uncleanness: that of the flesh and that of the spirit, that is, external and internal. As to the external, under the Law those were considered unclean who had touched a carcass, a leper, or menstrual blood, or had tasted some forbidden food. But nothing of this is prescribed now, since all those ceremonies have been abrogated in Christ. Therefore the defilements of the flesh are said to be those sins which pollute the body itself, while they are committed through its agency: such as fornication and every unlawful lust, of which it is said in the former epistle: "He who commits fornication sins against his own body." Likewise drunkenness, which defiles the whole man and does not stop in the body but extends its powers even to the soul. Blasphemies and curses, by which we pollute our mouth and tongue. Unlawful worship and strange rites, whose participation generally defiles the body as well, as is told of the Israelites, who polluted themselves with the rites of Baal-Peor and, moreover, committed fornication with the daughters of Moab. The Corinthians too were being polluted when they reclined at feasts instituted in honour of the gods; and it is especially of this that Paul speaks here, as is clear from what precedes. Today the same thing happens to many who take part in Papistical rites, when they bring their infants to Papistical baptism and so take care to have them enrolled in their church; when they likewise keep holidays with them, go on pilgrimages, hear Masses, and prostrate themselves before images. All these things (I say) and whatever is of this kind pertain to defilements of the flesh, or to external uncleanness. On the other hand, the defilement of the spirit comprehends all those things which cling to the mind: namely false and impious opinions about God, impure thoughts, depraved desires and all vicious affections, envy, emulation, hatred, anger, avarice, the desire for revenge, and things similar to these. Paul wants us to abstain from all of these, so that we may be clean both in body and in mind; and we should abstain not only from those things which lie open to the eyes of God alone, but also from all external things which are at odds with the profession of true faith and piety. The particle "all" has emphasis: for it is not enough to have avoided one kind of defilement if meanwhile you are polluted in another, as regards body or soul.

units.la: Obseruandum hoc diligenter propter eos, qui externam idololatriam excusant animi synceritate: quod nimirum, etsi ad sacra illicita accedant, fidem tamen in unum Deum per solum IESVM CHRISTVM habeant inuiolatam. Est horum magnus numerus hodie. At ut sese excusent, nunquam tamen negare poterunt, sacris illis corpus atq; externam fidei professionem pollui. Id vero homines Christianos facere Paulus in praesenti prohibet. Et aperte in Christi mandatum peccant, quo is fidei confessionem synceram a nobis exigit. Imo quam parui faciant Christum non obscure testantur, quando eos non mouet gravis illa sententia: Quem mei & sermonum meorum puduerit in natione hac adultera & peccatrice, illius pudebit & Filium hominis, vbi venerit in gloria Patris sui cum Angelis sanctis. Adde his quod vanissimum est, quicquid isti de cordis & fidei suae synceritate garriunt. Nam ut alias diximus, adulteras imitantur, quae de coniugali fide & amore magnifice loquuntur, corpus autem suum quibusuis obuijs prostituunt. Et quia Deus a nobis diligi vult ex toto corde & ex omnibus viribus nostris, eidem corpus nostrum negare nullo iure possumus.
units.tr: This must be observed carefully on account of those who excuse external idolatry by the sincerity of their mind: that is, that even if they approach unlawful rites, they nevertheless keep their faith in the one God through Jesus Christ alone inviolate. There is a great number of these today. Yet however they excuse themselves, they will never be able to deny that by those rites both the body and the external profession of faith are polluted. Paul forbids Christian men to do this here. And they sin plainly against Christ's command, by which He requires of us a sincere confession of faith.
