Indeed, how little they value Christ is not obscurely shown when that grave saying does not move them: "Whoever is ashamed of Me and of My words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him also will the Son of Man be ashamed, when He comes in the glory of His Father with the holy angels." Add to these that whatever those men babble about the sincerity of their heart and faith is most empty. For, as we have said elsewhere, they imitate adulterous women, who speak grandly of conjugal faith and love, yet prostitute their bodies to whomever they meet. And since God wills to be loved by us with the whole heart and with all our strength, we can by no right deny our body to Him.

units.la: Et facit ad huius confirmationem, quod Paulus modum quoq; aut rationem tradit, quam in toto hoc negotio sequamur. Nam addit: Perficientes sanctificationem cum timore Dei. Perficien di verbo vitur, cui etsi Graeca vox respondeat, eius tamen vsus fuit olim in sacrificijs, quae & per se integra ac perfecta esse, & rite perfici oportebat. Proprie autem eandem vocem nobis accommodat, qui alibi iubemur nos Deo hostiam viuentem sistere. Nec enim ea grata erit Deo, nisi perfectae sanctificationi studeamus, & illi tam corpora quam animas nostras sistamus per veram fidei obedientiam. Etenim dimidius modo cultus erit, si alterutram tui partem Deo neges. Et huc pertinent, quaecunq; de sanctificatione in Scripturis traduntur. In Lege clamat Deus: Eritis mihi sancti, quia ego Dominus sanctus sum, & segregaui vos de populis, ut sitis mei. Cui conuenit, quod Christus de suis discipulis dicit: Ego elegi vos de mundo. Si ergo a reliquis gentibus segregati sumus, ut Deo possemus consecrati esse, quid obsecro in nobis erit, quod ei negare, & quo hominibus prophanis cum nostrae professionis detrimento gratificari possimus? Et Christi precatio est pro discipulis: Pater, sanctifica illos tua veritate. Qualis ergo erit sanctificatio, quae cum dolo & perfida simulatione coniuncta fuerit? Apostolus certe noster ait: Pacem sectemini cum omnibus, & sanctimoniam: sine qua nemo videbit Deum. Id vero de vera & perfecta sanctimonia dicit, de qua in praesenti agitur. Quia vero nobis semper aliquid deest, adhaec mundus quotidie nouas nobis labes atq; maculas aspergit, studio iugi & assiduo opus est, vt indies promouendo & proficiendo tandem ad perfectionem illam perueniamus, quam hic nobis Paulus praecipit. Huc pertinet Christi praeceptum, quo eos, qui ipsius sanguine & merito abluti sunt, pedes tamen itidem abluere iubet. Itaq; vehementer seipsos fallunt, qui se iam perfectos esse sibi persuadent, & quasi nihil agendum reflet, ignauo otio & desidiae sese dedunt. Atqui solidam perfectionem in coelis tandem obtinebimus: quoad ergo hic viuimus, indesinenter proficere debemus, & nobis applicare quod Paulus alibi de semetipso scribit: Ego meipsum nondum arbitror metam apprehendisse, unum autem hoc ago, ea quidem quae a tergo sunt obliuiscens, ad ea vero quae a fronte sunt contendens: Scopum versus feror, ad palmam supernae vocationis Dei per CHRISTVM IESVM. Vide locum ad Philippenses tertio Capite.
units.tr: And it serves to confirm this that Paul also hands down the manner or rule which we should follow in this whole matter. For he adds: "perfecting holiness in the fear of God." The word "perfecting" is used, and although the Greek word corresponds to it, its use was once in sacrifices, which had to be both whole and perfect in themselves and duly perfected. Properly, however, he applies the same word to us, since elsewhere we are bidden to present ourselves to God as a living sacrifice. For this will not be pleasing to God unless we strive for perfect sanctification, and present to Him both our bodies and our souls through true obedience of faith. For the worship will be only half-done if you deny Him either part of yourself. And to this pertain whatever things are taught about sanctification in the Scriptures. In the Law God cries out: "You shall be holy to me, for I the Lord am holy, and I have separated you from the peoples, that you may be mine." To this agrees what Christ says of His disciples: "I have chosen you out of the world." If therefore we have been separated from the rest of the nations so that we might be consecrated to God, what, I beg you, will there be in us that we could deny Him, or by which we could gratify profane men to the detriment of our profession? Also Christ's prayer is for the disciples: "Father, sanctify them by your truth." What sort of sanctification, then, will it be that is joined with deceit and treacherous pretence? Our Apostle certainly says: "Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no one shall see God." He speaks there of true and perfect holiness, which is the matter under discussion now. But since something is always lacking in us, and the world daily sprinkles fresh stains and spots upon us, we need a constant and unremitting zeal, so that by advancing and making progress day by day we may at last reach that perfection which Paul enjoins on us here. To this pertains Christ's precept, by which He bids those who have been washed in His blood and merit nevertheless to wash their feet as well. Therefore those greatly deceive themselves who persuade themselves that they are already perfect, and, as if nothing remained to be done, give themselves over to idle sloth and laziness. Yet we shall attain solid perfection only in heaven; so long as we live here, we must advance unceasingly, and apply to ourselves what Paul writes elsewhere about himself: "I do not think that I have already laid hold of the goal; but this one thing I do: forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forward to those which are before, I press toward the mark, to the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus." See the passage in Philippians, chapter three.

units.la: Porro exhortationi huic stimulum adhibet, quo omnino opus est, eo quod hic nobis multa obstant. Iubet enim, ut sanctificationem nostram perficiamus cum timore Dei: hoc nimirum monens, ut nunquam non Deum nobis ob oculos ponamus, deque eo cogitemus, quod ille ignavos et perfidos sui nominis professores impunitos non dimittat. Ista enim meditatio, si in ea assidui et diligentes simus, sanctum illu atque salutarem Dei timore in animis nostris gignit, qui nos efficacissime et urget et confirmat, ne defatigemur aut succumbamus in iis perficiendis, quae nobis a Deo mandata esse scimus: ut supra Cap. 5. dictum est. Idem etiam initium sapientiae dicitur, quod caecos affectus ex cordibus nostris expellit, qui si illis locus detur, nos ea cernere non sinunt, quae nos facere conveniebat. Qui vero illum excusserunt, ii aut effrenes ruunt in omne nefas, dum carnis propriae et mundi cupiditatibus indulgent: aut quicquid faciunt, id ex hypocrisi et vana ambitione faciunt, et proinde Deo probari non possunt. Semper ergo cogitemus, nos in Dei conspectu versari, qui fuco externo falli nequit, cum corda et renes scrutetur. Et hoc ad se transferant omnes Ecclesiarum ministri. Idem faciant, qui in Repub. versantur, privatim quoque singuli in omnibus suis actionibus atque studiis. At hodie omnium malorum haec causa est, quod Dei timor ubique locorum exulat. Hinc petulantius omnia pro sua libidine faciunt Antichristiani antistites: negligentius vero etiam ii agunt, qui Euangelium profitentur. Quid, quod ijdem contentionibus non necessariis Ecclesias turbant? quod nunquam facturi essent, si vero Dei timore afficerentur. Eadem causa principes viros audaciores facit, ut sub Euangelij praetextu quae sua sunt quaerant, et Ecclesiarum bona non minus impudenter quam iniuste diripiant. Quod deniq omnis loci et ordinis homines in religione ludunt, et eam ad suos affectus detorquent, dum cum superstitionibus Dei quoq timorem ex cordibus procul eijciunt. Meminerimus ergo promissionum Dei, et ingenuo Dei timore nos ipsos ad veram sanctificationis studium excitemus, ut nos IESVS CHRISTVS pro suis agnoscere possit, quos regni sui caelestis coheredes faciat. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria et potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, Paul adds a spur to this exhortation, which is indeed needed, since many things here stand in our way. For he bids us perfect our sanctification in the fear of God: thereby admonishing us never to set God aside from before our eyes, and to think about this, that He does not let slothful and treacherous professors of His name go unpunished. For this meditation, if we are assiduous and diligent in it, begets in our minds that holy and salutary fear of God, which most effectively both urges us on and strengthens us, so that we do not grow weary or give up in performing those things which we know God has commanded us, as was said above in chapter five. The same fear is also called the beginning of wisdom, because it casts out of our hearts blind affections, which, if they are given room, do not allow us to see those things which we ought to do. Those who have shaken off this fear, however, either rush headlong into every wickedness while they indulge the desires of their own flesh and of the world; or whatever they do, they do out of hypocrisy and empty ambition, and therefore cannot be approved by God. Let us therefore always think that we live in the sight of God, who cannot be deceived by outward paint, since He searches the heart and the reins. And let all the ministers of the Churches apply this to themselves. Let those who live in the commonwealth do the same, and let each individual do so privately too, in all his actions and pursuits. Yet today the cause of all evils is this: that the fear of God is exiled from every place. Hence the Antichristian prelates act more wantonly in everything according to their own lust, while even those who profess the Gospel act more carelessly. What of this, that the same men disturb the Churches with unnecessary quarrels? They would never do so if they were moved by the fear of God. For the same cause makes princes bolder, so that under the pretext of the Gospel they seek their own interests and tear apart the goods of the Churches no less shamelessly than unjustly. And finally, men of every place and rank toy with religion and bend it to their passions, while along with superstitions they also cast the fear of God far from their hearts. Let us therefore remember God's promises, and stir ourselves by a sincere fear of God to a true zeal for sanctification, so that Jesus Christ may acknowledge us as His own, whom He makes heirs of His heavenly kingdom. To Him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXI.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXI.

units.la: Accipite nos: neminem iniuriam fecimus, neminem corrupimus, neminem expilauimus. Non ad condemnationem loquor. Nam ante dixi, vos in cordibus nostris esse ad simul moriendum, et simul viuendum. Multa mihi loquendi libertas apud vos, multa mihi gloriatio de vobis: impletus sum consolatione, vehementer exundo gaudio in omni afflictione nostra.
units.tr: Receive us. We have wronged no one, corrupted no one, taken advantage of no one. I do not say this to condemn you, for I have said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together. I have great freedom of speech toward you and great boasting about you. I am filled with comfort, and in all our affliction I overflow exceedingly with joy.

units.la: Quemadmodum in Repub. multum refert, ut populus de principum suorum studio praeclare sentiat, et liberi se a parentibus suis amari intelligant: Ita in Ecclesia hoc imprimis necesse est, ut omnibus persuasum sit, se a verbi Dei administris diligi, et hos quaecunque faciunt, non nisi publicae omnium salutis studio facere. Quia enim mundus hic veritatis lucem natura odit, nunquam se ab illis coerceri aut in ordinem redigi patietur, nisi intelligant ipsos serio agere, et non suum commodum privatum, sed singulorum salutem quaerere. Hoc Mosem olim monuit, ut suum erga filios Israelis amorem tam multis tamque gravibus argumentis declaraverit. Et hoc ipsum Prophetas quoque fecisse scimus. Obseruauit hoc Paulus quoque cum apud alias Ecclesias, tum maxime apud Corinthios. Quia enim sciebat, se multis apud eos exosum esse, diligenter et saepe de suo erga illos studio disserit, idq; imprimis in hac epistola, cum priore illos nonnihil offensos esse videret. Itaq; cum eos nuper aliquanto gravius monere vellet, ut ab idololatrarum commerciis abstinerent, multis praefatus est, quam ardenti amore eos complectatur. Idem nunc quoq; facit, postquam admonitionem illam absoluit: et verbis eiusmodi utitur, quae singula illorum animos quam efficacissime poterant commouere. A precibus orditur, perinde ac si pater aliquis liberis suis, quos contumaciores esse, & incurabili malitia in exitium proprium ruere videt, supplex fiat, & eosdem humiliter roget, ut suis admonitionibus apud se locum dent. Accipite nos, inquit: vel, Capaces quaeso nostri estote. Quo dicto ad illud alludit, quod supra Cap. 6. dixerat: Non habitatis angustè in nobis, sed in vestris visceribus angusti estis. Itaq; ut filijs loquor de pari compensatione: Dilatamini & vos. Itaq; huius loci sensus est: Cùm ego meum animum iam pridem erga vos dilatarim, vosq; omnes toto corde meo complexus sim, vos precor, ut vicissim vestra quoque corda mihi aperiatis, neque vos ullo affectu coarctari aut constringi patiamini, quò minus mihi & doctrinae meae apud vos locus sit, &c.
units.tr: In a commonwealth it matters greatly that the people think well of the zeal of their rulers, and that children understand that their parents love them. So in the Church it is above all necessary that everyone be persuaded that they are loved by the ministers of God's Word, and that whatever these men do, they do only out of concern for the common salvation of all. For this world, which by nature hates the light of truth, will never allow itself to be restrained by them or brought into order unless it understands that they act in earnest, and seek not their own private advantage but the salvation of each person. Moses once gave this warning, and he declared his love toward the children of Israel with so many and such weighty proofs. We know that the Prophets did the same. Paul also observed this, both among other churches and especially among the Corinthians. Because he knew that he was hated by many among them, he speaks often and carefully of his zeal for them, and above all in this letter, since he saw that they had been somewhat offended by the earlier one. So when he wished to admonish them more sharply a little while ago, to abstain from dealings with idolaters, he first made clear how ardently he embraced them with love. He does the same now, after he has finished that admonition, and he uses words that could move each of their hearts as powerfully as possible. He begins with an entreaty, as a father who sees his children becoming stubborn and rushing to their own ruin through an incurable wickedness would become a suppliant and humbly ask them to make room for his admonitions. "Receive us," he says, or "Be roomy toward us, I beg you." With these words he alludes to what he had said above in chapter 6: "You are not restricted in us, but you are restricted in your own affections." So, speaking to them as to children, he asks for a fair return: "Open wide to us too." The sense of the passage, then, is this: since I have long since opened my heart to you and embraced you all with my whole heart, I beg you in turn to open your hearts to me, and not to allow yourselves to be narrowed or confined by any feeling that would keep my teaching from having a place among you, and so on.

units.la: Venit autem hoc loco nobis observanda admirabilis & paterna plane Dei bonitas, qui simili ratione cum omnibus agit, quibus verbum suum praedicari curat. Offert his, imò effundit in eos bonorum suorum thesaurum, & plerunq; ministros dat qui nos ipsius nomine & verbis precentur (ut sub finem Cap. 5. dictum est) seq; totos nobis impendant. Patet hoc ex eo, quòd ut aliorum saluti consulant, seipsos omnium odijs exponunt, adhaec curis atq; laboribus conficiunt. Iure igitur & magno suo merito petunt, ut recipiantur & locus detur ipsorum admonitionibus. Et hoc sane auditores omnes facere decebat. Quid verò fit? Pleriq; hoc nolunt facere, & iniuriam sibi fieri putant, si verbi administris ex Dei verbo salutaria mandantibus obedire iubeantur. Estq; haec mundi contumacia & ingratitudo vetus admodum, vel potius omnium seculorum exemplis confirmata. De ea enim acerbissima extat Dei querela, in Psalmo dicentis: Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, qui eduxi te de terra Aegypti: dilata os tuum, & implebo illud, id est, satisfaciam omnibus tuis votis atq; desiderijs. Quid autem ibidem sequitur? At populus meus vocem meam non audiuit. Israel noluit me. Id autem verè dictum esse infinita exempla docent. Quis enim nescit, quàm indignis modis Mosem tractarint, cuius beneficio ex dura & immani Pharaonis tyrannide erepti fuerant? Quis verò sufficeret exponendis iniurijs omnibus, quibus Prophetas, aeterni Dei legatos atq; interpretes, affecerunt? Et quod olim factum fuit illis docentibus, hoc ipsum aeternus Dei Filius, IESVS CHRISTVS, expertus est, ut non absq; graui causa neq; fine acerbi doloris significatione tandem diceret: Hierusalem, Hierusalem, quae occidis Prophetas, & lapidas eos, qui ad te missi sunt: Quoties volui congregare filios tuos, quemadmodum gallina congregat pullos suos, & noluistis? Et eandem Apostolorum sortem fuisse inter eos, quibus illi Euangelium praedicarunt, unicum hoc Pauli & Corinthiorum exemplum abunde docet. Nam enormem fuisse oportet eam contumaciam, quae tantum Apostolum ad preces non tam paternas quam feriles (si carnis iudicium audias) recurrere coegit. Est autem eadem tam frequens & vulgaris hodie, ut non solis verbi administris negotium faciat, verumetiam si quando pij ac boni principes saluti publicae consultum & Dei gloriam propagatam volunt, pleriq; id impatientissimè ferant, multi quoque ex eo tumultuandi occasionem arripiant.
units.tr: Here we must notice the wonderful and truly fatherly goodness of God, who deals in the same way with all those to whom he takes care to have his Word preached. He offers to them, indeed he pours out upon them, the treasure of his good things, and he usually gives them ministers who beseech us in his name and by his words (as was said near the end of chapter 5), and who give themselves wholly for us. This is clear from the fact that, to care for the salvation of others, they expose themselves to the hatred of all and wear themselves out with cares and labours. Rightly, therefore, and by their great merit, they ask to be received and given a place for their admonitions. Indeed, all the hearers ought to do this. But what actually happens? Most are unwilling to do it, and they think they are wronged if they are told to obey the ministers of the Word who deliver what is salutary from the Word of God. This stubbornness and ingratitude of the world is very old, or rather it is confirmed by the examples of all ages. For there is a most bitter complaint of God about it in the Psalm, where he says: "I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt: open your mouth wide, and I will fill it," that is, I will satisfy all your prayers and desires. But what follows in the same place? "But my people did not hear my voice; Israel would not have me." That this was truly said, countless examples show. For who does not know in how shameful a way they treated Moses, by whose help they had been rescued from the harsh and savage tyranny of Pharaoh? And who could be sufficient to list all the wrongs with which they treated the Prophets, the envoys and interpreters of the eternal God? What once happened to those who taught, the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, also experienced, so that not without grave cause and not without a sign of bitter grief he finally said: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the Prophets and stone those who are sent to you! How often would I have gathered your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks, and you would not!" And that the same lot fell to the Apostles among those to whom they preached the Gospel, the single example of Paul and the Corinthians teaches us abundantly. For that stubbornness must have been enormous which forced so great an Apostle to resort to entreaties not so much paternal as, if you judge by the flesh, almost those of a slave. This same attitude is today so frequent and common that it not only causes trouble for the ministers of the Word, but also, whenever godly and good rulers wish to provide for the public welfare and the spread of God's glory, most people bear it with the greatest impatience, and many seize on it as an occasion for stirring up tumults.

units.la: Sed debebant omnes isti meminisse, quàm infeliciter hoc olim Iudaeis cesserit. Nam in Psalmo supra adducto, mox subijcit Dominus: Permisi igitur eos libidini cordis ipsorum, ut incesserint secundùm consilia sua. Quibus verbis comprehendit quaecunq; ad extremum hominis exitium faciunt. Quia enim ex nobisipsis non videmus quae salutaria sunt, imò quia ex nobis nihil aliud est quàm perditio, non potest ea non sequi, ut primùm nos nostrae libidini permittit. Tunc enim effrenis equi instar proteruire non definimus, donec nosipsos in barathrum perditionis praecipitauerimus. Quod Iudaeis accidisse, historiae testantur. De istis ergo diligentius singuli cogitent, quando se à Dei ministris suppliciter rogari sentiunt, ut respiscant. Qui enim ad Dei preces aures suas obturant, ij ipsi quoq; illum postea surdum inueniunt, quando periculis undiq; pressi ad eum clamitant.
units.tr: But all these people ought to remember how unhappily this turned out for the Jews of old. For in the Psalm quoted above, the Lord goes on at once: "So I gave them up to the lusts of their hearts, that they walked in their own counsels." In these words he sums up whatever leads to the utter ruin of man. For since we do not see of ourselves what is salutary, indeed since nothing comes from us but destruction, it cannot fail to follow that God first lets us have our own lust. For then, like an unbridled horse, we do not stop running wild until we have hurled ourselves into the pit of perdition. The histories testify that this happened to the Jews. Therefore let each of these people think more carefully about this, when they feel that they are being humbly asked by the ministers of God to repent. For those who stop their ears to the entreaties of God will later find him deaf to them, when, pressed on every side by dangers, they cry out to him.

units.la: Porrò rationem adducit Paulus, cur ipsum admittere & recipere debeant Corinthij. Nemini iniuriam fecimus, neminem corrupimus, neminem expilauimus per nostram scilicet auaritiam & insatiabilem habendi cupiditatem. Summa & sensus verborum est, non esse aliquam causam iustam, cur animis ab ipso alienis esse debeant. Quasi diceret: Nemo administrorum verbi excludi aut reijci debet, quàm qui iniurijs Christi fideles afficit, vel hominum mentes corrumpit atq; peruertit, vel etiam suis potius rebus quàm publicæ saluti intentus pecunias colligit, & ad hoc multorum simplicitate abutitur: At ego nihil horum feci, & meæ innocentiæ vos testes habeo. Ergo iustissima est mea petitio, vt me accipiatis, iniusti autem & iniqui fueritis, si me velitis à vobis alienum ducere.
units.tr: Further, Paul gives the reason why the Corinthians ought to admit and receive him: we have wronged no one, corrupted no one, taken advantage of no one, namely through our greed and insatiable desire for gain. The sum and sense of the words is that there is no just cause why they should be alienated from him in their minds. As if he were saying: no minister of the Word ought to be excluded or rejected more than the one who wrongs Christ's faithful, or corrupts and perverts people's minds, or even, intent on his own affairs rather than on the common salvation, collects money and abuses the simplicity of many for this purpose. But I have done none of these things, and I have you as witnesses of my innocence. Therefore my request is most just: that you receive me. You would be unjust and unfair if you wished to regard me as a stranger to you.

units.la: Comprehendit autem tribus lisce membris omnia, propter quæ doctores merito nobis suspecti esse & cauleri debent. Primum est Iniuria, quæ ex feroci & insolenti potestatis commissæ abusu nascitur, & eum manifesta læsione vel corporis vel famæ coniuncta est. Alterum corruptio est, quæ per doctrinam solet fieri, quando Dei verbo hominum traditiones admiscentur, quæ simplicem populum superstitionibus excæcatum à Deo, vnico salutis authore, abducunt, & siquidem multorum euertunt. Tertium est, πλεονεξία, quam proprie plus habendi studium dixeris: quod si apud doctores locum inuenerit, mox sub religionis prætextu rudes ac imperitos circumueniunt, & conscientijs eorum laqueos iniiciunt, quibus quasi captiuos ducunt, quod ipsis deinde aucupium est longè quæstuosissimum. Tales olim Scribæ & Pharisæi erant, qui sub prætextu longæ precationis domus viduarum deuorabant, & à liberis eas emungebant pecunias, quas in parentum senio confectorum alimoniam debuissent impendere. Tales etiam fuerunt, qui Apostolorum tempore in familias opulentiores irrepebant, vt captiuas ducerent mulierculas, quarum conscientiæ peccatis oneratæ erant. At ab omnibus iste se abstinuisse dicit Paulus, & id quidem verissime.
units.tr: He sums up in these three members all the things on account of which teachers ought rightly to be suspect and avoided by us. The first is injury, which arises from a fierce and arrogant abuse of the power entrusted to one, and is joined with a manifest harm either to body or to reputation. The second is corruption, which usually happens through teaching, when human traditions are mixed with the Word of God, and they lead the simple people, blinded by superstitions, away from God, the sole author of salvation, and so overturn the faith of many. The third is πλεονεξία (greed), which one could properly call the desire to have more. If this finds a place among teachers, then at once, under the pretext of religion, they deceive the untaught and ignorant, cast snares upon their consciences, and lead them away as captives; and this then becomes for them a most profitable hunt. Such were the scribes and Pharisees of old, who under the pretext of long prayers devoured the houses of widows and squeezed out of their children the money which should have been spent on the support of their aged parents. There were also such men in the time of the Apostles who crept into wealthier households to lead captive weak women whose consciences were burdened with sins. But Paul says that he kept himself from all of these, and indeed most truly.

units.la: Quoad primum enim, ab omni tyrannide & iniusto potestatis Apostolicæ abusu tam alienus fuit, vt potius instar patris indulgentissimi omnibus omnia facere fuit, & cum suo detrimento saluti aliorum consulere voluerit. Deinde nihil scire se putabat, præter IESVM CHRISTVM, & hunc quidem crucifixum: & quia hunc solum prædicabat, qui via, veritas & vita est, neminem vtiq; sua doctrina corrumpere aut peruertere potuit. Postremò, adeò non captauit alicuium pecunias, vt stipendio quoq; abstineret, quod optimo iure & ex Christi institutu ab Ecclesijs exigere poterat. Dum vero ista de se dicit, non obscure pseudoapostolos perstringit, qui vt tyranni & fidei dominatores in seruitutem adigebant, discipulos sibi ipsis mancipabant: fidem multorum labefactabant, & licentiæ authores erant, quoad idolothytorum epulas, fornicandi libidinem, incestus, lizes forenses, & multa alia, quæ cum Christiani nominis professione minus conueniunt: neq; iis contenti, insuper defraudabant quosvis, & suas res agendo sub pietatis prætextu, cum aliorum perditione atq; exitio ditescebant.
units.tr: As for the first point, Paul was so far from any tyranny or unjust abuse of apostolic authority that he chose to act like a most indulgent father, becoming all things to all people and seeking the salvation of others even at his own expense. Next, he thought he knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. Since he preached only him who is the way, the truth and the life, he could in no way corrupt or pervert anyone by his teaching. Lastly, he so little sought the money of anyone that he even refrained from the stipend which he could rightly and by Christ's own ordinance have demanded from the churches. In saying these things about himself, he plainly strikes at the false apostles, who, like tyrants and lords over faith, reduced the disciples to slavery and made them their own property. They undermined the faith of many, and were authors of licence regarding meals of idol-offerings, the lust of fornication, incest, lawsuits, and many other things that agree poorly with the profession of the Christian name. Not content with these, they also defrauded whomever they could, and under the pretext of piety they grew rich by the ruin and destruction of others while managing their own affairs.

units.la: Habemus igitur hoc loco discrimen inter veros & falsos Ecclesiarum ministros siue pastores. Illi nemini iniuriam faciunt, neq; aliquem grauant: hi onera imponunt intolerabilia, quæ tamen ipsi ne minimo quidem digito (vt Christi verbis vtar) attingunt. Illi verum Christum tradunt, cum sciant nullum prætereà nomen sub cælo hominibus datum esse, in quo nos seruari oporteat: hi per mille ambages & infinita auia miseros circumducunt, quos semel in naufragium suam illexerunt. Illi nullius opes aut pecunias, sed omnium salutem quærunt: isti cum ditescere velint, & fere ventrem Deum habeant, religionem sibi ipsis quæstum faciunt, & templa quoq; in emporia vel domus mercatus conuertunt. Ex his ergo iudicare discito de omnibus, qui Ecclesiæ pastores haberi volunt. Sunt inter hos hodie præcipui Pontifices, qui Apostolicorum titulo sese venditant. At si ijdem illi cum Paulo possunt dicere: Neminí iniuriam fecimus, neminem corrupimus, neminem per auaritiam expilauimus: bene est, & merito recipi atq; audiri debent. Sed quàm hæc verba ipsis conueniant, res ipsa loquitur. Quis enim iniurias omnes enumerauerit, quibus totum orbem Christianum grauarunt? Reges è solijs suis eiecerunt, regna transtulerunt, Imperatoriam Maiestatem conculcarunt. Certè, qui ista omnia recitare velit, is dicendi exordium facilius quàm finem inuenerit. Quàm horribilem verò doctrinæ corruptelam ijdem illi inuexerunt, quæ nullum omnino Christianæ fidei atq; religionis articulum intactum reliquit? Quid verò de illorum auaritia dicemus, cuius rapaces manus ne moriendo quidem effugere licet, cùm à mortuis quoq; tributum exigant? Vtinam verò Euangelici ab omnibus istis immunes essent, & non multa inter hos quoq; fierent, quæ Pauli exemplo minus conueniunt. Quis enim nescit inter hos quoq; inueniri, qui titulis ambitiosis superbi in fymmystas suos & clerum Domini imperium sibi vsurpant, quo deinde facilius tyrannicè abutuntur? Sunt præterea, qui Euangelij doctrinam quæstionibus non necessarijs inuoluunt, & ita scandala imperitis obijciunt, & multorum conscientias grauant. Nec àturpis lucristudio omnes abhorrent, dum ex defunctis quoque quaestum habent, quos interdum per iu- nebres conciones in cœlum vsque euehunt, vt plus pecuniarum ab haeredibus recipiant. Taceo multa alia, quae hic adduci poterant. Sufficiunt enim ista cordatis, vt de officio suo diligentius cogitent, & si quid ab ipsis peccatum est hactenus, emendent.
units.tr: In this place, then, we have the difference between the true and the false ministers or pastors of the churches. The true ones do wrong to no one and burden no one; the false ones impose intolerable burdens, which yet they do not touch even with the tip of a finger (to use Christ's words). The true ones deliver the true Christ, knowing that no other name under heaven has been given to men by which we must be saved; the false ones lead wretched people about through a thousand windings and endless byways, people whom they once enticed into shipwreck. The true ones seek not the wealth or money of anyone, but the salvation of all; the others, since they wish to grow rich and almost make their belly their god, make a gain of religion, and turn temples into markets or trading houses. From these marks, then, learn to judge all who wish to be held as pastors of the Church. Among these today the chief are the Pontiffs, who peddle themselves under the title of apostles. But if these men could say with Paul: "We have wronged no one, corrupted no one, plundered no one through greed," then it would be well, and they would deserve to be received and heard. But how little these words suit them the thing itself declares. For who could list all the injuries by which they have burdened the whole Christian world? They have cast kings from their thrones, transferred kingdoms, and trampled on the imperial majesty. Certainly, anyone who wished to recite all these things would find it easier to find a beginning of his speech than an end. And how horrible is the corruption of doctrine which these same men have introduced, a corruption that has left no article of the Christian faith and religion untouched? And what shall we say of their avarice, whose grasping hands cannot even be escaped by dying, since they exact tribute even from the dead? Would that the Evangelicals were free of all these things, and that many things were not done among them too which agree poorly with Paul's example. For who does not know that among them too there are those who, proud of their ambitious titles, usurp dominion over their fellow-initiates and over the clergy of the Lord, and then abuse it all the more easily and tyrannically? Besides, there are some who entangle the doctrine of the gospel in unnecessary questions, and so throw stumbling-blocks before the unlearned and burden the consciences of many. Nor do all shun shameful love of gain, while they make profit even from the dead, whom they sometimes carry up to heaven through funeral sermons, so that they may receive more money from the heirs. I pass over many other things that could be brought forward here. For these things are enough for the thoughtful, that they may consider their duty more carefully and amend whatever wrong they have hitherto done.

units.la: Sed vt ad praesentis loci tractatione redeamus, poterant haec Pauli verba Corinthij accipere, quasi in ipsorum contumeliam ista diceret, vt in ingratos atq; iniquos beneficiorum spiritualium, quae in ipsos contulerat, aestimatores. Ideo vt omnem suspicione declinet, praeoccupatione diligenti sese excusat, dicens: Non ad condemnationem loquor, id est, non ideo haec dico, vt aliquem ex vobis accusem vel condemnem. Cur ergo? Vt meam tuear innocentiam, & eadem ratione doctrinam meam a contemptu vindicem. Est autem hic videre singulare modestiae & mansuetudinis exemplum. Multis & indignissimis modis in Paulum Corinthij peccauerant. Nam ingratissimi erant in optime de ipsis meritum. Impostorum calumniis locum dederant. A fidei simul & externi cultus simplicitate recesserant. In coetibus sacris multa erat confusio: morum disciplina nulla, & insuper de ipso contemptim & scurriliter loquebantur. Attamen nihil horum illis amarulentius exprobrat, nec accusationem contra eos instituit, sed simplici suae innocentiae defensione contentus est. Imò solicitè cauet, ne in suspicionem veniat, quasi animo sit in eos alieno. Vere ergo Christum imitatur, & secundum huius praeceptum vitat omnem offensae occasionem. Hoc ipsum si omnes facerent, plus pacis esset in Ecclesia & Repub. priuatim quoque inter singulos. Sed quia plerique mutuis exprobrationibus certant, plerunque ex paruis initijs lites & turbae nunquam finiendae enascuntur.
units.tr: But to return to the treatment of the present passage: the Corinthians could take these words of Paul as if he were saying them to their insult, as judges ungrateful and unjust of the spiritual benefits which he had conferred upon them. Therefore, so that he may avoid all suspicion, he excuses himself with a careful preliminary statement, saying: "I do not speak to condemn you," that is, I do not say these things so that I may accuse or condemn any of you. Why then? So that I may defend my innocence and, by the same reasoning, vindicate my teaching from contempt. Here we may see a singular example of modesty and gentleness. The Corinthians had sinned against Paul in many and most unworthy ways. For they were most ungrateful for his merit toward them, which was very great. They had given a hearing to the slanders of impostors. They had fallen away both from the simplicity of the faith and from the simplicity of outward worship. In their sacred assemblies there was great confusion, there was no discipline of morals, and besides, they spoke of him with contempt and in a buffoonish way. Yet he reproaches them with none of these things more bitterly, nor does he bring an accusation against them, but is content with a simple defence of his innocence. Indeed, he takes anxious care lest he come under suspicion of being ill-disposed toward them. Truly, then, he imitates Christ, and according to this precept avoids every occasion of offence. If all people did this same thing, there would be more peace in the Church and in the commonwealth, and also privately between individuals. But because most people contend with mutual reproaches, quarrels and tumults that never end usually arise from small beginnings.

units.la: Porro argumentis aliquot probat, se nihil odiose dicere in ipsorum contumeliam. Primum est: Nam ante dixi, vos in cordibus nostris esse ad simul moriendum, & simul viuendum. Id est, ita vos complector, & in corde meo quasi conclusos gesto, vt omnem fortunam vobiscum subire paratus sim, & me neq; mors neq; vita a vobis diuellere, aut meum illud studium extinguere queat. Est hoc verae charitatis argumentum, quando non solum viuentes & fortunis florentes colimus, sed cum ijsdem pericula quoque adimus, imò hac vita defunctos amore prosequimur. Talis olim Dauidis amor fuit in Ionathanum. Ita mulieres quoque illae Galilaeae Christum dilexerunt, de quibus Lucas scribit, quòd vt viuum & miraculis clarum ex suis facultatibus aluerant, ita mortuo quoque & sepulto extremum honorem impendere voluerint, quàmuis id cum periculo manifesto esset coniunctum. Ollae amici sunt, qui non nisi eos sectantur, ex quibus commodum aliquod sperant. Imprimis tamen hoc ad Verbi Dei ministros pertinet, vt cum Ecclesijs suae fidei creditis viuere ac mori parati sint. Etenim mercenarij sunt, qui viso lupo, aut periculo aliquo immi nente fugiunt. Quis vero Pauli imitatores dixerit eos, qui oblato pinguiori stipendio, ab Ecclesijs suis discedunt, vel etiam lucri causa stationem suam omnino deserunt, & ministerium Ecclesiae, ad quod vocati fuerunt, vel cum principum aulis, vel quocunq; alio vitae genere commutant?
units.tr: Furthermore, he proves by several arguments that he says nothing spitefully to their reproach. The first is this: "For I have said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together." That is, I embrace you so, and carry you in my heart as if enclosed there, that I am ready to undergo every fortune with you, and neither death nor life can tear me from you or extinguish that zeal of mine. This is a proof of true charity, when we cherish not only the living and those flourishing in their fortunes, but also incur dangers with them, and indeed continue to love them even after they have departed this life. Such was David's love for Jonathan of old. So also those Galilean women loved Christ, of whom Luke writes that, just as they had supported him from their means while he was living and famous for his miracles, so they wished to pay him the last honour even when he was dead and buried, although this was joined with manifest danger. Those are friends only of those from whom they hope for some advantage. Above all, however, this applies to the ministers of the Word of God, that they should be ready to live and die with the churches entrusted to their faith. For they are hirelings who flee when they see a wolf or some imminent danger. But who would call those imitators of Paul who, when a fatter stipend is offered, leave their churches, or even for the sake of gain altogether desert their post, and exchange the ministry of the Church, to which they were called, for the courts of princes or any other kind of life?

units.la: Alterum argumentum amoris est: Multa mihi loquendi libertas apud vos: Id est, dum ista dico, mea libertate vtor, cuius mihi non alia causa est, quàm quòd vobis fido, & mihi de vobis omnia amica polliceor. Atqui hoc non postremum animi amici & benevoli argumentum est, libere effari quod sentis, & quod ex re eius fore putas, quo cum agis. Nam nisi bene speremus de hominibus, facile nobis ab ista dicendi libertate temperabimus. Itaque Ecclesiae male constitutae certissima nota est, si ministri aut nolint, aut non audeant liberius dicere quod animo sentiunt, & quod res ipsa exigit. Illud enim animos ignauos arguit, sui potius commodi quàm publicae salutis amantes: hoc vero populi & magnatum insolentiam prodit, qui vel minantur ministris, vel etiam vim apertam tentant, qua fidos monitores coerceant. Quapropter dicendi libertas tam ministris quam Ecclesijs honorifica est, & non minus utilis. Nam & in viam multos reuocat, qui alioqui in peccatis suis perituri erant, & paci publicae seruit. Qui enim aliorum sceleribus offensi murmurabant, mox placantur, si eos correptionem patienter ferre videant, qui publici scandali authores fuerunt. Ideo Christus dicebat: Habete in vobisipsis salem, & pacem habete inter vos alij cum alijs. Marc.9.
units.tr: The second argument from love is this: "I have much freedom of speech towards you." That is, while I say these things I use my liberty, of which I have no other reason than that I trust you and promise myself everything friendly from you. Indeed, this is no small sign of a friendly and well-disposed mind, to speak freely what you feel and what you think is for the good of the one with whom you deal. For unless we hope well of people, we will easily refrain from such freedom of speech. Therefore it is a most certain mark of a badly constituted Church if the ministers either are unwilling or do not dare to speak more freely what they feel in their hearts, and what the matter itself demands. For the former betrays cowardly minds, lovers of their own advantage rather than of the public welfare; the latter reveals the insolence of the people and of the great, who either threaten the ministers or even attempt open violence by which to restrain faithful admonishers. Hence freedom of speech is as honourable for ministers as for the Churches, and no less useful. For it both calls back to the way many who otherwise were going to perish in their sins, and serves public peace. For those who, offended by the wickedness of others, were murmuring, are soon appeased if they see that those who were the authors of public scandal patiently endure correction. Therefore Christ said: "Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves, one with another." Mark 9.

units.la: Marc. 9.
units.tr: Mark 9.

units.la: Tertio, vt suum erga illos amorem amplius testetur Paulus, ait: Multa mihi gloriatio de vobis. Quasi diceret: Etsi apud vos liberius reprehendam, quae reprehensione merentur, id tamen me non odiose aut ex animo hostili facere, vel ex eo apparet, quod interea apud alios de vobis honorifice loquor, imò glorior quoq; de vestra fide & obedientia. Huc facit, quod eos sigillum apostolatus sui dicebat, deq; ipsorum in pauperes munificentia apud alias Ecclesias gloriabatur, vt sub finem Cap. proximi audiemus. Et hac vera atq; solida ministrorum gloria est, si de Ecclesijs bene constitutis, deq; earum fide, obedientia, morum honestate & charitate mutua gloriari possint. Sic Christus de discipulis suis probè custoditis atq; seruatis apud Patrem gloriabatur. At qui hodie sunt Episcopi, quia de nemine, quem ipsi Christo lucrifecerint, gloriari possunt, ditiones & dioeceses late patentes, redditus annuos & feuda iactant, adhaec pedis, crucibus argenteis, mitris & alio ornatu theatrico superbiunt. Inter alia autem hic imprimis obseruari debet verae charitatis ingenium. In faciem libere monet, corripit, hortatur, nec quicquam dissimulat: absentes verò laudat, & quantum potest, eorum honori consulit. Hoc veros amicos decet. E contra adulatores & impostores, in faciem laudant, à tergo obtrectant, deridbent & ex aliorum stoliditate voluptatem capiunt. Hos ergo caveant, alteros autem illos in honore & pretio habeant omnes, quibus sua salus cordi est.
units.tr: Thirdly, so that Paul may bear further witness to his love for them, he says: "I have great boasting about you." As if to say: even though I speak more freely among you about what deserves rebuke, I do not do this out of spite or a hostile spirit. This is shown by the fact that meanwhile I speak honourably of you among others, and indeed I also glory in your faith and obedience. To this belongs what he called them, the seal of his apostleship, and his boasting about their generosity towards the poor before other churches, as we shall hear at the end of the next chapter. And this is the true and solid glory of ministers: when they can boast of well-ordered congregations, of their faith, obedience, moral integrity and mutual love. So Christ boasted before the Father about his disciples, carefully kept and preserved. But those who today are bishops, since they cannot boast of anyone whom they have won for Christ themselves, flaunt their wide-spreading domains and dioceses, their annual revenues and fiefs, and besides take pride in their pedestals, silver crosses, mitres and other theatrical finery. Among other things, however, the nature of true love must especially be observed here. It warns, rebukes and exhorts frankly to a person's face and conceals nothing; but in their absence it praises and, as far as it can, looks after their honour. This befits true friends. On the other hand, flatterers and deceivers praise to a person's face, carp behind their back, mock and take pleasure in the folly of others. Let everyone whose salvation is dear to them therefore beware of these, and hold the others in honour and esteem.

units.la: Addit his Paulus: Impletus sum consolatione, vehementer exundo gaudio in omni afflictione nostra. Sensus est: Quomodo possem vos odisse, cùm ex vobis non ita pridem dulcissima consolatione perfusus sim, quae me totum exhilarauit? & quidem in afflictionibus meis, quae mihi vndique imminent? Quae autem haec consolatio, quodue gaudium fuerit, mox exponet. Nunc discant Christiani homines Paulum imitari, vt omnium honori & saluti consulant, libere moneant alios, & ex aliorum in vera pietate profectu mutuam capiant consolationem in CHRISTO IESV, Domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Paul adds to these words: "I am filled with comfort; I overflow with joy in all our affliction." The sense is: how could I hate you, when from you, not long ago, I have been drenched with the sweetest comfort, which has wholly cheered me, and that in my afflictions, which press upon me on every side? What this comfort and joy was, he will shortly explain. Now let Christians learn to imitate Paul: to look after the honour and salvation of all, to admonish others frankly, and to draw mutual comfort from the progress of others in true godliness, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXII.

units.la: Etenim cùm venissemus in Macedoniam, nullâ habuit relaxationem caro nostra, sed in omnibus fuimus oppressi: foris pugnæ, intus terrores. Sed qui consolatur humiles, cōsolatus est nos Deus, aduentu Titi. Non solùm autem aduentu illius, sed etiam consolatione, quam ille accepit ex vobis: cùm renuntiaret nobis vestrum vehemens desiderium, vestrum eiulatum, vestrum pro me zelum, adeò vt magis gauisus fuerim.
units.tr: For when we came into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest, but we were troubled on every side: fightings without, fears within. Nevertheless God, who comforts those who are cast down, comforted us by the coming of Titus. And not only by his coming, but also by the comfort with which he was comforted in you, when he reported to us your earnest desire, your mourning, and your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced even more.

units.la: Paulus Apostolus multis de suo erga Corinthios studio loquitur, & quanti eos faciat nuper diligenter exposuit: idq; non adulatorie facit, vt ex eo commodum aliquod priuatum percipiat, sed vt doctrinæ suæ authoritatem conciliet, & eos sibi propitios reddat, qui insidiosis impostorum blanditijs decepti, animos suos ab ipso nonnihil alienauerant. Debet exemplum hoc imitari omnes Ecclesiarum ministri. Quia enim hominum salus maximè in eo consistit, vt Dei Verbo obediant, Satan hoc imprimis agit, vt huius ministros siue præcones omnibus inuisos atq; exosos, vel saltem contemptos reddat. Id verò non alia ratione commodiori efficere potest, quàm si in suspicionem veniant, quasi ex odio omnia dicant & faciant. Quare necesse omnino est, vt ea suspicione sese liberent. In eum ergo finem à Paulo dicta sunt quæ nuper audiuimus: quòd nimirum Corinthios in corde suo gestet, quòd paratus sit cum illis viuere & mori, quòd ex amore syncero coràm quidem liberius cum ipsis agat, absens verò apud alios de ipsorum fide & pietate glorietur: deniq;, quòd ex ipsis consolationem & gaudium percipiat, quo in omni afflictionum genere recreetur. Id nunc exemplo recenti probat, quod sic narratur, vt in eo luculentissimè appareat, vt inter se mutuò affici debeant ministri & Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: The apostle Paul speaks at length about his eagerness toward the Corinthians, and recently set out carefully how highly he values them. He does not do this in flattery, to gain some private advantage from them, but to win authority for his teaching and to make those well disposed to him who, deceived by the treacherous flattery of impostors, had somewhat estranged their minds from him. All the ministers of the Churches ought to imitate this example. For since the salvation of men consists chiefly in obeying the Word of God, Satan above all works to make the ministers or heralds of that Word hated and detested by all, or at least despised. He can achieve this most easily if they come under suspicion, as if they said and did everything out of hatred. It is therefore absolutely necessary that they free themselves from that suspicion. To this end Paul has said what we have heard recently: namely, that he carries the Corinthians in his heart, that he is ready to live and die with them, that out of sincere love he deals more frankly with them when present, and when absent boasts to others of their faith and piety; and finally, that he receives from them comfort and joy with which he is refreshed in every kind of affliction. Now he proves this by a recent example, which is related in such a way that it shows most clearly how ministers and Churches ought to be mutually affected toward one another.

units.la: Nam sic scribit: Etenim cùm venissemus in Macedoniam, nullam habuit relaxationem caro nostra, sed in omnibus fuimus oppressi, &c. Loquitur autem non de primo suo in Macedoniam aduentu, quem Lucas in Actis Cap.16. descripsit (quæ enim illic narrantur, multò ante facta sunt, prius quam Paulus Corinthum venisset) sed de eo, cuius supra Cap.2. mentionem fecit. Etenim Tiuum Titum ex Asia ad Corinthios miserat, ut res Ecclesiæ illius inspiceret, & inde ad ipsum Troadem rediens, de omnibus ipsum certiorem faceret. Illi vero, cum Titum diutius apud se detinuissent, in causa fuerunt, ut ipse Troadem veniens illum non inveniret, sicuti inter eos convenerat. Ideo rerum incertus & anxius Paulus in Macedoniam traiecit, ut illic Tito occurreret. Ubi cum rursus nova mora intercederet, novas animo suo curas concepit, quibus discruciabatur. De eo in præsenti scribit: Cum venissemus in Macedoniam, nullam habuit relaxationem carò nostra, id est, quoad carnem sive externum hominem, nihil habui aut vidi, quod me recreare aut consolari posset. Foris enim ab ijs, qui à fide & Ecclesiæ contubernio alieni sunt, pugnæ & certamina movebantur, cum illi contra me & fidem Christianam omnia hostiliter tentarent. Intus vero, id est, intra Ecclesiæ parietes à domesticis fidei novi quotidie terrores excitabantur, partim ex multorum infirmitate, quorum saluti timebamus, partim ex insidijs Satanæ, quem nihil non tentare ac moliri videbam, ut fidem quorundam everteret, & illius loci Ecclesias turbaret. Ista vero in eum finem commemorat Paulus, ut ostendat, non vulgarem fuisse eam consolationem, quæ in tam gravibus certaminibus laborantem confirmare potuerit. At quia eam ex Corinthijs acceperat, non potuit non eosdem maximi facere, &c.
units.tr: For he writes thus: "For when we came into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest, but we were troubled on every side," etc. He is speaking not of his first arrival in Macedonia, which Luke describes in Acts chapter 16 (for the things narrated there happened long before Paul came to Corinth), but of that visit which he mentioned above in chapter 2. For he had sent Titus from Asia to the Corinthians, to look into the affairs of that Church, and then, returning to Troas, to inform him about everything. But they, having detained Titus for a long time with them, were the cause that when Paul came to Troas he did not find him, as had been agreed between them. Therefore Paul, uncertain of affairs and anxious, crossed over into Macedonia, so as to meet Titus there. When a new delay again intervened there, he conceived fresh cares in his mind, by which he was tormented. Of this he writes now: "When we came into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest," that is, as regards the flesh or the outward man, I had nothing or saw nothing that could refresh or comfort me. For fightings and conflicts were stirred up outside, from those who are alien to the faith and to the fellowship of the Church, since they attacked me and the Christian faith with every hostile device. Within, that is, within the walls of the Church, new terrors were daily aroused by those of our own household of faith, partly from the weakness of many, whose salvation we feared, and partly from the snares of Satan, whom I saw attempting and striving in every way to overthrow the faith of some and to disturb the Churches of that region. Paul recalls these things in order to show that the comfort which could support him while labouring under such grave conflicts was no ordinary one. And because he had received it from the Corinthians, he could not but hold them in the highest esteem, etc.

units.la: Debet autem hoc loco observari fors ministrorum Ecclesiæ, adeoq; omnium fidelium. Quia enim in mundo hospites ac peregrini sunt, undique premuntur. Etenim si eos respiciant, qui extra Ecclesiæ societatem & à fide prorsus alieni sunt, nihil quàm certamina invenient. Constat enim totus hic mundus partim ex hypocritis, qui iustitiæ & sanctitatis fuco sese vendicant: partim ex carni & seculo huic per omniaediti atq; palàm impij. At neq; hi neq; illi Veritatis lucem ferre possunt, ut qui sua opera prava (sicuti Christus ait) nolunt argui. Utriq; ergo hostiliter agunt, & cum ipsam Veritatem vincere aut extinguere non possint, aduersus eius præcones sive jactatores insurgunt. Neq; inter eos discrimen est aliquod, nisi quòd hypocritæ affluentiores sunt & crudeliores. Itaq; semper locum habet quod dicitur: Multæ sunt afflictiones iustorum. Item: In mundo afflictionem habebitis. Omnes, qui volunt pie vivere in Christo, persecutionem patientur. Et revera fluctuati sunt, qui sibi ipsis ex mundo vel pacem vel inducias tutas pollicentur. Nam ut apud Jeremiam dicit Dominus, sicuti neq; Æthiops cutem suam, neq; pardus maculas suas mutare potest, ita neq; infelix hic mundus ingenium suum mutabit. Ierem. 13.
units.tr: Moreover, in this place we ought to observe the lot of the ministers of the Church, and therefore of all the faithful. For since they are strangers and pilgrims in the world, they are pressed on every side. For if they look to those who are outside the fellowship of the Church and wholly estranged from the faith, they will find nothing but conflicts. For this whole world consists partly of hypocrites, who claim for themselves the false appearance of righteousness and holiness, and partly of those who are wholly given over to the flesh and to this age, and openly ungodly. But neither the one nor the other can bear the light of truth, since, as Christ says, they do not want their evil deeds to be exposed. Both therefore act with hostility, and since they cannot conquer or extinguish the truth itself, they rise up against its heralds or proclaimers. Nor is there any difference between them, except that the hypocrites are more prosperous and more cruel. Thus what is said always holds true: "Many are the afflictions of the righteous." Likewise: "In the world you shall have affliction." "All who want to live godly in Christ shall suffer persecution." And indeed those are deceived who promise themselves from the world either peace or safe truces. For, as the Lord says through Jeremiah, just as the Ethiopian cannot change his skin, nor the leopard his spots, so this unhappy world cannot change its nature. Jer. 13.

units.la: Quòd si vero ad ipsam Ecclesiam oculos suos minister converterit, aut quivis alius ex Christi cultorum numero, hic quoq; plena curarum atq; terroris omnia invenient. Nam hic falsi fratres occurrent, ex quibus plus periculi est, quàm ex apertis hostibus: in quibus ferendis multa devorare oportet, ne publica pax Ecclesiæ turbetur. Et hi revera sunt zizania illa, quæ neq; bene ferri possunt, cum multis noceant, neq; etiam cuelli possunt absq; totius segetis periculo. Sunt præterea, qui non nisi sua quærunt, & nisi ipsorum votis, atq; desiderijs satisfiat, mox turbas dant. Sunt item homines contentiosi, qui novis figmentis atq; constitutionibus dissensionum indies authores sunt. Adde his infirmos, qui ab impostoribus facile seducuntur, aut hostium tyrannide atq; crudelitate devicti succumbunt. Accedunt omnibus istis publicæ & communes calamitates, utpote multorum egestas, exilia, morbi, carceres, tentationes omnis generis: quæ omnia hodie passim inter Christianos homines cernuntur. Hæc igitur omnia quisquis probè consideraverit, is cum Paulo cogetur dicere: Non habet relaxationem caro mea, sed in omnibus premimur: foris pugnæ, intus terrores. Is deniq; verum esse experietur illud Christi: Qui vult post me venire, is abneget seipsum, tollat crucem suam quotidie, & sequatur me, &c. Ad ista ergo præparemur, nec aliquid tribuamus mundo & eius studijs, sed his relictis ad cœlestia aspiremus.
units.tr: But if a minister, or anyone else of the number of Christ's worshippers, turns his eyes to the Church itself, he will find here too everything full of cares and terror. For here false brothers will meet him, and they are more dangerous than open enemies; in bearing with them one must swallow much, lest the public peace of the Church be disturbed. And these are truly those tares, which cannot well be borne, since they harm many, nor can they be uprooted without danger to the whole crop. Besides these there are those who seek only their own ends, and unless their wishes and desires are satisfied, they straightway cause disturbances. There are likewise contentious men, who daily become the authors of dissensions by new inventions and regulations. Add to these the weak, who are easily seduced by impostors, or who, overcome by the tyranny and cruelty of enemies, give way. To all these are added the public and common calamities, such as the poverty of many, exiles, diseases, prisons, temptations of every kind; all of which are seen today everywhere among Christian people. Therefore whoever considers all these things carefully will be compelled to say with Paul: "My flesh has no rest, but we are pressed on every side: fightings without, fears within." Finally he will learn by experience the truth of Christ's words: "Whoever wants to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me," etc. Let us therefore prepare ourselves for these things, and attribute nothing to the world and its pursuits, but leaving these aside, aspire to heavenly things.

units.la: Verumtamen ut minus succumbamus certaminibus istis, audi quid Paulus præterea dicat: Sed qui consolatur humiles, consolatus est nos, Deus, adventu Titi. Sensus verborum est: Cum omnia essent deplorata, & ne spes quidem aliqua relaxationis in humanis appareret, tunc Deus, qui afflictos et ab omnibus derelictos respicere solet, mihi quoq; consolationem adhibuit per adventum Titi, quem tam diu tamè, solicitè expectaveram. Quo loco observabis, quòd vbiq; omnis consolationis authorem inducit Deum. Hunc in primo Cap. patrem omnis misericordiæ & Deum omnis consolationis dixit. Et sanè hic solus proprie consolator dici meretur: quia novit nos, qui fimus,& vnde ortum habeamus:neq; nostri obliuisci potest, cùm eius in nos amor naturales illas parentum erga liberos affectiones longe superet, vt alibi ex Ifaia docuimus. Deinde solus ille consolari potest in quauis necessitate, cùm & mala imminentia auertere possit, & omnium hominum corda in sua manu habeat, & proinde ex hostibus amicos facere, & odium in commiseratio nem subito mutare queat. Cuius rei exempla Scripturæ infinita exhibent. Esauus certè,qui Iacobi vitæ prius insidias struxerat, & ex Mesopotamia redeunti cum hostili apparatu occurrebat, illo viso,in lachrymas soluitur,inq; eius amplexum ruit. Idem Sauli accidit, qui cùm affectum parentis erga Ionathanum filium iampridem exuisset,& Dauidem cum copijs armatis quæreret, vt inuentum male perderet,non semel eo inuento flere cæpit, & dicere: Iustior me es Dauid,fili mi. Talis ergo cùm sit Deus,rectè ei hoc epitheton Paulus tribuit: quo admonemur,ipsum solum inuocari debere.
units.tr: Yet, that we may succumb less to these conflicts, hear what Paul adds: "But God, who comforts the humble, comforted us by the coming of Titus." The sense of the words is this: when all things had been given up for lost, and no hope of relief appeared in human affairs, then God, who is accustomed to look upon the afflicted and those forsaken by all, brought me consolation also through the coming of Titus, whom I had nevertheless so long and anxiously awaited. Here you will observe that he everywhere presents God as the author of all consolation. In the first chapter he called him the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation. And indeed he alone truly deserves to be called Consoler: because he knows us, of what we are made and whence we have our origin; nor can he forget us, since his love toward us far surpasses the natural affections of parents toward their children, as we have taught elsewhere from Isaiah. Next, he alone can console in every necessity, since he can both avert impending evils and holds the hearts of all men in his hand, and therefore can turn enemies into friends and suddenly change hatred into compassion. Scripture offers countless examples of this. Esau certainly, who had earlier plotted the life of Jacob and was coming to meet him with a hostile force as he returned from Mesopotamia, on seeing him dissolved into tears and fell upon his neck. The same happened to Saul, who, although he had long since laid aside a father's affection for his son Jonathan, and was seeking David with armed forces so as to destroy him once found, began more than once, when David had been found, to weep and to say: "You are more righteous than I, my son David." Since God is such, Paul rightly attributes this epithet to him, by which we are reminded that he alone ought to be called upon.

units.la: Quos verò consolatur ille? Humiles,id est,eos,qui calamitatibus oppressi,ad extrema iam deuenerunt,vt nulla ipsis auxilij siue consilij spes sit reliqua. Et obserua, Paulum hac quasi Periphrasi Deum describere,vt eius ingenium atque proprietatem exprimat. Nec enim hoc ex suo cerebro fecit,sed sciebat,illum passim se patrem peregrinorum, viduarum atq; orphanorum profiteri. Neq; etiam potest aliter facere,cùm ipsissima sit charitas,& in omnibus eius operibus misericordia primas teneat. Exemplum memorabile olim in Israelitis ædidit. Quid his abiectius & infelicius dici potuit,cùm Pharaonica tyrannide in Ægypto premerentur? Sed respexit eos Deus, neq; eos consolatus modò est, verumetiam manu sua, quasi cœlitus extensa eos eripuit. Idem in Babylone factum, cùm sub impio Baltazare de reditu in patriam vix cogitare auderent. Quò etiam tota Hestera historia pertinet, qua narratur, vt tam illam quàm Iudæos omnes, iam ad exitium damnatos,consolatione simul & manu potenti subleuarit. Quid,quod humanis rebus afflicissimis & omnino deploratis consolationem simul & salutem,misso in carnem Filio suo Vnigenito,attulit? Nemo igitur in periculis & angustijs desperet, sed cum Philone sentiamus,illic diuinum auxilium incipere,vbi humanum desinit.
units.tr: Whom then does he console? The humble, that is, those who, crushed by calamities, have come to the very end, so that no hope of help or counsel is left them. Observe that Paul here describes God by a kind of periphrasis, so as to express his nature and character. He did not invent this from his own head, but knew that God everywhere professes himself the father of strangers, widows and orphans. Nor can God do otherwise, since he is love itself, and mercy holds the first place in all his works. He showed a memorable example of this long ago among the Israelites. What could be more abject and wretched than they, when they were oppressed by Pharaoh's tyranny in Egypt? Yet God looked upon them, and not only comforted them but also rescued them with his hand, as if stretched out from heaven. The same happened in Babylon, when under the impious Belshazzar they hardly dared to think of returning to their homeland. To this also pertains the whole history of Esther, in which it is told how he raised up both her and all the Jews, already condemned to destruction, with consolation and at the same time with a mighty hand. What of the fact that, when human affairs were most afflicted and utterly desperate, he brought consolation and salvation together, by sending his only-begotten Son into the flesh? Let no one therefore despair in dangers and distress, but let us agree with Philo that divine help begins where human help ends.

units.la: Facit autem ad Paulini dicti confirmationem quod sequitur,quo diligentius exponit,quæ & qualis consolatio ista fuerit. Diceret enim aliquis: Quid verò ad nos,quòd suo aduentu Titus te consolatus est? Ex eo certè apparet,te Titum pluris quam nos facere,cùm hucusq; nunquam nos viseris,sicuti pollicitus eras. Præoccupat ergo obiectionem istam, & se non tam propter Titum gauisum esse docet,quàm propter ipsos,de quibus per illu certior factus fuerit. Quod sic enuntiat: Non autem solùm aduentu illius,sed etiam consolatione,quam ille accepit ex vobis:cùm renuntiaret nobis vestrum vehemens desiderium, vestrum eiulatum, vestrum pro me zelum: adeò vt magis gauisus fuerim. Sensus verborum est: Amo quidem Titum,idq; magno suo merito,sed non tam recreauit me, quòd tam fidi discipuli opera rursus vti possem, quàm quòd viderem illum ex vobis veram & solidam consolationem accepisse,quam mihi quoq; communicauit,cùm mihi renuntiaret quis vobis erga me animus esset. Tria autem tribuit Corinthijs,quæ ipsi consolationis huius materiam præbuerint. Primum est ardens sui ad ipsos aduentus desiderium: quod argumentū erat, Paulum ab illis magni fieri, vtpote eum,qui rebus ipsorum afflicissimis posset salutem afferre. Alterum,fletus & luctus,vel eiulatus,qui exortus fuerat ex prioris epistolæ recitatione,qua ipsorum vitia,& imprimis neglectam ab ipsis disciplinam accusauerat. Erat is signum reuerentiæ, & quòd ex animo pæniterent. Tertiò zelum nominat,quo ipsum prosequantur. Huius indicia erant,quòd eius nomen atq; authoritatem contra æmulos & calumniatores tuerentur. Nam etsi quidam de ipso malignius sentirent,pleriq; tamè eum amabant,nec ferre poterant,vt eius nomen proscinderetur. Hæc (inquit) mihi consolationem & gaudium pepererunt,quo plenissimè recreatus sum. At non poterat his gaudere Apostolus,nisi Corinthios amauisset,& maximi fecisset ipsorum Ecclesiam. Nam si quos contemptu dignos iudicamus, de illis non multum soliciti sumus, neque etiam eorum de nobis iudicia magni facimus.
units.tr: Moreover, what follows serves to confirm Paul's statement, as he explains more carefully what and what kind of consolation it was. Someone might say: "But what is it to us that Titus comforted you by his coming? Surely this shows that you value Titus more than us, since you have never yet visited us, as you promised." He forestalls this objection, and teaches that he rejoiced not so much on account of Titus as on account of the Corinthians themselves, about whom Titus had made him more certain. He states it thus: "Not only by his coming, but also by the comfort which he received from you, when he reported to us your earnest desire, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced the more." The sense of the words is this: I indeed love Titus, and that for his great merit, but he refreshed me not so much because I could again use the work of so faithful a disciple, as because I saw that he had received from you a true and solid consolation, which he also shared with me, when he reported what your disposition toward me was. He attributes three things to the Corinthians which supplied the matter of this consolation. (1) The first is their ardent desire for Paul's coming to them; this was a sign that they held him in high regard, as one who could bring salvation to their most afflicted circumstances. (2) The second is the weeping and mourning, or lamentation, which had arisen from the reading of his earlier letter, in which he had accused their faults, and above all the discipline they had neglected. This was a sign of reverence, and that they repented from the heart. (3) Thirdly he names their zeal with which they followed him. Signs of this were that they defended his name and authority against rivals and slanderers. For although some thought more maliciously of him, most loved him, and could not bear that his name be torn to pieces. "These things," he says, "have brought me comfort and joy, by which I have been most fully refreshed." But the Apostle could not rejoice in these things unless he had loved the Corinthians and held their Church in the highest esteem. For if we judge some to be worthy of contempt, we are not much concerned about them, nor do we set much store by their judgements of us.

units.la: Admonet autem huius loci exemplum,quis affectus inter Ecclesias & ministros esse debeat. Idem nimirum,qui inter pios parentes & bonæ indolis liberos esse solet. Hi illos peregre agentes, quàm ocyssimè domum redire vellent,& eorum aduentum maximo cum desiderio expectant: cùm è contra filij nequam suos parentes perpetuò abesse cupiant, imò in mortem quoq; eorum ceu vultures & corui intenti sint. Deinde dolet vehementer filijs ingenuis, si quid se fecisse sentiant, quod parentibus displicet. At hoc quoque improbi filij susque deque ferunt. Denique pro parentum honore & existimatione aemulantur boni filij, & vt hanc contra quosuis tueantur, sedulò laborant: quam scelerati illi & degeneres proscindere & calcare solent, quàm primùm parentes prauis ipsorum desiderijs aduersari sentiunt. Vicissim pij ac fidi parentes toto animo gaudent, quando se à suis desiderari, amari, coli, honorari & timeri vident. Ista ad se transferant omnes Christiani. Ardeant fidelium doctorum & doctrinae syncerae desiderio, & huic thesauro omnium pretiosissimo quotidie aliquid adijcere studeant. Doleant item delictorum suorum conscientia, & correptionem cum lachrymis ferant, quas non disciplinae impatientia, sed vera peccati agnitio & ex ea enatus dolor secundum Deum illis extorqueat. Sic Dauidem olim fecisse legimus, qui totas noctes cum suspirijs transfigebat, & lachrymis perpetuis lectum suum rigabat, quod se libidine sua Deum offendisse sciret. Imitati sunt illum Hierosolymitani illi, ad quos primam concionem Petrus habuit. Cum enim immane illud scelus, quod in Dei Filium patrauerant sibi exprobrari audirent, & de eo intra animos suos propriae conscientiae testimonio convincerentur, mox toto corde compuncti salutis consilium ab Apostolis petierunt. Idem ergo hodie etiam faciant, qui inter Dei filios censeri volunt. Faueant praeterea honori & existimationi ministrorum siue pastorum suorum, & hos profuis in Christo patribus agnoscant. Etenim qui hos odisse & nomen eorum laedere possunt, ij neque Christum amant, cuius illi legati sunt, neque magni faciunt regenerationis & aeternae salutis beneficium, quod ipsis per illorum ministerium Deus contulit. Rursus haec gaudia ministri quaerant, vt Ecclesias bene institutas habeant: recreet item eos & alacriores faciat populi ad doctrinam ipsorum concurrentis studium, adeoq; Christi exemplum imitati, hunc suum cibum esse putent, vt quod ipsis Deus mandauit, sedulò exequantur. Gaudeant item publica eorum, qui peccata sua pijs lachrymis deplorant, poenitentia. Hoc enim Angelos in coelis facere, Dominus testatur. Gratus quoque & iucundus ipsis sit zelus fidelium, quos Euangelij authoritatem fortiter asserere atque tueri vident. Haec vera & solida decora atque ornamenta sunt, quae de ministrorum fide, industria & studio testimonium ferunt: non pretio empti tituli, non pilei rubri aut mitrae, non togae, & quaecunque alia huius generis caeca ambitio nuuissimus hisce temporibus in Ecclesiam introduxit.
units.tr: Moreover, this passage shows what feeling there ought to be between Churches and ministers. It is surely the same as is usually found between godly parents and children of good character. These desire their children, when they are abroad, to return home as quickly as possible, and they await their arrival with the greatest longing; whereas wicked sons wish their parents to be absent continually, and indeed they watch for their deaths like vultures and ravens. Again, noble sons grieve deeply if they perceive that they have done anything displeasing to their parents. But wicked sons take this lightly and care nothing for it. Finally, good sons strive for their parents' honour and reputation and labour diligently to defend it against anyone; whereas those wicked and degenerate sons are accustomed to tear it apart and trample it underfoot as soon as they perceive their parents opposing their depraved desires. In turn, godly and faithful parents rejoice with their whole heart when they see themselves desired, loved, honoured, revered and feared by their own. All Christians should apply these things to themselves. Let them burn with desire for faithful teachers and for pure doctrine, and let them strive daily to add something to this treasure, the most precious of all. Let them likewise grieve over the consciousness of their sins, and bear correction with tears, which should be wrung from them not by impatience with discipline, but by a true recognition of sin and the sorrow arising from it, according to God. So we read that David once did, who spent whole nights in sighs and with perpetual tears watered his bed, because he knew he had offended God by his lust. Those men of Jerusalem imitated him, to whom Peter gave his first sermon. For when they heard that monstrous crime, which they had committed against the Son of God, thrown in their faces, and were convicted in their minds by the testimony of their own conscience, straightway, pricked in their whole heart, they sought counsel of salvation from the Apostles. Therefore let those who wish to be counted among the sons of God do the same today. Let them favour the honour and reputation of their ministers, and acknowledge them as fathers in Christ. For those who can hate them and harm their name neither love Christ, whose ambassadors they are, nor value the benefit of regeneration and eternal salvation, which God has bestowed through their ministry. Again, let ministers seek these joys, that they may have well-ordered Churches; likewise let the eager zeal of the people flocking to their teaching refresh them and make them more eager. Thus, imitating the example of Christ, let them think this is their food: to carry out diligently what God has commanded them. Let them also rejoice in the public repentance of those who lament their sins with godly tears, for the Lord testifies that the angels in heaven do this. Let the zeal of the faithful, whom they see boldly asserting and defending the authority of the gospel, be pleasing and welcome to them as well. These are the true and solid adornments, which bear witness to the faith, diligence and zeal of ministers: not titles bought with money, not red caps or mitres, not gowns, nor any other such blind ambition as these most recent times have introduced into the Church.

units.la: At non minus diligenter hoc quoque obseruari debet, quod Paulus tam seueriter cum Corinthijs agendum sibi esse putauit, quibus ista aderant, quae veros Christianos decere diximus. Nemo igitur tam perfectus est, qui non stimulis opus habeat. Quia etsi magna sit in credentibus Spiritus alacritas, caro tamen infirmior est, & ingenium suum retinet, cui vt sedulò resistamus necesse est. Quid vero Paulum facturum putabimus, si in terras reuersus, hodie in Ecclesijs tam inter ministros quàm verae fidei professores omnia his contraria fieri videret? Etenim Verbi studium friget, & aut omnino nullum est, aut tale, quale Deus apud Ezechielem Iudaeis tribuit, qui ex communi & recepto more potius quàm discendi studio ad sacras conciones veniebant, quibus non aliter quàm cantiuncula aliqua nihil ad ipsos pertinente afficiebantur. At huius negligentiae causa non postrema in multis ministris haeret, qui vel in docendo frigidi & indiligentes sunt, vel morum licentia authoritatem suam profitentur, sed ipsos populo partim ridiculos, partim exosos faciunt. Quòd si poenitentiam requiras, quàm paucos inuenies, qui de peccatis suis doleant, & ea cum lachrymis pijs deplorent? Plures certe sunt, qui illis tanquam praeclare factis gloriantur, & ex eorum commemoratione voluptatem capiunt. Et quid aliud faceret vulgus hominum, quando ministros suos siue pastores, vel canes mutos esse, vel assiduis comessationibus vacare, deq; rebus sacris scurriliter loqui videt? Fit ergo, vt neq; Ecclesiae ministros suos magni faciant, neque hi illarum cura tangantur, vtrinq; vero Euangelij professione vel ad morum licentiam, vel ad turpem quaestum abutantur. Oremus ergo aeternum Dei Filium, Dominum nostrum IESVM CHRISTVM, vt is medicam manum vitijs istis adhibeat, vt omnes sancto zelo accensi ipsum quaerant, ament & colant, vt olim cum ipso viuant & regnent. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But this too must be observed no less carefully: Paul thought he had to deal so severely with the Corinthians, among whom were present those things which we have said befit true Christians. No one therefore is so perfect that he has no need of goads. For although in believers there is great eagerness of the Spirit, the flesh is weaker and keeps its own nature, which we must diligently resist. But what would we think Paul would do, if, returning to earth today, he saw all these things contrary to them occurring in the Churches, both among ministers and among those who profess true faith?
