For zeal for the Word grows cold, and either there is none at all, or it is such as God, through Ezekiel, attributed to the Jews, who came to the sacred sermons out of common and accepted custom rather than eagerness to learn, and were moved by them no differently than by some little song having nothing to do with them. And the cause of this negligence lies not least in many ministers, who are either cold and careless in teaching, or who, by license of morals, profess their authority while making themselves partly ridiculous and partly hateful to the people. But if you ask about repentance, how few will you find who grieve over their sins and lament them with godly tears? Surely there are many who boast of them as if they were nobly done, and take pleasure in recounting them. And what else would the common crowd do, when they see their ministers to be either dumb dogs or given over to constant feasting, and speaking scurrilously about sacred things? So it comes about that neither do the people value their ministers, nor are the ministers concerned for the Churches, and on both sides the profession of the gospel is abused, either for licence of morals or for shameful gain. Let us therefore pray to the eternal Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, that he may apply his healing hand to these vices, so that all, kindled with holy zeal, may seek, love and worship him, and live and reign with him for ever. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: Nam etiamsi tristitia vos affeci per epistolam, non me poenitet, etiamsi poenituerit: Video enim epistolam illam, tametsi ad tempus, tristitia vos affecisse. Nunc gaudeo, non quod tristitia affecti fueritis, sed quod tristitia affecti fueritis ad resipiscentiam: nam tristitia affecti fuistis secundum Deum, ut nulla in re detrimento affecti sitis per nos. Nam qui secundum Deum est dolor, is resipiscentiam efficit ad salutem, cuius nunquam poeniteat: at mundi dolor mortem efficit. Ecce enim istud ipsum, quod secundum Deum tristitia affecti fuistis, quantum in vobis effecit studium: imo defensionem, imo indignationem: imo timorem, imo vehemens desiderium, imo zelum, imo vindicationem.
units.tr: For even if I grieved you with my letter, I do not regret it, though I did regret it. For I see that the letter grieved you, though only for a time. Now I rejoice, not that you were grieved, but that you were grieved into repentance. For you were grieved in a godly way, so that you suffered no loss from us in anything. For godly sorrow produces a repentance that leads to salvation and leaves no regret, but worldly sorrow produces death. For see, this very thing, that you were grieved in a godly way, how much earnestness it produced in you: indeed defence, indeed indignation, indeed fear, indeed vehement longing, indeed zeal, indeed vengeance.

units.la: QUamvis Verbi Dei ministerium in eum finem institutum sit, ut per illud homines Deo adducantur & salvi fiant, multis tamen hoc adeo non prodest, ut potius ex eo perditionis & exitii sui occasionem arripiant, dum correptionis & disciplinae impatientes, adversus Verbi precones se insolentius gerunt. Ideo Prophetae & Apostoli frequenter de suo ministerio differunt, ut ostendant, se quicquid faciunt, ex officio facere. Quo etiam referri debent, quaecunque Paulus hucusque de suo apostolatu atque doctrina disseruit. Nam ut saepe diximus, erant aliqui inter Corinthios, qui de ipso iniquius iudicabant, quasi insolentius & nimis pro imperio ageret: & hi imprimis rigorem prioris epistolae exagitabant, per quam multa illorum vitia graviter corripuerat, & hominem incestum Satanae tradi iusserat. Poterant isti ex eo, quod proxime de consolatione & gaudio dixerat, quod ex ipsorum fletu atque eiulatu perceperit, occasionem novam arripere, dicendi: Ergo ut tu laetari & gaudere possis, nobis lugendum atque eiulandum est? Quid vero nobis de tuo in nos studio polliceri possumus, quando propter unius hominis scelus universam Ecclesiam nostram tam duriter tractavisti? Et num nostri amantem putabimus esse te, qui ex nostris lachrymis voluptatem capis? Rursus ergo hanc quoq; obiectionem praeoccupat, & ea occasione nunc diligentius exponit, quod supra Cap. secundo cepit de hac causa dicere.
units.tr: Although the ministry of God's Word was instituted for this end, that through it men might be brought to God and saved, for many it does not help at all; rather they seize on it as an occasion of their own ruin and destruction, since they cannot bear correction and discipline and behave more insolently towards the heralds of the Word. Therefore the prophets and apostles often speak about their own ministry, to show that whatever they do, they do from duty. To this also must be referred everything Paul has so far said about his apostleship and teaching. For, as we have often said, there were some among the Corinthians who judged him unfairly, as if he acted too insolently and too much like a lord. Chiefly they attacked the severity of the earlier letter, in which he had sharply rebuked many of their faults and had ordered the incestuous man to be handed over to Satan. From what he had just said about consolation and joy, which he had perceived from their weeping and wailing, they could seize a new occasion and say: "So that you may rejoice and be glad, we must mourn and wail? And what can we promise about your concern for us, when because of one man's crime you have treated our whole Church so harshly? And shall we think you love us, when you take pleasure in our tears?" So again he anticipates this objection too, and now, on this occasion, he explains more carefully what he began to say about this matter in chapter two.

units.la: Initio fatetur simul & excusat rigorem illum, de quo aemuli eius querebantur. Nam etiamsi (inquit) tristitia vos affeci per epistolam, non me poeniter, etiamsi poenituerit. Quibus verbis hoc vult dicere: Nemo mihi obiiciat, quae prius scripsi. Fateor ipse, me vobis tristitiae authorem fuisse. Non autem me eius facti poenitet, etiamsi me aliquando eius poenituerit. Quae particula postrema non ita intelligi debet, quasi Paulus praecipiti carnis affectu abreptus scripserit, quae postea nollet scripta fuisse. Scimus enim spiritum Sanctum Apostolorum linguas & calamum direxisse, ut nihil quam quod ille dictabat dicerent aut scriberent. In praesenti ergo hoc solum vult dicere, quod quoad affectum suum privatum, non sine dolore, adeoq; invitus, illa scripserit, ex quibus sciebat optimos quosque dolorem concepturos esse. Ideo supra dixit: Ex multa tribulatione & anxietate cordis scripsi vobis, per multas lachrymas. Itaque hic praesentis loci sensus est: Maluissem ego mitius vobiscum agere, & ut pater pius, dum filios suos durius tractare cogitur, dolorem fere acutiorem, quam ipsi, in corde suo sentit: ita ego quoque non minus quam vos contristatus fui, cum illa scriberem. Verumtamen ita fieri oportebat, & nunc adeo non poenitet me facti illius ut potius gaudeam: quia video epistolam illam, tametsi vos ad tempus contristaverit, non tamen caruisse suo fructu.
units.tr: At the outset he both admits and excuses that severity of which his rivals complained. "For even if," he says, "I grieved you with the letter, I do not regret it, though I did regret it." By these words he means this: let no one object to me what I wrote earlier. I myself admit that I was the author of your sorrow. But I do not regret that deed, even if at some time I did regret it. This last clause ought not to be understood as if Paul, carried away by a hasty impulse of the flesh, wrote things he afterwards wished had not been written. For we know that the Holy Spirit guided the tongues and pens of the apostles so that they said or wrote nothing except what he dictated. So in the present passage he wants to say only this: with regard to his private feeling, he wrote those things not without pain, and indeed reluctantly, knowing that all the good people would be grieved by them. Therefore he said above: "Out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you, with many tears." So the sense of the present passage is this: I would have preferred to deal with you more gently, and like a loving father who is compelled to treat his sons more harshly, I feel in my heart a pain almost sharper than theirs. So I too was no less saddened than you when I wrote that. Nevertheless it had to be so, and now I do not regret that deed so much as rejoice in it, because I see that the letter, though it grieved you for a time, did not lack its fruit.

units.la: Est autem hic observatu dignum, quod ita se excusat Paulus, ut nihil eorum retractet, quae prius severius aut acrius scripserat, & quae multis displicuisse sciebat. Imo aperte illa pro suis agnoscit & defendit. Discant ergo eius exemplo ministri, non cedere improbis & contumacibus, sed potius constanter urgere quod semel ex Dei mandato instituerunt. Debent enim (ut infra dicet Paulus) Christi in se loquentis experimentum praebere: quod non poterunt facere, si in suis dictis & scriptis non semper sibi constet. Et huc pertinent multorum aliorum exempla, quos Dei fideles seruos fuisse scimus. Moses certè, etsi Pharaonem iniquissimè ferre videret Dei mandatum de dimittendis filijs Israelis, illud tamen constantissimè vrsit, neque vllis comminationibus aut periculis se perterrefieri passus est, vt segnius ageret. Idem simili constantia cum Israelitis murmurantibus & aduersus ipsum atque fratrem Aaronem tumultuantibus suam authoritatem defendit. Talis quoque Elias fuit, quando ei cum Achabo impio & contumaci res erat. Idem de omnibus Prophetis dici potest, Ieremia imprimis, qui quamus se proditionis & perfidiae in patriam suspicione grauari sentiret, nunquam tamen adduci potuit, vt aliter loqueretur, quam ei in mandatis Deus dederat. Sic Apostoli fecere, cum illis a Senatu mandaretur, ne posthac in nomine IESV CHRISTI praedicarent. Responderunt enim: Oportet Deo magis obedire quam hominibus: Non possumus quae vidimus & audiuimus, non loqui. Et Paulus postea, cum Romae captiuus detineretur, ex vinculis non alia scripsit, quam quae prius docuerat, neque eorum calumnias veritus est; qui illum contra Romanas leges nouum Dei cultum inuebere vociferabantur. Debet hoc ipsum hodie etiam fieri ab Ecclesiae ministris. Aegre ferunt multi, si superstitiones & illicitas cultus liberius arguantur, si scelera publice accusentur, si poenitere nescijs ira Dei denuntietur: multi etiam silentium ministris praecipere audent. Sed qui obsecro nos sumus, vt aliter loquamur, quam ex Dei ore, ex Scripturis nimirum sacris didicimus? Stulti profecto, & nimium arrogantes sunt, qui hoc a nobis exigunt. Aut quis prudentem & cordatum diceret eum, qui legatos Regis potentissimi ad se missos alia loqui vellet, quam a Rege suo in mandatis acceperunt? Et tu a Dei Opt. Max. legatis hoc postulare audes? Quod si vero id obtineas, quae inde ad te vtilitas redibit? Etenim propter legati fui perfidiam non mutabit sententiam suam Deus, quo minus puniat eos, quos poena dignos esse prius iudicauit. At non in Deum modo impij & perfidi, verum etiam terque quaterque miseri atque infelices sunt, qui vt hominibus placeant, aut canes muti fiunt, aut quae bene dixerunt retractant, aut illa saltem ambigua & dubia expositione aliqua mitigant, eo quod nonnullis duriora aequo videntur. Atqui finis ministerij sacri est, non vt hominibus placeamus, sed vt quam plurimos feruemus. Etenim qui hominibus placere studeat (vt de semetipso Paulus ait) ij Dei serui non sunt. Itaque huius exemplum imitentur, quotquot cum lande & fructu aliquo in Verbi ministerio versari volunt. Nam qui mundi huius applausum quaerunt, ij neque Deo neque hominibus probantur, imo eos tandem sibi acerrimos hostes esse sentiunt, quorum prauis desiderijs ipsi nimis seruiliter indulserunt.
units.tr: It is worth noting here that Paul excuses himself in such a way that he retracts none of the things he had written earlier, more severely or sharply, which he knew had displeased many. Indeed he openly acknowledges and defends them as his own. Let ministers therefore learn from his example not to yield to the wicked and stubborn, but rather to press constantly what they have once established by God's command. For they ought (as Paul says below) to give proof of Christ speaking in them; this they cannot do if they are not always consistent in their words and writings. To this point also belong the examples of many others whom we know were faithful servants of God. Moses certainly, although he saw Pharaoh most unjustly resisting God's command to release the sons of Israel, nevertheless pressed that command most steadfastly, and did not allow himself to be frightened by any threats or dangers into acting more feebly. In the same way, with similar constancy, he defended his authority against the murmuring Israelites who stirred up tumult against him and his brother Aaron. Elijah was such a man too, when he had to deal with the impious and obstinate Ahab. The same can be said of all the prophets, Jeremiah above all, who, although he felt himself burdened with suspicion of treachery and disloyalty to his country, could never be brought to speak otherwise than God had commanded him. So the apostles acted, when the Senate ordered them not to preach any more in the name of Jesus Christ. For they answered: "We must obey God rather than men. We cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard." And Paul afterwards, when he was held captive at Rome, wrote from his chains nothing other than what he had taught before, and did not fear the slanders of those who cried out that he was introducing a new worship of God contrary to Roman laws. The same must be done today by the ministers of the Church. Many people are displeased if superstitions and illicit forms of worship are argued against too freely, if crimes are publicly denounced, if the wrath of God is proclaimed against those who will not repent; many even dare to order ministers to be silent. But who are we, I ask, that we should speak otherwise than we have learned from the mouth of God, that is, from the holy Scriptures? Those who demand this of us are certainly foolish and far too arrogant. Or who would call wise and sensible the man who wished the envoys of a most powerful king, sent to him, to say something other than what they had received as instructions from their king? And do you dare to demand this of the envoys of God, the Best and Greatest? But even if you were to obtain it, what advantage would come back to you from it? For God will not change his judgment because of the treachery of his envoy, so as to spare those whom he has previously judged worthy of punishment. Indeed the wicked and faithless are not only wicked and faithless towards God, but are also three and four times wretched and unhappy, who, in order to please men, either become dumb dogs, or retract what they said well, or at least soften it with some ambiguous and doubtful explanation, because some things seem to some people harsher than is fair. Yet the purpose of the sacred ministry is not that we should please men, but that we should kindle as many as possible. For whoever seeks to please men (as Paul says of himself) is not a servant of God. Therefore let all who wish to serve in the ministry of the Word with praise and some fruit imitate his example. For those who seek the applause of this world are approved neither by God nor by men; indeed in the end they find that those whose wicked desires they indulged too servilely have become their bitterest enemies.

units.la: Caeterum tausam indicat Paulus, cur ipsum facti non poeniteat, dicens: Gaudeo nunc, non quod tristitia affecti fueritis ad resipiscentiam. Est verborum constructio obscurior, & aliquid deesse videtur. Nam ex omnibus loci totius circumstantijs satis constat, Apostolum hoc voluisse dicere: Gaudeo, non quod tristitia per me affecti fueritis, sed quod tristitia haec vobis ad resipiscentiam adiumento fuit, qui prius securi in peccatis vestris pergebatis. Vbi discimus, in correptionibus non tam dolorem & gemitum eorum, qui corripiuntur, quam resipiscentiam spectari debere. Nam inhumanum prorsus & barbarum est, imo tyrannicum nimis, aliorum cruciatibus gaudere, aut ex eorum querelis atque gemitibus voluptatem captare. Rursus pharisaicum est, in externa luctus specie acquiescere, aut pro peccatis satisfactu putare, si qui haec aut ista patiantur. Sola resipiscentia testatur dolorem nostrum ex animo vere pio manare, neque fictos esse gemitus quibus interea dum corripimur, suspiramus. Satisfactio autem extra Christum nulla potest esse, qui solus nobis scelerum omnium expiatio simul & iustitia a Patre factus est: inutilis autem est dolor omnis, nisi ad Deum conuertamur per Christum, & ex huius semine renati vitam moresque emendemus. Huc referri debent exempla de filio prodigo, de latronibus cum Christo crucifixis, de Dauide ac similibus. Et ideo Petrus iis, qui toto corde compuncti salutis consilium petebant, praecipit, vt resipiscant, in nomine IESV CHRISTI baptizentur, eiusdem Ecclesiae sese coniungant, separentur autem a natione Iudaeorum praua atque degenere. Id vero simul officij admonet eos, qui disciplinae praefecti sunt: Vt nimirum non prius remittant huius rigorem, quam homines emendatos viderint. Denique vt bonus atque prudens pater, virgas tunc demum retrahit, quando filium ex disciplina meliorem factum esse videt, & tunc hac se vsum esse vehementer gaudet: Ita illi quoque sibi agendum esse cogitent. Et hunc finem sibi propositum habere debent non solum Ecij, quibus Legum executio mandata est: ne indulgentia sua eos perdant, qui seueriori disciplina corrigi & in ordine retineri poterant.
units.tr: Otherwise Paul gives the reason why he does not regret the deed itself, saying: "I now rejoice, not that you were grieved into repentance." The construction of the words is rather obscure, and something seems to be missing. For from all the circumstances of the whole passage it is clear enough that the apostle meant to say this: "I rejoice, not that you were grieved through me, but that this sorrow was a help to you towards repentance, since before you had gone on secure in your sins." Here we learn that in reproofs one should look not so much to the pain and groaning of those who are corrected as to their repentance. For it is utterly inhuman and barbarous, indeed too tyrannical, to rejoice in the sufferings of others or to take pleasure in their complaints and groans. On the other hand, it is Pharisaical to rest in an outward show of mourning, or to think that satisfaction has been made for sins if people suffer this or that. Only repentance shows that our sorrow flows from a truly pious heart, and that the groans with which we sigh while we are being corrected are not feigned. But satisfaction can be made only in Christ, who alone has been made for us by the Father both the expiation of all sins and our righteousness; and all sorrow is useless unless we turn to God through Christ and, born again from his seed, amend our life and morals. To this must be referred the examples of the prodigal son, of the thieves crucified with Christ, of David and similar cases. And so Peter commanded those who, pricked to the heart, sought counsel for salvation, that they should repent, be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, join themselves to the same Church, and separate themselves from the perverse and degenerate nation of the Jews. This, at the same time, is a reminder of duty to those set over discipline: namely, that they should not relax its severity until they see that people have been amended. Finally, like a good and wise father, he withdraws the rod only when he sees that his son has become better through discipline, and then rejoices greatly that he has used it: so they too should think they must act. And not only the magistrates, to whom the execution of the laws has been entrusted, ought to have this end in view, lest by their indulgence they ruin those who could have been corrected and kept in order by a stricter discipline.

units.la: Sed diligentius narratur à Paulo, ut Corinthij ad resipiscentiam contristati fuerint. Nam tristitia affecti fuistis (inquit) secundum Deum, ut nulla in re sitis detrimento affecti per nos. Argumentum ita formari poterit: Qui secundum Deum tristitia afficiuntur, ij nullum ex illis detrimentum accipiunt, qui ipsis tristitiae illius authores sunt: At vos secundum Deum tristitia affecti estis: Ergo nihil ex me damni accepistis, neque habetis quod de meo rigore conqueramini. Ad Maioris confirmationem pertinet quod subijcitur. Nam qui secundum Deum est dolor, is resipiscentiam efficit ad salutem, cuius nunquam poeniteat: at mundi dolor mortem efficit. Duas facit doloris species. Dolor secundum Deum dicitur, qui in unum Deum respicit, ita ut hoc unum homini doleat, quod peccando Deum offenderit, & hunc sibi iratum habeat, alioqui quiduis ferre paratus, modo cum illo in gratiam edire possit. Mundi vero dolor dicitur, quando propter res humanas saeculi dolemus, utpote propter opes amissas aut coniugis & liberorum obitum, aut propter amicos nobis ereptos, vel quod infamia notati simus: item, quando aliena felicitate ringimur, vel metu poenarum nobis imminentium discruciamur, nihil interim de Deo soliciti, aut de scelerum emendatione, quibus iram illius provocauimus. Ille dolor mortem efficit, partim quoad corpus, dum consolationem nullam admittens ossa exiccat (ut sapiens ille Solomon dicebat) virésque omnes consumit: partim quoad animam, quia nisi Deus remedium adhibeat, ad desperationis praecipitium deducit. E contra dolor ille, qui secundum Deum concipitur, resipiscentiam efficit ad salutem, cuius numquam poeniteat. Nam qui ita dolent, ij sibi ipsis displicent, de vitijs corrigendis cogitant, & ad Deum reuertuntur, vbi certa eis spes gratiae & salutis portus tutissimus paratus est. Etenim Dei promissiones sunt: Nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut conuertatur, & viuat. Reuertimini ad me, & ego reuertar ad vos. Item: Respicite ad me, & salui eritis omnes fines terrae.
units.tr: But Paul gives a fuller account of how the Corinthians were brought to repentance. "For you were grieved," he says, "in a godly way, so that you suffered no loss through us in anything." The argument can be framed like this: those who are grieved in a godly way suffer no loss from those who caused that grief; but you were grieved in a godly way; therefore you have suffered no harm from me, and you have no reason to complain of my severity. What follows serves to confirm the major premise: "For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation and is never regretted, but worldly grief produces death." He makes two kinds of grief. Grief is called godly when it looks to the one God, so that a person grieves for this alone, that by sinning he has offended God and made him angry, and is ready to endure anything, provided he can be reconciled to him. Worldly grief is what we feel over the affairs of this age: the loss of wealth, the death of a spouse or children, friends snatched from us, or disgrace. It is also what we feel when we are tormented by another's good fortune, or when we are racked by fear of the punishments hanging over us, while we are not at all concerned about God or about amending the sins by which we provoked his anger. This grief produces death, partly in the body, since, admitting no comfort, it dries up the bones (as the wise Solomon said) and consumes all strength; and partly in the soul, since unless God applies a remedy, it drives a person over the precipice of despair. By contrast, that grief which is conceived in a godly way produces a repentance that leads to salvation and is never regretted. For those who grieve in this way are displeased with themselves, think about correcting their faults, and turn back to God, where a sure hope of grace and a most secure harbour of salvation are ready for them. For these are God's promises: "I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live." "Turn back to me, and I will turn back to you." Again: "Look to me, and be saved, all you ends of the earth."

units.la: Exempla, quibus haec doloris distinctio confirmetur, vbiq; sunt obuia, & mox res totasuidentissime patebit, si Cainum & Dauidem inter se conferas. Ille secundum mundi doluit, non quod Deum offendisset, sed quod se à Deo minus quam fratrem Abelum curari, & hunc sibi praeferri videret. Inde vero mors animae secuta est, & vita in hoc corpore ipsa morte acerbior, sicuti vox ista desperationis plena testatur: Maior est iniquitas mea, quam ut remitti possit. At Dauid, cum turpissime peccasset, secundum Deum doluit, deq; eius gratia & reconciliatione solicitus clamauit: Miserere mei Deus secundum multitudinem misericordiarum tuarum, &c. Et mox sibi dici audiuit: Transtulit Deus peccatum tuum. Itaque dolor ille veram resipiscentiam ad salutem in ipso peperit. Idem videbis adhuc clarius si eundem cum Saule contuleris. Dolebat is quoque huius mundi dolore, quod Regnum sibi diuina sententia negari, & successorem iam sibi a Deo electum esse audiret. At dolore hoc exacerbatus, mortem sibi ipsi accelerauit, dum nobiles infamnes duxit, cor proprium exedit, Dauidem insontem, imo meliora de se & toto regno meritum, persecutus est, & tandem bello implicitus artes fatidicas, vel potius harum praesidem diabolum consuluit, qui ipsi mortis violentae simul & desperationis author fuit. Quod si Dauidem inspicias, is etsi a filio Absalone ex solio regali deturbaretur, tamen sui sceleris non immemor, secundum Deum doluit, & proinde de hoc potius placando quam de regno per vim retinendo solicitus, dicebat: Si inuenero gratiam coram Domino, restituet me, offendetque mihi & se & habitaculum suum: Quod si dixerit mihi: Non mihi places: praesto sum, faciat mecum quod sibi bonum videbitur. Ita vero resipiscentiam salutarem sibi acquisiuit Dauid, cuius eum nunquam potuit poenitere. Possunt hic adnumerari Iudas & Petrus, ex quibus hic secundum Deum dolens a Christo in gratiam receptus & pristinae dignitati restitutus est: ille vero mundi dolore absorptus desperauit, seq; ipsum suspendit. Caeterum in his obseruari debet.
units.tr: Examples confirming this distinction of grief are everywhere to hand, and the whole matter will be quite plain if you compare Cain and David. Cain grieved in a worldly way, not because he had offended God, but because he saw that he was cared for less by God than his brother Abel, and that Abel was preferred to him. From this indeed came the death of the soul, and a life in this body more bitter than death itself, as that voice full of despair bears witness: "My iniquity is greater than can be forgiven." But David, when he had sinned most shamefully, grieved in a godly way, and, anxious about God's grace and reconciliation, cried out: "Have mercy on me, O God, according to the multitude of your mercies," and so on. Soon he heard it said to him: "God has taken away your sin." So that grief brought forth in him a true repentance that leads to salvation. You will see the same even more clearly if you set him beside Saul. Saul too grieved with worldly grief, because he heard that the kingdom had been denied him by divine sentence, and that a successor had already been chosen for him by God. But, exasperated by this grief, he hastened his own death: he killed the priests, consumed his own heart, persecuted the innocent David, who deserved better of him and of the whole kingdom, and at last, entangled in war, consulted the arts of the fortune-tellers, or rather the devil, the lord of those arts, who was himself the author of his violent death and of his despair. If you look at David, though he was driven from the royal throne by his son Absalom, yet, not forgetful of his own wickedness, he grieved in a godly way; and therefore, anxious rather to placate God than to keep the kingdom by force, he said: "If I find grace in the sight of the Lord, he will bring me back and show me both himself and his dwelling. But if he says to me, 'I am not pleased with you,' here I am; let him do with me what seems good to him." So David won for himself a saving repentance, which he never regretted. Judas and Peter may be numbered here. Of these, Peter, grieving in a godly way, was received back into favour by Christ and restored to his former dignity; but Judas, swallowed up by worldly grief, despaired and hanged himself. Moreover, the following should be observed in these cases.

units.la: Primo, vera & salutaris poenitentiae initium esse dolorem illum secundum Deum. Verum tamen non potest is in nobis locum habere, nisi peccata nostra vere & ex animo agnoscamus. Quia vero id innata nobis vitiositas non permittit, nobisq; ipsis inter peccandum delitias facere solemus, redargutione seria et diligeti opus est: quod ipsum in Dauidis exemplo apparet, qui secure in suo scelere periisset, nisi Natha ipsum induxisset in eius agnitionem. Ideo qui nos peccates arguu & corripiunt, ij nullo nos detrimento (vt Paulus hîc ait) afficiunt, sed potius beneficium nobis conferunt, quo nullum nobis salutarius magisque necessarium conferri poterat. Idem enim faciunt, quod pij parentes, qui filios immorigeros castigant: aut quod fidi medici, qui vt toti corpori consulant, vitiosum membrum secant & vrunt, vel aegrotanti pharmacum amarum propinant. Sed in eo potissimum elucet peruersitas humani ingenij, qua fit, vt poenitentiae authores odio prosequamur, impostores vero blandulos amemus, qui nostrum nobis exitium acceleravant.
units.tr: First, that godly grief is the beginning of true and saving repentance. Yet it cannot take place in us unless we truly and sincerely acknowledge our sins. Since our innate vice does not allow this, and we are wont to indulge ourselves in our sins, a serious and careful rebuke is needed. This appears in the example of David, who would have perished securely in his sin unless Nathan had led him to recognize it. Therefore those who reprove us for our sins and correct us do us no harm (as Paul says here), but rather confer a benefit on us, than which nothing more salutary or more necessary could be given to us. They do what godly parents do when they chastise undutiful children, or what faithful physicians do when, to care for the whole body, they cut out and burn a diseased limb, or give a bitter medicine to the sick. But the perversity of the human mind shines out most clearly in this: we come to hate the authors of repentance, and love the smooth-tongued impostors who hasten our ruin.

units.la: Deinde fructum quoq; doloris istius diuini diligentius considerasse prodest. Respipiscentiam ad salutem efficit ἀμεταμέλητον, id est, cuius nos nunquam poenitere. Qui propter res huius sae culi tristitia afficiuntur atq; dolent, eos plerunq; suae tristitiae poniter, quādo se nihil proficere vident, imo sibi eo peius esse sentiunt, quo maiori & acerbiori cum luctu sese inaniter excruciant. Ac quae secundum Deum est tristitia, duo comoda sibi coniuncta habet. Primum, quod desperationi metur: quia ad hunc modum afflictis Deus gratiae suae Solem seu iubar aliquod ostendit. Alterum, quod eo fructu beat vere poenitentes, quae pij & electi vnice quaerunt. Nam de gratia Dei certos facit, & simul scandalum e medio tollit, quod ex nostris flagitijs enatum fuerat. Quapropter tristitia haec omnibus huius mundi gaudijs praestat. Haec enim rebus fluxis & caducis constant, quae cum amittuntur, post se relinquunt dolores atque cruciatus intolerabiles. Illa vero vtilis est, vt & hic bene viuamus, & olim felicitatem veram atque aeternam consequamur. Denique haec non postrema pietatis illius pars est, quam Paulus quaestum maximum esse dixit, eo quod promissiones habeat praesentis & futuri saeculi. 1. Tim. 4.
units.tr: Next, it is useful to consider more carefully the fruit of this godly grief. It produces a repentance that leads to salvation and is "not to be regretted" [ἀμεταμέλητον], that is, one that we shall never regret. Those who are saddened and grieved over the things of this age, for the most part come to regret their sorrow, since they see that they accomplish nothing, and indeed feel that they are worse off, the more vainly and bitterly they torment themselves with mourning. But the sorrow that is according to God has two advantages joined to it. First, it guards against despair, because God shows to those so afflicted some sunrise or ray of his grace. Second, it brings the fruit that truly repentant people, the godly and the elect, seek above all: it makes them certain of God's grace, and at the same time removes the scandal that had arisen from our wickedness. Therefore this sorrow surpasses all the joys of this world. For those joys rest on fleeting and perishable things, and when these are lost they leave behind pains and intolerable torments. But godly sorrow is useful both so that we may live well here and so that we may one day attain true and eternal happiness. Finally, this is not the least part of that godliness which Paul called "great gain," because it has the promise of the present and of the future life. 1 Tim. 4.

units.la: Porro cum Paulus & Scripturarum testimonijs & exemplis pluribus confirmare posset quod di xeratipsos Corinthios compellat, vt quot & quanta bona ex hac tristitia ipsis enata sint, consideret: Ecce enim (inquit) istud ipsum, quod secundum Deū tristitia affecti fuistis, quantum in vobis effecit studium? imo defensionem, imo indignationem, &c. Demonstrandi particula eos excitat, et simul laudat, quod certis argumentis probauerint, se vere & ex animo poenituisse. Sunt illa septem numero. Primum est studium serium poenitentiae. Qui enim hucusq; securi in vitijs suis dormierant, horum agnitione compuncti, in illis corrigendis alacres cernebantur & industrij. Ita enim solent, quicunque vere poenitent. Nam militum bonorum similes sunt, qui qua ignobili fuga sibi inuulerunt infamiae notam, postea omni studio eluere satagunt. Sic Dauidem olim fecisse legimus, sic Petrum quoque, quorum exempla plerosque Corinthiorum imitatos fuisse, hic locus docet. Secundo defensio ne ponit. Graece est ἀπολογία, quod excusationem aut criminis purgationem significat. Eam Corinthijs tribuit Apostolus, quia & apud Deum sese pijs precibus purgauerant, & toti mundo suâ probarant innocentiam, quoad incestum illum hominis, vt paulo post sequetur. Tertium est, indignatio. Sibijpsis enim irascebantur, quod in coercenda quorunda licentia tâ fuissent negligentes. Quarto timore eis tribuit: Dei nimirū, quo tunc continebantur in officio. Quinto vehemens desiderium, cum Deo videlicet redeundi in gratiam. Quod quàm ardens sit in sanctis, Dauid eleganti similiter exprimit, dicens: Vt cerua rugit ad torrentes aquarum: sic anima mea rugit ad te ô Deus: Sitit anima mea Deum, Deum viuum, quando veniam tandem, vt appaream in conspectu Dei? Sexto zelus siue aemulatio sancta nominatur, qua se mutuo ad studium placandi Dei accendebant. Addit his postremū, Vindicationē, qua nimirū vsi fuerant in homine incestum, publici illius scandali authorem. Et ea imprimis opus est, ne a Deo iudicemur, & cum mundo infelici condemnemur, vt in prioris epist. Cap. vndecimo audiuimus. HAEC ergo sunt verae poenitentiae indicia, & fructus illi, de quibus Baptista olim concionatus est: Ferte fructum dignum ijs, qui respuerint. His hodie etiam nos studere oportebat, quando Deus vbiq; flagella sua exerit. Sed poenitentia hodie aut nulla, aut momentanea, aut fucata est, qualem Israelitis Hoseas Cap. sexto tribuit.
units.tr: Now, since Paul could confirm by the testimonies of Scripture and by many examples what he had said, he addresses the Corinthians themselves, that they should consider how many and how great good things have arisen for them from this sorrow: "For behold," he says, "this very thing, that you were grieved in a godly way, how much earnestness it produced in you; yes, defence, yes, indignation," and so on. The particle of showing stirs them up, and at the same time praises them, because by certain proofs they had shown that they had truly and sincerely repented. There are seven of these. (1) The first is earnest zeal for repentance. For those who had hitherto slept securely in their vices, pricked by the recognition of them, were seen to be eager and active in correcting them. This is what all who truly repent are wont to do. For they are like good soldiers who, after a shameful flight that brought them the stain of infamy, strive with all their zeal to wipe it away. So we read that David did, and so did Peter, and this passage shows that many of the Corinthians imitated their examples. (2) Second, defence. In Greek it is apologia, which means excuse or the clearing of a charge. The Apostle attributes this to the Corinthians, because they had cleared themselves before God by devout prayers, and had proved their innocence to the whole world regarding that man's incest, as will follow shortly after. (3) Third, indignation. For they were angry with themselves, because they had been so negligent in restraining the licence of certain persons. (4) Fourth, fear, namely fear of God, by which they were then kept in their duty. (5) Fifth, a vehement desire, namely to return to God's favour. How ardent this is in the saints David expresses elegantly, saying: "As the hart cries out for the water-brooks, so my soul cries out for you, O God. My soul thirsts for God, the living God; when shall I come at last, that I may appear before the face of God?" (6) Sixth, zeal, or holy emulation, by which they stirred one another on to the eagerness to placate God. To these he adds a final item, vindication, which they had certainly exercised against the man who had committed incest, the author of that public scandal. This is especially necessary, so that we may not be judged by God and condemned with the unhappy world, as we heard in the first epistle, chapter eleven. These, therefore, are the true signs of repentance and those fruits of which the Baptist once preached: "Bring forth fruit worthy of repentance." We too ought to be zealous for these things today, when God everywhere stretches out his scourges. But today repentance is either none at all, or momentary, or feigned, like that which Hosea in chapter six ascribed to the Israelites.

units.la: Obseruabis autē, quid in Ecclesia cum ijs fieri debeat, qui istis argumentis se respipuisse testantur? Deus poenitetes absq; mora in gratiā recipit, vt alibi prolixè docuimus. Vt ergo idem ipsi quoque faciamus iubet Christus, dicens: Si peccauerit in te frater tuus, obiurga eū: & si respuerit, remitte ei: Et si septies in die peccauerit in te, & septies in die conuersus fuerit ad te, dicens: Poenitet me: Remitte ei. Hoc in praesenti Paulus obseruat, & neq; tempus gratiae diutius extrahit, neque satisfactiones theatricas praescribit alicui. Imo quia vidit, illos simul omnes, aut saltē maiorē eorū partem, peccata sua agnoscere, de illis dolere, sibi ipsis irasci, & serio Deum quaerere, dignos iudicat, qui publicis quoque praeconiis atque laudibus ornentur. Posteris demum temporibus propter Novatianos & hypocritas novae satisfactionum formulae excogitatae, & paenitentiae certum tempus pro delictorum ratione constitutum est. Sed humanum figmentum gemella prole mox sese prodidit: Tyranide nimirum episcoporum, & Hypocrisi, matre scelerum omnium fecundissima. Et memorabilis est historia, quam Socrates narrat. Cum enim Constantinopoli paenitentiarius presbyter mulieri nobili ob nescio quam causam paenitentiae exercitia & satisfactiones diuturniores mandavisset, interea dum his vacat, in ipso templo cum Diacono stupri consuetudinem habuit. Quo scandalo populus irritatus, in sacerdotes saevire coepit. Itaque Nectarius paenitentiarium presbyterum suffulit, & Pauli doctrinam secutus sufficere censuit, si unusquisque seipsum probet, priusquam ad sacra Domini coenam accedat. Neque reduxit bene & merito abrogatum paenitentiariorum ordinem successor Nectarij Chrysostomus, quamvis acerrimus morum & disciplinae vindex fuerit: nimirum quod videret rem hanc periculi plenam esse, & quod semel factum fuerat, sapius fieri posse: neque frustra hoc illum timuisse, abunde testantur exempla, quae inter Papistas postea acciderunt. Scio Socrati factum hoc displicuisse, qui se Eudaemone Alexandrinum, qui Nectario huius consilij author fuerat, ideo reprehendisse scribit: sed quam friuolo & Sophistico argumento id fecerit, quanto facile intelliget, qui illud propius inspexerit. Nam ita abolitas fuisse dixit mutuas redargutiones sive correptiones una cum apostolico illo praecepto: Ne commercium habueritis cum operibus illis infructiferis tenebrarum, sed potius etiam arguite. Quid vero hoc ad paenitentiarios presbyteros sive Seniores? Et quae ratio est, quae ne alij alios monent, arguant, corripiant, prohibeat: etiamsi paucis quibusdam non permittatur, ut ipsi Senatum novum atque extraordinarium in Ecclesia constituant? Ego certe nihil utilius & tutius esse video, quam ut Apostolorum & primitivae Ecclesiae vestigijs insistamus. Minime tamen iis patrocinamur, qui & Christiani haberi volunt, & impudenter sese ingerunt absque omni paenitentiae indicio. Ferent illi suum iudicium; neque impunitos dimittet Deus. Oremus Patrem misericordiarum, ut omnium animos suo Spiritu excitet, ut ad ipsum reuertantur, & cum ipso vere in gratiam redeant per Mediatorem unicum IESVM CHRISTVM: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: You will observe, moreover, what ought to be done in the Church with those who testify by these signs that they have repented. God receives the penitent into grace without delay, as we have taught at length elsewhere. Christ therefore commands us to do the same, saying: "If your brother sins against you, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him. And if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turns back to you, saying, 'I repent,' forgive him." Paul observes this in the present case: he neither prolongs the time of grace any longer, nor prescribes theatrical satisfactions to anyone. Indeed, because he saw that they all together, or at least the greater part of them, acknowledged their sins, grieved over them, were angry with themselves, and sought God earnestly, he judges them worthy to be honoured with public proclamation and praise. In later times, however, on account of the Novatians and hypocrites, new formulas of satisfaction were devised, and a fixed period of repentance was laid down according to the seriousness of the offences. But the human invention soon revealed itself with a twin offspring: namely, the tyranny of the bishops and hypocrisy, the most fruitful mother of all crimes. There is a memorable story that Socrates relates. When a presbyter in charge of penance at Constantinople had imposed longer exercises of penance and satisfactions on a noble woman, for some reason I do not know, while she was occupied with these, she had an adulterous relationship with a deacon in the very church. The people, roused by this scandal, began to rage against the priests. So Nectarius removed the penitentiary presbyter, and, following the teaching of Paul, judged that it was enough for each one to examine himself before approaching the Lord's Supper. Nor did Chrysostom, Nectarius' successor, restore the order of penitentiaries, which had been well and rightly abolished, although he was a most zealous guardian of morals and discipline: plainly because he saw that the matter was full of danger, and that what had once happened could happen often. That he was not wrong to fear this, the examples that later occurred among the Papists abundantly testify. I know that Socrates disliked this act, and he writes that he rebuked Eudaemon of Alexandria, who had been the author of this plan for Nectarius; but how frivolous and sophistical his argument was, anyone will readily understand who looks at the matter more closely. For he said that mutual rebukes and corrections had been abolished along with that apostolic precept: "Have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather even reprove them." But what has this to do with penitentiary presbyters or elders? And what reason is there that forbids men to admonish, reprove and correct one another, even if it is not granted to a few to set up for themselves a new and extraordinary senate in the Church? For my part, I see nothing more useful and safer than to follow in the footsteps of the Apostles and the primitive Church. Yet we by no means defend those who wish to be regarded as Christians and thrust themselves forward shamelessly, without any sign of repentance. They will bear their own judgment; nor will God let them go unpunished. Let us pray to the Father of mercies that he may stir up the minds of all by his Spirit, so that they may turn back to him and truly be reconciled with him through the one Mediator, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXIIII.

units.la: Per omnia testatu fecistis, vos esse puros in hoc negotio. Nempe etiamsi scripsi vobis, non scripsi eius causa, qui iniuriam fecerat, nec eius causa, qui iniuria affectus fuerat: sed ut apud vos manifestum fieret studium illud nostrum pro vobis in conspectu Dei. Propterea consolatione accepimus ex consolatione vestri: sed longe plurimum gaudii sumus ob gaudium Titi, quod refocillatus sit spiritus eius ab omnibus vobis. Et si quid apud eum de vobis gloriatus sum, non fui pudefactus: sed ut omnia vere locuti sumus vobis, ita & gloriatio nostra, qua usus eram apud Titum, vera comperta sit. Et viscera eius amplius erga vos affecta sunt, dum reminiscitur obedientiae omnium vestrum, utque cum timore ac tremore ipsum excepperitis. Gaudeo igitur quod penitus confidam de vobis.
units.tr: You have shown by every means that you are pure in this matter. Indeed, even though I wrote to you, I did not write for the sake of the one who had done the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who had been wronged, but so that our zeal for you might be made plain to you in the sight of God. Therefore we have been comforted by your comfort; but we rejoiced far more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit was refreshed by all of you. And if I boasted anything to him about you, I was not put to shame; but just as we spoke everything to you truthfully, so our boasting, which I made before Titus, has proved true. His affection for you has grown even greater as he remembers the obedience of you all, and how you received him with fear and trembling. I rejoice, therefore, that I can be fully confident about you.

units.la: Quemadmodum homo natura ad malum proclivis est: ita admonitiones & correptiones impatienter ferre solet, & plerunque fidos monitores pro hostibus habet. Exempla huius mali passim occurrunt, in Prophetis maxime, quos multi turbarum omnium authores & pacis publicae inimicos esse dixerunt, eo quod ab illis liberius corriperentur. Quare multum prodest, ut omnes intelligant, non utile modo, verumetiam imprimis necessarium esse, ut admoneamur, & interdum gravius quoque accusemur. Est enim haec propria ratio, qua nos Deus in officio continet. Et huc referri debet, quod toto hoc Capite Paulus agit. Cum enim prioris epistolae rigorem multi indignè ferrent, quasi insolentior æquo sibi ius quoddam & imperium in Corinthios vendicaret, non ideo retractat quæ scripserat, neque responsatoribus istis seruiliter blanditur: sed diligenter docet, se omne hoc partim ex officio fecisse, partim propter ipsos, quorum salus hoc exigebat. Id autem proprio ipsorum exemplo probauit, dum exponit, quàm pulchris effectibus demonstrauerint, se vere & ex animo resipuisse. Eum locum in præsenti concludit & absoluit.
units.tr: As human nature is inclined to evil, so people usually bear admonitions and rebukes impatiently, and they often regard faithful advisers as enemies. Examples of this evil occur everywhere, especially among the Prophets, whom many have called the authors of all disturbances and enemies of public peace, because they rebuked people too frankly. So it is very useful that everyone understand that it is not only helpful but even especially necessary that we be admonished, and sometimes accused more sharply. For this is the very means by which God keeps us in our duty. And to this must be referred what Paul is doing throughout this whole chapter. For when many took badly the severity of his earlier letter, as if he were claiming for himself a right and authority over the Corinthians more arrogant than was fair, he does not retract what he had written, nor does he slavishly flatter those who answered him back. Instead he carefully teaches that he had done all this partly from his office, and partly for their own sakes, whose salvation required it. He proves this by their own example, as he sets out with what fine results they showed that they had truly and sincerely repented. He concludes and finishes this point here.

units.la: Per omnia (inquit) testatum fecistis, vos esse puros in hoc negotio. Prius impuri censeri poterant, quando omni disciplina quasi sublata & extincta, ad quæuis vitia conniebant, adeo vt nec incesta hominis turpissimi libidine ad iustam indignationem commouerentur, et ideo digni fuerat, qui aliquanto durius tractarentur. Quia autem admoniti & correpti tam serio egerant in scelere illo vindicando, & ita animi dolorem & indignationem non simulatam declarauerant, nunc puros pronuntiat, & sibi abunde satisfactum esse testatur.
units.tr: "You have shown by every means," he says, "that you are pure in this matter." Before, they could have been judged impure, since, with discipline almost removed and extinguished, they had overlooked every kind of vice, so that they were not moved to just indignation even by the incest of a most vile man; and therefore he deserved to be dealt with somewhat more harshly. But because, once admonished and rebuked, they had acted so seriously in avenging that crime, and had so declared their sorrow and unfeigned indignation, he now pronounces them pure and testifies that he is fully satisfied.

units.la: Quo loco discimus, alienis peccatis eos pollui, qui illis vel communicant, vel cum ea puniri possent, non puniunt. Et hæc causa est, quòd interdum propter paucorum delicta tota gentes aliquo infortunio publico multantur. Exemplum eius rei in Achan sacrilego historia Iosuæ proponit. Quid, quòd Ionas sua inobedientia hominibus alienigenis, ad quorum ciuitatem ipse non pertinebat, periculum attulit, cum eadem cum ipsis naue veheretur? Debent nos ista admonere, primum, ne quid commercij habeamus cum improbis, qui contumaciter in sceleribus suis pergunt: ne videlicet nostra amicitia ferociores facti, nos eodem secum reatu inuoluant. Deinde, ne aliquem illis consensum præbeamus. Nam qui id faciunt, ij easdem cum illis pœnas merentur, vt Paulus in epistola ad Romanos docet. Postremo, vt resistamus pro virili improbis eorum conatibus, & vt qui puniendi ius habent, eo vt decet vtantur in illis coercendis. Pertinet hoc ad omnis loci & ordinis homines. Nam vt ab Ecclesiæ ministris exordiamur, nisi hi eos qui peccant, in tempore & liberè admoneant, imò corripiant quoque seuerius si opus fit, iam illorum peccatis communicant, & vna cum illis puniuntur. Quid verò, si insuper colludant cum sceleratis, & (vt apud Ezechielem dicitur) puluillos supponant, quibus illi suauiter indormire possint, qui seueriori prædicatione ad pœnitentiam excitari debebant? Sic qui magistratum gerunt, si bonas leges violari, disciplinam morum dissolui, & huius loco scelerum licentiam atque impunitatem introduci patiantur, si item ad munera publica adhibeant homines improbos ac venales, tunc scelerum simul atq; pœnarum seipsos confortes faciunt: & plerumque hæ ad totam Rempub. redundant, quando licentia illa omnes publicè gaudent, & eam coërceri nolunt. Exemplum, quo hoc confirmetur, horribile in Iudicū libro extat, vbi effrenis & scelerata quorundam libido non punita, sed potius publica authoritate defensa, belli ciuilis causa fuit, in quo virorum sexaginta quinq; millia cæsa, & tribus Beniamin ferè tota deleta fuit. In Romana historia Catilinam, Lentulum, Cethegum & horum similes habemus, quorum licentia, cum à nemine coercerentur, tandem Rempub. in extremum periculum adduxit. Quid verò sperari potest, quando qui legum authoritatem & disciplinam publicam tueri debebat, hanc ipsi dissoluunt, & toti populo pessimi exempli authores sunt, dum ipsi primi perpetrant, ludunt, scortantur, vsuras exigunt, omnia denique faciunt, quæ bonos mores corrumpere possunt & publicam authoritatem euertere? De his certè graue illud Solomonis dictum intelligi debet: Væ terræ, cuius rex puer est, & cuius principes manè comessantur. Debent de his priuatim quoque parentes cogitare, ne filijs suis nimium indulgendo, eorum proteruiæ & libidini communicent. Cessit hoc olim infelicissimè Heli Sacerdoti, qui cum filiorum scelera non qua poterat seueritate punirèt, tandem cum ipsis pœnas dedit. Peccauit in eo Dauid quoque, Rex quidem optimus, sed pater plus satis indulgens, sicuti Ammonis & Absolonis historia testatur. In quanta autem discrimina seipsum simul & Rempub. hac sua indulgentia ille adduxit? Erant hæc diligentius consideranda hodie. At paucos ista cura tangit. Plerique affectuum suorum libidine abrepti pessima quæq; designant. Alij conniuent ad omnia, multi insuper hominibus ebriosis, scortatoribus, adulteris, vsurarijs & fenératoribus, militibus mercenarijs legum, omniū violatoribus patrocinantur. Ne ergo miremur calamitates, quibus publicè & priuatim infestamur. Cū enim effrenis illa vitiorū licentia nemini, aut saltem paucissimis, displiceat, nemo iusta indignatione & zelo commoueatur, quomodo nos Deus pro puris agnoscere, aut virgas à nobis retrahere poterit? Ad nos enim pertinet reuera, quod Isaias de fui sæculi calamitatibus olim dixit: Atqui in omni hoc non remittit ira eius, sed manus eius adhuc extensa est: quia populus ille non redit ad eum, qui ipsos percussit, & Dominum exercituum non quaerunt. Vide Isa. 9. & 10. Cap.
units.tr: From this place we learn that those are polluted by the sins of others who share in them, or who, though they could punish them, do not punish them. And this is the reason why sometimes whole peoples are punished with some public calamity on account of the offences of a few. The history of Joshua sets before us an example of this in Achan the sacrilegious. What of the fact that Jonah, by his disobedience, brought danger upon men of foreign nations, to whose city he did not belong, when he was sailing in the same ship with them? These cases ought to warn us: first, that we have no dealings with the wicked who persist stubbornly in their crimes, lest, made bolder by our friendship, they involve us in the same guilt with themselves; second, that we give them no consent, for those who do so deserve the same punishments as they, as Paul teaches in his letter to the Romans; last, that we resist their attempts to the best of our ability, and that those who have the right to punish use it as is fitting in restraining them. This applies to men of every place and rank. To begin with the ministers of the Church: unless they admonish those who sin in good time and freely, and indeed, if need be, rebuke them more severely, they now share in their sins and are punished together with them. What if, moreover, they collude with the wicked and (as is said in Ezekiel) put cushions under the elbows on which those men may sleep soundly, men who ought to have been roused to repentance by a more severe preaching? So too those who hold the magistracy, if they allow good laws to be violated, discipline of morals to be dissolved, and in its place licence and impunity for crimes to be introduced, and likewise if they admit wicked and venal men to public offices, then they make themselves partners in the crimes and in the punishments; and these often spill over upon the whole commonwealth, when everyone publicly rejoices in that licence and does not want it restrained. A dreadful example confirming this stands in the book of Judges, where the unbridled and wicked lust of certain men, not punished but rather defended by public authority, was the cause of a civil war, in which sixty-five thousand men were slain and the tribe of Benjamin was almost wholly destroyed. In Roman history we have Catiline, Lentulus, Cethegus and men like them, whose licence, since no one restrained it, at last brought the commonwealth into extreme danger. And what can be hoped for when those who ought to defend the authority of the laws and public discipline themselves dissolve them, and become the authors of the worst example to the whole people, while they themselves are the first to commit crimes, gamble, whore, exact usury, and in short do everything that can corrupt good morals and overthrow public authority? Certainly that grave saying of Solomon ought to be understood of such men: Woe to the land whose king is a child, and whose princes feast in the morning. Parents too ought to consider these things privately, lest by indulging their sons too much they share in their wantonness and lust. This once turned out most unhappily for Eli the priest, who, when he did not punish his sons' crimes with all the severity he could, at last paid the penalty together with them. David also sinned in this way, an excellent king indeed, but a father who indulged too much, as the story of Amnon and Absalom bears witness. Yet into how many dangers did he, through this indulgence, bring both himself and the commonwealth? These things ought to be considered more carefully today. But few are touched by such concern. Most, carried away by the lust of their passions, pursue the worst things. Others wink at everything, and many moreover defend drunkards, whoremongers, adulterers, usurers and moneylenders, mercenary soldiers, and violators of all laws. Let us not wonder, therefore, at the calamities by which we are afflicted both publicly and privately. For since that unbridled licence of vices displeases no one, or at least very few, and no one is stirred by just indignation and zeal, how can God acknowledge us as pure, or withdraw his rods from us? For what Isaiah once said of the calamities of his own age truly pertains to us: Yet for all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out; because that people does not return to him who struck them, nor seek the Lord of hosts. See Isaiah chapters 9 and 10.

units.la: Sed vt ad Paulum redeamus, obijceret aliquis: Si vero puri fumus, & id re ipsa tectatum fecimus, cur ergo tanta cum acerbitate & vehementia in nos inuectus es? & quid correptio ne tam acri opus fuit? Quis item nos indigne abs te tractatos esse negauerit, qui propter vnius delictum totam Ecclesiam nostram in publicum ludum & tristitiam coniecisti? Ad ista ergo respondet, & facti sui rationem amplius reddit: Equidem etiam si scripsi vobis, non scripsi eius causa qui iniuriam fecerat, nec eius causa qui iniuria affectus fuerat: sed vt apud vos manifestum fieret studium illud nostrum pro vobis in conspectu Dei. Non negat simpliciter, se propter hominem illum inceptum scripsisse (quomodo enim hoc negaret, cum illum iussisset Satanae tradere, ne totum Ecclesiae corpus inficeret, & vt ipse aliquandiu à Satana vexatus ad mentem meliorem rediret atque sanaretur?) sed suspicionem declinat, quam fere incurrunt in eiusmodi casu, qui aliquos liberius admonent atque corripiunt. Nam aut odio eorum quos accusant, aut amore illorum, quos ipsi leserunt, hoc omne facere putantur. Ad id ergo respiciens Paulus sic vult dicere: Nolo aliquis suspicetur, me aut illum miserum odio habuisse, aut eius patri impensius fauisse. Nam etiamsi vtrinque vicem doluerim, & mea correptione illum ad poenitentiam studuerim adducere, simul tamen aliud quoque mihi propositum fuit: Vt nimirum studium hoc nostrum, quo ego vos prosequor in conspectu Dei (id est, cuius Deum testem habeo) omnibus manifestum fieret. Etenim non immerito multi de illo dubitare poterant, si tantum scelus dissimulauissem. Quis enim pater filium amare putetur, quem inter scorta & ganeones corrumpi sinit? Quis principe populi sui studiosum dixerit, quem nimia licentia perire videns, nullis legibus aut disciplina coercet? Itaque quicquid ego feci, id ex amore & fido salutis vestrae studio feci, ne eorum similis essem, qui vos eo vsque infamiae prolabi passi sunt sua indulgentia, &c.
units.tr: But to return to Paul: someone might object, "If we are indeed pure, and have shown this by the fact itself, why then did you attack us with such bitterness and vehemence? Why was there any need for such a sharp rebuke? Who, moreover, would deny that we have been treated unworthily by you, when for the offence of one man you have thrown our whole Church into public mockery and sorrow?" To these things, then, he replies and gives a further account of his action: "Indeed, even though I wrote to you, I did not write for the sake of the one who had done the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who had been wronged, but so that our zeal for you might be made plain to you in the sight of God." He does not simply deny that he began the matter because of that man (for how could he deny it, since he had ordered him to be handed over to Satan, so that he would not infect the whole body of the Church, and so that he, being harassed for a time by Satan, might come to a better mind and be healed?). Rather, he avoids the suspicion which those usually incur in such a case who admonish and rebuke others rather freely. For they are thought to do all this either out of hatred for those whom they accuse, or out of love for those whom they themselves have injured. Looking to this, Paul wishes to say: "I do not want anyone to suspect that I held that wretched man in hatred, or favoured his father too much. For even if I grieved on both sides, and by my rebuke I was eager to bring him to repentance, yet I had another purpose as well: namely, that this zeal of ours, with which I pursue you in the sight of God (that is, whose God I call as witness), might be plain to all. Indeed, many could rightly have doubted about me if I had concealed so great a crime. For who would be thought to love his son, whom he allows to be corrupted among harlots and wastrels? Who would call a ruler zealous for his people, when he sees them perishing through excessive licence and does not restrain them with any laws or discipline? So whatever I have done, I have done out of love and faithful zeal for your salvation, so that I might not be like those who, by their indulgence, allowed you to slide so far into infamy," and so on.

units.la: Hic loci huius sensus verus, & haec eiusdem lectio germana est, quam olim Chrysostomus quoque & Ambrosius secuti sunt. Conuenit enim cum his, quae Cap. secundo dixit: Ex multa angustia & anxietate cordis scripsi vobis, per multas lachrymas: non vt tristitia afficeremini, sed vt cognoscueretis charitatem, quam habeo abundantissimam erga vos. Hodie tamen Graeca exemplaria sic habent ἵνα γνῶτε τὴν ἀγάπην ... id est, vt manifestum fieret studium vestrum pro nobis apud vos in conspectu Dei. Sed facile fuit lapsus inter literas u & v vt pro τὴν ἀγάπην ὑμῶν scriberetur ὑμῶν. Et ineptam esse lectionem istam, satis ostendit particula, πρὸς ὑμᾶς, id est, apud vos. Quis enim Corinthiorum tam stupidus erat, vt ignoraret, quomodo ipse erga Paulum esset affectus? Imo, qui eius studiosiores adhuc erant, hac correptione potuissent offendi, si quasi dubitans de ipsorum erga se studio voluisset eius experimentum sumere. Etenim ambitiosum quid spirat, velle de aliquibus periculum facere, quanti te faciant. Paulus certe, non quanti ipse fieret quaerebat, sed hoc potius, vt sublato omni scandalo, ipsi omnes serio disciplinae retinendae studio accenderentur. Quia vero nomen suum multis inuisum, aut saltem suspectum esse, multos item de se contemptius loqui sciebat, necesse erat, vt ipsius erga Ecclesiam illam studium, & quanta salutis eorum cura tangeretur, omnes intelligerent. Et ideo tanta verborum & argumentorum vehementia vsus fuit, quando in priori epistola hoc ipsum argumentum tractauit.
units.tr: Here the true sense of the passage is clear, and this is the genuine reading, which Chrysostom and Ambrose also followed long ago. It agrees with what Paul said in the second chapter: "Out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you, with many tears; not that you should be grieved, but that you might know the love which I have most abundantly toward you." Today, however, the Greek copies read ἵνα γνῶτε τὴν ἀγάπην ... [that you may know the love ...], that is, "that your zeal for us might be made manifest before you in the sight of God." But an easy slip occurred between the letters u and v, so that ὑμῶν was written for τὴν ἀγάπην ὑμῶν. That this reading is absurd is shown well enough by the particle πρὸς ὑμᾶς [before you]. For which of the Corinthians was so dull as not to know how Paul himself was disposed toward them? Indeed, those who were already more devoted to him could have been offended by this rebuke, if he had seemed to doubt their zeal toward him and wished to test it. For it breathes a certain ambition to want to put others to the test to see how much they value you. Paul, certainly, was not seeking how much he himself was valued, but rather that, every offence being removed, they might all be seriously fired with zeal for keeping up discipline. Since he knew that his name was hateful to many, or at least suspect, and that many spoke of him more contemptuously, it was necessary that all should understand his zeal for that Church and how deeply he cared for their salvation. And so he used such vehemence of words and arguments when he treated this same matter in the earlier letter.

units.la: Porro quoad causam, de qua hic agitur, obseruatu dignissima est Pauli modestia. Poterat ut multis aliis rationibus factum suum tueri, & quidem his ipsis, quas in praesenti negat, vel saltem dissimulat: denique scelus hominis incesti odiosius exagitare poterat, vt ex eius atrocitate constaret, ipsum merito eis tantopere succensuisse. Sed cum illos simul omnes suae negligentiae vere poeniteret, non voluit refricare iam obdurata vulnera. Et hac ratione agi debet cum omnibus iis, qui admoniti & correpti resipuerunt. Sic olim Nathan consolationem Dauidi adhibuit, cum eum sceleris admissi dolore consternatum de poenitentia serio cogitare videret. Et huc referri possunt omnes promissiones, quibus Prophetae eos qui in Babylone adducedi erant, praemunire voluerunt, ne de liberatione & reditu suo desperaret, quin potius in verae poenitentiae studio essent ardentiores. rit. Imprimis tamen hic Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI exemplum observari debet, qui ut pharisaeos & hypocritas omnes acerrime corripuit in suis concionibus, ita indulgentissime tractauit meretrices & publicanos, quos saepe de peccatis suis dolere, & de resipiscentia cogitare videbat. Quo etiam referri debet filij prodigi parabola, quem redeuntem & peccata sua ingenue confitentem pater tenerrimo amore complexus in integrum restituit. Sunt ergo nimium morosi, qui diutius adhuc suspendunt eos, qui iam totis animis contriti sunt, qui deniq; nouis itidem satisfactionibus eos fatigant, quorum fidem gratia Dei praedicatione debebant confirmare. Alia est contumacium ratio, in quibus nulla cernuntur vitae emendatae aut doloris ex peccatorum agnitione concepti indicia. Horum enim scelera acrius corripere, & eosdem poenarum denuntiatione terrere indies oportet, sicuti olim Isaiae praecepit Deus, dicens: Clama ex gutture, exalta instar tubae vocem tuam, & annuntia populo meo scelera sua. Et Paulus Timotheum suum, non solum monere, verum etiam arguere & increpare, adeoque tempestiue & intempestiue instare iubebat. Vide Isa. 58. 2. Timoth. 4.
units.tr: Further, as to the matter under discussion here, Paul's moderation is most worthy of observation. He could have defended his action on many other grounds, and indeed on those very grounds which he here denies or at least passes over. Finally, he could have railed at the crime of the incestuous man more bitterly, so that it would be clear from its atrocity that he had justly been so angry with them. But since he truly grieved that they had all been so negligent, he did not want to reopen wounds that had already hardened. And this is the way one ought to deal with all those who, having been admonished and rebuked, have come to their senses. So long ago Nathan offered consolation to David, when he saw him dismayed by grief for his sin and seriously thinking about repentance. To this can also be referred all the promises by which the prophets wished to fortify those who were to be led away to Babylon, lest they despair of their deliverance and return, but rather be the more eager in the pursuit of true repentance. Above all, however, the example of our Lord Jesus Christ must be observed here, who, while he rebuked the Pharisees and all hypocrites most sharply in his sermons, treated harlots and publicans with the greatest gentleness, seeing that they were often grieved over their sins and thinking about repentance. To this also belongs the parable of the prodigal son, whom his father, as he returned and frankly confessed his sins, embraced with the tenderest love and restored to full standing. Therefore those are too stern who keep waiting those who are already utterly contrite, and who finally weary them with new satisfactions, when they ought to have confirmed their faith by the preaching of the grace of God. Different is the method for the stubborn, in whom no signs of an amended life or of grief conceived from the recognition of sins can be seen. For it is right to rebuke their crimes more sharply and to terrify them daily by the announcement of punishments, just as God long ago commanded Isaiah, saying: "Cry aloud, lift up your voice like a trumpet, and declare to my people their transgressions." And Paul bade his Timothy not only to admonish but also to rebuke and reprove, and to press on, in season and out of season. See Isa. 58. 2 Tim. 4.

units.la: Sed ad Titum redit Paulus, cuius supra mentionem fecit, & diligentius exponit, ut huius aduentu fit recreatus. Narrationem vero hanc ita contexit, ut & Corinthios in suo instituto confirmet, & Titum ijsdem amplius commendet. Sic enim scribit: Propterea consolationem accepimus ex consolatione vestri: sed longe plurimum gauisi sumus ob gaudium Titi, quod refocillatus sit spiritus eius ab omnibus vobis, &c.
units.tr: But Paul returns to Titus, whom he mentioned above, and explains more fully how he was refreshed by his arrival. He weaves this narrative so as both to confirm the Corinthians in his course of action and to commend Titus to them still more. For he writes: "Therefore we have been comforted in your comfort; but we rejoiced exceedingly the more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit was refreshed by you all," and so on.

units.la: Primo, se consolationem accepisse ait, ex ipsorum consolatione. Consolatio illa erat, quod admoniti per epistolam, omnes simul certatim operas suas contulerant ad tanti flagitij correctionem, ideoq; instaurato Ecclesiae suae statu iam tranquillius & quietius agebant, qui prius varias ob causas inter se tumultuabantur. Hoc (inquit) vbi resciui, sensi ex eo efficacissimam consolationem. Id vero synceri amoris certissimum est argumentum, si quis gaudium & consolationem ex aliorum incolumitate percipiat. Addit tamen aliud, quo hoc ipsius gaudium magis fit confirmatum: Sed longe plurimum gauisi sumus ob gaudium Titi, quod refocillatus sit spiritus eius ab omnibus vobis. Etenim credibile est, Titum non fine metu Corinthum profectum fuisse, eo quod periculum esset, ne durius & inhumanius exciperetur, aut etiam reiceretur ab ijs, quos de Paulo, electo illo Christi organo, iniquius iudicare sciebat. Itaque cum praeter expectationem se reuerenter excipi, epistolam Pauli magnum pondus habere, & absq; mora res in melius restitui videret, non potuit non toto animo exhilarari. Id vero mihi (inquit Paulus) redundantissimi gaudij causa fuit. Et huius causam indicat: Quia si quid apud eum gloriatus sum de vobis, non fui pudefactus: sed ut omnia vere locuti sumus vobis, ita & gloriatio nostra, qua vsus eram apud Titum, vera comperta fit.
units.tr: First, he says that he received comfort from their comfort. That comfort was this: when they had been admonished by the letter, they had all together eagerly applied themselves to the correction of so great a disgrace, and so, with their Church's condition now restored, they were acting more calmly and quietly, though before they had been in turmoil among themselves for various reasons. "When I learned this," he says, "I felt from it the most effective comfort." Indeed, it is a most certain sign of sincere love if someone receives joy and comfort from the well-being of others. He adds, however, something else by which this joy of his is made the more certain: "But we rejoiced exceedingly the more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit was refreshed by you all." For it is credible that Titus went to Corinth not without fear, because there was a danger that he might be received too harshly and inhumanly, or even rejected, by those whom he knew to judge Paul, that chosen instrument of Christ, too unfairly. So when, beyond expectation, he saw that he had been received with respect, that Paul's letter carried great weight, and that matters were set right without delay, he could not but be cheered with his whole heart. "This indeed," says Paul, "was the cause of my most abundant joy." And he states the reason for it: "For if I have boasted anything to him about you, I have not been put to shame; but just as we spoke everything to you in truth, so also our boasting, which I made before Titus, has been found to be true."

units.la: Debet hic probe observari exemplum Pauli, qui cum Corinthios coram & per epistolam acriter corripuisset, eosdem tamen Tito (ut & multis aliis) commendauit, & de eorum fide atq; fiducio bene sperare iussit. Est hoc candidi pectoris & amoris non fucati argumentum. Hodie fere diuersum fit. Qui enim ex officio suo imprimis corripere debebant eos, qui peccarunt, ij pisce magis muti sunt illis praesentibus: absentes autem proscindunt, ut apud quosuis in contemptum vel odium adducant. Et haec praecipua dissidiorum causa est inter eos, qui ex Christi mandato dilectioni mutuae & concordiae studere debebant.
units.tr: The example of Paul must be carefully observed here. Though he had sharply rebuked the Corinthians both in person and by letter, he nevertheless commended them to Titus (as to many others) and bade him hope well of their faith and loyalty. This is a sign of a candid heart and of love without pretence. Today it is almost the reverse. Those who, by virtue of their office, ought above all to rebuke those who have sinned, are as dumb as fish when those people are present, but when they are absent they tear them to pieces, so as to bring them into contempt or hatred before anyone at all. And this is the principal cause of the quarrels among those who, by Christ's command, ought to strive for mutual love and concord.

units.la: Admonemur praeterea eodem Pauli exemplo, Verbi administros ex doctrinae suae professu & bona Ecclesiarum constitutione consolationem & gaudium concipere debere. Ista enim eos fideles IESV CHRISTI seruos esse testantur, qui in negotiatione illa sancta & salutari, de qua ille in Euangelio loquitur, sedu li sint & inducentur. Minime autem apostolici spiritus argumenta sunt, si mundi huius gaudia quaerant, epulentur, perpotent, ludant, venationibus & aucupijs vacent, potentum amicitijs superbiant, stipendijs immodicis inhient, ut studijs hisce pessimis possint sufficere: nihil interim soliciti de auditorum profectu & Ecclesiarum incremento. Vtinam vero de his hodie diligentius pleriq; cogitarent, qui vel Ecclesiae vel Reipub. praefecti sunt.
units.tr: We are further admonished by the same example of Paul that ministers of the Word ought to take consolation and joy from the profession of their teaching and from the good constitution of the Churches. For these things testify that they are faithful servants of Jesus Christ, who are and will be busy in that holy and saving trade of which he speaks in the Gospel. But it is by no means a sign of the apostolic spirit if they seek the joys of this world, feast, drink deep, play, devote themselves to hunting and fowling, take pride in the friendships of the powerful, and crave excessive stipends, so that they may have enough for these wicked pursuits, meanwhile being in no way concerned about the progress of their hearers and the growth of the Churches. Would that many who are set over the Church or the commonwealth today thought about these things more carefully!

units.la: Porro non contentus de se dixisse Paulus, Titi quoq; gaudium, quod ex Corinthijs perceperat, describit, ut ipsit illum magis conciliet: Vtscera eius (inquit) amplius erga vos affecta sunt, dum reminiscitur obedientiæ omnium vestrûm, vt cum timore & tremore ipsum exceperitis. Viscera nominat, quæ sedes sunt dilectionis & misericordiæ, vt ostendat Titum ipsos toto animo complecti, adeò vt vel sola ipsorum recordatione recreetur & gaudeat. Quid vero illud erat, cuius recordatio eum tantopere reficiebat? Obedientiam dicit, quam præstiterant, quando tam ex illius ore, quàm ex Pauli epistola intelligebant, quid ipsos facere deceret. Deinde, quòd ipsum quoque cum timore & tremore exceperant. Loquitur autem non de seruili timore, sed hoc dicit, quòd ingenuo suorum delictorum pudore percalsi fuerint, & apostolici Spiritus vim atque authoritatem reueriti sint, quæ & in Pauli epistola & ipsius Titi persona relucebat.
units.tr: Moreover, not content to have spoken about himself, Paul also describes Titus's joy, which he had received from the Corinthians, so as to win him over to them all the more: "His inward affections," he says, "are more and more drawn out toward you, while he remembers the obedience of you all, how you received him with fear and trembling." He names the inward parts, which are the seat of love and compassion, to show that Titus embraced them with his whole heart, so that he was refreshed and rejoiced by the mere recollection of them. But what was that thing, the memory of which so greatly restored him? He speaks of the obedience they had rendered, when they understood from his lips as well as from Paul's letter what it became them to do. Then, that they had received him, too, with fear and trembling. He does not mean a servile fear, but that they were pierced with a noble shame for their offences, and revered the power and authority of the apostolic Spirit, which shone both in Paul's letter and in the person of Titus himself.

units.la: Rursus ergo hic quoque de boni pastoris officio admonemur, vt nimirum totis visceribus & corde toto eos complectatur, quos fidei ipsius credidit Dominus. Etenim amor maximè commendat eos, qui aliis præfecti sunt. Et quod Chrysostomus annotauit, parentes non tam generatio arguit, quàm amor, quo ex se genitos complectuntur: cuius rei exemplum historia sacra proponit in meretricibus, quæ ad Solomonis tribunal pro puerulo viuo litigabant. Ita ergo affectos esse decet Ecclesiarum ministros simul & Reipub. præsides. Talis olim affectus in Mose fuit, qui vt initio aula delitias atque opes propter miseros Israelitas reliquerat: ita postea, cùm eos propter idololatriam perdere vellet Deus, caput proprium pro illis obijciens, clamabat: Aut remitte illis Deus hanc noxam, aut dele me ex libro tuo, quem tu scripsisti. Huius similem videmus Dauidem fuisse, qui cùm Angelum videret, qui peste percutiebat populum Israeliticum, mox exclamauit: Ego peccaui, ego iniquè egi, oues autem istæ quid fecerunt?
