Sit quæso manus tua contra me, & contra domum patris mei. Quem animum Prophetis quoq; fuisse, acerbissima illa querela testantur, quibus eorum interitum deplorant, quos prius propter scelera sua grauiter accusarant. Quid de ipso Paulo dicemus, qui dies & noctes pro Iudæis precatus est, & pro ijsdem anathema fieri optabat, qui ipsius hostes erant plus quàm capitales? Qua exempla nostri seculi principes aliquos arguunt, qui nulla alia populi sui cura tanguntur, quàm quòd illum deglubendi rationes quotidie nouas excogitant. Quibus iure adnumerauerit Ecclesiarum ministros, qui præter ventrem & quæstum nihil sapiunt, & ob qualemcunq; causam suæ fidei commissas Ecclesias deserunt.
units.tr: Here again we are reminded of the duty of a good shepherd, namely to embrace with his whole heart and entire soul those whom the Lord has entrusted to his faith. For love above all commends those who have been set over others. As Chrysostom noted, it is not so much begetting that makes parents as the love with which they embrace the children they have brought forth. Sacred history offers an example of this in the harlots who quarrelled before Solomon's tribunal over a living little child. So ought the ministers of the churches and the rulers of the commonwealth to be affected. Such an affection was once in Moses, who at the start had left the court's delights and riches for the sake of the wretched Israelites, and later, when God wished to destroy them for their idolatry, offering himself in their place, cried out: "Either forgive them this sin, O God, or blot me out of your book, which you have written." We see that David was similar, who, when he saw the Angel striking the Israelite people with the plague, at once cried out: "I have sinned, I have done wrong, but what have these sheep done? Let your hand, I beg, be against me and against my father's house." The Prophets too had this same spirit, as their most bitter lamentations bear witness, in which they mourn the destruction of those whom they had earlier sharply accused for their wickedness. What shall we say of Paul himself, who day and night prayed for the Jews, and wished himself to be made an anathema for them, though they were his enemies more than deadly ones? Our own age's princes are shown up by such examples, for some of them are moved by no care for their people except how they may devise new ways of flaying them every day. Rightly will they be counted among the ministers of the churches who think of nothing but their belly and gain, and who desert the churches committed to their faith for whatever cause.

units.la: At non minus omnes Christianos de suo erga ministros officio hic locus admonet. Sunt, qui se omni officio defunctos putant, si stipendio liberaliori eis prospiciant, conuiuijs lautis ac sumptuosis excipiant, honorificè deducant, aut etiam illis de via cedant. Sunt hæc quidem amoris & ciuilitatis officia, sed quæ ab hypocritis & palàm impijs non minus quàm à bonis præstari possunt. Vera officia sunt, vt eos ex animo diligant, vt patres in Christo: vt tanquam Christi ministros atque legatos reuereantur: vt tanquam mysteriorum Dei dispensatores colant, vt deniq; doctrinæ ipsorum, quam ex Christi ore tradunt, obtemperent. Vbi ista locum habent, ibi externa illa reuerentiæ signa non deerunt.
units.tr: But this passage admonishes all Christians no less about their duty toward ministers. There are those who think they have done every duty if they provide them with a more generous stipend, entertain them with lavish and costly banquets, escort them with honour, or even give way to them on the road. These are indeed offices of love and courtesy, but they can be performed by hypocrites and openly impious people no less than by good ones. The true duties are these: to love them sincerely as fathers in Christ; to revere them as the ministers and ambassadors of Christ; to honour them as stewards of God's mysteries; and finally to obey their teaching, which they deliver from the mouth of Christ. Where these are present, those outward signs of reverence will not be lacking.

units.la: In Tito autem memorabile gratitudinis exemplum Spiritus sanctus proponit. Fuit ille meritor beneficiorum, quæ à Corinthijs acceperat, & eadem apud Paulum atq; alios magnificè prædicauit, eoruḿ recordatione frequenti tam seipsum quàm alios amore & studio Corinthiorum accendit. Arguuntur ingrati, qui vt beneficia accepta non magni faciunt, ita eorundem facilè obliuiscuntur, neq; vnquam de referendis gratijs cogitant. Sunt hi aridorum truncorum & arborum emortuarum siue agrorum sterilium similes. Vt enim hi fructum nullum ferunt, siue arentur, siue serantur & rigentur: Ita isti quoque sibi solis addicti ita viuunt, vt nemo aliquem fructum ex illis percipiat. Est autem hoc scelus cumprimis detestabile. Pugnat enim cum naturæ legibus, quæ brutis animantibus sensum & recordationem beneficiorum acceptorum infeuit: & amicitias dissoluit, sine quibus vita hominum consistere non potest. Etsi vero omnis loci & ordinis homines gratitudo deceat, maximè tamen eos, qui rebus præfecti sunt: ea enim populi animos sibi deuinciunt, vt omnes se ipsis obsequentiores præbeant. Vehementer ergo peccant, qui sese insolentius efferunt, & cùm sibi nihil non à populo deberi putent, ipsi nemini nihil conferunt, imò se plus satis beneficos esse putant, si miseros & infelices non totos excorient aut deglubant.
units.tr: In Titus the Holy Spirit sets before us a memorable example of gratitude. He was a repayer of the kindnesses he had received from the Corinthians, and he praised them highly before Paul and others; by frequently recalling them he kindled both himself and others with love and zeal for the Corinthians. Those are rightly called ungrateful who do not value the benefits they have received, and therefore easily forget them, and never think of returning thanks. They are like dried-up stumps, dead trees, or barren fields. For as these bear no fruit, whether they are left dry or are sown and watered, so these people, devoted only to themselves, live in such a way that no one derives any fruit from them. This sin is especially detestable. It fights against the laws of nature, which have implanted in brute animals a sense and memory of benefits received; and it dissolves friendships, without which human life cannot endure. Although gratitude becomes men of every rank and station, it becomes most of all those who are set over affairs, for kindness binds the hearts of the people to them so that all become more obedient to them. Those therefore sin grievously who carry themselves with too much insolence, and, thinking that everything is owed them by the people, confer nothing on anyone, and even think themselves beneficent enough if they do not utterly flay or skin the wretched and unfortunate.

units.la: Restat huius tractationis conclusio, quam Paulus sic infert: Gaudeo igitur quòd penitus, siue in omnibus, confidam de vobis. Id est, quòd tales vos esse deprehenderim, vt nihil non mihi de vobis possim bis possim polliceri. Isto autem Epiphonemate aculeum animis eorum inijcit, quo extimulentur, ne spem de se conceptam fallant. Etenim cum hoc semper turpe sit; turpissimum tamen est, eorum spei non respondere, qui aliquod in nos ius habent. Quacunque enim (vt Poëta ait) ex merito spes venit, aequa venit. Admonentur autem hoc exemplo primum ministri, vt moderata gravitate cum suis agant, & neq; ignava dissimulatione quiduis audendi licentiam inuehant, neq; immoderata & nimia austeritate infirmioribus desperationis authores sint. Deinde discat quoque vulgus Christianorum, ministros & pastores suos obedientia & voluntario pietatis studio exhilarare, & spei de se conceptae respondeant. Ita vtrinque probari poterunt Domino nostro IESV CHRISTO, qui Ecclesiae suae caput est: Huic debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: There remains the conclusion of this discussion, which Paul draws thus: "I rejoice therefore that I may be confident of you in all things." That is, I have found you to be such that I can promise myself everything from you. By this exclamation he pricks their minds with a goad, so that they may be stirred not to disappoint the hope conceived of them. For although such a thing is always shameful, it is most shameful not to answer the hopes of those who have some right over us; for whatever hope comes from merit, as the poet says, comes just as fairly. By this example ministers are first admonished to deal with their people with measured seriousness, neither letting in by idle dissimulation a licence to dare anything, nor by immoderate and excessive harshness becoming authors of despair to the weaker. Next, let the common run of Christians also learn to cheer their ministers and pastors by obedience and by a willing zeal for godliness, and to answer the hope conceived of them. Thus on both sides they may be approved before our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the head of his Church: to him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXV.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXV.

units.la: PORRO notam facimus vobis, fratres, gratiam Dei, quae data est in Ecclesiis Macedoniae: Nam in multa probatione afflictionis abundantia gaudij ipsorum, & profunda eorum paupertas redundavit in divitias simplicitatis ipsorum. Nam pro viribus (testor) & supra vires voluntarij fuerunt: multis cum precibus nos rogantes, vt gratiam & societatem ministerij quod est in sanctos, suscipieremus. Et non vt sperabamus, sed semetipsos dediderunt primum Domino, deinde & nobis per Dei voluntatem: Vt adhortaremur Titum, vt sicut ante coepit, ita etiam absoluat apud vos hanc quoque gratiam.
units.tr: Moreover, brothers, we make known to you the grace of God that has been given in the churches of Macedonia. For in a great trial of affliction, the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty have overflowed into riches of generosity. For I testify that they gave according to their means, and even beyond their means, of their own accord, begging us with many entreaties to accept the grace and the partnership in the ministry that is for the saints. And they gave not as we had hoped, but first gave themselves to the Lord and then to us, by the will of God, so that we urged Titus that, as he had begun before, so he would also complete among you this grace as well.

units.la: PRIMIS septem Capitibus suae doctrinae & ministerij rationem Paulus diligenter reddidit Corinthijs, & eosdem simul in genere hortatus est, vt sibi factam Dei gratiam constanter tueantur, seq; ipsos impollutos seruent. Nunc ad id transit, quod tunc passim in Ecclesijs gentium agebatur, & de quo ipsi quoq; imprimis erant admonendi: Nimirum vt fratribus in Iudaea subueniretur. Constat enim, illo tempore Christianos homines vbique inuisos & exosos fuisse. Prae aliis tamen periclitabatur & laborabant, qui in Iudaea quasi inter lupos medij agebant, qui eos iam pridem bonis & facultatibus suis omnibus spoliauerant. Accedebat his malis fames sub Claudio Caesare: quae ita premebantur, vt vix vitam sustentare possent. Ideo fratribus, qui in tutioribus locis erant, visum fuit, illos aliquo subsidio iuuare, & eius operis pulcherrimi initium fecerunt Antiocheni, vt Lucas in Actis perhibet. Deinde, cum necessitas maior passim ingrueret, Apostoli causam hanc passim egerunt apud Ecclesias, & imprimis quidem Paulus, cui hoc praecipue in mandatis datum fuerat, vtpote peculiari gentium Apostolo. Quapropter de hac re cum Corinthijs agere coepit in prioris epistolae Cap. vltimo: & insuper misso ad illos Tito amplius instituit. Videntur autem remissius egisse: Ideo nunc diligentius causam istam tractat in duobus Capitibus quae proxime sequuntur.
units.tr: In the first seven chapters Paul carefully set out for the Corinthians the principle of his teaching and ministry, and he urged them all in general to hold firmly to the grace of God given to them and to keep themselves undefiled. Now he turns to what was then being done everywhere in the churches of the Gentiles, and about which they in particular needed to be reminded: namely, that help should be given to the brothers in Judea. For it is certain that at that time Christians were hated and detested everywhere. Yet those who lived in Judea, as if in the middle of wolves, were in more danger and distress than the others, since they had long since been stripped of all their goods and property. To these evils was added a famine under the emperor Claudius, by which they were so oppressed that they could scarcely sustain life. Therefore it seemed good to the brothers who were in safer places to help them with some support, and the Antiochenes made a beginning of this most excellent work, as Luke reports in the Acts. Then, when greater need pressed everywhere, the Apostles pleaded this cause in the churches on every side, and Paul above all, to whom this had been especially entrusted, as the apostle peculiarly of the Gentiles. Hence he began to deal with the Corinthians about this matter at the end of the former epistle, and besides, after sending Titus to them, he pressed the matter further. But they seem to have responded rather lukewarmly; therefore he now treats this cause more diligently in the two chapters that immediately follow.

units.la: Est autem multa consideratione dignissimum Apostolorum exemplum; qui cum occupatissimi essent, hanc tamen causam tam feruide egerunt. Sciebant enim quam curae sint Christo pauperes, & quod idem non postrema Ecclesiae Christi membra sint. Debent ergo hodie quoq; ministri illorum stros pertinet, causam diligenter agere, neq; pudeat eos huius officij, cuius aeternum Dei Filium adeo non puduit, vt sponsorem quoq; seipsum pro illis fecerit. Ne ergo patiantur se illorum improbitate abstirreri, qui ista nihil ad ipsos pertinere clamant, sed sufficere ipsis debere, si Euangelij praedicandi potestas libera ipsis detur. Etenim magna Euangelicae doctrinae pars est charitas, per quam fides potissimum agit, & quae in pauperibus amplissimam habet se exercendi materiam. Et si Apostolis licuit apud Ecclesias gentium pro exteris, qui in Iudaea habitabant, intercedere, quanto magis pastores bodie sua fidei creditas Ecclesias monere & vrgere debent, vt domesticus fidei prospiciant, neque eos publica egestatis exempla fieri patiantur: & vt opes in hunc vsum maiorum liberalitate donatas fideliter dispensent.
units.tr: The example of the Apostles, who, although they were very busy, pleaded this cause so ardently, is most worthy of careful consideration. For they knew how much Christ cares for the poor, and that the poor are not the least members of the Church of Christ. Therefore ministers today too ought to plead this cause diligently, as far as it concerns them, and let them not be ashamed of this duty, in which the eternal Son of God was so far from being ashamed that he even made himself a surety for them. Let them not, then, allow themselves to be turned aside by the wickedness of those who cry out that these matters do not concern them, and that it should be enough for them if the power of preaching the Gospel is left free to them. For charity is a large part of evangelical doctrine, the chief means by which faith works, and it has in the poor a very ample matter for its exercise. And if it was lawful for the Apostles to intercede on behalf of those who lived in Judea, before the churches of the Gentiles, how much more ought ministers today to admonish and urge the churches entrusted to their faith, so that they take care of the household of faith, and do not allow public examples of want to occur among them, and that they faithfully dispense the wealth given for this purpose by the generosity of their forebears.

units.la: Sed Paulum cum Corinthijs agentem audiamus, qui artificiosa & prudenti insinuatione vtitur apud eos, quos hucusque remissius egisse videbat, & qui facile offendi poterant. Ne enim pro imperio agere videatur, aut aliquid ab eis postulare, quod apud alias Ecclesias non fit receptum, Macedonum exemplo eos excitare studet. Et facit attentionem Exordium, quod est eiusmodi: Porro notam vobis facimus, fratres, gratiam Dei, quae data est in Ecclesijs Macedonia. Docet, se dicturum de re minime vulgari, sed in qua Macedones iam ex singulari Dei gratia magnam sibi laudem pararuerint: debere ergo ipsos quoq; hanc Dei gratiam agnoscere, & anniti omni studio, ne illis inferiores esse inueniantur.
units.tr: But let us hear Paul pleading with the Corinthians, who uses a skilful and prudent approach with those whom he saw had hitherto been rather lukewarm, and who could easily be offended. For lest he seem to be acting by command, or to demand from them something not received in other churches, he takes care to rouse them by the example of the Macedonians. And he makes his opening so as to win their attention, and it runs thus: Moreover, brothers, we make known to you the grace of God that has been given in the churches of Macedonia. He teaches that he is going to speak about a matter by no means ordinary, but one in which the Macedonians have already, by the singular grace of God, won great praise for themselves; therefore they too ought to acknowledge this grace of God, and strive with all zeal lest they be found inferior to them.

units.la: Admonemur autem Pauli exemplo, obseruari debere aliarum Ecclesiarum exempla, quas bene instituras esse constat, vt nimirum illa ministri suis hominibus imitanda proponant. Id vero nemo auditorum iniquius ferre debet, quasi quae alibi fiunt, nihil ad ipsos pertineant. Est enim Christi Ecclesia vnica (vt Solomon canit) quam ideo Catholicam dicimus, eo quod ad eam colligantur omnium seculorum atq; locorum credentes, & cuius membra sunt siue partes, quacunq; per orbem hinc inde dispersae sunt: omnes autem ad vnum caput, IESVM CHRISTVM, pertinent. Non possumus ergo a nobis alienum putare quod vel in ista vel illa recte & pie fit secundum Christi doctrinam. Imo talibus nos congratulari decet, & Dei gratiam in illis agnoscere, gaudere item occasionem nobis dari, qua & ipsi excitemur, & alios quoq; ad officium faciendum hortemur. Et sane scelerata est eorum inuidia, qui Ecclesiarum aliarum laudibus ringuntur, quas potius imitari debebant.
units.tr: We are also admonished by Paul's example that the examples of other churches, which are known to be well ordered, ought to be observed, so that ministers may set them before their people to be imitated. Indeed, none of the hearers ought to take this amiss, as if what is done elsewhere had nothing to do with them. For the Church of Christ is one (as Solomon sings), and we call it Catholic for this reason, that believers of all ages and places are gathered into it, and that its members or parts are scattered here and there throughout the world; all, however, belong to one head, Jesus Christ. We cannot therefore regard as foreign to us what is rightly and piously done according to the teaching of Christ in this place or that. Indeed, it becomes us to rejoice with such churches, and to acknowledge the grace of God in them, and also to rejoice that an occasion is given us by which we ourselves may be stirred up and may also urge others to do their duty. And truly, the envy of those is wicked who are wounded by the praises of other churches, which they ought rather to imitate.

units.la: Caeterum exponit Paulus, quae illa gratia Dei sit, initio summam totius negotij duobus capitibus comprehendens. Primum est, quod afflictiones grauissimas cum gaudio suffinuerint. Idque sic enuntiat: In multa probatione afflictionis, id est, in multis tribulationibus & aduersis, quibus ipsorum fidem Deus probauit, abundantia gaudij ipsorum redundauit. Intelligit autem gaudij nomine consolationem Spiritus, qua confirmati aduersa omnia vicerint. Facit ad loci huius expositionem quod Philippensibus scribitur: Quia vobis datum est pro Christo, non solum in eum credere, sed etiam pro eo affligi, idem certamen habentes, quale vidistis in me, &c. Et ad Thessalonicenses: Vos imitatores nostri facti fuistis & Domini, admisso sermone cum affliction multa, cum gaudio Spiritus sancti: adeo vt fueritis quasi exemplaria omnibus credentibus in Macedonia & Achaia. Item: Vos imitatores facti estis, fratres, Ecclesiarum Dei, quae sunt in Iudaea, in CHRISTO IESV, quod eadem passi fitis & vos a propriis contribulibus, sicut & ipsi a Iudaeis. Et rursus in posteriori epistola: Gloriamur de vobis apud Ecclesias Dei, nempe de tolerantia vestra & fide in persecutionibus vestris & afflictionibus, quas toleratis, &c. Ex quibus liquido apparet, Ecclesias illas post Pauli ab eis discessum grauissime concussas fuisse. Nam procul dubio non quieuerunt seditiosi illi, qui (vt in Actis narratur) contra Paulum leges Romanas implorauerant. Laudat ergo eos, quod in his omnibus non modo patientes fuerint & constantes, verumetiam laeto & alacri animo per omnia aduersa sint eluctati.
units.tr: Besides, Paul explains what that grace of God is, at the outset summing up the whole matter under two heads. The first is that they bore the most grievous afflictions with joy. And he states it thus: in a great trial of affliction, that is, in many tribulations and adversities, by which God tested their faith, the abundance of their joy overflowed. By joy he understands the consolation of the Spirit, by which, strengthened, they overcame all adversities. What is written to the Philippians helps the exposition of this passage: For to you it has been granted on behalf of Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for his sake, having the same conflict that you saw in me, etc. And to the Thessalonians: You became imitators of us and of the Lord, receiving the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit, so that you became an example to all believers in Macedonia and Achaia. Likewise: You, brothers, became imitators of the churches of God that are in Judea in Christ Jesus, because you suffered the same things from your own countrymen as they did from the Jews. And again in the second epistle: We boast of you among the churches of God, namely of your endurance and faith in your persecutions and afflictions which you endure, etc. From these things it plainly appears that those churches were very severely shaken after Paul had departed from them. For without doubt those seditious men were not quiet who (as is related in the Acts) had accused Paul under the Roman laws. He therefore praises them because in all these things they were not only patient and steadfast, but also struggled through all adversities with a glad and cheerful mind.

units.la: Non temere autem probationem afflictionis dicit, pro afflictionibus grauissimis. Ea enim locutione proprium afflictionum vsum exprimit, qui est vt illis fides nostra, perinde vt aurum igne, probetur. Sic eandem Petrus explicat, de credentibus scribens: Vt exploratio fidei vestrae multo pretiosior probatione auri, quod perit, & tamen per ignem exploratur, comperiatur vobis esse laudi & gloriae & honori, cum patefiet IESVS CHRISTVS. Item: Charissimi, ne tanquam hospites percellamini explorationem illa per ignem, quae fit vobis ad vestri experimentum, ac si peregrinum aliquid vobis accideret. Vt enim auri glebis aut granis terreni quid inhaeret, quod per ignem excoqui oportet: ita in electis quoque multa vitiosa naturae scoria inuenitur: quam dum res nobis secundae sunt facile dissimulamus, adeo vt ne ipsi quidem de nostra fide & eius constantia certi simus. At cum ignis probationis, afflictio nimirum omnis generis adhibetur, tunc demum sentire incipimus quantum nobis desit, quam item nihil sit in nobis praesidij, quam deniq; fallacia sint. sint quæcunq; in mundo eximia habentur. Itaq; ab vno Deo pendere discimus, & nouis indies gratiæ Dei experimentis confirmati (vt Paulus ad Român. scribit Cap.5.) magis atq; magis proficimus in vera fidei constantia.
units.tr: Nor does he call it a trial of affliction without reason, meaning the most grievous afflictions. For by that expression he expresses the proper use of afflictions, which is that our faith be tested by them, just as gold is tested by fire. Peter explains the same thing in this way, writing to believers: So that the proof of your faith, much more precious than gold, which perishes and yet is tested by fire, may be found to bring praise and glory and honour when Jesus Christ is revealed. Again: Beloved, do not be dismayed as if some strange thing were happening to you, by the fiery trial which comes upon you for your testing. For just as clods of gold or grains of ore contain something earthy that must be burned out by fire, so among the elect too much vicious dross of nature is found; while things go well for us we easily dissemble it, so that we ourselves are not even sure of our faith and its constancy. But when the fire of trial, that is, affliction of every kind, is applied, then at last we begin to feel how much we lack, how little help is in us, and how deceptive are the things in the world that are held in high regard. Thus we learn to depend on the one God, and, strengthened daily by new experiences of the grace of God (as Paul writes to the Romans, chapter 5), we make ever greater progress in the true constancy of faith.

units.la: Obseruabis etiam, quòd gaudium ipsorum redundauisse dicit. Respicit ad id, quòd Deus nos non supra vires tentari sinit, sed consolationibus suis æstum afflictionum temperat. Idem ergo experti sunt Macedones, quod supra de semetipso dixerat: Sicuti abundant passiones Christi in me, ita abundat consolatio nostra per Christum. Ergo solius Dei opus est lœta illa & alacris inter medias afflictiones fidei constantia. Nam si nos spectes, facilè succumbimus, vt qui thesaurum hunc in vasis quouis vitro fragilioribus gestamus. Solari autem nos debet, quòd non nostram, sed Dei causam agimus, & quòd per nostram crucem Christus triumphat. Facile etiam omnem tristitiam ex animis nostris eijcere, & eosdem nouo gaudio perfundere poteš multiplicis gratiæ Dei, sese per crucem exerentis, consideratio. Primò enim hæc (vt modò diximus) scoriam nostram excoquit, & fidem nostram reddit illustriorem. Deinde consortes siue socios facit Deus crucis Filij sui IESV CHRISTI, vt & gloriæ ipsius olim cohæredes simus, quam ille nobis pollicitus est, dicens: Volo, vt vbi ego sum, ibi etiam sit minister meus. Item: Volo Pater, vt vbi ego sum, ibi etiam sint quos dedisti mihi. Quibus addè, quòd ipse iam nunc nobis adest, & vires subinde nouas sufficit, quibus possumus omnibus aduersis atq; periculis superiores fieri.
units.tr: You will also observe that he says their joy overflowed. He has in view the fact that God does not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength, but tempers the heat of afflictions with his consolations. So the Macedonians experienced the very thing he had said of himself: "As the sufferings of Christ abound in me, so our consolation also abounds through Christ." The cheerful and eager constancy of faith amid the midst of afflictions is therefore solely the work of God. For if you look at ourselves, we easily give way, since we carry this treasure in vessels more fragile than any glass. But we ought to be comforted that we are fighting not our own cause but God's, and that through our cross Christ triumphs. The consideration of the manifold grace of God, showing itself through the cross, can also easily drive all sadness from our minds and fill them again with new joy. For first, as we have just said, it purges our dross and makes our faith more radiant. Then God makes us partners, or companions, in the cross of his Son Jesus Christ, so that we may also one day be fellow heirs of the glory which he promised us, saying: "I desire that where I am, there my servant also may be." And again: "Father, I desire that where I am, there also may be those whom you have given me." To these may be added that he is already now present with us, and from time to time supplies new strength by which we can become superior to all adversities and dangers.

units.la: Alterum gratiæ diuinæ apud Macedones argumentum Paulus indicat, quòd profunda eorum paupertas redundarit in diuitias simplicitatis ipsorum. In Græco legitur, ἡ κατὰ βάθος πτωχεία, id est, quæ ad fundum usque exhausta iam erat paupertas: & ideo à Chrysostomo exponitur, ἡ πολλὴ καὶ ἀφατος, id est, multa & ineffabilis. Est autem in Apostoli verbis Metaphora à vasis aut scrinijs sumpta, quæ ad fundum usque exhausta sunt, vt nihil aut modicum in illis superfit. Itaq; sensus est: Macedones, cùm ad extremam egestatem redacti, & iam prorsus exhausti essent, liberalissimos tamen fuisse in facienda collecta qua sanctorum in Iudæa egestas subleuaretur. Id verò amplificat per contraria, dum sibijpsis opponit Paupertatem & Diuitias, Exhaustionem & redundantiam. Atqui impossibile & naturæ legibus contrarium est, ex paupertate diuitias nasci, & vasa ad fundum vsque exhausta redundare. Sed, vt Chrysostomus annotauit, hæc verissimè dicuntur, quia eleemosynas Deus non pro mensura eorum, quæ dantur, æstimat, sed ex animi promptitudine & alacritate, qua illas pij contribuunt. Exemplum, quod ad huius loci illustrationem faciat, in vidua habemus paupercula, cuius duo oboli magnificis diuitum donarijs à Christo præferuntur, eò quòd illos ex imo fundo scrinioli sui prorsus exhausti depromps̄isset, cùm alij ne ea quidem omnia darent, quæ ipsis erant superflua. Et hunc sensum Paulus nobis ceu digito indicat, quando paupertatem Macedonum redundauisse dicit in diuitias simplicitatis ipsorum. Nam simplicitatis nomine animi ingenuum atq; liberalem candorem intelligit, cui opponitur malignitas & fraudis dolinæ plena simulatio, quæ prætextus quærit, ne quid largiatur, & quod dat inuita dat. Facit huc quod Apostolus ad Romanos monet, vt qui distribuit, id faciat in simplicitate. In præsenti autem argumentum subest à Comparatis, quo Corinthij vehementer permoueri poterant, & ita colligere: Si Macedones pauperrimi & tantum non exhausti tam fuerunt liberales, quantò magis vos liberaliter conferre decet, qui & illis opulentiores estis, & otio atque pace magis quàm illi abundatis?
units.tr: Paul points out another proof of divine grace among the Macedonians, namely that their deep poverty overflowed into the riches of their simplicity. In the Greek it reads ἡ κατὰ βάθος πτωχεία [hē kata bathos ptōcheia], that is, poverty drained right down to the bottom; and so Chrysostom explains it as ἡ πολλὴ καὶ ἄφατος [hē pollē kai aphatos], that is, abundant and unspeakable. Now in the apostle's words there is a metaphor taken from vessels or chests that have been emptied right to the bottom, so that nothing or very little remains in them. The sense, then, is this: the Macedonians, though reduced to extreme want and already completely drained, were nevertheless most generous in making the collection by which the saints in Judaea in their need might be relieved. Paul amplifies this by contraries, setting poverty against riches and exhaustion against overflow. Yet it is impossible and contrary to the laws of nature for riches to be born from poverty, and for vessels emptied to the bottom to overflow. But, as Chrysostom observed, these things are said most truly, because God does not measure alms by the amount that is given, but by the readiness and eagerness of mind with which devout people contribute them. We have an example that illustrates this passage in the poor widow, whose two mites were preferred by Christ to the magnificent gifts of the rich, because she had drawn them from the very bottom of her little chest, which was completely emptied, whereas the others did not give even all that was superfluous to them. Paul points to this sense, as it were with his finger, when he says that the poverty of the Macedonians overflowed into the riches of their simplicity. For by the name of simplicity he understands a frank and generous openness of mind, which is opposed to malice and to pretence full of deceit, which seeks excuses so as to give nothing, and gives unwillingly what it does give. To this belongs what the apostle advises to the Romans: that the one who distributes should do it in simplicity. In the present case, moreover, the argument rests on comparison, by which the Corinthians could be powerfully moved and so reason: If the Macedonians, very poor and almost exhausted, were so generous, how much more ought you to contribute liberally, who are richer than they are and abound more in leisure and peace than they do?

units.la: Docet autem locus hic, quæ regula nobis tenenda sit, dum eleemosynam facimus: Nimirum, vt animo simplici & candido demus egenis. Continet hæc fere omnia quæ in hoc negotio exigi possunt. Primùm hypocrisim excludit, ne quid simulate faciamus, sed ex animo. Deinde, vt non alius nobis finis propositus sit, quàm vt pauperibus subueniamus. Tertiò, vt posthabitis omnibus nostræ carnis rationibus, in vnum Deum respiciamus, qui remunerator est fidelissimus. Etenim qui carnem audiunt, non possunt non æquo tenaciores fieri. Vident enim omne hoc suo aceruo decedere, quod egenis largiuntur. Idem solicitas rationes secum ineunt, quàm multis ad vitam honestè sustentandam opus sit. Nec eo contenti curas suas vlterius ad liberos siue posteros suos extendunt, vt singulis tantum relinquant, quantum ad tuendum statum suum possit sufficere. Adhæc proximi opem ipsorum implorantis mores examinant, vt ex his causas vænentur, ob quas eius preces possint respuere. Hæc igitur corda illorum indurant, vt nullo egentium aspectu moveantur. At qui simplici oculo in vnum Deum respiciunt, & huic placere student, hi omnes istos nodos vno quasi ictu abrumpunt: eò quòd plus apud eos valeat mandati diuini authoritas & ab illo promissæ remunerationis spes, quàm quicquid caro stulta & infelix obijcit. Toti enim à Dei gratia pendent, cuius fontes inexhaustos esse sciunt: & promissiones habent, nihil defuturum ijs, qui in pauperes benefici sunt: eò quòd Deo fœnerentur, vt Solomon inquit. Itaque etiamsi ad fundum vsque exhausti sint, semper tamen cum vidua illa euangelica aliquid inueniunt, quod in aliorum subuentionem redundet.
units.tr: This passage also teaches the rule we must keep when we give alms: namely, that we give to the needy with a simple and sincere mind. It contains nearly everything that can be required in this business. First, it excludes hypocrisy, so that we do not act feignedly, but from the heart. Next, that no other end be set before us than to help the poor. Thirdly, that, setting aside all considerations of our flesh, we look to the one God, who is the most faithful rewarder. For those who listen to the flesh cannot but become rather stingy. They see that everything they give to the needy is lost from their heap. The same flesh makes anxious calculations of how much is needed to sustain life decently. Not content with this, they extend their cares further to their children or descendants, so that they leave to each only as much as may suffice to keep up their station. Moreover, they examine the habits of a neighbour who implores their help, so as to search out from these the causes on account of which they may reject his prayers. Thus these things harden their hearts, so that they are moved by no sight of the needy. But those who look with a single eye to the one God, and strive to please him, break all these knots as if with a single blow: because the authority of the divine command and the hope of the reward promised by him carry more weight with them than whatever foolish and unhappy flesh objects. For they depend wholly on the grace of God, whose fountains they know to be inexhaustible; and they have the promise that nothing will be lacking to those who are generous to the poor, since they lend to God, as Solomon says. So even if they have been drained right to the bottom, they always, like that gospel widow, find something which overflows into the help of others.

units.la: Cæterùm vt Macedonum exemplo magis monerentur Corinthij, quod vno quasi verbo dixerat Paulus, nunc diligentius expolit & amplificat, dicens: Nam pro viribus (testor) & supra vires voluntarij fuerunt: multis cum precibus nos rogantes, vt gratiam & societatem ministerij, quod est in sanctos, susciperemus, &c. Primùm testandi verbo vtitur, ne quid fingere putetur. Et eos non pro virili modo contulisse, sed plus fecisse dicit, quàm vires ipsorum ferre potuerint. Et quia hoc quoque impossibile & (vt Dialectici loquuntur) implicatio contradictionis videri poterat, disti huius rationem vno verbo explicat, quando αὐθαίρετος, id est, voluntarios fuisse scribit, aut sponte eos, qui ipsi nemine eos impellente hoc iampridem apud se constituerint. Etenim qui tales sunt, ij plus præstant, quàm præstare posse videbantur. Exempla eius rei vsus quotidianus nobis præbet in ijs, qui ad artes discendas animum serio studio ardentem afferunt, in militia item & quouis alio vitæ genere. Quo loco apparet, cur hodie plerisq; videatur impossibile esse, vt singulæ Ecclesiæ suis egenis prospiciant, ne qui mendicare cogantur. Nimirum quia id facere nolunt, neq; feria pauperum cura tangantur. Etenim ijdem illi maioribus impensis sufficiunt, quas faciunt in gulæ studium, in scorta, aleam, vestitum superbum & insana ædificia, ad quæ toto animi impetu feruntur. Hoc vnû certè nobis omnem excusationis prætextum eripit.
units.tr: But so that the Corinthians might be more admonished by the example of the Macedonians, Paul, having said it in a single word, now polishes and amplifies it more carefully, saying: "For to their power, I bear witness, and beyond their power, they were willing, urgently begging us to receive the grace and fellowship of the ministry which is for the saints, etc." First, he uses the word of testifying, so that nothing may be thought to be invented. And he says that they contributed not merely according to their means, but did more than their resources could bear. And because this too might seem impossible and (as the dialecticians say) an implication of contradiction, he explains the reason for this paradox in a single word, when he writes that they were αὐθαίρετοι [authairetoi], that is, voluntary, or that they, with no one urging them, had of their own accord long since resolved upon this. For those who are such do more than they seem able to do. Daily experience gives us examples of this in those who bring to the learning of arts a mind burning with earnest zeal, and likewise in soldiering and in every other kind of life. At this point it appears why today it seems impossible to most people for individual churches to provide for their needy, so that none are compelled to beg. Clearly it is because they are unwilling to do it, and are not touched by the care of the poor at all. For those same people suffice for greater expenses, which they incur for the pursuit of gluttony, for harlots, dice, proud clothing, and mad buildings, to which they are carried with their whole force of mind. This alone certainly snatches away from us every pretext for excuse.

units.la: Secundò, Rogarunt nos (inquit) multis precibus, vt gratiam & societatem ministerij, quod est in sanctos, susciperemus. Sensus est, Non expectarunt, donec ego eos monerem, sed illi nos prævenientes, multis precibus contenderunt à nobis, vt nos socios præberemus, & nostram operam ipsis conferremus, vt hanc suam beneficentiam maiori cum fructu possent egenis in Syria fratribus præstare. Et morem illis gessit Paulus, quando pecuniam istam passim collectâ ad se recepit, & Hierosolymam detulit. Videntur autem Macedones ideo eius opera voluisse vti, vt eò alacrius singu-li contribuerent, neq; aliqua sinistra suspicione absterrerentur, quando curam huius dispensationis audiebant penes illum fore, cuius maxima erat apud omnes pios authoritas. Etenim tunc demum cum aliquo fructu instituuntur quæ ad pauperum subuentionem faciunt, quando ad hoc officium deliguntur viri, quorum fides & probitas omnibus spectata est, & qui non seipsos obtrudunt priuati commodi studio, sed potiùs rogati munus istud suscipiunt, vt Deo & Ecclesiæ seruiant. Hodie infeliciter de re tanti momenti deliberatur, eò quòd aut improbi suarum facultatum concoctores, aut auari & insatiabiles ministeria ista ambiunt, vt ex ijs ipsi ditescere possint, quæ pauperum alimoniæ debebant seruire. Taceo eos, qui muneribus & pretio illa obtinent: de quibus quid aliud speres, quàm quòd quæstum ex eis velint facere?
units.tr: Second, "They begged us," he says, "with many prayers, that we would receive the grace and fellowship of the ministry which is for the saints." The sense is: they did not wait until I should admonish them, but, anticipating us, they earnestly asked us with many prayers to join them and lend our effort to them, so that they might bestow their beneficence on the brothers in need in Syria with greater fruit. And Paul complied with their wish when he received that money, gathered everywhere, and carried it to Jerusalem. Now the Macedonians seem to have wished to use his labour for this purpose, so that each would contribute the more eagerly and would not be deterred by any sinister suspicion, when they heard that the care of this distribution would rest with the man whose authority was greatest among all the pious. For those things that are done to relieve the poor are then carried out with some fruit, when men are chosen for this office whose faith and integrity have been tested before all, and who do not thrust themselves forward out of a desire for private gain, but rather accept this charge when asked, so that they may serve God and the Church. Today such matters of great moment are decided unhappily, because either dishonest men who squander their own resources, or greedy and insatiable men, seek these ministries so that from them they themselves may grow rich, whereas they ought to serve the maintenance of the poor. I say nothing of those who obtain such offices by bribes and purchase: of whom what else would you expect, than that they wish to make profit from them?

units.la: Tertiò addit: Non vt sperabamus, scilicet fecerunt, sed communem beneficentiæ regulam prætergressi sunt, quæ monet, vt ex fontibus nostris ipsi bibamus riuos autem eorum communicemus alijs: Nam se totos dederunt, primùm Domino, deinde & nobis per Dei voluntatem. Ergòne (inquis) peccauit Paulus in charitatis leges, quando non satis honorificè de Macedonibus sperauit? Nequaquam. Sperauit enim quod in tali causa sperari potest, facturos nimirum quantum possent. Quoad verò summam Collectæ huius, non poterat tantam sperare, quantam illi contulerunt, cùm eos egentiores esse sciret. In ea igitur spem ipsius illi superarunt. Fit hoc frequenter, vt aliqui plus præstent, quàm optimi quiq; & qui illius amicissimi sunt, de eis sperare ausint. Et hoc fere in persecutionibus publicis fieri solet, quando interdum constantissimi sunt in perferendis suppliciis pro Christi nomine, qui infirmiores esse putabantur, quàm vt aliquid susferre possent. Nemo igitur temere de alijs iudicet, multò minus autem alios damnet. Cor hominis est in Dei manu: nos autem scire non possumus, quid ille de vnoquoq; statuerit.
units.tr: Thirdly, he adds: "Not as we hoped, namely, they did, but they went beyond the common rule of generosity, which advises that we drink from our own springs and share their streams with others. For they gave themselves wholly, first to the Lord, and then to us by God's will." "Did Paul then (you ask) sin against the laws of charity when he did not hope well enough of the Macedonians?" By no means. He hoped what can be hoped in such a matter, namely that they would do as much as they could. As for the total of this collection, he could not have hoped for as much as they gave, since he knew they were poorer. So they surpassed his hope. This often happens: some give more than the best people, and those who are most friendly to them dare to hope for them. This usually happens in public persecutions, when sometimes those who were thought too weak to bear any suffering prove the most steadfast in enduring punishments for the name of Christ. Therefore let no one judge others rashly, and much less condemn them. The heart of man is in God's hand, and we cannot know what he has decided about each one.

units.la: Est autem hoc verae pietatis enconium, cuius praecipuae partes sunt, quae hic Macedonibus tribuuntur. Primum, ut nos ipsos demus Domino, id est, nos totos eius gratiae permittamus, nosque ad omnia offeramus paratos, quae ille de nobis constituerit. Ita se totum Deo dedidit Abrahamus, quando Deo vocante patrium solum reliquit, filium quoque dilectum eodem iubente immolare voluit, deinque ad omnia obsequens fuit, quae ille mandabat. Idem Dauid fecit, quando se totum Dei voluntati permittebat, sive hic ipsum in regnum restituere, sive perpetuo exilio multare vellet. Sed & Paulus huius subiectionis egregium specimen dedit, quando IESV CHRISTI manu ad Damasci portas prostratus quaerebat: Domine, quid me vis facere? Non possunt autem haec fieri absque nostrijpsius abnegatione & carnis mortificatione. Quam vero durum sit innatis carni desiderijs valedicere, mox experiuntur, quos ad graviora certamina Deus vocat. At ut hoc faciamus plus quam necessarium est. Quia nisi eo vsque progrediamur, neque in aduersis constantes erimus, neque liberales in subleuanda aliorum egestate. Deinde ut ministris quoque IESV CHRISTI nos dedamus connenit, nimirum quatenus illius ministri sunt. Est enim hic coniunctius cum suo ministerio, & ut eos audiamus iubet, quos ad nos miserit. Hinc locutiones illae: Credidit populus Deo & Mosi. Item: Audiat populus me loquentem ad te, & credat tibi: quatenus scilicet ea proponis, quae ex me profecta esse sciunt. Etenim ut qui Regis legatis credunt & obediunt, ij Regi credidisse & obediuisse dicuntur: Ita etiam qui fidos Christi praecones audiunt, & ijsdem obtemperant. Cauendum tamen, ne qui hoc praetextu hominum serui fiant. Ideo Macedones se Domino simul & Paulo dedidisse dicuntur secundum voluntatem Dei. Hodie vtring, peccatur. In Papatu ius sibi omne in populum vendicant mali antistites, quibus non satis est, si quis germanis Christi Apostolus sese subijciat, nisi simul ipsos quoque dominos agnoscat. Nota est enim Alexandri III. historia, qui cum Imperatoris Friderichi collum impuro pede calcaret, & hunc audiret protestantem: Non tibi, sed Petro: mox respondit: ET MIHI, & Petro. Attamen infelix populus ab illis pendere cogitur, dum putat esse ex necessitate salutis, ut omnis anima Romano Pontifici subdita fit, sicuti Bonifacij VIII. Canon docet. Inter Euangelicos partim licentia regnat, dum qui Antichristi iugum excusserunt, Christi quoque iugum abijcere satagunt: partim tyrannis, qua principes viri Euangelicae doctrinae praeconibus pro suo arbitrio leges dicendi & tacendi praescribere audent: de quibus nunquam vere dixeris, quod se Domino primum, deinde ministris quoque eius dediderint, quando ipsi potius Domino & eius ministris imperare volunt. Subiectionis enim huius propria nota est obedientia, quae Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI mandatis debetur.
units.tr: This is the true praise of godliness, and its chief parts are those attributed here to the Macedonians. First, that we give ourselves to the Lord, that is, that we surrender ourselves wholly to his grace, and offer ourselves ready for all that he has determined concerning us. So Abraham gave himself wholly to God, when, at God's call, he left his native land, and was willing to sacrifice his beloved son at the same command, and then obeyed in all that he was commanded. David did the same when he yielded himself entirely to God's will, whether God wished to restore him to the kingdom or to punish him with perpetual exile. Paul too gave a notable example of this submission, when, prostrate at the gates of Damascus under the hand of Jesus Christ, he asked: "Lord, what do you want me to do?" These things cannot be done without our own self-denial and mortification of the flesh. How hard it is to bid farewell to the desires innate in the flesh, those whom God calls to harder struggles soon experience. Yet we must do this more than is strictly necessary, for unless we advance so far we shall be neither steadfast in adversity nor generous in relieving the want of others. Next, it is fitting that we also give ourselves to the ministers of Jesus Christ, namely insofar as they are his ministers. For he is here more closely joined with his ministry, and he bids us listen to those whom he has sent to us. Hence those phrases: "The people believed God and Moses." Likewise: "Let the people hear me speaking to you, and believe you," that is, insofar as you set forth those things which they know have come from me. For just as those who believe and obey a king's envoys are said to have believed and obeyed the king, so too those who hear the faithful heralds of Christ and obey them. Yet we must take care that we do not become slaves of men under this pretext. Therefore the Macedonians are said to have given themselves at once to the Lord and to Paul, according to the will of God. Today both are done wrongly. In the Papacy, evil prelates claim for themselves every right over the people; it is not enough for them that anyone submit himself to the apostle of Christ, unless he also acknowledges them as lords. The story of Alexander III is well known: when he trod on the neck of the Emperor Frederick with his unclean foot, and heard him protest, "Not to you, but to Peter," he at once replied, "And to me and Peter." Yet the unhappy people is forced to depend on them, while it thinks it is necessary for salvation that every soul be subject to the Roman Pontiff, as the canon of Boniface VIII teaches. Among the Evangelicals, on the one hand, licence reigns, since those who have shaken off the yoke of Antichrist are eager to cast off the yoke of Christ as well; on the other hand, tyranny, in which princes presume to prescribe laws to the heralds of evangelical doctrine, to speak and to be silent as they please. Of these men one could never truly say that they gave themselves first to the Lord and then also to his ministers, when they themselves wish to command the Lord and his ministers. For the mark of this submission is obedience, which is owed to the commands of our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Sed ad Macedones redeamus, quos Paulus hoc etiam abs se impetrauisse scribit, ut adhortaretur Titum, ut sicut ante coeperat, nunc apud ipsos Corinthios quoque hanc gratiam absoluerat. Addit hoc partim ut studium Macedonum amplificet, qui huius operis longe pulcherrimi socios habere voluerint Corinthios (quod hos vehementer extimulare poterat, ne spem de se conceptam fallerent) partim, ut & seipsum excuset, et Tito authoritatem maiorem conciliet, ut qui non tam ex ipsius mandato quam ex Macedonum rogatu ad ipsos veniat. Et absoluendi verbo vtitur: quia non satis est bene coepisse, nisi quod coeptum est perficiatur. Nam ut non magnus vsus est operum, quae adhuc imperfecta sunt: ita neque charitatis et beneficientiae professio quicquam proderit, nisi reipsa praestetur quod profitemur. Ideo Ioannes monebat, ne diligamus verbis, sed opere.
units.tr: But let us return to the Macedonians, whom Paul writes that he also obtained this from them: that he might encourage Titus, so that, as he had begun before, now he might also complete this grace among the Corinthians themselves. He adds this partly to magnify the zeal of the Macedonians, who wanted the Corinthians as companions in this most excellent work (which could strongly spur them on, so that they would not disappoint the hope conceived of them), and partly to excuse himself and to win greater authority for Titus, so that he might come to them not so much by Paul's command as at the request of the Macedonians. He uses the word "complete," because it is not enough to have begun well unless what has been begun is brought to completion. For just as works that are still unfinished are of little use, so the profession of love and beneficence will profit nothing unless what we profess is actually shown in deed. Therefore John warned: "Let us not love in word, but in deed."

units.la: Quoad vero statu huius loci, obseruabis Paulum in tota hac causa subinde gratiae vocabulo vti, quo beneficentiam in pauperes & collectas, quae propter hos fiunt, denotat. Rationes huius dicti multae adduci possunt. Prima, quia nihil ex nobis ipsis possumus, nisi Dominus nos sua gratia praeueniat & excitet. Natura enim tenaces sumus & ad rem attenti, quae causa est, ut egentium miseria minus tangamur. Deus autem is est, qui & animos nostros emollit, & egenis dat gratiam in oculis nostris, ut quae volunt a nobis impetrent. Id vero confutat meriti fiduciam, quam multi (ut olim pharisaei) in eleemosyna collocant. Altera ratio est, quod ex illis bonis largimur pauperibus, quae nobis ex gratuita Dei misericordia obtigerunt, ideoque gratiae Dei dispensatores sumus, ut Christus in Euangelio docet. Quibus adde, quod eleemosyna a misericordia sic dicitur, & proinde eleemosyna non erit, nisi ex gratuita beneficentia fiat, idque animo laeto & voluntario, qui a priuati
units.tr: As to the purpose of this passage, you will observe that Paul uses the word "grace" throughout this whole matter, by which he denotes the beneficence towards the poor and the collections which are made on their behalf. Many reasons can be given for this usage. The first is that we can do nothing of ourselves unless the Lord goes before us with his grace and stirs us up. For by nature we are tenacious and attentive to our property, which is why we are less moved by the misery of the needy. But God is the one who both softens our hearts and gives grace to the needy in our eyes, so that they obtain from us what they wish. This indeed refutes the confidence in merit which many (as once the Pharisees did) place in almsgiving. The second reason is that we give to the poor from those goods which have fallen to us from God's free mercy, and therefore we are dispensers of the grace of God, as Christ teaches in the Gospel. To these add that alms are so called from mercy, and therefore it will not be alms unless it is done from free beneficence, and that with a cheerful and willing mind, one that is most remote from the hope of private advantage.

units.la: Macedones eum piunt Corinth. habere socios. commodi spe sit alienissimus. Quò referri debet, quod Christus monet, ne sinistram manû eius, quod dextra facit, consciam faciamus, id est, ne quo affectu sinistro beneficentiâ nostram adulteremus.
units.tr: The Macedonians have the Corinthians as companions. To this should be referred what Christ warns, that we should not let our left hand know what our right hand does, that is, that we should not corrupt our beneficence with any sinister motive.

units.la: Facit ad huius explicationem quod de Macedonibus in præsenti narratur, quorum exemplo vera eleemosynæ aut beneficentiæ Christianæ ratio perfectè traditur. Primò enim voluntarios & spontaneos fuisse dicit. Deinde Corinthios in eiusdem operis societatem adducere studuerunt. Postremò se totos Domino & eius ministris dediderunt: nimirum quòd se illius debitores esse scirent. Istos ergo imitemur, & primò αὐθαίρετοι siue voluntarij faciamus omnia, quos proprius misericordiæ affectus moueat. Hic procul remouebit obstacula, quæcunq; sui amans caro obijcit: sicuti in Samaritani parabola est videre, qui in terra peregrina & latronibus infesta, hominis ignoti seminecis curam suscepit solo misericordiæ affectu ductus. Volupe item sit multos habere rei omnium laudatissimæ socios, ut & egenis liberalius subueniatur, & plures Deo probentur. Imprimis autem meminerimus nos Dei debitores esse, qui eius verbo obsequium negare nullo iure possimus. Ita excitabimur, ut pro viribus faciamus omnia, imò voluntas nostra vires superabit. Hæc quia olim Christiani homines serió expenderunt, non graue illis visum fuit, pauperes suos alere. At no bis hodie illud impossibile videtur, quia ab animis nostris misericordia exulat. Apparet hoc ex principum exactionibus, quibus infelice populum exhauriunt, bellis item non necessarijs, & sumptibus immodicis, quos in res partim inutiles, partim turpes et inhonestas faciunt. Idé cernitur in privatorum hominum vsuris & monopolijs, quibus rerum omnium pretia non sine acerbis multorum querelis augentur. Quibus adde, quod multi ex ijs ditescere student, quæ maiorum liberalitate in pauperum vsus olim consecrata sunt. Quid, quod gulæ studium multorum immites animos arguit, quando pauperum clamores cum diuite illo epulone facilè negligunt, modò ipsis quotidie comessari licet. Hæc (inquam) nobis graue & impossibile faciunt, quod leuissimum atq; facillimum erat, imò iucundum quoq;, si corda nostra commiserationis igne calerent. Discant ergo omnes Macedonum exemplo se totos Deo addicere, hunc diligere, & simul omnes homines syncero dilectionis affectu completi in CHRISTO IESV, Domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: What is related here about the Macedonians helps to explain this, for by their example the true rule of almsgiving or Christian beneficence is fully set forth. For first, he says they were voluntary and spontaneous (αὐθαίρετοι [authairetoi]). Next, they were eager to bring the Corinthians into partnership in the same work. Lastly, they gave themselves wholly to the Lord and to his ministers, namely because they knew they were his debtors. Let us therefore imitate them: first, let us do everything voluntarily, moved by a genuine feeling of mercy. This will drive far off the obstacles which the self-loving flesh throws in our way, as can be seen in the parable of the Good Samaritan, who, in a foreign land and dangerous because of robbers, took up the care of a half-dead stranger, moved by mercy alone. It is also a pleasure to have many companions in the most praiseworthy of all things, so that the needy may be helped more generously and more may be approved before God. Above all, let us remember that we are debtors of God, who cannot by any right refuse obedience to his word. So we shall be stirred to do everything within our strength; indeed, our will will surpass our strength. Because Christians of old considered these things seriously, it did not seem a burden to them to feed their poor. But today this seems impossible to us, because mercy has been banished from our hearts. This is evident from the exactions of princes, by which they drain the unhappy people, and from unnecessary wars and excessive expenses, which they incur partly on useless and partly on shameful and dishonourable things. The same is seen in the usury and monopolies of private persons, by which the prices of all goods are raised, not without bitter complaints of many. To these add that many strive to grow rich from what was long ago dedicated to the use of the poor by the generosity of our forebears. And what of the eagerness for gluttony, which reveals the cruel hearts of many, when they easily ignore the cries of the poor, provided they themselves may feast every day with that rich glutton? These things (I say) make impossible for us what would be very light and very easy, indeed even pleasant, if our hearts were warmed with the fire of compassion. Let all therefore learn from the example of the Macedonians to devote themselves wholly to God, to love him, and at the same time, filled with sincere affection of love, all men in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXVI.

units.la: Itaq; sicut in omnibus abundatis fide, & sermone, & cognitione, & omni studio, & vestra in nos charitate, videte vt in hac quoq; gratia abundetis. Non pro imperio loquor, sed aliorum studio vestræ quoq; dilectionis syncere-itatem exploratam reddens. Nostis enim gratiam Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, quòd propter vos pauper factus est, cùm esset diues, vt vos illius paupertate ditescere-tis.
units.tr: Therefore, as you abound in all things, in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in all earnestness, and in your love for us, see that you abound in this grace also. I do not speak by way of command, but by testing the sincerity of your love through the zeal of others. For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that by his poverty you might be enriched.

units.la: EST quidem charitas communis omnium Christianorum nota, qua omnis loci & ordinis homines se mutuò completi debent: attamen eius officia illis potissimum debentur, qui in alia qua grauiori necessitate constituti seipsos iuuare non possunt. Nam si in eos modò officiosi & bene ci simus, qui sibi ipsis sufficiunt, & ex quibus ipsi aliquam retributionem sperare possumus, tunc suspecta merito est charitas nostra, quasi sub eius prætextu negotiationem aut quæstum instituamus. Ideo in Scripturis passim pauperes commendantur, quibus in Lege Deus sic iubet prospicere, ne quem illorum auersemur, aut ostiatim victum quærere patiamur. In Nouo testamento eosdem nobis IESVS CHRISTVS ita commendat, vt iis impendi velit, quæ in ipsum velle-mus conferre, si adhuc in terris viueret. Quapropter Apostoli non temere putarunt hac curam ad se pertinere, & hanc causam apud Ecclesias ita egerunt, vt eis non satis fuerit, si vnaquæq; Ecclesia suos pauperes aleret, sed vt quæ opulentiores erant exteris quoq; aliquod subsidium mitterent postularunt. Et huc pertinet tota hæc tractatio, quæ duobus hisce Cap.8. nimirum & nono, continetur. Exorsus est hanc Apostolus ab exemplo Macedonum, quorum liberalitatem præclaro encomio celebrauit: vt nimirum intelligerent Corinthij, inexcusabiles se fore, si ipsi diuites se à tenuioris fortunæ hominibus vinci patiantur. Nunc propius ad rem ipsam accedit. Nam proprio exemplo eos vrget, ne qui in multis alijs excellunt, in hac causa alijs sint inferiores. Itaq; sicut in omnibus abundatis fide, & sermone, & cognitione, & vestra in nos charitate, videte vt in hac quoq; gratia abundetis. Etenim fuit Ecclesia illa donis spiritualibus egregiè ornata, vt in priori epistola vidimus. Monet ergo, vt in hac etiam causa prae alijs industrij sint & eximij. Nullus enim aliorum donorum vsus est, quàm vt per ea ad pietatem excolamur, cuius praecipua pars est charitas, per quam fides agere dicitur. Et semper ratum erit illud Christi: Cui multum datum est, ab eo plus exigetur. Quia ergo Corinthij donis plurimis instructi erant, quibus & opes huius seculi accedebant, turpè fuisset, eos quoad liberalitatem in pauperes alijs inferiores inueniri. At simul obseruatu dignum est, à quibus dotibus commendentur, vt eorum exemplo discamus, quibus virtutibus Ecclesias, adeoque singulos Christianos instructos esse conueniat.
units.tr: Love is indeed a mark common to all Christians, by which people of every place and rank ought to help one another. Yet its duties are owed chiefly to those who, held by some heavier necessity, cannot help themselves. For if we show kindness and goodwill only to those who are self-sufficient, and from whom we can hope for some return, then our love is rightly open to suspicion, as if we were using it as a cover for trade or profit. This is why the Scriptures everywhere commend the poor, and why God in the Law commands us to provide for them, so that we turn none of them away and do not allow them to beg from door to door for food. In the New Testament Jesus Christ commends the same people to us in such a way that he wishes us to give them what we would have wished to give him had he still been living on earth. Therefore the Apostles did not rashly think that this care pertained to them, and they pressed this cause upon the churches so that it was not enough for each church to feed its own poor; they demanded that the wealthier churches also send some help to others. To this belongs the whole of the discussion contained in these two chapters, namely 8 and 9. The Apostle began it with the example of the Macedonians, whose generosity he praised with a splendid commendation, so that the Corinthians might understand that they would be inexcusable if, being rich themselves, they allowed themselves to be outdone by people of more modest means. Now he comes closer to the matter itself. For he presses them with their own example, that those who excel in many other things should not be inferior to others in this cause. Therefore, as you abound in all things, in faith, in speech, in knowledge, and in your love for us, see that you abound in this grace also. That church was indeed richly adorned with spiritual gifts, as we saw in the former epistle. He therefore advises them to be diligent and outstanding in this cause too, above others. For the use of all other gifts is only that through them we are trained in godliness, whose chief part is love, through which faith is said to work. And that saying of Christ will always stand: to whom much has been given, of him more will be required. Since the Corinthians were therefore furnished with very many gifts, to which the riches of this age were also added, it would have been shameful for them to be found inferior to others in generosity towards the poor. But at the same time it is worth noting by what qualities he commends them, so that from their example we may learn with what virtues the churches, and indeed each individual Christian, ought to be equipped.

units.la: Prima hic fides nominatur, ea nimirum, quae solo Deo nititur per Mediatorem vnicum IESVM CHRISTVM. Huic primae partes debentur, quia sine ea ne Christiani quidem erimus: eò quòd haec sola Christum apprehendit, & eidem nos inserit, per quem Deo Patri reconciliamur. Quae ratio est, quòd sine fide neminem Deo placere posse dicit Apostolus, imò peccatum est omne illud, quod absq; fide fit. Vnde sequitur eos frustra ceremonijs & externis exercitijs gloriari, qui fide destituuntur. Sunt enim ex eorum numero, qui etsi ore appropinquent Deo, & labijs eum honorent, cor tamen ab illo procul remotum habent. At hic probè tenendum est, fidem non esse, quae nos non vni Deo consecrat, vt nec coniugalis fides in vxore fuerit, quae non vnum & solum maritum colit & obseruat. Arguit hoc ambidextros, qui cum fide in Deum glorientur, huic tamen Diuos caelites & infinita alia coniungunt, in quae salutis fiduciam partiuntur. Hos Elias olim in vtrumq; latus claudicare dixit, & de ijsdem dici potest, quòd non recto pede incedant secundùm Euangelij veritatem.
units.tr: Here faith is named first, namely that faith which rests on God alone through the one Mediator, Jesus Christ. First place is owed to this, because without it we will not even be Christians, since this alone apprehends Christ and grafts us into him, through whom we are reconciled to God the Father. This is why the Apostle says that without faith no one can please God; indeed, everything that is done without faith is sin. From this it follows that those who lack faith boast in vain of ceremonies and outward exercises. For they belong to the number of those who, though they draw near to God with their mouths and honour him with their lips, nevertheless keep their heart far from him. But here it must be firmly held that faith is not faith if it does not consecrate us to the one God alone, just as a wife's fidelity would not be fidelity if she did not cherish and keep only one husband. This refutes the double-dealers, who boast of faith in God but at the same time join to him the heavenly saints and countless others, in whom they divide their hope of salvation. Elijah once said that such people limp on both sides, and of the same people it can be said that they do not walk with a straight foot according to the truth of the Gospel.

units.la: Secundò Sermo ponitur. Non potest, neq; debet hic alius intelligi quàm Euangelij praedicatio, ex qua fides discitur, vt Paulus ad Romanos testatur, & in quo solo certa fidei regula habetur. Nec enim fides erit, quae non secundùm Dei verbum dirigitur. Admonet de eo Christus nō obscurè Iudaeis dicens: Amen dico vobis, qui sermonem meum audit, & credit ei qui misit me, habet vitam aeternam. En praemittit sermonem suum, qui non alius quàm Euangelium est, & vt secundùm hoc credamus docet. Simile huic est, quod apud Lucam, mulieri, quae vterum beatum dixerat, qui ipsum gestasset, & vbera, quae eundem lactassent, respondit: Quin imo beati, qui audiunt sermonem Dei, & custodiunt illum. Imprimis tamen huc facit postremum Christi mandatum in quo discipulis dicit: Praedicate Euangelium omni creaturae: qui crediderit (scilicet Euangelio) & baptizatus fuerit, saluus erit. Est ergo praeclarum & necessarium Ecclesiae donum, libera & syncera verbi Dei praedicatio. Agnoscunt hoc electi, & proinde eidem vnicè studeant: quod ipsum Christus quoque testatur: Qui ex Deo est, verba Dei audit. Item: Oues meae vocem meam audiunt. Arguit hoc eorum impietatem, qui coetus sacros oderunt, verbi praedicationem fugiunt & auersantur. Qui fere, ne impij videantur, hoc vnum in ore habent: Fidem Dei donum esse, & neminem cogi debere. Atqui eodem argumento agricultura aboleri poterat, & quaecunq; ad rem domesticam & Reipub. faciunt, quando haec quoq; vnà cum toto telluris prouentu Dei dona sunt gratuita. Sed indigni sunt tales, quibus cum prolixius agatur. Seruit illis, quod Christus olim Iudaeis dicebat: Vos ex patre diabolo estis, &c. Ioan. 8.
units.tr: Second, the word is mentioned. Here nothing else can or should be understood than the preaching of the Gospel, from which faith is learned, as Paul testifies to the Romans, and in which alone the sure rule of faith is found. For there will be no faith that is not directed according to God's word. Christ clearly points to this when he speaks to the Jews: Truly, truly I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. Behold, he puts his word first, which is nothing other than the Gospel, and teaches us to believe according to it. Similar to this is what he said in Luke to the woman who had called blessed the womb that bore him and the breasts that nursed him: Yes indeed, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it. Yet especially to this purpose belongs Christ's last command, in which he tells his disciples: Preach the Gospel to every creature; he who believes (namely the Gospel) and is baptized will be saved. Therefore the free and sincere preaching of the word of God is an excellent and necessary gift of the Church. The elect acknowledge this and accordingly devote themselves to it alone, which Christ himself also attests: he who is of God hears the words of God. Likewise: My sheep hear my voice. This exposes the impiety of those who hate sacred assemblies and shun and turn away from the preaching of the word. They commonly have only this on their lips, lest they seem ungodly: that faith is a gift of God, and no one ought to be compelled. And yet by the same argument agriculture could be abolished, and everything that serves domestic and civil life, since these too are free gifts of God together with the whole produce of the earth. But such people are unworthy to be dealt with at greater length. What Christ once said to the Jews suits them: You are of your father the devil, etc. John 8.

units.la: Tertiò Cognitione numerat, quae est scientia rerum spiritualium, quae ex Dei verbo discitur. Etenim homo animalis non percipit ea, quae sunt Spiritus Dei. At in Euangelio nobis Christus loquitur, qui ab aeterno est in sinu patris, & nobis annuntiauit omnia. Rursus ergo nobis studiu audiendi verbi commendatur, & ideo hoc in praesenti Paulus cū cognitione coniungit. Et in Psalmo beatus pronuntiatur, qui procul relictis hominum malorum & illusorum studijs dies & noctes meditatur in Lege Domini. Quàm ergo infelices & miseri sunt, qui cum Euangelio glorientur & Christiani dici velint, nihil tamen norunt imò ne volunt quidem aliquid scire, & eo nomine seipsos excusant, si quando de controuersijs fidei articulis ipsorum quoq; sententia requiritur. Atqui non tales fuerunt Corinthij, Paulo teste. Et aliter Ecclesiam Isaias describit, quando
units.tr: Third, he counts knowledge, which is the understanding of spiritual things learned from God's word. For the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God. But in the Gospel Christ speaks to us, who from eternity is in the bosom of the Father, and has declared all things to us. Once again, therefore, the eagerness to hear the word is commended to us, and for this reason Paul here joins knowledge to it. In the Psalm the man is pronounced blessed who, having far abandoned the pursuits of wicked and deluded men, meditates on the Law of the Lord day and night. How unhappy and wretched, then, are those who boast of the Gospel and wish to be called Christians, yet know nothing, indeed do not even want to know anything, and excuse themselves on this ground whenever their opinion is asked about controverted articles of faith. Yet the Corinthians, as Paul testifies, were not like this. And Isaiah describes the Church otherwise, when

units.la: Ioan. 8. dicit: Erunt omnes filij tui à Deo docti. Item: Plena erit terra scientia Domini, perinde ut cum aquæ maris inundant. Isa. 54. & 11.
units.tr: John 8. says: All your children shall be taught of God. Likewise: The earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord, just as the waters of the sea cover it. Isa. 54 and 11.

units.la: Quarto charitatem illorum erga se Paulus prædicat. Exprimitur hic mutuum inter Ecclesias & verbi administros officiu. Vt enim hi illas amare, & pro ijsdem (si ita opus fit) animas suas deponere debent: ita vicissim Ecclesiæ ipsos ament, & (quod in Galatis Paulus commendat) proprijs oculis chariores habeant. Sunt enim parentum instar, eò quòd ipsorum ministerio regenerantur in filios Dei, ut in prioris epist. Cap. 4. audiuimus. At quæ nostri seculi infelicitas est, qui hodie ex Euangelio maxima commoda percipiunt, ij fere pra alijs huius ministros oderunt: quo argumento animos suos egregiè produnt, ut nimirum erga Euangelium & huius authorem, IESVM CHRISTVM, affecti sint. Est autem obseruatu dignissima Pauli modestia, qui cum Corinthi æmulos haberet multos & graues, contra quos hucusque suam authoritatem tam constanter asseruit: non tamen odium illorum toti Ecclesiæ imputat, sed potius eam charitatem prædicat, qua alij vere credentes ipsum prosequebantur. Imitentur exemplum hoc omnes ministri. Hocipsum enim temporibus corruptissimis Prophetas fecisse, eorum sermones, imo preces & querelæ testantur, quas pro incurabilibus & pœnitere nescijs fuderunt. Peccant hodie multi pastores nö leui ter, qui nulla vere credentiu ratione habita, de solis aduersarijs conqueruntur, & ab his acceptas iniurias ita exagitant, ut Ecclesias totas damnent, vel etiam non sine magno scandalo deserant.
units.tr: Fourth, Paul proclaims their love towards himself. Here the mutual duty between the churches and the ministers of the Word is expressed. For just as the ministers ought to love the churches and, if need be, lay down their lives for them, so in turn the churches ought to love the ministers and (as Paul commends in the Galatians) hold them dearer than their own eyes. For they stand in the place of parents, because through their ministry they are born again as sons of God, as we heard in chapter 4 of the former epistle. But what unhappiness of our age is this: those who today receive the greatest benefits from the Gospel are for the most part the ones who hate its ministers above others, and by this argument they clearly betray their minds, namely that they are disposed in this way towards the Gospel and its author, Jesus Christ. Moreover, the modesty of Paul is most worthy of note: although at Corinth he had many serious rivals, against whom he had so steadfastly maintained his authority up to that point, he nevertheless does not impute their hatred to the whole Church, but rather proclaims the love with which the other truly believing people followed him. Let all ministers imitate this example. For that the Prophets did the same in the most corrupt times, their sermons, indeed their prayers and complaints, bear witness, which they poured out for those who were incurable and did not know how to repent. Many ministers today sin no slightly, who, taking no account of the truly believing, complain only of their opponents, and so inflame the wrongs they have received from them that they condemn whole churches, or even abandon them not without great scandal.

units.la: Est præterea confideratu dignum, quod tam multis tamen egregijs virtutibus instructos hortatur, ut his beneficentiam in pauperes addant, vel potius ut Ecclesijs Iudaicis subsidium mittant. Ex eo discimus, vana & mania esse omnia alia studia, nisi charitate gubernentur. Admonemur item, neminem debere sibi placere, quasi iam ad metam perfectionis peruenerit. Hoc enim nemini datur, quoad in hac carne mortali viuimus. Nam manent semper in membris nostris peccati reliquiæ, vel (ut alibi Paulus loquitur) Lex peccati, quæ nos præter voluntatem nostram transfuersos abripit. Quare nos semper proficere conuenit, nec quantum profecerimus, sed quàm multum adhuc nobis desit, videre debemus: quod proprio exemplo in epistola ad Philippenses diligentius explicat. Imprimis verò hæc sibi ipsis applicent Ecclesiæ, quibus primis datum est Euangelium audire, & quarum fides, cognitio, doctrina passim apud exteros prædicatur. Meminerint præterea, hoc abs se quoq; exigi, ut quoad officia charitatis in fratres egenos, exteros & exules, se à nemine vinci patiantur. Quia enim alijs in exemplum propositæ sunt, turpe fuerit, si minus alijs præstent, quarum fama non ita celebratur.
units.tr: It is also worth noting that he urges those who already have so many excellent virtues to add to them beneficence towards the poor, or rather, to send help to the Jewish churches. From this we learn that all other pursuits are empty and worthless unless they are governed by charity. We are also reminded that no one should please himself, as if he had already reached the goal of perfection. For this is granted to no one as long as we live in this mortal flesh. Remnants of sin always remain in our members, or (as Paul says elsewhere) the law of sin, which drags us off, turned aside against our will. Therefore we ought always to make progress, and we should look not at how much we have advanced but at how much is still lacking to us. He explains this more carefully by his own example in the epistle to the Philippians. Above all, let the churches to whom the gospel was first given to hear apply these things to themselves, those whose faith, knowledge and teaching are proclaimed everywhere among foreigners. Let them also remember that this is required of them too: that in the duties of charity towards needy brothers, strangers and exiles, they allow themselves to be outdone by no one. For since they have been set before others as an example, it would be shameful if they gave less than others whose reputation is not so widely celebrated.

units.la: Quia verò qui alijs opulentiores & in aliqua dignitate constituti sunt, indignius ferre solent, si quis ipsis aliquid ex imperio mandet, mitigat exhortationem, & eius rationem reddit, quia hoc omne ad ipsorum honorem & dignitatem facere docet. Non ex imperio loquor, ait, &c. Ex imperio loqui dicuntur, qui præcise mandant, & obediendi necessitate aliquem obstringunt. Id vero in præsenti causa minimè locum habebat. Nam etsi Deus charitatis officia omnibus præcipiat, & ut his fidem nostram testemur atq; exerceamus necesse sit, tamen non coactos aut inuitos, sed voluntarios siue spontaneos, imo hilares datores requirit, ut in proximo Capite dicetur. Atqui tales dici non possunt, quibus ex imperio mandatur quid facere debeant.
