Quia ergo Paulus hoc agebat, ut Corinthij sponte conferrent eleemosynam, & ita se vere Christianos esse testarentur: quia item iampridem hoc facere cœperant, & proinde de illis spes bona erat, debuit mitius cum illis agere Apostolus. Aliter cum illis agendum, qui malitiose cunctantur, vel etiam Dei præceptis se pertinacius opponunt. Hos vehementius vrgere, ad Christi tribunal citare, & ijsdem laruam falsæ professionis detrahere oportet. At si Pauli modestiam, qua in causa non minus necessaria quàm honesta & bona vtitur, cum Pontificum insolentia conferas, qua illi quæuis decreta sua, ea etiam quæ cum aperto Dei verbo pugnant pro imperio & sub pœna Excommunicationis obtrudunt, facile videbis quàm parum eis conueniat Apostolicorum titulus.
units.tr: But because those who are wealthier than others and placed in some position of dignity are wont to take it badly if anyone commands them by authority, Paul softens the exhortation and gives his reason, teaching that all this serves their own honour and dignity. "I speak not by way of command," he says, etc. Those are said to speak by command who lay down orders outright and bind someone by the necessity of obedience. That had no place in the present case. For although God commands the duties of charity to all, and it is necessary that we bear witness to and exercise our faith through them, yet he requires givers who are not compelled or unwilling, but willing, or rather cheerful, as will be said in the next chapter. Those who are ordered by authority to do something cannot be called such. Therefore, since Paul's aim was that the Corinthians should give the alms of their own accord, and so show themselves to be truly Christians; and since they had already long begun to do this, and so there was good hope concerning them, the apostle rightly dealt more gently with them. Those who hang back maliciously, or who oppose God's precepts more stubbornly, must be dealt with differently. These must be pressed more vehemently, summoned before the judgment seat of Christ, and stripped of the mask of a false profession. But if you compare Paul's moderation, which he uses in a matter no less necessary than honourable and good, with the arrogance of the popes, who thrust upon men their own decrees by authority and under penalty of excommunication, even those that clash with the plain word of God, you will easily see how little the title of "apostolic" suits them.

units.la: Sed videamus Pauli rationem, quam ille hic secutus est. Aliorum studio (inquit) vestræ quoq; dilectionis fynceritatem exploratam reddens: ut nimirum ea omnibus innotescat. In Græco quidem est ðοκιμάζων, quod probare significat. Sed ut infra ex Capitis noni principio patebit, Paulus iampridem exploratam habebat Corinthiorum promptitudinem, & odiosum plane videri poterat, si
units.tr: But let us look at Paul's reasoning, which he followed here. "Through the zeal of others," he says, "testing the sincerity of your love too," namely so that it may become known to all. In the Greek it is dokimazōn [δοκιμάζων], which means to prove. But as will be clear below from the beginning of the ninth chapter, Paul already had the readiness of the Corinthians well tested, and it could have seemed quite odious if he had said that he was seeking a proof of it, as though he doubted it.

units.la: Charitas. terat, si se eius experimentum quaerere dixisset, quasi de illa dubitaret: Ideo in praesenti se non aliud quaerere dicit, quam ut charitas & studium, quo iam nunc accensi sint, omnibus conspicuum fiat. Iure autem & merito hoc agebat. Nam ut proximo Capite audivimus, de illis apud quosfus gloriari solebat, & magna de illis spem conceperat. Ne ergo & ipse pudefieret, & Corinthij infames haberentur, opus omnino fuit, ut publicum darent verae pietatis specimen. Nihil autem haec Pharisaeorum hypocrisi patrocinantur, qui eleemosynas suas ambitiose ostentabant, ut sibi ipsis sanctitatis existimationem pararent. Hic enim de eiusmodi specimine agitur, quod ad Dei gloriam & fidei Christianae commendationem faciebat, & quo multorum pauperum egestas subleuabatur: quae res Christiano homini cumprimis cordi esse debent. Sed & ministrorum est, Ecclesiarum suarum honori & dignitati consulere, ne ea per aliquorum socordiam vel petulantiam collabatur.
units.tr: Therefore in the present passage he says that he seeks nothing else than that the love and zeal with which they are already burning should become visible to all. He did this rightly and deservedly. For, as we heard in the previous chapter, he used to boast of them to the Macedonians and had conceived great hope concerning them. So, lest he himself be put to shame and the Corinthians be thought disreputable, it was entirely necessary that they give a public sample of true piety. Nothing here, however, lends any support to the hypocrisy of the Pharisees, who ostentatiously displayed their alms so as to win for themselves a reputation for holiness. For what is meant here is a demonstration that serves the glory of God and the commendation of the Christian faith, and by which the want of many poor people is relieved. These things ought to be especially dear to a Christian. But it also belongs to ministers to look after the honour and dignity of their churches, lest these fall into disrepute through the carelessness or wantonness of some.

units.la: Porro admonet nos locus iste, quis nobis exemplorum usus esse debeat, eorum imprimis, qui aliquid cum laude faciunt. Ut nimirum quae bene facta sunt, imitemur. Haec aemulatio sanctissima atq; saluberrima est, quando in virtutis studio & beneficentiae palaestra nemo ab altero vinci vult. At Christi autem Spiritu alienissimi sunt, qui ex aliorum egregie factis & laude invidiae atque odij semina concipiunt, & calumniandi occasionem venantur. Illud enim Cainus olim fecit, hoc vero diaboli proprium est, ut ex Iobi historia apparet. Praecipue vero discimus hoc loco, observanda diligenter esse veterum Ecclesiarum exempla, ut secundum ea mores & studia nostra instituamus. Inter illa perfectissimum est, quod in primitiua Ecclesia habetur, Summam eius Lucas his verbis comprehendit: Erant perdurantes in doctrina Apostolorum, & in communicatione, & fractione panis & orationibus. Multitudinis autem eorum qui crediderant, erat cor & anima una: nec quisquam aliquid eorum quae habebat, suum esse dicebat: sed erant illis omnia communia (voluntate nimirum & mutua beneficentia, ut alibi demonstrauimus) & nemo egens siue mendicus erat inter eos, &c. Huic ergo formulae se accommodent, qui Ecclesiam recte constitutam habere cupiunt. Debet hoc ipsum ad Rempub. quoq; transferri, ut diligenter eorum exempla inspiciamus, qui olim res suas cum laude & utiliter instituerunt: videamus item, quid multis alijs turbas dederit, aut etiam exitio fuerit.
units.tr: Moreover, this passage reminds us what use we ought to make of examples, especially of those who do something to their credit: namely, that we imitate what has been done well. This emulation is most holy and most wholesome when, in the pursuit of virtue and in the arena of beneficence, no one wishes to be outdone by another. But those are utterly alien to the Spirit of Christ who conceive seeds of envy and hatred from the excellent deeds and praise of others, and hunt for occasions to slander. Cain once did this, and this is the proper work of the devil, as appears from the history of Job. Above all, we learn in this place that the examples of the early churches must be carefully observed, so that we may shape our conduct and pursuits according to them. Among these the most perfect is what is found in the primitive Church. Luke sums it up in these words: "They continued steadfastly in the doctrine of the apostles, and in fellowship, and in the breaking of bread, and in prayers. And the multitude of those who believed had one heart and one soul; nor did anyone say that any of the things he possessed was his own, but everything was common to them" (of course by will and mutual beneficence, as we have shown elsewhere), "and there was no one among them who was needy or a beggar," etc. (Acts 2.) Let those who wish to have a rightly ordered church conform themselves to this pattern. This same principle ought also to be applied to the commonwealth, so that we carefully examine the examples of those who in former times conducted their affairs with credit and to good effect; and we should likewise consider what has brought disorder to many others, or even ruin.

units.la: Caeterum ad Paulum reuertamur, qui confirmationis loco exemplum Christi adducit, quo simul Macedonum liberalitas magis commendatur, ut quae huic conueniat. Nostis (inquit) gratia Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, quod propter vos pauper factus est, cum esset dives, ut vos illius paupertate ditesceretis. Atqui praecepta eius allegare poterat, quae multa & praeclara in Euangelio occurrunt. Sed quia voluntarios esse volebat, & ad hoc maior est exemplorum efficacia, illud potius adducit. Sunt autem figulae eius partes diligentius excutienda, quia paucis hisce verbis tota salutis nostrae ratio continetur, vna cum ijs, quae ad vitam recte & pie instituenda faciunt.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who, as a confirmation, adduces the example of Christ, by which the generosity of the Macedonians is also more highly commended, as it befits that case. "You know," he says, "the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that through his poverty you might become rich" (2 Cor. 8.). Yet he could have cited Christ's precepts, which are many and excellent and occur throughout the gospel. But because he wanted them to give freely, and because the example has greater force for this purpose, he adduces that instead. Each of its parts must be examined carefully, because in these few words the whole reasoning of our salvation is contained, together with those things which serve to order life rightly and piously.

units.la: Primo Christum divitem fuisse scribit. Dicitur hoc non ex Papae Ioannis vigesimi tertij sententia, qui Christum ratione huius seculi divitem fuisse dicebat, & pertinaces atq; haereticos pronunciauit eos, qui illum & Apostolos nihil proprium habuisse sentirent: & ne de eo in scholis porro disputaretur per bullas Apostolicas mandauit. At Paulus altius quid & sublimius docere vult. Divitem enim dicit Christum, utpote Deum verum & Dei Filium aeternum atq; Patri consubstantialem, qui omnia cum Patre communia habet, sicuti ipse testatur: Omnia quae habet Pater, mea sunt. Item. Mea omnia Pater, tua sunt: & mea, tua sunt. Deinde quod ad humanitatem assumptam diues etiam dici potest, ut cuius haereditas sunt gentes & termini orbis terrarum, quiq; pro suo nutu omnibus uti semper potuit. Etenim quamuis neq; domum propriam, neq; praedia, neq; auri argentiq; thesauros humano more possederit, imo non habuerit quo caput suum reclinaret: eidem tamen, quoties voluit, omnium aedium fores patuerunt, omnium hominum facultates & iumenta seruierunt, ut & ipse illis uti posset, & ex ijsdem totum suorum discipulorum sodalitiu alere: sicuti Euangelica historia abunde docet. Et quis diuitem esse negauerit eum, qui mari et ventis, spiritibus item impuris & morbis pro suo arbitrio mandauit, & ad cuius seruitium Angeli nunquam non praesto fuerunt?
units.tr: First, he writes that Christ was rich. This is said not in the sense of Pope John the Twenty-third, who maintained that Christ was rich in the manner of this world, and who pronounced obstinate heretics those who thought that he and the apostles had possessed nothing of their own, and who by apostolic bulls ordered that the matter should not be disputed any further in the schools. But Paul wishes to teach something higher and more sublime. For he calls Christ rich as the true God and the eternal Son of God, consubstantial with the Father, who has all things in common with the Father, as he himself testifies: "All that the Father has is mine" (John 16.), and again: "All mine are yours, and yours are mine" (John 17.). Then, with respect to the humanity he assumed, he may also be called rich, since the nations are his inheritance and the ends of the earth his possession, and he was always able to use everything at his own pleasure. For although he did not possess a house of his own, or estates, or treasures of gold and silver in the manner of men, indeed had nowhere to lay his head, yet the doors of every house were open to him whenever he wished, the resources and beasts of all men were at his service, so that he could use them himself and feed the whole company of his disciples from them, as the evangelical history amply shows. And who could deny that he was rich, who commanded the sea and the winds, as well as unclean spirits and diseases, at his own will, and whose servants the angels were always at hand?

units.la: At hunc ipsum Paulus pauperem factum esse dicit. In Graeco πτωχευσω ponitur, quod proprie mendicorum est. Vtitur eo Paulus de Christo loquens, non quod mendicum egerit ostiatim per factum. panem aut stipem petendo, sed quòd nihil proprium habuit, vt ipse in Euangelio fatetur. Non habuit autem aliquid proprium, quia habere noluit, neq; cum posset vti voluit ijs, quorum ⁊ unicus hæres erat & dominus. Quare hoc membrum de paupertate eius voluntaria exponi debet. Nam etsi hominem verum assumpsisset, nunquam tamen desijt esse is qui erat, æternus nimirum Dei Filius, neq; etiam potestati suæ renuntiauit, sicut tot huius specimina testantur: sed pauper factus esse dicitur, quia voluntarie abstinuit ab vsu eorū, quæ ad ipsum iure pertinebant. Id Paulus ad Phil. alia phrasi explicat, dicens: Cùm esset in forma Dei, non duxit rapinam, parem esse cum Deo: sed seipsum exinaniuit, forma serui sumpta. Et facit ad huius dicti expositionem tota vitæ eius in terris transactæ historia. Qui enim cælum & terram implet, Bethlehemi in stabulo natus est: Qui potestatem habet omnem in cælo & terra, in Ægypto per annos aliquot exulat: Qui homines, pecudes, feras, aues, pisces omnes alit, partim labore suo victum sibi quærit, partim ex aliorum beneficentia accipit: Qui omnibus de amictu prospicit, nudus in cruce pendet: Qui cælis vt throno insidet, & terra vt scabello pedum vtitur, in sepulchro alieno & aliorum impensis conditur. Itaq; vt vnus idemq; Christus, Deus & homo est, ita in eodem diuina rerum omnium potestas & voluntaria omnium inopia concurrunt.
units.tr: But Paul says that this same Christ became poor. In Greek the word is πτωχευσω [ptōcheuō], which properly belongs to beggars. Paul uses it of Christ, not because Christ went from door to door begging for bread or alms, but because he had nothing of his own, as he himself confesses in the Gospel. He had nothing of his own because he did not want to have anything, and although he could have used the things that were rightly his, as the sole heir and Lord of them, he chose not to. So this clause about his poverty should be understood as voluntary. For even though he had taken on true human nature, he never ceased to be who he was, the eternal Son of God, nor did he give up his power, as so many examples of it attest. He is said to have become poor because he voluntarily refrained from using what by right belonged to him. Paul explains this in another form of words in Philippians, saying: "Though he was in the form of God, he did not count it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant." The whole history of his life on earth bears this out. He who fills heaven and earth was born in a stable at Bethlehem. He who has all power in heaven and earth spent some years in exile in Egypt. He who feeds all men, beasts, wild animals, birds and fish, partly earns his own food by labour and partly receives it from the kindness of others. He who provides clothing for all hangs naked on the cross. He who sits on heaven as his throne and uses the earth as a footstool is buried in another man's tomb, at other men's expense. Thus, just as one and the same Christ is God and man, so in him the divine power over all things and his voluntary lack of all things come together.

units.la: Sunt hæc mirabilia valde, & omnem humani ingenij captum superant: Quare finem huius voluntariæ paupertatis & subiectionis Christi Paulus indicat: Propter vos (inquit) pauper factus est, vt vos illius paupertate ditesceretis. Poterat in prima persona loqui: Propter nos, &c. Sed oportuit Christi pauperis exemplum Corinthijs propius applicari, quos suarum opum fiducia arrogantiores faciebat. Et multum prodest, vt singuli quæcunq; Dei Filius fecit & passus est, sibi-ipsis applicent, & nunquam non sibiipsis occinant: Christus propter te homo factus est, propter te suriuit, sitiuit, alsit: propter te captus, damnatus, flagellis cæsus & in cruce suffixus est. Ita enim & fides nostra magis confirmabitur, & ad officij nostri meditationem efficacius accendemur.
units.tr: These things are truly wonderful and exceed the whole grasp of human understanding. Therefore Paul points out the purpose of this voluntary poverty and submission of Christ: "For your sakes he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich." He could have spoken in the first person: "for our sakes," and so on. But it was fitting that the example of the poor Christ be applied more closely to the Corinthians, whom confidence in their own wealth made too proud. It is also very profitable for each of us to apply to himself whatever the Son of God did and suffered, and never to cease singing it to himself: Christ became man for your sake, he thirsted, hungered, and grew cold for your sake; for your sake he was seized, condemned, scourged, and nailed to the cross. In this way our faith will be strengthened more, and we will be kindled more effectively to meditate on our duty.

units.la: Porrò summa argumenti, quod hinc Paulus colligit, hæc est: Quia Christiani estis, Christi exemplum debetis imitari, vt quod ille propter vos fecit, idem vos quoq; faciatis propter cos, quos ille vobis perinde vt seipsum commendauit. Ille cùm dives esset, vos pauperes & plus quàm miseros non neglexit: Ergo neq; vos debetis pauperes negligere. Ille pauper factus est, vt vos diuites faceret: Ergo non pigeat opes, quas habetis, expendere, vt alij vestra liberalitate subleuentur. Nam etiamsi multum detis, imò si omnes facultates expendatis, nunquam tamen tantum feceritis, quantum ille, qui vitam quoq; pro vobis effundere dignatus est. Quæ vero excusatio vobis reliqua erit, si cum vobis liceat tantum seruare, quantum vestræ necessitati sufficere potest, in ijs quæ superflua sunt tenaciores, imò dispensatores iniqui fueritis? Hæc (inquâ) præsentis loci summa est.
units.tr: Moreover, the sum of the argument that Paul draws from this is this: because you are Christians, you ought to imitate the example of Christ, so that you may do for those whom he has commended to you, just as he commended himself, what he did for you. Although he was rich, he did not neglect you, who were poor and more than wretched. Therefore you too ought not to neglect the poor. He became poor so that he might make you rich. Therefore do not be reluctant to spend the wealth that you have, so that others may be relieved by your generosity. For even if you give much, indeed even if you spend all your resources, you will never have done as much as he did, who also deigned to pour out his life for you. What excuse will remain for you, if, while you may keep only as much as your own need can require, you are the more grasping about what is superfluous, or rather become unjust stewards? This, I say, is the sum of the present passage.

units.la: Cæterum quoad alia, quæ hic concurrunt, non oscitanter videre oportet, quas & quales diuitias nobis Christus acquisierit. Errant enim hic pernitiosissimè, quotquot in illo terrena quærunt, inter quos facilè primas tenent Pontifices cū Senatu suo purpurato, Episcopi & reliquis eius farinæ præsulibus: qui omnes sub eius nomine non opes modò, verumetiam regna huius mundi ad se rapiunt. Neq; extra culpam sunt, qui Euangelica professione ad eundem finem abutuntur. At volui quidem Dei Filius, quoad hoc seculum, in terris pauper viuere: non autem ideo, vt nos, quoad hoc seculum, diuites faceret, sed vt thesaurum nobis in cælo pararet, quem neq; fures rapere, neq; erugo aut tineæ corrumpere possunt. Continet thesaurus iste opes incomparabiles, nimirum gratiam Dei, remissionem peccatorum, veram Dei cognitionem, iustitiam, sanctificationem, Spiritum adoptionis, ipsos deniq; cælos, & beatæ immortalitatis hæreditatem. Hæc in solo Christo habentur, & soli diuites sunt, qui ista in illo per fidem possident: Pauperrimi verò & plus quàm mendici sunt, qui extra hunc vagantur. Hic ergo vere locum habet paradoxon illud, quo solum sapientem diuitem esse, olim saniores philosophi dixerunt. Quia enim animalis homo non percipit ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, nemo sapiens est, nisi cuius sapientia Christus est. At qui hunc habet, is de Dei gratia & bonitate certus, & proinde sua sorte contentus, nihil præterea expetit: Ad has ergo opes aspiremus ô fratres, neq; nobis graue fit interea, dum eas sectamur, pauperiem perpeti, quam nobis suo exemplo & merito consecrauit æternus Dei Filius, IESVS CHRISTVS, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: As for the other matters that come together here, we must look carefully at what sort of riches Christ has gained for us, and how great they are. Those who seek earthly things in him err most destructively here, and among them the Popes, with their purple-clad Senate, and the bishops and the other prelates of that kind easily hold first place. Under his name they seize for themselves not only wealth but even the kingdoms of this world. Nor are those free of blame who abuse the profession of the gospel to the same end. But the Son of God chose to live poor on earth for this age, not so that he might make us rich in this age, but so that he might prepare for us a treasure in heaven, which neither thieves can steal nor rust or moths destroy. That treasure contains incomparable riches: namely, the grace of God, the forgiveness of sins, the true knowledge of God, righteousness, sanctification, the Spirit of adoption, and finally the heavens themselves and the inheritance of blessed immortality. These things are found in Christ alone, and only those are rich who possess them in him through faith. But those who wander outside him are the poorest, more than beggars. Here, then, that paradox truly applies, by which the wiser philosophers of old said that only the wise man is rich. For "the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God," and so no one is wise except the one whose wisdom is Christ. Whoever has him is certain of God's grace and goodness, and therefore content with his lot, desires nothing further. So let us aspire to these riches, brothers, and let it not be hard for us in the meantime, while we pursue them, to bear the poverty that the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, has consecrated for us by his example and merit. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMI Et sententiam in hac re meam edo. Nam hoc vobis conducit, qui non solum facere, sed etiam velle ante cepistis anno superiore. At nunc etiā illud ipsum facere absoluite, vt sicut adfuit promptum illud velle, ita etiā adsit ipsum perficere ex eo quod habetis. Etenim si prius adsit promptus animus, aliquis acceptus est pro eo quod habet, non pro eo quod non habet. Non enim vt alijs relaxatio sit, vobis autem oppressio: sed pari conditione hoc tempore vestra abundantia illorum defectum [suppleat:] Vt & illorum abundantia vestrum defectum suppleat, vt fiat æquabilitas. Sicut scriptum est: Qui multum collegit, non habuit amplius; & qui paulum, non habuit minus.
units.tr: I also give my opinion on this matter. For this is useful to you, who began a year ago not only to do this but also to will it. But now finish the doing itself, so that just as the ready will was present, so also the completion may be present, out of what you have. For if the ready mind is present first, a gift is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have. The aim is not that others be relieved while you are burdened, but that by equal terms, in this present time, your abundance may supply their lack, so that their abundance may in turn supply your lack, and there may be equality. As it is written: "He who gathered much had nothing over, and he who gathered little had no lack."

units.la: Inter multa vitia, quæ mortalibus ex naturæ nostræ prauitate inhærent, præcipuum fere est philautia. Parit hæc priuati commodi studium, & difficulter admittit ea, quæ huic aliqua ex parte derogare videntur. Et hæc etiam causa est, quòd plerique pauperes fastidiunt, aut saltem negligunt: qui etiam iniquius secum agi putant, si illorum inopiam sua liberalitate subleuare iubeantur. Prodest ergo nos in hac causa diligenter instituì, & rationibus idoneis atq; validis vrgeri, quibus philautiæ malum expugnetur. Extant hæ passim in Scripturis. In Lege certè non solum commendat nobis pauperes Deus, verumetiam rationem præscribit, quam in illis alendis Israelitæ publicè & priuatim obseruare debeant: adhæc promissionibus quoq; amplissimis excitat eos, qui egestatis metu à beneficentia abstinent. Sic etiam Prophetæ in hoc admodum diligentes sunt, & eorum duritiem grauiter accusant, qui egenos inhumanius negligunt. Præ aliis tamen Scripturæ locis conspicitur dignissima est Pauli tractatio, quam duobus hisce Cap. proponit, vt Corinthios hortetur, vt Iudæ fratribus aliqua collecta extraordinaria succurrant. Et quia magna est exemplorum vis, primò Macedones produxit, qui etiamsi magnam suarum facultatum iacturam passi essent, plus tamen fecerant, quàm ab eis honestè petere licuisset. Deinde ipsius Christi exemplum subiecit, quod à nemine contemni potest, qui Christianus dici & haberi volet. At quia noua subinde effugia captat caro nostra, plura adhuc congerit.
units.tr: Among the many vices that cling to mortals from the depravity of our nature, self-love is almost the chief. It gives birth to a zeal for private advantage, and it admits with difficulty those things which seem in some way to detract from this. And this is also the reason why most people despise the poor, or at least neglect them, and think they are treated too unfairly if they are ordered to relieve their poverty by their own generosity. It is therefore profitable for us to be carefully instructed in this matter, and to be urged with suitable and strong reasons, by which the evil of self-love may be overcome. These are found everywhere in the Scriptures. In the Law God not only commends the poor to us, but also prescribes the manner in which the Israelites ought to observe the support of them, both publicly and privately. Besides, he also rouses with the most ample promises those who abstain from beneficence through fear of want. The Prophets too are very diligent in this, and grievously accuse the hardness of those who negligently and inhumanly neglect the needy. Yet among the other passages of Scripture, Paul's treatment is the most worthy to be noted, which he sets forth in these two chapters, to exhort the Corinthians to help the brethren in Judea with an extraordinary collection. And because the force of examples is great, he first brought forward the Macedonians, who, although they had suffered a great loss of their resources, had nevertheless done more than it would have been honourable to ask of them. Then he set before them the example of Christ himself, which no one who wishes to be called and considered a Christian can despise. But because our flesh constantly seeks new escapes, he piles up still more.

units.la: Kursus autem præfatiunculam interserit, qua cauet, ne quid imperiosius mandare videatur. Sententiam in hac re meam edo, inquit. Ita vero loquitur, quia (vt modo diximus) de extraordinaria collecta agebatur, qua exteris deberent subuenire. Quòd si de Corinthiacæ Ecclesiæ pauperibus sermo fuisset, procul dubio cū authoritate Apostolica illis mandasset quod Deus olim in Lege statuit, & quod Christus confirmauit, quodq; apud omnes Ecclesias iam erat receptum. Quia autem nusquam expresso Dei præcepto iubemur eleemosynas ad exteros mittere, qui longioribus locorum interuallis à nobis distant, noluit Apostolus ex imperio mandare, sed quid ipsi in hac causa honestum, pium & vtile videatur, ingenuè proponit. Est ergo hoc nouum modestiæ Apostolicæ exemplum. Meminerunt hi semper se Christi serui esse, huius autem domum simul atq; sponsam esse Ecclesiam. Vt ergo fidelis seruus in heri domo nihil temere constituit, nihil mutat aut innouat, multo minus autem in ipsam heram sibi ius sumit, fideliter autem monet quid sibi videatur agendum esse, si quis nouus casus incidat: Ita Apostoli olim fecerunt: quorum vestigijs si insistere voluissent successores, sua Ecclesi libertas salua mansisset, et minus haberemus superstitionum, plus autem pietatis syncerioris.
units.tr: Paul, however, prefaces his words with a short remark, to guard against seeming to issue a command in an imperious manner. "I give my opinion in this matter," he says. He speaks this way because, as we have just said, the matter concerned an extraordinary collection to help outsiders. Had he been speaking of the poor of the Corinthian Church, he would undoubtedly have commanded them with apostolic authority what God had long since established in the Law, what Christ had confirmed, and what was already accepted in all the churches. But since we are nowhere commanded by an express precept of God to send alms to foreigners who live far from us across long distances, the Apostle chose not to command by authority. Instead he sets out frankly what seems to himself honourable, godly and useful in this case. This, then, is a new example of apostolic modesty. The apostles always remembered that they were servants of Christ, and that the Church is at once his house and his bride. Just as a faithful servant in his master's house decides nothing rashly, changes or alters nothing, and much less claims any right over the mistress herself, but faithfully advises what seems to him must be done should some new case arise, so the apostles acted in former times. If their successors had been willing to follow in their footsteps, the liberty of the Church would have remained safe, and we would have fewer superstitions and more of a purer piety.

units.la: Interim tenere hoc conuenit, non temere contemni debere Apostolorum consilia atq; sententias, quasi inter res medias & indifferentes numerentur. Adfuit enim illis consultor ille fidelissimus, quem Christus promiserat, Spiritus Veritatis nimirum, qui eos falli non est passus. Si quid ergo pro suorum temporum ratione constituerunt, attentius nos videre oportet, num eadem sit nostri seculi conditio, & si omnia conueniant, tunc illorum consilijs atq; placitis, perinde vt diserto Dei oraculo obedire debemus. Id vero si in præsenti causa obseruetur, mox patebit, ad nos non minus quàm ad Corinthios pertinere, quæ Paulus istis consulit. Vt enim tunc aliæ Ecclesiæ alijs magis premebantur: ita hodie, quando aliæ sub principibus veræ Christianis, aliæ sub moderatioris ingenij magistratibus, aliæ sub crudelissimis tyrānis degunt. Vt ergo tunc quæ otiò & pace liberius fruebantur, & alijs opulentiores erant, pauperioribus debuerunt subuenire: Ita hodie fiat oportet, quando perpetua est & semper rata erit mutuæ dilectionis lex, qua Christus suos discipulos constrinxit. Similiter, vt olim Apostoli errones ignauos atq; ἀτάκτως, id est, inordinatè viuentes in ordinem redigere & coercere iusserunt, ne Ecclesijs oneri & dedecori essent: ita hoc ipsum hodie necessario fieri debet, quando maior est, quàm vllis seculis fuerit, morum licentia. Sed audiamus rationes, quibus Corinthios Paulus vrget.
units.tr: Meanwhile, it is fitting to hold to this: the counsels and opinions of the apostles must not be lightly despised, as if they were counted among indifferent and neutral matters. For that most faithful counsellor whom Christ had promised, the Spirit of truth, was with them, and he did not allow them to err. So if they decided something in accordance with the circumstances of their own times, we ought to look more carefully whether the condition of our own age is the same. If everything agrees, then we must obey their counsels and decisions just as we would obey a clear oracle of God. Indeed, if this is observed in the present case, it will soon become plain that what Paul advises here pertains to us no less than to the Corinthians. For just as in that time some churches were more oppressed than others, so today some live under princes who are true Christians, others under magistrates of a milder disposition, and others under the most cruel tyrants. Therefore, just as those who then enjoyed greater leisure and peace more freely, and were richer than others, ought to have helped the poorer, so it must be done today, since the law of mutual love, by which Christ bound his disciples, is perpetual and will always remain in force. Similarly, just as the apostles of old ordered idle and disorderly people, that is, those living in an unruly and disorderly way, to be brought back into order and restrained, so that they would not be a burden and a disgrace to the churches, this same thing must necessarily be done today, since the licence of morals is greater than it has been in any age. But let us hear the reasons by which Paul urges the Corinthians.

units.la: Prima est ab vtili. Nam hoc vobis conducit, ait. Ab ea autem orditur consultò, eò quòd in omni deliberatione pleriq; emolumentum ante omnia spectare solent, in eo autem falluntur, quòd quid reuera vtile sit, non semper vident, imò non raro quod noxium & pernitiosum est eligunt, dum inter vtile & honestum non probè distinguunt. Solet hoc ipsum in præsenti causa multis accidere: qui dum eleemosynas facere debent, hoc vnum spectant, quantum ex suo aceruo decessuru sit, & ideo non modò vtilitate nullam videre possunt, sed insuper damnum luculentum se accepturos esse arbitrantur, & ita eius metu se absterreri sinunt, quò minus faciant, quod sui erat officij. Vt ergo istis occurrat Paulus, simpliciter & absq; omni exceptione hoc conducere pronuntiat. Ratio huius dicti in promptu est: Quia Christus in suas rationes ascribit ea, quæ in pauperes conferuntur. Quod olim sapientissimus ille Solomon intelligens, eos Domino fœnerari dicebat, qui sua pauperibus distribuunt. Quid, quod idem, Christo teste, thesaurum sibi ipsis in cœlo recondunt, & amicos sibi parant fidelissimos, qui illos olim ad se in tabernacula æterna recipiant? Olim quidè ethnicorum sapientes hanc quoq; vtilitatem beneficentiæ coniunctam esse viderunt, quòd extra omne periculū sunt ea, quæ aliis erogauimus, adeò vt eorum causa nos porrò neq; metu, neq; solicitudine discrutiari oporteat, retributione verò ex illis sperare possimus, quos nostra liberalitate iuuimus. Sed quia homines pleruq; ingrati sunt, & benefactores suos fallunt, Christiani longius prospicere debent: In ipsum Deum videlicet, qui remunerator est fidelis, & multas habet remunerationis rationes, quibus hominum ingratitudinem farciat. Itaq; carnis nostræ philautiæ, quæ nos tenaciores facere solet, semper Paulinum hoc opponamus, non posse quæstuosiorem institui opum huius seculi dispensationem, quàm qua & homines & Deum nobis obstringimus.
units.tr: The first is drawn from what is useful. "For this is to your advantage," he says. He begins with this deliberately, because in every decision most people habitually look above all to their own gain. Yet they are mistaken in this, for they do not always see what is truly useful; indeed they often choose what is harmful and destructive, because they do not properly distinguish between the useful and the honourable. This very thing happens to many in the present matter. When they ought to give alms, they look only at this one thing: how much will be taken from their heap. Therefore they not only cannot see any advantage, but they even think they will suffer a plain loss, and so they allow themselves to be frightened by that fear from doing what belongs to their duty. So that Paul may meet such people, he declares plainly and without any exception that this is advantageous. The reason for this statement is ready to hand: Christ counts to his own account whatever is given to the poor. Wise Solomon, understanding this, said that those who distribute their goods to the poor lend to the Lord. And what of the fact that, by Christ's testimony, such people lay up for themselves a treasure in heaven, and make for themselves most faithful friends who will one day receive them into the everlasting tabernacles? The wise men of the heathen indeed saw this advantage too in beneficence: that what we have given to others is beyond all danger, so that we need not be racked by fear or anxiety on its account, and we may hope for a return from those whom we have helped by our generosity. But since most men are ungrateful and deceive their benefactors, Christians ought to look further ahead: namely to God himself, who is a faithful rewarder and has many ways of rewarding by which he makes up for human ingratitude. Therefore let us always set this Pauline saying against the self-love of our flesh, which is wont to make us more grasping: the management of worldly goods cannot be arranged more profitably than by a way in which we bind both men and God to ourselves.

units.la: Altera ratio ab honesto est, qua quòd de vtili dixerat, diserte ad Corinthios restringit, vt hoc ipsis imprimis vtile fore ostendat: quia ipsi non solùm facere verumetiam velle iam ante cœperint anno superiore: Nam vt in priori epist. audiuimus, de eadem re ad illos scripserat, & Titum quoq; miserat, qui opus istud pulcherrimum vrgeret. Et vt ex his verbis colligi potest, mox manum admoliri cœperant, & non modò contribuerant aliquid, verumetiam animi voluntatem conceperant bonam & propensam. Ideo dicit: Cœpistis iam ante nō solum facere verumetiā velle. Quæ locutio huic causæ proprie conuenit: Quia multa faciunt homines non volentes, quando aut coguntur vi aliqua, aut saltem pudore mouentur. At quæ ita coferuntur eleemosynæ, Deo placere non possunt, qui (vt suo loco audiemus) hilarem datorem requirit. Hoc ergo in Corinthijs laudat Apostolus, quòd vltroneo benefaciendi studio accensi opus istud inchoauerint. Quia autem zelus iste subitus (vt fieri solet) cito deferbuerat, remissiores factı, quod bene cœperant intermiserunt. Id ergo in mentem illis reuocat, vt intelligant, quàm turpe hoc ipsis futurum sit, si non perficiant, quod factô opus esse iampridem intellexerint. Ideo infert: At nunc etiam illud ipsum facere absoluite. Nec enim sufficit voluntas bona, si perficiendi facultas adsit.
units.tr: The second reason is from what is honourable, which, having said what is useful, he expressly restricts to the Corinthians, to show that this will be especially useful to them: for they had not only begun to do this but to want to, already the year before. For, as we heard in the earlier letter, he had written to them about this same matter, and had also sent Titus, who was to press on this most excellent work. And, as may be gathered from these words, they had soon begun to lay hands to it, and not only had contributed something but had also conceived a good and ready will. So he says: "You began before, not only to do, but also to be willing." This expression fits this case well, because people often do things unwillingly, when they are either compelled by some force or at least moved by shame. But alms given in such a way cannot please God, who (as we shall hear in its place) requires a cheerful giver. Therefore the Apostle praises this in the Corinthians: that, kindled by a zeal to do good of their own accord, they had begun the work. But because that sudden zeal (as usually happens) had quickly cooled, they became more lax and abandoned what they had well begun. So he calls this to their minds, so that they may understand how shameful it will be for them if they do not finish what they have already recognised needed doing. Hence he adds: "But now also finish the doing of it." For a good will is not enough, if the ability to bring it to completion is present.

units.la: Debet hoc loco obseruari carnis ingenium. Reliquæ sunt in nobis aliquæ notitiæ honesti & boni ex naturæ Lege, quam omnium cordibus inscriptam esse Paulus ad Romanos docet. Hæsi vel per Dei Verbum, vel aliqua alia ratione efficacius excitentur, mox ad opus accingimur, & multos videre est, qui tunc magno cum conatu res pulcherrimas aggrediantur. At quia maior in nobis est innatæ vitiositatis vis, nòn durabilis esse potest zelus iste, sed vt flamma ex stipulis aut aridioribus sarmentis subitò in altum emicat, mox autem euanescit, eò quod nulla solidiori aut pinguiori materia foueatur: ita illic etiam fieri solet. Exempla huius impetus videre est in Ecclesiarū reformationibus, quando pleriq; modum quoq; excedūt, & importunius multa faciunt, quæ si prudentia & moderatio grauis adhiberetur, maiori cum fructu perfici poterant: at ijdem fere alijs languidiores fiunt, ubi primus ille animi motus deferbuit. Idem in pœnitentia quoq; solet fieri, si quæ propter imminens aliquod periculum publica authoritate instituitur. Nam hic quoq; multorum studia feruent, qui ut primum periculi metus euanuit, ad priorem vitæ licentiam revertun tur, sicuti in Niniuitis, & hodie in multis horum similibus esse videre. Quid ergo de illis spere- mus, qui inviti ad rem aliquam accedunt? Hi ad primam periculi alicuius suspicionem pedem re- ferunt, aut spe commodi privati oblata, vel anteactorum recordatione moti, cum Lothi uxore a tergo respiciunt. Meminerimus ergo non satis esse bene coepisse, nisi in finem usq; perseueremus: ideoq; stimulis quoq; opus esse, quos & ipsi nobis adhibere, & si ab alijs admonentur, patienter fer- re debemus. Miseri & stulti nimium sunt, qui hos superuacaneos esse putant. Nam si seipsos nos- sent, facile videret, nullam diligentiam, quæ nobis excitandis adhibetur, nimiam esse posse. Et quid hodie nimium dicetur, quando paucissimi sunt, qui in deploratissima scelerum licentia adduci possint, ut de reformatione facienda seriò cogitare incipiant?
units.tr: Here the nature of the flesh ought to be observed. There remain in us some notions of what is honourable and good, from the Law of nature, which Paul teaches in the Letter to the Romans is written in the hearts of all. When these are stirred up more effectively, whether by the Word of God or by some other means, we immediately set ourselves to the work, and one may see many who then undertake the finest things with great effort. But because the power of our innate wickedness is greater in us, this zeal cannot last; like a flame that from straw or drier twigs suddenly shoots up high and then soon vanishes, because it is not fed by any more solid or richer matter, so it is also wont to happen there. Examples of this impulse are to be seen in the reformations of churches, when many go beyond the measure and do many things too eagerly, which could have been accomplished with greater fruit if serious prudence and moderation had been applied; yet the same men often become more sluggish once that first movement of the mind has cooled. The same is usually the case with repentance too, when it is undertaken by public authority because of some impending danger. For here too the zeal of many burns hot, but as soon as the fear of danger has vanished, they return to their former licence of life, as among the Ninevites, and as one may see today in many similar cases. What then should we hope for from those who approach some matter unwillingly? At the first suspicion of any danger they draw back their foot, or, moved by the hope of some private advantage offered, or by recollection of what was past, they look back like Lot's wife. Let us remember, therefore, that it is not enough to have begun well unless we persevere to the end; and so there is need of spurs as well, which we ourselves ought to apply, and which we should patiently bear when others admonish us. They are too wretched and foolish who think these are superfluous. For if they knew themselves, they would easily see that no diligence applied to stirring us up can be excessive. And what can be called excessive today, when there are very few who can be brought, amid the most desperate licence of sins, to begin seriously to think about making a reformation?

units.la: Sequitur in Pauli verbis tertia ratio à facili: Sicut adfuit promptum illud velle, ita etiam adsit ipsum perficere ex eo quod habetis, &c. Id est, quantum facultates vestræ ferunt, tantum facite. Quasi dicat: Si quæcunq; habetis, iuberemini in commune deponere, aut alijs largiri, esset aliqua hoc detrectandi occasio in speciem, quàmuis ne tunc quidem de Dei iustitia possetis conqueri. Qui enim omnia dedit, is pro suo in nos iure omnia potest repetere, vel etiam inuitus eripere, ut Iobus olim dixit. At non eo iure rigidius in nos ille utitur, neq; aliud petit, quàm ut ex eo quod habetis, pars aliqua egenis in Iudæa fratribus decidatur. Id vero factu facillimum est, neq; causam quiritandi habetis aliquam. Et ut magis moveat, diligentius hoc expolit: Etenim si prius adsit promptus animus, aliquis acceptus est pro eo quod habet, non pro eo quod non habet, id est, Quicquid pro tuarum facultatum modulo dederis, id Deus gratum habebit, qui non quantum detur respicit, sed quo animo detur, qui si recte affectus fuerit, procul dubio faciet, quantum facultates vniuscuiusq; ferre possunt.
units.tr: Next comes Paul's third reason, drawn from what is easy: "As there was first the ready will, so let there also be the completion out of what you have," and so on. That is: do as much as your means allow. As if he were saying: even if you were ordered to lay everything down in common, or to give it to others, there might seem to be some pretext for refusing, though even then you could not complain of God's justice. For he who gave all things may, by his right over us, reclaim all things, or even take them away against our will, as Job once said. Yet God does not use that right more harshly against us, and he asks only that some part of what you have be set aside for the needy brothers in Judea. This is very easy to do, and you have no cause for complaint. To move them more, Paul expresses it more carefully: "For if the willing mind is present first, it is accepted according to what one has, not according to what one does not have." That is, whatever you give according to the measure of your means, God will count as pleasing, for he looks not at how much is given but at the mind in which it is given. If that mind is rightly disposed, he will undoubtedly accept as much as each person's means can bear.

units.la: Hæc ut omnem prætextum duris & immitibus eripiunt, ita eos quoq; confutant, qui cum nihil aut certè non multum habuerint, per illicitas artes & modos iniquissimos diuites facti, eleemosynarum magnificentia & liberalitate Deum placare instituunt. Falluntur hi vehementer sua ratione. Etenim Deus eleemosynas ex eo quod quisq; habet æstimat. Habere autem hic dicitur pro eo quod est, iusto & legitimo titulo possidere, quod ex illius benedictione datum est. Ex eo beneficentia exerceri debet, ut Thobias olim filium suum monuit. Quod autem vel rapinis, vel furto, vel vsuris iniquis partum est, id nemo iustè habet, sed ut raptor & iniquus rei alienæ vsurpator, qui totum illud diuinis legibus vel duplum vel quadruplum, aut etiam quintuplum restituere tenetur: quod Zachæum quoq; intellexisse, Euangelica historia docet. Si qui ergo ex eo eleemosynas faciunt, ij aliena bona in vsum quoq; alienum transferunt, & tantum non Deum suarum rapinarum atq; furtorum socium facere conantur. Id vero illi gratum & acceptum esse non potest, qui preces quoque eorum abominatur, qui manus sanguine pollutas ad ipsum attollunt. Et quis non tales eius similes dicat, qui patrem spolijs filij ab ipsis occisi placare velit? Dei vox est: Misericordiam volo, & non sacrificium. At quæ illa misericordia est, si alijs ad inopiam extremam redatis, tu ex illorum bonis voluptueris, vel etiam inani pietatis fuco te ostentes?
units.tr: These words snatch from the hard and merciless every pretext, and they also refute those who, having had nothing, or certainly not much, have become rich by unlawful arts and the most unjust means, and then set out to placate God by the lavishness and liberality of their alms. These men are gravely mistaken in their reasoning. For God judges alms by what each person has. "Has" here means to possess by a just and lawful title what has been given by his blessing, and it is from this that beneficence ought to be exercised, as Tobit once advised his son. But whatever has been gained by robbery, theft or unjust usury, no one rightly has. Rather, the robber and unjust usurper of another's property is bound by the divine laws to restore the whole of it, double, fourfold or even fivefold, as the Gospel history teaches that Zacchaeus also understood. If therefore people make alms from such things, they transfer other people's goods to another's use, and they try almost to make God a partner in their robberies and thefts. This cannot be pleasing and acceptable to him, who abhors even the prayers of those who lift up hands polluted with blood. And who would not call such people like someone who wishes to placate a father with the spoils of a son whom they have themselves killed? The voice of God says: "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice." But what kind of mercy is it, if you reduce others to extreme want, and then revel in their goods, or display yourself with the empty paint of piety?

units.la: Quia vero multi obijciunt: An vero æquum est, ut ego mea alijs elargiri iubear, ut ipsi quidem bene & comodè viuant, ego vero cum inopia conflictor? Respondet horum querelis Apostolus, & quod modo dixerat, diligentius exponit: Non enim (inquit) hoc agitur, ut alijs relaxatio fit, vobis autem oppressio siue afflictio. Qui enim nos pauperum curam habere iubet Deus, idem ut nostris quoq; prospiciamus, mandat. Et facit ad huius loci confirmationem, quòd alibi infidelibus ac ethnicis deteriores dicit eos, qui nulla suorum cura tanguntur, neq; necessitatibus eorum prouident. Ita vero rursus omnem quiritandi occasionem ijs eripit, qui iniquius secum agi dicunt, si sua in aliorum vsus erogare iubeantur. Quid enim queratur is, cui salua manet suarum facultatum possessio, & cui retinere licet, quantum ipsi ad vitam comodè & honestè agendam sufficiat? At simul ignauos fucos hoc Pauli dictum iugulat, qui sub voluntariæ paupertatis prætextu vitam inertem atq; otiosam viuunt, & relaxatione siue immunitate ab omnibus oneribus fruuntur, alijs interim cum egestate & fame luctantibus, ex quorum laboribus ipsi voluptuantur. Sunt bi Monachi & Sacrifici, de quibus verissimè illud dixeris, quod in Psalmo habetur: Pingues sunt & præualidi, in labore hominũ non sunt, & malorum quibus alij affliguntur, immunes sunt. Quibus non immerito adnumeraueris nostros, qui ex paupertate quæstum sibi faciunt, & ostiatim atq; à quibusuis obuijs impudenter petunt, & ne ab ijs quidem abstinent, qui ipsis pauperiores vi-tam vix duro manuum suarum labore sustentant. Sunt vtriq; ex ἀτάκτων numero, & digni qui disciplina seueriori atq; Christianis hominibus digna coerceantur.
units.tr: But since many object: "Is it really fair that I should be ordered to give my own to others, so that they may live well and comfortably, while I struggle with want?" the Apostle answers their complaints and explains more carefully what he has just said: "For this is not meant," he says, "that others should be relieved while you are burdened or afflicted." For God, who commands us to care for the poor, also commands us to provide for our own. This also supports the point, since elsewhere he says that those who are untouched by the care of their own and do not provide for their needs are worse than unbelievers and heathens. In this way again he takes away every occasion for complaint from those who say they are treated too unfairly if they are ordered to spend their own for the use of others. For what can someone complain of, whose possession of his means remains safe, and who may keep as much as suffices for living comfortably and honourably? At the same time, this saying of Paul strangles the idle drones, who under the pretext of voluntary poverty live an inert and leisured life, enjoy relief and immunity from all burdens, while others meanwhile struggle with want and hunger, and they revel in their labours. These are the monks and priests, of whom one could most truly say what is written in the Psalm: "They are fat and strong; they are not in the labour of men, and they are free from the troubles with which others are afflicted." Not undeservedly one may add to them our own people, who make a gain out of poverty and beg shamelessly from door to door and from everyone they meet, and do not even spare those who sustain themselves by the hard labour of their hands, though they are poorer than the beggars themselves. Both sorts belong to the number of the "disorderly" [ataktōn], and deserve to be restrained by a stricter discipline, fitting for Christian people.

units.la: Sed audiamus quartam Pauli rationem, quam his verbis proponit: Pari conditione hoc tem-pore vestra abundantia illorum defectum suppleat, vt & illorum abundantia vestrum defectum suppleat, vt fiat æquabilitas. Quem locum pleriq; interpretum de spiritualium bonorũ remunera-tione exposuerũt, quasi sensus sit, si fore, vt si ipsi fratres in Iudæa laborantes pecuniario subsidio iu-uent, hi vicißim ipsis bona spiritualia communicent, quæ apud illos sint abundantiora. Sed est hic sensus à Pauli instituto alienissimus. Totus enim in eo est, vt Iudæos fratres Corinthijs cõciliet. At quàm obsecro his iniuriam maiorem facere, quomodo item eosdem magis offendere poterat, quàm si quoad fidem & dona Spiritus Sancti egenos esse dixisset, quos aliorũ fide & pietate sub-leuari oporteat? Deinde sibi ipsi contradixisset Apostolus, cùm alibi Corinthios à donorũ illorum abundantia magnificè commendauerit, & ab initio statim huius tractationis hoc argumento erga eos sit vsus, ne qui in alijs omnibus excellant, in hac causa se ab alijs vinci patiantur. Adhæc pu-gnat hoc cum religionis Christianæ principijs, quæ vnumquenq; sua fide viuere & seruari docent. Deniq; ex hoc fonte Monachi opera supererogationis deriuarũt, quibus nihil magis impium, ipsis autem nullum aucupium quæstuosius fingi poterat. Nihil ergo huius Paulo in mentem venit, & verba ipsa nobis alium sensum monstrant. Nam primo de præsentis temporis necessitate loquitur, cuius nunc rationem habere debeant Corinthij, vt pote homines opulenti & in pace bona agentes: & ostendit fore, vt aliquando similem beneficentiã sentiant eorum qui nunc ipsorum liberalitate subleuentur. Itaq; verbis hisce argumentum subest à necessario, quo docet, necessitatem ipsam hoc monere, vt qui præ alijs abundant, aliorum inopiæ succurrant, eò quòd non eadem semper sit for-tunæ facies, sed vicißitudine quadam res humanæ itidem mutentur: Posse ergo fieri, vt qui nunc Macedonum & Corinthiorum opem requirunt, aliquando commodius agant, & vicißim ipsis tunc laborantibus suppetias ferre possint.
units.tr: But let us hear Paul's fourth reason, which he sets out in these words: "In the present time, on equal terms, your abundance should supply their lack, so that their abundance may supply your lack, and there may be equality." Most interpreters have explained this passage of the reward of spiritual goods, as if the sense were that, if the brothers in Judea, who are labouring, help them with financial support, these in turn should share with them spiritual goods, which are more abundant among them. But this sense is most alien to Paul's purpose. For his whole aim is to win the Judean brothers over to the Corinthians. But, I beg you, how could he do them a greater wrong, or offend them more, than by saying that they were lacking in faith and the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and needed to be supported by the faith and piety of others? Moreover, the Apostle would have contradicted himself, since elsewhere he praises the Corinthians magnificently for the abundance of those gifts, and from the very beginning of this discussion he has used this argument with them: that they, who excel in all other things, should not allow themselves to be surpassed by others in this matter. Besides, this fights against the principles of the Christian religion, which teach that each person lives and is saved by his own faith. Finally, from this source the monks derived their works of supererogation, than which nothing could be more impious, though for them no more profitable snare could be devised. Nothing of this therefore came into Paul's mind, and the words themselves show us another sense. For first he speaks of the necessity of the present time, which the Corinthians must now take into account, as men who are wealthy and enjoying good peace. And he shows that it will happen that at some time they will feel a similar beneficence from those who are now relieved by their liberality. So there lies in these words an argument from necessity, by which he teaches that necessity itself advises those who abound beyond others to help the want of others, because the face of fortune is not always the same, but human affairs change by a certain vicissitude. Thus it can happen that those who now seek the help of the Judeans will at some time fare better, and in turn will be able to bring aid to them when they are in trouble.

units.la: Debet igitur diligenter considerari rerum humanarum vicißitudo, quæ vt in alijs rebus, ita in hac causa multùm nos iuuare potest, si recte cognoscatur. Plerofq; enim inflatos & confiden-tiores facit, quòd se opibus abunde instructos esse sibijpsis persuaserunt, qui nullius opera siue au-xilio opus habeant. Quæ persuasio eosdem ergà egenos quoq; inhumaniores reddit, vt absq; omni commiseratione illorum inopiam spectare possint. Quid, quòd multi stolidam hanc confidentiam verbis quoq; indignißimis palàm produnt. Sed meminerimus, nihil in humanis stabile & perpe-tuum esse, & Dei hoc institutum esse, vt alij aliorum opera indigeant. Quod quia multi non agno-scunt, iusto illius iudicio frequenter fit, vt qui in summo felicitatis culmine extra omnem teli ia-ctum constituti videbantur, subito casu ruant, & vilißimorum hominum auxilia implorent. Quid olim florentius, beatius & opulentius fuit terra Ægyptiaca? Quis Pharaone Rege felicior? At nisi Josephi seruuli & captiui prudentia adiutus fuisset, totus cum suo regno famis tempore periisset. Similis Nabuchodonoȝoris conditio fuit, qui cùm paulò ante debellata Iudæorũ gente & euersa vrbe cum templo, Danielem captiuum abduxisset, postea eodem non minus necessario quàm fido consultore vsus est. Quid Xerxes, qui cum maria nauibus vt ponte strauisset, piscato-riæ scaphæ beneficio seruatus est? Semper ergo cogitemus, ab hominibus nihil humanum alienum, nihil autè tam humanum esse, quàm incertis casibus iactari. Itaq; æquabilitati omnes studere di-scant, non quidem ei, quæ confusam & iniquissimam omnium bonorum communionem inducat, sed ei, de qua in præsenti Paulus agit. Inter prophanos & à Christo alienos confusio illa & inæqua-bilitas illa cernitur, vt alijs splendidè ac lautè epulantibus alij esuriant: alij item vestitu molli & sumptuoso superbiant, alij nudi æstu aut frigore pereant: alij iubilent, alij plorent. At Chri-stiani homines, quos Christi Spiritus in vnum corpus redegit, res longè aliter instituere debent: vt nimirũ sanĉta illa συμπαθέια, de qua alibi diximus, afficiantur, & alij aliorum onera in sese recipiant: sicuti Paulus ad Galatas quoq; monet. Accusantur hic nostrorum temporum mores, quando inter eos, qui Christo & Euangelio eius gloriantur, æquabilitas illa rarissima, vel potius nulla est. Imo multi ex aliorum egestate & publica rerum penuria sibi ipsis quæstum faciunt, ut illorum opera gratis abutantur, aut vsuras voraciores faciat: Multi ex bonis Ecclesiæ luxuriantur simul & ditescunt, esurientibus illis, quorum necessitati illa imprimis seruire debebant.
units.tr: The changing course of human affairs must therefore be carefully considered, which, as in other matters, so in this case can greatly help us, if it is rightly understood. For it makes many people puffed up and overconfident, since they have persuaded themselves that they are abundantly provided with wealth and have need of no one's work or help. This persuasion makes them also harsher toward the needy, so that they can look upon their want without any pity. What more? Many openly betray this foolish confidence even in the most unworthy words. But let us remember that nothing in human affairs is stable and everlasting, and that it is God's ordinance that some people need the work of others. Because many do not acknowledge this, it often happens by his just judgment that those who seemed placed on the highest peak of happiness, beyond every range of missiles, suddenly fall and implore the help of the basest men. What was more flourishing, blessed and wealthy in former times than the land of Egypt? Who was happier than King Pharaoh? Yet unless he had been aided by the prudence of Joseph, a slave and captive, he would have perished with his kingdom in the time of famine. Similar was the condition of Nebuchadnezzar, who, shortly after he had subdued the nation of the Jews and overthrown the city with its temple, led Daniel away as a captive, and afterwards used the same man as a counsellor, no less necessary than faithful. What of Xerxes, who, when he had bridged the seas with ships, was saved by the help of a fishing boat? Let us therefore always consider that nothing human is alien to men, and nothing is so human as to be tossed about by uncertain chances. Let all learn, then, to strive for equality, not that kind which brings in a confused and most unjust sharing of all goods, but that of which Paul is speaking here. Among the profane and those alienated from Christ, that confusion and that inequality can be seen: while some feast splendidly and luxuriously, others go hungry; some swell with soft and costly clothing, others perish naked from heat or cold; some rejoice, others weep. But Christians, whom the Spirit of Christ has brought into one body, ought to order things quite otherwise: namely, that they be moved by that holy sympatheia [συμπάθεια], of which we have spoken elsewhere, and that they take one another's burdens upon themselves, as Paul also advises the Galatians. Here the morals of our own times are accused, when among those who glory in Christ and his Gospel that equality is very rare, or rather there is none at all. Indeed, many make a profit for themselves from the want of others and from the public scarcity of goods, either misusing others' labour for nothing or making their usury more voracious. Many luxuriate and grow rich from the goods of the Church, while those are starving whose need those goods above all ought to serve.

units.la: Porro quia lucri studio multi inescantur, ut neglecta Dei benedictione, res omnes suo labore & studio confici oportere putent, illis quoq; Paulus occurrit, & anxium illud acquirendi & acquisita seruandi studium prorsus inutile & superuacaneum esse docet. Sicut scriptum est: Qui multum collegit, non habuit amplius: & qui paulum, non habuit minus. Habent autem verba hæc eclipsim, quæ ita farciri poterit: Studeant coaceruandis opibus, quibus ita libet, nihil tamen proficient. Oportet enim æquabilitate illam, de qua modo dixi, inuitis quoq; omnibus aliqua ex parte seruari, ut nimirum vnius abundantia alterius inopiam suppleat. Itaq; vtut seipsos torqueant multi, semper fiet, quod olim factum fuisse scribitur: Qui multum collegit, non habuit amplius, &c. Exstant verba hæc Exo. 16. Cap. vbi dati Mannæ historia describitur. Dabat hoc Deus de cælo quotidie recens absque Israelitarum labore aut industria. Mane autem ad illud colligendum exibant agminatim, & congerebant in aceruos: in quo haud dubie alij alijs agiliores erant & feruentiores. Attamen singulis non nisi suum homer aut sextarius cedebat, nec licebat cuiquam vel plus accipere, vel aliquid in crastinum reseruare. Itaq; reuera in diem (quod dicitur) Israelitæ viuebant. Etenim qui contra Dei mandatum aliquid seruabant, his omne illud in vasis suis computruit & vermes genuit. Fuit hoc ingens Dei beneficium, cuius simile nullum in historijs habetur: cuius inter alia hic vsus esse debebat Israelitis, ut procul relicta solicitudine victus, discerent à solius Dei providentia pendere, neq; vnquam obliuiscerentur, hominem non solo pane viuere, sed omni Verbo, quod exit ab ore Dei, id est, per omnis generis media, quibus Deus vitam nobis seruare statuit. Continet ergo historia hæc vtilem doctrinam de opibus, quæ de omnibus nos admonet, quæ hic nobis cognitu necessaria sunt.
units.tr: Moreover, since many are enticed by the desire for gain, so that, neglecting God's blessing, they think all things must be accomplished by their own labour and effort, Paul meets them too and teaches that this anxious zeal for acquiring and for keeping what is acquired is entirely useless and superfluous. As it is written: "He who gathered much had nothing over, and he who gathered little had no lack." These words have a gap which could be filled thus: let men strive to heap up wealth as they like, yet they will gain nothing. For that equality of which I have just spoken must be kept in some measure even against everyone's will, so that the abundance of one may make up for the want of another. So, however much men torment themselves, what was once written as having happened will always happen: "He who gathered much had nothing over," etc. These words are found in Exodus 16, where the history of the giving of the manna is described. God gave this from heaven every day, fresh, without any labour or industry on the part of the Israelites. In the morning they went out in troops to gather it and heaped it up in piles; in this, no doubt, some were quicker and more eager than others. Yet to each one there fell no more than his omer or measure, nor was anyone allowed to take more or to keep anything over until the morrow. Thus the Israelites truly lived, as the saying goes, from day to day. For those who kept something against God's command, all of it rotted in their vessels and bred worms. This was a great benefit of God, of which there is no like instance in history; among other uses it was meant for the Israelites here, that, having put aside all anxiety about food, they might learn to depend on the providence of God alone, and never forget that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God, that is, by all the means by which God has determined to preserve our life. This history therefore contains a useful teaching about wealth, which warns us of all those things that we need to know here.

units.la: Primò docemur, omnia quæ ad victum faciunt, instar Mannæ esse. Cœlitus enim dantur ex diuinæ prouidentiæ penu siue thesauro. Ipsi enim nudi ex matris vtero nascimur, & vt nihil in mundum inferimus, ita etiam in acquirendo frustra laboramus, nisi sua benedictione Deus labores & curas nostras fructuosas reddat. Notum etenim est illud Psalmi: Nisi Dominus ædificet domum, frustra laborant qui ædificant. Et illud Pauli: Nihil est qui plantat, nihil qui rigat, sed Deus qui dat incrementum. Vt ergo omnia à Deo creantur, ita nobis ex eius solius benedictione obtingunt & salutaria fiunt. Vnde sequitur ab hac omnes pendere, & hanc vnam expectare debere, ne curas & studia sua nimio acquirendi studio præcipitent. Nam qui id faciunt, ij coturnices sibi accersunt, ex quibus aliquantisper delitiantur, sed cum certo suo exitio. Imo ignem domi suæ recondunt, qui tandem omnia ipsorum deuorat. Exemplis hic non opus est, cum quotidie fiant, quæ his possunt fidem facere.
units.tr: First, we are taught that all things which serve for our sustenance are like the manna. For they are given from heaven, out of the store or treasury of divine providence. For we are born naked from our mother's womb, and just as we bring nothing into the world, so too we labour in vain in acquiring, unless God by his blessing makes our labours and cares fruitful. Well known is that saying of the Psalm: "Unless the Lord build the house, they labour in vain who build it." And that of Paul: "Neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase." Therefore, as all things are created by God, so they come to us and become beneficial solely by his blessing. Hence it follows that all depend on this, and ought to wait for this alone, lest they hurry their cares and efforts by an excessive zeal for acquiring. For those who do this summon quails for themselves, with which they delight for a little while, but to their own certain destruction. Indeed they hide fire in their own house, which at last devours everything they have. There is no need for examples here, since they happen every day and can give proof of these things.

units.la: Deinde vsus opum legitimus indicatur, qui nō alius est, quam ut necessitati nostræ seruiant: vt nimirum ex ijs edamus, bibamus, vestiamur & commode habitemus. Etenim præter ista nihil ex illis ad nos redire potest. Atqui natura paucis contenta est, & de singulis istorum dici potest, quod de Sallum sive Ioachaz apud Ieremiam dicitur: Annon pater quoq; tuus edit & bibit, & fecit iudicium & iustitiam, & bene illi erat? Equidem exempla quotidiana docent, comodius ac tutius viuere eos, qui modico contenti sunt, quam qui circa ingentes opum aceruos inter exquisitas dapes & seruorum vndique strepentium cateruas tumultuantur. Quod si quaeras, quid ergo facient de ijs diuites, quæ ipsis superflua sunt? Paulum respondentem audi, qui iubet, ut sua abundantia inopia aliorum suppleant. Nam vt Christus docet, dispensatores constituti sunt, ut æquabilitati studeant, de qua modo est dictum. Quam nisi probè obseruent, epulonis illius & fatui diuitis similes erunt, quorum mores cauere iubet Dominus. Vide Luc. 16. & 12. Cap.
units.tr: Next, the lawful use of wealth is pointed out, which is nothing other than to serve our necessity: namely, that from it we may eat, drink, clothe ourselves and live decently. For beyond these things nothing from them can return to us. Yet nature is content with few things, and of each of these it can be said what is said of Shallum, or Jehoahaz, in Jeremiah: "Did not your father eat and drink, and do judgment and justice, and was it not well with him?" Indeed, everyday experience teaches that those who are content with a modest amount live more comfortably and more securely than those who bustle about among huge heaps of wealth, amid exquisite dishes and troops of slaves shouting on every side. But if you ask, what then will the rich do with those things which are superfluous to them? Listen to Paul answering, who bids them to supply the want of others from their abundance. For, as Christ teaches, they have been appointed stewards, so that they may strive for the equality of which I have just spoken. If they do not observe this well, they will be like that glutton and foolish rich man, whose ways the Lord bids us beware of. See Luke 16 and chapter 12.

units.la: Postremò pœnam quoque adumbrat Mannæ historia, quæ omnibus à Deo constituta est, qui per fas & nefas congerunt: Vermes in sinum suum congerunt, qui corda ipsorum arrodant. Adhæc serui diuitiarum fiunt, dum in illis asseruandis cura simul & labore immodico seipsos conficiunt. Et quis enim seruus herum suum, quis iuuenis amatam abs se virginem tam solicitè obseruat, quàm auari thesauros suos asseruare solent? Attamen inutilis est cura ista omnis: quia putrescunt & inutilia fiunt tandem, quæcunq; illi indefessó studio congesserunt. Accedit his, quòd tam ipsi quàm opes malis artibus partæ in Dei conspectu fætent, & ab imminenti interitu ipsos adeò non possunt eripere, vt illum potius accelerent. Exempla, quibus hæc probentur, tam vulgaria sunt, vt si quis ea commemorare velit, dicendi initium citius quàm finem inueniat. Horum itaque singuli memores, à Dei benedictione pendeant, eidem pro acceptis donis grati sint, ijsdem pie ac modestè vtantur, pauperibus item benefaciant, vt tandem cum electis omnibus cœlestis illius thesauri hæredes fiant, quem nobis sanguinis sui pretio acquisiuit æternus Dei Filius IESVS CHRISTVS, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Lastly, the history of the manna also sketches the punishment which God has appointed for all who gather by right and wrong alike: "They gather worms into their bosom, which gnaw their hearts." Besides, they become slaves of riches, while in preserving them they wear themselves out with anxious and excessive labour. And what slave watches over his master, or what young man watches over the maiden he loves, as carefully as misers are wont to guard their treasures? Yet all that care is useless, because whatever they have gathered with tireless zeal at last rots and becomes worthless. To this is added that both they and the wealth gained by wicked arts stink in the sight of God, and so far from being able to rescue themselves from impending destruction, they rather hasten it. The examples by which these things are proved are so commonplace that, if anyone wished to recount them, he would find the beginning of his speech sooner than its end. Therefore, let each of them, mindful of these things, depend on God's blessing, be thankful to him for the gifts received, use them piously and modestly, and do good to the poor as well, so that at last, together with all the elect, they may become heirs of that heavenly treasure which the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, acquired for us at the price of his blood, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXVIII.

units.la: Gratia autem sit Deo, qui cordi Titi indidit idem studium pro vobis: quòd tum exhortationem illam receperit, tum etiam cum studiosior esset, vltrò ad vos abierit. Misimus autem vnà cum eo fratre illum, cuius laus est in Euangelio per omnes Ecclesias. Nec id solùm, sed etiam suffragijs delectus est ab Ecclesijs socius peregrinationis nostræ cum hac gratia quæ à nobis administratur ad ipsius Domini gloriam & promptum animum vestrum comprobandum: Vitantes hoc, ne quis nos vituperet in hac exuberantia, quæ administratur à nobis: vt qui procuremus honesta non solùm coram Domino, sed etiam coram hominibus. Misimus autem cum eis fratrem nostrum, quem sæpe in multis probauimus studiosum, nunc autem multò studiosiorem, ob multam fiduciam de vobis. Quoad ergo Titum, socius meus est, & apud vos adiutor: quoad fratres nostros, legati sunt Ecclesiarum, & gloria Christi. Itaque demonstrationem charitatis vestræ, & nostræ de vobis gloriationis edite in eos, in conspectu Ecclesiarum.
units.tr: But thanks be to God, who put the same earnest care for you into the heart of Titus. He not only accepted our exhortation but, though he was already the more eager of the two, went to you of his own accord. We sent with him the brother whose praise is in the Gospel throughout all the Churches. Nor is that all: he was also chosen by the Churches to travel with us, bringing this grace which is administered by us, to the glory of the Lord himself and to show your ready mind. We do this so that no one may blame us for this abundance administered by us, since we aim at what is honourable not only before the Lord but also before men. We sent with them our brother, whom we have often proved zealous in many matters, and who is now far more zealous because of his great confidence in you. As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow-worker among you; as for our brothers, they are messengers of the Churches and the glory of Christ. Therefore show them, in the sight of the Churches, the proof of your love and of our boasting about you.

units.la: Multis hucusque Paulus Corinthios hortatus est, vt pro subleuanda pauperum in Iudæa fratrum egestate collectam faciant. At quia multi in contribuendo parciores sunt ideo, quòd metuunt, ne quà fraus ab illis fiat, qui collectarum dispensatores constituti sunt: simulq; res ista tunc temporis aliquibus suspecta esse poterat, eò quòd Apostoli & quicunque his ministrabant, homines essent peregrini, & pecuniæ istæ in terras longinquas procul deportandæ essent: postrema huius Cap. parte eos diligenter commendat, quos huius negotij causa ad ipsos mittebat: idq; sic facit, vt simul hic quoque rationes multas & graues congerat, quibus ad liberalitatem excitentur. Fuerunt autem legati tres numero, de quibus singulis ex ordine disserit.
units.tr: Paul has urged the Corinthians many times to make a collection to relieve the poverty of the brothers in Judea. But because many are rather sparing in giving, fearing that some fraud might be committed by those appointed as stewards of the collections, and because the matter could at that time have seemed suspect to some, since the apostles and those who served with them were foreigners and the money had to be carried far away to distant lands, Paul, in the last part of this chapter, carefully commends those whom he was sending for this business. He does so in such a way that he also heaps up many weighty reasons by which they may be stirred to generosity. There were three envoys, and he speaks of each of them in turn.

units.la: Primus est Titus, quem ex præcipuis Pauli discipulis fuisse, ex eius ad illum scripta epistola apparet, & alijs locis multis, in quibus honorificam facit illius mentionem. Hunc autem primum nominat, quòd Corinthijs notus esset, vt qui iam antea quoque apud illos fuerat, sicut Cap. septimo audiuimus: & commendationem eius a gratiarum actione exordiens ait: Gratia autem sit Deo, qui cordi Titi indidit idem studium pro vobis, &c. Est ergo hæc gravis admodum & multiplex commendatio. Primò enim Dei hoc opus esse docet, qui hunc motum in Titi animo excitarit. Ex eo cuius facile erat colligere, non debere eum spernì, quem Deus ipse huic muneri destinauisset. Deinde à Deo excitatum esse probat: quia exhortationem suam, qua apud eum ex Macedonum rogatu (vt supra dictum est) visus fuerat, ratam & acceptam habuerit, adeò vt qui iam ante ardentiori ipsorum studio tenebatur, iam etiam vltrò ad ipsos abierit. Itaque Paulus (quod prouerbio dicitur) sponte currentem insitabat. Quis vero hominis tam amici & propensi officium aspernetur? Nimium certè ingratus & inhumanus esset, qui hoc faceret. Est autem hic imprimis notatu dignum, quòd Apostolus pium hunc in Titi animo motum ad Deum authorem refert. Debet hoc de omnibus ijs intelligi, quaecunque in toto Christianae pietatis negotio bene & rectè facimus. Sumus enim noštrapte natura modis omnibus corruptissimi, neq; ex nobisipsis vel cogitare possumus quod bonum est. Si quid ergo boni volumus aut cupimus, id omne ex Deo est, qui in nobis agit tam velle quàm facere, dum foris quidem per omnis generis media, intus verò animos nostros Spiritus sui suggestionibus excitat. Unde sequitur, omnem bonorum operum, quae à nobis fiunt, gloriam uni Deo in solidum transcribi, nihil autem nostris sive viribus sive meritis tribui debere. Interim officij nostri fuerit, nosmetipsos Deo accommodare, nec loquentem in nobis Spiritum sanctum contemnere, neq; conscientiae dictatis atq; stimulis reluctari.
