Eo enim argumento constat, nos à Deo efficaciter moveri & trahi, si Verbi sui adhortationes non aspernemur, si item voluntarij & strenui simus in opere eius, cui nos videmus esse destinatos. Etenim frustra Dei Spiritu gloriantur, qui Verbum eius contemnunt, & ad pietatis officia desides & ignaui sunt.
units.tr: The first is Titus, who appears from Paul's letter to him, and from many other places where he speaks of him with honour, to have been one of Paul's chief disciples. He names him first because he was known to the Corinthians, having already been among them before, as we heard in the seventh chapter. Beginning his commendation with thanksgiving, he says: "Thanks be to God, who put the same zeal for you into the heart of Titus," and so on. This commendation is therefore very weighty and manifold. First, he teaches that this is God's work, who stirred this impulse in Titus' mind. From this it is easy to conclude that he should not be despised, since God himself had destined him for this office. Next, he shows that Titus was roused by God, because he received and accepted Paul's exhortation, given at the request of the Macedonians (as said above), so that he, who was already held by an more ardent zeal for them, now went to them of his own accord. So Paul, as the proverb goes, was urging on one who was already running willingly. Who would spurn the service of so friendly and well-disposed a man? Anyone who did so would surely be too ungrateful and inhuman. What is especially worth noting here is that the Apostle refers this pious impulse in Titus' mind to God as its author. This must be understood of everything we do well and rightly in the whole business of Christian piety. For by our own nature we are utterly corrupt in every way, nor can we of ourselves even think what is good. If, therefore, we will or desire anything good, all of it comes from God, who works in us both to will and to do: outwardly through all kinds of means, and inwardly by stirring our minds with the suggestions of his Spirit. Hence it follows that the whole glory of the good works done by us is to be ascribed wholly to God alone, and nothing ought to be credited to our strength or merits. Meanwhile, it is our duty to accommodate ourselves to God, not to despise the Holy Spirit speaking within us, nor to struggle against the dictates and goads of conscience. For by this sign it is clear that we are effectually moved and drawn by God: if we do not spurn the exhortations of his Word, and if we are willing and vigorous in the work to which we see ourselves destined. Those who despise his Word and are idle and sluggish in the duties of piety boast of the Spirit of God in vain.

units.la: Deinde debet hoc praesenti causae applicari, ut discamus Dei hoc opus, & eius paternae providentiae argumentum esse, si qui excitantur, qui nobis in aliqua necessitate constitutis benefaciant. Admonent de eo locutiones illae, quae in Scripturis passim occurrunt: Inuenit gratiam in oculis eius. Item: Deus dedit gratiam populo coram Aegyptijs, ut quae petebat, darent eis. Et Nehemias orabat Deum, ut gratiam inueniret apud Regem Artaxerxem, cui causam populi sui commendare statuerat. Et hoc illud ipsum est, quod Christus pollicetur, dicens: Omnis qui reliquerit domus, aut fratres, aut sorores, aut patrem, aut matrem, aut uxorem, aut filios, aut agros, centuplum accipiet, &c. Cuius promissionis ratio est, quòd quorumcunque vult corda ille flectere & movere potest, ut suis ea officia praestent, quae fratres fratribus, parentes filijs, filij parentibus debent. Exempla promissionis huius in Elia habentur, quoad Sareptanam viduam, & in Apostolis, quibus nihil unquam defuit, ex quo omnibus reliquis Christum secuti sunt. Discant ergo omnes pro acceptis beneficijs Deo gratias agere, nec in solo hominum fauore acquiescant, quo multi decipiuntur, eò quòd omnis homo mendax est, & omnes sibi melius esse volunt quàm alteri. Admonet praeterea consideratio ista, ne quid contra Dei praecepta faciamus in hominum gratiam. Potest enim ille facile horum animos mutare, qui nunc hostes sunt, vel etiam eos omnino perdere, aut saltem aliqua ratione obstare, quo minus noceant. At si Dei iram provocemus, quis nos defendet? quis ignemir ae eius restinguet? Horrendum est incidere in manum Dei viuentis. Adhaec consolationis quoque plena est haec doctrina, ne de Dei gratia & animarum salute dubitemus. Qui enim corporibus nostris tam benignè prospicit per eos, qui nobis prius facie & nomine ignoti erant, num animam, quae nostri pars melior est, negligeret? Huius certè beneficium est, quòd Verbi sui praecones dantur, quòd corda nostra aperiuntur, illuminantur, trahuntur. Huic ergo nos totis animis consecremus, neq; eorum minis terreamur, qui Verbum eius nobis eripere conantur. Non patietur ille, ut animae electorum suorum fame pereant.
units.tr: Next, this should be applied to the present case: we learn that when some are stirred up to do us good in our need, this is God's work and a sign of his fatherly providence. Those phrases which occur everywhere in the Scriptures remind us of this: "He found grace in his eyes." Likewise: "God gave the people grace before the Egyptians, so that they gave them what they asked." Nehemiah prayed that God would let him find grace before King Artaxerxes, to whom he had resolved to commend the cause of his people. This is exactly what Christ promises when he says: "Everyone who has left houses, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields, will receive a hundredfold," and so on. The reason for this promise is that he who can bend and move the hearts of whomever he wills can cause them to render those duties which brothers owe to brothers, parents to children, and children to parents. Examples of this promise are found in Elijah, with regard to the widow of Zarephath, and in the Apostles, who never lacked anything from the time they left everything to follow Christ. Let all, therefore, learn to give thanks to God for benefits received, and let them not rest in the mere favour of men, by which many are deceived, since every man is a liar and everyone wishes to be better off than his neighbour. This consideration also warns us not to do anything against God's precepts to win men's favour. For he can easily change the minds of those who are now enemies, or utterly destroy them, or at least in some way prevent them from harming us. But if we provoke God's anger, who will defend us? Who will quench the fire of his wrath? It is a dreadful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. Moreover, this doctrine is full of comfort, so that we need not doubt concerning God's grace and the salvation of our souls. For if he so kindly cares for our bodies through those who were previously unknown to us by face and name, would he neglect the soul, which is the better part of us? Certainly it is his gift that heralds of his Word are given, that our hearts are opened, enlightened, and drawn. Let us therefore devote ourselves to him with all our hearts, and let us not be terrified by the threats of those who try to snatch his Word from us. He will not allow the souls of his elect to perish of hunger.

units.la: Sed alterum quoque legatum videamus, quem ita Paulus commendat: Misimus autem unà cum eo fratrem illum, cuius laus est in Euangelio per omnes Ecclesias. Nomen huius reticet, quia ut hoc posteri scirent, non multum referebat. Corinthijs tamen satis notum fuisse puto, saltem ex fama, quae de illo ubiq; spargebatur. Chrysostomus Barnabam denotari putauit, quem plerique ex nostris sequuntur propter ea quae Lucas in Actis Cap.12. & 13. scripsit. Sed illic eius modò subsidij mentio fit, quod statim post Agabi de fame imminente vaticinium Antiocheni Hierosolymam miserunt per Paulum & Barnabam. Deinde ijdem missi fuisse dicuntur, ut Euangelium gentibus hinc inde praedicarent. Et postea contentione inter ipsos propter Ioannem Marcum orta, alter ab altero discessit, priusquam Corinthij essent ad fidem conuersi, nec demonstrari potest, eos ab eo tempore rursus conuenisse. Itaq; si quem nominare libeat, verisimilior mihi eorum sententia videtur, qui Hieronymum & Sophronium secuti, Lucam intelligi existimant, quem in postrema profectione Hierosolymitana Paulo indiuulsum comitem adhaesisse constat. Nam etsi verba haec nolim simpliciter ad Euangelij historiam à Luca descriptam restringere (quemadmodum illi fecerunt) non dubito tamen singularem fuisse Lucae authoritatem apud Ecclesias gentium, cùm
units.tr: But let us also consider the second envoy, whom Paul commends thus: "We sent with him the brother whose praise is in the Gospel through all the churches." Paul does not name him, since it mattered little to posterity to know it. Yet I think he was sufficiently known to the Corinthians, at least by the reputation that spread about him everywhere. Chrysostom thought Barnabas was meant, and many of our writers follow him because of what Luke wrote in Acts 12 and 13. But there mention is made only of that single relief which the Antiochenes sent to Jerusalem through Paul and Barnabas, immediately after Agabus' prophecy of the coming famine. Then the same men are said to have been sent to preach the Gospel to the Gentiles here and there. Afterwards, a dispute arose between them over John Mark, and one departed from the other before the Corinthians had been converted to the faith; nor can it be shown that they met again from that time. So if one wishes to name someone, the opinion of those who, following Jerome and Sophronius, think Luke is meant seems more likely to me, since it is certain that he was attached to Paul as an inseparable companion on his last journey to Jerusalem. For although I would not wish to restrict these words simply to the Gospel history written by Luke (as they did), I do not doubt that Luke's authority was singular among the churches of the Gentiles, since

units.la: Secundus legatus, Lucas fuisse videtur. quòd Paulo comes esset fidelißimus, tum quòd eundem in Euangelio longè latè propagando diligenter adiuuaret. Hunc certè suum in præsenti magnificè commendat. Primùm ab eo, quòd laus eius apud Ecclesias sit in Euangelio, id est, quòd celebris sit propter operam suam, quam in Euangelij prædicatione Ecclesijs plurimis dederit. Qui in Papatu imagines & earum cultum defendunt, ij Lucam à pictura commendant, & Christi atq; Mariæ Virginis aliorumq; imagines ab illo depictas esse fabulantur, quas hodie adhuc in certis locis monstrant. At professione medicus fuit, Christum verò non coloribus & penicillo in tabulis, sed stilo & calamo in opere suo Euangelico itá depinxit, vt qui talem fide vera recipiunt, ipsi ad eius imaginem, quæ ipsius Dei imago est, reformentur. Illi verò nugatores atrocem viro sanctissimo iniuriam faciunt, quàdo eum superstitionum & idololatriæ authorem fingunt. Nos potius in eius commendatione obseruemus, laudem deberi illis, qui de Ecclesijs bene merentur. Sancti equidem nihil priuatæ laudis aut gloriæ studio faciunt, illa tamen eis, nequaquam negari debet, cùm Spiritus sanctus dixerit, memoriam iusti fore gloriosam & laudabilem. Optimè autem merentur de Ecclesijs, qui Euangelij doctrinam prouehunt, siue id docendo fiat, siue scribendo, siue ministros submittendo, in quo principum quoq; virorum pietas maximè spectatur, qui eam potissimùm ob taufam nutritij Ecclesiæ dicuntur. Nimium autem iniqui & ingrati sunt, qui tales oderunt, & studium eorum calumnijs suis proscindunt.
units.tr: The second legate seems to have been Luke, both because he was Paul's most faithful companion and because he diligently helped him in spreading the Gospel far and wide. Certainly Paul commends him here in lofty terms. First, he commends him because his praise is "in the Gospel among the churches", that is, because he is famous for the work he did in preaching the Gospel to many churches. Those among the Papists who defend images and their worship commend Luke as a painter, and they invent stories that he painted images of Christ, of the Virgin Mary and of others, which they still show today in certain places. But he was a physician by profession. He did not paint Christ with colours and brush on panels, but with stylus and pen in his Gospel work, so that those who receive him thus in true faith are themselves reformed into his image, which is the image of God himself. Those trifling fellows do a monstrous injury to that most holy man when they pretend he was the author of superstitions and idolatry. Rather, let us observe in his commendation that praise is owed to those who deserve well of the Churches. Holy men certainly do nothing for the sake of private praise or glory, yet such praise ought by no means to be denied them, since the Holy Spirit has said that the memory of the righteous will be glorious and praiseworthy. Now those deserve best of the Churches who advance the doctrine of the Gospel, whether by teaching, by writing, or by sending ministers. In this the piety of even princes is chiefly seen, who are said to be the nursing fathers of the Church especially for this reason. But they are exceedingly unjust and ungrateful who hate such men and tear their zeal to pieces with their slanders.

units.la: Altera Lucæ commendatio est, quòd eü Ecclesiarum suffragijs deleētum dicit, vt ipsi sit peregrinationis socius in administranda gratia ista, quæ & Dei gloriam prouebat, deq; animi ipsorum pro pensione ac beneuolentia publicè testetur. Rursus enim Gratiæ vocabulo pecunias intelligit, quæ à piis ex gratuita misericordia in subsidium pauperum conferebantur. Obiter verò commendat hoc institutum, vt Corinthios magis excitet, quando intelligant hoc omne ad gloriam Dei facere, simulq; ad ipsos quoq; gloriam non vulgarem redire. Sunt ergo res coniunctæ, Gloria Dei & Beneficentia in pauperes: quia hac testamur, quanti Deum faciamus, dum ab eo nobis commendatos benignè foueamus & iuuamus. Sed & illis occasionem damus glorificandi Deum: adhæc prophani quoq; homines & à fide alieni eadem occasione in Dei cognitionem adducuntur, dum propter præclara illa Christianorum in pauperes officia de religione & fide Christiana rectius iudicare incipiunt. Caius rei memorabile exemplum habetur apud Euseb. Ecclesiast. hist. lib. 9. Cap. 8.
units.tr: Luke's second commendation is that he is said to have been chosen by the votes of the Churches to be the companion of Paul's journey in administering this grace, which also brought glory to God and publicly bore witness to the goodwill and devotion of their minds. For by the word "grace" Paul again means the money which the pious gave out of free mercy to relieve the poor. In passing, he commends this arrangement so that he may stir the Corinthians up more, since they understand that all this is done for the glory of God and that at the same time no common glory returns to themselves as well. So the things are joined: the glory of God and beneficence towards the poor. For by these we show how highly we esteem God, when we kindly cherish and help those whom he has commended to us. But we also give them an occasion of glorifying God. Moreover, profane men and those alien from the faith are led by the same occasion to the knowledge of God, when on account of those splendid services of the Christians to the poor they begin to judge more rightly about the Christian religion and faith. A memorable example of this matter is found in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 9, chapter 8.

units.la: At nos Pauli modestiam obseruemus, qui non priuato consilio mittit legatos, qui pecuniam istam ab Ecclesijs exigant, sed eos, qui ab Ecclesijs probati & legitimè ad hoc electi erant: id quod χειροτονίας vocabulo innuit. Ita Apostolos quoque fecisse legimus, quando primi Diaconi instituti sunt. Et sanè necessarium est valde, vt publica authoritate muniantur, qui negotium istud tractare debent. Nam nisi id fiat, multi nihil, multi parcius conferunt. Quales verò ad hoc munus deligi debeant, in vltimo prioris Epistolæ Cap. diximus. In præsenti tamen repetendum videtur, tales eligendos esse, qui laudem mereantur ex Euangelio per ipsos promoto. Quis enim illis fidem habeat, qui Euangelium non magni faciunt, aut etiam aperte oderunt? Aut quomodo pauperibus Christi fideles erunt, qui in ipsum Christum sunt perfidi? Deinde scientia rerum accedat, & indu-stria laboriosa, ne vel ignorantia peccent, vel tædio molestiarum, quæ hic deuorandæ sunt, superati succumbant. At hodie plerunq; omnia secus fiunt, & sæpe tanta prouincia ijs creditur, qui non solùm homines ineptissimi, verumetiam Ecclesiæ labes sunt.
units.tr: But let us observe the modesty of Paul, who does not send legates on his own private counsel to demand that money from the Churches, but those who were approved by the Churches and lawfully chosen for this task. This he indicates by the word "elected by show of hands" [χειροτονίας]. We read that the Apostles did the same when the first deacons were instituted. And indeed it is very necessary that those who ought to handle such business be protected by public authority. For unless this is done, many give nothing and many give more sparingly. What sort of men ought to be chosen for this office, we discussed at the end of the chapter of the former Epistle. Yet it seems right to repeat here that such men should be chosen as deserve praise from the Gospel advanced through them. For who would trust those who do not hold the Gospel in high esteem, or even openly hate it? Or how will those be faithful to the poor of Christ who are faithless towards Christ himself? Next, let them have knowledge of affairs and diligent industry, lest they either sin through ignorance or, overcome by the weariness of the troubles they must undergo here, give way. But today almost everything is done the other way round, and often such a great charge is entrusted to those who are not only most unfit men but even blemishes on the Church.

units.la: Poterat autem aliquis morosior obijcere: Quid verò opus est tam multos mittere? Annon sufficeret Titus, qui iam ante nobis probè notus est? Vel quid opus fuit publica Ecclesiarũ authoritate? Num verò hi, de quibus toties gloriaris, tibi non tantum fidei habent, vt negotiũ hoc eibi soli committerent? Etenim scimus quàm auidè omnes calumniandi occasiones arripiant, qui amulatione vruntur: quales multos apud Corinthios fuisse constat. Quapropter præoccupatione vtitur Paulus, qua suspicionem omnem declinat, dum seipsum Ecclesijs huius consilij authorem fuisse fatetur. Vitantes hoc (inquit) ne quis nos vituperet in hac exuberantia, quæ administratur à nobis: vt qui procuremus honesta nõ solum coram Domino, sed etiam coram hominibus. Sensus verborũ est: Ideo sic faciendũ putaui, vt suspiciones vitentur, quæ aliquibus nos reprehendendi occasionē præbere poterant, quasi non pauperum causa nobis cordi sit, sed Ecclesias expilare libeat, vt priuato cõmodo nõ stro consulamus. Et vt de eo diligentius cogitarem, mouit me exuberantia ista, id est, ingens & immensa mensa pecuniarum, quæ ab Ecclesijs conferuntur, summa. Itaq; ne quis ad suspiciones proclivior aliquam in nobis occasionem inveniat, decoro & honestati studere decreuimus non solum coram Domino, qui corda novit, verumetiam coram hominibus, qui externa modò specie ducuntur.
units.tr: Some more peevish person might object: "Why indeed is it necessary to send so many? Would not Titus suffice, who is already well known to us? Or what need was there for the public authority of the Churches? Do these men, of whom you boast so often, not have enough trust in you that they would commit this business to you alone?" For we know how eagerly all who practise rivalry seize every occasion for slander, and such men are known to have been numerous among the Corinthians. Therefore Paul uses a precaution, by which he avoids all suspicion, while confessing that he himself was the author of this plan to the Churches. "Avoiding this," he says, "lest anyone blame us in this abundance which is administered by us, so that we take care of honest things not only before the Lord but also before men." The sense of the words is this: "I thought it should be done in this way so that suspicions might be avoided, which could give some people an occasion to blame us, as if we did not have the cause of the poor at heart, but wished to plunder the Churches in order to look after our own private advantage. And that I might think about this more carefully, that abundance moved me, that is, the huge and immense sum of money that is contributed by the Churches. Therefore, lest anyone who is more prone to suspicion find an occasion against us, we have decided to strive for what is seemly and honourable, not only before the Lord, who knows the hearts, but also before men, who are led only by outward appearance."

units.la: Fuit hæc singularis Pauli modestia, qua in re omnium honestissima vti voluit. Magna erat eius apud omnes Ecclesias authoritas. Donus Spiritus sanctí præ aliis clarus erat. Malignos & suspiciosos calumniatores apostolica potestate coërcere poterat, ut desinerent maledicere. Veruntamen nihil insolenter, nihil ex priuato arbitrio agere voluit. Sciebat enim hominem natura ad malũ proclivem, imprimis vero habendi cupiditatem omnibus innatam, & proinde alienæ pecuniæ tractatio nem periculosam esse: sicut in Iudæ exemplo apparet. Caute ergo & circumspectè agit omnia, ne vel sibiipsi tentationis aliquius grauioris materiam, vel alijs sinistræ suspicionis occasionem præbeat. Vide autem quàm alieni sint ab eius spiritu Pontifices, qui & Ecclesiæ opes impudenter sibi vendicant, vt ijs pro sua libidine abutantur, & in ijs etiam quæ ad Dei cultum & animarum salutem spectant, pro suo arbitrio omnia agunt, & interea vulgi infelicis stoliditatem deridۥent, dum cum Alexandro VI. dicunt: O bonam persuasionem, per quam nos regnamus. Quò cumprimis referri debet, quod in Pontificis inauguratione fieri alibi diximus: quando plus quam Lucianica scurrilitate Scripturis abutuntur, & cum Deo simul atq; Ecclesia ludunt. Vide homil. 20. in Actis Apostolorum.
units.tr: This was the singular modesty of Paul, in which he wished to use the most honourable course. His authority among all the Churches was great. He was more distinguished than others by the gift of the Holy Spirit. He could restrain malicious and suspicious slanderers by apostolic power, so that they would stop speaking evil. Yet he wished to do nothing insolently and nothing by his own private judgement. For he knew that man is by nature prone to evil, and above all that the desire for possessions is innate in all, and that therefore the handling of another's money is dangerous, as appears in the example of Judas. So he acts carefully and circumspectly in everything, lest he provide either himself with the material of some more serious temptation or others with an occasion of unfavourable suspicion. But see how far the Popes are from his spirit, who both shamelessly claim the riches of the Church for themselves, so that they may abuse them at their own pleasure, and in matters which concern the worship of God and the salvation of souls they do everything at their own discretion, and meanwhile mock the stupidity of the unhappy crowd, while they say with Alexander VI: "O what a good persuasion, through which we reign!" To this should especially be referred what we said elsewhere about the inauguration of the Pope, when they abuse the Scriptures with more than Lucianic buffoonery, and make sport of both God and the Church at once. See homily 20 on the Acts of the Apostles.

units.la: Continet autem locus iste generalem doctrinam, decere nimirum Christianos homines, vt non modo conscientiæ suæ rationem habeant apud Deum, verumetiam suæ existimationis apud homines. Præcipuum quidem est & semper necessarium, vt bene nobis conscij innocentiam nostram ipsius Dei testimonio possimus probare, quod Dauidem non semel fecisse legimus, quando iniquis soceri sui calumnijs premebatur. At simul, quoad eius fieri potest, hominibus quoq; testatum facere debemus, nos extra culpam esse: ne videlicet Euangelium & fides, quam profitemur, propter nos male audiant. Et hoc Paulum imprimis mouit, quòd nimirum per latus suum syncerioremEuangelij doctrinam ab improbis peti videret. Et debet nos quoq; excitare mundi nequitia & calumniarum licentia, quam ne sanctissimi quidem homines vnquam effugere potuerunt, quò minus pro beneficijs maximis pessimam gratiam referret. Docent hoc Mosis & Prophetarũ exempla, quos non veriti sunt proditores dicere ij, pro quorum salute ipsi dies noctesq; excubabant. At quid opus est de illis dicere, quando ne Christus quidem immunis fuit à calumnijs, quas atrocissimas sustinuit? Quapropter diligenter cauere oportet, vt à specie etiam mali abstineamus, ne quam calumniandi occasionem aduersarij ex ijs arripiant, quæ nos non quidem male, sed tamen leuiter & imprudenter facimus. Transferant hoc ad se omnes homines, & præ aliis quidem ij, qui in altiori gradu constituti minus latere possunt. Gloriantur hodie multi de fide sua & conscientiæ suæ puritate. Cur verò ijdem illi alios offendunt morum petulantia, ebrietate, libidine et quiduis designandi licentia? Et qualis rogo est conscientia, quæ non terreatur Christi maledictione, qua is horrendum illud Væ omnibus scandalorum authoribus denuntiat?
units.tr: This passage contains a general teaching, namely that it becomes Christian people to take account not only of their conscience before God but also of their reputation before men. Indeed, it is especially and always necessary that we be able to prove our innocence, being well aware of it, by the testimony of God himself, as we read David did more than once, when he was pressed by the unjust slanders of his father-in-law. At the same time, as far as it can be done, we ought also to make it evident to men that we are free from blame, lest the Gospel and the faith which we profess suffer ill repute on our account. This especially moved Paul, since he saw that through his side the purer doctrine of the Gospel was being attacked by the wicked. The wickedness of the world and the licence of slanderers, which not even the most holy men have ever been able to escape, should also stir us up, lest we return the worst thanks for the greatest benefits. The examples of Moses and the Prophets teach this, whom those for whose salvation they themselves watched day and night did not hesitate to call traitors. But why say more about them, when not even Christ was free from slanders, which he endured most atrocious? Therefore we must take diligent care to abstain even from the appearance of evil, lest our adversaries seize on some occasion for slander from those things which we do, not indeed wickedly, but yet lightly and imprudently. Let all men apply this to themselves, and especially those who, being placed in a higher rank, can hide less. Many today boast of their faith and the purity of their conscience. But why do the same people offend others by the wantonness of their conduct, by drunkenness, by lust, and by the licence to abuse anyone they like? And what sort of conscience, I ask, is it that is not terrified by the curse of Christ, by which he pronounces that dreadful "Woe" upon all the authors of scandals?

units.la: Sed pergamus in verbis Apostoli, qui tertium quoq; legatũ duobus prioribus addit, qui & ipse ἀνόνυμος est. Theodoretus Apollo fuisse putat, quod mihi nullo modo verisimile videtur. Cur enim eius nomen tacuisset, cuius maxima erat apud Corinthios authoritas? & qui commendatione nulla opus habebat, cùm multi illum Paulo præferrent? Alij Syluanum intelligi sentiunt. {Sed quisquis fuerit, non multum refert. Commendatur autem hic quoq;, quòd frater sit, id est, Christianus & verè fidelis. Deinde, quòd eius studium & diligentiam ipse in multis negotijs expertus sit. Addit tertium, quòd in hac causa seipsum quodammodo vincat, & solito studiosiorem sese præstitierit: & huius causam dicit fiduciam illam præclaram, quam ipsum de illis concepisse videat. Vbi rursus discimus, eos demum rebus magnis & arduis debere destinari, quorum fides & industria prius sufficientibus argumentis probata est. Peccatur in eo multum, quando non solum ad opum Ecclesiæ dispensationem eliguntur homines malæ frugis & Euangelij ofores, verumetiam Reipub. gubernaculis tales adhibentur. Imprudens merito & insanus diceretur, qui tempestate exorta clauum nauis homini inepto & nautica artis imperito traderet. Quales ergo dicendi, qui hisce turbulentissimis temporibus hoc in Reipub. faciunt?
units.tr: But let us go on to the words of the Apostle, who adds a third envoy to the two earlier ones, and he too is anonymous. Theodoret thinks it was Apollos, which seems to me in no way likely. Why would he have concealed the name of a man who had the greatest authority among the Corinthians, and who needed no commendation, since many preferred him to Paul? Others think Silvanus is meant. But whoever he was, it matters little. He is commended here too, in that he is a brother, that is, a Christian and truly faithful. Next, in that his zeal and diligence have been tested by Paul himself in many affairs. He adds a third point, that in this matter he has in a way surpassed himself and shown himself more zealous than usual; and the cause of this he says is that splendid confidence which he sees Paul to have placed in them. Here again we learn that men should be appointed to great and difficult tasks only when their faith and industry have first been proved by sufficient evidence. There is great fault in this, when men of bad character and enemies of the Gospel are chosen not only for the stewardship of the Church's wealth but are even placed at the helm of the commonwealth. Would not a man be rightly called imprudent and mad who, when a storm had arisen, handed the ship's tiller to someone unskilled and ignorant of the seaman's art? What, then, shall we say of those who do this in the commonwealth in these most turbulent times?

units.la: Porrò vt semel locum hunc Paulus absoluat, summatim comprehendit quæ in istorum comen dationem hucusq; sigillatim dixit: Quoad ergo Titum, socius meus est, & apud vos adiutor: quo ad fratres nostros, legati sunt Ecclesiarum & gloria Christi. Quasi diceret: Quid verbus opus est? Si de Tito quaeritur quis sit, & num hac provincia dignus sit? socius meus est, & meus apud vos, vel erga vos adiutor. Sin de fratribus sermo sit, qui ipsum comitantur, Ecclesiarum legati sunt, & tales quidem, per quos gloria Christi hucusq; egregie illustrata est: & proinde digni, quos in pretio habeatis. Rursus vero novi modestiae suae specimen Paulus praebet. Fuit Titus ipsius discipulus. Non tamen dedignatur eum socium & collegam suum dicere, imo quam apud Corinthios ipse habere debebat authoritatem (utpote ipsorum Apostolus & pater in Christo) cum Tito partitur. Deinde alteros illos, non suos, sed Ecclesiarum ministros esse dicit. Hodie longe aliter Pontifices agunt. Nam etiamsi Cardinales & Episcopos fratres suos dicere soleant, eosdem tamen non nisi suo charactere signatos agnoscunt, & insuper sibi subiectos & iuramento quoq; obstrictos esse volunt. Deinde legatos suo nomine mittunt, & hos ideo a latere missos dicunt: idq; non minus vere quam insolenter, cum tales legati non nisi illorum negotia agant, Ecclesias vero, quarum titulis superbiunt, non modo negligant, sed insuper tam eas quam alias expilent atq; depraedentur.
units.tr: Furthermore, so that Paul may finish this passage once for all, he sums up briefly what he has hitherto said in detail in commendation of these men: "As for Titus, he is my partner and your helper; as for our brothers, they are envoys of the Churches and the glory of Christ." It is as if he said: "What need is there of words? If you ask who Titus is, and whether he is worthy of this task, he is my partner and, with me, your helper or aide to you. But if the talk is of the brothers who accompany him, they are envoys of the Churches, and such men as through whom the glory of Christ has hitherto been splendidly displayed; and therefore they are worthy to be held in esteem by you." Again, Paul here gives an example of his own humility. Titus was his own disciple. Yet he does not disdain to call him his partner and colleague, and indeed he shares with Titus the authority which he ought to have among the Corinthians (as their Apostle and father in Christ). Then he says that the others are not his own ministers but the ministers of the Churches. Today the Pontiffs act quite differently. For although they are wont to call Cardinals and Bishops their brothers, yet they acknowledge them only as marked with their own character, and moreover they want them to be subject to themselves and bound by oath too. Then they send legates in their own name, and call these "sent from the side"; and they say this no less truly than insolently, since such legates do nothing but transact their business, while the Churches, whose titles they boast of, they not only neglect but moreover plunder and pillage both these and others.

units.la: Observabis praeterea gloriam Christi dici iustos, quorum fides & industria hucusq; multis argumentis spectata fuerat. Potest autem hoc bifariam accipi. Primum, quia in talibus Christi gloria elucet, qui eos donis Spiritus sancti instruit, & per eosdem efficaciter agit ea, quae vires humanas superant. Deinde sic dici possunt, eo quod ipsi donis omnibus vtuntur ad Christi gloriam, dum huc omnes adducere studeant, ut a plurimis agnoscatur atq; celebretur. Haec diligentius meditentur, quicunq; inter Christianos vel in Ecclesia, vel in Repub. excellunt. Vanissima enim est vniuersa huius mundi gloria, nisi simul Christi gloria sit. Sed & singuli hoc curent priuatim, ne dedecori sint Christo, qui eos sanguine suo pretio redimere dignatus est. Graues ergo illorum culpa est, qui vel sibi ipsis tribuunt dona illa, quae a Domino ex gratuita misericordia acceperunt, vel iisdem turpiter abutuntur, & ita viuunt, ut & fides Christiana & Euangelium Christi propter ipsos male audiant.
units.tr: Moreover, you will observe that those whose faith and industry had hitherto been proved by many evidences are called the glory of Christ. This may be understood in two ways. First, because in such men the glory of Christ shines forth, since he endows them with the gifts of the Holy Spirit and through them effectively accomplishes things that exceed human powers. Second, they may be so called because they use all their gifts for the glory of Christ, while they strive to bring everyone to this, that he may be acknowledged and celebrated by very many. Let all who excel among Christians, whether in the Church or in the commonwealth, meditate on this more carefully. For the whole glory of this world is utterly vain unless it is at the same time the glory of Christ. But let individuals also take care of this in private, lest they be a disgrace to Christ, who deigned to redeem them with his own blood. Therefore those are greatly to blame who either attribute to themselves those gifts which they have received from the Lord out of free mercy, or shamefully abuse them, and so live that both the Christian faith and the Gospel of Christ are ill spoken of on their account.

units.la: Sequitur huius loci Conclusio, qua fine & vsum omnium, quae hucusq; dicta sunt, indicat: Itaq; de monstratione charitatis vestrae, & nostrae de vobis gloriationis, edite in eos, in conspectu Ecclesiarum. Demonstratione pro documento dixit: & sensus est, ut suam charitatem luculento aliquo specimine & contributione siue liberalitate se digna declarent, & ita testatum faciant, non inanem aut fictitiam fuisse ipsius de illis gloriationem, cum revera tales sint, qui celebrari mereantur. Est haec ratio ab honesto, & apud generosioris animi homines efficacissima est. Nam ut omnis fraus & deceptio tur pis est, ita longe turpissimum est eorum spem fallere, qui de nobis praeclare meriti nihil non tam sibi ipsis quam alijs de nostra virtute pollicentur. Legatis vero istis Ecclesias coniungit, ita admonens, quod licet illi per se mereantur amice tractari, simul tamen Ecclesiarum quoq; rationem habendam esse, quarum legati sint, & quas hoc beneficio sibi ipsis sint obstricturi. Ita clausulam hanc Theodoretus expos uit, & ut isto sensu accipiatur, Graeci contextus constructio requirit.
units.tr: There follows the conclusion of this passage, in which he indicates the end and use of all that has been said so far: "Therefore, show to them, in the sight of the Churches, the proof of your love and of our boasting about you." He has said "demonstration" as proof, and the sense is that they should declare their love by some clear example and by a contribution or liberality worthy of them, and so make it evident that his boasting about them was not empty or feigned, since they are truly such men as deserve to be celebrated. This argument is drawn from honour, and it is most effective among men of more generous spirit. For just as all fraud and deception is base, so it is by far most shameful to disappoint the hopes of those who, having deserved well of us, promise themselves no less than good things from our virtue, and of others too. But by this he joins the Churches to these envoys, thereby admonishing that, although these men deserve to be treated kindly on their own account, yet regard must also be had for the Churches of which they are envoys, and whom they will bind to themselves by this kindness. Theodoret expounded this clause in this way, and the construction of the Greek context requires that it be taken in this sense.

units.la: Interim discamus hoc loco, non satis esse, ut fidei & charitatis nomine gloriemur, nisi publice quoq; tam huius quam illius praebeamus documenta. Vult enim Deus in Veritate coli, & corda ipsa requirit, qui fons est consiliorum & actionum nostrarum omnium. At fidei documenta in aduersis potissimum elucet, si videlicet periculis vndiq; pressi ab vno Deo pendere pergimus, & aduersus minas atq; furores intrepidi consistimus, patienter deniq; ferimus quaecunq; ferenda sunt. Fidei enim vox est: Quis nos separabit a dilectione Dei? &c. Vide locum Rom. 8. Charitatis vero decla randa materiam nobis fratrum egestas & pericula exhibent, ut in Samaritani parabola docemur, qui ut primum vidit faucium & seminecem, eius commiseratione motus curam illius suscepit. Unde Ioannes Apostolus recte scripsit: Qui habuerit facultates mundi, & viderit fratrem suum egentem, & clauserit viscera sua coram eo, quomodo charitas Dei manet in eo? Putemus ergo ad nos pertinere Conclusionem istam o viri Germani. Multa de nostra fide & professione praedicatio apud exteras gentes auditur. Praebeamus ergo illius documenta, ne dedecori simus Domino & Seruatori nostro, IESV CHRISTO, qui nos tanto honore dignatus est. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Meanwhile let us learn from this place that it is not enough to glory in the name of faith and love unless we also give public proofs of both. For God wills to be worshipped in truth, and he requires the heart itself, which is the source of all our counsels and actions. But the proofs of faith shine forth chiefly in adversity, namely when, pressed on every side by dangers, we continue to depend on God alone, and stand fearless against threats and rages, and at last patiently bear whatever must be borne. For the voice of faith is: "Who shall separate us from the love of God?" etc. See Rom. 8. The occasion for declaring love is supplied to us by the need and dangers of the brothers, as we are taught in the parable of the Samaritan, who, as soon as he saw the man half dead, moved by compassion for him, took up his care. Whence the Apostle John wrote rightly: "Whoever has the goods of the world, and sees his brother in need, and shuts up his bowels against him, how does the love of God abide in him?" Let us therefore think that this conclusion pertains to us, O German men. Much is heard among foreign nations about the preaching of our faith and profession. Let us therefore give proof of it, lest we be a disgrace to our Lord and Saviour, JESUS CHRIST, who has deigned to honour us so greatly. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT IX. HOMILIA XXXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX. HOMILY XXXIX.

units.la: NAm de ministerio quidem in sanctos superuacaneum est scri-bere vobis. Noui enim promptum animum vestrum, quem de vobis iacto apud Macedones: Achaiam videlicet paratam esse ab anno superiore, & ex vobis ortus zelus prouocauit complures. Misi autem hos fratres, ne gloriatio nostra de vobis inanis fiat hac in parte: vt (sicut dicebam) parati sitis. Ne quo modo si mecum venerint Macedones, & offenderint vos imparatos, nos pudefiamus (vt ne dicam Vos) in praesidente ista gloriatione. Itaq; necessarium putaui adhortari fratres, vt prius eant ad vos, & prius absoluant antea indictam benedictionem vestram, vt ea sit parata, ita vt benedictio, non vt extortum aliquid.
units.tr: It is indeed superfluous for me to write to you about the ministry for the saints. For I know your ready mind, which I boast of to the Macedonians: that Achaia has been prepared since last year, and the zeal that arose among you has stirred up many. But I have sent these brothers so that our boasting about you may not prove empty in this matter, and that you may be ready, as I was saying. Otherwise, if the Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we will be put to shame (not to mention you) for having boasted so confidently. So I thought it necessary to exhort the brothers to go to you first and to complete beforehand the blessing you promised earlier, so that it may be ready, and so that it may be a gift freely given and not something wrung out of you.

units.la: VEMADMODVM aeternus Dei Filius propter nos in mundum venit, nec homo solum, verumetiam pauper factus est, vt nos pauperes atq; nudos bonis caelestibus & aeternis beatos atq; diuites faceret: ita homines egenos & inopes Ecclesiae suae atque singulis credentibus diligentia singulari commendauit. Quae causa est, quod illorum causam Apostoli apud Ecclesias tanto studio egerunt, vt illis non satis visum sit, si vnaquaeque suos aleret, sed insuper exterorum quoque rationem haberi voluerunt: sicut ex tota hac tractatione apparet: Monet enim Corinthios Paulus, vt collectam faciant extraordinariam, per quam famis tempore egenis Syriae fratribus subueniatur. Tantam vero in hac causa diligentiam adhibendam esse putauit, vt quamvis proximo Cap. omnia dixisse videri queat, quae de hac causa dici possunt, eandem tamen nunc quasi de novo agat: & ideo magna cum circumspectione adhuc quaedam subijcit, quae ad illos excitandos efficacissima esse videbantur.
units.tr: Just as the eternal Son of God came into the world for our sake, and became not only man but also poor, so that he might make us, who were poor and naked, blessed and rich in heavenly and eternal goods, so he has committed the needy and destitute to his Church and to each believer with a singular diligence. This is why the Apostles pursued their cause among the churches with such eagerness, and it did not seem enough to them that each church should feed its own, but they also wished account to be taken of outsiders. This is clear from the whole of this discussion. For Paul urges the Corinthians to make an extraordinary collection, by which help may be given to the needy brothers in Syria in a time of famine. Indeed, he thought such great diligence was to be applied in this matter that, although it might seem that in the previous chapter he had said everything that can be said about it, he now treats the same matter again, as if anew; and so, with great caution, he still adds certain things which seemed most effective for rousing them.

units.la: Ec principio quidem Caput hoc cum ijs quae proximè praecesserunt connectens, rationem reddit eius quod dixerat: Documentum charitatis vestrae, & nostrae de vobis gloriationis edite, &c. Pote-rant enim hoc ita accipere Corinthij, quasi suspecta ei esset ipsorum tenacitas siue sordities, & pro inde indignius ferre, quod tantopere ab ipso vrgerentur. Itaq; vt omni suspicione seipsum liberet, haec subijcit: Nam de ministerio in sanctos superuacaneum est scribere vobis, &c. Rursus autem de Collectis loquitur, & eas ministerium dicit, quia dum egentibus subuenimus, debitum illis ministerium siue officium praestamus. Adhaec, non pauperes siue inopes, sed Sanctos itidem nominat, ita docens, illos non quales sint mundi iudicio, sed quales Deus aestimet, spectari debere: Fideles nimirum, quos in Filio suo IESV CHRISTO sibi consecrauerit. Quod vnum si in tota hac causa nobis perpetuo in mentem veniat, frustra nobis caro suipsius amans rationes suas obijciet, quibus beneficentiam nostram impedire conatur. Interim pauperes quoq; qui nomine Christi petunt sibi benefieri, huius semper meminerint, ne vel ignauo otio vel turpi eorum quae accipiunt dilapidatione sanctitatem suam prophanent, dum Christi nomine absq; causa necessaria ad quaestum abutuntur. Quoad vero Pauli verba, hic sensus est huius loci: Nemo putet, me ideo vobis tam vehementer instare, quod vos suspectos habeam. Quoad enim me, noui ego animi vestri alacritatem, imò de ea gloriari soleo apud Macedones, quod nimirum omnes Achaiae Ecclesiae ad collectas hasce faciendas paratae sint iam ab anno superiore: & ita hoc vestrum studium praedico, vt qui ex eo enatus est zelus multos prouocauerit, vt etiam ipsi alacriùs & liberaliùs contribuerint, ne officio suo defuisse videantur, &c.
units.tr: At the start, this chapter connects with what immediately preceded and gives the reason for what he had said: "Show to the churches, therefore, the proof of your love and of our boasting about you," and so on. For the Corinthians could take this to mean that he suspected their stinginess or meanness, and so they might bear it more indignantly that he pressed them so hard. Therefore, in order to free himself from every suspicion, he adds: "For it is superfluous for me to write to you about the ministry for the saints," and so on. Again he speaks of the collections and calls them a ministry, because while we help the needy we render to them the service or duty owed to them. Besides, he calls them not poor or needy but also saints, thereby teaching that they should be regarded not as the world judges them but as God judges them: namely, faithful people whom he has consecrated to himself in his Son Jesus Christ. If this one thing comes to our mind throughout this whole matter, our self-loving flesh will in vain object its reasons by which it tries to hinder our beneficence. Meanwhile, let the poor also, who ask in the name of Christ to be helped, always remember this, so that they do not profane their holiness either by idle laziness or by shameful squandering of what they receive, while they abuse the name of Christ for gain without any necessary cause. As for Paul's words, the sense of this passage is this: let no one think that I press you so vehemently because I hold you under suspicion. For as far as I am concerned, I know the eagerness of your mind; indeed, I am accustomed to boast of it among the Macedonians, that all the churches of Achaia were ready to make these collections already from last year. And so I so praise your zeal that the enthusiasm born from it has stirred up many, so that they too might contribute more eagerly and generously, lest they seem to have failed in their duty, and so on.

units.la: Quo loco non debet ofcitantius praeteriri studium Pauli, quod in tota hac causa nouis subinde argumentis se exerit. Sciebat quid anno priore iam coepissent facere Corinthij, & spem de illis optimam conceperat. Attamen subinde illis instat, & omni generis rationes congerit, quibus illos
units.tr: Here we must not pass over carelessly Paul's zeal, which in this whole matter he shows by fresh arguments again and again. He knew what the Corinthians had already begun to do the year before, and he had conceived the best hope about them. Yet again and again he presses them and heaps up every kind of reason by which he makes them more eager. [The text breaks off here]

units.la: Ratio redditur eorum, quae praemisit.
units.tr: An account is given of the things he had premised.

units.la: Pauperes, Sancti dicuntur.
units.tr: The poor are called saints.

units.la: Studium Pauli in hac causa. alacriores reddat. Est hoc charitatis non fucatæ ingenium. Qui huius igne ardent, optimè quidem sperant de omnibus, quia ex seipsis alios omnes æstimant. At quia ijdem non possunt ignorare, quanta sit ingenij nostri infirmitas, & quàm facilè mutentur aut fatigentur, quos nihil non facturos esse putaveras, non possunt non soliciti esse & eos etiam vrgere, qui sponte officium faciunt. Ideo Paulus admirabili prudentia & divino (vt Theodoretus scribit) artificio causam iflam agit. Nam apud Macedones, qui sponte coeperant collectas facere, Corinthiorum studium prædicauit, vt illos confirmaret, ne ab eis se prævenīri paterentur, & vt eos etiam excitaret, qui fortassis inter illos nondum tam proclives erant ad largiendum. Rursus apud Corinthios Macedonum liberalitatem commendauit, vt horum exemplo illos etiam extimularet. Sunt enim homines (vt Chrysostomus annotauit) natura ζelotypi, & ideo aliorum æmulatione multi vehementius quàm vllis aliis rationibus permouentur ad faciendum officium. Et hac illa prudentia atq; fides est, quam in domus suæ dispensatoribus Christus requirit.
units.tr: Paul's zeal in this matter [may make them more eager]. This is the nature of unfeigned charity. Those who burn with its fire hope the best of everyone, because they judge all others by themselves. But since they cannot fail to know how weak our nature is, and how easily those whom you thought would do everything are changed or tired, they cannot but be anxious and press even those who perform their duty willingly. Therefore Paul handles this cause with admirable prudence and with divine artifice, as Theodoret writes. For among the Macedonians, who had of their own accord begun to make collections, he proclaimed the zeal of the Corinthians, so as to strengthen them, lest they allow themselves to be outdone by them; and so as to stir up even those who perhaps were not yet so inclined to give. Again, among the Corinthians he commended the liberality of the Macedonians, so that by their example he might spur them on as well. For people are (as Chrysostom observed) by nature jealous, and so many are moved far more vehemently to do their duty by the rivalry of others than by any other reasons. This is that prudence and faithfulness which Christ requires in the stewards of his house.

units.la: Discant ergo Pauli exemplo ministri, quid ipsos facere conueniat. Etiamsi norint qui & quales sint ij, quibus cum agunt, nihilo tamen remissius agant. Qualescunque enim sint, homines tamen sunt, & Legem peccati circumferunt in membris suis, quæ sæpe inuitos quoq; abripit quò nolunt, vt Paulus de semetipso fatetur. Nec vnquam feriatur Satan, qui dormientibus ferè zizania sua aspergit, quæ præter omnem expectationem interdum fructus ferunt nostra professione indignos. Exemplis hac demonstrare nequaquam opus est, eò quòd quotidie fiunt, quæ nos excitare possunt, ne ofcitanter in nostro munere versemur. Quòd si verò cura & studio vigilanti opus est, quando res in tuto consistere videtur, & pleriq; officium faciunt: quæ diligentia, quæ exhortatio nimia esse potest, quando plerique dormitant in ijs, quæ fidei causam & charitatis officia concernunt: interim verò ijs moribus viuitur, quos nouissimis temporibus regnaturos esse olim Christus prædixit? Debet ergo eadem consideratio auditores etiam mouere, vt admonitiones & exhortationes seueriores patienter ferant: nec sufficere sibi putent, quòd iam ante norint, quid factu & creditu opus sit. Non enim qui norunt voluntatem Domini, sed qui faciunt illam, feruantur. Qui verò norunt, & non faciunt, ij pluribus plagis vapulant. Et vt ministros eadem subinde dicere decet, ita illud nobis tutum est. Denique exempla quotidiana docent, nullam diligentiam hic superuacaneam esse. Qui verò se institutione aut admonitione nulla opus habere putant, ij se omnium mortalium ignorantissimos & arrogantissimos esse produnt, vt qui ne seipsos quidem nouerint.
units.tr: Let ministers, then, learn from Paul's example what they ought to do. Even if they know who and what sort of people those are with whom they deal, they should not deal with them any less earnestly. For whatever they are, they are still human, and they carry the law of sin in their members, which often drags even unwilling people where they do not wish to go, as Paul confesses of himself. Nor does Satan ever rest, who sows his tares while people are almost asleep, and these sometimes bear fruit unworthy of our profession, beyond all expectation. There is no need to demonstrate this by examples, since things happen every day which can rouse us so that we do not carry out our office carelessly. But if care and watchful zeal are needed when matters seem to stand safe and most people are doing their duty, what diligence or exhortation can be excessive when most are sleeping in those matters which concern the cause of faith and the duties of charity? Meanwhile, do we live by the customs which Christ foretold long ago would reign in the last times? Therefore the same consideration ought to move the hearers too, so that they patiently bear stricter admonitions and exhortations, and do not think it enough for them that they already know what must be done and believed. For it is not those who know the will of the Lord, but those who do it, who are saved. And those who know and do not do it are beaten with many blows. And as it is fitting for ministers to say the same things again and again, so for us that is safe. Finally, daily examples teach that no diligence in this matter is superfluous. But those who think they have no need of instruction or admonition show themselves to be the most ignorant and arrogant of all mortals, since they do not even know themselves.

units.la: Quia verò non vulgaris diffidentiæ argumentum videri poterat, quòd non per literas modo, verumetiam legatos certos vrgebantur, nunc cur hos miserit, apertius ac diligentius docet. Misi autem hos fratres, ne gloriatio nostra de vobis inanis fiat hac in parte, &c. Causas legationis huius duas allegat. Primam, ne falso de ipsis gloriatus esse dicatur. Id verò restringit ad præsentem causam de collectis in pauperum subsidiū faciendis, quando dicit: Hac in parte. Quia enim præcipuum fidei argumentum est charitas, & eadem propria discipulorum Christi nota est: merito administri Verbi cauere debent, ne hæc gloria in Ecclesijs ipsorum inanis fiat. Nam qui hic deficiunt, ij certè frustra fide in Christum gloriantur. Altera causa priori similis, vel potius eius expositio est: Ne quo modo, si mecum venerint Macedones, & inuenerint vos imparatos, nos pudefiamus (vt ne dicam Vos) in præsidente ista gloriatione. Quibus verbis docet, non tam de sua quàm ipsorum gloria & exi-stimatione hic agi, quam apud Ecclesias amissuri sint maxima ex parte, si in opere tam sancto, tam honesto, tam necessario alijs remissiores aut sordidiores inueniantur. Et sanè non multum de sua gloria solicitus erat Paulus, qui alibi testatur, sibi non curæ esse, vt ab humano die iudicetur, & iampridem seipsum omni gloria spoliauerat, qua inter Iudæos præ alijs fuerat clarus. Attamen non sine causa cauere debebat, ne vanus iactator videretur, & ita alij quoq; remissiores fierent. Apostolici verò candoris euidens argumentum est, quòd tam solicitè cauet, ne Corinthiorum existimatio in periculum veniat.
units.tr: But since it could seem to be a sign of no ordinary distrust that they were pressed not only by letters but also by certain envoys, he now teaches more clearly and carefully why he sent them: "But I have sent these brothers so that our boasting about you may not prove empty in this matter," and so on. He gives two reasons for this embassy. The first is that he should not be said to have boasted falsely about them. He restricts this to the present cause of making collections for the relief of the poor, when he says: "in this matter." For since charity is the chief proof of faith, and is the peculiar mark of the disciples of Christ, the ministers of the Word rightly ought to take care that this boast does not become empty in their churches. For those who fail here certainly boast in vain of faith in Christ. The second reason is similar to the first, or rather is its explanation: "lest, if the Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we be put to shame (not to mention you) for having boasted so confidently." By these words he teaches that the matter here concerns not so much his own glory and reputation as theirs, which they would lose for the most part among the churches if they were found more careless or meaner in a work so holy, so honorable, and so necessary as the others. And indeed Paul was not very anxious about his own glory, for he testifies elsewhere that it was no concern of his to be judged by a human day, and he had long since stripped himself of all the glory by which he had been famous among the Jews above others. Yet he rightly had to take care not to seem an empty boaster, and thus that others too would become more careless. And the clear evidence of his apostolic candor is that he takes such care lest the good opinion of the Corinthians come into danger.

units.la: Continet autem locus iste generalem doctrinā, quæ etsi ad omnes Ecclesias ex æquo pertinet, ad eas tamen imprimis, quæ apud exteros præ alijs celebrantur: Vt nimirum curet, ne gloriatio eorum falsi conuincatur, & ita pudefiant, quicunq; illarum virtutes alijs prædicauerunt. Fit hoc si famæ de ipsis diuulgatæ non respondeant. Quò cumprimis pertinet, si in fide languidiores sint, si in latus utrumque claudicent (vt olim de Israëlitis suis Elias dicebat) si item vitam viuant prophanam & sceleratam, quoad intemperantiam, ebrietatem, gulæ & crapulæ studium, libidines vagas, incestus, execrationes, deierationes, auaritiam, fraudes, vsuras, rapinas, & quæ alia sunt huius generis: si præterea religione & Euangelij prætextu ad quæstum abutantur: si à charitate & humanitate alieni sint, cùm quoad suos, tum maximè quoad peregrinos & hospites. Hæc enim hos vehementer offendunt, & simul pudore suffundunt eos, qui aliquando de Ecclesiis eiusmodi honorificum testimonium tulerunt. Erant hæc nobis serìo cogitanda, quibus hoc nouissimo sæculo primùm innotuit Euangelij lux, & quorum in abolendis superstitionibus inque reducenda veri cultus forma studium, iampridem in toto terrarum orbe vulgatum multos ad nostri admirationem atq; imitationem accendit. At pauci sunt, qui ignominiam istam metuant, de qua in præsenti Apostolus loquitur: multi autem fronte plus quam meretricia prediti adeò non erubescunt, vt in petulanti & effreni licentia laudem quærant, & illam verbis quoque indignißimis testentur, dum admoniti responsant: Quid ad nos exterarum nationum homines? Num propter hoc aut illum ego nouam vitæ rationem instituerem? Si offenduntur isti nostris moribus, ad sua redeant. Quis eos, vt huc venirent, vocauit? Quis inuitos retinet? Hæc & alia multa huius generis hodie audiuntur inter eos, qui Euangelicæ doctrinæ fautores præcipui dici volunt. At sunt hæc indigna Christianis hominibus. Et eho quis tu es, qui peregrinos nihil ad te pertinere dicis, & quidem eos qui vel propter religionem sedibus patrijs eiecti ad te confugiunt, vel discendi causa veniunt? Tune alienos dicis eos, quos nisi pro fratribus agnoscas, tu in filiorum Dei numero censeri non poteris? Vel, num tu gentium aut personarum discrimen facies in CHRISTO IESV, qui absque omni delectu omnis loci & conditionis homines ad se vocat? Paulus Apostolus à carnium esu prorsus abstinere voluit, ne quem eorum offenderet, pro quibus Dei Filius mori dignatus est: Et tu tibi iniuriam fieri putas, si propter infirmiores, siue illi peregrini siue cives sint, modestius, temperantius & religiosius viuere, & ab illis sceleribus abstinere iubearis, quorum atrocitas per se, etsi nullum ex illis scandalum publicum nascatur, tanta est, vt à Regno Dei excludat eos, qui in illis contumaciter perseuerant? Expendite ista diligenter ô fratres, quibus inter nostri sæculi terribiles motus, quibus multarum nationum Christiani exercentur, datum est in pace viuere: ne quando idem vobis eueniat, quod olim Galilæa ciuitatibus ingratis & pœnitere nescijs, Bethsaida nimirum, Corozaimo & Capernao Christus minatus est. Vide Matth. 11.
units.tr: This passage contains a general teaching, which applies equally to all churches but especially to those that are famed above others among foreigners. Paul's concern is that their boasting should not be shown to be false, and so those who have praised their virtues to others should not be put to shame. That happens when the reputation spread about them does not match what they are. This applies especially if they are weaker in faith, if they limp on both sides (as Elijah once said of his Israelites), if they live a profane and wicked life, given to intemperance, drunkenness, gluttony and carousing, wandering lusts, incest, curses, oaths, greed, frauds, usury, robbery, and other things of this kind, if besides they abuse religion and the pretext of the Gospel for profit, or if they are strangers to charity and kindness, both towards their own people and above all towards foreigners and guests. For these things offend such people greatly and at the same time fill with shame those who once gave such churches an honourable testimony. These are things we must seriously consider, we to whom the light of the Gospel first became known in this last age, and whose zeal for abolishing superstitions and restoring the true form of worship has long been spread throughout the whole world and has kindled many to admire and imitate us. Yet there are few who fear that disgrace of which the Apostle speaks here. Many, however, endowed with a face more brazen than a harlot's, are so unashamed that they seek praise in wanton and unbridled licence, and they bear witness to it even in the most unworthy words when they are admonished and reply: "What are foreigners to us? Should I adopt a new way of life because of this or that man? If those people are offended by our customs, let them go back to their own homes. Who called them to come here? Who keeps them against their will?" These and many other things of this kind are heard today among those who want to be called the chief supporters of evangelical doctrine. But such things are unworthy of Christians. And tell me, who are you who say that foreigners are nothing to you, and indeed those who, having been driven from their homeland for the sake of religion, flee to you, or who come to learn? Do you call them strangers, when you cannot be counted among the sons of God unless you acknowledge them as brothers? Or do you make a distinction of nations or persons in Christ Jesus, who calls men of every place and condition without any distinction to himself? The Apostle Paul wished to abstain entirely from eating meat, lest he offend any of those for whom the Son of God deigned to die. And do you think you suffer injury if you are bidden to live more modestly, temperately and religiously for the sake of the weaker, whether they are foreigners or citizens, and to abstain from those crimes whose atrocity is so great in itself, even if no public scandal arises from them, that it shuts out from the kingdom of God those who persist obstinately in them? Consider these things carefully, brothers, you to whom it has been granted to live in peace amid the terrible upheavals of our age, by which Christians of many nations are afflicted; lest the same thing ever happen to you that Christ once threatened against the ungrateful cities of Galilee that could not repent, namely Bethsaida, Chorazin and Capernaum. See Matt. 11.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum reuertamur, qui amplius exponit instituti sui rationem, sic dicens: Itaque necessarium putaui adhortari fratres, vt priùs eant ad vos, & priùs absoluant antea indictam benedictionem vestram, vt ea sit parata, ita vt benedictio, non vt extortum aliquid. Quasi diceret: Cùm huius rei gratia ad vos proficisci statuerim, & fortassis aliqui Macedonum, qui vestram in quoscunque liberalitatem me multoties prædicare audiuerunt, me comitaturi sint, omnino è re vestra & mea esse putaui, vt fratres hosce cum Tito priùs ad vos excurrere iuberem, vt ante promissam & iam decretam benedictionem vestram absoluerent, id est, vt quod anno superiore cœpistis, ipsi ad finem perducerent, sic, vt cùm eam ego paratam inuenero, omnibus constet, eam reuera benedictionem esse, non munus violenter aut improbè ab inuitis extortum.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who explains further the reason for his plan, saying: "So I thought it necessary to exhort the brothers that they should go on ahead to you and arrange beforehand the blessing you promised earlier, so that it may be ready, as a blessing and not as something extorted." As if he were saying: since I have decided to set out to you for this purpose, and perhaps some of the Macedonians, who have often heard me praise your generosity towards anyone, will accompany me, I thought it altogether fitting for your sake and mine to order these brothers to go on ahead to you with Titus, so that they might complete the blessing you promised and have already decided upon, that is, so that they might bring to completion what you began the previous year. Thus, when I find it ready, it will be plain to everyone that it is truly a blessing and not a gift forcibly or wrongly extorted from the unwilling.

units.la: Quo loco obseruabis, collectam siue pecuniam, quæ in pauperum subuentionem conferri debebat, & quam hucusque Gratiæ vocabulo denotauit, nunc benedictionem dici. Ita verò ex Hebræorum more in sacris literis vsitatissimo Paulus loquitur. Apud illos enim Berachah, quod vulgò benedictionem dicimus, proprie faustam imprecationem, gratiarumactionem, laudem item, & quæcunque ex gratuito fauore Dei nobis obtingunt, significat. Inde benedicti & benedici dicuntur, qui Dei fauore luculento vtuntur quoad rem domesticam, pacem, bonam valetudinem, agrorum proventus & alia quæ incolumitati nostræ seruiunt. Vide Deut. 27. & 28. Cap. Inde verò Benedictionis vocabulum ad ea quoque transfertur, quæ homines ex gratuita liberalitate & animo benevolo donant alicui, vt suum erga eum studium siue reuerentiam testentur. Sic Abigael de comeatu, quem ad Dauidem ferebat, dixisse legitur: Et nunc hæc est benedictio, quam attulit ancilla tua domino meo, quæ datur pueris, &c. Dauid quoq; de muneribus honorarijs, quæ ad Seniores Iu 30. da mittebat, similiter loquebatur: En vobis benedictione de preda inimicorum Domini Naamã item Eliseo pro recuperata sanitate donum offerens, dicebat: Accipe nunc benedictionem à seruo tuo. Ratio huius nominis est, quòd ad Dei ingenium proxime accedimus, quando egenos & pauperes nostra beneficentia subleuamus: simulque ipsi quoque diuina gratia ac benedictionis participes efficimur, Deo liberaliter retribuente ea, quae in suos conferuntur. Promissiones ea de re passim in Lege extant, quoties inopes nobis Deus commendat. Quapropter rectè monuit Siracbides: Beneficentia cuiusque, quasi sacculo reposita apud ipsum, gratiam eius conseruabit veluti pupillam, & tandem emicans premium in suum caput cuique regeret. Apertius vero Isaias: Sieffuderis esurienti animam tuam, & animam afflictam saturaueris, tunc orietur in tenebris lux tua, & erit caligo tua sicut meridies: Et deducet te Dominus semper, & saturam reddet in siccitatibus animam tuam, & ossa tua saginabit: & eris vt hortus irriguus, & sicut scaturigo aquarum, cuius aquae nunquam fallunt, &c. Quòad vero praesente locum, voluit Paulus benedictionis voce potissimum ideo vti, vt Corinthij memores se bonorum, quae ex Dei benedictione acceperint, dispensatores esse, illius exemplum imitentur, & non maligne, sed liberaliter & ἁφθόνως (vt Graeci loquuntur) contribuant. Ideo benedictioni opponit πλεονεξίαν, quae vox proprie nimiam & insatiabilem plus habendi cupiditatem significat: Et quia qui hac laborant, aegre aliquid largiuntur (adeo vt, tenacitas eorum proverbio locum dederit, quo ex pumice citius aquam elici dicimus, quam ab auaro munus aliquod) per Metalepsim hic pro dono multa precandi importunitate extorto vsurpatur. Monet ergo Corinthios, vt in ipsius aduentum sic omnia praeparent, vt constet eos alacri & laeto animo dare quicquid dant. Sed de eo ipse amplius dicet in ijs, quae sequuntur.
units.tr: Here you will observe that the collection of money, which was to be contributed for the relief of the poor, and which Paul until now called by the name of "grace," is now called a "blessing." Paul speaks in this way in accordance with the Hebrew custom, which is most common in the sacred writings. For among them berakhah, which we commonly render as "blessing," properly signifies a favourable prayer, thanksgiving, and also praise, and whatever comes to us from the free favour of God. Hence those are called blessed, and are said to be blessed, who enjoy the manifest favour of God in domestic affairs, in peace, good health, the produce of the fields, and other things that serve our well-being. See Deut. 27 and 28. From there the word "blessing" is also transferred to those things which people freely and kindly give to someone to show their goodwill or respect towards him. Thus we read that Abigail said of the provisions she was bringing to David: "And now this is the blessing which your handmaid has brought to my lord, which is given to the young men," etc. David too spoke in a similar way about the honorary gifts he sent to the elders of Judah: "Behold, a blessing for you from the spoil of the enemies of the Lord." Naaman, too, offering a gift to Elisha for his recovered health, said: "Accept now a blessing from your servant." The reason for this name is that we come very close to God's own nature when we relieve the needy and the poor by our beneficence; and at the same time we ourselves become partakers of divine grace and blessing, since God generously repays what is bestowed on his people. Promises about this are found throughout the Law, as often as God commends the poor to us. Therefore the son of Sirach rightly warned: "The beneficence of each man, stored up as in a purse with him, will keep his grace like the apple of the eye, and at last it will rise up and repay each man's reward on his own head." More plainly Isaiah says: "If you pour out your soul to the hungry and satisfy the afflicted soul, then your light shall rise in darkness, and your gloom shall be like midday. And the Lord shall guide you always, and will satisfy your soul in dry places, and will fatten your bones; and you shall be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water whose waters never fail," etc. As for the present passage, Paul wished to use the word "blessing" chiefly so that the Corinthians, mindful that they are stewards of the good things they have received from God's blessing, should imitate his example, and contribute not grudgingly but generously and aphthonōs (as the Greeks say) [ἁφθόνως], that is, without envy. Therefore he sets against "blessing" pleonexia [πλεονεξία], a word which properly signifies an excessive and insatiable desire to have more. And because those who are afflicted with this rarely give anything willingly (so that their stinginess has given rise to the proverb by which we say that water is more readily squeezed from a pumice stone than a gift from a miser), by metalepsis the word is here used for a gift extorted by much importunate begging. He therefore warns the Corinthians to prepare everything for his coming in such a way that it is clear they give whatever they give with a willing and cheerful mind. But he will say more about this himself in what follows.

units.la: Nunc extra statum causae, de qua hic agitur, Pauli exemplum obseruari debet, qui toties & tam sollicitè de suo aduentu loquitur, cùm tamen nunquam ad eos venerit, quantum ex Actorum historia per Lucam descripta poterit colligi. Ergo non semper consiliorum suorum certi sunt sancti Dei homines, sed ad eos quoque pertinet illud Solomonis: Homo cogitat de via sua, Dominus autem dirigit gressum eius. Quod cum probè norint, consilia sua Dei voluntate metiuntur, sicuti Iacobus Apostolus docet. Fecit hoc semper Paulus, vt alibi quoque diximus. Imitentur eius exemplum omnes, & consilia sua sic frenent, ne quid vel ex praecipiti affectu, vel confidentia incon-sulta temere instituant. Feramus item patienter, si quid nobis praeter voluntatem accidat. Idenim cum optimis & sanctissimis quibusque nobis commune est. Tutissimum vero fuerit, si calcatis per fidei obedientiam rationis nostrae consilijs atque desiderijs, ab vnius Dei prouidentia pendeamus, qui vt nos in Filio suo IESV CHRISTO elegit, ita eundem nobis vindicem & seruatorem dedit, qui nobis adsit, nosque regat & seruet ad nominis sui gloriam & Ecclesiae suae aedificationem. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Now, apart from the particular matter under discussion here, Paul's example should be observed, for he speaks so often and so anxiously about his coming, although he never came to them, as far as can be gathered from Luke's account in the history of the Acts. Therefore the holy men of God are not always certain of their plans, and for them too applies that saying of Solomon: "A man plans his way, but the Lord directs his step." Since they know this well, they measure their plans by the will of God, as the Apostle James teaches. Paul always did this, as we have said elsewhere. Let all imitate his example, and so restrain their plans that they do not rashly undertake anything either from headlong passion or from unconsidered confidence. Let us also bear patiently if anything happens to us contrary to our will, for this is common to all the best and holiest people. It will indeed be safest if, trampling underfoot through the obedience of faith the counsels and desires of our own reason, we depend on the providence of the one God, who has chosen us in his Son Jesus Christ, and has given us the same Christ as our defender and saviour, who may be present with us, rule us and keep us to the glory of his name and the building up of his Church. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XL.
units.tr: HOMILY XL.

units.la: Illud autem dico: Qui serit parce, parce etiam metet: & qui serit benedictione fretus, cum benedictione metet. Quisque sicut prae optat corde, non ex tristitia aut necessitate. Nam hilarem datorem diligit Deus. Potens est autem Deus efficere, vt omnis gratia in vos redundet: vt in omnibus semper omnino quantum sufficiat penes vos habentes, abundetis in omne opus bonum: Sicut scriptum est, Dispersit, dedit pauperibus, iustitia eius manet in saeculum.
units.tr: I say this: he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and he who sows relying on a blessing will reap with a blessing. Let each give as he has decided in his heart, not out of sadness or necessity, for God loves a cheerful giver. God is able to make all grace abound toward you, so that always, in all things, having enough for yourselves, you may abound in every good work. As it is written: "He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever."

units.la: Paulus Apostolus Corinthios ad beneficentiam erga pauperes ita hortatur, vt simul diligenter ea omnia remoueat, quae nos in hoc studio impedire solent. Est inter ea praecipuum solicitudo carnis, quae fere metuit, ne dum alijs nostra largimur, ipsi ad egestatem redigamur. Quae causa est, quòd multi vel omnino nihil dant, vel maligne & animo invito fuerit et tiante dant. Itaque huic malo Apostolus mederi studet. Et nuper quidem dixit, se Titum & alios fratres eo misisse ob causam ad ipsos praemittere, vt ipsis tempus & occasio suppetat conferendi: ne si ipse cum Macedonicedonibus aduenerit, imparatos inueniat, sed tales tunc sint, vt omnibus constare possit, collectam illam ab ipsis alacri & laeto animo ex Dei benedictione factam, non autem munus esse, quod necessitas aliqua aut vis inuitis extorserit. Id vero in praesenti diligentius explicat, & est locus hic confideratu dignissimus.
units.tr: The Apostle urges the Corinthians to show kindness to the poor, and at the same time he carefully removes the things that usually hinder us in this effort. Chief among them is the anxiety of the flesh, which fears that if we give to others, we ourselves will be reduced to want. This is why many give nothing at all, or give grudgingly and with an unwilling mind. The Apostle therefore takes pains to remedy this evil. Earlier he said that he had sent Titus and other brothers ahead to them for this reason, so that they would have time and opportunity to collect the gift, lest, if he himself came with the Macedonians, he would find them unprepared. He wanted them to be such that everyone could agree that the collection was made by them with a willing and cheerful mind, out of the blessing of God, and was not a gift which some necessity or force had wrung from unwilling people. Now he explains this more carefully, and this passage deserves the closest attention.

units.la: Principio rationem adducit, cur liberaliter conferre aut largiri debeant. Illud autem dico, id est, haec mea est sententia, vel potius ratio, quae me vt istud moneam, monet: Qui serit parce, parce etiam metet: & qui serit benedictione fretus, cum benedictione metet. Opponit haec illis, qui metuunt, ne ipsis aliquid decedat: et sensus est, tales adeo falli, vt potius egentiores fiant, qui tenaciores aequo sua seruare satagunt: cum e contra remunerationem a Deo largissimam recipiant, qui benefici sunt & liberales. Quod autem simpliciter dicere poterat, id similitudine expolit, quae ratione quoq; huius dicti continet: eo quod beneficentia in pauperes eadem sit ratio, quae sementis est. Ita enim solet Spiritus sanctus parabolis & similibus ea illustrare, quae maioris momenti sunt, vt penitius animis insideat, & frequentius occurrat de ijsdem cogitandi occasio. Quae etiam causa est, quod Paulus in praesenti propositionibus vniuersalibus vtitur, vt nimirum singuli ista ad se pertinere intelligant, vtpote doctrinam generalem, quae apud omnes & omni tempore rata sit. Et debet diligentius considerari haec sementis & messis parabola, vt quae omnia complectitur, quae de toto hoc negotio dici possunt.
units.tr: First, he gives the reason why they ought to give generously and bountifully. "I say this," that is, "this is my opinion, or rather the reasoning which advises me to give you this counsel: he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and he who sows relying on a blessing will reap with a blessing." He sets this against those who fear that something will be taken from them, and the sense is that such people are deceived to such an extent that those who are too stingy in keeping their goods become poorer, whereas those who are beneficent and generous receive from God the most abundant reward. What he could have said plainly, he sets out in a comparison, which in its reasoning also contains the force of this saying, since kindness to the poor follows the same principle as sowing. The Holy Spirit is accustomed to illustrate weightier matters in this way, through parables and similitudes, so that they sink more deeply into the mind and the occasion for thinking about them recurs more often. This is also why Paul here uses universal statements, so that each person may understand that these things apply to himself, since it is a general teaching, valid for all people and at all times.
