And this parable of sowing and reaping should be considered more carefully, since it embraces everything that can be said about this whole matter.

units.la: Qui sementem facit, hoc ipsum seminat, quod prius ex Dei benedictione accepit. Quis enim semen propria industria aut arte creare possit? Ita pauperibus no alia damus, quam quae nobis ita ante a Deo data sunt. Hic enim de fidelium siue piorum eleemosynis sermo est, qui ex suo largiuntur, id est, ex ijs, quae a Deo accepta iusto titulo possidet: no ex alienis, quae vel rapto, vel dolo, aut alijs medijs illicitis acquisiuerunt. Deinde qui seminat, no omne frumentum terrae aut sulcis mandat, sed partem modo eorum, quae in horreis condita habet, reliqua vero vsui necessario seruat: Ita nemo iubetur omnem suam substantiam egenis largiri, sed licet vnicuique retinere, quae sibi & suis alendis sufficiant: quia de re in proximo Cap. est dictum. Praeterea in sementem frumentum in terram proijcitur, sic vt nunquam ad agricolam rediturum putetur. Nam in agro sparsum occa subigitur, subactu emorimur & computrescit. Ita qui facultates suas pauperibus largiuntur, eas videntur perdere. Sunt enim bi infir agri, vacui & sterilis, cum ex seipsis neque habeant, neque possint aliquid. Quid, quod ijdem saepe ne in conspectum quidem nostrum amplius veniunt, postquam beneficium a nobis acceperunt? Quis ergo ex illis speret aliquid? Vt autem Dei Benedictione semen germinat, & messis tandem agricolam exhilarat, qui de illa ne dubitare quidem potest, quia Deum sic instituisse nouit: Ita beneficentiam in egenos retributio sequitur, de qua nemo pius dubitare potest, cum hanc Deus promiserit, & exempla infinita occurrant, quae promissionibus illis fidem faciunt. Et huc impri-mis pertinet quod in praesenti Apostolus dicit. Qui enim sementem facit parcius, is messem quoque habet tenuiorem. Rursus, qui in benedictione, id est, liberali & alacri diuinae benedictionis fiducia fretus (Germani dicimus, vff Gottes sägen hin) sementem facit largam & copiosam, idem ille messe quoque vberiori donatur: Ita qui ad rem attentior est, & ideo in inuandis egenis sordidior, is Deum quoque minus liberalem erga se sentiet, qui interea remunerator est prodigalissimus (vt ita dicam) erga omnes, qui in suos munificentiam exercent.
units.tr: He who sows seed sows what he first received from God's blessing. For who could create seed by his own industry or skill? So we give nothing to the poor except what has likewise been given to us beforehand by God. Here the discussion concerns the almsgiving of believers or the godly, who give from what is their own, that is, from what they possess by a just title received from God, and not from what others have acquired by robbery, fraud, or other unlawful means. Next, the one who sows does not commit every grain of wheat to the furrows, but only part of what he has stored in his barns, and keeps the rest for necessary use. Thus no one is commanded to give all his substance to the needy, but each is permitted to keep what suffices for himself and his family, as was said in the preceding chapter. Moreover, in sowing, the grain is cast into the earth in such a way that it is not thought ever to return to the farmer. For the scattered seed is covered by the harrow, and in being covered it dies and rots. So those who give their means to the poor seem to lose them. For those fields are empty and barren, since they have neither anything of their own nor the power to produce anything. And what of the fact that these same people often no longer even come into our sight after they have received a benefit from us? Who then could hope for anything from them? But just as the seed sprouts by God's blessing, and the harvest at last gladdens the farmer, who cannot even doubt this because he knows God has so ordained it, so the repayment follows kindness to the needy, about which no godly person can doubt, since God has promised it, and countless examples present themselves which give credit to those promises. And to this especially the Apostle's words here pertain: "For he who sows sparingly also reaps sparingly." Again, he who sows in blessing, that is, relying on the generous and cheerful confidence in God's blessing (as we Germans say, "auf Gottes Segen hin," on God's blessing), sows generously and abundantly, and he is likewise rewarded with a richer harvest. So he who is too attentive to his property, and therefore too stingy in helping the needy, will find God less generous toward himself, while God, as the most lavish rewarder (so to speak) of all who exercise kindness toward their own, remains so.

units.la: Ex quo euidentissime sequitur, eos qui sua egenis distribuunt, illa non amittere, sed potius seruare & augere. Et simul hoc loco causam monstrat Spiritus sanctus, cur hodie multorum opes parum faustae sint & euanidae? Nimirum quia pauci in benedictione Dei respiciunt, sed diuitias suis cuiusque laboribus parari arbitrantur. Fit ergo, vt per fas & nefas corradant, neq; vlla aequitatis aut charitatis ratione ducantur. Idem postea opibus quaesitis vel turpissime abutuntur, vel etiam vti non audent, dum aceruo suo malis artibus cogesto metuunt. Itaq; parcissimi sunt in eos, qui ipsis quam maxime commendati esse debebant, & eode argumento se a Dei quoq; dilectione alienos esse produnt. Est enim non minus verum quam graue istud Apostoli dictum: Qui non diligit fratrem suum quem videt, Deum quem non videt quomodo potest diligere? Hinc vero inexhausta omnis generis malorum seges nascitur. Nam vero et proprio opum suarum vsu homines seipsos spoliant: conscientiam suam curis & sollicitudinibus assiduis grauant: corda sua ad Dei Verbum obturat: deniq; mandatione sibi ipsis acceperunt, qua fit, vt aut ipsis adhuc viuentibus opes male dilabantur, aut ipsis praeter expectationem mors inopina obrepat, quae inuitos & nequicquam quiritantes abripit. Sequitur fere, quod de diuite illo epulone Christus tradidit, vt apud inferos horribili siti excruciet ur, qui absque misericordia inter suarum opum aceruos delitiati sunt. In horum meditatione frequentiores sint, quotquot se natura ad rem attentiores esse sentunt.
units.tr: From this it follows most clearly that those who distribute their goods to the needy do not lose them but rather keep and increase them. At the same time, the Holy Spirit shows here the cause why the wealth of many today is so unlucky and short-lived. Surely it is because few look to God's blessing, but suppose that riches are acquired by each man's own labors. So it comes about that they heap up wealth by right and wrong alike, and are guided by no principle of justice or charity. Afterward they either abuse their hoarded riches most shamefully or do not dare to use them at all, since they fear for their pile, gathered by wicked arts. Therefore they are most stingy toward those to whom they ought especially to be commended, and by the same token they show that they are estranged from God's love as well. For the Apostle's grave saying is no less true than it is serious: "He who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?" From this indeed springs an inexhaustible harvest of evils of every kind. For men also rob themselves of the proper use of their goods: they burden their conscience with constant cares and anxieties; they stop up their hearts against the Word of God; and finally they receive for themselves a curse, so that either their wealth slips away badly while they are still living, or sudden death creeps upon them beyond expectation and snatches them away, unwilling and crying out in vain. What Christ taught about that rich man who feasted sumptuously follows almost of necessity: that he is tormented in Hades by dreadful thirst, since he lived in luxury without mercy amid heaps of his goods. Let those who feel that by nature they are more attentive to such things reflect on these matters more often.

units.la: Caeterum ne putaretur Apostolus benedictionem siue remunerationem Dei ad donorum, quae pauperibus conferuntur, magnitudinem siue pretium restringere, & ita eos abterreret, quibus facultates tenuiores sunt, quàm vt multa aliis largiri possint, huc quoque nodum soluit & explicat, dicens: Quisque sicut praeoptat corde, nō ex tristitia aut necessitate, &c. Quasi diceret: Nolim quod de semente dixi, ad eleemosynas ita referr, vt has ex pretio æstimari putetis. In semente quidē quò plus feritur, eò plus metitur: qui vero minus ferunt, quia vel nolunt vel non possunt aliter, idem minus quoque metunt. At hic ratio longè alia est. Vt enim non omnes eadem possunt, ita neque Deus eadem ab omnibus requirit. Faciat ergo quisque sicut praeoptat corde, id est, sicuti apud se statuit, & quantum animus ipsi praescribit aut mandat: & hoc solum curet, ne quid ex tristitia aut necessitate faciat, id est, animo inuito & coacto. Rationem huic admonitioni subijcit: Nam hilarem datorem diligit Deus. Quo loco obseruari debet Dei bonitas paterna, qui cum omnia a nobis exigere posset pro suo iure, nō plus tamen postulat, quàm fortunae aut facultates nostrae ferunt. Itaq; eleemosynas nō ex donorū multitudine aut pretio æstimat, sed ex eius animo qui largitur. Quae ratione fieri potest (vt Chrysostomus scribit) vt qui obolum dedit, Dei iudicio liberalior sit eo, qui cētum aureos contulit. Et huc pertinet exemplum viduae illius pauperculae, quam Christus diuitibus omnibus praefert, quòd ex tenuitate sua duo aera minuta in gazophylacium deposuisset. Vide Mar.12.
units.tr: Moreover, lest it be thought that the Apostle limits God's blessing or reward to the size or value of the gifts given to the poor, and so frightens off those whose means are too slender to give much to others, he resolves this knot as well and explains it, saying: "Let each give as he has decided in his heart, not out of sadness or necessity," and so on. As if he said: "I would not want what I said about sowing to be applied to alms in such a way that you think these are measured by their price. In sowing, indeed, the more that is sown, the more is reaped; but those who sow less, because they are unwilling or unable to do otherwise, likewise reap less. But here the reasoning is quite different. For just as not all can give the same, so neither does God require the same from all. Let each one therefore do as he has decided in his heart, that is, as he has settled within himself, and as his mind prescribes or commands him; and let him take care only that he does nothing out of sadness or necessity, that is, with an unwilling and forced mind." He adds a reason for this admonition: "For God loves a cheerful giver." Here we ought to observe the fatherly goodness of God, who, although he could demand everything from us as his right, requires no more than our fortunes or means can bear. Therefore he does not measure alms by the multitude or the price of the gifts, but by the mind of the giver. In this way (as Chrysostom writes) it can happen that he who gave a small coin is, in God's judgment, more generous than he who contributed a hundred gold pieces. To this also belongs the example of that poor widow, whom Christ placed above all the rich, because out of her poverty she had put two small coins into the treasury. See Mark 12.

units.la: Imprimis autem caueri debent vitia, quorum in praesenti Paulus meminit. Primum est tristitia, quae auaros perpetuò comitari solet, eò quòd se amittere putant quaecumque egenis largiuntur. Quare ita fere his subueniunt, vt interea perditos vellent, & plerumque inter largiendum ijf dem exprobrant atque conuiciantur. Hi omnem beneficij gratiam amittunt, & ipsis etiam egenis nouae tristitiae authores sunt, qui non alia re magis quàm dantis hilaritate delectantur. Imò neque eleemosynae nomen meretur quòd isti faciunt. Haec enim a misericordia dicitur, quae vt aliorum miserijs mouetur, ita benefaciendo gaudet. Quod alibi quoque Paulus monet, dicens: Qui miseretur, cū hilaritate. Alterū vitiū, quod hic caueri debet, est necessitas: ne quid nimirum faciamus coacti. Nec enim de absoluta necessitate loquitur, qua omnes ad Dei & proximi dilectionem, ad beneficentiam, vitae sanctimoniā obstringimur, adeò, vt sine his neq; Christi discipuli esse, neque Deo placere possimus: sed de coactione, quae aliunde accedit, quando iftafectamur quidem, non autē ideo, vt Deo debitum praestemus obsequium, sed quia vel ambitione et gloriae studio impellimur, vel publico reipub. aut Ecclesiae decreto vrgemur, vt pro facultatū nostrarum ratione contribuamus in pauperū subuentione. Tales nihil merentur, quia inuiti faciunt quicquid faciunt, & (quod Christus in primis vetuit) sinistram manum conscium faciunt eorū, quae facit dextera. Neque tamen damnantur hic qui inter largiendum pugnam carnis & spiritus sentiunt, quae frequenter in electis quoq; sese exerit. Vincat modò spiritus, & subigatur caro, vt vel inuita officium faciat. Nam ex cordis voluntate æstimatur beneficentia, et vt in aliis rebus exercitia prosunt, vt tandem leue nobis fiat, quod initiò intolerabile videbatur: ita hic quoque fieri solet, vt quò plura in pauperes conferimus, eò magis assuescamus beneficentiae, & ex ea voluptatem quoque capiamus.
units.tr: First, the vices that Paul mentions here must be guarded against. The first is sadness, which usually accompanies the miserly, because they think they lose whatever they give to the needy. So they help the poor in such a way that they would rather the poor perish, and while they give they often reproach and abuse the very people they are helping. These people lose all the grace of the benefit, and they become the authors of fresh sadness even for the needy, since they take their greatest pleasure in nothing so much as the giver's cheerfulness. Indeed, what such people do does not deserve the name of almsgiving. For alms come from mercy, which is moved by the miseries of others and rejoices in doing good. Paul also warns of this elsewhere, saying: "He who shows mercy, let him do it with cheerfulness." The second vice to be guarded against here is necessity, that is, that we should do something under compulsion. He is not speaking of that absolute necessity by which all of us are bound to love God and neighbour, to beneficence and holiness of life, so that without these we cannot be disciples of Christ or please God. He means the compulsion that comes from elsewhere, when we do these things not so that we may render God the obedience owed to him, but because we are driven by ambition and the desire for glory, or are pressed by a public decree of the commonwealth or the Church to contribute to the relief of the poor according to our means. Such people merit nothing, because whatever they do, they do unwillingly, and (which Christ especially forbade) they let the left hand know what the right hand is doing. Yet those who, while giving, feel the struggle of flesh and spirit are not condemned, a struggle that often breaks out even in the elect. Let only the spirit conquer and the flesh be subdued, so that even if unwilling, it performs the duty. For beneficence is measured by the will of the heart, and just as in other matters practice helps, so that what at first seemed intolerable at last becomes light to us, so it usually happens here too: the more we contribute to the poor, the more we grow accustomed to beneficence and take pleasure in it.

units.la: Et debet hic semper animis nostris obuersari, quòd hilarem datorem Deus diligit. Quia enim hic cor hominis totum requirit, nunquam poterit eorum officia probare, qui tristes & inuiti ea obeunt. Cur enim tales probaret Deus, qui nullius est indigus, quando ne homines quidem ingenui sibi ab inuitis seruiri nolunt? Tyrannorum vox est: Oderint, dum metuant. Deus populum spiritualem requirit qui ipsum colat in spiritu & veritate. Deinde eleemosyna sacrificium est, quo vix aliud Deo magis gratum est & acceptum. Nam apud Prophetam ille ait: Misericordiam volo, & non sacrificium. Et ad Hebraeos scribit Apostolus: Beneficentiae & communicationis ne obliui scamini: talibus enim victimis delectatur Deus. At sacrificia voluntaria esse oportebat olim, & dies festos cum laetitia Deus celebrari voluit. Recte ergo Sirachides ille monuit: Quicquid donatu rus es, vultu induas hilarem: & decimas cum laetitia consecra. Quia vero datores eiusmodi Deus diligit, ijsdem haud dubiè benedicit quoque, & quæcunque ipso iubente in egenos conferunt libera-lissimè remunerabitur, vt supra diximus.
units.tr: And we should always keep before our minds that God loves a cheerful giver. Since he requires the whole heart of a man, he can never approve the duties of those who perform them sadly and unwillingly. For why would God approve of people who are in need of nothing, when even free men do not want to be served by the unwilling? It is the voice of tyrants: "Let them hate, provided they fear." God requires a spiritual people who worship him in spirit and in truth. Moreover, almsgiving is a sacrifice, and scarcely anything else is more pleasing and acceptable to God. For the Prophet says: "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice." And the Apostle writes to the Hebrews: "Do not forget beneficence and fellowship, for with such sacrifices God is delighted." But sacrifices had to be voluntary of old, and God wished feast days to be celebrated with joy. Rightly, then, that son of Sirach admonished: "Whatever you give, put on a cheerful countenance, and consecrate your tithes with joy." And because God loves such givers, he doubtless also blesses them, and whatever they bestow on the needy at his command he will repay most generously, as we said above.

units.la: Quapropter in præsenti subijcit Paulus: Potens est autem Deus efficere, vt omnis gratia in vos redundet, vt in omnibus semper omnino quantum sufficiat penes vos habentes, abundetis in omne opus bonum. Confirmat his verbis quod de remuneratione aut retributione dixit, & ita quidem, vt omnibus argumentis occurrat, quæ caro auara & sordida solet prætexere, si quid liberaliter agendum est. Præcipuè in his est, quòd solis præsentibus intenta, impossibile putat aliquid ex illis recipere qui & nihil habent, et nihil etiam possunt eorum præstare, quibus nobis opus est. Adhuc videre nō potest caro, quomodo non aliquando inopes fiant, qui sua aliis largiuntur. Ideo nos Paulus ad Deū remittit, et huius omnipotentiā nobis commendat, ne in nostro sensu et carnis rationibus subsistamus, sed meminerimus nihil esse, quod illi factu non sit facillimum. Et ita nos facere convenit in omnibus, de quibus voluntatem suam Deus nobis disertis verbis manifestauit. Sed præstat singula verba diligentius excutere. Primò Deum potentem esse dicit. Quid enim non posşit, qui in rerum principio omnia solius Verbi sui virtute ex nihilo produxit, & cuius nutus ad omnia sufficit, vt vocet quæ non sunt, vt sint? Sed ad præsentem causam hoc restringens Paulus, ait: Potens est Deus efficere, vt omnis gratia in vos redundet. Gratia vocabulo benedictionem gratuitam intelligit: per redundantiam verò bonorum omnium tam corporalium quàm spiritualium copiam, adeoq; superfluitatem. Quomodo enim non bearet homines sua benedictione, quando huius virtutem terra rudis & omnes aliæ creaturæ sentiunt? Tu aperis manum tuam (inquit Dauid) & saturas desiderium omnium animantium. Item: Qui dat pecori pabulum suum, & pullis coruorum, qui eum invocant, &c. Id verò Corinthijs applicans Paulus, addit. Vt in omnibus semper omnino quantum sufficiat penes vos habentes, abundetis in omne opus bonum. In Græco vox αὐτάρκεια habetur, quæ partim sufficientem omnium, quæ nobis necessaria sunt, facultatem siue copiam significat: partim animum quoque sua sorte contentum, qui nihil præter ea, quæ Deus dedit, desiderat siue expetit. Hinc αὐτάρκης dicitur, qui ipse sibi sufficit, vt non opus habeat quicquam aliunde emendicare: qui item suis contentus ab alienis abstinet, & inordinatas carnis cupiditates refrenat. In præsenti vterque sensus commodè potest coniungi.
units.tr: Therefore Paul adds in the present passage: "God is able to make all grace abound toward you, so that always, in all things, having all sufficiency, you may abound in every good work." By these words he confirms what he said about reward or recompense, and he does so in such a way as to meet all the arguments that a greedy and sordid flesh is accustomed to put forward when something must be given generously. Chief among these is the thought that the flesh, intent only on present things, judges it impossible to receive anything back from those who have nothing and cannot provide any of the things we need. The flesh cannot yet see how those who give their own to others do not sometimes become poor. So Paul sends us back to God, and commends to us his omnipotence, so that we do not rest on our own judgment and the reasoning of the flesh, but remember that there is nothing which is not most easy for him to do. And we ought to act in this way in all matters concerning which God has made his will known to us in plain words. But it is worth examining each word more carefully. First, he says that God is powerful. For what could he not do, who in the beginning of things produced all things out of nothing by the sole power of his Word, and whose nod suffices for all things, so that he calls the things that are not, that they may be? But restricting this to the present case, Paul says: "God is able to make all grace abound toward you." By "grace" he understands free blessing; by "abounding," the abundance and even superabundance of all good things, both bodily and spiritual. For how could he not make men blessed by his blessing, when even the rough earth and all other creatures feel its power? "You open your hand," says David, "and satisfy the desire of every living thing." Likewise: "He gives to the beast its food, and to the young ravens that call upon him," and so on. Applying this to the Corinthians, Paul adds: "that always, in all things, having all sufficiency, you may abound in every good work." In the Greek the word is αὐτάρκεια [autarkeia], which signifies partly a sufficient supply or abundance of all the things we need, and partly also a mind content with its lot, which desires or seeks nothing beyond what God has given. Hence one who is self-sufficient is called αὐτάρκης [autarkēs], that is, one who has enough in himself, so as not to need to beg anything from elsewhere; likewise one who, content with his own, abstains from what belongs to others and restrains the disordered desires of the flesh. In the present passage both senses can conveniently be joined.

units.la: Admonet ergo locus iste, quæ & qualis sit retributio illa, qua Deus suorum munificentiā siue liberalitatem compensat. Primo dat illis unde viuant. At hic non adeo multis opus est, neque in multarum opum abundantia (vt Christus ait) hominis vita consistit. Et ferè commodius viuitur inter modicas fortunæ facultates, cùm è contra diuites circa multa occupati, neque cibum neque somnum quietè & tutò possint capere. Quàmus interdum opes quoque ingentes Deus suis largitur, vt in Abrahamo, Iobo & similibus esse videre. Id tamen neque perpetuum est, neque omnibus contingit. Scit enim Deus, quantum nobis vtile sit dari, & vnicuique dat quantum sufficit. Itaque etsi non omnes diuitiis abundent, generale tamen est, quod Dauid se obseruauisse dicit: Iuuenis fui, & nunc senui, nec vidi iustum desertum, neque posteros eius mendicantes panem. Exemplo nobis sunt Apostoli, qui etsi absque pecuniis & commeatu à Christo emissi essent, sibi tamen nihil vnquam defuisse testantur. Deinde animos dat suis Deus, qui forte sua contenti nihil præterea expetant. Est hic quæstus longè uberrimus (vt alibi Paulus docet) qui omnes huius mundi thesauros superat. Nam si hos omnes in unum aceruum congeras, auari tamen animum saturare non possunt, cui tam deest quod habet, quàm quod non habet. Et vt Satyricus dicebat, Crescit amor nummi, quantū ipsa pecunia crescit. Solus ille dives, cui nihil deest. At nihil deest solis ijs, qui certa animi fiducia in vnū Deum reumbunt, & ab eo solo pendent. Nam quicunq; circa res huius sæculi occupantur, ij perpetuo desiderijs æstuāt, quæ nunquā satiantur. Solus Deus summū illud ac æternū bonū est, quòd fide vera apprehensum, hominis animā per se insatiabile saturat & vere securā reddit. Ex eo autem tertium sequitur, quòd qui in Deo omnia reposita habent, ijdem abundent in omne opus bonum: Vt nimirum non solum benefici sint, verumetiam alijs virtutibus conspicui. Vt enim omnium scelerum fons est philautia, quæ facit vt nemo sua sorte contentus sit, sed plerique aliena appetant, unde impostura, furta, rapinæ, vagæ libidines, ambitiones, concertationes, seditiones, cædes, bella denique nascuntur: Ita qui à Dei benedictione toti pendent, & ijs contenti viuunt,quæ ab illo in diem accipiunt, ij non solùm ab omnibus istis abstinent, verumetiam omnibus prodesse student,humiles & modesti sunt,pacifici itẽ & temperantes, vitam denique viuunt sanctam & innocuam, & insuper aduersam quoque forturam patienter ferunt. Atqui hæc sunt,quæ vitâm in hoc sæculo nobis vere beatam & iucundam reddunt,& proinde am plissima est retributio illa,qua Deus suorum beneficentiam remunerat.
units.tr: This passage, then, shows what and what sort of recompense it is by which God repays the generosity or liberality of his people. First, he gives them what they live on. Yet they do not need very much, and, as Christ says, a man's life does not consist in the abundance of many possessions. And one lives more comfortably, as a rule, with modest means, whereas the rich, occupied with many concerns, cannot take food or sleep quietly and safely. Although God sometimes grants great wealth to his own, as we see in Abraham, Job and others like them, this is neither permanent nor given to all. For God knows how much it is useful for us to be given, and he gives each one as much as is sufficient. Therefore, even if not all abound in riches, it is nevertheless the general rule, which David says he himself observed: "I have been young, and now I am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his children begging bread." The Apostles are an example for us: although they were sent out by Christ without money or provisions, they nevertheless testify that nothing ever failed them. Next, God gives his people minds which, content perhaps with what they have, desire nothing further. This gain is by far the richest (as Paul teaches elsewhere), and it surpasses all the treasures of this world. For even if you heap all of these into one pile, the miser's mind still cannot be satisfied, since he lacks as much what he has as what he does not have. And as the satirist said: "The love of money grows as money itself grows." Only that man is rich to whom nothing is lacking. But nothing is lacking only to those who rest with a firm confidence of mind in the one God and depend on him alone. For all who are occupied with the things of this age are perpetually burning with desires which are never satisfied. God alone is that highest and eternal good, which, when apprehended by true faith, satisfies the human soul, which is insatiable in itself, and makes it truly secure. Moreover, from this there follows a third point: those who have all things laid up in God abound in every good work, so that they are not only beneficent but also distinguished by other virtues. For just as self-love is the source of all wickedness, since it makes no one content with his lot, but leads most people to covet what belongs to others, from which deceit, thefts, robberies, wandering lusts, ambitions, quarrels, seditions, murders, and finally wars are born, so those who wholly depend on God's blessing and live content with what they receive from him day by day, not only abstain from all these things but also strive to benefit everyone; they are humble and modest, peaceful and temperate, and in short they live a holy and blameless life, and moreover they bear adversity patiently too. And these are the things that truly make our life in this age blessed and pleasant; therefore that recompense by which God rewards the beneficence of his people is most abundant.

units.la: Ista vero auaros & insatiabiles arguunt,qui non contenti necessarijs, iniquius secum agi putant,si non sit quo luxurientur & sese ostentent. Atqui non ea nobis pollicetur Deus, sed αὐτάρ- κειαν, quæ (vt Chrysostomus rectè admonet )ijs limitatur, sine quibus non potest viui. Sunt ea victus & amictus,sub quo domicilium quoque comprehenditur. Itaque nobis à Deo destinata dicit,τροφὰς,ϰ τρυφὰς,ϰ ἱματισμάτα,ϰ καλλωπισμάτα, id est, alimenta, non voluptatum & libidinum fomenta:amictum, non ornatum fastui aut luxui seruientem : domicilium item sufficiens, non insana palatia.Quibus consentit quod Paulus alibi scribit: Nihil intulimus in mundum, videlicet nec efferre quicquam possumus : Sed habentes alimenta & quibus tegamur,his contenti eri mus. Et sanè(quod supra quoque monuimus) commodius & suauius viuunt qui his contenti sunt, quàm alteri illi,qui in sua abundantia tumultuantur,& sibi ipsis labores,curas, vigilias,multorum odia,pericula,morbos denique & inortem immaturam accersunt.
units.tr: These words, however, rebuke the greedy and insatiable, who, not content with what is necessary, think they are treated too unfairly if they have no means to indulge in luxury and display themselves. Yet God does not promise us that, but self-sufficiency [αὐτάρκειαν], which (as Chrysostom rightly reminds us) is limited to those things without which one cannot live. These are food and clothing, and a dwelling is included under them. So he says that God has appointed for us nourishment [τροφὰς], delicacies [τρυφὰς], clothing [ἱματισμάτα] and ornaments [καλλωπισμάτα], that is, food, not fuel for pleasures and lusts; clothing, not decoration serving pride or luxury; and likewise a sufficient dwelling, not mad palaces. Paul agrees with this elsewhere when he writes: "We brought nothing into the world, and clearly we can carry nothing out. But having food and things to cover us, we shall be content with these." And indeed (as we noted above as well) those who are content with these live more comfortably and pleasantly than those others who bustle about in their abundance and heap upon themselves labours, cares, sleepless nights, the hatred of many, dangers, diseases, and finally an untimely death.

units.la: Cæterùm ne quod de retributione Dei Dixit Apostolus, ex suo capite finxisse putetur,hoc ipsum Scripturæ veteris testimonio confirmat,dicens:Sicut scriptum est : Dispersit,dedit pauperibus, iustitia eius manet in sæculum. Extat locus hic in Psalmo 112: qui doctrinam vtilissimam & assiduâ meditatione dignam continet. Docet enim , quæ vera sit hominis felicitas tam in hoc præsenti quàm futuro sæculo,& qua ratione ad eam peruenire possimus.
units.tr: Moreover, lest it be thought that the Apostle invented what he said about God's reward from his own head, he confirms it by the testimony of the Old Scripture, saying: "As it is written: He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever." This passage is found in Psalm 112, which contains teaching most useful and worthy of constant meditation. For it teaches what the true happiness of man is, both in this present age and in the age to come, and by what means we may attain to it.

units.la: Propositio totius Psalmi est: Beatus vir, qui timet Dominum, & præceptis eius delectatur. Dei timorem veræ felicitatis quasi fundamentum collocat,eò quod idem ille sapientiæ principium est, sine qua nemo beatè aut feliciter viuit. Distinguit autem inter salutarem Dei timorem & terrificum illum atque noxium,quem apud impios quoq;imò apud dæmones locum habere constat. Nam de eo loquitur Psaltes, qui non nisi filijs Dei proprius, & cum fidei obedientia coniunctus est,& facit, vt ex Dei præceptis voluptatem capiamus.
units.tr: The theme of the whole Psalm is: "Blessed is the man who fears the Lord and delights in his commandments." He lays the fear of God down as the foundation of true happiness, because it is the beginning of wisdom, without which no one lives blessedly or happily. He distinguishes, however, between the saving fear of God and that terrifying and harmful fear which is known to have a place among the impious, and even among demons. For the Psalmist speaks of that fear which belongs only to the sons of God, is joined with obedient faith, and makes us take pleasure in God's precepts.

units.la: Deinde quæ & qualis sit horum felicitas,docet:Potens erit in terra semen eius,& generationi rectorum benedicitur.Id vero ex fœdere Dei desumit,quod is cum Abrahamo ea conditione percussit, quòd tà ipsius quàm seminis sui Deus esse velit. Addit: Copia rerum & diuitiæ erunt in domo eius, & iustitia eius æterna stabit.Vbi rursus inter Dei timentes & impios distinguit. Nam hi quoq;interdum opulentissimi sunt,sed absq; iustitia,& quia ferè opes iniquè partas possident,eadem infelices & fluxæ sunt. Alia autem est piorum conditio,qui ex Dei benedictione habent quicquid habet, & proinde titulo iustissimo sua possident.Vnde sequitur: Oritur in tenebris lux probis, beneficio, misericordi & iusto.Id est,Licet interdum aduersa incidant, Deus tamen talibus inter pericula vndè que imminentia suæ bonitatis luce assulget,eosdem consolatur,& viam effugij monstrat.
units.tr: Then he teaches what this happiness of theirs is and what kind it is: "His seed will be mighty on earth, and the generation of the upright will be blessed." He draws this from the covenant of God, which God struck with Abraham on the condition that he would be God both to Abraham and to his seed. He adds: "Plenty and riches will be in his house, and his righteousness will stand forever." Here again he distinguishes between those who fear God and the impious. For the latter too are sometimes very wealthy, but without righteousness; and since they mostly possess wealth unjustly acquired, they are for that very reason unhappy and transitory. But the condition of the pious is different: they have from God's blessing whatever they have, and therefore possess their goods by the most just title. Hence it follows: "Light rises in darkness for the upright, the gracious, the merciful and the just." That is, although adversities sometimes befall them, God nevertheless shines upon such people with the light of his goodness amid dangers threatening on every side, comforts them, and shows them the way of escape.

units.la: His tertio loco mores & studia istorum subijcit:Vir bonus benefacit, & dat mutuò : res suas agit cum iudicio:Vt nimirum non cæcis carnis affectibus ducatur.Ideo non mouetur in æternum, sed sibi ipsi semper constat,ideò memoria quoque iusti ʃsq; durat. Adsamem tristem non expauescet:vtpote bene sibi conscius.Nam cor eius firmum est,& Domino fidit.Cor(inquam )eius stabile est,vt non expauescat,donec spectet in hostibus suis quod cupit.Istis subijcit Propheta, quod in præsenti Paulus citat:Dispersit, dedit pauperibus, iustitia eius manet in sæculum, cornuq; eius altum erit cum gloria,&c.Quibus verbis omne illud continetur,quod de vera liberalitate & iusta opum dispensatione dici potest. Vbi hæc nobis consideranda veniunt.
units.tr: To these things he adds, in the third place, the morals and pursuits of these people: "A good man does good and lends; he manages his affairs with judgment," namely so that he is not led by blind fleshly passions. Therefore he is not moved forever, but always remains consistent with himself, and therefore the memory of the just also endures. He will not be terrified by evil tidings, being conscious of his own goodness. For his heart is firm and trusts in the Lord. His heart, I say, is steadfast, so that it will not be terrified until it sees in his enemies what it desires. To these things the Prophet joins what Paul cites in the present passage: "He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever; his horn will be exalted with glory," and so on. In these words is contained everything that can be said about true liberality and the just dispensing of wealth. Here these matters come before us for consideration.

units.la: Primò modu liberalitatis & munificentiæ exprimit Dispergedi verbo. Dicitur hoc de rebus nò magni pretij,quas nò multu curamus,vel etiam noxijs,ex quib. periculu tiemetur. Admonet hoc, quales æstimari debeat diuitiæ.Vulgus hominũ nihil his præstatius , vtilius et beatius esse putat. Sed fluxæ sunt,caducæ sunt,et nihil in illis solidu est & perpetuu.Pertinet enim ad carnis cœsum, de qua Deo iubere clamat Propheta:Omnis caro fœnû & omnis gloria carnis flos agri.Et quàm- uis ad huius vitæ vsum faciat,in carũde tamẽ abundatia(vt Christus testatur)hominis vita ne quaquam consistit. Quis enim vniuersis huius seculi facultatibus vel propriæ vitæ diem vnû adij cere, vel animam suam ab interitu liberare potest? Adde his, quod eadem plurimum incommo- dant: quia scelerum causa & (vt poeta ait) irritamenta malorum sunt, pacem publicam turbant, charitati officiunt, lites indefinentes de Meo & Tuo pariunt, & ad cœlum tendentibus remora sunt omnium pernitiosissima, sicuti in diuitis illius exemplo apparet, qui cùm in pietate maximos progressus fecisset, tristis abijt, quando diuitias sibi relinquendas esse audiuit. Hæc ergo considerans quisquis Deum timet, adeo non addicit illis cor suum, vt potius dispergat, id est, liberaliter & absque omni tristitia in eos vsus eroget opes, quibus eas Deus destinauit. Nec enim hic incon-sultam prodigalitatem Spiritus sanctus præcipit, neque etiam vt pecunias in mare aut profluentem abijciamus, quod olim Crates ille Thebanus fecisse legitur: sed hac locutione ad sementis parabolam nos remittit, in qua semen cum gaudio proijci, adeoque dispergi solet.
units.tr: First, he expresses the manner of liberality and generosity by the word "scattered abroad." This is said of things of no great value, which we do not much care about, or even of harmful things from which danger is feared. It warns us what value riches ought to be esteemed at. The common crowd of men thinks nothing better, more useful or more blessed than these. But they are fleeting and perishable, and nothing in them is solid and lasting. For they belong to the flesh, concerning which the Prophet bids us cry out to God: "All flesh is grass, and all the glory of flesh is like the flower of the field." And although riches serve for the use of this life, nevertheless man's life by no means consists in the abundance of possessions, as Christ testifies. For who can add to his own life even one day by all the resources of this age, or free his soul from perishing? Add to these that riches do great harm: since they are the cause of crimes and (as the poet says) the incitements of evils, they disturb public peace, injure charity, give rise to endless quarrels over "mine" and "yours," and are the most pernicious hindrance to those who strive toward heaven, as appears in the example of that rich man, who, though he had made very great progress in piety, departed sad when he heard that he must leave his riches behind. Therefore whoever fears God, considering these things, does not so attach his heart to them that he would rather scatter them, that is, dispense his resources liberally and without any sadness, for those uses for which God has destined them. For the Holy Spirit does not here enjoin reckless prodigality, nor that we cast our money into the sea or a flowing river, as that Theban Crates is said to have done; rather, by this expression he sends us back to the parable of the sower, in which seed is cast with joy and in this way is usually scattered.

units.la: Ideo additur mox, quibus dispergat, aut largiatur? Pauperibus nimirum. Ergo non helluo- nibus, compotoribus, scortis, mimis, ambubaijs, sartoribus, cupediarijs distribuunt opes suas pij, neque eadem turpi aleæ committunt, aut in insanis ædificiorum non necessariorum structuris insumunt: neque etiam domi congerunt, vt nummos auidi contemplentur in arca, quibus nec ipsi vtantur, neque alios vti sinant. Sed quæ superflua habent, ea in pauperes distribuunt, non quidem impostores illos, qui voluntariam paupertatem profesi religionem sibi quæstum faciunt, quales sunt fratres illi, quos mendicantes dicunt, & tota fere sacrificulorum cohors: sed in vere pauperes, qui vel morbis confecti seipsos alere non possunt, vel alijs aduersis ad egestatem redacti ab aliorum liberalitate pendere coguntur. Hos enim nobis Christus commendauit, seq; pro illis sponsorem dedit, vt iam sæpe diximus. Sed o præposteram hominum prodigalitatem. Quam multi enim sua in homines turpissimos & omni scelere infames profundunt? Quam multi item pecunias cum valetudinis dispendio dilapidant, dum gulæ, ventri, & ijs quæ sub ventre sunt inseruiunt? Quàm multos etiam esse videre, qui in canes, accipitres, simias, cercopithecos, psitacos & alia peregrina animalia sumptus faciunt immodicos? At ijdem fere in egentia Christi membra parcissimi sunt, & omne illud sibi perijsse putant, quod in pauperes impenditur. Quis vero tales venia dignos dixerit?
units.tr: Why is it then added at once to whom they scatter or bestow? To the poor, surely. Therefore the pious do not distribute their wealth to gluttons, drinking companions, whores, mimes, jugglers, tailors and confectioners, nor do they entrust it to shameful dice, nor spend it on mad constructions of unnecessary buildings; nor do they even pile it up at home so that the greedy may gaze at their coins in a chest, which they themselves do not use and do not allow others to use. But what they have over and above they distribute to the poor: not indeed to those impostors who, professing voluntary poverty, make a profit out of religion, such as those brothers whom they call mendicants, and nearly the whole crowd of little priests; but to the truly poor, who, worn out by sickness, cannot support themselves, or who, reduced to want by other adversities, are forced to depend on the liberality of others. For Christ has commended these to us and has given himself as their surety, as we have often said. But oh, the monstrous prodigality of men! How many pour out their substance on the most vile men, infamous for every crime? How many likewise squander money to the detriment of their health, while they serve the belly, the gullet, and those things that lie below the belly? How many are seen to spend immoderately on dogs, hawks, apes, long-tailed monkeys, parrots and other foreign animals? Yet these same people are very stingy toward the members of Christ in need, and think that everything spent on the poor is lost to themselves. Who would call such people worthy of pardon?

units.la: Sed præmium audiamus, quod benefico & misericordi Psaltes pollicetur. Iustitia eius (in- quit) manet in seculum, cornu eius altum erit cum gloria. Iustitiæ vocabulum varie in Scripturis vsurpatur. Quoad præsens argumentum, sensus erit, beneficentiam piorum perpetuam esse, quia semper habituri sint quod egenis largiantur, & quod ipsi quoq; benefaciendo non fatigentur, sed potius quotidie in melius proficiant. Sed potest etiam de ea iustitia intelligi, quæ nos apud Dei tribunal tuetur. Est enim beneficentia hæc proprius charitatis effectus, quæ simul argumentum est fidei, per quam iustificamur. Quod si vero iustitia hæc æterna est, præmium quoq; eius æternum erit, & qui illi student, olim in tabernacula æterna (vt Christus ait) recipientur. Et rectissimè vtrumq; sensum coniunxeris. Hoc enim tam multiplici præmio Deus piorum beneficentiam remunerat. Primò enim dat illis, quæ ad vitam sustentandam sufficiunt. Agit præterea in illis Spiritu suo, vt indies in melius proficiant. Seruat item in aduersis & periculis. Adhæc Filij sui iustitiam ijsdem communicat. Sequitur tandem corona illa immarcescibilis, quam in cœlo olim obtinebunt cum omnibus electis, qui diligunt illustrem illum aduentum Domini & Seruatoris nostri, IESV CHRISTI cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: But let us hear the reward which the Psalmist promises to the beneficent and merciful man: "His righteousness," he says, "endures forever; his horn will be exalted with glory." The word righteousness is used in various ways in Scripture. As to the present argument, the sense will be that the beneficence of the pious is perpetual, because they will always have something to give to the needy, and because they themselves are not wearied by doing good, but rather day by day make progress for the better. But it can also be understood of that righteousness which defends us before the tribunal of God. For this beneficence is the proper effect of charity, which is at the same time a proof of the faith through which we are justified. And if this righteousness is indeed eternal, its reward too will be eternal, and those who strive for it will be received, as Christ says, into eternal tabernacles. And you would rightly join both senses together. For God rewards the beneficence of the pious with so manifold a recompense. First, he gives them what suffices to sustain life. Moreover, he works in them by his Spirit so that they daily make progress for the better. He also preserves them in adversities and dangers. Besides, he communicates to them the righteousness of his Son. Finally there follows that unfading crown, which they will one day obtain in heaven together with all the elect, who love the illustrious coming of the Lord and our Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power forever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLI.
units.tr: HOMILY XLI.

units.la: Porrò qui suppeditat semen serenti, is quoq; pane ad escam suppeditabit, & multiplicabit sementem vestram, & augebit fructus beneficentiæ vestræ: Vt in omnibus ditati ad omnem simplicitatem, quæ per nos efficit, vt gratiæ agantur Deo. Nam ministerium functionis istius non solum supplet inopiam sanctorum, verum etiam redundat per multas gratiarum actiones Deo; Dum per hoc documentum ministerij huius Deum glorificant de subiectione vestrae confessionis in Euangelium Christi, decp simplicitate communicationis in ipsos & in omnes. Et in illorum preces pro vobis, expetentium vos propter gratiam Dei in vobis exuberantem. Gratia autem sit Deo super inenarrabili suo munere.
units.tr: Now he who supplies seed to the sower will also supply bread for food, and will multiply your seed and increase the fruits of your beneficence, so that you, being enriched in everything, may have all simplicity, which through us produces thanksgiving to God. For the ministry of this service not only supplies the needs of the saints, but also overflows in many thanksgivings to God. Through the proof of this ministry they glorify God for the obedience of your confession to the Gospel of Christ and for the simplicity of your sharing with them and with all. They pray for you, longing for you because of the grace of God abounding in you. But thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift.

units.la: Quemadmodum fiduciae in Deum nihil perinde officit, atq; carnis solicitudo, qua decepti propria industria & labore nobismetipsis consulere studemus: Sic eadem, quo minus charitatis fraternae officia egenis praestemus impedit. Nec enim videre potest carnis ratio retributionem, quae beneficiis a Deo promissa atq; parata est: & idcirco metuit, ne dum aliis largimur, ipsi ad egestatem redigamur. Quapropter Spiritus sanctus in Scripturis frequenter solicitudinem illam oppugnat, & adversus eam nos rationibus atq; exemplis instruit. Huc enim Israelitarum exemplum pertinet, quos totis annis quadraginta Deus in deserto Manna caelitus demisso aluit, ut eo documento constaret, hominem non solo pane & ordinaria illa ratione viuere, sed quovis verbo, quod ex Dei ore egreditur. Eodem promissiones quoq; referri debent, quae passim in Psalmis et Prophetis occurrunt, & quas omnes Christus confirmat, dicens: Quaerite ante omnia regnum Dei atq; iustitiam eius, & reliqua omnia vobis adijcientur. Quibus accenseri debent quae Paulus in hac tractatione prolixe tradit. Et nuper quidem omnia carnis auarae argumenta quasi uno ictu abrumpens, Corinthios ad Dei omnipotentiam remisit, qui possit & velit abunde compensare quicquid in pauperes conferant: adeo ut & ipsis abunde sit unde viuant, & simul aliis benefacere possint, & in omne opus bonum redundent. At quia quaedam obscurius dicta videri poterant, quae consideratu plus quam necessaria sunt, eadem nunc diligentiori expositione illustrat.
units.tr: Just as nothing hinders trust in God more than anxious concern for the flesh, by which, deceived, we strive to provide for ourselves by our own industry and labour, so the same anxiety prevents us from performing the duties of brotherly love towards the needy. For the reasoning of the flesh cannot see the reward that God has promised and prepared for benefactions, and so it fears that, while we give generously to others, we ourselves may be reduced to want. Therefore the Holy Spirit frequently attacks this anxiety in the Scriptures and equips us against it with arguments and examples. To this belongs the example of the Israelites, whom God fed for forty years with manna sent down from heaven in the desert, so that by this lesson it would be established that man does not live by bread and ordinary means alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God. The promises also, which occur everywhere in the Psalms and the Prophets, and which Christ all confirms, saying: Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all the rest will be added to you, should be referred to the same point. To these must be added what Paul sets out at length in this discussion. Having just now broken off, as with a single blow, all the arguments of greedy flesh, he sent the Corinthians back to the omnipotence of God, who is able and willing to repay abundantly whatever they bestow on the poor, so that they themselves will have abundantly enough to live on, and at the same time can do good to others and overflow in every good work. But because some things said there might seem rather obscure, and yet are very necessary to consider, he now clarifies them by a more careful exposition.

units.la: Porro (inquit) qui suppeditat semen serenti, is etiam panem ad escam sive cibum suppeditabit &c. Rursus ad Dei omnipotentiam remittit, & hunc periphrasi describit, quae huic argumento optime convenit. Nam sementis parabolam denuo inculcat, & argumento vtitur a minori ad maius: Deus agricolis semen suppeditat, quod ex eius ordinatione sulcis mandatum germinat & mirifice multiplicatur: Idem ergo nequaquam eos negliget, qui quae ex eius liberalitate acceperunt, in pauperes conferunt, qui ipsius ager sunt, quem omni officiorum genere excolere debent, quotquot ipsius serui & cultores esse volunt. Ita locum hunc D. Chrysostomus intellexit, qui inter alia sic scribit: Si agricolis terram colentibus Deus retribuit, quanto magis illos remunerabitur, qui caelum colunt, & animae curam gerunt? Id vero faciunt, quicunq; fide in IESVM CHRISTVM, quae sola nos caelorum incolas facit, dilectionis fraternae operibus & beneficentia exercent.
units.tr: "Now," he says, "he who supplies seed to the sower will also supply bread for food, or sustenance, etc." Again he refers us to the omnipotence of God, and describes him by a periphrasis which is very well suited to this argument. For he again presses the parable of the seed and uses an argument from the less to the greater: God supplies the farmers with seed, which by his ordinance, once committed to the furrows, sprouts and is wonderfully multiplied. Therefore the same God will by no means neglect those who give to the poor from what they have received from his generosity; the poor are his field, which all who wish to be his servants and cultivators must tend with every kind of duty. So Chrysostom understood this passage, who among other things writes thus: If God rewards those who cultivate the land, how much more will he reward those who cultivate heaven and care for the soul? Those who do this, whoever they are, who through faith in Jesus Christ, which alone makes us inhabitants of heaven, practise brotherly love and beneficence, do indeed do so.

units.la: Est autem hic dignissimum observatu, quod Paulus nos ad Dei omnipotentiam remissurus, eum esse dicit, qui semen det seminanti. Est enim haec proprissima Dei descriptio, quae ad hunc omnia refert, nobis vero omnem gloriandi occasionem sive materiam eripit etiam quoad ea, quae ad victum & vitae huius mortalis sustentationem faciunt. Multos equidem ea persuasio dementat, quod suo labore & industria haec parari arbitrantur: quae causa est, quod quaesita domi suae congeruunt, & inutilibus frugum aceruis gaudent: vel ijsdem secure ad luxum & carnis voluptates abutuntur, ut fatuus ille, quem Christus dixisse ait: Anima, habes multa bona repostia in annos multos: requiesce, comede, bibe, obleętare. Sed dicant illi qui ita sentiunt, quis primus Adamo feminam dederit? quis item feminibus vim germinandi & fructificandi inseruerit? Annon Deus is est, cuius virtute illa ex terra enata sunt? Aut quis mortalium tam ingeniosus, industrius & exercitatus est, qui ex materia qualicunq; semen fabricare, & eidem vim generandi inserere possit? Quis vero rudem tellurem vi procreandi donauit? Quis tempestates regit ac moderatur, sine quibus nullae fruges proueniunt? Quis incrementum dat, postquam semina tam germinauerunt? Non ne solus Deus is est, de quo Scripturae haec passim praedicant, & cuius virtutem gentes quoq; agnouerunt? Verissime ergo ab Ambrosio dictum est: Omnia Dei sunt: & semina & nascentia Dei nutu crescunt & multiplicantur. Prodest autem multum haec consideratio ad fidem confirmandam, quando vbiq; occurrunt, quae nobis Dei admirabilem potentiam simul & prouidentiam plus quam paternam commendant. Deinde eadem nos de vero & legitimo opum huius seculi vsu admoneant, monet, nos ad gratiarum actionem & beneficentiae studium excitat. At simul haec latius ad ea quoq; extendi debent, quae ad salutem aeternam faciunt: ne videlicet in illis aliqua nostri vel meriti vel dignitatis fiducia superbiamus. Nam nisi renascatur homo, non potest videre regnum Dei. At quis verbum, quod semen regenerationis est, cordibus nostris inserit? quis illud vivificat? quis animos nostros immutat & innovat, ut homines novi efficiamur? Quid hic habes o homo, quod non acceperis ab eo, qui solus in corda & corpora nostra ius habet & imperium?
units.tr: Here, however, what is most worthy of notice is that Paul, in sending us back to the omnipotence of God, says that he is the one who gives seed to the sower. For this is the most proper description of God, which refers everything to him, and it takes away from us every occasion and matter for boasting, even as regards those things that serve food and the sustenance of this mortal life. Indeed, many are deluded by the belief that these things are obtained by their own labour and industry. This is why they heap up what they have gathered at home and delight in useless piles of crops, or else they securely abuse them for luxury and the pleasures of the flesh, like that foolish man of whom Christ says: "Soul, you have many good things laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, make merry." But let those who think this way tell us: who first gave the woman to Adam? Who also implanted in seeds the power to sprout and bear fruit? Is it not God, by whose power those things came up from the earth? Or what mortal is so clever, industrious and skilled that he can make seed out of any matter whatever and implant in it the power of generating? Who indeed gave the rough earth its power to produce? Who governs and regulates the weather, without which no crops come forth? Who gives the increase after the seeds have sprouted? Is it not God alone, of whom the Scriptures everywhere speak, and whose power the nations too have acknowledged? Therefore Ambrose spoke most truly: All things are God's; both seeds and things that are born grow and are multiplied at God's nod. This consideration is very useful for confirming faith, since everywhere there occur things which commend to us God's wonderful power and at the same time a providence more than paternal. Then these same things admonish us concerning the true and lawful use of the wealth of this age, and stir us up to thanksgiving and zeal for beneficence. But at the same time these things ought to be extended more widely to those matters too which pertain to eternal salvation, so that we may not take pride in any confidence in our own merit or dignity. For unless a man is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God. But who implants in our hearts the word, which is the seed of regeneration? Who makes it live? Who changes and renews our minds, so that we become new men? What do you have, O man, that you have not received from him who alone has right and rule over our hearts and bodies?

units.la: Porrò ad huius loci argumentum doctrinam istam Paulus accommodans, docet, quae & quanta beneficia in eos conferat Deus, qui pauperibus & egenis sua liberalitate subveniunt. Primo, dabit panem (inquit) in cibum. Panem nominat solum, ut rursus περὶ τῆς αὐταρκείας admoneat, ne quid praeter ea, quae necessaria sunt ad vitam serundam sufficere possunt, expetamus. Et sensus huius membri est: Deum, qui omnia pascit, nobis quoq; daturum victum necessarium & sufficientem. Et huc pertinent promissiones, quas alibi ex Scripturis adduximus. Interim observabis, homines Christianos necessariis contentos esse debere, neq; praeter ea aliquid postulare importunius. Nec enim superflua Deus omnibus pollicetur. Et Christus inter orandum nos panem quotidianum petere iubet, ita docens, sufficere nobis debere, si in diem (quod dici solet) viviamus. Vidit hoc Iacobus patriarcha, qui à fratris Esau facie profugus votum eiusmodi concipiebat: Quoniam Deus mihi adfuit, si idem ille me custodiat in via ista, qua proficiscor, & det mihi panem ad comedendum, & vestes ad induendum, reversus q; fuero incolumis & salvus ad domum patris mei: erit mihi Dominus in Deum, &c. Hac frugalitatis mensura si omnes homines vota sua circumscriberent, minus tumultuarentur circa non necessaria, & non sanctius modò verumetiam commodius atq; tranquillius viverent.
units.tr: Moreover, applying this doctrine to the subject of this passage, Paul teaches what and how great benefits God bestows on those who help the poor and needy by their generosity. First, he will give bread (he says) for food. He names only bread, so that again, concerning self-sufficiency [περὶ τῆς αὐταρκείας], he may remind us that we should not desire anything beyond what is sufficient and necessary for sustaining life. The sense of this clause is: God, who feeds all things, will also give us sustenance that is necessary and sufficient. The promises which we have adduced from the Scriptures elsewhere also pertain here. Meanwhile you will observe that Christian men ought to be content with what is necessary, and not demand anything beyond it too importunately. For God does not promise superfluities to all. And Christ bids us, in prayer, to ask for our daily bread, thus teaching that it should be enough for us if we live from day to day, as the saying goes. The patriarch Jacob saw this, who, fleeing from the face of his brother Esau, made a vow of this kind: "Since God has been with me, if he keeps me on this way on which I am going, and gives me bread to eat and clothes to wear, and I return safe and sound to my father's house, then the Lord will be my God," etc. If all men limited their wishes by this measure of frugality, they would be less troubled about unnecessary things, and they would live not only more holily but also more conveniently and more quietly.

units.la: Deinde, Deus ille (inquit) multiplicabit semen tuum. Sic vocat ipsas facultates & bona huius saeculi, ex quibus beneficentiam in pauperes exercemus: & sensus est, Deum non modò daturum quae necessitas exigit, sed insuper benedictione sua opes nostras multiplicaturum esse, ut indies plura largiri possimus. Rursus vero hoc eorum solicitudini opponit, qui sibi decedere putant quicquid in pauperes distribuunt. At multùm illi falluntur, cum beneficentia (ut iam saepe diximus) instar seminis sit, quam suo tempore messis sequitur. Ut ergo agricola, dum semen ex horreo suo in agrum defert, acervum quidem quem illic reconditum habet, minuere videtur, adeò tamen nihil damni patitur, ut quò liberaliorem facit sementem, eò uberiorem quoq; messem colligat, & proinde in annum venturum sit opulentior: Ita etiam iis accidere solet, qui ex divitiis suis eleemosynas liberaliter faciunt, quas Deus uberiori benedictione rependit. Exempla, quibus hoc confirmetur, passim occurrunt. Abrahamus relicto natali solo exul spontaneus ad Chananaeos venit, inter quos hospitalitate & liberalitate erga quosvis claruit. At idè in terra peregrina remunerator fidelissimum habuit Deum, cuius benedictione divitias sibi amplissimas paravit. Idem de Iobo possumus dicere, quem fortunis omnibus spoliatum Deus mox opulentissimum fecit, cum prius beneficentiae liberaliter fluduisset. Et huius generis multa hodie fiunt: cùm è contra qui æquo tenaciores sunt, opes suas indies decrescere sentiant, & saepe praeter omnem expectationem ad inopiam extremam redigantur.
units.tr: Next, "that God," he says, "will multiply your seed." He calls by this name the very resources and goods of this age, from which we practise beneficence towards the poor. And the sense is that God will not only give what necessity requires, but will moreover multiply our wealth by his blessing, so that we can give more and more each day. Again, he opposes this to the anxiety of those who think that whatever they distribute to the poor is lost to them. But they are greatly mistaken, since beneficence (as we have often said already) is like seed, which a harvest follows in its time. Thus, when a farmer carries seed from his barn into the field, he seems indeed to diminish the heap he has stored there, and yet he suffers no loss at all; the more generously he makes the sowing, the more abundant the harvest he gathers, and so he becomes richer in the coming year. So it is also wont to happen to those who generously give alms from their riches, which God repays with a more abundant blessing. Examples confirming this occur everywhere. Abraham, leaving his native soil, came as a voluntary exile to the Canaanites, among whom he was renowned for hospitality and generosity towards all. And yet, in a foreign land, he found God a most faithful rewarder, by whose blessing he acquired for himself very ample riches. We can say the same of Job, whom God, after stripping him of all his fortunes, soon made most wealthy, since before that he had freely poured forth his beneficence. Many instances of this kind happen today as well, whereas, on the contrary, those who are too tenacious find their wealth decreasing day by day, and often they are reduced to utter want beyond all expectation.

units.la: Tertio addit: Et augebit germina sive fructus iustitiae vestrae. Exponit quod modò dixerat, & opera beneficentiae fructus iustitiae vocat, rursus ad seminis parabolam alludens, ut ostendat illa esse proprios & germanos fructus verae illius iustitiae, quae per fidem in IESVM CHRISTVM obtinetur. Testantur enim de charitate, quae fidei iustificantis evidentissimum argumentum est, ut ad Galatas Paulus docet. Illa (inquit) augebit Deus, ut ditati abundetis in omnem simplicitatem, id est, ut posthabitis omnibus carnis auaritiae & solicitae rationibus, animo simplici & liberali beneficentiam indies exerceatis erga quosvis, quos vestra ope videtis indigere. Est hoc imprimis necessarium, ut supra quoq; diximus. Na ut Theodoretus ait, qui circa rationes & computationes superfluas occupantur, ij facile decipiuntur auaritiae fascino, ut parciores sint aequo, ubi liberalissimos esse decebat. Quid, quòd in simplicitate illa praecipuae & maximae opes piorum consistunt? Ea enim causa est, ut in solius Dei providentiam recumbant, cuius thesauri inexhausti sunt, & quae eis nihil deficeri patitur.
units.tr: Third, he adds: "And he will increase the fruits of your righteousness." He explains what he had just said, calling the works of beneficence "fruits of righteousness," again alluding to the parable of the seed. He shows that these are the proper and genuine fruits of that true righteousness which is obtained through faith in Jesus Christ. For they bear witness to charity, which is the most evident proof of justifying faith, as Paul teaches to the Galatians. "He will increase them" (he says), "so that, being enriched, you may abound in all simplicity," that is, so that, setting aside all the cares and calculations of the flesh and greed, you may exercise beneficence towards whomever you see in need through your help, with a simple and generous mind. This is especially necessary, as we also said above. For, as Theodoret says, those who are occupied with superfluous calculations and reckonings are easily deceived by the charm of avarice, so that they become more sparing than is fitting when they ought to be most generous. Moreover, do the greatest and chief riches of the godly not consist in that simplicity? For this is the reason they rest upon the providence of God alone, whose treasures are inexhaustible and which allows nothing to fail them.

units.la: At simul admonet nos locus iste, quid de auarorum hominum thesauris iudicari debeat. Quae animo simplici & benefico in pauperes erogantur, ea iustitiae germina atq; fructus sunt. Ergo quae his fraudatis vel neglectis congeruntur, iniustitiae & iniquitatis fructus sunt, & olim iustam damnationem afferent suis possessoribus. Ideo apud prophetam auaris, raptoribus & fraudatoribus Deus olim dicebat: Annon adhuc ignis in domo impij? thesauri nimirum iniquus. Et Habakuk: Vae ei qui adauget non sua. Quousque tandem? & qui aggravat super se denum lutum. Nam non nostra dicuntur, non modo quae aliis per vim aut dolum malum extorsimus, verumetiam quae non distribuimus ex charitatis praecepto egenis, quos nobis Deus commendauit. Attales simul lutum densum super se congerunt: quia opibus immersi neq; ad caelestia bona suspicere, neq; pedes suos extricare possunt, vt in vijs Domini ambulent. Quibus adde quod Iacobus scribit: Agite nunc diuites, plorate vlulantes super miserijs vestris, quae aduenient vobis. Diuitiae vestrae putrefactae sunt, vestes vestrae a tineis erosae sunt: aurum & argentum vestrum erugine vitiatum est, & erugo eorum in testimonium vobis erit, & exedet carnes vestras sicut ignis, &c. Iacob. 5.
units.tr: At the same time this passage warns us what should be judged of the treasures of greedy men. What is poured out in a simple and bountiful spirit upon the poor is the seed and fruit of righteousness. Therefore, what is heaped up by those who have defrauded or neglected the poor is the fruit of injustice and iniquity, and will one day bring just condemnation upon its possessors. Hence God, speaking through the prophet to the greedy, plunderers and defrauders, said: "Is there still fire in the house of the wicked, and the accursed treasure of iniquity?" And Habakkuk: "Woe to him who increases what is not his own. How long? And who loads himself with thick mud." For those things are not called ours only when we have wrung them from others by force or wicked deceit, but also when we do not distribute them to the needy, whom God has committed to us by the command of charity. Such men heap thick mud upon themselves, because, sunk in riches, they can neither look up to heavenly goods nor extricate their feet so as to walk in the ways of the Lord. Add to these the words of James: "Come now, you rich, weep and howl over your miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted, your garments are moth-eaten, your gold and silver are corroded, and their rust will be a witness against you and will eat your flesh like fire," etc. James 5.

units.la: Sed alium adhuc beneficentiae fructum Paulus subijcit, dicens: Quae per nos efficit, vt gratiae agantur Deo, id est, haec causa est, quod multi ad gratiarum actionem excitantur. Ita vero docet eleemosynas ad Dei gloriam redundare, cui hic gratissimus cultus est, si homines ipsi gratias publice agant pro acceptis beneficijs. E contra vero graviter peccant, qui sua duritia & sorditie egenis murmurandi & de Deo quaeritandi occasionem praebent, quorum linguas sua liberalitate in Dei laudes & gratiarum actionem soluere debebant.
units.tr: But Paul adds yet another fruit of beneficence, saying: "which works through us that thanks be given to God." That is, this is the reason why many are stirred to thanksgiving. He teaches that alms redound to the glory of God, to whom this is the most welcome worship, if people themselves publicly give thanks for the benefits received. On the contrary, those sin grievously who by their hardness and meanness give the needy an occasion to murmur and complain against God, when their tongues ought to have been loosed by their liberality into the praises of God and thanksgiving.

units.la: Caeterum quia haec particula consideratu dignissima est, diligentius eam explicat, & quae de tota hac causa dici possunt, in breuem summam contrahit. Nam ministerium functionis illius non solum supplet inopiam sanctorum, verumetiam redundat per multas gratiarum actiones Deo: dum per hoc documentum ministerij huius Deum glorificant de subiectione vestrae confessionis in Euangelium Christi, &c. In Graeco λειτουργίας vocabulum habetur, quod proprie quoduis munus publicum significat, tam in Repub. quam Ecclesia. Et hinc mos obtinuit, vt diuini cultus actiones, inter quas antiquitus sacrificia primum locum habebant, λειτουργίαι dicerentur. Seruit vtraq; significatio causae praesenti: Nam pauperum subuentio proprissimum Ecclesiae munus est, quod publice simul & priuatim ab omnibus debet administrari. Deinde eleemosynae sacrificia sunt Deo longe gratissima, quae de fide nostra testantur, & quibus ipse Dei Filius, IESVS CHRISTVS, in pauperibus suis alitur atq; iuuatur. Voluit ergo in praesenti ista locutione vt Paulus vt vehementius eos excitaret, qui adhuc cunctabantur. Et quia pauperes plerisq; videntur non tanti fieri apud Deum, vt aliquam rationem habeat eorum, quae in eos conferuntur, ostendit non in horum vili aspectu nos haerere debere, sed animi oculos longius extendere, vt quid in tota hac causa fit consideremus. Quo loco rursus nobis occurrit multiplex beneficentiae in pauperes fructus, qui nos de spe liberalissimae retributionis certos facit.
units.tr: Moreover, because this clause is most worthy of consideration, he explains it more carefully and gathers into a brief summary what can be said about this whole matter. For "the ministry of this service," he says, "not only supplies the want of the saints, but also overflows through many thanksgivings to God, while through the proof of this ministry they glorify God for the subjection of your confession to the gospel of Christ," etc. In the Greek the word is leitourgias [λειτουργίας], which properly signifies any public office, both in the commonwealth and in the Church. From this usage arose the custom by which the acts of divine worship, among which sacrifices held the first place in antiquity, were called leitourgiai [λειτουργίαι]. Both meanings serve the present case. For the relief of the poor is the most proper office of the Church, which ought to be administered by everyone, both publicly and privately. Next, alms are sacrifices most pleasing to God, which bear witness to our faith, and by which the Son of God himself, Jesus Christ, is fed and helped in his poor. Therefore in this expression Paul wished to stir up more vehemently those who were still hesitating. And because the poor seem to most people to count for so little with God that any account is taken of what is bestowed upon them, he shows that we should not fix our gaze on their humble appearance, but extend the eyes of our mind further, so that we may consider what is done in this whole matter. Here again there presents itself to us the manifold fruit of beneficence towards the poor, which makes us certain of the hope of the most generous reward.

units.la: Primus est, quod inopiam sanctorum supplet. Sancti autem dicuntur fideles, quos Christus sanguinis sui pretio ablutos Deo Patri suo consecrauit: & ab his Ecclesia illa catholica, quam in Symbolo profitemur, communio sanctorum dicitur. At hi in terris peregrini & hospites sunt, neq; habent hic ciuitatem permanentem siue durabilem: & ideo ijsdem multa desunt & varie exercentur, dum in hoc mundo degunt. Nam etsi in Christo abunde habeant omnia, quae ad salutem aeternam faciunt, vita tamen haec illis perpetua militia est, laborum & periculorum plena. Et vt ita exerceantur necesse est: nimirum vt & caro in officio contineatur, quae dum otio & pace abundat proteruire solet, & eorundem fides atq; patientia probetur, simulq; semper occasio fit, qua beneficentiam exerceamus, quae nulla esset, si nemo nostra ope indigeret. Est autem hic eximius & praeclarus beneficentiae usus, quod per hanc eorum defectus sine inopia sublevatur, quos Christus sanguinis sui pretio redimere dignatus est, & quos nobis, quoad externa haec officia, perinde vt seipsum commendauit. Ideo in tota hac causa non tam quid nobis utile sit, quam quibus illi opus habeant videre conuenit, ne ipsi illorum inopiae authores efficiamur.
units.tr: The first is that it supplies the want of the saints. Now the saints are called the faithful, whom Christ, cleansed by the price of his blood, has consecrated to God his Father; and from these is called that catholic Church, which we profess in the Creed, the communion of saints. But these are strangers and sojourners on earth, and have here no abiding or lasting city; and therefore many things are lacking to them and they are variously exercised while they live in this world. For although in Christ they have in abundance all things that pertain to eternal salvation, yet this life is to them a perpetual warfare, full of labours and dangers. And it is necessary that they be so exercised: namely, that the flesh may be kept in obedience, which, when it abounds in leisure and peace, is wont to grow wanton, and that their faith and patience may be tested; and at the same time an opportunity is always given us for exercising beneficence, which would not exist if no one needed our help. Now this is a distinguished and remarkable use of beneficence: that through it the lack of those whom Christ has deigned to redeem by the price of his blood is relieved without want, and whom he has commended to us, as to these external duties, just as he commended himself. Therefore in this whole matter it is fitting that we look not so much at what is useful to us as at what they need, lest we ourselves become the authors of their want.

units.la: Sed deplorandum hic venit peruersum & praepostorum multorum iudicium, qui sub Sanctorum nomine non alios quam Diuos caelites intelligunt, & toti circa horum cultum occupantur, neglectis.
units.tr: But here we must lament the perverse and inverted judgment of many, who under the name of saints understand none but the heavenly gods, and are wholly occupied with their worship, while neglecting

units.la: 1. Supplet inopiam sanctorum. neglectis interea sanctis qui ipsis videntibus esuriunt, algent & omnibus necessariis destituuntur. At cœlites illi, vt olim suo seculo deseruierunt (vt de Dauide scriptum extat) & huius vitæ laboribus atq; curis defuncti sunt: ita nunc nullius egent, sed beati & felices in Dei conspectu bonorum omnium satietate fruuntur, & eorundem corpora cum læta & beata resurrectionis spe quiescunt. Nihilominus tamen illis superstitiosi homines templa palatiorum regalium instar extruunt, aras dicant, statuas locant, pecunias, vestes & quæuis alia offerunt, deniq; fraudatis quoq; legitimis hæredibus amplissimas opes illorum cultui consecrant. Et dum ista faciunt, viua Christi membra non negligunt modo, verumetiam defraudant, spoliant, iugulant, vt sit quod truncis inutilibus & omni sensu carentibus offeratur. Quis hic non exclamet cum Satyrico poeta: O cæcas hominum mentes, o pectora cæca?
units.tr: 1. He supplies the want of the saints. Meanwhile the saints are neglected, who, before their very eyes, hunger, freeze and are destitute of all necessities. Those heavenly ones, as they once served in their age (as is written of David) and have been released from the labours and cares of this life, so now they lack nothing, but being blessed and happy in the sight of God they enjoy the satiety of all good things, and their bodies rest in the joyful and blessed hope of the resurrection. Nevertheless, superstitious men build for them temples like royal palaces, dedicate altars, set up statues, offer money, garments and whatever else, and finally, defrauding even the lawful heirs, consecrate their vast wealth to their worship. And while they do these things, they not only neglect but actually defraud, despoil and butcher the living members of Christ, so that there may be something to offer to useless logs devoid of all sense. Who here would not cry out with the satirist: "O blind minds of men, o blind hearts"?

units.la: Sed alterum quoq; beneficentiæ fructum Apostolus indicat, dum eam redundare dicit per multas gratiarumactiones Deo. Et mox modum quoq; & rationem huius describit: Dum per hoc documentum siue specimen ministerij huius Deum glorificant de subiectione confessionis vestræ in Euangelium Christi, deq; simplicitate communicationis in ipsos & in omnes. Sensus est, multorum piorum ora & linguas in gratiarumactionem & Dei laudes solui, dum ex tam luculento liberalitatis specimine intelligunt, vos Euangelium vere amplexos esse, & ita quidem, vt vnanimi consensu vos & omnia vestra illi subijciatis, & non in ipsos modo, verumetiam in omnes alios benefici, vos vera & germana corporis Christi, quod Ecclesia eius est, membra esse testamini.
units.tr: But the Apostle also points out another fruit of beneficence, when he says that it overflows through many thanksgivings to God. And he immediately describes the manner and reason of this: "While through the proof or specimen of this ministry they glorify God for the subjection of your confession to the gospel of Christ, and for the simplicity of your communication towards them and towards all." The sense is that the mouths and tongues of many godly people are loosed into thanksgiving and the praises of God, when from so clear a display of liberality they understand that you have truly embraced the gospel, and that you so submit yourselves and all that you have to it with one accord, and that you are beneficent not only towards them but towards all others, and so testify that you are true and genuine members of the body of Christ, which is his Church.

units.la: Admonemur hoc loco, Christianos decere, vt non modo Euangelij doctrinam & fidem in Christum profiteantur, verumetiam fidei suæ documenta præbeant, ex quibus appareat, ipsos Euangelio vere credidisse. Nam vt Christus ait, non omnis qui dicit, Domine Domine, ingredietur in regnum eius, sed qui fecerit voluntatem Patris cœlestis. Et Iacobus inanis aut mortuæ fidei professoribus dicebat: Ostende mihi fidem tuam ex factis tuis. Sunt autem veræ fidei documenta, quæ Paulus in præsenti attingit. Primum, consensio in veritatis doctrina. Hanc nobis Christus vnicè commendat, quando Patre precatur, vt discipuli eius omnes vnum sint in ipso & Patre. Et sane absurdum fuerit eos dissentire aut inter se scindi, quorum omnium vnus & idem est Pater, idem Dominus, idem Spiritus, eadem vocationis spes, idem baptismus & eiusdem fidei professio.
