Alterum est subiectio siue obedientia fidei, quam Euangelicæ prædicationis finem & scopum esse, in sequenti Capite audiemus. Tertium, beneficentia in fratres, quos nostro auxilio videmus indigere. Accedit his gaudium quod ex aliorum profectu concipimus, quodq; Dei laudes & gratiarumactionem in nobis parit. Et tales quidem olim fuisse constat Christianos homines quado Ecclesia vere floruit. Hodie in omnibus ipsis peccatur. Consensio in verbi doctrina rara aut nulla est, sed pleriq; vt magni habeantur, nouis dogmatibus student, & ita de rebus nihili aut etiam scandali plenis, contentiones excitant minime necessarias: in quibus eò vsq; progrediuntur, vt propter eas diris anathematismis damnent eos, qui eundem Christum cum ipsis profitentur, & quos pro fratribus suis debebant agnoscere. Deinde Euangelio paucissimi obediunt, plerique autem illud torquent pro affectuum suorum libidine, vt ex eo vel peccandi licentiam, vel priuatum commodum venentur. Fit ergo vt rebus secundis lasciuiant, & inter atrocissima scelera fibijpsis impunitatem perpetuam polliceantur: in aduersis verò ad carnis consilia & infelicis mundi auxilia respiciant, & si hæc fallant, turpiter quoque à fide deficiant. Interim pauperes non negliguntur modò, verumetiam deglubuntur, & ex publicis Ecclesiæ bonis homines auari, raptores, helluones, blasphemi, ditescunt, quæ vt egentium necessitati seruirent olim ab hominibus piissimis consecrata sunt. Quòd si qui meliores pietati studeant, & in ea proficiunt, mox illi omnium odijs subijciuntur, proscinduntur, lœduntur denique ab omnibus. Ita fit, vt propter nos male audiat nomen Domini, qui exemplo quosuis alios in eius cognitionem & amorem excitare debebamus.
units.tr: We are reminded at this point that it befits Christians not only to profess the doctrine of the gospel and faith in Christ, but also to give evidence of their faith, by which it may appear that they have truly believed the gospel. For as Christ says, not everyone who says "Lord, Lord" will enter the kingdom of his Father, but he who does the will of the heavenly Father. And James said to those who professed an empty or dead faith: "Show me your faith from your works." The evidences of true faith, which Paul touches on here, are these. First, agreement in the doctrine of truth. Christ especially commends this to us when he prays to the Father that all his disciples may be one in him and the Father. And indeed it would be absurd for those to disagree or be split among themselves whose Father is one and the same, whose Lord is one and the same, whose Spirit is one, who share one hope of calling, one baptism and one profession of faith. The second is submission or obedience of faith, which we shall hear in the following chapter is the end and aim of the gospel preaching. The third is beneficence toward brothers whom we see need our help. To these is added the joy we feel at the progress of others, which produces in us praise of God and thanksgiving. And indeed it is established that such Christians existed in former times, when the Church truly flourished. Today sin is committed in all these respects. Agreement in the doctrine of the Word is rare or nonexistent. Most men, so that they may be thought great, pursue novel dogmas, and so stir up quarrels quite unnecessary, about matters of no value or even full of scandal. In these they go so far that on account of them they condemn with dire anathemas those who profess the same Christ as they do, and whom they ought to acknowledge as their brothers. Then very few obey the gospel, and most twist it to the lust of their passions, so that from it they hunt either licence to sin or private advantage. Thus it happens that in prosperity they grow wanton, and among the most atrocious crimes promise themselves perpetual impunity; in adversity they look to the counsels of the flesh and the helps of the unhappy world, and if these fail, they shamefully fall away from the faith as well. Meanwhile the poor are not only neglected but even stripped, and from the public goods of the Church greedy men, robbers, gluttons and blasphemers grow rich, goods which were once consecrated by most pious men so that they might serve the needs of the needy. But if some who are better devote themselves to piety and make progress in it, soon they are subjected to the hatred of all, torn apart, and finally wounded by everyone. So it happens that the name of the Lord is ill spoken of because of us, who ought to have stirred up others more than anyone to his knowledge and love.

units.la: Sequitur tertius beneficentiæ fructus, quod nimirum Iudææ fratres ea excitandi sint, vt preces pro Corinthijs fundant, & ipsos videre cupiant propter gratiam Dei in ipsis exuberantem. Videtur autem hoc prioribus adiecisse, vt dissensionis & simultatis suspicionem declinaret, quæ apud gentes ex Iudæorum morositate nascebatur, qua plerique eorum gentes vt prophanas abominabantur, & ne eos quidem, qui iam ab idololatria ad Christum conuerserant pro fratribus agno scebant, nisi insuper circumciderentur, & Legis Mosaicæ disciplinam reciperent. Videbatur hæc multis iusta & grauis causa, ob quam ipsi quoq; vicißim Iudæos odissent, & suos ab illis animos alienarent. Necesse ergo erat, Corinthios admoneri, non eundem esse omnibus animum, imò plures esse in Iudæa, qui non solum honorificè sentiant de gentium Ecclesijs, verumetiam pro illis frequen ter orent, & præclara illa Dei dona in illis exosculentur: & proinde aliquorum morositatem ne- quaquam istis fraudi esse debere.
units.tr: The third fruit of beneficence follows, namely that the brothers in Judea are to be stirred up to pour out prayers for the Corinthians, and to long to see them because of the grace of God abounding in them. But this seems to have been added to the earlier point so that he might turn aside the suspicion of division and enmity which arose among the Gentiles from the stubbornness of the Jews, by which most of them abhorred the Gentiles as profane, and did not even acknowledge as brothers those who had already turned from idolatry to Christ, unless they were also circumcised and received the discipline of the Mosaic Law. This seemed to many a just and weighty reason for which they in turn also hated the Jews and turned their minds away from them. It was therefore necessary for the Corinthians to be warned that the mind is not the same in all; indeed there are many in Judea who not only think honourably of the churches of the Gentiles, but also pray for them frequently and rejoice in those excellent gifts of God in them. Therefore the stubbornness of some ought by no means to be a disadvantage to those people.

units.la: At simul hic pauperes officij sui admonentur: quod est, gratias agere Deo pro acceptis benefi-cijs. Non enim ab hominibus pendere debent, sed à Deo, qui omnium hominum corda in manu sua habet, & eadem flectere & mouere potest, vt quibus ille vult benefaciant. Simul autem se bo- nam gratiam benefactoribus suis debere meminerint, & ideo si non aliud possunt, saltem pro illis orent, vt Deus ipsorum laboribus & familijs benedicat, & eosdem Spiritus sui donis augeat. Amant deniq; & bene velint illis, à quibus iuuantur. Adhæc bene vtantur ijs quæ accipiunt, non ab- liguriant ea, non dilapident comessando, ludendo aut alijs studijs inhonestis ac turpibus. Imò me- minerint hoc sacrilegium esse, si publicis eleemosynis ad otium ignavum aut intemperantiam & luxum abutantur. Arguit hoc multorum corruptissimos mores, qui cùm pauperes Ecclesiæ haberi velint, tamen neq; Dei neq; religionis aliquam curam habent: divites omnes odërunt, benefactoribus suis inuidene, morosi & queruli eos accusant, quibus gratiam bonam debebant: gaudent deniq; eo- rundem calamitatibus: acceptis verò turpissimè abutuntur, & sub egestatis prætextu otio dediti belluantur ac intemperantissimè viuunt. Quæ causa est, quòd nihil illis sufficiat, & querelis non necessarijs omnium aures fatigent. Non talis Lazarus, qui immanem quoq; diuitis epulonis sa- stum patienter tulit, seque totum paternæ Dei providentiæ commisit.
units.tr: At the same time the poor are reminded of their duty, which is to give thanks to God for the benefits they have received. For they ought not to depend on men but on God, who holds the hearts of all men in his hand, and can turn and move them so that they do good to whom he wills. At the same time they should remember that they owe a good grace to their benefactors, and therefore, if they can do nothing else, at least let them pray for them, that God may bless their labours and households and increase them with the gifts of his Spirit. Finally, let them love and wish well those by whom they are helped. Moreover, let them use well what they receive, not squander it, nor waste it on feasting, gambling or other dishonourable and base pursuits. Indeed, let them remember that it is sacrilege if they abuse public alms for idle sloth, intemperance and luxury. This points to the very corrupt morals of many who, although they want to be counted as the Church's poor, yet have no care for God or for religion. They hate all the rich, grudge their benefactors, and with peevish and complaining mouths accuse those to whom they ought to owe good grace; finally they rejoice in their calamities. Yet they abuse what they receive most shamefully, and, given over to idleness under the pretext of need, they revel and live most intemperately. This is why nothing is enough for them, and they weary everyone's ears with unnecessary complaints. Not such was Lazarus, who patiently bore even the monstrous pride of the rich feaster, and committed himself wholly to the fatherly providence of God.

units.la: Admonet præterea locus iste, quàm turpiter fallantur suis rationibus, qui ideo parciores sunt in egenos, quòd ea sibi perire putant, quæ illis largiuntur. Atqui nullæ opes sunt præstantiores, quàm quas hic Paulus beneficiis pollicetur, neq; aliunde maior quæstus & gloria sperari potest. Tales enim sanctorum inopiam supplent, imò ipsum Christum in membris suis alunt, & proinde (vt Solomon ait) ipsi Domino fœnerantur. Deinde alios ad gratiarum actionem excitant, quo nullus cultus Deo magis gratus & acceptus est. Adhæc euidens præbent fidei suæ documentum, ex quo pro germanis Christi discipulis agnosci possunt. Præterea alios sibi obstringunt, vt qui prius ipsos oderant, nunc eos in honore & pretio habeant, & absentes quoq; magni faciant. Deniq; eosdem ad preces pro ipsis faciendis excitant, quibus nihil vtilius, nihil magis necessarium fingi potest. In Dei aures penetrat clamor pauperum, qui vel negliguntur vel etiam opprimun- tur, vt Iacobus docet. Quid ni ergo eorundem preces quoq; ille exaudiat, quas pro benefactori- bus suis fundunt? I nunc, & pauperes habere nega, quod tibi rependant, cum maiora sint multò quæ ad te ab illis redeunt, quam quæ tu illis largiris.
units.tr: This passage further shows how shamefully people are deceived by their own reckoning, who are therefore more sparing toward the needy because they think that what is given to them is lost to themselves. Yet there are no riches more excellent than those which Paul here promises through beneficence, nor can greater gain or glory be hoped for from anywhere else. For such people supply the want of the saints; indeed they nourish Christ himself in his members, and therefore (as Solomon says) they lend to the Lord himself. Then they stir others to thanksgiving, and no worship is more pleasing and acceptable to God. Moreover, they give clear evidence of their faith, by which they may be recognised as true disciples of Christ. Besides, they bind others to themselves, so that those who formerly hated them now hold them in honour and esteem, and value them even when they are absent. Finally, they stir those same people to pray for them, and nothing can be imagined more useful or more necessary than this. The cry of the poor penetrates the ears of God, the poor who are either neglected or even oppressed, as James teaches. Why then should he not also hear the prayers they pour out for their benefactors? Go now, and deny that you have poor people to repay you, since what comes back to you from them is far greater than what you give them.

units.la: Porrò concludit Paulus totam hanc tractationem ἀοξολογία seu gratiarumactione admo- dum pathetica: Gratia autem sit Deo super inenarraabili suo munere. Loquitur autem de toto isto negotio. Etenim ineffabile Dei donum erat, quòd Ecclesiæ passim constitutæ erant, quòd eæ- dem inter tot insidias & pericula seruabantur, quod charitatis mutuæ vinculo inter se cohære- bant, et mutuis auxilijs sese iuuabant. Nouo autem artificio vtitur, dum pro ijs gratias agit, quæ Corinthij nondum contribuerant. Ita enim spem bonam, quam de eis conceperat, testatur, vt eos magis extimulet: simulq; ipsos etiam reprimit, ne munificentia sua superbiant, sed hanc Dei opus esse agnoscant, qui suo Spiritu in ipsis agat, & bonos hosce motus excitet. Debemus ergo nos quoq; Deo gratias agere pro omnibus, quæ bene & rectè à nobis fiunt. Ex nobis ipsis enim nihil possu- mus, sed Deus est, qui in nobis agit & velle & facere. Oremus autem ipsi quoq; Deum patrem mi- sericordiæ, vt Ecclesias nostro etiam seculo fidei vnanimis & charitatis mutuæ vinculo con- stringat, vt omnes idem sentiant & loquantur in CHRISTO IESV, fidemq; suam publicè testentur, dum ab eo sibi commendatis pauperibus benefaciunt. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, glo- ria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Finally Paul concludes this whole discussion with a thanksgiving of great warmth: "Thanks be to God for his unspeakable gift." He is speaking of the whole of this matter. For the unspeakable gift of God was that churches had been established here and there, that they were preserved amid so many snares and dangers, that they were bound together by the bond of mutual charity, and helped one another with mutual aid. He uses a novel device, however, when he gives thanks for things which the Corinthians had not yet contributed. For thus he testifies to the good hope he had conceived of them, so that he may stimulate them the more; and at the same time he restrains them, lest they be puffed up with their generosity, but acknowledge that this is the work of God, who acts in them by his Spirit and stirs up these good impulses. So we too ought to give thanks to God for all things that are done by us well and rightly. For of ourselves we can do nothing; it is God who works in us both to will and to do. But let us also pray to God the Father of mercies, that he may bind the churches in our own age too with the bond of unanimous faith and mutual charity, so that all may think and speak the same in CHRIST JESUS, and publicly testify to their faith as they do good to the poor commended to them by him. To him are due blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: HOMILIA XLII.
units.tr: HOMILY XLII.

units.la: Cæterum precor vos per clementiam & æquitatem Christi, ego ipse Paulus, qui coram quidem humilis sum inter vos, absens vero confidens sum erga vos. Rogo autem, ne cum præsens adero, confidens sim ea fiducia, qua cogito audax esse in quosdam, qui nos æstimant, quasi secundum carnem incederemus. Nam in carne incedentes, non secundum carnem bellum gerimus.
units.tr: But I beg you by the gentleness and fairness of Christ, I, Paul myself, who am humble when face to face with you, but bold toward you when absent. I ask, however, that when I am present I may not have to be bold with that confidence which I intend to use against certain people who judge us as though we walked according to the flesh. For though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh.

units.la: ETSI Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS, discipulos suos, & cum his omnes Ecclesiæ suæ ministros, modestiæ & humilitati studere iubeat, & hanc suo quoq; exemplo eis commendet: idem tamen vt suam authoritatem contra hostes suos & calumniatores tueantur præcipit, & ideo promissionibus quoq; illos armat, quando dicit: Qui vos audit, me audit: Qui vos spernit, me spernit. Et vt in eo illi fortes ac seduli sint, admodum necesse est: ne videlicet in illis Dei Verbum contemnatur, quod sine certa salutis æternæ iactura non potest fieri. Ideo olim in authoritate sua defendenda constantissimi fuerunt Prophetæ: Et Christus etiamsi hominum modestissimus fuerit, & servi quoq; formam suscipere dignatus sit, acerrime tamen iis respondit semper, qui doctrinam eius in contemptu adducere conabantur. Huius ergo exemplum Paulus secutus, etsi prius multa pro se dixisset, nunc tamen post interpositam tractationem de Collectis & pauperum subuentione, redit ad sui ministerij defensionem de sua authoritate graviter disserit: idq; facit, partim vt exhortationi, quæ præcesserat, pondus addat: partim vt vniuersam doctrinam suam amplius commendet.
units.tr: Although our Lord Jesus Christ bids his disciples, and with them all the ministers of his Church, to strive after modesty and humility, and commends this to them by his own example, nevertheless he also commands them to defend their authority against his enemies and slanderers, and so he arms them with promises when he says: "He who hears you hears me; he who rejects you rejects me." It is absolutely necessary that they be brave and diligent in this, lest the Word of God be despised in them, which cannot happen without the certain loss of eternal salvation. Therefore the prophets of old were most steadfast in defending their authority. And Christ, although he was the most modest of men, and deigned to take the form of a servant, nevertheless always answered most sharply those who tried to bring his teaching into contempt. Paul, then, following this example, though he had already said much in his own defence, now, after the discussion about the collections and the relief of the poor, returns to the defence of his ministry and argues weightily concerning his authority. He does this partly to add weight to the exhortation that had gone before, and partly to commend his whole teaching more fully.

units.la: Vt vero causam hanc totam rectius intelligamus, initio videre oportet, quæ nam aduersariorum eius calumniæ fuerint: vbi quædam altius erunt repetenda. Paulus cum Corinthi docueret, vitæ genus secutus fuerat humile & nulla externi splendoris specie conspicuum. Nam vitium sibi manuum labore parabat, ne cui grauis esset: in docendo autem multa lenitate & mansuetudine vtebatur, vt ciuitatem quæ diuitijs sidebat, & luxui atq; libidini assueuerat, paulatim ad ferendum Christi iugum assuefaceret. Ita vero multos ad fidei obedientiam adduxit, & Ecclesiam illic constituit omni donorum spiritualium genere illustrem. Ipso autem inde digresso, subierunt homines ambitiosi, qui doctrinam ad ostentationem instituebant, Ecclesiam in sectas distrahebant, disciplinæ nervos labefactabant, adeo, vt nihil fere inter illos sanum esset & integrum. Quapropter Paulus per priorem epistolam grauissime cum illis expostulavit. Inde vero occasionem arripuerunt homines ambitiosi & disciplinæ impatientes, vt eum toti Ecclesiæ calumniis suis suspectum & exosum facerent. Itaq; apud homines faslui & splendori deditos humile illud & abiectum vitæ genus petulanter nimis exagitabant, vt hominem nullius existimationis & proinde indignum esse euincerent, qui in ciuitatem tam illustrem & opulentam ius aliquod haberet. Adhæc manuetudinem quoque & lenitatem eius calumniabantur, quasi ea fraudulenter vsus esset, vt per eam sese insinuaret. E contra epistolæ prioris rigorem accusabant, quasi Corinthiorum facilitate insolentior factus, nunc nimis imperiose cum illis ageret. Denique iactabundum Thrasonem esse clamabant, qui præsens nihil auderet, absens vero literis minacibus fulminaret, & inanibus terriculamentis homines simplices & rerum imperitos in metum & solicitudinem conijceret. Ad ista ergo omnia respondendum erat, ne simplex Euangelij doctrina prorsus in contemptum veniret.
units.tr: To understand this whole matter more rightly, we must first see what the calumnies of his opponents were, and for this some things must be recalled from further back. When Paul taught at Corinth, he had lived a humble way of life, showing no outward splendour. He earned his living by the labour of his own hands, so as not to be a burden to anyone; and in teaching he used great gentleness and mildness, so that he might gradually accustom the city, which sat in riches and was given to luxury and lust, to bear the yoke of Christ. In this way he brought many to obedience of faith, and established there a Church distinguished by every kind of spiritual gift. But after he had departed, ambitious men came in, who taught for display, divided the Church into factions, and undermined the sinews of discipline, so that scarcely anything among them was sound or whole. For this reason Paul rebuked them very severely in his first epistle. The ambitious men, however, who were impatient of discipline, seized on this as an occasion to make him suspect and hateful to the whole Church by their slanders. Thus among men devoted to show and splendour they insolently mocked his humble and abject way of life, to prove that he was a man of no standing and therefore unworthy to have any right in so famous and wealthy a city. Besides this, they also slandered his mildness and gentleness, as though he had used them deceitfully in order to worm his way in. On the other hand, they accused the severity of his first letter, as if, having become more arrogant through the Corinthians' easygoing nature, he now dealt with them too domineeringly. Finally they cried out that he was a boastful braggart, who dared nothing when present but thundered threats by letter when absent, and who filled simple people, inexperienced in affairs, with fear and anxiety by empty bugbears. Everything of this kind, then, had to be answered, lest the simple teaching of the gospel fall altogether into contempt.

units.la: Apparet autem in hoc exemplo, quæ nam ministrorum Ecclesiæ fors sit inter homines mundo & carni deditos. Paulus etsi quoad viuendi rationem nemini grauis esset, moribus placidissimis & sanctissimis commendaretur, in docendo autem simplicitati & perspicuitati studeret, & Verbi rigorem Spiritus lenitate moderaretur, non potuit tamen effugere calumniatorum dentes, qui & mansuetudinem & seueritatem ipsi vitio vertebant. Accidit hoc multis alijs. Quis merita Mosis & beneficia eiusdem in Israelitas dignis laudibus posset prosequi? Et nonne idem ipsius Dei testimonio mortalium omnium mansuetissimus fuit? At nihilominus illum impostorem, latronem & ambitiosum imperij affectatorem esse clamant ij, pro quorum salute ille dies & noctes excubabat. Quid de Ioanne & Christo dicemus, quorum hunc quidem propter facilem conuictum, belluonem esse, illum vero propter vitae genus austerius solito à dæmone malo exagitari Iudæi dixerunt? Quis ergo à calumnijs tutus aut immunis fuerit? Falluntur vehementer qui hoc sibi-ipsis pollicentur, & hac spe illecti se hominum moribus atque ingenijs accommodant. Nam vt ve teipsum torqueas, retinebit tamen ingenium suum infelix mundus, quod est, Veritatis lucem odisse, & proinde illam mendacijs & calumnijs obscurare. Illi ergo si placere cupias, Christo fidele obsequium præstare non poteris: & quàmuis in omnes formas te vertas, inq; eo Vertumnum & Protheas superes, semper tamen inuenient improbi quod inuido dente arrodant. Id ad se transferant omnis loci & ordinis homines, & discant nihil tutius esse, quàm Deum vocantem sequi, & ab hoc creditam funQionem constanter obire. Quod ij demum facient, qui cum Paulo dicere didicerunt: Mihi pro minimo est, vt à vobis dijudicer, aut ab vllo humano die, &c. His præmissis, videamus vt hanc causam egerit.
units.tr: This example also shows what fate awaits the ministers of the Church among men given over to the world and the flesh. Although Paul, as to his manner of life, was a burden to no one and was commended for the most peaceable and holy conduct, and although in teaching he aimed at plainness and clarity and tempered the rigour of the Word with the gentleness of the Spirit, he could not escape the teeth of slanderers, who found fault with both his gentleness and his severity. This has happened to many others. Who could praise worthily the merits of Moses and his benefits toward the Israelites? Was he not, by God's own testimony, the meekest of all mortals? Yet those for whose salvation he kept watch day and night cry out that he was an impostor, a robber, and a seeker after power. What shall we say of John and Christ, of whom the Jews said that one was a glutton because of his easy company, and the other was troubled by an evil demon because of his life more austere than usual? Who, then, will be safe or free from slanders? They are gravely mistaken who promise this to themselves, and, lured by this hope, adapt themselves to the morals and natures of men. For however you twist yourself, the unhappy world will keep its nature, which is to hate the light of truth and therefore to obscure it with lies and calumnies. If you wish to please such people, you will not be able to render faithful service to Christ; and however you turn yourself into every shape, and outdo Vertumnus and Proteus in changing, the wicked will always find something to gnaw with their envious teeth. Let men of every place and rank apply this to themselves, and learn that nothing is safer than to follow God when he calls, and to discharge constantly the office entrusted by him. Those who have learned to say with Paul will certainly do this: "It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you, or by any human day," and so on. With these things premised, let us see how he pleads this cause.

units.la: Exordio vtitur amico & pathetico, quo aduersarios suos acriter perstringit. Caeterum precor vos per clementiam & æquitatem Christi, ego ipse Paulus, qui, &c. Nomen suum exprimit, vt authoritatem suam fortius asserat contra eos, qui illa extenuabant, & fortassis scurrili quoq; petulantia in eius nomen ludebant. Paulus enim Latinis idem quod modicum aut pusillum sonat. Græcis vero quietum vel otiosum, ἀπὸ τῆς παύλης. Itaque non caret Emphasi particula ista: Ego ipse Paulus, &c. Quasi diceret: Scio quid de me aliqui dicant, quibus volupe est scurriliter in Christi seruos iocari. Sed qualis qualis sim, ego ipse Paulus, qui quando præsens sum, humilis & nullius pretij videor, absens vero confidens & audaculus dicor, vos precor & hortor (vtrumq; enim vox Græca significat) per clementiam & æquitatem Christi, &c. Ita vero cordatioribus, qui inter illos erant, suam vocationem in mentem reuocat, & quæ apud illos ædita erant veri Apostoli opera atq; specimina, quorum consideratio eum facile ab omni contemptu vindicabat. Similis locus in epistola ad Galatas habetur, vbi contra eos, qui Legis iustitiam cum fide miscebant, differens, inter alia dicit: Ecce ego Paulus dico vobis, quod si circumcidamini, Christus nihil vos iuuabit, &c.
units.tr: He uses a friendly and emotional opening, by which he sharply censures his opponents. "But I beg you by the gentleness and fairness of Christ, I, Paul myself, who," and so on. He states his own name so that he may assert his authority more strongly against those who belittled it, and who perhaps even mocked his name with buffoonish impudence. For "Paul" in Latin means the same as "small" or "little"; in Greek it means "quiet" or "at rest" [ἀπὸ τῆς παύλης]. So this particle, "I, Paul myself," has emphasis. As if he were saying: "I know what some people say about me, people who delight in jesting coarsely at the servants of Christ. But whatever I am, I, Paul myself, who when present seem humble and of no worth, and when absent am called bold and too daring, I beg and exhort you (for the Greek word means both) by the gentleness and fairness of Christ," and so on. In this way he recalls to the more discerning among them his own calling, and the works and proofs of a true apostle that had been displayed among them, the consideration of which would easily free him from all contempt. A similar passage is found in the Epistle to the Galatians, where, arguing against those who mixed the righteousness of the Law with faith, he says among other things: "Behold, I, Paul, say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing," and so on.

units.la: Est hoc magnum fiduciæ argumentum, qua ministros armatos esse oportet, vt se fortiter opponere possint aduersariorum calumnijs atq; criminationibus. Hanc vero obtinebunt, si Dei vocatione expectent, & in ea sic viuant, vt improbi contemptores non habeant, quod in ipsis possint reprehendere, & proinde ad scurrilia dicteria & frigidas atq; pueriles nominum aut cognominum allusiones confugere cogantur, vt sui similibus, aut rerum plane imperitis contemptos faciant. Est hoc hodie nimis vulgare, quod vel ad nomina ministrorum improbi petulanter alludunt, vel natales obscuros, aut vitæ genus humile, aut inopiam illis exprobrant. Sed his ministri suum nomen forti & intrepida fiducia opponere, & ad vocationem suam illos remittere debent, quæ sola ipsos tueri potest, si ex Deo sit. Ita olim Amos propheta fecisse legimus. Cum enim Amasias Sacerdos ipsi fraudulenter consuleret, vt ex terra Israelitica in regnum Iuda confugeret, vbi tuto posset Dei Verbum annuntiare, non autem cum capitis periculo illic prophetare pergeret, vbi regiis edictis id esset prohibitum: mox illi respondit: Ego non sum Propheta, neq; filius Prophetæ, sed homo pecuarius ego sum, sycomora strmgens: Tulit autem me Dominus cum greges sequerer, dixitq; ad me Dominus: Vade, & propheta populo meo Israel, &c. Et simile quid Apostoli Sacerdotibus & Senioribus Hierosolymitanis responderunt, se non posse non loqui ea, quæ & comperta habeant, & quæ Deus annuntiare iusserit.
units.tr: This is a great argument of confidence, with which ministers ought to be armed, so that they can bravely oppose the calumnies and accusations of their opponents. They will obtain this confidence if they wait for God's calling and live in such a way that wicked despisers have nothing in them to find fault with, and so are not forced to take refuge in buffoonish sayings and cold and childish puns on names or surnames, by which they may make them contemptible to their like-minded followers or to people altogether ignorant of affairs. Today it is far too common for the wicked to make wanton puns on the names of ministers, or to reproach them with obscure birth, a humble way of life, or poverty. But ministers ought to oppose such things with a strong and fearless confidence, and refer their critics to their calling, which alone can protect them, if it is from God. So the prophet Amos did long ago, as we read. For when Amaziah the priest tried to trick him into fleeing from the land of Israel into the kingdom of Judah, where he could safely proclaim the Word of God, instead of continuing to prophesy at the risk of his life where royal edicts forbade it, Amos immediately answered him: "I am not a prophet, nor the son of a prophet, but I am a herdsman, gathering sycamore figs. The Lord took me as I followed the flock, and the Lord said to me: Go, prophesy to my people Israel," and so on. And the apostles answered the priests and elders of Jerusalem in a similar way, that they could not but speak the things they had seen and heard, and which God had commanded them to proclaim.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui ne arrogantius putetur solius nominis sui fiducia ferocire, gra uem admodum & huic causæ conuenientissimam obtestationem interserit. Adhortor, siue precor vos (inquit) per clementiam & æquitatem Christi. ἐπιεικεια proprie dicitur iuris moderatio, qua eius rigor temperatur, ne (quod prouerbio dicitur) summum ius summa iniuria fiat. Est hæc in CHRISTO IESV perfectissima. Etsi enim ideo in mundum venijset, vt Legem impleret, & huius
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who, lest he be thought to be puffed up with arrogance from confidence in his own name alone, interposes a grave and most fitting appeal to this cause. "I exhort you," he says, "or rather I beg you, by the gentleness and fairness of Christ." Epieikeia is properly the moderation of law, by which its rigour is tempered, so that (as the proverb says) the highest right does not become the highest wrong. In Christ Jesus this is found in its most perfect form. For although he came into the world in order to fulfil the Law, and to

units.la: Exordiū graue & pathericum
units.tr: A grave and pathetic exordium.

units.la: Ministros fiducia armatos esse oportet.
units.tr: Ministers ought to be armed with confidence.

units.la: Amos 7.
units.tr: Amos 7.

units.la: Hortatur per Christi æquitatem & mansuetudinem. huius sensum germanum sic tradat, ut in ipsas hominum mentes penetret, & omnes homines peccati reos agat: idem tamen sub hoc pondere laborantes atque oneratos non fastuose aut crudeliter abijcit, sed amicè ad se invitat, imò reatum nostrum in se recipit, & quod nobis praestitu impossibile erat, ipse praestitit, sicuti de illo olim Isaias praedixerat. Denique, ut Paulus ipse testatur, illle nostra iustitia, imò peccatum pro nobis factus est, ut nos efficeremur iustitia Dei per ipsum. Et quamvis adhuc infirmos & imperfectos nos esse videat, mitis tamen & mansuetus ille seruator est, qui linum fumigans non extinguit, neque arundinem quassatam conterit. Per hanc mansuetudinem Christi Paulus Corinthios obtestatur: & ita simul offendit, quam pernersum sit ipsorum iudicium, qui hoc ipsum ei vitio vertant, cuius exemplum nobis Christus praebuit, qui adhuc hodie plus quam paterna indulgentia nostras infirmitates ferat.
units.tr: He exhorts them by the gentleness and mildness of Christ. He so delivers the true sense of this law that it penetrates into men's very minds and makes all men guilty of sin; yet he does not cast off, proudly or cruelly, those who labour and are burdened under this weight, but kindly invites them to himself. Indeed he takes our guilt upon himself, and what was impossible for us to accomplish, he himself accomplished, just as Isaiah had long ago foretold of him. Finally, as Paul himself testifies, he who knew no sin was made sin for us, that we might be made the righteousness of God through him. And although he sees us still weak and imperfect, he is nonetheless the mild and gentle Saviour, who does not quench the smoking flax nor break the bruised reed. By this gentleness of Christ Paul appeals to the Corinthians, and at the same time shows how perverse the judgement is of those who find fault with him for this very thing, of which Christ has given us the example, he who even today bears our infirmities with more than fatherly indulgence.

units.la: Atqui eadem obtestatione non minus hodie nobis opus est, quando eandem perversitate & iudicij inopia, quam in Corinthijs Paulus perstringit, etiam hodie passim cernere licet. Odio enim prosequimur mundus hic Veritatis lucem, nec ferre potest, ut per hanc opera eius prava coarguantur. Interim nihilominus non desunt, qui in verbi administris acrimoniam maiorem requirunt, & eos plus aequo indulgentiores esse queruntur, si non minus seueris ribus contra eos fulminent, quibus ipsi male volunt. Sed, ut nuper diximus, non debent ista aliquem movere, quo minus officium suum sedulo faciat, & Euangelici salis acerbitatem Christiana lenitate aut mansuetudine moderetur. Singuli vero obtestationem illam sibi ipsis applicent, & meminerint se quoque similiter ab ipso Christo rogari, ut suae facilitati atque indulgentiae locum dent. Quam vero indignum fuerit, si illum audire dedigneris, qui propter te ex Patris sinu in mundum hunc venire, homo fieri, & tam multa tamque grauia subire dignatus est, ut miseros nos ex interitu sempiterno redimeret?
units.tr: Yet we need the same appeal no less today, since the same perversity and lack of judgement that Paul censures in the Corinthians can be seen everywhere today. For this world hates the light of truth and cannot bear that its wicked works should be exposed by it. Meanwhile there are not lacking those who demand greater harshness in the ministers of the Word, and complain that they are more lenient than they ought to be if they do not thunder against those whom they themselves wish ill with equal severity. But, as we said a little while ago, such things ought not to hinder anyone from carrying out his duty diligently, and from tempering the sharpness of the Gospel's salt with Christian gentleness and mildness. Let each one apply that appeal to himself, and remember that he too is similarly asked by Christ himself to give place to his kindness and indulgence. How unworthy it would be if you were to refuse to hear him who, for your sake, deigned to come into this world from the bosom of the Father, to become man, and to undergo so many and such grievous things, in order to redeem us wretched men from eternal destruction!

units.la: Quid vero tam graui obtestatione effectum aut impetratum vult Paulus? Hoc rogo (inquit) ne cum praesens adero, confidens sim ea fiducia, qua cogito audax esse in quosdam, qui nos aestimant, quasi secundum carnem incederemus. Quorum verborum hic sensus est: Precor ita vos geratis, ne cum venero, cogar coram uti mea illa fiducia & potestate, quam nunc in animo habeo exercere aduersus aliquos, qui nos petulantius contemnunt, quasi secundum carnem ambulemus, id est, quasi carnis affectu ducar, neque alio quam carnis praesidio nitar, & proinde contemni merear. At hoc dicendo alludit ad illud, quod in prioris epist. Capite quarto dixit: Quid vultis? cum virga veniam, an cum spiritu lenitatis? Et hoc ipsum infra Capite vltimo apertius edicet: Praedixi, & ut praesens secundo praedico, quod si venero denuo, non parcam, quandoquidem experimentum quaeritis in me loquentis Christi, &c.
units.tr: But what does Paul wish to achieve or obtain by such a weighty appeal? "I ask," he says, "that when I am present I may not have to be bold with that confidence with which I think of being bold against certain people, who regard us as though we walked according to the flesh." The sense of these words is this: "I beg you to so conduct yourselves that when I come I may not be compelled to use in your presence that confidence and authority which I now intend to exercise against certain people who despise us too insolently, as though we walked according to the flesh, that is, as though I were led by fleshly affection, relied on nothing but fleshly protection, and therefore deserved to be despised." But in saying this he alludes to what he said in the fourth chapter of his earlier epistle: "What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in the spirit of gentleness?" And he states this same thing more plainly in the last chapter below: "I have told you before, and as though present a second time I tell you again, that if I come again I will not spare, since you seek proof of Christ speaking in me," etc.

units.la: Habemus autem in Paulo singularis modestiae & lenitatis exemplum, qui etsi iniurijs atrocissimis provocatus esset, noluit tamen adhuc suo iure uti, imò quasi supplex hoc deprecatur, ne ipsum cogant illud persequi. Adhaec, etsi quoduis supplicium iam illis meruissent, non tamen insolentius eis minatur, sed solummodo se de vindicta cogitare dicit, si videlicet sua contumacia ipsum cogant, ut eam exequatur. Quam vero alieni sunt ab hoc spiritu lenitatis hodie Romani Pontifices, qui Apostolicorum nomine gloriantur? Hi certè si sui nominis existimationem, aut sedis suae authoritatem, vel vnico verbulo laedi sentiant, illico ad excommunicationis fulmen recurrunt, nec contenti vnius caput petiisse, insuper seditionibus, bellis, incendijs omnia miscent.
units.tr: Moreover, in Paul we have an outstanding example of modesty and gentleness, who, though provoked by the most atrocious injuries, nevertheless was unwilling to use his right, but even as a suppliant begs that they not compel him to pursue it. Besides, although they had already deserved any punishment whatever, he threatens them no more insolently, but says only that he is thinking of vengeance, namely if their obstinacy compels him to carry it out. How far removed from this spirit of gentleness are the Roman Pontiffs today, who glory in the name of the Apostles! If they feel that the esteem of their name or the authority of their see has been harmed even by a single word, they at once have recourse to the thunderbolt of excommunication, and not content with attacking one head, they throw everything into confusion with seditions, wars and burnings.

units.la: Interim meminerimus, veros Christi ministros per modestiam & mansuetudinis leges nequaquam prohiberi, quo minus digna seueritate vtantur aduersus praefractos, qui incurabili contumacia contra Dei Verbum proteruiunt. Sic Mosem scimus fecisse, quando ei cum Cora & huius coniuratis res erat, qui impia temeritate à Deo institutum ordinem vna cum legitimo cultu euertere conabantur. Similia exempla in Prophetis extant. Quis mitior fuit Isaia, qui tam blandis consolationibus eos confirmat, quos propter scelera in Babylonem abducendos esse sciebat? Quis Ieremia indulgentior, qui sanguinariae vrbis excidium tam multis tamq; amaris lachrymis defleuit? Quam grauiter autem idem illi tonant & fulminant contra incurabiles & poenitere nescios Verbi Dei illusores? Possumus his Christum connumerare, qui etsi mirifica indulgentia hoflies suos tulerit, ijsdem tamen Væ illud horrendum denuntiat, cum eos nulla ratione emendari posse videret. Hæc exempla si cum nostri seculi moribus conferamus, mox patebit, quid Verbi ministros facere conueniat, quando fatalis quædam securitas & letalis ἀναλγησία omnium fere hominum animos occupauit, vt nec scelerum atrocitate moueantur, neque ipsos percutientis Dei manum agnoscant.
units.tr: Meanwhile let us remember that true ministers of Christ are by no means prevented by the laws of modesty and gentleness from using due severity against the stubborn, who with incurable obstinacy rebel against the Word of God. Thus we know Moses acted when he had to deal with Korah and his conspirators, who with impious rashness tried to overthrow, together with the lawful worship, the order instituted by God. Similar examples exist among the Prophets. Who was milder than Isaiah, who confirmed with such gentle consolations those whom he knew were to be led away to Babylon because of their crimes? Who was more indulgent than Jeremiah, who mourned the destruction of the bloody city with so many and such bitter tears? Yet how gravely those same men thunder and lightning against the incurable and unrepentant mockers of the Word of God! We may add Christ to these, who, though he bore with his enemies with wonderful indulgence, nevertheless pronounced that dreadful Woe upon them, since he saw that they could by no means be amended. If we compare these examples with the manners of our own age, it will soon be plain what it befits the ministers of the Word to do, when a certain fatal security and deadly insensibility have seized the minds of almost all men, so that they are moved neither by the atrocity of their crimes nor recognise the hand of God striking them.

units.la: Porro ne frustra hac deprecatione vti videretur Apostolus, eius rationem reddit, & sefub vili illa & contemptibili specie potestate instructu esse docet maiori quam ipsi ferre possint. Nam in carne (inquit) incedentes, non secundum carnem bellum gerimus. In carne ambulare hoc loco idem est, quod in carne viuere, aut in hoc mundo versari. Quo sensu ad Philippen. quoq; scribit: Vt in carne permaneam, magis necessarium est propter vos. Et hoc pijs cum impijs commune est, quod nimirum vtriq; vitam hanc mortalem in carne viuunt. At secundum carnem viuere, est carnis sensu atq; desideriis duci, & consiliis carnalibus regi. Habent ergo verba hæc Concessionis speciem, qua aduersariorum calumniæ respondet. Quasi diceret: Non est, quod mihi aliquis infirmam & vilem speciem sine persona, quam sustineo, exprobret. Nam ego ipse fateor, me in carne viuere, & hominem esse, à quo nihil humanum alienum sit, & proinde infirmum, caducum, mortalem & infinitis casibus obnoxium esse. Sed qualis qualis sum, non tamen secundum carnem hoc bellum gero, quod mihi Christus mandauit. Id est, minister meum non humanum aut carnale est, neque in eo obeundo carnis affectibus indulgeo, aut huius consilia sequor: sed totum hoc negotium diuinum est, & à Dei spiritu gubernatur.
units.tr: Furthermore, lest the Apostle should seem to use this entreaty in vain, he gives the reason for it, and teaches that under that lowly and contemptible appearance he was furnished with a power greater than they could bear. "For walking in the flesh," he says, "we do not wage war according to the flesh." To walk in the flesh here is the same as to live in the flesh, or to dwell in this world. In this sense he also writes to the Philippians: "To remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake." And this is common to the godly and the ungodly, that both alike live this mortal life in the flesh. But to live according to the flesh is to be led by the sense and desires of the flesh, and to be ruled by carnal counsels. These words therefore have the form of a concession, by which he answers the calumny of his adversaries. As if he said: "There is no reason for anyone to reproach me for the weak and lowly appearance under which I labour. For I myself confess that I live in the flesh and am a man, to whom nothing human is foreign, and therefore weak, frail, mortal, and subject to countless accidents. But whatever I am, I do not wage this war which Christ has committed to me according to the flesh." That is, my ministry is not human or carnal, nor do I in discharging it indulge the affections of the flesh or follow its counsels; but this whole business is divine and is governed by the Spirit of God.

units.la: Docet nos locus iste, Veritatis doctrinæ nihil decedere propter eius precones viles & contemptibiles. Vtuntur fere hoc argumento, qui illam in contemptum adducere, & inuisam facere conantur. Clamant enim: Annon homines fuerunt Apostoli & Prophetæ? Annon homines sunt, qui hodie concionantur? Cur ergo vt illis credamus, vrgemur? Annon omnis homo mendax est? Quid item homini tam facile est, quàm falli simul & fallere? Quibus nos cum Paulo respondemus: Fuerunt quidem illi homines mortales & nobis ὁμοιοπαθεῖς, id est, ijsdem nobiscum affectibus atq; casibus obnoxij: at quoad officium, ipsis commendatum, non vulgares homines fuerunt, qui humanis affectibus & consiliis ducti docuerint, quæ in ipsorum ore temere nata sunt: sed Dei homines fuerunt, quos ille totos sibi consecrauit, vt eorum ministerio in voluntate sua manifestan da vteretur. Sic ipse de Patriarchis olim testatus est, Chananæis dicens: Ne tetigeritis Christos meos, & prophetis meis quid mali faciatis. Prophetis quoq; idem ille dicebat: Ecce, ego posui verba mea in os tuum, & quæcunq; ego tibi mandauero, loqueris. Item: Accipies verbum ex ore meo, & monebis eos ex me. De Apostolis autem Christum pronuntiauisse scimus: Qui vos audit, me audit, &c. Si qui ergo hodie non alia docent, quàm quæ ex Scripturis propheticis & apostolicis deprompta sunt, illi quoq; non vt homines vulgares contemni, sed vt Dei serui atq; interpretes audiri debent. Eadem enim horum ratio siue conditio est, quæ Legati, qui Regis sui nomine bellum gerit: quod simile huic negotio probe conuenit, vt in proximo Sermone dicetur Nunc discamus Dei bonitatem agnoscere, qui Verbi sui thesaurum, quo nullus pretiosior & miseris nobis magis necessarius est, vasis testaceis credit (vt supra Cap. quarto Apostolus monuit) sed tam familiariter ad captum nostrum demittit. Audiamus ergo loquentè in seruis suis IESVM CHRISTVM, & huic nos totos consecremus, qui nobis doctor & seruator catholicus datus est. Huic debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: This passage teaches us that the doctrine of truth loses nothing because of its heralds being base and contemptible. Those who try to bring it into contempt and make it hateful commonly use this argument. For they cry: "Were not the Apostles and Prophets men? Are not those who preach today men? Why then are we pressed to believe them? Is not every man a liar? And what is so easy for a man as to be deceived and to deceive at the same time?" To these things we answer with Paul: those men were indeed mortal and like us in their passions (homoiopatheis), that is, subject to the same affections and accidents as we are; but as regards the office committed to them, they were not ordinary men, who, led by human affections and counsels, taught what had rashly sprung up in their own mouths; they were men of God, whom he wholly consecrated to himself, that he might use their ministry to make known his will. So he himself testified of the Patriarchs long ago, speaking to the Canaanites: "Do not touch my anointed ones, and do no harm to my prophets." To the Prophets too he said: "Behold, I have put my words in your mouth, and you shall speak whatever I command you." Likewise: "You shall receive the word from my mouth, and you shall warn them from me." And we know that Christ declared concerning the Apostles: "He who hears you hears me," etc. If therefore any today teach nothing other than what has been drawn from the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures, they too ought to be heard, not to be despised as ordinary men, but as servants and interpreters of God. For the position and condition of these men is the same as that of an envoy who wages war in the name of his king; which fits this matter well, as will be said in the next sermon. Now let us learn to recognise the goodness of God, who entrusts the treasure of his Word, than which none is more precious and none more necessary for us wretched men, to earthen vessels (as the Apostle warned above in the fourth chapter), yet stoops so familiarly to our capacity. Let us therefore hear Jesus Christ speaking in his servants, and let us wholly consecrate ourselves to him, who has been given to us as our catholic teacher and saviour. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XLIII.

units.la: Arma enim militiæ nostræ non carnalia sunt, sed Deo valida ad subuersionem munitionum: dum ratiocinationes euertimus, omnemq; sublimitatem: quæ extollitur aduersus cognitionē Dei, & captiuam ducimus omnem cogitationem ad obediendum Christo: & in parato habemus quo vindicemus omnem contumaciam, postquam impleta fuerit vestra obedientia.
units.tr: For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds, casting down imaginations and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ, and being in readiness to avenge all disobedience, when your obedience is fulfilled.

units.la: Paulus Apostolus primis septem Capitibus. multa dixit de suo ministerio, & qua fide in illo obeundo vsus fit. At quia hominibus, qui Veritatis odium semel conceperunt, nihil sufficit, redit nunc ad illud argumentum, et aliquanto acrius confutat aduersariorum suorum calumnias. Erat autem illis hic scopus propositus, quod eum apud Ecclesiam Corinthiacam in contemptum & odium adducere conabantur. Quia ergo ipsum, quando Corinthi docuerat, nullo splendore commendabilem, sed modestum & erga quosuis facilem atq; mansuetū viderant, nunc vero illius epistolas audiebant apostolica seueritate graues, quibus ipsorum vitia acerrime corripiebat, ex eo ipsum calumniabantur: quod nimirum Thrasonico & minaci fastu in absentes fulminaret, qui coram vix hiscere auderet. Ad ista ergo respondurus, initio incredibili lenitate eos rogat, ut cauere velint, ne quando cogatur coram seuerius agere: & illic simul monuit, non debere eos de ipso secundum carnem & speciem externam iudicare: Quia etsi homo sit, & in carne vitam mortalem agat, bellum tamen se contra mundum & huius principem, non carnis praesidijs, sed ipsius Christi auspicijs gerere. Id nunc diligentius explicat, & ea occasione paucis comprehendit, quæcunq; de ministerio Verbi Dei dici possunt. Quo loco ista nobis consideranda veniunt.
units.tr: In the first seven chapters the Apostle Paul said much about his ministry and about the faith with which he had discharged it. But since nothing is enough for men who have once conceived a hatred of the truth, he now returns to the same subject and refutes the slanders of his opponents with somewhat more vigour. Their aim was this: they tried to bring him into contempt and hatred in the Church at Corinth. When he had been at Corinth, they had seen him as a man without any show of distinction, modest and easy and gentle towards everyone. But now they heard his letters, weighty with apostolic severity, in which he rebuked their faults most sharply, and on this ground they slandered him: that he thundered against absent people with a boastful and threatening arrogance, though in person he scarcely dared to open his mouth. Therefore, to answer these charges, he begins by pleading with them, with incredible gentleness, that they should take care not to force him to deal more severely when he is present. At the same time he warns them that they ought not to judge him according to the flesh and his outward appearance. For although he is a man and lives a mortal life in the flesh, he wages war against the world and its prince, not with the defences of the flesh but under the leadership of Christ himself. He now explains this more carefully, and on this occasion he touches briefly on everything that can be said about the ministry of the Word of God. Several points here deserve our attention.

units.la: Primum, quod illud militiae confert, aut bello, quod vt Legatus gerat à Christo sibi mandatum. Conuenit simile hoc quàm maximè Apostolis. Scimus enim Christum iam inde ab initio destinatum fuisse, vt caput serpentis conculcaret, id est, vt veterem humani generis hostem, diabolum, debellaret & eius opera destrueret. Id verò partim fecit merito mortis suæ & resurrectione, partim spiritu oris sui (vt Isaias ait) id est, Euangelij sui praedicatione, per quam superstitiones, idololatriam & omne id per quod ille inter homines regnabat, euertit. Ad hanc autem vsus est Apostolorum ministerio, qui ab ipso emissi, Euangelium in toto orbe diuulgarunt, & expugnato vbique gentium Satanæ regno, homines Christo adduxerunt. In quo cum Pauli fides & industria prae cæteris eluxerit (vt alibi demonstrauimus) recte se huic militiae ascribit, & se bellum istud gerere profitetur.
units.tr: First, he compares it to military service, or to a war which he wages as an ambassador, with a commission given him by Christ. This comparison suits the Apostles extremely well. For we know that Christ, from the very beginning, was destined to crush the serpent's head, that is, to make war upon the ancient enemy of the human race, the devil, and to destroy his works. He did this partly by the merit of his death and resurrection, and partly by the breath of his mouth (as Isaiah says), that is, by the preaching of his gospel, through which he overthrew superstitions, idolatry, and everything by which that enemy held sway among men. For this purpose he used the ministry of the Apostles, who, sent out by him, spread the gospel throughout the whole world, and, when the kingdom of Satan had been overthrown everywhere among the nations, brought men to Christ. Since Paul's faith and diligence shone out above the rest in this work (as we have shown elsewhere), he rightly counts himself among this soldiery and declares that he is waging this war.

units.la: Interim debet hoc omnibus Verbi Dei administris applicari, quorum omnium idem est officium. Nam licet iam olim debellatus sit Satan, no quiescit tamen, sed indesinenter de possessione, è qua eiectus est, recuperanda cogitat, & regnum suum inter homines instaurare conatur. In eum ergo finem submittit falsos doctores, qui sub Veritatis praetextu incautos à Christo abstrahant. Seruiunt eidem peccatorum illecebræ, mundi exemplum & carnis nostræ desideria, quæ omnia securos reddunt, & peccandi licentiam pariunt. Et quia hæc pauci obseruant, pleriq; verò ijsdem sponte locum dant, ministros Verbi sui Christus constituit, quos statione suam constanter tenere, & Speculatorum instar pro publica salute excubare decet, ne qui ipsorum incuria & negligentia pereant. Debent ergo in horum meditatione diligenter versari, ne sibijpsis otium & pacem polliceantur, sed potius (vt Christus admonet) ratione ineant, quibus copijs & armis hosti aduenienti occurrere, & irruentem repellere possint. Nam licet is omnibus insidias struat, qui Christo nomen dederunt, prae alijs tamē Verbi administros petit, quia his ex statione sua deiectis, facilem sibi deinde reliquo vulgo victoriam pollicetur. Et hoc facit Christi admonitio, qui Petro in vltima Cæna dicebat: Simon, Simon, ecce Satanas expetiuit vos, vt ventilaret sicut triticum: sed ego rogaui pro te, ne deficiat fides tua: & tu aliquando conuersus confirma fratres tuos. Quantum item negotij Paulo fecerit, infra Cap.12. audiemus. Et hoc illum adhuc facere, exempla multorum quotidie docent. Quod si verò Ecclesiae ministros constantiores esse videt, quàm vt eius artibus se circumueniri, aut blanditijs capi patiantur, tunc alia via eos aggreditur, & tyrannos excitat, qui aut calumnijs improborum hominum, aut priuatis suspicionibus fascinati, odia & iras aduersus illos concipiunt, & eò vsq; progrediuntur, vt neq; regna sua consistere posse, neque se salvos fore sibi persuadeant, nisi illi è medio tollantur. Hinc apertæ persecutiones initium sumunt, quas olim quoq; semper à ministris coepisse, historiæ Ecclesiasticæ testantur.
units.tr: Meanwhile this must be applied to all the ministers of God's Word, whose duty is one and the same. For although Satan was long ago overcome, he does not rest, but without ceasing he plots to recover the possession from which he was cast out, and he strives to restore his kingdom among men. To this end he sends false teachers, who under the pretext of truth draw the unwary away from Christ. The allurements of sin serve the same purpose, along with the example of the world and the desires of our flesh; all these make men careless and produce a license to sin. And because few guard against these things, while many willingly give them room, Christ has appointed ministers of his Word, who ought to hold their post steadfastly and keep watch for the public safety like sentinels, lest any perish through their carelessness and negligence. They must therefore apply themselves diligently to considering these matters, not promising themselves ease and peace, but rather (as Christ admonishes) reckoning with what forces and weapons they may meet the approaching enemy and repel his attack. For although he lays snares for all who have given their name to Christ, he seeks above others the ministers of his Word, because once these have been thrown from their post he promises himself an easy victory over the rest of the crowd. Christ's warning does this, who said to Peter at the last supper: "Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brethren" [Luke 22:31-32]. How much trouble he caused Paul we shall hear below, in chapter 12. That he still does this, the examples of many show every day. But if he sees the ministers of the Church too steadfast to be deceived by his arts or to be taken by his flatteries, then he attacks them by another way and stirs up tyrants, who, bewitched by the slanders of wicked men or by private suspicions, conceive hatred and anger against them, and go so far that they persuade themselves that their kingdoms cannot stand, nor they themselves be safe, unless those men are removed. From this the open persecutions take their beginning, which the histories of the Church testify have always likewise begun with the ministers.

units.la: Ea autem tunc ferè est illorum infelicitas, quod infidos sentiunt eos, quorum saluti illi con fultum volunt, & qui ipsorum consilijs atq; conatibus imprimis fauere debebant. Differt enim in eo huius seculi militia à spirituali illa, quam homines Christiani faciunt. In illa milites suis dubus eò fideliores sunt, quò acriores & in oppugnando hoste fortiores ipsos esse vident, neq; ho-
units.tr: Their misfortune is then this: they find faithless those whose salvation they wish to promote, and those who ought above all to favour their counsels and efforts. For in this the warfare of this age differs from that spiritual warfare which Christian men wage. In the former, soldiers are the more faithful to their commanders the fiercer and braver they see them to be in attacking the enemy, nor

units.la: Lucæ 13. Lucæ 22. Isa. 11. stium calumnijs mouentur, quò minus illis obtemperent. At hic quò fortius hosti, diabolo nimirũ & mundo, ministri instant, eò magis suis quoque exosi siunt, & pleriq; sibi persuaderi patiuntur, dissidiorum & turbarum omnium authores esse solos Verbi Dei præcones, qui sua morositate & nimio rigore eos etiam offendant, qui pacis amantissimi sunt, & quosuis alios facile ferrent. Fit ergo, vt multi illorum capitibus pacem redimendam putent, nec videre volunt, his sublatis hostium rabiem longius progressuram esse. Potest huc referri Demosthenis Apologus de ouibus, quæ lupis de canibus conquerentibus fidem habuerunt, his autem procul remotis sub pacis prætextu lupis præda factæ sunt.
units.tr: Luke 13. Luke 22. Isa. 11. are they moved by the enemy's slanders so as to obey them less. But here the more fiercely the ministers press upon the enemy, the devil and the world, the more they become hateful even to their own people, and many let themselves be persuaded that the Lord's heralds alone are the authors of all quarrels and disturbances, since by their peevishness and excessive severity they offend even those who love peace most and would readily put up with anyone else. So it comes about that many think the heads of these men must be bought off for peace, and they do not see that once these are removed the rage of the enemies will proceed further. To this may be applied the fable of Demosthenes about the sheep, who believed the wolves when they complained of the dogs; but when the dogs were sent far away, under the pretext of peace the sheep were made the wolves' prey.

units.la: Sed ad Pauli verba accedamus, qui quia dixerat, Apostolos bellum hoc non secundum carnem, id est, non armis aut viribus carnalibus gerere, nunc quæ & qualia ipsorum arma sint, docet. Arma militiæ nostræ (inquit) non carnalia sunt, sed Deo valida, &c. Carnalia arma dicit, quæ à carne suggeruntur, qualia sunt, opes, honores, amicitiæ, fœdera, milites, doli, eloquentia, & quicquid aliud huius generis apud homines carni & mundo deditos magnificum & inuictum videtur. Atqui omnibus his Apostoli destituti fuerunt, vt Christus quoq; qui apud Pilatum regnum suum non de hoc mundo esse probat, quia neminem habeat, qui pro se pugnet. Et quoad Apostolos, scimus pauperes fuisse, extorres, contemptibiles, omnibus exosos, simplices & absque omni dolo, & prædicatione etiam vsos fuisse simplici, neque vllis humanæ eloquentiæ phaleris ornata. Quibus ergo armis pugnauerunt? Spiritualibus, Verbo Dei nimirum & Spiritus sanêti virtute, qui donis varijs & mirificis sese exeruit: qualia fuerunt, linguarum omnium cognitio, quæ omnibus admirabiles fecit: miraculosæ morborum sanationes, & dæmonum expulsiones: prophetia, fides in Deum inuicta: conscientiæ integritas, quam scuti instar conuitijs & calumnijs omnibus opposuerunt: Spiritus prudentia, qua diaboli artes & mundi astutiam eluserunt: zelus ardens gloriæ Dei & publicæ salutis, quo aduersa & pericula quæuis superarunt. Et hæc illa arma sunt, quibus etiam hodie verbi administros armatos esse oportet. Stulti sunt & malè fidi milites, qui istis neglectis ad mundum respiciunt, & huius amicitiam venantur, aut principum fauore nituntur. In his fere impletur, quod olim per Ieremiam dixit Dominus: Maledictus, qui fidit homini, & facit carnem brachium suum.
units.tr: But let us come to the words of Paul, who, having said that the apostles waged this war not according to the flesh, that is, not with carnal arms or strength, now teaches what and what kind of arms they are. "The weapons of our warfare," he says, "are not carnal, but mighty through God," etc. He calls carnal those arms which are supplied by the flesh, such as wealth, honours, friendships, alliances, soldiers, trickery, eloquence, and whatever else of this kind seems grand and invincible among men devoted to the flesh and the world. Yet the apostles were without all these things, just as Christ also, who before Pilate proved that his kingdom is not of this world, because he had no one to fight for him. And as for the apostles, we know they were poor, exiles, despised, hated by all, simple and without any guile, and that they used a plain preaching, adorned with none of the rhetorical polish of human eloquence. With what arms, then, did they fight? With spiritual arms: the Word of God, namely, and the power of the Holy Spirit, who showed himself in various and wonderful gifts. Such were the knowledge of all tongues, which made them admired by everyone; miraculous healings of diseases and expulsions of demons; prophecy; faith in God that could not be conquered; integrity of conscience, which they set against all reproaches and slanders as a shield; the wisdom of the Spirit, by which they eluded the arts of the devil and the cunning of the world; and burning zeal for the glory of God and the public salvation, by which they overcame every adversity and danger. These are the arms with which the ministers of the Word ought to be armed even today. They are foolish and faithless soldiers who, neglecting these, look to the world and hunt for its friendship, or rely on the favour of princes. In such men is fulfilled what the Lord once said through Jeremiah: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm" [Jer. 17:5].

units.la: Obseruabis autem, non excludi propterea à gubernatione & defensione Ecclesiæ principes Christianos: vt quidam malè feriati sentiunt, qui huius loci authoritate abutuntur, vt euincant, neminem publica magistratus authoritate ad certam fidei & religionis formulam cogi & astrin- gi debere, sed cuius permittendum esse, vt quod animo sentit, liberè profiteatur. Est horum dogma pestilentissimum & prorsus intolerabile. Nam sub libertatis Christianæ prætextu ex Ecclesia stabulum Circeum fabricare conantur, in quo omnis generis animalia vocibus diuersis tumultuentur, id est, diuersissimarum opinionum hæretici suos errores publicè tradant, & eosdem quibusuis obuijs obtrudant. Atqui pugnat hoc cum primitiuæ & Apostolicæ Ecclesiæ exemplo, in qua credentium omnium cor vnum fuisse, & illi omnes in Apostolorum doctrina perseuerauisse dicuntur. Deinde confundunt isti homines functiones Ecclesiasticas & Politicas. Quod enim de ministerio Verbi dicitur, hoc illi ad magistratus extendunt: nec obseruant, Paulum de ministrorum functione loqui, qualis tunc erat: omni nimirum carnali præsidio nudata. At non obstare hoc debuit, quò minus suo tempore impleretur, quod Deus Ecclesiæ per Isaiam promisit: Dabo Reges nutritios tuos, & Reginas nutrices tuas. At quales illi nutritij erunt Ecclesiæ, qui hæreses impunè grassari patiuntur? Quo item argumento probari poterit, abrogatam esse Legem Dei de occidendo falso propheta, qui Deos alienos colere docet, & à Deo traditam cultus formam euertit? Scio olim D. Augustinum in ea sententia fuisse, ne magistratus gladio coercerentur hæretici: sed Donatistarum indomiti furores & longus rerum vsus illum sententiam mutare coegit, quòd Ecclesiæ & fidei vnitatem non aliter conseruari posse videret.
units.tr: You will notice that Christian princes are not for that reason excluded from governing and defending the Church, as some idle fellows think, who misuse the authority of this passage to prove that no one should be compelled or constrained by the public authority of the magistrate to a fixed formula of faith and religion, but that each person should be permitted to profess freely whatever he thinks. This doctrine is most pestilential and wholly intolerable. For under the pretext of Christian liberty they try to turn the Church into a stable of Circe, in which animals of every kind make a din with their different voices; that is, heretics of the most diverse opinions publicly propagate their errors and press them on whoever they meet. Yet this is at odds with the example of the primitive and apostolic Church, in which, it is said, all believers had one heart and all of them persevered in the teaching of the Apostles. Moreover, these men confuse ecclesiastical and political functions. What is said of the ministry of the Word, they extend to the magistrates, and they do not observe that Paul is speaking of the office of ministers as it then was, stripped of all carnal protection. Yet this should not have stood in the way of what God promised the Church through Isaiah being fulfilled in its own time: "I will give kings to be your nursing fathers, and queens to be your nurses." But what sort of nursing fathers will those be who allow heresies to rage with impunity? By the same argument, could it be proved that the law of God concerning the killing of a false prophet, who teaches people to worship other gods and overturns the form of worship delivered by God, has been abrogated? I know that St Augustine once held the view that heretics should not be restrained by the sword of the magistrate; but the unbridled fury of the Donatists and long experience of affairs forced him to change that opinion, because he saw that the unity of the Church and of the faith could not otherwise be preserved.

units.la: Sed pergamus in Pauli verbis, qui armorum istorum vim & efficaciam describit, dicens illa Deo valida esse ad subuersionem munitionum. Quod Deo valida esse dicit, bifariam exponi potest. Primum, quòd Dei virtute valida & efficacia sint, qui per illa agat in ministris: & hic sensus Chrysostomo placuit. Deinde, quòd Apostoli his vni & soli Deo militent. Vtrq; sensus præsenti arguti argumento probè conuenit, & Paulum sic locutum existimo, vt vtrumque simul coprehenderet. Nã officij sui ministros hac locutio admonet, vt se Dei milites esse meminerint, & proinde huius solius gloria quærant. Vt item se absq; huius ope nihil posse cogitet, ideoq; nihil suæ industriæ aut meritis tribuant. Deniq; vt perpetuò memores, se Dei armis instructos esse, nõ metuat sibi ab hoc mundo, sed cũ Dauide dicant hostibus suis: Vos venitis contra nos cũ gladio, lancea & clypeo, nos autem venimus ad vos in nomine Domini exercituum. Est autem hoc Dei ingenium, quòd virtutem suam per ea exerit, quæ hominibus infirma & nullius pretij esse videntur, vt alibi quoque diximus.
units.tr: But let us go on with Paul's words, in which he describes the power and efficacy of these weapons, saying that they are mighty before God for the overthrowing of strongholds. That they are mighty before God can be explained in two ways. First, that they are mighty and effective by the power of God, who acts through them in the ministers; and this sense pleased Chrysostom. Second, that the Apostles fight with these weapons for the one and only God. Both senses agree well with the present argument, and I think Paul spoke in such a way as to embrace both at once. For this expression reminds the ministers of their office, that they should remember they are soldiers of God, and so seek the glory of him alone. Likewise, that they should recognise that they can do nothing without his help, and therefore attribute nothing to their own diligence or merits. Finally, that, always mindful that they are armed with the weapons of God, they should not fear this world for themselves, but say with David to their enemies: "You come against us with sword, spear and shield, but we come to you in the name of the Lord of hosts." It is, moreover, God's way to exercise his power through those things which seem weak and of no value to men, as we have said elsewhere.

units.la: Sed videamus, ad quid valida sint arma illa Apostolorum? Ad subuersionem munitionũ. Quasi diceret: Nemo nobis obijciat munitiones siue obstacula, quæ contra nos parantur. Nam quicquid mundus hic cum suo principe ædificauerit, ei demoliendo & euertendo hæc arma nostra sufficient. Vtq; res sit evidentior, omnia ista in duas species diuidit, dicens: Dum ratiocinationes euertimus, omnemq; sublimitatem, quæ extollitur aduersus cognitionem Dei. Sub ratiocinationum vocabulo omnia carnis seu rationis humanæ consilia comprehendit, per quæ Satan mille doloru artifex, vires suas maximè ostentat. Nam primum zelo inconsulto multos seducit, vt se Deo seruire putent, quando huius cultum extinctum volunt: quod olim Iudæis accidisse, & hodie multis accidere videmus. Deinde astutos facit, & mirifica consilia illis suggerit, quibus plures alios in suas partes trahunt. Accedit his Sophistica, in qua verè exercitatissimi sunt, quotquot Euangelij doctrinæ aduersantur. Alterum est omnis sublimitas, quæ aduersus cognitionem Dei extollitur. Hæc comprehendit omnem mundi gloriam, potentiam, fœdera, & quicquid hostes aperta vi moliuntur. His omnibus Paulus spiritualia illa arma opponit, quæ sola aduersus ista sufficiant: quod ab ipso verissimè dici, res ipsa indicat. Fuit enim Apostolis res cum Iudæorum Sacerdotibus, cum gentium philosophis, cum Romano Imperio, quòd viris tam politica prudentia instructis quàm militaribus abundabat. Perruperunt tamen per omnia ista obstacula, & sola Euangelij prædicatione ac Spiritus virtute munitiones istas diaboli omnes euerterunt: quod fore olim Propheta prædixerant.
units.tr: But let us see: for what purpose are those weapons of the Apostles mighty? For the overthrowing of strongholds. As if he were saying: let no one throw in our faces the fortifications or obstacles that are being prepared against us. For whatever this world with its prince has built up, these weapons of ours will be sufficient to pull down and overthrow. And so that the matter may be clearer, he divides all those things into two kinds, saying: "while we overthrow reasonings, and every height that is raised up against the knowledge of God." Under the word "reasonings" he includes all the counsels of flesh and human reason, through which Satan, the artificer of a thousand wiles, chiefly displays his power. For first, by ill-considered zeal he leads many astray, so that they think they are serving God when they want his worship extinguished; this we see happened to the Jews of old and happens to many today. Then he makes men crafty and suggests wonderful plans to them, by which they draw many others to their side. To these is added sophistry, in which all who oppose the doctrine of the gospel are truly most practised. The second kind is every height that is raised up against the knowledge of God. This comprehends all the glory, power, alliances of the world, and whatever enemies attempt by open force. Against all these Paul sets those spiritual weapons, which alone are sufficient against them; and the event itself shows that he spoke most truly. For the Apostles had to deal with the priests of the Jews, with the philosophers of the Gentiles, and with the Roman Empire, which abounded in men as well versed in political prudence as in military affairs. Yet they broke through all those obstacles, and by the preaching of the gospel alone and the power of the Spirit they overthrew all those strongholds of the devil; this the prophets had foretold would happen.

units.la: Porro finem quoque huius militiæ attingit Paulus, dum addit: Et captiuam ducimus omnem cogitationem ad obediendum Christo, & in parato habemus quo vindicemus omnem contumaciam, &c. Duo dicit, quorum alterum ad electos, alterum ad reprobos pertinet. Illos (inquit) nostris armis deuictos quasi captiuos ducimus, vt qui prius diabolo seruierunt, nunc Christo voluntariam & salutarem seruitutem seruiant. Hos autem coërcemus singulari Spiritus virtute, qua armati vindictam in parato habemus aduersus omnes, qui sese contumacius Veritati opponunt. Respicit ad potestatem illam ligandi & soluendi, quæ sub clauium typo alibi adumbratur: item ad singulare illud donũ Spiritus, quo rebelles multare potuerunt, & Satanæ affligendos tradere, vt suo loco diximus. Comprehendit autem hoc loco omnes ministerij Euangelici partes.
units.tr: Moreover, Paul also touches on the end of this warfare, when he adds: "and we take captive every thought to the obedience of Christ, and have in readiness to avenge every disobedience, etc." He mentions two things, one of which pertains to the elect and the other to the reprobate. The former (he says) we lead captive by our weapons, as captives, so that those who once served the devil may now serve Christ in a willing and salutary servitude. The latter we restrain by the singular power of the Spirit, by which, armed, we keep vengeance in readiness against all who set themselves more stubbornly against the truth. He refers to that power of binding and loosing which is foreshadowed elsewhere under the figure of the keys; likewise to that singular gift of the Spirit by which they could punish rebels and hand them over to Satan to be afflicted, as we have said in its place. Indeed, in this passage he embraces all the parts of the evangelical ministry.

units.la: Primũ in illo est, vt ministri demoliantur et euertat omnes munitiones quæ aduersus veram Dei cognitionem excitantur. Confultò autè sic loquitur: quia nè Satan quidè ipse videri vult ut esse, qui cum Deo bellũ gerat: & quia hoc omnibus detestabile videtur, cognitionè Dei veram obscurare satagit. In hunc sinè ergo falsam doctrinã affert, opiniones itẽm hominũ mentibus instillat vel superstitiosas vel Epicureas, quarum illæ quidem cultus illicitos & inutiles pariunt, hæ verò effrænis scelerum licentiæ causa sunt. In his ergo demoliendis ministros sedulos & strenuos esse oportet. Hoc enim illud est, quod Ieremiæ dicitur, ipsum constitutũ esse super gentes & super regna, vt euellat & extirpet, perdat & dissipet. Nam nisi id fiat, plantationi & ædificationi locus esse non potest. Obseruarũt hoc diligenter Apostoli, qui Legis quoq; statuta oppugnarunt, cũ his aliqui ad euertenda fidei iustitiã abuterentur, neq; eos terruit, quòd ideo contra Mosem & templũ concionari dicebantur. Inter gentes verò idololatriã et falsorũ Deorum cultus acerrimè debellarunt, quàmuis non ignorarent, quanto cum periculo hoc esset coniunctũ. Quid, quòd de futuris quoq; admonuerũt, vt posterorũ quoq; saluti consulerent? Est hoc obseruandũ propter eos, qui Euangelium hodie ita prædicari posse sibi persuadent, vt neque Antichristi artes & doli arguantur, neque scelera manifesta accusentur. Quod perinde est, ac si quis bellum gerere, hosti autem parcere velit, ne eum irritet. Atqui à pœnitentiæ doctrina prædicandi initium Apostoli facere debuerunt, quæ nulla esse poterit, nisi errores, superstitiones & scelera arguantur.
units.tr: The first part of it is that the ministers should pull down and overthrow all the strongholds that are raised up against the true knowledge of God. He speaks deliberately in this way, because Satan himself does not want to appear to be waging war against God; and since this seems detestable to everyone, he strives to obscure the true knowledge of God. To this end he brings in false doctrine and instils into men's minds opinions that are either superstitious or Epicurean; of these the former produce unlawful and useless forms of worship, while the latter are the cause of unbridled licence in sin.
