Therefore, in pulling these down the ministers must be diligent and vigorous. For this is what is said of Jeremiah, that he was set over nations and over kingdoms, to pluck up and to pull down, to destroy and to overthrow. For unless this is done, there can be no place for planting and building. The Apostles observed this carefully; they attacked even the statutes of the Law, since some were using them to overthrow the righteousness of faith, and they were not deterred by the fact that they were said for this reason to preach against Moses and the temple. Among the Gentiles they fought most fiercely against idolatry and the worship of false gods, although they were not unaware of how great a danger this involved. What of the fact that they also gave warning about the future, so that they might provide for the salvation of those who came after them? This must be observed on account of those who persuade themselves today that the gospel can be preached in such a way that neither the arts and deceits of Antichrist are exposed nor manifest wickedness is accused. This is just as if someone wanted to wage war but spare the enemy, lest he provoke him. Yet the Apostles ought to have begun with the teaching of repentance, which cannot exist unless errors, superstitions and wicked deeds are exposed.

units.la: Deinde ministrorum est, Captiuam ducere omnem cogitationem siue intelleƈtum ad obedien-diendum Christo. Nec enim satis est liberari à superstitionum iugo & peccati seruitio, nisi insuper Christo consecremur, in quo vno salus omnis habetur, & illum vnum audiamus. Hoc enim filijs Dei & omnibus suis proprium esse Christus docet, quòd ipsius solius vocem audiant & sequantur. Et fidei obedientiam alibi quoque totius Euangelicæ prædicationis finem atque scopum esse Apostolus scribit. At quia ad hanc homines adduci non possunt, quoad carnis ratione & sensu ducuntur, illam prorsus subigi & captiuam duci necesse est. Et huc pertinent, quæcunque de hominis regeneratione, nostrijpsius abnegatione, carnis mortificatione passim traduntur. At hoc illud est, in quo plerique cessant atque deficiunt. Nam gloriantur quidem multi Euangelio, sed qui eius captiui esse volunt, paucos est videre. Hinc est, quòd sub Euangelij prætextu licenter viuunt, & si quid aduersum incidat circa carnis cæca consilia, infeliciter tumultuentur, neque aliquid certum habeant. Meminerint ergo Christiani homines, nos ideo ex Satanæ tyrannide redemptos esse, vt Christo mancipati simus, & huic seruiamus. Nec enim liberi erunt ex Satanæ seruitio, nisi qui se Christo captiuos sistunt. Estque hæc omnium felicissima captiuitas, quia (vt Chrysostomus ait) assertio est ex seruitute in libertatem, ex morte in vitam, ex perditione in salutem. E contra verò infelicissima mancipia sunt, qui excusso Christi iugo, quiduis audendi licentia lasciuiunt.
units.tr: Next, it is the task of ministers to lead captive every thought or understanding to the obedience of Christ. For it is not enough to be freed from the yoke of superstitions and the slavery of sin, unless we are also consecrated to Christ, in whom alone all salvation is found, and hear him alone. For Christ teaches that it is proper to the children of God and to all his own that they hear and follow his voice alone. And the Apostle writes elsewhere that obedience of faith is the aim and goal of all evangelical preaching. But since men cannot be brought to this while they are led by the reason and senses of the flesh, it is necessary that these be utterly subdued and led captive. To this belong all the things that are everywhere taught about the regeneration of man, self-denial and the mortification of the flesh. But this is where most people stop and fail. For many boast of the gospel, but few are to be seen who want to be captives of it. Hence it is that they live licentiously under the pretext of the gospel, and if anything adverse arises against the blind counsels of the flesh, they are unhappily thrown into confusion and have nothing certain to hold to. Let Christians therefore remember that we have been redeemed from the tyranny of Satan so that we may be bound to Christ and serve him. For no one will be free from the servitude of Satan unless he presents himself as a captive to Christ. And this is the happiest of all captivities, because (as Chrysostom says) it is a passage from servitude to liberty, from death to life, from perdition to salvation. On the other hand, those are the most unhappy slaves who, having shaken off the yoke of Christ, grow wanton in the licence to dare anything whatever.

units.la: Tertio, ministri vindiƈtam quoque paratam habere debent aduersus eos, qui Dei Verbo contumaciter eluƈtantur. Illa autem ex Dei Verbo dependet, & per hoc exercetur, dum pœna denuntiantur transgressoribus, & ad Dei tribunal citantur qui admonitionibus & correptionibus pijs nolunt cedere. Fuerunt in eo olim acerrimi Prophetæ, qui etsi se rideri scirent ab improbis, subinde tamè Dominũ exercituũ illis inculcabant. Et qua constantia Paulus vsus fit, infra sub finem Cap. duodecimi & postremi initium patebit. Nec est quòd aliqui ferociores fiant, eò quòd vindiƈta non semper moxminas ministrorum sequitur, vt olim quando Ananias & Sapphira subito mortui sunt, & Elymas Magus cæcitate illico percussus est. Singulis enim suum diem destinauit Deus, & interdum pœnæ propter eleƈtos differuntur, vt hi resipiscendi tempus & occasionem habeant. Venietautem hora, quandoque incurabilibus certò vindiƈta sumetur.
units.tr: Thirdly, the ministers ought also to have vengeance ready against those who stubbornly struggle against the Word of God. That vengeance depends upon the Word of God and is exercised through it, when punishments are announced to transgressors and those who refuse to yield to pious admonitions and rebukes are summoned to God's judgment seat. Of old there were very fierce prophets in this matter, who, although they knew they were mocked by the wicked, nevertheless kept urging the Lord of hosts upon them from time to time. And with what constancy Paul acted will become clear toward the end of the twelfth chapter and at the beginning of the last. Nor is there any reason for some to become more savage because vengeance does not always follow the threats of ministers at once, as when Ananias and Sapphira died suddenly, and Elymas the sorcerer was struck immediately with blindness. For God has appointed a day for each, and sometimes punishments are deferred on account of the elect, so that these may have time and opportunity for repentance. But an hour will come when vengeance will certainly be taken on the incurable.

units.la: Et huc pertinet huius loci clausula: Postquam impleta fuerit vestra obedientia. Hac enim causam indicare vult, cur non nunc vindiƈtam contra contumaces illos exerat: Nimirum quia nõ omnes deplorati erant, sed multi ex infirmitate, multi communi exemplo abrepti peccauerant, qui iam cœperant in viam redire. At quia nondum perfeƈta erat eorum obedientia, rigorem isium & vindiƈtæ executionem differri oportuit, donec isti ad metam suam peruenirent, & non cum incurabili rebellium turba eodem exitio implicarentur. Distinxit ergo Paulus inter proteruos illos & alteros, de quibus adhuc bona spes erat, quorum rationem habendam esse putauit, ne in medio pœnitentiæ cursu interciperentur.
units.tr: To this belongs the closing clause of this passage: "after your obedience shall be fulfilled." For by this he wishes to indicate the reason why he does not now inflict vengeance on those stubborn men: namely, because not all of them were past hope; many had sinned through weakness, and many had been carried away by the common example, and these had already begun to return to the way. But since their obedience was not yet complete, the severity and the execution of vengeance had to be deferred until these men reached their goal, and so that they would not be caught up in the same destruction with the incurable crowd of rebels. Paul therefore distinguished between those headstrong men and the others, of whom there was still good hope, and he thought their case must be taken into account, lest they be cut off in the middle of their course of repentance.

units.la: Debet hinc generalis doƈtrina peti, quomodo vindiƈta & castigatio in Ecclesia exerceri debeat. Non quidem parcendum est impijs, sed ita tamen agendum, ne horum contumacia fraudi sit pijs & tractabilioribus. Docet hoc suorum iudiciorum exemplis Deus. Nã etsi is olim mundũ incurabile diluuij aquis perderet, Noã tamen iustitiæ præconẽ ab vniuersali illo exitio eripuit. Ideo Sodomas cũ vicinis vrbibus igne cœlitus immisso exussit, Lothũ autẽ cũ suis seruauit. Et cũ Ægyptum varijs plagis affligeret, inter filios Israëlis & hostes eorum diligenter distinguebat, ne illi quoque cum his multarentur. Et Moses ex Dei mandato populum à Cora & coniuratorum eius tentorijs procul secedere iubebat, ne idem cum his supplicium innoxij subirent. Nõ ergo probari potest inconsultus eorum rigor, qui flagitiosis ita infcuntur, vt cum his alios quoque extinƈtos velint. Tales sunt, qui propter paucos enormiter viuentes totas Ecclesias damnant: qui item in se ditionibus ab improbis quibusdam excitatis promiscue in innoxiam populi turbam seuiunt. Fidos medicos potius imitari conuenit, qui partes vitiosas sic vrunt & secant, ne saniores simul periclitentur. At simul piorum est, vt ipsi sese separent, neq; communicent aliorum sceleribus. Neq; sufficit hic bene cæpisse, sed (vt in præsenti Paulus monet) obedientiam implere oportet. Continet ergo locus hic œconomiam Ecclesiæ ab ipso Deo institutam. In hanc itaque intenti pastores demo-liantur liantur sedulò quæcunque aduersus Dei cognitionem extolli vident: è contra omnes captiuos ducere studeant ad obediendum Christo: improbis verò & præfractis fortiter resistant: rationem autem diligentem habeant eorum, qui adhuc cunabiles sunt. His verò se accommodent quicunque Christiani dici & haberi volunt, vt IESVM CHRISTVM in seruis suis loquentem audiant, & eidem se totos consecrent: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: From this a general teaching ought to be drawn about how vengeance and correction ought to be exercised in the Church. Indeed the wicked are not to be spared, but yet it must be done in such a way that the obstinacy of these people does not bring harm to the godly and the more teachable. God teaches this by the examples of his judgments. For although he once destroyed the incurable world with the waters of the flood, he nevertheless rescued Noah, the herald of righteousness, from that universal destruction. So he burned Sodom and the neighbouring cities with fire sent from heaven, but preserved Lot with his own. And when he afflicted Egypt with various plagues, he carefully distinguished between the sons of Israel and their enemies, so that they too would not be punished along with these. And Moses, by God's command, ordered the people to withdraw far from the tents of Korah and his conspirators, so that the innocent would not undergo the same punishment with them. Therefore that ill-considered severity cannot be approved, of those who so attack the wicked that they want others destroyed along with them. Such are those who condemn whole churches on account of a few who live scandalously; likewise those who, when factions have been stirred up by certain wicked men, rage indiscriminately against the innocent crowd of the people. It is fitting rather to imitate faithful physicians, who cauterise and cut away the diseased parts in such a way that the healthier parts are not endangered at the same time. But it is also the part of the godly to separate themselves and not share in the crimes of others. Nor is it enough here to have made a good beginning; but (as Paul warns in the present passage) it is necessary to fulfil obedience. This passage therefore contains the economy of the Church instituted by God himself. Keeping this in view, let ministers diligently pull down whatever they see raised up against the knowledge of God; on the contrary, let them strive to lead all captives to obey Christ; let them resist the wicked and the stubborn with courage; and let them take careful account of those who are still infants. Let whoever wishes to be and be called Christians accommodate themselves to these things, so that they may hear Jesus Christ speaking in his servants, and consecrate themselves wholly to him, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XLIV.

units.la: Quæ ob oculos sunt aspicitis? Si quis apud se confidit se Christi esse, hoc vicissim cogitet ex sese, quòd quemadmodum ipse Christi est, ita & nos Christi esse. Nam si amplius etiam quippiam gloriner de potestate nostra, quam dedit Dominus nobis ad ædificationem, & non ad subuersionem vestri, non pudefiam: Ne videar ceu perterrefacere vos per epistolas. Nam epistolæ quidem (inquit) graues sunt & validæ: sed præsentia corporis infirma est, & sermo nihili. Hoc cogitet qui istiusmodi est, quòd quales sumus verbo per epistolas cum absumus, tales etiam fore reipsa cum aderimus.
units.tr: Do you look at what is before your eyes? If anyone trusts in himself that he belongs to Christ, let him think this in turn: just as he himself belongs to Christ, so do we. For if I should boast somewhat more of the authority which the Lord gave us for building you up and not for tearing you down, I would not be ashamed, lest I seem to frighten you with letters. For his letters, he says, are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech is worthless. Let whoever is such a man consider this: that such as we are in word through letters when we are absent, such we shall be in deed when we are present.

units.la: Quoniam Deus Verbi sui præcones fere ex illis eligit, qui mundi huius iudicio hominies abiectissimi & nullius pretij esse videntur: non vtile modò, verumetiam necessarium est, vt in Dei consilium penitius inspiciamus, & ipsam ministrorum conditionem atque munus, quod sustinent, consideremus. Nisi enim hoc fiat, propter illos æternæ Veritatis doctrina in contemptum venit, & cum Dei gloria etiam salus nostra periclitatur. Hæc causa est, quòd Christus, qui Apostolos passim ad modestiam & humilitatem exhortatur, de eorundem tamen functione & dignitate admodum magnificè disserit. Et ipsi Apostoli authoritatem sui ministerij aduersus huius contemptores acerrimè tuentur, non quidem sui honoris causa, sed vt Deo suam gloriam vindicent, & hominum saluti consulant. Facit hoc ipsum Paulus in tota hac tractatione, qua suam existimationem aduersus æmulorum & impostorum quorundam calumnias defendit. Cum enim à nonnullis ideo contemneretur, quòd Corinthi humilius sese gessisset, ostendit nuper, se qualiscunque videatur, Christi militem esse, qui armis spiritualibus ipsum abundè instruxerit, quibus non modò debellare possit omnia, quæ aduersus Dei cognitionem erigitur, verumetiam de cotumacibus vindictam sumere. Id verò nunc propter aliquos, qui præfractiores erat, maiori cū grauitate Corinthijs applicat.
units.tr: Since God chooses the heralds of his Word mostly from those whom the world's judgment regards as the most abject men and of no worth, it is not only useful but necessary that we look more deeply into God's counsel and consider the very condition and office of ministers, and the task they undertake. For unless this is done, the doctrine of eternal Truth comes into contempt because of them, and our salvation is endangered along with God's glory. This is why Christ, who everywhere exhorts the apostles to modesty and humility, nonetheless speaks very magnificently of their function and dignity. The apostles themselves defend the authority of their ministry most fiercely against those who despise it, not for their own honour, but so that they may vindicate God's glory and look after men's salvation. Paul does exactly this throughout this whole discussion, in which he defends his reputation against the slanders of rivals and certain impostors. For since some despised him because he had conducted himself rather humbly at Corinth, he shows that, however he may seem, he is a soldier of Christ, who has amply equipped him with spiritual arms. With these he can not only overthrow everything that is raised up against the knowledge of God, but also take vengeance on the stubborn. Now he applies this with greater seriousness to the Corinthians on account of some who were more headstrong.

units.la: Orditur autem à graui increpatione, qua peruersum & iniquum quorundam de se iudicium corripit. Quæ ob oculos, aut secundùm faciem, id est, quæ in conspectu sunt aspicitis? Intelligit autem per ea, quæ ob oculos sunt, externam laruam, qua æmuli eius sese venditabant, vt ipsius authoritatem propter vilem & contemptibilem speciem, qua inter ipsos vixerat, eleuarent. Et podus orationi addit Interrogatio. Nam perinde hoc est, ac si diceret: Ita ne vos, qui alijs præstantiores & prudentiores habeti vultis, in ipsum iuris principium peccatis, dum personas, id est, laruas externas respicitis, & in pretio habetis opulentos, eloquentes et externi splendoris superbos ostentatores, neglecta interim iusti iudicij ratione, quæ in res ipsas diligentius inquirere, & secundum eas pronuntiare debet? Est enim hæc communis regula, quà Deus passim iudicibus præscribit. In Lege enim dicit. Ne feceritis iniquum quid in iudicio, neque suscipias faciem pauperis, nec reuereberis faciem potentis, iustè iudicabis proximo tuo. Et Moses iudicibus dicebat: Audite causas fratrum vestrorum, & iudicate iustè inter virum & fratrem eius, & inter peregrinum eius. Non agnoscetis faciem in iudicio, vt magnum sic & parùm audiatis, nec aliquem mortalium formidetis: iudicium enim hoc Dei est. Et his consentiunt, quæ Iosaphat, Rex optimus, abs se constitutis iudicibus præcepit, & quæ passim apud Prophetas fusius explicantur, qui hoc potissimum nomine magistratus iniquos accusant, quòd personarum respectu aut priuati commodi studio ducerentur. Quod quam fœdum & perni-
units.tr: He begins with a grave rebuke, by which he chides the perverse and unjust judgment some passed on him. "Do you look at what is before your eyes, or according to appearance, that is, at what is in sight?" By "what is before the eyes" he means the external mask behind which his rivals were showing off, so that they could raise up their own authority over his, on account of the lowly and contemptible appearance he had among them. The question also adds weight to the speech. For it is as if he said: Are you, who want to be thought more distinguished and wiser than others, sinning against the very principle of justice when you look at persons, that is, at external masks, and hold in high regard the wealthy, the eloquent, and the proud showy displayers of outward splendour, while neglecting the principle of right judgment, which ought to inquire more carefully into the things themselves and pronounce according to them? For this is the common rule which God everywhere prescribes to judges. In the Law he says: "You shall do nothing unjust in judgment; you shall not favour the face of the poor, nor revere the face of the mighty; you shall judge your neighbour justly" (Lev. 19). And Moses said to the judges: "Hear the causes of your brethren, and judge justly between a man and his brother and the stranger with him. You shall not show partiality in judgment; you shall hear the small as well as the great; you shall not fear any mortal, for this judgment is God's" (Deut. 1). These agree with what Jehoshaphat, that excellent king, commanded the judges he had appointed, and with what the Prophets explain at greater length throughout their writings, who accuse unjust magistrates chiefly on this ground, that they were swayed by respect of persons or by the pursuit of private gain. How foul and pernicious this is

units.la: Leuit. 19. Deut. 1. 2. Par. 19. trìfum fit, gentium quoque sapientes intellexerunt. Cambyses, tyrannus cum esset crudelissimus, iu- diciorum tamen æquitatem necessariam esse vidit, & ideo iniquo & corrupto iudici pellem detra- hi, & ea tribunal vestiri iussit, ut exemplo tam truculento alij absterrerentur. Thebani vero Se- natus typum expresserunt per cæcos & mancos, ut docerent iudices neque personas spectare, neque manus admunera capessenda habere debere. Et ex historijs constat, nullam Respub. diu incolu- mem mansisse, quæ iudicia venalia habuit.
units.tr: Lev. 19. Deut. 1. 2 Par. 19. it is, the wise men of the nations also understood. Cambyses, though he was a most cruel tyrant, nevertheless saw that fairness in judgments was necessary, and therefore ordered that the skin of an unjust and corrupt judge be stripped off and the tribunal be covered with it, so that others might be frightened away by so grim an example. The Theban Senate, however, expressed the image through blind and maimed men, to teach that judges ought neither to regard persons nor to keep their hands ready for taking bribes. And from histories it is clear that no commonwealth which had venal judgments remained unharmed for long.

units.la: Imprimis autem hoc observari debet in causa doctrinæ & religionis, de quo Christus Iudæos, iniquos sua doctrinæ & factorum æstimatores, graviter admonet, dicens: Ne iudicetis secundum aspectum, sed iusto iudicio iudicate. Etenim qui hic personas respiciunt, ij non possunt non falli perniciosissime. Ita enim comparatum est, ut qui numero plures, & dignitate præstantiores sunt, mendacium sequantur, aut proprijs persuasionibus seipsos decipiant. Estque hoc vetus malum, quod multis imposuit. Moses certe neminem præter Aaronem habuit, qui causam Dei cum ipso tueretur: aduersarios autem habuit, Pharaonem regem, aulicos omnes, Magos item, & ipsos Israe- litas, pro quorum libertate ille laborabat. Sic solus Elias cum Baalis sacerdotibus quadringentis & quinquaginta committitur. Et paulo post Micheas solus contra pseudoprophetas quadringen- tos Dei sententiam profert. Quid de Christo dicemus, qui cum lapis ille esset, quæ caput anguli Deus Pater destinauerat, ab illis tamen reprobatus est, qui tunc Ecclesiæ architecti haberi voluerant? Hoc ipsum de Apostolis dici potest, quos omnes cum sua doctrina damnari oportebit, si secundum ea, quæ in carnis sensus incurrunt, iudicare velimus. Et hoc Corinthijs imposuit, ut nequissimos impostores fido & germano Christi Apostolo anteferrent. Non est ergo, quod eorum clamoribus moueamur, qui nobis hodie aduersariorum multitudinem, authoritatem & consensum obijciunt, nobis vero paucitate & contemptibilem nostrorum doctorum & sectatorum conditionem expro- brant. Merentur illi cum Corinthijs grauem correptionem, quod cum Christi nomen & fidem pro- ficiantur, ad argumenta eiusmodi friuola confugiunt.
units.tr: Above all, this must be observed in the matter of doctrine and religion, about which Christ sternly admonishes the Jews, unjust assessors of his teaching and works, saying: "Do not judge according to appearance, but judge with a just judgment" (John 7). For those who here regard persons cannot help being most perniciously deceived. For it is so arranged that those who are more numerous and more distinguished in dignity follow falsehood, or else deceive themselves by their own persuasions. This is an old evil, which has deceived many. Moses certainly had no one besides Aaron who defended God's cause alongside him; he had adversaries, however: Pharaoh the king, all his courtiers, the magicians as well, and the Israelites themselves, for whose freedom he was labouring. So Elijah alone was pitted against the four hundred and fifty priests of Baal. And a little later Micaiah alone pronounced God's sentence against four hundred false prophets. What shall we say of Christ, who, though he was the stone which God the Father had destined to be the head of the corner, was nonetheless rejected by those who then wished to be regarded as the builders of the Church? The same may be said of the Apostles, all of whom, with their doctrine, would have to be condemned if we were willing to judge according to what falls under the senses of the flesh. And this is what deceived the Corinthians, so that they preferred the most wicked impostors to the faithful and genuine apostle of Christ. There is therefore no reason for us to be moved by the clamours of those who today throw in our faces the multitude, the authority and the consensus of our adversaries, while they reproach us with the paucity and contemptible condition of our teachers and followers. Those men deserve, together with the Corinthians, a severe rebuke, because, although they profess the name and faith of Christ, they take refuge in such frivolous arguments.

units.la: Sed obijciebant Corinthij: Atqui non possumus contemnere istorum sermones, cum Chri- sti ministri sint, & huius nomen profiteantur. Etenim impostores illi hoc potissimum nomine Pauli authoritatem eleuabant, quod se Christum vidisse, cum germanis eiusdem Apostolis fa- miliariter conuersatos esse, ab his denique missos esse gloriarentur. Huic ergo ille respondet: Si quis apud se confidit se Christi esse, hoc vicissim cogitet ex se, quod quemadmodum ipse Christi est, ita & nos Christi esse. Non negat illos Christi nomen profiteri, neque etiam (quod optimo iure poterat) falsi eos arguit, ne aliquos exasperet: sed se propter illos non debere viliorem æstimari doc- cet, cum etiam ipse Christi minister sit. Id vero sic enuntiat, ut aduersariorum conscientias com- pellet, adeoque hos proprio testimonio conuincat. Si (inquit) Christi sunt, haud dubie pro fratribus & conseruis suis agnoscent eos, qui cum ipsis Christo seruiunt, & hunc solum prædicant. Atqui ego illud non minus facio quam ipsi, quod res ipsa testatur, cum quotidie quam plurimos Christo lucrifaciam: & huic vni homines adducam. Cur ergo me ita despicatui habent? cur meam exi- stimationem extinctam volunt? cur me & doctrinam meam tam odiose vellicant? Latet au- tem sub his verbis magnum fiduciæ Apostolicæ argumentum, quando se Christi esse ita testatur, ut non obscure innuat, à Christo & eius Spiritu alienos esse eos, qui ipsum nolint pro conseruo & fratre agnoscere.
units.tr: But the Corinthians objected: "Yet we cannot despise the words of these men, since they are ministers of Christ and profess his name." For those impostors especially used this name to raise Paul's authority, since they boasted that they had seen Christ, had lived on familiar terms with the other Apostles, and had finally been sent out by them. To this he replies: "If anyone trusts in himself that he belongs to Christ, let him think this in turn from himself: that just as he himself belongs to Christ, so do we." He does not deny that they profess Christ's name, nor, though he could justly do so, does he charge them with falsehood, lest he provoke some of them. Rather, he teaches that he should not be valued any less on their account, since he too is a minister of Christ. He puts it in such a way as to press upon the consciences of his adversaries and thus convict them by their own testimony. "If (he says) they are Christ's, they will undoubtedly acknowledge as brothers and fellow servants those who serve Christ with them and preach him alone. Yet I do this no less than they do, as the thing itself bears witness, since every day I win very many for Christ and bring men to him alone. Why then do they despise me so? Why do they want my reputation extinguished? Why do they pick at me and my doctrine so spitefully?" Moreover, under these words lies a great argument of apostolic confidence, since he testifies that he belongs to Christ in such a way as to hint plainly that those who are unwilling to acknowledge him as a fellow servant and brother are alien from Christ and from his Spirit.

units.la: Est hoc omnibus Verbi administris summo studio curandum, ut idem de seipsis possint di- cere. Id vero poterunt, si vnum CHRISTVM IESVM fideliter prædicent, huic vni omnes adducant, in vita vero & moribus honestati & sanctimonia studeant. Qui tales asternatur, is eo ipso se Christi germanum discipulum esse negat. Debebant horum meminisse, qui hodie nos damnant, eo quod carnalem & crassam illam corporis Christi in Cœna mysticâ præsentiam atque manducatio- nem negamus. Quod si ipsi Christi sunt, cur non id respiciunt, quod Christianis hominibus proprium est? Atqui Christus omnes eos pro suis agnoscit et Deo patri commendat, qui in ipsum credunt, sicut Apostoli credere docuerunt. Non pro his rogo tantum (inquit) sed et pro iis qui creditur sunt per sermonē eorum in me. At summa prædicationis et doctrinæ Apostolicæ in Symbolo contineri, nemo pius vnquam negauit. Quid vero, quo ad illud, aduersarij nostri in nobis desiderant? Aut nū aliquæ articu-
units.tr: Every minister of the Word must take the greatest care that he can say the same of himself. He will be able to do so if he faithfully preaches the one Christ Jesus, brings all people to this one alone, and strives for honesty and holiness in his life and conduct. Whoever is found otherwise thereby denies that he is a true disciple of Christ. Those who condemn us today, because we deny the carnal and crude presence and eating of Christ's body in the mystical Supper, ought to remember this. But if they are Christ's, why do they not look to what is proper to Christian people? Yet Christ acknowledges all who believe in him, as the Apostles taught them to believe, as his own, and commends them to God the Father. "I pray not for these only," he says, "but also for those who shall believe in me through their word." No pious person has ever denied that the sum of the Apostolic preaching and teaching is contained in the creed. What then do our opponents demand of us with regard to that? Or can they say that any articles of faith are denied by us?

units.la: Ioan.17. articulorum fidei à nobis negari dicere possunt? Annon enim IESVM CHRISTVM agno scimus verum & aeternum Dei Filium esse, qui praefinito tempore ex Virgine homo natus, nunc in vna indiuidua persona Deus simul & Homo sit? Annon eundem pro nobis passum & mortuum peccata nostra expiauisse, resurrectione sua mortem atque inferos vicisse, ascensione nobis caelum aperuisse, & illic ad dexteram Patris sedere, & secundum vtramque naturam Mediatorem nostrum esse credimus & docemus? Annon illum in nouissimo die ad iudicium venturum fatemur, vt suis promissa fidei praemia tribuat, impios autem ad sempiternas poenas damnet? Cur ergo Christi esse negamur? Num quia illum vero suo & naturali corpore cum pane corporaliter coniunctum esse, fateri nolumus? aut quod corpus eius perinde vt Deitatem omnipraesens esse, & in Caena oraliter à dignis simul & indignis manducari negamus? At quis Apostolorum hoc vnquam tradidit? Vel qui nam Symboli Apostolici articulus, vt ita sentiamus, iubet? Scio quidem aduersarios nostros multa dicere, nosq; omnipotentiam Filij Dei negare, calumniari. Sed ista tam putida sunt, vt mirum sit illos non pudere eiusmodi figmentorum, ad quae toties iam responsum est. Idem ergo nouis illis Areopagitis & alienae fidei censoribus dicere possumus, quod Paulus in praesenti suis aemulis dicit: Si qui apud se confidunt se Christi esse, hoc vicissim cogitent ex sese, quod quemadmodum ipsi Christi sunt, ita & nos Christi esse.
units.tr: John 17. For do we not acknowledge that JESUS CHRIST is the true and eternal Son of God, who at the appointed time was born of a Virgin as a man, and who now, in one undivided person, is both God and Man? Do we not believe and teach that he suffered and died for us, expiated our sins, overcame death and hell by his resurrection, opened heaven to us by his ascension, sits there at the right hand of the Father, and is our Mediator according to both natures? Do we not confess that he will come to judgment on the last day, to give to his own the rewards promised to faith and to condemn the wicked to everlasting punishment? Why then are we denied to be Christ's? Is it because we refuse to affirm that he is bodily joined to the bread with his true and natural body, or because we deny that his body, just like his Deity, is everywhere present, and is eaten orally in the Supper by the worthy and unworthy alike? But did any of the Apostles ever hand this down? Or what article of the Apostles' Creed commands us to think so? I know indeed that our opponents say many things, and accuse us of denying the omnipotence of the Son of God. But these charges are so foul that it is astonishing they are not ashamed of such fictions, to which an answer has already been given so many times. So we can say the same to those new Areopagites and censors of another's faith that Paul says in the present passage to his rivals: "If anyone trusts in himself that he is Christ's, let him think this again within himself, that just as he is Christ's, so also are we Christ's."

units.la: Sed & auditores hoc loco admonentur, vt Euangelij praecones pro Christi seruis & legatis agnoscant, neque in ignobili eorum specie aut infelicis mundi de illis iudicio haereant. Nam nisi in Christum respiciant, qui de illis pronuntiauit, Qui vos audit, me audit: nunquam eos patienter ferent, sed aut impostores esse putabunt, aut stultos & insanos, vel etiam seditiosos rerum turbatores esse dicent. Hoc certe olim Achabo imposuit, qui neque Eliam neq; Micheam audire dignatus est, quod hunc quidem morosum obiurgatorem, illum vero regni totius turbatorem, vtrumque vero hostem suum esse sibi ipsi persuasisset. At e contra Dauid Nathanum magno cum fructu audiuit, quia Dei seruum esse & ex huius mandato loqui credebat.
units.tr: But because Paul had associated himself with others who in no way could be compared with him, he adds a qualification to that statement, by which he asserts and defends his own authority more forcefully against those who could answer thus: "If you are not Christ's in any other way than those teachers of ours whom you confess to be Christ's servants, what prevents us from listening to and following them rather than you? Indeed, it is fair that we should do so, since they are always with us, while you are far away, busied with the care of other churches." To this objection he replies: "For if I should boast somewhat more of our authority, which the Lord gave us, etc." These words have an ellipsis. For the sense is that Paul, although he claims for himself a greater authority than the rest or ordinary ministers have, will nevertheless not be a vain boaster. For although the Lord of all is one, and the same ministry is committed to all, and the same Spirit works in all, there are nevertheless diverse gifts of the Spirit, and therefore there are also certain grades among ministers, so that one is more excellent than another.

units.la: Quia vero Paulus se aliis accensuerat, qui ipsi nullo modo erant conferendi, correctionem eius dicti subijcit, qua suam exististimationem fortius asserit atq; tuetur aduersus eos, qui sic respondere poterant: Si tu non aliter Christi es quàm nostri illi doctores, quos Christi seruos esse fateris, quid obstat, quo minus te posthabito illos potius audiamus atque obseruemus? Imò vt id fiat aequum est, cum ipsi perpetuò nobiscum sint, tu vero procul absens circa aliarum Ecclesiarum curam occuperis. Huic obiectioni occurrit, dicens: Nam si amplius etiam quippiam glorier de potestate nostra, quam dedit Dominus nobis, &c. Habent verba haec Eclipsim. Nam sensus est, Paulum etsi aliquam potestatem sibi vendicet maiorem, quàm reliqui aut vulgares ministri habeant, non tamen vanum ostentatorem fore. Etenim licet idem omnium sit Dominus, idem quoq; ministerium omnibus commissum sit, & idem Spiritus in omnibus agat, sunt tamen diuersa dona Spiritus, & proinde certi etiam inter ministros gradus sunt, vt alius alio sit praestantior.
units.tr: This moderation of Paul's is to be carefully observed: he so humbles himself that at the same time he does not conceal the authority by which God had equipped him above others. For many today sin in this respect, for they are not sufficiently mindful of their condition. In order to win everyone's approval of their modesty and affability, they shamefully prostitute their authority. Some ministers of the Church do this, and many of those who have been called by God to the helm of the commonwealth also do it, although they ought to discharge their office with due seriousness. This is a grave sin, and Christ calls such people "salt that has lost its savour," which is of no use at all, not even fit for the dunghill. Let all therefore imitate the example of him who, however modest a man he was, never allowed his authority to be trampled underfoot with manifest contempt for his teaching. Rightly, then, in the present passage Paul acknowledges his colleagues, and does not claim lordship over the churches for himself alone; at the same time, he openly testifies that he has some greater power, which he ought not to dissemble. The words of Christ, who said of Ananias concerning him, "This man is a chosen instrument to me, to bear my name before the Gentiles and kings and the sons of Israel," agree with this. And again, Paul heard Christ speaking to him: "I have appeared to you for this purpose, to appoint you a minister and witness both of those things which you have seen and of those in which I will appear to you, delivering you from this people and from the Gentiles, to whom I send you, to open their eyes, that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, etc." To this may also be referred what took place between him and the Apostles, who, on account of the singular gifts of the Spirit which were found in him, appointed him Apostle to the Gentiles.

units.la: Estque diligenter obseruanda haec Pauli moderatio, qua ita se se humiliat, vt interim non dissimulet authoritate qua ipsum Deus prae aliis instruxerat. Peccat enim in eo multi hodie, quod nō satis memores suae conditionis, vt suam modestiam & facilitatem omnibus approbent, authoritatem suam turpiter prostituunt. Faciunt hoc aliqui ex ministris Ecclesiae. Multi item ex ijs, qui ad Reipub. gubernacula à Deo vocati sunt, & proinde debita grauitate functionem suam obire debebant. Est hoc graue peccatum, & tales falsem infatuatum vocat Christus, cuius adeo nullus vsus est, vt ne sterquilinio quidem seruiat: Quin ergo huius exemplum omnes imitentur, qui etsi hominum modestissimus esset, nunquam tamen passus est authoritatem suam conculcari cum manifesto doctrinae suae contemptu. Recte ergo in praesenti Paulus collegas quidem suos agnoscit, neq; solus sibi in Ecclesias dominium vendicat, simul tamen aperte testatur, se potestatem aliquam maiorem habere, quam dissimulare non debeat. Faciunt autem ad horum confirmationem verba Christi, qui Ananiae de ipso dixerat: Instrumentum electum est mihi iste, vt perferat nomen meum coram gentibus & Regibus, & filijs Israël. Et rursus illum sibi loquentem audierat: Ad hoc apparui tibi, vt designarem te ministrum ac testem tum eorum quae vidisti, tum eorum in quibus apparebo tibi: eximens te ex hoc populo & gentibus, ad quos te mitto: Vt aperias oculos eorum, vt se conuertant à tenebris ad lucem, & à potestate Satanæ ad Deum, &c. Quo etiam referri potest, quod inter ipsum & Apostolos transactum fuit, qui propter singularia Spiritus dona, quæ in ipso deprehendebantur, eum gentibus Apostolum destinauerunt.
units.tr: Lest, however, anyone think he has said something too arrogant here, he adds two things by which he softens the statement. First, that he has all this power not from himself, but received it from God. Second, that the same power was given to him for the building up of the churches, not for their destruction. In this way he at the same time strikes at the false apostles, who, though they themselves founded no churches, destroyed those that others had built. Some ambitious men do the same today: by unnecessary innovations they unhappily disturb churches that others have happily planted through their labour and diligence. We say nothing now of the Anabaptists, for whom this is almost their proper work. He also strikes at the perverse judgment of the Corinthians, who gave a place to such men, through whom they themselves were split into sects, and many things were overthrown that he had well established.

units.la: Ne tamen hic aliquid arrogantius dixisse putetur, duo adijcit, quibus hoc dictum mitigat. Primum, quòd potestatem hanc omnem, non ex semetipso habeat, sed à Deo acceperit: Alterum, quòd eadem ipsi data sit ad ædificationem Ecclesiarum, non ad destructionem. Ita verò simul pseudoapostolos perstringit, qui cùm ipsi Ecclesias nullas constituerent, ab aliis ædificatas destruebant. Vt hodie ambitiosi quidam faciunt, qui non necessarijs innouationibus Ecclesias aliorum labore & industria feliciter plantatas, infeliciter turbant: vt iam de Anabaptistis nihil dicamus, quorum hoc quasi proprium opus est. Sed & peruersum Corinthiorum iudicium perstringit, qui eiusmodi hominibus locum dabant, per quos ipsi in sectas scindebantur, & multa labefactabantur, quæ ab ipso bene constituta fuerant.
units.tr: Lest, however, anyone think he has said something too arrogant here, he adds two things by which he softens the statement. First, that he has all this authority not from himself but has received it from God. Second, that the same authority was given to him for the building up of the churches, not for their destruction. At the same time he thereby rebukes the false apostles, who, since they founded no churches themselves, destroyed those that others had built. Some ambitious men do the same today, who with unnecessary innovations unhappily disturb churches that others have happily planted with their labour and diligence; to say nothing yet of the Anabaptists, for whom this is almost their own work. But he also rebukes the perverse judgment of the Corinthians, who gave room to such men, through whom they themselves were split into sects and many things were overthrown that he himself had well established.

units.la: Rursus verò totam ministerij ecclesiastici rationem Paulus tradit, in qua hoc obseruatu dignissimum est, quòd ministros non aliam potestatem habere testatur, quàm quæ illis à Deo data est. Atqui hæc Verbo alligata est, neq; in dominio externo consistit, quale hodie Episcopi et Pontifices exercent. Imò ne quid huius Apostoli affectarent, Christus non semel grauiter prohibuit. Ita verò Dei verbo alligata est omnis ministrorum potestas, vt non aliud quàm hoc ipsis prædicare liceat. Nam ad omnes pertinet quod Ieremiæ dictum fuit: Ecce ego pono verba mea in os tuum, & quæ tibi mandauero loqueris. Et Ezechieli: Sumes verbum ex ore meo, & monebis eos ex me. Neque maiorem libertatem Apostolis datam esse, ex eo apparet, quòd non aliis gentibus tradere iubeatur, quàm quæ à Christo acceperant. Sed & ipsum Euangelium Dominus in prædicationem pœnitentiæ & remissionis peccatorum partitur, & vt vtramque in suo nomine annuntient præcipit. Ista igitur eos arguunt, qui cùm antistites Ecclesiæ haberi velint, vel à prædicandi munere omnino cessant, & circa res huius sæculi occupantur, vel sui capitis figmenta prædicant. Quid verò ea, quæ de sua potestate Apostoli dicunt, ad Pontifices & Episcopos faciunt, qui in vtroq; peccant, nec eo contenti sunt, quòd ipsi tacent, insuper alios quoq; non patiuntur prædicare, & templa simulachris complent, ex quibus discere debeant rudiores, quid facto opus sit?
units.tr: Again, Paul sets out the whole plan of the ecclesiastical ministry, in which this is most worthy of notice: that he testifies that ministers have no other power than that which has been given them by God. But this power is bound to the Word, and does not consist in external dominion, such as bishops and popes exercise today. Indeed, lest they should aim at anything of this kind, Christ more than once sternly forbade it. So completely is all the power of ministers bound to the Word of God that it is lawful for them to preach nothing but this. For what was said to Jeremiah applies to all: "Behold, I have put my words in your mouth, and you shall speak whatever I command you." And to Ezekiel: "You shall take the word from my mouth, and you shall warn them from me." Nor is it apparent that the Apostles were given greater freedom, since they are not ordered to hand on to other nations anything except what they had received from Christ. Moreover, the Lord himself divides the Gospel into the preaching of repentance and the forgiveness of sins, and commands them to proclaim both in his name. These things, therefore, condemn those who, while wishing to be regarded as leaders of the Church, either altogether cease from the office of preaching and occupy themselves with the affairs of this world, or preach the inventions of their own head. But what the Apostles say about their own authority has nothing to do with popes and bishops, who sin in both respects, and are not content that they themselves are silent, but moreover do not allow others to preach, and fill the temples with images, from which the cruder folk are supposed to learn what needs to be done.

units.la: Deinde vsum quoque & finem huius potestatis indicat Apostolus, quando datam dicit ad ædificationem, non ad destructionem. Deo eo dictum etiam in prioris epistolæ 14. Cap. Modus & regula ædificationis est, vt omnes super fundamentum IESVM CHRISTVM extruantur in domum spiritualem, quam Deus inhabitare possit, & in qua hic regnet atque glorificetur. At quia hic destructionem simpliciter excludit, quæri potest, annon ibi ipsi contradicat, cùm paulò ante se armis instructum esse dixerit diuina virtute & potentia validis ad subuersionem munitionum? &c. Sed obseruabis, Paulum illic loqui de subuersione eorum, quæ contra Dei cognitionem extolluntur, & quæ Dei siue Ecclesiæ ædificium impediunt: quæ destructio ad modum necessaria est: In præsenti autem de ea, per quam destruuntur fides & religio vera, dum homines à Christo abstrahuntur in diuersas sectas scinduntur, & Dei domus esse desinunt. Rursus ergo æmulos suos perstringit, qui multa bene ab ipso ædificata petulanter destruxerant, multa item sua incuria & negligentia passi erant corruere. Vide ergo quid de illis iudices, qui hodie destruunt quæ Deus ædificata vult, ædificant autem quæ deiici & euerti oportet, si Ecclesiam habere velimus rectè institutam? Gloriantur illi plenitudine potestatis: sed huius loci authoritate palàm conuincuntur, quo docemur, ne ipsis quidem Apostolis hanc potestatem concessam fuisse. Sunt ergo architecti eorum similes, qui pretiosum illum lapidem, Christum, reijciendo, fidem & religionem omnem euerterunt.
units.tr: Next the Apostle also indicates the use and the end of this power, when he says it was given for building up, not for destruction. He said this also in the fourteenth chapter of the earlier epistle. The measure and rule of building is that all be built upon the foundation of Jesus Christ into a spiritual house, which God may inhabit, and in which he may reign and be glorified. But since here he simply excludes destruction, it may be asked whether he does not contradict himself there, when a little before he said that he was armed with divine virtue and power, strong enough for the overthrow of strongholds, etc.? But you will observe that Paul there speaks of the overthrow of those things which are raised up against the knowledge of God, and which hinder the building of God or of the Church; that destruction is in a manner necessary. In the present passage, however, he speaks of that destruction by which faith and true religion are destroyed, while men are drawn away from Christ into divided sects and cease to be the house of God. Again, then, he rebukes his rivals, who had wantonly destroyed many things that had been well built by him, and had also suffered many things to fall through their own carelessness and negligence. See, then, how you should judge those who today destroy what God wills to be built up, and build up what ought to be pulled down and overthrown, if we wish to have the Church rightly ordered? They boast of the fullness of their power; but by the authority of this passage they are plainly convicted, since we are taught that this power was not granted even to the Apostles themselves. They are therefore like those architects who, by rejecting that precious stone, Christ, overthrew all faith and all religion.

units.la: At ne propter hoc quoque dictum insolentiorem dicerent Paulum, mox subijcit: Ne videar ceu perterrefacere vos per epistolas, &c. Est hæc quoque oratio ecliptica, quam ita supplere poteris: Sed nolo de mea potestate plura dicere, ne aduersarijs nouam calumniandi occasionem præbeam. Scio enim quid de me quidam dicat: Epistolæ quidem graues sunt & validæ: sed præsentia corporis infirma est, & sermo nihili. Quibus verbis certum quendam perstringit, qui aliorum antesignanus erat. Et talem quendam fuisse apparet ex ijs, quæ de eodem infra dicet: Si is qui venit alium IESVM prædicet, quem non prædicauimus, &c. Solebant autem isti omnes de ea Pauli præsentia contemptius loqui, qua cum ipsis fuerat, cùm Corinthi primùm prædicaret. Et erat hoc peruerfissimi iudicij argumentum, quòd humile illud & contemptibile vitæ genus ipsi vitio verterent, quod non alia de causa secutus erat, quàm vt eorum saluti consuleret. Solent hoc ipsum hodie multi facere, qui Verbi administros propter ea contemnunt; quæ illi propter ipsos patiuntur & ferunt.
units.tr: But lest on account of this saying they should call Paul too arrogant, he immediately adds: "Lest I seem as if I would terrify you by letters," etc. This also is an elliptical expression, which you may supply thus: "But I do not wish to say more about my power, lest I give my adversaries a new occasion for slander. For I know what some say about me: 'The letters indeed are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech is worthless.'" By these words he rebukes a certain man who was the leader of others. And that he was such a man appears from what he says below about the same person: "If he who comes preaches another Jesus, whom we have not preached," etc. Now all these men were accustomed to speak more contemptuously of that presence of Paul which he had had with them when he first preached at Corinth. And this was a very perverse sign of judgment, that they found fault with that humble and despised manner of life, which he had followed for no other reason than to provide for their salvation. Many today do the very same, who despise the ministers of the Word for those things which these men endure and bear on account of them.

units.la: Porrò calumniam istam Paulus grauiter excipit & confutat, dicens: Hoc cogitet qui istiusmodi est, quòd quales sumus verbo per epistolas cùm absumus, tales etiam fore reipsa cùm adesse rimur. Sibijpsi applicat, quod prius in genere de communi omnium Apostolorum functione dixit. Per Verbum autem doctrinam & correptiones intelligit, quas literis comprehensas ad illos miserat, & sensus huius loci est, quòd reipsa declarare velit, se non inanibus minis aduersus ipsos tonuisse, sed ita cum ipsis actu rum esse vbi venerit, vt se Christi virtute instructum esse sensuri sint.
units.tr: Moreover, Paul takes up this calumny gravely and refutes it, saying: "Let him who is such consider this, that such as we are in word by letters when we are absent, such we shall be also in deed when we are present." He applies to himself what he had said before in general about the common function of all the Apostles. By "word" he understands the teaching and the corrections which he had sent to them in writing; and the sense of this passage is that he wishes to show in fact that he has not thundered against them with empty threats, but that when he comes he will so deal with them that they will feel he is armed with the power of Christ.

units.la: Quo loco admonemur, ministros Ecclesiæ constantiam & grauitatem decere, vt sibi ipsis similes sint. Ab hac certè Ioannem Baptistam Christus ipse commendauit. Talem quoque Eliam fuisse legimus, quem ne Regis quidem ferocissimi conspectus terrere potuit, vt in doctrina semel ex Dei mandato tradita aliquid mutaret. Quod ipsum de omnibus etiam alijs Prophetis dici potest. Et Apostolos constantissimos fuisse, Lucas in Actis perhibet, adeo vt Senatui coram in faciem dicerent, Deo magis quam hominibus esse obtemperandum. Quod autem de Verbi administris dicitur, hoc ijs quoque plus quam necessarium est, quibus Reipub. gubernacula commissa sunt. Nihil enim illic turpius, nihil nocentius est leuitate aut temeraria bonarum legum mutatione. Quæ enim potest magistratuum esse authoritas, si hanc eo vitio ipsi profituantur, quod in priuatis hominibus omnes boni detestantur? Debet ergo hæc admonitio ad omnis loci & ordinis homines extendi, & vt eam omnes meditentur necesse est, eò quòd leuitate & inconstantia vbique peccatur. In religione, qua nihil nobis augustius, nihil sanctius esse debebat, plerorumq; animi cum fortuna mutantur. Idem in amicitijs fieri solet, quas vulgus fere vtilitate metitur. In contractibus quoque fides rara est, eò quòd lucro plerique ducuntur, neque magnam æqui, & honesti rationem habent. Hinc verò lites nascuntur, & horribilis rerum omnium confusio, quæ nihil certum & inuiolatum esse finit.
units.tr: In this passage we are reminded that the ministers of the Church ought to have constancy and gravity, so that they are like themselves. Christ himself certainly commended John the Baptist for this quality. We read that Elijah also was such a man, whom not even the sight of the most fierce king could terrify into changing anything in the doctrine once delivered by God's command. The same may be said of all the other Prophets. And Luke in the Acts relates that the Apostles were most steadfast, so much so that they said openly to the Senate's face that God must be obeyed rather than men. What is said of the ministers of the Word is necessary also, and more than necessary, for those to whom the helm of the commonwealth has been entrusted. For nothing there is more shameful, nothing more harmful, than levity or rash change of good laws. For what authority can magistrates have, if they profess themselves to have this vice which all good men detest in private persons? This admonition ought therefore to extend to men of every place and rank, and all must necessarily meditate upon it, since everywhere people sin by levity and inconstancy. In religion, than which nothing should be more venerable or holy to us, the minds of many change with their fortune. The same is usually done in friendships, which the common crowd for the most part measures by advantage. Faith is also rare in contracts, because most men are led by gain and do not have a great regard for what is fair and honorable. From this, indeed, lawsuits arise, and a dreadful confusion of all things, which allows nothing to be certain and inviolate.

units.la: Est præterea obseruandum, Apostolos coràm non alia docuisse in Ecclesijs, quàm quæ scriptis suis complexi sunt. Est ergo detestabilis eorum vanitas, qui sub illorum nomine traditiones & nescio quos Canones nobis obtrudere audent, qui cum eorum scriptis prorsus pugnant. At ne quid huius fieret, doctrinam Euangelij & quæcunq; ad Ecclesiæ œconomiam faciunt, Spiritus sanctus non solùm viua voce ab eis tradi, verumetiam scriptis mandari voluit. Ad ea ergo examinemus quæcunque alij proferunt, & in illis loquentem audiamus Dei Filium, IESVM CHRISTVM, qui Via est, Lux & Veritas. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, it must be observed that the Apostles, when present, taught in the Churches nothing other than what they embraced in their writings. It is therefore detestable vanity of those who dare to force upon us traditions and I know not what canons under the names of the Apostles, which are wholly at odds with their writings. But so that nothing of this kind should happen, the Holy Spirit willed that the doctrine of the Gospel and whatever pertains to the economy of the Church should be committed not only to be delivered by them with the living voice, but also to be entrusted to writings. Let us therefore examine by these whatever others put forward, and in these let us hear the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who is the Way, the Light and the Truth. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLV.
units.tr: HOMILY XLV.

units.la: Non enim audemus nos inferre aut conferre cum quibusdam, qui seipsos commendant: sed non intelligunt quòd ipsi sese seipsis metiuntur, & sese sibijpsis comparant. At nos non gloriabimur de ijs, quæ mensuræ nostræ non sint, sed secundum mensuram regulæ, quam Deus nobis partitus est, vt ad vos vsque peruenerimus. Non enim vt si non vsque ad vos peruenerimus, nosipsos supra modum extendimus. Nam vsque ad vos etiam peruenimus in Euangelio Christi: Non de ijs quæ non sunt nostræ mensuræ gloriantes in alienis laboribus: sed sperantes, quòd augescente fide vestra nos in vobis abundanter magnificandos fore secundùm nostram mensuram: Vt in locis quæ vltra vos sunt euangelizem: non vt in aliena mensura de præparatis gloriemur. Cæterum qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur. Non enim qui seipsum commendat, is probatus est, sed is quem Dominus commendat.
units.tr: For we do not dare to class or compare ourselves with some who commend themselves. But they do not understand that they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves. We, however, will not boast beyond our measure, in things that are not ours, but according to the measure of the rule which God has apportioned to us, to reach even as far as you. For we are not overstretching ourselves, as though we had not reached as far as you; we have indeed come as far as you in the gospel of Christ. We do not boast beyond our measure, in other men's labours, but we hope that, as your faith grows, we shall be greatly magnified among you according to our measure, so that we may preach the gospel in regions beyond you, and not glory in what is already prepared within another's measure. But he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord. For it is not he who commends himself who is approved, but he whom the Lord commends.

units.la: QVemadmodum Deus, qui homines vult saluos fieri & in Veritatis cognitionem pervenire, fidos Verbi sui præcones excitat, qui Veritatis & salutis æternæ doctrinam longè lateq; diuulgent: Ita Satan totus in eo est, vt fructum Verbi Dei impediat, ideoq; passim organa sua submittit, vt ζizania aspergant, & quæ bene ædificata sunt destruant. Factū hoc apud Corinthios quoq;. Nam Paulo inde digressso, obrepserunt homines ambitiosi & inquieti, qui omnia turbarunt, quæ ille per saniorem Euangelij doctrinam recte constituerat. Quare priorem ad illos epistolā dedit, qua acriter eos corripuit. Hi ergo vt imperium in illa Ecclesia retinere possent, & Paulum omnibus exosum facerent, vndique conuiciandi & calumniandi materiam venabantur. Inter alia autem vanum & ambitiosum ardelionem esse dicebant, qui absens epistolis minacibus fulminaret, præsens autem nihil auderet contra eos qui se ipsi opponerent. Hic respondit nuper, quòd non alius sit in literis, quam præsens coram, neq; alia scribat, quam quæ in faciem ipsis dicturus sit, si ita res poposcit. Id nunc diligentius explicat.
units.tr: As God, who wishes men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, raises up faithful heralds of his word to spread the teaching of truth and eternal salvation far and wide, so Satan is wholly intent on hindering the fruit of God's Word. Therefore he everywhere sends out his instruments to sow tares [ζιζάνια] and to destroy what has been well built. This happened among the Corinthians too. For after Paul had departed, ambitious and restless men crept in, who threw into confusion everything he had rightly established through the sounder teaching of the gospel. Therefore he wrote them an earlier letter, in which he sharply rebuked them. These men, so that they might keep control of that church and make Paul hated by all, hunted everywhere for material with which to revile and slander him. Among other things they said he was a vain and ambitious busybody, who, when absent, thundered with threatening letters, but when present dared nothing against those who opposed him. He has now replied that he is no different in his letters from what he is in person, and that he writes nothing other than what he would say to their faces, if the situation demanded it. He now explains this more carefully.

units.la: Principio vanitatis crimen declinat, & offendit, se nequaquam esse ex eorum numero, qui virtutes suas verbis magnificis iactent, cum re ipsa nihil præstent laude dignum, nec etiam præstare possint. Sic autem loquitur: Non enim audemus nos inferre aut conferre cum quibusdam, qui seipsos commendant, &c. Audendi verbo vtitur, partim vt æmulorum suorum vanissimam & inconsultam temeritatem perstringat, partim vt huic suam opponat modestiam. Alioquin non tam pusillanimis erat Apostolus, vt ardelionum & Thrasonum iflorum congressum expauesceret, qui præter inanem verborum apparatum nihil afferebant: Sed suæ modestiæ & officij memor, nefas ducebat talibus associari aut similem fieri. Habent ergo verba ista sanctam Ironiam, perinde ac si quis vir honestus & vere dives, qui intra honestatis & temperantiæ metas se continet, interrogatus, cur non prodigos aliquos & ambitiosos imitetur, qui tum vix modicas opes habeant, eas tamen superbè ostentant, & effraeis legum omnium repagulis eadem luxu ambitioso & effraeni dilapidant? respondeat: Ego non ausim me illis inferre tam opulentis & magnificis, qui se tantis sumptibus perpetuò sufficere posse putant, atq; opum suarū thesaurcs inexhaustos esse sibi persuaserunt, &c. Eodem plane sensu Paulus hic loquitur, & quæ æmuli eius scurrili dicacitate contra ipsum eiaculabantur, ea ipse facetè quidem, sed non sine salis Apostolici acrimonia in illos retorquet. Propositum illis erat, ipsius authoritatem eleuare, & omnibus contemptum facere. Ideo eum nihil præter epistolas habere dicebant, quibus acerbissimas correptiones & terribiles minas spirare, non audere autem eum cum aliquo coram congredi. Imò nihil eius præsentia abiectius, nihil eiusdem sermone elumbius esse. Istud autem illi exprobrando sibi ipsis grauitatem verè Apostolicam tribuebant, qui omnibus coram in faciem resistere auderent, simulq; suas victorias atque triumphos plenis buccis decantabant. Hanc ergo illorum leuitatem, quæ durius castigari merebatur, Paulus cum sancta sua authoritatis fiducia deridens, ait: Ego sanè non ausim me inferre gigantibus istis, multò minus autem me conferre aut similem dicere ausim tantis heroibus, qui iampridem totum orbem terrarum debellauerunt. Nam ego meæ mihi tenuitatis probè conscius, meo mepede metior. Simul autem quàm ridiculi sint illi docet: Seipsos commendant, inquit. Vno verbo leuitatem eorum turpissimam perstringit. Sordet enim laus propria, & vulgo suspecti sunt ambitiosuli suarum virtutum ebuccinatores. Addit tamen stupidam ignorantiam, qua seipsos fallant, dicens: Sed ipsi non intelligunt, quòd ipsi sese seipsis metiuntur, & sese sibi ipsis comparant. Sensus est: Volunt isti omnium hominum eruditissimi & sapientissimi videri, sed ne hoc quidem intelligunt quod vulgo notum est: stultè nimirum & ridiculè eos facere, qui se seipsis metiuntur, & sese sibi ipsis comparant. Qui enim aliquid metiri volunt, ijs mensura certa opus est. At illi nulla alia adhibita seipsis suas virtutes metiuntur. Et vt hoc rectius intelligatur, per Expositionem addit: Sese sibi ipsis comparant, id est, non respiciunt ad alios, qui donis pluribus instructi sunt, & qui plus quàm ipsi in propagando Christi Regno laborauerunt: sed suis modò intenti, illa extollunt & magnificè prædicant. Id verò perinde est, ac si quis pigmæus aut Therfites deformior, de sui corporis statura aut forma gloriari volens, se solum intueatur, non autem alios spectet, qui ipso procti-riores & formosiores sunt. Quis verò talem non dicat risu dignum? quis non vecordem & plus quàm stultum esse pronuntiet? Quid verò mei illi æmuli aliud faciunt? Quòd si ijdem in germanos Christi Apostolos respicerent, & cum horum laboribus suum otium & ignauiam, cumq; eorundem modestia suam arrogantiam conferrent, mox viderent quàm nulli sint, & procul dubio suijpsius eos puderet.
units.tr: First he avoids the charge of vanity, and makes clear that he is by no means one of those who puff up their virtues with grand words, while achieving nothing praiseworthy in fact, nor even being able to achieve it. He speaks thus: "For we do not dare to class or compare ourselves with some who commend themselves," and so on. He uses the word "dare" partly to brand the most vain and ill-considered rashness of his rivals, and partly to set his own modesty against it. Otherwise the Apostle was not so faint-hearted that he would shrink from meeting those busybodies and braggarts, who brought nothing but an empty display of words. But mindful of his modesty and his office, he judged it wrong to associate with such men or to become like them. So these words carry a holy irony, just as if an honest man, truly wealthy, who keeps within the bounds of honesty and temperance, were asked why he does not imitate those prodigal and ambitious men who, though they have scarcely modest means, nonetheless proudly display them and squander them in extravagant, unrestrained luxury, breaking through every barrier of the laws. He would answer: "I would not dare to put myself on a level with those so splendid and grand, who think they can always keep up such expense, and who have persuaded themselves that their treasuries of wealth are inexhaustible," and so on. Paul speaks in exactly this sense here. What his rivals hurled against him with buffoonish sharpness, he turns back on them wittily, but not without the apostolic bite of salt. Their aim was to lower his authority and make him despised by all. So they said he had nothing but letters, in which he breathed the bitterest rebukes and terrible threats, yet did not dare to meet anyone face to face. Indeed, they said, nothing was more abject than his presence, and nothing more feeble than his speech. By reproaching him with this, they claimed for themselves a truly apostolic gravity, since they dared to resist everyone openly to their faces, and at the same time they sang their victories and triumphs with full cheeks. Paul, therefore, mocking this levity of theirs, which deserved harsher rebuke, and confident in his holy authority, says: "I would certainly not dare to set myself among those giants; much less would I dare to call myself equal to, or like, such heroes, who long ago subdued the whole world. For I, being well aware of my own slightness, measure with my own measure." At the same time he shows how ridiculous they are: "They commend themselves," he says. In one word he brands their most shameful levity. For self-praise is contemptible, and ambitious men who trumpet their own virtues are generally suspect. He adds, however, the foolish ignorance by which they deceive themselves, saying: "But they do not understand that they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves." The sense is this: these men wish to seem the most learned and wise of all, yet they do not even understand what is commonly known, namely that it is foolish and ridiculous to measure oneself by oneself and to compare oneself with oneself. For whoever wishes to measure anything needs a fixed standard. But these men, applying no other standard, measure their own virtues by themselves. So that this may be understood more correctly, he adds by way of explanation: "compare themselves with themselves." That is, they do not look to others, who are endowed with greater gifts and have laboured more than they in spreading Christ's kingdom. Intent only on their own affairs, they extol and loudly proclaim their own gifts. This is just as if some pygmy, or a Thersites more misshapen than most, wishing to boast of the stature or form of his body, looked only at himself and not at others, who are much more handsome and better formed than he. Who would not call such a man worthy of laughter? Who would not pronounce him mad and more than foolish? And what else do my rivals do? If they looked to the genuine apostles of Christ, and compared their own idleness and sloth with the labours of these men, and their arrogance with their modesty, they would soon see how little they are, and doubtless they would be ashamed of themselves.

units.la: Obseruabis autem hic commune vitium notari, quo vix aliud Ecclesiæ & Reipub. nocentius est: Ambitionem nimirum, qua alij se alijs præferunt, ut qui soli sapiant, & proinde soli excellere & regnare debeant. Qui eo laborant, ij fere se meliores contemnunt & deprimunt, & ut ipsi emineant, sanioribus quoq; consilijs obstant: Vel saltem sua insolentia sapientiores eo adducunt, ut sponte illis locum cedant, & ipsi à publicis negotijs abstineant. Exempla sunt passim in historijs obuia, quæ docent, quàm graues turbas sæpe tales in Repub. excitarint, & in quanta pericula patriam communem adduxerint. Procul ergo arceri debent, & si nihil aliud accedat, cordatis omnibus suspectti esse debent, quicunq; hac tam confidenti ambitione laborant.
units.tr: You will observe here that a common vice is being noted, and hardly any vice is more harmful to the Church and the commonwealth: namely ambition, by which some set themselves above others, as if they alone were wise and therefore alone ought to excel and rule. Those who labour for this commonly despise and depress their betters, and, so that they themselves may stand out, they also oppose wiser counsels. Or at least, through their insolence, they bring wiser men to the point of giving way to them of their own accord, and of abstaining themselves from public affairs. Examples are met everywhere in histories, which teach how grave the disturbances such men have often stirred up in the commonwealth, and into what dangers they have brought the common fatherland. They must therefore be kept far away, and, even if nothing else followed, all sensible people ought to regard as suspect whoever labours under this so confident ambition.

units.la: At simul causam huius mali intueri proderit, quò facilius illud possimus euitare. Ea est, quòd plerique se solos spectant atque mirantur, neque cum suis donis aliorum dona aut merita conferunt, qui plus ipsis laborauerunt. Fit ergo ut propria philautia excæcati se solos admirentur atque suspiciant, de omnibus autem alijs contemptissimè iudicent. Accedunt deinde adulatores, vanissimum & turpissimum hominum genus, & vilissima ventris mancipia, qui plus satis superbientes magis inebriant, & insolentiores reddunt. Et tales omnino erant scioli illi Corinthiorum, quos inanis scientiæ fiducia & inutilis docendi facultas eò usque extollebat, ut quosuis alios præ se contemnerent. Tales in Repub. fuerunt Alcybiades, Marius, Sylla, Iulius, quorum ambitio Leges & libertatem publicam euertit. Tales hodie sunt Monachi, & qui in pulueribus scholasticis consenescunt, nec unquam in theatrum Ecclesiæ descenderunt, ut propius cum apertis fidei hostibus, aut cum sceleratis publicorum scandalorum authoribus congrederentur. Quibus etiam non nulli merito adnumerari debent, qui etiamsi in Ecclesiæ ministerio constituti sint, tamen cum διδάσκαλοι sint, se solos sapere sibijpsis persuadent, & proinde neminem alium audire, nullius alterius scripta legere, neque se præstantiorum labores inspicere dignantur. Isti omnes sese sibi metiuntur, seque non nisi sibijpsis comparant, & proinde in sua superbia non minus pernitiosa quàm stulta indies cum publico multorum detrimento proficiunt atque confirmantur. Et ut ad inferiores quoque hominum gradus descendamus, horum similes sunt, qui opum suarum fiducia elati, eas ambitiosè ostentant. Nam hi quoque dum non respiciunt in aliorum fortunas & mores, qui cum ipsis multò opulentiores sint, modestius tamen de seipsis sentiunt, thesauros se inexhaustos possidere sibijpsis persuadent, & proinde immodico & petulanti luxu seipsos ad egestatem redigunt.
units.tr: But it will also be useful to look at the cause of this evil, so that we may avoid it more easily. It is this: most people look only at themselves and admire themselves, and do not compare their gifts with the gifts or merits of others who have laboured more than they. So it happens that, blinded by their own self-love, they admire and esteem only themselves, and judge all others with the utmost contempt. Then flatterers come in, the most vain and base kind of men, slaves of the belly, who, puffing them up beyond measure, inflate them further and make them more insolent. The Corinthians' pseudo-learned men were certainly of this sort, whom confidence in empty learning and the useless ability to teach so raised up that they despised every other man by comparison. Such in the commonwealth were Alcibiades, Marius, Sulla and Julius, whose ambition overthrew laws and public liberty. Such today are the monks, and those who grow old amid scholastic dust, and who never came down into the theatre of the Church to meet more closely the open enemies of the faith or the wicked authors of public scandals. To these must also rightly be added some who, although placed in the ministry of the Church, nevertheless, since they are teachers [διδάσκαλοι], persuade themselves that they alone are wise, and therefore deign to hear no one else, to read no one else's writings, nor to look at the labours of better men. All these measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves only with themselves, and therefore, in their pride, they advance and are confirmed day by day, no less pernicious than foolish, to the great public harm of many. And to descend also to the lower ranks of men: like them are those who, puffed up with confidence in their wealth, display it ambitiously. For these too, while they do not look at the fortunes and manners of others who are far richer than they, nevertheless think more modestly of themselves; they persuade themselves that they possess inexhaustible treasures, and so by immoderate and wanton luxury they reduce themselves to poverty.

units.la: Itaq; communis horum omnium pœna est, quòd suam stultitiam produnt, seq; ipsos ridiculos faciunt, ut olim simia, quæ suos catulos aliorum animalium catulis præferendo sese omnium risui exposuit. Vel potius asini Cumani similes, ut ut leoninam induant, aures tamen tegere non possunt, quibus tandem deprehensis fabula fiunt ijs, qui ipsos prius admirabantur. Itaque tales dum supra omnes eminere volunt, ignominiam sibijpsis indelebilem accersunt. Discant ergo singuli, quando de seipsis iudicare volunt, eam mensuram siue regulam sibijpsis adhibere, quam in Scripturis Spiritus sanctus vnicuique pro sua vocationis aut functionis ratione præscribit: & primo quidem ad hanc seipsos & facta sua diligenter examinent: deinde verò aliorum quoque labores & egregia opera intueantur. Ita mox videbunt, quàm multum adhuc ipsis desit, & quàm exiguam habeant de suis virtutibus gloriandi materiam.
units.tr: Therefore the common punishment of all these people is that they betray their own folly and make themselves ridiculous, like the monkey of old, who, preferring her own young to the young of other animals, exposed herself to everyone's laughter. Or rather, they are like the asses of Cumae, who, though they put on a lion's skin, cannot cover their ears, and when these are at last detected, they become a fable to the very people who had admired them before. So such people, while they want to stand above everyone, bring upon themselves an indelible disgrace. Let each person therefore learn, when he wishes to judge himself, to apply that measure or rule which the Holy Spirit prescribes in the Scriptures for each person according to the nature of his calling or office. First of all, let them examine themselves and their deeds carefully by this rule; then let them also look at the labours and outstanding works of others. In this way they will soon see how much they still lack, and how little material they have for boasting of their own virtues.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui vanæ & stultæ aduersariorum suorum iactantiæ suam modestiam opponit, & omnia ea abs se remouet, quæ ipsum eiusdem culpæ reum facere poterant. At nos (inquit) non gloriabimur εἰς τὰ ἄμετρα, id est, in immensum, vel de ijs, quæ nobis Deus non admensus est. ἀμετρα enim proprie dicuntur quæ immensa sunt, aut quæ nemo metiri potest. Itaque εἰς τὰ ἄμετρα gloriari dicuntur, qui quæ non habent, neque vnquam assecuti sunt, iactant, adeoque quæ solius Dei sunt sibijpsis arroganter tribuunt: quod hodie nimis insolenter faciunt Pontifices, dum se Christi in terris vicarios esse, & omnem potestatem in cælo & in terra habere arroganter iactant. Quia tamen æmuli Pauli non eo vsque insolentiæ progressi erant, nihil huius vult dicere, sed præsentis loci argumento insistens, eorum calumniam confutat, qui ipsum falso gloriari dicebant de ijs, quæ per ipsum non essent confecta. Etenim vt ex contextu colligere licet, conuersæ etiam Corinthi laudem ipsi eripere conabantur. Dicit ergo: At nos non gloriabimur de ijs, quæ non sint nostræ mensuræ, sed secundum mensuram regulæ, quam Deus nobis partitus est, vt ad vos vsque peruenerimus, &c. Quibus verbis hoc dicere videtur: Si non ad vos vsque peruenissem, poteram dici gloriari supra mensuram mihi à Deo assignatam, & proinde isti horum similis censeri, qui quæ nunquam fecerunt, insolentius iactant. At non vt si non ad vos vsque peruenerimus, nosipsos supra modum extendimus, id est, laborum nostrorum narrationem non extendimus ad ea, quæ per nos non confecta sunt, quando de vobis ad fidem Christi conuersis gloriamur. Nam negari hoc non potest, me vsque ad vos peruenisse in Euangelio Christi, id est, ministerio nostro, quo Euangelium Christi prædicamus. Quis enim ante me vobis prædicauit? Annon ego vos in CHRISTO IESV genui, vt qui prius à Deo alieni in superstitionibus vanissimis & omni scelerum genere volutabamini, nunc Christi Ecclesiæ & filij Dei sitis? Iure ergo de vobis glorior, neq; ijs accenseri mereor, qui sibi plus æquo tribuunt: cum ego intra mensuram regulæ, id est, iustam sive regularem dimensionem eius mensuræ me contineam, quam mihi Deus partitus est. Mensuræ autem vocabulo intelligit eam partem orbis terrarum, quam Deus ipsi assignauerat, vt per eius ministerium Euangelij doctrina illuminaretur. Ita vero ista de seipso dicit, vt rursus æmulorum suorum iactantiam perstringat, qui longinquis peregrinationibus gloriabantur, & vt ambitiosi imperatores solent gentes abs se deuictas magnificis verbis enumerabant, cum tamen Ecclesias nullas (vt alibi diximus) ipsi constituissent, sed ab alijs constitutas turbarent.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who sets his modesty against the empty and foolish boasting of his opponents, and removes from himself everything that could make him guilty of the same fault. "But we," he says, "will not boast eis ta ametra [εἰς τὰ ἄμετρα], that is, beyond measure, or about those things which God has not measured out to us." For ametra [ἄμετρα] properly means things that are immeasurable, or that no one can measure. So those are said to boast eis ta ametra who vaunt things they do not have and have never obtained, and arrogantly attribute to themselves what belongs to God alone; which the Pontiffs do today all too insolently, when they arrogantly boast that they are Christ's vicars on earth and have all power in heaven and on earth. Yet since Paul's rivals had not gone so far in insolence, he says nothing of this. Keeping to the argument of the present place, he refutes the calumny of those who said he boasted falsely of things not accomplished by him.
