But since nothing of this kind can be said, and since nobody can hand on to you anything concerning the heads of faith and salvation which you have not first learned from us, and since you already excel in every knowledge, understanding, faith, love, prophecy, and the gift of tongues and of interpretation, while he brings nothing but figments of human wisdom, cloaked in the false polish of speech composed for show, you are truly far too credulous, or rather too light-minded, who, despising me, hold him in such esteem, and who, without any necessary cause, by this your instability bring the whole cause of the Christian religion into suspicion among your fellow citizens and neighbours.

units.la: At in his primùm obseruabis, quòd non diserte nominat impostorem illum, sed vocat τὸν ἐρχόμενον, id est, Venientem, vel Eum qui venit, nec etiam exprimit, vnde venerit, aut à quo missus venerit. Ita enim docere vult, vel hoc solo nomine ipsis debuisse suspectum esse. Veri enim doctores vocationem Dei expectant, & non nisi ab ipso missi docendi munus suscipiunt. Nec quisquam sibi ipsi (vt ad Hebraeos de sacerdotibus scribitur) sumit hunc honorem, &c. Exempla sunt in veteribus Prophetis, qui suam vocationem constantissimè vrgent, si quando ipsis cum aduersarijs res fuit. Quod ipsum Apostolos quoque fecisse scimus. Denique non minus necessarium quàm utile est, vt noti sint omnibus Verbi praecones, & (vt alibi Paulus monet) ab exteris quoque bonum testimonium habeant. Alia est pseudoprophetarum & impostorum conditio, de quibus olim conquestus est Dominus, per Ieremiam dicens: Currebant, & ego non mittebam eos. Et idem fere homines ignoti sunt, qui non nisi blanditiis, promissis item magnificis & dolo malo se insinuant. Debent ergo tales diligenter caueri. Nam ad eos proprie pertinet Christi admonitio: Cauete à pseudoprophetis, qui veniunt (scilicet non missi) in pellibus ouium, intus verò sunt lupi rapaces. Sed quae nostri seculi calamitas est, plerique tales sibi ipsis sponte accersunt, neglectis illis, quorum vocatio legitima est, & insuper doctrina atque morum dexteritate confirmatur.
units.tr: But in these words you will observe first that he does not plainly name that impostor, but calls him "the one who comes" (τὸν ἐρχόμενον), that is, "the Comer" or "he who comes," nor does he express whence he came or by whom he was sent. For he wishes to teach that they ought to have been suspicious of him on this ground alone. True teachers wait for God's calling and take up the office of teaching only when sent by him. Nor does anyone take this honour to himself (as it is written of priests in the letter to the Hebrews), etc. There are examples in the ancient prophets, who most firmly insist on their calling whenever they had to deal with opponents. We know that the apostles did the same. Finally, it is no less necessary than it is useful that the heralds of the Word be known to all and, as Paul advises elsewhere, have a good testimony even from outsiders. The condition of false prophets and impostors is different; the Lord complained of them long ago, speaking through Jeremiah: "They ran, and I did not send them." Such men are generally unknown, and they insinuate themselves only by flattery, by magnificent promises and by evil deceit. Such men must therefore be carefully guarded against. For Christ's warning applies properly to them: "Beware of false prophets, who come (that is, not sent) in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves." But it is a calamity of our age that many men of this sort summon themselves of their own accord, neglecting those whose calling is lawful and who are, moreover, confirmed by sound doctrine and the uprightness of their lives.

units.la: Deinde admonemur hoc loco, quid in doctrina potissimùm spectari debeat? Nimirum tria haec, quorum hic fit mentio. Primum, an hic ipse IESVS praedicetur, quem Apostoli tradiderunt? In eo enim salutis nostræ cardo versatur. Alterum, an idem ille spiritus conferatur, quem adoptionis spiritum Apostoli vocant, qui nos salutis certos facit, in quo clamamus Abba pater, qui denique Regnum Dei in nobis inflaurat, nosque per fidei obedientiam Deo captivos ducit. Tertium, an hoc ipsum Evangelium annuntietur, quod Apostolis à Christo traditum est, cum diceret: Oportet prædicari in meo nomine pænitentiam & remissionem peccatorum. Ubi ista traduntur, ibi à seductione non est aliquid periculi, & audiri debent qui hæc fideliter prædicant, etiamsi quoad alia insolentiores sint, aut etiam petulantiores & minus honeste viuant: sicuti de Scribis in Mosis cathedra sedentibus Christus pronuntiat. Quàm primum vero doctrinæ argumentum mutatur, & alia traduntur quàm quæ modo commemorauimus, tunc aures & animos procul auertere debet Christiani homines. Nam oues Christi vocem alienam non audiunt. Ioan. 10.
units.tr: Next we are reminded here what ought chiefly to be looked for in doctrine. Surely these three things, which are mentioned here. First, whether Jesus himself is preached, whom the apostles handed down? For the hinge of our salvation turns on him. Second, whether that same Spirit is conferred, which the apostles call the Spirit of adoption, who makes us sure of our salvation, in whom we cry "Abba, Father," who finally restores the Kingdom of God within us and leads us captive to God through the obedience of faith. Third, whether that very gospel is announced which was handed down to the apostles by Christ, when he said: "Repentance and the remission of sins must be preached in my name." Where these things are taught, there is no danger of seduction, and those who preach them faithfully ought to be heard, even if in other respects they are more insolent, or even more wanton, and live less honourably; just as Christ pronounces concerning the scribes who sit in Moses' seat. But as soon as the argument of the doctrine changes, and other things are taught than those we have just recalled, then Christian men ought to turn their ears and minds far away. For Christ's sheep do not hear the voice of a stranger. John 10.

units.la: Quoad autem in præsenti Corinthijs Paulus exprobrat, hodie etiam illis obijci poterat, qui Anabaptistarum prophetis siue doctoribus locum dant, & eosdem ita admirantur, ut eis legitimi Ecclesiarum ministri præillis sordeant. Quid enim illi tradunt, quod non ex ijs plenius discipositi, qui Euangelium syncere & ordinarie prædicant? Certè, quoad IESVM CHRISTVM, si non eundem nobiscum prædicant, anathema sunt. Quoad Euangelium, idem dici potest, & dicti huius authorem habemus Paulum, qui Angelum quoque anathema dicere audet, qui præter id quod prædicatum est euangelizat. Neque alia est spiritus ratio, & totius spiritualis œconomiæ, quæ ex Euangelio hauritur. At vrgent isti homines disciplinam morum, Quid verò hic desiderant? Annon corripiuntur scelera? annon pænitentia omnibus ex æquo præcipitur? Imò, annon hoc potissimum nomine exosi sunt plerisque Euangelij ministri, quod in corripiendis hominum vitijs liberiores aut acriores, quàm par sit, censentur? At nulla (inquiunt) est apud vos Excommunicatio, quæ à Cœnæ Dominicæ vsu excludatur homines flagitiosi & peccatores? Quis verò vt id fiat, iusşit? Vel quo iure arcentur, qui se pænitere dicunt, & pænitentiam vnà cum gratiæ Dei desiderio eo ipso testantur, quòd cum Ecclesia communicare, & beneficium Christi celebrare cupiant? Vel num disciplina esse nulla potest, nisi contra Pauli edictum nos in aliorum conscientias nobis ius vendicemus? Et tu quis es, qui nouis satisfactionibus eum fatigas, quem Christus iam in gratiam recepit? Quid multis? Leuitas est inexcusabilis, hypocritas illos ita admirari, ut propter ipsos Ecclesiæ vnitatem scindas, & eos temere condemnes, qui & ipso & illis meliores sunt.
units.tr: As for what Paul rebukes in the Corinthians, it could today be laid against those who give a hearing to the prophets or teachers of the Anabaptists and admire them so much that the lawful ministers of the Churches seem worthless beside them. For what do they teach that cannot be learned more fully from those who preach the Gospel sincerely and in the ordinary way? Certainly, as regards Jesus Christ, if they do not preach the same Christ as we do, they are anathema. The same holds for the Gospel, and we have Paul as the author of this saying, for he dares to call even an angel anathema if he preaches anything beyond what has been preached. Nor is there any other rule of the Spirit, or of the whole spiritual economy, that is drawn from the Gospel. But these men press the discipline of morals. What then do they really want here? Are sins not rebuked? Is repentance not enjoined on all alike? Indeed, are the ministers of the Gospel not for the most part hated for this very reason, that they are judged too free or too harsh in rebuking men's vices? "But," they say, "among you there is no excommunication that shuts wicked and sinful people out from the use of the Lord's Supper." Who ordered this to be done? Or by what right are those shut out who say they repent, and by that very profession show that, along with a longing for the grace of God, they desire to communicate with the Church and to celebrate the benefit of Christ? Or can there be no discipline unless, contrary to Paul's edict, we claim for ourselves a right over other people's consciences? And who are you, that you weary with new satisfactions the one whom Christ has already received into grace? In short, it is inexcusable levity to admire those hypocrites so much that you rend the unity of the Church on their account, and rashly condemn those who are better than both you and them.

units.la: Ut verò ad Paulum redeamus, quærat aliquis, cur Corinthios qui subreptitium hunc doctorem admiserant, reprehendat, si ille neque alium Christum neque aliud Euangelium prædicabat? Ad id sic respondemus: quod etsi eundem IESVM in ore haberent, & eodem spiritu gloriarentur, idemque Euangelium profiterentur, tamen inani modo eloquentiæ fuco turgidi, non col-limabant ad verum scopum, ut omnes uno Christo contenti essent, huic se totos subijcerent, & ei so liviuerent: sed sua loquacitate & indulgentia nimia morum licentiam inuexerant, disciplinam euerterant, imo idololatriam quoque & sacrorum illicitorum communionem inter Christiani nominis professores ferre poterant, ut ipsi plures fierent. Habes ego quod ijs respondeas, qui Papistica religionem hoc nomine tuentur, quòd Papistici doctores non alium IESVM prædicent, quàm quem nos profitemur: quòd eundem nobiscum spiritum profiteantur: quòd Euangelium idem in Missa & ex suggestu recitent: quòd denique eiusdem Symboli apostolici articulos nobiscum recipiant. Sed non sufficit ista dixisse, res ipsa inspiciatur, ut num hæc vere dicantur intelligamus. Apostoli nobis illum IESVM prædicarunt, qui solus nobis à Patre iustitia factus, solus inter hunc & nos Mediator sit, solus ad salutem sufficiat, cuius regnum item non sit de hoc mundo, quique peracto in terris redemptionis nostræ negotio, corpus suum in cælos euexerit, nunc illic ad dexteram Patris sedeat, Rex & Sacerdos Ecclesiæ suæ, quam spiritus & Deitatis suæ præsentia feruet, regat atque tueatur. Quòd si verò Papistas audire libeat, talem isti prædicant, cuius iustitia atque meritum nostrorum operum meritis farciatur, apud quem Mediatoribus Diuis, & imprimis matre Virgine, opus sit: qui solus ad salutem non sufficiat, qui item regnum in terris habeat potentia, opibus, victorijs illustre, in quo ipsi dominentur & ditescant: qui denique in sacra ædicula inclusus detineatur, quotidie in Missa immoletur: adhæc vicarium in terris habeat, etiamsi ipse nobis realiter.
units.tr: But to return to Paul: someone may ask why he rebukes the Corinthians, who had admitted this sneaking teacher, if the man preached neither another Christ nor another Gospel. We answer thus. Even though they had the same Jesus on their lips, boasted of the same Spirit and professed the same Gospel, yet, swollen with the empty paint of eloquence, they did not aim at the true goal, namely that all should be content with the one Christ, submit themselves wholly to him and live for him alone. Instead, by their chatter and excessive indulgence they had introduced licence in morals and overturned discipline. Indeed, they were even able to tolerate idolatry and communion in unlawful rites among those who professed the Christian name, so that they themselves might become more numerous. Here you have what to answer those who defend the Papist religion on this ground: that Papist teachers do not preach another Jesus than the one we profess; that they profess the same Spirit as we do; that they recite the same Gospel in the Mass and from the pulpit; and that, in short, they accept the articles of the same Apostles' Creed along with us. But it is not enough to say these things. Let the matter itself be examined, so that we may understand whether these things are truly said. The Apostles preached to us that Jesus who alone was made righteousness to us by the Father, who alone is the Mediator between God and us, who alone suffices for salvation, whose kingdom likewise is not of this world, and who, having finished the work of our redemption on earth, lifted up his body into heaven, and now sits there at the right hand of the Father, as King and Priest of his Church, whose Church is warmed by the presence of his Spirit and his Deity, ruling and protecting it. But if we are willing to listen to the Papists, they preach a Christ whose righteousness and merit must be filled out by the merits of our works; with whom there is need of Mediators, the saints, and above all the Virgin Mother; who alone does not suffice for salvation; who likewise has a kingdom on earth, renowned for power, wealth and victories, in which they themselves rule and grow rich; who, lastly, is shut up and held in a sacred little shrine and is sacrificed every day in the Mass; and who, moreover, has a vicar on earth, even though he himself is really present to us

units.la: & corporaliter præsens adsit, &c. Quis ergo eos eundem IESVM cum Apostolis prædicare dixerit? Quoad spiritum, qui per Apostolos olim credentibus collatus fuit, est ut diximus) adoptionis Spiritus, qui nos salutis certos reddit, & ideo huius arrhabo alibi dicitur. Idem homines, ex æterno Verbi semine regenerat, & totos Deo consecrat. At Pontificij doctores, de salute & gratia Dei nos certos fieri posse negant, & ideo homines dubitare docent, an Deum sibi propitium atque placatum habeant: ijdem Ecclesiam in sectas distrahunt, & hominum seruos faciunt ex ijs, qui Christo nomen dederunt in baptismo, & huic vni debebant esse consecrati. Denique infelices in superstitionibus detinent, bellis, sanguine, incendijs omnia miscent vindictæ spiritu accensi, neque audiunt Christum dicentem: Nescitis cuius Spiritus sitis? Quoad Euangelium, decantant quidem illud in Missis suis, ex suggestu recitant, in libris magnifice ornatis descriptum habent: sed illud peregrina lingua decantant, contra Apostoli traditionem: deinde nec totam IESV CHRISTI historiam, aut integros Euangelistarum libros populo exponunt, sed excerpunt ex illis frustillatim sua illa Euangelia, quæ Dominicalia vocant: quæ morem demum sub annum Domini D.CCCVI. ex Caroli Magni mandato à Paulo Vuarnenfrido institutum esse, historici testantur. Admisceat præterea sanis literis Philosophiam, quam nisi quis prius imbiberit, ad illarum studium non admittitur. Hinc traditionum humanarum chaos, quibus tota religio adulterata est. Neque pudet eos dicere, illas necessarias esse, eo quod in Scripturis non omnia continentur, quæ cognitu & credita necessaria sunt, & ideo canones & decreta quotidie nova pro suo arbitrio fingunt. Id vero huius loci authoritate euidentissimè confutatur. Quis ergo ab illis idem Euangelium annuntiari fateatur, quod ab Apostolis est traditum? Quoties ergo isti homines suam doctrinam nobis obtrudunt, & vt hanc recipiamus necessarium esse contendunt, semper ex hoc loco illis occinamus: Aut idem est cum Apostolorum doctrina quod vos traditis, aut ab ea diuersum est. Si idem docetis, quid opus aliqua innouatione? aut cur propter vos, si nihil noui affertis, receptum Ecclesiæ ordinem turbaremus? Quòd si vero aliquid præter illud quod Apostoli tradiderunt profertis, religio nobis est eos audire, quos Paulus iam olim anathema pronuntiauit.
units.tr: and bodily, and so on. Who then would say that they preach the same Jesus as the Apostles? As for the Spirit, which was once conferred on believers through the Apostles, it is, as we have said, the Spirit of adoption, who makes us certain of salvation, and for that reason is called the earnest of it elsewhere. He regenerates men from the eternal seed of the Word and consecrates them wholly to God. But the Papist teachers deny that we can be made certain of God's grace and salvation, and so they teach men to doubt whether they have God as propitious and reconciled to them. The same men tear the Church into sects, and make slaves of men out of those who have given their name to Christ in baptism and ought to have been consecrated to him alone. Lastly, they keep wretched people in superstitions, and, kindled with a spirit of vengeance, throw everything into confusion with wars, bloodshed and burnings, and do not listen to Christ saying: "You do not know what spirit you are of." As for the Gospel, they indeed chant it in their Masses, recite it from the pulpit, and have it written out in magnificently decorated books; but they chant it in a foreign tongue, contrary to the tradition of the Apostles. Then they do not expound to the people the whole history of Jesus Christ, or the complete books of the Evangelists, but pick out from them, piece by piece, those little Gospels which they call Sunday Gospels. Historians testify that this custom was finally established around the year of the Lord 806, at the command of Charlemagne, by Paul Warnefrid. Moreover, they mix philosophy into sound learning, and unless a person has first soaked it up, he is not admitted to the study of those sound letters. Hence comes the chaos of human traditions by which the whole of religion has been corrupted. Nor are they ashamed to say that these traditions are necessary, because not all the things that must be known and believed are contained in Scripture; and so every day they invent new canons and decrees at their own pleasure. Yet this very passage most evidently refutes that claim. Who then would admit that the Gospel announced by them is the same as that handed down by the Apostles? Whenever these men thrust their teaching upon us and insist that we must accept it, let us always answer them from this passage: either what you teach is the same as the doctrine of the Apostles, or it differs from it. If you teach the same, why is any innovation needed? Or why should we disturb the established order of the Church on your account, if you bring nothing new? But if you put forward anything beyond what the Apostles handed down, it is a matter of conscience for us not to listen to those whom Paul long ago pronounced anathema.

units.la: Porrò gloriabantur impostores illi, quòd suum Euangelium accepissent à germanis Christi Apostolis, qui huic in terris agenti conuixerant, & ideo ab imperitis rerum plurimis fiebant. Occurrit ergo etiam huic perfuasioni Paulus dicens: Puto enim me nihilo inferiorem fuisse ijs, qui sunt summi Apostoli. Quasi diceret: Audio quidem qua authoritate illi sese venditent, & quid plerosq; vestrum moveat, vt illis fidem habeatis. Sed quid hic verbis opus est? Annon etiam ego sum Apostolus? Annon (quod alias dixi) sigillum apostolatus mei vos estis? Et si comparatio fieri debeat, puto me cum summis Apostolis conferri posse. Summos autem Apostolos dicit per Mimesim ex aduersariorum sententia, qui vt se gloriosius venditarent, inter Apostolos gradus fingebant, quasi alius alio esset sublimior aut maior. Atqui omnes illi Christi serui erant, nec voluit vt aliquê supra alios eminere, quoad apostolici muneris dignitatem: imò omnes in ipso vnum esse & mutuâ operam sibi inuicem præstare voluit.
units.tr: Moreover, those impostors boasted that they had received their Gospel from the true Apostles of Christ, who had lived with him while he was on earth; and for this reason they were believed by the many who were ignorant of affairs. Paul meets this claim too, saying: "For I consider that I am not in the least inferior to those who are the chief Apostles." It is as if he said: "I hear by what authority they put themselves forward, and what moves most of you to put your faith in them. But what need is there of words here? Am I not an Apostle too? Are you not (as I have said elsewhere) the seal of my apostleship? And if a comparison must be made, I think I can be set alongside the chief Apostles." He calls them the chief Apostles by mimesis, in the opinion of his opponents, who, in order to make themselves look more glorious, invented ranks among the Apostles, as if one were more exalted or greater than another. Yet all of them were servants of Christ, and he did not want anyone to stand out above the rest in the dignity of the apostolic office; rather, he wanted all of them to be one in him and to render mutual service to one another.

units.la: Itaque Paulus hoc non arroganter de seipso dixit, sed quia sic eum cogebat necessitas, vt pseudoapostolos retunderet, qui eius authoritatem ideo eleuabant, vt supra fundamentum, quod ipse iecerat, suas stipulas & paleas possent ædificare. Alibi enim humillimè de seipso loquitur, & se Apostolorum minimum, imò Apostoli nomine indignum esse dicit, eò quod Ecclesiam Christi persecutus sit. Et cùm in præsenti, se alijs parem esse, constanter affirmare posset, dicit: Puto me non esse inferiorem, &c. Quid, quod alibi non fastidit collegas agnoscere eos, qui quoad dona Spiritus & merita in Ecclesiam Christi, ipsi minimè conferendi erant, vtpote Softhenē, Syluanum, Timotheum & similes alios? Sed & cum Apostolis omnibus ipsi optimè conueniebat, sicuti acta Synodi Hierosolymitanæ testantur. Denique hoc loco non alia ratione se alijs æquat, quàm quòd suum ministerium æque efficax atque fructuosum esse videret, neque eius authoritas labefactari posset, quin simul gloria Dei & multorum salus in periculum veniret. Imitentur omnes modestiâ hanc Pauli: interim non desint suo muneri, si Dei Gloria ita postulet. Nam etsi præclaris Dei donis nemo superbire debeat, eadem tamen nemo in semetipso contemnere aut negligere debet, vt neque in alijs. Qui enim id faciunt, ij in Deum ingrati sunt, & graviter peccant. Sibijpsis ergo Pauli exemplum plum omnes applicent, qui Dei gratiam in se efficacem esse sentiunt, neque aliquid admittant suae functione indignum, quod Dei gloriae derogare queat.
units.tr: Paul did not say this out of arrogance about himself. He was compelled by necessity to refute the false apostles, who exalted his authority only so that they could build their own straw and stubble upon the foundation he had laid. Elsewhere he speaks of himself very humbly, saying that he is the least of the apostles and not worthy to be called an apostle, because he persecuted the Church of Christ. Yet here, where he could firmly affirm that he is equal to the others, he says: "I think I am not inferior," and so on. Moreover, elsewhere he does not disdain to acknowledge as colleagues those who, in respect of the gifts of the Spirit and their merits, were in no way to be compared with him in the Church of Christ, such as Sosthenes, Silvanus, Timothy and others like them. He also agreed very well with all the apostles, as the acts of the Synod of Jerusalem bear witness. Finally, in this passage he makes himself equal to the others for no other reason than that he saw his own ministry to be as effective and fruitful as theirs, and that his authority could not be weakened without the glory of God and the salvation of many being put in danger. Let all imitate this modesty of Paul: meanwhile, let them not fail in their office if the glory of God so requires. For although no one ought to be proud of the excellent gifts of God, yet no one ought to despise or neglect those same gifts in himself, any more than in others. Those who do so are ungrateful to God and sin grievously. Let all, therefore, apply Paul's example to themselves, those who feel that the grace of God is effective in them, and let them admit nothing unworthy of their function that could detract from the glory of God.

units.la: Rursus autem aliqui in impostoribus eloquentiam & eximiam dicendi facultatem admirabantur, & Paulo econtra contemptum ac humile dicendi genus exprobrabant. Quamobrem his quoque respondet: Quod si rudis sum sermone, non tamen cognitione. Non negat se dicendi peritum esse, multo minus barbariem aut infantiam profitetur. Nam illum dicendo plurimum potuisse, plerique veterum prodiderunt: & eius rei argumentum evidens habes in iis, quae apud Lystrenses acciderunt, quibus Mercurius esse visus est, quem a facundia gentium poetae commendant. Itaque verba haec Concessionis speciem habent (quod D. Augustinus quoque observavit) ut obtrectatoribus fortius respondeat. Et non nisi fucatam illam eloquentiam abs se remouet, quae inani verborum splendore constat, qua impostores illi sese vendita-bant. Itaque sensus huius loci est: Esto non tantum dicendo posse videar, quantum aemuli mei, nemo tamen me rudem putare debet, quoad rerum divinarum cognitionem, quae in Ecclesia tradi debent, & sine quibus salus non potest constare. Haec autem cum mihi adsit solida, & eandem vobis quoque fideliter tradiderim, iniqui nimium est, si me propter Logodaedalos istos minoris faciatis.
units.tr: On the other hand, some admired eloquence and an outstanding gift of speech in the impostors, and cast up to Paul his contemptible and humble manner of speaking. For this reason he answers these people too: "But even if I am rude in speech, yet not in knowledge." He does not deny that he is skilled in speaking, much less does he confess to barbarism or childishness. For many of the ancients have reported that he was very powerful in speech, and you have clear evidence of this in what happened at Lystra, where he was taken for Mercury, whom the poets commend for the eloquence of the nations. Thus these words have the appearance of a concession (as Augustine also observed), so that he may answer his detractors more strongly. And he rejects only that painted eloquence, which consists in the empty splendour of words, by which those impostors were selling themselves. The sense of this passage, therefore, is: "Granted that I seem to have less power in speaking than my rivals, nobody ought nevertheless to think me ignorant as regards the knowledge of divine things, which must be taught in the Church and without which salvation cannot stand. Since I possess this solid knowledge, and have faithfully handed the same on to you also, it is altogether unjust if you value me less on account of those word-artisans."

units.la: Est hoc observatu dignum, quod non pugnat pro eloquentiae laude Paulus, sed potius rerum cognitionem sibi vendicat. Hanc enim magis quam illam necessariam esse sciebat. Quid enim loquetur, qui nihil novit? aut quem erudiet copia verborum, si res nullae adsint? Sed & Regnum Dei non in sermone est, sed in virtute. Quid quod crucis gloria & Evangelii virtus, quae per Spiritum se exerit atque agit; verborum splendore obruitur potius quam illustratur; ut in priori epistola est dictum? Eadem vero luculentior est & omnibus admirationem parit, si eam homines idiotae & illiterati constanter atque simpliciter proponant? Exemplu eius rei evidens in Apostolis habemus, qui Iudaeorum Sacerdotibus & Senioribus ideo potissimum admirationi fuerunt, quod eos homines illiteratos esse scirent. Et huius generis multa quotidie fiunt inter eos, qui Evangelium hostiliter persequuntur. Nemo igitur fuco verborum se decipi sinat, ut simplicem Veritatis doctrinam fastidire velit. Quod ipsum in Repub. quoque debet observari. Nam illic etiam magis prosunt, qui solida legum & iuris publici cognitione instructi & patriae communis amantes ea dicunt, quae dici opus est, quam qui artificiosis orationibus aures demulcent, & fere sub illis res suas agunt: Quales olim Graeciae oratores fuisse constat, qui sua eloquentia patriam pessum dederunt.
units.tr: It is worth noticing that Paul does not fight for the praise of eloquence, but rather claims for himself knowledge of the things themselves. For he knew that this was more necessary than that. For what will someone say who knows nothing? Or whom will a wealth of words instruct, if there is no substance? "For the kingdom of God is not in speech, but in power." Moreover, the glory of the cross and the power of the Gospel, which works and acts through the Spirit, is overwhelmed rather than illumined by the splendour of words, as was said in the earlier epistle. Is that same power not far more brilliant, and does it not win everyone's admiration, if uneducated and unlettered men set it forth constantly and simply? We have a clear example of this in the apostles, who were especially an object of admiration to the priests and elders of the Jews precisely because they knew them to be unlettered men. And many things of this kind happen every day among those who bitterly persecute the Gospel. Therefore let no one allow himself to be deceived by the paint of words, so as to want to despise the simple doctrine of the truth. This same principle must be observed in the commonwealth too. For there they are of greater use who, instructed in the solid knowledge of the laws and of public right and loving their common country, say what needs to be said, than those who soothe the ears with artful orations and for the most part pursue their own affairs under cover of them. Such, it is well known, were the orators of Greece of old, who ruined their country by their eloquence.

units.la: Nemo tamen vel Paulum vel nos ignavus & stolidus omnis eruditionis oforibus patrocinari putet, qui a stirpe aut ex sutrinis elapsi in suggestum temere ascendunt, & docendi munus sibi sumunt. Ut enim inanis verborum splendor damnatur, neque rhetoricis coloribus Spiritui Sancto opus est: ita tamen Verbi administrum αὐλαχικὸν esse vult Paulus, qui commode, apte & perspicuè dicere possit ea quae dici debent. Et ideo Christus piscatores quidem fecit Apostolos, sed eosdem ad praedicandum noluit prodire, donec eos Spiritu suo donasset, qui illos tam Scripturarum quam linguarum cognitione instruxit. Quid multis? Oratio & dicendi facultas cognitioni rerum servire, non autem sine hac luxuriari aut superbire debet.
units.tr: Yet let no one think that Paul, or we, defend the cause of the ignorant and dull enemies of all learning, who, having slipped out from the stock or from the cobblers' shops, rashly climb into the pulpit and take upon themselves the office of teaching. For just as empty splendour of words is condemned, and the Holy Spirit has no need of rhetorical colours, so Paul wants the minister of the Word to be a rustic [αὐλαχικὸν], yet one who can speak fitly, aptly and clearly what ought to be said. And therefore Christ made fishermen apostles, but was unwilling that they should go forth to preach until he had endowed them with his Spirit, who instructed them in the knowledge both of the Scriptures and of languages. What more need be said? Speech and the faculty of speaking ought to serve the knowledge of things, and ought not to revel or take pride in themselves apart from this knowledge.

units.la: Caeterum ne quid ambitiosius dixisse putaretur Paulus, ipsos Corinthios testes, vel potius iudices appellat: Sed omnino manifesti (inquit) facti sumus in omnibus erga vos. Id est, nihil mihi temere arrogo, quod non abunde praestiterim. Vos autem testes appello, ut de me meisque laboribus atq; studiis pronuntietis. Fatebimini (sat scio) me nihil occulte, nihil simulater aut fraudulenter egisse, sed in omnibus luci studuisse, ita ut omnes quid vellem, & quae mea esset sententia, intelligere potuerint, neque unquam alius videri volui, quam reuera sim. Ita vero aemulos suos perstringit, qui artibus & dolis utebantur, & faciunt ad huius loci expositionem, quae supra Cap. 2. dixit: Non ut plerique cauponantes sermonem Dei, sed ut ex sinceritate, sed ut ex Deo in conspectu Dei in Christo loquimur. Et rursum Cap.quarto: Abdicauimus latebras turpitudinis, non incedentes cum calliditate, neque falsantes sermonem Dei, sed declaratione veritatis commendantes nosipsos apud omnem conscientiam hominum, in conspectu Dei, &c.
units.tr: But lest Paul be thought to have said anything too boastful, he calls the Corinthians themselves as witnesses, or rather as judges: "But we have been made fully manifest," he says, "to you in all things." That is: "I do not presume anything rashly, which I have not abundantly performed. I call you as witnesses, so that you may pronounce concerning me and my labours and endeavours. You will confess (I know well) that I have done nothing secretly, nothing feigned or fraudulent, but have sought the light in all things, so that everyone could understand what I wished and what my opinion was, and I never wished to appear other than I really am." He thus strikes at his rivals, who used tricks and deceits, and what he said in chapter 2 pertains to the explanation of this passage: "not like many who peddle the word of God, but as of sincerity, as from God, in the sight of God, we speak in Christ." And again in chapter 4: "We have renounced the hidden things of shame, not walking in craftiness, nor adulterating the word of God, but by the manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every human conscience, in the sight of God," and so on.

units.la: Id vero omnes Verbi administros decet, ut sincere agant, nec aliquid simulent. Suc enim lucis ministri & veritatis, cui nihil magis contrarium, imo magis infestum est, quàm hypocrisis, quae semper cum mendacio coniuncta est. Arguit hoc tenebriones & simulatores, qui interdum dolo sancto utendum esse putant, & ideo aliter loquuntur quàm animo sentiunt, & ita verborum coturnis multos fallunt. At nullus dolus sanctus esse potest in religionis causa, ubi omnia liberè, ingenuè & constanter dici debent, ne ex eorum numero esse deprehendamur, quos veritatis pudet. Pertinet idem ad omnes Christianos, qui ita viuere debent, ut aduersarios quoque suae integritatis testes habeant. Ita enim Christus fecit, qui acerrimis hostibus audebat dicere: Quis ex vobis arguet me de peccato? Et hoc veteribus Christianis olim studium fuisse, Plinij ad Traianum epistola testantur. Id verò facilè consequemur, si hic nobis omnium nostrarum actionum atque studiorum scopus sit, ut in nobis glorificetur IESVS CHRISTVS, Seruator & Dominus noster unicus, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: This indeed becomes all ministers of the Word, that they act sincerely and feign nothing. For they are ministers of the light and of the truth, to which nothing is more contrary, indeed nothing is more hostile, than hypocrisy, which is always joined with lying. This rebukes the men of darkness and the dissemblers, who sometimes think that a holy deceit must be used, and therefore speak otherwise than they feel in their minds, and so deceive many with the buskins of words. But no holy deceit can exist in the cause of religion, where everything ought to be said freely, openly and steadfastly, lest we be discovered to belong to the number of those who are ashamed of the truth. The same applies to all Christians, who ought so to live that even their adversaries have witnesses to their integrity. For so Christ did, who dared to say to his most bitter enemies: "Which of you will convict me of sin?" And that this was an earlier aim of the Christians of old is attested by Pliny's letter to Trajan. This we shall easily attain if this alone is the goal of all our actions and endeavours, that Jesus Christ, our only Saviour and Lord, may be glorified in us, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XLVIII.

units.la: Num peccaui cùm meipsum demitterem, ut vos extolleremini? quòd item gratuitò Euangelium Dei euangelizauerim vobis? Alias Ecclesias spoliaui, accepto ab eis stipendio, ut vobis inseruirem. Et cum apud vos essem & egerem, non obtorpui cum cuiusquam incommodo. Inopiam enim meam suppleuerunt fratres qui venerant ex Macedonia: & in omnibus me praestiti vobis minimè onerosum, & praestabo. Est Veritas Christi in me, quòd haec gloriatio non obstruetur in me in regionibus Achaiae. Quapropter? an quòd non diligam vos? Deus nouit: Sed quod facio, etiam faciam: ut amputem occasionem iis qui cupiunt occasionem, ut in eo de quo gloriantur, reperiantur quales & nos.
units.tr: Did I sin when I humbled myself so that you might be exalted? Or because I preached the Gospel of God to you free of charge? I robbed other churches, taking wages from them, so that I might serve you. And when I was with you and in need, I was not a burden to anyone. For the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my want, and in everything I have kept myself, and will keep myself, from being a burden to you. As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting shall not be silenced in me in the regions of Achaia. Why? Is it because I do not love you? God knows that I do. But what I do, I will go on doing, so that I may cut off the opportunity from those who seek an opportunity, that in the matter of which they boast they may be found to be like us.

units.la: Diluus Paulus authoritatem siue existimationem suam apud Corinthios itatuetur, ut ad omnia diligenter respondeat, quae hanc labefactabant. Erat inter ea fere praecipuum nimia & praepostera pseudoapostolorum admiratio, qui humana sapientia, verborum splendore & magnificentia multorum oculos ita perstrinxerant, ut eis Paulus quasi sorderet. Ostendit ego nuper, illos nimis stultè agere, qui istis capiantur, cùm nihil praeterea afferant, quod non iam antea ex ipso didicerint. Id verò sic probat, ut ipsos Corinthios testes faciat. Vbi didicimus, licere quidem iis, qui aliis praefecti sunt, ut suam existimationem propugnent, ne Dei gloria in ipsis periclitetur: sed eosdem hoc simul diligenter debere cauere, ne ab aliquo possint conuinci aut falsi argui. Caterùm Corinthios, qui fastui & splendori, quae opulentiam comitantur, assueuerant, hoc imprimis offendebat, quòd Paulus, cùm apud eos ageret, ut vulgaris aliquis & plebeius homo manuum labore victum sibi parauerat. Indignum enim videbatur, vrbis tam celebris & opulentae ciues à sordido opifice gubernari: & credibile est, hoc illis frequenter à suis vicinis, vel etiam exteris, qui commerciorum causa illuc confluebant, exprobratum fuisse. Quapropter nunc hoc quoque scandalum remouere incipit.
units.tr: Paul, a divine man, defends his authority, or reputation, among the Corinthians, so that he may answer carefully everything that undermined it. Among these things, the chief was the excessive and perverse admiration for the false apostles, who by human wisdom, by the splendour and grandeur of their words, had so dazzled the eyes of many that Paul seemed contemptible to them. I have shown earlier that those who are caught by such men act very foolishly, since these men bring nothing new that they had not already learned from him. He proves this in such a way that he makes the Corinthians themselves his witnesses. From this we learn that those who are set over others may indeed defend their reputation, lest the glory of God be put at risk in them; but at the same time they must take great care not to be refuted by anyone or shown to be false. Moreover, what especially offended the Corinthians, who had grown used to the pomp and show that accompany wealth, was that Paul, while living among them, had earned his living by manual labour like some common and plebeian man. For it seemed unworthy that the citizens of so famous and wealthy a city should be governed by a lowly craftsman; and it is believable that this was often thrown in their faces by their neighbours, or even by foreigners who flocked there for trade. Therefore he now begins to remove this stumbling block too.

units.la: Narrat enim quomodo inter ipsos versatus sit, & ostendit, nullam in ipso culpam haerere, propter quam contemni mereatur, illos autem ingratos & iniquos esse laborum suorum aestimatores, qui ipsum propter ea contemnant quae ipsorum causa fecerit. Id Ironia eleganti, vel potius Sarcasmo exprimit, dicens: Num peccaui cùm meipsum demitterem, ut vos extolleremini? quòd item gratuitò Euangelium Dei euangelizauerim vobis? Quasi diceret: Quid obsecro in tota mea conuersatione inuenire potestis reprehensione dignum? Num vitam vixi dissolutam & luxu diffluentem? Num ego auarus aliorum opibus insidiatus sum? Num què laesi calumniis aut obtrectationibus? Certè nemo, opinor, haec de me dixerit. Quid ergo reliquum est, quàm quòd mea modestia & humilitate offendamini, & voluntaria subiectione, qua meo iure cessi, ut me infra omnes demitterem? Id ne verò tantum scelus est, ut minus apud vos valere debeat mea doctrina & ministerij
units.tr: For he tells how he conducted himself among them, and shows that there is no fault in him that could deserve contempt, and that those who despise him on account of the things he has done for their sake are ungrateful and unfair judges of his labours. He expresses this with an elegant irony, or rather with sarcasm, saying: Did I sin when I humbled myself so that you might be exalted? Or because I preached the Gospel of God to you free of charge? As if he were saying: What, I beg you, can you find in my whole conduct that deserves reproach? Have I lived a dissolute life, given over to luxury? Have I, a covetous man, plotted against the wealth of others? Have I wounded anyone with slander or detraction? Surely, I think, no one would say such things about me. What remains, then, except that you are offended by my modesty and humility, and by the voluntary submission by which I gave up my own right, so as to lower myself beneath everyone? But surely it is not such a great crime that my teaching and the authority of my ministry should count for less among you?

units.la: Sue apud Corinthios contemerfationis reddit. nisterij authoritas? Atqui humilitas eiusmodi apud omnes bonos laudem meretur, & Christi ministros quàm maximè decet, qui illius exemplum in illo habent, qui pedes quoque discipulorum abluere dignatus est. Quid, quòd quicquid huius feci, propter vos feci & gratuitò vobis prædicaui Euangelium, vt vos ex peccatorum sordibus & potestate tenebrarum ereptos in libertatem atque dignitatem filiorum Dei eueherem.
units.tr: Is the authority of my ministry to be held in contempt among the Corinthians? And yet such humility deserves praise from all good people, and it becomes the ministers of Christ above all, who have the example of him who deigned to wash even the feet of his disciples. Moreover, whatever I have done of this kind, I have done for your sake, and I preached the Gospel to you free of charge, so that I might lift you, rescued from the filth of sins and from the power of darkness, into the liberty and dignity of the sons of God.

units.la: Apparet hoc loco, quàm iniqua sint mundi huius de Verbi Dei administris iudicia. Finis totius ministerij hic est, vt qui prius in luto peccatorum iacebant & mortis æternæ reatu tenebantur, inde extracti euehantur ad cœlestis Regni & immortalis gloriæ possessionem. Id enim non alia ratione, sed per solum Euangelium fit, ex cuius semine renati iustitiæ Dei, quam hic nobis in Filio suo IESV CHRISTO donauit, participes efficimur, & ad nuptias illas cœlestes vocamur, in quibus tota electorum Ecclesia cum sponso suo æternum gaudebit. Ad quas vt nobis peruenire liceat, Deus ministros suos laboribus, iniurijs, contumelijs, inopia & omni periculorum genere exercet, perque illos nobis thesaurum hunc pretiosissimum gratuitò offert. Sed ea est hominum peruersitas, vt plerisque ideo sordeat tota salutis ratio, quòd ἀιδἀπανος sit. Volunt enim ipsi cœlos vel pecunijs vel suorum operum meritis redimere: adhæc præsulibus fastuosis & luxu plus quàm Persico sese venditantibus delectantur; Christi verò ministros humiles & sub cruce gementes fastidiunt. Quod perinde est, ac si quis seruum fidelißimum, ideò minoris faciat, quòd ille ei gratuitum seruitium præstet, neque vllum laborem detrectet, quem hero vtilem esse intelligit. At non debet ingratitudo ista Dei ministros offendere, quo minus in officio suo fideles sint, vt ab illo præmium recipiant, qui remunerator est liberalissimus.
units.tr: Here it is evident how unjust are the judgments of this world about the servants of the Word of God. The whole purpose of the ministry is this: that those who once lay in the mire of sin and were bound by the guilt of eternal death may be drawn out and raised to the possession of the heavenly kingdom and immortal glory. This does not happen by any other means, but only through the Gospel, from whose seed we are born again and made partakers of the righteousness of God, which he has given us in his Son Jesus Christ, and we are called to those heavenly weddings, in which the whole Church of the elect will rejoice eternally with its bridegroom. So that we may attain to these, God exercises his ministers with labours, injuries, insults, want and every kind of danger, and through them freely offers us this most precious treasure. But such is human perversity that for most people the whole plan of salvation is cheap because it is without cost [ἀδάπανος]. For they want to buy heaven, either with money or by the merits of their own works; they delight in haughty prelates who display themselves in luxury more than Persian, but they despise the humble ministers of Christ who groan under the cross. This is just as if someone were to value less a most faithful servant because he renders his service freely and shrinks from no labour that he understands to be useful to his master. But this ingratitude toward God's ministers should not offend them so that they are less faithful in their duty, so that they may receive their reward from him who is the most generous rewarder.

units.la: Docemur præterea exemplo Pauli, quæ sit humiliationis siue humilitatis Christianæ ratio: Ea ninirum, vt alij per nos exaltentur, & ex nobis beneficium accipiant. Obseruandum hoc propter hypocritas, qui humilitatem simulant, vt ipsi euehantur, & ea ratione in quosuis alios dominium siue imperium obtineant. Sic Papa, qui se Seruum seruorum dicit, sed eo prætextu Romæ gentium domitricis dominus est, humeris hominum gestatur, regibus cum imperio mandat quæ vult, & eosdem adpedem suorum oscula compellit: vt non inscis, nec minus vere quidam dixerit: Roma tibi quondam fuerant domini dominorum, Seruorum serui nunc tibi sunt Domini.
units.tr: Moreover, we are taught by Paul's example what the manner of Christian humbling or humility is: namely, that through us others may be exalted, and receive a benefit from us. This must be observed on account of hypocrites, who feign humility so that they themselves may be raised up, and by that means obtain dominion or power over whomever they like. Thus the Pope, who calls himself the servant of servants, yet under that pretext is lord of Rome, the mistress of nations, is carried on the shoulders of men, commands kings with authority what he wishes, and compels those same kings to kiss his feet. As someone, not unskilfully and no less truly, once said: "Rome, once you had lords of lords; now the servants of servants are your lords."

units.la: Idem in Monachis est videre, qui vestitu, gestu, incessu humilitatem extremam præferunt: sed (vt Germanico prouerbio dicitur) claues quærunt, quibus in arcem potentiæ & opulentiæ penetrent, nec solum homines omnes præse contemnunt, verumetiam contra Deum efferuntur, dum suorum operum iustitiam (vt olim Iudæi) stabiliunt atque iactant, Dei verò iustitiam, quam ĩs nobis in Filio suo IESV CHRISTO offert, non nodò contemnunt, verumetiam persequuntur. adhæc alijs quoque authores sunt, vt similiter suam iustitiam erigendo à iustitia Dei excidant. Longè aliter Apostoli fecerunt, qui Christi exemplum imitati sese demiserunt, vt alios exaltarent: quemadmodum ille è cœlo descendit, vt nos illuc euheret: Filius hominis factus est, vt nos filios Dei faceret: omnibus seruiuit, vt nos in libertatem assereret: ignominiam denique & omnis generis contumelias, adhæc diram & infamem mortem sustinuit, vt nobis gloriæ cœlestis & vitæ æternæ hæreditatem acquireret. Ad hunc ergo modum, vt alijs prosint, sese demittant quotquot Christianam humilitatem profiteri volunt. Cur enim humiliare seipsum dicatur, qui nemini seruit, & nemini vtilis vitam viuit otiosam, telluris inutile pondus?
units.tr: The same can be seen in the monks, who display the utmost humility in dress, gesture and bearing; but, as the German proverb says, they seek keys with which to enter the citadel of power and wealth, and not only do they despise all men, but they also rear themselves up against God, while they establish and boast of the righteousness of their own works (like the Jews of old), and not only despise but also persecute the righteousness of God, which he offers us in his Son Jesus Christ. Besides, they also are the authors for others too, that by raising up their own righteousness in the same way they fall away from the righteousness of God. The apostles acted very differently: they imitated the example of Christ and humbled themselves so that they might exalt others; just as he came down from heaven so that he might raise us up thither; he became the Son of man so that he might make us sons of God; he served all so that he might set us free; finally, he endured disgrace and every kind of insult, and besides a cruel and infamous death, so that he might acquire for us the inheritance of heavenly glory and eternal life. In this way, then, let all who wish to profess Christian humility humble themselves, so that they may be of benefit to others. For why should he be said to humble himself who serves no one, and lives an idle life useful to no one, a useless weight upon the earth?

units.la: Quia verò Paulus se Corinthijs gratuitò euangelizauisse dixit, nunc qua ratione id fecerit, docet: Alias Ecclesias spoliaui, accepto abeis stipendio, vt vobis inserùrem. Sensus est, se ab alijs habuisse vnde viueret. Rursus autem opsonij militaris meminit (vt in priori epistola) vt ad militiæ parabolam alludat, & sibi licuisse ostendat, ab ipsis stipendium exigere. Vt enim milites partim ex stipendio ordinario viuunt, partim ex deuictarum gentium spolijs: itase ex illis victum habuisse testatur, quos iam ante per Euangelij prædicationem deuictos Christi imperio subiecerat. Vtitur autem odioso depræ-dandi vocabulo, non quòd aliquid violenter ab inui-tis extorserit, sed vt innuat, Corinthios adeò non habere quod in ipso accusent, vt potius alij iustam de illis quiritandi causam habeant, quos ipsi sua tenacitate coegerint ad eum Corinthiace Ecclesiæ ministrantem subsidium mittere, quo ipsius egestas subleuaretur. Potest idem hodie de multis dici. Quis enim aliquid de suo largitur Ecclesiæ ministris? Vel, à quo nam aliquid exigitur? Etenim olim Christiani principes & Maiores nostri religionis & pietatis studio excitati sua liberalitate Ecclesias & Cœnobia ditarunt, vt & Scholæ essent, ex quibus ministri prodirent, & qui iam in ministerio sunt absque aliorum incommodo alerentur. Attamen plerique non aliter fremunt, ac si de suo dare cogerentur. Imò, cum ipsi ex Ecclesiæ bonis ditescant, ministris tenuem victum inuident. Est hæc plus quàm Corinthiaca ingratitudo, quam Deus aliquando fame Verbi sui puniet, sicuti olim per Amos Prophetam minatus est.
units.tr: But since Paul has said that he preached to the Corinthians free of charge, he now teaches by what means he did so: "I robbed other churches, taking wages from them, so that I might serve you." The meaning is that he had received from others the means by which he lived. Again he mentions soldier's pay (as in the earlier letter), to allude to the parable of military service, and to show that it was lawful for him to demand a stipend from them. For just as soldiers live partly on regular pay and partly on the spoils of conquered peoples, so he testifies that he had his sustenance from those whom he had already conquered by the preaching of the Gospel and brought under the rule of Christ. He uses the hateful word "plunder" not because he extracted something violently from unwilling people, but to suggest that the Corinthians had so little to accuse him of that others rather had a just cause for complaint against them, since by their own stinginess they had forced them to send to the Corinthian Church, which he served, a help by which his poverty might be relieved. The same can be said today of many. For who gives anything of his own to the ministers of the Church? Or, from whom is anything even demanded? For in former times our Christian princes and forefathers, moved by zeal for religion and piety, enriched churches and monasteries with their generosity, so that there might be schools from which ministers would come forth, and so that those already in the ministry might be supported without loss to others. Yet most people complain as though they were being forced to give from their own. Indeed, although they themselves grow rich from the goods of the Church, they grudge the ministers a meagre living. This ingratitude is more than Corinthian, and God will one day punish it with a famine of his Word, as he once threatened through the prophet Amos.

units.la: Debet etiam diligenter obseruari Pauli exemplum, qui ab Ecclesijs accepit subsidia victus, non autem vt ignauo otio torpesceret, aut vt opum thesauros congereret, sed vt quàm plurimis seruiret, denique vt ingratissimis illis prædicaret, qui Euangelio potius carere, quàm eius gratia sumptum facere voluissent. Conferamus ad hoc exemplum nostri sæculi Apostolicos, qui cum nulli Ecclesiæ seruiant, omnes tamen expilant & depredantur per suos legatos, qui aut Indulgentias diuendunt, aut putres atque ementitas Diuorum reliquias superstitiosis pro pecunia exscalandas obtrudunt, vel etiam principes viros minis inanibus territant. Possunt hi cum Apostolo dicere: Omnes Ecclesias depredamur: sed non possunt adijcere: Vt his aut illis per Euangelij prædicationem seruiamus. Quin, si verum fateri velint, dicendum erit: Vt Veneri, Bacchio, Mammonæ seruiamus, & totum terrarum orbem bellis non necessarijs turbemus. Illis ergo conueniunt, quæ apud Ezech. Cap. 34. & in posteriori Petri Epistola Cap. secundo habentur. Nos Deo gratias agamus, qui nos ex laqueis eorum eripuit, & libertatem nostram constanter tueamur.
units.tr: The example of Paul should also be carefully observed. He received support for his living from the churches, not so that he could grow sluggish in idle leisure or amass hoards of wealth, but so that he could serve as many people as possible and, above all, preach to those most ungrateful men who would rather go without the Gospel than bear its cost. Let us set beside this example our own Apostolic men of today. Though they serve no church, they plunder and strip everyone through their agents, who either sell indulgences or foist rotten and fabricated relics of the saints on superstitious people, to be scraped clean for money, or who frighten even princes with empty threats. These men can say with the Apostle, "We rob other churches," but they cannot add, "in order to serve these or those by preaching the Gospel." Indeed, if they were willing to tell the truth, they would have to say: "We serve Venus, Bacchus and Mammon, and we disturb the whole world with unnecessary wars." What is written in Ezekiel chapter 34 and in the second chapter of the second epistle of Peter applies to them. Let us thank God, who has snatched us from their snares, and let us steadfastly defend our liberty.

units.la: Porrò ne cum aliquo iniquius egisse putaretur Apostolus, rationem sui consilij diligentius explicat: Cùm apud vos essem & egerem, non obtorpui cum alicuius incommodo, id est, non otio mededi, vt aliquibus oneri essem, sed in docendo assiduus, simul opificio & manuum labori omne tempus quod mihi reliquum erat consecraui, vt absque aliorum incommodo viuerem. Quod si quis obijciat, me non potuisse tantum lucrari, quantum mihi opus erat, Respondeo: Quod mihi deerat supleuerunt fratres, qui venerant ex Macedonia. Itaque victum mihi paracui partim manuum mearum labore, partim ex Macedonum liberalitate. Denique in omnibus me præstiti vobis, ἀβαρῆ, id est, minime onerosum, & talem me in posterum quoque præstabo. Ita verò turpem & pudendam Corinthiorum ingratitudinem arguit, & eandem exemplo Macedonum amplificat. Quasi diceret: Vos me vobiscum agentem, & vobis seruientem neglexistis, adeò vt ne egenti quidem aliquid dederitis: Illi verò absenti & in alieno seruitio occupato subsidium miserunt. Vos item, cum in otio agatis & diuitijs abundetis, erga me tamen tenacissimi fuistis, quem Macedones fortunis suis magna ex parte exhausti subleuarunt. Vos denique me, qui nunquam vobis onerosus fui, adhuc me fastiditis, cùm alteri illi me venerentur & in pretio habeant.
units.tr: Moreover, lest the Apostle be thought to have acted unfairly towards anyone, he explains the reasons for his decision more carefully: "When I was among you and working, I did not grow idle at anyone's expense." That is, he did not pass his time in idleness so as to become a burden to some; rather, while he was constant in teaching, he devoted all his remaining time to manual labour and craft, so that he might live without burdening others. But if someone objects that he could not earn as much as he needed, I answer: the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what was lacking. So I provided for my living partly by the labour of my hands and partly from the generosity of the Macedonians. In short, I have been "without burden" [ἀβαρῆ], that is, not at all burdensome to you in anything, and I will continue to be so in future. Thus he charges the Corinthians with shameful and disgraceful ingratitude, and magnifies it by the example of the Macedonians. It is as if he said: "You neglected me while I was dealing with you and serving you, so that you did not give me anything even when I was in need. But they sent help to me when I was absent and occupied in another's service. Likewise, although you live in idleness and abound in riches, you have been very stingy towards me, whom the Macedonians, having been largely drained of their own resources, have relieved. Finally, you despise me, who was never a burden to you, while those others revere me and hold me in high esteem."

units.la: At quærat aliquis, cur à Macedonibus, qui pauperiores erant, Paulus stipendium accepe-rit, Corinthijs autem opulentis pepercerit? Id certè primo intuitu non minus iniquè quàm imprudenter factum videri poterat. At hic tenere oportet, iure quidem nihil illum tunc temporis à Macedonibus exigere potuisse, oblationes verò siue dona voluntaria ipsi accipere licebat, cum necessitas urgeret. Et potest illum excusare Dauidis exemplum, qui contra morem in Lege traditum panes propositionis comedit, & eosdem suis distribuit, cùm non aliud esset quo famem urgentem posset placare. Deinde quia vnum est omnium Ecclesiarum corpus, & omnium gentium credentes ad vnam illam Catholicam Ecclesiam pertinent, quam in Symbolo Apostolico profitemur, nihil præter officium faciebant Macedones: quin potius vt hoc facerent, gratitudinis & charitatis Christianæ legibus admonebantur. Etenim vt in corpore humano membra infirmiora & contemptibiliora præstantioribus seruiunt: ita pauperiores opulentioribus operam suam præstare debent, si hac eos indigere videant. Quoad Paulum verò, prudentiæ hoc erat quòd Corinthios stipendij debiti postulatione noluit offendere, quos sciebat Euangelio potius carituros esse, si sumptus aliquos facere cogerentur. Itaque parcendum eis erat, donec in fide confirmati magis arderent. Et est hæc prudentia ministris imitanda, ne procacitate sua eos offendant, qui adhuc teneriores & infirmiores sunt in fide
units.tr: But someone may ask: why did Paul accept support from the Macedonians, who were poorer, yet spare the wealthy Corinthians? At first glance this might seem to have been done as unfairly as it was unwisely. But here we must keep in mind that at that time he could by right demand nothing from the Macedonians, though he was allowed to accept offerings or voluntary gifts when necessity pressed. The example of David may also excuse him, who against the custom handed down in the Law ate the bread of the Presentation and shared it with his men, since there was nothing else with which he could relieve pressing hunger. Again, because the body of all the churches is one, and believers of all nations belong to that one Catholic Church which we profess in the Apostles' Creed, the Macedonians were doing nothing beyond their duty. Indeed, they were rather reminded by the laws of gratitude and Christian charity to do this. For just as in the human body the weaker and more despised members serve the more honourable ones, so the poorer ought to lend their help to the richer when they see them in need. As for Paul himself, it was a matter of prudence that he did not wish to offend the Corinthians by demanding the stipend owed to him, since he knew they would rather go without the Gospel than be forced to incur any expense. So they had to be spared until, confirmed in the faith, they would burn with greater zeal. This prudence ought to be imitated by ministers, so that they do not offend by their boldness those who are still tender and weaker in the faith.

units.la: Interim debet hoc loco diligenter obseruari Macedonum pietas, qui cum ipsi pauperiores es-sent, Apostolum suis impensis aluerunt, vt Corinthijs ditissimus posset Euangelizare. Debent itaque multo magis facere, qui otio abundant, & occasiones habent multas Euangelium ad alios propagandi. Est enim hic Deo gratissimus cultus, & hominibus nullum beneficium praestantius & salutarius conferri potest. At hodie Macedones quidem pauci, plures autem Corinthijs deteriores sunt, qui quae ab alijs olim Ecclesijs & Scholis collata sunt, insatiabili rapacitate intercipiunt, liberalissimi autem videri volunt, si ex ingenti praeda, quam sacrilego ausu congesserunt, vix tenuem victum Verbi ministris demetiantur. Debet tamen exemplum istud ad alia quoque extendi. Vulgo enim fit, vt qui tenuiores sunt, ditioribus sint liberaliores. Vt enim illos propriae egestatis sensus ad commiserationem excitat: ita hi accipere assueuerunt, & proinde insatiabiles facti iniuriam sibi fieri putant, si quid dare iubeantur. Est ergo magnum & tantumnon immedicabile Auaritiae malum. Abundabant Corinthij scientia & cognitione rerum diuinarum, vt alibi Paulus testatur. Verumtamen ditescendi studium adeo tenaces fecit, vt tantum Apostolum alere noluerint, cui seipsos totos debebant. Tales hodie multos est videre, qui cum in egenis ipsum Christum ali & vestiri audiant, nunquam tamen adduci possunt, vt id liberaliter & ex animo faciant. Sed vt hic Corinthiorum auaritia Macedonum exemplo aggrauatur: ita illi olim a tenuioris fortunae hominibus conuincentur ad Christi tribunal, qui ipsis benigniores & liberaliores fuerunt.
units.tr: Meanwhile, in this place, the piety of the Macedonians must be carefully observed. Although they were themselves poorer, they supported the Apostle at their own expense, so that he could preach the Gospel to the wealthy Corinthians. Therefore those who abound in leisure, and have many opportunities to spread the Gospel to others, ought to do much more of the same. For this is the most pleasing worship to God, and no greater or more healthful benefit can be conferred on men. Today there are few Macedonians, but there are many Corinthians, and worse ones, who with insatiable greed seize what was once given by others to the churches and schools, and who wish to be thought most generous if, out of the huge spoil they have gathered by sacrilegious daring, they scarcely measure out a meagre living to the ministers of the Word. Yet this example ought to be extended to other cases as well. For it commonly happens that those who are humbler are more generous than the wealthier. As the sense of their own want stirs the poor to compassion, so the rich have grown accustomed to receiving, and therefore, having become insatiable, they think they are wronged if they are told to give anything. This is therefore a great evil of avarice, and one that is almost incurable. The Corinthians abounded in knowledge and understanding of divine things, as Paul testifies elsewhere. Yet their eagerness to grow rich made them so stingy that they were unwilling to support the Apostle, to whom they owed themselves entirely. Today one may see many such people who, when they hear that Christ himself is fed and clothed in the poor, can never be brought to do this generously and from the heart. But just as the avarice of the Corinthians is made worse by the example of the Macedonians, so those of the Corinthian sort will one day be convicted before the judgement seat of Christ by people of humbler means who were kinder and more generous to them.

units.la: Deinde ad omnes Ecclesiarum ministros pertinet Pauli exemplum, qui tam solicite cauit, ne cuionerosus esset. Cur enim cuiquam oneri sint, qui ideo mittuntur a Deo, vt liberent, feruent atq; consolentur? Nam hic proprius Euangelij effectus est, quod conscientijs pace & gaudium conciliat. At hic tenere oportet, quid illos facere quidue cauere oporteat, vt nemini graues aut onerosi sint. Vbi primum fuerit, ne Ecclesias hominum traditionibus grauent, quibus neque Deus colitur, neq; conscientijs pax paratur. Nec item aliquem ad suas satisfactiones remittant, quibus nequicquam fatigantur, qui animae sitim alibi quam apud Christum, vnicum aquae viuentis fontem, restingue-re volunt. In vita vero & moribus frugalitati & temperantiae studeant, vt modicis stipendijs contenti viuere possint, neque alicui exactionibus importunis molestiam exhibere cogantur. Hodie in vtroque peccant Papistici praesules atque sacrifici. Inter Euangelij vero professores non desunt, qui doctrina quidem sana conscientias exhilarant, luxu autem & intemperantia sua molesti sunt omnibus, dum nihil ipsis sufficit.
units.tr: Next, the example of Paul pertains to all the ministers of the churches, for he took such careful pains that he would be a burden to no one. For why should those be a burden to anyone who are sent by God so that they may free, feed and console? For this is the proper effect of the Gospel, that it brings peace and joy to consciences. But here we must consider what they ought to do and what they ought to avoid, so that they are not burdensome or oppressive to anyone. First, they must take care not to weigh down the churches with human traditions, by which God is neither worshipped nor peace prepared for consciences. Nor should they send anyone to their own satisfactions, by which those are in vain wearied who wish to quench the thirst of the soul anywhere other than with Christ, the only fountain of living water. In their life and morals, they should practise frugality and temperance, so that they can live content with modest stipends and are not forced to cause trouble to anyone by importunate exactions. Today the Papistical prelates and sacrificing priests sin in both respects. Among the professors of the Gospel, there are not lacking those who by sound doctrine cheer consciences, but who by their luxury and intemperance are a burden to everyone, since nothing is enough for them.

units.la: At quod de ministris dicitur, in genere ad omnes Christianos pertinet: Ne aliquibus onerosi sint. Ergo hoc pauperes quoq; sibi dictum putent. Nam iubet hoc charitatis Lex, quae ipsis non minus quam diuitibus data est. Poterat Paulus optimo iure a Corinthijs debitum sibi stipendium exigere: sed cum alia esset victus parandi ratio, iure suo cessit volens, ne cui molestiam exhiberet. Est ergo hoc graue scelus & nulla venia dignum, si qui suo labore victum sibi parare poterant, abs-que omni iure illum ab alijs postulent. At quam magnus illorum numerus est hodie, qui ignauo otio addicti hinc inde discurrunt, & obtiatim omnes fatigant ab alijs improbe petendo, quae ipsi manuum suarum labore acquirere poterant, nisi cum religione pudorem quoque omnem exuissent. Debebant tales publica authoritate coerceri, ne (quod Apostolus iussit) ex publico ederent qui laborare noluHnt. 2. Thes. 3.
units.tr: But what is said of the ministers applies in general to all Christians: they should not be burdensome to anyone. Therefore let the poor also consider this said to themselves. For the law of charity commands this, and it has been given to the poor no less than to the rich. Paul could with the best right have demanded from the Corinthians the stipend owed to him, but since his method of providing for his living was different, he willingly yielded his right, so that he would cause trouble to no one. Therefore it is a grave sin and deserving of no pardon if those who could earn their living by their own labour demand it from others without any right. Yet how great is the number today of those who, given over to idle leisure, run hither and thither and wearisomely plague everyone by shamelessly asking others for what they could have acquired by the labour of their own hands, unless, having cast off religion, they had also shed all shame. Such people ought to be restrained by public authority, so that (as the Apostle commanded) those who would not work should not eat at the public expense. 2 Thess. 3.

units.la: Caeterum quia Paulus videri poterat hac ideo scribere, vt Corinthijs posthac liberalioribus vteretur, se in posterum quoque talem velle se praestare dicit, qualis hucusque fuerit, & id mox cum graui assueratione confirmabit. Nec enim satis est bene coepisse, nisi in finem vsque perseueres. Quod vt in omni re fieri necesse est, ita maxime in ijs, quae ad fidem & religionem spectant: vt nimirum a Deo vocati, non modo ingrediamur iter, sed cursum nostrum perficiamus, vt metam nobis propositam possimus attingere. In eo olim Lothi vxor & Israelitae peccarunt, dum illa ad Sodomas & illic relictas opes, hi vero ad ollas carnium & Aegypti delitias respectarunt. Et hoc ipsum multos hodie in salutis via remoratur, dum vrgentibus periculis poenitentiam magno quidem cum conatu inchoant, at in medio cursu subsistunt, quam primum melior fortuna affulgere incipit.
units.tr: Moreover, since Paul might seem to write these things so that the Corinthians would be more generous from now on, he says that in future also he wants to show himself such as he has been hitherto, and he will soon confirm this with a solemn assertion. For it is not enough to have begun well unless you persevere to the end. As this is necessary in every matter, so it is especially necessary in those things that concern faith and religion: that we, called by God, not only enter upon the way but complete our course, so that we may reach the goal set before us. In this Lot's wife of old sinned, while she looked back to Sodom and the wealth left there, and the Israelites to the pots of meat and the delicacies of Egypt. And this same thing holds many back today on the way of salvation: while dangers press, they begin repentance with great effort, but they stop in mid-course as soon as better fortune begins to shine upon them.

units.la: Porrò vt diximus, assueratione aut iuramento confirmat Paulus quod dixit: Est Veritas Ts Christi in me, quòd hæc gloriatio non obstruetur in me in regionibus Achaiæ. Gloriationem dicit, quòd gratuitò illis prædicauerat: vt innuat, si non pænitere huius facti, imò non passurum, vt hæc gloria ipsi intercidat. Habent autem verba ista iurandi formulam, cuius sensus est: Per Veritatem Christi hoc testor. Vel: Quàm certò in me est Veritas Christi, cuius ego minister sum, tam certò ego hoc facere constitui, &c. Est autem Veritas Christi Euangelium, cuius prædicatio Apostolis fuit mandata: & ita dicitur, non modò quia doctrina illa veracissima est, verumetiam quia omnium promissionum & vaticiniorum veterum complementum continet. Quia ergo Christus ipse cum Euangelio suo coniunctus est, & Paulus suam salutem in eo consistere sciebat, vt illius seruus esset fidelis, rectè per illud iurat. Et debet huius consideratio ministros omnes excitare, ne leues & vani sint in suis dictis aut factis, vt ne Euangelium aliquo modo suspectum reddant. Quòd si verò Euangelium Veritas Christi est, certè ipsum Dei Filium mendacij insimulant, quotquot illi contradicunt. Quod cum hodie passim fiat, non est quòd nostri sæculi calamitates, quæ nos vndique circumstant, miremur.
units.tr: Moreover, as we have said, Paul confirms by a solemn assertion or oath what he said: "As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting shall not be stopped in me in the regions of Achaia." He calls it a boasting because he had preached to them free of charge, implying that, if he did not regret this deed, he would not in fact allow this glory to be taken from him. These words have the form of an oath, whose sense is: "By the truth of Christ I testify this." Or: "As surely as the truth of Christ is in me, whose minister I am, so surely have I resolved to do this," etc. The truth of Christ is the gospel, whose preaching was committed to the apostles; and it is so called not only because that doctrine is most true, but also because it contains the fulfilment of all the promises and prophecies of old. Since, therefore, Christ himself is joined with his gospel, and Paul knew that his own salvation consisted in it, so that he might be a faithful servant of it, he rightly swears by it. The consideration of this ought to stir up all ministers, lest they be light and vain in their words or deeds, and so in any way make the gospel suspect. But if the gospel is the truth of Christ, certainly all who contradict it charge the Son of God himself with lying. Since this happens everywhere today, we should not wonder at the calamities of our age, which surround us on every side.

units.la: At obseruari debet hoc loco, quòd Paulus suū illud institutū ad Ecclesias Achaiæ restringit. Nec enim absque omni exceptione iurat, se à nemine aliquid accepturum esse, sed nunquā passurū se, vt hæc gloria ipsi obturetur aut obstruatur apud Achaiæ Ecclesias, inter quas facile prima erat Corinthiaca. Causam paulò ante exposuimus, & ipse eam mox diligentius explicabit. Paralogizant ergo, qui ex particulari exemplo doctrinam vniuersalem colligunt, & ita argumentantur: Paulus nihil accepit ab Ecclesijs Achaiæ, neque se quicquam accipere velle iurauit: Ergo ministris non licet stipendia habere, aut ex ministerio viuere. Nam conuerti potest argumentum hoc, vt dicamus: Paulus à Macedonibus accepit vitæ subsidia: Ergo idè licet facere omnibus, qui Euangelium prædicant. Imò si literam vrgere libeat, colligetur hinc quod nō minus iniquū quàm absurdum fuerit: Paulus nihil accepit à Corinthijs, quibus seruiebat, sed ab alijs: Ergo ministri stipendia sua non ab Ecclesijs, quibus seruiunt, sed aliunde accipere debent. Quis verò non videat huius argumenti absurditatem? Non debent ergo ista trahi extra Apostoli institutum. Quoad enim stipendia ministrorū, nota est IESV CHRISTI sententia, qui illos operarijs adnumerat, quibus sua merces debetur. Et quid Paulus de hac causa senserit, alibi audiuimus. Vide 1. Cor. 9. & 1. Timoth. 5. Hæc igitur rata sint, nisi quæ causa grauior nos cogat iure nostro cedere.
units.tr: But it must be observed here that Paul restricts that resolution of his to the churches of Achaia. For he does not swear without any exception that he will receive nothing from anyone, but that he will never allow this glory to be stopped or obstructed for him among the churches of Achaia, among which the Corinthian church was easily first. We explained the cause a little earlier, and he himself will soon explain it more carefully. Those therefore reason falsely who draw a universal doctrine from a particular example and argue thus: Paul received nothing from the churches of Achaia, nor did he swear that he wished to receive anything; therefore ministers may not have stipends or live from the ministry. For this argument can be turned around, so that we say: Paul received support for his living from the Macedonians; therefore it is lawful for all who preach the gospel to do the same. Indeed, if one wishes to press the letter, there would follow from it something no less unjust than absurd: Paul received nothing from the Corinthians, whom he served, but from others; therefore ministers ought to receive their stipends not from the churches they serve but from elsewhere. Who does not see the absurdity of this argument? These things therefore ought not to be drawn beyond the apostle's intention. As for the stipends of ministers, the saying of Jesus Christ is well known, who counts them among the workers to whom their wage is due. And what Paul thought about this matter we have heard elsewhere. See 1 Cor. 9 and 1 Tim. 5. Let these things therefore stand, unless some weightier cause compels us to yield our right.

units.la: At obijcere poterant Corinthij: An ergo nos fastidiis, aut indignos putas, à quibus aliquid accipias? Ita enim comparatum est, vt quos magni facimus, eos etiam amemus, & proinde familiariter quoque ijsdem vtamur, adeoq; donis quoq; illorum delectemur. Itaq; suspicionem, quam de illo concipere poterant Corinthij, præoccupatione diluit, dicens: Quapropter? An quòd non diligā vos? Deus nouit. Rursus autem testem citat Deum, & proinde iterum iurat. Arguit hoc fanaticos qui omne iuramentum illicitum esse dicunt, & Christi verbis ad suam sententiam stabiliendam abutuntur, qui dixerit: Ne iuretis omnino, sed sit sermo vester, Est est, Non non. Atqui eo loco de temerarijs & non necessarijs iuramentis agitur, qualia hodie etiā apud homines leues in vsu sunt, & commendatur veritatis studiū, cui ita assuescere debent Christiani homines, vt in colloquijs priuatis, in contractibus item & alijs eiusmodi negotijs iurare non sit opus, neque hoc quisquam ab eis exigat. Quid verò hoc ad controuersias, quas iureiurando interposito finiri Apostolus ad Hebræos testatur? Quid itē hoc ad magistratus & subditos, vel etiam ad socios siue confæderatos, quos mutui iuramenti vinculo obstringi necesse est? Dicant etiam nobis religiosi isti homines, num Deus iubeat quod illicitū est, & salua religione aut pietate non potest fieri? Atqui leges diserta extant, quibus vt per nomen eius iuremus præcipitur, et hoc inter vera fidei exercitia Spiritus sanctus numerat. Obijciunt illi, hæc in Veteri testamento olim facta esse. Fatemur hoc ipsi quoq; Sed quid hoc obstat, cùm ex Dei iussu & mandato facta sint? Quid verò illi Isaiæ respondebunt, qui de Ægypti coniuersione ad Christum, quæ Noui testamenti tempore demū fieri debuit, vaticinans, inter alia ait: In die illa erunt quinq; ciuitates in terra Ægypti, quæ loquuntur lingua Chanaan, & quæ iurabunt per Dominum exercituum. Quid multis? Sub pietatis prætextu isti homines Reipub. dissipationem quærunt, & proinde eorum verbis nemo moueri debet. Caueatur modò leuitas iurandi, seruetur autem formula à Deo tradita, qua qui sancte & religiose viuntur, minimè peccant.
units.tr: But the Corinthians might object: "Do you then despise us, or think us unworthy to receive anything from? For it is so ordered that those whom we esteem highly we also love, and therefore we make familiar use of them and take delight in their gifts." So he removes by anticipation the suspicion the Corinthians might conceive about him, saying: "Why? Because I do not love you? God knows." Again he calls God as witness, and so swears once more.
