This refutes the fanatics who say that every oath is unlawful, and who abuse the words of Christ to establish their opinion, who said: "Do not swear at all, but let your speech be, Yes, yes; No, no." Yet that passage deals with rash and unnecessary oaths, of the kind that even today are in use among frivolous men, and it commends love of truth, to which Christians ought to be so accustomed that in private conversations, in contracts too and in other such affairs, there is no need to swear, nor does anyone demand it of them. But what has this to do with disputes which, as the apostle to the Hebrews testifies, are ended by an interposed oath? What has it to do with magistrates and subjects, or even with allies and confederates, who must be bound by the bond of mutual oath? Let these religious men also tell us: does God command what is unlawful, and can it be done without loss of religion or piety? Yet clear laws exist commanding us to swear by his name, and the Holy Spirit counts this among the true exercises of faith. They object that these things were done in the Old Testament. We admit this too. But what does that matter, since they were done at God's command and bidding? And what will they answer to Isaiah, who, prophesying of the conversion of Egypt to Christ, which was to happen only in the time of the New Testament, says among other things: "In that day there shall be five cities in the land of Egypt that speak the language of Canaan and that swear by the Lord of hosts"? What more is there to say? Under the pretext of piety these men seek the dissolution of the commonwealth, and therefore no one should be moved by their words. Let levity in swearing be avoided, but let the formula given by God be kept, and those who live holy and religious lives do not sin at all.

units.la: Sed causam audiamus, quæ Paulum mouit, vt hanc gloriationem sibi eripi nollet. Sed quod facio (inquit) etiam faciam, vt amputem occasionem ijs qui cupiunt occasionem, vt in eo, de quo gloriantur, reperiantur quales & nos. Quæ verba plerique intelligunt, quasi pseudapostoli gratuito prædicauerint, & ideo Paulum idem fecisse aiunt, ne illis in hac parte esset inferior. Sed pugnat cum hac sententia, quod infra dicet: Toleratis, si quis vos in seruitutem adigit, si quis exedit, si quis accipit, &c. Deinde noluit Paulus illorum similis fieri, sed potius illos ad sui exempli imitationem excitare, & simul calumniandi occasionem præripere, quam vænabantur. Volebant enim ipso præstantiores videri, & ideo Zelum pietatis ardentissimum simulabant, magnifice de diuinis loquebantur, interim vero rem suam agebant. Vt ergo illis omnem occasionem amputaret, ipse gratuito docebat, quod illos nunquam facturos satis nouerat, cum toti ambitione simul & auaritia flagrarent, imo ventris quoque mancipia essent. Itaque sensus verborum est: Illi vellent me quoq; à vobis aliquid exigere, vt ita in hac parte ipsis æquarer, illi vero quoad reliqua inuenirent aliquam gloriandi occasionem. At ego hanc illis nunquam concessero. Quin potius, si mihi pares esse volunt, ipsi etiam gratuito prædicent oportet, & ita habebunt fortasse, quo aduersus me glorientur. Itaque Paulus ita voluit gloriandi occasionem æmulis suis præscindere, vt eos sibi pares fieri cuperet: vt nimirum posthabito lucri priuati studio, solius Dei gloriam & Ecclesiæ salutem quærerent, id quod animi vere Christiani argumentum est.
units.tr: But let us hear the cause which moved Paul not to want this boasting taken from him. "But what I do," he says, "I will also continue to do, so that I may cut off the occasion from those who desire an occasion, that in that in which they boast they may be found like us." Most people understand these words as if the false apostles preached free of charge, and so they say Paul did the same, so as not to be inferior to them in this respect. But this view clashes with what he says below: "You put up with it if anyone brings you into bondage, if anyone devours you, if anyone takes from you," etc. Moreover, Paul did not wish to become like them, but rather to stir them up to imitate his example, and at the same time to snatch away the occasion for slander which they were hunting. For they wanted to seem more eminent than he, and therefore they feigned the most ardent zeal for piety, spoke magnificently of divine things, yet meanwhile pursued their own affairs. So, to cut off every occasion from them, he himself preached free of charge, which he knew they would never do, since they burned with ambition and avarice together, and were indeed slaves of their belly. So the sense of the words is: "They would wish me also to demand something from you, so that in this respect I might be made equal to them; but as to the rest, they would find some occasion for boasting. But I will never grant them this. Indeed, if they wish to be equal to me, they too must preach free of charge, and so perhaps they will have something to boast of against me." Thus Paul wished to cut off the occasion of boasting from his rivals in such a way that he desired them to become equal to him: namely, that, setting aside the pursuit of private gain, they would seek the glory of God alone and the salvation of the Church, which is a true mark of a truly Christian mind.

units.la: Continet autem locus hic vniuersalem doctrinam, ne qua occasio ijs detur, qui eam captant contra nos & veritatem. Paulus, ne id fieret, à licitis quoque abstinebat. Quanto magis ergo ab illicitis nos abstinere conuenit? Debet hoc ad omnes vitæ nostræ actiones extendi. Cogitemus nos in totius mundi theatro versari, & omnium oculos in nos, ceu in ciuitatem in edito monte sitam, esse intentos: nec vnquam animis nostris excidat, mundum totum in malo iacere, & in omnem occasionem intentum esse, vt aduersus veritatem & huius professores calumniandi argumentum inueniat. Nec dormitat Satan, qui vbique sua flabella habet, quibus eorum etiam, qui adhuc quiescunt, animos accendat. Vigilemus ergo, & ab omni specie mali abstineamus. Imprimis autem cura sit, ne Deum tentemus ea nobis temere accersendo, quæ vel nobis alicuius lapsus, vel aliis calumniandi occasionem præbere possunt. Denique vocationem suam singuli sedulo sequantur, & in omni actione CHRISTI IESV doctrinam atque exemplum respiciant, qui nos non patietur errare, cum sit Via, Veritas & Vita. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: This passage contains a general teaching, that no occasion be given to those who seek one against us and the truth. Paul, to prevent this, abstained even from things that were lawful. How much more, then, ought we to abstain from things that are unlawful? This should be extended to all the actions of our life. Let us consider that we live on the stage of the whole world, and that the eyes of all are fixed on us, as on a city set on a high mountain; and let it never slip from our minds that the whole world lies in evil, and is intent on every opportunity to find a ground for slandering the truth and those who profess it. Satan does not sleep either; he has his fans everywhere, with which he kindles the minds even of those who are still at rest. Let us therefore keep watch, and abstain from every appearance of evil. Above all, let us take care not to tempt God by rashly taking on those things which can either give us a fall or give others an occasion to slander us. Finally, let each one diligently follow his own calling, and in every action look to the teaching and example of Christ Jesus, who will not suffer us to err, since he is the Way, the Truth and the Life. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLIX.
units.tr: Homily XLIX.

units.la: Nam istiusmodi pseudapostoli, operarij dolosi sunt, transformati in Apostolos Christi. Neque id mirum: ipse enim Satanas transformatur in Angelum lucis. Non magnum est igitur, si transformentur vt ministri iustitiæ, etiam eius ministri; quorum finis erit secundum opera eorum.
units.tr: For such false apostles are deceitful workers, transformed into apostles of Christ. Nor is this surprising, for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light. It is no great wonder, then, if his ministers too are transformed into ministers of righteousness; their end will be according to their works.

units.la: Quemadmodum omnes Apostoli magno studio & zelo se se falsis doctoribus opposuerunt, ne qui rudiores & in fide infirmiores ab illis decepti a Veritate & vnica salutis æternæ via declinarent: Ita Paulus tota hac tractatione constantissimè aduersus eos dimicat, qui apud Corinthios eius authoritatem eleuabant, vt sua figmenta Ecclesiæ obtrudere possent, quibus syncerior Euangelij doctrina corrumpebatur. Et quia sciebat eos in omnem occasionem intentos esse, nuper protestatus est, se nunquam passurum vt sibi pares æstimentur, nisi procul relicto lucri & gloriæ priuatæ studio, ipsum in omnibus imitentur. Quia vero hoc poterat ambitiosius dictum videri, ideo nunc eius rationem reddit, quam ab illorum persona desumit, ita nimirum eos describens, vt offendat, indignos esse, quibus cum ipse aliquid commune habeat, simulque hic omnia comprehendit, quæ de falsis doctoribus dici possunt. Docet enim, qui & quales illi sint: Deinde quibus artibus sese insinuent: Quis item eorundem finis futurus sit, adeoque omnium qui eos imitantur.
units.tr: Just as all the apostles opposed false teachers with great zeal and earnestness, so that the cruder and weaker in the faith might not be deceived by them and turn aside from the truth and the one way of eternal salvation, so Paul in this whole discussion fights most strenuously against those who were raising up his authority among the Corinthians, so that they could impose their own fictions on the Church, by which the purer doctrine of the gospel was being corrupted. And because he knew that they were watching for every opportunity, he recently declared that he would never allow himself to be counted their equal, unless, far from any pursuit of gain or private glory, they imitated him in all things. But because this might seem a rather boastful statement, he now gives the reason for it, which he draws from their own person, describing them in such a way as to make it plain that they are unworthy of having anything in common with him. At the same time he gathers together everything that can be said of false teachers. For he teaches who and what sort of men they are; then by what arts they insinuate themselves; and again what the end of these men will be, and so of all who imitate them.

units.la: Principio sic scribit: Nam isti huiusmodi pseudapostoli, operarij dolosi sunt transformati in Apostolos Christi. Diserte pseudapostolos dicit, ut per praeoccupationem illis respondeat, quibus durum & periculosum videbatur eos contemnere aut reijcere, qui Christi nomen profitebantur, Christum item praedicabant, & eiusdem Apostoli volebant censeri. Nam sensus verborum est: Scio quo nomine aut titulo se fe pallient, & quales nonnullis inter vos videantur: Sed qualescunque dicantur aut aestimentur, Pseudapostoli sunt, qui seipsos in Apostolos Christi transformarunt, & proinde cauendi sunt, nec aliqua ipsis dari debet res suas agendi occasio. Significat autem Pseudapostoli vox legatum falsum, qui se legatum esse mentitur: & talis proprie dicitur, qui vel non missus est ab eo, cuius nomen praetexit: vel quod in mandatis accepit, non bona fide exequitur, dum vel falsa alia affingit, vel non ad finem verum omnia dirigit, sed sub publico nomine res suas agit. Est hoc turpissimum flagitium, & antiquitus παραπρεσβεία dicebatur, cuius criminis convicti poenas gravissimas dabat. Ut enim legatorum nomen apud omnes gentes sacrosanctissimum & bono ratissimum erat: ita vix ulla venia dignus iudicabatur, qui tanta dignitate, sibi a Repub. mandata, sua vel negligentia vel cupiditate aliqua prava prophanauisset. At quanto gravius is peccare dicetur, qui in Christi Ecclesia sub ipsius Christi nomine falsum legatum tunc agit, quando aeternae salutis negotium agitur? Atqui tales erant isti, de quibus hic Paulus disserit. Nam primo non missi erant, sed subdole in Ecclesias irrepebant, falso Apostolorum authoritatem praetexentes.
units.tr: He writes at the outset: "For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, transformed into apostles of Christ." He expressly calls them false apostles, so that by anticipating the objection he answers those for whom it seemed hard and dangerous to despise or reject men who professed the name of Christ, preached Christ, and wished to be counted apostles of Christ. For the sense of the words is this: "I know under what name or title they cloak themselves, and what sort of men some among you think them to be. But whatever they are called or thought to be, they are false apostles, who have transformed themselves into apostles of Christ, and therefore they must be guarded against, and no opportunity must be given them to carry on their business." The word "false apostle" signifies a false envoy, one who falsely claims to be an envoy. Properly speaking, such a man is one who either was not sent by him whose name he puts forward, or who does not faithfully carry out what he has received in his instructions, while either inventing other things falsely, or not directing everything to the true end, but pursuing his own affairs under a public name. This is a most disgraceful crime, and in antiquity it was called [paraprεsbeia], and those convicted of it paid the heaviest penalties. For just as the name of envoys was most sacred and most firmly held to be good among all nations, so one who had profaned by his negligence or some wicked desire such a dignity entrusted to him by the commonwealth was thought scarcely worthy of any pardon. But how much more grievously will he be said to sin who, in the Church of Christ, under the very name of Christ, acts as a false envoy at the very time when the business of eternal salvation is being transacted? And yet such were those of whom Paul is here speaking. For first, they were not sent, but craftily crept into the churches, falsely pretending the authority of the apostles.

units.la: Et hoc de illis Apostoli in Synodali sua epistola testantur, in qua sic scribunt: Quidam ex nobis egressi turbauerunt vos verbis, quibus hoc non mandaueramus. Deinde praedicabant isti quidem Christum, sed huius doctrinam partim legis Mosaicae additionibus, partim philosophia ethnica adulterabant: adeo ut Christi meritum exinanirent, & illum suis sectatoribus inutilem facerent, ut in epistolis ad Galatas & Colossen. Est videre. Postremo, res suas agebant, nihil de Christi gloria aut hominum salute solliciti. Argumentum eius nimis euidens erat ignaua & turpis illa indulgentia, qua sceleratissimos quosque ferebant, disciplinam collabi patiebantur, nec ad priuatorum modo hominum vitia, verumetiam ad ea conniuebant, quae in publicis Ecclesiae coetibus praeter Christianae professionis decorum fiebant: sicuti in priori epistola vidimus. Sufficiebat enim hominibus ambitiosis & auaris, si ipsi magni fierent, & opibus augerentur. Ideo operarios quoque dolosos dicit: quia etsi operarentur, id tamen non bona fide faciebant, cum omnia ad quaestum & gloriam priuatam instituerent, cum eorum periculo atque damno, qui ab ipsis seducebantur. Quo nomine in epistola ad Philippenses eosdem operarios malos dicit, nimirum ad illud Christi respicies, qui olim talibus se dicturum ait: Discedite a me, qui operamini iniquitatem.
units.tr: The apostles bear witness to this about them in their synodal letter, in which they write thus: "Some who went out from us have troubled you with words, to which we had not given any commandment." Moreover, these men indeed preached Christ, but they corrupted his doctrine partly with additions from the Mosaic law, partly with ethnic philosophy, so that they emptied Christ's merit and made him useless to their followers, as may be seen in the epistles to the Galatians and the Colossians. Finally, they pursued their own affairs, caring nothing for the glory of Christ or the salvation of men. The evidence for this was all too plain in that lazy and shameful indulgence, by which they tolerated the most wicked men, allowed discipline to collapse, and winked not only at the sins of private persons but also at those things that were done in the public assemblies of the Church contrary to the decorum of the Christian profession, as we saw in the former epistle. For it was enough for ambitious and greedy men that they themselves should become great and be enriched with wealth. Therefore he also calls them deceitful workers, because although they did work, they did not do it in good faith, since they directed everything to gain and private glory, to the peril and loss of those who were led astray by them. For this reason, in the epistle to the Philippians he calls the same men evil workers, no doubt with an eye to that saying of Christ, who said that he would one day speak thus to such men: "Depart from me, you who work iniquity."

units.la: Docet autem locus iste, quales censeri debeant, qui hodie Apostolicos se dicunt, horum autem per omnia sunt similes: Pontifices nimirum Romani, cum tota suorum Cardinalium & Episcoporum cohorte. Gloriantur hi omnes successione apostolica, & potestatem iactant, quam ex successionis illius iure ab ipso Christo acceperint. Sed si quis rem propius inspiciat, illos & falsos legatos esse, et insuper παραπρεσβεύειν, id est, legatione (si quae ipsis comissa est) mala fide obire patebit. Nam omnia faciunt, quae et Christi mandato, & Apostolorum exemplo aduersantur. Quis ergo illos missione legitimam habere, aut in illa eos bona fide agere dixerit? Christi quidem nomen in ore habet, & Euangelium eius profitentur, sed sexcenta alia addunt, quibus illius meritum prorsus exinanitur & inutile redditur: & ea quidem addunt, quae ab hominibus superstitiosissimis confictana non alia quam sui similium authoritate nituntur. Adhaec non nisi suas res agunt, cum circa ea sola occupentur, quae neque Christi gloriam, neque Ecclesiae salutem atque aedificationem adiuuant, ipsis autem quaestuosa sunt, & stolidum vulgus in ipsorum admirationem rapiunt. Quod si vitam atque mores eorum inspicere libeat, nihil illis petulantius, nihil impurius inuenies. Itaque operantur quidem, sed dolosi & iniqui operarii sunt, qui vel ea faciunt, quae palam iniqua & impia sunt: vel simulate agunt, quicquid recte & bene agere videntur. Quibus adde quod manifesta & gravissima quaeque scelera patienter ferre & dissimulare possunt, modo suam existimationem ipsis apud omnes salvam manere videant. Quis enim Inquisitorum, quos ipsi ceu vigiles publicos constituunt, vnquam in hominum mores inquisiuit? quis alicui propter stupra, & adulteria, vsuras, caedes, veneficia, litem mouit? At si cui verbulum excidat, quo vel Romanae sedis authoritas læditur, vel superstitiones ab illis confictæ reprehenduntur, mox in illius fide inquiritur, & hæretica prauitatis suspectus habetur. Sunt ergo reuera pseudoapostoli, qui publice argui debent, ne qui incautiores sunt, illorum artibus circumuenti capiantur.
units.tr: This passage also teaches what sort of men ought to be counted those who today call themselves apostolic, and these are in every respect like them: namely the Roman pontiffs, with the whole retinue of their cardinals and bishops. All of these glory in apostolic succession, and they boast of the power which they say they received from Christ himself by right of that succession. But if anyone looks into the matter more closely, it will be plain that they are false envoys, and moreover that they [paraprεsbeuein], that is, carry out in bad faith the legation (if any has been committed to them). For they do everything that is contrary both to the command of Christ and to the example of the apostles. Who, then, would say that they have a lawful sending, or that they act in good faith in it? They indeed have the name of Christ on their lips, and they profess his gospel, but they add six hundred other things, by which his merit is utterly emptied and rendered useless. And these additions they make are devised by most superstitious men, and rest on no other authority than that of their like. Besides, they pursue only their own affairs, since they are occupied only with those things which serve neither the glory of Christ nor the salvation and edification of the Church, but are profitable to themselves, and carry the foolish crowd away into admiration of them. And if one cares to look into their life and morals, you will find nothing more wanton, nothing more impure. Thus they do indeed work, but they are deceitful and wicked workers, who either do things that are openly unjust and impious, or pretend to do well whatever they seem to do rightly. To this add that they can patiently bear and overlook every manifest and most grievous crime, provided they see their own reputation remaining safe with everyone. For which of the Inquisitors, whom they set up as public watchmen, has ever inquired into men's morals? Who has ever brought a suit against anyone on account of fornication, adultery, usury, murder, or poisoning? But if anyone lets slip a little word by which the authority of the Roman see is injured, or by which the superstitions devised by them are rebuked, at once his faith is investigated, and he is held under suspicion of heretical depravity. They are therefore truly false apostles, who ought to be publicly exposed, lest the more incautious among you be taken in by their arts and ensnared.

units.la: Porrò, quia Paulus suos illos aduersarios in Apostolos Christi trasformatos esse dixerat, eius dicti rationem reddit propter stolidos eorum admiratores, quos fucatæ sanctimoniæ simulatio sic cœperat, vt illos tales esse vix posse putarent. Quæ persuasio hodie etiam multos decipit, vt indigne ferant Monachos aut Sacrificulos reprehendi, qui vel dicendo aliquid possunt, vel morum simulata probitate & mirifica humanitatis specie sese apud illos insinuarunt. Tunc enim mox audiuntur voces illæ: Et quis credat istos homines de re Christiana male sentire, qui venerabile illud IESV CHRISTI nomen nunquam non in ore habent? qui ad eius mentionem caput reuerenter inclinant? Quis vero de illorum sanctitate dubitet, in quorum vita & moribus extrema humilitas, modestia rara, & pudor plus quam virgineus elucent? Sed Paulus omnibus istus vno argumento respondet, & hoc diaboli singulare aucupium esse docet, quo optimis quibusque insidias struit. Neque id mirum (inquit) ipse enim Satanas transformatur in Angelum lucis. Argumentum est à Maiori, quod ita formari potest, vt sensus sit euidentior: Si Satan omnis nequitiæ & impietatis princeps siue caput, se transformare potest in Angelum lucis, quanto magis homines, quos Deus ad suum seruitium condidit, ministros iustitiæ simulare possunt? Atqui Satan in Angelum lucis se transformare potest. Cur ergo alicui mirum videatur, aut impossibile, si qui huius ministri & organa semel facti sunt, personam ministrorum iustitiæ suscipiant? Sunt autem ministri iustitiæ, qui CHRISTVM IESVM prædicant, qui nobis à Patre iustitia factus est, & ita ad veram iustitiam homines erudiunt, vt Daniel de illis loquitur. Ad Maioris confirmationem facit rerum experientia, & quæ passim nobis occurrunt exempla. Etenim Angeli lucis dicuntur & reuera sunt, qui in Dei conspectu stant, & luce illa æterna, quæ hic inhabitat, delectantur, quique ad eius obsequium parati, omnes homines ad illius cultum & æternæ salutis hæreditatem adducere cupiunt: vt in eorum Angelorum exemplis esse videre, qui cum Daniele & Ioanne Apostolo egerunt. Contra tenebrarum Angelus atque princeps dicitur Satan, qui vt tenebris gaudet, ita eadem omnibus hominibus offundere cupit, vt eos secum ad æternas inferni tenebras, ad quas ipse iampridem damnatus est, abripiat. Hic vero, etsi nihil perinde atque lucem Veritatis oderit, tamen in Angelum lucis se transformare solet, id est, celata sua persona Dei ministrum mentitur, qui & huius gloriam promotam, & hominum saluti consultum esse velit. Exemplum huius astutiæ in ipsa statim rerum origine edidit. Nam serpentis, animalium omnium sapientissimi, forma assumpta ad Euam accessit, & colloquium cum illa à Deo exorsus, hoc sibi dolere simulauit, quod hunc cum ipsa & Adamo malignius agere, & perfectiorem gloriam eis inuidere videat: neque eo contentus, scientiam boni & mali, & quod Dei similes facere velit pollicetur, si suis monitis obtemperent. Ita vero infelicem decepit, & cum illa omnem posteritatem in eas miserias adduxit, ex quibus non alio pretio quam Filij Dei sanguine redimi potuimus. Simili ratione Achabum quoque seduxit, quando spiritus mendax fuit in ore Prophetarum eius; & victori- am contra Syros Dei nomine illi pollicitus est. Sed & gentes omnes sub sapientiæ & veritatis prætextu dementauit, vt Deos infinitos fingerent, idolis seruirent, seque ipsos nefarijs libidinibus polluerent, sicuti Paulus ad Romanos scribit. Quid quod Christum tentaturus perinde egit, ac si de ipsius salute & gloria solicitus esset, & laqueos, quos ei parabat, Scripturis sacris velare ausus fuit? Talem nos quoque adhuc experimur: nec enim ab eo tempore ingenium mutauit. Quando enim nos ad defectionem à Deo, ad fidei abnegationem, ad superstitiosas & illicitas artes, idololatriam, vagas libidines & immanissima quæque scelera solicitat, non aperte quod vult dicit, neque initio statim vngues & cornua exerit, sed amicum & nostræ salutis amantem se esse simulat: falsa dogmata veritatis specie fucat: defectionem à Deo necessitate excusat: manifesta scelera utilitatis prætextu & communi omnium exemplo commendat. Opus igitur est de his frequenter cogitare, vt vigilemus, neque temere locum demus suggestionibus ipsius, vel etiam eorum blandiloquentiæ, quorum opera in nobis decipiendis vtitur. Nam qualis ipse est, tales etiam facit ministros suos: quod multis exemplis probari potest. Olim certè Veritatis & communis patria atque diuini cultus vindex acerrimus videri volebat Hananias, qui Ieremia vrbi & templo excidium minati sese opposuit. At idem ille infelices falsis promissis inscatos decepit, vt incurabi‑li sua cotumacia exitiù sibijpsis maturarent. Pharifaei itē & Sadducaei iustitiæ ministri et cultores præcipui esse putabantur, cum pro Legis iustitia acerrime pugnarent, & sanctitatis studium vesti‑tu, verbis, nomine & operum suorum fuco publice profiterentur. Sed ijdē Dei iustitiā reijciebant, & multorum animos suo exemplo & authoritate seducebant, quò minus Christū & in hoc oblatā ipsis salutem reciperent. Horū omnino similes sunt, qui hodie idololatriam & superstitiones vanif‑imas propugnant. Quid enim magnificentius & sanctius est titulis, quibus illi sese vendicant? Pō‑tifices certe Vicarij Christi dicuntur, Apostolici, Serui seruorum Dei, Sanctissimi. Qui ab his pro‑ximi sunt, Cardinalium nomine ornantur, vel quòd præ aliis excellant, vel quòd circa ipsos, ceu cardines, orbis terrarum vertatur. Alij Episcopi siue Speculatores, alij Abbates siue Patres, alij Monachi vel Solitarij & mundo mortui, multi Presbyteri, Doctores, Magistri nostri, Sera‑phici, Cherubici, candelabra Ecclesiæ, luminaria mundi, hæreticorum mallei, & quid nō præterea? dici solent. At si omnes istos vnà cùm sua doctrina atq; studijs omnibus excutias, nō alios inuenies, quàm quales isti fuerunt, de quibus in præsenti Paulus scribit. Quid enim habent, quod titulis is‑tis respondeat? Aut quis operarios dolosos, imò perfidos, imò noxios esse negauerit, qui saluberrimū illud opus Dei impediunt, fidem videlicet in IESVM CHRISTVM, quo solo (vt ipse do‑cet) panis ille cœlestis paratur, qui nos alit & seruat ad vitam æternam? Ioan. 6.
units.tr: Moreover, because Paul had said that these adversaries of his had been transformed into apostles of Christ, he gives the reason for that statement, on account of their foolish admirers, whom the pretence of a painted holiness had so captivated that they could hardly believe such men could be anything but genuine. That same belief deceives many today, so that they take it badly when monks or little priests are rebuked, men who, by speaking well or by a feigned goodness of life and a remarkable show of courtesy, have worked their way into people's favour. For then at once those voices are heard: "And who would believe that these men think wrongly about the Christian religion, when they always have that venerable name JESUS CHRIST on their lips? Who bows his head reverently at the mention of it? And who could doubt their holiness, when extreme humility, rare modesty and a shame more than virginal shine forth in their life and conduct?" But Paul answers all such objections with a single argument, and teaches that this is the devil's particular snare, by which he lays traps for the best of men. "Nor is that surprising," he says, "for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light." This is an argument from the greater, which may be framed so that its sense is more evident: If Satan, the prince and head of all wickedness and impiety, can transform himself into an angel of light, how much more can men, whom God created for his service, simulate the ministers of righteousness? But Satan can indeed transform himself into an angel of light. Why, then, should it seem strange or impossible to anyone that those who have once become the instruments and tools of this minister should put on the character of ministers of righteousness? Now the ministers of righteousness are those who preach CHRIST JESUS, who has been made righteousness for us by the Father, and who thus teach men to true righteousness, as Daniel speaks of them. The experience of things, and the examples that meet us everywhere, confirm the greater argument. For those are rightly called angels of light, and truly are so, who stand in the sight of God, delight in that eternal light which dwells here, who are ready for his service, and who desire to bring all men to his worship and to the inheritance of eternal salvation; as we may see in the examples of those angels who dealt with Daniel and with the apostle John. On the other hand, Satan is called the angel and prince of darkness, who, as he delights in darkness, so he wishes to pour the same over all men, so as to snatch them with himself into the eternal darkness of hell, to which he himself was condemned long ago. Yet he, although he hates the light of truth no less than before, is accustomed to transform himself into an angel of light, that is, with his own person hidden, he pretends to be a minister of God, one who wishes his glory to be advanced and the salvation of men to be cared for. He gave an example of this craftiness at the very beginning of things. For, taking the form of a serpent, the wisest of all animals, he approached Eve, and, opening a conversation with her, he pretended to grieve that God dealt more harshly with her and Adam and begrudged them a more perfect glory; and, not content with this, he promised her the knowledge of good and evil, and that they would be made like God, if they obeyed his counsel. So he deceived the unhappy woman, and with her led the whole posterity into those miseries, from which we could be redeemed at no price but the blood of the Son of God. In a similar way he also seduced Ahab, when a lying spirit was in the mouth of his prophets, and promised him victory over the Syrians in the name of God. But he also drove all the nations mad under the pretext of wisdom and truth, so that they made for themselves infinite gods, served idols, and defiled themselves with unlawful lusts, as Paul writes to the Romans. What of the fact that, when he was about to tempt Christ, he acted as though he were concerned for his safety and glory, and dared to veil the snares he was preparing for him with the holy Scriptures? We still experience him in the same way, for he has not changed his nature since that time. For when he incites us to defection from God, to denial of the faith, to superstitious and unlawful arts, to idolatry, to wandering lusts and to every most monstrous crime, he does not openly say what he wants, nor at the start does he at once show his claws and horns, but pretends to be a friend and a lover of our salvation. He paints false doctrines with the appearance of truth, excuses defection from God by necessity, and commends plain crimes under the pretext of usefulness and the common example of all. It is therefore necessary to think often on these things, so that we may stay watchful, and not rashly give place to his suggestions, or even to the smooth words of those whose work he uses to deceive us. For as he himself is, so he also makes his ministers; this may be proved by many examples. Long ago, certainly, Hananiah wished to appear the most zealous champion of truth, the common fatherland and divine worship, when he set himself against Jeremiah, who threatened the city and temple with destruction. Yet that same man deceived the unwary, poor fools, with false promises, so that by their incurable obstinacy they hastened their own ruin. The Pharisees and Sadducees likewise were thought to be the chief ministers and cultivators of righteousness, since they fought most fiercely for the righteousness of the Law, and publicly professed a zeal for holiness by their dress, their words, their name and the show of their works. But these same men rejected the righteousness of God, and by their example and authority led the minds of many astray, so that they would not receive Christ and the salvation offered to them in him. Those who today defend idolatry and the most empty superstitions are altogether like these. For what is more magnificent and holy than the titles by which they claim distinction for themselves? The Popes, certainly, are called Vicars of Christ, Apostolic, Servants of the servants of God, Most Holy. Those who are next to these are adorned with the name of Cardinals, either because they excel the others or because the whole world turns on them as on hinges. Others are called bishops or overseers, others abbots or fathers, others monks or solitaries and dead to the world, many presbyters, doctors, our masters, seraphic, cherubic, candlesticks of the Church, lights of the world, hammers of heretics, and what else besides are commonly said. But if you shake out all these men, together with their doctrine and all their pursuits, you will find none other than those very men of whom Paul is writing here. For what do they have that answers to those titles? Or who would deny that these are deceitful workmen, nay faithless, nay harmful, who hinder that most salutary work of God, namely faith in JESUS CHRIST, by which alone (as he himself teaches) that heavenly bread is prepared which nourishes and preserves us to eternal life? John 6.

units.la: Quapropter nemo se titulorum eiusmodi splendore temere capi patiatur, neque professionem veritatis ex fuco externo æstimet. Ecenim olim nos Christus præmonuit, venturos lupos, qui se o‑uium pellibus vendicent: & eosdem ex Ecclesiæ ministris siue Episcoporum ordine exituros esse Paulus testatur. Nec vnquam nobis excidere debet, quòd magna illa mater scortationum phil‑tra sua, quibus Reges terræ & populos dementat, in aureo calice propinare dicitur. At nos ones Christi esse conuenit, quibus hoc ille proprium tribuit, quòd inter veri sui pastoris & mercenarij vocem possint discernere. Ecenim vehementer falluntur, qui se excusatos esse, culpam vero omnē erroris in doctoribus hærere putant. Notum est enim illud Christi: Si caecus cæco dux fuerit, am‑bo cadunt in foueam. Matth.15.
units.tr: Therefore let no one allow himself to be rashly taken in by the splendour of titles of this sort, nor judge the profession of truth by its outward paint. For Christ forewarned us long ago that wolves would come, clothing themselves in sheepskins, and Paul testifies that these same men would arise from among the ministers of the Church, that is, from the order of bishops. Nor should it ever escape us that that great mother of harlotries, who makes the kings of the earth and the peoples drunk with her love potions, is said to pour them out in a golden cup. But it becomes us, the sheep of Christ, to whom he gives this as their peculiar mark, that we can distinguish between the voice of his true shepherd and that of the hireling. For those are gravely mistaken who think they are excused and that all the blame for error sticks to the teachers. For that saying of Christ is well known: If the blind lead the blind, both fall into the ditch. Matth.15.

units.la: Sed pœnam quoque istorum omnium audiamus, quam Paulus his verbis denuntiat: Quo‑rum finis erit secundùm opera eorum. Vbi primùm obseruabis, quòd finem aliquando habituros dicit. Est hoc plenum consolationis. Nam plerumque videntur impostores & superstitionum anti‑stites regnum suum ita stabiliuisse, vt nemo eorum tyranidi resistere possit. Et hoc pios sæpe offen‑dit, vt cum Propheta clament: Quousque Domine? Sed non durabunt perpetuò, & iam nunc illis metam fixit Deus, quam neque declinare neque transilire poterunt. Exempla, quibus hoc probe‑tur, passim habetur. Magna fuit olim in Ægypto Magorum existimatio, qui Mosi et Aaroni se‑se opponebant, & ipsius Regis fauore protegebatur. Sed tandē sine illa habuit, & vel inuiti digitū Dei agnouerūt, cui se resistere nō posse sentiebant. Idem de Baalis mystis atque pseudoprophetis di‑cipotest, qui sub Achabo & Iezabele perpetuò dominaturi videbantur: Sed hi quoque ad finē suū decurrerunt, viuente adhuc et florente fidelis serui Dei, Eliæ, memoria. Idē Iudæorū Sacerdotibus & Scribis accidit. Et nouissimus bisce temporibus, magna quidē est Pontificū Romanorū potētia, quæ diu Regibus quoque & Imperatoribus potentissimis formidabilis fuit. Attamen iam nunc il‑los ad finem suum tendere videmus, & nemo non nouit, quantum in illis expugnandis dicendo & scribendo profecerint à Deo excitati Veritatis præcones, qui nihil omnino posse videbantur.
units.tr: But let us also hear the punishment of all these people, which Paul announces in these words: "Their end will be according to their works." Here, first, you will observe that he says they will at some time come to an end. This is full of comfort. For impostors and the leaders of superstitions often seem to have so firmly established their rule that none of them can resist their tyranny. This often offends the godly, so that they cry out with the prophet, "How long, O Lord?" But they will not last forever, and God has already fixed a limit for them, which they can neither turn aside from nor leap over. Examples proving this are found everywhere. Long ago in Egypt the Magi were held in high esteem and opposed Moses and Aaron, and they were protected by the favour of the king himself. But in the end that esteem was gone, and even unwillingly they recognised the finger of God, against which they felt they could not stand. The same can be said of the priests of Baal and the false prophets, who seemed sure to rule forever under Ahab and Jezebel. Yet they too came to their end, while the memory of God's faithful servant Elijah was still alive and flourishing. The same happened to the priests and scribes of the Jews. And in our own times, the power of the Roman Pontiffs is indeed great, and for a long time it was feared even by the most powerful kings and emperors. Yet already we see them heading to their end, and everyone knows how much the heralds of the truth, raised up by God, have achieved in overthrowing them by speaking and writing, though they seemed able to do nothing at all.

units.la: Qualis autem erit finis ille? Secundùm opera ipsorū. Id est, respondebit eorum factis & studi‑js. Ergo qui fuco & laruis suis diu illudunt omnibus, tandem ipsi quoque omnibus ludibrium fi‑unt. Et qui multos seducunt, ipsi quoque à diabolo seducti tandem toti excæcantur, vt in viam re‑dire non possint. Denique, qui diabolo, patri mendaciorum seruiunt, olim cum eodem in æternum cruciabuntur. Est hæc talionis Lex, quæ vt iustissima & ab ipso Deo sancita, ita etiam ineuita‑bilis est, & omnium sæculorum exemplis confirmata. Nam vt ad Ægyptios Magos redeamus, annon hi cùm in pediculo creando hærerent, ludibrium factì sunt? Et ijdem annon excæcati perrexe‑runt in sua contumacia, quàmuis Dei digitum & ore confiterentur, & vlceribus pleni in corpore suo sino sentirent? Et quis dubitet, eos, qui Regi indurationis causa fuerunt, & innumeram hominum turbam suis praestigiis in exitium adduxerunt, nunc aeternis supplicijs multari? Sic Balaam, celeberrimus ille totius Orientis propheta, toti mundo ludos praebuit, quando ab asina reprehensus est, qui Deum loquentem audire nolebat: quando item Israelitas execrari volens, ijsdem fausta precari cogitur. Quàm horribilis autem fuit eiusdem excaecatio, qua deceptus cum ipso Deo in certamen descendere non dubitauit? Et idem non multò post cum Madianitarum gente, quam diu seduxerat, se dignum interitum sortitus est. Accidit hoc ipsum fere omnibus pseudoprophetis. De Iudaeorum vero Sacerdotibus quid attinet dicere? Quoties istos toti populo deridendos Christus propinauit, si quando colloquia cum illo insidiosa instituerunt? Quàm ridiculos ipsi se praebuerunt in causa caeci, cuius oculos ille aperuerat? Quoties intra animos suos conuicti perrexerunt Veritatem persequi, quod excaecationis certum est argumentum? Quàm triste vero tandem excidium ijdem passi sunt cum tota gente, quam suis mendacijs diu lactauerant? Atqui in nostris haec omnia fieri cernimus. Nam quasi retectis & supra caput reductis vestibus (vt Prophetae verbis vtar) toti mundo ostenditur turpitudo eorum, & duplicia illis reddunt multi, quos illi nimis diu ludibrio habuerunt. In omnium ore sunt fraudes, doli, sacrorum nundinatio, tyrannis, rapinae, quibus orbem Christianum oppresserunt. Canitur de illis in triuijs, compitis, tonstrinis, & in theatris populo laeta spectacula praebent quae de ipsis aguntur fabulae. At illi fatali caecitate fascinati ista non vident, & quasi adhuc salua ipsis sit sua authoritas, Concilia indicunt, ad reddendam fidei & doctrinae rationem omnes imperiosè citant, minantur & bullarum fulminibus pugnant, atq; orientem vbiq; terrarum Veritatis Solem flamineis suis structuris impedire & fumis suis obscurare satagunt. Quid ergo aliud fiat, quàm quòd illos tandem digno excidio euertet Deus, vt nimirum magnam illam meretricem (vt in Apocalypsi praedicitur) hi ipsi sploDent, exurant, deuorent, qui cum ea fornicati sunt: & olim draco ille immanis cum pseudopropheta praecipitetur in lacu igne & sulphure inextinguibili ardentem? Neminem ergo illorum successus offendant. Excitent autem haec omnes homines, ne operibus illorum malis communicent, multò minus eos tueantur. Si enim sectatores eorum poena digni sunt, quid de illis fiet, qui eosdem armis defendere audent, quos Deus vult perditos? qui denique vt horum regnum stabiliant, in Dei electos crudeliter saeuiunt? Exiget de matribus istorum sanguinem seruorum suorum aeternus Dei Filius, IESVS CHRISTVS, Dominus & Seruator noster: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But what will that end be? "According to their works." That is, it will answer to their deeds and pursuits. Thus those who have long deceived everyone with their paint and masks finally become a laughingstock to everyone themselves. And those who lead many astray are themselves led astray by the devil, and at last are so utterly blinded that they cannot return to the right way. Finally, those who serve the devil, the father of lies, will one day be tormented forever with him. This is the law of retaliation, which, as most just and sanctioned by God himself, is also unavoidable, and is confirmed by the examples of all ages. For, to return to the Egyptian magicians, did they not become a laughingstock when they were stuck in producing lice? And did they not, blinded, persist in their obstinacy, although they confessed the finger of God with their mouths, and, full of sores in their body, did they feel nothing? And who could doubt that those who were the cause of the king's hardening, and by their trickery brought an countless crowd of men to destruction, are now punished with eternal torments? So Balaam, that most famous prophet of the whole East, offered sport to the whole world, when he was rebuked by his donkey, he who was unwilling to hear God speaking; and again, when he wished to curse the Israelites, he was forced to pronounce blessings upon them. But how dreadful was his blindness, by which, deceived, he did not hesitate to enter into a contest with God himself? And not long afterwards he met a well-deserved death along with the nation of the Midianites, whom he had long led astray. Almost the same happened to all the false prophets. But what need is there to speak of the priests of the Jews? How often did Christ make them a laughingstock before the whole people, whenever they set up treacherous discussions with him? How ridiculous did they make themselves in the case of the blind man whose eyes he had opened? How often, convicted in their own minds, did they press on to persecute the truth, which is a sure sign of blindness? And how sad was the final ruin they suffered along with the whole nation, which they had long flattered with their lies? Yet we see all these things happening in our own times. For, to borrow the prophet's words, as if their garments were stripped away and lifted over their heads, their shame is displayed to the whole world, and many whom they long held in mockery now pay them back double. Frauds, deceits, the peddling of sacred things, tyranny and robberies, by which they have oppressed the Christian world, are on everyone's lips. They are sung about in the streets, at crossroads, in barbershops, and the stories told about them give the people happy spectacles in the theatres. But they, bewitched by a fatal blindness, do not see these things, and as if their authority were still safe, they summon councils, arrogantly cite everyone to give an account of their faith and teaching, threaten, and fight with the thunderbolts of their bulls, and they strive to block the Sun of Truth rising everywhere on earth with their fiery structures and obscure it with their smoke. What else, then, will happen than that God at last overthrows them with a deserved destruction? Indeed, those who committed fornication with that great harlot (as is foretold in the Apocalypse) will tear her apart, burn her, and devour her; and that huge dragon, together with the false prophet, will one day be cast into the lake burning with fire and unquenchable sulphur. Therefore let no one be offended by their successes. Rather, let all people be roused not to share in their evil works, and much less to defend them. For if their followers are worthy of punishment, what will become of those who dare to defend with arms those whom God wills to be destroyed, and who, finally, to make their kingdom secure, cruelly rage against God's elect? The eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, our Lord and Saviour, will require the blood of his servants from their mothers, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power forever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA L.
units.tr: HOMILY L.

units.la: Rursus dico, ne quis me putet insipientem esse: alioqui etiam vt insipientem accipite me, vt paululum quiddam & ego glorier. Quod dico, non dico secundum Dominum, sed vt per insipientiam in praesidente ista gloriatione. Quandoquidem multi gloriantur secundum carnem, & ego gloriabor. Libenter enim toleratis insipientes, cum sitis sapientes. Toleratis enim si quis vos in seruitutem adigit, si quis exedit, si quis accipit, si quis attollit sese, si quis vos in faciem caedit. Quantum ad contumeliam dico: nimirum quia nos infirmi fuimus.
units.tr: Again I say, let no one think me foolish. But if you must, receive me even as a fool, so that I may boast a little myself. What I say, I do not say as the Lord would have it, but as in foolishness, in this confident boasting. Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast. For you gladly put up with fools, being wise yourselves. You put up with it when someone enslaves you, devours you, takes from you, exalts himself, or strikes you in the face. I say this to our shame, as if we had been weak.

units.la: Quoniam pseudoapostoli partim ignavia & nimia indulgentia, partim improbitate sua totum Ecclesiae Corinthiacae statum turbauerant, cumq; faniori doctrina disciplinam quoque morum sustulerant, & (vt vulgò fieri solet) ideo apud plerosq; in honore & pretio erant, Paulus nuper magna cum vehementia in eos inuectus est, & docuit qui nam illi sint, & cuius serui sint, quae denique tandem ipsorum fors aut finis sit futura. At quod de illis dicitur, ad omnes extendi debet, qui horum similes fidem & disciplinam Christianam labefactant: Vt nimirum tales caueamus, imò procul arceamus ab Ecclesiae septis, ne quando omnes simul in exitium adducant. Postquam vero hos depinxit Apostolus, nunc ad seipsum redit, & quanto ipsis praestet ostendit. Et hoc quoque ita facit, vt & impostoribus illis fucum amplius abstergat, & Corinthiorum leuitatem acriter perstringat, qui tales tam diu tamq; patienter tulerint.
units.tr: Since the false apostles had thrown the whole state of the Corinthian Church into turmoil, partly through sloth and excessive indulgence, and partly through their own wickedness, and since, with a corrupt teaching, they had also overthrown the discipline of morals, and (as commonly happens) were for that reason held in honour and high regard by many, Paul lately inveighed against them with great vehemence, and taught who they are, whose servants they are, and what their fate or end will finally be. But what is said of them ought to be extended to all who undermine the faith and Christian discipline by being like them, so that we may of course guard against such people, or rather keep them far from the fences of the Church, lest at some time they bring everyone together to ruin. Having now portrayed these men, the Apostle returns to himself and shows how far he surpasses them. And he does this so that he may further wipe away the paint from those impostors, and sharply rebuke the levity of the Corinthians, who have put up with such people so long and so patiently.

units.la: Initio rationem reddit, cur iterum de se dicere velit, & vt eum ferant, rogat: Rursus dico, id est, redeo ad id vnde digressus sum, ne quis me insipientem putet esse, cui (vt fatuis fieri solet) ea quæ hactenus dixi, temere exciderint. Nam solent qui non satis sanæ mentis sunt, effutire quicquid in buccam venit, & ab vno ad aliud transilire, quod etiam prouerbio dicitur, ἀπροσδιόνυσα λοqui. Veruntamen ex hac occasione attentionis argumentum captat, dum infert: Alioqui etiam vt insipientem accipite me, vt paululum quiddam & ego glorier. Id est: Esto, sim insipiens, ferte tamen me aliquantisper, vt de me aliquid dicam, quod gloriæ meæ afferendæ seruiat. Et paululum quiddam se dicturum protestatur, quia vt multis ageret non opus erat, cum ipsius virtus & mirifici in propagando regno Christi ministerij sui effectus omnibus abunde noti essent. Ne quis tamen ipsi initio exciperet: Quid vero opus est nos istis obtundere, quæ ad te potius quam ad nos spectant? Nunc quæcunque tu pro te dicis, nos vt oracula ad nos pertinentia audire cogemur? Respondet obiectioni huic per Concessionem: Quod dico, non dico secundum Dominum, sed vt per insipientiam in præsidente ista gloriatione. Sensus verborum est: Fateor hanc afferendi gloriam & existimationem meam, rationem, quæ confidentis cuiusdam ambitionis speciem præ se ferre videtur, non per omnia conuenire Domini IESV CHRISTI præceptis, si ea secundum τὸ ῥητὸν siue literam accipiamus. Ille enim nos ad humilitatem & patientiam instituit, vt iniurias & contumelias quasuis ferre, & pro malo bonum rependere discamus. Idem, etsi omnia fecerimus quæ nobis mandata sunt, tamen vt nos seruos inutiles esse fateamur, præcipit. At æmulorum meorum improbitas me in istam arenam protrahit, vt in hac mea existimationis assertione tam confidenti tantumnon desipere cogar.
units.tr: At the start he gives a reason why he wishes to speak about himself again, and asks them to bear with him: "Again I say," that is, I return to the point from which I digressed, "let no one think me foolish," as people who are not quite sane are often thought to be, whose words have carelessly slipped out. For those who are not fully in their right minds tend to blurt out whatever comes into their mouth, and to leap from one thing to another; this is also what the proverb calls [ἀπροσδιόνυσα λαλεῖν], to talk at random. Nevertheless, from this occasion he seeks to win their attention, when he adds: "But if you must, receive me even as a fool, so that I may boast a little myself." That is: granted, let me be foolish; bear with me for a while, so that I may say something about myself that serves to win me credit. He also declares that he will speak only a little, since there was no need to say much, when his own virtue and the remarkable effects of his ministry in spreading the kingdom of Christ were already well known to all. Yet, lest someone object to him at the outset: "But why must we be wearied with these things, which concern you rather than us? Now, whatever you say on your own behalf, are we forced to hear it as oracles that pertain to us?" He answers this objection by a concession: "What I say, I do not say as the Lord would have it, but as in foolishness, in this confident boasting." The sense of the words is this: I admit that this way of asserting my glory and reputation, a line of argument which seems to show a kind of boastful ambition, does not altogether agree with the precepts of the Lord Jesus Christ, if we take them according to [τὸ ῥητὸν], the letter. For he trained us to humility and patience, so that we might learn to bear all kinds of injuries and insults, and to repay evil with good. Likewise he commands that, even if we have done everything that has been commanded us, we should still confess that we are unprofitable servants. But the wickedness of my rivals drags me into this arena, so that in this assertion of my reputation I am compelled to act almost foolishly in so confident a way.

units.la: Est hic obseruatu dignum, quod gloriationem, qua vti cogebatur, rursus insipientiæ tribuit. Denuo igitur modestiæ admonet, & cauet ne quis suo exemplo ambitiose abutatur. Est enim hoc valde necessarium, eo quod naturali quadam gloriæ studio ardemus: quo interdum ita abripimur, vt in vetitis quoq; laudem quæramus, atque alios superbe aspernemur. Semper ergo meminerimus, nos peccatores esse, ex gratia autem accepisse quicquid boni habemus. Itaque nunquam debemus insolentius gloriari de iis quoq; quæ bene & recte fecimus, nisi ita nos cogat necessitas: vtpote quando Dei gloria in nobis periclitatur, & aliorum infirmitas id requirit, vt nominis nostri famam aut existimationem contra calumnias afferamus.
units.tr: It is worth noting here that he again attributes to folly the boasting which he was forced to use. Therefore he once more gives a reminder of modesty, and takes care that no one abuse his example in an ambitious way. This is indeed very necessary, because we burn with a certain natural desire for glory, by which we are sometimes so carried away that we seek praise even in what is forbidden, and proudly despise others. Let us therefore always remember that we are sinners, and that whatever good we have we have received from grace. Thus we must never boast too arrogantly even of those things which we have done well and rightly, unless necessity compels us to do so: namely, when the glory of God is endangered in us, and the weakness of others requires that we defend the fame or reputation of our name against slanders.

units.la: Etenim sæpe coguntur serui Dei, vt præter ea, quæ ad salutis æternæ rationem & hominis Christiani officium pertinent, de aliis quoque rebus dicant: nimirum de sua vocatione, de fide item & industria sua, qua in illa obeunda vsi sint. Sed tunc illos Paulũ imitari conuenit, cuius solicita & circumspecta in scribendo diligentia singulari consideratione digna est. Primò enim diligenter cauet, ne quid Christi nomine proponat, quod ab eo non acceperit. Sic in priori epist. quoque Cap.7. & 11. illum fecisse videmus. Facit hoc ad commendationem doctrinæ Apostolicæ, ne illos ex carnis affectu aliquid dixisse aut scripsisse suspicemur. Quod enim de Prophetis Petrus dicit, illos ex Spiritus Dei suggestione locutos esse, hoc ipsum de Apostolis quoque debet intelligi, quibus à Christo dictum est: Non vos estis qui loquimini, sed Spiritus Patris vestri, qui in vobis est. Id vero simul ministros officij admonet, ne quid temere dicant, neque pro oraculis venditent omnia quæ ipsis in ore nascuntur: sed meminerint se ijsdem cum aliis hominibus affectibus obnoxios esse, & proinde Spiritus gubernaculis opus habere. Ne tamen quod in præsenti dicit Paulus, se non secundum Dominum loqui, aliquis de doctrina sua dictum putaret, & sic illa in dubium vocaretur, diligenter illud ad præsentis causæ argumentum restringit. Ita ergo modestiæ & humilitati ministros studere conuenit, ne Veritatis doctrina in periculum veniat. Ideo Prophetæ, homines quoad alia modestissimi, in suis concionibus subinde repetunt: Dicit Dominus. Item: Factum est ad me Verbum Domini. Et quàta cum gravitate Paulus Euangelij abs se prædicati Veritatem affirmauerit, in principio epist. ad Galatas est videre.
units.tr: For the servants of God are often compelled to speak, besides those things which pertain to the way of eternal salvation and the duty of a Christian, also about other matters: certainly about their calling, and likewise about their faith and diligence, with which they have discharged it. But then it is fitting to imitate Paul, whose careful and cautious diligence in writing deserves special consideration. For first he takes great care not to propose anything in Christ's name that he has not received from him. We see him doing this in his earlier letter too, in chapters 7 and 11. This serves to commend the apostolic teaching, so that we do not suspect that they said or wrote anything from fleshly feeling. For what Peter says of the prophets, that they spoke from the prompting of the Spirit of God, must also be understood of the apostles, to whom Christ said: "It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who is in you." At the same time this reminds ministers of their office, that they should not speak rashly, nor pass off as oracles everything that arises in their mouths, but remember that they are subject to the same passions as other men, and therefore need the guidance of the Spirit. Yet, lest anyone take what Paul now says, that he is not speaking according to the Lord, as referring to his teaching in general, and so his teaching be called into doubt, he carefully restricts it to the argument of the present case. Thus it is fitting that ministers aim at modesty and humility, so that the doctrine of truth may not be endangered. For this reason the prophets, who in other respects were most modest men, repeat again and again in their sermons: "Thus says the Lord," and "The word of the Lord came to me." And how solemnly Paul affirmed the truth of the gospel he preached, may be seen at the beginning of his letter to the Galatians.

units.la: Sed argumenta audiamus, quibus institutum suum Apostolus excusat, vtque ipsum ferant æquum esse docet. Primum ab exemplo petit, dicens: Quandoquidem multi gloriantur secundum carnem, & ego gloriabor. Quæ verba non ita accipi debent, quasi liceat nobis coram Deo quic-quid multi alij faciunt (nam in plerisque vitari debet multitudinis exemplum, vtque per angu-stam portam & viam asperam ingrediamur, Christus iubet, qua pauci ingrediuntur) sed ad Co-rinthiorum iudicium respicit Paulus. Quasi diceret: Quoniam per vos multis alijs licet ambitiosius gloriari, cur hoc mihi vitio vertatur, si æmulorum improbitate coactus vilissim gloriér, vt mei nominis existimationem afferam? Dicit autem eos secundum carnem gloriari, quia (vt ex ijs, quæ mox sequuntur, apparet) gloriabantur gentis aut generis prærogatiua, Circumcisione, sa-pientia seculari, amicitijs, nominis splendore, vulgi applausu, diuitijs denique, & alijs eiusmodi, quæ mundi iudicio magnifica videntur, ad ostentationem vero magis faciunt, quàm ad conscien-tiæ integritatem.
units.tr: But let us hear the arguments by which the Apostle excuses his course, and teaches that it is fair for them to bear with it. First he appeals to example, saying: "Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast." These words should not be taken as if we were allowed before God to do whatever many others do (for in most matters the example of the multitude must be avoided, and Christ bids us enter by the narrow gate and the hard road, which few enter). Rather, Paul is looking at the judgment of the Corinthians. As if he were to say: since through you many others are allowed to boast more ambitiously, why should this be counted against me, if, compelled by the wickedness of my rivals, I boast in a humble way, so as to defend the reputation of my name? He says that they boast according to the flesh because (as appears from what follows) they boasted of the privileges of nation or family, circumcision, worldly wisdom, friendships, splendour of name, the applause of the crowd, and finally riches and other such things, which seem splendid by the judgment of the world, but serve more for display than for integrity of conscience.

units.la: Obseruabis autem Paulum ijsdem gloriari voluisse, non quòd ea alicuius momenti aut pre-tij esse putaret apud Deum: sed quia alij se istis insolentius efferebant, & propter ista apud impe-ritum & rude vulgus in pretio habebantur. Perinde ergo facit, ac si quis ex nobili familia natus & diuitijs clarus, sacrarum literarum & Theologiæ studium serio amplexus, se totum Christi & Ecclesiæ suæ ministerio consecret, & aduersus eos, qui sola professione Theologi, reliquis propter genus & Doctoris titulum præstare volunt, suam quoque nobilitatem in medium adducat, dicens: Debebant quidem ista Theologi & Christi ministri pro stercoribus ducere, sed quia vobis lubet his gloriari, agedum videamus qua in re hic etiam me superetis. Hoc sensu Paulus quoq; in præsenti loquitur, & ista contemni potius quàm magni fieri debere suo exemplo docet, cùm illis non nisi ab alijs provocatus glorietur.
units.tr: You will observe, however, that Paul wished to boast of these same things, not because he thought they had any weight or value before God, but because others were puffing themselves up more insolently over them, and because among the unskilled and uneducated crowd they were held in esteem on account of them. He acts, then, just as if someone born of a noble family and famous for wealth, who has seriously embraced the study of the sacred letters and theology and dedicated himself wholly to the ministry of Christ and his Church, and who, against those who want to excel by the bare profession of theologian and by the title of Doctor, while others surpass them by birth, brings forward his own nobility too, saying: "Theologians and ministers of Christ ought indeed to count these things as dung, but since it pleases you to boast of them, come now, let us see whether in this matter too you can outdo me." In this sense Paul also speaks in the present passage, and by his own example teaches that such things ought to be despised rather than valued highly, since he boasts of them only when provoked by others.

units.la: Alterum apologiæ huius argumentum à Corinthiorum persona petit. Libenter enim (inquit) toleratis insipientes, cùm sitis sapientes. Habent ista Ironiam acrem, vel Sarcasmum, & ex com-muni hominum more loquitur, quo fit, vt magnates & qui præ alijs excellere volunt, fatuis ac mo-rionibus delectentur: & fit hoc iusto Dei iudicio, vt quæ nemo alius illis dicere auderet, ex fatuis audiant. Sed & inter opulentos & mercatores, qui variarum gentium moribus atq; delitijs affue-erunt, illud hominum genus facile locum inuenit. Adde, quòd qui verè sapiunt, ij non facilè fuc-censent ex stultitia aut ignorantia peccantibus. Ad ista ergo respiciens Paulus ait: Quia præ mul-tis alijs sapere vobis videmini, vel hoc argumento sapientiæ vestræ specimen præbete, vt hanc meam insipientiam patienter feratis.
units.tr: The second argument of this defence is drawn from the persons of the Corinthians. For he says: "You gladly put up with fools, since you yourselves are wise." This carries a sharp irony or sarcasm, and he speaks in the ordinary manner of men. Great people, and those who want to excel above others, delight in silly flatterers and buffoons. By God's just judgement it comes about that they hear from fools what no one else would dare to say to them. Such a class of men also easily finds a place among the wealthy and the merchants, who have grown used to the customs and pleasures of many nations. Add to this that those who are truly wise are not quick to be angry with those who sin through folly or ignorance. Looking to these things, Paul says: "Since you seem wise above many others, give at least this proof of your wisdom, that you bear my folly patiently."

units.la: Admonemur itaque hoc loco, hanc non postremam sapientiæ partem esse, si quis aliorum in-eptias, aut etiam contumelias æqui bonique consulat. Qui id facere nolunt, sibijpsis frequenter mo-lestiam accersunt, seque ipsos sæpius cum ineptis illis altercando ridiculos præbent. Recte ergo Diogenes, cùm ab improbo quodam petulanter percussus esset, & ab astantibus moneretur, vt il-lum in ius vocaret, respondit: Num vero idem mihi suaderetis, si me asinus calce ferijsset? Ita admonens stolidorum hominum, qui absque ratione quiduis dicunt & faciunt, non maiorem quàm asinorum rationem habere debere. At hic meminisse oportet, hoc ad ea modo debere restringi, quæ cum nulla Dei contumelia aut æternæ salutis periculo coniuncta sunt. Nam vbi de his agi-tur, ibi nullus patientiæ locus est{ζ}, eo quòd illa non sunt nostri iuris, vt de eis pro nostro arbi-trio dispensare liceat. Ideo Hieronymus olim dicebat, in hæreticos crimine neminem debere esse patientem.
units.tr: Here we are reminded that it is no small part of wisdom to take the silly behaviour, and even the insults, of others calmly and fairly. Those who will not do this often bring trouble on themselves and make themselves ridiculous by constantly quarrelling with such fools. So Diogenes rightly replied, when a wicked man had struck him insolently and his bystanders urged him to take the man to court: "Would you give me the same advice if an ass had kicked me?" By this he meant that men who say and do whatever they please without reason deserve no more regard than asses. But we must remember that this should be restricted to matters not joined with any insult to God or any danger to eternal salvation. Where those things are at stake, there is no room for patience, because such matters are not ours to dispose of as we please. So Jerome once said that no one ought to be patient in the case of heretics.

units.la: Et huc faciunt quæ sequuntur. Probat enim quod dixerat, ipsos libenter tolerare insipientes, & ostendit quales hucusque tulerint, vt & pseudoapostolorum mores depingat, & Corinthiorum stoliditatem arguat, qui ea tulerint hucusque, quæ Christianis hominibus sint indignissima. To-leratis enim (inquit) si quis vos in seruitutem adigit, si quis exedit, si quis accipit, si quis at-tollit se, si quis vos in faciem cædit. Accusat illos (inquam) quòd plus quàm seruili ignauia ab impostoribus illis patiantur, quæ nemo in Veritatis doctore ferre deberet. Quæ autem illa erant?
units.tr: What follows also bears on this. For Paul proves what he had said, that they gladly tolerate fools, and he shows what sort of men they had put up with until now. In this way he both paints the character of the false apostles and rebukes the stupidity of the Corinthians, who had endured things utterly unworthy of Christian men. "For you suffer it," he says, "if anyone brings you into bondage, if anyone devours you, if anyone takes from you, if anyone exalts himself, if anyone strikes you on the face." He accuses them, I say, of suffering from those impostors more than servile cowardice, things that no one should tolerate in a teacher of the truth. What were these things?

units.la: Primò, Fertis (inquit) si quis vos in seruitutem adigit. Faciunt hoc, qui in hominum conscien-tiam sibi ius vendicant, vt superbè dominentur clero Domini: qui item pro imperio quiduis man-dant, & eos qui Christo nomen dederunt, hominum traditionibus circumducunt, & oneribus partim inutilibus, partim noxijs grauant. Id vero impostores illi faciebant. Nam ementita Apostolorum authoritate superbi ius sibi vendicabant in Corinthiorum Ecclesiam, Christi fideles in seruitutem stas distrahebant, cum abs se illos vellent denominari: adhæc iugum Legis ijsdem imponebant, quod ne patres quidem (vt Petrus ait) olim ferre potuerant. Atqui quid hoc aliud erat, quàm in seruitutem adigere Christiano homini intolerabilem? Quid enim indignius est, quàm hominum seruum fieri eum, quem æternus Dei Filius proprij sanguinis pretio redemptum in libertatem filiorum Dei asseruit? Hæc certè causa Martyres dedit, qui quiduis potius ferre voluerunt, quàm in ijs quæ ad Deum spectant, hominum edictis parere.
units.tr: First: "You suffer it if anyone brings you into bondage." This is done by those who claim for themselves a right over men's consciences, so that they may lord it proudly over the clergy of the Lord. Likewise they command whatever they like by their own authority, and they lead those who have given their name to Christ around by human traditions, burdening them with some burdens that are useless and others that are harmful. This is exactly what those impostors did. For by falsely invoking the authority of the apostles, these proud men claimed a right over the Church of Corinth. They dragged the faithful of Christ into servitude, wanting them to be called by their name. Moreover, they laid on the same people the yoke of the Law, which, as Peter says, not even the fathers could bear. And what else was this than bringing a Christian man into intolerable bondage? For what is more unworthy than for one to become the slave of men, whom the eternal Son of God redeemed with the price of his own blood and claimed for the freedom of the sons of God? Surely this is the cause that produced martyrs, who preferred to bear anything rather than obey human edicts in matters that concern God.

units.la: Secundò, Fertur (inquit) si quis exedit. Perstringit hoc membro auaritiam & insatiabile studium pecuniæ, quo impostores illi ardebant, vt non contenti ijs, quæ commodè dari poterant ab auditoribus, insuper exedebant eos, quos vt pastores debebant pascere. Et videtur alludere ad locum Ezechielis, in quo idem pastoribus populi sui Deus exprobrauit, quòd seipsos pascerent, pinguiores oues mactarent & ederent, atque earundem lana vestirentur. Erant autem horum similes Corinthij illi Logodædali, qui hunc suæ sanctitatis & grandiloquentiæ scopum sibi proposuerant, vt eo prætextu plures pecunias ab incautis emungerent. Simul autem exedendi verbo innuit, illos gulæ deditos esse, & male quæsitas pecunias turpiter dilapidare. Est hoc fere proprium pseudoprophetis & pseudoapostolis, quòd nimirum ventris & gulæ mancipia sunt, & intemperantissimè viuunt. Sic olim ex Iezabelis mensa epulabantur Baalis sacerdotes. Et Isaias sui seculi seduCtoribus has voces tribuit: Venite, vinum adferam, vt perpotemus ad ebrietatem vsque, &c. Et Paulus de illis, qui tunc oberrabant, alibi dicit: Quorum Deus venter est. Quid verò hodie faciant Papisticæ doctrinæ & religionis mystæ, quid attinet dicere? Norunt ista quicunque illorum conuiuijs funebribus, Encænijs & aliis festis intersunt, vt iam de priuatis compotationibus nihil dicam.
units.tr: Second: "You suffer it if anyone devours you." In this member he touches on the greed and insatiable desire for money that burned in those impostors. Not content with what could be given them readily by their hearers, they devoured them besides, though they ought to have fed them as shepherds. He seems to allude to the passage in Ezekiel where God likewise rebuked the shepherds of his people, because they fed themselves, slaughtered and ate the fatter sheep, and clothed themselves with their wool. The Corinthian word-spinners were like these men. They had set this as the aim of their supposed holiness and grand talk: under that pretext they might squeeze more money out of the unwary. At the same time, by the word "devour" he hints that these men were given to gluttony and shamefully squandered money gained by dishonest means. It is almost a characteristic of false prophets and false apostles that they are slaves of the belly and of gluttony and live with the utmost intemperance. So of old the priests of Baal feasted at Jezebel's table. Isaiah also ascribes these words to the seducers of his age: "Come, I will fetch wine, that we may drink ourselves full," and so on. And Paul says elsewhere of those who were then wandering about: "whose god is their belly." What the Papist teaching and the mystics of their religion do today, why should I say? Anyone who attends their funeral banquets, dedication feasts and other festivals knows these things, not to mention their private drinking parties.

units.la: Tertio ait: Toleratus si quis attollit se. Est hoc prioris consequens. Nam vbi tales vident se ab omnibus in pretio haberi, sibi omnes obedire in ijs quæ nimis pro imperio mandant, iam alios omnes præ se contemnere & immani fastu supra omnes extolli incipiunt, ac sibi nihil non licere arbitrantur. Est hoc in Republ. intolerabile vitium, quod (vt historiæ docent) ferè omnibus seculis seditiones dedit, ex quibus periculosæ legum & magistratuum mutationes enatæ sunt. At in religionis & salutis æternæ negotio illud impium quoque & detestatione dignum est, vbi nulla est præeminentia, nisi quam Christus sanciuit, vt is aliis maior censeatur, qui omnibus aliis seruierit. In externis quidem sunt personarum discrimina, quæ Christiani homines diligenter obseruare debent, vt suum vnicuique tribuant. At in Christo non est mas aut fœmina, non seruus aut liber: & proinde ferri non debent, qui vt dominentur sese attollunt cum aliorum contemptu.
units.tr: Third, he says: "You suffer it if anyone exalts himself." This follows from the previous point. For when such men see that they are held in high regard by everyone, and that all obey them in things they command with too much authority, they begin to despise all others in comparison with themselves and to raise themselves above everyone with monstrous pride, and they think that nothing is forbidden to them. In the commonwealth this is an intolerable vice, which (as the histories teach) has produced seditions in almost every age, from which dangerous changes of laws and magistrates have arisen. But in the business of religion and eternal salvation it is also impious and worthy of detestation, where there is no pre-eminence except that which Christ has sanctioned: that he be counted greater than the rest who has served all the rest. In external matters there are differences of persons, which Christians ought to observe carefully, so that each is given his due. But in Christ there is neither male nor female, neither slave nor free. Therefore those who raise themselves up to lord it over others, with contempt for the rest, ought not to be tolerated.

units.la: Addit hïs quartum Paulus, dicens: Toleratus si quis vos in faciem cædit. Est hoc extremi contemptus argumentum, ideo per Expositionem subijcit: Quantum ad contumeliam dico, id est, non dico quòd quoad literam & ipso actu vos in faciem cædant, sed indignitatem contumeliæ significo, qua vos afficiunt, quæ non minor est, quàm si vos in faciem cæderent & conspuerent. Id verò faciebant partim doctrina, partim negligentia sua. Ad doctrinam pertinet, quòd Legem & Circumcisionem vrgendo, omnes eos Goijm dicebant, qui hanc non admittebant, & proinde vt pro phanos & à Dei regno alienos aspernabantur. Faciunt hoc etiam hodie Iudæi, dum Christianos omnes Goijm dicunt, & insuper ipsum Christum execrantur atque diris devouent. Deinde negligentia sua & nimia indulgentia Corinthios in contemptum adduxerant, qui prius inter Christianos homines præ multis aliis celebrabantur. Quòd enim in sestas scissi erant, quòd scortatoribus & hominibus incestis abundarent, cum idololatria & dæmoniorum mensa communicarent, & ita si-bijpsis apud alias Ecclesias infamiam conciliarent, hæc (inquam) omnia istorum indulgentiæ debebant. Itaq; hoc dicendo illis turpem ignauiam exprobrat, qui ista ferant, nolint autem ipsum fer re, qui ipsorum honori & saluti consultum cupiat. Et ideo amplificationis causa addit: Nimirum quia nos infirmi fuimus. Habet hoc membrum acrem Apostopesim. Quasi diceret: Ideo hæc fertis sub istis, quia scilicet nos infirmi, id est, abiecti & mille periculis obnoxij, vitam egimus in egestate, & manuum labore inter vos vitium quæsiuimus. At cur non obseruatis exerentem se in hac infirmitate virtutem Spiritus sancti? Ego enim qui talis sum, vos ab idolorum cultu ad fidem Christi conuerti, ego apud vos plantaui quæ isti destruunt? Cur item non cogitatis, me sponte nunc ad ista demitti, vt vos extollam? Quæ ergo hæc ingratitudo est & iniquitas, quòd me contemptò, eos in pretio habetis, qui vos deprimunt & conculcant, vt ipsi de vobis gloriari & in delitijs viuere possint?
units.tr: Paul adds a fourth, saying: "You suffer it if anyone strikes you on the face." This is a proof of extreme contempt, and so he adds an explanation: "I speak of dishonour," that is, "I do not mean that they literally strike you on the face with their hands, but I point to the indignity of the insult with which they treat you, which is no less than if they struck and spat upon your face." They did this partly through their teaching and partly through their own carelessness. To their teaching belongs the fact that, by insisting on the Law and circumcision, they called all who did not accept these "Goyim" and so despised them as profane and alien to the kingdom of God. Even today the Jews do this, when they call all Christians "Goyim," and moreover curse Christ himself and devote him to dreadful destruction. Next, by their own carelessness and excessive indulgence the Corinthians had brought themselves into contempt, although they had once been celebrated among Christians above many others. For that they were split into factions, that they abounded in fornicators and incestuous men, that they shared in idolatry and the table of demons, and thus brought infamy on themselves among other Churches: all these things, I say, were owed to their indulgence of these men. Therefore by saying this he rebukes them for their shameful cowardice, since they put up with these things and yet would not put up with Paul himself, who desired their honour and salvation. And so, for the sake of amplification, he adds: "Indeed, because we were weak." This member contains a sharp aposiopesis, as if he said: "You endure these things from them because we were weak, that is, abject and exposed to a thousand dangers, and we lived in poverty and sought our livelihood by the labour of our hands among you. But why do you not observe the power of the Holy Spirit showing itself in this weakness? For I, who am such a man, converted you from the worship of idols to the faith of Christ; I planted among you the things these men are destroying. Why do you also not consider that I now voluntarily humble myself in these ways in order to exalt you?
