What, then, is this ingratitude and injustice, that you despise me and hold in esteem those who oppress and trample you, so that they may boast about you and live in luxury?

units.la: Continet exemplum hoc generalem doctrinam siue admonitionem, quid illis fieri soleat, qui salutare Christi iugum ferre nolunt, & spreuerunt Euangelij doctrinam fastidiunt. Manet hos seruitus omnium miserrima & contumeliosissima, qua merito multantur, qui libertate à Deo data frui nolunt. Typus huius rei olim in Israelitis præcessit, qui reiecto Samuele, fidelissimo Dei seruo, Saulem, crudele ambitionis mancipium sibi ipsis imposuerunt. Hoc ipsum Corinthijs accidisse, hic locus docet. Imò eandem omnium Ecclesiarum Orientis fortem fuisse videmus, quæ postquam diu inter se pugnarunt, & spreta saniori doctrina, blasphemis nefandissimarum hæresum authoribus locum dederunt, tandem Mahumeti impostori sceleratissimo præda facti sunt, sub cuius iugo infelici hodie gemunt. Occidentales autem Ecclesiæ eadem ratione Antichristum Romanum sibi ipsi accersiuerunt, sicuti Paulus in posteriori ad Thessalonicenses prædixit: sub cuius iniusto dominio omnia ea fiunt, quæ in præsenti de Corinthiorum pseudoapostolis dicuntur.
units.tr: This example contains a general teaching, or warning, about what usually happens to those who are unwilling to bear the saving yoke of Christ and who scorn and reject the doctrine of the Gospel. Slavery, the most wretched and humiliating of all conditions, awaits them, and they rightly suffer it, because they refuse to enjoy the liberty God has given them. The type of this was long ago given among the Israelites, who, after rejecting Samuel, God's most faithful servant, set Saul over themselves, a cruel slave of ambition. This passage shows that the same thing happened to the Corinthians. Indeed, we see that the same fate befell all the Churches of the East, which, after fighting among themselves for a long time and spurning the sounder doctrine, gave a place to the blasphemies of the authors of the most impious heresies. At last they became the prey of Mahomet, that most wicked impostor, under whose yoke they groan in misery today. The Western Churches, for the same reason, summoned the Roman Antichrist upon themselves, just as Paul foretold in the second letter to the Thessalonians. Under his unjust lordship everything happens that is now said of the false apostles of the Corinthians.

units.la: Etenim qui illum admittunt, ij serui fiunt miserrimi quoad corpus & animam. Et quis hoc nescit, quando Papa Reges & Imperatores sibi iureiurando obstringit, & eosdem ad pedum suorum oscula cogit? Quid verò Abbates & Episcopi? Annon hi olim abolitam inter Christianos hominum seruitutem instaurant, quam ne moriendo quidem licet effugere, cum ideo sibi omnes mancipatos velint, vt à mortuis possint tributum exigere? Animas verò traditionibus grauant nō minus noxijs quàm impijs? Nam coniugio & cibis à Deo datis & concessis interdicunt: ad confessionem quosfuis adigunt, per quam in omnium conscientias penetrant, & ita sibi obstringunt summos, infimos, diuites & pauperes, principes & subditos, vt nemo contra illos vel mutire audeat: adhæc in sectas scindunt, & hominum seruos faciunt eos, quos Christus in filiorum Dei libertatem vindicauit. habet, imò defendit illos, proque ipsis bella gerit, quæ sæpe eò vsque progrediuntur, vt principes in suæ fidei commissum populum crudelissimè sæuiant, parentes verò ex senatos propter solam fidei purioris professionem abdicare non vereantur. Interim suaue illud & salutare Christi iugum nemo vult ferre: & qui sub Papatu ista omnia patientissimè toleraverunt, nunc modicam disciplinam recusant ferre, quæ non alia ab eis exigit, quàm quæ communis sensus factu salutaria & necessaria esse docet. Quæ verò huius mali causa? Nimirum, quòd Euangelij præcones mundi iudicio infirmi sunt, & nullo splendore commendantur. At non illis hærere debent, qui ad salutem æternam aspirant, sed in illis se exerentem Spiritus sancti virtutem & illustria Euangelicæ prædicationis effecta obseruare. Terreant etiam multorum exempla, qui sua ingratitudine iugum gratuitum sibi ipsis accersunt. His consideratis agnoscamus Dei beneficium, qui nos per Filium suum IESUM CHRISTUM liberauit, & huic consecrati ipsi seruiamus in spiritu & veritate: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: For those who admit him become the most wretched slaves, in body and in soul. And who does not know this, when the Pope binds kings and emperors to himself by oath and forces them to kiss his feet? What of the abbots and bishops? Do not these restore that human servitude, long abolished among Christians, which cannot even be escaped by dying, since they want all men bound to them so that they can exact tribute even from the dead? Do they not burden souls with traditions no less harmful than impious? For they forbid marriage and the foods given and permitted by God; they force people to make confession to them, by which they penetrate the consciences of all and so bind to themselves the highest and lowest, rich and poor, princes and subjects, so that no one dares even to murmur against them. Besides this, they split people into sects and make slaves of those whom Christ has claimed for the liberty of the sons of God. He holds them, indeed defends them, and wages wars on their behalf. These often go so far that princes rage most cruelly against the people entrusted to their charge, and parents do not hesitate to cast off their children from the senate merely for professing the purer faith. Meanwhile, no one wants to bear that sweet and saving yoke of Christ. Those who patiently endured all these things under the Papacy now refuse to bear a moderate discipline, which asks of them nothing other than what common sense teaches to be beneficial and necessary. And what is the cause of this evil? Clearly, it is that the heralds of the Gospel are weak in the judgment of the world and are commended by no splendour. But those who aspire to eternal salvation ought not to cling to such things; rather, they should observe the power of the Holy Spirit shining forth in them and the notable effects of the Gospel preaching. Let the examples of many who by their ingratitude bring a voluntary yoke upon themselves also serve as a warning. With these things considered, let us acknowledge the benefit of God, who has freed us through his Son Jesus Christ, and let us, dedicated to him, serve him in spirit and in truth, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LI.
units.tr: HOMILY LI.

units.la: Imò, in quocunque audacia vti velit aliquis (insipienter loquor) audacia vti velim & ego. Hebræi sunt? sum & ego. Israelitæ sunt? sum & ego. Semen Abrahami sunt? sum & ego. Ministri Christi sunt? (desipiens loquor) supero ego: In laboribus, amplius; in verberibus, supra illos; in carceribus, amplius; in mortibus sæpe.
units.tr: Indeed, in whatever boldness anyone wishes to indulge (I speak foolishly), I too will be bold. Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they the seed of Abraham? So am I. Are they ministers of Christ? (I speak as one beside himself) I am more so: in labours more abundantly, in stripes above measure, in prisons more abundantly, in deaths often.

units.la: GRauiter accusauit hucusq; Paulus nimiam Corinthiorum facilitatem, qui impostores pseudoapostolos plus quàm seruiliter ferebant, à quibus indignissimè tractabantur. Nam præter id, quòd syncheriorem Euangelij doctrinam corrumpebant, sua ambitione simul & auaritia omnibus erant intolerabiles, & vt ipsi dominarentur, eos quos CHRISTVS IESVS sui sanguinis pretio redemit, sibi ipsis mancipabant, spoliabant, & non sine contumelia eorundem facilitate abutebantur. Est hoc memorabile exemplum peruersitatis mundi, qui (vt prouerbio dicitur) vult decipi: & constat, hoc antiquum & commune vitium esse, quòd in pretio habentur seductores, contempti autem & exosi sint, qui Veritatem fideliter docent, & omnium saluti consultum cupiunt. Porrò fallebantur Corinthij pseudoapostolorum magnificentia & ostentatione, & e contra vili atque contemptibili Pauli specie offendebantur, & (quod perinde reprehendi merebatur) hoc ei vitio vertebat, cuius causa ipsum debebant maximi facere. Ideo nunc liberius digreditur in suipsius commendationem, vt & inanem pseudoapostolorum iactantiam confutet, & Corinthios de toto Euangelicæ prædicationis ministerio rectius iudicare doceat.
units.tr: Up to this point Paul has sharply rebuked the excessive pliancy of the Corinthians, who put up with false apostles more than slavishly, though these men treated them most shamefully. For, apart from the fact that they corrupted the pure doctrine of the Gospel, by their ambition and greed they were intolerable to everyone; in order to lord it over people, they enslaved and plundered those whom Christ Jesus had redeemed at the price of his own blood, and they abused the people's compliance with insult. This is a notable example of the perversity of the world, which (as the proverb says) wishes to be deceived. And it is clear that this is an old and common vice: impostors are held in high esteem, while those who faithfully teach the truth and seek the salvation of all are despised and hated. Moreover, the Corinthians were taken in by the pomp and showiness of the false apostles, and on the other hand were offended by the lowly and contemptible appearance of Paul; and (which deserved equal reproof) they held this against him as a fault, when they ought to have esteemed him most highly for the very reason they despised him. So now he digresses more freely into praise of himself, both to refute the empty boasting of the false apostles and to teach the Corinthians to judge more rightly of the whole ministry of the Gospel preaching.

units.la: Propositio omnium, quæ ad finem Capitis vsque sequuntur, hæc est: In quocunque audacia vti velit aliquis (insipienter loquor) audacia vti velim & ego. Audaciam dicit, ambitiosam illam & confidentem iactantiam aduersariorum: qui cùm homines nihili essent, quiduis tamen sibi ipsis arrogabant, adeò vt contra germanos Christi Apostolos sese extollerent. Itaque sic vult dicere: Age, quia mea infirmitate offendimini, rogo vos, vt omissis paulisper personis, rem ipsam examinetis: & mox patebit istos homines, qui vobis tanti viri esse videntur, nihil habere præter inanem confidentiam cum audacia impudenti coniunctam, qua sese venditant, & quæ illos vobis debebat suspectos facere. Quia verò illam tanti facitis, age ego quoq;, vt causæ communi consulam, nolo illis meticulosior videri, & proinde liberè hoc vobis edico, illos quantùmuis audaces & arrogantes sint, tamen non aliquid habere, in quo ego illis cedam, neque etiam mihi animus deest, vt cum illis pedem propius conferre verear. Rursus verò excusationem interponit, qua se insipientius loqui fatetur: vt ostendat se inepto & præposter o Corinthiorum iudicio cogi, vt cum Thrasonibus illis ineptire velit. Accidit hoc sæpe ijs, qui in Ecclesia & Repub. versantur, & in eo magna eius prudentiæ pars sita est, quam Christus in suæ domus dispensatore requirit.
units.tr: The proposition of everything that follows to the end of the chapter is this: "In whatever boldness anyone wishes to indulge (I speak foolishly), I too will be bold." By "boldness" he means the ambitious and confident boasting of his opponents, who, though they were nobodies, claimed for themselves whatever they pleased, so much so that they set themselves up against the genuine apostles of Christ. So he means to say something like this: "Come now, since you are offended by my weakness, I ask you to set aside persons for a little while and examine the matter itself. It will soon become plain that these men, whom you think so great, have nothing but empty self-confidence joined with shameless audacity, by which they puff themselves up, and which ought to have made you suspicious of them. But since you hold this in such high regard, come, I too will act, for the sake of the common cause; I do not want to appear more timid than they are. Therefore I tell you freely that, however bold and arrogant they may be, they have nothing in which I would yield to them, nor am I lacking in spirit, so that I should fear to measure my steps against theirs." Then again he interposes an apology, admitting that he is speaking more foolishly, so as to show that he is forced, by the foolish and perverse judgement of the Corinthians, to play the fool with those braggarts. This often happens to those who hold office in the Church and the commonwealth, and a large part of the prudence that Christ requires in the steward of his house consists in it.

units.la: Etenim debent isti diligenter videre, vt quàmuis humilitati & modestiæ studeant, animo tamen præsenti sint, vt audeant (si quando necessitas exigit) se improbis & gloriosis ostentatoribus opponere. Nam humilitatis hic finis esse debet, ut Deo sua gloria vindicetur, & ut hic supra omnes emineat. Itaq; modestia praepostera & reprehensione digna est, quae permittit, ut improbi se contra Deum attollant impune. Vidit hoc Moses, qui cum mortalium omnium mansuetissimus esset, inuicta tamen magnanimitate omnibus sese oppõsuit, qui Ecclesiae & Reipub. statum turbabant. Quod ipsum Prophetas fecisse legimus, qui non veriti sunt Regibus quoq; in faciem resistere. Recte ergo hos in praesenti Paulus imitatur. Et poterunt idem facere, qui primo legitimam vocationem habent, & eo nomine sibi ipsis bene sunt conscij: quae causa est, quod hanc Prophetae & Apostoli frequenter suis hostibus atq; eorundem minis opponunt. Deinde si in ijs seduli sint, quae vocatio ipsorum requirit, & ea fide bona exequantur. Tunc etenim aduersariorum ora & linguas facile frenare poterunt, si horum calumnijs & inani iactantiae ipsi res & opera opponant. At hodie omnis ὐαγεγίας atque confusionis haec praecipua causa est, quod plerique ad Ecclesiae & Reipub. gubernacula malis artibus irrepunt, qui deinde affectibus prauis indulgent, & ita suam authoritatem turpiter proflituunt.
units.tr: For such men must take care that, however much they cultivate humility and modesty, they nevertheless have the courage, when necessity demands it, to set themselves against wicked and boastful showmen. For the purpose of humility should be that God's glory is vindicated and that he stands out above all. Therefore a modesty that permits the wicked to exalt themselves against God with impunity is perverse and deserves reproof. Moses saw this: though he was the meekest of all mortals, he nevertheless opposed with unconquered greatness of spirit all those who disturbed the state of the Church and the commonwealth. We read that the prophets did the same; they did not fear to resist even kings to their face. Paul therefore rightly imitates them in the present passage. And those can do the same who first have a lawful calling and are conscious of having it; this is why the prophets and apostles often set this against their enemies and their threats. Next, they must be diligent in those things which their calling requires, and carry them out in good faith. For then they will easily be able to restrain the mouths and tongues of their adversaries, if they set deeds and works against their slanders and empty boasting. But today the chief cause of all disorder [ἀταξίας] and confusion is that many creep into the helm of Church and commonwealth by wicked arts, and then indulge depraved desires, and so shamefully prostitute their authority.

units.la: Sed Paulum audiamus, qui cum aduersarijs suis congressurus a genere aut gente orditur, & hic eos nihil habere ostendit, propter quod sibi debeant praeferri. Et quia in hoc argumento nimium futilis erat aemulorum iactantia, ne quid ipsis reliquum faciat, omnes titulos congerit, quibus sese venditabant. Erat inter hos primus, quod Hebraei essent, quo nomine de gentis vetustate gloriabatur. Heber enim (ut Moses tradit) Semi abnepos, filium habuit Phalegum, sub quo linguarum diuisio facta est. Erat ergo hoc praeclarum prouidentiae & studij Dei erga gentem illam argumentum, quod cum aliae gentes vel prorsus interijssent, vel sedibus suis relictis, cum alijs permixtae essent, sola Hebraeorum gens, ex qua promissus ille humani generis redemptor nasci debebat, suam originem vna cum lingua primis parentibus vsitata retinuit, & ab alijs distincta mansit. Deinde Israelitas se esse dicebant, nimirum a Iacobo, qui primus nomen istud ab Angelo accepit, quod ei in lucta praevaluisset. Et eo posteri imprimis superbiebant, perinde ac si principes & victores Dei essent, ut apud Hoseam est videre. Imprimis tamen gloriari solebant Abrahami nomine, cuius filij vocabant dici, propter promissiones & foedus, quod cum illo & posteritate eius Deus sanciuerat. Et erat propter istud apud fideles magna Iudaicae gentis dignitas, quod ex ea CHRISTVS IESVS secundum carnem natus esset, & ex eadem prodijssent Apostoli. Itaq; non temere factum fuit, ut pseudoapostoli his titulis sese venditarent, ut nimirum ipsi quoq; pluris fierent. Addebant his (ut alibi monuimus) quod Christum in carne vidissent, & quod ab eius Apostolis germanis essent missi. Ut ergo hanc laruam eis detraheret Paulus, graviter cum illis agit, & interrogationibus vrget stolidos illorum admiratores. Quasi diceret: Age, quid obsecro habent illi, quoad hanc suae gloriationis partem, quo me superent? Num quod Hebraei sint? Atqui ego quoq; Hebraeus sum. Num quod Israelitae sint? At me quoq; Israelitam non minus quam illos esse constat. Num quod Abrahami semen siue filij sint? At ipse quoq; ex Abrahami posteritate natus sum. Et facit ad huius loci interpretationem, quod in epist. ad Philip. scribitur: Si quisquam alius videtur fiduciam habere in carne, ego magis habeo: Circumcisus octauo die, ex gente Israelis, tribus Beniamin, Hebraeus ex Hebraeis, &c. Quibus adde, quae Acto. 22. & 26. de seipso dicit.
units.tr: But let us hear Paul, who, about to engage his adversaries, begins with birth or nation, and here shows that they have nothing on account of which they ought to be preferred to him. And since the boasting of his rivals was very trifling on this point, he gathers together, lest he leave them anything, all the titles by which they advertised themselves. The first of these was that they were Hebrews, and on this title they boasted of the antiquity of their race. For Heber, as Moses records, was a great-grandson of Shem, and had a son Peleg, in whose time the division of tongues took place. This was therefore a notable proof of God's providence and care for that nation: while other nations had either utterly perished, or, having left their dwellings, had been mingled with others, the Hebrew nation alone, from which that promised Redeemer of mankind was to be born, retained its origin, together with the language used by the first parents, and remained distinct from others. Next, they said that they were Israelites, namely from Jacob, who was the first to receive that name from the Angel, because he had prevailed in the wrestling. And his descendants above all took pride in this, as though they were princes and victors of God, as may be seen in Hosea. Yet they were accustomed to glory especially in the name of Abraham, whose sons they called themselves, on account of the promises and the covenant which God had sanctioned with him and his posterity. And because Christ Jesus was born of that people according to the flesh, and the Apostles had sprung from it, the Jewish nation enjoyed great dignity among the faithful. So it was not without reason that the false apostles advertised themselves with these titles, so that they too might be held in greater esteem. To these they added (as we have noted elsewhere) that they had seen Christ in the flesh, and that they had been sent by his genuine Apostles. So, to strip away this mask from them, Paul deals with them severely and presses with questions their foolish admirers. As if he were saying: "Come now, I beg you, what do they have, in respect of this part of their boasting, by which they surpass me? Is it that they are Hebrews? But I too am a Hebrew. Is it that they are Israelites? But it is plain that I am an Israelite no less than they. Is it that they are of the seed or children of Abraham? But I too was born of the posterity of Abraham." And what is written in the Epistle to the Philippians bears on the interpretation of this passage: "If anyone else seems to have confidence in the flesh, I have more: circumcised on the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, etc." Add to these what he says of himself in Acts 22 and 26.

units.la: In praesenti vero non obscure Corinthiorum stupiditatem perstringit, qui in pseudoapostolis ea magni faciebant, quae in Paulo negligebant. Ita solet vulgo fieri, ut si cui bene volumus, omnia eius admiremur, quae in multis alijs non observamus. Ita hodie si quis Episcopus aut Abbas aliquae blandius alloquatur, mox is incredibilem illius humanitatem praedicat, & huius praetextu superstitiones simul & aperta flagitia, quibus illud hominum genus pollutum est, excusat: at aeternum Dei Filium, Regem & Sacerdotem verum & vnicum, nos quotidie expansis vlnis ad se & bonorum caelestium communionem inuitantem, plerique negligunt. Similiter, si Sacrificulo pro concione dictum aliquod plausibilius excidat, omnes illud excipiunt, mirantur, laudant: nō autem attendunt fidis Christi ministris, hoc ipsum quotidie ad rauim vsq; clamantibus.
units.tr: In the present passage, however, he plainly rebukes the stupidity of the Corinthians, who valued in the false apostles those things which they neglected in Paul. It is customary for people to do this: if we are well disposed towards someone, we admire all his traits, while in many others we do not notice them. So today, if some bishop or abbot speaks somewhat more agreeably to someone, at once that person proclaims his incredible kindliness, and under cover of this excuses the superstitions as well as the open scandals with which that class of men is polluted; but the eternal Son of God, the true and only King and Priest, who daily invites us with outstretched arms to himself and to the fellowship of heavenly goods, most people neglect. Likewise, if some little priest lets slip a more pleasing remark in a sermon, everyone catches it up, marvels at it, and praises it; but they do not attend to the faithful ministers of Christ, who cry out this very thing daily until they are hoarse.

units.la: In Paulo autem obseruemus, eum ista non ideo dixisse, quod (ut ambitiosi illi solebant) ex genere & natalibus gloriam captarit, sed potius, ut horum vanitatem argueret. Dum enim se eandem habere ostendit gloriandi materiam, ea autē non vtitur, non obscure testatur, se ideo abstinere,
units.tr: In Paul, however, we should notice that he did not say these things because, as ambitious men usually did, he sought glory from his family and birth. He said them rather to expose the emptiness of such boasting. For while he shows that he has the same ground for boasting, and yet does not use it, he makes it plain enough that he refrains for this reason.

units.la: Generis fiducia confutat. Gen.10. Gen.32. Hos.12. Corinthiorum stupiditas. Generis fiducia & gloriamanis est. quòd illa nullius sit momenti. Fuit hoc sanè proprium Iudæis, quòd gentis suæ nobilitate gloriantur, & extant ambitionis illius exempla passim apud Prophetas, vt iam de illis nihil dicam, quæ Ioanni Baptistæ & ipsi Christo aliquando nimis insolenter obiecerunt. Quin hodie, etsi omnibus modis miseri atq; infelices sint, tamen adhuc se solos Dei peculium & gentem sanctam esse sibi persuadent, reliquos verò omnes (vt nuper diximus) prophanos Goijm dicere consueuerunt. At semper grauissimè cófutata est à Prophetis hæc illorum arrogantia, qui eos non veriti sunt Amorrhæos & Chananæos dicere: & Christus eosdem diaboli filios esse demõstrat, cùm Abrahami patris sui titulo aduersus ipsum arrogantius superbirent. Obseruandum hoc erat illis, qui hodie maiorum suorum virtutes & stemmata iactant. Est quidem singulare Dei donum, ex præclaris parentibus natum esse: Sed nisi tu natalium splendori respondeas, eò illustrior est tua nequitia. Et quis (vt Satyrici poëtæ verbis vtar) generosum dixerit hunc, qui
units.tr: Pride of birth refuted. Gen. 10. Gen. 32. Hos. 12. The folly of the Corinthians. Pride of birth and boasting in it: that it counts for nothing. Boasting in noble descent was certainly a peculiar mark of the Jews, and examples of that ambition appear everywhere among the Prophets, not to mention those things which they once too insolently threw at John the Baptist and at Christ himself. Even today, though they are wretched and unhappy in every way, they still persuade themselves that they alone are God's own people and the holy nation, and they customarily call all others profane, Goijm (as we said recently). Yet this arrogance of theirs has always been most severely refuted by the Prophets, who did not hesitate to call them Amorites and Canaanites. And Christ shows that these same men are the children of the devil, since they proudly boasted against him of the name of their father Abraham. This was something those people had to note, who today vaunt the virtues and pedigrees of their ancestors. It is indeed a singular gift of God to be born of illustrious parents; but unless you live up to the splendour of your birth, your wickedness is all the more conspicuous. And who (to use the words of the satirical poet) would call a man noble who is "unworthy of his race, and marked only by a famous name? It is a wretched thing to lean on the reputation of others."

units.la: Indignus genere, & præclaro nomine tantum Insignis? miserum est aliorum incumbere famæ.
units.tr: Unworthy of his race, and marked only by a famous name? It is a wretched thing to lean on the reputation of others.

units.la: Ideo idem ille non minus grauiter quàm prudenter in degeneres patriæ virtutis decantatores dicebat:
units.tr: For that same poet, no less weightily than wisely, said against those degenerate praisers of their country's virtue:

units.la: Malo pater tibi sit Therfites, dummodo tu fis Æacidæ similis, Vulcaniaque arma capessas: Quàm te Therfitæ similem producat Achilles.
units.tr: I would rather you had Thersites for a father, provided you were like Achilles the son of Aeacus and took up the arms of Vulcan, than that Achilles should produce you as a Thersites like himself.

units.la: Vt verò ad huius seculi solidam gloriam nihil facit generis nobilitas: ita multò minus hæc iuuat in æternæ salutis negotio, sicuti in Ismaelis, Esau & similium exemplis est videre. Et notum est illud Apostoli, filios Dei non ex voluntate carnis, neque ex voluntate viri, sed ex solo Deo nasci. Et germanos Abrahami filios esse dicit Christus eos, qui illius fidem atque mores imitantur. Transferamus hoc ad nostri seculi Apostolicos, Pontifices nimirum & Episcopos, qui Petri successione superbiunt. Nam vt hanc illis demus, imò vt insuper eos ex Petri genere natos esse fateamur, quid tamen hoc proderit, nisi se Petri Spiritu agi operibus suis testentur? Et rectè olim orthodoxi patres monuerunt, non personarum, sed doctrinæ successionem spectari debere.
units.tr: Just as noble birth contributes nothing to the solid glory of this age, so it helps even less in the business of eternal salvation, as the examples of Ishmael, Esau and their like show. And the saying of the Apostle is well known, that the children of God are born not of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God alone. Christ also says that those who imitate the faith and conduct of Abraham are his true children. Let us apply this to the apostolic men of our own age, namely the Popes and bishops, who pride themselves on succession from Peter. For even if we grant them this, indeed even if we confess that they are born of Peter's stock, what will it profit them, unless their works show that they are driven by Peter's Spirit? And the orthodox Fathers rightly warned that it is the succession of doctrine, not of persons, that must be looked to.

units.la: Sed pergamus in Pauli verbis, qui ad id transit, quod præcipuum huius tractationis caput est, Ipsum videlicet Verbi Euangelici ministerium. Ministri Christi sunt? (desipiens loquor) supero ego. Rursus autem insipientiæ hæc verba tribuit: quia vix vllum aliud huius argumentum est euidentius, quàm si quis se alijs præferat nulla necessitate coactus. Nam qui id faciunt, ij plerunque seipsos & communem hominum sortem ignorant. Est autem in Pauli exemplo probè obseruandum, quòd qui quoad generis nobilitatem alios ferre potuit æquales, nunc vbi ad ministerium Verbi deuentum est, se supra illos extollit: primò quidem, quia hoc exigebat donorum excellentia, in quibus non debuit negligere gloriam Dei, qui ipsum præ multis alijs instruxerat, vt organum sibi esset electum: Deinde, quia toti in hoc erant pseudoapostoli, vt ipsum contemptui exponerent: quod fieri non poterat absque doctrinæ & religionis Christianæ contumelia. Adde, quòd nisi illis fuisset præstantior, Christi seruus esse non poterat, & proinde neque fidem meruisset ipsius doctrina. Itaque non tam pro sua authoritate, quàm Euangelij doctrina pugnat, vt illos euincat non esse germanos Christi Apostolos, imò indignos esse, qui audiantur. Habent ergo verba hæc Concessionis speciem. Quasi diceret: Esto, Christi ministri sint, non tamen mihi conferri merentur, neque eadem indicia proferre possunt, quibus ego me Christi ministrum esse probo. Et est hic obseruatu dignissimum, quòd à generis nobilitate ad ministeriu transfit. Vera enim nobilitas est Christi ministrum esse. Nisi hoc accedat, turpissima diaboli mancipia, aut saltem ignaui ventres sunt, quicunque alijs donis superbiunt. Id verò non modò Ecclesiarum ministri, verumetiam principes Reipub. ad se transferre debent: quorum hæc summa gloria est, quòd ipsi quoq; in Scripturis serui Dei dicuntur.
units.tr: But let us go on with Paul's words, who now passes to what is the main subject of this discussion: namely, the ministry of the Gospel Word itself. "Are they ministers of Christ? (I speak foolishly) I am more so." Yet he again attributes these words to foolishness, since there is hardly any other argument more evident than when a man sets himself above others without being compelled by any necessity. For those who do this usually fail to know themselves and the common lot of humankind. In Paul's example, however, we must carefully note that he, who could put up with others as his equals in respect of noble birth, now, when it comes to the ministry of the Word, raises himself above them. This he did, first, because the excellence of his gifts required it, and in these he ought not to neglect the glory of God, who had equipped him above many others so that he might be a chosen instrument for him. Second, because the false apostles were wholly intent on exposing him to contempt, which could not happen without insult to the teaching and the Christian religion. Add that unless he had been superior to them, he could not be the servant of Christ, and therefore his teaching would not have deserved faith. So he fights not so much for his own authority as for the doctrine of the Gospel, to prove that they are not the true apostles of Christ, and indeed are unworthy to be heard. These words therefore have the appearance of a concession, as if he said: "Grant that they are ministers of Christ; yet they do not deserve to be compared with me, nor can they produce the same evidence by which I prove myself to be a minister of Christ." And it is most worthy of note here that he passes from noble birth to the ministry. For true nobility is to be a minister of Christ. Unless this is added, all who pride themselves on other gifts are most shameful slaves of the devil, or at least lazy bellies. And this is something not only the ministers of the Churches but also the rulers of the commonwealth must apply to themselves, since their highest glory is that they too are called servants of God in the Scriptures.

units.la: Cæterùm probat Paulus, se quoad ministerium alteris illis præstare: id verò non inanibus verbis aut hominum testimonijs probat, sed reipsa, ijs nimirum, quæ hucusque fecerat & passus est: In laboribus (inquit) amplius: in verheribus, supra illos: in carceribus amplius: in mortibus, sæpe.
units.tr: Moreover, Paul proves that in respect of the ministry he excels those others; and he proves it not by empty words or the testimonies of men, but in fact, namely by those things which he had done and suffered up to that point: "In labours," he says, "more abundantly; in stripes above measure; in prisons more frequently; in deaths often."

units.la: Quain re Pau lus alijs præ- stantior fuerit sæpe. Laborum nomine continuas peregrinationes, docendi molestiam & infinitas, quæ ei obijciebantur, difficultates intelligit: quibus accedebat, quòd interdum victum sibijpsi manuum labore parare cogebatur. Quod de verberibus & plagis dicit, ipse mox interpretabitur. In carceres quoque & vincula sæpe coniectum fuisse, Actorum liber docet. Mortes graviora pericula dicuntur, quæ præsens vitæ periculum minantur. Tale quid fuit, de quo in primo Cap. scripsit, & quòd se cum reliquis Apostolis mortificationem IESV CHRISTI in corpore suo circumferre dicit. Vide 2. Cor. 4. & 5.
units.tr: In what respect Paul was more excellent than the others: often. By "labours" he understands his continual journeys, the trouble of teaching and the countless difficulties that were thrown in his way, to which was added that at times he was forced to earn his own living by the labour of his hands. What he says about stripes and blows he will explain himself shortly. That he was often cast into prisons and chains the Book of Acts teaches. "Deaths" are dangers more serious, which threaten present danger to life. Something of this kind was what he wrote of in the first chapter, and that he says he bears about in his body the dying of the LORD JESUS in his body. See 2 Cor. 4 and 5.

units.la: Debet hic non ofcitanter obseruari, quòd non inanibus titulis aut bullis superbit Paulus, sed reipsa & operibus se Christi Apostolum esse probat. Hæc enim vera est {ei} ipsum commendandi ratio, si res & facta loquantur. Pontifices Romani, ut se Apostolicos esse probent, ipsi otiosi adducunt Conciliorum decreta, Imperatorum donationes, successionem Apostolicam, & quæ alia sunt huius generis. Atqui omnia ista in pessimis quibusque locum inueniunt, & proinde non possunt Christi ministros facere, quorum ministerium, non in dignitate & eminentia externa, sed in opere consistit, quod illis Deus mandauit. Peccant etiam priuatim, qui fidem in Christum magnifice profitentur, factis vero eandem negant. Quibus omnibus Diuus Iacobus dicit: Ostende mihi fidem tuam ex factis tuis, & ego tibi ostendam fidem meam ex factis meis. Quod ipsum ad se quoque debent transferre, qui magistratum aliquem gerunt. Nam hic quoque præstant reliquis, qui plus aliis in Repub. laborant.
units.tr: Here we must observe, not carelessly, that Paul does not pride himself on empty titles or bubbles, but proves in fact and by his works that he is an apostle of Christ. For this is the true way of commending oneself, if things and deeds speak. The Roman Pontiffs, to prove that they are apostolic, idly bring forward decrees of Councils, donations of emperors, apostolic succession, and other things of this kind. Yet all these things are found in the worst men of all, and therefore they cannot make ministers of Christ, whose ministry consists not in external dignity and eminence, but in the work which God has committed to them. Those also sin privately who profess faith in Christ in grand terms, but deny it in their deeds. Of all such St James says: "Show me your faith by your works, and I will show you my faith by my works." Those who hold any magistracy must also apply this to themselves. For they too excel others, since they labour more in the commonwealth than the rest.

units.la: Est præterea hoc loco obseruatu digna admirabilis rerum vicissitudo, quam Paulus subijt. Priusquam enim ad fidem Christi conuerteretur, ipse otio, diuitijs & dignitatibus abundans, aliis labores exhibebat, qui ipso authore in carceres ducebantur, cædebantur & egebant, sicuti ipse in Actis testatur. Nunc eadem ipse patitur ab ijs, apud quos prius in pretio & honore fuerat. Accidit hoc multis olim, & exempla huius generis passim in historijs occurrunt: & hodie vix quicquam frequentius est in illis locis, vbi persecutiones feruent. Admonent ista, primum, ne temere desperemus de alicuius hominis salute. Qui enim apertos Verbi sui hostes & crudeles Ecclesiæ suæ persecutores in gratiam recipit, multò magis eos admittet, qui in ijs modò delinquunt, quæ ad hoc seculum pertinent. Et exempla sunt quæ nos in fide ista confirmant: inter quæ perquàm memorabile est, quod in Paulo habemus, qui eius considerationem nobis serio commendat in priori ad Timoth. dicens: Fidus est hic sermo, & modis omnibus dignus quem amplectamur, quòd CHRISTVS IESVS venit in mundum, vt peccatores seruaret, quorum primus sum ego: verum ideo misertus est mei, vt in me primo ostenderet IESVS CHRISTVS omnem clementiam, vt essem exemplar ijs, qui crediturî erant ipsi in vitam æternam. 1. Tim. 1.
units.tr: Moreover, there is in this passage a remarkable reversal of fortune, which Paul underwent, worthy of notice. Before he was converted to the faith of Christ, he himself, abounding in leisure, riches and dignities, inflicted labours on others, who at his instigation were led into prisons, beaten and made needy, as he himself testifies in the Acts. Now he suffers the same things from those among whom he had formerly been held in esteem and honour. This has happened to many in the past, and examples of this kind occur everywhere in histories; and today there is hardly anything more frequent in those places where persecutions rage. These things teach us, first, not to despair rashly of anyone's salvation. For he who receives into favour those who were open enemies of his Word and cruel persecutors of his Church will much more readily admit those who sin only in matters that pertain to this world. And there are examples which confirm us in this faith, among which it is most memorable what we have in Paul, who earnestly commends his case to us in the first letter to Timothy, saying: "This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief. But for this reason I obtained mercy, that in me first Jesus Christ might show all longsuffering, as a pattern to those who would believe on him to eternal life." 1 Tim. 1.

units.la: Deinde peruersum mundi ingenium atq; iudicium hic locus arguit. Quia enim totus in malo iacet, eorum modò amicitiâ gaudet, & eos solos amat, qui ipsi perditionis authores atque scelerum ministri sunt. Eosdem vero odit & immani impietate persequitur, quàm primùm ipsos ad Deum conuersos hoc agere videt, vt plures alij per ipsos conuertantur & salui fiant. Exemplis non opus est, vbi res ipsa loquitur. Olim certè ab Imperatorum gratia illico excidisse legimus eos, qui Christo nomen dabant, in pretio autem habitos fuisse, qui ipsorum rabiem adiuuabant. Consolentur illorum exemplis sese pij hodie, neq; dubitent de Dei bonitate, qui remunerator est fidelissimus.
units.tr: Next, this passage exposes the perverse disposition and judgment of the world. Because the world lies entirely in evil, it delights in the friendship of those who are authors of destruction and ministers of wickedness, and it loves only them. But it hates those who have been converted to God, and it persecutes them with monstrous impiety as soon as it sees them working to bring many others to conversion and salvation through their labours. No examples are needed where the matter speaks for itself. We certainly read that long ago those who gave their name to Christ at once fell out of the favour of the emperors, while those who abetted their rage were held in high esteem. Let the godly today take comfort from their examples, and let them not doubt the goodness of God, who is the most faithful rewarder.

units.la: Tertio discimus Pauli exemplo, Deum non impunitos dimittere eos, qui Ecclesiam eius persequuntur, aut molestiam atq; labores ei exhibent. Illius enim vox est: Qui vos tangit, tangit pupillam oculi mei. Quare tanti æstimat illis factas iniurias, vt has in illis quoq; vlcisci soleat, qui ad ipsum conuertuntur. De Paulo certè, cùm ad Damasci portas prostratus esset, iamq; Deo obedientiam vouisset, Ananiæ Dominus dicebat: Ego ostendam ei, quàm multa oporteat eum pati pro nomine meo. Quid ergo de contumacibus fiet, & pœnitere nescijs? Hoc nimirum, vt in sua contumacia male pereant, & tandem cum magno illo Christi aduersario sempiternis inferni cruciatibus multentur.
units.tr: Third, we learn from Paul's example that God does not let go unpunished those who persecute his Church or cause it trouble and hardship. For the saying of God is: "He who touches you touches the apple of my eye." Therefore he counts the injuries done to his people so highly that he is accustomed to avenge them even in those who are converted to him. Indeed, when Paul had been thrown to the ground at the gates of Damascus, and had already vowed obedience to God, the Lord said to Ananias: "I will show him how much he must suffer for my name." What then will become of the stubborn, who know not how to repent? Surely this: that they perish miserably in their obstinacy, and at last, together with that great adversary of Christ, are punished with the everlasting torments of hell.

units.la: Postremò, qui iam ab impietate conuersi & à Christo in gratiam recepti sunt, agnoscant iustum Dei iudicium, qui magno ipsorum merito eos durius tractet, exosculentur autem eiusdem bonitatem, qui ipsos Verbi sui luce illuminare dignatus est, vt iam gratiæ suæ vasa sint, qui prius ira & ignominia vasa videri poterât. Fuit in ista consideratione admodum frequens Paulus, quæ ipsum in Dei seruitio feruentiorem fecit, simulq; patientia inuicta armauit, qua per omnes aduer- forum procellas eluctatus est. Faxit æternus Dei Filius, IESVS CHRISTVS, vt qui hodie eius Ecclesiam persequuntur, similî exemplo conuersi, ipsi seruiant, & illius merito partæ salutis participes fiant. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, those who have already been converted from impiety and received back into favour with Christ should acknowledge the just judgment of God, who treats them more harshly on account of their great guilt, and should embrace the goodness of him who has deigned to illuminate them with the light of his Word, so that those who could formerly be seen as vessels of wrath and dishonour are now vessels of his grace. Paul was very frequent in this consideration, which made him more fervent in the service of God and at the same time armed him with an unconquered patience, by which he struggled through all the storms of opposition. May the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, grant that those who today persecute his Church, converted by a similar example, may serve him themselves and become sharers in the salvation won by his merit. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LII.
units.tr: HOMILY LII.

units.la: A Iudæis quinquies accepi quadragenas plagas, vna minus. Ter virgis cæsus fui, semel fui lapidatus, ter naufragium feci, noctem ac diem in profundo egi: In itineribus sæpe, in periculis fluminum, periculis latronum, periculis à meis gentilibus, periculis à gentibus, periculis in ciuitate, periculis in deserto, periculis in mari, periculis inter falsos fratres: In fatigatione & ærumna, in vigiliis sæpe, in fame & siti, in ieiuniis sæpe, in frigore & nuditate: absque iis quæ extrinsecus, vrget agmen illud in me quotidie consurgens, solicitudo nimirum pro omnibus Ecclesiis. Quis affligitur, quin ego affligar? quis offenditur, quin ego vror?
units.tr: Five times I received from the Jews forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I spent in the deep. On journeys often, in dangers of rivers, dangers of robbers, dangers from my own countrymen, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers; in toil and hardship, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness: besides those things which are from outside, there is that crowd that rises up against me every day, namely anxiety for all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?

units.la: Quoniam pseudoapostoli apud Corinthios externo splendore sese venditabant, Paulus è contra illis opponit labores & omnis generis pericula, quibus ipse exercetatur: & ne quis eum de illis loqui putet, quæ ipse sibi absque causa necessaria accersiuerit, diserte narrationem omnem ad ea reflringit, quæ ipsi in IESV CHRISTI ministerio, apostolatu nimirum, accidederant. Continent autem hæc generalem doctrinam, Ecclesiarum ministros non ex ijs, quæ mundo magnifica videntur, æstimari debere, sed ex curis & laboribus, quos in promouenda gloria Dei & hominum salute sustinent. Quoad vero narrationem hanc, nuper in genere dixit, se in hac parte aduersarijs suis multum præstare, vt qui ipsis in otio inter amicos & admiratores suos secure deliciantibus, omnis generis labores subeat, verbera patiatur, carcerum squalorem sentiat, adeoque inter mille mortes versetur. At ne quid illum fingere dicerent, quod in genere dixerat, nunc in speciem diducit. Ita vero & aduersariorum segnitiem arguit, & Dei gratiam in se agentem magnifice commendat.
units.tr: Since false apostles among the Corinthians were boasting of their outward show, Paul on the other hand sets against them his labours and dangers of every kind, with which he himself was beset. And lest anyone think he is speaking of those things which he had brought upon himself without necessity, he restricts his whole account plainly to what had happened to him in the ministry of Jesus Christ, that is, in the apostleship. These words contain a general teaching: that the ministers of the churches ought not to be judged by those things which seem splendid to the world, but by the cares and labours which they undergo in advancing the glory of God and the salvation of men. As for this account, he had recently said in general terms that in this respect he far surpassed his opponents, who, idle among their friends and admirers, live securely in luxury, while he undertakes labours of every kind, suffers stripes, endures the squalor of prisons, and lives, as it were, amid a thousand deaths. But lest they should say that he was inventing what he had said in general, he now sets it out in particular. In this way he both exposes the sloth of his opponents and magnificently commends the grace of God working in him.

units.la: Orditur à singularibus, quæ ipsi quasi propria & cum paucis aliis communia erant. Inter quæ primum est, quòd à Iudæis se quinquies plagas quadragenas, vna minus, accepisse scribit. Et consultò Iudæos primo loco adducit, vt magis perstringat æmulos, qui quòd Iudæi essent, superbiebant, cùm vel hoc solo nomine boni & cordati quibusque deberent suspecti esse. Nam illo tempore nulli erant hostes Christi illis truculentiores, qui non Paulo soli vbique terrarum negotium faciebant, verumetiam pedibus manibusque obstabant, ne Euangelium gentibus prædicaretur, vt in priori ad Thessalonicenses scribitur. Sed & numerum plagarum exprimit Apostolus, vt ostendat, Iudæos extrema, qua licebat, crudelitate in ipso multando vsos fuisse. Extat enim Lex Dei, quid cum illis agi debeat, qui etsi capitis supplicium non meruerunt, tamen in corpore mulctari debent. Non vult Deus talibus omnino parci, aut eos indulgentius tractari, sed vt virgis aut flagris cædantur præcipit, vt seruile supplicium luant, qui seruiliter peccarunt. Verumtamen moderationem præscribit, ne odio aut irâ aliquid detur, sed pro delicti ratione plagæ plures aut pauciores talibus infligantur: monet autem, ne numerum quadragenarium excedant: & causa huius præcepti hæc redditur: Ne vilescat frater tuus in oculis tuis, id est, ne eum, qui tuus cius & fratris instar est, videaris habere vilis bestiæ aut iumenti loco. Ne quid ergo hic peccaretur, à Rabbinis conflitutum fuit, ne ad quadragesimam vsque plagam cædendo procederetur, sed in trigesima nona finis fieret: ne videlicet ad quadragesimam vsque progressi, impetu irae abriperentur, & temere adhuc vnam & alteram addendo in Dei legem peccarent. Fuit hæc quoq; cautio hypocritica, quales multas Rabbini excogitarunt: & hanc in Paulo Iudæi obseruauerunt. uauerunt, quasi moderatius cum eo vellent agere, cum interim in Dei legem non vno modo peccarent. Nam & innocentem cædebant, & ad extremum vsq; numerum procedebant, procul dubio plures plagas addituri, si licuisset. Attamen qualescunque fuerint, nostris moderatiores fuerunt, qui Christiani dici & haberi volunt. Nam contenti extremo Legis rigore, non putarunt vlterius esse progrediendum. Item cæsum dimiserunt, non autem coegerunt fidem abnegare, neq; spectaculum ex illo fecerunt theatricum, multò minus occiderunt. Hodie omnia ista faciunt Inquisitores, qui eò sanctiores se fore putant, quò crudelius in Christi germanos cultores sæuiunt. Quæ causa est, quòd publica quoq; iura silent, si qui verè fideles in illorum manus incidant.
units.tr: He begins with the particular things which were peculiar to himself, or shared with only a few others. Among these the first is that he writes that he received from the Jews five times forty lashes less one. And he deliberately names the Jews first, so that he may sting his rivals more sharply, who took pride in being Jews, although on that very ground alone every good and sensible person ought to regard them with suspicion. For at that time there were no enemies of Christ more savage than they, who not only harassed Paul everywhere in the world, but even with hands and feet stood in the way of the gospel being preached to the Gentiles, as is written in his earlier letter to the Thessalonians. But the Apostle also states the number of stripes, to show that the Jews, in punishing him, used the utmost cruelty that was permitted. For the law of God exists, laying down what must be done with those who, though they have not deserved the death penalty, nevertheless ought to be punished in the body. God does not wish such people to be spared altogether, or treated with excessive leniency, but commands that they be beaten with rods or whips, so that those who sinned in a servile way may bear a servile punishment. Yet he prescribes moderation, so that nothing is given to hatred or anger, but more or fewer blows are inflicted according to the nature of the offence; and he warns that they must not exceed forty. The reason for this precept is given thus: lest your brother be cheapened in your eyes, that is, lest you seem to regard as a vile beast or a beast of burden one who is yours and is like a brother. Therefore, so that no wrong might be committed here, the rabbis decreed that the beating should not proceed up to the fortieth stroke, but should end at the thirty-ninth: lest, namely, those who had advanced almost to forty should be carried away by the rush of anger and, rashly adding one or another stroke, sin against the law of God. This was also a hypocritical caution, of the kind the rabbis devised in great number; and the Jews observed it in the case of Paul, as if they wished to deal with him more moderately, while in fact they were sinning against the law of God in more than one way. For they beat an innocent man, and proceeded to the full number, doubtless adding more blows if it had been allowed. Yet whatever they were, they were more moderate than ours, who want to be and be called Christians. For they, content with the extreme rigour of the Law, did not think they should go further. Likewise, having beaten a man, they let him go, and did not compel him to deny his faith, nor did they make a theatrical spectacle of it, much less kill him. Today the inquisitors do all these things, who think they become the holier the more cruelly they rage against the genuine worshippers of Christ. This is why the public laws also fall silent when any truly faithful persons fall into their hands.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui se ter virgis cæsum fuisse ait: nimirum inter gentes, apud quas hoc supplicium vulgare fuit, apud Romanos imprimis, quorum apparitores securibus & virgis armati Consulem comitabantur. Et hoc Paulo apud Philippenses accidisse, Lucas in Actis scribit. Act. 16. & 14. Addit bis, semel etiam se lapidatum fuisse, apud Lystrenses nimirum: quod etiam Iudæis authoribus factum fuit, & tunc quidem, cum ingens beneficium dedisset Lystrensibus, & ad veri Dei cultum eos revocaret, qui ipsi & Barnabæ divinum cultum exhibere volebant. Fuit hoc memorabile leuitatis humanæ exemplum. Quem Deum esse proclamauerunt Lystrenses, mox lapidibus obruunt, & seminecè ex vrbe eiiciunt, idq; ab hominibus peregrinis persuasi. Quid, quod Iudæi, ne Lystrenses relictis idolis ad sui Dei cultum conuertantur, obstant: quando vident fore, vt eadem ratione Christiani fiant? Similes horum sunt hodie nonnulli ex Euangelicæ doctrinæ professoribus, quibus dolet, si qui Papisticis superstitionibus abnegatis ad Euangelium & syncériorem Christi fidem transeunt, non autem ab ipsis conscriptæ aut receptæ Confessioni subscribunt. Sed debet Christi cultores animosos facere hoc Pauli exemplum. Qui enim hunc inter medios lapidum grandines serua re potuit, ne periret, ipsos quoq; tuebitur, quoad illorum operam Ecclesiæ suæ vtilem fore viderit.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who says that he was three times beaten with rods: namely among the Gentiles, among whom this punishment was common, above all among the Romans, whose attendants, armed with axes and rods, accompanied the consul. Luke writes in the Acts that this happened to Paul at Philippi (Acts 16). He adds that twice, and once more, he was stoned, namely at Lystra; this also was done at the instigation of Jews, and indeed at a time when he had just conferred a great benefit on the Lystrans, calling them back to the worship of the true God, when they wanted to offer divine worship to him and to Barnabas. This was a memorable example of human fickleness. The Lystrans, who had proclaimed him to be God, soon overwhelmed him with stones and dragged him half dead out of the city, persuaded to do so by men from elsewhere. And what of the fact that the Jews opposed the Lystrans turning from their idols to the worship of their God, since they saw that in the same way they would become Christians? Some of the professors of evangelical doctrine today are like them: they are grieved if anyone, having renounced Papistical superstitions, passes over to the gospel and the purer faith of Christ, but does not subscribe to the confession drawn up or adopted by themselves. But this example of Paul ought to make the worshippers of Christ bold. For he who was able to preserve him amid the hail of stones, so that he did not perish, will also protect them, as long as he sees that their work will be useful to his Church.

units.la: Præterea terni quoq; naufragij meminit, quibus quartum tandem accessit, quando ex Iudæa vinctus Romam missus fuit. Addit in præsenti: Noctem ac diem in profundo egi. Chrysostomus illum tanto tempore à fluctibus iactatum esse, & natauisse putat. Sunt qui in ipsa maris abysso eum miraculosè (vt Ionam in ventre ceti aut lamiæ) seruatum fuisse dicant. At qua ratione hoc factum sit, non certò constat: mihi tamen non dubium est, hic singulare quid accidisse, in quo admirabili Dei virtute seruatus sit.
units.tr: Besides, he also recalls three shipwrecks, to which a fourth was finally added, when he was sent bound from Judaea to Rome. In the present passage he adds: a night and a day I spent in the deep. Chrysostom thinks that he was tossed by the waves for so long a time and swam. Some say that in the very abyss of the sea he was miraculously preserved, as Jonah was in the belly of the whale. But how this came about is not clearly known. Yet I have no doubt that something singular happened here, in which he was preserved by the wonderful power of God.

units.la: Obseruabis autem multa hoc loco recitari, quorum Lucas in Actis ne verbo quidem vno meminit. Huic enim satis fuit historiæ seriem cotexuisse, vt doceret, quibus progressibus aut incremen-tis Christiana religio propagata & aucta fuerit: non autem Pauli laudes conscribere. In præsenti vero Paulus aduersariorum improbitate & calumniandi libidine coactus ea etiam commemorat, quæ alioqui nunquâ voluisset iactare: & tamen modestiæ Christianæ memor in necessitate ista subinde insipientiæ culpam fatetur. Facit hoc ad commendationem sacræ historiæ, & eius scriptores in ea condendâ nihil affectui priuato dedisse, sed bona fide ea narrauisse docet, quæ cognitu vtilia & necessaria esse, Spiritus sanctus admonebat. Arguuntur etiam exemplo isto nostri seculi scriptores, qui dum bene meritorum de Ecclesia virorum vitam atque obitum describere instituunt, minutissima quæq; commemorando, & ipsi inepti fiunt, & illorum existimationi plurimùm derogant. Accidit hoc D. Luthero, cuius sermones quoque conuiuales & quæ in familiarioribus colloquiis dixit, quidam nescio quo genio ducti vulgarunt: in quibus multa tam inepta, tam absurda, imò scurrilia quoque sunt, vt ea tanto viro nunquam vel in mentem venisse, nedum ab eo dicta esse crediderim: nec poterat quicquam in illum scribi contumeliosius, & quod aduersarijs maiorem daret calumniandi occasionem. Sed ita accidere solet ineptis & nimijs hominum admiratoribus.
units.tr: You will notice, however, that many things are recounted in this place of which Luke in the Acts does not make even a single mention. For it was enough for Luke to weave together the sequence of the story, to show by what advances or increases the Christian religion was spread and grew, and not to write panegyrics on Paul. But here Paul, compelled by the wickedness of his opponents and their itch for slander, recalls even those things which otherwise he would never have wished to boast of; and yet, mindful of Christian modesty, under this necessity he from time to time confesses the fault of folly. This serves to commend sacred history, and it teaches that its writers, in composing it, gave nothing to private feeling, but related in good faith those things which the Holy Spirit showed to be useful and necessary to know. By this example our own century's writers are also rebuked, who, while they set about describing the lives and deaths of men who have deserved well of the Church, by recording the most trivial details make themselves foolish and greatly diminish those men's reputation. This has happened to Dr Luther, whose table talk and whatever he said in more familiar conversations certain persons, led by I know not what spirit, have published. In these there are many things so silly, so absurd, indeed even buffoonish, that I cannot believe such things ever came into that great man's mind, let alone that he uttered them. Nothing more insulting could be written against him, and it gave his opponents a greater occasion for slander. But this is what usually happens with foolish men and with admirers who go too far.

units.la: Sed omissis illis cum Paulo ad rerum ab ipso gestarum narrationem redeamus, qui à singularibus istis ad generaliora reuertitur, & multa congerit, quæ ei quotidie accidisse non est dubium. Inter quæ itinera & profectiones siue peregrinationes crebras primo loco ponit. Etenim quando primùm ad Christi fidem conuersus fuit, ex Damasco in Arabiam profectus, ei genti Euangelium prædicauit. Inde Damascum redijt, & inde mox fuga se recepit Hierosolymam propter Aretæ Regis insidias, vt in sequenti sermone dicetur. Hierosolymæ cum Iacobo & Petro contulit, tum. illis mansit diebus quindecim. Mox oraculo admonitus abijt ex vrbe, & à fratribus Cæsaream deductus est, qui eum inde Tharsum ablegarunt, quod ei erat solum natale: cui ista occasione annuntiauit Verbum salutis ac vitæ æternæ. Illic inuentum Barnabas abduxit Antiochiam. Vbi cum annum integrum egissent, Hierosolymam venerunt. Inde assumpto Marco Antiochiam reuersi, & mox ex Spiritus revelatione ab Ecclesia missi sunt, vt Euangelium longè lateque gentibus annuntiarent. Primò igitur Seleuciam profecti, inde in Cyprum traiecerunt, quam totam vnà cum Procos. Sergio Paulus ad Christi fidem converti. Hinc in Pamphyliam venit, mox in Pisidiam & Lycaoniam contendit, vbi eum (vt modò diximus) Lystrenses lapidarunt. Inde in Pamphyliam reuersi, per Pergam & Attaliam tandem Antiochiam redierunt. Vbi cum aliquandiu substitissent, lis exorta est de Circumcisione, quam aliqui gentibus ad fidem conversis obtrudere conabantur. Ideo per Phœniciam & Samariam cum Barnaba rursus Hierosolymam abijt ad Synodum, in qua de causa ista Apostoli statuerunt, vt Acto 15. Cap. scribitur, deq; ista professione intelligi debet, quod in epistola ad Galatas Cap. 2. habetur: vbi etiam indicatur, illum annum à conversione Pauli decimum quintum fuisse. Cùm verò Antiochiam redijsset, Ecclesias inuisere statuit, & assumpto Syla, Syriam atque Ciliciam lustrauit: vnde in Lycaoniam transiuit, & Lystris inuenit Timotheum, quo postea discipulo & collega fidissimo vsus est. Inde cùm Phrygiam & Galatiam peragrauissent, in Mysiam venerunt, cumq; in Troadem appulissent, Paulus ab Angelo in Macedoniam euocatus ad Philippos iter instituit. Ibi captus & virgis cæsus, tandemque dimissus per Amphipolim & Apolloniam ad Thessalonicenses venit, & ab his Berrhœam seconsulit. Ex Berrhœa Athenas profectus est, & inde Corinthum contendit. Ex Corintho, cùm illic sesquiannum docuisset, in Asiam traiecit, & venit Ephesum. Inde Hierosolymam adsestum ascendit, vnde Antiochiam redijt. Postea Phrygiam & Galaticam regionem denuo lustrauit, & tandem Ephesum iterum venit. Quo tempore priorem ad Corinthios epist. ab eo scriptam fuisse, suo loco diximus. Ex Epheso in Macedoniam traiecit, ex qua in Græciam quoq; transijt, cùm prius ex Macedonia posteriorem hanc epist. ad Corinthios misisset. Hæc ex ordine commemorare libuit, vt seriem rerum ab ipso gestarum & profectiones eius omnes complecterer: ex quibus satis euidenter apparet, non temere hic ab eo dici, quòd in itineribus sæpe fuerit. Id verò absq; multis laboribus & magna molestia fieri non potuit. Sunt enim peregrinationes longinquæ per se graues & laboriosæ, graviores autem fiunt, si ob causam aliquam, quæ cum odio & periculo coniunctæ est, suscipiantur: qualis omnino erat, quam Paulus agebat. Etenim cùm Iudæi iam ante gentibus exosi essent, Apostolis cum vtrisq; dimicandum erat, & iam in omnium ore erant voces illæ: Hi qui turbant orbem terrarum, venerunt etiam ad nos.
units.tr: But leaving those matters aside, let us return with Paul to the narrative of what he himself did. He moves from these particular events to more general ones and gathers many things that were certainly happening to him day by day. Among these he first lists his frequent journeys and travels. When he was first converted to faith in Christ, he went from Damascus into Arabia and preached the gospel to that people. He then returned to Damascus, and soon fled from there to Jerusalem to escape the plots of King Aretas, as will be said in the next sermon. At Jerusalem he conferred with James and Peter and stayed with them for fifteen days. Then, warned by an oracle, he left the city, and the brothers escorted him to Caesarea, from where they sent him away to Tarsus, which was his native place. There, on this occasion, he proclaimed the word of salvation and eternal life. Barnabas found him there and led him to Antioch. After they had spent a whole year there, they went to Jerusalem. Then, taking Mark with them, they returned to Antioch, and soon, by revelation of the Spirit, they were sent out by the Church to proclaim the gospel far and wide among the Gentiles. So they first set out for Seleucia, then crossed over to Cyprus, the whole island of which, together with the proconsul Sergius Paulus, was converted to faith in Christ. From there he came to Pamphylia, then made for Pisidia and Lycaonia, where, as we have just said, the people of Lystra stoned him. Then they returned to Pamphylia and, through Perga and Attalia, at last came back to Antioch. When they had stayed there for some time, a dispute arose about circumcision, which some were trying to impose on Gentiles who had come to the faith. So Paul, with Barnabas, went up again to Jerusalem through Phoenicia and Samaria, to the council, in which the apostles decided the matter, as is written in Acts chapter 15. What was said at that conference must be understood in the light of what is found in the letter to the Galatians, chapter 2, where it is also shown that this year was the fifteenth after Paul's conversion. When he had returned to Antioch, he resolved to visit the churches, and, taking Silas with him, he traversed Syria and Cilicia. From there he passed into Lycaonia and found Timothy at Lystra, whom he afterwards used as a most faithful disciple and colleague. Then, having travelled through Phrygia and Galatia, they came to Mysia, and when they had reached Troas, Paul was summoned by an angel into Macedonia and set out for Philippi. There he was seized, beaten with rods, and finally released; he passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia and came to the Thessalonians, and from them went on to Berea. From Berea he set out for Athens and from there hastened to Corinth. From Corinth, after he had taught there for a year and a half, he crossed over into Asia and came to Ephesus. From there he went up to Jerusalem for the feast, and from there returned to Antioch. Afterwards he again travelled through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, and at last came again to Ephesus. At that time, as we said in its place, he wrote the first letter to the Corinthians. From Ephesus he crossed into Macedonia, and from there he also passed into Greece, having earlier sent this second letter to the Corinthians from Macedonia. I have chosen to recount these things in order, so that I might embrace the sequence of what he did and all his journeys. From them it is quite clear that he does not say this here carelessly, that he was often on the road. Yet this could not be done without great toil and much hardship. Long journeys are in themselves burdensome and laborious, and they become more burdensome when they are undertaken for some cause joined with hatred and danger, which was entirely the case with Paul's journeys. For since the Jews were already hated by the Gentiles, the apostles had to fight on both fronts, and those words were already on everyone's lips: "These who have turned the world upside down have come here too" (Acts 17).

units.la: Quapropter, quàm multa quamque grauia in profectionibus istis passus sit, narrat amplius: In periculis fluminum, periculis latronum, periculis à meis gentilibus, periculis à gentibus (notari) periculis in ciuitatibus, propter seditiones, quæ passim per Iudæos aut alios improbos excitabantur, vt Corinthi, Ephesi & multis alijs in locis accidisse scimus: periculis in deserto, vbi ferè sitis, bestiæ & latrones infesti sunt: quæ omnia hodie adhuc experiuntur, qui per Arabiam iter faciunt: periculis in mari, quod toties traijciendum erat: periculis inter falsos fratres, qui passim obrepebant in Ecclesias, & quales erant, qui Corinthiacam quoque turbauerant. Denique in fatigatione (inquit) & ærumna mihi perpetuò versandum est. Est autem ærumna (vt Cicero definit) ægritudo laboriosa, vel labor qui effugi aut declinari nec potest, nec debet, quales reuera erant omnes illi, quibus Apostolus fatigabatur, vtpote à Deo impositi, & cum eius vocatione coniuncti, quam deferere non poterat. Addit his vigilias, famem, sitim & ieiunia (voluntaria nimirum) quæ interdum sibijpsi indicebat, vt precibus posset ardentius vacare. Denique frigora quoque & nuditatem se passum dicit, quæ duo in longinquis peregrinationibus vix possunt ca- ueri, ne ab opulentissimis quidem.
units.tr: Therefore he goes on to tell in more detail how many and how grievous were the things he suffered on these journeys: "In perils of rivers, perils of robbers, perils from my own countrymen, perils from the Gentiles (note this), perils in the cities, on account of the seditions that were stirred up everywhere by the Jews or other wicked men, as we know happened at Corinth, Ephesus and in many other places; perils in the wilderness, where thirst, wild beasts and robbers are usually a menace, dangers which people who travel through Arabia still meet today; perils at sea, which had to be crossed so often; perils among false brothers, who crept into the churches everywhere, and such as those who had also disturbed the church at Corinth." Finally he says: "In weariness and toil I must constantly labour." Now toil (as Cicero defines it) is a painful sickness, or a labour that cannot and should not be escaped or avoided. All those burdens with which the apostle was wearied were of exactly this kind, since they were imposed by God and joined with his calling, which he could not abandon. He adds to these his watchings, hunger, thirst and fastings (voluntary, of course), which he sometimes imposed on himself so that he might give himself more ardently to prayer. Lastly, he says that he suffered cold and nakedness, two things which in long journeys can scarcely be avoided even by the very wealthy.

units.la: Docet autem diligens huius loci consideratio, quanto cum labore & quàm multis cum periculis sanctissimorum hominum Euangelij doctrina per orbem terrarum propagata fit. Est hoc magnum bonitatis Dei argumentum, qui seruos suos ita exerceri voluit, vt infelicis & ingrati mundi salutì consuleret.
units.tr: A careful consideration of this passage teaches us with how much labour and how many dangers the doctrine of the gospel was spread throughout the world by these most holy men. This is a great proof of the goodness of God, who wished his servants to be so exercised in order to provide for the salvation of an unhappy and ungrateful world.

units.la: Peregrinatio Paulina s. num periculorum. Lib. 4. Thusc. (vt Cicero) & 2. de Finib. Euangelium quanto cum labore propagatum? consuleret. Nimirum ergo improbi & ingrati sunt, qui de illius veritate dubitant, vel etiam illud insolenter contemnunt. Quis enim credat, sanctos IESV CHRISTI apostolos, qui domi suae quiescere poterant, pro re dubia & incerta voluisse tot tantaq; pericula subire, cum nulla in terris vel opum vel honorum spes affulgeret? Dei ergo hoc opus fuit, qui & ipsos incitavit, & ad ista ferenda fortes atque robustos fecit, & ab ipsis praedicatam doctrinam inter tot obstacula in hunc usque diem defendit. Quam vero absurdi & iniqui sunt hodie, qui cum Apostolorum cultores dici & haberi velint, doctrinam tamen eam persequuntur, quam ipsi tanto cum labore propagaverunt, & tandem proprio sanguine confirmarunt? Sunt illi praeponere religioni, & ideo neminem movere debet eorum exemplum: nostrum autem fuerit, doctrinam salutis constanter tenere & sequi. Quis enim venia dignos dixerit eos, qui sua ignavia sibi vel eripi, vel ex manibus elabi patiuntur salutem, quae Filij Dei sanguine nobis parta, & per tot discrimina sanctissimorum hominum nobis annuntiata est?
units.tr: Paul's journeys, or the number of his dangers (Cicero, Tusculan Disputations, book 4; and On Ends, book 2). How great a labour it was to spread the gospel? Surely, then, they are wicked and ungrateful who doubt its truth or even insolently despise it. For who would believe that the holy apostles of Jesus Christ, who could have rested at home, wished to undergo so many and such great dangers for a matter that was doubtful and uncertain, when no hope of wealth or honours shone upon them on earth? So this was the work of God, who both stirred them up, and made them brave and strong to bear these things, and has defended the doctrine they preached amid so many obstacles down to this very day. How absurd and unjust, then, are those today who want to be called and considered worshippers of the apostles, and yet persecute that same doctrine which they propagated at such great cost, and at last confirmed with their own blood! They prefer something else to religion, and therefore their example ought to move no one; rather, it is our part to hold fast to the doctrine of salvation and follow it. For who would count worthy of pardon those who by their own sloth allow salvation to be snatched from them or to slip from their hands, a salvation won for us by the blood of the Son of God and proclaimed to us through so many dangers of most holy men?

units.la: At postquam Paulus ea, quae ipsi prae aliis Apostolis extraordinarie accidebat, recensuit, nunc ad id transit, quod ipsi perpetuum erat, sic dicens: Absq; ijs quae extrinsecus, scilicet mihi accidunt, urget agmen illud in me quotidie consurgens, solicitudo nimirum pro omnibus Ecclesijs. Per ea quae extrinsecus accidebant, intelligit labores & molestias, quae ipsi ab alijs exhibebantur, qui eum vel dolo vel aperta vi infestabant, & quibus poterat carere, si illi fuissent aequiores: & ideo distinguit ea ab illis curis atque laboribus, quos ipse sibi imponebat, ut proprie ad suam functionem pertinentes. Hos autem vocat ἐπιπρυσχον quotidianam. Ita dicitur proprie incursus aut agmen multorum, qui nobis circumquaque imminent, ut armis atque telis aliquem comminus & eminus opprimant. Itaque verborum Pauli sensus est: Etsi hostes illi aperti vnà cum falsis fratribus quiescerent, tamen quae mihi quotidie incumbit negotiorum atque curarum moles abunde sufficeret ad me fatigandum. Et mox, quae illa sit, indicat: Solicitudo nimirum pro omnibus Ecclesijs. Hanc vero sibi ut propriam tribuit, quia eam non poterat deponere, cum peculiaris & a Deo destinatus esset gentium Apostolus. Erat autem ea multiplex. Passim enim multi inueniebantur rudes adhuc & rerum imperiti, quos erudiri oportebat: infirmi, quos confirmari necesse erat: affligti & tentationibus obnoxij, qui consolatione efficaci opus habebant: delinquentes item & vitijs dediti, qui in viam erant revocandi. Accedebant hus publica pericula ex persecutionibus, quibus & Romani Imperatores & Iudaei nascentem vbique terrarum veri Dei cognitionem opprimere conabantur. Hinc tristia nascebantur multorum fratrum exilia, qui incertis sedibus oberrabant, & plerumque ad ipsum confluebant, ut eius consilio atque consolationibus subleuarentur. Accedebant his frequentes nuntij & literae de Ecclesijs vel turbatis vel euersis, aut saltem dissipatis, quae novos dolores atque curas pariebant. Merito igitur se agmine quodam laborum atque curarum vr geri dicit. Etenim grauis & laboriosa est vnius domus amplioris administratio, etiamsi omnes in e i officium faciant: quod si vero plerique vel ignavi sint, vel etiam contumaces, habet paterfamilias iustam & amplam quiritandi materiam. Quam grauem ergo prouinciam Paulus sustinuit, cui Deus omnium, quae inter gentes tunc fuerunt, Ecclesiarum curam imposuerat? Apparet hoc ex assiduis (de quibus paulo ante dictum est) peregrinationibus, hoc solo nomine suscepit: ex precibus, quas dies noctesq; fundebat: ex epistolis, quibus Ecclesias vel afflictas consolatus est, vel secuturas & oscitantes admonuit, vel etiam vitijs infectas corripuit atque correxit.
units.tr: But after Paul has recounted those things that happened to him in an extraordinary way beyond the other apostles, he now passes to what was constant for him, saying thus: "Apart from those things that come from outside, namely, that crowd which rises against me every day presses upon me, that is, anxiety for all the churches." By "the things that came from outside" he means the labours and troubles that were inflicted on him by others, who harassed him either by treachery or by open force, and from which he could have been free had they been more fair to him. Therefore he distinguishes these from the cares and labours which he imposed on himself, as belonging properly to his office. These he calls the daily pressure [ἐπίστασις]. Thus the word properly refers to the onrush or crowd of many people who press on us from every side, so as to overwhelm someone with arms and missiles, at close quarters and from a distance. So the sense of Paul's words is this: even if those open enemies, along with the false brothers, were at rest, still the mass of business and cares that falls upon me every day would be more than enough to wear me out. And then he indicates what that is: "anxiety, that is, for all the churches." He claims this as his own, because he could not lay it down, since he was a special apostle to the Gentiles, appointed by God. Now this anxiety took many forms. Everywhere there were many who were still raw and ignorant of things, who needed to be taught; weak ones, who needed to be strengthened; afflicted ones, exposed to temptations, who needed effective consolation; and also those who were sinning and given over to vices, who had to be called back to the right way. To these were added public dangers from persecutions, by which both the Roman emperors and the Jews tried to crush the knowledge of the true God, which was beginning to spread everywhere. From this arose the sad exiles of many brothers, who wandered about without fixed homes and for the most part flocked to him, to be supported by his counsel and consolations. In addition, there were frequent messages and letters about churches that were either disturbed, or overthrown, or at least scattered, which produced fresh sorrows and cares. Rightly, then, he says that he is borne along in a kind of crowd of labours and cares. For even the management of one large household is hard and laborious, even if all the members do their duty; but if most of them are either lazy or even stubborn, the head of the household has a just and ample reason for complaint. How heavy, then, was the charge Paul bore, to whom God had entrusted the care of all the churches that then existed among the nations! This appears from his constant journeys (of which we spoke a little earlier), undertaken for this one purpose alone; from the prayers which he poured out day and night; and from the letters by which he consoled churches that were afflicted, admonished those who were lukewarm and slow to act, and rebuked and corrected those infected with vices.

units.la: Docent ista, Ecclesiae gubernationem non esse prouinciam eiusmodi, quae carni voluptate pari at, sed plena laboris & periculi. Retinet enim perpetuo ingenium suum mundus, & semper erit curarum atque laborum materia ijs, quibus cum illo res est. Imo, ut Cap.decimo audiuimus, militia instar est Ecclesiae & Verbi Dei ministerii: & eo grauius fit onus istud laborum, si cogitemus, olim ad Christi tribunal rationem reddendam esse, qua fide in illo quisq; versatus sit. Idem dici potest de ijs, qui Reipub. administrant. Nam si hi quoque officium velint facere, nunquam non se ad nouas curas, vigilias & labores vocari sentient. Sunt ergo parum prudentes, qui non expectata vocatio ne legitima sese intrudunt: ingrati autem nimis, qui illos oderunt, atq; contumacia sua negotium facessunt pro publica salute laborantibus. Qui vero vel ad Ecclesiae vel Reipub. gubernacula legitime vocati sunt, ij Paului imitentur, neque eos laborum siue curarum pigeat. Etenim ad laborem
units.tr: These things teach that the governance of the Church is not a task of the sort that offers pleasure to the flesh, but one full of labour and danger.
