For the world keeps its nature always, and it will always be a source of cares and toils for those who have to deal with it. Indeed, as we heard in the tenth chapter, the ministry of the Word is like a warfare, and the burden of these labours becomes heavier if we consider that one day an account of how faithfully each has conducted himself must be rendered at the tribunal of Christ. The same can be said of those who administer the commonwealth. For if they too wish to do their duty, they will always feel themselves called to new cares, watches and labours. Those therefore are not very wise who thrust themselves in without a lawful and expected calling; and those are too ungrateful who hate them and make trouble for the men who labour for the public welfare by their own obstinacy. But those who have been lawfully called to the helm of the Church or of the commonwealth should imitate Paul, and not be wearied by labours or cares. For Paul bore the care of all the Churches upon himself with labour.

units.la: Paulo omnium Ecclesiarum cura incubuit.
units.tr: Paul bore the care of all the Churches upon himself with labour.

units.la: Ecclesiae gubernatio laboriosa. omnes in primo parente nostro damnati sumus. Quid ergo optabilius fuerit, quàm si quod omnino ferendum ess, in Dei domo ferre contingat, qui cùm remunerator sit liberalissimus, debito præmio nunquam fraudabit eos, qui hìc officium suum fideliter fecerint. At qui ignauiores se præbent, vel etiam mala fide agunt, ij fere laboribus & periculis grauioribus sese intricant, & tandem pœnas acerbissimas luunt.
units.tr: The governance of the Church is laborious. We are all condemned in our first parent. What therefore would be more to be wished for than that, if something altogether burdensome must be borne, it should happen to be borne in the house of God, which, since its Rewarder is most bountiful, will never defraud of the due reward those who here faithfully perform their office? But those who show themselves more slothful, or who even act in bad faith, entangle themselves for the most part in heavier labours and dangers, and at last pay the most bitter penalties.

units.la: Porrò explicat Paulus quod de solicitudine pro omnibus Ecclesijs sibi incumbete dixit. Quis affligitur (inquit) quin ego affligar? Quis offenditur, quin ego vrar? Duorum meminit, quibus Ecclesiæ plerunque exercentur atque turbantur, Afflictionum nimirum & Scandalorum. Quoad primum, vocabulo ἀσθενεῖ vtitur, quod proprie significat infirmum esse, id quod ferè ex afflictionibus accidit, quæ tam animi quàm corporis vires debilitant. Atqui tunc plena afflictionum & periculorum erant omnia. Hïc verò συμπάθειαν sibi tribuit, qua aliorum afflictionibus perinde atque proprijs tangatur. Et sanè aliter fieri non poterat. Qui enim tanto gloriæ Dei & salutis hominum desiderio flagrabat, vt se sponte laboribus & periculis obijceret, non potuit non toto animo discruciari, si Ecclesias abs se constitutas turbari & credentes ab hostium immanissimorum rabie infestari, eos denique vel in exilium eiectos, vel in carceribus conclusos, vel etiam crudeliter neca-tos esse audiebat, cum quibus amicitiam nouam paulò ante contraxerat in Christo. Eadè fuit scandalorum siue offendiculorum ratio, quibus tunc similiter omnia scatebat. Aliù enim offendebat inuista hostiū Euangelij, & imprimis Iudæorū, contumacia: aliū Romani Imperij successus, et latior vicinorum siue ciuium idololatriæ deditorum fortuna: alios sciolorum leuitas, qui cum idolothytis communicabant: alios multorum licentia, qui sub Christianæ professionis prætexru quidùis impunè designabant, cùm politicis legibus scelera non punirentur, Ecclesiæ verò disciplinam proteruiores illi contemnerent. Vrebant ista omnia non sine acutissimo dolore sanctissimum illud Apostoli pestus: eoque grauior erat dolor iste, quòd non semper in promptu erat remedium, quo scandala illa vel è medio tolli, vel saltem leniri possent. Nec caret Emphasi, quòd infinitè de omnibus, qui vel affligebantur vel offendebantur, loquitur, vt se absque personarum respectu de omnibus solicitum esse testetur.
units.tr: Paul goes on to explain what he said about the care that rests upon him for all the Churches. "Who is weak," he says, "and I am not weak? Who is offended, and I do not burn?" He mentions two things by which the Churches are for the most part harassed and troubled: afflictions, namely, and scandals. As to the first, he uses the word ἀσθενεῖ [is weak], which properly means to be infirm, something that mostly comes from afflictions, which weaken the strength both of mind and of body. And indeed at that time everything was full of afflictions and dangers. Here he ascribes to himself συμπάθειαν [sympathy], by which he is touched by the afflictions of others just as by his own. And indeed it could not be otherwise. For he who burned with such a desire for the glory of God and the salvation of men, that he willingly exposed himself to labours and dangers, could not but be tormented in his whole mind when he heard that the Churches he had founded were disturbed, and that believers were harassed by the raging of most savage enemies, and finally that some had been cast into exile, or shut up in prisons, or even cruelly put to death, men with whom he had a little before formed a new friendship in Christ. The same was the nature of the scandals or stumbling-blocks, with which everything was similarly teeming at that time. For the unbending obstinacy of the enemies of the Gospel, and above all of the Jews, offended one man; another was offended by the successes of the Roman Empire and the wider prosperity of neighbours or fellow citizens given over to idolatry; others by the levity of the half-learned, who communicated with idol-offerings; others by the licence of many, who under the pretext of the Christian profession committed whatever crimes they pleased with impunity, since crimes were not punished by the civil laws, while those more shameless men despised the discipline of the Church. All these things burned that most holy breast of the Apostle not without the sharpest pain; and this pain was the heavier because a remedy by which those scandals could be removed from the midst, or at least softened, was not always at hand. Nor is there lack of emphasis in his speaking so universally of all who were either afflicted or offended, so that he testifies that he is anxious about all, without regard to persons.

units.la: Discant autem hoc exemplo Ecclesiarum ministri, vt erga suæ fidei credito s affecti esse debeant: Vt nimirum sibi ipsis accidere putent, quod illis vel omnibus publicè, vel singulis priuatim accidit. Deinde, vt vrantur scandalis, & vt ferre nequeant ea, quæ vel Dei gloriæ vel aliorum saluti incommodant. Pertinet hoc ipsum ad magistratus quoque, & huius studij exemplum memorabile in Dauide habemus, qui vt populo parceretur, gladium Dei in se & domum suam conuerti cupiebat. At si nostri sæculi mores consideremus, quàm multa hïc vbique desiderantur? Quotus enim quisque est, quem aliena pericula serió tangant? Ministri certè Ecclesias, quibus aliquandiu præfuerunt, priuati commodi causa vel commutant, vel deserunt, & ita se mercenarios esse produnt. Principes bella mouent non necessaria, & ipsi publicarum calamitatum præcipui authores sunt. Alij ex populi oppressione ditescunt, aut saltem luxuriantur. Et qui neutrum faciunt, ignaui tamen ad omnia conniuent. Quem verò dabis, quem verè vrant, quæ vbique cernuntur, scandala? Vtinam non darent ea, qui debebant è medio auferre. Sed & in vulgo eadem oscitantia obtinuit, vbi omnis loci & ordinis homines, dummodo ipsis bene sit, facilè negligunt omnia, quæ Ecclesijs totis & singulis priuatim aduersa accidunt. Oremus ergo summum illum pastorum principem, Dominum nostrum IESVM CHRISTVM, vt ille rebus afflictis opem ferat, & fidos operarios extrudat, quibus & ipsius gloria & Ecclesiarum salus cordi sit. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let the ministers of the Churches learn from this example to be affected towards the trust committed to their faith: namely, that they should think that what happens to these individuals in private, or to all of them publicly, happens to themselves. Then, that they should be burned by scandals, and be unable to bear those things which hinder either the glory of God or the salvation of others. This applies also to the magistrates, and we have a memorable example of this zeal in David, who, that the people might be spared, desired the sword of God to be turned against himself and his house. But if we consider the manners of our age, how many things are everywhere lacking here? For how few are there whom the dangers of others touch seriously? Ministers indeed either change or desert the Churches over which they have presided for a time, for the sake of private advantage, and so they show themselves to be hirelings. Princes wage unnecessary wars, and they themselves are the chief authors of public calamities. Others grow rich, or at least live in luxury, from the oppression of the people. And those who do neither, yet, being idle, turn a blind eye to everything. And whom will you give, whom truly do the scandals that are seen everywhere burn? Would that those who ought to remove them did not themselves supply them. But the same carelessness has also prevailed among the common people, where men of every place and rank, provided that things go well for themselves, easily neglect all the things that go badly for the Churches, both for all and for each individually. Let us therefore pray to that highest Prince of pastors, our Lord Jesus Christ, that he may bring help to afflicted affairs, and send forth faithful workers to whose hearts both his own glory and the salvation of the Churches may be dear. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LIII.
units.tr: HOMILY LIII.

units.la: Si gloriari oporteat, de iis quæ infirmitatis meæ sunt, gloriabor. Deus & Pater Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, qui est benedictus in sæcula, nouit quòd non mentiar. In vrbe damasci gentis præfectus nomine Aretæ regis præsidio tenebat Damascenorum vrbem, cupiens me præhendere. Et per fenestram in sporta demis- sus fui per mœnia, & manus eius effugi.
units.tr: "If I must boast, I will boast of the things that concern my infirmity. The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ever, knows that I do not lie. In Damascus the governor of the nation, acting under King Aretas, kept guard over the city of the Damascenes, wishing to seize me. And I was let down through a window in a basket over the walls, and escaped his hands."

units.la: Quamuis fideles Dei serui suæ infirmitatis sibi probè conscij nequaquam superbiant, sed po- tius de officio faciendo soliciti sint: ijdem tamen aduersariorum calumniis & mundi ingrati- tudine sæpius coguntur de seipsis liberius & honorificentius aliqua dicere, ne Dei gloria in ipsis periclitetur. At tunc diligenter videndum est, vt in hunc vnum scopum respiciant, neue eo prætextu aliquid ambitiosius faciant cum aliorum contemptu. Et proderit hic Pauli exemplum obseruauis- se, qui etsi multis sese tueatur aduersus eos, qui ipsum & doctrinam eius apud Corinthios conaban- tur in contemptum adducere, hunc tamen scopum sibi solum propositum habet, vt illos in fidei pu- ritate retineat, & Christo suam gloriam vendicet. Ideo rerum abs se gestarum narrationem ita instituit, vt se omnia pro Christo, & non propria, sed illius virtute fecisse testetur. Facit ad horum confirmationem præsens iste locus, quem modò recitauimus.
units.tr: Faithful servants of God, aware of their own weakness, are never proud but are rather anxious to do their duty. Yet they are often forced by the slanders of their opponents and the ingratitude of the world to speak of themselves more freely and with more honour, lest the glory of God be put at risk through them. In such cases we must take care that they look to this one goal, and that they do not use that pretext to do anything more ambitious, to the contempt of others. Here it will be useful to observe the example of Paul, who, although he defended himself against those who tried to bring him and his teaching into contempt among the Corinthians, nevertheless had this one aim before him: to keep them in the purity of the faith and to claim for Christ his glory. Therefore he framed his account of what he had done so as to testify that he had done everything for Christ, and by Christ's power and not his own. The present passage, which we have just read, supports this.

units.la: Initio enim protestatur, se inutilem de istis rebus dicere, & simul aduersarios perstringit, qui suis calumniis ipsum hæc dicere cogant. Si gloriari oporteat (inquit) de ijs quæ infirmitatis meæ sunt, gloriabor. Sensus est: Ego quidem malim ab istorum commemoratione prorsus abstinere, sed quia me huc adigit aduersariorum meorum iniquitas, qui toti in eo sunt, vt me oppresso Veritatis quoque doctrinam è medio tollant, agedum glorientur illi, vt lober generis nobilitate, eloquentia, vulgi applausu, & aliis eiusmodi, quæ mundi iudicio magnifica videntur: me tamen illi nunquam eo adducent, vt eorum exemplum secutus me ijsdem venditem: quin potius, cùm omnino aliquid dicendum sit, ego de illis gloriabor, quæ meæ infirmitatis sunt, id est, quæ me hominem infirmum, & vt alij homines casibus omnis generis obnoxium, ideoque opis diuinæ indigum esse ostendunt. Itaque infirmitatis nomine omnia ea intelligit, quæ ipsum exercebant, vt se nihil posse sentiret, nisi Dei gratia & virtute sustentaretur.
units.tr: At the outset he declares that he speaks of these things reluctantly, and at the same time he rebukes those opponents who force him to say them by their slanders. "If I must boast," he says, "I will boast of the things that concern my infirmity." The sense is this: I would rather abstain altogether from mentioning those men; but since the injustice of my opponents compels me to it, who strive by every means, once I am crushed, to remove also the teaching of the truth from the midst, let them boast, if they like, of their noble birth, their eloquence, the applause of the crowd, and other such things that seem splendid by the world's judgement. Yet they will never bring me to follow their example and sell myself by the same means. Rather, since something must be said, I will boast of the things that concern my infirmity, that is, of what shows me to be a weak man, subject like other men to every kind of misfortune, and therefore in need of divine help. Thus by "infirmity" he means all those things that afflicted him, so that he felt he could do nothing unless he was sustained by the grace and power of God.

units.la: Cernitur hoc loco discrimen inter Christi ministros veros & fucatos. Hi ijs superbiunt, quæ apud mundum gloriosa sunt & magnifica, qualia sunt, opes, dignitates, principum fauores, amici- tiæ multorum, victoriæ, pompa externa, &c. Quia enim de Dei gloria non multum soliciti sunt, eam quæ ex hominibus est, gloriam captant, sicuti de Iudæorum scribis Christus olim dixit. E contra illi, quia huius mundi gloriam iampridem calcauerunt, in eo suum decus & honorem con- sistere putant, si multa faciant & ferant propter Christum, interque ea se præsenti Dei auxilio subleuari sentiant. Tantum ergo inter germanos Dei seruos & personatos siue perfidos discri- men est, quantum inter matronam frugi & impudentem adulteram. Hæc mundo muliebri immodicum delectatur, amatorum præconijs & cantilenis ad libidinem prouocandam composi- tis, donis item & munusculis adulterorum suorum superbit. Illius verò animum gaudio iucun- dissimo reficit, si domum fideliter administret, si suum studium atque labores marito probari, & hunc propter ipsam (vt Solomon ait) apud alios in honore & pretio esse videat. Arguunt i- sta fastuosos & delicatos nostri sæculi antistites, qui Apostolicorum nomen sibi vendicant, cùm Sardanapalos vita, luxu autem & fastu Persarum satrapas atque Reges superent. Pudeat e- tiam hic suæ vanitatis Euangelicæ doctrinæ professores aliquos, qui potentum atque diuitum a- micitias ambitiosè venantur, eos autem sua familiaritate non meliores, sed insolentiores, imò fidis Christi ministris iniquiores reddunt. Quo vno argumento facile colligi potest, illos Christi ne gotium non bona fide apud istos agere, qui ipsos non in tanto pretio haberent, si Domino fideles es- sent. Debent ista ad se quoque transferre, qui magistratum gerunt: ne videlicet gloriosum hoc sibi esse putent, si magni fiant ab improbis Legum bonarū dissipatoribus, & religionis hostibus, vel si ex publico aut iniquis largitionibus ditescat: sed potius ex eo laudè quærat, si improbis exosi, ijsdem terrori sint, si respub. fideliter curent, si denique cū Samuele possint dicere: En testificamini de me coram Domino, cuius bouem aut asinum accepi: num alicui vim feci aut iniuriam: num ab aliquo munus accepi expiatorium, vt ipsi conniuerem? Eadem debet omnibus cura esse priuatim. Impri- mis tamen hoc in religione obseruandum est. Putant aliqui gloriosum plane esse, si omnibus probetur: at hoc plerunque vel ignauiæ vel perfidiæ argumentum est. Etenim gloria Christianorum est.
units.tr: In this place a distinction is seen between true ministers of Christ and counterfeit ones. The latter take pride in what is glorious and splendid in the eyes of the world: such things as wealth, dignities, the favour of princes, the friendship of many, victories, outward display, and so on. Because they are not much concerned for the glory of God, they seek the glory that comes from men, as Christ once said of the scribes of the Jews. The true ministers, on the other hand, having long since trampled underfoot the glory of this world, think that their honour and dignity consist in doing and bearing many things for Christ, and in feeling themselves upheld by the present help of God in the midst of them. So great, then, is the difference between the genuine servants of God and the masked or faithless ones, as great as between a respectable matron and a shameless adulteress. The one delights immoderately in womanly adornment, in the praises and songs of lovers composed to stir up lust, and she prides herself on the gifts and little presents of her paramours. The other is refreshed in her heart by the most pleasant joy if she manages the household faithfully, and sees her labour and diligence approved by her husband, and sees him, because of her (as Solomon says), held in honour and esteem among others. These things rebuke the proud and pampered bishops of our age, who claim for themselves the name of Apostles, though in their way of life they outdo Sardanapalus, and in luxury and pride they surpass the satraps and kings of Persia. Some professors of the Gospel doctrine should also be ashamed of their vanity, who hunt eagerly after the friendship of the powerful and the rich, and who by that familiarity make them not better but more insolent, and indeed more hostile to the faithful ministers of Christ. From this one argument it can easily be gathered that those who do not have so high an esteem for these men would not deal in good faith with Christ's business among them, if they were faithful to the Lord. These things ought also to be applied to those who hold the magistracy: lest they think it glorious to be held in high regard by wicked dissipators of good laws and enemies of religion, or if their wealth grows from public funds through unjust gifts. Rather, let them seek praise from this, that they are hated by the wicked and a terror to them, that they faithfully care for the commonwealth, and that finally they can say with Samuel: "Behold, testify against me before the Lord: whose ox or ass have I taken? Have I done violence or injury to anyone? Have I received a bribe from anyone, to close my eyes to it?" The same care ought to be taken by everyone in private. Yet above all this must be observed in religion. Some think it is plainly a glory if they are approved by everyone; but this is for the most part a proof of either cowardice or faithlessness. For the glory of Christians is:

units.la: 1. Sam. 12. Crux, quæ vt patientiæ materiam nobis præbet, ita diuinæ gratiæ experimenta sentit, & tandem coronam iustitiæ ijs propinat, qui in finem vsque perseuerauerint. At quæcumque in hoc mundo magnifica videntur, ea vana, fluxa & momentanea sunt. Nam omnis caro fœnum, & omnis gloria carnis flos agri. Vide Isa. 40. Eccles. 1. &c.
units.tr: 1 Sam. 12. The cross, which provides us with the matter of patience, likewise experiences the trials of divine grace, and at last bestows the crown of righteousness on those who persevere to the end. But whatever seems splendid in this world is vain, fleeting and momentary. For "all flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is as the flower of the field." See Isa. 40; Eccles. 1, etc.

units.la: At poterat superbis illis & ambitiosis incredibile videri quod Paulus dicebat. Solent enim huiusmodi homines quosuis alios ex semetipsis æstimare. Ideo quod dixit, grauissima asseueratione confirmat: Deus & Pater Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, qui est benedictus in sæcula, nouit quòd non mentiar. Iusiurandum interponit, quia (vt iam sæpe diximus) non tam de eius existimatione, quàm Dei gloria & multorum aliorum salute agebatur. Testem vero sistit Deum, & eum quidem, qui sit Pater IESV CHRISTI. Sunt enim duo hæc contrahenda, ne putemus aliud esse Deum, alium vero Patrem Christi. Etenim non alius est verus Deus, nisi qui idem IESV CHRISTI Pater est, & hunc vnum Christiani homines agnoscunt & colunt, vt in prioris epist. Cap. nono Apostolus diserte docuit. Confutantur ergo Iudæi & Turcæ, qui Deum quidem illum profitentur, qui Cæli & terræ Creator sit, at Filium huius IESVM CHRISTVM aperte negant. Quia enim (vt diximus) hic solus est Deus verus, qui Filium ex seipso sibi consubstantialem & coæternum genuit, quique vnus est in tribus distinctis personis, illi Deum falsum sibi ipsis fingunt, dum Filium ab illo diuellunt. Particula autem quæ additur: Qui est benedictus in sæcula, tam ad Patrem quàm ad Christum referri potest. In epist. ad Romanos diserte Christo tribuitur, & euidens est diuinitatis eius æternæ testimonium.
units.tr: Yet to those proud and ambitious men what Paul said might have seemed incredible, for such people are accustomed to judge everyone else by themselves. Therefore he confirms what he said with the gravest oath: "The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ever, knows that I do not lie." He interposes an oath because, as we have often said already, the matter concerned not so much his own reputation as the glory of God and the salvation of many others. He calls God as witness, and God as the Father of Jesus Christ. These two things must be held together, lest we think that God is one and the Father of Christ another. For there is no other true God than the one who is also the Father of Jesus Christ, and this is the one whom Christian people acknowledge and worship, as the Apostle clearly taught in the ninth chapter of the earlier epistle. Therefore the Jews and the Turks are refuted, who indeed profess that God is the Creator of heaven and earth, but openly deny his Son, Jesus Christ. For, as we have said, he alone is the true God who from himself begat a Son consubstantial and coeternal with himself, and who is one in three distinct persons. Those who tear the Son away from him fashion for themselves a false God. The clause that follows, "who is blessed for ever," can be referred both to the Father and to Christ. In the epistle to the Romans it is clearly attributed to Christ, and it is a manifest testimony to his eternal divinity.

units.la: Quoad vero huius loci argumentum, obseruatu dignum est, quòd rursus iurat Apostolus. Nam eius exemplo docemur, licitum esse, vt iuremus in causa seria & graui. Nam quod Anabaptistæ obijciunt, partim friuolum, partim seditiosum est, vt alibi demonstrauimus. Interim meminerimus, nonaliam esse formam iurisiurandi legitimam, quàm quæ per Dei nomen concipitur, & qua hic testis citatur, qui vt solus omnia nouit, ita solus veraces tueri, periuros autè punire potest. Ideo diserta de hac re Dei præcepta extant, de quibus cum alibi dictum sit, eadem in præsenti repetere non est opus.
units.tr: As for the subject of this passage, it is worth noting that the Apostle again swears an oath. From his example we are taught that it is lawful to swear an oath in a serious and weighty matter. As for what the Anabaptists object, it is partly frivolous and partly seditious, as we have shown elsewhere. Meanwhile let us remember that there is no other lawful form of oath than the one that is framed by the name of God, and by which this witness is called upon, who, as he alone knows all things, so he alone can defend the truthful and punish perjurers. Therefore God's precepts on this matter are plain, and since these have been discussed elsewhere, there is no need to repeat them here.

units.la: Porro quod initio profeslatus est Paulus, id narratione rei gestæ confirmat, quæ singulare habet infirmitatis exemplum: quia periculum fuit maximum, & ipse fugam sibi consuluit: interea autem Dei ope seruatus, non modò incolumis euasit, verumetiam animosior & fortior ad officium redijt. Et probè seruiebat exemplum hoc causæ præsenti. Primò, quia tyrocinij instar fuit, quo Paulum Deus voluit exerceri. Itaque simul arguebat pseudapostolorum ignauiam, qui nihil simile vnquam passi erant, imò ita se gerebant, vt nihil huius ipsis esset timendum à mundo, cui soli cupiebant placere. Deinde plurimum faciebat ad diluendum omnem suspicionem, cum res omnibus nota esset, & eandem ita narret, vt de se quidem nihil aliud quàm metum, tripidationem, fugam denique prædicet, fratrum vero virtutem commendet, qui contra Regis voluntatem & leges publicas pro ipso periculum subierint maximum: adhæc omnem liberationis suæ gloriam cum omnibus, quæ ab eo tempore fecerit, ad vnum Deum authorem referrat. Narrat historiam hanc Lucas Act. nono Cap. series autem temporis, quo hoc factum est, ex Capite primo epistolæ ad Galatas peti debet, & ex vtriusque loci collatione talis potest colligi: Paulus cum ad fidem Christi conuersus & ab Anania baptizatus esset, illico prædicandi occasionem captauit: & quia sciebat, se gentibus designatum esse Apostolum, in vicinam Arabiam se contulit, vbi nemo Apostolorum adhuc Euangelium prædicauerat: & vbi hanc Euangelij prædicatione illustrauit, Damascum redijt, nimirum alio profecturus. Attamen cum multa se offerret quotidie contra Iudæos disputandi occasio, aliquandiu illic hæsit: donec Iudæorum insidiæ ipsum de loci mutatione cogitare coegerunt. Hi enim Aretæ Regis præfectum instigarunt, vt eum comprehendere tentaret. Et credibile est, non absque Regis voluntate hoc factum fuisse, qui procul dubio propter religionis flatum, in regno suo mutatum Paulo iniquior fuit. Itaque portis præsidia imposuit, ne qua effet elabendi via: quæ causa fuit, vt qui illic iam erant Christiani, illum sportæ impositum ex muro demiserint, &c. Habet autem historia hæc multa dignissima obseruatu, quæ ex ordine considerabimus.
units.tr: Moreover, what Paul professed at the beginning, he confirms by the narrative of the event, which provides a singular example of weakness: for the danger was very great, and he himself sought flight for his own safety. Meanwhile, however, preserved by the help of God, he not only escaped unharmed but returned to his duty more spirited and braver. And this example served the present cause well. First, because it was like an apprenticeship through which God willed Paul to be trained. Thus it at the same time rebuked the cowardice of the false apostles, who had never suffered anything similar, indeed who so conducted themselves that they had nothing of this kind to fear from the world, whose favour alone they desired to win. Next, it did very much to dispel every suspicion, since the matter was known to all, and he relates it in such a way that he speaks of himself only as fear, trembling, and finally flight, but commends the courage of the brothers, who, against the king's will and the public laws, undertook the greatest danger on his behalf. Besides, he ascribes all the glory of his deliverance, together with everything he has done since that time, to God alone as author. Luke relates this history in Acts chapter 9. The sequence of time in which this happened ought to be sought from the first chapter of the Epistle to the Galatians, and from comparing the two passages the following can be gathered: when Paul had been converted to the faith of Christ and baptized by Ananias, he at once seized the opportunity to preach; and because he knew that he had been designated an apostle to the Gentiles, he betook himself to nearby Arabia, where no apostle had yet preached the Gospel. And when he had made the preaching of the Gospel known there, he returned to Damascus, intending evidently to go elsewhere. Yet since many opportunities for disputing with the Jews presented themselves daily, he lingered there for some time, until the plots of the Jews compelled him to think of changing place. For these men stirred up the prefect of King Aretas to try to seize him. And it is credible that this was done not without the king's will, who, no doubt because of the fervour of religion, had become more hostile to Paul in his kingdom. Therefore he set guards at the gates, so that there would be no way of escape; which was the reason why the Christians who were already there let him down from the wall in a basket, and so on. This history, however, contains many matters most worthy of observation, which we shall consider in order.

units.la: Primùm est periculum, quo Paulum tam citò Deus exerceri & probari voluit, cum suae fidei & diligentiae tyrocinium egregium in Arabia dedisset. Mox ergo expertus est veritatem oraculi, quod Ananiae de ipso revelatum fuerat: Ego ostendam ei, quàm multa eum oporteat pro nomine meo pati. Id verò testatur, quàm strenuè causam Christi egerit. Nisi enim in Arabia fructum fecisset eius doctrina, nisi item eiusdem virtutem & in illa se exerente Spiritus Dei efficaciam Iudaei simul & Aretas cum suo praefecto sensissent, non opus erat ut tantopere commoverentur. Est autem hoc memorabile exemplum, quo docemur, quid sibi de hoc mundo polliceri debeant, qui cum Christo fideliter serviunt. Primo in honore & pretio erat Paulus, & quamuis iuvenis adhuc esset, causis capitalibus iudex adhibebatur (ut in Stephani Protomartyris historia est videre) & cum publica authoritate Damascum mittebatur, ut illic pullulantem IESV CHRISTI fidem extingueret: At nunc ibidem ei non licet tutò agere, & propter ipsum ceu publicum hostem tota civitas tumultuatur. Ita fore praedixerat Christus discipulis & causam eius rei ostenderat, quòd mundus hic eos non posset nō odisse, quos ipse ex eo selectos sibi consecravit. Si de mundo essetis (inquit) mundus quod suum est diligeret: Quia verò de mundo non estis, sed ego vos elegi ex mundo, propterea odit vos mundus. Exempla sunt ab origine rerum, quibus hoc confirmatur. Abelus certè, cùm ex fide promissi feminis potiorem victimam obtulisset, mox fratrem sibi inimicum habuit, qui eum crudeliter trucidavit. Abrahamus, cùm inter suos honoraretur, quàm primùm Dei vocationem sequi coepit, variis & periculosis casibus iactatus est. Idem de aliis patribus, Isaaco, Iacobo, Iosepho, Mose & similibus dici potest. Prophetas quoque hoc potissimum nomine inuisos fuisse scimus, quòd inanem externorum sacrorum fiduciam oppugnarent, & ad promissum Messiam populum remitterent. Et quod Paulo accidit, hoc Apostolis quoq; aliis omnibus accidisse scimus. Quod si Ecclesiastica historiae exempla quis commemorare velit, is vix unquam dicendi finem inveniet. Nemo igitur offendatur, si quid huius vel sibijpsi vel aliis pijs evenire videat: quin potius praeparemus nos ad hanc palaestram, & meminerimus non temere ab Apostolis olim dictum esse, quòd per multas afflictiones oporteat nos ingredi in regnum Dei. Act. 14.
units.tr: First is the danger by which God so quickly wished Paul to be exercised and tested, after he had given him an excellent apprenticeship of his faith and diligence in Arabia. Soon, therefore, he experienced the truth of the oracle which had been revealed to Ananias concerning him: "I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name." This bears witness to how vigorously he pleaded the cause of Christ. For if his teaching had not borne fruit in Arabia, and if the Jews along with Aretas and his prefect had not perceived the power of Paul and the efficacy of the Spirit of God working in him there, there would have been no need for them to be stirred so greatly. Now this is a memorable example, by which we are taught what those who serve Christ faithfully may promise themselves from this world. At first Paul was held in honour and esteem, and although he was still young, he was employed as a judge in capital cases (as may be seen in the history of Stephen the first martyr), and he was sent to Damascus with public authority to extinguish the faith of Jesus Christ as it was springing up there. But now he is not permitted to act safely there, and the whole city is in tumult on account of him as if he were a public enemy. Christ had foretold that this would happen to the disciples, and had shown the reason for it: that this world cannot but hate those whom he has chosen out of it and consecrated to himself. "If you were of the world," he says, "the world would love what is its own; but because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you." There are examples from the beginning of things confirming this. Abel, when from faith in the promised seed he offered a more excellent sacrifice, straightway had a brother as his enemy, who cruelly slew him. Abraham, while he was honoured among his own people, as soon as he began to follow God's calling, was tossed about by various and perilous chances. The same may be said of the other fathers, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses and the like. We know also that the prophets were especially hated on this account, because they attacked the empty confidence in external rites and sent the people back to the promised Messiah. And what happened to Paul, we know also happened to all the other apostles. But if anyone wished to recall examples from ecclesiastical history, he would hardly ever find an end to speaking. Let no one, therefore, be offended if he sees anything of this kind befall himself or other godly people; rather let us prepare ourselves for this wrestling-ground, and remember that it was not rashly said by the apostles that we must enter the kingdom of God through many afflictions. Acts 14.

units.la: Et hic nos consolari debet, quòd aliquantum temporis, trium videlicet fere annorum spatium intercessisse audiuimus inter Pauli conversionem & periculum iudud, de quo hic agitur. Ergo otium illi datum est, ut interea Evangelium Arabibus praedicaret, neque sine fructu Damasci quoque versaretur: & potuit Deus tam Iudaeorum quàm Aretae Regis rabiem cohibere, quàm diu voluit, & causa Veritatis requirebat. Non ergo possunt semper impij quod volunt, imò non audent semper, quod posse videbantur. Instigantur quidem semper à Satana, & ut mare aestuant: sed ut Satan etsi nobis nunquam non nocere cupiat, nihil tamen potest, nisi Deo permittente: ita neque eius satellites semper effectum dare possunt, quod animo suo conceperunt. At quia Deus non iustus modo, verumetiam fidelis & humani generis amantissimus est, nunquam aliquid permittet mundo & eius principi, quàm quod nobis salutare esse novit, neque (ut alibi Apostolus docet) nos supra vires tentari patietur.
units.tr: Here too we ought to be consoled that a considerable time, namely about three years, we have heard, passed between Paul's conversion and the danger of which we are speaking here. Therefore leisure was granted to him, so that in the meantime he might preach the Gospel to the Arabs, and he was not without fruit while he remained also at Damascus. And God was able to restrain the rage both of the Jews and of King Aretas for as long as he wished, and as the cause of the truth required. The wicked, therefore, cannot always do what they will; indeed they do not always dare to do what they seemed able to do. They are indeed always stirred up by Satan, and they boil like the sea; but just as Satan, although he always desires to harm us, can do nothing unless God permits it, so neither can his henchmen always bring about what they have conceived in their minds. And because God is not only just but also faithful and most loving of the human race, he will never permit the world and its prince to do anything to us except what he knows to be salutary for us; nor (as the Apostle teaches elsewhere) will he suffer us to be tempted beyond our strength.

units.la: Deinde docet historia ista, ut mundus Deo ac Veritatis doctrinae resistere soleat. Paulus praesidij meminit, & portas insuper custoditas fuisse Lucas scribit. Atqui ille neque armis instructus erat, nec milites habebat, à quibus vis aliqua posset fieri, sed verbis & argumentis solummodo agebat. Itaque verba verbis & argumenta argumentis erant opponenda. At quia argumentis & rationibus nihil profici vident adversarij, ad vim convertuntur. Videmus autem hic ceu in speculo, quàm ridiculos sese praebeant Veritatis hostes, quando suas vires cotra Christum ostentare, & huius cultores illis terrere volunt. Paulus cùm publica authoritate munitus & satellitiū caterua stipatus Damascum veniret contra fideles, qui illic erant, tunc timere debebat Aretas, ne Iudaeorum principes, qui cum Romanis praesidibus mirificè colludebant, eo praetextu aliquid molirentur. Sed tunc nemo obstitit, & aduentanti urbs tota patebat. At nunc, cùm omni dignitate exutus nihil habet formidabile, contrahitur praesidium, custodes adhibentur portis, & omnia belli cuiusdam imminentis specie referunt. Ita hodie Reges atq; principes facere solent. Quando enim Pontifices & horum coniurati sibi in illorum terris ius & imperium sumunt, perque suos Inquisitores omnium fortunis & vitae insidiantur, imò iurisdictionem quoque aperte inuadunt: nihil timent, sed voluntariam seruitutem seruiunt. Quàm primùm verò pauperculus aliquis & ob scurus IESV CHRISTI minister Euangelium praedicare incipit, & illi aures praebet aliqui: mox regna sua & omnem suam authoritatem periclitari putant, tumultuantur, concurrant, & fit non raro, ut propter unicum homunciónem totae gentes armis strepant. Sic fore Christo exhibito, olim Dauid in Psalmo secundo praedixit, & eius rei typum ipse nobis praebuit, quando totius regni vires contra illum, ceu publicum communis patriae hostem Saul concitauit. Et ad Christum inermen cum inermibus discipulis exiuerunt cum militibus Sacerdotes, ut illum comprehenderent. Ridiculum plane hominum genus. Etenim eorum similes dixeris merito, qui armati ad lepores aut cuniculos venandos exeunt, lupos verò & vrsos impune grassari patiuntur. Sed ita hostes suos Deus ludificat, simulq; eorundem conatus facile frangit.
units.tr: Further, this history teaches how the world is wont to resist God and the doctrine of the truth. Paul made mention of a guard, and Luke writes that the gates were moreover watched. Yet Paul was neither armed nor had soldiers by whom any force could be used; he acted only with words and arguments. Therefore words were to be opposed to words and arguments to arguments. But since the adversaries see that nothing is gained by arguments and reasons, they turn to force. Here we see, as if in a mirror, how ridiculous the enemies of the truth make themselves, when they wish to display their strength against Christ and to terrify his worshippers with it. When Paul came to Damascus against the faithful who were there, armed with public authority and surrounded by a band of attendants, then Aretas ought to have feared that the princes of the Jews, who were colluding wonderfully with the Roman governors, might undertake something under that pretext. But then no one opposed him, and the whole city lay open to the man arriving. Now, however, when he has been stripped of all dignity and has nothing formidable about him, a guard is assembled, sentries are posted at the gates, and everything has the appearance of some impending war. Thus kings and princes are wont to act today. For when the Pontiffs and their conspirators assume right and rule in the lands of those princes, and lay snares for the fortunes and lives of all through their Inquisitors, and even openly invade jurisdiction, they fear nothing, but serve a willing servitude. But as soon as some poor and obscure minister of Jesus Christ begins to preach the Gospel, and some few lend him their ears, straightway they think their kingdoms and all their authority are in danger; they grow tumultuous, they run together, and it often happens that whole nations clatter with arms on account of a single little man. That this would happen when Christ was revealed, David foretold long ago in the second Psalm; and he himself gave us a type of this when Saul stirred up the whole strength of the kingdom against him as a public enemy of the common fatherland. And the priests went out with soldiers against Christ, who was unarmed, with his unarmed disciples, to seize him. Surely a ridiculous kind of men! For you would rightly liken them to those who go out armed to hunt hares or rabbits, but allow wolves and bears to roam with impunity. But thus God mocks his enemies, and easily breaks their attempts at the same time.

units.la: Factum hoc etiam hic. Nam Damasceni fratres Paulum sportae impositum ex muro demittunt, & ita insidijs ipsi struetis absque magno labore eripiunt. Fuit tamen factum hoc cum periculo magno coniunctum, & proinde fidei non vulgaris exemplum habet. Rebellionis enim speciem prae se ferre videtur, si quis eum feruet, quem princeps siue magistratus vult extinctum. Et ne ab excubitoribus deprehenderentur, periculum erat. Quid, quod antiquitus capitale scelus visum fuit moenia violare, aut transfilire: eò quod illa numini alicui certo consecrari solerent? At nihil horum iflos mouet, quò minus periclitanti opem ferant. Qui enim sciebant, Sabbati religionem charitati cedere debere, adeò ut illo die asinum & bouem seruare liceat, multò magis succurrendum esse intelligunt Christi ministro, cuius fides & industria iam multis praeclaris argumentis erat perspecta. Est ergo hoc (ut diximus) memorabile fidei exemplum, quo officij sui admonentur omnes, qui Christiani dici & haberi volunt: Vt nimirum pios sub tyrannis periclitantes iuuent, si qua commoda ratione possunt, neque se aliquo modo tyrannidis & crudelitatis socios siue ministros praebeant. Laudantur hoc nomine obstetrices Aegyptiae, quòd contra Regis edictum Hebraeorum infantes seruarunt. Et Rachab meretrix fidei testimonium meruit, inque Dei societatem adoptata est, quòd exploratores Israelitas abscondisset ne ab Hierichuntinis occiderentur. Arguunt haec nostri saeculi ignauiam: quando vbique terrarum grassante impiorum tyrannide paucis cordi est piorum salus, plerique verò his laborantibus genio suo indulgent: requisiti autem, ut illorum causam suscipiant, frigidissimis rationibus sese excusant. At ijdem, dum omnia tuta metuunt, plerunque seipsos periculis grauioribus immergunt, & tunc talionis lege eos multat Deus, ut ipsi quoque ab omnibus derelicti pereant. Quid verò de illis dices, qui si quid periculi imminet, ministrorum Verbi capitibus pacem redimendam esse clamant? Sunt hi indigni Christiano nomine. Imitentur ergo Damascenorum fratrum fidem atque fortitudinem omnes ij, quibus datum est liberius in pace & otio viuere.
units.tr: The same thing happened here as well. For the Damascene brothers let Paul down from the wall in a basket, and so rescued him without great effort from the snares that had been laid for him. Yet this deed was attended by great danger, and so it offers an example of no ordinary faith. For it seems to carry the appearance of rebellion if someone helps a man whom the prince or magistrate wants put to death. And there was danger that they might be caught by the sentries. Moreover, in ancient times it was regarded as a capital crime to breach or leap over the walls, because these were customarily consecrated to some particular deity. Yet none of these things deterred them from bringing help to a man in peril. For they knew that the observance of the Sabbath must yield to charity, so that on that day it is lawful to save an ass or an ox; so much the more, they understood, ought help to be given to a minister of Christ, whose faith and diligence had already been proved by many notable evidences. This, then, as we have said, is a memorable example of faith, by which all who wish to be and be called Christians are reminded of their duty: namely, that they should help the godly who are in peril under tyrants, by whatever fair means they can, and that they should in no way make themselves partners or ministers of tyranny and cruelty. The Egyptian midwives are praised for this, because against the king's edict they saved the Hebrew infants. And Rahab the harlot earned a testimony of faith and was adopted into fellowship with God, because she hid the Israelite spies so that they would not be killed by the people of Jericho. These examples expose the sloth of our own age: when everywhere the tyranny of the wicked is raging, few care for the safety of the godly, and most indulge their own ease while others are in distress; and when they are asked to take up their cause, they excuse themselves with the coldest of reasons. Yet these same people, while they fear every step as unsafe, often plunge themselves into graver dangers, and then God punishes them by the law of retaliation, so that they too perish, abandoned by all. What, then, will you say of those who, whenever any danger threatens, cry out that the peace must be purchased with the heads of the ministers of the Word? Such people are unworthy of the name of Christian. Let all those, then, who are granted the freedom to live in peace and leisure imitate the faith and courage of the Damascene brothers.

units.la: Postremò Paulus ipse considerandus venit, qui hoc officium admisit. Ergo non scrupulosas & ineptas quaestiones mouit de dicto Christi, Ne resistatis malo, &c. ut hodie Anabaptistae faciunt: Neque etiam securus de Dei prouidentia inutiliter garrit, qui si ipsum velit seruare, facile medium & rationem abfq; fratrum periculo inuenturus sit: sed quod Deus iam ipsi offerebat, quoq; salua fide & pietate vti poterat, gratus recipit. Quo exemplo primum docemur, licere nobis vti ordinarijs medijs, si quando periclitamur. Inter ea autem legitimum & ordinarium debet censeri, quicquid ex fide & syncero charitatis studio pij faciunt; & imprimis quod magistratus publica authoritate facit. Huius enim praecipuum munus est, pios tueri, malorum verò temeritatem reprimere & coercere. Vt ergo hic fratrum auxilijs Paulus vtitur, ita alibi ad Leges Romanas & legitimam magistratus defensionem confugit. Nemo igitur fanaticorum disputationibus moueatur, qui Christi dicto (quod paulo ante adduximus) abutuntur, vt magistratu inter Christianos aboleant. Est enim duplex resistendi modus, legitimus nimirum & illegitimus: & ab hoc quidem Christiani homines abstinere, illo autem cum fide & gratiarum actione debent vti. Vide Lucam nostrum in Cap. sexto Homil. 60.
units.tr: Lastly, Paul himself deserves our consideration, for he undertook this duty. He did not raise scrupulous and foolish questions about the saying of Christ, "Do not resist evil," etc., as the Anabaptists do today; nor did he, carelessly, babble uselessly about God's providence, supposing that if God wished to preserve him, He would easily find a means and a way without danger to the brothers. Rather, he gratefully accepted what God was already offering him, which he could use with faith and piety intact. From this example we are first taught that we may make use of ordinary means when we are in danger. Among these means, whatever the godly do out of faith and sincere zeal for charity ought to be counted lawful and ordinary; and especially what the magistrate does by public authority. For it is his chief task to protect the godly and to restrain and check the recklessness of the wicked. Therefore, just as Paul here makes use of the help of the brothers, so elsewhere he takes refuge in the Roman laws and the lawful defence of the magistrate. Let no one, then, be moved by the arguments of the fanatics, who abuse the saying of Christ (which we cited a little earlier) in order to abolish the magistrate among Christians. For there are two ways of resisting, the lawful and the unlawful; Christians ought to abstain from the latter, but use the former with faith and thanksgiving. See our Luke on chapter six, Homily 60.

units.la: Deinde fugam quoque Christianis licitam esse, hoc exemplo admonemur. Quod enim hic factum est, Christum quoque non semel fecisse scimus. Nam infans adhuc in Aegyptum se deferri voluit, vt Herodis insidias effugeret, quem multis alijs modis poterat coercere: & postea saepe hostium manus secessione aut fuga declinauit. Quid, quòd discipulis idem ille dixit: Si vos persecuti fuerint in vna ciuitate, fugite in aliam? Et extant passim piorum exempla, qui hoc Christi consilio non minus vtiliter quàm piè vsi sunt. Minime ergo probari debet Tertulliani (doctissimi aliàs scriptoris & non male de Ecclesia meriti) sententia, qui inconsulto Zelo abreptus omnem fugam simpliciter damnauit: cuius de hac re librum D. Hieronymus nominatim contra Ecclesiam scriptum esse, non dubitauit dicere. Attamen, qui fugere volunt, primò cauere debent, ne quid faciant cum gloriae Dei detrimento: Deinde ne temere ab officio discedant, neq; eorum salutem negligant, quos ipsis Deus commendauit. Quòd si salua Dei gloria, & absq; aliorum detrimento locum mutare possunt, nihil obstat, quò minus id faciant.
units.tr: Next, we are reminded by this example that flight is also permitted to Christians. For what was done here, we know Christ also did more than once. For as an infant he was willing to be carried into Egypt, so that he might escape Herod's plots, though he could have restrained him by many other means; and afterwards he often evaded the hands of his enemies by withdrawing or by fleeing. Moreover, he himself said to the disciples: "If they persecute you in one city, flee to another." And everywhere there are examples of the godly who used this counsel of Christ no less profitably than piously. Therefore the opinion of Tertullian (otherwise a most learned writer who deserved well of the Church) must by no means be approved, for he, carried away by ill-considered zeal, condemned all flight outright; and Jerome did not hesitate to say that a book on this subject was written by him expressly against the Church. Nevertheless, those who wish to flee ought first to take care that they do nothing to the detriment of God's glory; then that they do not rashly abandon their duty or neglect the safety of those whom God has committed to them. But if they can change place with God's glory preserved and without harm to others, nothing stands in the way of their doing so.

units.la: Praeterea docemur, ne periculis grauioribus erepti otio ignavo nos dedamus, sed prima quaq; occasione oblata eò feruentius redeamus ad officium, cui nos Deus destinauit. Id fecit in praesenti Paulus. Mox enim Hierosolymam contendit, unde ceu ex fonte quodam omnes persecutiones deriuari sciebat, & vbi plus periculi poterat timeri, cùm illinc missus esset à principibus Iudaeorum, à quibus secessionem fecerat. Sed nihil territus illic se Ecclesiae credentiū coniungit, & quamuis initiò repulsam pateretur, modestè tamen hanc quoq; fert, ini officio suo constanter perseuerat. Idem postea etiam saepe fecit, sicuti totus Actorum liber prolixè testatur. Arguit eius exemplum eos, qui vno & altero periculo defuncti ferias sibi ipsis indicunt. Atqui in finem vsq; perseuerandum esse, Christus monet. Et si Dei manum nobis periclitantibus adfuisse sensimus, eò maiori studio nos eius causam agere decet, ne ingratos nos illi praebeamus. Nam si nos iterum atq; iterum liberare velit, hoc illi facile erit. Sin illi aliter visum fuerit, nulla nobis mors gloriosior obtingere poterit, quàm vt pro nomine aeterni Filij Dei, Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI moriamur, qui propter nos homo factus & mortuus, ex morte item resuscitatus est, vt nos ipsi viuamus & moriamur, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, we are taught that, having been rescued from graver dangers, we should not give ourselves over to idle sloth, but, whenever any opportunity offers, return all the more eagerly to the office to which God has appointed us. Paul did this in the present case. For he immediately made for Jerusalem, whence, as from a certain fountain, he knew all persecutions were derived, and where the danger was greatest to be feared, since he had been sent from there by the leaders of the Jews, from whom he had withdrawn. But, undismayed, he joined himself there to the company of the believers, and although at first he suffered rejection, he bore this too with moderation and persevered steadfastly in his office. He did the same afterwards also often, as the whole book of Acts bears witness at length. His example condemns those who, after escaping one or another danger, grant themselves a holiday. Indeed, Christ bids us to persevere to the end. And if we have felt the hand of God present with us in our dangers, we ought all the more eagerly to plead His cause, lest we show ourselves ungrateful to Him. For if He wishes to deliver us again and again, this will be easy for Him. But if He should decide otherwise, no death can befall us more glorious than to die for the name of the eternal Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who, made man and dead for our sake, was likewise raised from the dead, so that we might live and die in Him; to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 12.

units.la: HOMILIA LIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 54.

units.la: Gloriari sanè non expedit mihi. Veniam enim ad visiones & revelationes Domini. Noui hominem in Christo ante annos quatuordecim (an in corpore, nescio, an extra corpus, nescio, Deus novit) raptum in tertium vsq; coelum. Et noui huiusmodi hominem (an in corpore, an extra corpus, nescio: Deus novit) raptum fuisse in paradisum, & audisse ineffabilia verba, quae non liceat homini loqui. De huiusmodi gloriabor, de meipso vero non gloriabor nisi in infirmitatibus meis.
units.tr: "Indeed, it is not expedient for me to boast. For I will come to visions and revelations of the Lord. I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago (whether in the body, I do not know, or outside the body, I do not know; God knows) was caught up to the third heaven. And I know that such a man (whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows) was caught up into paradise and heard unspeakable words, which a man may not utter. Of such a man I will boast, but of myself I will not boast, except in my infirmities."

units.la: Vtitur quidem Deus electorum suorum ministerio ad res magnas & quae vires humanas longè superant, ijdem verò suae infirmitatis probè memores, de sola eius gratia gloriari solent, qua ille ipsos dignos iudicat, qui pro eius nomine aliquid facere aut ferre debeant. Exemplum huius rei euidens in Paulo Apostolo habemus. Fuit is electum IESV CHRISTI organum, & plus omnibus aliis Apostolis laborauit. Idem tamen (vt fieri solet) aduersarios habuit multos, interq; hos acerrimos omnium pseudoapostolos, qui toti in eo erant, vt eum apud omnes in contemptum & odium adducerent. Cogebatur ergo auctoritatem suam tueri, ne Dei gloria & Euangelij fides in ipso periclitaretur. Etsi verò hic amplissimam haberet gloriandi materiam, omissis tamen omnibus, quae vt multarum gentium domitor magna cum laude gesserat, de solis infirmitatibus suis gloriatur, & in ijs commemorandis adeò nihil dissimulat, vt ne fugam quidem tacuerit, qua per Damasci moenia euaserat. At quia aemuli eius visiones quoq; & reuelationes iactabant, nunc de his ipse etiam aliquid dicit, ne illis hac in re putetur inferior esse. Tanta vero modestia rursus vtitur, vt perspicuè appareat, ipsum praeter animi voluntatem in hanc narrationem ingredi.
units.tr: God indeed uses the ministry of his chosen servants for great things, far beyond human strength; yet they, mindful of their own weakness, are accustomed to glory only in his grace, by which he judges them worthy to do or suffer anything for his name. We have a clear example of this in the apostle Paul. He was a chosen instrument of Jesus Christ and laboured more than all the other apostles. Yet, as often happens, he had many adversaries, the most bitter of them the false apostles, who devoted themselves wholly to bringing him into contempt and hatred before everyone. He was therefore compelled to defend his authority, lest the glory of God and the faith of the gospel be endangered in him. Although he had the most ample material for boasting, since he had accomplished so much with great praise as conqueror of many nations, he sets all of this aside and boasts only of his infirmities. In recounting them he hides nothing, so that he does not even pass over his flight, when he escaped through the walls of Damascus. But because his rivals also boasted of visions and revelations, he now says something about these himself, lest he be thought inferior to them in this respect. Yet he uses such modesty again that it clearly appears he enters upon this account against the desire of his own mind.

units.la: Nam à protestatione exorsus ait: Gloriari sanè non expedit mihi. Quasi diceret: Quò feror? aut quò me abripit aduersariorum improbitas, dum me de ijs gloriari cogunt, quae per me gesta sunt? Etenim id mihi nequaquam expedire scio & fateor, ideoq; nolim aliquis existimet, me ex eo voluptatem capere, vt ambitiosi solent, quibus nihil iucundius est, quàm laudes suas vel ex aliis audire, vel earum commemoratione animum suum pascere. Et merito hac protestatione Paulus vtitur. Facile enim in suspicionem veniunt, quasi nimia gloriae inanis cupiditate vrantur, quicunq; de rebus abs se gestis sermonem instituunt: eo quòd illa omnibus quasi cognata est, vt Cicero alicubi philosophorum exemplo probat, quos dicit illis ipsis libris, quos de contemnenda gloria scribunt, nomina sua praefigere, & ita gloriam venari, dum alios ab eius cupiditate deborantur. Nec dissimulauit hoc humani ingenij vitium Themistocles, qui cùm theatrum ingressus à quodam interrogaretur: Quod nam acroama, aut cuius vocem libentissimè audiret? ingenue & libere respondit: Eius, à quo mea virtus praedicatur. Quem animum Alexandro quoq; Macedoni fuisse constat, qui Achillem hoc nomine felicem praedicauit, quòd mortuus Homerum rerum abs se gestarum praeconem nactus esset. Quae omnia cùm Paulus non ignoraret, non abs q; causa timuit, ne se cordatis suspectum faceret.
units.tr: For he begins with a protest: "Indeed, it is not expedient for me to boast." It is as if he said: Where am I being carried? Or where does the wickedness of my adversaries drag me, when they force me to boast of those things which were accomplished through me? For I know and confess that this is in no way expedient for me. Therefore let no one think that I take pleasure in it, as ambitious men do, for whom nothing is more pleasing than to hear their praises from others or to feed their minds by recalling them. Paul uses this protest with good reason. For those who begin to speak of deeds they have done easily fall under suspicion of being burned with an excessive desire for empty glory, because that desire is, as Cicero somewhere shows by the example of the philosophers, almost innate in all people. He says that these philosophers put their own names on the very books in which they write about despising glory, and so hunt for glory while they seek to deprive others of the desire for it. Themistocles, too, did not conceal this flaw of human nature. When he entered the theatre and someone asked him what performance or whose voice he would most gladly hear, he answered frankly and openly: "The voice of the one by whom my virtue is proclaimed." It is well known that Alexander the Macedonian had the same spirit, who called Achilles happy for this reason, that after his death he had found Homer as the herald of his deeds. Since Paul was not unaware of all this, it was not without cause that he feared he might make himself suspect to sensible people.

units.la: Sed aliae etiam causae ipsum mouerunt, quae ad ipsius functionem propius pertinebant. Nam fi (inquit) gloriandum sit, veniam ad visiones & revelationes Domini. Id est, si semel hunc campum ingrediar, vt commemorare velim quae per me gesta sunt, & quaecunq; in hoc argumento dici poterunt, tandem de visionibus quoq; mihi dicendum erit, quibus Deus seipsum & multa arcana, quae vulgus Christianorum ignorat, mihi manifestauit. Ita vero duplex periculum mihi imminere video. Nam multi vix fidem adhibebunt mihi ista narranti, qui me fabulatorem esse dicent, & inde nouam occasionem de mea doctrina contemptius loquendi arripient. Deinde ipse etiam gloriae & propriae laudis dulcedine abreptus fortasse extollar, vt ambitione atque superbia peccem. Nam quò maiora sunt dona, quibus nos Deus ornauit, eò periculosiori in gradu consistimus, si illorum admirationi aut praedicationi nimium indulgeamus. Facile enim nobisipsis persuadebimus, nos communem hominum sortem iam transiluisse, & ita inani noströ ipsius fidutia ebrij nihil non nobis ipsis permittemus. Quòd si vero illa ab alijs quoq; celebrari, nosq; propter illa in honore & pretio esse videamus, difficile fuerit superbia criptas reprimere, quo minus in gloriando modum omnem excedamus. Ita enim plerique sibi ipsis placent, vt interea non obseruent infirmitatem suam & inhaerentem nobis naturae vitiositatem, imò ne in Deum quidem, vnicum omnis boni authorem respiciunt. Exempla insolentiae huius in prophanis hominibus multa extant. Pharaonem certè opum & potentiae fiducia cum insatiabili gloriae cupiditate coniunctam tam insolentem fecit, vt dicere auderet: Quis est Iehoua ille Hebraeorum, cuius vocem ego audire debeam? Quem Sennacherib imitatus non de gentibus solum verumetiam earum Diis abs se deiectis gloriabatur. Et Nabuchodonosorem gloriae dulcedo eò adduxit, vt diceret: Annon haec est Babylon, quam ego aedificaui & illustrem feci? Taceo nunc eos, qui cum in mortali corpore agerent, & se omnis generis affectionibus obnoxios esse quotidie sentirent, diuinos tamen honores affectarunt, seq; ex Dijs genitos esse mentiti sunt: quales Herculem, Alexandrum & aliquos Romanorum Imperatorum fuisse legimus. Et hodie exempla huius generis multa extant in opulentioribus & potentissimis Monarchis, qui vera Dei cognitione destituuntur. Estq; arrogantia haec multorum vitiorum mater, & proinde (vt Solomon dicebat) plerunque exaltationem ruina sequitur. At omnium nocentissima fit, si in ijs locum inueniat, quos Deus donis spiritualibus liberalius donauit. Tunc enim ita hominum mentes excaecat, vt aduersus Dei gratiam sese attollere, & non sine Filij eius vnigeniti IESV CHRISTI contumelia suorum operum meritis confidere, alios verò omnes prae se contemnere ac fastidire audeant. Quod olim Pharisaeos fecisse constat, quorum vestigijs nimium pertinaciter insistunt hodie Monachi, & quotquot horum traditionibus decepti suarum virium atque operum fidutia efferuntur. Ne quid ergo huius Paulo quoque accideret, non libenter se de visionibus & alijs donis excellentioribus loqui testatur, quibus eum bus eum Deus instruxerat, non ut ipse illis superbiret, sed ut aliorum saluti consuleret.
units.tr: But other causes also moved him, which pertained more closely to his own office. For, he says, if I must boast, I will come to the visions and revelations of the Lord. That is: if I once enter this field, so as to recount what has been accomplished through me and whatever can be said on this subject, then at last I must also speak of the visions by which God has revealed himself to me and many hidden things which the common run of Christians does not know. Yet I see a double danger hanging over me in this. For many will scarcely give credence to me as I tell these things, and they will say I am a teller of tales, and from this they will seize a new occasion to speak of my teaching more contemptuously. Then too I myself, carried away by the sweetness of glory and of my own praise, might perhaps be elated, so that I sin through ambition and pride. For the greater the gifts with which God has adorned us, the more perilous is the standing we hold, if we indulge too much in admiring or proclaiming them. For we will easily persuade ourselves that we have already passed beyond the common lot of humanity, and so, drunk with our own empty confidence, we will permit ourselves everything. But if we see that these gifts are also celebrated by others, and that we are held in honour and esteem on account of them, it will be hard to restrain the hidden recesses of pride, so that we do not go beyond all measure in boasting. For most people are so pleased with themselves that meanwhile they do not observe their own weakness and the wickedness of nature that clings to us; indeed they do not even look to God, the sole author of every good. There are many examples of this arrogance among profane men. Certainly, the confidence of Pharaoh in his wealth and power, joined with an insatiable desire for glory, made him so insolent that he dared to say: "Who is Jehovah, the god of the Hebrews, whose voice I should obey?" Sennacherib, imitating him, boasted not only of the nations but also of their gods, which he had cast down. And the sweetness of glory brought Nebuchadnezzar to say: "Is not this Babylon, which I have built and made illustrious?" I now pass over those who, while they lived in mortal bodies and daily felt themselves subject to every kind of passion, nevertheless aspired to divine honours and falsely claimed to be born of the gods. We read that Hercules, Alexander and some Roman emperors were of this kind. And today there are many examples of this sort among the wealthier and more powerful monarchs, who lack the true knowledge of God. This arrogance is the mother of many vices, and therefore, as Solomon said, ruin usually follows exaltation. But it is most harmful of all when it finds a place among those whom God has endowed more generously with spiritual gifts. For then it so blinds men's minds that they dare to raise themselves against the grace of God, to trust in the merits of their works, not without contumely to Jesus Christ, the only begotten Son of God, and to despise and scorn all others in comparison with themselves. It is well known that the Pharisees did this, and in their footsteps stubbornly walk today the monks and all who, deceived by their traditions, are puffed up with confidence in their own strength and works. So that nothing of this should happen to Paul as well, he testifies that he is unwilling to speak of visions and other more excellent gifts with which God had equipped him, not so that he might take pride in them, but so that he might provide for the salvation of others.

units.la: Habet autem locus hic utilissimam doctrinam, ut nimirum in donorum Dei consideratione versari debeant, quicunque illa sibi ipsis & aliis utilia atque salutaria esse cupiunt? Hic ante omnia necesse est, ut nunquam nobis excidat, qui nam simus quoad naturam nostram & conditionem. Etenim si corpus spectemus, nos non aliud quam terram esse & in terram redityros esse videbimus, sicuti Adamo olim Deus dixit: ut iam omittamus mille morborum species & casus innumeros, quibus vita haec obnoxia est. Quoad animam vero, etsi haec spiritus sit immortalis & corpore dignior multo, eadem tamen vitiosa est & desideriis pravis atque illicitis ardet, quibus abrepta a Dei semitis declinamus, in proprium exitium sponte ruimus. Itaque licet nos Deus ex gratuita misericordia donis maximis dignetur, ut multis aliis praestemus, thesaurum tamen istum in vasis testaceis (ut supra dictum est) gestamus, & (quod Christus discipulos monebat) etsi magna sit agentis in nobis spiritus alacritas, caro tamen infirmior nunquam non nobis obstaculo est, quo minus in salutis via progrediamur. Ut ergo humiliemur necesse est sub potenti manu Domini, quod unicum est remedium, adeoque fulcrum unicum, quo homo alioqui ruiturus sustentatur. Et haec causa est, ob quam Paulus toties priorem vitae suae in Iudaismo transactae conditionem in mentem revocat: ut nimirum eius recordatione ad humilitatem & preces ardentiores erudiretur. Et Davidem olim hoc unum in officio continuit, ne Saulem imitatus regia potentia superbiret, quod se opilionem fuisse nunquam oblitus est. Quod ipsum in aliorum quoque exemplis apparet, quorum fides & pietas in Scripturis commendatur. Deinde authorem omnium, quae habemus, agnoscamus esse Deum, qui ut primum hominem condidit, ita omnium nostrum creator est, qui & corpus nostrum in utero matris (ut Dauid docet) mirabili artificio formal, & eidem adhuc illic quasi sepulto animam instillat immortalem, & utrumque postea suis viribus atque facultatibus instruit. Semper ergo nobisipsis Apostolica haec apophthegmata occinamus: Omne donum bonum e supernis est a Patre luminum. Item: Quid habes, quod non accepisti? Haec ut feroces superbiae spiritus reprimunt, ita nos ad gratias Deo agendas efficacissime extimulant. Accedat his diligens nostri officii consideratio, ut in quem usum nobis dona sua Deus largiatur, sedulo cogitemus: Nimirum, non ut nobis solis serviant, sed ut per ea ipsius gloria illustretur, & plures alii iuvenitur. Nam ad Dei gloriam nos conditos, & a Christo redemptos esse, nemo negaverit, qui vel prima tenet religionis Christianae principia, deque eo Oratio Dominica nos admonet, cuius haec prima petitio est: Sanctificetur nomen tuum. Charitas autem sive dilectio fraterna totius vitae regula est, quae omnia nostra tam dicta quam facta ad aliorum aedificationem dirigit, ut alibi prolixe docuimus. De his si serio cogitemus, si quando nos ambitiosa nostrae dignitatis fiducia sentimus titillari, facile poterimus illius adulacionibus resistere.
units.tr: But does this passage contain a very useful teaching: that those who wish these gifts of God to be useful and salutary both to themselves and to others ought to be occupied with considering the gifts of God? Here it is above all necessary that we never forget who we are, in respect of our nature and condition. For if we look at the body, we shall see that we are nothing but earth and will return to earth, as God once said to Adam; not to mention the thousand kinds of sickness and countless accidents to which this life is subject. As for the soul, although it is an immortal spirit and far more worthy than the body, it is nevertheless corrupt and burns with depraved and unlawful desires, by which, carried away, we turn aside from the paths of God and rush willingly to our own destruction. Therefore, although God in his free mercy deigns to honour us with the greatest gifts, so that we excel many others, we nonetheless carry this treasure in earthen vessels (as was said above), and, as Christ warned his disciples, although the spirit in us is eager, the flesh is always weaker and is always an obstacle to our progress on the way of salvation. It is necessary, then, that we be humbled under the mighty hand of the Lord, which is the only remedy and therefore the only prop by which a man who would otherwise fall is upheld. This is the reason why Paul so often calls to mind the former condition of his life spent in Judaism: namely, that by remembering it he might be taught humility and more fervent prayers. Likewise David, once, was kept in this one duty, that, imitating Saul, he should not grow proud in royal power, since he never forgot that he had been a shepherd. This appears also in the examples of others whose faith and piety are commended in the Scriptures. Next, let us acknowledge that God is the author of all that we have, who, as he first formed the man, so is the creator of all of us; who (as David teaches) fashions our body wonderfully in the mother's womb, and infuses into it, while it is still there as if buried, an immortal soul, and afterwards equips each with its powers and faculties. Let us therefore always sing to ourselves these apostolic maxims: "Every good gift is from above, from the Father of lights." Also: "What have you that you did not receive?" As these restrain the fierce spirit of pride, so they most effectively stir us to give thanks to God. Let there be added to these a careful consideration of our duty, so that we diligently think to what use God bestows his gifts upon us: certainly not that they should serve us alone, but that through them his glory may be made illustrious and many others may be helped. For no one will deny that we were created for the glory of God and redeemed by Christ, as anyone holds even the first principles of the Christian religion, and the Lord's Prayer admonishes us of this, whose first petition is: "Hallowed be your name." Moreover, brotherly charity or love is the rule of the whole of life, which directs all our words and deeds to the edification of others, as we have shown at length elsewhere. If we think seriously about these things, whenever we feel ourselves tickled by the ambitious confidence in our own dignity, we shall easily be able to resist its flattery.

units.la: At quoad huius loci argumentum, ex visionibus, quas multas & eximias habuerat, unam modo adducit Paulus. Novi (inquit) hominem in Christo, id est, Christianum, aut Christi servum, ante annos quatuordecim, &c. Alienam personam suscipit, proinde ac si non de seipso, sed alio quodam loquatur, & ita rem narrat, ut ex singulis prope verbis constet, ipsum maluisse tacere. Etenim hoc facit temporis notatio, quae hoc ipsi ante annos quatuordecim accidisse docet. Qui enim tam diu id celauerat, procul dubio amplius caelauisset, nisi aduersariorum importunitas ipsum coegisset de eo verba facere. Deinde visionis quidem excellentiam exprimit, sed ita ut sibi ipsi prorsus nihil tribuat. Nam primo se raptum fuisse scribit: Id vero divinae virtutis & gratiae opus est, neque in ullius hominis arbitrio sive potestate est, ut extra se rapiatur. At quia raptus tam corpore fit quam animo, se quid ipsi acciderit, nescire fatetur, dicens: An in corpore, scilicet raptus sim, ut hoc quoque alio fit subiectum aut translatum, nescio: An extra corpus, sola nimirum mens sit rapta, idem nescio. Oportuit ergo huius visionis modum admirabilem fuisse, qui nullo corporis sensu, imo ne intellectu quidem naturali potuit percipi, cum ne postea quidem resciuerit, quid passus esset. Id vero unum nobis sufficere debet aduersus eorum curiositatem, qui de hoc Apostoli raptu quaestiones movent minime necessarias, & circa disputationes inutiles seipsos atque alios fatigant. Nam ut recte monuit D. Augustinus: Quis audet dicere se scire, quod se nescire negat Apostolus? Quò verò raptus est? In tertium cœlum, quod mox paradisum dicet. Vbi non opus est ex philosophorum aut physicorum libris de cœlorum numero disputare, aut de paradiso terrestri, in quem Adam initio collocatus fuit, quæstionem mouere, quando hunc in Oriente situm & in diluuio abolitum fuisse constat. Etenim Paulus hic de fede gloriæ siue maiestatis Dei (quem alibi lucem inaccessam inhabitare scribit) loquitur, qui idem beatæ immortalitatis locus est, in quo olim Deum facie ad faciem videbimus, & in eius conspectu (vt Dauidis verbis vtar) satietate gaudiorum fruemur. Et conuenit nostræ sententiæ, quòd Enoch in paradisum translatum fuisse, in Ecclesiastico scribitur: quòd item Christus in cruce pendenti latroni iam moriturus dixit: Hodie mecum eris in paradiso: cum paulò post ipse animam suam in manus Patris commendaret. Ex istis enim apparet, beatas illius æternæ felicitatis sedes vulgò tunc Paradisum dictas fuisse, vt omnes admonerentur, in Christo nobis restituendam fore eam beatitatem, quam Adam in paradiso olim amisit. Quoad cœli vocabulum, Hebræi hoc Shamaijm dicunt (quod duális numeri vocabulum est) idq; propter duo hemisphæria, quorum alterum supra Orizontem à nobis cernitur, alterum verò adhuc abscon-sum oculos nostros latet. Eodem autem vocabulo partim aerem denotant (vnde aues cœli dicuntur) partim expansionem illam siue firmamentum, in quo stellæ sunt. At quia hoc vnà cum sphæris suis à Deo creatum est, & initium habuit, ideoq; in fine seculi abolebitur, & (vt Petrus ait) cum stridore præteribit: Verè & proprie tertium cœlum dicitur in Scripturis beatorum mansio siue sedes, quæ extra hunc mundum corruptibilem nobis IESV CHRISTI merito quæsita & parta est, quam idem ille domum Patris sui vocat, quò & ipse spectantibus discipulis suis supra omnes cœlos siue sphæras cœlestes corpore suo ex Maria virgine assumpto ascendit, & nos eodem ad se transferet in nouissimo suo ad iudicium aduentu, vt cum ipso æternum viuamus. In eum locum Apostolum raptum fuisse dicimus, & id totus verborum istorum contextus docet. Quid verò illic fecit? Audiuit ineffabilia verba, quæ non licet homini loqui. Istud verò Paulus non superstitiosè dicit, quasi religio nostra (vt olim de sacris suis Eleusinis gentes fabulabantur) mysteria habeat, de quibus nemini fas sit loqui: neque etiam ex Iudæorum more nomina quædam peculiaria Dei intelligit (quale illi suum illud Schem Hamphoras esse nugantur) sed potius docere vult, non posse vllis verbis ea explicari, quæ nobis in cœlo parata sunt, & proinde nefariam esse temeritatem, si quis ista vel curiosius scrutari, vel etiam exponere conetur. Huc ergo referri potest illud Isaiæ: Quæ oculus non vidit, & auris non audiuit, & in cor hominis non ascenderunt, quæ Deus præparauit diligentibus ipsum. Nec est, quòd aliquis obijciat, cur ea Paulus audiuerit, quæ verbis explicari non possunt? Etenim ei soli hæc visio seruire debuit, quem Deus ad dura certamina vocabat, in quibus multiplici consolatione erat opus. Quæ etiam causa fuit, vt totis annis quatuordecim de illa nemini verbum fecerit, eo nimirum contentus, quòd ipse ex ea fructum efficacem sentiret.
units.tr: But as to the subject of this passage, Paul mentions only one of the many remarkable visions he had. "I know a man in Christ," he says, that is, a Christian or a servant of Christ, "fourteen years ago," and so on. He takes on another person, as if he were speaking not of himself but of someone else, and he relates the matter so that from nearly every word it is clear that he would rather have kept silent. The indication of time does this, for it shows that the thing happened to him fourteen years earlier. Someone who had hidden it for so long would undoubtedly have hidden it still longer, had not the importunity of his opponents forced him to speak of it. Then he sets forth the excellence of the vision, yet in such a way that he attributes nothing at all to himself. For first he writes that he was caught up. This is truly a work of divine power and grace, and it lies in no man's choice or power to be caught up out of himself. But because a rapture takes place in both body and mind, he confesses that he does not know what happened to him, saying: "whether in the body, that is, whether I was caught up in the body, or whether this too was subject to or carried over by another, I do not know; or whether outside the body, that is, whether only the mind was caught up, I likewise do not know."
