The manner of this vision must therefore have been wonderful, since it could be grasped by no bodily sense, nor even by natural understanding, seeing that afterwards he did not learn what had happened to him. This alone ought to suffice us against the curiosity of those who raise questions about the rapture of the Apostle that are by no means necessary, and who weary themselves and others with useless disputes. For, as Augustine rightly warns: "Who dares to say he knows what the Apostle says he does not know?" Where was he caught up? "To the third heaven," which he will presently call paradise. Here there is no need to dispute about the number of the heavens from the books of philosophers or natural scientists, or to raise the question of the earthly paradise in which Adam was first placed, since it is agreed that this lay in the East and was destroyed in the Flood. Paul here speaks of the seat of the glory or majesty of God (whom he elsewhere writes as dwelling in unapproachable light), which is the same place of blessed immortality, where we shall one day see God face to face and, in his presence (to use the words of David), enjoy fullness of joys. And it agrees with our view that Enoch is written in Ecclesiasticus to have been translated into paradise, and likewise that Christ, when hanging on the cross, said to the thief who was about to die: "Today you will be with me in paradise," shortly after he commended his soul into the hands of the Father. From these things it appears that the blessed abode of that eternal happiness was commonly called paradise at that time, so that all might be reminded that the blessedness which Adam once lost in paradise is to be restored to us in Christ. As for the word heaven, the Hebrews call it Shamaijm, which is a word in the dual number, and this on account of the two hemispheres, of which one is seen by us above the horizon, while the other remains hidden from our eyes. By the same word they denote partly the air (whence the birds of heaven are called) and partly that expanse or firmament in which the stars are. But since this, together with its spheres, was created by God and had a beginning, and therefore will be abolished at the end of the age, and (as Peter says) will pass away with a great noise, the third heaven is truly and properly called in Scripture the dwelling or seat of the blessed, which outside this corruptible world has been rightly sought and obtained for us by Jesus Christ, whom that same One calls the house of his Father, and into which he himself, with his disciples looking on, ascended above all the heavens or celestial spheres, with his body taken from the Virgin Mary, and at his final coming to judgment he will bring us to himself in the same place, so that we may live eternally with him. We say that the Apostle was caught up into that place, and the whole context of these words shows this. But what did he do there? He heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter. Paul does not say this superstitiously, as if our religion (as the nations once told tales of their Eleusinian rites) had mysteries about which it is not right for anyone to speak; nor does he mean certain peculiar names of God after the manner of the Jews (such as they foolishly claim that their Schem Hamphoras is), but rather he wishes to teach that the things which are prepared for us in heaven cannot be explained by any words, and that it is therefore a wicked rashness if anyone tries either to investigate these things too curiously or even to expound them. To this, then, may be referred that saying of Isaiah: "Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man, the things which God has prepared for those who love him." Nor is there reason for anyone to object: why did Paul hear things that cannot be expressed in words? For this vision was to serve him alone, whom God was calling to hard conflicts, in which he needed manifold consolation. This was also the reason why for all fourteen years he spoke of it to no one, being content, of course, with the fact that he himself felt its effective fruit.

units.la: Sed omissis curiosis potius quàm vtilibus quæstionibus, Dei morem obseruemus, qui visionibus & reuelationibus varijs eos instruit, quorum opera siue ministerio ad res arduas vult vti: & vt ita fiat necesse est, vt & fortiores sint in periculis, & in rebus agendis magis idonei. Exempla huius rei in Abrahamo & aliis Patriarchis extant: Mose item & omnibus Prophetis. Et Christus inter discipulos hunc delectum habuit, vt suæ clarificationis spectatores atq; testes facere ret Petrum, Ioannem & Iacobum, quos graujoribus periculis atque laboribus deflinauerat. Et hoc ipsum cum Paulo quoque factum est. Debebat is electum organum esse, cuius ministerio regnum Dei longè lateq; propagaretur. Ne ergo (vt Chrysostomus annotauit) reliquis Apostolis inferior haberetur, qui cum Christo in terris agente versati erant, & diuinitatis eius argumenta in operibus eius miraculosis & gloriosa à mortuis resurrectione viderant, ipsum rapi & cœlestis suæ maiestatis spectatorem in spiritu, aut etiam in corpore (nam vtro modo id factum sit, ne ipse quidem sciuit) fieri voluit. Facit ad doctrinæ propheticæ & apostolicæ commendationem, ne de eorum veritate dubitemus, quos inusitatis rationibus Deus in altiorem rerum cœlestium cognitionem introduxit: neue illis aures præbeamus, qui in æterna salutis causa ea tradunt, quorum neq; Prophetæ neq; Apostoli meminerunt. Confutantur praeterea Pauli exemplo omnes, qui de futura vita statu curiosius disputant, neq; ijs contenti sunt, quae de hoc in sacris literis traduntur: quales sunt, qui hierarchias & choros Angelorum atq; Diuorum finxerunt. Quibus non immerito adnumerauerit nostri seculi doctores, qui contra Scripturarum veritatem & diserta Christi verba supra coelos locum aliquem esse negant. (Aristotelem fortasis in hoc dogmate aeterno Dei Filio praeferendum esse putantes) & vna cum Christi corpore ipsos etiam coelos ad omnia loca, supera, infera, extendunt. Fuit equidem Moses verus & familiarissimus Dei veri oeconomus, cum quo per totos dies quadraginta colloquutus est, vt nunc infinita alia colloquia taceamus. Quid vero ille pronuntiat? Praeceptum istud (inquit) quod ego tibi praecipio hodie, non est abconditum abs te, neq; remotum: Non est in coelis, vt dicas: Quis ascendet nobis in coelos, vt ipsum nobis afferat, &c? En praeceptis a Deo iam traditis nos instituere iubet, non ea quaerere, quae Dei verbo non traduntur. Vidit & Isaias gloriam Domini: sed idem ille (vt supra annotauimus) de caelestium bonorum statu & conditione verba facturus, ait: Quae oculus non vidit, & auris non audiuit, &c. Et Paulus, cum in tertio coelo haec coram audiuisset, tamen ineffabilia esse fatetur. Constat item aliquos ex mortuis olim resuscitatos fuisse, inter quos fuit Lazarus ille Bethanienfis, quem Christus amicum suum vocare dignatus est. Quid vero illi vel de coelis vel inferis retulit? aut quid ex eius ore nobis Apostoli tradiderunt? Vnum hoc ex Euangelio nobis constat, quod vita huic redditus perinde vt antea Christi discipulus atq; auditor fuit: quem haud dubie relicturus erat, si aliam quam ab illo tradi audiebat, alterius vitae conditionem esse comperisset. Quid, quod ipse Dominus rediuius ex Scripturis concionatus est, non noua & prius inaudita vitae futurae mysteria discipulis exposuit. Atqui omnes isti multo rectius & verius de coelis disputare potuissent, quam nostri illi, qui suis portentosis de omniprasentia corporis Christi disputationibus reuera coelum cum terra, & beatas coelicum sedes cum inferis miscent.
units.tr: But let us set aside questions that are curious rather than useful, and observe the custom of God, who instructs by various visions and revelations those whose work or ministry he wishes to use in weighty matters. And so that this may be done, it is necessary that they be stronger in dangers and more fit for the business at hand. Examples of this are found in Abraham and the other patriarchs, likewise in Moses and all the prophets. Christ too had this choice among his disciples: he wished Peter, John and James, whom he had destined for heavier dangers and labours, to be spectators and witnesses of his glorification. And this was done also in the case of Paul. He was to be a chosen instrument, through whose ministry the kingdom of God would be spread far and wide. Lest therefore (as Chrysostom observed) he be thought inferior to the other Apostles, who had lived with Christ while he was acting on earth and had seen the proofs of his divinity in his miraculous works and in his glorious resurrection from the dead, God willed that he too be caught up and become a spectator, in spirit or even in body (for in which way it happened, not even he himself knew), of his heavenly majesty. It serves to commend the prophetic and apostolic teaching, so that we may not doubt the truth of those whom God has led by unusual means into a higher knowledge of heavenly things, and that we may not give ear to those who hand down, as necessary to eternal salvation, things of which neither the Prophets nor the Apostles made mention. Moreover, by Paul's example all are refuted who dispute too curiously about the state of the future life, and are not content with what is handed down about it in the Sacred Scriptures: such as those who have invented hierarchies and choirs of angels and of the saints. Among these, not undeservedly, our teachers of this age may be numbered, who, against the truth of Scripture and the plain words of Christ, deny that there is any place above the heavens (perhaps thinking that Aristotle is to be preferred to the eternal Son of God in this matter), and who extend the heavens together with the body of Christ to all places, above, below and beyond. Moses indeed was a true and most intimate steward of the true God, with whom he talked for forty whole days, not to mention the countless other conversations. But what does he declare? "This commandment," he says, "which I give you today, is not hidden from you, nor far off: it is not in heaven, that you should say, Who will go up for us into heaven to bring it to us, etc.?" See, he bids us be instructed by the precepts already delivered by God, and not to seek those things which are not handed down in the word of God. Isaiah too saw the glory of the Lord; but the same man, when about to speak of the state and condition of heavenly goods (as we noted above), says: "Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, etc." And Paul, although he had heard these things in the third heaven, nevertheless confesses that they are unspeakable. It is also agreed that some were raised from the dead in former times, among whom was that Lazarus of Bethany, whom Christ deigned to call his friend. But what did he report to us either of heaven or of hell? Or what did the Apostles hand down from his mouth? From the Gospel we know only this: that, returned to this life, he was just as before a disciple and hearer of Christ; and undoubtedly he would have left this life again, had he discovered that the condition of another life was other than what he heard taught by him. Moreover, when the Lord himself, risen again, preached from the Scriptures, he did not set forth to his disciples any new mysteries of the future life that had not been heard before. Yet all those men could have disputed about the heavens far more rightly and truly than those of our time, who by their monstrous disputations about the omnipresence of the body of Christ in fact mix heaven with earth, and the blessed seats of heaven with the underworld.

units.la: Sed Paulum audiamus, qui narrationem hanc concludens ait: De huiusmodi gloriabor: de meipso vero non gloriabor, nisi in infirmitatibus meis. Duos ex seipso homines facit. Vnum, quem hac gratia dignatus fit Deus, & de illo se gloriari velle dicit: nimirum, non vt seipsum venditet, sed gratiam sibi a Deo factam praedicet. Alterum, qui erat quoad suam naturam & conditionem, quam cum aliis hominibus habebat communem. Quoad hunc, se quicquam gloriaturum negat, nisi de infirmitatibus, quas in semetipso sentiat. Verissime autem sibi ipsi nihil aliud quam infirmitates tribuit. Quid enim ex nobis ipsis habemus, quam quod infirmum, caducum, vitiosum, mortale est? Ex eo autem nobis vberrima praebetur gloriandi materia, si simul Dei bonitatem & mirificam eius virtutem in nobis se exerentem consideremus. Rursus aut docemur, suspectos nobis esse debere eos, qui visiones ambitiose iactant. Fuit hoc semper peculiare impostorius, vt Valentinianorum & Gnosticorum, Mahumetis item exempla docent: quos hodie Monachi & Anabaptistae imitantur. Longe aliter sancti, quos visionibus territos & consternatos fuisse alibi exemplis multis demonstrauimus. Sunt ergo alteri illi impostores nequissimi, quibus procul relictis nos in Prophetis & Apostolis loquentem audire debemus aeternum Dei Filium, Dominum ac Seruatorem nostrum, IESVM CHRISTVM: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But let us hear Paul, who, concluding this narrative, says: "Of such a one will I glory; yet of myself I will not glory, but in my infirmities" (2 Cor. 12:5). He makes two men out of himself. One is the man whom God has honoured with this grace, and of him he says he wishes to glory: not, of course, so as to puff himself up, but to proclaim the grace granted to him by God. The other is the man he was in his own nature and condition, which he shared in common with other men. Concerning this man, he denies that he will glory in anything except the infirmities he feels in himself. And most truly he attributes to himself nothing but infirmities. For what do we have from ourselves but what is weak, fleeting, sinful and mortal? Yet from this there is offered to us a most abundant matter for glorying, if at the same time we consider the goodness of God and his wonderful power displayed in us. Again, we are taught that those who boast ambitiously of visions ought to be suspect in our eyes. This has always been the peculiar mark of impostors, as the examples of the Valentinians and Gnostics teach, and likewise of Muhammad; and today the monks and Anabaptists imitate them. The saints were quite otherwise, whom we have shown elsewhere by many examples to have been terrified and dismayed by visions. Those other impostors, then, are most wicked, and, leaving them far behind, we ought to hear in the Prophets and Apostles the eternal Son of God, our Lord and Saviour, JESUS CHRIST, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LV.
units.tr: HOMILY 55.

units.la: Nam si voluero gloriari, non ero insipiens: veritatem enim dicam: sed parce loquor, ne quis de me cogitet supra id, quod videt me esse, aut quod audit ex me. Et ne excellentia reuelationum super modum efferrer, datus est mihi surculus infixus carni, angelus Satanae, vt me colaphis caedat, ne supra modum efferar. Super hoc ter Dominum rogaui, vt abscederet a me. Et dixit mihi: Sufficit tibi gratia mea; nam potentia mea in infirmitate perficitur.
units.tr: For if I wish to boast, I shall not be foolish, for I shall be telling the truth. But I refrain, so that no one may think of me beyond what he sees me to be, or beyond what he hears from me. And lest I be lifted up beyond measure by the greatness of the revelations, a thorn in the flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to buffet me, so that I might not be exalted above measure. Concerning this I besought the Lord three times that it might leave me. And he said to me: My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.

units.la: Diligenti & longa narratione exposuit Paulus labores atq; pericula, quæ pro Christi nomine subierat. Id verò non fecit priuatæ gloriæ studio, sed quia sic opus erat, ne æternæ salutis doctrina propter ipsum in contemptum veniret, & pseudoapostolis locus daretur, qui passim Ecclesias turbabant. Postremò autem ad revelationes deuenit, quibus ipsum Deus hucusq; instruxerat atq; confirmarat, vt tot tamq; duris certaminibus posset sufficere. In quo argumento etsi amplissimam haberet gloriandi materiam, modestissimè tamen agit. Nam ex multis revelationibus vnam modò narrat: & ita quidem, vt non dissimulet infirmitatem suam, quam tunc senserat: & simul omnem gloriam vni soliq; Deo transcribit, qui ipsum ista gratia dignatus fit. Caeterum obijcere poterant aduersarij, ipsum ideo nolle huic argumento diutius insistere, quòd non haberet quod vere dicat: & fortasis illud omne quod dixerat, nihil aliud quàm somnium aut ex cerebri infirmitate obortam illusionem fuisse: istud nunc præoccupatione diluit, & rem omnem diligentius illustrat.
units.tr: Paul set out, in a careful and lengthy account, the labours and dangers he had undergone for the name of Christ. He did not do this out of a desire for private glory, but because it was necessary, so that the teaching of eternal salvation would not be held in contempt on his account, and so that no room would be given to the false apostles, who were throwing the churches into confusion everywhere. Finally he came to the revelations by which God had instructed and strengthened him up to that point, so that he could endure such harsh and numerous conflicts. In this matter, although he had very ample material for boasting, he speaks most modestly. For, out of many revelations, he relates only one, and that in such a way that he does not conceal the weakness he had felt at that time, and at the same time he ascribes all the glory to the one and only God, who deigned to bestow this grace upon him. Moreover, his opponents could object that he did not wish to dwell longer on this subject because he had nothing true to say; and perhaps everything he had said was nothing but a dream or an illusion arising from a sickness of the brain. He now forestalls this objection and explains the whole matter more carefully.

units.la: Propositio huius loci est: Si voluero gloriari, non ero insipiens. Rationem subijcit: Quia veritatem dicam. Itaq; insipientem dicit pro vano & mendace, quare sensus est: Etiamsi pergam ea narrare, quæ mecum egit Deus, nemo tamen me stultitiæ aut vanitatis accusauerit. Nam quæ vera sunt dicam, neque hic aliquid affingam. Verumtamen alias ob causas parcius loquar de ijs, quæ prolixè narrare poteram. Quo loco rursus admonemur, parum prudentes esse eos, qui falsis atque ementitis laudibus sese venditant. Etenim sordet laus propria, etiamsi nihil falsum habeat: & non sine causa viris grauibus atque cordatis suspecti sunt, qui res abs se gestas ambitiosius iactant. Quis ergo non extremè stultos atque intolerabiles eos esse dixerit, qui insuper mentiuntur? Hi enim aut ea iactant, quæ omnino facta non sunt (quod vanitatis inexcusabilis argumentum est) aut quæ alij fecerunt, in se transferunt: quod cum iniustitia coniunctum est. Quare modestè de seipsis omnes sentire & loqui decet, ne dum virtutis existimationem sibi parare volunt, infames fiant. Sed audiamus Pauli rationes, propter quas breuitati in hac causa studuit.
units.tr: The proposition of this passage is: If I wish to boast, I shall not be foolish. He gives the reason: because I shall be telling the truth. Thus he calls "foolish" what is empty and false. The sense is: even if I go on to relate what God has done with me, no one will be able to accuse me of folly or vanity, for I shall tell what is true, and I shall add nothing fictitious here. Nevertheless, for other reasons I shall speak more sparingly about those things which I could narrate at length. At this point we are again reminded that those are not wise who puff themselves up with false and invented praises. For self-praise is unseemly even when it contains nothing false, and men of weight and sound judgment are rightly suspicious of those who boast of their achievements too ambitiously. Who, then, would not say that those are utterly foolish and intolerable who, on top of that, lie? For they either boast of things that were never done at all (which is an inexcusable proof of vanity), or they claim as their own what others have done, which is joined with injustice. Therefore everyone ought to think and speak modestly of himself, lest, while he wishes to win for himself a reputation for virtue, he become infamous. But let us hear Paul's reasons, on account of which he was eager to be brief in this matter.

units.la: Primam his verbis completitur: Ne quis de me cogitet supra id, quod videt me esse, aut quod audit ex me. Id est, ne quis mihi plus tribuat, quàm homini tribui debet: sed talem me omnes agnoscant, qualem esse vident, & quem me esse audiunt ex meis sermonibus, aut etiam aliorum fidelium relatione, qui rectius de omnibus iudicant. Videbant omnes, Paulum hominem esse, variis casibus (vt & reliqui homines sunt) obnoxium. Audiebant vero, eundem Dei seruum esse, & mysteriorum Dei dispensatorem. Vult ergo intra hos limites subsistere omnium hominum de se & suo ministerio iudicia: & ideo abstinet ab eorum commemoratione, quæ vires humanas superabant. Nec absq; causa cautione ista tam diligenti vsus est: cum adhuc recens apud eum esset Lystrensium memoria, qui propter paralyticum ab eo miraculose curatum, ipsum Mercurium esse putarant, & diuinos honores ei exhibere voluerant: quando scilicet vestibus in mediam turbam cum Barnaba insiliens, orationem habuit, quæ propriam continet eorum, quæ hic scribit, interpretationem: Nam sic dixit: Viri, cur ista facitis. Nos quoque ijsdem quibus vos affectionibus obnoxij sumus, annuntiantes vt ab istis vanitatibus conuertamini ad Deum illum viuum, &c. Vide Actor. 14. Capite.
units.tr: He completes the first reason with these words: "that no one may think of me beyond what he sees me to be, or what he hears from me." That is, that no one may ascribe to me more than is due to a man; rather, let all recognise me as I am seen to be, and as they hear me to be from my own words, or also from the report of other faithful men, who judge all things more rightly. All saw that Paul was a man, subject to various misfortunes, as other men are. But they heard that he was a servant of God and a steward of God's mysteries. He therefore wishes that the judgments of all men about himself and his ministry should remain within these limits; and for this reason he refrains from mentioning those things which exceeded human powers. Nor without cause did he use such careful caution, since the memory of the Lystrans was still fresh with him. On account of a paralytic whom he had miraculously healed, they had thought he was Mercury, and had wished to offer him divine honours; when, namely, leaping with Barnabas in their garments into the midst of the crowd, he gave a speech which contains a fuller explanation of the things he writes here. For he spoke thus: "Men, why do you do these things? We too are subject to the same passions as you, proclaiming that you should turn from these vanities to the living God," etc. See Acts, chapter 14.

units.la: Habet ergo locus hic generalem doctrinam, quid de sanctis Dei seruis sentire debeamus? Nimirum secundum id quod videmus, & quod ex illorum ore audimus. At in sacris literis videmus eos homines fuisse mortales, infirmos, imò peccatores & suis vitijs obnoxios. Et hoc illos ipsos audimus fateri. Abrahamus enim cum Deo colloqui volens, se puluerem & cinerem esse protestatur. Dauid se in peccatis conceptum esse ait, & delictorum iuuentutis suæ meminit, orat denique, ne Deus velit cum ipso ingredi in iudicium. Apud Isaiam verò vna omnium sanctorum vox est: Iustitia nostræ sunt panni centonum, &c. Idem vno ore omnes homines ad vnum Deum remittunt, qui solus inuocari, solus coli, & cui soli omnis nostræ salutis gloria transcribi debeat. His ergo insistamus, & exosculemur gratiam Dei, qui in illis efficax fuit, obediamus autem ipsorum doctrinæ, quam proprij sanguinis testimonio obsignarunt. At hodie fere diuersum fit. Nam plerique in celebrandis sanctorum laudibus occupantur, doctrinam verò illorum negligunt: quæ omnium superstitionum præcipua causa est.
units.tr: Does this passage therefore contain a general teaching on what we ought to think about the holy servants of God? Surely, according to what we see, and what we hear from their own mouths. But in the sacred writings we see that they were mortal men, weak, indeed sinners, and subject to their own vices. And we hear these very men confess this. For Abraham, when he wished to speak with God, declares that he is dust and ashes. David says that he was conceived in sins, recalls the offences of his youth, and finally prays that God may not wish to enter into judgment with him. In Isaiah, moreover, there is one voice of all the saints: "All our righteousnesses are as filthy rags," etc. All men alike refer themselves to the one God, who alone is to be invoked, alone worshipped, and to whom alone the glory of all our salvation must be ascribed. Let us therefore dwell on these things, and embrace the grace of God, who was effective in them; let us obey their teaching, which they sealed with the testimony of their own blood. Today, however, it is almost the reverse. For most people are busy celebrating the praises of the saints, but neglect their teaching, and this is the chief cause of all superstitions.

units.la: Videm sibi ipsi conciliat.
units.tr: They win favour for themselves.

units.la: Quod autem de seipso Paulus dicit, hoc singuli sibijpsis accommodare debent. Nam omnes homines perinde cauere debent ne quis illos maioris quàm æquum est faciat, quàm ne ab aliquibus contemnantur. Etiamsi enim nos aliqui nunc minoris faciant, imò etiam conuitientur, erit tamen tempus, quando existimatio nostra afferetur, & notum est illud Prophetæ: Memoria iusti erit laudabilis. At si nos pluris fieri patiamur, nosq; ementitis laudibus venditemus, detegetur aliquando fraus, & exaltationem istam ruina sequetur. Arguit locus hic totum Papatum, qui fere in eo consistit, quòd homines alij videri volunt, quàm revera sint, & de seipsis quoque aliter loquuntur. Nam si à capite, Papa nimirum, exordiaris, vult is Semideus quidam dici, imò IESV CHRISTI vicarius, cui omnis potestas non in cœlo modò & in terra, verumetiam in nouo illo mundo omnibus insulis fortunatis quæstuosiore, Purgatorio nimirum, datasit. Idem se tantum non ἀναμάρτητον fingit, qui nec peccare aut errare possit nec ab aliquo reprehendi debeat. Ad hæc Sanctissimus, & ipsa Sanctitas, denique Seruus seruorum Dei vocatur. Atqui vident simul & audiunt omnes homines, Papam hominem esse mortalem, omnis generis affectionibus obnoxium, imò hominem peccati, ambitiosum, auarum, sanguinarium, & quid non? Ad capitis vero exemplum Clerus totus (vt illi loquuntur) spirituales sese dicunt, cùm toti carnales sint. Monachi item, id est, solitarij censeri volunt, qui suis examinibus vrbes & agros implent. In vulgo item iusti censentur, qui quanti quanti sunt, peccatores sunt: & operum suorum meritis gloriantur, qui propter manifesta scelera exitium merentur, vt nunc de occultis nihil dicamus. Quis ergo mendax, nisi Antichristus? Aut num isti idem cum Paulo dicere possunt: Ne quis cogitet de nobis supra id, quod nos videt esse, aut quod audit ex me?
units.tr: What Paul says about himself, each person ought to apply to himself. For all men should take equal care that no one makes them greater than is fair, as that they are not despised by some. For even if some now think less of us, or even revile us, there will nevertheless come a time when our reputation will be restored, and that saying of the Prophet is well known: "The memory of the righteous will be praiseworthy." But if we allow ourselves to be held in higher esteem than we are, and sell ourselves with false praises, the fraud will one day be revealed, and a fall will follow that exaltation. This passage condemns the whole Papacy, which consists almost entirely in this, that men wish to appear other than they really are, and speak of themselves differently too. For if you begin from the head, the Pope namely, he wishes to be called a certain demigod, indeed the vicar of Jesus Christ, to whom all power has been given not only in heaven and on earth, but also in that new world, Purgatory, more profitable than all the fortunate islands. He likewise pretends to be utterly sinless [ἀναμάρτητον], one who can neither sin nor err and ought not to be rebuked by anyone. Besides, the Most Holy, and Holiness itself, finally the Servant of the servants of God, is what he is called. Yet all men see and hear at the same time that the Pope is a mortal man, subject to every kind of passion, indeed a man of sin, ambitious, greedy, bloodthirsty, and what not? Following the example of the head, the whole clergy (as they put it) call themselves spiritual, when they are wholly carnal. The monks likewise wish to be regarded as solitaries, though they fill cities and fields with their swarms. Among the common people, too, those are considered righteous who, however many they may be, are sinners, and who glory in the merits of their works, though on account of manifest crimes they deserve destruction, not to mention, for now, their hidden sins. Who, then, is the liar, if not Antichrist? Or can they say the same thing as Paul: that no one should think of us beyond what he sees us to be, or what he hears from me?

units.la: Altera ratio, propter quam Apostolus de laudibus suis parcius loqui voluit, haec est, quòd Deus ipsum gloriari vetet. Nam dicit: Et ne excellentia reuelationum supra modum efferrer, data est mihi surculus infixus carni, &c. Argumentum verbis istis subest eiusmodi: Pij hominis est non luctari cum Deo, neq; id velle, quod ille aperte vetat: Atqui Deum video me nolle superbire aut efferri donis, quæ in me contulit: Ergo id ego nec velle nec etiam facere debeo. Ad Minoris confirmationem facit, quòd dicit: Datus est mihi σκόλοψ, id est, surculus siue palus carni infixus, qui nimirum carnem meam pungat atq; discrutiet, meq; ad humilitatem erudiat. Quis verò ille surculus siue palus fuerit, varie & multum inter se diuersæ sunt interpretum sententiæ. Alij de morbo aliquo, qui ei familiaris fuerit, exponunt: & hunc alij acutos & certis vicibus recurrentes capitis dolores fuisse dicunt: alij Iliaca laborasse illum putant. Alij non sine notoria, quam electo Dei organo faciunt, iniuria de libidinis æstro hoc dici intelligunt. Atqui facile erat huic malo mederi legitimo connubio, quod ipse alijs mandat, qui vruntur. Quid, quod sibi donum castitatis à Deo datum esse alibi fatetur? Chrysostomus hostes denotari putat, quos ei Deus vbiq; locorum multos atq; graues obiecerit, & inter hos nominatim recenset Alexandrum fabrū ærarium, Hymenæum, Phi letum, sub quibus omnes alios horum similes comprehendit. Sunt, qui locū hunc de vno aliquo certo aduersario exponant, qui ipsum vbiq; locorum insecutus sit, vt ei negotiū faceret. Sed quia tot tantisq; laboribus non potuisset sufficere corpus infirmū & morbo alicui familiari obnoxium, & non de hoste aliquo externo, sed de surculo carni ipsius infixo loquatur, ego tentationē graviorem notari arbitror, qua Deus illū non in corpore solum affligi, verumetiā intra animum & conscientiam suam exerceri voluerit, ne donorum excellentia superbiret. Et huic sensui fauet, quod ad Rom.7. Cap. de graui illa luctā scribit inter Legem Dei & Legem peccati quā in corde suo sentiebat, adeò vt ea quasi in extremas angustias adactus clamaret: Miser ego homo, quis me liberabit ex hoc corpore mortis? Etenim credibile est, obrepsisse simul ei vitæ anteactæ & crudelitatis, qua in fideles Christi seuierat, recordationē, quam ipsi Satan suggerebat, vt quam in Dei gratia fiduciam collocata habebat, labefactaret. Nam qui scadalis, quæ aliunde pijs obijci videbat, totus verebatur, quomodo potuit non totus exhorrescere & intra conscientiā suam æstuare, quoties cogitabat, quàm diris quamq; indignis modis ipse Christi membra tractauisset, quàm multos item fide coegisset abnegare? Nec enim cum sono, qui aures feriebat, simul intra animū eius terribilis illa vox Christi euanuerat: Saul Saul, cur me persequeris? Et quàmuis non dubitaret de gratia Dei, manebant tamen stimuli conscientiæ, qui acerbissimam istorum scelerum recordationem innouabant. Augebat dolorem istum angelus malus, Satan nimirum, qui insuper illum quotidie novis terro-ribus exagitabat, & simul hostes externos excitabat, ut eum tantumnon colaphis cæderet, id est, conuitijs, calumnijs, persecutionibus, carceribus, flagris & omni iniuriarum genere exagita-ret. Id tamen omne ad Deum refert Paulus, qui ita fieri velit, ne ipse supra modum suæ conditio-nis efferretur, cui erat destinatus. Continet autem locus hic eximiam doctrinam de tentationi-bus & aduersis, quibus in huius vitæ curriculo exercemur.
units.tr: A second reason why the Apostle wished to speak sparingly of his own praises is that God forbids him to glory in them. For he says: "And lest I should be exalted above measure by the abundance of revelations, there was given me a thorn in the flesh," etc. The argument in these words runs as follows: it is the mark of a godly man not to struggle against God, nor to will what he plainly forbids. But I see that God does not want me to be puffed up or elated by the gifts he has bestowed on me. Therefore I neither ought to will this nor actually do it. The lesser premise is confirmed by his words: a thorn (σκόλοψ), that is, a stake or stick fixed in the flesh, which surely pricks and tears my flesh and trains me to humility. Opinions differ widely and variously among the interpreters about what that stake or thorn was. Some explain it as a certain illness familiar to him, and others say it was sharp headaches that recurred at set intervals. Others think he suffered from iliac disease. Still others, not without a notorious insult to God's chosen instrument, understand it to mean a goad of lust. Yet it would have been easy to remedy such an evil by lawful marriage, which he himself commends to those who use it. What of the fact that he elsewhere confesses that the gift of chastity was given him by God? Chrysostom thinks that enemies are meant, whom God set against him in many places and grievous ones, and among these he names Alexander the coppersmith and Hymenaeus and Philetus, under whom he includes all others like them. Some expound this passage of one particular adversary who pursued him everywhere to make trouble for him. But since a weak body, liable to some familiar disease, could not have sufficed for such great and many labours, and since he speaks not of an external enemy but of a thorn fixed in his own flesh, I judge that a more severe temptation is meant, by which God wished him to be afflicted not only in body but also to be exercised within his mind and conscience, so that he would not grow proud of the excellence of his gifts. This sense is also supported by what he writes in Romans 7 about that heavy struggle between the law of God and the law of sin which he felt in his heart, so that, driven as it were to the utmost straits, he cried out: "Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?" For it is credible that there crept over him at the same time the recollection of his former life and of the cruelty with which he had raged against the faithful of Christ, a recollection which Satan himself suggested to him in order to shake the confidence he had placed in the grace of God. For since he was wholly fearful of the scandals which he saw were thrown at the godly from elsewhere, how could he not utterly shudder and seethe within his conscience whenever he thought in what dreadful and unworthy ways he himself had treated the members of Christ, and how many he had forced to deny the faith? For that terrible voice of Christ had not vanished from his mind along with the sound that struck his ears: "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" And although he did not doubt the grace of God, the goads of conscience remained, which renewed the most bitter memory of these sins. The angel of evil, Satan indeed, increased this pain, who moreover harassed him daily with new terrors and at the same time stirred up external enemies, so that they all but struck him with fists, that is, harassed him with insults, slanders, persecutions, prisons, scourgings and every kind of injury. Paul, however, refers all of this to God, who wills that it happen so that he himself would not be exalted above measure in the condition to which he was destined. This passage contains, moreover, an outstanding teaching about the temptations and adversities with which we are exercised in the course of this life.

units.la: Et primò quidem admonemur, ista omnia à Deo immitti, quæ nos vel intus vel foris infe-stant. Innuit hoc Paulus, quando furculum hunc sibi datum esse dicit. Nam quàmuis simul Sata-næ mentionem faciat, hic tamen non aliter quàm ut sententiæ diuinæ executor considerari debet: quando constat, eum nihil contra nos posse, nisi hoc ei permittat Deus. Et quid obsecro contra nos posset, qui ne porcos quidem audet inuadere, nisi Christus iubeat, sicuti Euangelica historia do-cet? Seruit hoc primum consolationi, ne in hac palæstra desperemus. Est enim Deus fidelis no-striq; amans, & quia nos saluos vult, nunquam nos supra vires nostras tentari patietur. Deinde officij quoque nos ista admonent. Quia enim hæc per Satanæ ministerium fiunt, qui nostra per-ditione gaudet, procul dubio concessa sibi potestate strenuè vtitur. Itaq; vt vigilemus necesse est, & in precibus assidui simus, ne nostra securitate illi maiorem & liberiorem demus nobis nocen-di occasionem.
units.tr: And first of all we are warned that all those things which trouble us, whether inwardly or outwardly, are sent by God. Paul hints at this when he says that this thorn was given to him. For although he at the same time mentions Satan, he is to be regarded here only as the executor of the divine decree, since it is clear that Satan can do nothing against us unless God permits it. And what, I ask you, could he do against us, when he does not even dare to attack swine unless Christ commands it, as the Gospel history teaches? This serves first for consolation, so that we may not despair in this contest. For God is faithful and loves us, and since he wills our salvation, he will never allow us to be tempted beyond our strength. Then these things also admonish us of our duty. For since these things come about through the ministry of Satan, who rejoices in our destruction, he undoubtedly uses the power granted him vigorously. Therefore we must be watchful, and be constant in prayers, lest by our carelessness we give him a greater and freer occasion to harm us.

units.la: Obseruabis etiam, quòd Paulo datus fuit surculus ille, & quòd idem à Satana colaphis cæ-sus est. At quantus ille fuit, quem Dei Filius organum electum nominare dignatus est? Ergo ne sanctissimi quidem à tentationibus liberi atq; immunes sunt. Sensit has acerrimas Iobus, quàm-uis ipsius Dei testimonio probaretur. Et Patriarchas olim in hac palæstra ad extremum usque spiritum desudauisse legimus. Quod ipsum de Prophetis, Apostolis & innumeris aliis dici potest. Prodest hoc imprimis considerauisse, ne aduersa & tentationes grauiores Dei irati argumenta esse putemus: quin potius nos sanctissimorum Dei seruorum, imò Filij eius vnigeniti & dilecti, IESV CHRISTI, socios hac ratione fieri cogitemus, neq; dubitemus de dicti illius Apostolici veritate: Si cum eo morimur, cum eodem viuemus: si sufferimus, etiam cum eo regnabimus.
units.tr: You will also observe that the thorn was given to Paul, and that Satan likewise struck him with fists. But who was so great that the Son of God deigned to call him a chosen instrument? Therefore not even the most holy are free and exempt from temptations. Job felt these most bitter trials, although he was approved by the testimony of God himself. And we read that the patriarchs of old sweated in this contest right to the last breath. The same can be said of the Prophets, the Apostles and countless others. It is especially useful to consider this, so that we do not think adversities and heavier temptations are signs of God's anger. Rather, let us reflect that by this means we are made companions of the most holy servants of God, indeed of his only begotten and beloved Son, Jesus Christ, and let us not doubt the truth of that saying of the Apostle: "If we die with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him."

units.la: Facit ad huius consolationis confirmationem finis totius pugnæ, quam Paulus sustinuit. Nam hæc ideo sibi accidisse ait, ne excellentia visionum atque donorum Dei supra modum effer-retur. Ergo nostro bono nos exerceri & affligi finit Deus. Est enim caro ad omne malum procli-uis, superbia autem, quæ omnibus insita est, immodico gloriæ studio plerunque eos inflammat, qui se prærogatiuis aliquibus ornatos esse vident. Et sane magna esse oportet huius mali vim, quan-do in tanto Apostolo adhuc locum habere potuisset, nisi illud tam duro tamq; acerbo antidoto re-pressisset Deus. Quid ergo de te speres ô infelix, qui in vmbra & otio quantumuis leui occasione oblata cristas attollis? Quin potius tuæ infirmitatis memor vigilas, & quoties aduersum quid pa-teris, hoc à Deo tibi immitti cogitas, ne efferaris? Habet præterea hæc quoque pars non vulga-rem consolationem. Voluit Satan Paulum perdere: sed iuuit potius, & eum ad humilitatem eru-dijt, sic volente Deo, cui infelix ille vel inuitus obtemperare cogitur.
units.tr: The purpose of the whole struggle which Paul endured contributes to the confirmation of this consolation. For he says that these things happened to him so that he would not be exalted above measure by the excellence of God's visions and gifts. Therefore God allows us to be exercised and afflicted for our good. For the flesh is prone to every evil, and pride, which is implanted in all, often inflames with an immoderate desire for glory those who see themselves adorned with some privileges. And indeed the force of this evil must be great, since it could have still found a place in so great an Apostle, had God not repressed it with so harsh and bitter a remedy. What, then, can you hope for yourself, O unhappy one, who raise your crests at the least opportunity offered in shade and leisure? Rather, mindful of your weakness, do you not keep watch, and whenever you suffer anything adverse, do you not think it has been sent to you by God, so that you may not be puffed up? Moreover, this part also holds no ordinary consolation. Satan wanted to destroy Paul, but he helped him rather, and trained him to humility, as God willed, to whom that unhappy one, even against his will, is compelled to submit.

units.la: Sed audiamus, quid interea fecerit Apostolus. Super hoc (inquit) ter Dominum rogaui, vt abscederet à me, scilicet Angelus ille Satanæ. Ergo non ad Exorcistas aut Magos, infelicia dia-boli mancipia, confugit, sed ad Deum, & huius opem pijs precibus implorauit. Id vero se ter secis-se scribit, quod plerique pro Sæpius exponunt, quasi numerus finitus pro infinito positus sit, vt in illo Vergilij: O terq; quaterq; beati, &c. Sed ego minimè opus esse puto, vt aliam exposi-tionem quæramus, cùm verba hæc quàm simplicissimè & secundum literam intelle-cta ad præsen-tem causam probè faciant. Nam oraculi meminit, quo admonitus Deum ita velle, didicit hanc crucem patienter ferri, neque liberationem posthac peti debere. Itaque Christi exemplum secutus est Paulus, qui cùm ad montem oliuarum ter precatus esset Patrem, vt calicem diræ illius pas-sionis abs se transferret, vbi ab Angelo confirmatus, vidit aliter Patri visum esse, mox hosti-bus obuiam processit. Docent autem exempla ista, sanctos non esse ἀπαθεῖς, qui nullis affectio-nibus moueantur, qualem Stoici suum virum bonum finxerunt. Etenim nisi Paulus grauem in corde suo molestiam sensisset, nunquam tam serio orauisset Dominum, vt ab ista tentatione libe-raretur. raretur. Quod ipsum in aliorum quoque sanctorum querelis obseruari debet, quibus illi inhæren-tes sibi infirmitates non dissimulant. Sunt ergo nimis temerarij, qui præcipiti iudicio omnes eos damnant, quos periculis imminentibus moueri & perterrefieri vident. Imprimis tamen in Pauli exemplo hoc nobis imitandum est, vt ipsi quoque in periculis ad vnum Deum confugiamus per Mediatorem vnicum IESVM CHRISTVM. Ille enim solus curas & labores nostros omnes nouit: solus vbique præsens est, vt nos audiat: solus omnia potest. Neque est, quòd de eius voluntate dubitemus, qui ne Filio quidem proprio parcere voluit, vt nos seruaret, qui mille mortes & sempiternos inferorum cruciatus merebamur. Obseruarunt hoc omnes sancti, vt mirum sit hodie in tam clara Euangelij luce multos ita hallucinari, vt Deos cælites inuocent, cùm hoc & expresso Dei mandato prohibeatur, qui vt in die tribulationis ipsum inuocemus iubet, & nullum ex Scripturis exemplum produci possit, quo defunctorum inuocatio probetur.
units.tr: But let us hear what the Apostle did meanwhile. "Concerning this," he says, "I besought the Lord three times that it might leave me," namely that angel of Satan. Therefore he did not flee to exorcists or magicians, unhappy slaves of the devil, but to God, and implored his help with godly prayers. Now he writes that he did this three times, which many often explain as if a definite number were put for an indefinite one, as in that line of Virgil: "O thrice and four times blessed," etc. But I think there is no need to seek another explanation, since these words, understood as simply as possible and according to the letter, serve the present case well. For he recalls the oracle by which, once admonished that God wished it so, he learned that this cross must be borne patiently and that deliverance should not be sought from then on. Thus Paul followed the example of Christ, who, when he had prayed three times to the Father on the Mount of Olives that the cup of that dreadful passion might pass from him, was strengthened by an angel, saw that it seemed otherwise to the Father, and at once went out to meet his enemies. Moreover, these examples teach that the saints are not without passions [ἀπαθεῖς], those who are moved by no affections, such as the Stoics imagined their wise man to be. For unless Paul had felt a grave distress in his heart, he would never have prayed so earnestly to the Lord to be delivered from this temptation. This must also be observed in the complaints of other saints, in which they do not hide the weaknesses that cling to them. Therefore those are too rash who with hasty judgment condemn all those whom they see moved and terrified by impending dangers. Above all, however, in Paul's example this must be imitated by us: that we too, in dangers, flee to the one God through the one Mediator, Jesus Christ. For he alone knows all our cares and labours; he alone is present everywhere to hear us; he alone can do all things. Nor is there reason to doubt his will, who did not even wish to spare his own Son, so that he might save us, who deserved a thousand deaths and everlasting torments of hell. All the saints have observed this, so that it is strange that today, in the so clear light of the Gospel, many go so astray as to invoke the heavenly saints, although this is forbidden by the express command of God, who bids us invoke him in the day of trouble, and no example can be produced from the Scriptures by which the invocation of the dead is approved.

units.la: Quid verò Deus Paulo respondit? Audiuit quidem precantem, & procul dubio animum eius grauiter laborantem respexit, non tamen eius petitione ratam habuit, & vehementius instantem de sua voluntate admonuit, dicens: Sufficit tibi gratia mea: nam potentia mea in infirmitate perficitur. Quærunt aliqui, quomodo Dominus Paulum allocutus sit. At est quæstio ista superuacanea. Quid enim nostra interest hoc scire? Ita verò hoc factum esse constat, vt Paulus sciret hæc sibi non ab alio quàm à Domino dici. Propositio est: Sufficit tibi gratia mea. Id est, Ne petas te hac molestia liberari, qua te ego exerceo, quia sic opus habes. Interim verò tibi sufficere debet mea gratia, qua nimirum tibi hactenus adfui, ne succumberes, & qua in posterum quoq; te iuuabo, vt tentationibus omnibus possis sufficere.
units.tr: What then did God answer Paul? He indeed heard him praying, and no doubt looked upon his soul, which was sorely troubled, yet he did not approve his request, and, admonishing him of his own will as Paul pressed more vehemently, said: "My grace is sufficient for you: for my power is made perfect in weakness." Some ask how the Lord spoke to Paul. But that question is superfluous. For what does it matter to us to know this? It is certain, however, that this happened in such a way that Paul knew these words were spoken to him by the Lord and by no one else. The statement is: "My grace is sufficient for you." That is, do not seek to be freed from this affliction with which I am exercising you, since you have need of it in this way. Meanwhile my grace ought to be sufficient for you, that grace by which, I assure you, I have hitherto stood by you, so that you did not give way, and by which I will also help you in future, so that you may be equal to all temptations.

units.la: Docent ista, preces piorum nunquam esse prorsus irritas aut inutiles. Licet enim non impetrent quod petunt, exaudit tamen illos Deus, & pro ijs quæ petunt, dat magis necessaria. Sic olim Dauid, non quidem liberabatur statim ex periculis, quibus illum Saul exagitabat, at inter ista Deum sibi adesse sentiebat, qui ne illis opprimeretur, ipsum seruabat. Oremus ergo indesinenter, at interea non præscribamus Deo temere, sed preces nostras eius voluntati subijciamus, sicut Christus non solùm in precandi formula, quam nobis tradidit, verum etiam proprio exemplo docet. Etenim diuinæ misericordiæ opus est, quòd ea nobis negantur, quæ nocitura erant, si illa obtineremus. Sufficiat ergo nobis quoque, quòd nos Deum propitium habere scimus, qui vt promissionibus amplissimis nos instruxit, ita istarum omnium nobis complementum dedit in Filio suo IESV CHRISTO, qui iam ex terris hisce abiturus dixit: Ecce, ego vobiscum sum vsque in consummationem seculi. Itaque nobis quoq; illum loqui putemus, quoties vel egestate, vel perse-cutionibus, vel alijs periculis vndique premimur: Sufficit tibi gratia mea, &c.
units.tr: These words teach that the prayers of the godly are never altogether vain or useless. For although they do not obtain what they ask, God nevertheless hears them, and in place of what they ask, gives what is more necessary. So once David, though he was not at once freed from the dangers with which Saul harassed him, yet among these things he perceived God to be present with him, who preserved him so that he was not overwhelmed by them. Let us therefore pray without ceasing, but meanwhile let us not rashly prescribe to God, but submit our prayers to his will, just as Christ teaches, not only in the form of prayer which he handed down to us, but also by his own example. For it is a work of divine mercy that those things are denied us which would have harmed us had we obtained them. Let it therefore be enough for us also that we know we have God propitious to us, who has furnished us with the most ample promises, and in his Son Jesus Christ has given us the fulfilment of all of them, who, about to depart from this earth, said: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the world." Therefore let us also think that he speaks to us whenever we are pressed on every side, whether by want, by persecutions, or by other dangers: "My grace is sufficient for you," etc.

units.la: Sed rationem audiamus, qua Paulum Deus confirmat. Nam potentia mea in infirmitate perficitur. Emphaticè loquitur, Potentia mea: qua scilicet ego per te & alios collegas tuos hucusque egi, qua item seruos meos erigo, confirmo, recreo & seruo, qua denique regnum meum longè lateque propago. Ea (inquam) perficitur in infirmitate meorum seruorum, id est, tunc vberrimam habet sese exerendi materiam, quando tu aut alij ad extremas angustias redacti, vos infi-miores esse sentitis, quàm vt oneribus ferendis possitis sufficere. Apparet hoc euidentissimè in Apo-stolis, qui si huius seculi authoritate atque viribus instructi fuissent, negotium hoc quod agebant, humanum videri poterat. At quia homines idiotæ, illiterati, obscuri, infirmi & omnium iniurijs expositi fuerunt, diuinum illud opus esse & Dei auspicijs perfectum fuisse constat. Recte ergo Theodoretus scripsit: Eorum qui prædicant infirmitas, aperte ostendit eius, qui prædicatur, potentiam. Et adumbratur hic nobis euidenter, quæ sit ratio quisue modus diuini auxilij. Etenim si ipsi nobis sufficeremus, Deo nequaquam nobis opus esset, neque etiam intelligeremus nos eius manu seruari. Cùm enim ne nunc quidem omnes illud agnoscant, quid fieret, si loco essemus meliore? Patitur ergo nos Deus ad extrema vsque deuenire, vt nostræ infirmitatis sensus & ex eò enatus dolor nos cogat ad ipsum confugere, vtque ipsius virtute nos liberari fateamur. Et huc multa pertinent, quæ in Psalmis habentur, imprimis autem querelæ piorum, quibus fatentur, se in profundo calamitatum hærere, in abyssum demersos esse, ab hostibus vndique cingi, vt nulla sa-lutis spes in humanis sit reliqua. Discamus igitur hoc loco, cur Deus humanum genus tot malis atq; aerumnis obnoxium fieri velit? Nimirum ut haec ipsi quasi officina sit, in qua suam potentiam, bonitatem & misericordiam exerceat. Ex eo autem consolationis argumenta petamus in omni genere tentationum, & cogitemus, Deum (ut ipse apud Isaiam fatetur) saepe alienum opus facere, ut occasionem habeat nos iuvandi, quod opus eius est proprium. Exempla, quibus hoc probetur, habes in liberatione Israelitarum ex Aegypto, in exilio Babylonico, in Davide, Ezechia, & infinitis aliis. Et nostro tempore multa huius generis vidimus, ut non dubium sit, Dei auxilium (ut olim Philo dicebat) tunc incipere, quando humanum deficit. Observandum hoc etiam in salutis aeternae negotio. Nam hic imprimis salutifica Dei nos per Christum liberantis potentia in nostra infirmitate perficitur: quando nimirum peccatorum nostrorum agnitione intra conscientiam nostram conviti ad throunum gratiae cogimur confugere. Humiliemur ergo omnes sub potenti manu Dei, & in periculis intrepidi salutis fiduciam omnem in illius gratia collocemus, cuius nobis Mediator unicus est Filius eius dilectus, IESVS CHRISTVS: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But let us hear the reason by which God confirms Paul. "For my power is made perfect in weakness." He speaks emphatically: "My power," namely that by which I have hitherto worked through you and your other colleagues; that by which I also raise up, strengthen, refresh and preserve my servants; that by which, in short, I spread my kingdom far and wide. This (I say) is made perfect in the weakness of my servants, that is, then it has the amplest opportunity to show itself, when you or others, brought to extreme distress, feel yourselves too weak to be able to bear the burdens. This appears most evidently in the Apostles, who, if they had been furnished with the authority and strength of this age, might have seemed to be doing a human work. But because they were uneducated men, unlettered, obscure, weak, and exposed to the injuries of all, it is plain that this was a divine work and was accomplished under God's auspices. Theodoret rightly wrote: "The weakness of those who preach plainly shows the power of him who is preached." And here is clearly set before us what is the reason and manner of divine help. For if we were sufficient for ourselves, we would by no means need God, nor would we understand that we are kept safe by his hand. For since even now not all acknowledge this, what would happen if we were in a better position? God therefore allows us to come to the extremity, so that the sense of our weakness, and the pain arising from it, may compel us to flee to him and confess that we are freed by his power. Many things pertaining to this are found in the Psalms, especially the complaints of the godly, in which they confess that they cling in the depths of calamities, have been sunk into the abyss, are surrounded on every side by enemies, so that no hope of salvation remains among men. Let us learn, then, from this place, why God wishes the human race to be subject to so many evils and troubles? Surely that these may be, as it were, a workshop in which he exercises his power, goodness and mercy. From this let us seek arguments of consolation in every kind of temptation, and let us consider that God (as he himself confesses through Isaiah) often does a "strange work," so that he may have occasion to help us, which work is properly his own. You have examples by which this is proved in the deliverance of the Israelites from Egypt, in the Babylonian exile, in David, Hezekiah, and infinite others. And in our own time we have seen many things of this kind, so that there is no doubt that the help of God (as Philo once said) begins then when human help fails. This is also to be observed in the business of eternal salvation. For here above all the saving power of God, who frees us through Christ, is made perfect in our weakness: namely, when, convicted within our conscience by the recognition of our sins, we are compelled to flee to the throne of grace. Let us therefore all be humbled under the mighty hand of God, and in dangers, fearless of salvation, let us place all our confidence in his grace, of which his beloved Son Jesus Christ is our sole Mediator: to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LVI.
units.tr: HOMILY LVI.

units.la: Libentissime igitur gloriabor potius de infirmitatibus meis, ut inhabitet in me potentia Christi. Propterea oblector in infirmitatibus, in contumeliis, in necessitatibus, in persecutionibus, in angustiis, pro Christo. Cum enim infirmus sum, tum potens sum.
units.tr: Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me. Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses, for Christ's sake. For when I am weak, then am I strong.

units.la: Quoniam Paulus electum illud Dei organum fuit, cuius ministerio Euangelium per totum orbem inter gentes propagari debebat, necesse omnino erat, ut sui nominis existimationem contra calumniatores sedulo tueretur, ne propter ipsum veritatis doctrina vilesceret. Id vero sic facit, ut simul suo exemplo doceat, quae omnium administrorum verbi Dei studia esse, & quibus idem potissimum gloriari debeat. Cum enim multa posset narrare, quae Deus cum ipso privatim egerat per varias revelationes, imo cum ut imperator aliquis gentes per Euangelij praedicationem deuictas & ad Christi obsequium adductas recensere posset, & quasi triumphis atque trophaeis gloriosissimis superbire: abstinet tamen ab istorum commemoratione, ne quis rerum ab ipso gestarum magnitudine deceptus, de ipso sublimius sentiret, quam de homine sentire fas est. Sed neque consilium Dei dissimulat, qui ipsum hucusque crebris atque variis tentationibus ad modestiam & humilitatem erudierit. Ubi perquam memorabilis est illa sententia, qua Deus ipsum sua gratia contentum esse iussit, qui tunc nos iuvandi & suam potentiam exercendi materiam habeat uberrimam, quando nos in extremis periclitamur, nec aliqua in humanis auxilij spes nobis affulget.
units.tr: Since Paul was that chosen instrument of God through whose ministry the Gospel was to be spread among the Gentiles throughout the whole world, it was absolutely necessary that he should diligently defend his good name against his slanderers, lest the teaching of the truth itself be held in contempt because of him. He does this in such a way that, by his own example, he also teaches what the zeal of all the ministers of God's Word ought to be, and in what they ought above all to glory. For although he could recount many things that God had done with him privately through various revelations, indeed although, like some general, he could list the nations conquered by the preaching of the Gospel and brought into obedience to Christ, and could boast as if in most glorious triumphs and trophies, he nevertheless refrains from mentioning these things, lest anyone, deceived by the greatness of his achievements, should think of him more highly than it is right to think of a man. Nor does he disregard the counsel of God, who has trained him up to this point through frequent and various temptations to modesty and humility. Here is that most memorable saying by which God bade him be content with His grace: He who wishes to help us and to exercise His power has the richest material precisely when we are in the greatest danger, and no hope of human help shines upon us.

units.la: Porro pergit Paulus, & oraculum hoc causae praesenti applicans ait: Libentissime igitur gloriabor potius de infirmitatibus meis, ut inhabitet in me potentia Christi. Quasi diceret: Gloriantur alij hominum applausu & favore, dignitatibus, eloquentia, & aliis huius generis rebus, quae mundi iudicio magnifica sunt, sese ostentent: at mihi longe alia mens est. Etenim nihil mihi iucundius fuerit, quam gloriari in infirmitatibus meis, id est, iis rebus, quae ut mundo infirma videntur, meq; apud multos contemptibilem faciunt: ita mihi causa sunt, ut infirmitatem meam agnoscam, & humilius de me sentiam. Rationem vero huius dicti reddit: Ut inhabitet in me potentia seu virtus Christi. In Graeco habetur verbum ἐπισκηνώσῃ, & Metaphora est à tabernaculis aut tentorijs sumpta: Nam proprie idem significat, quod aliquem quasi tentorio supra ipsum expanso tueri atque protegere. Quo sensu in Psalmis Angelus Domini castrametari aut tentoria figere dicitur circa eos, qui hunc timent. Docet ergo hac locutione Paulus, se adeo non pudere aut pigere afflictionum, ut potius eis delectetur propter dulcissimam illam protectionem IESV CHRISTI, cuius divina virtute & potentia se seruari & recreari sentiat.
units.tr: Paul goes on, applying this oracle to the present case, and says: Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me. It is as if he said: Others glory in the applause and favour of men, and in dignities, eloquence, and other things of this kind, which are magnificent by the world's judgement, and they display themselves. But my mind is quite different. For nothing is more pleasing to me than to glory in my infirmities, that is, in those things which seem weak to the world and make me contemptible in the eyes of many. They are so much a cause to me that I recognise my weakness and think more humbly of myself. He gives the reason for this saying: that the power or strength of Christ may dwell in me. In the Greek there is the verb ἐπισκηνώσῃ [may tabernacle upon], and the metaphor is taken from tents or pavilions. For properly it means the same as protecting and shielding someone as if a tent had been spread over him. In this sense in the Psalms the Angel of the Lord is said to encamp or pitch tents round those who fear Him. Paul therefore teaches by this expression that he is so far from being ashamed or weary of afflictions that he rather takes delight in them because of that most sweet protection of Jesus Christ, by whose divine strength and power he feels himself preserved and refreshed.

units.la: Observabis autem hoc ita ab ipso dici, ut afflictiones sive aduersa, quibus exercebatur, causam esse fam esse doceat diuinæ protectionis. Quasi diceret: Nisi ita exercerer, hæc non haberet locum apud me, & proinde maxima ista voluptate ego carerem, quam ex illa percipio. Rursus igitur hic de multiplici afflictionum vsu admonemur. Primus est, quòd nos in propriæ infirmitatis cognitionem adducunt, qui primus ad salutem gradus est. Alter quòd humiles atq; modestos reddunt, vt sicuti pauones conspectis pedibus caudam demittere solent, ita nos nostræ imbecillitatis sensu ter riti confidentiæ cristas supprimamus. Sequitur ex eo tertius, quòd salutificæ virtutis Christi capa ces reddunt. Nec enim temere dictum est, Deum humilibus gratiam conferre, superbis autem resistere. Item: Dissipauit superbos cogitatione cordis ipsorum, detraxit potentes de sedibus, & exaltauit humiles. Quod Iacobus obseruans monebat: Humiles vos præbete in conspectu Dei, & eriget vos. Etenim, vt alij eleganter & rectè annotarunt, sicuti valles pluuijs cœlestibus rigantur, & fœcundiores fiunt, fulminibus autem feriuntur summa altissimorum montium cacumina, quæ ne pluuijs quidem cedunt, vt asperitatem suam & sterilitatem exuant: Ita quos propriæ infirmitatis & innatæ vitiositatis sensus ad humilitatem erudiuit, vt inter alios homines instar vallium sint, ijs sua gratia & benedictione Deus adest, vt indies proficiant, & (vt Psalmus dicit) de virtute in virtutem progrediantur: E contra vero, qui suarum virium & propriæ virtutis fiducia superbi sese attollunt, ijdem seipsos Christi Spiritu & virtute spoliant, adeoq; sibijpsis ostium præcludunt, quò minus illa ad ipsos possit pertingere. Docent ista, cur hodie tam pauci sint, in quibus præclari illi virtutis atque gratiæ Dei effectus conspiciantur, vt olim in primitiua Ecclesia vulgo factum fuisse legimus: Nimirum, quòd plerique vel superstitionibus dementati suam iustitiam iactant, vel huius seculi bonis addicti stolida ambitione turgent atque superbiunt, pauci vero sese Deo subijciunt, vt vel verbo suo vel eiusdem virgis paternis ad modestiam erudiantur.
units.tr: Observe, moreover, that he says this in such a way as to show that the afflictions or adversities with which he was exercised are the cause of the divine protection. It is as if he said: Unless I were so exercised, this protection would have no place with me, and so I would lack that greatest joy which I receive from it. Here, then, we are again reminded of the manifold use of afflictions. The first is that they lead us to a knowledge of our own infirmity, which is the first step to salvation. The second is that they make us humble and modest, so that, just as peacocks are wont to lower their tails when they see their feet, so we, sensing our own weakness, may suppress the crests of our bold confidence. From this follows a third: they make us capable of the saving power of Christ. For it was not without reason said that God gives grace to the humble but resists the proud. Likewise: He has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts, has put down the mighty from their seats, and has exalted the humble. James, observing this, warned: Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up. Indeed, as others have elegantly and rightly observed, just as valleys are watered by heaven's rains and become more fruitful, while the highest peaks of the loftiest mountains are struck by lightning and do not even yield to the rains, so that they do not shed their roughness and barrenness, so God, with His grace and blessing, is present to those whom the sense of their own infirmity and innate sinfulness has taught humility, so that they are like valleys among other men, that they may advance daily and (as the Psalm says) go from strength to strength. On the contrary, those who, trusting in their own powers and their own virtue, lift themselves up in pride, these same men strip themselves of the Spirit and power of Christ, and so shut the door against themselves, so that it cannot reach them. These considerations explain why today there are so few in whom the remarkable effects of the virtue and grace of God are seen, as we read was commonly the case in the early Church. Namely, because most either, driven mad by superstitions, boast of their own righteousness, or, addicted to the goods of this age, swell and grow proud with foolish ambition, while few submit themselves to God, so that they may be trained to modesty either by His Word or by the fatherly rods of the same.

units.la: Quia ergo res ista maximi est momenti, amplius explicat quod dixit: Propterea oblectior in infirmitatibus, in contumelijs, in necessitatibus, in persecutionibus, in angustijs pro Christo. Oblectari se dicit, vt ostendat se infirmitates, quas Deus ipsi imponat, non modò patienter ferre, sed voluptatem quoque ex illis percipere singularem. Et ne infirmitatis nomine leuiculum quid notare putetur, species eius præcipuas ex ordine subtexit, primum locum contumelijs tribuens, quas sustinere cogebatur, eò quòd Iudæi ipsum impium patriæ Legis desertorem, religionis prophanatorem, Mosis & cultus diuini hostem, gentes verò nugiuendum & (quod grauius erat) totius orbis turbatorem esse dicerent. Secundò necessitates numerat, quibus imprimis rerum penuriam denotat (vt Cap. sexto diximus) & quà illum frequenter laborauisse scimus, adeò vt manuum labore victum sibi pararet. Potest tamen vocabulu istud hoc loco latius extendi ad pericula omnis generis, in quibus sæpenumero, quoad humana nulla auxilij aut salutis spes apparebat. Tertiò, persecutionum nomine comprehendit infesta sibi hostium consilia, insidias, seditiones, fugas, exilia, carceres, plagas & verbera: de quibus omnibus supra quoque est dictum. Postremò angustias nominat, quæ proprie pericula grauiora significant, quæ rerum incertos faciunt, vt quid consilij capi debeat, nesciamus. Et videtur Metaphora petita esse ex re militari, vbi interdum copiæ abhostibus in loca angustiora & inuia coguntur, vt neque perfugij via sit, neque etiam pugnandi copia illis detur. Tale quid fuit, quod in Asia Paulo accidisse supra Cap. primo audiuimus, quando ipse sibi mortis sententiam tulerat.
units.tr: Since this matter is of the greatest moment, he explains more fully what he has said: Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses, for Christ's sake. He says that he takes pleasure in them to show that he not only bears patiently the infirmities that God lays upon him, but also derives from them a singular delight. And lest anyone think that by the name of infirmity something trivial is meant, he sets out its principal kinds in order. He gives first place to reproaches, which he was forced to endure because the Jews called him an impious deserter of the law of his country, a profaner of religion, an enemy of Moses and of divine worship, and the Gentiles called him a babbler and (what was more serious) a troubler of the whole world. Second, he enumerates necessities, by which he chiefly means scarcity of goods (as we said in the sixth chapter), and we know that he often suffered from this, so that he had to earn his living by the labour of his hands. Yet this word can in this place be extended more widely to dangers of every kind, in which very often, when no hope of human help or salvation appeared, he was caught. Third, under the name of persecutions he includes the hostile plots of his enemies, their ambushes, seditions, flights, exiles, prisons, blows and beatings, all of which were also mentioned above. Lastly he names distresses, which properly denote more serious dangers, which make men uncertain of their affairs, so that we do not know what counsel ought to be taken. The metaphor seems to be drawn from military affairs, where sometimes troops are forced by enemies into narrower and trackless places, so that there is neither a way of escape nor any opportunity of fighting for them. Something of this kind happened to Paul in Asia, as we heard in the first chapter, when he had himself passed the sentence of death.

units.la: Quo loco rursus apparet, quæ piorum atque ministrorum Christi fors sit, dum in terris vi-uunt. Odit illos mundus propter Veritatis lucem, qua ipsius impietas & opera prava arguuntur. At tanta tamen, venerabilis est Veritatis maiestas, vt nemo eius ofor aut hostis videri velit. Hinc illæ impijssimorum quoque hominum voces audiuntur: Et quis Dei Verbum reijciat? aut Veritatem oderit? Interim verò ijdem odio Veritatis implacabili extimulati in huius cultores atque ministros impetum faciunt, quos calumnijs petunt, & omni genere contumeliarum adobruunt. Fit ergo, vt multi non mali suspicionibus sinistris imbuantur, & ipsi quoq; illos odisse incipiant. Quæ deinde persecutionum grauissimarum causa est, per quas optimi quique fortunis suis spoliantur, natali solo pelluntur, vt incertis sedibus oberrent, & in extrema rerum omnium penuria in singulas horas de vita quoque periclitentur. Factum hoc omnibus seculis. Olim certè Eliæ temporibus, hic quidem apud Sareptanam viduam, alij verò Prophetæ in diuersis spelunci delitescentes pane & aqua alebantur, impijs Baalis sacerdotibus ex Reginæ Iezabelis mensa seducere voluptuantibus. Imo plerosq; Prophetas tunc crudeliter occisos fuisse, Elias queritur. Idem posteris quoq; temporibus contigit, vt in historijs Ecclesiasticis esse videre. Quid hodie multis in locis fiat, deploratione potius quàm commemoratione dignum est. Plerique enim Christi ministros omni contumeliarum genere afficiunt, ijsdem insidias struunt & omnia infesta reddunt, adhæc in necessitates & angustias adigunt, vt cum fame conflictentur, qui vitæ æternæ Manna toti mundo ex Dei penu depromere satagunt.
units.tr: Here again it appears what the lot of the godly and of the ministers of Christ is while they live on earth. The world hates them because of the light of the truth, by which its impiety and wicked works are exposed. Yet so great and venerable is the majesty of the truth that no one wishes to be seen as its enemy or opponent. Hence those voices of even the most impious men are heard: Who would reject the Word of God, or hate the truth? Meanwhile, however, these same men, goaded by an implacable hatred of the truth, attack its worshippers and ministers, assail them with slanders, and overwhelm them with every kind of insult. So it comes about that many, imbued with unfavourable suspicions, though not wicked themselves, begin to hate them too. From this arises the most grievous persecutions, by which the best men are stripped of their goods, driven from their native soil, wander about without settled homes, and, in the utmost lack of all things, are endangered in their lives every hour. This has happened in every age. Certainly in the times of Elijah, some were fed with bread and water at the widow's house at Zarephath, and other prophets hiding in various caves, while the impious priests of Baal were feasting at the table of Queen Jezebel. Indeed, Elijah complains that many prophets were then cruelly put to death. The same happened in later times, as can be seen in the ecclesiastical histories. What is done today in many places is more worthy of lamentation than of recounting. For many treat the ministers of Christ with every kind of insult, lay snares for them, make everything hostile to them, and moreover reduce them to necessities and distresses, so that they struggle with hunger, although they strive to bring forth for the whole world the manna of eternal life from God's store.

units.la: Quid vero inter ista facere debent pij? Paulus se aduersis istis oblectari ait. Atqui idem alibi de illis queritur, & nuper Dominum se ter precatum esse fatetur, vt angelum Satanæ ab ipso auferret, qui eum colaphus cædebat. Porro hic meminisse oportet, eandem esse rationem IESV CHRISTI & ministrorum eius. Ille quia humanæ salutis cupidissimus erat, & æterno Patris decreto cupiebat obedire, desiderio desiderauit vltimam Cœnam cum discipulis agere, vt ea facta opus nostræ redemptionis aggrederetur. At quia idem ille hominem verum assumpserat, vnà cum infirmitatibus nostris, diræ illius mortis recordatione turbabatur sæpius. Nunc (inquit) anima mea turbata est, & quid dicam? Pater, serua me ex hac hora. Item: Nunc anima mea turbata est vsq; ad mortem. Imo precatur quoque Patrem, vt calycem istum à se transferat. Ita sanctis quoq; solet accidere. Non sunt enim hi truncorum aut lapidum instar ἀναισθήτως, qui nihil sentiant, neq; dolore vllo permoueantur: & hoc quoque in illorum precibus atque querelis euidentissimè apparet. Sed præualet in omnibus certaminibus, quæ sustinent, Spiritus Christi, qui animos eorum huius amore atq; desiderio accendit, vt ipsis volupe fit aliquid pro Christo sufferre, quo testentur, quanti illum faciant: denique ad quæuis parati sunt, modo illius sint, & hic ipsos pro seruis atque membris suis agnoscat. Exemplum huius rei Apostoli sub initium statim suæ functionis præbuerunt, quando in Senatu virgis cæsi cum gaudio exibant, & Deo gratias agebant, qui eo honore dignos iudicarat, vt pro ipsius nomine talia paterentur. Et huc respiciens Paulus, credentes in afflictionibus gloriari scribit, vt quæ noua gratiæ experimenta ipsis indies supeditent, & quia ipsdem persuasissimum sit, nihil esse, quod ipsos possit separare à dilectione Dei, qua nos hic in Christo complexus est. Vide Rom.5. & 8.
units.tr: What, then, ought the godly to do amid these things? Paul says he takes delight in such adversities. Yet elsewhere he complains about these same people, and recently he confesses that he prayed three times to the Lord that he might take away the angel of Satan who was buffeting him. Here we must remember that the case of Jesus Christ and that of his ministers is the same. He, being most eager for human salvation and wishing to obey the eternal decree of the Father, earnestly desired to eat the last supper with his disciples, so that, once it was done, he might undertake the work of our redemption. But because he had assumed a true human nature, along with our infirmities, he was often troubled by the memory of that dreadful death. "Now," he says, "my soul is troubled, and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour." Likewise: "Now my soul is troubled, even unto death." Indeed he even prays the Father to take this cup from him. So it commonly happens to the saints too. For they are not like trunks or stones, [ἀναισθήτως] insensible, feeling nothing and moved by no pain; and this appears most plainly in their prayers and complaints. But the Spirit of Christ prevails in all the struggles they undergo, kindling their minds with love and longing for him, so that it is a joy to them to suffer something for Christ, by which they bear witness how highly they esteem him. In short, they are ready for anything, provided they belong to him and he acknowledges them as his servants and members. The apostles gave an example of this at the very beginning of their office, when, scourged in the council, they went out rejoicing and gave thanks to God, who had judged them worthy of that honour, to suffer such things for his name. Looking to this, Paul writes that believers glory in afflictions, because these bring them fresh experiences of grace day by day, and because they are fully persuaded that nothing can separate them from the love of God, with which he has embraced us in Christ. See Rom. 5 and 8.

units.la: Quia tamen quod Paulus dixit, se oblectari afflictionibus, carnis iudicio πεποιθότες & absurdum, imo etiam impossibile videtur, dicti eius rationem reddit his verbis: Cum enim infirmus sum, tunc potens sum. Infirmus siue impotens erat Paulus, quando circumquaque aduersis & periculis præssus nihil auxilij aut consilij videbat, quo iuuaretur. Tunc enim simul sentiebat carnis cum fide & spiritu luctantis certamina, & quàm exigua, vel potius nullæ essent suæ vires, si Deus manum suam ipsi subduceret. At tunc idem se robustissimum esse dicit, nimirum in CHRISTO IESV, & in ijs, quæ ad salutis æternæ negotium faciunt. Ita enim noxiæ & illicitæ carnis cupiditates reslinguebantur, è contra vero spiritus præualebat, vt animum ad Deum attolleret, huius solius ope niteretur, quam ita sibi præsentem esse sentiebat, vt nouis quotidie diuini auxilij exemplis confirmaretur.
