units.tr: Yet because what Paul said, that he takes delight in afflictions, seems to the judgment of the flesh absurd, and even impossible, he gives the reason for his saying in these words: "For when I am weak, then I am strong." Paul was weak or powerless when, pressed on every side by adversities and dangers, he saw no help or counsel by which he might be aided. For at such times he felt at once the struggles of the flesh against faith and the Spirit, and how slight, or rather how nonexistent, his own strength would be if God withdrew his hand from him. But then he says that he is most robust, namely in Christ Jesus, and in those things that pertain to the business of eternal salvation. For thus the harmful and unlawful desires of the flesh were checked, while on the contrary the Spirit prevailed, so that he raised his mind to God and leaned on his help alone, which he felt to be so present to him that he was strengthened by fresh examples of divine aid every day.

units.la: Rursus ergo fructus afflictionum nobis commendatur. Debebamus ipsi carnem siue membra nostra terrestria (vt alibi Paulus loquitur) mortificare: quia quo magis illa præualent, eo magis spiritus Dei laborat atque fatigatur. Quæ causa est, quod ieiunia sæpe præcipiuntur, non quidem superstitiosa illa, quæ inepti homines pharisaico more ad certos dies & ciborum delectum astringunt, sed per quæ carni omnia ea subducuntur, quæ eius libidinem accendunt atque fouent. At quia hoc non facimus sponte, sed potius illam, quoad nobis illud per otium & quacunque occasione licet, securam atque petulantiorem facimus, Deus fidi patris instar virgas adhibet, & crucè nos coercet. Idem tamen paternæ suæ indulgentiæ memor, crucem temperat, & (vt in Psalmo scribitur) pro æstu multarum cogitationum consolationes suggerit, quibus recreentur, qui tentationibus succubituri videbantur. Ea ratione fit, vt in Domino robusti fiant, qui prius langue bant: adhæc omni virtutum genere & egregijs fidei documentis floreant, qui paulò ante emortui trunci videbantur. Aduersis enim & ærumnis (vt Chrysostomus scribit) anima purgatur à crassis desiderijs & impuris cogitationibus, vt verè philosophari incipiat, cum securitate (quæ nocentissima
units.tr: Therefore again the fruit of afflictions is commended to us. We ought to mortify the flesh, or our earthly members (as Paul says elsewhere). For the more the flesh prevails, the more the Spirit of God labours and is wearied. This is the reason why fasts are often prescribed; not those superstitious fasts which foolish men bind upon themselves in the Pharisaic manner, on certain days and with a selection of foods, but those by which everything is withdrawn from the flesh that kindles and feeds its lust. Yet because we do not do this willingly, but rather make the flesh secure and more wanton whenever we have leisure or any opportunity, God, like a faithful father, applies the rod and restrains us with the cross. Yet he, mindful of his fatherly indulgence, tempers the cross and, as is written in the Psalm, in the heat of many thoughts he supplies consolations by which those are refreshed who seemed about to succumb to temptations. By this means those who were formerly weak become strong in the Lord, and those who had seemed like dead trunks flourish with every kind of virtue and with outstanding proofs of faith. For, as Chrysostom writes, the soul is purged of gross desires and impure thoughts by adversities and troubles, so that it begins to philosophise truly. Security, which is the most harmful plague, is shaken off with its pride and self-confidence; it despises earthly things, resists the affections of the flesh, and by a truly Christian patience overcomes whatever is set against it.

units.la: Psalm.94. centissima pestis est) saltum atque confidentiam excutiat, res terrenas fastidiat, affectibus pecuniis resistat, & patientia vere Christiana vincat quaecunque ipsi obijciuntur. Exempla sunt passim, quibus hoc probari potest. Abrahamus quasi nullus erat, cum in natali solo inter opes & suos cognatos otio abundaret, & apud omnes in pretio & honore esset. At ex patrijs aedibus quasi in palaestram evocatus, novas fidei vires animo concepit, quibus grauissima omnis generis tentationum certamina superauit. Iobum quoque semper quidem pietati studuisse, & ipsius Dei testimonio probatum fuisse constat. At idem nunquam haec tam praeclara fidei & patientiae trophaea statuisset, nisi ipsum diabolo diuexandum permisisset Deus. Quid de Dauide dicemus? Nonne hic, cum vicinarum gentium domitor, belli pericula procul a finibus suis repulisset, omnium infirmissimus fuit? Etenim foeda libidini cessit, quae adulterum & latronem fecit eum, qui prius de mundo & huius principe toties triumphabat, quando a socero Saule proscriptus se pulici & cani mortuo conferebat. Sunt etiam publica huius generis exempla Israelitae, quando in Aegypto feliciter agebant, foederis diuini immemores idololatrae facti sunt, & multorum scelerum illecebris succubuerunt: oppressi autem & libertate exuti cum fiducia ad Deum clamauerunt, qui hostibus suis superiores fecit. Et huc totus Iudicum liber debet referri, qui exemplorum eiusmodi plenus est. Idem in primitiua Ecclesia est videre, quae dum exigua esset & contemptibilis, mirifice floruit: quam primum vero crescere coepit, & indies auctior fieri, mox dissensiones exortae sunt, quae illius pacem magna ex parte labefactauerunt. Facit ad huius confirmationem vniuersa Ecclesiastica historiae series, qua docemur, Ecclesias semper sub Cruce floruisse, plerumque vero arridente fortuna laetiori vitiis contraxisse, et remissiores fuisse factas. Et quid hodie passim fiat, plus satis notum est. Quae enim perseuutionibus exagitantur Ecclesiae, in Domino fortes impiorum conatibus sese opponunt, in pietate feruent, & martyrum exemplis indies nouis celebres fiunt. E contra quibus fide in Christo licet tuto profiteri, ij fere languent, et sibijpsis nescio quid magni ex ignaua dissimulatione et turpi cum impijs collusione pollicentur. Nemo igitur miretur, nos nouis quotidie periculis exercemur. Neminem quoque impiorum conatus terreant: Nec enim meta transfilire poterunt, quam illis Deus praefixit: & ut Christum regnare oportet, ita quicquid illi faciunt, credentium saluti seruiet. Itaque exultemus in medijs afflictionibus, & ad Deum totis animis conuersi amplectamur, quam is nobis simul offert, gratiam atque consolationem: disciplina autem eius salutifera vtamur ad cari nis castigationem vitaeq; totius emendationem. Sic enim fiet, ut qui cum aeterno Dei Filio, Domino nostro IESV CHRISTO periclitati sumus, cum eodem olim in coelis viuamus & regnemus. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Psalm. 94. There are examples everywhere by which this can be proved. Abraham was as it were nothing when, in his native land, he abounded in wealth and leisure among his kinsmen, and was held in esteem and honour by all. But called out from his father's house, as if into the wrestling-ground, he conceived new strength of faith in his mind, by which he overcame the most grievous struggles of every kind of temptation. It is also established that Job had always devoted himself to piety, and was proved so by God's own testimony. Yet he would never have set up these most splendid trophies of faith and patience, unless God had allowed him to be harassed by the devil. What shall we say of David? Was he not, though the conqueror of neighbouring nations who had driven the perils of war far from his borders, most feeble of all? For he yielded to shameful lust, which made him an adulterer and a robber, he who had earlier so often triumphed over the world and its prince, when, proscribed by his father-in-law Saul, he compared himself to a flea and a dead dog. There are also public examples of this kind among the Israelites: when they fared happily in Egypt, they forgot the covenant of God and became idolaters, and yielded to the allurements of many sins; but when they were oppressed and stripped of their liberty, they cried to God with confidence, and he made them superior to their enemies. The whole book of Judges should be referred to this, for it is full of examples of this sort. The same can be seen in the primitive Church, which, while it was small and despised, flourished wonderfully; but as soon as it began to grow and increase day by day, dissensions arose which largely undermined its peace. The whole series of ecclesiastical history supports this confirmation, teaching us that the Churches have always flourished under the cross, but, when fortune smiled more pleasantly, they have often been contaminated by vices and have grown more lax. And what is done everywhere today is more than sufficiently known. For the Churches that are harassed by persecutions stand firm in the Lord against the attempts of the impious, glow with piety, and become more famous day by day through the examples of martyrs. On the other hand, those among whom it is safe to profess faith in Christ are for the most part languid, and promise themselves I know not what great things from idle dissimulation and shameful collusion with the impious. Let no one therefore wonder that we are exercised by new dangers every day. Nor let the attempts of the impious terrify anyone. For they cannot leap over the boundary which God has set for them; and just as Christ must reign, so whatever they do will serve the salvation of believers. Let us therefore rejoice in the midst of afflictions, and, turning to God with all our minds, embrace the grace and consolation which he offers us at the same time; and let us use his saving discipline for the correction of the flesh and the amendment of our whole life. For thus it will come about that we who have suffered with the eternal Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, shall live and reign with him in heaven. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LVII.
units.tr: HOMILY LVII.

units.la: Fui insipiens in gloriando: vos me coegistis, nam ego debueram a vobis commendari. Nulla enim in re inferior fui summis Apostolis, tametsi nihil sum. Signa quidem Apostoli aedita sunt inter vos in omni tolerantia, in signis & prodigijs & virtutibus. Nam quid est in quo fueritis inferiores caeteris Ecclesijs, nisi quod ego ipse vos non grauaui meo otio? Condonate mihi hanc iniuriam.
units.tr: I have become foolish in boasting; you forced me to it, for I ought to have been commended by you. In no respect was I inferior to the chief apostles, although I am nothing. The signs of an apostle were indeed performed among you with all patience, by signs and wonders and mighty deeds. For in what were you inferior to the other churches, except that I myself did not burden you with my idleness? Forgive me this wrong.

units.la: Multis hucusque exposuit Paulus, quid per ipsius ministerium fecerit Deus, & quam multa quamq; grauia pericula propter Euangelium Christi subierit, ut quam plurimos in eius cognitionem adduceret. Id vero (ut saepe diximus) non ambitiose fecit, ut ardelliones solent, sed in eum solum finem, ut suae doctrinae authoritatem tueretur, quam aliqui in ipsius persona euertere conabantur. Ideo narratione iam ita contexuit, ut non obscure appareat, ipsum de Christi gloria potius quam de sua solicitum fuisse. Omnia enim refert ad Deum authorem, qui ipsius ministerio ut dignatus sit: & omissis ijs, quae magna cum laude fecerat, ea narrat, quae ipsum hominem infirmum & diuinae opis indigum esse declarabant. Imo, si rem propius consideres, in illis ipsis Dei potentiam praedicat, qui ipsum inter certamina ista seruarit, atque omnibus aduersis fecerit superiorem. Decet hoc ipsum nos quoque, vt si quid praeclari per nos fecit Deus, eo non gloriemur info-lentius, sed propriae infirmitatis memores illius gratiam celebremus. Praeterea ex ijs, quae iam fa-cta sunt, consolationem petamus, ne facile succumbamus ponderi: quin cogitemus, nobis a Deo ma-teriam offerri, in qua nos fidei & patientiae nostrae specimina edamus, ille vero suam potentiam at-que bonitatem erga nos declarat. At non ignorabat Paulus, Corinthios pro suo more haec omnia calumniaturos esse: ideo excusationem subtexit, qua culpam, si quae admissa sit, in ipsos retorquet.
units.tr: Paul has already set out at length what God has done through his ministry, and how many and how grave the dangers he endured for the sake of the Gospel of Christ, so that he might bring as many people as possible to knowledge of him. He did this, as we have often said, not out of ambition, as busybodies usually do, but for this one purpose only: to defend the authority of his teaching, which some were trying to overthrow by attacking his person. So in his narrative he has arranged things so that it is clear that he was concerned for the glory of Christ rather than his own. He refers everything to God as the author, who deigned to use his ministry; and, leaving aside the things he had done that were worthy of great praise, he recounts those that showed him to be a weak man in need of divine help. Indeed, if you consider the matter more closely, he proclaims God's power even in those very trials, which preserved him in the midst of these conflicts and made him superior to all adversities. This ought to be our own practice too: if God has done anything commendable through us, we should not boast of it the more arrogantly, but, mindful of our own weakness, celebrate his grace. Moreover, from what has already happened let us take comfort, so that we do not easily give way under the burden; rather let us consider that material is offered us in which we may display the proofs of our faith and patience, while God himself declares his power and goodness toward us. But Paul was not unaware that the Corinthians, as is their habit, would slander all these things; so he added an excuse by which he turns back upon them the blame, if any was incurred.

units.la: Factus sum (inquit) insipiens in gloriando: vos me coegistis, &c. Fatetur aliquo modo culpa, quod insipientius ista dixerit quae hucusque audiuimus: Nimirum ad id respiciens, quod vulgo sa-pienti sunt, qui seipsos laudant. Et ideo non simpliciter se excusat, vt ij solent, qui quicquid faciunt & dicunt, omnibus volunt probari, & ne manifestos quidem errores fatentur. At Christiana mode-stia est ea agnoscere & fateri, quae vel in speciem vitiosa sunt. Interim in Corinthios culpam traf-fert Apostolus, dum addit: Vos me coegistis, scilicet haec dicere. Et quia hoc illi negare poterant, rursus id quoque probat: Nam ego debueram a vobis commendari. Id est, veritum erat meum studium atque fidem, qua vobis seruiui, agnoscere, meique nominis existimationem contra improbos calum-niatores illos tueri, qui mihi maliciose detrahunt. Cum vero vos hucusque vestro officio defuerint, & iam non tam de me & mea existimatione, quam de Euangelij doctrina & omnium vestrum sa-lute agatur, ego diutius tacere non potui, neque etiam debui.
units.tr: "I have become foolish in boasting," he says, "you forced me, etc." He admits in some measure a fault, that he has spoken more foolishly than what we have heard so far; clearly he has in view what is commonly regarded as foolish, namely that people praise themselves. And so he does not simply excuse himself, as those do who want to be approved by everyone in whatever they do or say and do not confess even manifest errors. But Christian modesty is to acknowledge and confess even those things that seem faulty. Meanwhile the Apostle shifts the blame onto the Corinthians when he adds: "You forced me," that is, to say these things. And since they could deny this, he proves it again: "For I ought to have been commended by you." That is, my zeal and the faithfulness with which I served you ought to have been acknowledged by you, and you ought to have defended my reputation against those wicked slanderers who maliciously disparage me. But since you have hitherto failed in your duty, and now the matter concerns not so much me and my reputation as the doctrine of the Gospel and the salvation of you all, I could not and ought not keep silent any longer.

units.la: Reprehenditur ergo hic Corinthiorum ingratitudo. Sunt enim nimis ingrati & graui repre-hensione digni, qui bene de ipsis meritorum famam non tuentur, & eorundem dona, quibus illi ipsis seruierunt, ab alijs conculcari patiuntur. Et est hoc proprium Ecclesiae, adeoque singulorum cre-dentium officium, vt doctoris sui, siquidem dignus est, nomen sedulo a contemptu & contumelia vindicent. Quia enim (vt alibi dictum est) parentum instar sunt Verbi praecones, ad illos quo-que pertinet praeceptum de honorandis parentibus. Et si olim capitalem poena merebatur, quisquis summi Pontificis sententiae contumaciter resistebat, quo supplicio non digni erunt, qui Euangelij ministros ideo contemni & eorundem exististimationem labefactari patiuntur, vt illius doctri-nam licentius reijcere & calcare possint? At hodie inter eos, qui Euangelio gloriantur, vix ali-ud vulgarius est, quam quod plerique in eo sunt, vt doctores suos in contemptum adducant, & ex eo summam voluptatem capiant, si quos vel scurrilibus dictis in illos ludere, vel etiam eo-rum famam conuitijs proscindere audiant. Qua causa est, vt undique calumniandi occasio-nem avide captent, sicut olim Iudaei in Ioanne Baptista & Christo factitarunt. Excusant qui-dem aliqui petulantiam suam corruptis quorundam ministrorum moribus, quos hoc ita mereri dicunt. Sed cur non illi eosdem mores in alijs quoque carpunt? cur impostores monachos & sacrificos in pretio habent, quorum maior est in omni vita scurrilitas atque impudentia? cur tam patienter eos ferunt, in quibus ἀδελφοί ... ἴδεῖ, nihil sanum est (vt prouerbio dicitur) siue doctrinam siue mores eorum inspicias? Quare vtut culpam suam maledici illi palliare stu-deant, satis aperte seipsos produnt, quod non nisi Veritatis & verbi Dei odium, quod animis suis iam pridem conceperunt, illos huius administris tam infestos reddat. Solet hoc ipsum in Repub. quoque fieri, vbi minima quaeque vitia aliqui in illis odiose notant, qui pure religionis amantes & bonarum legum strenui vindices sunt: eos autem in caelum vsque ementitis laudibus euehunt, qui religionem omnem extinctam, bonas leges euersas, morum disciplinam e medio sublatam vo-lunt, qui denique vitam omnem in ebrietate, nequitia & omnis generis licentia transfigunt.
units.tr: Here, then, the ingratitude of the Corinthians is rebuked. For those are very ungrateful and deserve severe reproof who do not defend the good name of those who have served them well, and who allow the gifts by which those men served them to be trampled underfoot by others. It is the particular duty of the Church, and indeed of each individual believer, to guard diligently the name of their teacher, if he is worthy, against contempt and insult. For since (as we have said elsewhere) heralds of the Word are like parents, the command to honour parents applies to them as well. And if of old a man was liable to capital punishment who stubbornly resisted the sentence of the supreme Pontiff, what punishment will be deserved by those who allow the ministers of the Gospel to be despised and their reputation undermined, so that they may reject and trample on its teaching more freely? Yet today, among those who boast of the Gospel, scarcely anything is more common than that many people set out to bring their teachers into contempt, and take the greatest pleasure if they hear that someone is mocking them with scurrilous remarks or tearing their reputation apart with abuse. This is why they eagerly seize every opportunity to slander, just as the Jews once did with John the Baptist and Christ. Some excuse their insolence by the corrupt morals of certain ministers, whom they say deserve this treatment. But why do they not also attack the same faults in others? Why do they hold in high regard impostor monks and priests, whose whole life is marked by greater buffoonery and shamelessness? Why do they tolerate so patiently those in whom, whether you look at their teaching or their morals, nothing is sound, as the proverb says [ἀδελφοί ... ἴδεῖ]? Therefore, however much those slanderers strive to cover up their fault, they betray themselves quite plainly: nothing but hatred of the Truth and of the Word of God, which they have long harboured in their minds, makes them so hostile to its ministers. The same thing usually happens in the commonwealth, where some men invidiously brand the smallest faults in those who love pure religion and are vigorous defenders of good laws, while they raise to the heavens with false praises those who want all religion extinguished, good laws overturned, and the discipline of morals abolished, and who in the end spend their whole life in drunkenness, wickedness and every kind of licence.

units.la: Deinde admonemur hoc Pauli exemplo, quae causa sit, cur ministri multa dicant in-terdum, quae plerisque displicent, aut etiam molesta sunt? Ea nimirum, quod sic coguntur face-re ab ijs, qui sui officij minus memores vel ignaua socordia vel etiam aperta malitia peccant. Na-vt de veteribus Prophetis aliquid dicamus, quis dubitet Samuelem maluisse olim Sauli ea dicere,
units.tr: Next, we are taught by this example of Paul the reason why ministers sometimes say many things that displease most people, or even cause annoyance. The reason, surely, is that they are compelled to do so by those who, forgetful of their office, sin either through idle sloth or even through open malice. To say something of the ancient prophets: who would doubt that Samuel was once unwilling to say to Saul the things he was compelled to say,

units.la: ex quibus ille voluptatem potuisset capere? Etenim patet hoc ex eo, quod huius repulsam lachry-mis amaris & diuturnis eo vsque defleuit, donec a Domino corriperetur. At vt acerbius & durius cum illo ageret, eius contumacia merebatur, imo etiam exigebat. Idem de Nathano pos-sumus dicere, qui quanti Dauidem fecerit, ex ijs apparet, qua cum eo de Messia ex ipsius posteris nascituro nasciturò disseruit. Idem tamen illi Dei iram & vindicem gladium minitari coactus est, cùm tur-pi adulterio & indigna Vriæ cæde pœnas graues mertisset. Eundem omnibus Prophetis animum fuisse, non est dubium. Ieremias certè de sua sorte conqueritur, & se mortalium infelicissimum pu-tat, cui perpetuò rixandum sit cum hominibus pœnitere nescijs : nequè falsas fuisse querelas istas, aut simulatas, illius threni post miserabile vrbis & templi excidium conscripti restantur; quibus nihil tristius fingi poterat. De Christo verò quid attinet dicere, qui horribilis illius calamitatis, quæ vrbem atque gentem Iudaicam manebat ne recordari quidem potuit absque lachrymis : ve-rumtamen Sacerdotum incurabili impietate, & totius populi ingratitudine atque contumacia quasi superatus, non potuit non ea dicere, quæ ipsi merebantur? Idem Apostolis omnibus acci-dit, & Paulum Corinthij coègerunt, vt præter animi sui voluntatem nunc ipsos acrius corripe-ret, nunc in pseudapostolos maiori verborum vi inueheretur, nunc suas quoque laudes prædicaret. Horum meminisse debebant hodie, quibus Verbi administri nimij esse videntur in confutandis superstitionibus, in oppugnando Antichristo & eius infelicibus monstris, Monachis nimirum atque tota rasorum & vnctorum cohorte, in arguendis item sceleribus, & pœnis horum denun-tiandis. Atqui coguntur ista facere ab illis ipsis, qui superstitiones abolitas postliminio redu-cere satagunt, qui impostores maximi faciunt, qui denique perruptis omnium legum repagulis in omnem licentiam effunduntur. Et quid obsecro nimium dici potest, quando impietas vbique gen-tiũ triumphat, scelus verò intolerabile putatur fidem in CHRISTVM IESVM profiteri, et reliquis superstitionibus vitam viuere Christiana professione dignam?
units.tr: things from which Saul might have taken pleasure? For this is clear from the fact that Samuel mourned Saul's rejection with bitter and long-lasting tears, until he was rebuked by the Lord. But that he dealt with him more harshly and sternly was deserved by Saul's obstinacy, indeed it demanded it. The same we can say of Nathan, who showed how highly he regarded David from the things he discussed with him about the Messiah who was to be born from David's offspring. Yet he was nonetheless compelled to threaten David with God's wrath and the avenging sword, since he had deserved severe punishment for his shameful adultery and his unworthy slaying of Uriah. There is no doubt that all the prophets had the same spirit. Jeremiah certainly complains of his lot, and thinks himself the most wretched of mortals, since he must constantly quarrel with men who do not know how to repent; and the laments he wrote after the miserable destruction of the city and temple remain to show that those complaints were neither false nor feigned; nothing more mournful could have been imagined. And as for Christ, what need is there to say that he could not even recall without tears that dreadful calamity which was hanging over the city and the Jewish nation? Yet, as if overcome by the incurable impiety of the priests and the ingratitude and obstinacy of the whole people, he could not but say the things they deserved. The same happened to all the apostles, and the Corinthians forced Paul, against the wishes of his own heart, now to rebuke them more sharply, now to attack the false apostles with greater force of words, and now also to proclaim his own praises. They ought to remember these things today, those for whom the ministers of the Word seem too severe in refuting superstitions, in attacking the Antichrist and his unhappy monsters, namely the monks and the whole troop of shaven and anointed men, and likewise in condemning crimes and announcing the punishments for them. Yet they are compelled to do these things by those very people who strive to bring back the superstitions that have been abolished, who hold impostors in the highest esteem, and who finally, having broken down all the barriers of the laws, pour themselves out into every licence. And, I ask, what can be said too much when impiety everywhere triumphs among the nations, and it is thought an intolerable crime to profess faith in Jesus Christ and to live a life worthy of the Christian profession rather than in the other superstitions?

units.la: Debet tamen huius loci doctrina latius extendi. Nam ita fieri solet in genere, vt qu̇ utquot officium non faciunt in aliqua re exequenda, hi alios illud facere cogant. Oportet enim omnino fie-ri quod Deus statuit, cuius decreta æterna sunt & irreuocabilia. Si ergo ij, quibus Deus aliquid mandauit, & qui locum legitimum vel in Ecclesia vel in Repub. tenent, in officio suo cessent, facile est Deo aliquos excitare extraordinarie, qui quod iussit effectum dent. Quapropter si extraordinarij illi aliquid vel imprudentius vel immodestius faciant, non tam hi quàm alteri illi reprehendi me-rentur, qui sua ignauia istis occasionem dederunt. Exemplo res fiet illustrior. Religionis cura im-primis ad Episcopos vel Ecclesiæ pastores & Magistratus pertinet, quorum est videre, vt tam doctrina quàm cultus externus atq; Sacramentorum vsus secundùm Dei Verbum rectè instituatur, aboleantur verò superstitiones noxiæ & quæcunq; contra Dei voluntatem irrepserunt. Fit autem feré vt veteré ordo hominum hæc vt nihil ad se pertinentia negligat. Nolunt enim manum huic operi admouere Antistites, quibus omnis Ecclesiæ reformatio inuidiosa & suspeĉta est, dum suæ existimationi & quæstui metuunt. Magistratus verò vel hanc à suo officio alienâ esse putant, vel etiam sui emolumenti causa cum superstitionum magistris colludunt. Vt ergo olim cessantibus in suo munere Sacerdotibus, Dominus Prophetas excitabat extraordinarie, homines rusticos & opifices, vel etiam generis nobilitate illustres, qualem Isaiam fuisse constat: Ita hodie etiam Euangelij præ-cones excitat, obscuros prius, qui opus istud aggrediantur, quod ipse confectum vult. Fit tunc, vt dolis per Euangelij prædicationem detectis, vulgus exardescat, & motus publici surgant, per quos non sine periculo ea tollantur, quæ facile & decenter tolli possent, si alteri illi vellent officio suo fungi. Fremunt tunc idololatriæ patroni, & quouis supplicio dignos esse clamant alteros illos, qui multa importunè & immodestius fecerunt. Atqui maior est illorum culpa, qui tam diu per Dei Verbum admoniti cessarunt in eo, quod facere debuissent, & quod ipsi commodius facere poterant. Fatentur hoc aliqui, & tamen vociferantur: Esto, cessarint hucusque Pontifices, Episcopi, Reges & magistratus, non tamen isti debebant hisce rebus sese immiscere. At eho quisquis es, dic mihi, qui scis istos quoque cessare debuisse? Deus equidem superstitiones tol-li, idololatriam euerti, doctrinas falsas è medio auferri, & scandala omnia remoueri vult. Qui id ex officio facere debebant, nolunt. Num ergo incredibile est, alteros illos à Deo ex-citari, vt omni periculo contempto rem istam aggrediantur? Ne ergo hic aliquis iudicium su-um præcipitet, sed potius discipulos imitemur, qui cùm Christum flagello facto sacrorum nun-dinatores è templo eiecisse & nummulariorum mensas euertisse, atque pecunias eorum effudisse viderent, illum (etsi functionis, cui eum Pater destinauerat, mysterium nondum intelliges) rent) non tamen vel imprudentem vel seditiosum dixerunt, sed hoc totum Zelo sancto tribuerunt, & eius quod in Psalmis habetur, recordati sunt: Zelus domus tuae devoravit me. Sunt enim Spiritus Sancti motus in electis admirabiles, & vere Heroici: quorum exempla nemo quidem temere imitari debet, at eadem neque etiam damnanda sunt temere, cum non semper nobis pateat iudiciorum & consiliorum Dei ratio.
units.tr: Yet the teaching of this passage ought to be extended more widely. For it is generally the case that when those who should carry out a duty fail to do so, others are compelled to do it. For what God has decreed must certainly come to pass, since his decrees are eternal and irrevocable. So if those to whom God has entrusted something, and who hold a lawful office either in the Church or in the commonwealth, neglect their duty, it is easy for God to raise up others by extraordinary means to bring about what he has commanded. Therefore, if these extraordinary men do something too rashly or immoderately, they deserve blame not so much themselves as those others, whose idleness gave them the occasion. The matter will become clearer by an example. The care of religion belongs above all to the bishops or ministers of the Church and to the magistrates. It is their task to see that both doctrine and external worship, and the use of the sacraments, are rightly ordered according to the Word of God, and that harmful superstitions and whatever has crept in against God's will are abolished. But it usually happens that these men, in the old manner, neglect this as if it did not concern them. The prelates do not wish to lay a hand to this work, for every reform of the Church is hateful and suspect to them, since they fear for their reputation and their profit. The magistrates either think this has nothing to do with their office, or else they collude with the masters of superstition for their own gain. So, just as in former times, when the priests failed in their office, the Lord raised up prophets by extraordinary means, men of humble rank and tradesmen, or even men famous for noble birth, as Isaiah is known to have been, so today too he raises up heralds of the gospel, men previously obscure, to undertake that work which he himself wills to be done. Then, when the deceits are exposed by the preaching of the gospel, the common people blaze up and public disturbances arise, by which those things are removed, with danger, which could have been removed easily and decently if those others had been willing to perform their duty. Then the patrons of idolatry rage and cry out that those men, who have acted without restraint and too immoderately in many things, deserve any punishment. Yet the greater fault lies with those who, though so long admonished by the Word of God, have ceased to do what they ought to have done, and what they could have done more fittingly themselves. Some admit this, and yet they clamour: "Granted, the popes, bishops, kings and magistrates have hitherto been negligent, but still these men ought not to have meddled in such affairs." But tell me, whoever you are, how do you know that those others too ought to have ceased? God certainly wishes superstitions to be removed, idolatry overthrown, false doctrines taken away and every stumbling-block cleared. Those who ought to have done this as part of their office are unwilling. Is it then incredible that God should stir up others to tackle this business, despite every danger? Let no one therefore rashly pass judgement, but rather let us imitate the disciples, who, when they saw Christ make a whip and drive the sellers of sacred things out of the temple, overturn the tables of the money-changers and pour out their coins, did not call him rash or seditious (although they did not yet understand the mystery of the office for which the Father had destined him), but attributed the whole thing to holy zeal, and remembered what is written in the Psalms: "The zeal of your house has consumed me." For the movements of the Holy Spirit in the elect are admirable and truly heroic. No one ought rashly to imitate their examples, yet neither ought they rashly to be condemned, since the reason of God's judgements and counsels is not always open to us.

units.la: Solent etiam saepe hisce similia in Repub. fieri, quoad vitam & mores. Etenim magistratuum officium est coniugij tura & publicae honestatis leges tueri, stupra, incestus, adulteria & vagas libidines dignis supplicijs coercere. Et notum est illud Pauli: Scortatores & adulteros Dominus iudicabit. At quia scelera haec iudicio mundi huius leviscula, adeoque lusus iocusque videntur, & proinde magistratus in illis puniendis dormitant, imo saepe ipsi illis polluti sunt, sic iusto Dei iudicio, ut multi priuatam vindictam sumant de illis, qui vel filias vel sorores ipsarum constupraverunt, vel thoros ipsorum violarunt, adeo ut multi in ipso scelere confossi animam infelicem absque omni peccati detestatione aut numinis invocatione exhalent, atque aeternum pereant. Taceo nunc seditiones, bella & publicos motus, periculosas item Reipub. mutationes, quae omnia ex vagis libidinibus saepius exorta esse omnium saeculorum historia testantur. Vbi fateor, multa fieri ab iratis & iniuria impatientibus, & crudele nec Christiana professione dignum facinus esse, ita maechus vel ciscis, ut animam eius simul cum corpore perdas. Atqui culpa maior in ignaris magistratibus haeret, qui invitos ad tam immania facinora cogunt. Discant ergo singuli pro sua functionis ratione officium facere, & minus turbarum erit in Ecclesia & Repub.
units.tr: Similar things often happen in the commonwealth, in matters of life and morals. For it is the duty of magistrates to protect the laws of marriage and of public decency, and to restrain fornication, incest, adultery and wanton lusts with fitting punishments. And that saying of Paul is well known: "Whoremongers and adulterers God will judge." But because these crimes seem rather slight and mere sport and jest in the judgement of this world, magistrates grow lax in punishing them, and indeed they themselves are often defiled by them. Thus, by the just judgement of God, many take private vengeance on those who have debauched their daughters or sisters, or violated their marriage beds, so that many, struck down in the very act of sin, breathe out their unhappy souls without any repentance for sin or invocation of the divine name, and perish for ever. I say nothing now of seditions, wars and public uprisings, nor of the dangerous overthrows of commonwealths, all of which the history of every age testifies have very often arisen from wanton lusts. Here I admit that many things are done by men who are angry and impatient of wrong, and that it is a cruel deed, and not worthy of the Christian profession, so to avenge an adulterer that you destroy his soul together with his body. Yet the greater fault clings to the ignorant magistrates, who force unwilling men to such monstrous deeds. Let each therefore learn to perform his duty according to the nature of his office, and there will be fewer disturbances in the Church and the commonwealth.

units.la: Sed redeamus eo unde digressi sumus. Quia Paulus se a Corinthijs commendari debuisse dixit, id argumento a propria persona probat, dicens: Nulla enim in re inferior fui summis Apostolis, tametsi nihil sum. Quibus verbis simul Corinthiorum stoliditatem & iniqua iudicia perstringit, qui impostores illos hoc potissimum nomine tanti faciebant, quod se a principibus Apostolorum missos esse dicerent. Itaque sensus est: Si ita vos movet Apostolici nominis splendor, quin me species, qui non ab illis, sed ab ipso Dei Filio, IESV CHRISTO, missus, & proinde germanus Apostolus sum, & tantus quidem, ut si omnino libeat gradus fingere inter Apostolos (quod aemuli sti mei ambitiose magis quam pie faciunt) ego summus etiam conferri merear. At ne hoc infalentius dictum putetur, per Correctionem subijcit: Tametsi nihil sum.
units.tr: But let us return to where we digressed. Because Paul said that he ought to have been commended by the Corinthians, he proves it from his own person, saying: "For I was in no way inferior to the chief apostles, although I am nothing." In these words he at the same time rebukes the foolishness and unjust judgements of the Corinthians, who held those impostors in such high esteem chiefly on this ground, that they said they had been sent by the chief apostles. The sense therefore is: "If the splendour of the apostolic name moves you so much, why do you not look at me, who was sent not by them but by the Son of God, Jesus Christ himself, and so am a true apostle, and indeed so great that, if one should wish to devise degrees among the apostles (as my rivals ambitiously rather than piously do), I too might deserve to be counted among the highest." But lest this be thought too arrogant, he adds by way of correction: "although I am nothing."

units.la: Vbi quis obijceret: An ergo nihil sunt etiam alij Apostoli? Vel annon sibijpsi contradicit Paulus, qui se passim Seruum Christi, patrem item Corinthiorum & aliorum vocat, quos in Christo genuerat ex Verbi semine? Num denique nihil est esse Christi seruum & Apostolum? Atqui Christus ait: Sicut me misit Pater, ita & ego mitto vos: Qui vos audit, me audit. Non ignorabat ista Paulus, neque voluit aliquid in Apostolici ministerij contemptum dicere: sed in praesenti distinguit inter seipsum, qualis erat sua natura, & Apostoli personam, quam sustinebat. Itaque se nihil esse dicit, quoad naturam suam, in qua natus erat. Secundum hanc enim homo erat. At quid homo aliud quam bulla? quid vita hominis, nisi vapor surgens & transiens? Adde, quod peccator erat, in peccatis conceptus & genitus. Et quamuis Iudaeus esset, nihil tamen hoc ad salutem confererat: quod vero Pharisaeus fuerat & Legis aemulator, id persecutorem & non tam CHRISTI IESV quam propriae salutis hostem fecerat. Haec omnia in seipso agnoscens, se nihil esse dicit. Quoad vero personam, quam tunc sustinebat, Christianus erat, Apostolus sive Christi legatus erat, & quidem summis aut praecipuis in eo ordine non inferior: utpote organum illud electum, quo Dei Filius in regno suo longe lateque propagando utebatur. Ita ergo se hominem esse agnovit, ut non neglexerit dignitatem suam, qua ipsum Christus donauerat. Et rursus hanc ita consideravit, ut non obliuisceretur sua infirmitatis & miseria, quam cum alijs hominibus communem habebat, ut nec pristinae suae conditionis.
units.tr: Here someone might object: "Then are the other apostles also nothing? Or does Paul not contradict himself, who everywhere calls himself the servant of Christ, and the father of the Corinthians and of others whom he begot in Christ from the seed of the Word? Is it nothing, finally, to be a servant and apostle of Christ?" Yet Christ says: "As the Father sent me, so I send you. He who hears you hears me." Paul was not ignorant of these things, nor did he wish to say anything in contempt of the apostolic ministry; but here he distinguishes between himself, as he was by nature, and the apostolic person which he sustained. So he says that he is nothing as regards his nature, in which he was born, for according to this he was a man. But what is a man other than a bubble? What is human life, except a vapour that rises and passes away? Add that he was a sinner, conceived and born in sins. And although he was a Jew, this contributed nothing to his salvation; and that he had been a Pharisee and a zealot for the Law had made him a persecutor, and an enemy not so much of Christ Jesus as of his own salvation. Acknowledging all this in himself, he says that he is nothing. But as regards the person he then sustained, he was a Christian, he was an apostle or legate of Christ, and indeed not inferior to the highest or chief men in that order, being that chosen instrument by which the Son of God used to spread his kingdom far and wide. So he recognised himself as a man in such a way that he did not neglect the dignity which Christ had bestowed on him; and again he so considered this dignity that he did not forget his own weakness and misery, which he shared with other men, nor his former condition.

units.la: Debet hinc generalis doctrina peti, ut nimirum omnes meminerint, se in conspectu Dei nihil esse, quatenus homines sunt, utut coram mundo diuites, sapientes, magnifici siue gloriosi appareant. Etenim Christo teste, quod sublime est coram hominibus, abominabile est coram Deo. Quare nimium imprudentes, imo infelices sunt, quirebus bisce friuolis atque caducis superbiunt. Simul tamen singuli diligenter attendant, in quem gradum Deus ipsos euexerit, & huius dignitatem sedulò tueantur. Laudatur Romanus ille, qui Consularem maiestatem reverentia, quam patri suo debebat, anteposuit. At quantò constantius debent authoritatem suam tueri, qui ab ipso Deo in gradum aliquem sublimiorem euecti sunt? Hodie in utramque partem peccatur, dum alij quidem Dei donis atque honoribus publicis efferuntur; alij verò nullum inter priuatam & publicam personam discrimen faciendo, dum modestiâ laudem venantur, authoritatem suam turpiter prostituunt.
units.tr: From this we ought to draw a general teaching: that all of us should remember that, in the sight of God, as men we are nothing, however rich, wise, magnificent or glorious we may appear before the world. For, as Christ testifies, what is lofty among men is an abomination before God. Those who take pride in these frivolous and fleeting things are therefore very foolish, indeed wretched. At the same time, each person should attend carefully to the rank to which God has raised him and diligently guard its dignity. That Roman is praised who put the majesty of the consul before the reverence he owed his father. How much more steadfastly, then, ought those to guard their authority who have been raised by God himself to some higher rank? Today people sin in both directions: some are puffed up by God's gifts and public honours, while others, making no distinction between their private and public persons, shamefully throw away their authority while hunting for praise for their modesty.

units.la: Caeterùm pergit Paulus, & se summis Apostolis nihilo inferiorem esse probat argumento ab Euangelij effectis inter ipsos editis. Signa quidem Apostoli (inquit) edita sunt inter vos in omni tolerantia, in signis & prodigijs & virtutibus. Priori loco signa generalium dicit pro indicijs certis, quibus Deus Apostolatum ipsius quodammodo obsignauerat, & vt publicis testimonijs confirmarat. Quare sensus est: Ego ita inter vos versatus sum, vt res ipsa loquatur, me IESV CHRISTI Apostolum esse, neque ampliori demonstratione opus fit. Nam quaecunque per germanos & summos Apostolos vnquam facta sunt Spiritus virtute, ea in me quoque conspicua fuisse, nemo vestrum (opinor) negabit. Ea autem ex ordine recenset.
units.tr: Paul goes on and proves that he is in no way inferior to the highest Apostles, by an argument drawn from the effects of the Gospel produced through him. "The signs of an Apostle," he says, "have been wrought among you in all patience, in signs and wonders and mighty deeds." By "signs" he means first of all the sure indications by which God had in some way set his seal on the Apostleship, and confirmed it by public witnesses. The sense, therefore, is this: "I have so conducted myself among you that the thing itself speaks, showing that I am an Apostle of Jesus Christ, and no further demonstration is needed. For whatever was ever done by the true and chief Apostles through the power of the Spirit, I think none of you will deny was also manifest in me." He then lists these things in order.

units.la: Et primo quidem loco (vt supra quoque sexto Cap.) tolerantiam nominat, sub cuius nomine intelligitur partim inuicta in ferendis laboribus atque molestijs constantia, quas in Ecclesiae ministerio sustinebat, vbi infirmi indulgentius fouendi erant, mali ferendi, ingratis condonandum, tot denuoranda taedia: partim patientia in omni afflictionum genere, quae ab hostibus inferebantur. In omnibus autem istis inuictum perstitisse scimus, cum alibi tum maximè apud Corinthios, vbi non sine periculo docebat propter Iudaeos, qui ipsi insidias subinde struebant, & interea inops & egens victum manuum labore sibi quaerere cogebatur. Opus autem est hac virtute omnibus, qui in Verbi ministerio non sine fructu versari volunt, vt alibi prolixius est dictum. Imò eadem omnibus Christianis plus quàm necessaria est, cùm omnes nos ad crucem ferendam Dominus vocet, & ideò (vt Apostoli monuerunt) nos per multas afflictiones oporteat ingredi in regnum Dei.
units.tr: First of all (as also above in the sixth chapter) he names "patience." Under this word is understood, partly, an unconquered steadfastness in bearing the labours and troubles which he endured in the ministry of the Church, where the weak had to be indulgently cherished, evils endured, the ungrateful forgiven, and so many tedious tasks repeated; and partly, patience in every kind of affliction inflicted by enemies. We know that he remained unconquered in all of these, both elsewhere and especially among the Corinthians, where he taught not without danger because of the Jews, who kept laying plots against him, and meanwhile, poor and needy, he was forced to seek his living by the labour of his hands. This virtue is needed by all who wish to labour fruitfully in the ministry of the Word, as has been said at greater length elsewhere. Indeed, it is more than necessary for all Christians alike, since the Lord calls all of us to bear the cross, and therefore (as the Apostles warned) we must enter the kingdom of God through many afflictions.

units.la: Deinde miracula adducit, quae inter Corinthios per ipsum ediderit, quae tribus nominibus describit. Nam signa dicit, quia his partim Apostolorum doctrina, partim auditorum fides obsignabatur: & vt ita fieret opus erat, quod noua & gentibus inaudita prorsus esset doctrina de IESV CHRISTO crucifixo. At eadem prodigia vocat, quod contra naturae leges fierent, & omnium animos raperent in admirationem. Virtutes item sue potentias, quod in illis se exereret virtus Christi per Verbum suum operantis. Nec dubium est, multa huius generis per Pauli ministerium Corinthi facta fuisse, vt alibi quoq; quae illis in mentem reuocat, vt suam eis ofcitantiam exprobret, qui istorum tam cito erant obliti. Est enim hoc commune vitium, quod hodie etiam passim regnat. Nam etsi Euangelij doctrinam hodie non opus sit ijsdem signis probari inter eos, qui Christiani haberi volunt: fiunt tamen multa alia, quae vt magis necessaria sunt, ita non minorem merentur admirationem: qualia sunt, subitae animorum mutationes, mirifici Euangelicae praedicationis progressus, eiusdem victoriae & triumphi, quos de potentissimis Monarchis agit, quorum consilia & machinationes non sine ludibrio plerunque dissipantur: denique Ecclesiae inermis & infirmae inter medios hostes conseruatio. Equidem ipsis hostibus admirationem parit, quod se per annos totos quinquaginta consilijs suis, faederibus, bellis tam ciuilibus quàm exteris, dirissimis suppliciorum tormentis, dolis, fraudibus nihil proficere vident contra eos, quos nulla hominum authoritas siue potentia defendit. Magna autem est multorum ex nostris stupiditas atque ignauia, qui ista non obseruant, vel etiam eorundem tam cito obliuiscuntur.
units.tr: Next he adduces the miracles which he had worked among the Corinthians, and describes them by three names. He calls them "signs," because by them the Apostles' teaching was partly sealed, and the faith of the hearers partly confirmed; and for this to happen there was need of a doctrine about Jesus Christ crucified that was new and wholly unheard of by the Gentiles. He calls them "wonders," because they happened against the laws of nature and filled all minds with amazement. He calls them "mighty deeds" (powers), because in them the power of Christ, working through his Word, showed itself. Nor is there doubt that many works of this kind were done at Corinth through Paul's ministry, as he also recalls elsewhere, to rebuke them for their slowness, since they had forgotten these things so quickly. For this is a common fault, which even today reigns everywhere. For although there is no need today for the Gospel teaching to be proved among those who wish to be called Christians by the same signs, yet many other things are done which, though more necessary, deserve no less admiration: such as sudden changes of hearts, the marvellous progress of evangelical preaching, its victories and triumphs over the most powerful monarchs, whose counsels and schemes are for the most part scattered to their mockery; and finally, the preservation of the Church, unarmed and weak, amid the middle of her enemies. Indeed, it amazes the enemies themselves that, for fifty whole years, with their plans, their treaties, their wars both civil and foreign, their most dreadful tortures, their deceits and frauds, they see themselves achieving nothing against those whom no human authority or power defends. Great, however, is the dullness and sloth of many among us, who do not observe these things, or even forget them so quickly.

units.la: Sed propius cum Corinthijs congreditur Apostolus, vt ingratitudinem ipsorum magis arguat. Nam quid est (inquit) in quo fuerit inferiores caeteris Ecclesijs, nisi quod ego ipse vos non gratuito meo otio? Sensus est: Si quae in re alijs effectu inferiores, aliqua esset de me quiritandi occasio. Sed agedum dicite, quid vobis defuerit? Quid inter vos per me omissum sit? quidue neglexerim? Non poteritis quicquam dicere, nisi fortassis hoc indignius fertis, quod ego meo otio aut desidia ignaua nemini vestrum molestus fui, sed manuum labore potius victum mihi parare, quàm à vobis exigere volui. Quòd si hoc vos tantopere offendit, condonate mihi quaeso hanc iniuriam. Est autem hac mordax Ironia, qua ipsorum ingratitudinem acriter pungit, perinde ac si quis pater filio
units.tr: But the Apostle comes closer to the Corinthians, so that he may the more sharply accuse them of ingratitude. "For what," he says, "is there in which you were inferior to the other Churches, except that I myself was not burdensome to you?" The sense is this: "If I were in any respect less effective than the others, there would be some ground for your complaining about me. But come, tell me, what did you lack? What has been left undone among you through me? Or what have I neglected? You will not be able to say anything, unless perhaps you take it more amiss that, in my leisure or idle sloth, I was burdensome to none of you, but preferred to earn my living by the labour of my hands rather than to demand it from you. But if this offends you so much, I beg you to forgive me this wrong." This is a biting irony, by which he sharply stings them for their ingratitude, just as if a father were to say to a stubborn and rebellious son:

units.la: Proprio testimonio Corinthios conuincit. contumaci & rebelli dicat: Quid habes mi fili, quod de me conqueraris? qua in re inferior fuisti aliis eiusdem loci atque ordinis iuuenibus? Num vitu? num vestitu? Vel num me vnquam in tuis studijs promouendis difficilem aut tenaciorem esse senseristi? Cercè nihil horum te dicere posse sat scio. Num ergo hoc tibi dolet, quòd ego vt tibi prospiciam, me curis, laboribus & vigilijs confi-cio? quòd meum genium defraudo? quòd sumptus pro te quotidie maiores quàm pro meipso fa-cio? Condona mihi fili hanc iniuriam, &c. Poterat hoc bodie multis dici, qui nimium ingratos & inquos se præbent Verbi administris, qui modestiæ memores humilius agunt, neque insolentes & Perfido luxu diffluentes Episcopos, aut stolidos illos Superintendentes imitantur, qui sub Euan-gelij nomine quorumuis capitibus arrogantiam insultant.
units.tr: He convicts the Corinthians by their own testimony. "What have you, my son, to complain of in me? In what were you inferior to other young men of the same place and rank? In food? In clothing? Or have you ever found me difficult or too strict in promoting your studies? I am quite sure you can say none of these things. Is it then grieving you that I wear myself out with cares, labours and watchings, to provide for you? That I cheat myself of my own comforts? That every day I spend more on you than on myself? Forgive me, son, this wrong, etc." This could be said today to many who show themselves far too ungrateful and unjust to the servants of the Word, who, mindful of modesty, behave humbly, and do not imitate the insolent bishops who wallow in faithless luxury, nor those foolish superintendents who, under the name of the Gospel, insult the heads of anyone whatever with arrogance.

units.la: At omissis illis, hoc potius observemus, Corinthiorum Ecclesiam nihilò inferiorem fuisse ali-js, quæ tunc optimè fuerunt instituta. Sufficiunt ergo eiusdem Ecclesiæ ea, quæ illis Paulus tradidit. At hunc nihil eis prædicauisse constat, præter IESVM CHRISTVM, & hunc quidem cruci-fixum. Idem fuit minister effectum atq; omnem humanæ salutis gloriam vni Deo transcripsit, qui solus det incrementum, vt quæ per homines plantantur & rigantur, succrescant. Quoad vero Ec-clesiæ œconomiam, cætus instituit, in quibus Verbi prædicatio siue prophetia primas teneret, preces fierent, Cœna item Dominica administraretur ritu & ordine nobis per Christum tradito. Inter-seruit his frequentes admonitiones de disciplina conseruanda, de morum honestate & vitæ sanctì-monia, de mutuæ charitatis studio. Adhæc resurrectionis nostræ certitudinem diligentissimè af-feruit. Nullam verò mentionem fecit eorum, quæ posterius demum temporibus per homines superstitiosè introducta sunt: qualia sunt, Diuorum intercessio & inuocatio, Missæ sacrificium, purgato-rius ignis, exequiæ pro defunctis, ciborum delectus, feria, cælibatus monasticus, rosaria, cerea, lam-pades, cruces argenteæ, imagines, indulgentia, confessio auricularis & sexcenta alia, pro quibus ho-die contenditur. Sunt ergo omnia ista superuacanea & inutilia, imò noxia sunt, cùm à Deo abdu-cant, & Christi merito derogent. Itaque procul relictis omnibus istis, in simplici Euangelij doctri-na constantes maneamus, & fide syncera seruiamus vni IESV CHRISTO, Domino & Ser-uatori nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But setting those aside, let us rather observe this: the Church of Corinth was in no way inferior to others that were then best established. The things which Paul handed down to them are therefore enough for that same Church. Yet it is clear that he preached nothing to them except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. He was the minister by whom the work was done, and he ascribed all the glory of human salvation to the one God, who alone gives the increase, so that what is planted and watered by men may grow. As for the order of the Church, he set up assemblies in which the preaching of the Word, or prophecy, held the first place, prayers were made, and the Lord's Supper was also administered in the rite and order handed down to us through Christ. Among these he interspersed frequent admonitions about keeping discipline, about the honesty of morals and the holiness of life, and about zeal for mutual charity. Besides this, he most diligently affirmed the certainty of our resurrection. But he made no mention of those things which were introduced superstitiously by men only at a later time: such as the intercession and invocation of saints, the sacrifice of the Mass, purgatorial fire, funeral rites for the dead, the choice of foods, holy days, monastic celibacy, rosaries, wax candles, lamps, silver crosses, images, indulgences, auricular confession, and six hundred other things, for which today people contend. All these things are therefore superfluous and useless, indeed harmful, since they lead us away from God and detract from the merit of Christ. Let us therefore leave all those things far behind, remain constant in the simple doctrine of the Gospel, and with sincere faith serve the one Jesus Christ, our Lord and Saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LVIII.
units.tr: Homily 58.

units.la: Ecce, tertiò paratus sum venire ad vos, neque vos grauabo oti-o meo. Non enim quæro quæ vestra sunt, sed vos. Non enim de-bent filij parentibus thesauros congerere, sed parentes filijs. Ego verò libentissimè impendam & expendar pro animabus vestris: et-iamsi abunde vos diligens, minus diligar.
units.tr: Behold, I am ready to come to you the third time, and I will not burden you with my leisure. For I do not seek what is yours, but you. Children ought not to lay up treasure for their parents, but parents for their children. I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls, and even if I love you abundantly, I may be loved less.

units.la: Quemadmodum infelix hic mundus Veritatis lucem odit atque auersatur, & ideo facilè qua-uis occasionem arripit, qua eius ministros siue præcones reijciat: ita si ijsdem semel in suspicio-nem veniant, difficile fuerit eis suam authoritatem recuperare, eò quòd apud malevolos & odij af-fectu occupatos vix vllæ excusationes possunt sufficere. Exemplum huius rei euidens in Paulo & Corinthijs habetur. Vixerat ille ita inter ipsos, vt neq; in eius vita atq; moribus, neq; etiam do-ctrina quicquam posset reprehendi. Nam quoad mores, frugalitati studuerat, & ne cui oneri es-set, ipse sibi victum proprijs manibus quæsiuerat. Quoad hanc verò, nihil præter IESVM CHRI-STVM prædicarat, neque aliquos ritus inuexerat, quos ille non tradidisset. Verumtamen non po-tuit calumnias improborum quorundam effugere, qui doctrinæ purioris adulteratione & indulgen-tia nimia inter illos multorum studia sibi parauerant. Qui cùm non aliud possent reprehendere, eius tenuitatem ipsi vitio vertebant, & indignissimum facinus esse clamitabant, hominem obscu-rum & tentoriorum textorem tantæ vrbi tamque celebri leges prescribere, quibus homines opu-lentos & multo rerum vsu exercitatos parere oporteat. Quapropter non abs ratione Paulus tam multis hanc causam agit, vt demonstret, se ab illis hoc nomine magis amari debuisse, ipsos autem non tam ingratos quàm iniquos esse laborum suorum æstimatores, qui tam malitiosè de ipso iudicent. Ut ne suspicaretur, ipsum aliquid captare in posterum, supra dixerat testatus fuit, se talem per petuò fore, qualis initio fuerit: qui nimirum nemini grauis aut onerosus sit. Id in præsenti amplius explicat, & suo exemplo docet, perseuerandum esse in eo, quod semel rectè cœpisti.
units.tr: Just as this unhappy world hates and turns away from the light of truth, and therefore readily seizes any opportunity to reject its ministers or heralds, so, once such men fall under suspicion, it is hard for them to recover their authority. Among malicious people who are possessed by hatred, scarcely any excuse can suffice. A clear example of this is found in Paul and the Corinthians. He had lived among them in such a way that nothing could be found fault with, either in his life and conduct or in his teaching. As to conduct, he had devoted himself to frugality, and so as not to be a burden to anyone, he had earned his living by his own hands. As to teaching, he had preached nothing but Jesus Christ, nor had he introduced any rites that he had not handed down. Nevertheless, he could not escape the slanders of certain wicked men, who, by corrupting pure doctrine and by excessive indulgence, had won over many to themselves among them. Since they could find nothing else to blame, they turned his lowliness into a fault, and kept crying out that it was a most shameful thing for a man of obscure birth, a weaver of tents, to prescribe laws for so great and famous a city, laws to which wealthy men, practised in the use of many goods, ought to submit. Therefore it is not without reason that Paul argues this cause at such length, to show that they ought to have loved him more on this account, and that they were not so much ungrateful as unfair judges of his labours, since they judged him so spitefully. Lest they suspect that he was seeking any advantage in future, he had already testified that he would always be such as he had been at the beginning, namely one who is a burden to no one. In the present passage he explains this more fully, and by his own example teaches that one must persevere in what one has rightly begun.

units.la: Ecce (inquit) tertiò paratus sum venire ad vos, neque vos grauabo otio meo. Non dicit se tertiò venisse, sed tertiò iam paratu fuisse, ut profectionem ad ipsos suscipert. Facit ad huius locl expositionem, quod supra Capite primo dixit: Volui ad vos venire primum, ut secundam gratiam haberetis, & per vos transire in Macedoniam, & rursus ex Macedonia venire ad vos, & à vobis deduci in Iudæam. Quæ docent, eum in eadem profectione bis voluisse Corinthum venire. At quia hucusque alijs negotijs impeditus & retentus fuerat, nunc tertiò idem consilium suscepit. Nec tamen ex Actorum libro aut epistolis eius certò definiri potest, an vnquam ab eo tempore Corinthum venerit. Estq; hoc memorabile exemplum, quo docemur, non semper procedere, quæ optimi & sanctissimi serui Dei ex bono sanctoque zelo de rebus suis statuunt. Sunt enim horum quoque actiones in Dei manu, cuius prouidentia ad omnia extenditur: & non minus de illis, quàm de alijs dictum est à Solomone: Homo proponit, sed Dominus dirigit greßus eius. Et sunt huius generis multa cum Scripturæ testimonia tum exempla, quæ alibi adduximus. Nobis verò omnium hic vsus esse debet, ut primùm non temere aliquid statuamus, quasi in nostra manu sit facere quod nobis visum fuerit: Deinde, ne impatientius feramus, si quod instituimus, non procedat pro nostro arbitrio aut nutu. Quoties enim euentus rerum probat, neq; utile neq; tutum fuisse quod instituera-mus? Semper ergo animis nostris obuersetur, quod inter precandum dicimus: Fiat voluntas tua, quemadmodum in cœlo, sic etiam in terra, &c.
units.tr: "Behold," he says, "I am ready to come to you the third time, and I will not burden you with my leisure." He does not say that he has come a third time, but that he is now already prepared to undertake the journey to them. This agrees with what he said in the first chapter: "I wished to come to you first, that you might have a second grace, and to pass through you into Macedonia, and again to come from Macedonia to you, and to be brought on my way to Judea by you." These words show that in that one journey he twice wished to come to Corinth. But since he had until now been hindered and held back by other business, he now undertook the same plan a third time. Yet from the book of Acts or from his letters it cannot be determined with certainty whether he ever came to Corinth after that time. This is a memorable example, by which we are taught that the things which even the best and most holy servants of God decide from good and holy zeal concerning their affairs do not always turn out as they plan. For their actions too lie in the hand of God, whose providence extends to all things; and what Solomon said applies no less to these than to others: "A man plans, but the Lord directs his steps." There are many testimonies and examples of Scripture of this kind, which we have cited elsewhere. For our part, this lesson ought to be of use to us in this way: first, that we should not decide anything rashly, as if it lay in our power to do whatever seems good to us; and second, that we should not bear it too impatiently if what we have undertaken does not go forward according to our judgement or will. For how often do the outcomes of events prove that what we had undertaken was neither useful nor safe? Therefore let this always be before our minds, what we say in prayer: "Thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven," and so on.

units.la: Quoad verò huius loci statum, addit Apostolus: Nec grauabo vos otio meo, id est, Sicut antea non otiosus inter vos vixi, neque cum alicuius incommodo meæ quieti consului: ita ne nunc quidem hoc faciam, sed vitam & res meas sic instituam, ut nemini incommodem. Quod autem de ipso Paulus dicit, hoc omnes Christianos decet. Requirit enim hoc charitatis lex, quam nobis totius vitæ regulam Deus fecit, & ex qua, ceu nota certissima, veri Christiani dignoscuntur. Quæ causa est, quod alibi ... id est, de ijs qui inordinatè viuunt, & ex aliorum laboribus otiantur, tam grauiter præcipit Spiritus sanctus, ne qui illis locum dent, sed eos sedulò in ordinem redigant. Quid ergo de ijs hodie iudicari debet, qui vt luxurientur & voluptatibus nefarijs indulgere possint, omnes grauant? in quorum numero facile principes sunt Furarij & Monopolæ, quos olim inter gentes in bene constituta Repub. sapientissimi quique indignos esse iudicarunt, qui viuerent. Cur enim viuat, qui non nisi cum aliorum incommodo viuit, & ideo non tam hominibus quàm bestijs & feris accenseri meretur? Sed Pauli rationes audiamus, quibus se mouerit docet, ne quid huius ipse faciat.
units.tr: As to the state of this passage, the Apostle adds: "Nor will I burden you with my leisure," that is, just as I did not live idly among you before, nor did I consult my own ease at anyone's inconvenience, so I will not do so now either, but I will order my life and my affairs so that they are a burden to no one. What Paul says of himself, all Christians ought to do likewise. For the law of charity requires this, which God has made the rule of the whole of life, and by which, as by a most certain mark, true Christians are recognised. This is why the Holy Spirit so gravely commands, elsewhere, concerning those who live disorderly and live idly at the labours of others, that no one should give them place, but that they should be diligently brought back into order. What then ought to be judged today of those who, in order to be able to indulge in luxury and nefarious pleasures, burden everyone? Among these the chief are easily the thieves and monopolists, whom the wisest men among the nations, in well-ordered commonwealths, judged unworthy to live. For why should he live who lives only at the expense of others, and therefore deserves to be counted not so much among men as among beasts and wild creatures? But let us hear Paul's reasons, by which he teaches what moved him to do nothing of this kind himself.

units.la: Prima est: Quia non quæro quæ vestra sunt, sed vos. Id est, non pecunijs vestris inhio, ut ex vobis ego ditescam, sed quod maius est quæro: Vos nimirum totos, ut vos IESV CHRISTO lucrifaciam, & huic sistam virginem puram, vosq; in illo æternùm felices & beati sitis. Hæc vt mihi omnium laborum causa est, ita etiam me mouet, ut iure meo libenter cedam, & ne tunc quidem velim ab aliquo exigere victum, quando id facere licet.
units.tr: The first is: "Because I do not seek what is yours, but you." That is, I am not greedy for your money, so that I might grow rich from you; but what I seek is greater: namely, you entirely, so that I might win you for Jesus Christ, and present you to him as a pure virgin, and that you might be happy and blessed in him for ever. Just as this is the reason for all my labours, so it also moves me to give up my right willingly, and not even then to wish to demand maintenance from anyone, when it is in my power to do so.

units.la: Debet hoc animo omnes Ecclesiarum pastores & Verbi Dei præcones prædicti esse. Sunt enim à Christo constituti piscatores (sicuti ille olim Apostolus dicebat) non opum, honorum, dignitatum, sed hominum: & horum quidem piscatores sunt, non ut eos sibijpsis discipulos faciant, quibus pro suo arbitrio abutantur, & quos pecunijs emungant: sed ut Christo adductos ita huic consecrent, ut eius Spiritu animati vitam in hac carne mortali nouam viuant, donec huius corporis vincu-lis soluti in cœlestè regnum transferantur, & cum illo æternùm gaudeant. Talem fuisse constat Ioannem Baptistam, qui ægerrimè ferebat, quòd discipulos cæca æmulatione sibi addictiores Christo suum honorem & gloriam inuidere cerneret, & inter alia fatebatur: Hunc oportet crescere, me verò minui. Imitati sunt hunc omnes Apostoli, quorum hoc vnicum studium fuit, ut omnes homines IESV CHRISTI cognitione illuminarentur, & hunc suum Seruatorem agnoscerent: adeò, ut ipsis non absurdum modò, verumetiam nefarium, imò impium & cum summa blasphemia coniunctum scelus visum fit, fi qui Christo debitum honorem in ipsos transferre vellent. Vide Actho. 3.10. & 14. Cap. At quàm procul ab horum vestigijs recesserunt, qui hodie Apostolicorum nomine sese vendicant? Enimuero Romanus ille piscator,seu potius pirata,quid aliud facit,quàm quòd bullis suis,anulo piscatoris signatis,omnium fortunis retia tendit,imò totas gentes & vrbes venatur, dum alios superstitiosæ persuasionis philtro insecatos, alios excommunicationis fulmine territos cogit, vt ad pedum suorum oscula prolapsi obedientiam ipsi præstent, plus quàm seruilem:idque non in alium finem, quàm vt omnes homines sibi vendicet, & ijs pro suo nutu imperitet? Quod si ab illis impetrauerit,non multum solicitus est de illorum salute, siue illi in superstitionibus oberrent, siue in sectas scindantur, siue etiam vitam in apertis flagitijs atque sceleribus transigant. Etenim præcipuum apud illos homines fidei articulus est, vt omnes de Romana sede honorificè sentiant, & (vt Bonifacius VIII. loquitur)de necessitate salutis esse credant, vt huic subijciantur. Sed sentient illi aliquando,quid sit sub religionis prætextu cum Deo ludere. Discant ergo Ecclesiarum ministri Paulum imitari, vt quosuis Christo adducentes tam buius gloriam, quàm illorum salutem promebant. Quod autem de illis dicitur, non minus ad principes & omnes alios pertinet,quibus Reipub.gubernacula credita sunt. Nam horum quoq; est, non pecunias populi venari, sed in illud potius incumbere,vt morum honestas & bona disciplina floreat, religio à sordibus superstitionum repurgetur, & pace publica omnes fruantur. At hodie plerique imperare & suarum ditionum fines propagare cupiunt, vt plures habeant,quos exactionibus non minus iniquis quàm immodicis exhauriant: pacis verò studio adeò non tangun-tur,vt bellis non necessarijs tam suæ fidei creditum populum quàm alios turbent. Quis verò pastorem bonum dixerit eum,qui oues non tondeat modò,verumetiam deglubat?
units.tr: All the ministers of the Churches and heralds of the Word of God ought to be endowed with this spirit. For they have been appointed by Christ as fishers (as that Apostle of old used to say), not of riches, honours or dignities, but of men. And they are fishers of men not so that they may make them their own disciples, to be exploited at their pleasure and drained of their money; but so that, having been brought to Christ, they may be consecrated to him, that, animated by his Spirit, they may live a new life in this mortal flesh, until, loosed from the bonds of this body, they are carried over into the heavenly kingdom and rejoice with him for ever. John the Baptist is known to have been such a man: he bore it very ill that his disciples, too attached to him through blind rivalry, were grudging to Christ his honour and glory, and among other things he confessed: "He must increase, but I must decrease." All the Apostles imitated him, whose only zeal was that all men should be enlightened by the knowledge of Jesus Christ and should acknowledge him as their Saviour; so much so that if anyone wished to transfer the honour due to Christ to themselves, it seemed to them not merely absurd but a nefarious, indeed impious crime, joined with the utmost blasphemy. See Acts 3.10 and chapter 14. But how far have those who today claim for themselves the name of the Apostles withdrawn from these footsteps? Indeed, that Roman fisherman, or rather pirate, what else does he do than spread his nets over the fortunes of all, with his bulls sealed with the fisherman's ring, and hunt down whole nations and cities? He drives some, pursued with the philtre of a superstitious persuasion, and others, struck with the thunderbolt of excommunication, to fall at his feet, and to kiss them, and to render him obedience more than servile; and this for no other end than that he may claim all men for himself and rule over them at his nod. And if he has obtained this from them, he is not much troubled about their salvation, whether they wander in superstitions, or are torn into sects, or even pass their lives in open crimes and wickedness. For indeed the chief article of faith among those men is that all should think highly of the Roman see, and (as Boniface VIII says) believe that it is necessary for salvation that they be subject to it. But they will one day perceive what it is to trifle with God under the pretext of religion. Let the ministers of the Churches, then, learn to imitate Paul, so that, in bringing whomever to Christ, they may advance his glory no less than their salvation. What is said of those men pertains no less to princes and all others to whom the helm of the commonwealth has been entrusted. For it is their business too not to hunt after the money of the people, but rather to apply themselves to this, that the honesty of morals and good discipline may flourish, that religion may be cleansed of the filth of superstitions, and that all may enjoy public peace. But today most men desire to rule and to extend the borders of their domains, so that they may have more people to drain by exactions no less unjust than immoderate; and they are so little moved by zeal for peace that they disturb, with unnecessary wars, the people entrusted to their faith no less than others. Who, then, would call a good shepherd one who not only shears the sheep but even flays them?

units.la: Sed alteram rationem audiamus, quæ Paulum monuit, vt Corinthijs nollet grauis aut molestus esse quicquam ab illis exigendo. Non enim debent(inquit)filij parentibus thesauros congerere,sed parentes filijs. Sumitur hæc ratio ex communi Lege vel more inter homines recepto, & ad illud alludit, quod in prioris epist. Capite quarto, se illorum patrem esse dixit, qui ipsos in Christo genuerit. Ex eo autem sequitur, eos qui sub ministerij Ecclesiastici prætextu hoc vnum agunt, vt ab omnibus accipiendo aliquid ipsi disescant, non autem de alijs ditandis, quoad bona cœlestia, soliciti sunt, non patres esse Ecclesiarum, sed vitricos,adeoque indignos,qui ministri aut pastores dicantur. Quoad verò similitudinem, ex qua Paulus argumentum istud deducit, obseruari debet, illum de parentibus loqui, qui liberos habent adhuc teneriores ætatis, qui sibi ipsis nondum possunt prospicere, & ideo parentum cura opus habent. Quo loco hæc consideranda veniunt.
units.tr: But let us hear the second reason, which led Paul to warn that he did not want to be a burden or a nuisance to the Corinthians by demanding anything from them. "For children ought not to lay up treasure for their parents, but parents for their children," he says. This reasoning is drawn from the common law or custom received among men, and it alludes to what he said in the fourth chapter of the first epistle, that he was their father, who had begotten them in Christ. From this it follows that those who, under the pretext of the ecclesiastical ministry, do only this, namely take something from everyone for themselves, and are not concerned to enrich others with heavenly goods, are not fathers of the Churches but stepfathers, and so are unworthy to be called ministers or pastors. As for the comparison from which Paul draws this argument, it must be observed that he speaks of parents who have children still of tender age, who cannot yet provide for themselves and so need their parents' care. Several points deserve consideration here.

units.la: Primò, parentum esse,vt liberos suos non solum honestè educent,verumetiam ijsdem recondant,quo possint aliquando honestè,piè & commodè viuere. Est hoc natura insitum brutis animalibus, quæ catulos siue pullos suos tantisper educant & nutriunt, donec ipsi possint sibi victum parare. Et inter homines hoc apud omnes gentes sic semper receptum fuit, vt non temere Paulus infidelibus deteriores esse dicat eos,qui suis non pro virili prospiciunt. Inter Athenienses certè legibus sancitum erat,vt liberi parentes senio confessos alerent, excipiebantur tamen ij, qui liberos suos neglexerant, sed vlla arte instituerant, qua alimoniam sibi parare possent. Videbant enim sapientissimi homines,non debere illos frui communis naturæ legibus,qui bas in suis si-lijs educandis neglexissent.
units.tr: First, it is the duty of parents not only to bring up their children honourably but also to lay up provision for them, so that they may someday live honourably, piously and comfortably. Nature has implanted this in brute animals, which rear and feed their whelps or chicks only until they can get their own food. Among men this has always been accepted among all peoples, so that Paul does not rashly say that those who do not provide for their own as far as they can are worse than unbelievers. Among the Athenians it was certainly enacted by law that children should support parents worn out with age; yet excepted were those who had neglected their children and had not taught them any skill by which they could earn their living. For the wisest men saw that those who had neglected to bring up their children in this way ought not to enjoy the laws of common nature.

units.la: At quia hoc loco de thesauris loquitur Apostolus, proderit tenere, quæ vera sit thesaurorum congerendorum ratio. In ea enim à multis varie peccatur. Sunt enim, qui vt liberis suis diuitias magnas relinquant,non laboribus modò immodicis sese conficiunt,verumetiam genium suum defraudant, & curis mordacibus atque inutilibus ita sese dedunt, vt cœlestium bonorum meditationi vacare non possint.Sunt item, qui longius progressi, ad vsurarias artes animum adjiciunt, imposturis suis incautos circumueniunt, rapiunt, furantur, & omnes tam iniuriæ ciuilis quàm charitatis Christianæ terminos transgrediuntur. Sed his omnes adeò nihil proficiunt, vt potius infelicissimi mortalium dici mereantur. Congerunt enim non sua (vt Prophetæ verbis vtar) & nihil quàm lutum densum supra se coaceruant, quo obruti & impediti neque animi oculos ad cœ-los atlot attollere, neque pedes suos extricare possunt, ut in via praeceptorum Dei ambulent: Quid de lutro dico? Imo ignem domi suae recondunt (ut Micheas ait) inimirum maledictionem Dei, quae ipsos persequitur, ut ne ijs quidem feliciter frui possint, quae legitime prius acquisierunt.
