Liberis vero suis ijdem non aliud relinquunt, quam intemperantiae, libidinis, fastus, nequitiae & impietatis materiam, dum illi opum abundantia freti nihil non audent, & ex illa fibijpfis impunitatem policentur. Accedit hus, quod nec gratiam bonam parentibus suis liberi referunt. Hi enim parentes senio confectos plerunque oderunt, & vitam quoque illis inuident. Itaque fit, ut quemadmodum illi in colligendis opum thesauris Mammonae seruierunt: ita liberi eosdem in diaboli seruitio dilapident, & vtrinque exitium sibijpfis accersant. Quis ergo diuitias eiusmodi ignem esse negarit? Quis non miseros & infelices dixerit eos, qui se totos illis mancipant? Meminerint ergo omnes homines, veras diuitias in coelis nobis reconditas esse, quas nobis IESVS CHRISTVS sanguinis sui pretio acquisiuit: & proinde procul relicta anxia illa solicitudine acquirendi opes huius saeculi, ante omnia (sicuti ille praecipit) quaerant regnum Dei & huius iustitiam, neque dubitent de eius liberalitate, qui cum aues caeli & pullos coruorum pascat, suos nunquam negliget, qui ab ipso vno pendere didicerunt. Est enim reuera vberrimus quaestus pietas, quae praesentis & futuri saeculi promissiones habet. Quapropter ij demum veras atque solidas opes liberis suis reconduunt, qui eos in veri Dei cognitione & pietatis studio instituunt. Praecipit hoc olim Deus in Lege, & idem Abrahamum hoc nomine commendat, quod filijs suis & nepotibus ea traderet, quae Dei timorem ipsis incutere poterant. Cuius exemplum si omnes imitarentur, haud dubie & ipsi felicius viuerent, & filios post se relinquerent vere diuites & beatos.
units.tr: But since the Apostle speaks here of treasures, it will be useful to grasp what the true way of laying up treasure is, for many people go wrong in various ways. Some, in order to leave great riches to their children, not only wear themselves out with excessive labours but also defraud their own spirit, and give themselves over to such gnawing and useless cares that they cannot find time for meditation on heavenly goods. Others, going further, apply their minds to usurious practices, cheat the unwary with their deceits, seize, steal, and overstep every boundary of both civil justice and Christian charity. Yet all these gain nothing; rather they deserve to be called the most miserable of mortals. For they gather what is not theirs (to use the words of the Prophet) and heap up nothing but thick mud upon themselves, and, buried and hindered by it, they can neither lift the eyes of their mind to heaven nor free their feet to walk in the way of God's commands. Why do I speak of mud? Rather, they store up fire in their house (as Micah says), that is, the curse of God, which pursues them, so that they cannot even happily enjoy what they have lawfully acquired before. To their children they leave nothing but material for intemperance, lust, pride, wickedness and impiety, since the children, relying on the abundance of wealth, dare anything, and claim impunity for themselves from it. Add to this that the children do not repay their parents with a good return of gratitude. For they often hate their parents when they are worn out with age, and even envy them their lives. So it happens that, just as the parents served Mammon in gathering their treasures, the children squander them in the service of the devil, and both bring ruin upon themselves. Who then will deny that such riches are fire? Who would not call miserable and unhappy those who give themselves wholly over to them? Let all men remember, then, that the true riches are stored up for us in heaven, which Jesus Christ acquired for us at the price of his blood. Therefore, leaving aside that anxious care for acquiring the wealth of this age, let them seek first (as he instructs) the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and let them not doubt his generosity, for he who feeds the birds of the air and the young ravens will never neglect his own, who have learned to depend on him alone. For piety is truly the most abundant gain, since it has the promises of the present and the future age. Therefore those alone lay up true and solid riches for their children who bring them up in the knowledge of the true God and in the pursuit of godliness. God commanded this of old in the Law, and he commends Abraham for this very reason, that he handed on to his sons and grandsons those things which could instil the fear of God in them. If all men imitated this example, without doubt they too would live more happily, and would leave behind sons who were truly rich and blessed.

units.la: At non minus liberos quoque sui officij hic locus admonet: Vt nimirum sese a parentibus instituti patiantur, & meminerint institutione & disciplina opus esse propter insitam nobis naturae vitiositatem, in qua concipimur & nascimur. Nam vt sapiens ille Solomon inquit, flultitia colligata est in corde pueri, sed ferula castigatrix expellit eam. Itaque (vt idem ille ait) Qui diligit disciplinam, diligit scientiam: qui vero castigationem odit, obbrutescit. Deinde gratos quoq; suis parentibus sese liberi praebeant, & praecipua eius cura sit, ne illos vel adiram provocent, vel maerorem atque tristitiam ipsis concilient. Sapiens filius exhilarat patrem: at fluitus maeror est matri suae. Nec vnquam excidat iuniorum animis memorabile illud Sapientis dictum: Eius oculos, qui patrem subsannat, & matris doctrinam spernit, eruant corui torrentis & aquilarum pulli devorent.
units.tr: But this passage no less reminds children of their own duty: namely, that they should allow themselves to be instructed by their parents, and remember that instruction and discipline are needed on account of the innate corruption of our nature, in which we are conceived and born. For as the wise Solomon says, folly is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of correction drives it out. Therefore (as the same writer says) he who loves discipline loves knowledge, but he who hates correction grows brutish. Next, let children also show themselves grateful to their parents, and let their chief care be not to provoke them to anger or to bring sorrow and grief upon them. "A wise son makes a father glad, but a foolish son is the grief of his mother." Nor let that memorable saying of the Wise Man ever slip from the minds of the young: "The eyes of him who mocks his father and despises his mother's teaching shall be picked out by the ravens of the valley, and the young eagles shall devour them."

units.la: Sunt haec confirmata multorum exemplis, inter quae admodum memorabile est, quod in Absolone Deus edidit, qui ex propria caesarie suspensus, adhaec lancea confossus & infami lapidum aceruo obrutus rebellionis contra patrem poenas dedit. Nec temere factum aliquis putabit, quod Deus vitam longaeuam iis pollicetur, qui parentes honorant. Ne tamen in inani aut otiosa reuerentia pietas ista subsistat, insuper ἀντιπελαργεῖν discant liberi, vt nimirum (quod de ciconijs scribitur) parentes multo senio debilitatos alant, neq; ipsos alicuius laboris, molestiae aut sumptus pigeat. Quid enim facient, quo parem gratiam illis referant? Peccatur hodie vtrinque, quae non postrema malorum causa est, quibus orbis infelix afflictur.
units.tr: These things are confirmed by the examples of many, among which is that very notable one which God displayed in Absalom, who, hanging by his own hair, pierced with a lance, and buried under a heap of stones in disgrace, paid the penalty for rebellion against his father. Nor will anyone think it without reason that God promises long life to those who honour their parents. Yet lest this dutifulness stand as empty or idle reverence, let children also learn to repay in kind [ἀντιπελαργεῖν], as it is written of storks: that is, let them feed their parents, worn out with great age, and let them not shrink from any labour, trouble or expense on their account. For what will they do to repay them with equal gratitude? Today people fail in both respects, and this is no small cause of the evils with which the unhappy world is afflicted.

units.la: Caeterum ad Paulum reuertamur, qui simile hoc parentum non solum ad se transfert, verum etiam amplificat, dicens: Ego vero libentissime impendam & expendar pro animabus vestris: etiamsi abunde vos diligens, minus diligar. Id est, Non solum paratus sum ex meo labore mihi vitiu quae vere, laborare, egere, esurire, vt vobis consulam: sed vt pater aliquis indulgentissimus proprium cor pus & vitam exponit potius periculo, quam vt liberos dulcissimos periclitari aut perire sinat: ita si necesse sit, ego me totum expendere malim, quam mea socordia admittere, vt vestra salus in periculum veniat. Neq; me abster ret quorundam ingratitudo, qui me vestri amore flagrantem non modo non redamant, sed mea omnia inuidiose calumniantur.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who not only applies this comparison of parents to himself but also enlarges it, saying: "I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls, even though, loving you abundantly, I am loved less." That is to say: I am not only ready to toil with my own labour, to earn my own living, to be in want and hunger, so that I may provide for you; but, as an exceedingly indulgent father exposes his own body and life to danger rather than allow his dearest children to be imperilled or to perish, so, if it is necessary, I would rather spend myself entirely than by my negligence allow your salvation to come into danger. Nor does the ingratitude of certain people deter me, who not only do not love me in return, though I burn with love for you, but even maliciously slander all my actions.

units.la: Notatur his Pauli verbis commune vitium, quo fit, vt pauci respondeant amori, quo alij ipsos prosequuntur. Nam vt a parentibus, de quibus modo dictum est, exordiamur, quid illi non faciunt pro liberis suis? quas curas atq; labores non suscipiunt sponte, vt illorum commodis prospiciant? Sed quam paucos est videre filios, qui simili amore parentes complectantur? Idem de pijs magistratibus dici potest. Quantus obsecro Mosis amor fuit, qui eum mouit, vt propter miseros Israelitas aulæ honores atque delitias cum certa regni spe relinqueret, ut denique pro illis deleri vellet ex libro Dei? Quam vero isti in tandem ingrati, quàm iniqui, imò quàm impij & crudeles fuerunt? Quid de Dauide dicemus, qui ab eo tempore, quo cum Goliatho singulari certamine congressus esset, multis argumentis & non sine manifesto vitæ discrimine multoties declarauit, quanti populum Israeliticum faceret? Quàm pauci verò erga ipsum simili affectu praediti fuerint, persecutiones Saulinæ & seditio per Absolonē filium excitata abundè docent. Et hodie multi principes, dum cum Epaminunda Thebano pro publica salute excubant, & curis publicis distracti noctes insomnes ducunt, ut alijs securis & quietis esse liceat, fere non modò nō amantur à suis, verumetiam illis exosi sunt. Inter primatos verò homines hoc nimis vulgare est, ut minus diligantur, qui impensissimè diliguntur. Est hoc ingens vitiositatis nostræ argumentum, quæ homines beslijs deteriores facit, quas beneficiorum memores esse, & benefactores suos redamare constat.
units.tr: In these words of Paul a common fault is noted, by which it happens that few respond to the love with which others pursue them. For, to begin with the parents just mentioned, what do they not do for their children? What cares and labours do they not undertake willingly, so as to provide for their advantage? But how few children are there to be seen who embrace their parents with similar love? The same can be said of godly magistrates. What great love for Moses, I ask, moved him to leave the honours and luxuries of the court, with the certain hope of a kingdom, for the sake of the wretched Israelites, and finally to wish to be blotted out of the book of God for their sake? But how ungrateful, how unjust, indeed how impious and cruel, were those very people afterwards? What shall we say of David, who from the time when he fought in single combat with Goliath, often and by many proofs, not without manifest danger to his life, declared how much he valued the people of Israel? How few, however, were endowed with a similar affection towards him, the persecutions by Saul and the rebellion stirred up by his son Absalom abundantly show. And today many princes, while they keep watch with Epaminondas the Theban for the public welfare, and, distracted by public cares, pass sleepless nights so that others may be safe and at rest, are scarcely loved by their own people, but are even hated by them. Among the great men of the world it is only too common that those who are most lavishly loved are loved less. This is a great proof of our vice, which makes men worse than beasts, which, as is well known, remember benefits and love their benefactors in return.

units.la: At non debet aliquem mouere ingratitudo ista, ut eò minus ipse diligat eos, quos erga se tam duros & iniquos esse experitur. Nam proprium verae dilectionis est, non commoueri aliorum ingratitudine, sed potius miseri eorum, qui hoc vitio tam noxio tamque fædo laborant. Quia enim eo igne ardet, quem Dei Spiritus in animis nostris accendit, illius quoque exemplar imitatur, qui pluuiam suam bonis & malis depluit, quiq; Solem tam gratis quàm ingratis oriri finit. In Christi deniq; exemplum respicit, qui cùm inimici essemus, seipsum pro nobis in mortem tradidit, proq; ijs apud Patrem intercessit, à quibus in crucem suffigebatur. Quotquot ergo aliorum improbitate siue ingratitudine ita commouentur, ut diligere desinant, ij non obscurè testantur, dilectionem suam fuisse, ut qui suum potius quàm proximi commodum quæsiuerint. Imitemur nos Domini & Seruatoris nostri IESV CHRISTI exemplum, ut huius discipuli & coheredes simus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But we should not let this ingratitude move us to love them any less, those who we find so harsh and unjust toward us. For it is the mark of true love not to be stirred by the ingratitude of others, but rather to feel pity for those who suffer from so harmful and so foul a vice. For since it burns with that fire which the Spirit of God kindles in our hearts, it also imitates the pattern of him who sends his rain on the good and the evil, and who lets the sun rise on the grateful and the ungrateful alike. Finally, it looks to the example of Christ, who, when we were enemies, gave himself up to death for us, and interceded with the Father for those by whom he was being nailed to the cross. Therefore, whoever are so moved by the wickedness or ingratitude of others that they cease to love, they bear clear witness that their love was of the kind that seeks its own advantage rather than the good of the neighbour. Let us imitate the example of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, that we may be his disciples and fellow heirs, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LIX.
units.tr: HOMILY LIX.

units.la: Sed esto, ego vos non grauaui: sed cùm sim callidus, dolo vos cepi: Num per quenquam eorum quos misi ad vos, expilaui vos? Precatus sum Titum, & cum eo misi fratrem illum: Numquid vos expilauit Titus? Nonne eodem spiritu incesimus? nonne ijsdem vestigijs?
units.tr: "But granted, I did not burden you; yet being crafty, I caught you by deceit. Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you? I urged Titus, and sent with him that brother. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not walk in the same spirit? Did we not walk in the same steps?"

units.la: Sicuti nullus ager tam felix, nulla vinea tam bene culta est, quæ non iugi & continuo agricola studio atque labore opus habeat: sic in Ecclesia, quæ Dei ager & vinea est, res nunquam tam bene instituti possunt, quin adhuc opus sit rigatione, sarritura, runcatione & alijs eius generis laboribus, quibus ea remouentur, quæ fidei fructum impediunt. Semper enim fit, de quo in parabola nos Christus admonet, quòd nimirum dormientibus illis, quos Verbi sui semine Deus conferre dignatus est, communis ille humani generis hostis Satan bono semini vel infelix humanarum traditionum lolium, vel scelerum vrticas atq; sentes aspergit, quibus illud suffocetur. Exemplum huius mali memorabile in Corinthijs habemus. Fuerant hi à Paulo Apostolo optimè instituti, ut quoad veram Christi cognitionem, rerum diuinarum scientiam & omnis generis χαρίσματα sive dona spiritualia, nullis Ecclesijs essent inferiores. Illo autem ab ipsis digressio intra paucos annos ita depravati fuerunt, ut vix quicquam eorum integrum haberent, quod ad veram Ecclesiæ constitutionem pertinet. Et quod inter ista mala pessimum erat, tantum Pauli odium, aut saltem fastidium, conceperant, ut alios quidem illius puderet, alij verò omnia eius improbè calumniarentur. Quapropter cùm videret illos in viam reduci non posse, nisi suam apud eos authoritatem rursus obtineret, multa de seipso & suo in proue hend a omnium salute studio disserit. Fuit inter ea postremum, quòd apud ipsos gratis prædicarit Euangelium, & hoc ipsum in posterum quoq; facere velit: ut qui non pecunias, sed ipsos quærat, ut nimirum Christo lucrifacti æternum seruentur: Se deniq; paratum esse testatur, ut se totum pro ipsis impendat, quàmuis hactenus expertus fit, se non ita ut par erat ab ipsis redamari. Sed restabant adhuc nonnulla, quæ æmuli eius calumniabantur, quæ nunc diluere incipit.
units.tr: Just as no field is so fruitful and no vineyard so well tended that it does not need the constant and unceasing care and labour of the farmer, so in the Church, which is God's field and vineyard, things are never so well established that they do not still need watering, weeding, clearing and other labours of that kind, by which those things are removed that hinder the fruit of faith. For what Christ warns us of in the parable always happens: while those men sleep whom God has deigned to sow with the seed of his Word, that common enemy of the human race, Satan, scatters over the good seed either the wretched tares of human traditions or the nettles and brambles of wickedness, by which the good seed is choked. We have a memorable example of this evil among the Corinthians. They had been excellently instructed by the apostle Paul, so that in respect of true knowledge of Christ, understanding of divine things and every kind of spiritual gifts [χαρίσματα], they were inferior to no churches. But within a few years after his departure from them they had been so corrupted that scarcely anything they had remained sound with regard to the true constitution of the Church. And what was worst among these evils, they had conceived such hatred, or at least disdain, for Paul that some were ashamed of him, while others wickedly slandered everything he did. Therefore, seeing that they could not be brought back to the right way unless he regained his authority among them, he speaks at length about himself and about his zeal for the salvation of all. Among other things, last of all, he says that he preached the Gospel among them free of charge, and that he wishes to do the same in future, since he seeks not their money but themselves, that they, won over to Christ, may be kept for eternity. Finally he testifies that he is ready to spend himself wholly for them, although hitherto he has found that he was not loved in return as he ought to be. But there still remained some matters which his rivals slandered, and these he now begins to refute.

units.la: . Primum, quòd dolo seu astu singulari vsus nihil ab eis petijsset, vt ira vel pâr suos nuntios deinceps plura emungeret, vel hac facilitate insecatos in nassam pertraheret, atque illis pro suo spicione se arbitrio abuteretur. Nam, vt supra audiuimus, Titum & duos alios fratres ad ipsos miserat, qui colleƈtam facerent qua fratrum Syriæ & Iudææ egestati subueniretur: adhæc de nonnullis se-uerius cum ipsis expostulauerat, quòd eum satis pro imperio fecisse existimabant. Id nunc diluit, & ità quidem, vt ipse per Concessionem sibi objiciat id, cuius ipsum maleuoli illi insimulabant. Sed esto (inquit) ego vos non grauaui: sed cùm sim calidus, dolo vos cæpi, &c. Ita enim solent imposto-res. Fingunt se zelo gloriæ Dei ardere, publicam omnium salutem sitire, mundo & carni mor-tuos esse, denique non solùm sanƈtimoniam Apostolicam, sed portentosam abstinentiam præ se fe-runt, dum pro vetitis ea ducunt, quorum vsum Deus omnibus liberum esse voluit. Quis verò fi-nis aut scopus ipsis propositus est? Num vt hominės salui fiant? aut vt Dei gloria illustretur? Nequaquam: Sed vt simplices & incautos in sui admirationè rapiant, & tandem regno suo per hypocrisim stabilito, quiduis ab omnibus impetrare possint, & nemine prohibente pro suo nutu & libidine omnia faciant.
units.tr: First, that he had used a singular craft or cunning and had asked nothing from them, so that, either through Titus or the other two he might afterwards squeeze out more, or by winning them over by this apparent ease might draw them into a net and abuse them at his own pleasure. For, as we heard above, he had sent Titus and two other brothers to them to make a collection for the relief of the poverty of the brothers in Syria and Judaea; and besides, he had rebuked some of them rather severely, since they thought he had done this more than his authority warranted. He now refutes this, and does so in such a way that he himself raises by way of concession the very charge that his malicious critics brought against him. "But granted," he says, "I did not burden you; yet being crafty, I caught you by deceit," and so on. For this is how impostors usually act. They pretend to burn with zeal for the glory of God, to thirst for the public salvation of all, to be dead to the world and the flesh; finally they display not only apostolic holiness but an extraordinary abstinence, while they count as forbidden those things whose use God wanted to be free for all. But what end or aim is set before them? Is it that men may be saved? Or that the glory of God may be made illustrious? By no means. Rather, it is that they may snatch the simple and the incautious into admiration of themselves, and, once their kingdom is established by hypocrisy, may obtain whatever they like from everyone and do all things at their own nod and lust, with no one forbidding them.

units.la: Tales iam seculis aliquot fuerunt Romani Pontifices cum suis emissarijs & legatis à late-re(vt ipsorum phrasi vtar)qui mirificis dolis non rude modò hominum vulgus, verumetiam Re-ges potentissimos in retia & casses suos adducere potuerunt. Initio enim Romam à barbaris intra paucos annos sæpius captam & ruinis deformatam, ideoq; ab Imperatoribus & eorum Exarchis reliƈtam, sub religionis & Ecclesiæ prætextu sibi vendicarunt, vt illic regni fundamenta iacerent, quod vel veteris nominis maiestate commendaretur. Postea cum in Occidente Imperator nullus esset, Romæ autem imperium asseƈtarent Longobardi, eoq; nomine Pontificibus graues atq; molesti essent, neq; vllum auxilium à Constantinopolitanis Imperatoribus, qui & varijs bellis atque moti-bus in Oriente distinebantur, & propter acceptas iniurias Pontificibus infensi erant, assulgeret, nouam bestiam ad veteris exemplum parturire cœperunt Pontifices, & primò quidem Pipinum Franciæ regem fecerunt, vt hoc beneficio insecatum sibi manciparent, & eo tutore atq; defensore contra Longobardos vterentur. Mox huius filium Carolum, qui propter res præclarè gestas Magni nomen accepit, Imperatorem Occidentis creauerunt, vt nimirum in propinquo haberent vin-dicem, qui ipsos aduersus quosuis tueretur. Itaq; dum isti se Reges & Imperatores faƈtos putant, non viderunt, se Pontificum artibus circumuentos & horū mancipia faƈtos esse. Carolus certè præ ter inanem Imperij titulum nihil accepit, suis autem impensis ad Pontificis nutū bella multa gessit, illum præterea donationibus amplíssimis diuitem & potentem fecit, quas postea filius Ludouicus non modò confirmauit, verumetiam auxit, dum ipsam Romam cum tota sua iurisdiƈtione, omni-busq; circa eam terris, ciuitatibus, portubus ac maritimis Hetruriæ locis adiecit. A quo tempore Romani Imperij titulo superbierunt Imperatores, Romam verò cum omnibus, quæ ex Imperio lacero & euerso reliqua erant, Pontifices possederunt. Nec melior fuit Germanorum sors, ad quos tandem titulus Imperij translatus, ipsos quoque Pontificum seruos fecit, & bellis infinitis, tam ciuilibus quàm exteris, implicuit. Quid cum maioribus nostris, viris fortissimis, aƈtum sit, notius est, quàm vt multis commemorare oporteat. Hos enim Sixtus IIII. monasticis dolis instruƈtus (nam Franciscanus prius fuerat) per suos emissarios magnificis promissis insecatos contra omnes Romanæ sedis inimicos armauit, & bellis obiecit continuis, in quibus per multos annos cùm bel-licosissimis totius Europæ populis fuit dimicandum. Quo autem præmio tot illorum labores, im-pensas & sanguinem largissimè profusum remuneratus est? Vexillo rubro & inani defensorum Ecclesiasticæ libertatis titulo. Addidit his diploma siue bullam, quam (vt de Draconis legibus quidam olim dicebant) sanguine scriptam non immeritò dixeris. In ea enim inter multa alia etiam hæc leguntur: Ea propter, quod huic sanƈtæ sedi ac vobis faustum & felix sit, læto & magno ani-mo vexillum hoc, quod præfata sedes vobis donat, accipientes, contra eiusdem sedis inimicos, vir-tutem vestram ostendite. Ite animis lætis contra hostes Ecclesiæ, & illam ab oppressoribus Eccle-siasticæ libertatis ac facientibus contra illam, solita magnanimitate vestra defendite. Inferat præ-potens exaratus vir vexillum hoc altissimi nomine inuocato, contra dictæ sedis inimicos, &c. Quis verò ista vel Monachi vel pastorū Ecclesiæ, & non potius Imperatoris iam classicum canentis verba esse dixerit? Et poterant huius generis multa commemorare. Sed quid verbis opus est, quando res ipsa loquitur, istos homines, quando liberalissimi esse & sua benedictionis thesaurros gratis profundere videntur, nihil aliud quam inanes titulos & bullas quauis aquatili bulla leuiores largiri, eo autem praetextu in populosissimas gentes, in ciuitates munitissimas, in principes potentissimos denique sibi ipsis ius & imperium vendicare, ut omnium hominum fortunis, laboribus, imo sanguine etiam ad suam tyrannidem stabiliendam abutantur? Imitantur hos Monachi, dilectissimi ipsorum filij, qui dum obedientiam vouent & voluntariam paupertatem, hoc unum agunt, ut sibi immunitatem parent, ne vlli vel politico vel ecclesiastico magistratui parere cogantur, & ut ex alienis opibus securi in otio & deliciis viuant. Et tales tunc quoque fuisse aliquos, ex posteriori ad Timoth. patet, vbi illorum mentionem facit Apostolus, qui in familias subdole irrepebant, & captiuas ducebant mulierculas, quarum conscientia iam ante nimium erant grauata. Quia ergo hic vetus impostorum mos est, Paulum quoque hoc nomine aduersarij suspectum facere conabantur.
units.tr: Such for some centuries have been the Roman pontiffs with their emissaries and legates from the side (to use their own phrase), who by wonderful tricks were able to draw into their nets and snares not only the rude common people but even the most powerful kings. For at first they claimed for themselves, under the pretext of religion and the Church, Rome, which within a few years had been captured many times by the barbarians and disfigured by ruins, and which had therefore been abandoned by the emperors and their exarchs, so that they might lay there the foundations of a kingdom, which might be recommended by the majesty of the old name. Afterwards, when there was no emperor in the West, and the Lombards were claiming dominion over Rome and were troublesome and burdensome to the pontiffs on that account, and no help was forthcoming from the Constantinopolitan emperors, who were occupied in the East with various wars and disturbances and were hostile to the pontiffs because of injuries received, the pontiffs began to bring forth a new beast after the example of the old one. First of all they made Pepin king of France, so that, bound to them by this favour, he might be their servant and they might use him as guardian and defender against the Lombards. Soon they created Pepin's son Charles, who received the name Great on account of his illustrious deeds, emperor of the West, so that they might have near at hand an avenger who would protect them against whatever enemies. So while these men think they have been made kings and emperors, they do not see that they have been ensnared by the arts of the pontiffs and made their slaves. Charles certainly received nothing beyond the empty title of empire, but at his own expense he waged many wars at the pontiff's nod; moreover, the pontiff made him rich and powerful with very ample donations, which his son Louis afterwards not only confirmed but also increased, when he added Rome itself with its whole jurisdiction, and all the lands, cities, ports and maritime places of Etruria around it. From that time the emperors took pride in the title of the Roman empire, while the pontiffs possessed Rome together with all that remained from the torn and overthrown empire. The lot of the Germans was no better: to them the title of empire was at last transferred, and it made them too slaves of the pontiffs and entangled them in endless wars, both civil and foreign. What was done with our forefathers, men most brave, is better known than that it need be recounted at length. For Sixtus IV, trained in monastic deceits (for he had previously been a Franciscan), armed them through his emissaries, who pursued them with magnificent promises, against all enemies of the Roman see, and hurled them into continual wars, in which for many years they had to fight with the most warlike peoples of all Europe. And with what reward did he repay the great labours, expenses and blood so lavishly poured out by all those men? With a red banner and the empty title of defenders of ecclesiastical liberty. To these he added a diploma or bull, which one may not unfairly call written in blood, as some once said of the laws of Draco. For among many other things these words are read in it: "Therefore, that it may be fortunate and happy for this holy see and for you, receive with a joyful and great spirit this banner, which the aforesaid see gives you, and show your valour against the enemies of the same see. Go with glad hearts against the enemies of the Church, and defend her with your accustomed greatness of spirit from her oppressors and from those who act against her. Let the mighty man who is anointed bear this banner, with the name of the Most High invoked, against the enemies of the said see," etc. Who would say these words were those of monks or ministers of the Church, and not rather the words of an emperor already sounding the trumpet? And they could recount many things of this kind. But why use words, when the thing itself speaks: these men, while they seem most generous and lavishly pour out the treasures of their blessing for nothing, grant nothing but empty titles and bulls lighter than any water-bubble, and under that pretext claim for themselves right and rule over the most populous nations, the most fortified cities and finally over the most powerful princes, so that they may abuse the fortunes, labours and even the blood of all men to establish their tyranny? These monks imitate them, their most beloved sons, who, while they vow obedience and voluntary poverty, have this one aim: to secure for themselves immunity, so that they may not be compelled to obey any civil or ecclesiastical magistrate, and so that they may live in leisure and delights, secure, on the wealth of others. That such men existed even then is clear from the later letter to Timothy, where the apostle mentions those who craftily crept into households and led captive silly women, who were already heavily burdened in conscience. Since, then, this is the old habit of impostors, they also tried to make Paul suspect under this very name.

units.la: Debet igitur hic obseruari eorum improbitas, qui Veritati contradicere semel in animum induxerunt. Nam quicunq; malitiosi sunt, ij suo pede quosuis alios metiri consueuerunt. Itaq; si eorum, quos oderunt, virtutes & praeclara facta negare non possunt, ea calumnijs suis apud rerum imperitos suspecta, vel etiam exosa facere studeant. Sic olim Sacerdotes cum Prophetis egisse legimus. Non poterant illi negare multa in Israele & in Iuda contra Dei legem fieri. At eadem si Prophetae accusabant, mox hos seditiose id facere calumniabantur, & lasa maiestatis reos agebant, ut qui a Regibus instituto cultus contumeliose proscinderent. Sic Amasias prophetam Amos apud Ierobeam Regem deferebat, quod ea diceret, quae terra ipsa non posset ferre. Idem Ieremiae accidit. Quae hic accusabat scelera tam manifesta erant, ut ne pseudoprophetae quidem & impij sacerdotes ea possent inficiari. Calumniam ergo ex eo isti struunt, quod tempore importunissimo illa corripiendo Babylonijs, qui vrbem cbsidebant, animum faceret, populum vero & milites terreret: id quod cum proditionis suspicione erat coniunctum: quod item contra locum sanctum non sine diuini nominis & cultus contumelia inueheretur. Quid autem de istis attinet dicere, quando aeternus Dei Filius calumniatorum dentes effugere non potuit, qui miraculosa eius facta, quibus alij a morbis incurabilibus, alij ex diaboli tyrannide liberabantur, illicitis & nefarijs artibus fieri dicebant, imo illa aperte ad diabolum authorem referre audebant? Hoc ipsum Paulus cum apud Corinthios tum alibi passus est. Et solet idem in prophanis etiam rebus fieri, ut multorum optime de Republica meritorum exempla, quae passim in historijs extant, testantur. Est enim hoc impijs proprium, qui in eo patris sui Diaboli ingenium referunt, cui hoc nomen apud Graecos a calumnia impositum est. At non debent ista aliquem offendere, quasi noua sint & insolita: multo minus autem abterrere, ut in officio faciendo sit remissior. Novit enim Deus, quo animo quisque agat, & idem suorum innocentiam atque famam suo tempore asserit. Veruntamen memores simus semper, quibus cum nobis res sit, nosque ad ista praeparemus, simulque circumspecte & caute omnia nostra instituamus, ne improbi & malitiosi homines facile calumniandi occasionem possint inuenire.
units.tr: We should therefore notice the wickedness of those who have once made up their minds to oppose the truth. Malicious people always measure everyone else by their own standard. So when they cannot deny the virtues and outstanding deeds of those they hate, they try to make those deeds suspect, or even hateful, in the eyes of people who do not know the facts. We read that the priests once acted this way against the prophets. They could not deny that many things were being done in Israel and Judah contrary to God's law. But when the prophets pointed these things out, the priests at once accused them of stirring up sedition and brought them to trial for treason, claiming they insulted the cult the kings had established. So Amaziah reported the prophet Amos to King Jeroboam, saying that he spoke things the land could not bear. The same thing happened to Jeremiah. The sins he denounced were so obvious that not even the false prophets and the wicked priests could deny them. So his accusers invented a charge: that by rebuking these things at a most inopportune time, while the Babylonians were besieging the city, he discouraged the people and terrified the soldiers, which carried a suspicion of treason. They also said that he attacked the holy place, to the insult of God's name and worship. But why say more about these men, when the eternal Son of God could not escape the teeth of the slanderers? They said his miraculous works, by which some were freed from incurable diseases and others from the tyranny of the devil, were done by unlawful and wicked arts. Indeed they dared to attribute these works openly to the devil as their author. Paul suffered the same thing, both among the Corinthians and elsewhere. The same thing also happens in secular affairs, as the examples of many who deserved very well of the commonwealth, found everywhere in histories, bear witness. This is the mark of the wicked, who show in this the nature of their father the devil, whose name the Greeks derived from slander. Yet these things should not trouble anyone as though they were new and unusual, and still less should they frighten us into being less diligent in doing our duty. God knows with what intention each person acts, and in his own time he vindicates the innocence and good name of his own people. Nevertheless, let us always remember with whom we have to deal, and prepare ourselves for such things, and at the same time conduct all our affairs with care and caution, so that wicked and malicious people will not easily find an occasion for slander.

units.la: Sed Paulum audiamus respondentem ijs, qui ipsum dolo vsum dicebant, cum stipendium nullum a Corinthijs acciperet. Num (inquit) per quenquam eorum quos misi ad vos, expilaui vos? In Graeco ponitur verbum πλεονεκτεω: quod proprie significat per auaritiam & immoderatam plus habendi cupiditatem alijs sua eripere. Id vero se fecisse, negat. Et interrogatione vtitur, ut proprio testimonio illos conuincat. Quasi diceret: Si quid huius feci quod mihi obijcitur, imo si quid huius vel cogitaui facere, age prodeat qui vult, & dicat aperte quid a quoquam per meos exegerim? aut quod nam huius mea cupiditatis dederim indicium? Atqui scio neminem tam impudentem aut malitiosum esse, qui hoc ausit dicere. Quia vero ad illos Titum miserat cum quodam fratre (de quo Cap. 8. dictum est) quibus tertius accesserat nomine Ecclesiarum, ut Corinthi collectam facerent, de illis nominatim agit, dicens: Precatus sum Titum, & cum eo misi fratrem illum, de quo supra dixi: Numquid vos expilauit Titus? Sensus verborum hic est: Fateor Titum cum suis comitibus ad vos venisse ex meo rogatu. At isti non mihi pecuniam colligere debuerunt, sed pauperibus in Iudea, quibus subsidium fidium mittere Ecclesiæ iampridem decreuerant. Nec etiam ab inuitis aliquid extorserunt, sed quæ pij sponte conferrent debuerunt colligere. Quid ergo hic mihi poterit fraudi verti? Num quòd vos hortatus sum, ne in re non minus necessaria quàm honesta & sancta vestram benefi- centiam cum alijs Ecclesijs coniungeretis? Vel quòd feruentius apud vos institi, vt opus semel inchoatum procederet? Atqui omne hoc ex officio feci, & sic mihi Apostoli mandarunt, vt paulo probè memor essem. Imò velim vestri illi mihi respondeant, annon ego & Titus eodem spiritu incesserimus, & eadem secuti simus vestigia? Id est, an non eundem spiritum Christi, & proinde eundem quoq; animi affectum, eosdem mores eademq; studia in illis deprehenderitis, quæ prius in me vidistis? Quid ergo habent æmuli illi mei, quòd vel in me vel in collegis meis reprehendant? Hæc & alia huius generis Paulus vult Corinthijs obijcere, vt se contra Zoilorum calumnias tueatur: quo loco quædam nobis consideratu dignissima occurrunt.
units.tr: But let us hear Paul answering those who said that he had used deceit, since he accepted no support from the Corinthians. "Did I," he says, "take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you?" The Greek word is πλεονεκτέω [pleonekteō], which properly means to rob others of their goods through greed and an immoderate desire to have more. Paul denies that he did this, and he uses a question so as to convict his accusers by their own testimony, as if he were saying: "If I have done anything of this kind that is laid to my charge, or even if I have thought of doing anything of the kind, let whoever wishes come forward and state plainly what I have exacted from anyone through my agents, or what evidence of such greed I have given. But I know that no one is so shameless or malicious as to dare to say this." Because he had sent Titus to the Corinthians with a certain brother (about whom it was said in chapter 8), and a third man had joined them in the name of the churches, to complete the collection at Corinth, he speaks of them by name, saying: "I urged Titus, and I sent with him that brother of whom I spoke above. Did Titus take advantage of you?" The sense of his words is this: "I admit that Titus came to you with his companions at my request. But they were not required to collect money for me, but for the poor in Judea, to whom the churches had long since decided to send relief for the faithful. Nor did they extort anything from unwilling people; they were obliged to collect only what the godly gave of their own accord. What, then, can be twisted into a fault for me here? Is it that I urged you not to withhold your generosity, in a matter no less necessary than it is honourable and holy, from joining the other churches? Or that I pressed you more eagerly so that a work once begun might be completed? Yet I did all this as my duty, and the apostles have so charged me, as you well know. Indeed, I would like your critics to answer me: did Titus and I not walk in the same spirit and follow the same footsteps? That is, did you not find in them the same spirit of Christ, and therefore the same disposition of mind, the same manners and the same zeal that you first saw in me? What, then, have my rivals to find fault with in me or in my colleagues?" Paul wishes to lay these and other charges of this kind before the Corinthians, so that he may defend himself against the slanders of the carping critics. Several points here deserve our careful consideration.

units.la: Primum, quòd ei nequaquam sufficere visum est, si ipse bona & integra fide ageret cum Ecclesijs, nisi idem collegæ aut conservi sui facerent, quorum ministerio vtebatur. Sciebat enim si- bi iure imputari debere, si quid illi peccauissent. Debet ergo hinc generalis doctrina peti. Etenim qui homines ineptos, adhæc leues & mali exempli ordinant, vt Ecclesiarum ministri sint, ij omnium eorum, quæ per ipsos designantur, reatu seipsos grauant. Idem de illis iudicari debet, qui doctores falsos & superstitionum magistros Ecclesijs submittunt. Et hæc causa Paulum monuit, vt Timotheo quoque mandaret, ne alicui manus cito imponeret, & ita cum peccatis alienis communicaret. Idem sentiendum est de magistratibus. Quis obsecro nauigaturus clauum aut nauis gubernacula credat furioso aut ebrioso homini? Cur ergo ad Reipub. gubernacula admittantur, quos cæca libido in omne flagitium abripit, vt nihil pensi habeant? Quid ex his aliud quàm naufragium vniuersale sperari possit? Vidit hoc sapientissimus ille Iethro, qui Mosem generum monebat, vt iudices populo præficeret, viros facultatum, id est, instructos ijs tam animi quàm corporis facultatibus, quibus ad hanc prouinciam opus esset: adhæc timentes Dei, veraces, & qui auaritiam odissent. Et hodie in bene constitutis Rebuspublicis receptum est, vt magistratuum electionem iusiurandum præcedat, quo fidem suam Reipub. obstringunt ij, penes quos est electionis ius atque potestas. Quod si isti fidem suam fallant, & homines vel indignos vel ineptos & improbos ad tantam functionem adhibeant, næ illi communem patriam parui faciunt, neque Dei vindicis manum effugient, qui fere per illos ipsos de eis pœnam sumit, quos ipsi in dignitatem istam euexerunt. Pertinet præterea cura hæc ad magistratus quoque, qui dum publicos ministros creare volunt, quibus inferiorum munerum officia committantur, similiter videre debent, ne priuatis affectibus abrepti eos deligant, qui Reipub. dedecori sint, aut sua vel insciitia vel negligentia malum dent, cuius culpa ipsis imputari queat. Etenim quantum accedat principum & magistratuum existimationi ex ministris & officialibus bonis atque fidelibus, Salomonis exemplo docemur, cuius sapientiam Sabæ regina ex ministrorum eius habitu & moribus prædicauit.
units.tr: First, it seemed to Paul by no means enough that he himself acted with good and sincere faith towards the churches, unless his colleagues and fellow workers, through whose ministry he acted, did the same. For he knew that he would rightly be held accountable if they sinned. From this we should draw a general teaching. Those who appoint unfit, frivolous and badly behaved men to be ministers of the churches make themselves guilty of all the wrongs committed through them. The same judgment must be made of those who put false teachers and purveyors of superstitions over the churches. This is why Paul also warned Timothy not to lay hands hastily on anyone, lest he share in the sins of others. The same must be said of magistrates. I ask you, who would entrust the helm of a ship, or its steering gear, to a madman or a drunkard before setting out to sea? Why then should those be admitted to the government of the commonwealth whom blind lust carries off into every shameful act, so that they have no concern for anything? What can be expected from such men but a general shipwreck? That most wise man Jethro saw this, when he advised his son-in-law Moses to set over the people judges who were men of ability, that is, endowed with those gifts of mind and body that the task required, and also God-fearing, truthful, and hating covetousness. Today, too, in well-ordered commonwealths it is the custom that the election of magistrates is preceded by an oath, by which those who have the right and power of election bind their faith to the commonwealth. But if they break this faith and appoint men who are unworthy, unfit or wicked to so great an office, they make light of their common country, and they will not escape the hand of God the avenger, who often exacts punishment through those very men whom they themselves raised to that dignity. Moreover, this care also belongs to magistrates. When they wish to appoint public servants, to whom the duties of lesser offices are entrusted, they must likewise take care not to choose, carried away by private feelings, those who will bring dishonour on the commonwealth, or who, through their ignorance or negligence, cause harm for which they may be held to blame. For how much the reputation of princes and magistrates is enhanced by good and faithful ministers and officials, we are taught by the example of Solomon, whose wisdom the queen of Sheba praised from the bearing and conduct of his servants.

units.la: Deinde obseruabis, quòd Paulus se cum suis illis legatis eodem spiritu incessisse testatur. Spiritus vocabulo omnem propriæ dignitatis aut meriti gloriationem excludit, vt totum hoc opus solius Dei virtuti & gratiæ transcribat, qui ipsos suo Spiritu illuminarit atq; gubernauerit, vt ista possent perficere. Etenim singulare donum diuinæ gratiæ fuit, quòd qui patris sedibus eiecti indignissime tractabantur, egebant, esuriebant, nihil tamen ab illis exigerent, quibus omnis ipsorum labor deseruiebat. Quia verò idem fuit omnium istorum spiritus, ijdem quoq; illorum mores fuerunt, & eadem studia. Et Titus se eodem cum Paulo spiritu præditu esse testabatur, quando ip se etiam neminem expilabat sub suæ legationis aut ministerij prætextu.
units.tr: Next, you will observe that Paul testifies that he walked with his legates in the same spirit. By the word "spirit" he excludes all boasting of his own dignity or merit, so that he ascribes this whole work to the power and grace of God alone, who illuminated and guided them by his Spirit so that they could accomplish these things. For it was a singular gift of divine grace that men who had been cast out of their fathers' homes, who were treated most shamefully, who lacked necessities, went hungry, and yet demanded nothing from those for whom all their labour was spent. And since the spirit of all these men was one and the same, their manners were also the same, and so were their aims. Titus, too, testified that he was endowed with the same spirit as Paul, since he likewise did not rob anyone under the pretext of his mission or ministry.

units.la: Docet ergo locus hic, quæ propria nota sit, ex qua qui veri Apostolici sunt à personatis & falsis dignosci possunt. Ea nimirum, si eodem Spiritu ducantur, quo olim Apostolos ductos fuisse scimus. Id verò doctrina & moribus probent necesse est, quando satis constat spiritum illum neque otiosum esse, neque suijpsius dissimilem, qui à semetipso dissentiat. Vides ergo, quid de Apostolicis Romanensibus iudicari debeat, qui vt in doctrina ab Apostolis IESV CHRISTI dißentiunt: ita quoad mores & rabiem & sanguinis fludio nihil dicamus, à quibus Apostoli totis animis abhorruerunt, quis nescit illos per suos legatos in omnium principum aulas penetrare, & hos vbique gentium non munera modò regalia accipere, verumetiam opulentissimas quasque Abbatias, Episcopatus & sacerdotia occuparet? Quis item ignorat quàm vberem quæstum illis faciant indulgentiarum Papalium nundinatores, qui pro vili plumbo & tenui membrana aurum & argentum recipiunt? Aut quis bonus non detestatur Stationariorum (quos vocant) fraudes & impostura, qui ementitas Diuorum reliquias ostentant, & non nisi accepto pretio spectandas & exosculandas exhibent? Denique quid omnes illi aliud quàm petunt, exigunt, extorquent, expilant & deglubunt: & vtinam hæc solùm facerent, & non insuper hereditates alienas interciperent, populorum iura & ciuitatum priuilegia imminuerent, thorosq; alienos insatiabili sua libidine conspurcarent. Quis verò hæc Apostolici Spiritus opera esse dixerit? Aut quis non potius illos Simonis Magi successores esse videat: quem cum sua pecunia Petrus Apostolus execratus est?
units.tr: This passage therefore teaches what the mark is by which the true apostolic men can be distinguished from impostors and counterfeits: namely, if they are led by the same Spirit by whom we know the Apostles were once led. This must necessarily be shown by both doctrine and morals, since it is well established that that Spirit is neither idle nor unlike himself, so as to disagree with himself. You see, then, what judgement ought to be passed on the Romanist "apostolics," who differ from the Apostles of Jesus Christ in doctrine. As for their morals, their rage and their eagerness for blood, from which the Apostles shrank with their whole souls, I say nothing. Who does not know that they penetrate the courts of all princes through their legates, and that everywhere they not only receive royal gifts but also seize the richest abbeys, bishoprics and priesthoods? Who likewise does not know how rich a profit the sellers of Papal indulgences make, who receive gold and silver for cheap lead and a thin parchment? Or what good man does not detest the frauds and impostures of the so-called "stationers," who display fabricated relics of the saints and show them to be gazed at and kissed only once payment has been received? In short, what else do all these men seek, demand, extort, plunder and flay? And would that they did only this, and did not also seize other men's inheritances, diminish the rights of peoples and the privileges of cities, and defile other men's beds with their insatiable lust. But who would say these are the works of the Apostolic Spirit? Or who does not rather see them as the successors of Simon Magus, whom the Apostle Peter cursed together with his money?

units.la: Commendatur praeterea nobis hoc loco consensus ministrorum, quo nihil ad aedificationem Ecclesiae vtilius, nihil ad huius conseruationem magis necessarium est: vt è contra nihil nocentius fuerit, quàm sieiusdem Ecclesiae ministri & doctores in diuersas sententias scindantur, ritibus item & ijs quae per se adiaphora, id est, media aut indifferentia sunt, inter se digladientur. Faciunt hoc fere, qui ambitionis spiritu ducuntur, qui plerunque non aliam ob causam ab alijs dissentiunt, quàm ne quid ab alijs didicisse putentur. Est hoc nocentissimum hominum genus, & quantum mali dent ijdem Ecclesijs nostro tempore multis exemplis tristissimis didicimus. Sit autem consensionis regula Dei verbum, quod quicunque sequuntur, eos vnus idemque Christi spiritus regit, imò illos arctissimo vinculo constringit, vt in ipso vnum sint. Et hoc illud est, quod hic iam moriturus tam serijs atque ardentibus precibus à Patre flagitauit. Rogo (inquit) vt omnes vnum sint, sicut tu Pater in me, & ego in te, vt & ipsi in nobis vnum sint: vt credat mundus, quòd tu me misisti. Et ego gloriam, quam dedisti mihi, dedi eis: vt sint vnum, sicut & nos vnum sumus: Ego in eis, & tu in me, vt sint perfecti in vnum, & vt cognoscat mundus, quòd tu me misisti, & dilexisti eos, sicut me dilexisti. Hæc vtinam diligentius expenderent hodie, qui propter res leviculas & ritus inutiles, nec vlla verbi Dei authoritate confirmatos, odiose eos damnant, qui vnum eundemque cum ipsis Christum profitentur, & vnum cum ipsis esse cupiunt. Quia verò Apostoli olim & ipsorum discipuli atque collegae, quos Apostolicos antiquitus dixerunt, vnum eundemque spiritum secuti sunt, satis apparet, nihil pro apostolico hodie recipi debere, quod ab Apostolorum scriptis dissentit. Itaque procul reliquis ijs, qui talia Ecclesijs obtrudunt, nos illorum vestigijs insistamus, quos Deus orbis totius doctores esse voluit, & in his loquentem audiamus Filium Dei, Dominum & Seruatorem nostrum, IESVM CHRISTVM, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, the agreement of ministers is commended to us in this place, than which nothing is more useful for the building up of the Church, nor more necessary for its preservation. Conversely, nothing is more harmful than when the ministers and teachers of the same Church are torn apart into different opinions and fight among themselves over rites, and over those things which are in themselves adiaphora, that is, matters that are free or indifferent. Those who are led by a spirit of ambition mostly do this, who for the most part differ from others for no other reason than that they should not be thought to have learned anything from others. This is the most harmful kind of men, and in our own time we have learned from many very sad examples how much evil they bring to the Churches. Let the rule of agreement, however, be God's Word. Whoever follow it, one and the same Spirit of Christ governs them, and indeed binds them with the closest bond, so that they are one in him. And this is what he, now about to die, asked of the Father with such earnest and burning prayers: "I ask," he said, "that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us, that the world may believe that you sent me. And I have given them the glory that you gave me, that they may be one, as we are one: I in them, and you in me, that they may be made perfect in one, and that the world may know that you sent me, and that you have loved them as you have loved me." Would that those who today, on account of trivial matters and useless rites, not confirmed by any authority of God's Word, odiously condemn those who profess the same Christ as they do and wish to be one with them, would weigh these words more carefully. But since the Apostles of old, and their disciples and colleagues, whom they called "Apostolic" from ancient times, followed one and the same Spirit, it is sufficiently clear that nothing should today be received as apostolic which dissents from the writings of the Apostles. Therefore, far from those who thrust such things upon the Churches, let us follow the footsteps of those whom God wished to be teachers of the whole world, and in these let us hear the Son of God speaking, our Lord and Saviour, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LX
units.tr: Homily 60

units.la: Rursum putatis quòd nos vobis excusemus? In conspectu Dei, in Christo loquimur: omnia tamen haec charissimi, pro vestri aedificatione. Nam metuo, ne quo modo, cùm venero, non quales velim reperiam vos, & ego reperiar vobis qualem nolitis: ne quo modo sint lites, æmulationes, iræ, contentiones, obtrectationes, susurri, tumores, tumultuationes: Ne iterum vbi venero me deprimat Deus meus apud vos, & lugeam multos eorum qui antea peccarunt, nec resipuerunt super impuritate & fornicatione & proteruia, quam patrarunt.
units.tr: Do you think again that we are making excuses to you? We speak in the sight of God, in Christ. Yet all these things, beloved, are for your edification. For I fear that somehow, when I come, I may find you not as I would wish, and that you may find me not as you would wish: that there may somehow be quarrels, rivalries, anger, contentions, backbiting, whisperings, conceit, and tumults. And I fear that when I come again, my God may humble me among you, and I may mourn many of those who sinned before and have not repented of the impurity, fornication and wantonness they committed.

units.la: Diuus Paulus suam authoritatem contra æmulos suos hucusque tanto studio & diligentia defendit, vt postremò eos quoque excusauerit, quos pro collecta Corinthi facienda miserat. De nat. De his illud potißimùm prædicauit, quòd vt ipse nemini molestus fuerit aliquid petendo, ita illi quoque neminem expilauerint, sed eodem secum spiritu incesserint. Quia autem eius aduersarij neque in ipso neque in collegis ipsius aliquod flagitium aut delictum accusare poterant, hoc ipsum calumniabantur, quòd tam constanter tamç sedulò suam existimationem defenderet. Ex eo enim alij colligebant, eum male sibi conscium esse: alij verò ipsum nimis ambitiose de seipso subinde scribere clamabant, & proinde ex ipsius scriptis non multum vtilitatis percipi posse: Imò indignum esse dicebant, totam Ecclesiam rebus ad ipsius solius personam pertinentibus obtundi. Itaq; in præsenti istis quoq; respondet.
units.tr: For a long time the divine Paul has defended his authority against his rivals with such zeal and diligence that at last he also excused those whom he had sent to gather the collection at Corinth. Concerning these men he declared chiefly this: just as he himself had been a burden to no one by asking for anything, so they had not plundered anyone, but had walked in the same spirit as he did. But since his opponents could accuse neither him nor his colleagues of any disgrace or wrongdoing, they slandered him for this very thing, that he defended his reputation so firmly and so eagerly. For some inferred from this that he was conscious of some wrong in himself; others cried out that he wrote about himself too ambitiously from time to time, and that therefore not much profit could be drawn from his writings. Indeed, they said it was unworthy for the whole Church to be wearied with matters pertaining only to his own person. And so, in the present passage, he answers these people too.

units.la: Rursum putatis quòd non vobis excusemus? Præoccupatione vtitur, & ita vult dicere: Scio quid aliqui dicant; quibus volupe est vndique conquirere quod calumnientur. Sed sentiant & dicant illi quod lubet, ego tamen neque fingo aliquid, neque ambitiosius quàm IESV CHRISTI ministrum deceat ista scribo. Id verò grauissima asseueratione probat, dicens: In conspectu Dei, in Christo loquimur. Quæ verba duplicis iuramenti formam habent. Primò enim hoc perinde est ac si dixisset: Deum ipsum testor, qui omnia videt, omnia audit, in cuius conspectu omnes homines versantur, & qui cùm ipsissima sit veritas, eos qui mentiuntur & fallunt, inultos abire non sinit. Deinde in Christo se loqui dicit, vt qui non suam, sed Christi causam agat, & huius spiritu ducatur, qui fucatis commendationibus nequaquam opus habeat. Et simul scopum omnium, quæ dicit, vno verbo exprimit: Omnia tamen hæc, charißimi, pro vestri ædificatione. Charißimos dicit admodum pathetice, vt odij suspicionem declinet. Quasi diceret: Poteram quoad me, his omnibus super sedere, quando mihi in Dei conspectu mens sibi probè conscia sufficit. Sed aliud requirit mei ministerij conditio: quæ me in hoc incumbere iubet, vt vos ædificemini, & indies in melius proficiatis. Atqui sine veritatis doctrina ædificatio neq; perfici neque consistere potest. Illa enim medium illud ordinarium est, per quod homines Christo adducuntur, & in officio retinentur. Quia verò æmulorum calumniæ huc tendunt, vt doctrina mea in dubium veniat, & ideo meam existimationem extenuant, ego hic meo officio deesse non possum, neque etiam debeo.
units.tr: Do you think again that we are not excusing ourselves to you? He uses a figure of anticipation and wants to say: I know what some people say, those who take pleasure in searching everywhere for something to slander. But let them think and say what they please; I, however, neither invent anything nor write these things more ambitiously than becomes a minister of Jesus Christ. He proves this with the most solemn assertion, saying: We speak in the sight of God, in Christ. These words have the form of a double oath. For first, it is as if he had said: I call God himself to witness, who sees all things, hears all things, in whose sight all men live, and who, being truth itself, does not allow those who lie and deceive to go unpunished. Then he says that he speaks in Christ, as one who pursues not his own cause but Christ's, and who is led by his Spirit, a Spirit that has no need of false commendations. And at the same time he expresses in a single word the aim of all that he says: Yet all these things, beloved, are for your edification. He calls them beloved in a very emotional way, so as to avert any suspicion of ill will. As if he were saying: I could, as far as I am concerned, rise above all these things, since my mind, conscious of itself before the sight of God, is enough for me. But the condition of my ministry requires something else: it orders me to devote myself to this, that you may be built up and make progress daily into something better. Yet without the teaching of truth, edification can neither be brought about nor endure. For that teaching is the ordinary means by which men are brought to Christ and kept in obedience. But since the calumnies of my rivals aim at this, that my teaching may be called into doubt, and so they belittle my reputation, I cannot, and indeed ought not, fail in my duty here.

units.la: Debent autem omnes homines, cuiuscunque sint loci aut ordinis, sibijpsis applicare quod hic dicit Apostolus: vt nimirum se in Dei conspectu omnia loqui & facere meminerint. Adest hic suæ Ecclesiæ, quæ ideo ipsius domus dicitur. Videt ergo & audit, quæcunque in illa dicuntur & fiunt. Quapropter nouit idem ille, quæ doctrina prædicetur, qua fide item ministri votantur, & quis scopus isdem propositus sit. Sed & rationem ab illis exiget, & (vt apud Ezechielem habetur) ex manibus eorum requiret omnium illorum sanguinem, qui per ipsorum siue perfidiam siue negligentiam percunt. Nunquam ergo impune ferent, qui paleas suas (vt Deus per Ieremiam loquitur) ipsius verbo admiscent: qui item sub illius nomine priuatum honorem aut quæstum quærunt: qui vanis promissis lactant, & puluillos impijs atque pœnitere nescijs consuendo, ipsis exitij & perditionis authores sunt. Quibus recte adnumeraueris eos, qui in clerum siue hæreditatem eius dominium sibi vendicant, & in pios tyrannidem duram exercent, dum dogmata indies noua cudunt, conscientias grauant, & pro suo arbitrio omnia constituunt. Odit enim mendacium & omnis generis imposturas: nec ferre potest, vt hominum serui fiant, quos ipse sanguinis sui pretio in filiorum Dei libertatem asseruit. Et huc pertinent, quæ in Euangelio de pœnis perfidorum ministrorum habentur. Vide Matth.24. & 25.
units.tr: Moreover, all men, of whatever place or rank they are, ought to apply to themselves what the Apostle says here: namely, that they remember that they say and do everything in the sight of God. He is present in his Church, which for that reason is called his house. He therefore sees and hears whatever is said and done in it. Wherefore he himself knows what doctrine is preached, with what faith the ministers are devoted, and what aim is set before them. And he will demand an account from them and, as is found in Ezekiel, will require the blood of all those who perish through their faithlessness or negligence at their hands. Therefore those who mix their chaff (as God speaks through Jeremiah) with his word will never go unpunished; likewise those who seek private honour or gain under his name; those who lull people with empty promises, and by sewing cushions for the impious and those who know not how to repent, become the authors of their ruin and destruction. To these one may rightly add those who claim for themselves dominion over the clergy, or over their inheritance, and exercise harsh tyranny over the godly, while they daily coin new dogmas, burden consciences, and arrange everything at their own pleasure. For he hates lies and every kind of imposture, and he cannot bear that those whom he has claimed for the freedom of his sons by the price of his own blood should become the slaves of men. To this also belong the things said in the Gospel about the punishments of faithless ministers. See Matthew 24 and 25.

units.la: At quod de verbi administris dicitur, ad magistratus quoque pertinet. Etenim iudicium omne Dei est, qui illos etiam potestate armauit. Idem medius inter eos stat (vt in Psalmo dicitur) qui ad iudicandum confident. Videt ergo & audit voces siue sententias eorum, imò corda scrutatur, & quo animo vel in quem finem illas pronuntient, intelligit. Et qui nunc de alijs iudicandi potestatem habent, olim ad Christi tribunal sistentur, vt de omnibus suis dictis & factis rationem reddant. Semper ergo meminerint grauissimæ illius admonitionis, qua Iosaphat ad iudices vsus est. Dispicite quid agatis: non enim homini iudicatis, sed Domino, qui vobiscum est in causis, quas iudicatis: sit ergo timor Domini vobiscum, & cauti sitis atque satagite: quoniam nulla est peruersitas apud Dominum Deum nostrum, vt vel personas suspiciat, vel munera recipiat. Primò dispicere illos iubet quid agant. Quasi diceret: Non ideo vobis omnia licere putabitis, quod in gradu sublimiori estis constituti: sed potius quia lapsus ex alto periculosior est, diligenter videre vos decet, ne quid praeter officium à vobis fiat. Deinde causam huius praecepti subijcit: Non enim homini iudicatis, sed Deo. Veniunt quidem ad vos homines, & suas causas vobis dijudicandas committunt: sed vos Dei nomine iudicatis, qui simul vobis praesens adest, neque eos ferre potest, qui aliquem sub ipsius nomine fallunt. Itaque sit vobiscum timor Domini, qui sapientiae verae principium atque caput est: Denique cauti estote & seduli, id est, non pigeat vos alicuius laboris, morae, diligentiae, quo minus (ut Moses olim monuit) tam parvum quam magnum audiatis. Et rursus rationem aliam allegat ex Dei natura siue ingenio desumptam, apud quem neque persona hominis quicquam valeat, neque munera aliquid impetrent. Quibus verbis nocentissimas iudiciorum pestes perstringit. Haec enim integra & sancta esse non possunt, quando iudices vel personas hominum respiciunt, vel muneribus sese corrumpi patiuntur. Haec enim (ut Moses inquit) excaecant oculos sapientum, & causas iustorum peruertunt. Et quam vere hoc dicatur, omnium gentium historiae docent, & vtinam non fierent quotidie, quae his possunt fidem facere. Ista (inquam) nunquam non fibijpsis occinant iudices, neque se iura & leges in sua potestate habere putent, quas pro suo arbitrio torqueant.
units.tr: But what is said of the ministers of the Word pertains also to the magistrates. For all judgment belongs to God, who has also armed them with power. He likewise stands in the midst of those who sit in judgment (as it is said in the Psalm). Therefore he sees and hears their voices or sentences, and indeed searches the hearts, and understands with what mind or to what end they pronounce them. And those who now have the power of judging others will one day be brought before the tribunal of Christ, to give an account of all their words and deeds. Let them therefore always remember that most solemn admonition with which Jehoshaphat addressed the judges. Consider what you do, for you judge not for man, but for the Lord, who is with you in the causes you judge; let the fear of the Lord therefore be with you, and be careful and diligent, for there is no perversity with the Lord our God, so that he regards persons or accepts bribes. First, he bids them consider what they do. As if he said: Do not think that everything is permitted to you because you have been placed in a higher rank; rather, since a fall from a height is more dangerous, it becomes you to look carefully that nothing is done by you beyond your duty. Then he adds the reason for this command: For you do not judge for man, but for God. Men indeed come to you and entrust their causes to you to be decided; but you judge in God's name, and he, who is present with you at the same time, cannot bear those who deceive anyone under his name. Therefore let the fear of the Lord be with you, which is the beginning and the head of true wisdom. Finally, be careful and diligent, that is, let no labour, delay or diligence weary you, so that (as Moses once admonished) you hear the small as well as the great. And again he brings forward another reason, taken from the nature or character of God, before whom the person of a man counts for nothing and gifts obtain nothing. With these words he strikes at the most harmful plagues of judgments. For these cannot be sound and holy when judges look to the persons of men, or allow themselves to be corrupted by gifts. For these (as Moses says) blind the eyes of the wise and pervert the causes of the just. And how truly this is said, the histories of all nations teach, and would that those things which can give proof of this did not happen every day. These things, I say, let judges never cease to repeat to themselves, nor let them think that they have laws and rights in their own power, to twist them at their own pleasure.

units.la: Similiter singuli priuatim hoc ipsum obseruent, ut nunquam illis excidat, nos omnes in Dei conspectu versari, & ad singulos pertinere quod Abrahamo in foedere dixit Deus: Ambula coram me, & esto integer. Paulus certe hoc alibi seruis & heris applicat, sic scribens: Serui, auscultate ijs, qui Domini sunt secundum carnem, cum timore ac tremore, cum simplicitate cordis vestri, ut Christo: non ad oculum seruientes, ut qui hominibus placere student, sed ut serui Christi, facientes ex animo quae vult Deus: cum benevolentia seruientes Domino, & non hominibus: ut qui illud sciatis, singulos quicquid fecerint boni, hoc reportaturos à Deo, siue serus fuerit, siue liber. Et vos Domini eadem facite erga illos, remittentes minas: scientes quod & vester ipsorum Dominus in coelis, nec persona respectus est apud eum. Atqui ita inter homines comparatum est, ut alius alij seruire iubeatur, & vicissim alius in alium ius habeat pro sui ordinis aut conditionis ratione. Singuli ergo cogitent, se & in coelis Dominum habere, qui omnia videt, & huic olim rationem nos reddere oportere de omnibus, quae in hac vita facimus. Quam vero felices essent homines, si vel unum hoc sibi persuaderi paterentur?
units.tr: Likewise, let individuals privately observe this same thing, so that it never slips from their minds that we all live in the sight of God, and that what God said to Abraham in the covenant applies to each one: Walk before me and be perfect. Paul certainly applies this elsewhere to slaves and masters, writing thus: Slaves, obey those who are your masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, with simplicity of heart, as to Christ; not serving to the eye, as men-pleasers, but as servants of Christ, doing from the heart the things that God wills; serving with goodwill the Lord and not men, knowing that each one, whatever good he has done, will receive the same back from God, whether he be slave or free. And you masters, do the same to them, giving up threats, knowing that your own Master is in heaven, and that with him there is no respect of persons. Yet it is so ordained among men that one is commanded to serve another, and in turn one has rights over another according to the reason of his station or condition. Therefore let each one consider that he has the Lord in heaven too, who sees all things, and that we must one day give him an account of all that we do in this life. And indeed, how happy would men be if they were willing to be persuaded of this one thing alone?

units.la: Sed ut ad Paulum redeamus, is finem quoque & scopum, quem sibijpsi in omnibus suis dictis & factis propositum habeat, exprimit, quando se ista omnia dicere ait pro ipsorum aedificatione. Pertinet hoc quoque ad omnes, qui in Ecclesiae ministerio versantur. Est enim haec (ut supra diximus) domus Dei. Fundamentum eius est IESVS CHRISTVS, sicut ipse apud Matthaeum docet, neque aliud poni posse, Apostolus in priori epist. cap. tertio monuit. Super hunc homines, ceu viui lapides aedificantur, dum per Euangelij praedicationem instituuntur in fide, qua ipsum vnicum salutis suae authorem atque Mediatorem agnoscunt. Ad hunc ergo scopum ministri omnes collimare debent. Ut autem in aedificijs multa quotidie vel collabuntur, quae instauratione opus habent, multa etiam correctionem aut mutationem requirunt, ut commodius inhabitari queant: ita in Ecclesijs etiam bene constitutis fieri, vel vnum hoc Corinthiacae Ecclesiae abunde docet, & hodie passim experimur. Est enim hominis animus non prauus modo, verumetiam nouitatis appetens, & ideo se facile ex meliori statu in deteriorem, adeoque (ut de Galatis Paulus loquitur) à simplici & syncera salutis doctrina, quam nobis Apostoli tradiderunt, in aliud Euangelium transferri finit. Hic ergo Verbi administros sedulò aduigilare & nunquam non in opere esse conuenit, ut praesentibus vitijs medeantur, futuris vero prospiciant. Fuerunt in eo diligentes admodum Apostoli, qui ideo Ecclesias abs se instituas saepe inuiserunt, aut de rebus agendis per literas admonuerunt. Pudeat ergo hodie aliquos suae ignauiae, qua in Ecclesijs, quas à suis antecessoribus optime constitutas acceperunt, omnia collabi & euerti sinunt. Iniquissimi autem & propriae salutis inimici sunt, qui tantam sibi authoritatem vendicant, ut ministris in hac re suum officium facientibus sese opponere audeant, quasi illi res nihil ad se pertinentes agant. Quod vero de Ecclesia & huius ministris dicitur, non minus in Repub. debet obseruari, vbi similiter propter multorum licentiam non sufficit bonas leges condidisse, sed vt eadem sarta tecta maneant necesse est, & illorum proteruia occurratur, qui illas nouis indies artibus perrumpere conantur.
units.tr: But to return to Paul: he sets out the end and aim which he has in view in all his words and deeds, when he says that he says all these things for their edification. This applies also to all who are engaged in the ministry of the Church. For this (as we said above) is the house of God. Its foundation is Jesus Christ, as he himself teaches in Matthew, and Paul in the first epistle, chapter three, warned that no other can be laid. Upon this foundation men, like living stones, are built up, while through the preaching of the gospel they are instructed in faith, by which they acknowledge him as the only author and Mediator of their salvation. To this aim, therefore, all ministers ought to direct themselves. Just as in buildings many things daily either fall down and need restoring, or many things need correction or alteration so that they can be inhabited more conveniently, so it happens in Churches even when well established: the Corinthian Church alone teaches this abundantly, and we experience it everywhere today. For the human mind is not only wicked but also greedy for novelty, and so it easily passes from a better state to a worse, and thus (as Paul speaks of the Galatians) is allowed to be turned away from the simple and sincere doctrine of salvation which the apostles handed down to us, to another gospel. Here, therefore, it is fitting that the ministers of the Word watch carefully and are always at work, so that they may remedy present faults and look ahead to future ones. The apostles were very diligent in this, who therefore often visited the Churches they had founded, or admonished them about matters to be done by letter. Let those today be ashamed of their laziness, who allow everything to collapse and be overturned in Churches which they received well established from their predecessors. Yet they are most unjust and enemies of their own salvation who claim so much authority for themselves that they dare to oppose ministers doing their duty in this matter, as if the ministers were dealing with things that did not concern them. What is said of the Church and its ministers must equally be observed in the commonwealth, where likewise, because of the license of many, it is not enough to have enacted good laws, but it is necessary that they remain intact and that the insolence of those be resisted who daily try to break them by new tricks.

units.la: Porrò quia haec Pauli diligentia atque sedulitas aliquibus superuacanea videri poterat, eius rationem reddit, & vt ita faciat, necessarium plane esse docet. Nam metuo (inquit) ne quo modo, cum venero, non quales velim reperiam vos, & ego reperiar vobis qualem nolitis, &c. Sensus verborum hic est: Quicquid facio, id metu & solicitudine paterna motus facio. Nam siue vos siue meipsum spectio, periculu sese offert minimè contemnendum, quod me solicitum esse cogit. Vt enim ad vos venire iam diu optaui, vt vestra consuetudine recreer: ita vehementer metuo, ne vos longè alios quàm velim inueniam: qui videlicet loco dilectionis & vnitatis in Christo inter vos aemulatione mutua ardeatis, ex qua irae, lites et contentiones perpetuae, adhaec obtrectationes, susurri, tumores, & tumultuationes nascantur, quibus ecclesiae status labefactetur. Quòd si sic accidat, iam ego, qui ex vobis gaudium & consolationem percipere debebam, a Deo humiliabor, & toto animo deijciar, dum mei ministerij succeßum non tam felicem fuisse videbo, quàm ego putabam. Imò si inueniam aliquos nondum resipuisse, qui prius fornicatione & omni genere impuritatis turpißimè peccarunt, et admoniti licet adhuc contumaciter in peccatis pergunt, ego lugere cogar, qui me vobiscum gauisurum esse sperabam. At haec dicendo omnem seueritatis, qua hucusque fuit vsus, culpam in ipsos reijcit, qui sua contumaci proteruia ipsum cogant alium esse quàm velit. Perinde ergo hic facit Paulus, ac si pater aliquis peregre agens, familiae, quam dissolutius viuere resciuit, scribat: Ego quidem charißimi, domum redire cupio, & vestri desiderio totus ardeo, nunc tamen non ita vobiscum agere possum, sicuti vellem: Ea enim de vobis narrari audio, quae me vehementer solicitum reddunt, ne reuersus ad vos magis discrucier, adeò vt vestra illa petulantia & proteruia pudefactus, cogar alium me praebere quàm velitis, cùm vos quoque alij sitis, quàm ego vos esse velim.
units.tr: Moreover, because this diligence and earnestness of Paul might seem superfluous to some, he gives his reason for it, and teaches that it is plainly necessary for him to act thus. For I fear (he says) that somehow, when I come, I shall not find you such as I would wish, and I shall be found by you such as you would not wish, etc. The sense of the words is this: whatever I do, I do it moved by fear and paternal anxiety. For whether I look at you or at myself, a danger presents itself which is by no means to be despised, and which compels me to be anxious. For just as I have long desired to come to you, so that I may be refreshed by your company, so I greatly fear that I shall find you quite other than I would wish: namely, that instead of love and unity in Christ, you burn with mutual rivalry among yourselves, from which anger, perpetual quarrels and contentions arise, and besides these, detraction, whisperings, swellings and tumults, by which the state of the Church is weakened.
